en: I bow to the Supreme Brahman, the Brahman beyond the cosmic egg, to Śrī Nārāyaṇa, to Hari, the inner controller of all, the God who assumes all incarnations. || 1 ||
Salutation to that lineage, whose two wives are Śrī and Lakṣmī, whose mouth is considered to be the Brahmins and the sacrificial fire,
and whose heart is eternally the virtuous.
Salutations to that Śaṃvarṣin, whose true nature is attainable through meditation, who dwells in heaven, on the sacrificial grass, in the three worlds, among the ancestors, and in all beings.
On a delightful peak of the Himalayas, in his own hermitage on that best of mountains,
Nārāyaṇa indeed spoke this Saṃhitā to Lakṣmī.
Then, having obtained her at the holy site of Badarikāśrama, Śvetavyāsa, assuming his original form and possessing divine vision, spoke to his four disciples.
Śvaiti, Suśikha, Śvetāśva, and Śvetalohita—
these four high-souled ones were most devoted to Brahman and had reached the further shore of Brahman.
Having become that, they attained the abode of Hari from which there is no return;
for they were the wives of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Thus ends the narrative.
In the hermitage of Lomaśa, they affectionately questioned their lord Nārāyaṇa regarding the field of Kuṅkumavāpī and the Aśvapaṭṭasārasa lake in Saurāṣṭra.
And Nārāyaṇa indeed imparted this compendium to them,
known as the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, which contains all meaningful truths.
For there exist one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, the mere recitation of which bestows liberation. (1.1.10)
Once, Nārada set out to behold Vaikuṇṭha;
he saw the assembly hall presided over by Śrī Viṣṇu, where they were all seated.
The divine liberated ones are called the Akṣaras; others reside in Goloka, while the liberated ones dwell in Vaikuṇṭha and inhabit Śvetadvīpa.
Some dwell in the unmanifest nectar-abode, others reside in the abode of Śrī Lakṣmī,
some in the Badarī and the Ocean of Milk, and still others abide in other abodes.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the perfected ones (siddhas), the gandharvas and cāraṇas, the world-protectors, the Manus, the ascetics, and those who are virtuous; || 14 ||
The sages, possessing divine movements and divine, unassailable forms,
were all present there in that yoga, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
The assembly hall, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas and crowded at its borders, was indeed seen by Nārada; half of it was revealed by the men.
Wherever Lakṣmī is on the left side, there let the goddesses be stationed;
likewise, let there be Muktā, Vāsudevā, Gopī, and other female companions.
They are sovereign mistresses, divine ladies, and female attendants;
they are Brahmanīs, Mothers, goddesses, and human women with perfected forms. (18)
Nārada beheld the assembly hall, where half of it was revealed as a woman;
[he saw] the eternal Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Viṣṇu.
Nārada joyfully prostrated before Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Mahāmāyā;
then, having bowed to the entire assembly, he sat upon the excellent seat provided by Viṣṇu.
There the sage Āraṭa sat down, honored by them all;
"I am Vyāsa, known as Śveta, and the Sūta is named Suśikha. (21)
Likewise, other commentators led by Bṛhaspati were all endowed with divine forms through the will of Nārāyaṇa.
There they engaged in various discourses that increase devotion;
among them, Nārāyaṇa said: "This is the great sage Nārada."
One who is learned, possessed of great knowledge, a vast treasury of narrations,
and skilled in the ways of the world, should be questioned for the sake of understanding past events.
Lakṣmī said:
"O ascetic, O great yogin, O portion of Viṣṇu, O great sage! From where have you come? What is happening among the creations of Viṣṇu? (25)
What were the vows of the people on earth, and what was the social convention?
Likewise, [tell me] about the holy fords, the virtuous, the brahmins, and the cows on this earth. (26)
What is the current condition of the miserable, of those who perform virtuous deeds, of saintly women, and of renunciants? And is the path to liberation still intact? (27)
"Does knowledge accompanied by discernment shine among the brahmins? Does true devotion to Nārāyaṇa indeed exist among the people? (28)
Śrī Nārada said:
I always revere my parents, who are compassionate and bestowers of liberation;
indeed, nothing is unknown to my all-knowing parents, however small it may be. (29)
Nevertheless, because it is the duty of a disciple, I shall relate it in due order:
having wandered through many worlds and observed the condition of the Kṛta Yuga.
O Mother, beholding people endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu created by Viṣṇu, and subjects devoted to their husbands, I rejoice again and again. (31)
Blessed is this Lord Viṣṇu, and blessed am I, O Supreme Goddess, for by His majesty liberation is indeed obtained by human beings. 3.2.
Through hearing and chanting the names of Viṣṇu, through remembering Him, serving His feet, worshipping, bowing down, befriending, serving as a servant, or by the surrender of one's self; || 33 ||
Whether brought about by knowledge or ignorance, liberation is attained immediately through the removal of the impurities of saṃsāra; therefore, what indeed could be a greater fortune than this?
O Mother, those who recite the mantra even once, or utter the name of Hari with divine devotion, surely attain liberation. (35)
Indeed, those people— whether children, the elderly, or others— who receive the initiation of Viṣṇu, whether it be the general or the primary one, shall become inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha.
Constant conformity to Viṣṇu, the avoidance of all that is contrary to him, full faith in Viṣṇu, and the prayer "I am yours"—these are the boons [to be sought]. (37)
The renunciation of the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, ego, intellect, and the inner self into Viṣṇu, as well as constant dependence upon Hari for one's welfare; 38.
"Lord Hari alone is my everything; there is no other"—this firm conviction constitutes the sixfold surrender to Viṣṇu, known as taking refuge (śaraṇāgati). || 39 ||
Having approached that One, one who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa should accomplish either unity of being,
unity of action, or indeed unity of self.
In whatever manner and to whatever extent union with Śrī Hari is produced, to that same extent and in that same manner he himself enjoys the bliss of Nārāyaṇa. || 41 ||
The essence of love is liquid in nature, and the Self also partakes in liquidity;
having come together as two liquids, Viṣṇu himself becomes a liquid.
They are characterized by a mass of bliss, a mass of consciousness, and a mass of pure awareness;
they possess eternal contentment, eternal coolness, eternal happiness, and perfect nourishment. || 43 ||
Having attained oneness with Nārāyaṇa, he enjoys all desires; sometimes he is at his side, sometimes in his form, and sometimes he is absorbed into him. 44.
In one place he is liberated, in another he is Lakṣmī, and in another he proceeds as a servant;
he arises like his body, like his senses, and like his mind.
But I, O Mother, am called Nārada, the mind of Viṣṇu;
and you are Lakṣmī, said to be his half-body and his very self.
Hari is the manifest reality of pure existence, while you are indeed considered the half of consciousness;
the fluid union of these two is called Saccidānanda (Existence-Consciousness-Bliss). 47.
By whatever state of being one's self may indeed attain fluidity, having reached that fluidity of being, it shall proceed toward liberation consisting of Viṣṇu. 48.
The illustrious Śveta Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Nārada dissolved into a liquid form within Viṣṇu, who was an ocean of the experience of bliss at the supreme limit of love.
While all those present in the assembly were watching, this wonder occurred, causing great amazement: "Oh, the devotion of the devotee! (1.1.50)
Lakṣmī, who was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa and desiring to know [the truth], questioned the Supreme Self for the sake of the welfare of the world. (5.1)
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Aha! Many devotees of the Supreme Soul have been seen by me, but none such as this one has ever been seen who has gone to such a state of melting away within you. (52)
I believe, however, that the cause in this matter is your compassion, O illustrious one, for upon whomsoever you bestow your boundless grace, O Lord. (53)
O Lord, it is my conviction that you are not distinct from him;
for such is your intention regarding the attainment of this very self. (54)
"Or rather, what do you desire that must be done by you for the sake of obtaining grace?
Śrī Śvetavyāsa said: "Nārāyaṇa, having heard that, out of a desire for the welfare of all," (55)
With supreme affection, he spoke words that, though brief, contained incomparable meaning—words by which even ordinary living beings attain such a state as this. (56)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Marvelous Devotion of Nārada’s Melting Heart," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, set in the assembly of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare how my grace may be obtained for the sake of a devotee’s attainment of the state of melting devotion; understand that according to its true nature.
The Lord is the master over the creation of the liberated, the creation of [the world], and the creation of individual souls;
he created all embodied beings with their forms—such is the established doctrine.
The Self (Ātman), however, is declared to be Indra, the locus of all powers and qualities;
the mind, consciousness, and the ego-intellect are its internal instruments.
These four are declared to be the powers of Indra:
the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, feet, and hands. (4)
Indeed, the sense organs located in the anus and the genitals are the external instruments;
all these ten powers truly belong to Indra alone.
They move further and further outward toward external objects that are to be grasped;
having assumed the form of the object, they take on the appearance of the grasped.
But when all those [faculties], having turned back, assume the form of the Sustainer (dhātrī) and their internal organs are purified,
they indeed attain the Self.
Having assumed the form of objects of enjoyment, they then become the experience of Indra;
thereafter, this direct experience occurs within one's very own self.
I am directly established in Indra as the fulfiller of all powers; by virtue of my union with me, Indra is the locus of perfect power—such is the established truth.
Indeed, from that which is ungraspable arises the essence of affection (prema-tattva), which is considered to be fluidity;
it is present everywhere, and by means of it, all forms become cohesive.
I am Viṣṇu, full of affection, full of bliss, full of love, and the refuge of happiness; indeed, I am full of fluidity, for by union with me, he too becomes possessed of fluidity.
Everything—whether gross or subtle, sentient or otherwise—is melted by my grace; my favor alone is the cause here.
But if there should arise compassion for him, thinking, "May he become softened," then at that very moment he softens; otherwise, never.
The means for my grace, however, is considered to be the surrender of one's entire self.
I am always full of grace, compassionate, and an ocean of mercy. (14)
Filled with compassion, I shall shower the rain of grace out of love for my devotees;
for as the stream of my compassion enters Dhruva, so it shall continue.
In proportion as one is devoted, the reality repeatedly attains a state of fluidity;
I alone, without a second, abide in the imperishable abode.
In my form there, even the imperishable Brahman is released by me;
they flow forth due to the abundance of my love and also by the power of my grace.
Then, in the sovereign Virāj, nothing remains distinct;
this very liberation is attained by those who know the state of that [Virāj], through the realization of identity with it. (18)
If he, being alone, did not find delight, he desired a second from himself;
from that Great Self, the imperishable Brahman was manifested.
By the will of the Lord, that formless [reality] became twofold, both with form and without form;
it is the supreme abode from which all other abodes were born.
He, Hari, who possesses form— his own identical form, embodied and conforming to that embodiment— then further desired for himself a state of manifold forms.
Therefore, liberated souls, being free from destruction, have appeared there in infinite numbers;
in that immortal heaven consisting of three quarters, there exist those circles of worlds.
Muktā, Brahmā, and Parabrahmā are considered the triad of Brahman’s creation;
all of them are divine, possessing forms with limbs corresponding to their respective natures, and are endowed with beautiful features.
The senses are indeed identical in essence with the Tattvas;
their names are merely figurative designations, for they consist of the power of taste.

The mind, the ear, speech, the eye, the skin, and the sense of taste and so forth—these indeed remain concealed even when the signs are complete; neither is there delight in them, nor is there latent impression (vāsanā).
Since that [element] is not born of a mother, the six sheaths (kośa) are not found there;
therein, the vital breath (prāṇa) is the power of the Self, and space (kāśa) is its unobstructed nature.
Those whose hair, nails, teeth, and golden [complexion] are well-formed are never separated from Him;
for they shine as their own self, having the singular measure of being the nature of pure consciousness. 27.
All those divine luminaries shine in the celestial abode;
thus, this is called the world of Brahmā according to the Upaniṣads. (28)
The body of liberation is Brahmic; it is the state of experiencing the bliss of Brahman.
He eternally enjoys all desires together with Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Possession of Form through Liquid Liberation for the Supreme Brahman, Brahmā, the Liberated Souls, and Others in the Abode of the Imperishable," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, the desire of Hari—who resides upon the left side of the one whose nature is imperishable (Akṣara)—and who wishes to make that service fruitful by means of his female form, [arose]. || 1 ||
Like Nārāyaṇa from his left side, he manifested a beautiful form consisting of his own self-power (svātma-śakti),
which was the locus of all auspiciousness, good fortune, love, affection, and melting tenderness.
His own abode is conformable to his form; his field, his support, and his own [nature] consist of his qualities, sovereignty, power, passion, strength, and the cave as their refuge. (3)
The ocean of compassion assumed a manifested form consisting of Lakṣmī, which is the locus of the qualities of passion; desiring for Lakṣmī the fruitfulness of her unerring passion. || 4 ||
Assuming a form endowed with unfailing vigor known as Vāsudeva,
he is this very Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, proclaimed as Śrī Hari.
He, known by the name Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, became twofold;
for having seen all the liberated persons in the world of Brahmā, Lakṣmī [became divided].
She beheld only her own [reflection], identical in form to herself, and no other;
then, with joy, she prayed to the Lord Śrī Hari as her own husband.
O Lord, having understood the disposition of your beloved wife, please arrange a suitable place for her co-wife out of a desire for her welfare. (8)
The Lord fashioned the divine abode known as Vaikuṇṭha, indeed the world of Brahmā,
and he settled male and female servants there for the sake of service.
For that purpose, he created divine enjoyments and divine implements,
as well as that divine creation belonging to her, which was complete and whose desires were fulfilled.
Śrī Hari himself made her endowed with all means of accomplishment and possessed of prosperity and happiness; he truly recognized her perfection. || 11 ||
"I am he, you are she; these two worlds and Vaikuṇṭha belong to us two"—thus perceiving this great yoga consisting of husband and wife as a new reality.
The unborn power of Hari, consisting of the three qualities, is eternal and the progenitor of the principles.
Māyā, which is without beginning or end, chose Śrī Hari as her husband;
she is that wherein the creation, consisting of the principles of reality, is born and wherein it dissolves.
Then she again requested the Lord, the Master of All, the Protector Śrī Hari, to assume a form equal to Lakṣmī’s own, which was her desired wish.
Commanded by the Lord, she assumed a new form that causes infatuation—the beautiful form of Rādhā, which is indeed the vessel of countless delights. (15)
And she remained with him as his inseparable wife by his own will;
for that purpose, Śrī Hari indeed assumed the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The supreme Person is the support of all desires, the showerer of all essences;
he possesses unfailing and immeasurable heroism, glory, beauty, strength, and splendor.
The Lord, assuming the form of a youth worthy of Rādhā’s beloved,
was beheld by Rādhā as a handsome and suitable husband for herself.
In that abode, he requested a divine residence for himself, independent and serving as a great refuge for my delight, containing gardens for my pastimes. || 19 ||
The ultimate limit of my manifestations, gathered together as my own equipment,
consists of all the furnishings whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
"May everything be possible there for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa"—by Rādhā’s desire, everything came to pass, and millions of maidservants appeared. (21)
That supreme, divine, and imperishable abode of Goloka is exceedingly opulent;
it is perceived through its boundary as being extended throughout the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, Śrī Hari, having been commanded [by Brahmā], fashioned the beautiful abode of Goloka, which is graced by Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and honored by them. 23.
That eternal abode, Goloka, is established in the world of Brahmā;
there, assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa, He accepts the service performed by Rādhā.
In the world of Brahmā, in Goloka, and in Vaikuṇṭha, the stores of enjoyments belonging to Śrī Hari are equal, and they always bring bliss to his devotees.
According to their gender, their form, their fitness,
their merit, their pleasure, and their requirement, those [attendants] arise from the desire of Hari.
There is eternal divine pleasure and delight, and for those whose very selves are that,
divine love is perpetually born there through union with Hari.
Just as the Lord always delights among his beloveds in Vaikuṇṭha, so too does the Master rejoice among his dear ones in Goloka. (28)
In the supreme abode of the Imperishable, Hari delights among those who are liberated;
the Lord Himself sports with His liberated devotees, friends, and maidservants. (29)
Just as they worship me in one form or in a pair,
so do they take refuge in me as their master, their giver of happiness, and their husband.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Establishment of the Two Abodes of Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka for the Sake of Lakṣmī and Rādhā," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
That Supreme Self, Hari himself, thought, "May I be born as progeny.
The All-pervading Lord then emanated Mahākāla, his own power from Himself.
To him, the supreme creator of the agitation of Māyā and the end-maker of all, Hari issued this command: "Agitate Māyā! || 2 ||
Seeing that Māyā agitated by him, the man was indeed liberated by Hari;
however, another person was then joined with Māyā as its servant.
That Māyā is primordial nature (prakṛti), the root; but the Person (pums) is the Puruṣa, the Lord.
Thus, Nature and the Person brought forth their own creation.
From those two, indeed, millions of primary beings (pradhānapuruṣas) were born.
Pradhāna, however, is the principle of Mahat, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), and is called the field (kṣetra). || 5 ||
The Puruṣa is declared to be their lord; indeed, they exist as pairs. All Puruṣas are sovereigns who were previously merged within Prakṛti.
And they all appeared, possessing forms similar to those of the husband and wife;
from Pradhāna and Puruṣa, however, Mahāviṣṇu was born.
He is indeed declared to be the ego (ahaṃkāra), and he is also called the Golden Person (Svarṇapuruṣa).
She, the excellent daughter of Pradhāna, is remembered as Ahaṃkṛti.
She who is Hiraṇyā is Mahālakṣmī, the companion of Mahāviṣṇu;
Mahālakṣmī and Mahāviṣṇu together are proclaimed as that couple.
The embryo that was produced from Mahālakṣmī by Mahāviṣṇu was called Hiraṇyagarbha, and from that the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) was born.
The golden egg was split in two; from that, this Virāj was born. And the female born of Virāj is considered to be the wife of Virāj.
From the ego (ahaṃkṛti) of Mahāviṣṇu, the sixteen principles came into being;
from the sāttvika [ego], however, the ten sense organs along with the mind arose.
From the *tāmasa* [aspect] arises the group of subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and likewise from the *rājasa* [aspect] arise their deities:
the ear, skin, eye, tongue, speech, hands, feet, and anus. (12)
The generative organ, as well as the other senses, and the mind are the internal instruments;
the five organs of cognition and the five organs of action are to be understood [as the external ones]. (14)
But for the five [faculties] beginning with the ear, it is by virtue of their power to produce cognition;
and for the five beginning with speech, it is by virtue of their power to produce action. || 15 ||
The organs known as the faculties of cognition and action, as well as the mind (manas), are indeed of a dual nature.
[The presiding deities are] the Directions, Wind, Sun, Varuṇa, the Aśvins, Fire, Indra, Upendra, and Mitra. (16)
And Candra—these are considered the gods consisting of the creation of Īśa;
they dwell within the bodies and the orbs of the lords. 17.
The mind is one, yet it arises as fourfold due to the difference in its functions;
it is called by the knowers of reality as manas, ahaṃkāra, citta, and buddhi. (18)
By the will of the Lord, those elements were combined in the form of the Virāṭ;
nevertheless, when that Virāṭ did not rise up because it was devoid of vital breath (prāṇa), [the Lord acted].
Śrī Hari, indeed having become the very form of the vital breath (prāṇa), entered there;
for by him the life-force known as *jīvana* was placed within.
Because the conscious Prāṇātman is in essential identity with Śrī Hari. (1.4.20)
In that sense, his form became truly "Vairāja" (the sovereign king) for the sake of the task to be accomplished.
From the great stalk of the lotus at his navel, Brahmā was born;
then, from his forehead, Rudra emerged as the Rajasic creator.
He, however, was the tamasic Viṣṇu who became the destroyer of the heart;
he is declared to be the sāttvika nourisher, endowed with his own power.
Residing within the body of Brahmā, his wife is called Brāhmī.
She is indeed known as Sṛṣṭi, the half-body of Brahmā;
she is Rudraśakti, Rudrāṇī, Śivā, Harāṅganā, and Satī.
The power of Viṣṇu, which is Vaiṣṇavī, is also remembered as Lakṣmī;
these three [powers] bestow creation, destruction, and nourishment upon those three [deities].
Their wives, being identical with them, are considered to be the providers of assistance for those respective tasks;
by the command of Brahmā, they cause the flow of creation to proceed.
All those lords, from the primordial person down to the end of their hair, are recorded as having bodies of pure *sattva*; that *sattva* is indeed the manifestation (*bhūti*) of Hari.
Therefore, let all those lords be subject to Him; for the Lord shines forth, having entered into all those lords who are manifestations of the Supreme Brahman. (28)
Among them, Śrī Hari, assuming a form worthy of worship, came into being;
he is indeed called Vāsudeva, the regulator of the lords.
O Great King, this Lord, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the lords of lords, is accompanied by his own power, Vāsudevī. 1.4.30.
Having created that white abode for his own residence within the imperishable realm,
the Lord took up his dwelling in that divine, white abode of his own.
For he alone is indeed Vāsudeva in the supreme abode called Amṛta;
and Vāsudeva himself, for the sake of the creation of his own world, [acts] again.
For the sake of birth, nourishment, and dissolution, he assumed his own threefold form.
Aniruddha was born as the one who leads forth the creation of Īśa;
Pradyumna was born as the nourisher of that creation of Īśa.
He who was the destroyer of the creation of Īśa was born as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
for indeed, there are three manifest forms of Vāsudeva.
Śrī Hari himself, having cast aside [his original form], assumed four forms;
therefore, the knowers of the scriptures speak of the "fourfold manifestation" (vyūha-catuṣṭaya). || 35 ||
In that [manifestation], some lords are dependent on the cosmic array (vyūha); others have four faces, while yet others have eight faces, sixteen mouths, or even a hundred faces.

Some have a thousand faces, others ten thousand, others a hundred thousand; likewise, there are others with a billion faces, and as many again with ten million mouths, possessing an equal number of feet and hands.
There, the egg-spheres of Viṣṇu are said to be fourteen;
those of Sadāśiva Rudra are twenty-eight spheres.
The eggs of the primary Māyā are said to be fifty-six;
and those of Mahāviṣṇu are two hundred and twelve globes.
There are indeed five hundred Prakṛtis, Puruṣas, and Aṇḍas;
the worlds of Mahākāla are proclaimed to be one thousand.
The realms of Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa are divine, infinite, and innumerable; they are beyond the reach of words. ||41||
For all the lords (īśvaras), however, their own powers—consisting of mind, intellect, the senses, and so forth—are considered to be identical with their very selves and endowed with pure sattva. (42)
The objects of enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the grounds for the means of enjoyment exist as being composed of pure *sattva*, intermingled with supreme bliss. (43)
The Supreme Self, Hari, manifests there repeatedly, according to the task at hand and according to the specific nature of the Lord’s prayerful contemplation. 44.
Having accomplished the tasks of the lords, Śrī Hari then remains for the duration of each respective lord's lifespan and subsequently undergoes disappearance.
Through true devotion to each of their respective forms, they too attain the supreme goal;
having enjoyed perfect sovereignty, they go to the state of no-return.
Then, all of them, being liberated, worship Śrī Hari;
such is the eternal liberation even for the lords. ||47||
The glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa is their master, the Lord who grants liberation;
though He is the Supreme Brahman who governs all, He remains distinct from them.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Lords Beginning with Vāsudeva and Ending with Brahmā," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Vāsudeva, having come into existence, requested his own purpose: "What should be done by me here? How is it that I possess such a form? (1)
Having reflected thus, he remembered the Supreme One in His primordial form;
then Śrī Hari revealed three forms to him.
Born from Vāsudeva, they have returned to Vāsudeva;
these are Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and the other, Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Vāsudeva resides within Hara, and these three reside within Vāsudeva;
having seen and known this, he indeed reflected upon it once more.
"What should be performed by me with these three forms?"—
to him, Śrī Hari then granted the leadership over the creation of the Lord (Īśa).
That creation, consisting of the destruction of the stability of the earth, has been displayed and brought under her threefold dominion;
but what kind of creation is to be performed, and what is the extent of the world? (6)
While he was thus reflecting, Hari indeed showed to that Vāsudeva all his own forms, all his deeds, and all his arts.
In the infinite, illusory, and unfathomable body of Hari,
they all beheld their own respective abodes along with their own respective manifestations.
And Mahākāla, Prakṛtipuruṣa, Bhūmapuruṣa, Pradhānapuruṣa, and also Mahāpuruṣa. || 9 ||
Likewise, he likewise [meditated upon] Mahāviṣṇu, as well as the Vairāja-puruṣa,
and similarly Hiraṇyagarbha, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Goloka, Amṛta, Vaikuṇṭhaka, and the abode Śveta;
likewise the unmanifest abode and that which is the abode of Viṣṇu’s Śrī.
The abode created by Sadāśiva, the great sphere of Māyā,
and the various abodes of the twenty-four principles.
The arrangement of each [deity] according to their respective power and the arising of their strength,
and the manner in which their supreme divinity is established in each case according to its specific disposition.
And whatever kinds of wonders there may be, as well as sovereign powers, marvels, and the lakes of the essence of Brahman; || 14 ||

Desirable things, desirable creepers, prosperity, well-offered sacrifices, and desired manifestations of power—all those which are indeed most wonderful, existing for the sake of the flow of the essence of Brahman. (15)
The eons and sub-eons are like creepers that grow in accordance with their form; the trees of joy and delight are the very grounds of bliss and its continuation. (16)
The tasting of drinks that are both satisfying and unsatisfying, and the honoring of fragrant lotuses; the abundance of coolness and further coolness, and the delighting in joy and further joy. (17)
And whatever wonderful and marvelous things there were anywhere,
the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari displayed them all within his own body at that time.
But the Blessed Vāsudeva, repeatedly beholding the worlds of Īśa and their further limits, then declared: "It cannot be crossed. || 19 ||
King Vāsudeva himself reached the end of his own manifestation;
then he said to Hari, "You are Ananta, the Controller."
He described his form in many ways and chose eternal knowledge;
"So be it," Hari said, who brings about the creation of Brahmā.
"Manifest your own three sons, who are capable of bearing the burden of the Lord"—
thus he received this command from Vāsudeva, who was his very self.
Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa—these three are the creators, sustainers, and destroyers of all lords. (23)
From himself, the kings of kings were manifested;
of those, the three gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the portions. ||24||
They are the regulators of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) produced from the body of Vairāja;
they are the creators of the lower eggs and the governors of the creation of individual souls (jīvas). ||25||
Therefore, Aniruddha and the others are the directors of the Lord’s satisfaction;
they are the authors of the supreme creation and possess the very nature of the Supreme Self. ||26||
Thus, the diversity of creation is remembered as belonging to the various lords;
that state of being each respective lord is considered to be due to their connection with the Supreme Brahman. (27)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Vāsudeva’s Creation of the Lord," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: From the region of the navel of Vairāja, a lotus was born;
there, the four-faced Brahmā appeared just as before.
Then, from that region of his navel, a second lotus indeed arose;
there a second Brahmā appeared, who is known as Aṣṭānana.
Then, in the third lotus, Brahmā had sixteen heads;
in the fourth lotus, Brahmā indeed came to have thirty-two heads.
In the fifth lotus, Brahmā came to possess fifty faces;
when the sixth lotus was born, Brahmā indeed became hundred-faced.
Then, at the seventh lotus, Brahmā appeared with five hundred faces.
In the eighth lotus, the Creator became known as Sahasrānana (the Thousand-faced One).
In the ninth lotus, Brahmā was indeed born with five thousand faces;
in the tenth, Brahmā came to have ten thousand heads.
In the eleventh lotus, the unborn one indeed appeared with fifty thousand faces; likewise, in the twelfth, the unborn one appeared with a hundred thousand faces.
In the thirteenth lotus, the unborn one possesses two hundred thousand faces;
in the fourteenth lotus, the unborn one possesses fifty million faces.
Born in the fifteenth lotus, he was the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) with ten million faces;
indeed, in the sixteenth lotus, Brahmā was born with a hundred million heads.
Then, in the seventeenth lotus, Viśvasṛj had a head like a lotus;
likewise, in the eighteenth lotus, Brahmā had a head shaped like a dwarf.
In that nineteenth [kalpa], he indeed became Padmāsya;
in the twentieth, the Creator (Brahmā) became Kamala, possessing a face at every parārdha.
Thus, in each individual lotus there, millions of Brahmās have arisen;
those of the same kind are infinite in number.
In the same way, there are crores of Viṣṇus and Rudras of such a kind, produced from their respective abodes; there is no end to their number.
Just as there is no end to these [worlds] created by Īśa,
so too there is no end to the Vairājas, nor to their high-souled fathers.
Indeed, the limit of the number of those who are there— beginning with Mahāviṣṇu and including countless others— is impossible for anyone to reach.
Now, the authority for those sages, beginning with Caturāsya, has been well-determined within this work consisting of fourteen chapters.
The existence of the eight-faced ones shall be on twenty-eight levels;
likewise, that of the sixteen-faced creators within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) should be understood. || 17 ||
His authority extends over fifty-six Brahmāṇḍas consisting of various openings;
indeed, he dances upon a hundred rows of thirty-two heads. (18)
Authority over two hundred million Brahmāṇḍas was established by Virāja for fifty creators who possess fifty faces. (19)
Within the egg containing a thousand apertures, there is the leadership of fifty Brahmās with a hundred faces,
belonging to the five-hundred-faced Aja.
Furthermore, the office of leadership over the thousand-faced Brahmās was established,
and likewise, the leadership over two thousand cosmic eggs was ordained.
Likewise, the leadership of the Creator, who possesses five thousand mouths,
was stabilized by Virāja within the four-thousand-fold cosmic egg.
The eligibility for even the Creator, who possesses ten thousand mouths,
has been firmly established by Virāja within the cosmic egg consisting of ten thousand sections.
He indeed established the office of the one with fifty thousand faces within twenty thousand egg-universes.
In the forty-four billion cosmic eggs of the one with a hundred thousand faces, there resides that [Brahmā];
the Creator, possessing two hundred thousand faces, performs the work of the hundred thousand terrestrial eggs.
The leader was made with fifty lakhs of faces and two lakhs of apertures in his trunk;
then he had ten million mouths and five lakhs of testicles. (26)
Netār Arbuda-āsya was made the leader of ten lakhs of Tarāṇḍakas;
Abja-āsya attained the leadership of twenty lakhs of Bilāṇḍas. (27)
In the fifty-lakh *bilakāṇḍaka*, he was made Kharvāsya;
then, in the ten-million-fold *koṭistara* [kalpa], he was made Netā with a face like a lotus.

Brahmā, who has a face turned toward the far shore (*parārdha*), was established within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) consisting of one hundred million [worlds]; likewise, these others were also installed. (29)
They perform their respective duties according to their own jurisdictions.
Now, once, during the great Rājasūya sacrifice of Virāja—
In the house of Virāja, thousands of lords assembled—
Viṣṇus with many arms and Rudras with diverse eyes.
The Vairājas and other lords of lords likewise assembled there.
When the deliberation arose as to who indeed should receive the honor of being worshipped first at that festival assembly,
a great clamor ensued.
Some said, "Brahmā, whose face is turned toward the supreme limit (parārdha), should receive the honor of being worshipped first."
Others also say: "Śambhu, who perceives the highest limit (parārdha), shall receive the foremost honor."
Others, however, claimed that Viṣṇu, whose arms extend for a *parārdha*, was worthy of the first honor;
yet in this dispute and debate, they did not reach a final decision at all. (34)
Then, when a dispute arose among them, they all reflected:
"In matters such as disputes and confusion, the words of the elders must be accepted. (5)
But their great-grandfather was the wise Mahāviṣṇu;
whatever decision he established and demonstrated shall be considered authoritative. (36)
Having thus made this agreement in the presence of Mahāviṣṇu,
those lords bowed and reported the entire account to him.
Mahāviṣṇu, having meditated for a moment, said to his grandsons:
"You three are equal, possessing identical strength."
They are equally worthy of worship, equal in excellence, and likewise engaged in the same tasks; indeed, all three are worthy of honor, for none is inferior to the others.
Nevertheless, since in the Rājasūya sacrifice there should be worship of only one [deity],
may you lords, having deliberated thus, reach a decision.
"Honor should be shown to one, and compliance should be accepted from two"—
having thus commanded, Mahāviṣṇu remained established in silence.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Authorities and Offices of Brahmā and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||6||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, because of a great and persistent obsession on the part of those three to obtain the status of being the first to be worshipped, a supreme clamor arose.
"I should be worshipped first, not you, nor anyone else," said the lords;
thus they engaged in a quarrel to achieve their own status as the object of worship.
They treat one another with contempt and even hurl insults; with ill-spoken words as their arrows, they seem to pierce each other’s vital points. (3)
While they were thus engaged in quarreling, their followers—
Viṣṇus, Rudras, and Brahmās, numbering in the crores and equipped with weapons— also arrived.
They fought most fiercely and violently; that great slaughter occurred because they could not reach a decision regarding which one among them was worthy of worship.
Then, by the Vairāja-puruṣas accompanied by Mahāviṣṇu,
the Lord Hari himself was authorized to deliver the final decision.
Having personally understood their purpose, the Supreme Brahman indeed went to the supreme court,
that station which is the unmanifested abode of nectar.
Having himself established the system of justice within the abode of the syllable,
the Lord of Justice shines forth in the form of the Supreme Person (Bhūman-puruṣa).
Other lords, the administrators of justice, were appointed by him;
from his own left side, Lakṣmī was produced in abundance as Bhūmi.
She too is the presiding judge of justice, the dispenser of justice, and the Supreme Goddess;
and that abode is the unmanifest, made supreme over both the earth and the infinite.
Likewise, there are numerous judges who administer justice, as well as those who issue subordinate decisions and those who govern both the higher and lower courts. (11)
There exist those who consist of Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and Puruṣātman;
they provide definitive conclusions regarding Mahāviṣṇu, Virāṭ, Īśvara, and the others. || 12 ||
In various places and in those respective locations, there are indeed millions of lords who possess sovereignty that bestows both deficient and abundant happiness.
Viṣṇu, possessing arms as long as a *parārdha* and highly esteemed by kings, was worshipped; likewise, justice was abundantly administered, and the Rājasūya sacrifice was successfully completed.
By the command of justice, may the fruits of every righteous deed performed by those who have woven together all creations through logic be attained in each respective case. 15.
Upon the fall of one king, there is the festival for the coronation of another; when a change of affairs occurs, there is a rotation of leaders. (16)

In times of war, at the moment of destruction, or during sudden calamities, for the purpose of manifesting the splendor of the array's components, its manifestations, and its pervasive power. || 17 ||
The omnipresent Lord always possesses absolute authority in every respect regarding the dispatching and withdrawing of incarnations within the cosmic eggs.
Śrī Hari himself, manifest in the form of the Supreme Person (Puruṣa),
remained in his own unmanifest abode for the purpose of carrying out his judicial duties.
Whenever, wherever, and in whatever place within the cosmic egg a decline of dharma is perceived, He then impels His partial incarnation (aṃśa).
Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and all others are indeed distinct in age after age; infinite incarnations indeed arise separately within the cosmic egg. 21.
And in the worlds of the lords, indeed, there are infinite incarnations;
they possess the same character, the same form, and the same activities as He. (22)
There is no end and no limit to the number of the incarnations of Śrī Hari, due to the infinity of time, the boundlessness of creation, and the entirety of the infinite tasks to be accomplished. (23)
Then, for the sake of all lords to obtain happiness at all times,
Śrī Hari meditated in his heart upon austerity and the great vow.
May all lords always be happy, endowed with the essence of being; likewise may Prakṛti-Puruṣa and Pradhāna-Puruṣa be so. (25)
The Great Viṣṇus and Maheśvaras residing in the worlds of the Bhūmipuruṣas,
as well as the Hiraṇyagarbhas and Vairājas, are the lords of the eight enclosures.

Those residing in Goloka, those residing in Vikuṇṭha, as well as those situated in Śvetadvīpa, those situated in the unmanifest (avyākṛta), and those situated in the realms of Viṣṇu, Rudra, Māyā, and the Imperishable (akṣara). ||27||
"May all beings always be happy through my asceticism"—with such compassion, Hari established this abode for the sake of performing penance. (28)
In the region known as Akṣara, that divine Badarikāśrama is ever delightful, consisting of austerity and renunciation, and filled with peace and bliss. (29)
The divine form bearing the great vow was assumed by Śrī Hari;
He is indeed the Lord Nārāyaṇa, appearing as a divine youth of sixteen years.
Then, for the sake of serving him, a form was requested by Akṣara;
and that form assumed a human shape, sixteen years of age. || 3.1 ||
That man is a servant and Hari is the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
he is this very Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the Master who is beyond the imperishable and all else.
There shines the radiant lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, an ocean of spiritual luster, a celibate whose stream flows upward.
The lords go there repeatedly for the sake of beholding Hari;
indeed, countless liberated ones and those established in the final stage of life reside there, O descendant of Kaśyapa.
Those compassionate, peaceful, and virtuous ones are considered sages; indeed, they exist for the sake of bringing about the liberation of householders. (35)
Wandering through the worlds of the lords, they protect those who have come for refuge;
having imparted the very mantra of Nārāyaṇa, they lead them even to liberation.
They also promote the direct worship of Hari, the Supreme Brahman,
among the lords, and thereby liberate them from that [bondage].
It is known by the names Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Śvetadvīpa, Divyaka, Avyākṛta, and Badarikāśrama. (38)
The divine abodes being proclaimed exist within the abode of the Imperishable;
indeed, they were fashioned by Hari within the regions of the Imperishable.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Rāmacandra, Śrī Nārāyaṇa—this one;
Śrī Bhūmā, Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa, and indeed Śrī Hari. ||1.7.40||
Being himself the Lord Brahmā, the manifest sovereign of the Imperishable,
and the master of the world of Brahmā, he therefore assumes those forms.
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord known as Puruṣottama, who is established everywhere, shines forth in diverse forms. 42.
Indeed, other abodes have been established within the regions of that which is known as the Imperishable Abode;
for in all of them, the Imperishable truly exists.
Therefore, it is described that within Goloka and other realms, there exists the all-pervading, imperishable, supreme abode, the world of Brahman (Brahmaloka), which is present everywhere. ||44||
The boundary of the worlds of the lords is said to be Prakṛti;
for these abodes exist within that boundary, indeed joined to Brahman.
Therefore, they are designated as "immutables" (akṣara) and are pervaded by the immutable;
they are devoid of contact with primordial nature (prakṛti) and abide above primordial nature. ||46||
"Those worlds are called the stages of liberation by those who know the vital points;
thus, O Lakṣmī, this arrangement of the creation of the Lord should be understood correctly. (47)
All power belongs to you alone; all this is born from your majesty. The entire manifestation of the Lord would not shine at all without you.
Both you and I always assume the form of the Self of all there;
without you, I have no lordship, and without me, you have no delight.
O Saccit, bliss is said to be the happiness found there in every respect;
all the worlds and the lords enjoy the happiness of us two.
Therefore, that circle of the Lord, consisting of Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī,
manifested at that time from us both, and likewise vanished into us both.
"Reflecting that one becomes dissolved in ultimate dissolution and rises again at the beginning [of creation], the lords indeed always worship me. (52)
The lords who have attained their sovereignty are presided over by me;
through my yoga they have become lords, for without me they are not lords. ||63||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Abode of Avyākṛta and the Sacred Site of Badarikāśrama," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||7||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Salutations to the Supreme Deity, the Infinite, who possesses the three powers;
to the Witness among embodied beings, whose path as the Self is imperceptible.

Homage again to the lineage of the virtuous, which brings about the destruction of the wicked and the attainment of true prosperity; homage to that Abode which delights in a state free from both equality and superiority.
Salutations to you who are far removed from those of false yoga, yet close at hand;
the Vedas have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal, and the sacrifices have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal.
Knowledge has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme object; creation has Nārāyaṇa as its essence;
Nārāyaṇa is all this; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate goal.
Having assumed the three qualities (guṇas), Hari himself, though devoid of qualities,
became the Virāṭ Puruṣa and created the waters from his own body.
The waters are to be understood as *nārāḥ*, for the waters are the daughters of Nara;
having made his abode within them, he himself lies there, and thus he is Nārāyaṇa.
While he was lying there in the water, a thousand years passed;
then, from his navel, the lotus-stalk appeared.
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā came into being upon a lotus;
he beheld water on all sides and nothing else, and he became bewildered.
"How, why, and from where am I? What do I do here in this absolute [reality]?
Therefore, I truly desire to see my own root from its very foundation. (9)
Having thus resolved within himself, Brahmā entered the stalk;
he moved for a thousand cycles of four yugas until its end, yet he did not reach it.
Then, having rested, he turned back toward its stalk; but when he stood upon it with speed, aided by his perfection in yoga, [the stalk rose up]. || 11 ||
"For what purpose and how have I arisen as a lotus in the water?"—
as he was reflecting thus, an incorporeal voice spoke.
"Perform penance; when you are established there, at the proper time, knowledge will arise.
Having heard that [instruction], you shall understand the purpose for your own people once you have undertaken that penance. (13)
Then, indeed, knowledge arose within him: "This birth of mine is for the sake of creation.
He then applied his mind to the question, "What kind of creation should be performed by me? (14)
He beheld the creation of the former age within the form of Nārāyaṇa;
and having seen that which was even more ancient than the former, he rejoiced.
By the power of his asceticism, he indeed attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and beheld Hari, his own Guru, as the Cause;
the Great Lord who lies upon the waters, possessing diverse forms that comprise the entire creation.
With divine vision, he saw there, in the Vairāja realm, both the insentient and the sentient.
He beheld everything that was to be, consisting of creation, in the form of name and shape.
At the base of his feet he saw Pātāla, at the region of his heels Rasātala, and at his two ankles Brahmā saw the world Mahātala.
He indeed beheld the world of Talātala in his shanks;
the world of Sutala in his knees; and Vitala and Atala in his thighs.
Then he beheld the earth at the base of his thighs, the atmosphere at his navel, heaven in his heart, Maharloka in his neck, and Janaloka in his mouth.
He beheld the world of asceticism (tapas) upon his forehead, the world of truth (satya) upon his head, the gods beginning with Indra in his arms, and the very quarters of the sky in his ears.
He saw sound in the ears and the two Aśvins in the nostrils;
he saw smell in the sense of smell, fire in the mouth, and the sky within the two sockets of the eyes.
In her two eyes are the sun and the moon; in the lashes of those eyes, day and night;
in the play of her eyebrows, the station of Brahmā; and likewise, in her palate, the waters.
In his tongue was taste, in his fang Yama,
in his intellect the Vedas, and in his sidelong glance the dissolution of time.
Likewise, he saw shame upon his upper lip and greed upon his lower lip;
he saw righteousness on both breasts and unrighteousness on his back.
He beheld Prajāpati in his penis, Mitra and Varuṇa in his two testicles, the oceans in his belly, and the mountains in his bones.
He indeed explains the rivers as being in the channels, the trees in the body hairs,
the wind in the breath, time in the movement [of the vital energy], and the clouds in his hair.
One should place Sandhyā in the garment, Māyā in the heart, Candraka in the mind,
Rudra in the intellect and ego, and the elephants and horses in the nails.
In her skill she placed all birds within her intellect; in her two hips, Svāyambhuva Manu; in her memory, all deer; and in her recollection, the Gandharva singers.
In his valor were the armies of the Asuras; likewise, the Brāhmaṇas were in his mouth, the Kṣatriyas in his two arms, the Vaiśyas in his thighs, and the Śūdras in his feet. (1.8.3)
Whatever exists, from the immobile to the mobile, that which comes into being through its own nature—
all this Brahmā beheld clearly within the body of Vairāja.

Whatever effect belongs to whatever [cause], in whatever manner and to whatever extent; whatever instrument belongs to whatever [effect], in whatever manner—the majesty consisting of the conjunction with the effect, its attraction, its integration, and its manifestation. (32)
Like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of his hand, that Lord of Creatures saw everything;
then the Lotus-born One, having understood that [the world] is twofold—dependent on the principles (*tattva*) and dependent on the mind (*manas*).
Having regained his memory that had previously been lost, Brahmā rejoiced at the creation consisting of both the seed-born and the mind-born, and he praised Keśava.
Salutations to the one whose nature is creation; salutations to the embodiment of the Vairāja hymn;
salutations to the intermediate creation; salutations to the one who takes the form of Brahmā and the other progenitors. ||35||
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, whose form is that of Mahāviṣṇu;
salutations to the Lord of Pradhāna, the Master of Prakṛti. ||26||
Salutations to You, the Infinite and Unceasing; salutations to You as Pradyumna.
Salutations to You known as Saṃkarṣaṇa; salutations to You as Vāsudeva. ||27||
Salutations to the Great Being, salutations to you, the Great Time;
salutations to the abode of the imperishable, salutations to the liberated Inner Controller. ||30||
Salutations to You, the all-pervading, the Supreme Lord, who possesses manifold forms!
While You exist, there occur the errors of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*). (29)
Salutations to You who are truly non-different from this world; salutations again and again to the Witness, the Eye of all, and the Self-Ruling Sovereign. 1.8.40
To you who dwell in manifold wonders, who assume various forms, who previously perceived the self as manifold, and who later perceive it as a single self. ||41||
Salutation to you whose nature is both existent and non-existent, for the sake of both the related and unrelated meanings; salutation to you who are of the nature of atoms and yet all-pervading.
Salutations to the one who is devoid of the threefold division, whose nature consists of both female and male forms;
salutations to the divine knowledge, to that which is to be known, and to the one whose form is the knower. 43.
Salutations to you whose nature is the mind, salutations to the measure and the measurer; salutations be to you, the subject of cognition, and salutations to you who are the pre-existent effect. 44.
Salutations to you, whose nature is the pervasion of the fruit and who are the discourse of the Vedas;
salutations to you, whose nature is the cessation of the act of sowing and whose self is the dissolution of cognition. 47.
To Him whose body is light and space, whose nature consists of both divine and non-divine qualities;
from whom all proceed, in whom all abide, and who is the Lord whose very essence is everything. ||46||
Salutations again and again to you, the Teacher, whose purpose encompasses both the dream and the non-dream states;
O Compassionate Lord, you have awakened the door of my heart.
O Lord, do not forget that purpose for which I shall act;
through the awakening granted by you, I shall perform the creation of the universe.
May I not be bound there; I pray for your assistance.
In the undertaking of every task, be the one who provides the means and shows the way. (49)
Having thus praised him, Brahmā himself became silent for a moment; meanwhile, Nārāyaṇa also withdrew his manifold manifestations.
As soon as the Lotus-born Brahmā beheld the true form of Vairāja, Viṣṇu manifested from the region of Vairāja’s heart.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Attainment of Knowledge of Creation and Other Matters," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Viṣṇu is endowed with all auspicious qualities, possesses the power to nourish all,
is a treasure-house of all wonders, glorious, and intensely radiant with a jasmine-like navel.
His head was adorned with glossy hair of a tawny hue, curved at the ends;
he wore a golden crown set with many jewels and gems.
Wearing golden earrings upon his well-formed ears shaped like *śaṣkulī*, he bore a crescent moon upon his forehead marked by three broad and radiant lines. || 3 ||
Bearing a mark of kaisara on his forehead and anointed with aguru and sandalwood,
he was curved by the knitting of his eyebrows, which were worthy of being sprouts for the arrows of Kama.
His eyes have white edges with a reddish glow like the petals of a lotus, and the outer corners of his eyes are smeared with collyrium and ointment extending to his ears. || 5 ||
His nose has the luster of a blooming sesame flower; his cheeks are long, and his two cheeks are perfectly round and red. || 6 ||
Adorned with armlets of fragrant lotuses and divine flower-ear ornaments, his ears were beautified by earrings made of pure gold.
Beautiful with a beard arising from fine, dark, and golden tips;
his lips are even and rest upon a radiant smile resembling a red bimba fruit. || 8 ||
With a neck like a conch shell and a beautiful chin, his throat was encircled by a halo of splendor;
with his brilliantly shining body, he was the destroyer of the darkness within the heart.
Wearing golden flower-garlands and the Kaustubha gem upon his neck,
he possessed well-developed shoulders and arms whose foreparts were like the coils of a long, hanging serpent.
His arms reach down to his knees, his forearms are well-proportioned, and he possesses four arms; his two hands, with nails like the shining moon, are red. || 11 ||
His beautiful lotus-like hands were adorned with the luster of golden rings and set with excellent gems;
his palms bore the marks of the bow, the discus, the banner, the svastika, and the fish.
The Lord bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus as his weapons;
he wears a necklace, is marked with the Śrīvatsa, is the food of the gods, has teeth like jasmine buds, and possesses a beautiful back.
His broad and elevated chest is excellent, and his hips and private parts are well-developed.
His two thighs resemble the trunks of elephants, and his knees are even and rounded. || 14 ||
His calves were well-proportioned, tapering, and full; his feet were level, depressed in the center, and possessed of beautiful soles.
His lotus-like feet were lovely to behold, with reddish hues, beautifully arched in the middle, and elevated at the heels. || 15 ||
His feet are the source of merit for all who take refuge in them; his complexion is white, and he is resplendent with fine lines of hair upon his fingers.
With a beautiful line of fine body hair and a belly well-formed by that very vigor, he had three ankle-bones on his feet; glorious and adorned with every ornament.
He was resplendent with a divine forest garland, the Vaijayantī, which was moist with the excellent fragrance of various unfading flowers and honey.
The lotus, the goad, the vajra, the svastika, the javā flower, and the jambu fruit—these are the marks on the upper lines of the eight corners; there are nine [marks] on the right foot. 1.9.
Placing seven symbols on his left side— namely, a fish, a half-moon, a water-pot, a triangle, the sky, a cow’s footprint, and a bow.
With a broad line on his forehead that reached both edges without touching them,
he manifested the sixfold sovereignty of a *bhaga* and his birth from a *sāttvika* womb.
On his left thigh, he bore the beautiful mark of the moon, white with radiant luster,
which was the innate sign of the Goddess Lakṣmī.
Viṣṇu became such as this, the refuge of manifold forms and qualities;
seeing him, the self-born Brahmā, who takes pride in his role as the overseer of creation, [was moved].
Thinking, "Who was this other who excelled in beauty, virtue, heroism, and strength? he questioned Viṣṇu, the nourisher of the world.
"Who are you, O learned one, appearing as such an adversary of mine?
I alone am the creator of the universe, possessing the glory of all sovereignty. (25)
The sustainer of all, the nourisher of all, bringing about the state of leadership over all—
there is indeed no one other than me who is the creator, destroyer, and nourisher of the universe.
What indeed is the cause of your birth? Who is the doer? Who is the ordainer?
Truly, no one who creates enmity with me shall ever partake in happiness.
Having smiled, Viṣṇu replied to that Brahmā:
"The creation is in me, and I am in the creation; the all-pervading Lord is composed of the creation."
Many lotus-born ones like you rest merged within me;
I am without beginning or end, the Creator, facing in all directions.
He who stands pervading the universe through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader—
the God who consists of all creation, praised by Ananta, Brahmā, and the others.
I am that Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu; there is no other superior or equal to me.
Go far away from here, otherwise you will certainly meet your destruction.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said to Viṣṇu: "Do not be arrogant, you who are ignorant regarding true insight."
"Do not despise me, O God; here I am, I shall destroy you!
Having uttered this, they both became enraged, each desiring to slay the other.
Saying, "I alone am the excellent one, not you; I am the one supreme Lord," the two, desiring to slay each other, commenced a battle.
The two heroic warriors, scions of Manu and wielders of great weapons, fought as adversaries;
indeed, their battle arose from the deep-seated presence of egoism.
Lords equal to him in power arrived, desiring to behold the two engaged in combat, showering rains of flowers while watching them in the midst of battle.
Then, filled with rage, Hari discharged unbearable arrows and various weapons of great range at the chest of Brahmā. (37)
Then Brahmā, becoming exceedingly enraged, [discharged] at Viṣṇu’s chest unbearable arrows with the brilliance of lightning, as well as various other weapons.
He released them, and their battle immediately became truly wondrous;
seeing it, all the lords were deeply moved and offered their praise.
Viṣṇu, impelled by his own momentum, discharged the fire-weapon (*agny-astra*) at the Creator;
that weapon was then neutralized by the Creator with the rain-weapon (*parjanya-astra*).
The lightning-weapon accompanied by clouds, impelled there by Viṣṇu,
was indeed destroyed in the great sky by Brahmā with his wind-weapon.
Viṣṇu discharged the mountain-weapon, and who indeed released the thunderbolt-weapon?
Hari unleashed the serpent-weapon, while Brahmā hurled the Garuḍa-weapon. (42)
The burden sent by Hari was taken up with ease by the Brāhmaṇa;
then Viṣṇu, exerting his power of separation, struck him in the chest.
Brahmā, having severed her with his trident, discharged the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon;
and Viṣṇu, having dissolved that Jṛmbhaṇa with the Nidrā mantra.
As soon as Brahmā took up the Brahmāstra, Śiva also discharged it;
a most terrible battle between the two Brahmāstras then took place in the sky. ||45||
From that, great fires were born, capable of burning the creation of Īśa;
then Viṣṇu seized his own discus, Sudarśana.
Fierce like ten million suns, with sharp edges and destructive, the lords were terrified by it and raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
Just as the Lord prepared for the destruction of Brahmā,
Brahmā donned the armor known as the devotion to the name of Viṣṇu.
May the divine Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of suffering, dwell within me;
may the Supreme Brahman protect my head, and may Brahman protect my throat.
May Vāsudeva protect the chest; may Aniruddha protect the hips;
may Pradyumna protect the belly; and may Saṃkarṣaṇa protect the back.
May Bhūman protect my penis, and may Mahāviṣṇu protect my two thighs; may Hiraṇyagarbha protect my knees, and the Vairāja Puruṣa my shanks. ||5.1||
May Kṛṣṇa protect the two ankles as the Pradhāna-Puruṣa, Hari the feet as Prakṛti-Puruṣa, and Vaikuṇṭha the north. 52.
May Nārāyaṇa, the inner controller, protect me from behind on all sides;
O All-pervading Lord, you who are Viṣṇu, enter into all my limbs and protect me. (53)
May Nārāyaṇa himself protect my *sattva* (the quality of purity), which is the support of *sattva*; may the illustrious Lord himself protect my blood, which is the support of blood. ||54||
May the Discus-bearer, the giver of the gift of fearlessness, protect me who am the refuge of fear;
may the Lord, whose hand arises from the stalk, protect me as I stand upon that stalk.
Protect me, who have come to you for refuge, from this sudden and great suffering;
pacify the Brahma-weapon, withdraw the discus, and restore the heavens today! (56)
Having thus praised the supreme god, Brahmā became silent;
and Viṣṇu, recognizing his devotion to Brahman, did not release his discus.
Janārdana, who is Para-Brahman in his form as Saṃkarṣaṇa, set his mind upon withdrawing the splendor of your supreme Brahmāstras for the sake of their destruction. ||58||
Between the two of them, there appeared a pillar composed of great light;
meanwhile, those two Brahmā-missiles were capable of destroying everything.
Beholding that supreme and wonderful splendor which pacified the weapons, the two [Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa] instantly merged into a great fire consisting of light.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Īśa—whoever were assembled there—were struck with wonder and, being bewildered, exclaimed: "Aho! What is this light? (6.1)

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Devotion, Armor, and Other Matters," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Alas! What is this pillar-like form consisting of splendor that has arisen?
Both above and below it, this indeed consists of the splendor of Brahman."
While those two gods were thus deliberating and watching, in an instant,
the two Brahma-missiles they were fighting with dissolved away.
Because the two weapons, which were of the nature of Brahmā, had merged into the splendor of the pillar,
he was once again unable to decide which of the two was the greater.
But for this one who relies on the power to swallow the Brahmā-missile, he who can lead the lower limit of these two to the supreme limit—let him alone be great. (4)
Having thus established an agreement, those two who considered themselves heroes set out together; yet, it was impossible for both to achieve the same objective.
Having reflected thus, Hari Viṣṇu assumed the form of Garuḍa,
while Brahmā, having become embodied as a swan, went to see the end of it.
Viṣṇu traveled further and further for a hundred divine years;
yet, when he could not see the base of that pillar, he stopped.
Exhausted and despondent, he reached the eastern battlefield;
Brahmā had gone higher and ever higher for a hundred divine years.
Without reaching the end, he stood still for a moment and became absorbed in thought;
at that very moment, the supreme Lord appeared in the form of light.
He reflected: "Aha! What kind of gods are these, who, like children, have conceived such thoughts?
They are intent on showing contempt for me, who am infinite and immeasurable."
Even Vāsudeva himself would not be able to reach the end of even a single ray of mine; what then to say of others who merely imagine themselves to be lords?
Having thus made this jest, he indeed shook his head;
at that moment, a beautiful flower fell from the region of the crown of his head.
Brahmā beheld that ketakī flower, which possessed a fragrance fallen from a hundred divine yugas, as it was falling before him.
And Brahmā asked: "Who are you, and why do you fall, O King of Flowers?
Having heard this, Puṣpa said to Brahmā: "I have been seized by the Supreme Soul."
Therefore, I fall upon his head with my own nature as light;
even as I was falling from that head, a hundred yugas passed for me.
Nevertheless, the path traversed by me is indeed small in measure;
I do not see when the end of these rays will ever come.
Therefore, you too should abandon hope regarding the perception of an end to the Infinite;
at that time, Brahmā, having turned back, held counsel with Ketakī.
"O friend, you have done today that which was desired by me;
this must indeed be spoken by you along with me in the presence of Viṣṇu. (18)
"I have been seen within the light by the Creator; there, O Acyuta, I am the witness.
Thinking thus, Brahmā indeed bowed repeatedly to the Ketaka flower.
"Indeed, even that which is untrue may be commendable during a time of distress, according to the teaching;
for when the Brahma-flower arrived, it was indeed upon the field of battle."
Having observed that Viṣṇu was devoid of victory,
the deceitful eunuch Brahmā danced and spoke to Keśava, the upholder of truth.
Having indeed beheld the ultimate end of that which is of the nature of light, O God, I have now come here;
for this Ketaka tree is truly a witness to it.
He asked, "O Viṣṇu, am I indeed great? || 22 ||
Although that false testimony given by Ketaka was indeed a lie,
Brahmā reached its conclusion, and Viṣṇu considered it to be the truth.
Having paid homage to the Creator and considering him his own crest-jewel,
he worshipped the Creator with the sixteen types of offerings.
The Great Lord was there to inflict punishment upon Brahmā and Ketaka, for Brahmā had attained his greatness through force by acting as a false witness.
The Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa himself, manifested with a form from within his own nature as light,
assuming the form of Sadāśiva.
He is called an expansion (aṃśa) of Saṃkarṣaṇa; he is Sadāśiva, the agent of dissolution.
[This refers] to the Great Soul Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman. || 27 ||
Indeed, a single ray from his head became a pillar of light;
it possessed both the nature of an arrow and the form of a *liṅga*.
The nature of Brahman-splendor, the state of being the path of light, the mass of radiance of the Suṣumṇā, and Brahman itself which is formless—[these are the characteristics]. (29)
The formless reality of Śambhu is celebrated by many names,
arising from within the rays that emerge from the forehead of the Supreme Brahman.
The Veda also proclaims that the birth of Śiva occurred from the forehead;
indeed, having beheld Śiva as possessed of form, being existence-consciousness-bliss, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] [arose].
Trembling and with palms joined in reverence, he grasped Śiva’s feet along with his trident and said: "Forgive me, O Supreme Lord! (32)
O Mahādeva, you are the Lord who wields the rod of punishment for the destruction of my sins; you have manifested here—be gracious, O mine of compassion! 33.
Instruct me, who have fallen into delusion and resorted to falsehood;
O refuge of all, protect me, your brother, who have come to you for shelter. 34.
Out of deluded intellect, I committed an insult there toward Viṣṇu;
yet Viṣṇu is the Supreme Brahman, the Great One, and he is always worthy of my reverence.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, forgive me for my falsehood and mete out punishment;
you are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, and Hari is identical with the Supreme Brahman. (36)
One should not create a distinction between the two; he who perceives such a distinction falls downward.
If, through ignorance, I have failed to recognize this greatness of Śrī Janārdana, [may He forgive me]. (37)
Furthermore, having been utterly insulted, I spoke a falsehood;
therefore, O Blessed One, because I am a vessel for that fault, I ought to be punished by you.
Cut off my head, cut off falsehood, or cut off my sin;
cut off my perception of duality as well—do as you wish, O Śaṅkara! (39)
You are Viṣṇu, you are the Supreme Lord, you are the God, the Supreme Sovereign;
you are the light, you are formless, the all-pervading, and indeed Brahman.
You are the embodied Supreme Brahman and the very root of light;
O Brahman, that which is a ray from the circumference of the splendor of your face— ||41||
Its boundless shore has been beheld; great is its majesty.
Grant peace, grant forgiveness, and protect me who has come to you for refuge. 42.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of lords, the infallible one abiding in the light of Brahman—
the God who is Mahādeva, Sadāśiva, whose form is the Supreme Brahman— ||43||
Having paid homage, bowed again, and bowed repeatedly, Brahmā fell at his feet; when he remained silent, Śiva raised him up and spoke to him.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Śaṅkara Preceded by the Manifestation of the Effulgent Brahman-Liṅga," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Because the hidden meaning (liṅga) proceeds from that [source], it is therefore called a *liṅga*.
The glorious Keśava, the Supreme Person, is absorbed (līna) in the supreme Brahman. || 1 ||
He indeed causes that mere orb of splendor to go forth;
that splendor becomes the liṅga, which is proclaimed as Bāṇa. || 2 ||
Because there is no difference between light and the possessor of light, Hari himself is light;
therefore, Śiva as well as the Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman—so say the followers of the Vedas.
"Śiva, who assumes a form by his own will and bestows non-return [to saṃsāra], spoke to that bowing Brahmā: 'Do not fear, O elder brother.'"
I consider the humiliation of the great to be worse than the severing of one's head;
the loss of honor is a great ruin, regarded by the great as death itself.
I shall inflict upon you a punishment equal to the severing of the head, which removes all impurity;
for you, desiring honor as a Brahmin, have embraced the life of a gambler.
Consequently, there shall be no festivals for your chosen deity and the like in the world;
indeed, you yourself will not be worshipped by your chosen deity.
However, you shall have a place in sacrifices and domestic rites;
without you, a sacrifice complete in all its parts and accompanied by sacrificial fees would be fruitless.
"Therefore, when the offering to the gods is obtained at the sacrifice, let there be a share for you;
for the Grandfather, who is the object of honor for all, is established in you. (9)
"O Creator, people will address you with the word 'tvaṃ' (thou).
Then the Blessed Lord spoke to Ketaka, the false witness.
"You shall become unworthy of my worship, of this there is no doubt;
nor will any of the gods accept you in their own worship. (11)
Having heard this, Ketaka propitiated Mahādeva:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, salutations to you, the leader of all! (12)
Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; forgive my transgression.
O Protector, make my birth fruitful; salutations, salutations unto you!
Then Śambhu, the Lord who is the abode of compassion, said to him:
"My attendants shall support you; your birth shall become fruitful."
"I shall grant you a place under the canopy in my own abode; may you find peace.
Having thus commanded, Mahādeva himself ceased speaking.
Then that luminous liṅga gradually underwent contraction;
having become very small, it clearly entered there into the body of Sadāśiva.
Then indeed, by both Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the god Sadāśiva,
whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, was worshipped in his embodied form.
The *liṅga* there, consisting of the form of Brahmā and having the nature of the formless, is known as a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Brahman; it was worshipped by those two. (18)
And it was established in that very place where the creations of Īśvara exist; from that primordial time onwards, the worship of the *liṅga* has been practiced.
Indeed, the worship of Viṣṇu was performed by both Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
while the worship of Śiva was likewise established at that time by both of them.
Since the worship of the Creator, who is devoid of speech, has not been honored by anyone,
neither Viṣṇu nor Śiva is ever worshipped, but the Creator is never worshipped at all.
Śiva and Viṣṇu were worshipped by those very regions situated there;
that worship was initiated for the sake of attaining future creation.
Then, when the linga composed of light had become invisible,
the root of it was perceived in the form of a man, as he had been sought after.

That which is indeed called the Supreme Brahman, possessing two arms and consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss—by means of the rays known as the *liṅga* impelled by the halo of its splendor, [it manifests]. || 24 ||
From him comes Prakṛti-Puruṣa, from him Pradhāna-Puruṣa, from him Mahāviṣṇu, and from him the manifest Vairāja-Puruṣa, the Father,
who is beheld even by the triad of gods and in whom the three reside together.
Brahmā is in the navel, Viṣṇu in the heart, and Śaṅkara himself is in the forehead.
They each looked back at one another and thought, "It is our brothers.
Then the three gods closed their eyes, embraced him, and praised him.
Homage to the one of wondrous nature; homage again and again to the progenitor.
To him who, by his own will, is exceedingly remote, yet through compassion remains near at hand. (28)
"Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, the Vairāja Puruṣa;
for we three are your sons, since we carry out your commands. (29)
"Teach us, O Father; we shall do what must be done, without a doubt.
Then, by means of the Vairāja [sāman], the body was entrusted to the task of creation.
"To Viṣṇu belongs that which is called creation and nourishment; to Śiva, dissolution"—having observed this at that time, indeed, along with millions of lords of all [the worlds].
Likewise, those who were consecrated remained established in their respective stations,
adorned with crowns, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and jeweled earrings.
With linen garments, upper cloths, garlands, sacred threads, and finger-rings;
and with flowers, betel, camphor, sandalwood, and various other ornaments. || 33 ||
With incense, saffron, lamps, white umbrellas, fans, and chowries;
with divine offerings consisting of the excellent insignia and banners of a sovereign king of kings.
Those three gods were worshipped with divine offerings suitable for their respective manifestations, possessing a majesty beyond speech and mind, and they were duly honored by everyone.
The Vaiṣṇavī Lakṣmī arose from Viṣṇu, the Śāṅkarī from Śaṅkara, and the Brahmāṇī from Brahmā; they were born from their left sides. (36)
The abodes of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśa, together with their respective consorts, were also fashioned within the worlds of Īśa by Vairāja.
Vaikuṇṭha is one abode of Viṣṇu, while Kailāsa is another belonging to Hara; Satyaloka is another abode of the Creator (Brahmā), and they all departed for their respective dwellings.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Root of the Linga and the Administration of Instruction on the Unworthiness of Parameṣṭhin and Ketaka," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 11 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Padmā; I shall explain how he created the cosmic eggs from the midst of the body of Vairāja, which consists of the twenty-four principles.
Then Brahmā, taking a single lump from that mass with his joined palms,
kneaded it and fashioned it into innumerable minute portions.
Holding them in the palm of his hand, he caused them to fly up with a *phuṭ* sound;
they were then raised up on all sides into the great space whose nature is pure being (*sattva*).
O beloved, at that time, the cosmic eggs, the spheres, and the souls of the Brahmāṇḍas came into being;
then, many resolutions were made there by Brahmā.
"May all these innumerable atoms remain established separately in the great ether, always stable there and never colliding with one another. (5)
All exist in that very same way, mutually unimpeded;
thus, let there be a great space within each [atom] that provides room.
By the mere power of his resolve, the intermediate spaces then came into being,
and there the fourteen levels (bhūmikās) and so forth were manifested.
By mere such volition, fourteen worlds and so forth were produced within each cosmic egg; indeed, they were entirely pervaded by darkness.
In order to enter into them, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara assumed,
through the power of yoga, countless subtle forms of their own essential natures.
In various places within that egg, the three gods entered;
there, beholding the intense darkness, the Creator formed a resolve.
