"May there be substances of light within all these worlds"; then, in that supreme world, the lamp of truth was illuminated. || 11 ||
Because the lamp born of truth and self-restraint shines there,
this stage is therefore renowned as Satyaloka (the World of Truth).
Then, because of the manifestation of austerity in the lower realm, the name "Loka" was assigned to it by Brahmā. 1.3.
Below that, moreover, through the power of the merit of the ancestors, a light appeared; therefore, it was named Janaloka.
Then, on the lower level, the Great Lamp was indeed illuminated; it was firmly determined that this was the great light arising from the essence of the father’s body. (15)
Indeed, the name Maharloka was given because of its connection with the great lamp;
likewise, the world below that [Janaloka] is so called due to its contact with the lamp of the sun.
Likewise, the world of heaven (svargaloka) is known as "dyu" because of the shining of the stars;
below that, in the intermediate space, it is so called because of the illumination from the sight of the constellations.

The designation "antarīkṣa" (the intermediate space) applies to bhuvarloka and even to the cavities within the earth; below that, on the terrestrial level, it is so called because of the manifestation of the fire of Pṛthu.
The earth is named Agni; it is called "Bhūḥ" because of its blazing. Beneath that are the seven netherworlds (talas), each having seven lamps.
The gems are of divine significance; joined with their respective initial syllables and so forth, their names were properly established. Listen to those various names from me.
The medicinal herbs shine in the lower world, and from that [region] comes Atala; because of the luster of vaidūrya gems, the region below that is known as Vitala.
And Sūtala is considered to be below that, due to the splendor of the Kaustubha gem; Talātala is said to be [below] because of the lamp-like jewels on the hoods of the serpent's tongues.
That great netherworld (Mahātala) was illuminated by the light of emeralds,
while that subterranean realm (Rasātala) was illuminated by the light of various kinds of jewels.
And because of the radiance of the *puṣparāja* jewels situated upon its surface,
Brahmā himself gave it the name "Pātāla."

The Maharloka is said to consist of the masses of people, ascetics, and the truthful; it is born of merit and reality, possessing intense splendor in heaven, and is described as the layer of Vāyu within the Bhuvarloka.
The earth was fashioned from the earth, while the netherworlds beginning with Atala were formed from darkness;
in this manner, indeed, the arrangement of those layers was created by Brahmā.
Even within those, there are minute portions of earth for the sake of stability;
in some places, there are fiery portions, the elements mixed in layers.
In some places, there are also very firm watery portions that are tamasic; these layers, which serve as the support for living beings, are indeed called "cavities" (vivaras).
Then Brahmā fashioned a pillar as a support for the stars in the center;
it was made of gold, extending from Pātāla to Satyaloka, and was perfectly established.
In the world of truth (satyaloka), Brahmā indeed fashioned his own abode;
in the middle world (madhyaloka), Śambhu fashioned Kailāsa as his own.
But Viṣṇu, reclining upon Śeṣa, established for himself a dwelling in the milk ocean beneath Pātāla, which was suitable for his own yoga. || 31 ||
It is indeed for the sake of being seen by great-souled yogins such as Nārada and others,
and it is also the destination to which the gods and the Siddhas go.
That place where the sages go is considered their radiant abode;
it is also where those of other divine bodies attain a truly auspicious state.
He chose a second such place called Śvetadvīpa;
that divine island is indeed remembered as being in the northern part of the Ocean of Milk.
And beyond that, on the peak of the Snowy Mountain upon the earth, is his own third abode named Badarikāśrama, which is accessible to human beings and bestows all desired objects. (35)
There he performs penance in the form of Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the bringers of welfare to the world. (36)
They always strive in this manner for the sake of protection, because they are established therein;
their abodes here within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) are material and inferior.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Production of Innumerable Brahmāṇḍas, Their Extensive Arrangement, and the Dwelling of the Three Deities," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 12 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
This measurement of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is fifty crores of yojanas;
this is known as the covering of the earth, considered the first shell.
Then, indeed, when those innumerable cosmic eggs had arisen,
the terrestrial shell, heated by the heat produced within them, was on the verge of bursting asunder.
Having seen that, Brahmā then created another shell, possessing similar qualities, consisting of a covering of water, for the sake of pacifying those [disasters]. || 3 ||
That [egg] was deposited and enveloped by those [sheaths], surrounded by five lotuses and yojanas;
it was covered by a fiery sheath for the purpose of regulating the extreme cold of the waters.
The third is considered to be ten times greater than that of water;
for the sake of its restraint, that of wind is ten times more powerful than even that.
From that [the Self] comes space, from that the ego (ahaṃkāra), and from that indeed the Great One (mahat);
the Nature (prakṛti) is declared to be the eighth covering of the Great One.
These eight shells are indeed the coverings of the cosmic egg;
each is attached there, serving as that which provides their firmness.
Furthermore, for the purpose of regulating the lifespan of the cosmic eggs, of all created beings, and of Vairāja and the rest, Hari himself, the Supreme Brahman, [acted]. (8)
Then he manifested Mahākāla from his own body;
indeed, the form of Mahākāla is now described as the *samaya*.
Time impels the worlds; Time destroys all creatures;
from a single moment until the great dissolution, it performs its work.
That very same [time-unit] which Hari has conceived as the shortener of life is the *kṣaṇa*, which is the action that produces the separation of two atoms. (11)
That time, characterized by an action, then receives the name "moment" (kṣaṇa);
moreover, time pervaded even by a division [of that] is the second moment. || 12 ||
The third moment is that time characterized by the destruction of the prior conjunction;
the fourth moment is the moment pervaded by the subsequent conjunction with another location. || 13 ||
Time consisting of four kṣaṇas is called a kūṭa;
three kūṭas are said to be a truṭi, and three truṭis are considered a lava.
Three *lava*s constitute one *nimeṣa*; fifteen *nimeṣas* are declared to be one *kāṣṭhā*, and fifteen *kāṣṭhās* are one *nāḍikā*.
Two of those [ghatikās] are declared to be one muhūrta; six muhūrtas constitute a prahara.
Seven praharas make a yāma; by day, there are four yāmas.
Likewise, there are four yāmas; night and day together constitute two [yāmas]. Fifteen [days] make a fortnight (pakṣa), and two fortnights are called a month (māsa). || 17 ||

This month of humans is a day and night for the ancestors (pitṛs). Two such months constitute a season (ṛtu), and six such seasons are considered a southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and a northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
In heaven, the south is said to be night and the north is day;
the two solstices [constitute] the months, and twelve of those make a year. (19)
The Yugas are proclaimed to have a measure of divine years;
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali are known as the Yugas.
Four, three, two, and one thousand years respectively constitute the duration of those respective ages; [the total for] each age is ten thousand years. (2.1)
Likewise, the duration of their two twilight periods (sandhyāṃśa) is two thousand years each,
consisting respectively of eight, six, four, and two years.
Such a period of a thousand yugas is called a day of Brahmā;
his night is of the same duration, during which the three worlds perish.
Rising again in the morning and perishing in the evening in due order,
fourteen Manus indeed pass away during a single day of Brahmā.
Manu enjoys his own cycle of seventy-one caturyugas;
Indra likewise enjoys his own cycle of seventy-one caturyugas. (25)
Even for Brahmā, the supreme lifespan is one hundred of his own days;
it is held that the first half consists of fifty such years.
In this very manner, that parārdha, measured at fifty years, constitutes one year of Brahmā Vairāja; indeed, that [year] is his day.
That which is one year of Vairāja is a single day of Mahāviṣṇu;
and that which is one year of Mahāviṣṇu is a single day of Pradhānapuruṣa. ||28||
That which is a year for him, the primordial person (prakṛti-puruṣa), is a single day;
by that measure of days, his lifespan consists of one hundred years. (29)
That creative process is the unfolding of the imperishable Brahman;
its closing, however, is called the great dissolution.
The creations [occurring] during his closing and opening of the eyes are without interruption;
they dissolve and are born again, for there is no beginning to that continuous flow.
Alternatively, the subtle measure of time consists of four kṣaṇas;
sixty groups of four kṣaṇas are proclaimed to be one vipala. 32.
Sixty *vipalas* are considered to be one *pala*;
sixty *palas* are likewise recognized as one *ghaṭikā*.
The time of one *ghaṇṭā* is proclaimed to be two and a half *ghaṭikās*;
twenty-four *ghaṇṭās* constitute a day and night for humans. (34)
Three hundred and sixty-five days and nights pass;
in this manner, time always proceeds, bringing all things under its own control. (35)
In this context, that which is a fortnight for humans is considered a single day for the Moon;
the night is likewise of such duration, and thus a month constitutes a full day and night. (36)
The lunar and solar mandalas are likewise [defined by] the night and the void;
for in the Pole Star (dhruva), the day is eternal, since the creation proceeds from it in distinct divisions.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Measurement of Lifespans and the Delimitation of Time," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Brahmā desired a mental creation that possessed form.
Through the relationship of the ground and the grinders, he fashioned the creation of qualities.
Brahmā, through the power of his own creative consciousness, produced streams of many forms; through the power of the flow of his own will, he produced streams of desires;
and through his own qualities with great effort, he produced masses of manifold exertions and numerous activities for the purpose of creation.
Having made his own minds possessed of immeasurable qualities, and having made their number multiplied by a parārdha and even beyond that incalculable, he likewise made their measure small,
subtle, long, and great.
Having brought about separation from that which was created, he then brings about a supreme union.

Having fashioned from his own body the qualities of seniority, the excellence of wealth and pleasure, proximity, distance, the weightiness of meaning, fluidity, its opposite, and likewise affection, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] created them.
He established them in many different ways. || 4 ||
Having restrained Māyā who resided within his own mind,
he [restrained] her darkness (tamas) as well as her second form, delusion (moha),
and even that great delusion known as Turyasuparvan.
And he created five [more]: Tāmisra and Andhatāmisra.

Those very functions of ignorance, which serve as the support for creation and carry beings through existence, become the individual souls; yet, through a difference in form, they possess distinct designations, such as "the state of the non-existent" (āvidya) and "the state of being" (asmi-bhavana), as well as passion and its opposite.
Then Brahmā again created hatred, fear, and attachment to all embodied beings, as well as the valid means of knowledge (*sat-pramāṇa*),
conceptualization (*vaikalpaka*), error (*viparyaya*), and fierce sleep.
Then [he experiences] dreaming, deep sleep, and even more terrible states of existence.
Then the Creator indeed created folly, jesting, laughter, deceit, and illusion, as well as doubt;
and likewise logic, disputation, wrangling, and cavil.
Deceit, theft, and likewise fraud constitute untruthfulness. || 8 ||
Greed, thirst, as well as the state of being an asura, atheism, extreme mercilessness, lack of peace, harshness,
extreme coarseness, and affliction—
Then [he experienced] destruction, concealment, and the terrible state of being half-choked.
Having repeatedly observed that the creation was uniform and beset by calamities, and having reflected upon it as being composed of darkness,
he perceived it to be most sinful and contrary to his own nature.
The Unborn One did not attain peace of mind. || 1.14.10 ||
From the back of the Unpeaceful (Aśānta) Vidhi, Adharma was born;
along with him, Anīti indeed arose as his constant companion.
Likewise, his wives were anxiety, malice, envy, possessiveness, falsehood, hope, destruction, thirst, wickedness, deceit, and longing. (12)
Violence, harsh speech, lack of faith, lack of peace, and likewise mercilessness; as well as lack of wisdom, discontent, lack of nourishment, lack of friendliness, and inaction. || 13 ||
Lack of intellect, lack of movement, lack of endurance, as well as coming and going; lack of pride, formlessness, lack of attachment, and likewise impatience. (1.4)
From her were born Non-Memory (asmṛti) and Deep Sleep (suṣupti), which bring about worldly transmigration;
their sons, however, were Pride (mada), Greed (lobha), Passion (rasa), Delusion (moha), and Envy (matsara).
Hypocrisy, lust, anger, pride, harshness, falsehood, affection, arrogance, turbidity, malice, impurity, and strife; || 16 ||
Impurity, lack of trust, theft, drinking, gambling, as well as pride, atheism, negligence, and passion; 17.
Slander, calamity, suffering, hatred, ignorance, fear, as well as sin, death, lack of sovereignty, crookedness, and lack of self-restraint. (18)
Lack of gentleness, lack of contentment, lack of fortitude, as well as harmfulness, lack of generosity, lack of application, lack of serenity, and likewise lack of humility. (19)
Lack of gain, lack of effort, lack of self-control, and obstacles are known as the many daughters of Adharma who are born to bring great suffering. (1.14.20)
Repugnance, censure, contempt, loathing, as well as deceit, deception, injustice, violence, and reproach; ||21||
For there are the sounds *chicchikārā*, *ararrāṭī*, and *hāhākārā*, as well as painful sensation, affliction, burning of the heart, blackness, and delusion. (22)
Hṛtphālā, Prabhā, Yoni, Maladā, Phaṭprakāṇḍikā, Kāmanā, Rajasrotā, Liṭkarī, and likewise Kṣuvatī. ||23||
False view and evil conduct, hypocrisy and the wearing of religious marks;
miserliness, dependence on others, impurity, and poverty. (24)
Ariṣṭā, Cāpaśakunā, Duritā, Pāpiṇī, as well as Kuṇapā, Raktapā, Śukrapāyinī, and Pātinī. ||25||
Parasvabhedikā, Ṣaṇḍhā, Māriṇī, and likewise Vihvalā;
Abhānā, Tamaskarī, Ghorā, and likewise Digvibhramā. ||26||
Āḍambarā, Viḍambā, Cākasmikī, and Mṛtaṃkarī—these are said to be the daughters of Adharma, who are always terrifying. (27)
But seeing that unrighteousness accompanied by progeny, the Creator was not pleased;
he then desired in his heart once more to create a world that bestows peace.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of Guṇa, Ignorance, and Unrighteousness within the Mental Creation of Brahmā," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Lakṣmī, I must again create a world that brings happiness to all beings.
Having reflected thus, the Lotus-born One established Dharma from his own heart.
He is of brilliant white complexion, supremely luminous, and endowed with the power of knowledge;
he bestows the fruits of happiness, heaven, and liberation, and is dear to those of a sattvic nature. || 2 ||
Likewise, Dharma has for his wives Śraddhā, Śānti, Dayā, Gati,
Medhā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Maitrī, Lajjā, Kriyā, and Unnati.
Form, intellect, forbearance, devotion, worship, and so forth—
these were born from the heart of the Creator together with Dharma.
Their offspring were gentle-faced, of pleasing form, and bestowers of happiness;
they possessed sovereignty, straightforwardness, knowledge, dispassion, fearlessness, and austerity. (55)
Steadfastness, fortitude, happiness, security, truthfulness, purity, gentleness, renunciation, yoga, self-control, sacrifice, contentment, restraint, and tranquility. || 6 ||
Faith in the scriptures, serenity, splendor, self-study, exertion, humility, meditation, the meaning [of the teachings], equanimity, gain, and realization.
Freedom from greed, lack of envy, absence of hypocrisy, lack of desire, freedom from anger, and likewise absence of attachment to flavors;

freedom from delusion, absence of pride, lack of arrogance, absence of affection, lack of conceit, freedom from strife, and truthfulness; absence of harshness, purity, trustworthiness, and non-stealing—these are [the qualities].
Freedom from pride, lack of ostentation, fearlessness, absence of hatred, and likewise freedom from attachment. || 9 ||
Absence of backbiting, freedom from evil, merit, and virtuous action;
as well as straightforwardness, lack of deceit, absence of vice, and generosity. (1.15.10)
Thus these sons of Dharma were indeed born, as well as the maidens:
Compassion, Eloquence, Non-violence, Action, Memory, and Skillfulness.
Forbearance, cessation, knowledge, delight, mindfulness, equanimity, luster, gentleness, as well as dexterity and independence; || 12 ||
Profundity, steadfastness, fearlessness, eloquence, freedom from pride, non-violence, absence of arrogance, and lack of hypocrisy; || 13 ||
Non-stealing, as well as service, obedience, providing refuge, devotion to Brahman, protection, and likewise non-possessiveness. || 14 ||
Form, friendship, contentment, purity, clarity, holiness, transparency, and stainlessness have been revealed. (18)
Divinity, sovereignty, servability, and favorableness; prosperity, whiteness, success, happiness, and likewise delusion. (16)
Līlā, Pramodatā, Ujjvalatā, Rasatā, Viṣayārthā, Dhanavatī, Ratnavatī, and Vibhūṣikā. (17)
She is autumnal, rich in crops, abundant in grain, and full of song;
she possesses passion, sweetness, loveliness, and charm. (18)
Mādhavī is delight in pleasure, she is the lovely woman, she is loveliness;
she is beauty, wonder, power, and likewise the bearing of fruit. || 19 ||
Poṣikā, Śaktidā, Vilāsā, and Pravilāsikā;
likewise the Īśvarīs, the Divyas, the Mūrtas, and the Amūrtikas.
Thousands of young maidens, daughters of Dharma, were born;
with them and by them, the Creator himself was gratified in his own mind. ||21||
Having seen this creation of dharmas, he considered himself accomplished;
however, because of that supreme exertion, the Unborn One became exhausted. ||22||
At that moment, a drop of sweat indeed fell from his forehead;
as soon as that drop fell, Rudra came into being there.
White in form and delicate, though a child, he was of wondrous appearance;
he had five heads, three eyes, ten arms, and was composed of the quality of darkness (tamas).
His body was covered with bristling hair, he was misshapen, and he was naked;
his eyes were red, he wore matted locks, and he had sharp fangs and a topknot.
He holds a drum, a trident, rudrākṣa beads, a pināka bow, a staff, and a noose;
he bears the crescent moon upon his forehead and possesses a reddish glow at the corners of his eyes. (26)
Having been born, he wept; the Unborn (Aja) said to him, "Do not weep. Therefore he is called Rudra. Brahmā said to him, "Create progeny."
Then Rudra, having accepted his father’s command,
created beings who were characterized by darkness (tamas), equal to himself, and extremely troublesome.
They were formidable and agitated in mind, possessed by hunger and rage;
they were of many forms and misshapen, as well as black and reddish-brown.
Those progeny of Rudra pervaded the fourteen worlds;
they were all of the same nature as Rudra, existing in every direction.
Some had emaciated bodies with thick necks and noses;
others had long snouts and stout hips.
Some are stout and others are dwarfish; some are stunted, half-stunted, or with hanging limbs and protruding heads; some have short necks, long feet, and backs shaped like boxes.
Other bears had large bellies, trunks like pillars, and faces like caves;
some were like black mountains, while others were equal to Mahākāla.
Wherever they were, there were Rudras by the millions and even by the hundreds of millions;
throughout the fourteen worlds, there were only Rudras, and no others.
Cruel and enraged, they rushed to fight; they approached Brahmā to devour him, and they also ran toward Rudra, their own progenitor, to consume him.
Then Brahmā said to that son of his: "Withdraw these quickly;
never before has such a creation existed that brings peace to the world. (36)
Incomparable even in form and destructive of [all] qualities, she devours these devourers who perform terrifying deeds against the Rudras. (37)
"O son, destroy it quickly; such a creation is not desired by Rudra. Having received those words of his father, [he acted] within a moment. (38)

From Svāṭṭahāsa was born the one named Kṛtānta, who is terrifying, possessed of great strength, holding a noose and a sword in his hands, and appearing non-dual as if his testicles were crushed by his fangs. || 39 ||
"Having been thus produced, with my hands repeatedly joined in reverence, from what have I been produced? Tell me, what is my duty; instruct me. (1.15.40)
Rudra spoke thus regarding this creation that follows a wrong path—
fierce, terrifying, and established throughout all the worlds.
"Destroy it quickly; may you be blessed, and through this act toward me, you shall find favor.
Having received that command from his father, Kṛtānta set about his task.
For he produced fire from his mouth and likewise generated flames and fire from all his eyes in order to bring about the destruction of the Rudras.
In whichever of the fourteen worlds beings existed,
there he indeed brought about supreme destruction everywhere among those who were fierce.
From his eyes, mouth, and body, lightning-like flames were drawn forth;
these arose as long, flowing streams throughout every part of the universe and upon every spot of ground.
Having gone and gone, having searched and searched for those Rudras in their entirety, they seized them all without exception; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
They run away, they flee, and they leap up here and there;
they cry out piteously and say, "Save us! ||47||
Nevertheless, wherever they go, flames following at their very forefront approach for the sake of their destruction; there is not even the slightest place of refuge.
Finding no protection anywhere, those Rudras indeed turned back and fell; they met their destruction in the vast body of the flaming fire. 49.
When not even one remained among the fourteen hells, then Kṛtānta (Death) desisted; he became peaceful and unborn.
Then Rudra, together with his own son Kṛtānta, always requested his own father for his own abode as a place of residence. (51)
And Brahmā granted him that divine abode of Īśvara, established in truth;
it is known by the name Raudra, and indeed as the world of Mahas.
Wherever the intentions of the Brahmins are always true,
and wherever those established in truth desire something, it bears fruit accordingly.
The greatness of Satyaloka is indeed true;
moreover, the word "satya" is derived from Brahmā and is considered to signify pure existence (sattāmātra).
Beyond that is the Brahma-world, which is real and luminous by the very nature of Brahmā;
indeed, by the power of Brahmā, it is characterized by non-obstruction. ||55||
Therefore, this is indeed the World of Truth for those who have reached the state of no-return;
even there, it is taught that for those devoid of righteousness, the Lord of Death (Kṛtānta) is the dispenser of punishment.
It is known as Kṛtapura by name, and its court of justice is remembered [as such];
even for Brahmā, the assembly hall named Sudharmā is considered transcendent.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation and Other Matters of Dharma and Rudra," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 15 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate that which was performed by Brahmā himself for the sake of the world’s habitation and indeed for his own satisfaction. || 1 ||
Thereupon, Brahmā set his mind upon creating the Sāttvika creation;
he formed the resolve that all beings should become characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
From Rudra were born those who are indeed Rudras—sattvic, auspicious, pure, most pure, all wise, and of solid form. (3)
All those possess subtle bodies and always abide in the stable world; they are luminous, established in pure intellect, perfected beings who follow the path of yoga.
All of them, together with Brahmā, attained equal sovereignty;
they were all peaceful, their bodies composed of bliss, and consisting of pure contemplation.
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they have gone to immortality;
indeed, all are considered to be the nature of happiness through the purity of awakening. || 6 ||
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they indeed enjoy the bliss of immortality;
freed from the suffering of worldly existence, they are no longer overcome by those pairs of opposites.
Without [the status of] overlordship, those of great majesty were equal to Brahmā in their power,
victory, sovereignty, stability, dispassion, and insight.
All those belonging to the world of Brahmā, having attained the auspicious state of Brahmā,
were free from passion, had conquered anger, were devoid of delusion, and were speakers of truth.
Those who have fixed their minds upon the Self, who are compassionate, have conquered their senses,
are free from attachment, and are pure, are said to attain union with Brahman.
Those heroes who, through austerities free from desire, have burnt away their sins,
are said to possess undecaying worlds of immeasurable bliss.
This is the divine state of Brahman, supreme and radiant in the ether;
having gone there, the immortals, together with Brahmā, do not grieve.
They do not fall back from that state where they worship Brahmā;
for those who desire no further death, that is called the world of Brahmā.
Beyond the world of Brahmā and yet within the cosmic egg of the Creator,
in the center, is a divine, beautiful city, a realm consisting of the mind of Rudra.
The abode of that embodied Lord of immeasurable power is the city named Śiva; therein lies the refuge for those who dwell in Brahman.
It is a full hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
it is vast within and situated in the form of a circular expanse.
It was surrounded by a great rampart of gold, possessing the brilliance of the sun, which utterly overwhelmed the intense splendor of the midday sun and other luminaries.
Furthermore, it was adorned with golden elements decorated with strings of pearls;
it had four auspicious gates, was accessible, divine, and beautifully crafted.
And that city is situated in the sky, in the great void, in the world of truth;
there death does not prevail, nor does heat, nor old age, nor fatigue.
Indeed, that form cannot be attained anywhere by other cities;
such is that city of the one whose emblem is the bull, which is composed of light.
By his power, the mental ground was laid out as being of golden nature;
filled with jewel-sand, it exists pervaded by radiance. (21)
They have the brilliance of the autumnal moon and resemble the rising sun;
they are half-white and half-red, and likewise golden.
They were the size of chariot wheels, with stalks possessing the luster of emerald, and were endowed with exquisite form and incomparable fragrance. (23)
There, in the groves and pleasure gardens, were divine lotuses resembling the wings of bees and others made of refined gold.
Indeed, there are lotuses that are half-black and half-red, with delicate interiors,
and they are as large as parasols.
And divine rivers flow with streams of the nectar of merit,
possessing whirlpools and forms of foam, interspersed with the petals of lotuses and water-lilies.
The best of rivers carry water that resembles the surface of a jewel;
likewise, those who are undistracted, well-disciplined, and have conquered their senses [carry] that very meditation.
The high-souled ones behold here that city of the one whose self is the bull and the cow;
in the midst of that best of cities stands the divine [palace], endowed with auspicious splendor.
The great palace had a thousand pillars and was made of refined gold;
it was adorned on all sides with incomparable jewels,
with crystals resembling the moon and lapis lazuli possessing the splendor of the moon.
It shone with [ornaments] having the luster of the rising sun, made of gold and resembling fire,
as well as those made of silver and auspicious ones made of sapphire.
It was constructed with exceedingly vast materials made of firm adamant,
and it was consecrated by waters of various forms that were shimmering.
The city was adorned with banners possessing the brilliance of the moon,
and it was constantly filled with the sounds of golden bells and other instruments, as if perpetually engaged in festival.
The Rudradāsas, Gāndharvas, Kinnaras, and Sutamāgadhas praised the Lord Mahārudra together with his retinue.
This royal palace of Rudra shines with a hundred floors,
wherein stands a statue of Vāsantī in the residence of the Three-eyed Lord.
Rudrāṇī, the power of Śambhu, the goddess endowed with beauty and virtue, her body fragrant, indeed serves the god Rudra. (35)
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kīrti, Śobhā, and Sarasvatī—these goddesses were indeed accompanied by her, endowed with beauty and fragrance. (36)
Eternal and innumerable, they excel one another in their qualities;
indeed, these goddesses are the ornaments of all jewels, as well as of beauty and grace.
A hundred crores of highly fortunate ones, dividing themselves by their own selves,
joyfully attend upon the Blessed Mahārudra without weariness.
Behind them were another thousand female attendants,
all beautiful in form, endowed with splendor, and possessing lotus-like eyes.
Together with those Rudras— youthful and most excellent like fires— they rejoice, accompanied by states of being that are exceedingly captivating and endowed with playful charm.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Sāttvika Rudra and Rudrāṇī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 16 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall speak for those intent on many forms of worship:
of Rudra’s countless female servants and his hosts in the form of weapon-bearers.
They were delightful, gentle, and handsome, with limbs possessed of very firm joints; their thighs, hips, and shanks were symmetrical, and their waists were even, slender, and beautiful.
Some were hunchbacked, some were dwarfish, yet possessed of beautiful limbs and lovely faces; others were marked with spots, deformed, terrifying, or flat-faced. || 3 ||
Some had protuberant bellies and short arms, some were three-eyed and horse-faced;
some had the faces of lions and others had the faces of elephants with short feet. || 4 ||
Others had faces like those of elephants and bellies like those of lions; likewise, there were those with the faces of tigers, red eyes, large breasts, auspicious, and beautiful-eyed.
With short, curly hair, beautiful and with lovely cheeks,
all those excellent women were capable of assuming any form at will and possessed firm waists.
The Lord, the ten-armed Maheśvara, always delights with those women who speak sweet and excellent words, full of love, and endowed with graceful gestures and amorous expressions.
And with Nandin, together with the hosts of great-souled ones who possess universal forms,
as well as with the hosts of Rudras who are equal in magnanimity and prowess.
He was being saluted by those resembling the sons of Agni, whose faces were formidable with sacrificial posts for tusks,
and was being honored by those situated in celestial chariots who were intent upon that task.
He smelled the garland of flowers from all seasons resting upon his chest;
he was dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with broad, copper-hued, and long eyes.
His lips were slightly protruding and formidable, he was attended by hosts of sharp fangs,
possessed six upward-gazing eyes, was difficult to behold, yet beautiful, and clad in divine garments.
Unwearied in battles and the destroyer of all enemies,
he stood on his left side, having placed his arm upon [the king’s] arm.
In the range of his left forehand shines a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa),
possessing a roar as terrifying as a great Bhairava, with a strength and splendor beyond compare.
And a bow of ten colors shines exceedingly with its variegated beauty;
likewise, the trident, radiant as lightning, is unfailing and the destroyer of enemies. (14)
The axe blazed with its own form, endowed with ten thousand splendors;
and the sword was the best among those possessing vigor, as was the moon with its cool rays. || 15 ||
By its brilliance, form, and luster, resembling that of the high-souled Lord of Gods,
a great vessel made of gold stood before the God; beautiful, glorious, and auspicious, it was a water-pot for the subduing of all enemies.
Having placed her sword in its scabbard, she was dressed in white garments and graced by a large pearl resting upon her breast.
Four-armed, highly fortunate, victorious, and honored by the world. || 17 ||
The goddess’s first female doorkeeper, peerless like the supreme Śrī,
stood there resplendent, having placed her hands in añjali before the god.
Following behind her were other women accompanied by throngs of Apsarases;
they indeed waited upon Śaṅkara with ever-new and lovely offerings.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and accompanied by musical instruments,
the hosts born of the Gandharvas sing praises to the Lord of Gods.
Tall and broad-chested, with a luster like an autumnal cloud, the lowing bull shines in his house. (21)
His son Skanda, possessed of immeasurable heroism, accompanied by his retinue, wears crimson garments; he is glorious, with eyes like the petals of a choice lotus.
His disciples—Śākha, Viśākha, and the learned Naigameya—were free from all calamities and were devoted to the protection of the people. (23)
Together with them, that one of great heroism, whose vehicle is the peacock, shines resplendent;
indeed, he who faces all directions plays with the toys of children.
And tigers, golden-hued and swift, followed there;
they all moved at their own will, created by the God himself. (25)
They are indeed like death unto death, the destroyers of Yama’s pride;
they are lions, the hosts of Rudra, who abide under the control of Rudra’s will. (26)
Resembling Mount Mandara, they possessed incomparable splendor through their strength;
they were white as necklaces, jasmine, and the moon, and they roared like clouds charged with lightning.
They indeed wear crest-jewels and garments resembling clouds;
they are marked with the Śrīvatsa and the vajra, and hold finger-rings and tridents in their hands. ||28||
Such gods, endowed with divine splendor and possessed of such beautiful forms, took their place upon the pillars of his preeminent palace, which was like that of lions. (29)
Indeed, all those who were made angry by the wrath of that high-souled Lord out of his own anger became lions in form. (1.17.30)
Now, those by whom devotion to Rudramaheśa has been cultivated are modest, energetic, self-controlled, endowed with valor, and free from greed. ||3 1||
Those who have taken refuge in Maheśvara with purified action, mind, and speech, and with a pure inner self, having become single-minded in devotion; 32.
By them was attained the eternal and imperishable state of the same world as Rudra;
indeed, they were brought to the unsurpassed similarity of form with Bhava.
All of them had Vaiśvānara as their chief; they were universal in form, wore matted hair, had blue throats and white necks, possessed sharp fangs, and were three-eyed. ||34||
With uṣṇīṣas shaped like half-moons and wearing crowns of matted hair, all these heroes have ten arms and are fragrant with the scent of the interior of lotuses. (35)
All of them resembled the rising sun and were clad in yellow garments;
all held the Pināka bow in their hands and had white bulls as their vehicles. ||36||

Endowed with splendor, wearing earrings, and adorned with pearl necklaces, they were by divine power even more radiant than fire; they were omniscient and all-seeing, having divided themselves manifoldly and being free from old age and death. (37)
Having attained enjoyments that are very difficult to obtain, they sport in various forms;
these perfected beings (siddhas), moving according to their own will, were awakened by other perfected beings, and from them many millions of the eleven Rudras were created. || 38-39 ||
Together with these, the great-souled Maheśvara, the God of gods,
the Blessed Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees and the true master of his devotees, rejoices.
When the terrible dissolution of all beings has occurred, when all living creatures have perished, and when the dissolution has arrived at the end of the destruction of the great elements; ||41||
There were many tens of millions of Rudras, as well as numerous groups of female attendants,
many hosts of Gaṇas, tigers, and so forth, and various Siddhas and others.
Having gone to the world of Rudra, all those great-souled ones enter into dissolution in Maheshvara; all enter into dissolution in Rudra, and Rudra dissolves into Brahman. 43.
Having approached with supreme devotion and a mind endowed with knowledge,
one attains the eternal, imperishable state that is the same world as Rudra.
This creation of Rudra, the son of Aja, is indeed of the nature of Rudra;
it takes the form of hosts of male and female servants, tigers, and various vehicles.
It is adorned with weapons, perfected beings, gandharvas, apsarases, bards, maidservants, houses, gardens, great palaces, rivers, lotuses, and other such jewels.
All forms consist of the nature of being (*sattva*), and having the form of being, they bestow great happiness;
for that which is the fierce state (*raudrabhāva*) of Rudra does not exist here at all. (47)
Therefore, this creation of Raudrī, which is characterized by sattva and resides in Satyaloka, has indeed been made eternally stable by Brahmā.
Having seen this creation that bestows happiness, Brahmā indeed attained satisfaction;
however, those Sāttvika deities—the Rudras along with their male and female servants—[remained as they were]. (49)
Having attained sattvic happiness and acquired all forms of sovereignty,
they remained indeed absorbed in those sovereignties and pleasures, their power of discernment being weakened.
Therefore, they would be deceived by that knowledge which pertains to ultimate reality;
and if that were so, there might at some point be an obstruction to the path of liberation. (51)
Reflecting thus, "May there not be the attainment of misfortune through transgression," Brahmā himself created a creation that was auspicious and filled with knowledge. ||52||

Thereafter, he set his mind upon performing that mental [meditation] which bestows liberation, is connected to Brahman, and has the nature of Brahman; he then proceeded to meditate for the sake of perfection.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Sāttvika Rudras, Servants, Maidens, and Their Multitudes," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 17 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Brahmā, having resorted to yoga and attained meditative absorption (samādhi),
[merged] his very self into Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord in His own supreme abode.
Having unified it with effort through identity and having requested it, may creation be such that it bestows peace, and may men also become peaceful. (2)
Likewise, others, overflowing with the manifestation of Brahman, bestow liberation upon others;
they are the awakeners of all, untainted, and preeminent in the quality of sattva.
Always possessing the form of Brahman, fully nurtured by the contemplation of Brahman,
bathed in the bliss of Brahman, they are constant meditators upon the embodiment of Brahman.
The gurus are the creators of the worlds, the foundation for the perfection of dharma,
equal to the divine lords, and extend from Brahmā down to the crawling insects.
"O Lord, may I have sons by whom the worlds shall always be made happy"—
having recognized this supplication, the Supreme Brahmā then [responded].
The four liberated ones were commanded for the sake of the Supreme Lord's son;
these four liberated ones, who understand his will, [emerged] from the abode of the imperishable Brahman.
Having transcended the worlds and reached the world of truth (satyaloka),
they saw that even Brahmā had emerged from his yoga, having attained liberation equal to the four [deities].
"May these mental sons of mine become the causes of my liberation. Having thus resolved, he [gave] those five-year-old children, who were beautiful and liberated.
As soon as they were born, they were of the nature of Brahman, filled with the bliss of Brahman, supreme,
adorned with circles of light, clad in pure white garments, and possessing the brilliant luster of lotuses on dry land.
Having obtained four sons who were divine, always compassionate, and the sustainers of the existence of the entire universe, he indeed attained great satisfaction.
By name, your mind-born sons, who are the causes of the world's welfare,
are Sanaka, Sananda, Sanatana, and Sanātana.
They are virtuous, possessing the nature of the virtuous, meritorious, and ever composed of merit;
by their very sight they remove faults and bring about the dissolution of suffering and grief. (13)
They are compassionate, patient by nature, and desirous of the welfare of all creation; they are enduring, free from envy, tranquil, and have no rising enemies.
Free from envy, devoid of enmity, without pride, and without malice;
they are always worthy of honor, bestowers of honor, and their speech is always pleasant and truthful to all.
Free from pride, devoid of defects such as anger and greed, and stainless;
empty of the notions of "I" and "mine," they have conquered the impulses of desire.
Free from hypocrisy, pure, self-controlled, upright, moderate in speech, beyond the pairs of opposites, vigilant, steadfast, and having conquered their senses; || 17 ||
They are full of awakening, established in the Self, free from possessiveness, benefactors of all, and repositories of the qualities of faith, conviction, and devotion. || 18 ||
They were noble in their dedication to austerity, free from attachment to possessions,
devoid of malice and theft, and they did not disclose the secrets of others.
Having conquered the states of the body, they are contented, firm in intellect,
equal toward pleasure and pain, free from craving, and endowed with satisfaction.
Free from censuring others and the like, they rely on their own conduct;
endowed with divine fortune, they dwell within the lineage of Dharma. ||21||
They are great treasuries of the supreme flood of knowledge of Hari and are equal to Brahmā;
for them, not even a single moment passes fruitlessly without devotion to Hari. (22)
Resorting to hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and so forth, and endowed with such characteristics, they were Sanaka and the others. ||23||
With purified action, mind, and speech, and with a pure inner self,
they indeed constantly practice devotion to Hari with undistracted minds.
Having approached with supreme devotion, they shone with a splendor joined with knowledge;
their divine forms were radiant and pleasing to behold due to their gentle nature. (25)

Those who are deeply immersed in the bliss of the Self, whose nature is Brahman, and who bestow liberation, count even the attainments of supernatural powers and treasures as mere blades of grass. //26//
To the multitudes of living beings scorched by the forest fire of saṃsāra, the gurus—who rain down the nectar of their vision—are the bestowers of liberation. ||27||
They are the ancestors of the lineages of the virtuous, the saviors of those who have slain Brahmins, the paths for those who have gone astray, and the examples for those practicing celibacy. 28.

They are the foundations of all branches of knowledge, as well as the seeds of all that is auspicious; they are the treasuries of all scriptures and the embodiments of those whose nature is sattva. (29)

They are the foundation of all accomplishments, the refuge for those seeking shelter, the givers of liberation to those desiring release, and the bestowers of fruits upon all who perform actions. 1.18.30.
They are the inspirers of true blessings and the ornament of those possessing the luster of Brahman;
they are austerity itself among the ascetic, and likewise self-restraint among the disciplined.
Always divine, five years of age, with tender inner natures, they are devoid of the emergence of youth and free from old age and death.
The ignorant are considered young by virtue of their bodies, while the wise are considered old by virtue of their knowledge.
Having bowed to their own unborn father, they said, "O Auspicious One, what shall we do? (33)
Then indeed, they were consecrated by Brahmā with the waters of the Veda; they were invested with the sacred thread and established as lifelong celibates.
They were established in the world of Brahmā, in the true, celestial sphere of the beautiful mandala,
within a meritorious, delightful, wish-fulfilling, and supreme palace born of their own resolve.
In that layer where the city of Mahārudra is well-situated in the sky,
a perfectly designed abode was prepared for them on that level ground.
Divine, endowed with all supernatural powers, providing assistance through the attainment of one's own desires,
and possessing trees of rice with clusters of flowers and fruits arising from mere thought.
It consists of objects such as things to be enjoyed, instruments of enjoyment, food, drink, and so forth, which are obtained merely through the exertion arising from the reality of merit. ||38||
The merit is a radiant abode, possessing the fragrance presiding over the groves,
and endowed with gardens, orchards, fields, medicinal herbs, and elixirs.
There, the golden liquid is purifying and brings satisfaction;
the silver water, produced by the rivers of imagination, bestows happiness.
The Brahma-pools, the Cold-pools, and the Fire-pools are naturally arisen;
they are forever free from depletion, destruction, and the like, and they bestow the wealth of the submarine fire.
There were also large leaf-huts made from the great leaves of the Brahma-tree,
suitable for the dwellings of yogis and constructed for the sake of ascetics.
There, those born of pure resolve, equal to Sanaka and others, auspicious, rich in the wealth of knowledge and devotion, indeed dwell in youthful forms. (43)
Such was that celestial palace, constructed as a dwelling consisting of gardens;
it moved through the air at will and was gathered together by truth.
It was made of gold, possessed a hundred stories, and was vast, measuring a hundred thousand yojanas;
its various floors were distinguished by assembly halls, pavilions, pleasure gardens, fire-sanctuaries, and other such structures.
Having constructed such a dwelling worthy of habitation, Brahmā offered it to the four Kumāras out of a desire for them to reside there.
Then, indeed, Brahmā reflected upon how knowledge might be bestowed;
he meditated upon Hari, the Supreme Brahman, that Lord, for the sake of the knowledge of reality.
Then, impelled there by Śrī Hari, the personified Vedas arrived from the abode of Brahmā and stood before him. ||48||
Embodied in person, divine themselves, and filled with knowledge and realization, they have attained dissolution in the Grandfather (Brahmā); they are the forms of wisdom and the illuminators. 49.
In this [place], all forms of knowledge created by the Creator of all things indeed bestow complete liberation here and grant happiness in the hereafter. (1.18.50)
The unborn [Brahmā] praised those various Vedas, wherein the four aims of human life— known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— are always described.
He set his mind upon giving them [the Vedas] and instructed them according to the prescribed rules.
Those four sons of Brahmā, having studied the Vedas in their entirety, [attained perfection]. 52.
They constantly protect the Vedic knowledge and teach it;
furthermore, they provide millions of lifelong celibates who are fit for the study of those various branches.
And he made five eternal mental disciples who were equal to Sanaka and others in wisdom, form, splendor, strength, and other qualities. (54)
[He saw] the divine, supreme, and merit-filled forms of those devoted to the vow of celibacy, who possessed the sovereign power and prosperity enjoyed by the assembly of Sanaka and others.
There, in that abode of truth which is resorted to by Sanaka, he saw all those eternal, virtuous sons who were oceans of Vedic knowledge.
He caused all the virtuous qualities of the good, which are characterized by sattva,
immeasurable, mental, and eternal in form, to dwell within him.
He endowed them with blessings consisting of the qualities and forms of the state of equilibrium,
within this cosmic egg, from the beginning of creation until its dissolution.
"The treasures of Vedic knowledge remain with those who protect the Vedas.
Having performed this supreme service, Brahmā attained satisfaction once again. (59)
Having meditated for a moment upon Brahman as the supreme, he remained established, taking refuge in the Self;
beholding the creation that bestows happiness, he attained the fulfillment of his birth.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mental Creation of Sanaka and Others, Their Abodes Endowed with Virtues, and the Manifestation of the Vedas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 18 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, for I shall proclaim the excellence of the virtuous;
the virtuous bestow eyes, and the virtuous are my very heart. (1)
The path to liberation has been constantly raised up for me by such holy men and set in motion;
by means of it, living beings are liberated. || 2 ||
Knowledge of the Vedas, the conduct of people, and whatever rites are performed for the gods and ancestors proceed from these;
by means of them, living beings rejoice. || 3 ||
Through those [means], the power of devotion, detachment, and various forms of auspiciousness arise;
then, being truly detached, they indeed attain liberation.
The lineages of the virtuous, the lineages of the seers, and the channels of the celibate students proceed perpetually through them; by that means, liberation shall become certain. (5)
Equal to Sanaka and others, divine, celibate from childhood, these virtuous ones have realized Brahman by themselves; they alone are the Supreme Lords.
By the benedictions of the virtuous, I indeed became Nārāyaṇa;
by the benedictions of the virtuous, you became Lakṣmī, the embodiment of prosperity.
If the virtuous were to entreat me, "Bring Lakṣmī to us," then I would indeed surrender you, my beloved Lakṣmī, even to those virtuous ones.
What gift greater than this could there be for me to give for the sake of the virtuous, that I should respectfully bestow upon them you, who are most dear to me? (9)
Male and female servants, Vaikuṇṭha, the abundance of objects of enjoyment and means of attainment, Lakṣmī, and I myself—all these are for the enjoyment of the virtuous; of this there is no doubt.
When the merit accumulated over many lifetimes becomes manifest in the present, then virtuous people indeed come to one's own home by virtue of good fortune.
If the virtuous elders have been satisfied by many births,
then those noble ones will joyfully come to the homes of householders.
Whatever my virtuous ones desire from me— be it my home, wife, wealth, or other possessions— I shall undoubtedly offer all of that to them out of love.
Neither the world of Brahmā, nor Goloka, nor even Vaikuṇṭha has been fashioned;
neither Lakṣmī, nor Ramā, nor Rādhā exists for me—indeed, nothing is superior to the virtuous.
O Lakṣmī, the virtuous should always be served by body and mind every day;
for the virtuous are my very limbs, and the virtuous are indeed my own forms.
Indeed, from their nails to the tips of their hair, they become divine in body;
even the water from their feet purifies the surface of the earth.
The dust of their feet purifies when borne upon the head;
the soles of their feet purify when placed upon the chest. (17)
The touch of their feet indeed purifies the three worlds; for massaging their feet brings about the fulfillment of one's past karma (*prārabdha*). (18)
When one places the feet of the virtuous upon one's own head, the entire body becomes purified and becomes a vessel for liberation. || 19 ||
By licking their feet, one's own self is purified from sin;
by massaging their calves, a servant becomes a sovereign. (1.19.20)
By massaging their thighs, one shall become a sovereign king;
by massaging their hips, one will certainly become the lord of the three worlds.
By massaging their backs, one would attain the station of Parameṣṭhin;
by massaging their hands, one would attain the station of Vairāja.
By massaging their limbs, one shall attain the supreme kingdom of Viṣṇu;
by fulfilling the intentions of the virtuous, one's own everything becomes fulfilled. (23)
The body of the Blessed One resides within the bodies of the virtuous; the contemplation of the Blessed One resides within the contemplations of the virtuous;
the effort of the Blessed One resides within the efforts of the virtuous; therefore, the truly virtuous are indeed worthy of being propitiated. (24)
In the station of the virtuous is the power of Śrī Hari’s feet; in the hands of the virtuous is the power of Śrī Hari’s hands.
In the hearts of the virtuous resides the power of Śrī Hari’s dwelling; in the recreation of the virtuous lies the power accessible to Hari. || 25 ||
The mind of the virtuous is considered to be Śrī Hari’s own mind;
the knowledge of the virtuous is held to be identical with His knowledge;
and the desire of the virtuous is regarded as being the very same as Śrī Hari’s own desire.
In this matter, the wise have determined that it was Śrī Hari who acted. || 26 ||
But for the virtuous, the channels are the channels of the Supreme Lord; the blood of the virtuous is the blood of the illustrious Supreme Lord;
the bodily constituent of the virtuous is the constituent of the illustrious Supreme Lord; the breath of the virtuous is the vital air of the illustrious Supreme Lord. || 27 ||
The eye of the virtuous is the eye of the illustrious Supreme Lord; the ear of the virtuous is the ear of the illustrious Supreme Lord;
the mouth of the virtuous is the mouth of the illustrious Supreme Lord; the tongue of the virtuous is the tongue of the illustrious Supreme Lord. (28)
The food of the virtuous is the food of the glorious Supreme Lord; that which is to be accepted by the virtuous is obtainable from the glorious Supreme Lord;
the enjoyment of the virtuous is the enjoyment of the glorious Supreme Lord—through association with the virtuous, even a mundane object becomes divine. (29)
The saints are always equal to the Blessed Lord; they grant liberation to those who have come for refuge.
They indeed instantly wipe away sins and bestow infinite merits.
For the virtuous, the touch of their skin should be like that of divine syllables, bestowing supreme bliss;
it should be understood that for the virtuous, the attainment of the union of all the senses while in the state of Puṣya leads to liberation. 31.
Indeed, he by whom a son— a good son who purifies his lineage— was obtained from the presence of the virtuous,
was born indeed from the very body of Hari.
He is indeed equal to the virtuous and equal to Hari. || 32 ||
He by whom the grace of the lotus-face of the virtuous has been obtained here is a vessel for liberation;
he by whom the entire body of the virtuous has been touched possesses all happiness. (33)
People, placing the gift of food for the virtuous at the forefront,
receive the favor of the virtuous as they partake of most excellent and delicious delicacies that gratify the sense of taste.
To those who accepted [them], they granted excellent gifts to their disciples. || 34 ||
Every taste, such as sweet and the rest, when accepted as real, would fall into the state of being devoid of qualities;
likewise, form, when seen as white, beautiful, or gentle in appearance, would indeed fall into the state of being without qualities. (35)
Indeed, that sound which is heard by the virtuous attains divinity through association with the good;
likewise, that touch which is performed by holy men [attains the same].
For he indeed becomes the giver of liberation through association with the virtuous. || 36 ||
But that fragrance which is held by the virtuous during their perception becomes indeed devoid of qualities and is fit for divine worship;
yet it is merely the intention of the virtuous that must be awakened, for that bestows liberation, grants merit, and brings about prosperity. (37)
Whatever seat is occupied by the virtuous, whatever vehicle, or likewise the bodies of beasts and birds,
and whatever [place] the holy ones occupy to attain a measure of happiness— that too leads to liberation.
(38) If the holy ones experience happiness within the bodies of both the insentient and the sentient, [then all such states lead to liberation].
Know that through its union with this [consciousness], each respective insentient thing becomes divine and attains perfect liberation.

That house in which the touch of the soles of the feet of the virtuous is obtained is a desirable and divine house; that object upon which the touch of the hands of the virtuous falls is indeed a divine object. (1.19.4)
Speech that is employed in the praise of the virtuous attains divinity and does not lead to bondage;
through association with the virtuous, the mouth and the mind always become pure and divine in this world. (4.1)

Whatever constitutes the physical body—whether it be the organs of action, the organs of perception, each individual limb, or the entire body as a whole—whatever may be obtained through the service of the virtuous, that indeed becomes divine and brings about liberation. 42.
The objects of enjoyment for the body include well-crafted ornaments made of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as garments made of silk or cotton, in all their various types. (43)
There were fragrant oils for massage, sandalwood pastes for anointing and worship,
and beautiful, sweet-smelling flowers.
Those offered to the virtuous shall obtain a threefold [reward]. ||44||
Oh, what can I say of this distinction?
For the virtuous purify all—
whether they be sinful, extremely wicked, impure, or deceitful.
And the lowest living beings, in whom tamas predominates. ||45||
The Prajāpatis, Manus, gods, ṛṣis, and Pitṛs residing separately;
the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Asuras. ||46||
[He saw] Kimpuruṣas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, and Uragas, as well as Mātṛs, Piśācas, Rakṣases, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Vināyakas. ||47||
Vetālas, those possessed by madness, and Kūṣmāṇḍas; likewise, the seizing spirits of the elderly and children;
as well as domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, trees, mountains, and reptiles. ||48||
All beings, whether stationary or moving, dwelling on earth, in water, or in the sky—those of pure nature, those of mixed nature, as well as those of passionate and dark nature. ||49||

The virtuous purify all living beings, whether auspicious or inauspicious, who are overwhelmed by merit and demerit; through their mere sight, they lead them to liberation from their mental constructs.
Through association they make them divine; through service they make them prosperous;
through their word they make them lords; and through contact they make them peaceful.

Their superiority should be understood according to their sequence; that sequence, however, is to be understood by means of the measure of knowledge and also by devotion. Listen, O Lotus-born One, as I explain it. (52)

Compared to these living beings such as ourselves, grass and the like are superior; compared to them, food-grains, medicinal herbs, and so forth are superior; and compared to those, climbing plants (vīrudhas) are even more excellent. ||5.3||
Beyond those are the excellent celestial trees such as the mango;
beyond those, among the stationary beings, the mobile ones are superior—namely, those living creatures that are indeed subtle.
Ants are superior to them; locusts and the like are superior to those; bees and the like are superior to them; and sparrows and the like are considered superior to those. (55)
From them arose the hares and other animals, and from those, goats and others; superior to these were cows and other livestock.
From them came human beings, among whom the four castes are the most excellent.

Among them, the Brahmins are considered the best; among those, the ones established in Dharma are the best; among them, the possessors of knowledge are the best; and among those possessors of knowledge, tens of millions of gods are the best. (57)
The ancestors are superior to the gods, and the sages are supreme among them;
yet even more excellent than the sages is he who possesses exclusive devotion.
Among those devotees who are single-mindedly devoted, he is the best— a repository of the qualities of the virtuous—
who has offered his entire being and is dedicated to the state of the Blessed One.
The son born from the lap of Śrī Hari is a saintly person, a vessel of excellent qualities;
the disciple born from a portion of Śrī Hari is indeed a virtuous man and an heir to his legacy.
Liberation is his inheritance; he who possesses that share is a saint, for he is indeed Hari himself.
He is considered the lineage of Hari, the clan of Hari, and the very form of Hari. (61)
There is nothing small or inferior; Hari is directly present there, and thus it does not lack anything.
There is no one superior to it, for Hari dwells therein eternally. (62)
Having understood this gradation, those who take refuge in Hari are to be highly honored;
for those who have directly taken refuge in Hari are indeed the very essence of Hari’s heart.
But those who are gentle and saintly abide with you through a state of non-differentiation;
they are ascetics, holy men, divine beings, who are manifest forms of Śrī Hari himself. (64)
Having become like people of the world, they always please the people regarding their seats, beds, food, meals, vessels, and ointments. (65)
In lovemaking, in going, in laughing, in playing, in living together, in embracing, in seeing, in the best [of things], in festivals, and in riding vehicles— 66.
O Lakṣmī, for those who please people through entertaining activities, there is always eternal happiness once they have been propitiated. (67)

They are characterized by a disposition to assist others; they take the welfare of others as their own body; they accomplish the goals of others, bestow liberation, and are the saviors of living beings. ||68||
Those devotees of Hari are virtuous, bringing welfare to all living beings;
they are always patient, worthy of worship, and honorable, because they hold their own beloved [the Lord] as supreme. (69)
Through the refuge of the virtuous, the sinful become endowed with merit;
by serving the good, women and men attain the supreme goal.
By always renouncing one's body, wealth, and mind in the presence of the virtuous, or even by surrendering all that one possesses, liberation occurs without a doubt. (71)
Those who are indeed born under the influence of the virtuous, having become virtuous themselves and come under their sway,
lead [others] to the supreme liberation that is to be attained through their own power.
That my eyes are fixed upon seeing you; that my mind is intent on your thought; that my ears are well-disposed toward hearing the accounts of your divine deeds;
and that my nose is esteemed for grasping the fragrance arising from union with your form.
My tongue is engaged in chanting my own glory, and my palate is occupied with tasting [the nectar of] the Rāsa dance. ||73||
My lips indeed bestow supreme bliss during the act of kissing my form; their skin always touches my preeminent and stainless bimba-fruit [lips],
and for them, nothing other than embracing me is considered superior.
But for those very ones who are virtuous, I always provide protection, because they are mine. (74)
I always perform service for them and I also always maintain devotion toward them;
therefore, O devoted wife, I am always prosperous along with you. (75)
Just as I am, so indeed you too must always perform service to them;
for by that very act, I shall be served—even more so than through the threefold practice of devotion to one's husband.
Just as I have been served by you through your mind, body, and speech, so should virtuous people always be served by you; may it ever bring you well-being.
O Kamalā, because of their words of blessing, my separation from you shall never occur; therefore, they must always be served by you.
I bow down repeatedly to those who are always worthy of worship, always worthy of honor, always my attendants, and who have made renunciations for my sake. (79)
The desire of the virtuous is not for the sake of pleasure, nor is their greed for the sake of self-interest;
their anger does not result in agitation, nor does even their delusion lead to bondage. (1.19.80)
Intoxication does not lead to pride at all, nor does hope produce craving;
rivalry leads to the acquisition of good qualities, and compassion removes suffering. (8.1)
Thus, indeed, for the sake of assisting others in every way, the virtuous possess those natures which always bring about happiness and liberation. ||82||
Therefore, O virtuous ones, you who are divine and likewise intent on assisting others, I declare: "I, the Blessed One, dwell within the act of helping others. (83)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Holy Persons such as Sanaka and Others," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 19 ||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, bestower of fearlessness upon the worlds!
How are virtuous men who observe celibacy to be served daily by groups of people? (1)
Are even truthful women worthy of service, or not?
By whomsoever [served], the certain attainment of liberation for living beings may indeed be secured. ||2||
Indeed, service to those who are one's own kindred and elders brings delight;
but for women, virtuous, truthful, and elder women are indeed the givers of liberation.
In bathing, massaging, drinking, eating, sleeping, sitting, conversing, touching, traveling, riding, sporting, and honoring; ||4||
In embracing, in ornamentation, in beauty, in amorous passion, in bodily carriage, in jesting, in festivals, in assemblies, and even in exile; ||5||
In knowledge, in making known, in the heart, in the body, in worldly honor, in the menstrual flow, in purification, in a vow, in the acquisition of learning, and in the forest; ||6||

In the house or in the forest, on dry land or at night, by day or when alone among people; likewise during rites for the gods or ancestors, in thick crowds, or while performing worship of the deities or sweeping. ||7||
Whether during ritual purification, childbirth, sleep, fainting, or dancing; at a wedding, in times of calamity, during speech, in solitude, or while traveling abroad—(8)
In fleeing, in union with a female companion, in the recitation of Brahma-mantras and the like, in the practice of taking refuge, and in remaining in a state of nakedness; ||9||
In the matter of gestures, a woman is always to be properly served as a teacher;
for a virtuous and faithful wife becomes a weighty authority through her lack of hesitation, without a doubt.
Therefore, tell me whether virtuous women have arisen or not; for by knowing this, women who are auspicious to the world would always be worthy of worship.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall explain this unsurpassed question:
many virtuous young maidens were created by Brahmā as bestowers of liberation.
Their matted locks remain uncut, yet they are exempt from marriage;
they are eternally twelve years of age and never experience the onset of menstruation.
May they never undergo the menses, but be eternally devoted to Brahman;
may these virtuous women, dedicated to righteous dharma, be as if emerged from the limbs of the embodiment of Brahman.
Therein [he saw] the principal Mahāgītā, who is identical in form with Nārāyaṇa,
whose nature is Brahman, who has become Brahman, and whose characteristics are existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Divine, consisting of pearls yet free from them, abiding within the form of Śrī Hari;
eternally liquid in nature, ever peaceful, and supremely composed of eternal bliss. || 16 ||
The Lord Hari, the self-effulgent Supreme Master, brought forth from his own heart the singular Gītā-kumārikā, the supreme Brahman.

She who consists entirely of splendor, who is desirable in every limb, who is filled with all objects of desire, and who is worthy of being honored as the fulfillment of the goals of human existence. || 18 ||
Divine, beautiful, twelve years of age, fortunate and auspicious;
she who was filled with the bliss of every single limb, and perfectly firm in all her limbs. (19)
She is endowed with a form whose every limb is well-proportioned and perfectly joined;
she is the bestower of all illumination and the beloved who grants liberation to all.
Consisting of all-knowledge, beautiful, radiant, raining down the nectar [of truth], endowed with all virtues, and accessible to everyone through devotion. ||21||
She is the destroyer of sins and heaps of evil, filled with awakening;
she possesses beauty and charm corresponding to her form, and brings happiness to those who take refuge in her.
In whatever way possible, for those who approach their own surrender,
it leads them to the divine refuge of Śrī Hari, which brings about liberation.
She who possesses a single body with fourteen openings, who bestows the Supreme Brahman merely by being resorted to, and whose form is that of Brahman—[I bow to her]. 24.
Śrī Hari always abides within the imperishable Brahman;
therein, in that eternal Hari, she who is the nature of eternal knowledge shines forth eternally. (25)
She indeed goes everywhere together with Śrī Hari;
wherever the manifestation of Hari occurs, there she is present.
The Gītā, personified in a beautiful form, surely moves along with Śrī Hari;
sometimes it resides within the Lord's own form, and sometimes it exists externally. ||27||
She who bestows excellent liberation reaches heaven, earth, and the netherworld;
she always abides as the radiant one who destroys all sins. (28)
She was virtuous, devoted to the conduct of the righteous, and a faithful protector of the dharma of the good;
she dwelt within the hearts of the saintly and was the very embodiment of wisdom.
She is known as the one whose vows of conduct are Brahman, who removes all defects and bestows purity;
she is eternally pure, ever-enlightened, and possesses a form that is forever free from fault.
The supreme goddess Nārāyaṇī, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, was indeed formerly produced by Śrī Hari himself from his own being. 3.1.
Then, for the sake of attaining the bliss offered to those liberated while residing in the abode of Brahman, she was likewise offered to the Lords for the attainment of liberation. ||32||
Furthermore, she is eternally entrusted even to living beings for the sake of bestowing liberation, as long as the arrangement of creation fashioned by Māyā persists. ||33||
In all those creations, that Gītā was virtuous and well-nourished;
yet when the Blessed Lord sent forth the Gītā toward an inferior state, [it became otherwise]. (34)
Then, as Gītā prayed to the God for her own protection, Hari said, "May no one deceive me; let it be so. (35)
Indeed, he protects the Gītā in every way as long as it endures;
there are thousands and tens of thousands of those who serve the Gītā. (36)
Those [other songs] were indeed produced as counterparts to the Gītā;
they were all identical in form to the Gītā and equal to it in their qualities.
All these songs are liberating, bestowing what is desired upon those who practice celibacy;
they grant liberation, merit, and purity—sacred, purifying, and supreme. (38)
The female attendants, through song, serve the Great Goddess Mahāgītā;
for Mahāgītā, the Gītās, and likewise other Anugītās [are present]. (39)
Beautiful women, the beauties of the world, embodied and possessed of great strength,
always wander here in this sphere as virtuous female ascetics.
For women addicted to sin and non-sin alike, for sinners likewise, for children, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes, and for those who cause the mixture of castes; ||41||
[It is for] those who possess the sins of ancestors, gods, yakṣas, and others; of pretas and mortals; and of those haunted by bhūtas, vetālas, kūṣmāṇḍas, nāgas, serpents, and darkness. ||42||

The songs of the Gītās, which carry across all beings— whether moving or unmoving, and whether characterized by qualities, actions, or designations— move virtuously within the sphere of the world (golaka).
To those with divine vision, they are always directly perceptible;
however, to non-divine evildoers, they consist of knowledge and sound alone. (44)
These auspicious [scriptures], consisting of the science of knowledge, remain easily accessible;
by taking refuge in them, people cross the ocean of worldly existence. 45.

Those who are engaged in sexual intercourse, those who have reached their menses, those in a state of impurity following childbirth, those who are unclean, those seated upon the lap of a husband, those seated upon the lap of another, or those reclining on a bed of passion; ||46||
In times of misfortune, they fall into the hands of others or are ruined by lack of refinement; dependent on fate or dependent on others, they rely upon the same stage as actors and their props. (47)
Those who are performers of dance and drama, outcasts, those whose duties have fallen away, and those employed in menial tasks;
celestial nymphs, courtesans, women whose husbands are hidden, and those who kill children. ||48||

Devoid of devotion to their husbands and other virtues, lacking righteousness, and blinded by intoxication, they were devoted to liquor and meat, having fallen from their proper conduct and indulging in fine clothing, dwellings, and the like.
All women who are slaves—causing the faults of poverty such as calamities and the like, and bestowing their enjoyment upon others—cross over those [sufferings] by taking refuge in song. (1.20.50)
The faults arising from causing abortions or obstructing the pursuit of dharma and desire are indeed destroyed for those women by taking refuge in Goddess Gītā. 51.
"There is no sin greater than this, nor is there any fault so great; there is no action more base"—indeed, that which is sung thus one should not purify. (52)
Whichever body it has assumed, by that very name this song of knowledge is proclaimed; indeed, it is considered to consist of the essence of the word "knowledge. (53)
Of the sages and the ascetics, as well as those who know the supreme Brahman;
of the gods and the preceptors of the gods, and of the humans traveling in celestial chariots.
Because the incarnations of Śrī Hari, the lords, and the knowers of the Vedas are infinite, there is truly no end to the Gītās.
The Brahmagītā, the Muktagītā, and likewise the supreme Viṣṇugītā;
the Gītā composed by Nārāyaṇa, and then the Harigītā which is devoted to Him. 56.
There are indeed millions of songs—the Satīgītā and Vadhūgītā—and by taking refuge in them, even a barbarian immediately becomes pure. (57)
Having opened the door of the heart, it destroys craving within;
it gladdens the self and elevates that supreme abode.

Therefore, the Gītā—purifying like the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, the destroyer of worldly existence, the bestower of liberation, and the grantor of union with Brahman—should always be cultivated by women. (59)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the virtuous Mahāgītā, who, accompanied by her own maidservants and by her friends skilled in other songs, bestows liberation. 1.20.60.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Mahāgītā of the Great Satī-Sādhvī Who Bestows Liberation," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 20 ||
Śrī Lakṣmī said: "O Lord, O Teacher of the World, are there other virtuous women besides those mentioned in the Gītā who act for the welfare of the world? Please tell me."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Indeed, the Upaniṣads are even more excellent than the virtuous Gītās; they are exceedingly dear, virtuous, and, by providing refuge, they grant liberation.
By the constant service of which one quickly becomes absorbed in the form of Hari;
they bestow the nature of Brahman and lead to the attainment of non-difference from Brahman. (3)
Furthermore, by Śrī Hari himself, who abides in the abode of the imperishable Brahman,
they were manifested from the essence of the supreme bliss of the reality of his own self.
Others, liberated through their similarity to Brahman, possess divine forms with golden hair,
golden eyebrows, and golden eyeballs.
Their lips were as lovely as the petals of the land-lotus, red like the interior of a red lotus,
and their excellent cheeks shone like the center of a red water-lily.
They were charming with gentle smiles and the golden-hued luster of their faces;
their chests were beautifully adorned with breasts shaped like small *jaṃbīra* fruits.
Their beautiful hands were endowed with the granting of boons and the granting of fearlessness;
they had slender waists, small midsections, thick thighs, and excellent lotus-like feet.
They are eternally celibate, untouched by marriage, and remain inviolate;
they are celebrated as Upaniṣads, oceans of knowledge, and imperishable.
Both the lords and the individual souls, whoever they may be who move within the realm of the self,
attain supreme liberation in the state of Brahman by taking refuge in the Upanishads.
Having not yet reached the bloom of youth, these celibate self-sacrificing ones wander through the worlds in the forms of virtuous women, abodes of compassion. (11)
Innumerable are those virtuous women who are likewise composed of the nature of wisdom;
having known them and sought refuge in them, women attain the supreme goal. (12)
Whether they be goddesses, human women, or those born of lower wombs—
