Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Power of Origin and Other Qualities of the Devoted Wife," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. ||30||

That supreme, divine nectar is white as long as it has not gone outside.

She was white, endowed with all limbs, four-footed, and three years of age.
The auspicious Lakṣmī milked Surabhi with the utmost devotion. ||11||
Having obtained the milk, which was sweet, he thought, "What shall I do?

At that moment, Śrī Hari placed nectar upon the tip of his own tongue.
It has arisen in the form of rasa; it is pure, sweet, and supreme. ||14||
Having assumed the form of sugar, it was cast forth by the will of Hari.
When these three are combined, cooked, and thoroughly boiled, it is wholesome. ||15||

Therein, for the sake of another fragrance, [the offering] is then from the right nostril.

Indeed, from the portion of Hiraṇyaśmaśru, Keśara was manifested.
All that was indeed placed appropriately within the supreme food.
Having entered into meditative equipoise, he is like milk that has been mixed and well-cooked with fine sugar.

when it was poured by him into a vessel of milk, it produced a splashing sound.
But through its conjunction with that [sugar], the resulting curd becomes delightful, possessing both sweet and sour qualities.
There, by the will of Hari, matured butter was manifested.
Then, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, the goddess Lakṣmī prepared ghee—fragrant, supreme, and divine—considering how it might be useful. (23)
While she was thus reflecting, Nārāyaṇa transformed the remaining mass of grain into wheat and ears of corn.
Then, by the mere movement of his own eyebrows, Śrī Hari—

That very thing again became the true nature of Kālacakra;
Kālacakra always crushes living beings with extreme velocity. ||26||
A woman was fashioned from the powder of his fiercely knitted brows.

Through misfortune, all living beings are ground to dust moment by moment.

That cow was given to the brahmin for the sake of constant sacrificial attainment.

By the goddess known as Pātivratī, devoted wives have been made manifest. ||33||
In this place, filament-bushes were always produced from filaments;
likewise, trees bearing such fruits were born here from *jāti* fruits.

For from his unbroken [teeth] were born the rice grains and paddy;

From that, the world always produces saffron which is tawny in color;
and from the nectar and the essence of sandalwood, trees as cool as sandalwood are produced.
From that, the [Vaiṣṇava] traditions (bodhyas) were born, originating from Śrī Hari.
Then, sweet water was manifested there from the mouth of Hari. 39.
Having drunk some water and rinsed his mouth with a handful, he remains for as long as it takes.

Then, the nectar was manifested from his own mouth by Śrī Hari.

And from that other drop, when it has been made pungent, ||49||

For he, having undergone manifold division, remains established in the world during creation.

The redness of the twilight, the redness of fire, and the redness of bodies;
And upon his lips and cheeks were flowers that partake of the seasons.
Whatever redness there is that is beautiful and sweet, that belongs to the flavor.
The goddess Rati, who is fond of dalliance, arose from that very rasa. ||56||
Red, endowed with red juice, and the locus of all red qualities,
that maiden Rati is beautiful and has attained fresh youth.
She is filled with a fullness of red, golden-hued, and beautiful in every limb.
By the command of Śrī Hari, she was indeed Rati, devoted to her husband. ||58||
When they had arrived here and were established throughout the entire world, each in their own place,
those two came to this world and spread that knowledge.
The Khadira tree was born as Kathaka, while the Pūgī became Tṛṇarājaka.
And likewise, whatever other grasses have grown from that sap.
Thus, the cows and Brahmins, who possess the fragrance of the lotus and have arisen from the form of the illustrious Hari, are my most excellent body there. (61)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Production of Substances such as Saffron, Grains such as Unbroken Rice, Creepers such as Betel, Fruits such as Coconut and Mango, Minerals such as Red Ochre, and Flavors such as Passion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. ||31||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O all-pervading inner self, O Self of the self, O Lord of the imperishable!
O Master Nārāyaṇa, you are the one worthy of worship; O Lord, you fulfill everything.
Cows are indeed declared to be animals; how then can they deliver people?
One who is capable may deliver others, but one who is incapable cannot do so by any means.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "The noose is called bondage; bondage is considered to be of the nature of Māyā.
Wherever Māyā exists, all that is indeed designated as 'bound' (paśu)."
The body, indeed, is the same for both beasts and humans; it is dependent on food and drink, and pervaded by self-interest consisting of desire and greed. (4)
O Blessed One, that person who indeed attains the divine mantra of Manu—
He indeed is called a human being; otherwise, he is merely the best of animals. ||5||
But my cows in Goloka are in every way identical with my own self.
Chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," they indeed rejoice, being absorbed in that Brahman.
One who always firmly recites the mantra "Nārāyaṇa" is truly fortunate.
Chanting their sweet songs in heaven, they grant me liberation.
Even in Vaikuṇṭha, those cows and other liberated beings indeed dwell,
worshipping my name and overflowing with all-encompassing bliss.
For those [beasts] are not truly beasts; rather, it is ignorant men who are beasts.
In Vṛndāvana, they remember Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, day after day with devotion.
Those goddesses who reside in the heavenly realms and elsewhere are considered to have provided breast milk for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, for the sake of fulfilling their desires, they dwell there having become cows.
They are omniscient, knowers of all languages, and are considered to be the givers of liberation at all times.
They are the mothers who are the receptacle of nectar, being the morsels from the mouth of the Blessed One.
Since they were born from my own body, they are considered and worthy of worship on every single hair.
I indeed dwell within them, as does Dharma, whose nature is that of a bull.
I dwell among the cows as a cowherd; the cows are my Brahman-body.
On the forehead of cows, however, is the abode of Brahman; there I dwell.
On my two peaks are my flagstaffs; in the middle is my lion-throne.
My two eyes are considered to be the two abodes of Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha.
My nose is the unmanifest abode; my mouth is of the nature of Māyā.
The teeth are the sixteen principles (tattvas), and the tongue is the intellect (buddhi), for that is indeed the Great One (mahat). ||15||
The syllable *praṇava* is their introductory praise; the two lips are considered to be *rajas* and *tamas*.
The two ears were as vast as the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), and the dewlap was made of gold.
Of these, Sadāśiva is the throat, and the four Vedas are the feet.
The breasts are the four aims of human life, and the navel is the stalk of the lotus of dispassion.
Vairāja Mahāviṣṇu is considered their belly;
the fire of Brahmanic luster is their stomach; and Truth is the back of the Creator. (18)
Urine is considered divine Ganges water; feces is herself regarded as Lakṣmī;
menstrual blood is the water of the Sarasvatī, and the womb is the oceans. (19)
The womb is the opening of the anus; the tail-base is the source of beings and so forth; the tail is heaven; and the cluster of hair is the celestial sphere of the gods and other realms.
Śiva and Viṣṇu are the two hips; Brahmā is declared to be the waist.
The womb is the goddess Pārvatī, and the body hairs are the divine sources of birth. ||21||
"The bones are the ancestors, and their hooves are the beings born of the netherworld"—it was with this very intention that I then fashioned the funeral cake (piṇḍa). ||22||
May cows be my manifestations of power, since they dwell as the nectars of immortality.
From that morsel made of nectar, all who have me as their mouth are satisfied. ||23||
I am the cows, and I am the cows; they are considered the mothers of the worlds.
Because they nourish, rescue, and lead one to Brahman, they bestow prosperity and liberation. ||24||
Through worship they are said to bestow merit, but through the offering of grass they grant prosperity.
Through giving, one leads others to liberation; through service, one bestows heaven.
Through giving, they burn away sins; those who offer water go to the state of immortality;
and by warding off gadflies, they destroy poverty in every respect. (26)
Circumambulating them is declared to be equivalent to circumambulating the earth.
For embodied beings, the constant use of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) by them leads to heaven. ||27||
The water from their tails purifies the wicked and the sinful.
The dust from their hooves washes away the sacred bathing-place of the deceitful one.
By giving a cow with two faces, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
for a cow that has recently calved is considered to be "two-faced. (29)
Of the pretas, rākṣasas, and beings born as spirits who dwell in the state of no destination.
Through the gift of a cow, one attains a destination preceded by the destruction of evil.
And for the deceased who is joined with evil and has gone to the abode of Yama.
The crossing of the Vaitaraṇī river certainly comes about through the gift of a cow. ||31||
In heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, and even in the realm of the Lord, they are providers of assistance.
They should always be honored, saluted, given gifts, and fed by people. ||32||
They should always be served, honored, protected, bowed to, and touched.
If a great sinner should always sacrifice his own life in the midst of cows, [he attains liberation]. ||33||
He indeed goes to the divine realm; his followers go far away.
But here, one who tends to cows is protected by them in the next world.
Having obtained the grace of the cows here, one becomes possessed of all grace;
nothing else has been performed at all, but rather the service of the cows has been rendered. (35)
The fruit of that is the world of Brahmā and so forth; for that purpose, it should be eternal.
As well as the propitiation of cows and likewise the propitiation of Brahmins. ||36||
In this matter as well as the next, Hari himself has considered two things to be equal:
[the theft of] cows and that which is done here toward a woman, a maiden, a sister, or a mother. (37)
One who causes suffering to one who has sought refuge and is dependent shall himself become a partaker of suffering.
The householder who indeed protects the male calf, the female calf, the bull, and the cow; ||38||
By him indeed was the earth protected; may he obtain the fruit of being a protector of the earth.
They do not call mere substance "wealth"; it is said that wealth consists of cattle. ||39||
In this world it bestows flavors, and in the next world it acts as a companion.
They eat grass upon the ground and always dwell below.
They endure cold, heat, and other hardships; they offer many flavors [to others];
they nourish their own family and satisfy the gods and ancestors. ||41||
The divine cows, when remembered, deliver one from falling into the lower realms.
The Brahmins are declared to be the stars by means of the recitation of Vedic mantras and other such practices. ||42||
Even those who are overcome by sin cross over by the power of cows;
for cows and Brahmins are indeed one reality, manifested in two forms. (43)
For the mantras are deposited in one place, while the sacrificial oblation is offered elsewhere.
Through mantra and oblation, sacrifice arises; from sacrifice, rain then comes into being. ||44||
From rain comes food and water; from that, the elements; and from those, living beings.
Through progeny one attains heaven; from heaven comes happiness and great celebration. ||45||
From festival to festival they go; therefore, cows should be served daily.
What is the use of saying more? Cows are indeed my path to the state of Brahman.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Cow," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||32||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, my mind rejoices from chewing betel;
from tasting the flavor of betel, intoxication arises in my heart. (1)

Whom does he remember with affection? His heart sports with that which is heart-pleasing. || 2 ||

"O compassionate Lord, grant me peace; what was this disease that befell me? || 4 ||
Then, having heard of Lakṣmī’s fickleness arising from the juice of betel nut, he [spoke].

A trident with the luster of peacock feathers, its head-jewel like a flash of lightning.

The two beaks meeting in the midst of her lips, which were exerting effort to kiss; (9)
Manifesting a faintly dark and very subtle line of beard.

Having made the curved state of the knitted brow into a bow, O Kamaṭha.
Having first taken up an arrow made of mango blossoms there, he indeed [discharged it]. (13)
The second arrow is indeed fragrant oil for the eyes and so forth.

The fourth is called the attraction by the sight of the limbs of the youth;

The appearance of hair growing upon a body that resembles glowing gold.
Wearing a golden-colored garment as fine as the thread of a spider's web. ||16||
It causes the differentiation of the elements; it is a youth sixteen years of age.
Displaying his form, the wise one bowed down to Śrī Hari.
"What service may I perform for you, O Lord? he asked.
I have told you: "Becoming present in every individual, enter into the heart of Śrī."
You are indeed the progenitor of kings; therefore, always remain for the sake of pleasure.
Having entered therein, become in every way a producer of such vigor.
Entering into others during my creation, act as their instrument everywhere.
By which the creation, always bound to this or that state, may become stable. ||1.33.20||
Having thus received this command, he took it to heart;
at that time, O Lakṣmī, you were the first to embrace him.
O Lakṣmī, by contact with my body, your fever was indeed pacified.
"Because you dwelt in the womb during my period of heroic exertion, [your] son has become Dhanam."
Wealth was well-concealed by you at the time when it was our agreement; for indeed, through our union with a third desire, we have been joined together. (23)
Likewise, through the arrival of good fortune for both of us—myself and my son on our third day—and together with wealth, we three have attained an auspicious state. (24)
The tenth is known as Putravatī (the one possessing sons), and the thirteenth is considered Dhanatrayodaśī (the wealth-thirteenth).
Those who desire wealth and perform worship here [to these goddesses] indeed [attain their goal]. ||25||
Bring them wealth consisting of gold, silver, jewels, and so forth.
Then Kāma was commanded by me, with Bāṇa as his companion. ||26||
Go to the creation; enter into all youthful bodies, bringing about the production of passion and seed, acting as an assistant to the process of creation.
Requested by Kāma, she became his companion and went before him.
I have bestowed my youthful state upon Kāma as his former consort.
Then, once they had made their dwelling there, a second companion arrived.
Rati, the most beautiful woman, was created by me as a wife and given to Kāma.
I have offered myself as a slave to that Kāma, who expresses his own self-interest.
But that boy is the mind-born younger brother of Kāma. ||1.33.30||
Likewise, O son, Hāva and Bhāva were created by me as my two mind-born sons.
Those two were granted there to Kāma as his attendants, Sahasa and Sañcara.
Furthermore, I [created] two sons named Premā and Mānasa.
Having produced it, he gave it to him; and he too became his companion. ||32||
Then, from Gupta, a son named Saṃśleṣa was begotten and handed over [to him].
He too became an assistant to Kāmadeva in guarding his senses. ||33||
Therefore, a servant named Jāgara was given by me to this [consciousness] while it is awake;
and having produced the two servants Svāda and Bhoga, they were handed over to him. (34)
Then, a son named Śrāvaka was likewise produced by me and entrusted to him;
he too became there an accomplice to the impulses of desire for those [drops]. (35)
Then, the son named Ānanda was manifested by me from the root *dhā*;
he too was indeed bestowed upon him to act as an assistant in accomplishing the task. (36)
Likewise, the son Utsāhana was begotten by me and handed over to him.
For a long time, he has been rendered an ally by the harshness of his wakefulness and the fulfillment of his strength.
And my maidservant Nirvṛti was then surrendered by me to him as well.
Having reached the highest flow, he causes the two embodied beings to separate. ||38||
And then, having produced slackness in him, I delivered him over as a slave.
There resides a Ghaṭikā that makes known the cessation of desire. ||39||
Thus, O Goddess, this maṇḍala has been prepared by me for the purpose of creation.
What is done, given, and protected—these three each occur in pairs within the two [periods] of Īśa and Jīva.
Contemplating all this as consisting of me, one does not incur bondage;
by me the five fires were fashioned and revealed from my own self alone. (41)
Man, woman, desire, vigor, and passion—these are the five.
These five fires have been described by me; they have been revealed to you by me. ||42||
Likewise, these five fires are the various states of the element.
For the Puruṣa is the first fire; he is called the "puruṣa-element" (pauruṣa-dhātu). ||43||
The linga, accompanied by fire, is called the linga-element (laiṅga-dhātu).
Then the third fire is the womb; it is called the element in the womb. ||44||
Then the fourth fire is the *garbha* (womb) fire; it is called the *gārbha* (embryonic) child.
The fifth is the *apatya* (offspring) fire; it is called the *āpatyeya* (descendant) and is said to be embodied (*mūrta*). ||45||
Thus, from the seed of the elements (dhātu), creation indeed proceeds with certainty.
Having known them to be of my own nature, the composed individual meditates upon them.
Through the thorough contemplation of my true nature, one neither comes to nor goes toward me; for desire, born from affection between two embodied beings, is fashioned as a bond.

For from the perspective of Brahman there is a merit, whereas from the perspective of difference there is a defect. ||48||
Because Hari is devoid of qualities, all his actions, through their union with him, are likewise devoid of qualities.

For Kāma is called a god, and Rati is a goddess because she rests upon him.
Therefore, the divinity of that god [Viṣṇu] arises from the power of all the gods.
Kāma should be understood as the embodied form of Hari, bestowing the bliss and happiness of the embodied soul.
Bliss is the form of Brahman; when viewed as Brahman, it does not cause bondage. //51//
And you, Lakṣmī, have two sons indeed: Vyāja and Vyavasāyaka.
I give those two things, O people, by which men may become industrious and find refuge in happiness. ||52||

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Arising of Desire Caused by Betel and the Performance of its Consequent Rites and Sacrificial Fires," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 33 ||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa who was born from the body of Nārāyaṇa—"
Where did he go, and what did he do then? Tell me all that, O Hari.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"The primordial Puruṣa is a divine Brāhmaṇa sixteen years of age."
Indeed, instructed by his father, he became proficient in all branches of knowledge.
Equal to Nārāyaṇa in body and equal to him in virtues as well, he was like another Nārāyaṇa in form, age, and appearance. (3)
He praised the god Nārāyaṇa, his own father and teacher.
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of cows, you are the father and the teacher of the worlds. ||4||
"Instruct me: what task should I perform? I shall carry it out without any doubt."
He who protects is called the father, while the son is the protector of ignorance. ||5||
Viṣṇu is the father; the deity is the father; Aṃśa, born of Vāsudeva, is the father;
Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is the father; therefore, he is worshipped.
The Pitṛtīrtha is a supreme sacred site, a deliverer, bestowing merit, and most excellent.
The father is God, the supreme deity; the father is the eternal Brahman.
He who is the father, the provider of the seed, the nourisher, the protector, and the one who offers everything of his own—what other is considered superior to him? (8)
By him by whom the father is satisfied, Hari is satisfied;
and by him by whom the father is served, Hari is fully served.
Charity, merit, vows, hospitality, sacrifice, oblations, self-restraint, and so forth—even if unperformed, these become well-performed by one who serves his father. (1.34.10)
Even one who is a great sinner, an extreme evildoer, a slaughterer of animals, or a suicide,
is glorified in the world of Brahmā after drinking the water used for washing the feet of his father.
He is the father, the Brahman, the Supreme Brahman, and the refuge for those seeking shelter.
He is the giver, the nourisher, and the lord of the body, knowledge, wealth, and so forth. ||12||
By him who has carried out the father’s command, everything has been accomplished; nothing else remains to be done, for there is no duty other than obedience to the father’s blessings.
Whether refined or unrefined, a son is not truly regarded as such by his father alone.
He becomes fearless and is honored in every way even by the great. ||14||
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Mahādeva, nor Vairāja, nor the Īśvaras [are able to do so].
These become equal to a father, for the father himself is indeed considered the father. ||15||
He who performs service for his father in old age by providing water, food, clothing, and vehicles, and by massaging his feet and attending to him by his side; ||16||
He who does not respond with "no" when summoned or when being sent on a mission;
He who performs his desired rites with the thought "Om" alone shall partake of liberation; of this there is no doubt. ||17||
He who performs no action whatsoever without his father's consent.
He who acts solely by command is indeed the one who partakes of the fruit in every way. ||18||
One who is being led away by calamities, one who is oppressed by sufferings, and even one who is overcome by obstacles—such a person is indeed protected by devotion to the father. ||19||
Indeed, it is by such a good son that a father is truly considered to possess a son.
Indeed, a father does not truly possess a son if that son does not carry out his commands. ||1.34.20||
Therefore, father, I shall carry out your command so that the fruit of birth may be realized.
All that has been done would become well-done; therefore, grant your command quickly. ||21||
While he stood thus with palms joined in reverence, having demonstrated such devotion to his father,
his father Nārāyaṇa himself spoke to his excellent son.
"Oh, son! Live long; you have been strengthened by auspicious blessings. Devoted to filial piety toward your father, you increase day by day through righteousness. (23)
Such is your discernment, and your conduct is characterized by devotion to your father;
O son, I abide in the discrimination of filial devotion, which indeed bestows perfection.
He indeed should be known as a good son by whom his father has been well protected,
constantly saluted, served, honored, and revered.
Those sons who, having risen in the morning, [honor] their fathers, the gods, and likewise their teachers—
And those noble ones who pay homage and bow down partake in the light of inexhaustible meaning. || 25 ||
For them indeed are imperishable worlds; for them is imperishable immortality;
for them indeed is imperishable welfare; for them is supreme prosperity.
Their wives were always virtuous, devoted to their husbands, sweet-spoken, givers of sweet things, and likewise bestowers of sweet enjoyments. (28)
Their dwellings are divine, filled with millions of riches, and graced with the excellence of abundant liquids, materials, and treasures. (29)
Those people who serve their ancestors with clothing, food, and water, as well as through attendance, obedience, service, and other such acts; ||| 1.34.30 ||
For them, there shall be imperishable worlds and imperishable powers;
and there shall be imperishable divine happiness, free from obstacles, and long life. (31)
The supernatural powers abide where the ancestors are honored;
and prosperity comes to that place when it is joined with the blessings of the ancestors.
Gold, silver, wealth, grain, and various kinds of gems;
soft beds, the foam of milk, fair women, and likewise the objects of taste (rasas). || 33 ||
For those who serve their ancestors, there shine vehicles, carriages, and palaces;
as well as gardens, groves, dwellings, lakes, and grounds for recreation. (34)
Divine celestial chariots, cows, slender-waisted female servants, and gentle male servants who carry out one's commands come to those who serve their ancestors. (35)
Service to one's father is an inexhaustible gain; there is no other gain, nor any other like it, by which sons rejoice both in this world and in the next. (36)
Those by whom their father was previously served with devotion and fully satisfied have attained the supreme state of Brahmā and other realms, as well as the state beyond rebirth.
Yama does not approach one who is a vessel for the father’s favor;
even Kāla flees from such a person who is a vessel for the father’s favor. (38)
For Hari, who is the recipient of his father’s grace, there is the state of being a recipient of grace;
for those devoid of their father’s grace, the destination is miserable and brings enduring suffering.
The lineage of those who have obtained their father’s favor never perishes anywhere;
the well-being of those who have attained their father’s favor never decays anywhere. (1.34.40)
For those who have obtained the grace of the ancestors, calamities depart far away; indeed, spiritual sufferings are no longer seen at all. 41.
Indeed, their sense faculties always remain free from disease;
the father, as the provider of the seed, is worthy of honor, and the mother, who nurtures the embryo in the womb, is likewise venerable. (42)
In childhood, the mother who serves one should be served just as a father is;
the father is to be understood as Nārāyaṇa, and the mother is the very embodiment of Lakṣmī. 42.
He by whom service to the mother has been performed has served millions of deities;
for it is the mother who, established in her vow, bears the child in her womb for the sake of conception. (44)
Even having renounced desired objects of enjoyment, such as food and drink, she protects [her child];
she endures the supreme suffering of giving birth, as well as death and fainting. (45)
She makes the child, who is covered in urine and excrement, stainless;
even having abandoned sleep, she remains consumed by anxiety for the sake of the child. (46)
Like a meditating lord, she serves and nourishes the fool;
she always protects everything he has earned and gives it all for his sake. (47)
Does the debt of a mother toward her son ever truly pass away? Indeed, even in a hundred years, a son is not able to fully repay that debt.
Whatever their qualities may be, parents are regarded as equal to Brahmā;
they should always be honored, served, and saluted by sons who desire merit. 49.
Even if the parents are blind, diseased, impoverished, wretched, unchaste, thieves, or intent on violence, they are worthy of worship.
"You are blessed, my son, always, for you indeed carry out my command;
my command alone is your dharma—be a soul of dharma at all times. (51)
"O my little son, I shall perform for you that which is renowned as the 'Vow of the Wife' (Patnīvrata);
for you alone are the one who possesses the divine perfection of a Brāhmaṇa devoted to his wife. (52)
"Since you are my form and are exceedingly dear to me,
O son, become the preceptor known by the name Kṛṣṇavallabha."
You are indeed my own incarnation, O Blessed One, the creator of liberation for all;
become the sole and true husband of the countless virtuous women created by me. (54)
Having assumed a divine form throughout the entire creation and being all-pervasive,
dwell within every man and become endowed with ten million virtues.
Listen, I shall instruct you in the vow of a devoted wife according to its true essence;
by conducting yourself among men in that manner, you shall indeed become a bestower of liberation.
She who carries her husband’s portion into her own womb for his protection is called a wife;
she is a companion who bears witness before the sacred fire.
For that purpose and for the sake of her happiness, conducting oneself solely for the sake of her welfare is called a *vrata*; thus it is described as the "vow of the wife" (*patnīvrata*).

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Brāhmaṇa Consisting of a Man Devoted to Serving His Parents and Observing Chastity toward His Wife," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 34 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The true meaning of the term *patnīvratā* has been correctly explained by me;
I shall now tell you what various rites must be performed for the sake of your wife.
First there is the state of a religious student, and afterwards that of a householder;
having first been a student, one should thereafter live with a wife.
"Take up the life of celibacy (brahmacarya) and the sacred thread (yajñopavīta); learn the meaning of the Vedas, and afterwards become a householder with a wife."
Having thus commanded his own son, a brahmin who was approaching youth,
he waited for an auspicious moment and proceeded with the initiation ceremony.
Thus, with his mind eager to perform the investiture of his son,
he of great prowess prepared all the necessary materials.
Then auspicious musical instruments were indeed sounded again and again,
and Lakṣmī and the others sang songs there in joy at that time.
This supreme rite, consisting of the gift of three cows as a means for performing three *kṛcchra* penances,
was performed for the sake of pacifying the impurity resulting from eating according to one's own will.

One should eat in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, eat only what is unasked for (uninvited) for three days, and not eat at all for the final three days; this is declared to be the pure *kṛcchra* penance.

The worship of the Mātṛkās, as well as the Nāndī-śrāddha, the pronouncement of auspiciousness (svastivāca), the pacification of the house (gṛhaśānti), and likewise the feeding of the twice-born; || 1 ||
Then, upon the sacrificial ground, Śrī Hari himself performed the establishment of the fire born from the *samudbhava* mantra, as well as its worship and other rites.
Having bathed, eaten, had his hair dressed, and being fully adorned,
he performed the purificatory rites for his son who was seated on his right side.
Having performed an oblation of clarified butter, the Lord gave him a loincloth, a waist-thread, and a new sacred thread consisting of three strands, and spoke as follows.
Your Veda shall be the Sāmaveda, and your lineage (gotra) is Śrībrahma;
your three ancestral sages (pravaras) are Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari.
"Indeed, this branch shall henceforth be known by your name as the 'Patnīvratā. Now, understand that you have become a religious student (brahmacārī). (14)
Listen, I shall briefly declare the duties appropriate for you:
offer oblations into the fire at dawn, and likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). (15)
Perform service to your guru constantly, and likewise perform the recitation of the Veda;
receive this Gāyatrī mantra and always perform its recitation.
"Oṃ, we know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva;
may that Viṣṇu impel us"—with this mantra, rotate the rosary. (17)
"Accept this Brahmā’s staff and likewise this deerskin;
perform your twilight devotions, and avoid anger and falsehood. (18)
Likewise, protect your celibacy; do not enter into any state of mental distortion. Do not indulge in impure food or drink, and never commit an act of violence.
O Brahmin, do not fall into distress; do not engage in censure anywhere.
Perform your ritual bath, the twilight prayers, recitation, fire-oblation, Vedic study, and the libations for the ancestors.
"You should constantly practice self-knowledge, the worship of Hari, and the eight [limbs of yoga].
Having accepted those words with "Om," he likewise approached the Sun.
He performed a circumambulation of the fire and received alms from his mother:
cows, gold coins, garments, and ornaments from Śrī Hari.
He gave to the lords who had assembled there;
having provided them with food and sacrificial fees, they were fully satisfied. ||23||
Hari taught his son, whose very self was the praise of knowledge, the Veda;
[the son] wore matted hair, a water-pot, a staff, a hide, and bark garments.
He reflected upon the marriage of his son, named Patnīvrata,
with a girl named Pativratā, who was full of beauty and youth.
Nārāyaṇa indeed arranged the marriage of the girl with him;
having seen the birth-stars of both, he determined the auspicious moment for the wedding.
Having observed the auspicious moment and the strength [of the planets], he drew up the document for the wedding ceremony;
indeed, having caused auspicious songs and the recitation of benedictions to be performed.
Having likewise made the face of the bridegroom sweet with drops of unbroken rice, she massaged the body of the bridegroom with powdered flour and indeed worshipped him. ||| 28 ||
Having performed the raising of the pavilion and the installation of the ruby pillars,
he established Gaṇeśa and likewise worshipped the Mātṛkās.
Having performed the ritual installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), he had a sacrificial pit constructed;
then, having tied the "fruit of desire" (the *mīṃḍholaka*) to his hand, he brought the bridegroom to the excellent pavilion.
Having brought the maiden there, he had her place the bridegroom’s garland;
then, having established the Gārhapatya fire in the sacrificial pit, he offered oblations.
Having joined her hands together, he gave her sweet food to eat;
having tied a knot in her garment, he indeed caused her to perform circumambulations.
Having made the sound of Vedic recitation, he caused the auspicious hymns and others to be sung;
having delighted them with ritual gestures (mudrās) and the like, he offered the articles for the hands.
Having said, "Walk in righteousness together," he completed the rite of the auspicious union;
having removed all obstacles from their heads, he joined them with blessings. (34)
Having given away the bride and groom according to the Brāhma rite, he indeed led them away;
then Nārāyaṇa instructed the couple there.
A wife is indeed not separate from her husband, nor is a husband separate from his wife;
because the two loves are inseparable, there is a unity between the two born of their very nature.
For the wife indeed conceives in her womb the great power that was hidden in her husband;
and because of the union of those two limbs, the offspring is born as the union of the couple.
The father’s portion remains in the womb and is nourished by the mother’s portion;
thus the child becomes one for both, and therefore there is a unity between the two. (38)
When one person encounters what is undesirable, both will experience equal suffering;
when one person attains the perfection of happiness, both will experience equal joy. ||39||
Loss and gain, pleasure and pain—these two are experienced as equal;
for the self is attached to both within itself, and therefore there is unity between the two. (1.35.40)
When wealth is acquired by even one person, the ownership of another also comes into effect;
when merit is performed by one, a second person partakes in the fruit. (41)
For when one person has accomplished a task, another places his trust in him;
indeed, two people together enjoy that which was acquired by only one.
By day and by night, there is unity between the two bodies and even between the two minds;
my-ness and I-ness are certainly not distinct, therefore there is oneness of both.
In weeping it becomes weeping, likewise in rejoicing it becomes rejoicing;
in fainting it becomes fainting, and in thinking it becomes thought. (44)
Because of the unity of the two, all this arises; it does not arise from two things that are distinct.
Therefore, the supreme unity of husband and wife must be understood in every respect. (45)
Thus, by the power of this unity, unity also arises even regarding merit;
likewise, in the punishment of enemies and the punishment of kings, there is also unity through endurance.
In matters of pilgrimage, giving, assistance, auspicious rites, merit, and religious duty, the share of husband and wife is equal, both in this world and in the next. (47)
Therefore, half of one's own body belongs to another;
for a man, the left half is indeed the wife, and the wife’s right half is the husband.
For the husband always dwells in the wife, and the wife likewise abides in the husband;
therefore, the wife is considered half of the body, and the husband is considered half of the body. (49)
Therefore, having abandoned one's own self-interest and having understood the welfare of both,
one should remain for the sake of the livelihood of both, acting toward each other with mutual purpose.
Having recognized each other's own reflection as an ally,
even while enduring mutual friction, one must perform one's daily duties.
Just as a husband is to be served, honored, and worshipped like a god by his wife,
so too is a virtuous wife to be served, honored, and treated like a goddess by her husband during eating,
dressing, conversation, recreation, festivals, and play. (52)
In matters of love, laughter, honor, and ascending seats or vehicles; ||53||
In livelihood, in commerce, in ownership, in worship, in hospitality, and in honoring—indeed, in every way, a wife must be reckoned foremost by a man. (54)
Where pleasant things are honored, there the deities dwell;
where pleasant things are gratified, there prosperity resides. (55)
Where there are delightful things, people rejoice; indeed, prosperities flourish there.
Where there are delightful things, they find satisfaction; there, prosperities are drawn forth.
For women bring joy here, and through them, spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) arrive;
they must neither be provoked nor struck, since women are the bearers of the lineage. ||57||
But she who, having abandoned her father, has gone to her husband's house, being dependent on her husband and sharing his fortune—who that is wise would cause her distress? (58)
She who lives like a female slave, subsisting as a dependent; having become wretched and miserable, she follows after her husband alone. (59)
Or where she is driven like a cow, there she indeed drags herself in misery; who, then, being wise, would cause her pain, even as one might distress the shadow of one's own body? (1.35.60)
What is given away or consumed benefits others, and when she is pursued by another, she leaves behind only her remnants;
dependent on others, she yields herself to a husband—what wise man would not protect her? (61)
She who performs her domestic duties even while enduring hunger and thirst, and she who attends to her husband's business even while suffering through difficult times; ||62||
Abandoning sleep as well as indolence, and having disciplined her own mind,
she attends to her husband on the ground below for the sake of his sexual pleasure.
Whether she is beaten, reviled, shouted at, insulted, or even abandoned, the weak woman endures it all; who then would inflict suffering upon her? (64)
In such a virtuous wife, Lakṣmī resides—Rādhā, Ramā, Jayā, Padmā, Śāradā, and Sarasvatī. (65)
Ekādaśī, Rati, Sandhyā, Mohinī, and Jayantī—
these and other great goddesses indeed dwell there in the wife.
Whether she be blind, diseased, poor, ugly, or unfortunate; or one with deformed breasts, a distorted face, a hunchbacked back, or who is corpulent with a sagging waist. (67)
Even if she is ill-smelling, ill-footed, leprous, ill-favored, and of evil nature—even if she is wicked and of bad conduct—a wife must indeed be served, O Lotus-born One. (68)
One who desires their own welfare should never cause anyone to suffer;
for by her mere sigh, everything is consumed in that very instant.
From her sighs born of sorrow, a man is born who is without lineage;
his previously performed merit is destroyed by the fire at the end of the eon.
Therefore, my son, you should always honor your wife as is appropriate;
give her everything you have earned, even ten times more than for yourself. (71)
Having obtained the happiness of domestic life through that, and having entered heaven together,
you two shall at the end go to the divine state of Brahman, from which there is no returning to rebirth.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Duties of Celibacy, Householder Life, and the State of Husband and Wife of the Man named Patnīvratā," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. ||35||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Kamalā, to this discourse on worldly affairs, hearing which there will surely be wonder; I shall relate it to you according to the truth.
For in the world of karma, worldly activity arises from taking and giving;
through mutual assistance, it is always of the nature of bondage. (2)
The wealthy man always gives wealth and assistance to the poor, the destitute, and the helpless, so that they may carry on their bodily existence.
By that means, even a rigid commitment proceeds with ease;
when one's own practice is well-yoked, the commitment also becomes a source of gain. (4)
In that case, however, the wealth must be given in its entirety;
for if the debtor should die, the creditor would not receive it unless the receiver of the property returns it.
Then, for the sake of discharging his debts, if he is born again in another life as a human being,
he first becomes the father.
At that time, the sons who were previously givers become inactive;
even while remaining within their mother’s womb, they cause great expenditure.
Those who destroy wealth would even make his wife ill; at that time, those destroyers of wealth show no straightforwardness even regarding her birth.
After birth, there is no good health; at that time, those who cause the destruction of wealth, being entirely wicked even in childhood, cause great expenditure.
Through food, clothing, drink, ointments, and great festivities,
sons bring about the vast destruction of their father’s wealth.

Expenditure occurs during illness, expenditure during religious vows, and likewise expenditure during calamity; furthermore, expenditure is said to follow from further expenditure in the study of knowledge and in marriage. (11)
As long as they are not yet capable of earning, there is indeed only expenditure;
this continues until a time for earning is perceived.
For even a son who has been made young may die suddenly;
he departs taking with him everything that was given [to him] in a previous birth. (13)
Alternatively, if one who lives long becomes distracted or insane, for that reason there will undoubtedly be an expenditure of wealth in every way. || 14 ||
In this way, those who were donors in a previous life are born here as one's sons;
having exhausted the merit of the wealth they gave, they depart according to their karma.
Therefore, sons who do not return what was given to them in their own home should be known as those who first gave [to others]; even they become like cattle. || 16 ||
Having become bulls, horses, donkeys, or camels, they carry [the load];
through that means, having given their master's wealth, they go to another body. (1.7)
He who is liberated from debt owes nothing whatsoever to anyone;
he for whom a debt remains shall certainly not have offspring.
Therefore, sons should always be understood as having come for the purpose of destroying one's wealth;
however, virtuous sons bestow gain when the appropriate time has arrived. || 19 ||
In this cycle of existence bound by karma, whoever owes a debt to another takes that upon themselves and departs far away for a long time. || 1.36.20 ||
No one is anyone's son, nor is anyone anyone's father; the relationship between father and son is established only through the giving and receiving of debts. (21)
O sons, if they abandon the service of their own father and go astray,
they are consumed by the father's sighs and fall even to the lowest state.
If a wicked son, having lost his merit, expels from the home his mother, father, or even an elderly person who ought to be protected, he quickly becomes ruined.
If one treats the guru with "hūṃ" and the father and mother with "tūṃ," one will be born as a tree in a cremation ground, frequented by herons and vultures. (24)
If one does not give food to his mother or father when they have reached old age,
the gods will indeed be enraged with him and likewise become destroyers of his food.
He who does not provide clothing and a livelihood for them in their old age—his dwelling and his means of subsistence are taken away by the divine beings. (26)
That wicked son who subjects his parents to threats, beatings, or insults, shall experience those very same things in the hereafter. (27)
One must become a bad son, not a good son;
for by means of a good son, heaven is attained and even liberation is within one's grasp. (28)
Or else, by the propitiation of Sudeva, or by those two through whom merit was performed in the past, a son is obtained—a virtuous and pure son. (29)
A servant is one who always follows the commands of his master with humility, enduring pleasure, pain, and all else for the sake of his guru, and providing for his nourishment. || 1.36.30 ||
Auspicious conjunctions are always required for the birth of a virtuous son;
indeed, those excellent conjunctions that facilitate the retention of the embryo are the givers of a noble son. (31)
Whatever thought dwells in the father's heart regarding the gift at the time of the season—whether it be desire, anger, gain, reproach, or even theft—[that shall be the case]. (32)
Delusion, hypocrisy, impurity, deceit, or even crookedness;
heroism, learning, and goodness—these may be of the nature of rajas or tamas. (33)
Whether it be gambling, drinking, vice, or whatever else is undesirable, the drop becomes absorbed in that; even the son becomes absorbed in that.
If they should live with hearts tender with charity, righteousness, compassion, and love, then the drop [the son] would become identical with them; his son would possess those same qualities. (3.5)

If, at the time of the ritual gift, the barking of dogs or the braying of donkeys and the like is heard as inauspicious, or if sounds of distress or quarreling are likewise heard, then [it is unfavorable]. (36)
When drops, having become identical with that [semen], fall into your womb,
even sons are born like dogs or donkeys, possessing those very qualities.
Due to living with those of low birth and by adopting their ways and conduct, children are indeed born in such a manner when the drops are offered. (38)
Indeed, whatever forms exist everywhere in the house, on the walls and so forth, sons of such appearances as those come into being for them. (39)
They will be dark-complexioned and dominated by tamas; they will incite wars, act as deceivers, be thieves, full of lustful desires, and create causes for laughter and sorrow.
The poor and the wealthy, the victorious and the fugitives, as well as Rākṣasas, Pretas, Bhūtas, musicians, and dancers [all fled]. (4.1)
Just as whatever forms actors and actresses may assume—whether in a house, in public view, or in memory—the emission of the drop [occurs]. ||42||
In whatever manner those qualities manifest among the subjects, so indeed do they come to be;
therefore, a wise man should consider the merit even in the act of impregnation.
A man who is peaceful, endowed with righteousness, devoted, possessed of fame, virtuous, white (pure), meritorious, tranquil, and likewise possessed of good qualities. ||44||
A teacher, a husband, a father, a mother, or even a deity;
one who is learned, virtuous, heroic, handsome, and fortunate. (45)
One who is fair-complexioned, of renowned deeds, virtuous, and ascetic;
or one who acts for the welfare of the world and possesses faith in the worship of the gods. ||46||
He was industrious, knowledgeable in ethics, gentle, a mine of divine qualities,
devoted to helping others, fortunate, and distinguished by his generosity.
Then one should contemplate that pure abode of all excellent virtues—whether it be a man or a woman, or likewise a god or a goddess. (48)
One should [worship] the tranquil male deity and the virtuous female deity, both the Lord (Bhagavat) and the Goddess (Bhagavatī),
exactly as they were at the time of the impregnation ceremony.
And whatever she remembers, she obtains such offspring;
for in the act of conception during the fertile period, the nature of the offspring corresponds to the disposition of the two embodied beings.
For offspring are born endowed with the very dispositions of the couple;
yet in this creation, natures have been mixed in many ways. (5.1)
For indeed, through mutual intermingling, they do not remain pure;
nevertheless, one should contemplate that which bestows happiness as long as the power of the intellect persists. (52)
By that means, he shall have offspring that always bestows happiness and honor;
indeed, the quality of the menstrual flow certainly enters into all such offspring. (53)
From the commencement of the season, the embryonic lotus remains with its mouth wide open until the sixteenth day; thereafter, it no longer receives the embryo.
Having determined that it was after midnight and before the next midnight,
when the menses are clearly visible, the counting of days shall begin from that day.
Having excluded the four days of the moon's change and determining that the capacity for conception exists up to the limit of sixteen days; ||5-6||

Whether it be this or that, four nights associated with the *rajas* (dust/impurity) must be abandoned during the period following menstruation; on the fifth night, the daughter may be given away in marriage.
"The sixth night indeed bestows a son"—having counted thus according to the number, one should perform the conjunction as desired so that it yields fruit. (58)
Even-numbered nights grant sons to him, while odd-numbered nights grant daughters;
among them, the four nights associated with the onset of menstruation are censured. (59)
One must not engage in sexual union with them, for that would surely cause the destruction of the fetus;
therefore, having become firm in resolve and having performed purification, one may enter [the womb].
Having abandoned the wicked moon and having avoided the asterisms Maghā and Mūla,
one should approach his pure wife, especially under the Puṣya constellation.
Having performed purification together with his wife, the husband should enter the bedchamber;
he shall obtain a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human life.
If those two are impure, their sons will be impure and sinful;
during sexual intercourse, the woman should perform acts such as adornment and laughter.
By that, one shall have excellent offspring who enjoy happiness, possess a gentle appearance, are endowed with a sense of humor, have a divine form, and bring delight to the mind. ||64||
Having eaten sweet milk-porridge that is white in color, one should lie down;
by that, one's offspring will always be radiant, endowed with beauty, and very robust. (65)
If one should go to a woman after eating leafy vegetables (śāka), his child will be black-complexioned; therefore, leafy vegetables should not be eaten on that day.
Through brilliant food, one's vitality becomes brilliant;
therefore, at that time, both types of food—such as milk and other substances—should be consumed in a brilliant state.
Thereafter, the commencement of the seasonal rites (ṛtu-prasaṅga) should be performed, which brings about all auspiciousness,
at an auspicious time, in an auspicious conjunction (yoga), and likewise during an auspicious moment (muhūrta).

One should form an alliance and not otherwise for the sake of obtaining excellent offspring; however, those people who, disregarding the counsel of the virtuous, act out of the impulse of passion— (69)
Those who bestow embryos at the improper time have children who are unfortunate, lacking in vigor, lacking in strength, and performers of little merit. (1.36.70)
Those devoid of wisdom are born as givers of suffering and lead lives of misery; therefore, may you both always strive for the attainment of auspicious intelligence. (7.1)
May you both abide in the true nature of Dharma, never in anything else;
through that, may supreme happiness accrue to you two who are of one mind.
May those two conquerors of the two worlds bring you prosperity, and may you two always remain meaningful companions, never separated from one another. (73)
May you two, enjoying the bliss of married life, ever abounding in joy, endowed with physical excellence, and possessed of great fortune, remain thus when questioned. (74)
For the impurity of the menstrual flow is indeed a defilement that causes one to shine with impurity;
therefore, one should remain at a distance every day for as long as four days.
A woman who remains in the state of menstruation must never be touched;
by touching household objects and the like, they would become impure. (76)
Whether through ignorance or by chance, if a tactile defect should arise,
its cessation shall occur within a year by means of the Rishi-pañcamī vow.
On that day, a fast should be observed by women along with the worship of the gods; the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is Ṛṣipañcamī. (78)
During that vow, however, subsisting on fruit is considered auspicious for those who are incapable;
thus, even when this is done, there shall be no violation of the vow. (79)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Debt-Bondage, Marriage, Consecration, Offspring Corresponding to the Rite, and Vows for the Removal of the Defect of Menstruation," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O you who are devoted to your husband, O you who are faithful to your vows, having been married by Śrī Hari and having bowed to the Supreme God, they then wandered through the worlds.
By those two, through mere volition, millions of Brahmins were created;
indeed, all these Brahmins became masters of the fulfillment of their wills.
For them, there is no creation through sexual union, nor is it bound to any other means;
it is not dependent upon merit, nor does it require the assistance of piercing. || 3 ||
But these Brahmins, created by Brahmā, are indeed of the nature of Brahman;
they are all equal to Nārāyaṇa and possess the very form of Nārāyaṇa.
When Brahmā performed penance for the sake of his own creation,
at that time this creation was born solely from the Brahmins.
On the first day of Prajāpati, those Brāhmaṇas were all the creation of Nārāyaṇa; it was not the creation of Brahmā.
There, the lifespan of all those Brahmins is equal to that of Brahmā;
born together with the Creator, they perish along with him.
All those divine Brāhmaṇas go to the supreme city of Brahmā,
indeed to that divine and supreme abode of the Parameṣṭhin which consists of truth.
Remaining within the creation of Brahmā, those very same Brahmins in their entirety become the Brahmarṣis who exist throughout the duration of a day of Brahmā.
At the beginning of the first day, there were infinite [beings] even in Satyaloka;
they alone were also in Tapoloka, and in Janaloka as well, they were the Brahmins.
In Maharloka as well, those very same ones are Brahmins of divine form;
likewise in Svarga, in the intermediate space, on earth, and in the seven netherworlds (pātāla).
Everywhere, the divine brahmins were of one form and one disposition; they knew the single refined Sanskrit language and possessed a single caste and a single mode of livelihood.
All the men were sixteen years of age, and the women twelve;
they were all of equal condition, free from physical transformations and devoid of desire.
There is no impurity, nor any mental transformation born of desire for sexual union;
these are indeed meditators on Brahman, always devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman.
Capable of traveling to and fro throughout the fourteen worlds, they all move through the sky and can assume any form at will. || 16 ||
Those who know the nature of both the visible and the invisible, and who arise from the subtle and the gross,
are all of one kinship, having achieved their means through mental resolve alone.
Their food was nectar— the milk of cows and fruits—
and all those cows, who grant every desire, were bestowed by Hari.
Those very [beings] exist together upon the fourteen levels;
among those whose nature is that of Nārāyaṇa, none are ever deficient.
Whatever object is required indeed becomes available there for those ascetics who possess virtue, contentment, satisfaction, and so forth. (19)
There were no castes or stages of life there, nor were there villages and such;
there were no births of children and the like, nor was there death or old age.
There were no transformations of the body, no dwellers in houses, no fields for the purpose of cultivation, and no species of vehicles. ||21||
They dwell in rivers, mountains, lakes, caves, and highlands;
some live in water, some on land, and some in the sky.
Some have the wind as their support, some the stars, and some the vapors;
likewise, some have spiritual accomplishments as their support and others sovereignty—all of these are inhabitants.
Devoted to the worship of Brahman and intent upon meditation on Brahman and other such practices, those Brāhmaṇas are remembered as infinite pairs for all the worlds. ||24||
Indeed, all those hundreds of millions of *arbudas* of maidens were created by the vow of devotion to their husbands;
and all those hundreds of millions of *abjas* of youths were created by the vow of devotion to their wives.
As many as there are in the world of Truth (*satyaloka*), so many are there among the people of the ascetics (*tāpasa*).
And there are as many in Maharloka as there are in Svarga, Bhuvar, and the terrestrial realm.
Likewise in Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, and Pātāla, there were indeed Brāhmaṇīs and Brāhmaṇas. 27.
At that time, there were no established rules for anyone anywhere;
yet there existed bathing, meditation, chanting, and the worship of Śrī Hari. (28)
Hospitality, reverence, Vedic study, and the six acts of piety attend one through mere intention; for what purpose, then, is there the guarding of a treasury?
All who go to Vaikuṇṭha return again and again;
they depart for the next world and are joined with their dwelling places once more.
They truly become liberated just as those already liberated always are;
they possess unimpeded bodies and their objects of purpose are likewise unimpeded.
Their intentions were unimpeded and their splendor was unobstructed;
in Vaikuṇṭha, the world of Brahmā, there was not even the slightest difference between them.
In the fourteen worlds, there was not even the slightest inequality;
just as it was among men, so too among women there was no distinction in limb.
But with divine vision, they all appear radiant with one another's splendor;
they shine with divine forms, possessing the perfection of their own volitions.
The very grace of Śrī Hari that arises toward them through love and devotion is itself true dharma, itself right conduct, and itself the means to the attainment of bliss. (35)
All were indeed Vaiṣṇavas, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
having taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa, they were like those immersed in liberation.
And they dwell free from old age, birth, death, and disease; there is no anxiety, nor any mental affliction, nor obstacle, nor any untimely death.
In that regard, the object of focus is not fortune, because the object of focus is Hari alone;
nor is the teacher the object of focus, because the teacher is Śrī Hari himself.
Thus proceeds the first period of the undertaking;
for that is indeed the great divine time of the Creator. (39)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of All the Brāhmaṇas Alone on the First Day by Prajāpati," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, then the self-born Lord Brahmā, the Master,
desiring to create the multitudes of living beings, performed meditation.
"In the world of truth (Satyaloka), my creation shall be mental and characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
While he was meditating thus, those Brāhmaṇas who were endowed with goodness appeared there.
These very ones are the "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas), for they are established in the highest height; since they turned upward from there, they are known as the Upstreamers. || 3 ||
Abounding in happiness and joy, they were steadfast in their virtuous vows both internally and externally; they were luminous both within and without, and were indeed the very stream of Brahman.
Those sages are always considered sages because they are filled with the knowledge of the seer Brahmā;
through their realization of the Veda, those sages are eternally regarded as such.
The root *ṛṣ* is understood in the senses of "going," "hearing," "truth," and "asceticism. One who is fully disciplined in these is known as a *brāhmaṇa*, that is, a *ṛṣi*.
At the very moment of cessation, the Sage himself perceives the Unmanifest through his intellect;
because he perceives that which is supreme, he is therefore remembered as the Supreme Sage (Paramarṣi). || 7 ||
The derivation of the name "Ṛṣi" originates from the root *ṛṣ*, meaning "to go," from the very beginning;
because he is self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*), his status as a seer (*ṛṣitā*) is thus considered established.
The lords were born spontaneously as the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
because even when surrounded by great honors, he was not struck down by those very honors in his presence.

Because those wise ones perceive the Great One who is endowed with virtues in every respect, they are called "Great Seers" (Maharṣis), for they behold that which is beyond the intellect. || 1.38.10 ||
These very ones are celibate students, O Creator, possessing a lifespan equal to that of Brahmā;
they become equal to Brahmā in both form and domain.
Having attained the bliss of Brahman through sovereign power, they became equal to Him;
these were the eighty-eight thousand sages who had sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas).
All of them were born from the mind of Brahmā and dwell in truth;
the Unborn One bestows upon them their respective names according to their requirements.
Then, as he was meditating, the creation of the stream of knowledge emerged:
the divine seers, possessed of knowledge, whose essence is wisdom and who are preceded by the power of the self. (14)
From the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the renunciants (saṃnyāsas) were born from Brahmā:
the Vaikhānasas, the Bālakhilyas, the Audumbaras, and the Phenapas.
There are many types of Kuṭīcakas, Haṃsas, and Paramahaṃsakas;
these are the eight divisions of renunciants (saṃnyāsins), among whom the first [the Kuṭīcakas] are indeed in their thousands.
There are sixty thousand great sages known as the Bālakhilyas; others, such as the Audumbaraprabhṛtis, are to be understood as numbering in the tens of millions.
Then, as he was meditating, Ṛbhu and Agni were born;
and again, as he was meditating, ten sons were born to him.
The creators of the succession of worlds, preeminent in the knowledge of both theoretical and practical wisdom, were Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (19)
Bhṛgu, Vaśiṣṭha, and Dakṣa were there, with Nārada as the tenth;
Nārada was born from the lap, while Dakṣa was born from the thumb of the Creator.
Vasiṣṭha was born from his breath, Bhṛgu from his skin, and Kratu from his hand;
Pulaha was born from his navel, and the sage Pulastya from his ears.
Aṅgiras was born from his mouth, Atri from his eye, and Marīci from his mind;
Puṇya was born from his right breast, while Pāpa was born from his back.
From Chāyā was born Kardama; these three were also mind-born (mānasa).
Then, as he was meditating, Svāyaṃbhuva Manu was likewise born.
And Śatarūpā was his wife; thus they became a couple. Through the practice of the dharma of procreation, offspring increased from them.
Then, as he was meditating, these sages were born,
who were the expanders of the lineage and the causes for the continuation of the worlds.
In the first age, indeed, all are born from the mind;
but in another kalpa, some of them are also born from lineages.
Whether [a being] is born from a womb or not born from a womb, Viṣṇu’s will alone is the cause;
whenever and wherever He has a need for certain beings, He impels them at that time.
The directions, poetic compositions, passions, and subtle objects of the senses,
as well as the sense organs and the vital breaths, are indeed the mental faculties of Brahmā.
Ruci, Agni, and Medhā were the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
as were Kāvya, Bṛhaspati, Kaśyapa, and Uśanas.
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Sāyujya, and likewise Auśija; Kardama, Viśravas, Śakti, the Bālakhilyas, and the Adharas. || 1.38.30 ||
Śveta and the sages known as the Mānasas are considered to have originated from Brahmā through his mind; likewise Vatsara, Nagrahu, Bhāradvāja, and Analāyana.
Bṛhaduktha, Śaradvān, Agastya, and likewise Auśija;
the seer Dīrghatamas, Bṛhadgrantha, and Śaradvata. ||32||
Vājaśravas, Suvitta, Suvāg, Veṣaparāyaṇa, Dadhīca, Śaṅkha, Āma, and likewise King Vaiśravaṇa. ||33||
All these sages, though born of mind, are considered to be true;
so too are Bhṛgu, Kāvya, Pracetas, and the self-possessed Dadhīca.
Aurva, Jamadagni, Vida, Sārasvata, Adviṣeṇa, Arūpa, Vītahavya, and Sumedhas; ||35||
Vāstu, Pṛthu, Divodāsa, Paśvāsya, Gṛtsamān, Nabhas, Atri, Arciṣan, Śyāmavat, and Niṣṭhura; ||36||
Valgūtaka, the wise sage, and he who was Pūrvātithi—these are considered the ancient mental (mānasa) seers (ṛṣis) by means of these mantras. ||37||
Aṅgiras, Vaidhasa, Bhāradvāja, Bāṣkali, Amṛta, Gārgya, Śyenī, and Saṃhṛti as well. ||38||
Purukutsa, Ṛṣabha, Kaṇva, and Mudgala, as well as Utathya, Bharadvāja, and Vājaśravas. ||39||
Āpyāya, Suvitti, and likewise Vāmadeva;
Kakṣīvān, Aujasa, Dīrghatapas, Vyāsa, and Devala. ||1.38.40||
Kaśyapa, Vibhrama, Raibhya, Asita, Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, Yājñavalkya, and Maitrāvaruṇa. ||41||
Indrapramiti, Kuṇḍi, Kuśa, Pippalāyana,
Gopāla, and Kambharā— these couples were the progeny of Brahmā.
Thus were they formerly mind-born; later, they were also born from a womb.
Others too, though mind-born, were subsequently produced from a womb.
Their lineages and descendants arose, by whom the world was filled;
in every kalpa, others and yet others are born again by the command of Brahmā. (44)
Therefore, those who act for the welfare of the world attain truth;
they also come to share in the same world, the same life-span, and the same power as Brahmā.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mental Creation of the Sages and Others of Satyaloka," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the many mental sons of the Pitṛs;
indeed, while Brahmā was creating his sons, the Pitṛs were born from him.
The six seasons, beginning with spring (madhu), were born as the Pitṛs;
they are indeed the Agniṣvātta and Bārhiṣada ancestors, who are mental (mānasa) offspring. || 2 ||
These Pitṛs—both the drinkers of clarified butter (ājyapa) and the drinkers of Soma (somapa)—as well as the Mānasas, were likewise householders who did not perform sacrifices. || 3 ||
Those ancestors who have not maintained the sacred fires are indeed the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs;
those among them who were performers of sacrifices are the Soma-drinking Pitṛs.
Those who are the Bārhiṣads are indeed the ancestors of the Agnihotrins;
these are both the Ṛṣis and the Pitṛs, for they are born from the creative resolve of Brahmā.
Madhu and Mādhava are steeped in nectar; Śuci and Śukra are full of vigor; Nabha and Nabhasya are full of life; and Urja and Sahas are flooded with ambrosia.
Sahasa and Sahasya, Samanya and Tapas, Tapasya and Ghoraka— these are the pairs of seasons, whose nature consists of cause and effect.

Among them, those who are the mind-born sons of Brahmā are the presiding deities (abhimānins) over the sphere of effects, such as the divisions of time beginning with *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, months, and years.
The Pitṛs (Ancestors) are indeed conscious beings who possess knowledge and self-conceit;
the Great Year is Time, and its sons are known as the Seasons.
The ages (yugas) and the kalpas are indeed greater and greatest;
they are the ancestors born from the son of Brahmā, existing in the form of both cause and effect.
The sons of Ṛtu were Dinādi and others; their sons were Ārtava and others.
The sons of Ārtava were Sthāneśvara and others, who were also known as Sthānātman.
Prajāpati himself is Brahmā, assuming the form of the year and other such measures;
the year itself is Agni, for it signifies the Truth (Ṛta).
From the Seasons (Ṛtu) came those very Seasons, and from them the months were considered to arise;
likewise for bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, and reptiles.
Whatever flower belongs to stationary beings (sthāvara) is indeed considered to be produced by the seasons (kālārtava).
Because there is no distinction between the cause and the effect, the name is identical, signifying the ancestors (pitṛ). || 14 ||
Thus the Pitṛs are to be known, as well as the seasons (ṛtus) and the seasonal periods (ārtavas);
from them, at the time of the seasons, all beings were born.
Therefore, these Pitṛs were also created by Brahmā from the Ṛtus;
and from the Pitṛs, two daughters were born, Menā and Dhāraṇī.
Those two daughters of the Pitṛs, who were practitioners of yoga, exponents of Brahman, and highly esteemed, were given by the Bārhiṣads as wives to Himavat. || 17 ||
Maināka was born from Menā, and from Dhāraṇī, Mandara was born; furthermore, the daughters Velā, Niyati, and Āyati were also born.
Dhātṛ’s wife was Āyati, and Niyati is remembered as the wife of Vidhātṛ;
she gave birth to Velā, an auspicious daughter of the ocean, from Sāgara.
And Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Sāvarṇi;
they were the Prācīnabarhis, known as the ten Pracetas.
Then the Varkshas gave their daughter Vārkṣī to them; from her Dakṣa was born, the son of Pracetas. The Pitṛs (Ancestors) are remembered as ending with Dakṣa.
And those many wives of his dwell in the world of the ancestors (pitrya) and the world of austerity (tapas);
all of them were born from his mind, though in the Manvantara they are born from a womb.
Furthermore, those sages who are said to reside in Satyaloka, and those born in their lineages, are also celebrated as Pitṛs.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha—these eight are the sons of Brahmā. ||24||
Then, impelled by Brahmā, these mental sons produced the Pitṛs who dwell in the Tapoloka.
They were the Bhārgavas, the Āṅgirasas, and the Mārīcas;
likewise others who were the Paulastyas, the Paulahas, and the Krātus.
The Ātreyas and likewise the Vāsiṣṭhas, renowned throughout the world—
these are declared to be the hosts of the Pitṛs who dwell in the Tapoloka.
Among them, some are formless and luminous, while others are likewise radiant; indeed, those ancestors possess such diverse natures.
Furthermore, the sons of Dakṣa were the Haryaśvas and the Śabalāśvas,
numbering ten thousand and five thousand.
All of them, numbering one thousand and five hundred, possessed the splendor of Brahman;
having entered the path of austerity, they remained established in penance.
Intent on searching for Brahmā at the instruction of Nārada, they, possessing divine splendor, arrived at the world of Tapas and remained there. || 31 ||
These ancestors,
such as Ṛbhu, Sanatkumāra, and others, who bring about the welfare of all beings, sometimes reside among the ascetics.
For the sake of carrying out her duties in asceticism and for the purpose of meditation, she remained established there;
[there were] Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and others were likewise produced in the beginning; first, the Brahmin was born together with the mind.
Then, having established their subjects, all those hosts beginning with the Yāmas, who dwell in Maharloka, take refuge in Janaloka alone. (35)
But when Maharloka is destroyed, they take refuge in Janaloka alone;
having gone there, they all indeed exist with subtle bodies.
Possessing equal powers and likewise assuming identical forms,
they dwell in Janaloka for as long as the night of Brahmā lasts.
Even there, those who were the Prajāpatis in previous kalpas, endowed with the power of merit and renown, ceased from their status as lords. (38)
With their activities ceased, established in themselves, and likewise well-disposed,
they abandon the Janaloka and proceed to the Tapoloka together with them.
The maintenance of the Manvantaras, beginning with Svāyambhuva, occurs within the realm of the living;
the maintenance of the gods whose offices have ceased occurs within the realm of light.
Those who are the Manvantaras beginning with Śukra and ending with Cākṣuṣa reside in Maharloka and are born from the mind of Brahmā.
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, as well as Svāyambhuva, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and others such as these. ||42||
Indeed, for the sake of the continuous flow of worldly existence, all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) go even to Maharloka; they remain there together with them.
Even those established in truth come here repeatedly for the sake of some business;
once their business is accomplished, they all return again to their own homes. (44)
The worlds named Somapada are known as Maharloka;
the Pitṛs, such as the Agniṣvātta and others, reside there. (45)
The Vasus also exist, beginning with Amāvasu;
they are indeed the most subtle sparks of fire, who are the Pitṛs and the deities.
Those who were the sons of Virajā are the groups known as the Vairājas;
among them, the ancestors (pitṛs) are remembered as the Agniṣvāttas, possessing radiant splendor.
The sons of Svadhā and likewise the sons of Svāhā, who are radiant with light, are the Marīcigarbhas; there, indeed, are the ancestors (pitṛs) in the form of fire. ||48||
Those ancestors who are birds are known as the Ājyapās;
their world is called Mānasa, where they reside. (49)
The sons of Viraja, who are known by the name Vairājas, are radiant, partakers of merit, and indeed formless; they constitute those [divine] hosts.

Those who are considered the daughters of the ancestors and their sons (the dauhitras), as well as the ancestors who have expanded the lineage and reside in different dwellings, should be understood [as such]. ||5 1||

On earth they are in the form of virtuous women and holy men; in the intermediate space, they consist of the nature of wind; in heaven, they consist of the nature of gods; and in the realms of Maharloka, Janarloka, and Tapoloka, they are of mental birth.
The Pitṛs dwell together, possessing both embodied and unembodied forms;
they are all primordial deities, great beings of immense power. (53)
When satisfied, they grant all desires; when enraged, they are considered to take away everything. Therefore, they must always be propitiated with every effort. (54)
For those who indeed abide in Mahārāja and the other [stages], their accomplishment is mental;
everything desired by them arises immediately through the mind. 55.
Thus, O beloved Lakṣmī, all the great sages are established in the world of austerity (Tapoloka), and the ancestors are established in every way in the world of living beings (Janaloka). ||56||
In Maharloka, the world-protectors, the Rudras, the lords of progeny,
the Manus, and the ancestors likewise remained, each established according to their respective duties.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mental Creation and the Ancestors in the Mahar, Jana, and Tapa Lokas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
How many kinds of ancestors are to be understood? What is to be given, and likewise what is the fruit?
[This is asked] with reference to the father, and likewise the father of the father. || 1 ||

To whom among the three ancestors—namely the father and the grandfather—are the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be given by name? What kinds of śrāddhas should be offered, and how indeed do they reach the ancestors? || 2 ||
Whether on earth, in the intermediate space, or in heaven—whether they are suffering or happy—the ancestors who have attained a body may or may not be the *pitṛs*. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The gods, the sages, and indeed numerous living beings,
having come together in the world of action (karmaloka), performed manifold deeds.
Those ancestors are indeed born as inhabitants of the worlds beginning with the Earth;
some dwell upon the Earth, while others reside in the intermediate region (bhuvaḥ stara).
All of them, however, die suddenly due to their latent impressions (vāsanās);
yet some who are devoted to merit go indeed to heaven.
Some, through their merit, go to the worlds of Maharloka and Tapoloka; others likewise go to the world of Soma, the world of Sūrya, and the world of lightning.
They go to the world of Agni, the world of Indra, and to the stars, planets, and constellations according to their merit; they are remembered as the gods who are the ancestors (pitṛs).
The ancestors become gods, and the gods, in turn, become ancestors;
there are worlds known as Sāntānika, which are considered radiant for the ancestors.
Wherever the descendants may be situated, they should remember those ancestors for whom they perform the ancestral rites;
for it is necessary that the ancestors who are entitled to the lineage-offering must certainly come there.
Among the Pitṛs, however, Soma and Aryaman shall be kings;
and Aryaman daily stimulates Soma with his rays.
And Soma indeed nourishes the entire world with his rays;
therefore, all the ancestors are satisfied by drinking Soma.
But by gratifying Soma, their father, with śrāddha offerings, they shall attain satisfaction.
Those ancestors who dwell in the world of Soma and subsist on Soma; || 13 ||
Soma, nourished by those performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), will nourish the entire world—
including its mountains and forests, and all that is mobile and immobile.
Those men who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) while desiring prosperity,
to them the ancestors will always grant prosperity as well as progeny.
Those ancestors, including the great-grandfather, who exist everywhere, to whom they shall offer three rice-balls at the *śrāddha* ceremony according to name and lineage; ||| 16 ||
