And by the offering of the śrāddha, the ancestors, together with their latent impressions (vāsanas), will cause those offspring— whether happy or even miserable— to be nourished.
The descendants must certainly provide them with water and food according to their capacity;
by that, the ancestors—whether possessing form or being formless—shall be satisfied.
Seven groups of them are proclaimed, worshipped throughout the three worlds;
three of them are formless, while four possess form.
Above them, three exist as the embodiments of existence;
below them, four exist as the subtle embodiments. ||1.40.20||
Those whose form is composed of intention (bhāva) are satisfied by faith and meditation;
those whose form is subtle (sūkṣma) become satisfied by the merit of food and other offerings. ||21||
Moving with the speed of thought, devoted to their own nature, and possessing all desirable things as their wealth, they nourish themselves with food and Soma, their minds fully satisfied. (22)
In that regard, those who are faithful are satisfied at a funeral rite by offerings of water and food, through the disposition of giving;
whereas the wise devotees of Viṣṇu are satisfied by acts such as the ritual of offering everything to Brahman.
At the end of a full thousand yugas, those who discourse on Brahman are born;
casting off their physical bodies, they attain liberation as formless beings.
The embodied forms are satisfied by ritual actions and the worship of the guru;
furthermore, those ancestors, being satisfied at the śrāddha ceremony, drink the soma.
One should feed thousands of virtuous Brahmins and children;
by the feeding of these virtuous women as well, one's ancestors are satisfied. (26)
With a thousand Brahmins who have completed their Vedic studies, with a hundred *snātakas*, with a thousand who are without protectors, and with a hundred forest-dwellers; ||27||
One virtuous man and one virtuous woman excel in the matter of eating;
for they are the children of Hari, consisting of knowledge and meditation. (28)
"Divine, bestowers of liberation, contented, yogis who have become one with Brahman—whether it be a son, a grandson, or a great-grandson, those two boys shall feed you. (29)
His ancestors are satisfied, just as farmers are by a well-timed rain;
in the absence of virtuous men and women, one should feed two celibate students (brahmacārins).
But if he does not obtain him, he should feed his daughter's son or even a guest.
And the Siddhas wander in many ways every day in a concealed form.
One should always worship that guest, who is the very embodiment of the virtuous male and female practitioners;
for even the gods, the lords of yoga, and the earth bounded by the oceans [do so]. (32)
Moving about in various forms, these protectors of the dharma of living beings—accomplished ones, holy men, and virtuous women—wander upon the surface of the earth. (33)
One should perform their worship in the form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and offer them delightful food, side dishes, and fruits. (34)
The gods, the ancestors, and the sacred fire, having entered those who appear in the form of guests, partake [of the offerings]; therefore, one should always honor such guests. 35.
One should always regard children, those who have arrived from afar, the weary, virtuous men, and virtuous women without support, as well as devoted supplicants, as being of the nature of guests. 36.
A beggar is one who has arrived as a petitioner; a guest is one who has arrived without asking. [One should offer] to the thirsty, the weary, the wandering, and the intensely hungry. (37)
One who desires the fruit of sacrifice should, after honoring him, give [the gift] to one who is learned, virtuous, chaste, a child, or one who has no other refuge. (38)
And the virtuous, high-souled ones, having been honored and worshipped at the śrāddha ceremony, [bestow their blessings].
The ancestors bestow liberation, yoga, and even sovereign power. ||39||
Whatever is given by all [the ancestors] using silver vessels, or those adorned with silver,
while placing the word "svadhā" before it, truly gratifies the ancestors in that manner.
One truly delights the ancestors through devotion, and the ancestors delight him in return.
Furthermore, for one desiring prosperity or desiring worship, the Pitṛs [are the deities]. ||41||
They bestow nourishment, progeny, and a good heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Thousands of celestial chariots were joined by throngs of apsarases.
The ancestors bestow all desired objects that have been accomplished.
Wisdom, nourishment, mindfulness, intelligence, sovereignty, and even health; ||43||
Grandfathers bestow pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, tens of thousands of horses and elephants, and even crores of jewels.
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is said to be fit for the ancestors;
however, a vessel of silver or one coated with silver is the most excellent for the ancestors.
Even a mere conversation about silver, or seeing it, or giving it away—such a gift for the ancestors is said to be infinite, inexhaustible, and leading to heaven. (46)
Moreover, by this gift, those worthy recipients cause their ancestors to cross over.
Gold, silver, copper, a daughter's son, blankets from Kufa, and sesame seeds. ||47||
Clothing, purifying substances, and even a virtuous woman are called "good" (sādhu);
likewise, whatever food is delicious by which the ancestors are gratified [is also so called]. 48.
I shall indeed proclaim those [mantras] to you, which truly bestow all desires.
At the time of the śrāddha ceremony, one should indeed provide excellent foods for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Rice cooked with milk (paramānna), milk-porridge, pūrikās, polikās,
apūpas with a hundred holes, and sweet stuffed polikās.
And likewise rutalyas, ghāripūrikās, and praroṭakas.
Phāphaṭas, as well as sthirakas, ghee-powders, and rice mixed with jaggery. ||51||
Śaṣkulīs, khājakas, saṃyāvas, and likewise modakas;
kaṃsāras, parpikās, khaṇḍas, piṇḍakas, and likewise granthakas. ||52||
There were also *kalikālaḍukās*, as well as *kalikās* and *sevikās*;
*sohālikās*, *maṇḍakas*, *vaṭikās*, and *ghṛtapūraṇas*. ||53||
Cakes, pearls, garments, and thread-rolls.
Rice flour, mung bean dumplings, and ghurgharas provide happiness. ||54||
Tilaśrṛṅkhā, gundrapāka, and pītasārā sugars.
Inauspicious is the vessel of delusion; it is a heap of rice and flower-buds. ||55||
And likewise rice, barley, rājagava, and so forth.
Śṛṅgāṭakas, raktālavas, vaṭāṇas, and likewise dvidalas; ||56||
Vhālā, parpaṭas, parpaṭyas, kvathikā, curd, green mung beans, mung beans, tuvaryas, and milk. (57)
Vegetables seasoned with cinnamon, cloves, and cardamom; honey;
*gavāhāra* beans; *bhiṇḍaka* gourds; and red *cirbhaṭa* cucumbers. ||58||
Karkaṭī, kāravella, kūṣmāṇḍa, and likewise sūraṇa;
vṛntāka, śarkarākanda, śimbikā, and kharbuja as well. ||59||
Paṭola, gaṇḍaka, and parāvala are also prepared with sixfold ghee.
Lūnikā, methikā, rājñī, jīvantī, and suvamūlakā. ||1.40.60||
Indeed, there are tāṇḍulājya, hyamblalūnī, rājagraha, dugdhikā, kunarā, śarkarātiktā, and various kinds of patravallīs. 61.
Frying eggplants, eating snacks, and consuming butter—these are for those lacking the wisdom to distinguish between coriander and *kauthumī*. (6)
[One should offer] grapes, sugar-cane, plantains, mustard seeds, and bitter substances; curd-smeared mustard seeds, and various kinds of sour gruel (āranāla). 63.
There were sweet foods, all fresh, as well as excellent dishes fit for consumption.
There were also drinks mixed with sweets, fragrant and flavorful. ||64||
Sugarcane, nāraṅga, plantain, jambīra, aṅguda, santura, setu, rāmṛta, saphala, jananaspati, and jāmbava; ||65||
Iṅguda, coconut, mango, jackfruit, lipsikā, and cikā; likewise, jujube, aṅgura, pūpīya, nāna, and āmalaka. (66)
The fruits of the *rāmaphala*, *pāpanasa*, and *sītāphala*, along with the *subilvaka*;
these are the fruits, as well as the excellent leaves of betel and areca nut. (67)
Water originating from sacred fords and flowers that are very fragrant.
It should be given especially at a *śrāddha* ceremony for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors. ||68||
That by which it is given, that to whom it is given, that for the sake of whose satisfaction it is given, and indeed that wherein it is given;
In these three cases, the Blessed One is directly the giver, the receiver, and the leader. ||69||
The sacrificer [should meditate upon] Hari, who is the giver of one's own true nature and who is all-pervading.
Having meditated upon Hari in the form of the recipient, it should indeed be given.
That glorious Hari, the all-pervading one, dwells even within the father.
But through connection with Hari everywhere, satisfaction shall indeed come to the ancestors. ||71||
Having uttered the names of the ancestors, one should give [the offering] with the thought that it is for Hari.
That satisfaction shall be inexhaustible; even a very small amount shall become incomparable.
Maidens, widows, women, the elderly, and those without a protector should be fed with auspicious intent; at a śrāddha ceremony, the fruit of such an act is infinite.
A village may be consumed by the suppression of smoke for one seeking the fruit [of merit];
yet his reward exceeds that of a sacrifice, as it is enjoyed by beasts and birds. (74)
And where even insects and other creatures dwelling in the water consume [the offerings],
that Śrāddha is said to be the universal soul, the sovereign of all.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of Various Ancestors, Their Vessels, the Food and Fruits to be Offered to Them, and the Fruits of Attaining Those [Benefits]," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 40 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall proclaim for you their auspicious hymn of praise, which grants all desires, by means of which the ancestors are pleased through recitation and observance.
That should be recited at the time of the śrāddha ceremony for the sake of pleasing the ancestors.
By the sacrificer, by his son, and by the most virtuous Brāhmaṇa. || 2 ||
Of the formless ancestors and those with forms, who possess blazing splendor.
I always pay homage to those meditators who possess the eye of yoga.
I bow to those bestowers of desires, who are the progenitors of Indra and the others, as well as of Bhṛgu and Mārīca, and of the seven ṛṣis and the ancestors.
I bow to the Pitṛs, the bestowers of well-being, who are the progenitors of Manu and the other lords of the gods, as well as of the Sun and the Moon.
Then [he should offer to] the ancestors and grandfathers of the constellations, such as Carā and the others.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to Heaven and Earth and to the ancestors. ||6||
The progenitors of the divine sages, who are honored by all the worlds.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow down to those who always grant fearlessness. || 7 ||
To Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures, and to Soma and Varuṇa.
And with palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the masters of yoga. || 8 ||
Salutations to the seven groups of ancestors in the seven worlds.
Salutations to that Self-Existent One, to Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga.
By means of this supreme hymn of praise, a person obtains three boons.
The benevolent ancestors bestow food, long life, and sons.
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be food to be chewed or swallowed and so forth, one must not consume it without first offering it to the gods and the ancestors. (11)
But he who offers garlands and fragrant substances of every kind to both parents;
Endowed with prosperity, he who always gives shines like the sun. ||12||
He who offers incense such as guggulu and other fragrances to the ancestors;
If one consumes it combined with honey and clarified butter, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. ||13||
One who offers incense endowed with the quality of fragrance, which is pleasing and dedicated to the ancestors, obtains offspring through women—both in this world and in the next. (14)
He who, being self-restrained, always offers a lamp to the ancestors, [attains great merit].
He obtains in this world an incomparable eye that bestows divine vision. ||15||
By means of splendor, fame, beauty, and even strength,
he becomes self-luminous and shines in the triple heaven.
Surrounded by Apsarases, he rejoiced at the forefront of the celestial chariot.
One should indeed offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and oblations of clarified butter.
One should bring satisfaction to the ancestors with offerings of fruits, roots, and prostrations;
for at the time of the śrāddha, the grandfathers are always present in the form of the wind.
And upon seeing virtuous twice-born men and virtuous women, they enter them with joy.
With garments, food, gifts, and likewise with various kinds of eatables and delicacies. ||19||
One should honor those who have taken refuge as vessels with drinks, cows, and villages;
likewise, the kāśas, the punarbhavas, the barhiṇas, and the upabarhiṇas.
Those very ancestors are gods, and the gods are again ancestors.
One should carefully offer darbha grass and funeral cakes (piṇḍas) facing toward the twice-born.
Then, having brought the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the oblation is prescribed as follows:
"Svadhā to Agni Kavyavāha; salutation to Aṅgiras. (22)
To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! And obeisance to Aṅgiras!
And saying, "Svadhā and obeisance to Yama, the son of Aṅgiras," ||23||
Especially in a well-kindled fire, there is indeed an abundance of oblations.
And when the fire is smokeless and flickering, one should offer oblations for the successful completion of the rite. ||24||
He who offers oblations into a fire that is unkindled and full of smoke, [commits a fault].
The sacrificer would become blind, and he would also remain childless. ||25||
Whether it has little fuel, or is dry, or emits sparks in every direction.
If the flames and smoke move to the right, that fire does not lead to success.
It is foul-smelling, blue, and especially black.
One should know that wherever he penetrates the earth, there will be defeat. ||27||
Radiant, with a massed crest of flame, produced from clarified butter and gold.
A fire that is smooth and moving clockwise is favorable for the accomplishment of one's purpose. ||28||
"Perform it," he was thus authorized by those best of the twice-born.
Taking his wife and sons, he should offer oblations into the fire.
The *samidh* wood for the sacrifice consists of *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, and *vikaṅkata*, as well as *udumbara*, *bilva*, and *candana*. 1.41.30.
The sarala, the devadāru, the śāla, and likewise the khadira;
These trees, in particular, are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel.
And those who are called the Viśvedevas—these too are indeed the ancestors (pitṛs).
One should diligently offer them clarified butter and funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into the fire. ||3||
And likewise of flowers, fruits, and various kinds of edible foods.
Having extracted the foremost portion from all [the offerings], one should offer it into the Jātavedas fire.
At a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should respectfully perform the fire sacrifice (homa), the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa), and the ancestral rite (śrāddha).
Likewise, temples, the abode of a guru, mountains, and rivers [are also such places]. (34)
Where there are sacred trees, ponds, or where a Brahmin may be present.
Those various places shall be worthy of ancestral rites (śrāddha); therein, merit is incalculable.
Divine and virtuous persons always [protect] the earth bounded by the shores of the ocean.
They move about here in various forms, but through yoga, they attain liberation.
The Siddhas, the virtuous, and the holy women constitute the supreme pilgrimage site among all pilgrimage sites;
for Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa dwell here incessantly within those very forms.
To one who is thirsty, weary, hungry, or destitute, one should give something with due respect; thus one shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice. (38)
In the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the gross [self] eats the gross; the ancestors eat the merit (sukṛta). Through the offering to Brahman, the Self itself experiences satisfaction. 39.
In the world of action, having indeed performed [deeds] and having indeed given [gifts] again and again, these are obtained in the next world; therefore, one should give especially.
To those for whom the kinsmen shall offer three morsels of food, mentioning their names and lineages.
And upon the ground covered with Kuśa grass, according to the procedure prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas. ||41||
These rice-balls, offered everywhere, truly gratify the ancestors;
whatever food a living being consumes, that very food becomes theirs.
Just as a calf finds its mother who has wandered lost in the cow-pen, so does the mantra lead the person to wherever he abides. 43.
The name, the lineage, and the mantra lead him to the food that has been given.
Even if they obtain hundreds of wombs, thirst follows after them.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Hymns, Fire-offerings, the Sacred Tree, the Location, and so forth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, I shall describe the arrangement of the gods in brief.
All the mind-born gods of Brahmā are well-established in heaven.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you what happened after that; [I shall describe] those who nourish the ancestors through the splendor of their excellent penance. (2)
And kings, as the protectors of their subjects, are to be looked up to.
The Manus are indeed the protectors of the worlds and their observers as well.
For their sake, dwellings that are bright and conducive to nourishment were constructed.
Having reflected thus, Brahmā himself indeed performed meditative contemplation.
Having remembered the supreme Nārāyaṇa, he undertook what was to be done.
First, however, there is the great fire, which performs the functions of ripening and illuminating. ||5||
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he joyfully prayed to Śrī Hari for that second great splendor, which likewise bestows power and nourishment, while remaining in meditative absorption.
Then, even before that, from the eye of Śrī Hari on Dakṣa’s side,
a particle of splendor was born, which illuminates the universes.
Therefore, from that, countless particles were produced, and they became exceedingly fierce;
they too were introduced into the respective Brahmāṇḍas of those various Virañcis.
And in each of those places, at sunset, they became composed of light;
thus did the Sun come to be established by the Creator, the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, he was established in heaven for the sake of illuminating the worlds.
And Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, commanded him.
May you always be the Sun throughout the three worlds by your splendor—acting as the mere eyes for living beings and the perceivers of all objects. (11)
Where there is no illumination, how can there be the state of being an object of perception for things?
Therefore, the capacity to see will indeed arise through the close connection with light. ||12||
Therefore, the entire livelihood of the world shall indeed be rooted in seeing you; for that reason, do you become the maker of the day.
Thus commanded by Sūrya with the gift of his splendor,
he, fearing his own destruction, replied to Brahmā.
O God of gods, O Creator of the universe, I shall carry out your command.
Indeed, through the loss of my bodily luster, there may even be my destruction. ||15||
"I shall soon meet my destruction; therefore, become my protector!
Employ a means of protection here for me, so that I may remain unhurt. (16)
Having heard that from Brahmā, the imperishable Śrī Hari was remembered:
"Become yourself the fulfiller for the sake of filling the Sun. (17)
Nārāyaṇa Hari, having accepted that prayer of Brahmā, spoke to the god Brahmā like one who bestows fulfillment. ||18||
O Brahmin, I give it to you; may there be prosperity for you through the eye of the sun, which is mine.
For just as there would be an inexhaustible state, so too is form that which fulfills.
Having uttered this, Hari himself, a mass of splendor more dense than the densest, [appeared].
The person named Hiraṇmaya likewise has golden hair and a golden beard.
With golden hair down to his very nails, he was entirely made of gold;
at sixteen years of age, he was adorned with ornaments of gold.
But he whose forehead alone emits a thousand rays.
He whose head alone emits upward a million rays of light.
His body alone, indeed, emitted millions of rays of light.
Every single hair was filled with a mass of golden splendor. ||23||
Endowed with the beauty of form, sweetness, and auspicious qualities,
he wears a crown, earrings, and a garland, and is clad in a golden mantle.
A mass of inexhaustible splendor, illuminating with the brilliance of the sun.
The Blessed One, having become such as this, entered the orb of the sun. ||25||
Filling all splendors with the streams of his own radiance.
By Ravi, by Brahmā, and by others dwelling in Maharloka and the higher realms. ||26||
The Lord Sūryanārāyaṇa was worshipped and saluted with the sixteen-fold services; such is the worship of that Golden Man.
The eye of the world acts incessantly for the sake of bestowing [vision].
He utters this hymn of praise as a prayer for the fulfillment of his splendor. ||28||
Oṃ, salutations to You, the progenitor of splendor, the vast and imperishable light;
salutations to Brahman, the possessor of brilliance who bestows imperishable luster upon those who possess brilliance. ||29||
He whose many-horned, tireless cattle shine forth for the showerer [of rain].
Among the female lords and their male lords, his illustrious lineage attained splendor.
Salutation to that radiant one, the possessor of cows, who spreads forth with his rays;
salutation to you, the divine god, who dispels the darkness of the heart and possesses celestial splendor. ||31||
Salutation to the Sovereign Illuminator, who makes himself manifest.
Homage to the one who has cultivated the self, the sage of the awakening of knowledge. ||32||
Salutations to you, the ordainer of nourishment; salutations to you, the self that is the eternal Self;
salutations to the radiant one who, playing, bestows the seven vessels.
Homage to the one who dwells on earth, to the red one; homage to the celestial one, to the lightning;
homage to the sun, to the fierce one; homage to you, the golden one! (34)
Salutation to the true gold of the mine; salutation to the splendor of the belly;
salutation to the power of the moon; salutation to the self that extends as far as the dawn.
Salutations to the one whose nature is the effect, salutations to the one whose form is the cause;
to the golden-hued God, to Brahman, the Supreme Self. (36)
You are the creator, you are the nourisher, and you alone are indeed the destroyer;
you alone are the supreme splendor, the foremost among the radiant.
O Supreme Lord, always protect me by bestowing your splendor upon me.
And as many as possess vision shall worship the Lord of Light.
You alone are the Blessed One, the luminous one who illuminates all states of being and their powers;
you alone are the possessor of vision, the protector, the savior from distress, and the imperishable. (39)
O great eye, O heavenly eye, O eye of the mid-world, you alone are indeed the terrestrial eye and the eye of all; salutations to the Eye of eyes! 1.42.40.
Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ! Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! That Oṃ! We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. ||41||
Whoever, free from sloth, should recite this mantra and meditate upon it,
the supreme golden deity appears visibly before that person.
By reciting it ten thousand times, the great lord Sūrya himself [appears].
He becomes a granter of boons to him and bestows the state of a Blessed One. ||43||
It makes that eye divine and opens up the inner space;
it rouses the self and brings about that Brahman.
Therefore, being devoted to meditation, one should always recite this hymn composed by Sūrya for his own worship, for the sake of one's own spiritual welfare. 45.
Then indeed, by Brahmā, the golden Sun was provided with a male form.
Indeed, in the midst of all [the worlds], he shall be the bestower of all splendor. ||46||
Thus established in heaven, he alone is indeed the eye of the world;
for in his absence, those who possess eyes truly become sightless.
Through the radiance of its subtle atomic forms, it even becomes the divine eye;
it proceeds as the filler of the minute particles of light within the eyes.
Whatever living being there may be, by day or by night—indeed, every single one—[is sustained by this].
Whether it be very slight or even abundant, the eye possessing the brilliance of the sun—
its light becomes dense by day, but sparse at night.
And that [light] is born from the sun, consisting of the radiance obtained through a lineage of authoritative teachers.
Water, as well as leaves, flowers, and fruit, should be offered to Sūrya.
Salutations should always be offered, for he is indeed Jagannārāyaṇa. ||51||
The golden Puruṣa [beheld] Lakṣmī, whose body was golden.
Together with his own radiance, he constantly protected that mandala;
and when the end of the eon arrived and the destruction of heaven occurred, [he remained there].
Sūrya is golden, and Lakṣmī and the goddesses Sūryāṇīs are likewise. ||53||
They go indeed to the world of Brahmā, which is the supreme, imperishable, and undecaying;
there, for their residence, it was created by Śrī Hari himself. (54)
His own abode, named Hiraṇya, is divine within the imperishable realm;
there, the golden Person dwells together with the golden Lakṣmī.
Served by hundreds of billions of golden-hued male and female slaves,
the king of kings, the supreme lord, shines forever.
That divine, supreme abode is said here to be gross within the sun;
that root-abode situated in Brahman is the shadow of the solar orb.
That Puruṣa is the Supreme Brahman, golden-hued, and the Sun within the eye;
he is attained by those desiring liberation through the knowledge of the eye of meditation. 58.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Mental Sun, His Hymn of Praise, the Golden Person, and Other Matters," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When that singular, intense radiance was beheld by Brahmā,
it would have consumed everything, destroyed it, and caused nothing at all to flourish or remain.
Then, for the sake of pacification and prosperity, they prayed to the Lord,
the god Nārāyaṇa, from the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
From his resolve, a small amount of light emerged from his left eye—cool, nourishing, satiating, and raining down nectar. || 3 ||
Therefore, from a single atom, atoms of many millions and billions were produced;
indeed, by the will of the Creator, they became those great spheres.
They were indeed protected by the creators within their respective cosmic eggs.
And those moons born therein cause coolness to flow forth from this [place].
When he requested the Blessed One for the sake of fulfilling his splendor, the Lord replied,
"By me, who always dwell within the sun, through my rays."
There he will provide nourishment, and there your splendor shall reach fulfillment;
therefore, the Golden Man (Svarṇapuruṣa) bestows his brilliance day and night.
This nectar, which brings about peace and nourishment, should be drunk;
it is filled with bliss, moist, overflowing with joy, and is the cause for the cessation of all suffering.
Because it delivers one from the suffering of heat, that light is indeed the *tāraka* (the savior);
and because it binds together coolness, that light is also the lunar light.
And having thus fashioned that supreme moon, consisting of radiant light;
Brahmā protected it in heaven for the sake of the sweet bliss of embodied beings.
The moon, too, was always full and remained eternally constant; later, however, due to its partiality toward women, it fell into decline. ||11||
Furthermore, Śaṅkara also rescued him from half of that disease; likewise, because of his fitness, protection was then provided for half [of his body]. (12)
Śrī Lakṣmī said: "Tell me the story of the Moon, which concerns his partiality toward women."
O treasury of compassion, please cause me to hear that which brings about my destruction.
Who are his women, how many are they, and in what manner is he partial toward them?
How is there a curse? How is there liberation? And how is there partial destruction? ||14||
Listen to all of this, which is a supreme marvel to me.
O Lord, even for Your divine form, such is the suffering, O All-pervading One! 15.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen to his wonderful story, born of the impulse of desire, along with its full details;
having heard it, even though you suffer from the pain of rivalry with co-wives, you shall certainly not act in such a manner toward me.
In ancient times, Dakṣa, the Prajāpati and mind-born son of Brahmā,
mentally conceived daughters for the purpose of creation.
The twenty-seven maidens, headed by Rohiṇī, whom he gave to Candramas, became the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). ||18||
By name they are Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and likewise Rohiṇī.
Mṛgaśīrṣā, as well as Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Puṣya; ||19||
Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvāphālgunī, and Uttarāphālgunī.
Hasti, Citrā, as well as Svāti, Viśākhā, and Anurādhikā; ||1.43.20||
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, as well as Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā.
And Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and likewise Śatabhiṣaj (Śatatārā). ||21||
Likewise, both Pūrvabhādrapadā and Uttarabhādrapadā.
And Revatī; these are the twenty-seven wives of the Moon. ||22||
All divine, golden-hued, and red, they were twelve years of age.
Among them, she was preeminent, endowed with beauty, grace, good fortune, and excellent virtues.
Rohiṇī is always skilled in fulfilling desires, yet she is life-taking.
Just as the moon moves, so does Rohiṇī follow him. ||24||
The heart-stealing eye indeed displays an abundance of love toward him.
His face was gentle, filled with a smile, and possessed the radiant splendor of all erotic charm. ||25||
Even when displaying a contraction of her curved eyes and eyebrows, she captivates the heart.
With reddened lips and blooming cheeks, he indeed displays [a countenance] that bestows peace. ||26||
Holding a beautiful flower garland in his hand, he offers it as well.
Her breasts were small yet well-formed, and her bodice fit them firmly. ||27||
The young woman also displays her two lovely breasts, richly colored with saffron, as well as her gold-hued belly and her slender, very delicate waist. (28)
Her hips resemble the curves of a water-pot, and her garment reveals them;
she even displays her hairless, slender waist, which has the luster of gold. (29)
She even reveals her slow-moving anus between her golden thighs;
having come and given a slap on the cheeks, she departs in haste. (1.43.30)
Turning back again, placing her hand on his neck, and kissing him,
she touches his private parts and, offering her face, manifests her amorous grace.
Sometimes appearing even without a garment,
she displayed her own form and utterly stripped away the modesty of the moon, stealing his heart.
Although Candra was sixteen years of age, he was an inexhaustible treasury of vigor;
he took delight, he took delight again, he took delight, and with satisfaction he took delight again and again.
He always took delight with Rohiṇī, and he delighted with her again and again;
Rohiṇī, for her part, repeatedly assumed a fresh and lovely form.
Even after sporting with them, the Moon did not remember others;
yet at some time or another, he did sport with others as well. (35)
For even when their youth has fully blossomed and is equally radiant, all women do not find satisfaction from a lover here and there, just like Rohiṇī [alone] finds it from the moon. (36)
Because of her exclusive devotion to Rohiṇī, he did not treat all of them with equality;
consequently, they entreated their husband to come to them for their own happiness. (37)
Nevertheless, Rohiṇī did not consent to this for the sake of their happiness.
Exerting herself solely for her own sake, she displayed partiality. ||38||
At that time, however, others remained indifferent and did not feel grief for themselves.
What is the use of a fixed auspicious moment for those who do not possess the happiness of a husband? (39)
If the union of two people, both filled with desire and enriched by youth mounted upon passion, does not result in the pleasure of love, what is the use of that marriage? (1.43.40)
It provides the satisfaction of desire for both man and woman according to their wish.
It would not have been so, had he performed that rite with an auspicious moment while seeking its fruit in vain.
She whose body was filled with desire and who was endowed with fresh youth.
If one does not obtain happiness from her husband, what indeed is the use of having performed the marriage ceremony? ||4||
Rather than widowhood or remaining a maiden, therefore, this is said to be better.
While her husband is alive, she who is unfortunate does not obtain the pleasure of desire.
Better indeed is falling into a well, better is being consumed by fire.
It would be better to consume poison than to suffer the pain of burning desire.
Better is dwelling in one's father’s house, and better even is the state of being a virtuous wife;
but never, while a husband is alive, should one burn oneself with the fire of passion. (45)
May no man ever anywhere be the husband of any woman who is a eunuch.
Or let there be neither affection nor aversion, even for a single moment. ||46||
Or let there be no rivalry at all, nor even the slightest suffering born of enmity.
Having lamented thus in many ways, they all remained in their father's house.
Having gone, they reported their husband's suffering again and again.
O father, a daughter must not be given to one who is devoid of love and full of passion.
And for one who has fallen into partiality, or for a sick person lying among other women;
We must not go anywhere at all to the abode of Candra. ||49||
The moon never treats us with equality at all; it regards my father’s house as if it were dry wood, and my husband’s house as even more so. (1.43.50)
Everything becomes parched and withered, devoid of the bliss of passion.
"O Father, we speak the truth exactly as it was experienced, in every respect. (51)
Your son-in-law, however, constantly and repeatedly attends upon Rohiṇī.
If [the self] were not present in us anywhere at all, then even in that case there would be no fullness.
Therefore, we shall not go again to the abode of Candra.
One must certainly not go where there is nothing but suffering. ||53||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Birth of Candra from the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," followed by his partiality toward Rohiṇī and the subsequent report of this to Dakṣa by the other wives. ||43||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; hereafter I shall tell you what occurred next.
Having heard that, his father Dakṣa experienced great distress.
Gradually releasing his breath, he, overcome by compassion, said to the maidens:
"Let us go to the moon; I shall instruct him once again."
"One should not act thus; rather, one should maintain equal desire toward all.
Having resolved this, they all departed with reverence for the abode of Candra.
Dakṣa said: "O Lord Śaśin, you are my disciple, O observer of noble vows. You are already well-informed; what need is there for much instruction to be given to you? (4)
All these maidens, equal to one another and now young women, have been offered by me to you;
having seen them, they are all devoted to you and shall become your wives.
"Serve all women equally; indeed, abandon partiality. Serve all women with the desire for equal sensual pleasure. (6)
Do not be attached to one alone; be devoted to all of them. O Moon, desire all of them in such a way that they may each be satisfied.
He who brings to peace the burning desire of women shall possess prosperity, heaven, and manifold divine powers.
Those who please their wives, who give them life, always increase day by day, remaining uninjured and skilled in virtue; for such pleasing is ever a source of delight.
From the heart-born suffering of those women, a man may fall into hell;
for men there is indeed the True Dharma, but for women there is only the pacification of desire.
Therefore, one should not perform that marriage at such a time; a marriage performed then leads only to death.
It is better for a woman to remain without a husband than to enter a marriage devoid of the fulfillment of desire. 11.
If there is no auspicious result from the ascendant at the time of union between a woman and a man, then for either the woman or the man, that ascendant serves only as a burden. 12.
If, once the ascendant has been fixed, a person does not obtain the bliss of love, then that chosen ascendant was intended for the sake of union alone, and not for the sake of passion. 13.
How indeed could there not be a conjunction (dvandva) between two women or two men from the point of the ascendant?
In what manner would the Blessed Lord Hari fashion a man or a woman?
Or how is it that a woman is bestowed upon a man, but not a man upon a woman;
or how is it that there, a man takes a woman, but not a man? (15)
Thus, O Candra, having reflected, [he concluded that] all perfections of good fortune [reside therein].
Your wives should always be served by you for the sake of bestowing happiness. 16.
Having mentally identified himself with the syllable "Oṃ" as the Moon, and having worshipped Dakṣa with devotion,
he took all his wives and begot many offspring.
Furthermore, he gathered them all together and released them in many streams.
When a great deal of time had passed, he once again showed an abundance of affection toward Rohiṇī alone in every way, whereas his affection for the others was once more slight, just as before.
Then Dakṣa was properly informed by them again and again.
Then Dakṣa, having become enraged, spoke these beneficial words to Candramas: ||19||
"Candra, you have been properly instructed, and you shall be instructed by me once more:
you must always behave with impartiality toward all your wives. (1.44.20)
Then, may you always be prosperous and powerful like a yogi, possessing inexhaustible heroism and splendor, and bringing complete satisfaction to all. (21)
Thus, out of affection for your daughters, I shall grant you this favor;
for if I were to cast a curse upon you, it would bring suffering to your daughters. (22)
Therefore, I instruct you: be impartial toward all;
enjoy them all properly, and be a bestower of happiness according to their desire.
If you should proceed in this manner, then you will meet with destruction.
And through the exhaustion of your power and your vital energy, you shall experience suffering. ||24||
"You shall indeed live with but a single digit; of this there is no doubt.
Go now according to my word, and may you always remain full of all digits. (25)
Thus, having meditated again and again upon that which was spoken by Dakṣa, [he reflected].
He always and repeatedly delights with all his wives, remaining ever equanimous. ||26||
But Rohiṇī, the passionate woman, would forcibly restrain him right in her own home in many ways, her mind unsatisfied by desire.
Other wives waited for their husband’s path in the courtyard, looking for the moon;
when the lord did not come, they wept and uttered curses.
While you are our lord, we, as your wives, do not obtain the fulfillment of our desires.
Otherwise, however, at that time the maiden was like one without a protector, even though she had a protector. ||29||
If he were not our protector, may he likewise not be the protector of Rohiṇī.
Having thus reviled him, they all reproached their lord again and again.
O Moon, go always toward your decline; your splendor and vigor shall perish.
Whether you possess vigor or lack it, O winged one, you are but a mere being.
We do not even gain the opportunity for our seasonal rites; therefore, your vigor is wasted.
Let there be a loss of your physical form as well—what do you achieve by being so partial? (32)
This Rohiṇī causes excessive enjoyment, yet she may become afflicted by disease;
O Rohiṇī, you who suffer from menorrhagia and uterine disorders, become one who is diseased! 33.
Thus was this formidable pronouncement of the curse made by his wives;
it was a formidable fault incurred by Dakṣa as well, for he had caused their speech to be broken.
At that very moment, however, the moon’s luster, along with its vital power, was instantly exhausted;
he became impotent, surviving on a mere single digit. (35)
He became one who was always miserable and always to be shunned by women;
even Rohiṇī suffered from a discharge of blood and was afflicted by menorrhagia.
At that very moment, Candra abandoned his home and all his wives and went to the shore of the ocean in Saurāṣṭra to perform penance.
There he performed most rigorous penance for a hundred years for the sake of destroying his own disease, yet the disease did not cease at all. (38)
He fell into great sorrow and became despondent in mind.
Rohiṇī also constantly suffers from the discharge of blood and other such ailments even now. ||39||
Then, at that time, when a hundred years had passed on the surface of the earth,
all medicinal herbs perished except for the nectar of the moon.
But grains do not arise at all within husks or flowers.
And the essence of the earth does not grow in bulbs or roots. ||41||
Nourishment was then forever lost, and living beings were consequently filled with suffering.
The gods, moreover, have not attained their true essence, and the sages have exhausted their nectar.
Having approached Brahmā, he entreated him for the destruction of his suffering.
There, Candra, having diligently installed Mahādeva Śiva, [remained]. ||43||
Having again performed austerities for a hundred years, he propitiated Śaṅkara;
Śaṅkara, being pleased, said to him, "What indeed do you desire? (44)
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; be forever happy, O Śaśin!
Candra then said to Nandīśa: "O Lord, become Someśvara. (45)
And here, having propitiated me by performing most severe penance on the western frontier of Saurāṣṭra, in the vicinity of the shore of the ocean; ||46||
May Mahādeva Someśvara always be worthy of my worship.
O you who are born from the words of Dakṣa, destroy my consumption and disease. ||47||
"O God, O Mahādeva, I shall perform your installation;
having summoned Brahmā and the others here, I shall conduct a great festival of sacrifice. (48)
Having thus resolved, Candra [invoked] the deities beginning with Brahmā,
as well as the sages, the seers, and the lords of progeny there.
Humans, gods, gandharvas, bards, panegyrists, and dancers;
They arrived, having been summoned for the purpose of the installation of Śaṅkara.
That sacred field lies to the south of the Bhadrāvatī river.
From Ābhadrā, the field extending as far as the ocean brings liberation to human beings. ||51||
There, residing in the city named Kuṅkumavāpī,
the brahmin sage known as Patnīvrata arrived after having mastered the Vedas.
For this Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself, descended in person.
He caused the installation of Somanātha to be performed according to the prescribed rites. ||53||
After the installation was completed, Brahmā then said to the wielder of the trident:
"As many medicinal herbs as have perished due to the waning of the moon,"
All creatures, whose very root is that [moon], repeatedly go to their destruction;
therefore, O compassionate one, the waning of the moon must be prevented by you. (55)
Śambhu said to them all: "Let us go to Dakṣa, who is afflicted with grief."
Let us speak in order to bring about benefit, so that the world may be in great happiness. //56//
Having thus addressed him, they departed toward the abode of Dakṣa.
Dakṣa welcomed them, and they sat down in their respective places.

The skillful one, having inquired after my welfare and even expressed his desire to know more, [realized that] there would be no further purpose for me, for great-souled ones are free from worldly desire. (58)
Nevertheless, your arrival must be considered for my gain, security, and welfare; what may I, your servant, do for you? (59)
Having thus announced himself, Dakṣa, bowing with palms joined in reverence, remained there indeed.
And then, for the sake of Soma, Śambhu spoke these words to Dakṣa: ||1.44.60||

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Candra by Dakṣa, the Curse, the Disease, and the Installation of Somanātha," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Śambhu said to Dakṣa, "Destroy the disease of the Moon.
Dakṣa replied, "O Śaṅkara, I shall indeed take away my own curse."
Who, other than the Moon, will ever remove this constant sorrow born of despair for daughters, which arises again and again in the absence of the Moon? (2)
Furthermore, it was produced by the burning of the grief of his virtuous wives.
"Which god can ward off a curse? Do as you wish, O Śaṅkara! || 3 ||
Having thus heard the words of the self-restrained Guru Dakṣa, [he acted accordingly].
Then Śambhu said to Candra, "May the curse of Dakṣa be destroyed."
O cool-rayed one, be full of vigor; do not be one who takes flight.
Then, for the sake of destroying even the curse uttered by his wife, Śaṅkara— ||5||
The Lord then begged for forgiveness from Revatī and the others.
And then by his wives it was proclaimed: "O disease, go to destruction! || 6 ||
The disease of the loss of vigor was destroyed, though the loss of its parts was not;
it was expiated for the sake of destroying the fault of partiality. || 7 ||
The state of being cast down upon Rohiṇī alone was abandoned by the Moon;
the state of being cast down due to the loss of virility was destroyed by Śambhu.
The moon has accepted the state of waning in all its phases,
yet the state of decay in its digits was not destroyed by Śambhu.
Then Candra spoke again to the god Brahmā.
The loss of one's father’s splendor is a sorrow that excels all other sorrows. ||1.45.10||
Splendor is the self of those who possess splendor; honor is said to be splendor.
Fame, renown, wealth, and greatness are all established upon splendor. (11)
He who becomes lusterless in the world is excluded from the count.
But in the reckoning of the radiant, the truly radiant one is counted. ||12||
Even if devoid of other qualities, one who is endowed with the form of splendor will indeed be dear to the eyes, just like a flower born of the *kiṃśuka* tree.
Even if endowed with many virtues, one who is devoid of beauty and splendor would not be pleasing to the eye, just as blackness pervaded by darkness is not pleasing to the eye. ||14||
White, blue, yellow, red, green, brownish-red, and variegated—thus they manifest seven forms. (15)
Among all of them, white is indeed said to be the best form;
after that, yellow, then red, and immediately thereafter, brown. (16)
Then green is proclaimed, and after that blue is counted; then variegated, known as *citra*, is mentioned, and thereafter the beloved is spoken of here. (17)
The white splendor belongs to Brahmā, as well as to the Supreme Brahman;
it also belongs to those liberated ones known as Brahman who dwell in places such as Goloka. (18)
Form is always held to be white, which produces what is pleasing to the eye;
my form is always pure white, considered to be the support of splendor. (19)
Without that splendor, even I, Kṛṣṇa, am equal to iron or clay.
Therefore, O Lotus-born One, grant me my own eternal splendor.
O elder brother, I certainly do not wish to remain bereft of splendor.
And everyone treats me with total contempt because I am devoid of splendor. ||21||
And my women, too, will no longer honor me as they did before.
Formerly, due to the overflowing of my splendor, I shone resplendent in the assembly of the gods.
Now, being devoid of splendor, how shall I go to the abode of the gods?
Deprived of my splendor, I could not live; I shall die, and I speak these words in your presence.
He indeed entreats for as long as it takes until Soma [is obtained] there.
Various medicinal herbs, originating from different worlds, have assembled together. ||24||
Some medicinal herbs there sustain life with a single drop of nectar.
Some medicinal herbs there sustain life for two kalpas. ||25||
Some drink the nectar of three kalās, some possess the nectar of four kalās;
some are enjoyers of five kalās, and some possess the nectar of six kalās. ||26||
Some enjoy seven digits, while others are nourished by eight digits of nectar.
Some are enjoyers of the nine digits, while others have become immortal through the ten digits. ||27||
Some have eleven digits, some have twelve excellent digits;
some have thirteen digits, and some have fourteen nectars. ||28||
Some, having attained satisfaction through the enjoyment of the nectar of fifteen digits, consume their own respective nectar on those various days as they arrive. (29)
Thus, they possess distinct capacities and subsist upon different kinds of nectar.
Nourished by various arts, they had indeed gathered there.
A life seeking one's own self-interest has been sought through various medicinal herbs.
If the fortnightly moon were possessed of the digits of waning and waxing, [it would not be the true moon]. ||31||
But then our life would proceed in a nourishing manner.
It was fruitful, flavorful, and abundant, providing nourishment according to what was suitable for consumption.
According to its growth, according to its nourishment, according to the season, and provided with seed.
If the full moon were always present, then those [women] would likewise [always be so]. (33)
Unable to endure [this], we shall surely perish.
Because this nectar of all the digits is cool, it is incapable of being consumed by the fire. ||34||
All these charming maidens will meet their destruction day and night.
Therefore, [the earth] is incapable of enduring the perpetual coldness of the moon.
"May these tender creepers not perish even while still sprouting"—having heard this prayer of theirs, Brahmā and Śaṅkara [responded]. (36)
They both spoke these words, which bring happiness, to Candra, the lord of medicinal herbs:
"O Candra, you must indeed take to heart this request made by the creepers. (37)
I accept this here by force, for no other path is seen;
the life of these worlds has been made dependent solely upon medicinal herbs. (38)
The life-force of medicinal herbs is considered to consist of sixteen parts (kalās); since those various distinct parts sustain each respective herb day after day. (39)
"You have been declared the repository of all arts; if you were not to show compassion,"
Indeed, all would repeatedly perish by means of one another. ||1.45.40||
Therefore, once you have obtained a drop of fire, tell us and act accordingly.
Increasing on the side of worldly existence, may you meet with destruction on the other side. ||41||
Your fault of partiality has been directed toward the digits alone.
Indeed, there shall be a depletion of your digits, yet your splendor shall remain inexhaustible.
Indeed, by whom can the thunderbolt—a curse bestowed by a wife—be warded off?
But why is that which is desired for the sake of those to be supported not abandoned for the sake of supporting them? (43)
But those whose nature is to assist others do so for the sake of the happiness of others.
In ultimate reality, they abandon even their own self-interest and what is favorable to themselves. ||44||
O Candra, act with equal affection toward all your wives.
Do not take their sighs; indeed, be happy. ||45||
"O bearer of wings, accept this merit of the life-force of the herbs.
Having thus addressed the Moon, both Brahmā and Śaṅkara likewise [spoke].
Then the gods established the waning and waxing of the digits (kalās) in that very manner;
from that time forward, the moon has always been fully endowed with complete potency.
He sports with his wives, who have the forms of constellations, in a state of perfect equality.
The destruction of the digits and their increase, however, remain dependent upon the horse and the medicinal herbs. ||48||
And likewise, the gods beginning with Brahmā went to their own abodes.
Then Śambhu requested that moon as an ornament for his forehead.
Brahmā gave him that moon born from the ocean as his first; the second was the moon born from his own portion;
and the moon who was born from Atri was the third king.
Each of those moons is indeed to be understood as distinct, arising from different functions;
there are as many Śambhus as there are cosmic eggs.
There would be as many moons as there are kalpas, yet they are infinite due to the distinction between kalpas.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have explained to you the cause of even the moon’s waning.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Causes for the Waning, Waxing, and Stability of the Lunar Splendor," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the mental creation of the gods;
there, the Unborn One created the mental deities who possess self-consciousness.
Learn from me their names according to how they endure until the dissolution of all beings:
water, fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and likewise the directions. || 2 ||
Heaven, the sky, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the trees, and the creepers.
For they are indeed the selves of the herbs, as well as the selves of trees and creepers.
A lava, a kāṣṭhā, a kalā, a saṃdhi, and a muhūrta constitute a day and night.
A fortnight makes a month, a month an ayana, a month a year, and [a collection of years] a yuga, along with its additions.
The Unborn One created these gods who take pride in their respective stations.
And the deities who preside over the constellations, planets, and stars. ||5||
And he created twenty-eight crores of those of virtuous nature;
they are called the Vaimānikas, the celestial dwellers in the world of the gods.
The gods, the ancestors, the sages, and likewise the Manus.
And those who were their followers, as well as the sons of Manu. || 7 ||
By calculation, there are three hundred and ninety-two million, seven hundred thousand, and eight thousand [years]. (8)
For these deities are the presiding divinities of their respective spheres;
indeed, even without formal sovereignty, they possess a splendor resembling that of the sun.
These moving and stationary beings are the mind-born progeny of Brahmā;
[as well as] the Tuṣitas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the lightning-spirits.
And Stanayitnu, Bhānu, and likewise the eight Vasus—Droṇa, Prāṇa, Dhruva, Agni, Doṣa, Vasu, and Vibhāvasu. ||11||
As well as the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas.
And [he saw] Apsarases, Cāraṇas, Piśācas, Pretas, and Bhūtas.
Vidyādharas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Aśvamukhas, and Kinnaras; likewise Vetālas, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, and Yoginīs. ||13||
And the Vināyakas, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Vetālas, and even the Grahas; likewise the Yātudhānas, the Unmādas, the Mātṛs, the Guhyakas, and the Cāraṇas. ||14||
The lords of progeny, the sages, the nāgas, the serpents, as well as the uragas;
the birds, the wild animals, the domestic beasts, the trees, the mountains, mortals, and the reptiles. ||15||
And [he saw] the bards, panegyrists, and minstrels, as well as Bhāṭṭamindra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Īśāna, and likewise Nirṛti. ||16||
The Unborn One created the eight Siddhis, the nine Nidhis, as well as the eleven Rudras, and also the Daityas and Dānavas from his mind.
Sacrifices, meritorious beings, the vehicles of the gods, and even animals—such as the cow, goat, buffalo, black pig, gayal, and ruru deer. ||18||
These animals with cloven hooves are as follows: the camel and others;
likewise, the donkey, the horse, the śarabha, the gaur, and the camari—these are the animals with solid, single hooves.
A dog, a jackal, a wolf, a tiger, a cat, a hare, and a porcupine.
The lion, the monkey, the elephant, the tortoise, the iguana, the crocodile, and so forth. ||1.46.20||
Kanka-vultures, crows, owls, hawks, eagles, bhallas, peacocks, swans, cranes, cakravakas, ravens, owls, and cocks; ||21||

but the third he created as the subtle elements (tanmātra), which possess the potential for substance. ||23||
He created the sense organs as the fourth, consisting of both knowledge and action.
The fifth, however, he created as the mind-born gods (manodevas), and the sixth as those up to ignorance (avidya). ||24||
He emitted the seventh creation, that of the stationary beings, namely the plants;

He created the ninth creation, that of mortals, and the tenth, the divine creation; therein, he then created the secondary creation (gauṇasarga) as required in each respective case.

That Grandfather created the tenfold vital breaths (prāṇa), consisting of substance, action, and inherent nature, along with vitality (ojas) and strength (bala), as well as those pertaining to the mind.

The hair, the lord (the head), the hands, the feet, movement, bliss, and the phallus.

The anus, the penis, the seed, the semen, and the blood.
The navel is the downward breath (apāna) and death; the intestines are the channels (nāḍikā).
Contentment, the rivers, and the oceans; nourishment, and also the heart.
The mind, the moon, volition, desire, the skin, and the hide; ||31||

There, he established Varuṇa on the two palates and the deity of the tongue.
He established the two Aśvinī-kumāras as the presiding deities of the sense of smell. ||34||
But in the principle of Mahat, he established Vāgīśa as the presiding deity of the intellect.
Likewise, he established Viṣṇu as the deity of the feet upon his two feet. ||35||
In the eye, he established Tvaṣṭṛ, the Āditya, as the presiding deity of sight.

He established the wind in the hide and the god [of breath] in the skin for the sake of vital energy.
He established the deity of the ears in the direction of the ears, as was appropriate.

When an itch arose on his skin, he prepared as many medicinal herbs as there were.

He established the moon in his heart for the sake of transforming the mind. ||39||

This emission is the casting of sidelong glances, and the subsequent [act] is the biting of the upper lip.

The hips are the deer, the wings are the hoofed animals, the intellect is Manu, the mortal is the dwelling, and the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Apsarases are the musical notes. 49.
The Brāhmaṇas are the memory and the vigor, while the Kṣatriyas are the mouth and the arms.

Valor, the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, the meters, and the seven constituent elements; ||51||
The sacred fords (tīrthas) are the channels (nāḍīs); the attainment of desires is the feet, while the belly is indeed death.
The stone, iron, cloud, and lightning appear exactly like a treasure-house, a beard, and nakedness. ||52||
The penis is the rain-cloud from which flows the water of semen through the bliss of sexual union;
and the anus is also the friend who grants liberation through self-restraint. (53)
Violence is Nirṛti, hell is Death, and the anus is the Pradhāna;
darkness is unrighteousness and defeat, while the backbones are the mountains. (54)

All these mental [beings], whose tastes were unmanifest while they were previously meditated upon in the blood, having thus meditated upon the Supreme within their own selves, [constitute] the mental creation; therefore [it is called so]. (55)
Having prepared suitable abodes for them and having bestowed those upon them as well,

Then Brahmā, having conceptualized all that, explained it from his mind.
And here, the lords born in Satyaloka are the masters of the stream of sovereignty.

And here, the gods possess a stream of complete merit, as well as the perfection of virtues and other qualities.
And here, the pretas born from the meditation of those who dwell in the stream of existence are those produced by the meditation of latent tendencies.

In each respective place in the world, Brahmā established [the teachings] correctly.
For them, he fashioned food from his own body;
for the ṛṣis, however, he fashioned milk consisting of the Vedic meters as their nourishment.

For the Daityas, wine is prescribed; for the Dānavas, however, it is *āsava*.
The music of the Gandharvas and the beauty of the Apsarases.
He possessed the sky-faring knowledge of the Vidyādharas and was invisible even to the masters of illusion.
The flesh and blood of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and other pretas;

The flesh of fanged creatures, and the various juices of trees and creepers.
