Brahmā himself fashioned whatever was required for each being; by that means, this course of worldly existence proceeds until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus, in the first age, having performed the entire creation— including its primary and secondary limbs—
entirely through the mind, the Grandfather desisted.
Creation merely increases; it is never newly born. Just as it was, so it remains, exactly as it was before. //76//

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Creation of Devas, Yakṣas, Humans, Animals, Birds, Daityas, Dānavas, Nāgas, Serpents, and Immovable Beings, along with Their Corresponding Presiding Deities," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved, at the commencement of creation on the first day,
it is said that the creation was mental, for it consisted of the Satya Yuga.
Having created the various abodes for those who pride themselves on their stations, as well as the abodes themselves,
he indeed fashioned the state of the Yugas from the essence of those abodes.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and likewise the Kali age.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, in the Satya Yuga, he created mind-born progeny.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
its two twilights (sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa) are eight hundred divine years in number.
Three thousand years are considered the Tretā Yuga;
its two junctions (sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa) are, by number, six hundred divine years.
Two thousand years of such years is called the Dvāpara Yuga.
Its two twilight portions number four hundred divine [years] in total.
One thousand years of humans is called the Kali Yuga;
its two twilights (sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa) are, by calculation, two hundred divine years.
The Unborn One fashioned the cycle of four yugas consisting of twelve thousand years;
therein, O Lakṣmī, in the Kṛta-yuga, the subjects possessed perfections born of the mind.
In that Kṛta Yuga, dharma and adharma did not exist among them; those creatures were without distinction, possessing equal lifespan, happiness, and form.
In that age, they indeed frequent rivers, lakes, oceans, and even mountains; they roam about, partaking of water that is sometimes cold and sometimes hot.
They partake of sweet food produced through the power of their minds.
Moving at will in every respect, they have attained the perfection of the mind.
For them there is no obstruction, no duality, nor even a sequence.
Free from sorrow, abundant in sentient beings, and always exclusively happy. ||12||
The beasts and birds were always joyful in their minds.
This time brings all sensual pleasures and grants whatever the mind desires. ||13||
Indeed, by means of those [powers], the tastes and other qualities are meditated upon and arise within the earth.
The perfection that bestows youth and beauty upon them is that which destroys disease. ||14||
Those subjects had firm and well-nourished bodies and possessed stable youthfulness.
Then there arise truthfulness, non-greed, forbearance, contentment, happiness, and self-control. ||15||
All those women were indeed indistinguishable from one another in terms of their appearance, age, conduct, and movements;
yet, based upon truth, the social dealings of the people proceeded spontaneously. (16)
There was no engagement of living beings in either auspicious or sinful actions;
at that time, there were neither the established orders of castes and stages of life nor any intermixture of them.
Free from passion and hatred, they dwell together with one another; all possess equal success and lifespan, being devoid of the distinctions of low or high. (18)
Abounding in happiness, free from sorrow, filled with great energy, and full of great festivals.
These great beings possess minds that are eternally joyful and are endowed with great strength. ||19||
Let there be neither gain nor loss, neither friend nor foe, neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant among them.
The object proceeds for them by means of the mind, even though they are devoid of desire.
They do not desire one another at all, nor do they show them any favor.
Indeed, everything on earth ripens without being ploughed, even without the water of rain.
There, food is provided without effort and possesses a naturally excellent flavor;
likewise, there is neither the pain of childbirth nor the burden of carrying a fetus. (22)
There, women have no menstrual flow, nor do men have the emission of semen.
All cows are wish-fulfilling; all are the accomplishments of one's intentions. ||23||
In the fourteen worlds, however, all prosperities are indeed without distinction.
All his modes of movement were unimpeded, and likewise, all his words were perfectly refined.
The inhabitants of celestial palaces, though devoid of such vehicles, possess the power of yoga-perfection and austerity;
they are all indeed lords, as if their every desire were fulfilled. (25)
Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age; knowledge is said to be so in the Tretā;
sacrifice is practiced in the Dvāpara; and charity is best in the Kali age. (26)
Sattva constitutes the Kṛta age; Rajas, the Tretā; and both Rajas and Tamas together constitute the Dvāpara.
O you, the Kali age should be understood as darkness, according to the influence of the characteristics of the ages.
But the dharma of the age (yuga-dharma) remains entirely reduced to one quarter.
But when the Satya Yuga has completely ended, that perfection indeed vanished.
In that age, there was one kind of accomplishment; but in the Tretā age, it became otherwise once again.
But when the subtlety of the waters has vanished, they then [reappear] again in the form of clouds.
When rain has fallen but once from clouds accompanied by thunder, and the surface of the earth has been inundated by that single downpour; ||| 1.47.30 ||
At that time, the waters appeared, and the Kalpa trees stood as if situated within houses.
But from them, all their various enjoyments arise. ||31||
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsist by means of wish-fulfilling trees;
then, due to the nature of the Age (rājayuga), there occurs a reversal for them.
For at that time, the state consisting of passion and greed arises suddenly;
that which occurs for women at the end of their life is their menses.
He has now established that which was previously the mental creation of pairs—one thousand for each living being—in the form of the seasonal flow. (34)
Then, having attained joy, those beings became pairs; possessed by mutual desire for one another's hearts, they proceeded to engage in sexual union. (35)
From that time onwards in the Tretā age, the birth of twins is said to occur;
for at the end of their lifespan, women there experience menstruation only once.
They were born for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures and for the purpose of bearing fine offspring;
yet at that time, they did not give birth even though they engaged in sexual intercourse. (37)
At the end of their lifespan, they give birth only once to twins;
their birth and appearance are simultaneous, and they also die together. (38)
When that [Kṛta age] had waned and its purpose was fulfilled, the Tretā age arrived according to the law of time.
The powers of mental accomplishment, austerity, learning, and lifespan are exhausted. ||39||
And at that time, the dharmas performed [in previous lives] gradually diminish.
The power, reality, capacity, bliss, and majesty are each diminished by one quarter. ||1.47.40||
Then, when Vṛtra had been slain by Indra, the impurity consisting of the murder of a Brahmin [remained].
This [practice] is prescribed in four parts for women, trees, and caves. ||41||
From that time forward, that which constitutes the end of women's lives—their menses—began to recur for them month after month. 42.
Then, while they were living together as a couple by that very same yoga,
because of their state at that time, they approached one another month after month.
Indeed, the onset of menstruation and the conception of a fetus occurred out of season, due to the reversal of the proper time and because of their physical deficiencies. ||44||
Indeed, all the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) situated within every house have perished;
only here and there do some remain, bestowing success upon those who take refuge in them. (45)
When the wish-fulfilling trees had perished, they wandered about with their senses in utter agitation.
Having gone there, they covet the *vastuka* [substance] of the occasional wish-fulfilling trees. 46.
Then garments, fruits, and ornaments are produced.
In those very [beings] they are born; for them, there is fragrance, desired tastes, and so forth.
This honey, free from bees and of great potency, is found in every single cell.
In this way, all the preparatory rites proceed with diligent effort. ||48||
By that means, they lived happily during the half of the Tretā Yuga.
Thus they were joyful, well-nourished, contented, and free from all anxiety by means of the wish-fulfilling trees. ||49||
Then, as time passed, living beings were once again shrouded by greed.
By their power, they seized those trees, including honey, fruits, and other such things.
Due to those transgressions of theirs and likewise by the power of time,
those wish-fulfilling trees perished, and the subjects were left without any support.
Then, tormented by intense cold, wind, and heat, they became exceedingly distressed; being afflicted by these pairs of opposites, they constructed shelters.
Having provided remedies against the pairs of opposites, they indeed took up dwellings;
according to their needs, they occupied houses and fields for crops. (53)
While the Maruts, the mountains, and the rivers were bowing down before him.
They took refuge in difficult terrains and regions where water was perpetually available. ||54||
According to what is appropriate and according to one's desire, whether on even or uneven ground.
They indeed began to construct dwellings to ward off the cold and the heat.
And they established villages and cities there, on the sides of the agricultural fields where crops had been commenced.
And likewise, he may enter the villages and the inner apartments according to his pleasure.
Then, having measured it with their own fingers, they established the beginning of the planetary cycle. ||57||
The span from the little finger to the thumb is said to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
and by twenty-four such finger-breadths, a cubit (hasta) is formed.
A bow-staff is four cubits long, and an arrow is said to be two cubits;
two thousand bows are proclaimed there to be one *gavyūti*.
Four *gavyūtis* are proclaimed to be one *yojana*.
By this King Pṛthu, indeed, even the settlement [of the earth] was established.
A magnificent royal road, ten *dhanus* in width, was constructed.
It was a spacious and easy passage for men, horses, chariots, and elephants.
Amita is the house of ten archers, belonging to the middle class.
A king possesses a hundred bows, while a sovereign emperor possesses a thousand.
Thus it was for those dwelling in houses and palaces.
When the wish-fulfilling trees had perished, the loss of livelihood was considered. ||63||
The waters from the rains were indeed channeled into ditches and downward-flowing streams;
and from the union of the waters and the earth, medicinal herbs came into being within them.
Trees and shrubs bore flowers and fruits according to the seasons, and grain grew spontaneously in full abundance without being ploughed by the furrow. (65)
At that time, during the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsisted on medicinal herbs;
then, however, passion and greed arose among them once again due to the passage of time.
Then they also seized the rivers, the fields, and the mountains.
They forcibly [seized] the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs according to their strength. ||67||
Having made [the property] their own, those who are powerful forcibly and by violence consume it;
indeed, they seize it by sheer force from those of little luster.
Indeed, the earth was made their own by means of both their strength and their great power.
At that time, being of little strength, they indeed subsist by serving them.
Those who were then born as Śūdras became devoted to service;
while others, living by practicing agriculture, became Vaiśyas.
From *bala* were born the Kṣattras, the rulers of the earth, as well as others;
those who are peaceful and characterized by *sattva* are those who beg for alms there. (71)
Those brahmins were such great-souled beings, possessed of pure intentions.
Thus, by virtue of their actions, the social classes (varṇas) emerged from the Brāhmaṇas.
When human beings had thus fallen into mutual conflict,
by that very fault those medicinal herbs vanished from their sight at that time.
They were utterly destroyed, carried away, and indeed became devoid of essence once again.
Devoid of leaves, flowers, and fruits, they wither completely on all sides. ||74||
The subjects, deprived of their means of sustenance, were bewildered on all sides.
Overcome by hunger, they went to the self-born Lord Prajāpati.
Knowing that [the gods] had requested wealth for the sake of their livelihood, Brahmā reflected thoroughly and,
making Mount Sumeru the calf, milked this earth.
Then the cultivated and wild plants were born again:
rice, barley, wheat, millet, and sesame.
For there were fine priyaṅgu grains, udāra grains, kāruṣa grains, and satīnaka grains; as well as mung beans, green gram, lentils, flat beans, and horse gram.
Āḍhakī beans, chickpeas, śyāmāka millet along with gavedhuka, kuruvinda grains, bamboo seeds, nivāra rice, and likewise jartila seeds. (79)
And monkeys—all these are considered auspicious when they have not been ploughed over by the furrow.
Trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and species of grasses.
All medicinal herbs here were produced with flowers and fruits in their proper seasons; yet when those herbs, once released, did not sprout again, [the world was afflicted]. (81)
Then Brahmā indeed established the means of livelihood for the sake of its growth.
But through the livelihood of agriculture, those [plants] were born as crops that ripen on tilled soil. ||82||
The Vaiśyas there were farmers, the Kṣatriyas were protectors,
the Śūdras were attendants, and the Brāhmaṇas were dedicated to the offering to Brahman.
The status of the Brāhmaṇas who perform their duties is one of great dignity;
the status of the Kṣatriyas is sovereignty over those who do not flee from battle. (84)
The place for Vaiśyas, who live by agriculture and similar efforts, was established on the land;
the place for Śūdras, who subsist through service, was established at the edge of the village. ||85||
Then, while the social classes (varṇas) were established, he established the stages of life (āśramas):
the householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant.
The first great stage of life is the householder, consisting of the four castes; it is the foundation and indeed the source of the other three stages of life. (87)
For those established in their respective duties, Brahmā himself has ordained specific stations; I shall describe those very stations, so listen to me. 88.
For householder Brahmins, the Prājāpatya is considered the supreme [form of marriage].
For Kṣatriyas, it should be the temple of Indra; for renunciants, the abode of Brahmā.
But truth belongs to those practicing celibacy whose lives are dedicated to the forest-dwelling stage.
The station of the Maruts is for the Vaiśyas, and the Gāndharva station is ordained for the Śūdras.
The paths are those traveled by the gods, and the sun is remembered as their gateway.
In the same way, the Moon is said to be the gateway for those who travel by the path of the ancestors. ||91||
Thus, at the beginning of the Tretā age, this entire creation came into being.
At the end of the Tretā age, there is a reduction by two quarters in strength, vigor, and the quality of life. ||92||
In the Dvāpara age, beings live with their strength, vigor, and other qualities diminished by three-quarters.
In the Kali age, all living beings indeed subsist by any means whatsoever. ||93||

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Number of Years of the Yugas, the Attainment of Siddhis in the Kṛta Yuga, the Diminution of the Padas, the Creation of Couples, the Measurement of Cities and Other Matters, Food, Medicines, and the Establishment of the Castes and Stages of Life," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord, how did Indra come to incur the sin of killing a Brahmin? A great curiosity has arisen in my heart; please tell me that story."
Tell me, when was the earth leveled by Pṛthu?
O Lord, what was the goddess Earth like before that? || 2 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, for I shall relate from the beginning that auspicious narrative which,
when heard, becomes a destroyer of sins through its connection with the Blessed Lord.
Marīci was the son of Brahmā, and Kaśyapa was indeed his son;
and from Aditi, the auspicious Tvaṣṭṛ became the son of Kaśyapa.
Tvaṣṭṛ begot Viśvarūpa upon his wife Racanā.
There, Viśvarūpa became the domestic priest of the gods.
Once, Bṛhaspati arrived at the assembly hall of Indra;
however, Indra did not offer him the customary honors, such as rising from his seat to greet him.
From that time forward, Bṛhaspati, the king of preceptors among the denizens of heaven,
thereafter renounced his office as the domestic priest of the gods.
Thereafter, Indra bestowed the office of domestic priest upon Viśvarūpa.
When the sacrifice had been performed by Indra, Viśvarūpa became his domestic priest.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the gods, he also gave it secretly to the asuras;
for the Daityas were his maternal uncles, and therefore he gave the bali in secret.
Having discovered that the Bali had been offered secretly by him, the King of the Gods became enraged; he seized his weapon and cut off those three heads.
But one of his heads was indeed that which drank the Soma juice.
But from the cutting of that [hair], the Kapiñjala birds indeed came into being. ||11||
His second head indeed became a vessel for drinking the decoction.
But from the cutting of that [stalk], the kalaviṅka birds were born. ||12||
His third head became one that consumed food.
But upon its being cut, birds known as tittiras were born. ||13||
Upon the decapitation of the family priest, that sin of killing a Brahmin occurred.
Red, alkaline, green, black, terrifying, and multiform. ||14||
She indeed leaped toward Mahendra, for he had become Citravarṇa.
Then the gods, having assembled together, divided her into four parts.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, he clearly proclaimed: "She is indeed to be given in exchange."
Let those individual manifestations take a fourth part of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
A boon should be granted to them; there is no doubt that it shall be exactly as they desire.
Having heard this, the boon was sought by the women for the sake of satisfying their desires.
Even when requested for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and the practice of frequent sexual union, there is no fatigue; let the enjoyment of desires be constant and according to one's wish. (18)
After the gods had thus granted the boon, the fourth [sin], the killing of a Brahmin, [remained].
But the portion offered to the women became their menstrual blood. ||19||
From that time forth, for women, the god of love was ever new and fresh.
Month after month, she experienced the onset of menses; she even bore flowers and conceived a fetus.
Furthermore, wherever on this earth there may be a depression for me, or wherever there may be a hollow, may there always be a filling for me. (21)
Having given this boon to the Earth, [he gave] a fourth part as her share.
The excavated regions of the earth are filled by their very nature. ||22||
The result of that is that there is an alkaline portion in various places;
or rather, trees and such things are sought after there because they exist spontaneously. (23)
When wounded, severed, or bent, there shall be healing once again.
Having granted that boon there to the trees, he [assigned] a fourth part of the slaughter as their share. ||24||
And he gave [the gift] to the Drubhas, as well as the Kṛṣṇagundra-srava belonging to them.
That worm, which consists of the fruit of killing a Brahmin, is indeed not eaten.
Then, at the time of his departure, he requested a boon from the waters for whatever he desired therein.
In those places where there are springs and the like, there shall be an abundance of water on all sides. ||26||
In whatever substance water is poured, that substance shall always increase.
May our dwelling there take place in the form of the aesthetic flavor (rasa). ||27||
Having killed one-fourth of the slaughter among them, he indeed grants such a boon; by that, fulfillment is always observed in both water and on land. (28)
In water, the very form of killing consists of moss, foam, and bubbles.
Thus, four portions of the sin of killing a Brahmin have been described. ||29||
When they were given to those who desired them, Indra indeed attained purification;
from that time forward, the lord of the gods began to perform sacrifices.
Then, for the sake of Indra's livelihood and to obtain the ransom for his son—
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, his son having been slain, offered oblations into the fire accompanied by mantras.
"O Indra-slayer, grow strong! Slay Indra here with haste!"—with these words, by means of that very oblation, a man of terrible appearance appeared right there.
A massive body arose, assuming a form resembling the color of time (death).
Constantly increasing, he possesses a thousand hands and has the foremost smoky hue. ||33||
Resembling an evening cloud in luster, he stands brandishing his trident.
He had copper-colored hair matted into a topknot, and his fierce eyes were like the midday sun.
Roaring and making the earth tremble, as if licking the very sky;
devouring the light before him and vomiting forth blinding darkness. (35)
By him, whose very nature was darkness, the worlds were completely enveloped;
that terrible one was indeed summoned by Tvaṣṭṛ under the name Vṛtra.
The gods, having rushed toward him, struck him with divine weapons;
however, he himself swallowed all their missiles and arms from every side.
Then the gods were struck with wonder, despondent, and deprived of their splendor.
With their efforts frustrated, they praised the Lord God who dwells within. ||38||
Homage be to you, O Śrī Puruṣottama, the supreme deity of Brahmā, higher than the highest;
homage be to you, the self of Brahman who dwells within the bodies of the liberated—protect us who are shrouded in fear! 39.
In this scripture, offer salutations to the protectors, beginning with Śrī Vāsudeva—the lords of the abodes such as Vaikuṇṭha—and to the millions of lords beginning with Sadāśiva. 1.48.40.
The mountain was borne upon your own back, while the boat was held fast upon your horn;
the earth was supported by your teeth—may that very Lord grant us protection. (41)
We have been appointed for the sake of protection; may we not perish, utterly overwhelmed by the blinding darkness of ignorance.
Deprived of weapons and missiles, repeatedly afflicted by the enemy—may the God of Gods, the refuge and destroyer of suffering, grant protection. ||42||
Having praised him thus, the gods, led by Brahmā, ceased;
then the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari appeared there, bearing his weapons.
Captivating with his divine object of meditation and the beauty of every limb, the gods prostrated like staffs and, rising once more, offered praise. (44)
Protect us, O Lord, from the great terror of the most formidable Vṛtrāsura!
O Hari, we have indeed sought refuge in you, the infallible Lord and our protector. (45)
Śrī Hari said: "O Indra, go; may it be well with you. Ask the yogic sage Dadhīci, whose body consists of knowledge and austerity, and he will grant it to you."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari then vanished right there.
The gods, having gone, repeatedly entreated Dadhyañc for his body.
Indeed, at that very moment, Dadhīca, being exceedingly serene and devoted to the welfare of others, abandoned his body by resorting to yoga.
Indra, filled with joy, took up that vajra fashioned from his bones.
He rushed toward Vṛtra to slay him, gladdening the assembly of gods.
Therein were the gods— the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Agnis, and Vāyus—
as well as the Pitṛs, Ṛbhus, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and Kumārakas.
And other deities also gathered there, proceeding to the battle.
And the Asuras also, stationed with Vṛtra, were those who had fallen into the faction of Vṛtra. ||51||
Namuci, Śambara, Anarva, Dvimūrdhan, Ṛṣabha, Kāla, Hayagrīva, Śaṅkuśiras, Vipracitti, and Svayomukha; ||52||
The Dānavas Puloman, Vṛṣaparvan, Heti, and Praheti, as well as the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, let out lion-like roars. ||53||
They indeed carried all kinds of weapons, with maces and iron clubs in their hands,
[armed] with arrows, javelins, slings, spears, tridents, and battle-axes.
Indeed, he [was struck] with swords, weapons, missiles, śataghnīs, and bhūśuṇḍis.
Out of rage, they showered a tumultuous rain [of weapons] from all sides upon the bulls among the gods.
Their weapons were shattered in a thousand ways by the gods themselves.
The gods on Vṛtra’s side fled and regained their composure. ||56||

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fourfold Distribution of Viśvarūpa’s Slaughter, the Birth of Vṛtra, and the Battle with the Thunderbolt fashioned from Dadhyañc’s bones for the Destruction of Vṛtra," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. ||48||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Vṛtra, laughing, spoke to those who were broken and fleeing.
He [is the one] from whom Vipracitti, Namuci, Puloman, Śambara, and others [derive their power]. || 1 ||
Death is certain for all embodied beings who are born, even for the brave.
For that which has arrived by way of its own nature, no remedy exists. || 2 ||
Indeed, [it was] in the midst of battle, against the chests of their enemies, for those who were heroes.
How indeed is death not to be honored, both for the sake of fame and for the sake of spiritual welfare? (3)
However, two deaths are considered certain to grant liberation:
that which occurs for yogis through the aperture of yoga, and that which occurs for heroes through the opening of a weapon. (4)
Even though she was being exhorted in this manner, Vṛtra’s army fled.
With her mind distressed by the loss of her life-breath, she did not accept those words of the Dharma.
Then, enraged once more, Vṛtra spoke these words with a threat.
What is the use of those base matricides who destroy their own names and status?
For those who have brought death upon their backs and who mock the milk of their mothers,
there is no fame in flight, nor is there a higher world, nor a supreme goal.
This flight from battle is not praiseworthy; it causes distress like that of cowards.
May they remain healthy and victorious in my presence. ||8||
Having heard this and having regained their strength, they then turned back.
Terrifying the gods with their weapons, those fierce beings began to afflict them.
Vṛtra indeed hurled an iron mace at Indrabhakuṃbha.
The elephant retreated seven bow-lengths due to the blow of the strike.
When Indra seized that thunderbolt which slays the brothers of the Daityas, Vṛtra, becoming exceedingly enraged, said: "By good fortune, he has come before me! ||11||

"May I, who am a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of my guru, a slayer of my brother, and likewise a slayer of my disciple, fortunately become free from debt, now that he has been struck down by me with this trident. (12)
A Vedic scholar, a teacher, a child, one who trusts, and an initiated twice-born man—these should not be killed.
Having struck them with a sword, what destination will surely be theirs? ||13||
May vultures devour you on the ground—you who are devoid of modesty, prosperity, compassion, and the like—a corpse pierced by my trident yet untouched by fire. (14)
If I am destroyed by the thunderbolt, I shall go to the destination frequented by heroes.
If you have been destroyed by the trident, my position as Indra is certainly secure.
Or rather, what is the use of sovereignty, or even of hell, in my view?
May neither passion nor hatred arise within me; may Śrī Hari be gracious unto me. (16)
"Having been destroyed by your thunderbolt, he shall become your servant of servants;
may I be liberated by you from the ocean of suffering caused by the snares of saṃsāra. (17)
I shall serve the feet of the Blessed One; I shall perform service with devotion.
What is the use of this perishable body, worldly status, and so forth? ||18||
May my mind have no further attachment to home, children, and the like.
May my dwelling always be at his feet and other such places. ||19||
Thus speaking, he hurled his mace at Vṛtra.
Then Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, [beheld] that massive [form], resembling a mountain.
Vṛtra seized that mace with his hand as if in sport;
meanwhile, Indra hurled his own thunderbolt for the destruction of Vṛtra.
Then Vṛtra hurled a trident at Indra for his destruction; it was made of iron and possessed a vajra at its tip with a hollow opening at the front. ||22||
"O wicked one, you are slain here today; go to the abode of Yama!
Indra instantly shattered the trident with his hundred-edged thunderbolt.
As soon as Vṛtra seized a second trident with his hand,
Indra severed that arm along with the trident using another thunderbolt.
And then, with one hand, Vṛtra swiftly seized another trident.
Then, having seized another iron club, he hurled it at Indra and said to him: ||25||
"You are dead, O Indra! You have gone, O Indra, to the place where your ancestors dwell!
Having uttered this terrible roar, he struck Indra on the jaw with his fist.
The thunderbolt fell from his hand, and even Maghavan was thrown into a state of whirling confusion.
The gods, the Siddhas, and the heroes cried out loudly, "Alas! Alas! ||27||
Then Vṛtra said to Indra: "Take up the thunderbolt with your hand;
for what shame is there for those who have entered the field of battle in a contest of strength? (28)
Thinking that life, prosperity, fame, sovereignty, and the abundant blessings of home and wife do not truly exist, roam about upon the field of battle. 29.
Knowing that pleasure and pain, life and death, honor and dishonor, victory and defeat— all this is composed of illusion— move about upon the field of battle.
This is called the "Battle-Seat," the "Weapon-Eye," and the "Seizer of Life.
When life has departed, whose victory will there be? (31)
Having heard these words of Bhagavān uttered by Vṛtra,
he was greatly pleased with him and took up his thunderbolt in his hand.
Just as he hurled it at Vṛtra, the king of the Daityas quickly—
Having placed his lower jaw on the ground, Vṛtra raised his upper jaw toward the sky.
At that very moment, Vṛtra swallowed Indra along with his thunderbolt;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the great sages wailed aloud.
Then Indra, having split open that vajra-severed belly with his own thunderbolt,
emerged from the womb and cut off the head.
Vṛtra’s massive body fell to the earth as soon as it was severed.
Kettledrums resounded in the path of the gods, and the great seers were filled with joy. ||36||
The Gandharvas and Siddhas sang, and the Apsarases danced with joy;
then a rain of flowers was showered by the gods, accompanied by songs of victory.
The soul of Vṛtra, having been slain, then became merged in the splendor of Brahman for those who beheld it; and then the worlds indeed became free from feverish distress.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā, returned once again to their own respective abodes.
Indra, however, was distressed by the sin arising from the slaying of Vṛtra. ||39||
Yet he did not obtain even the slightest peace; therefore, in order to destroy that slaughter, he entreated the great seers: "Where shall I cleanse myself of this slaughter? (1.49.40)
The sages, however, said to him: "Cause him to be consecrated by means of a horse sacrifice."
Having worshipped the god Nārāyaṇa, you shall be liberated from the heap of sins.

The killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the killer of a father, the thief of a cow, the killer of a mother, and likewise the killer of a guru—such a person is purified by performing sacrifice for Him and by chanting and serving His name. 42.
Thus impelled and fleeing from the sin of Brahman-slaughter,
Indra took refuge in the northern direction at the lake named Mānasa.
Afflicted by the heat, he lived for one year within that great stalk;
there was a terrible, dark Caṇḍālī woman, clad in red garments and smeared with entrails and fat.
A foul odor spread all around there, following even from the lake.
The sages, having summoned him, [performed] for him in every respect the horse sacrifice.
They initiated her according to the prescribed rites through the propitiation of the Supreme Being;
and when the horse sacrifice was completed, the sin of slaughter was likewise destroyed.
Indra, having shaken off his sins, returned once more to the kingdom of heaven.
"O Lakṣmī, this divine story exists in a subtle form, composed by me. (47)
O Goddess, by means of this gross description, the power that bestows the movement of the sun and other planets has been shown to you in a way that is pleasant to hear; she is called Indra. 48.
The power (śakti) that is rich in the obstruction of the manifestation of water is called Vṛtra.
By virtue of their power to illuminate the waters, the planets always lead to happy rebirths. //49//
Vṛtra, who is of the nature of darkness, indeed creates an obstruction to movement.
For his destruction, the great Indra constantly wages war.
Especially in the autumn, Indra then slays the Asura;
thus everything has been told to you regarding the fruit of killing, which bestows what is undesirable.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Horse Sacrifice and Other Deeds that Destroyed the Brahmahatyā Following the Destruction of Vṛtra," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||49||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Mahālakṣmī, I shall tell you how the leveling of the earth was indeed performed by Pṛthu; this story bestows the gift of Brahman.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since his abode (*ayana*) was in them, he is therefore the Virāj, Nārāyaṇa.
From the navel of Virāj, indeed, there arose a great lotus;
there Brahmā himself was born and beheld it filled with a network [of veins].
But her own lotus was in that water in the form of mud;
the earth was pervaded by moisture, and no dryness was seen there.
Without dryness, how could the dwelling of those who serve the earthly-born (humans) there, as well as the growth of trees and creepers, possibly occur? (5)
Then a hymn of praise was uttered by Brahmā for Nārāyaṇa:
"O Nārāyaṇa, ocean of compassion, support of all, nourisher of all! (6)
Without a vast expanse, indeed, what beings could remain in the water?
Therefore, [the earth] remained in the water, moist and in the form of subtle mud.
O Lord, having brought it into a gross state, make it into the form of earth;
for without that, the human creation would be devoid of the four types of minerals.
Where will they stay, or from where will they obtain food? Homage to the one whose nature is infinite; homage also to the upholder of Dharma.
Salutations to the one whose nature is gross, salutations to the one whose nature is subtle;
salutations to the one whose nature is the lineage, salutations to the inner controller of all.
Homage to you whose nature is the imperishable syllable; homage to you whose self is liberated;
homage to you whose nature is the cosmic manifestation; homage to you who are the embodiment of time. ||11||
Salutations to Him who takes the form of Kṛṣṇa and others; salutations to the Golden One;
salutations to Him in the form of Vairāja; salutations to the Dweller in Goloka.
Salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to him who abides in the unmanifest;
salutations to the divine, peaceful one, whose inner self is the subtle reality.
Homage to the one whose nature is the effect; homage to the one whose form is the cause;
homage to the one whose nature is woman; homage to the bestower of the seed. ||14||
Salutations to the one whose nature is vast; salutations to the one who reclines upon the waters;
salutations to the one whose nature is fire and sun; and salutations to the one who consists of sacrifice.
"Have mercy, O Lord of Mercy; manifest solidity from the water!"—thus was Janārdana, the God of gods, being praised.
For the sake of accomplishing his purpose, the thousand-faced god assumed a divine, white, and gentle form,
with a thousand hanging tusks.
He had a thousand snouts for a face, a thousand hooves for feet,
two thousand great eyes, and his body was covered in great bristling hair.
In an instant, he became like Mount Meru, possessing the power of a thousand tails and two thousand ears. (19)
Laughing, he himself said to Aja:
"By my power, I shall indeed make the earth solid; therefore, I will bring that [water] back from there."
As my mouths and fangs hung down in every direction, I brought forth the power of the *piṇḍīkara* [mantra], which draws in all that is sour. ||21||
The waters from the contact of my teeth shall soon become pure there, and their gross state will be separated.
By the power of the clumping together of the lumps of clay, they become uneven;
having fashioned all those lumps, one should then unify them completely.
The earth, having attained a state of solidity, exists in the form of a sphere.
And in an instant, they will bring [the girl] standing above the water before you. ||24||
"May residence there for all of them become easily accessible through Brahman.
Having thus addressed him, the Lord Varāha, possessing a white form, departed.
Beholding all that water, he formed it into lumps of thick mud and placed them by the millions within his own nostrils.
Having unified all those [limbs] and fashioned them into a ball,
he held it between his nostrils and indeed came upon the surface of the water.
Having placed the globular great mass of the earth upon the waters,
the Supreme Lord, the Great Being in the form of a boar, ceased his labor.
Brahmā, all the sages, and the lords of munis headed by Nārada, praised that gentle Hari, the upholder of the earth, who had accomplished his task. (29)
Salutations to you whose nature is sacrifice, salutations to you who have the sacrificial altar as your mouth;
salutations to you who have the Vedas as your feet and tusks, and whose chest is the ritual acts prescribed by them.
Salutations to the one with a tongue of fire, whose hair is like *darbha* grass, the ascetic;
salutations to the head of Brahman, who wears the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs as a garland. ||31||
Homage to the one who sustains the moments of day and night, whose snout is the sacrificial ladle;
homage to the one whose nose is the clarified butter and whose sound is the resonance of the Sāman chants.

Obeisance to the Great One, whose nature is truth and righteousness, who is endowed with valor; obeisance to the one whose chariot is expiation, Oṃ, the Terrible One, whose consciousness is directed toward the sacrificial victim. 33.
Salutations to you, the deity who is the thread of the Udgātṛ priest, whose characteristic mark is the oblation;
salutations to the deity who is the seed of the sacred sites, the great medicinal herb. ||34||
Salutations to you who are the source of the power of mantras, the vast one; salutations to the inner self within the sacrificial altar;
salutations to you who touch the clarified butter and whose blood is Soma. ||35||
Salutations to you, the tranquil one who is the trunk of the Vedas, whose fragrance is the oblation;
salutations to him who possesses the great speed of offerings to gods and ancestors, and whose body is the eastern hall of the sacrificial shed.
Salutations to you who possess radiant splendor and are endowed with various initiations;
salutations to you whose heart is the sacrificial fee, the yogin whose form is the perpetual sacrifice.
Salutations to the Great Soul, adorned with the Pravargya-vitta and other ornaments;
salutations to the Source, the radiant Brahman, who is the object of the Upākarma sacrifice. ||38||
Salutations to you, the vital breath that traverses the various paths of meters and destinies;
salutations to you, the sacrifice seated upon the secret Upaniṣads.
Thus praised, the Supreme Lord, having granted his blessing, vanished;
and upon the vanishing of the Boar, the Unborn One himself beheld the Earth.
He constantly contemplated [the site] from all sides as being endowed with peaks, in some places low-lying and excavated, and in other places consisting of rocky mountains. ||41||
Having reflected correctly, the Creator again remembered that Lord;
then He appeared in a vast form, equipped with a bow.
On his right hand, the marks of a discus and a bow were seen.
Then, he was determined by Brahmā to be this very Lord, the Blessed One.
"O Lord, please level the earth by dividing its uneven parts.
Thus was the god Pṛthu entreated at that time by the Saṃvartaka fire.
He caused the Bhūtuṇḍas to be burned; they became shattered heaps of ashes, and all of them turned into earth; those are celebrated as "mṛttikās. ||45||
Having leveled the entire earth, which was beautiful with a covering of soil,
he sowed seeds upon that field and brought about an abundance of crops.
Where there were stones that had not been burnt, there he fashioned mountains;
where there were low-lying regions, there he fashioned lakes.
But by the venerable Pṛthu, the great-souled Nārāyaṇa,
his own fields were made into forests, villages, cities, and market towns.
The oceans, rivers, and great torrents of streams were made to flow in various channels, having observed the proper time and according to necessity. (49)
Having fashioned the worlds, he brought about the creation of living beings;
Pṛthu, having established the supreme kingdom, provided a stable order that grants security.
And having fashioned it and given it to Brahmā, he himself disappeared.
From that time on, the ground became level and even, covered with cloth. ||51||
The great goddess Pṛthvī became the appropriate resting place;
then, upon her destruction, the god Hari himself became Pṛthu once again.
Having become king again and again, he will indeed level the earth;
for at the end of Brahmā’s kalpa, the earth consists of the ten worlds.
When the earth sinks into the water,
then Hari himself, becoming Pṛthu, will repeatedly level the earth there.
Sometimes I am born as Pṛthu from the mind,
and sometimes my birth is taken from sages or from kings.
Thus, I have related to you all this regarding the form of Pṛthu that was assumed by me;
now, tell me what occurred at the end of the Dvāpara age.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Earth’s Elevation by Nārāyaṇa reclining upon the waters in the form of a Boar, and the Leveling of the Earth by Pṛthu," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 50 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how those subjects were born from the law of pairing; as the Creator was meditating, a husband and a wife came into being.
And before that, Svāyambhuva Manu and Śatarūpā, his wife,
caused progeny to increase through the practice of the law of the couple.
Having obtained his wife, Svāyambhuva took delight with her repeatedly;
that was the first act of sexual union which occurred at the beginning of the Kalpa.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were their two sons;
and two daughters were born, Ākūti and Prasūti. || 4 ||
He gave Prasūti to Dakṣa and Ākūti to Ruci;
from Ākūti a pair was born: Yajña and Dakṣiṇā.
From those two, the twelve gods known as the Yāmas were born;
and from Dakṣa, by Prasūti, twenty-four daughters were born.
All of them were expounders of Brahman, yoginīs, and mothers of the world:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and Kriyā.
Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti as the thirteenth—Dharma indeed accepted these as his wives. (8)
From them were born eleven beautiful-eyed daughters of Yaviyarya:
Khyāti, Satī, Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and Kṣamā.
Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā—
these eleven were then obtained by the great seers.
Bhava, Bhṛgu, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and the Pitṛs, as well as Agni—these are they. (11)
Satī gave Khyāti to Bhava and likewise to Bhṛgu;
she gave Saṃbhūti to Marīci and Smṛti to Aṅgīras.
He gave Prīti to Pulastya and Kṣamā to Pulaha; he gave Sannati to Kratu and likewise Anasūyā to Atri.
He gave Ūrjā to Vasiṣṭha and Svāhā to Agni; and he gave Svadhā to the Pitṛs. From sexual union with them, offspring were born.
Śraddhā gave birth to Kāma, and Darpa is remembered as the son of Lakṣmī;
Niyama was the son of Dhṛti, and Saṃtoṣa is said to be the son of Tuṣṭi. ||15||
From Puṣṭi comes gain as well as a son, Medhāputra, and likewise Śruta;
from Kriyā, however, Naya is said to arise, as well as Daṇḍa and Samaya. (16)

The son of Buddhi (Intellect) is Bodha (Knowledge), and Apramāda (Heedfulness) is her other son; Vinaya (Humility) is the son of Lajjā (Modesty), and Vyavasāya (Resolve) is the son of Vapuḥ (Form). ||17||
Kṣema was born from Śānti, and Sukha was born from Siddhi; Yaśas was also the son of Kīrti—these, indeed, were the sons of Dharma. (18)
Harṣa was born as the two sons of Kāma by the goddess Rati;
such indeed was this creation of Dharma through sexual union, which results in happiness. 19.
Bhava created countless Rudras of fierce nature;
however, when told by Brahmā, "Do not create," Hara remained with his vital energy drawn upward (a celibate).
From that time forward, Śambhu indeed produced no offspring;
remaining as a celibate ascetic (brahmacārī), he stood firm as Sthāṇu until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forgiveness, fortitude, the power of creation, self-awareness, and likewise the state of being the presiding controller. ||22||
These ten sovereign powers always abide in Śaṅkara; because he is eternally endowed with them, Maheśvara is a yogin possessed of yoga. ||23||
Indeed, by the grace of Maheśvara, a man becomes a Tridaṇḍin;
those three are the staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind. (24)
He for whom these three staffs are ever-restrained is indeed liberated, even though he is a bearer of the triple-staff;
having himself recognized the omens of misfortune, he beholds his own death. (25)
Listen, Lakṣmī; in this context, I shall indeed describe them in their entirety.
When one recognizes these signs, then one's own death should be known [to be imminent]. (26)
That man who cannot see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Soma-chāyā), and the white path (Sitam-patha) shall not live beyond one year.
He who sees the sun as devoid of rays and the purifier (fire) as possessed of rays shall certainly not live beyond eleven months. 28.
If one vomits urine or feces, or likewise gold or silver—
whether witnessed directly or in a dream— one lives for ten months.
If one's footprint should be broken either in front or behind,
whether on dusty ground or in mud, he shall live for seven months.
If a crow, a pigeon, a vulture, or any other flesh-eating bird should perch upon one's head, six months shall not pass before [his death]. (31)
Or he may be struck by a flight of crows, or again by a shower of dust;
or he may see his own shadow distorted—he lives for four or five [days].
One might see lightning in a cloudless sky, appearing to be situated in the southern direction.

that opening which caused terror among the gods was a hundred yojanas in width. 41.
I must fulfill it there, and I must also dwell there forever.
"For that purpose, I shall indeed grant a portion of the Imperishable to Raivata."
It was a divine, prosperous, and bliss-bestowing realm, a hundred *gavyūti*s in extent, where there were wells of liquid gold and likewise rivers of golden dust. (43)

It is the reviver, the remover of arrows, the healer of wounds, and that which prevents fainting; likewise, it is the giver of blood, the destroyer of hemorrhage, and the suppressor of hunger and thirst. ||44||
Various medicinal herbs shall be there with me,
where my wife Bhadrā Subhadrā is, by the river Bhadrāvatī.
Wherever my wife Ūrjā is, there let she be full of vigor;
wherever the saffron of Lakṣmī’s wet saffron-pool has been sprinkled, [there let her be]. 46.
There a Brahmin devoted to his wife, who is a portion of myself, shall come into being;
there the Sarasvatī, flowing toward the ocean, shall take up the Vāḍava fire.
Where I shall dwell for a moment in the shade of a Plakṣa tree, and where the beautiful city of Svarṇapura shall be located within my island. ||48||
Where King Khaṭvāṅgada shall become your son, and where the god Someśvara, the Great God (Mahādeva), shall be present. ||49||
Where, through the destruction of Tala, it shall indeed become Talaśyāma;
and where, because of sacrifices performed in secret, it shall also become Prayāga.
There, indeed, my great devotee named Dāma will appear;
there, three sages—Ekata, Dvita, and Trita—will also exist.
On that mountain where Dattātreya, who loves austerity, dwells, I shall reside;
there, the Gaṅgā, though appearing mad, shall flow for my sake.
Where the lions, the vehicles of the wife of the Lord of Beings (Bhavēśvara), shall stand;
where my path of devotion (bhaktimārga) shall exist, which bestows all things upon me. ||53||
Where Jayā and Lalitā shall become my Rādhā and Lakṣmī,
and where the Sun shall take birth in the form of the Arka tree.
There the goddess, having conquered her enemies, will take the form of a river;
there King Anarta will again go forth to perform ascetic penance.
Where the city shall dwell, obstructed by serpents and poison;
where Kṛṣṇa, marked by the bow, shall appear in the form of a virtuous man.
My parents shall be born upon the back of Gopālaka,
and there my incarnations shall take place, O great sages.
Where those who favor my kingdom shall become my sharers,
and where Devānīka shall be the one to consecrate the king.
"Where my permanent residence shall be, O Rajikuṭṭa, there Kṛṣṇa himself will establish my pair [of footprints]. (59)
That divine abode of mine shall be without beginning or end;
this divine island, which bestows liberation upon Kṛṣṇa, shall become such.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Future Reality, Beginning with the Arrival of Nārada at the House of Dharmarēvata during the Dvāpara Age within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, and the Bringing of the Portion of Brahmā to Fill the Chasm in the Western Region," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga. ||53||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, where is that region known as Vivara located?
It lies to the east of the region called Abrikta and to the south of Kaccha.
To the west of the Narmadā and north of the Siṃhāraṇya forest,
that region shall become Surāṣṭra, protected by the Suratrāṇa.
Extending from the western side of Mount Malaya to the eastern region of Abrikta,
it is five thousand yojanas long and wide in every direction.
There is a country known as Siṃhāraṇya, possessing an uninterrupted territory;
to the north of Siṃhāraṇya is the region named Devadamana.
One hundred *gavyūtis* to the north of the land of Devadamanabhū, there exists a great chasm in the earth; indeed, for the purpose of filling that very [chasm], [he went]. (5)
Śrī Hari will grant you His own abode according to your desire;
O sinless one, come with me toward Vaikuṇṭha.
"Take the land of Saurāṣṭra, which is to be given, and return to the surface of the earth;
having filled that opening, make that subterranean realm the terrestrial world. || 7 ||
O Protector of the Earth, remain steadfast in that land of Saurāṣṭra.
In that region, there is a great mountain named Brahmagiri, composed of jewels and gold.
O Somabhadrā, designate the Middle Country for your own residence;
and because of Raivata’s dwelling there, the mountain shall also be known as Raivata.
The great divine mountain known as Brahmagiri shall be named Revatācala.
Revata had a daughter named Revatī.
There, the place known as Tīrtha shall remain forever, even though it is situated in Goloka;
and Raivata, a devotee of the Lord, shall dwell there for a long time. (11)
"Having become the fifth Manu, you shall dwell there once again;
that Raivataka mountain-tīrtha will become a great tīrtha. (12)
Where Dāmodara Kṛṣṇa is, where Śambhu, the Lord of Existence, is, and where Brahmā, the Self-born, is—what indeed can be called illusory there? (13)
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, this divine earth is always black and full of essence;
likewise, it is so called because of its drawing away (karṣaṇa) of latent impressions (vāsanā) and its leading [the soul] to Vaikuṇṭha.
There is the mountain known as Saurāṣṭra, called Kṛṣṇa by name, which is equal to him in form, splendor, and power; and there is also Mount Kṛtasmara, located to the west of Raivataka. (15)
Because of that, a great conflagration will surely arise;
the goddess Sarasvatī, having carried [the fire], will travel along that path.
Then, for the purpose of throwing it into the great ocean, Smaragiri himself will rise up and create an obstruction near it. ||17||
Then the enraged submarine fire will reduce the mountain to ashes;
even the stones of that ash-bed become soft and white. (18)
By those artisans, palaces with white floors will be constructed;
the white powder, the material for the stucco, shall then be produced from the firing of clay in fire.
Then the ṛṣis, the ancestors, the perfected beings, the gods, the virtuous women and the virtuous men, the yogins, the ascetics, and the devotees shall dwell upon the Raivata mountain.

Encircled by ten mountain walls and adorned with the palace of Lakṣmyambā, it was circumambulated on the full moon day of Kārttika by a multitude of devotees eager for the festival of ten million circuits.
Its slopes are covered with clouds; its peaks are frequented by celestial sages;
its base is crowded with dark-skinned people; and its sides are the excellent path for divine chariots. ||22||
To the east is Śatruñjaya, and Vārāṇasī is four yojanas further;
the holy site known as Kuṅkumavāpī is three yojanas beyond that.
To its north lies the river named Bhadrā at a distance of two yojanas,
and to its south lies Somatīrtha at a distance of four yojanas.
To the west of which, protected by the very shadow of the Yoginī mountain, there is an extensive region of high ground measuring one *krośa* in width. (25)
There you must indeed create for yourself the city of Raivata;
from that, a son named Khaṭvāṅga shall be born to you.
Becoming a second moon, he will dispel the darkness of night;
by his name, that city shall be known as Khaṭvāṅgada.
In his lineage, there will be a king named Hāṭaka, a sovereign among devotees;
he shall bring forth from the netherworld the great god Hāṭakeśa-Mahādeva.
That city shall be known by his name as Hāṭakeśapura;
in his lineage, there will be a king named Maṇimān, who will be an attendant of Śambhu.
That city shall become famous by his name as Maṇipura;
and then, upon seeing the ancient fortresses, men [will be amazed].
In the course of time, they shall proclaim that city by the name Jīrṇadurgapura.
Then, after some time has passed there, the Lord’s attendant Vijaya [will arrive].
There a kingdom shall manifest, and he too shall rule it;
it shall acquire the name Vijayapura after his own name.
Virtuous women and virtuous men, embodiments of Brahman who bestow liberation, shall dwell there forever for the sake of the world's welfare. ||33||
Marvels will occur on that earth in age after age;
and there, in age after age, men shall become divine.
The protectors of the earth and the establishers of dharma, as well as the gopīs, repeatedly took refuge in Kṛṣṇa and Dāmodara. (35)
In various places there will indeed be women of great vows;
having become virtuous wives, they shall worship the holy and majestic Kṛṣṇa.
Men, women, beasts, and birds who make that their firm support shall be liberated from the snare of saṃsāra; such a stage [of practice] must come to be. (37)
Then, this future Raivata will be the refuge of the Mlecchas on all sides;
that will indeed be the evening of the Kalpa, at the end of the birth of Kalki.
Indeed, from the wrath of his eyes, he shall become Jvālāmukha;
scorched by the flames, even the region, tormented by the essence [of fire], shall turn into liquid. (39)
Having reached Vaikuṇṭha, Raso shall become as he was before;
born in Saurāṣṭra from Vaikuṇṭha, he shall return once more to Vaikuṇṭha.
Furthermore, it shall be exactly as before even in another kalpa;
therefore, O Indra among kings, come with me to Vaikuṇṭha.
"Śrī Hari will indeed grant you the region of Surāṣṭra";
having thus addressed him by Nārada, Raivata departed for that place.
Having arrived together at Vaikuṇṭha and prostrated before the Lord Hari,
he bowed his head like a staff and praised Him with palms joined in reverence.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Indication of the Holy Places and Other Sites that Filled the Cavities of the Earth," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, the Manu named Raivata attained Vaikuṇṭha;
and with great love, he praised me, the compassionate one, accompanied by you.
Salutations to you whose nature is existence and consciousness, the ocean of the mass of bliss;
salutations to you who are of a single nature and yet of both natures. 2.

Homage to the one with golden hair; homage to the one possessing a beard upon beard. Homage to the one possessing breasts and non-breasts; homage to the one who sustains both seed and non-seed. || 3 ||
Homage to you who have external marks; homage to you whose signs are on the outside.
Homage to you who are the sprout of the universe; homage to you who are sometimes like a child.
Homage to you, the being of the right; homage to you, the being of the left.
Homage to you whose nature is above; homage to you who are not of a nature above. || 5 ||
Salutations to you who are the form of that which is supported, salutations to you who are the form of the support;
salutations to you who are the form of the two-fold petals, salutations to the source from which the sprout is born.
Salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to you who dwell beyond all limits.
Salutations to you whose form is the mind; salutations to you whose form is devotion.
Salutations to you, O ocean of compassion; salutations to the prosperer of Saurāṣṭra;
salutations to the dweller of Raivata; salutations to you, Dāmodara.
Salutations to the one known as Patnīvrata; salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Viṣṇu;
salutations to the one whose nature is infinite, to my inner controller (antaryāmin).
"O Great Viṣṇu, you are independent; I do not know what you desire.
You ought to accomplish that for which your devotee has been summoned."
O Viṣṇu, by Your grace, may this servant be led to the further shore of the path of worldly existence;
for wherever Your two feet abide, that place shall indeed become my refuge from fear.
O Lord of Compassion, this servant who has come for refuge must certainly not be abandoned;
since he has been taken up by Your mercy, You ought not to forsake him.
"Whatever is desired that brings security in this world, let that be provided"—having praised him thus, Raivata, the best among devotees, fell silent. (13)
The glorious Lord, the Sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha, said to him:
"Accept this, which is like an atom, my portion of Vaikuṇṭha. (14)
Within the sphere of you, the four-faced Brahmā known as Svayambhū,
there is a great western aperture in the earthly realm of Priyavrata.
That gap in the path of the Suratrāsa, extending for a hundred *gavyūtis*, must be filled by you alone with the blossoming earth. (16)
By that [act], he shall become a protector (suratrāṇa) and attain the name Saurāṣṭra;
there, endowed with glory, I shall dwell for your sake. (17)
"Whatever else was spoken by Nārada, I shall ordain that as well;
having said this, the Lord bestowed upon him a minute particle of Vaikuṇṭha. (18)
Taking him by the command of Viṣṇu, Raivata returned;
he desired to place that minute object into the cavity exactly as it had been described.
It attained such vastness that it extended for a hundred *gavyūtis*;
in its density, it was equal to the surface of the earth; it was divine and composed of five qualities.
The gap situated according to its requirement and its proper place has been filled;
from the non-divine mixed with the divine, the junction consists of white and red. ||21||
The white ditch and the white ground turn back the circle;
that circle, extending for a hundred *gavyūtis*, is dark and pale.
He ruled over the divine, unbroken land of Surāṣṭra, which had been acquired by Raivata;
and in its central region, having meditated upon Viṣṇu, he established him there.
For Nārāyaṇa himself, casting aside his illusory form, remains intent on honoring all who worship him; he bestows upon such a person a compassionate glance. 24.
Then Hari gave him a thousandth part of his own jewel;
that [part], having attained bulk, assumed a supreme mountain-like form.
Thus, this mountain established in the middle of Surāṣṭra became famous by the name of its leader as Raivatācala.
There, Raivata built a city named Raivata;
Raivata was always engaged in the remembrance, chanting, and hearing of Viṣṇu. ||27||
For in service, worship, praise, servitude, and the offering of all things, that great devotee remained engaged throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (28)
In the burden of sovereignty, in legal affairs, in eating, and likewise in sleeping—in every way, O Lord of the gods, he worshipped Nārāyaṇa. (29)
Once, while lying upon a great couch in yogic sleep,
he entered into a state of meditative absorption (samādhi) as he meditated upon Śrī Hari within his own self.
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, from his right arm,
Svarṇāṅgada became liquid and fell onto the couch.
The youth became golden-colored, with a white radiance like that of the moon;
a halo of cool, white light appeared all around him. (32)
It became entirely pervaded on all sides by white rays;
thus, the palace, the city, and the country were filled with a luster as white as milk.
While he remained upon his couch dispelling all darkness, the great devotee Raivata happened to become awake by chance. (34)
Upon the couch, she received a boy born from her own body—one who was as bright as the moon, gentle, full of splendor, and auspicious. (35)
White-washing the entire world in all directions and intermediate points, he was fully consecrated as soon as he was born, appearing eternally radiant like a sixteen-year-old youth. (36)

Having recognized that Raivata was virtuous, possessed the mark of a universal monarch’s bow, and was endowed with the accumulation of formal requests, [the king] gave him the royal throne on Mount Raivataka.
He went to the Viśālā cave for the purpose of worship; there, Raivata remained constantly absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi) upon Hari. 38.
Remaining as a single self until the arrival of the fifth Manu,
he himself [will exist] in each successive great aeon (kalpa) during the subsequent time.
It is established that he will exist in the Satya age, known as Mahāvibhūti;
and here and there in his lineage will appear Khaṭvāṅga, Danu, Nṛpa, and others.
They shall be rulers of the earth for tens of millions of years.
Born from the armlet on the couch, he was named Khaṭvāṅgada. ||41||
A vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) like a golden line appeared on his forehead, and a natural tilaka mark, appearing like a drop of blood in its center, appeared upon his skin.
A golden garland was upon his neck, and a natural luster appeared upon his skin;
the mountain-like king was the refuge of all sovereignty, dispelling the darkness with his splendor. (43)
Then, having ascended his celestial chariot, he wandered repeatedly through the atmosphere,
seeing from afar what was even further away, like the darkness of night at the beginning of the month.
Wherever there was a region devoid of the moon, there he came through the air, destroying all darkness like a second moon. (45)
Wandering month after month through the sky and the empty quarters of the moon,
he makes the worlds luminous by spreading forth his cool rays.
But when this was done there, the oceans were perpetually in their full tide;
the earth became agitated, and the shores were repeatedly submerged by the waves. (47)
The waves rise up and do not indeed recede in that same way;
rather, at various times, the lands become overwhelmed by water.
At that time, medicinal herbs were generally nourished for only one, two, or three kalās;
due to the accumulation of excessive cold and indigestion, they went to ruin. (49)
Having thus perceived this loss, he withdrew his own celestial chariot;
it became such a great divine vehicle, consisting of cool radiance, as if it were a self-ruling lord.
He practices devotion to Śrī Hari and causes other people to do so;
at dawn he proclaims that Viṣṇu is always to be worshipped by all people. 51.
A forehead mark with a crescent moon should always be applied, and food should be offered to Hari;
having gone to the house of Viṣṇu in the evening, the Lord Janārdana should be praised.
Virtuous women and holy men should be highly honored with offerings of food, drink, and the like;
oblations should be offered into the fire and gifts should be given to the gods with devotion. (53)
Indeed, he who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa and always worships Nārāyaṇa—his hand must never be grasped by me. (54)
Thus, while he ruled, the entire earth was adorned with Vaiṣṇavas;
indeed, there was no one who was not a devotee during his reign.
Thus, in that circle filled with devotion, King Khaṭvāṅga remained peaceful;
having abandoned all anxiety for the kingdom, he constantly remembered the Blessed One. (56)
Having stationed his celestial chariot in a mountain cave, he himself became intent on propitiation;
for when many hundreds of millions of years had passed, he set his mind upon asceticism.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Lakṣmīśa, the Acceptance of Maṇibhūmi as a Follower, the Filling of the Earth’s Cavity, the Spreading of Radiance that Becomes a Second Moon, and the Establishment of Devotion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||55||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, then the king, overwhelmed by the force of his dispassion,
[went] three yojanas to the east of Mount Raivata.
The Aśvapaṭṭa lake is delightful, and the tiger forest is very extensive; it possesses uninterrupted waters and is surrounded by trees providing roots and fruits. || 2 ||
Knowing it to be solitary and free from danger, that king then went to a secluded spot not far from the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa river.
Having seen that region filled with cool shade, King Khaṭvāṅgada beheld it abounding in excellent trees such as the Badarī, pomegranate, jambu, tamarind, and guṇḍrā.
And in that region, which was pervaded and endowed with subterranean water-tanks,
the water of the tank flowed constantly in the form of a mountain stream.
Flowing from above, it indeed goes to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
there, at the foot of a banyan tree standing near the edge of that pool, on the surface of the earth—(6).
Placing a Śālagrāma stone before him, Khaṭvāṅga performed austerities;
for a thousand years, he subsisted on the eating of Jāmbū fruits.
He performed the consumption of *guṃdra* fruits for a second thousand [days],
and he performed the consumption of pomegranates for a third thousand [days].
He performed the fourth thousand [of days] subsisting on jujube fruits;
he performed the fifth thousand subsisting on sour tamarind.
Then he made the sixth thousand subsist on bulbs;
and the seventh thousand he made to subsist on leaves.
In the eighth thousand, he subsisted on water alone;
in the ninth thousand, he subsisted on air alone. ||11||
During the tenth thousand [years], however, remaining without food and established upon his big toe,
he stood meditating upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, his guru, at Śālagrāma.
Constantly meditating upon the glorious Lord Viṣṇu, he recited:
"O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Śrīman Nārāyaṇa, salutations unto You! (13)
At that moment, a great fire indeed burst forth from his head;
its smoke and mighty flames pervaded the three worlds.
Setting ablaze the gods, daityas, humans, and others stationed in the sky, the goddess Earth trembled and the oceans were likewise agitated. (15)
A great forest fire there arose from the fire of his ascetic heat;
when that forest fire had spread, the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa [appeared] there. ||16||
Out of compassion, for the protection of that ascetic who was devoid of physical luster,
he arrived there and sprinkled that nectar upon his head.
By that [act], the fire from his head was extinguished and the forest fire also turned back;
Nārāyaṇa, who had been won over by his devotion, spoke to him: "O devotee! (18)
O Khaṭvāṅgada, you shine brightly by practicing great devotion;
by performing penance consisting of devotion, you shall bring about the welfare of all creatures. (19)
Desist from such asceticism; show yourself to me, O sinless one!
For one like me, who is free from desire yet devoted, there is nothing that should not be given.
"What do you require? Choose, O King; I shall grant whatever you desire.
Having thus commanded, the glorious Hari then remained silent.
Opening his eyes, he beheld Nārāyaṇa standing before him;
filled with affection, he exclaimed, "Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! (22)
He performed a dance by beholding [the Lord], bearing the dust of His feet upon his head; he rolled about repeatedly at the feet of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. (23)
Becoming a servant, that sovereign of the discus (Cakrarāja) always chose to serve at his feet;
wherever penance was performed, there he remained in the presence of both himself and his own form.
Lakṣmī chose Nārāyaṇa, always desiring a vision of him;
then, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī replied, "So be it. (25)
Having spoken thus, an auspicious crescent moist with saffron was placed upon his forehead;
it was like drops of moist saffron held in the hand of Lakṣmī.
Many had fallen into the pond; likewise, having washed his hands, drunk water, bathed, and caused the king to drink as well, [he departed]. ||27||
The Lord made His eternal residence at Śālagrāma;
there the great Lord Nārāyaṇa, the leader of the glorious caravan, dwells forever.
From that time on, that pond became known by the name Kuṅkumavāpikā;
and there, by that king, a temple of Śrī Nārāyaṇa was established.
She herself performed service for him at his seven-storied palace;
and she was indeed Lakṣmī, while Kambharā bore that happiness. 1.56.30.
Indeed, Śrī Hari is that very Gopāla who always takes and accepts King Khaṭvāṅga as his refuge—the protector of the earth, which is like a cow. ||31||
They are called Lakṣmī and Narāyaṇa, known as Kambharā and Gopāl.
Their son is Patnīvrata, who is himself born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa. (32)
There, in that very world-cycle known as Prakalpaka, he remains performing austerities.
The son, who was dear to Kṛṣṇa, meditated upon his two divine parents. ||33||
At the auspicious holy site known as Kuṅkumavāpī, which bestows liberation upon those who take refuge there,
he dwells in a divine body, even though he is all-pervading everywhere.
This is the divine Aśvasaras lake and the vast tiger forest;
there is the divine Kuṅkumavāpī and the temple of Kambharā-Gopāla. (35)
In the region of Surāṣṭra, there were the holy ford of Patnīvratadvija, the city established by Khaṭvāṅga,
and the beautiful place known as Kuṅkumavāpī.
Taking with him all the requisites of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as hosts of male and female servants,
along with prosperity and sovereign power, Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent there.
Every particle of dust there is pure and bestows liberation;
it is a divine land with celestial waters, resembling the divine Vaikuṇṭha. (38)
It bestows liberation through sacrifice, ancestral rites, vows, charity, and sacred sites;
there, whether it be a woman or a man, whoever has entered any kind of womb [is liberated]. (39)
Abandoning the body there, one attains supreme liberation known as the imperishable Brahman;
all those men who are on that ground are indeed the attendants of Hari.
And those women who dwell there, all of whom move about in black;
likewise all the beasts, birds, and so forth, as well as the trees, creepers, and the like. (41)
Those liberated souls residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha are not to be perceived by one with human vision;
they are to be beheld with divine sight, and certainly not with the eyes of flesh. 42.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Direct Vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa through the Penance of Khaṭvāṅgada at Aśvapaṭṭasara, the Formation of the Kuṅkuma-candraka, the Emergence of the Tīrtha-pura known as Kuṅkumavāpī from the Flowing Drops, and the Abode of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of Kambharā and Gopāla," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The son of Khaṭvāṅga was indeed called Barhiṣāṅgada;
peacocks used to come and stand upon his head while he performed penance.
There they shed their feathers, yet he does not see them;
for there, a mass of peacock plumes has appeared. || 2 ||
Indeed, by means of their devotion to their wives, a great broom was fashioned for them;
it was kept near the deity's image for the task of cleaning the temple.
When she was seen by Khaṭvāṅgada and seized by his two hands, he proceeded to wipe her clean; at that very moment, rain began to fall from the sky.
Taking that broom, he entered a hut and stayed there;
day and night, a great rain occurred, falling in heavy torrents. ||5||
It was warm like a bundle of broom-grass, yet smooth,
soft, variegated, pleasant to the touch, and likewise dispelling the cold.
Having laid [her] by his side on the bed, he then became overcome by sleep;
there, by the will of Hari, he beheld a form of an Apsaras.
A dream-like emission of his vital essence occurred upon those sacrificial grasses;
very quickly, a son was born to him as soon as he looked at them in the morning.
Seeing that his son was a great adept who possessed youth from the very moment of birth, he then gave him the name Bāliṣāṅgada.
And he was consecrated as king in that realm— a proud, heroic archer—
honored in the beautiful capital city of Khaṭvāṅgapura.
Once that pure devotee, accompanied by a limited number of followers, was wandering through the forest of his father’s divine hunting grounds, roaming about in the tiger-infested wilderness. (11)
Then he arrived there at the excellent holy site of Kuṅkumavāpī, at the hermitage of the twice-born who were devoted to their wives, in order to behold those brahmins.
And having beheld his two gurus, his parents, who were the very embodiments of the divine Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, he returned to the presence of his true spiritual teacher (sadguru).
At that time, the Guru was established in meditative absorption nearby;
he did not perceive the king's sudden arrival while remaining within his inner state.
In that hermitage devoid of people, that royal sage received neither welcome, nor honor, nor a seat, nor even respect. (15)
When the king did not receive honor for even a moment, his intellect being ruined by his dependence on honor, he conceived a base self-interest. ||16||
"Alas! This mendicant, who eats our grain, treats us with contempt;
he does not show us even verbal respect, for he holds himself as a Brahmin. (17)
"Closing his eyes in deceit, what kind of meditation has he undertaken?
If I wake him, it will lead to the king’s showing me honor. (18)
"Therefore, this twice-born man is indeed treating me with contempt, putting forward the deception that one must remain established by relying on meditative concentration. (19)
Therefore, such a Brahmin must certainly not be neglected;
thus spoke King Bāhuśravas, who was like a great serpent with a dead snake around its neck.
Having entrusted [his wife] to Patnīvrata, he departed for his own city;
meanwhile, Brahmavrata arrived at that sage's hermitage.
Accompanied by the sage’s disciples, Svayamprakāśa and others, he remained there;
having seen a dead snake around the sage's neck, he understood it through meditative absorption (samādhi).
The king threw a dead snake at that wicked man, thereby sending forth a curse upon him:
"Alas! A dog, indeed, by barking at its master and insulting him with its paws," (23)
To throw dust [at him]—this is a great and extraordinary anomaly:
that a Malakīṭa, consecrated by Brahmins, has indeed attained the state of a serpent. 24.
He bites those very same people; what kind of unworthiness is this, that a mouse, having fallen into fear, has been joined with the state of a lion? (25)
What indeed is more wretched than this darkness that seeks to swallow it?
Like a sinful dog devouring its own food, he seeks to destroy the innocent vow of his wife. 26.
Disregarding his venerable father, who was like a god, she placed a serpent around his neck; she certainly deserves punishment. (27)
"Furthermore, those dogs shall not cause you any disrespect at all.
Having thus addressed them and taken water in his right hand, the son spoke. (28)
"May he by whom a snake was thrown around my neck through trickery meet his death within this very month!"—thus saying, he released water upon the ground. (29)
Having uttered a curse while observing the vow of celibacy, surrounded by his fellow students, he wept before his teacher; meanwhile, the teacher arose from his meditative absorption.
When he saw the carcass of a dead snake around his own neck,
he heard his own circle of sons and disciples weeping.
Then the teacher, devoted to his wife, consoled them all:
"Understand why you are all weeping here. (32)
Since a serpent is indeed worn as a corpse upon the human corpse [of Śiva],
it should be understood that this necklace is truly for the worship of the corpse by the corpse.
"There is no loss here, nor is there any fault; indeed, I am performing my bath.
Purity comes from the mere act of bathing; for what reason do you weep so bitterly? (34)
Peace must always be protected, and forbearance must be protected in every way;
through peace and forbearance, all the sages have attained a state of worshipfulness. (35)
Truth, virtue, austerity, meditation, self-study, peace, forbearance, and patience—this we always consider to be our divine and supreme wealth. (36)
That must never be abandoned, for it is our deity;
indeed, forgiveness is the supreme weapon, the destroyer of the weapon of anger. (37)
"Through forgiveness, all the Vāḍavas obtained worship from the gods;
my sons, I ask you: was anything harmful ever contemplated by you regarding him? (38)
