Thus questioned, the sons then informed the Ṛṣi that within a month the king, who had transgressed the bounds of propriety, would become the king of serpents.
"The deceiver will surely bite us"—this was indeed what had been intimated;
having heard that the sage possessed a terrible thunderbolt made of adamant, O King, which was destructive to men. (1.57.40)
He remained silent for a moment, as if burning within his own heart, and then said:
"Indeed, that which is self-luminous and cannot be taken away has been stolen by you! (41)
A great punishment for a very slight offense is indeed not just; you have acted improperly.
O Queen, when there is a ruler as a punisher, even thieves and the like do not oppress the subjects.
In a kingdom devoid of a king, the subjects kill one another and bandits plunder;
yet, O dear one, you, with your immature intellect, have uttered this terrible curse.
The Blessed One should forgive the fault committed through ignorance;
even when thousands of offenders exist, he does not grieve at all.
A devoted person suffers but does not seek recompense, even when they are treated with contempt, beaten, reviled, or insulted. (45)
Even when reviled, threatened, mistreated, or struck down—
even in times of adversity— the virtuous do not retaliate against the wicked.
Therefore, go quickly and announce your own self-luminosity;
for within a month, a rogue will surely bite you.
Thus urged, the disciple went to Barhiṣāṅgada;
the royal sage, overcome with grief, reflected upon his own wickedness.
"Alas! Even an ignoble person would not have committed such a deed as I have;
indeed, a great sin has been accumulated by me against a Brāhmaṇa worthy of worship. (49)
Prosperity, youth, pride, existence itself, and lack of discernment—these are [the causes of downfall].
They say that the causes of misfortune have found their true etymological meaning in me alone.
Alas! What world could there be for me, who have expanded as a hater of Brahman?
May the destruction of this sin necessarily become my adversary. ||51||
Furthermore, one should certainly not act in this way, as the Teacher, the Lord of Men, has taught;
rather, [one should act] so that kings may be secure and prosperous, and honored by the Brahmins. (52)
"Nevertheless, the Blessed One ought to inflict a great punishment upon me.
While he was thinking thus, [the power] accumulated for the purpose of the Brahma-punishment [manifested]. 53.
The voice of the disciple, arising from deceit, indeed arrived as a harbinger of death;
hearing it, the one endowed with discipline undertook a vow of fasting.
Having paid homage to the Brahmin, he merged his own self into Brahman on the Raivata plateau to the east of Khaṭvāṅgapura. (55)
Then, in the middle of the Bhaveśa lake, upon an island consisting of water,
he undertook a vow of fasting and sat down facing the north.
Having realized this through the practice of meditative concentration (samādhi), the sages, as well as the Manus,
the ancestors, gods, gandharvas, asuras, yakṣas, and human beings;
the brahmins, virtuous men, virtuous women, sacred fords, and likewise the mountains [attained their respective states].
The planets, constellations, and stars; divine medicinal herbs and wish-fulfilling trees. ||58||
The wish-fulfilling cows, the Surabhis, the Mothers, and the guardians of the world arrived;
having honored them, he prostrated himself like a staff before them again and again.
When they were seated comfortably, the king,
perceiving that the final duty must be performed, announced what he intended to do.
Oh, the sight of those who possess compassion, who bestow liberation, and who are endowed with merit, leads to the destruction of sins and to the attainment of the higher world! 61.
That the arrival of you both occurred as a pretext for the brahmin’s curse was a favor to me; it has become the root of my world-weariness and the impeller toward liberation. (62)
Whether sweet or bitter, that which is spoken by a Brahmin will lead to welfare in every way;
for you have come before my eyes at the very moment of my death. (63)
The compassionate ones should remain steadfast and likewise sing the *Daśa* of Hari;
let the deceiver bite his own desire, for today no anxiety dwells within me. (64)
May my vital breath go happily into the midst of the assembly of the virtuous;
wherever I go, may I enjoy the service of those who delight in Brahman.
Having done this and having bowed down at the Lake of the Lord of Existence (Bhaveśvara),
the lord of the earth sat down on the central island, abstaining from food.
Then, by the gods, the sages, and the apsarases, [he was praised] again and again.
A shower of flowers was offered in praise, accompanied by shouts of victory.
Just then, Vyāsa himself arrived there, the sage Śvetavyāsa,
who had assumed a white form and was born in the first Kalpa.
In brilliance he was like the sun, radiant with knowledge through his learning;
in yoga he was equal to Brahmā, and in sovereignty he was Hari himself.
Those who were there rose and paid homage to him as he arrived;
they then caused him to be seated upon a great, worthy throne.
As he sat there, the king bowed with palms joined in reverence and,
with humility, inquired after that auspicious and beneficial matter.
We are indeed heirs to the warrior class, yet by our actions we have become inferior; nevertheless, having encountered those such as you, we have been elevated above all people.

His palaces become sacred pilgrimage sites through the mere mention of his name, and by seeing them, touching them, being in their presence, serving them, massaging them, and bowing down before them. (73)
For when the virtuous are properly served, they indeed purify their servants;
by obtaining the dust of whose feet, householders become pure. (74)
Even houses are purified; how much more so by coming into contact with them!
How could the sight of you be possible for me without your compassion? (75)
Therefore, my liberation will surely come after eternal years;
now, what indeed should be done by me who am dying in every way? (76)
I ask: whether it be listening, recitation, or worship as is appropriate, or something else such as the *dīna-homa* and so forth—let that which brings about the highest good be shown to me. (77)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Barhiṣāṅgada, His Departure for the Hermitage of Patnīvratā, His Failure to Obtain Honor, the Casting of a Poisonous Serpent by a Great Sage onto His Neck, the Death Caused by the Sting of a Deceptive Snake within a Month by the Sage’s Son, the Curse, the Knowledge Thereof, the Vow of Fasting unto Death, the Meeting with the Sages, the Arrival of Śveta Vyāsa, and the Inquiry into the Means for One’s Own Spiritual Welfare," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. ||57||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, and understand from me what happened there after that;
the sage Śveta Vyāsa then spoke to Hāṭakāṅgada.
O King, such a hermitage as yours yields only meager benefit for the sake of the highest good;
the realization of the true nature of the self is not attained through sleep, sexual intercourse, or worldly activities.
One's youth passes away through desire; nights depart in sleep;
and days are spent in the mockery of exertion for the sake of filling the belly. (3)
The observer perceives incessantly the world dissolving moment by moment;
yet, though seeing his house, children, wife, and so forth as dead, he does not truly see them.
What was acquired yesterday may perish today or tomorrow;
yet the world does not realize that its own destruction has arrived. (5)
A frog, half-seized in the mouth by a serpent as it approached, strives to eat a fly; the hope for life is difficult to overcome.
Only someone through a mere fragment of compassion understands the liberation of the self;
only someone who is a vessel for compassion strives again for the highest good.
Even there, some fortunate person remains solely for the sake of liberation.
O King, you who desire liberation have indeed made a perfectly firm resolve.
The Lord Śrī Hari should be heard, glorified, and remembered, for the sake of attaining the perfection of yoga-practice and for the maintenance of the wisdom of Sāṃkhya. (9)
Likewise, from the study of the scriptures comes the attainment of the certain realization of liberation;
and the attainment resulting from birth as a human being is that which culminates in the remembrance of Śrī Hari at the end.
O King, the virtuous generally delight in the ocean of Hari’s qualities;
even those devoid of qualities engage in the narration and glorification of Hari. 11.
Indeed, the chanting of his deeds, the remembrance of his form, and the meeting with his devotees bestow the highest spiritual welfare. (12)
Hearing his stories and understanding his glories, as well as meditating upon him dwelling within the heart—this indeed bestows supreme liberation. (13)
Through the power of Śrī Hari’s grace, the first Śveta Vyāsa Muni was born from a ray of Śrī Hari; I am Nirguṇa, and I bow to Hari.
I meditate upon, remember, and glorify the stories of Hari;
those stories were heard by me from the mouth of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (15)
Through them, I have attained that state which is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa) and consists of liberation;
nevertheless, I cause these [teachings] to be heard by people for the sake of supreme liberation.
This Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā is indeed of the nature of Brahman;
for this speech, being a great Bhāgavata work, manifests the forms of Brahman. 17.
In whatever place this [text] is heard through a month-long recitation,
that very place indeed becomes the divine Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Sāra.
Those men to whose ears this [Veda] has come, established within their very self, should indeed be known as always liberated, even though they bear a body. (19)
O King, your father Ṣaḍānana heard this collection [of hymns] at Kuṅkumavāpī and went to Hari for fearlessness.
This Saṃhitā was indeed heard by Brahmā together with the Ṛṣis, and in the Tretā age, in Satyaloka, it was heard by the gods together with the Pitṛs. ||21||
Indeed, in Vaikuṇṭha, the goddess Lakṣmī herself recites this;
this complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) is considered superior even to all the Vedas.
From the very beginning, this scripture issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, the incarnations of the Supreme Brahman and the millions of His manifestations [are described therein]. (23)
Truly described according to their true meaning and heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, this well-composed Saṃhitā is the first scripture of them all. (24)
This [earth] was indeed made manifest by the primordial Vyāsa Śveta;
taking this as his foundation, he composed the collections of the Śāstras and Purāṇas. (25)
Other compositions, such as commentaries and the like, will merely string together ancient traditional narratives;
but this [work] is supremely worthy of being heard, for it leads to the attainment of the state of Nārāyaṇa.
With a one-pointed mind alone, one should contemplate its supreme meaning, by which liberation—consisting of reaching the world of Brahmā—may occur immediately. (27)
One should indeed practice the withdrawal of the senses from their objects,
and one should daily practice the dissolution of the mental modifications into the inner reality.
One should practice stability within one's own internal functions, and one should practice the yoga of union with Hari very firmly. (29)
Thus, for one whose conduct is that of a Brahmin, immediate liberation stands within reach;
seated in the svastika posture, he is devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having withdrawn the functions of the senses, one should first indeed concentrate upon the gross,
embodied form of Śrī Hari, consisting of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
His face was slightly smiling, a fountain of nectar, serene, a torrent of love, beautiful, captivating, gentle, radiant, and white.
A seeker of liberation should wear these two separately on his body:
the two eyes of Hari, which are as long as the petals of a blue lotus.
As if mocking the form of the God of Love, it was wide, white at the edges, and beautiful to behold, as though inflaming one with the flow of the nectar of love. 34.
The object of meditation for those two should be meditated upon separately by one seeking liberation:
the pair of eyebrows should be meditated upon as obliquely curved, smooth, and gradually tapering. (35)
With a peacock-feather fringe at the edge of its fine line of hair extending as far as the ear, it was radiant like a beautiful form, enriched in the middle by the moon of desire. ||36||
Then the Ālakās—slender, smooth, curved, and possessing a shimmering luster—were radiant, supported by the path of Brahman situated at their centers. ||37||
These two should be meditated upon separately, adorned with golden crowns, their hair either braided into a topknot or bound with a crest-jewel or a lock-jewel. (38)
One should fix the mind of oneself upon two cheeks rubbed with a string of pearls, or else one should fix the mind there upon an upward-pointing crescent moon. (39)
Their lips, with their mustaches just beginning to grow and resembling ripe bimba fruits,
were slightly joined and curved, revealing the moment of a kiss.
The two breasts on his chest, marked by the lines of the bow-scar, were filled with nectar.
One should maintain those two separately with devotion, and then gradually bring them into a state of oneness.
Their ears, adorned with golden ear-rings, should rest upon their chins, which are made beautiful by white gems and golden spots. 42.
With its ear-ornaments, crest-jewels, garlands, and the beauty of its blossoming jasmine, the face of Lakṣmī is thus desirable and lovely—the very face of Nārāyaṇa. (43)

One should draw into the activity of the self during meditation that which is intensely radiant, sweet, white, nectar-like, and perfectly circular; then, having drawn it in, the object of meditation (dhyeya) should be established there once again.
In that state, the subsiding of both the mind and the self is brought about by meditative concentration.
In this way, one should unite the self within the self, which is the supreme Brahman. ||45||
But by him who has performed one *yojana*, everything belonging to himself has been accomplished.
Thus [is performed] the touching of the throat, heart, arms, belly, and hips. 46.
The thighs, knees, shanks, calves, ankles, forefeet, and heels—
these are the limbs of Mahālakṣmī and Mahānārāyaṇa.
One should always maintain, meditate upon, and concentrate on each one individually. ||47||
By that, liberation occurs immediately, characterized by the state of non-return;
for in that case, the bondage-causing obscuration consists merely of the object itself. (48)
Even if there were a contradiction regarding what exists within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), one should still observe that [reality] therein at that time.
His two feet are in Pātāla, and his two heels are in Rasātala.
His two ankles were in Mahātala, his two shanks in Talātala, his two knees in Sutala, and his two thighs likewise in Vitala.
His penis was at the bottom and the base of his thighs was upon the surface of the earth.
The navel-pit is in the vault of the sky, and likewise, its heart is in heaven.
Indeed, at the great festival, one should cause the people to gaze upon his throat and his face.
One should observe his forehead, his austerity, his truthfulness, and his head. ||52||
One should observe his arms among Indra and the other [guardians] of the directions, his ears in the [region of] sound, and his two nostrils in those of the Aśvinīs. (53)
One should perceive his nose in the fragrance, his mouth in the fire of digestion,
his two eyes in the heavens, and one should behold his vision in the sun.
One should see his eyelashes by day and night, his eyebrows while seated in the Brahma-posture, his palate in water, and one should examine his tongue in taste.
In the Chāndas [Vedas] he has a sharp fang; likewise, in the Yama [Yoga] and in affection, he has the twice-born [teeth].
In the creation of Māyā, there is the laughter of Śrī Hari and the casting of his sidelong glances. ||56||
In the case of shame, the upper lip is [touched], and in the case of greed, the lower lip is situated [as the object].
One should contemplate the breast of Hari as being in Dharma, and His back in Adharma;
His penis in Brahmā, His testicles in Mitra and Varuṇa,
His bellies in the oceans, and likewise the collection of His bones in the mountains.
In the rivers he saw his veins; in the trees, the hairs born from his body;
in the wind, his breath; and in the birds, the gait of Śrī Hari.
One should perceive his actions within the flow of the qualities, his hair in the clouds,
his garments in the twilights, and his subtlety in the Pradhāna.
One should perceive the mind of Hara in the moon, the state of greatness in consciousness,
that internal organ in Rudra, and indeed the nails in horses and other animals.
He placed his hips and back upon the beasts, that dexterity upon the birds,
his intellect upon the self-born Brahmā, his leaf-hut upon the trees, and [his] manhood upon human beings.
His memory resides among the Gandharvas; his strength is in the armies of the Asuras;
his mouth is among the Brāhmaṇas; and his two arms are among the Kṣatriyas. (63)
Likewise, one should look at the two thighs for the Vaiśyas, and the feet for the Śūdras.
But his resolve regarding desires was fixed upon women who possessed the bodies of divine Hari.
Among men, one should perceive his divine vigor, his bliss, and his meditation on Brahman;
in the gross, the subtle, the great, and the small, one should behold the dark [form] within the Vairāja.
In this manner, one should perceive the glorious Nārāyaṇa everywhere.
Through hearing, reflection, and meditation, one should bring [the practice] to completion therein. ||66||
That is his bliss, that is his happiness, and that is certainly his sweet flavor.
One who always worships another [deity] should lead everything to consist of that [one deity]. ||67||
Thus, O King, that which is to be practiced for the sake of liberation has been shown to you.
By that path, Hari himself indeed becomes directly present. ||68||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Recitation of the Saṃhitā Composed by Śveta-Vyāsa, the Instruction on the Meditation on the Form of the Lord, the Manifestation of His Power, and the Meditation on Identity with Hari," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||58||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Nevertheless, if due to a trace of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the delusion of many births, the mind should again fail to attain stability; || 1 ||
At that time, one should maintain the conviction that "this mind alone is Brahman.
Whatever arises within it—whether white or even black—that is what must be contemplated.
Even that is Brahman alone; for it has no other object whatsoever.
Thus should the wise man who is about to die reflect; he should not pray for anything else.
Moreover, there might even be light there for various kinds of embodied beings.
Of the abundance of cattle, wife, sons, and other material possessions and dwellings. ||4||
One should indeed conceive that "all is Brahman" and not seek anything else;
for in that state of being Brahman, those very things are indeed of the nature of Brahman. (5)
Therefore, those [objects] do not at all become causes of bondage;
nevertheless, a person should themselves make that mind into the form of Brahman.
One should see everything as consisting of Brahman and perceive nothing else—
not by the external senses, nor by the internal ones, nor even by the rays of latent impressions (vāsanā).
For one should perceive that whatever else exists is devoid of one's own self and is not composed of it.
One's own mind, being of such a nature, should be understood as having the form of Brahman.
Having performed that, one should then meditate upon the Supreme Brahman with an undisturbed mind.
Just as one makes the supreme Brahman into one's own well-formed image.
One should contemplate him as having a gentle form, subtle, and the size of a span.
The Lord has four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
His lotus-face was exceedingly serene, his eyes were as long as lotus petals,
his lower garment was tawny like a flower-stamen, and he was beautifully adorned with ornaments set with jewels.
His head was adorned with a crown and earrings whose edges were embellished with great jewels;
he bore the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, along with a forest garland and the beautiful Kaustubha gem. ||12||
Her waist was adorned with a girdle, her lotus-feet were graced with golden anklets,
she wore delicate golden leaf-patterned garments, and was draped in a choice outer robe.
Adorned with golden chains, finger-rings, and bracelets;
possessing smooth, curved, dark-blue hair; and a face like nectar with a gentle smile. (14)
Her eyes overflow with the nectar of love, and she is supremely compassionate with the playfulness of her eyebrows.
Thus one should contemplate [the deity] within oneself as possessing divine splendor and beautiful form. (15)
Likewise, one should gaze upon each individual limb, beginning from the nails up to the hair, until it reaches a state of steadiness; one should practice for that duration. 16.
Seated in a comfortable and steady posture, desiring to leave this turbulent world behind,
one should restrain the vital breaths, restrain the mind, and restrain the intellect within the Self.
One should dissolve the self into Brahman, and Brahman into the Supreme Self; thus, restrained in this sequence, having become tranquil, one attains that very nature. (18)
One should gradually withdraw from activities; for virtues do not bestow bondage.
What else could it be? That state which transcends time, illusion, and the rest, is indeed the Vaiṣṇava state.
Contracting the navel and the anus, one should gradually leap over the cakras;
having meditated upon the Guru at the root of the eyebrows, one ascends upward through the suṣumṇā.
Then, having pierced the aperture at the crown of the head, he should depart together with those who are liberated;
having gone to the white Vaiśvānara, he reaches the Sun, the Moon, and the stars.
Having transcended the station of the ancestors as well as the circles of the sages.
Having completely transcended the world of truth (satyaloka) and the eight coverings of the Īśvaras.
Having passed beyond that, one should then go to the Lord Virāṭ Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having transcended Hiraṇyagarbha, one reaches the state of Mahāviṣṇu.
Having completely renounced even that, and having cast off the eternal abode of Brahma's world, one shall attain the primary, primordial state. ||24||
There is neither death nor old age there, neither time nor sorrow;
neither affliction nor agitation—this is called the world of Śrī Hari. 25.
Through that form, one who is composed of bliss attains supreme bliss;
thus does the seeker of liberation [attain it] through ritual action, meditation, or worship.
Having worshipped and meditated in that manner, one attains the Supreme Brahman;
thus have two paths been shown by the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari to Lakṣmī.
The yoga of action and the yoga of devotion, by which the self may attain liberation.
Hari is eternally present everywhere, and everything is indeed contained within Hari. ||28||
Therefore, with one's whole being, one should meditate upon the Seer within the inner self;
hence, by means of one's entire nature, one should always [meditate upon] Hari everywhere. 29.
Those who take refuge in Hari and constantly drink the nectar of his stories— hear them, recite them, and meditate upon them— will attain oneness with him.
Their hearts blaze with fervor, and they proceed to his lotus feet.
In this way, the knower of taste relies upon the faculty of consciousness called "taste. ||31||
Having made the earth his ball, his two arms his pillow, his joined palms his noble vessel, and having fashioned the directions into his garment; ||32||
Having obtained alms from trees, water from rivers, and likewise a cave for a dwelling,
the sage, finding contentment in Nārāyaṇa, rejoices in the Self.
Why, and for what reason, would one desire anything other than Nārāyaṇa?
Whether possessing desires or being free from them, one should meditate upon Hari with one's very self.
Whether in symbols or in the non-symbolic, one who is absorbed in that becomes identical with it;
by that very single deity, one's own manifestations arise from within oneself.
These [teachings] have been revealed for the sake of satisfying the desires of those who hold divergent views, because not every person becomes free from longing at the time of death;
indeed, even at the moment of dying, one continues to strive for many objects. (36)
Then, by him as well, that [was performed] repeatedly in that [state] through the contemplation of Brahman. ||37||
When contemplated with intentional application, that very Brahman is indeed the bestower of what is desired.
One who desires great brilliance should worship Hari through the vow of a devoted wife.
One desiring prosperity should always worship you, Lakṣmī, the bestower of gold;
one desiring excellence of the senses should worship Indra, the lord of Śacī.
One desiring offspring should worship Dakṣa and the other Prajāpatis here; one desiring invincibility should worship Agni, and one desiring wealth should worship the Vasus.
One who desires valor should worship Rudra; one desiring food should worship Aditi;
one desiring heaven should worship Sūrya; and one desiring sovereignty should worship the Viśvedevas. ||41||
One who desires mastery over progeny should indeed worship the presiding deities of the *sādhya* class.
One desiring long life should worship the Aśvins, and one desiring nourishment should worship the Earth.
One desiring to establish oneself in heaven and on earth, or one desiring a wife, should worship Urvaśī.
One who desires a beautiful form should worship the Gandharvas; one who desires fame should perform a sacrifice.
One who desires supreme sovereignty should worship Brahmā alone;
one who desires the accumulation of wealth should indeed propitiate Varuṇa.
One who desires knowledge should worship Śambhu; one who desires dharma should honor Viṣṇu.
One who desires conjugal love, however, should always worship the virtuous Umā. ||45||
One should worship the ancestors with diligence for the sake of increasing one's lineage.
One should perform sacrifices again and again in every way for the destruction of suffering. ||46||
One desiring strength should worship the Maruts; one desiring sovereignty, the Manu-deities; one desiring enjoyments, the Moon; and one desiring the destruction of enemies, the Rākṣasas. ||47||
But a person desiring liberation should constantly worship the Supreme Self, the Lord, as a devotee, with a mind consisting of both desire and desirelessness. 48.
One should pray to that very Supreme Self, the bestower of all one's own possessions.
There shall be the accomplishment of each respective desire; upon its accomplishment, there is satisfaction and the exhaustion of thirst. ||49||
From that as well, one should pray for the mass of eternal being, consciousness, and bliss.
In dwelling, eating, drinking, adorning, urinating, and in sexual pleasure. ||1.59.50||
Indeed, time passes separately even for axes; what then [of other things]?
For even trees live, and even bellows breathe.
Have you not even heard such stories regarding those who were likewise?
Without hearing such stories, the two ears of Vālmīki are considered to be mere holes.
Without the chanting [of his name], the material tongue is like that of a frog.
Except for bowing the head, which is worthy of a crown, it is merely a burden. ||53||
Without service to Hari, even hands worthy of gold become mere firewood;
without the sight of Hari, eyes become like the eye-spots on a peacock’s tail-feather. (54)
The two feet that have gone to Hari’s abode are indeed like a tree and a pillar;
for without obtaining the dust of Hari’s feet, a mortal is dead while still living. (55)
Without the fragrance of the flowers of Vṛndāvana belonging to Hari, even the nose is not truly functional;
and in the absence of melting devotion for Hari, the heart is like a stone.

When tears flow from the eyes during the narration of Hari’s deeds, when there is horripilation on the body hairs, when there is thrill in the limbs, and when there is melting in the heart— that is the state of sattva.
I myself dwell directly in the hearts of the Sātvatas as Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to that Supreme Lord, salutations again and again to Him who is the source of all.
Salutations again and again to you, whose inner self is the locus of infinite power.
Salutation to Brahman, whose form is invisible and whose path is imperceptible. ||59||
Salutations to you, who destroys evil deeds and whose form is that of all living beings.
Salutation to the Lord of the Sātvatas, whose name is Asannirasanana. ||1.59.60||
Salutations to you, the kinsman of the distressed; salutations to him who delights in his own abode;
salutations to the one possessed of sovereign qualities and power that have cast out all excess and equality.
Salutations to You, who abide in Your own heart, yet remain far beyond the reach of those who lack yoga.
In every way, [I offer] hymns of praise consisting of the recollection of the worthy one, whose fame flows forth and is visible. ||6||
Salutations to him who performs auspicious deeds and shakes off all impurities.
Having resorted to the worship of whose feet, they have shaken off all contact with the material elements.
Free from desire, they go to the state of Brahman; homage be to him and to them.
Virtue, charity, ritual action, mantra, sacrifice, renunciation, austerity, and vows; ||64||
Salutations to those who, without a mirror, find no security;
to the dog-eaters, the fish-eaters, the leather-workers, the Yavanas, the Ābhīras, and the mixed castes.
The Kaṅkas, Śabaras, Jhallas, Pārādhis, Gaṇikās, Pivas, Kirātas, Khasas, Ghātas, and other sinful beings as well. ||66||
Salutations again and again to Him, by depending upon whom and through His support they are swiftly purified;
this Lord consists of incarnations and is composed of virtuous men and women.
May the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who consists of the lords, the Īśas, and the unborn, be gracious;
he who embodies the sages, ancestors, and gods, and who sustains humans, asuras, and nāgas. (68)
May the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who consists of his consort as his very self, be gracious;
he is the Sovereign whose nature is both man and woman, and who is composed of the king and the queen. (69)
May my Lord, the sustainer of the world, the abode of the earth, and the master of modesty and glory, be gracious to me—
he whom those whose inner hearts are purified by meditation upon his feet perceive as the Sovereign.
In whatever form that [Supreme Being] is perceived through the intellect that is woven warp and woof throughout it,
in that very way do the seers describe Him in this world as the one beyond the supreme.
In the language of the Vedas He is the form of Brahman; in the worldly language He is the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa);
in both languages He is both sweet and bitter—may He, the granter of desired objects, be pleased. 72.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Meditation on the Lord, the Journey to the World of Brahmā, and the Meditation on His Various Manifestations," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||59||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, in this manner, King Hāṭakāṅgada [performed his duties] every single day.
He listens to the discourses from the mouth of Śveta Vyāsa together with his listeners.
Impelled by the curse uttered by the sage against the child,
the deceptive serpent approaches from the western quarter for the purpose of biting him.
Having assumed the form of a brahmin, that king of serpents rested in the shade of a banyan tree on the bank of the river named Vratadā while he stood there.
Then, another twice-born man, disguised as a physician, arrived there.
This very Dhanvantari is the physician who possesses the medicine that destroys poison.
Taking it, he goes to wherever its completion has been chosen.
"I shall remove the king's poison; I shall obtain much gold."
Considering it as a reward, he [gave] that golden armlet.
He too goes there, beneath a great banyan tree, to protect it.
Having reached a very cool shade, [Vratakā] [drank] the auspicious water from the Kaṅkalāsala [spring].
He sat down at the foot of a banyan tree there to drink and rest.
Then Dhanvantari, being questioned by Kuhaka,
spoke out of fear caused by the Brahmin’s curse upon the royal sage Hāṭakāṅgada,
and due to the obstacle consisting of poison arising from the bite of Kuhaka’s snake.
I am going there with the desire for a reward in order to liberate him. || 9 ||
But listen, O twice-born one, to what was said by the deceiver after hearing that.
How will you ward off the potent poison of the deceiver?
While he is performing it right here under the banyan tree, go there from this place, O friend!
O banyan tree, protect him and cause him to sprout once again. ||11||
Having spoken thus, he bit the banyan tree for as long as it took.
At that moment, the tree withered from its very roots due to the effect of the poison.
Then Dhanvantari, taking water and medicinal herbs from the river, [emerged].
Having bathed at its base, he performs the sprinkling as long as it takes. ||13||
Just as the banyan tree had previously been sprouted and laden with the essence of leaves,
so too did it suddenly become green once more.
Beholding this marvel, Kuhaka said to that brahmin:
"Do not go, O best of brahmins! Tell me, who are you? (15)
"I give you a substance, gold, worth a parārdha; go there and do not [hesitate].
The twice-born Dhanvantari said: 'I am born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa. (16)
"O giver of honor, I am going to protect my devotee Hāṭakāṅgada.
To him, Kuhaka said: "By good fortune, O Brahmin, this curse has come upon you. (17)
How indeed do you wish to bring about that very misfortune, given the exhaustion of his lifespan and the depletion of his merit? (18)
Because he was brought about by your secret signal, let the lord of the earth meet his destruction.
"Accept this wealth consisting of gold and jewels, indeed worth a parārdha."
"Go away, O Great King; I am going to see him.
Having spoken thus, Kuhaka took the jewel from his own head.
Since gold indeed becomes infinite from iron through contact,
Dhanvantari took the wealth and departed for his own abode.
But the rogue, due to his impending union, quickly went to the place of the assembly.
O banyan tree, by obtaining the medicine of immortality, you have quickly attained the state of being ageless.
Abounding with white and green leaves, it shall endure for the duration of a kalpa;
indeed, it will attain fame in the world by the name "Dhanvantari-vaṭa."
To the southwest of Mount Raivata,
at a distance of three yojanas, stands a small banyan tree, marking its location.
To the west of Mahālayakṣiti, there is a distance of one gavyūti.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) indeed removes poison; it is praised for the mere act of bathing there.
Merely by touching the *vaṭa* tree, the poison of embodied beings is destroyed;
this mantra for neutralizing poison was proclaimed by Dhanvantari. (26)
Withdraw, O poison; may it be well with you! Go away from here quickly, O poison!
Remember the power of Dhanvantari for the protection of Hāṭaka’s armlet. 27.
Having recited this mantra, he who administers the poison causes it to descend.
The most virulent poison is instantly brought to dissolution. ||28||
Then that rogue, assuming the form of a brahmin, quickly [entered] the assembly.
And having approached in secret, he constantly listens to their conversation. ||29||
But when the thirtieth day had arrived, specifically in the evening of the previous day.
Indeed, at the conclusion of the Pārāyaṇa, following the worship of Vyāsa, then—
When the Guru [performed the consecration] for King Hāṭakāṅgada, who was the patron (yajamāna).
Vyāsa departed at that moment to bestow his blessings.
But the king of serpents, having made his form subtle like a small stick, [entered].
He was indeed absorbed among the flowers of his necklace, appearing like a bodiless being of the same color as the blossoms.
While the necklace remained upon the king's neck by his own desire, the king also said: "O Vyāsadeva, salutations be unto you! (33)
"By your grace, I perceive that my obstacle has indeed vanished"—
even as he spoke, that rogue bit him gently on the neck.
He injected his own fierce and potent poison, though only a minute amount, through his fang;
it quickly entered the king's *brahmarandhra* via the channel.
Then the cry of "Alas! Alas! reached up to the tips of his own nails, and a great sound arose among the members of the assembly, whose minds were agitated by grief. (36)
But the king, his mind and self entirely absorbed in Kṛṣṇa like a sovereign of yogis,
assumed a divine form and went to the supreme city of Brahmā.
But Kuhuka, having shown his own form and then concealed it, fled swiftly and went to his own abode. 38.
Then, by the king’s noble son Svarṇāṅgada, a sovereign sacrifice was performed—
a snake-sacrifice— in which the serpents were offered as oblations into the fire.
Then, for the sake of repaying his father, for the cessation of his anger,
and for the destruction of the serpents, the knower of serpent-mantras acted.
Having quickly summoned the twice-born, he performed the snake-sacrifice.
Having kindled the fire and having recited the names of the serpents, ||41||
He offered many serpents as oblations, and they fell into the fire in great numbers;
it is said that at that time, the sorcerer Kuṭhaka sought refuge with Indra.
He said, "O Lord of the Gods, protect her from death; show her mercy.
Having heard this, Indra, the king who protects the three worlds, [acted accordingly]. ||43||
The king of serpents did not indeed fall, for he was protected by his own side;
however, through meditation, the brahmins then realized that he was well-guarded by Indra.
Then, the brahmins there quickly recited the mantras.
Those foremost of birds, the Suparṇas, having forcibly summoned the serpents, [spoke]. ||45||
And they offered into the fire both primary and secondary oblations on all sides.
And having uttered the mantra "sendraṃ ca kuhakam," he offered oblations according to the ritual.
"Oṃ, svāhā to Agni! I offer this mantra, together with Indra, against the deceiver.
As soon as he has uttered this and offers mustard seeds into the fire himself, [the deceiver is subdued]. (47)
Indra, indeed, being joined with illusion, fell from his own seat to the earth.
He fell into the fire with a serpent clinging to him and quickly blazed up, his waist enveloped in flames. ||48||
He was indeed restrained by Brahmā: "Do not act thus toward the gods in such a transgressive manner."
Then the twice-born Suparṇa and other twice-born ones of great strength [arrived]. ||49||
Having heard the words of the Grandfather, they then desisted from that action.
Dhanvantari approached Indra and treated him with medicinal herbs.
But having made him free from disease, he went to his own abode.
Indeed, that deceiver, half-burnt, was released by the remainder [of the fire] upon his arrival. ||51||
Then, having been restored to life by that medicinal herb which reconnects the vital breath, the serpents of deceitful nature [stayed] all around on the surface of his back. (52)
Due to the noose of fire, there always appear variegated moles—black, yellow, deep smoky, and so forth—as well as the sight of scorched skin. (53)
Thus ends the narrative concerning the first Dvāpara age.
At that time, indeed, Indra-deva experienced terror of death.
In the same way, terror certainly arises in living beings when their life is being taken.
Therefore, no one who is compassionate should commit an act of killing.
Thus has this divine narrative, originating from the time of the Kalpa and other periods, been told;
it is auspicious, rich in virtues such as devotion and non-violence, and brings about the highest welfare.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Examination of Kuhaka, Dhanvantari, and Bala; the Death of Hārāṅgada from the Bite of a Serpent; the Serpent-Sacrifice and the Oblation into the Fire; the Seizure of Indra by Kuhaka and the Compassionate Intervention of Brahmā, Śeṣa, and Others, Leading to the Protection of Indra," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 60 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall narrate to you, in accordance with your question,
the story of Yama and his city, wherein there is the atonement for living beings.
In the Dvāpara age, when the dispositions of living beings became devoid of truth, and when their intellect repeatedly turned toward sin and deceit; || 2 ||
At that time, partiality, theft, self-interest, false accusation,
and even the forcible seizure of another's property will become a source of reproach.
Having observed the worlds to be beset by such defects as violence, malice, contempt, censure, oppression by others, and plunder, Prajāpati [acted].
The self-existent Lord Brahmā reflected upon the matter for the sake of punishment.
He meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa for a moment, and in that very instant, Hari himself appeared.
Manifesting with a serene countenance, he said, "For what reason have I been remembered?"
Brahmā made a representation to the God, the Supreme Self.
Indeed, when the Dvāpara age has arrived, people are bereft of truth;
they seize one another's property, speak falsehoods, and are merciless.
But for their sake, O Blessed One, what indeed must be done by me?
O Lord, punishment must certainly be inflicted upon them.
Otherwise, there would be a lack of order, and the worlds would meet with destruction.
Even regarding food, clothing, houses, and dwellings, [one should act] with those who are most powerful. || 9 ||
From the harm they have inflicted, there shall never be happiness for them.
Therefore, impose some restraint upon them and bring about their welfare.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari, remembered Dharma as the instructor; and Dharma arrived there immediately.
And having prostrated and fully worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods.
And having paid homage to his father Brahmā, he spoke this: ||12||
"What task has come upon me? Give me your command; I shall perform it."
Then Hari said, "O Dharma, indeed take up the duty of wielding the rod of punishment."
Be the bestower of the fruits of the actions performed by the people themselves.
He bestows good fruits for virtuous deeds and yields evil results for non-virtuous deeds.
"O twice-born one, having assumed two forms, perform the task of punishment.
Encouraged by Brahmā, he too took that task upon his head.
Then Dharma again spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world.
What is the task, in what form, in what place, and by what means? ||16||
"O Śrī Parameśvara, instruct me on how he is to be punished.
Then the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa said: "Take up two bodies. (17)
One among them was of terrible form, causing terror and fear; the other, however, was of gentle form, always bestowing happiness and peace.
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining this form, may you soon become the offspring of the Sun.
You are Yama in form, possessing a terrifying appearance, and you are the source of fear.
Or rather, let this very form of yours become the second one.
Then they [sought] a place suitable for dwelling, situated in the southern direction.
I shall fashion that vast city known as Saṃyamanī;
I shall provide there a person named Daṇḍa and Yama’s messengers by the millions.

And I shall also appoint scribes, headed by the one named Citragupta, for the sake of the performers of actions, so that they may experience the fruits of their own deeds in their respective stations. (22)
I shall fashion various [forms]; go, become the son of Sūrya.
Having thus instructed him, Hari then vanished from that place.
Having paid homage to Brahmā, Dharma entered the Sun;
and the Sun, in turn, desired a wife who would ensure the continuation of his lineage.
Then his beloved wife, endowed with all virtues, arrived under the name of Saṃjñā.
The divine daughter of Viśvakarman was married by Ravi. ||25||
The sun, however, was intense with its brilliance, while Saṃjñā was mild by her own radiance.
Unable to endure the splendor of the sun, she even performs service for the sun.
When the Sun, out of desire, gazed upon Saṃjñā’s face, [he was transformed].
Then the perception [of the object] quickly becomes incapable of withstanding the splendor of the sun. ||27||
Due to the brilliance of the sun, Saṃjñā’s eyes were constantly closing;
yet, out of love, she would look at the sun even then, despite being overwhelmed by its radiance.
She is not able to look at him with wide-open eyes;
for the sun itself is by its very nature exceedingly hot even within the body.
Indeed, Saṃjñā was unable to endure the fierce brilliance of the Sun;
whenever the Sun would embrace that beloved wife, [she could not bear it].
But then, seeing the sun so scorching, she was indeed rendered helpless.
Upon seeing her husband, Saṃjñā repeatedly performed the closing of her eyes. ||31||
But Sūrya, at the moment of their meeting, [beheld] his beloved with her eyes closed.
Having looked at him repeatedly, being impatient, he spoke these words out of anger. ||32||
"O timid one, you have always practiced restraint of your senses during my yoga;
therefore, by my power, let your son also be self-restrained. (33)
He shall indeed be renowned by the name Yama, the great King of Death;
he will be the dispenser of punishment for the ripening of the karma of living beings. (34)
"By the power of my wrath, he too shall become one of cruel nature;
by the binding of your eyes, he too shall become just like that. (35)
But when he indeed inflicts the punishment that is the ripening of karma upon karma, then he will no longer see living beings who revile him with his own eyes. (36)
Closing his eyes, he will indeed mete out punishment according to the action;
for whatever the disposition of the parents at their union, such indeed shall it be in the child.
While Ravi was speaking thus, Saṃjñā remained exactly as she was.
Out of a desire to do what was pleasing to her husband, she then became fickle as well. ||38||
Displaying gestures and expressions, she indeed manifests affectionate delight.
Having opened his eyes with feeling, he [experienced] the enjoyment of desire and delight in the proper manner. ||39||
He brought about peace until he conceived a child from the sun.
Then Sūrya said to Saṃjñā: "O beloved, you are constantly fickle."
And again, with a gaze filled with intense and flickering restlessness, she looked at me.
You gaze at me from your lover and repeatedly delight me. ||41||
Then a second offspring shall be born to you, and it will be fickle;
that daughter also, indeed, will be as fickle as you.
Thus, out of a desire for [the son] Ravi, she conceived twins;
then, when the time had arrived, she gave birth to those twins.
From her words, which she had granted, Yama and Yamī were born.
But as soon as he was born, the two of them became sixteen years of age.
But when he delights in the house of the sun, that is the Yamaka; Yama and Yamī [are there].
The second son of Saṃjñā became Manu Śrāddhadeva. ||45||
Yama, however, became the King of Dharma in Saṃyaminī, the bestower of fruits [of karma].
But Yamī became the river Yamunā, devoted by the will of Kṛṣṇa. ||46||
Impelled by Kṛṣṇacandra from Goloka, she has arrived here.
Having herself become the daughter of the Sun, she will go to Vṛndāvana. ||47||
The daughter of Kalinda shall thereafter become the Kālindī;
she is the great goddess Yamunā, divine and the bestower of liberation. 48.
Until the end of the kalpa, she remains in the form of water, sporting in Vṛndāvana.
Delightful with the sporting pools of Kṛṣṇa, where cowherds and cowherd-maidens have performed their ablutions. ||49||
The great object of worship for gods and goddesses will go to the forefront of Gokula.
In this manner, Saṃjñā gave birth to two sons and a daughter for Ravi.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Manifestation of Śrāddhadeva, Yama, and Yamī, Born from the Womb of Saṃjñā, His Own Wife, Produced by the Sun," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 61 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account that occurred after that concerning Saṃjñā;
for her burning from constant contact with the Sun became truly unbearable.
Thus was the lady Saṃjñā afflicted by the great suffering caused by the heat of the sun.
As if unable to endure it, she constantly reflected thus in her mind.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? To what place of happiness shall I go?
If I go without his command, the Sun will surely be angry with me.
Therefore, having received my father's command, I am returning to his home.
Having reflected thus in many ways, he then spoke repeatedly to the Sun.
"O King, a constant anxiety arises within me regarding my father's house."
To go and bring together all her sisters, brothers, and female companions.
"Command me, O Lord; I shall go, if it pleases Your Majesty."
Sūrya said: "O Goddess, this is truly not the time for departure."
"O dear one, this is the time for nurturing your children and maintaining the household; this is the season for you to gain the full reward of service to your husband."
"Having gone there, O my beloved, what gain will there be for you, or what will happen to me?"
Leaving me behind while I remain in separation, how indeed will you stay there?
Uninvited, the daughter goes with speed to her father's house.
For she would surely encounter a miserable state, just like Satī, the wife of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, do not go, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks; you may come again at another time.
Indeed, before their marriage, maidens shine brightly in their father's house.
But after they have been married, they shine in their own husbands' homes through food, drink, ointments, massages, ornaments, and other such luxuries. (11)
With garments, vehicles, carriages, gardens, groves, and pleasure-parks—
various ever-new means for stimulating the memory of love.
They delight their husband with love and find satisfaction in their husband's happiness.
Or whose father is destitute and entirely incapable of providing for expenses. ||13||
For daughters, having come to that house, indeed cause him to be joined with suffering.
With garments, wealth, ornaments, and other objects of enjoyment.
"Since he is incapable of pleasing my daughter, let them not cause him distress;
having performed his daily duties with physical exertion and toil, let him rest. (15)
Having taken wealth for the sake of filling his own belly, he returned home in the evening.
In this way, however, one should daily acquire even a few small coins through one's own exertion. (16)
Having taken food and clothing, he buys them; do not cause him to fall into suffering.
Thus she was repeatedly instructed and entreated in many ways. ||17||
Overwhelmed by heat and unable to endure the suffering, she did not even speak to her husband.
But afterwards, having fallen into delusion and having reflected repeatedly by themselves, ||18||
Just as a husband assumes a second form so that he may not be recognized, this second body of his is a shadow produced from his own physical self. (19)
But having formed a resolution there, he indeed summoned his consciousness.
She was radiant, equal to fire, and likewise capable of enduring the brilliance of the sun.
Having entered into an equal portion of the earthly element, she became a shadow in the form of a woman;
thus that beautiful lady was endowed with consciousness in the form of a woman. 21.
And its form was similar to that of perception; indeed, everything became composed of perception.
Then the illustrious lady resolved to go to her father's house.
Having summoned his shadow, he honored it and gave it his house, wealth, and other possessions.
He said to her: "You must remain here just as I have remained for the Sun."
Likewise, you must behave toward your offspring exactly as you do toward the Sun;
even if they are wicked, you must not speak ill of them, so that they may remain highly esteemed in my eyes. O sinless one, you must say to them: "I am that very same Saṃjñā."
If the husband should ask out of anger, out of affection, or for any other reason; ||25||
Just as you indeed endure the heat of the sun, so too shall your body become cool. ||26||
Indeed, upon this body of yours, which is worthy of the practice of asceticism, peaceful, and a destroyer of fever, and which bestows happiness, the heat shall quickly be pacified. (27)
By causing the heat to dissolve, even the sun will attain peace;
therefore, you should always serve the sun with devotion, just as I do.
Whether in the face of threats, beatings, insults, or even severe crushing, you must not remain indifferent, nor should my secret be revealed. (29)
Chāyā said to Saṃjñā: "I shall endure everything with respect—from being seized by the hair to being cursed with a word. (1.62.30)
I shall do it and I shall protect it until the pulling out of the hair.
Or rather, when I perceive that suffering extends even unto death. ||31||
Nevertheless, I shall not speak of my own conduct nor yours;
go, O Goddess, you are my sister, to your father’s house and be happy.
"O sister, whenever you experience distress of mind, you should remember me.
Having made this agreement, Saṃjñā went to her father's house.
There he beheld Tvaṣṭṛ, whose body was strengthened by asceticism;
and having paid homage to his parents, he sat down near them.
And out of great respect, she was honored by Viśvakarman as well;
blameless, she dwelt happily in her father’s house for a long time. (35)
When the daughter did not wish to go to her husband's house,
then her father, who was knowledgeable in dharma, spoke to his daughter, who had lived with him for a long time.
But for me, O child, as I behold you, even many days pass by.
In a mere moment they may become equal; for whom would a child not be pleasing?
Whether it be a son or daughters, whether they possess virtues or lack them, whether they are well-disposed or ill-disposed, or however they may otherwise be. ||37-38||
Nevertheless, they should always be affectionate toward their parents and bring them joy.
"Daughter, you are in the prime of youth and have been married to Ravi. ||39||
By dwelling here for a long time, your dharma will be impaired;
for women, a prolonged stay among kinsmen does not bring glory. || 1.62.40 ||
Relatives desire that a lawful wife remain in her husband's house;
you, however, have been united with your husband Sūrya, the lord of the three worlds. (41)
"O daughter, you ought not to dwell for a long time in your father's house;
indeed, O daughter, you ought to make your residence in your husband's home. (42)

Therefore, go to your husband’s house; I have been seen by you and honored by me. You must come again at an auspicious moment for a further visit, should any sorrow regarding your son-in-law have arisen in your mind. (43)
"O daughter, you must certainly inform me of this here immediately."
If there is no suffering, go to the Lord who grants garments through service, and attain happiness.
By this, you will attain spiritual success both in this world and in the next. ||45||
Although addressed in this way, she, being modest, did not say anything to her father at that time regarding her own suffering, even after reflecting upon it again and again. (46)
Having said "So be it," and having bowed down and likewise honored his gurus;
Having embraced her brothers and sisters, she departed for the Northern Kurus. ||47||
Agitated by the heat of the sun, she was afraid of that splendor.
She did not go to the sun-house; having gone to the forest, she was devoted to asceticism.
There, unknown to others, she assumed the form of a mare and performed supreme asceticism, subsisting only on mouthfuls of grass and the like. (49)
Thinking that it was indeed Saṃjñā, the Sun-god begot two sons and one daughter, Manoramā, in her shadow.
By name, however, they were Sāvarṇi Manu, Tāpī, and likewise Śanaiścara.
The future Manu Sāvarṇi shall be the planet Śanaiścara.
But the river Tapatī, O beloved, will become the Tāpī in Gaurjara.
Having thus determined it to be a mere perception, the Sun [remained] in the shadow. ||52||
Engaged in dalliance with Rati, he indeed took delight for many years;
yet, by the power of fate, she did not perceive that it was anyone other than herself.
Day and night, she constantly and perfectly protects her own offspring.
He showed increased affection toward him in matters such as food and clothing. ||54||
Manu did not feel the same way toward Saṃjñā as he did toward his son and daughter;
he was patient with her, but Yama could not endure it.
He who formerly had great respect for his co-wife is now distressed by her.
He indeed gave way to anger for the sake of insulting his co-wife.
Then, out of anger, out of childishness, and indeed by the force of destiny to come, [he spoke].
But he raised his foot to strike that shadow. ||57||
But he, with a patient mind, did not strike her on the body.
Then his mother, the co-wife, cursed Yama out of anger.
Her lips were slightly quivering and her sprout-like hands were moving.
If you forcibly raise your foot against me, who am the wife of my father— ||59||
"Therefore, let this foot of yours fall upon the earth this very day!"
Having heard this curse, Yama became deeply apprehensive toward his mother.
Approaching his father, he spoke with a prostration:
"Father, this is a great marvel, the like of which has never been seen anywhere. (61)
She is constantly angry with me and even scolds me excessively;
casting aside her maternal affection, she utters a curse upon her own son. (6)
Even toward sons who are devoid of virtue, a mother does not become merciless.
Just as my mother spoke to me, so it is not the case that she is my mother.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Saṃjñā’s Departure for Her Father’s House after Entrusting a Woman in the Form of Her Own Shadow to the Sun, and of the Shadow’s Conduct Devoid of Affection toward Yama," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words of Yama, the Blessed One, the illuminator of the world, [spoke].
Having understood this very profound matter of the heart, he indeed spoke to Yama.
"Without doubt, my son, there must be a great reason for this,
by which such anger toward your mother has taken possession of you."
Then anger took possession of the mother even toward her son:
"O son, you are a knower of dharma, truthful in speech, and a bestower of honor. (3)
It is not possible, however, to make this word of your mother false.
Worms, having taken up your flesh, shall indeed go to the earth.
Then, O highly wise one, you shall again obtain your foot and find happiness;
thus your mother’s word shall indeed be made true.
And by the removal of the curse, you too shall be saved.
Āditya, however, said to Chāyā: "For what purpose [have you acted] toward my sons? (6)
Do you perhaps show partiality by bestowing affection unequally toward those who are equal?
How indeed could there be partiality toward one [side] without a second? (7)
"Who are you? Are you that very same second [wife]? Tell me the truth.
She replied, "I am Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, O Vibhāvasu."
"You are my wife; these children have been begotten by you upon me."
Thus, when Vivasvat had questioned her many times in this manner, || 9 ||
But the enraged Ravi did not speak then, as he was intent on cursing her.
Then she related everything exactly as it had happened to Vivasvat.
Having understood the matter, the blessed Sun then cursed her:
"May you always be dark-complexioned; become the shadow produced by trees and other such things. (11)
You are of the very nature of darkness, always separated from me.
May you always remain obstructed by the objects that hinder you, being of a dull and insentient nature. //12//
Go always far from my house; do not show your face to me.
But you, however, must always dwell beneath the object that obstructs my rays. 13.
Thinking, "I shall go forth," he indeed went toward the abode of Tvaṣṭṛ, taking his shadow with him.
There, Tvaṣṭṛ worshipped the Sun who had arrived.
O radiant one, why have you come to my house deprived of your power?
Then he questioned him, and he explained it to him according to the truth. ||15||
Tvaṣṭṛ said, "O Ravi, she has arrived here, sent by you."
O Maker of Day, she has gone from my house back to your abode.
Then Divākara declared that she, who had assumed the form of a mare and was performing penance, was in the Uttarakurus.
Desiring to curse her for her destruction, the Blessed Lord Ravi became enraged.
Tvaṣṭṛ, however, gradually consoled him in accordance with what was proper.
O Lord, being utterly overwhelmed by your splendor and unable to endure it,
she has abandoned her shadow-form, which resembles the brilliance of fire.
Having gone to a terrible forest, she performs difficult austerities.
Her body scorched by the fierce heat, she performs unbearable penance.
By which splendor you are unassailable, and even by your body you remain unconsecrated.
It had many high peaks and was covered with rough, coarse grass.
This extreme deformity of yours, which is harder than even a diamond to behold and impossible to endure, neither shines nor is it beautiful. (22)
That perception of his is powerless as he wanders in the grassy forest;
therefore, O slow-witted one, go and assume such a form that I may turn him back.
The form of Vivasvat was unstable and harsh to behold;
on one side it blazed with fire, while on the other it was neither hot nor cold.
Then Vivasvat, having heard that, became repeatedly ashamed at that time.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ was indeed authorized to make [his] form uniform.
Having placed the sun upon a lathe, he whetted it on a grindstone;
at that time, twelve distinct points from its tips were whetted away.
Then, O gentle one, the sun became level, beautiful, and well-formed.
The sun became one whose brilliance was endurable, whose touch was pleasant, and who could be dwelt with.
And from twelve portions, he fashioned the eight weapons.
Having fashioned the Sudarśana discus, he presented it to Viṣṇu.
Having fashioned a very great trident, he offered it to Śambhu.
Having fashioned a great spear, he presented it to Kārttikeya.
Having fashioned a vajra with eight edges, he presented it to the Lord of the Gods.
Having fashioned a most terrible staff, he presented it to Yama.
Having fashioned a jewel of great value, he presented it to Kubera;
and having fashioned a noose of lightning, he presented it to Varuṇa. ||31||
Having fashioned a great and formidable sword, he offered it to the goddess Kālī;
having fashioned a most terrible scimitar, he offered it to Agni.
Having fashioned a great arrow, he delivered it to Nara;
having fashioned a great divine firebrand, he delivered it to Vāyu.
Having made Kṛkaśā and Dantrikā into small pieces, he offered them to Nirṛti;
the others became diamonds and gems of very small fragments.
Then, having been well-prepared, the Sun assumed a divine form;
and employing yoga, Ravi beheld his own wife, Vaḍavā.
Having gone to that spot, he concealed his form and then touched it.
In the form of a horse, Mārtaṇḍa kissed her again and again. ||36||
Then, as he was walking behind her, she climbed up onto him of her own accord;
suspecting that the other man was making advances for the sake of sexual union, she [acted]. (37)
Having uncovered it, she stood there with her face turned toward him.
Although he was in the form of a horse, Sūrya was nonetheless agitated by the force of desire.
Leaping up onto her neck and placing his linga upon her nose,
he then indeed discharged his entire semen twofold into her nostrils.
She expelled that semen by means of the breath of her nostrils.
From that, the two gods, the Aśvins, the best of physicians, were born.
Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins.
Those two became like gods on a sacrificial altar, possessing most wonderful bodies. ||41||
Then, indeed, by means of his remaining vigor, from his very nose—
The third son was named Revata, who possessed a dark and handsome form. ||42||
Therefore, he went to the western direction in order to perform ascetic penance.
Having reached Mount Raivata, he indeed made his dwelling there.
This is that mountain Raivata, whose presiding deity is Ātivāhika.
Having become [that], he dwells right there until the end of the eon, performing ascetic penance.
Then Sūrya displayed his own form as the radiant Bhāskara.
Then Saṃjñā, feeling reassured, worshipped her husband’s feet. ||45||
Having asked forgiveness for her own transgression, she indeed departed to the solar orb;
that ever-divine goddess remained forever possessing a form identical to the Sun. 46.
He dwells in equality with them and rejoices together with the Sun in heaven.
Thus, in this manner, there is the divine birth of the nine sons of Sūrya. ||47||
Śrāddhadeva, Yama, Yamī, Sāvarṇi, and Śanaiścara.
Tapatī, Aśvinī, Bālā, and Revatī—these nine are recorded. ||48||
Therein, [the sacrifice] was offered by Yama to Sūrya and to Brahmā.
Having attained the status of a world-protector, he took his station in the southern quarter. ||49||
It is called Yamapurī because it is the destination for those who have committed forbidden acts.
For the sake of experiencing the fruit, an expiation for the self that is essentially suffering is performed therein.
In this world, through expiation, one becomes pure in terms of the fivefold elements; and by experiencing the fruits in the city of Yama, one becomes pure in terms of the self.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Saṃjñā’s Ascetic Practice in the Form of a Mare, the Sun Becoming a Horse and Uniting with Her to Procreate the Aśvinīkumāras and Revanta, and the Production of Divine Weapons such as the Discus and Trident from the Shards of the Sun’s Chariot-Wheel Ground by Viśvakarmā," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Between the regions of Yama and Nairṛta is the city of Vaivasvata;
it is entirely composed of diamond, divine, and impenetrable even by gods and asuras.
It is square, with four gates, seven walls, and archways;
Yama himself dwells within it, accompanied by his messengers.
Indeed, it is seen to measure one thousand yojanas;
it is entirely divine, composed of jewels, and circular like a garland of lightning or the sun.
It was twenty-five yojanas in height,
surrounded by thousands of pillars, and adorned with lapis lazuli gems.
It was adorned with lattices of pearls and windows, decorated with hundreds of banners,
enriched by the resonance of hundreds of bells, and surrounded by hundreds of archways.
Seated there upon a fixed, auspicious throne, ten yojanas in extent and resembling a dark blue cloud, was the Blessed Lord Dharma.
Yama knows the Dharma and is of righteous character; he is devoted to the principles of justice and the Dharma. He brings fear to those joined with evil, but bestows happiness upon the virtuous.
At the entrance into the middle of the city, indeed, is the house of Citragupta,
measuring twenty-five yojanas in extent.
Ten stories high, magnificent and divine, it was encircled by an iron wall;
it contained hundreds of thoroughfares and was adorned with hundreds of banners.
The house of Citragupta was crowded with hundreds of lamps, filled with the sound of singing, and adorned with paintings by skilled artists.
Seated comfortably upon a divine and most wonderful throne made of jewels and pearls,
he bestows long life upon Gaṇapati, upon humans, and upon others as well.
He is not deluded in any way regarding either good or evil deeds; he knows all that has been acquired throughout his births, whether it be virtuous or non-virtuous. (12)
He records the actions performed by means of the body, senses, and mind;
to the east of Citragupta’s house lies the great abode of Fever.
And on the south [is the seat] of the trident, as well as of spider-bites and eruptions; on the west [is the seat] of the noose of Death, as well as of indigestion and loss of appetite. (14)
In the north of the central seat, various types of cholera are to be known;
in the northeast, diseases of the head occur, while in the southeast, fainting occurs. (15)
In the southwest is Atisāra, and in the northwest is Dāhapīḍana;
Citragupta always remains surrounded by these.
Whatever action is performed and by whomsoever, all that he records at the gate of the abode of Dharmarāja; there, messengers stand by the millions. (17)
Indeed, the path between the world of Yama and that of humans is difficult;
through suffering do the sinners travel along the road of Yama, which is so hard to traverse. ||18||
Yama, having assumed a four-armed form bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
summons all the sinners through his messengers and indeed inflicts punishment upon them.
With a roar like the clouds at the dissolution of the world, possessing a luster like a mountain of collyrium,
mounted upon a buffalo, difficult to propitiate, and having a radiance equal to the brilliance of the sun.
His body was three yojanas in extent; he was cruel and a source of extreme terror. Holding a staff in one arm, the formidable one had a noose in his hand and possessed a hideous appearance. ||21||
With bloodshot eyes and inspiring extreme terror, the person the size of a thumb emerges from the corpse of the sinners, crying out "Alas! Alas! (hā hā).
When one is led by the messengers of Yama to the city of Yama,
the messengers indeed display intense fear and threaten him.
"Move away quickly, O evil-minded one! You shall go to the abode of Yama;
we will swiftly lead you to the Kumbhīpāka and other hells—act at once! (24)
Indeed, the deceased person travels along a path filled with forests of sword-leaves, thorns, heated sands, and poisonous mud. (25)
Day after day, that preta travels two hundred and forty-seven yojanas in a single day and night. (26)
On the thirteenth day, that deceased person is led away by the servants of Yama;
along that path he travels alone, like a captured monkey. (27)
For seventeen days he travels by way of the wind;
on the eighteenth day and night, he shall first go to the city of Yama.
The city of Yama is declared the first; Sauripura is the second;
Surendrapura is the third; and after that, Gandharvanagara. ||29||
The fifth is Śailapura, and the sixth is Krūrapura;
the seventh is Krauñcanagara, and Citrapura is the eighth.
After that, the tenth city is Bahvāpanna, which causes suffering;
then there is Daśaikam, the city of lamentation, and following that, Sutapta.
The thirteenth is Raudrapura, the fourteenth is Payovṛṣṭa;
the fifteenth is Śītapura, while the sixteenth is Bahubhaya.
The seventeenth is the city of Dharma, and the eighteenth is the city of Yama;
these cities indeed exist on the path for the sake of obtaining rest.
The sinner, having died, becomes a preta and obtains a preta-body;
that preta-body is firmly bound [with craving] within nine days and nights. (34)
For the sake of attaining the perfection of the body, morsels of food should be offered individually.
On the first day, by means of that first morsel, the head is produced. (35)
On the second day, however, the neck and shoulders [are formed]; on the third day, the heart comes into being;
on the fourth day, the heels appear; and likewise, on the fifth day, the navel.
In the sixth [month] the hips; in the seventh, however, the private parts are born complete;
on the eighth day the two thighs; and likewise the knees and feet in the ninth.
Having attained a body over nine days, on the tenth day he becomes hungry;
possessing a bodily form and being famished, he stands upon the roof of a house. (38)
On the tenth day, one should offer that funeral ball (piṇḍa) which wards off hunger;
on the eleventh and twelfth days, the deceased (preta) eats for two days.
On the thirteenth day, the deceased is indeed led along the great path;
until the seventeenth day, he travels by way of the wind.
On the eighteenth day and night, he first goes to the city of Yama;
there, on the bank of the river Puṣpabhadrā, is a great host of pretas.
Under the shade of a great banyan tree, a preta finds rest;
yet, afflicted by thirst and oppressed by fatigue, he cries out with piteous words. (42)
Śambala, the governor of that city, bestows [the gift] upon the preta, whether it has been given by sons or grandsons out of affection or out of compassion. (43)
Having consumed a mouthful of food once a month, he then goes to Sauripura;
there, indeed, is a king named Jaṅgama, who bears the form of Time (Kāla).
Indeed, he offers him a triple-portioned ball of rice for a good meal;
having consumed the water and food there, he passes beyond that city.
Within two months, he indeed reaches the city of the Lord of the Gods;
for the terrifying Surendra, its presiding deity, grants it to him.
If the funeral ball (piṇḍa) or food is offered within two months, and having passed that [period], it is offered again in the third month; ||47||
Having reached Gandharvapura, he eats a morsel of food for three months;
then, in the fourth month, the preta goes to Śailapura.
There, stones fall upon the back of the preta;
having consumed the fourth-month *śrāddha*, he goes to Krūra-pura.
Residing there in the fifth month, he consumes the fifth-month *piṇḍa*.
Having eaten there, he goes to the sixth city, Krauñcapura, which is inhabited by krauñca birds.
Having eaten the rice-balls and other offerings given at the śrāddha ceremony for a period of five and a half months, or likewise for slightly less than six months, he departs after resting.
Citrapura is the seventh; its king is Citraka, the younger brother of Yama, who is the presiding deity over the six-monthly funeral cake and water.
Then, having eaten, he travels ahead on the road;
there, thousands of fishermen come toward him from the opposite direction.
We shall ferry you across the great Vaitaraṇī river,
which is a hundred yojanas wide and filled with pus and blood.
By him who has given a cow there, which is covered by vultures, crows, fish, and crocodiles seeking flesh, that deceased person is swiftly delivered.
If a cow has not been given as a gift, he sinks into the Vaitaraṇī river;
therefore, while his body is still healthy, he should observe the vow for the Vaitaraṇī.
And a cow should be given to a learned man by one desiring to cross that river;
having eaten there, the Śrāddha performed six months prior moves forward. (57)
When the seventh month has arrived, he goes to a city of many calamities;
having eaten there what was offered as the result of the seven-month rite, [he returns]. 58.
Having passed beyond that city, he reaches a city that brings suffering;
having experienced great misery there, he cries out, tormented by heat. (59)
That which was given in the eighth month, having enjoyed that there, he goes;
staying in the city of Nānākranda, he enjoys the [offering] of the ninth month.
There, this empty-hearted one, afflicted by suffering, cries out;
having abandoned that city, he goes as a departed spirit toward the City of Heat.
Having reached Sutaptanagara in the tenth month, he enjoys [the fruits];
the fruit shall be obtained there through the offerings of food and the giving of funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
When the eleventh month is complete, he goes to the city of Rudra;
having enjoyed the milk-rain for ten months, he proceeds further.
There, clouds rain down, causing suffering for the pretas;
and there the deceased being partakes of that śrāddha offering which was performed on an inauspicious day. (64)
Then, when the year has fully elapsed, he goes from there to Śītapura; afflicted by great cold, the insentient preta wails repeatedly. (65)
Having passed beyond Śītapura, one should go to Bahubhītipura;
there, scorched by the fear of hunger and thirst, one then proceeds to Dharmapura.
There, scorched by heat and with tears flowing, he becomes dead;
the messengers of Yama devour him to dispel their own fatigue from the journey. (67)
Bahubhītipura and Dharmapura are the two outposts of Dharmakheṭaka;
these two are neighboring branch villages belonging to the city of Dharmarājapura.
Then these [messengers] lead the deceased to the supreme city of Yama’s Dharma,
which is presided over by eighty-four hundred thousand beings, both embodied and formless.
By the messengers of Yama, who are extremely cruel and come as tormentors.
In this palace of justice, messengers bring the deceased before you. ||1.64.70||

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the State of the Dead and the Journey through the Eighteen Cities on the Path to Citragupta’s Palace and the Extent of Yama’s City," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, in the city of Yama there are twelve attendants known as Śrāvaṇas;
they are the sons of Brahmā and serve as gatekeepers who observe the activities of human beings.
Having deliberated again and again upon their good and evil deeds,
they indeed cause them to be heard then by Citragupta and likewise by Yama.
Whatever action was performed by men, whether in a state of satisfaction or anger,
they reported it all exactly as it was and in its true nature.

The knowledge of hearing from afar, the range of vision from a distance, and the knowledge of the activities of those dwelling in the celestial realms, on earth, and in the netherworlds from afar. || 4 ||
Thus they possess the power to awaken [the deceased] secretly even among mortals and others;
for as long as they sing there concerning the karma of the departed spirit, [that power remains].
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Whose sons are those Śrāvaṇas, and how do they reside in the city of Yama?
O Lord, how do they know the karma performed by those residing in the three worlds?
How do they all hear? From what has knowledge arisen? And when did they come into being? Tell me everything, my beloved. (7)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the beginning, the world was produced; indeed, it was created by Brahmā.
It was protected by me, and Rudra is the agent of its destruction thereafter.
The King of Dharma was created by me together with Citragupta;
these three deities carry out their respective duties independently.
In the first age, the Kṛtayuga, all people were indeed independent;
all were like the three gods, so who could have authority over them? (1.65.10)
Likewise, in the Tretā age as well, they performed actions independently;
where, then, would the status of being a teacher be meaningful if it were unknown to those teachers? (11)
Then the three classes of gods assembled there for reflection:
"If we do not possess the knowledge of the karma of living beings who are independent, [how can we act]? (12)
"We do not know how living beings should be governed at that time.
