Having reflected thus, they deliberated: "Sons of such a kind must be created. (13)
Then Brahmā, having adopted the opinion of Śiva and Viṣṇu and being joined by the mantra,
took twelve kuśa blades and sprinkled water there.
He gave twelve conscious kuśa grasses with water to Dharmarāja;
Yama, taking them in his hand, consecrated them as his sons. (15)
Masses of splendor with large eyes, hearing and seeing from afar, perceivers of the self, knowers of gestures, and perceivers of the intentions of others. (16)
He created twelve sons who were invisible yet possessed visible forms;
these sons of Yama exist everywhere in this world, residing within the ears and eyes.
Whoever in this world speaks or performs an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, they swiftly bring it to the range of Yama's hearing. (18)
The cognition of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar—all of them hear everything; for that reason, they are all considered "those who hear" (śrāvaṇas). 19.
Moving in the form of wind while stationed in the path of space,
they perceive the activities of living beings and report them to Yama.
After death, they will experience according to their actions and according to what they have done—
whether it be dharma, artha, kāma, or whatever liberation they have practiced.
Likewise, they quickly report everything concerning all living beings to Citragupta, and afterwards, they indeed inform Yama.
Those disciples are capable of assuming many forms;
they move through the fourteen worlds in various guises. (23)
Those people who practice the Dharma go seated in celestial palaces;
those who bestow wealth go seated in celestial palaces, being honored by apsarases. (24)
Those who bestow gifts of desire travel in excellent chariots yoked with horses;
indeed, those destined for liberation proceed in celestial palaces drawn by swans and elephants.
But those who act unrighteously travel on foot along a path that is extremely difficult to endure, afflicted by stones and thorns, and consisting of forests of sword-leaves. (26)
Bound by nooses, they indeed proceed across a path covered with heated sand;
for their comfortable journey, one should give gifts according to one's ability. (27)
An umbrella, sandals, garments, a signet ring, and a water-pot.
A seat, a vessel, a vehicle, an ornament, and water. ||28||
Food, clarified butter, the sacred thread, and wealth such as cattle and buffaloes should be given on behalf of the deceased; thus the path shall become pleasant for him. (29)
O beloved, whatever is given in one's own home for the sake of the deceased,
Varuṇa, whose essence is water, is its witness and knows it in every way.
Varuṇa accepts the gift; he places it into my hand;
I, Nārāyaṇa, then offer it to the sun-god Bhāskara. (31)
And because that deceased spirit indeed seizes and eats [the offerings] from the sun,
O beloved, various kinds of gifts should be given for the sake of the deceased's happiness.
But he who has performed a religious duty yet does not subsequently give the gift, and has not earned merit for himself, goes to terrible hells. (33)
There are eighty-four lakhs of those hells that cause suffering;
among them, there are twenty-one which are the most prominent and principal. (34)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, and likewise Asipatravana. (35)
The Boar’s Mouth, the Blind Well, and the Feeding on Worms; the Pincers, the Heated Iron Image, and the Śālmali tree with its adamantine thorns. (36)
Pūyoda, Vaitaraṇī, Prāṇarodha, Viśaṃsana, Ayaḥpāna, Avīci, Śvādana, and Lālabhakṣaṇa. ||37||
These are indeed considered the primary ones in the city of Yama;
hear now the names of the other seven that exist below them. (38)
One is the Mire of Alkali, another is the Food of the Hosts of Rākṣasas;
likewise, there is the Impaled on a Spike, the Biting Snake, and the Confinement in a Pit.
Paryāvartanaka and Sūcīmukha are each distinct;
now learn of those other villages of hells that exist there. 1.65.40.
Talapāta, Mahājvāla, Śabala, Vikartana, Adhaḥśiras, Rudhirāndha, Cakṣuḥśūla, and Prapācana. (41)
The fall from a mountain, iron spikes, prods, and fetters; likewise, the iron machine, the kākola, and the tortures of reviving the dead. 42.
Furthermore, there are other hells, distinguished by various divisions; these indeed exist for the sake of the purification of those who have committed evil deeds. (43)

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Twenty-eight Hells Beginning with the Twelve Named Śravaṇa," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Those whose ancestors have indeed spent hundreds of years in a terrible hell, and for whom no progeny exists, they indeed go to the office of messengers.
Sent indeed by Yama, they seize day after day the lamps, food, water-pots, and other offerings belonging to a deceased human being. || 2 ||
For they offer [the food] specifically to the preta who desires food and is parched with thirst;
thus, they all attain satisfaction every day for an entire year.
The city of Citragupta is twenty yojanas in extent;
there, the scribes behold all manner of sins and merits.
The city of Vaivasvata extends for twenty-four yojanas;
having gone there, the servant-messengers speak to the gatekeeper.
The gatekeeper Dharmadhvaja speaks of his auspicious and inauspicious deeds;
for the messengers of King Yama are indeed the terrifying servants of Yama.
Terrifying, bearing nooses and staffs, sixteen thousand [demons] stand before each city, with one thousand stationed at the front of each.
The King of Dharma himself dispenses justice to this sinner;
listen now as to how he experiences various hells.
Those who forcibly seize the wealth, wives, children, and other possessions of others fall into that Tāmisra hell, severely tormented by hunger and thirst.
Those who deceive others by misappropriating their wealth, children, noble women, and other enjoyments,
fall into the Andhatāmisra hell, their vision and intellect utterly destroyed.
Indeed, those harmful embodied beings fall into the Mahāraurava hell;
having become flesh-eating ruru deer, they cause their own slayers to be killed.
Those who nourish their families through injury to living beings go to the Raurava hell;
for those beings, having become *ruru* deer and serpents, indeed injure those who have injured them. (12)
Indeed, those wicked ones who were like cattle and other animals fall into Kumbhīpāka;
the messengers repeatedly roast them in boiling oils. ||13||
Those who harm living beings such as gurus, parents, Brahmins, virtuous men, and virtuous women go indeed to the realm called Kālasūtra, which has a circumference of ten thousand yojanas.
They cause him to roll upon a copper floor heated by fire and burn him;
the heretic who destroys his own dharma goes to the forest of sword-leaves.
They are repeatedly cut and crushed by double-edged swords;
those who inflict unjust punishment go to the machine known as Sūkarāsya (the Boar-faced).
There, indeed, the limbs of lice,
mosquitoes, and birds— whose modes of existence are ordained by the Lord— are crushed and reduced to powder.
Indeed, those who cause the destruction of living beings fall into a blind well;
there, messengers in the form of creatures, having been wronged by them, in turn inflict harm upon them. (18)
Those who eat without sharing fall into the Kṛmibhojana hell;
there they are devoured by worms for hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
Those who forcibly steal the gold, jewels, horses, and other property of others from them by means of theft go to Saṃdaṃśa; there the servants of Yama cut them to pieces with iron pincers.
But those lustful men who have forcibly violated women who should not be approached,
they embrace a heated iron image and a heated iron doll.
Indeed, they forcibly place lustful men upon the *vajrakaṇṭaka* śālmali tree— trees that have thorns like thunderbolts— and there they saw them being cut to pieces.
Those who follow the conduct of beasts, devoid of purity, fall into the hell named Pūyodaka, which consists of phlegm, feces, urine, and pus; there they eat that very filth.
Having become devourers of those they were meant to protect, these instillers of fear destroy their charges;
they cause them to be carried away in the Vaitaraṇī river, which consists of feces, urine, pus, and blood.
Having cast down those who, addicted to hunting, kill animals and other creatures by obstructing their vital breaths with arrows, the servants of Yama pierce them there.
In the hell of Dissection, they tear apart and devour animals, birds, humans, and others; furthermore, they drink their blood. (26)
The Yamas forcibly compel those people who cause the destruction of countless living beings and who consume intoxicants to drink molten iron dross.
Furthermore, the servants of Yama repeatedly cast those who give false testimony down from a mountain two hundred *gavyūtis* in height into the Avīci hell.
The wicked who administer poison or set fires are devoured by dogs;
those who cause the consumption of semen are made to drink their own saliva by the attendants of Yama. (29)
But one who commits a transgression against the worship of those worthy of worship falls head-first into a mire of caustic matter; there he experiences the fruit of that action.
The followers of Yama devour beasts, birds, men, and women;
they eat their blood and drink it as food for the hosts of Rākṣasas.
The servants of Yama repeatedly pierce living beings with thorns, needles, and spikes; they impale those already transfixed by stakes with sharp-pointed instruments. (32)
And those with hundred faces, who cause agitation among living beings,
tear apart and repeatedly devour the venomous serpents.
In caves, hollows, granaries, pits, and the like,
those who obstruct living beings are bound by the Yāmyas with smoke and other substances, as well as with fire and molten lead.
The hungry messengers devour those who eat meat and other such things; when they are touched by their hands, the victims are restored to fullness, yet the messengers devour them once again. (35)
Having cast the one who is conceited about his wealth, who looks askance, and who commits evil deeds,
into the Sūcīmukha hell, they sew him up with threads.
If he looks upon a wretched, weak, and worthy recipient with an angry eye, birds with diamond-tipped beaks tear out his eyes. (37)
But as for others, the followers of Yama lift up even the thief of tree fruit and cause him to fall upon the ground from a palm tree. (38)
Having cast them into a great conflagration that burns the forest regions, the messengers of Yama indeed roast them in the fire again and again. (39)
For they cause the one who feeds them impure food to fall into sin.
There, the attendants of Yama feed them impure and foul-smelling food.
Those fierce [guardians] cast into Vikartana those who, having cut open the sheath-like covering, steal the contents;
they cut them to pieces and drink their blood.
And those who, having made a breach in a wall or other structure, steal wealth,
they cause to be weighed upside down in the sky by the fire of the lower world.
Men do not serve cattle with milk, grain, or water;
rather, they cast them into the blind darkness of blood, and it is their own blood that those cattle drink.
The attendants of Yama indeed inflict punishment upon one who employs evil eyes toward those unworthy of being seen,
by driving a spike right into his eyes.
Living beings roasted by fire cook him in turn;
indeed, those destroyers of living beings cause him to fall upon rocks with stones.
The one who binds the innocent is himself bound with iron fetters;
the one who knows and crushes living beings is crushed by iron machines. 46.
He who inflicts suffering upon living beings is tormented in Kākola;
likewise, he who causes misery throughout his life and he who utters false accusations [are tormented there]. (47)
Having killed, having devoured, and having restored to life, the followers of Yama— Yama himself—
cut, hack to pieces, and indeed devour that person.
He who causes suffering to his wife, she who causes suffering to her husband, and those who cause suffering to their dependents—they fall indeed into the Raurava hell. (49)
Thus, where those who should be protectors are instead devourers living by plunder.
All those hell-beings are split open by the servants of Yama.
Thus exist these hells for living beings, which serve as their means of purification;
there the most wicked are cleansed, and from there they proceed to rebirth. (51)
Yama leads a being along the very path that corresponds to whatever kind of birth and karma was previously accumulated by him. (52)

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Sin for Those Going to the Forty Hells," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having experienced great suffering in the hells, the denizens of hell indeed obtain a body through a remnant portion of their own karma.
Having entered a divine, ancestral, human, or even hellish womb,
liberation may then occur through the power of dharma.
In whatever manner a person has performed an action, he shall go to that very womb; experiencing the results exactly as they were done, he wanders through all wombs.
O Lotus-born One, hear from me how one becomes a partaker of hell through the ripening of karma, and what his subsequent birth shall be like.
At the end of their torments, they are liberated; having passed through many successions of lives, they enter a human womb, yet they remain marked by the signs of their sins.
In that regard, one who utters falsehoods has a throat that falters and a half-extinguished tongue;
or rather, he becomes mute, being a reviler of the gods and others.
One who takes life becomes consumptive; a drinker of liquor has black teeth; a thief of gold has deformed nails; and one who forcibly enjoys another's wife suffers from skin disease.
From stinginess one becomes blind from birth; by robbing the eyes of others, one is born blind from birth;
by stealing fruit, one becomes a monkey; and from eating what has been stolen, one becomes a crow.
One who reviles another's lineage will indeed be born without a lineage and childless; a stealer of property becomes a monitor lizard, and one who administers poison takes birth as a snake.
But one who seizes by force becomes a *piśāca* ghost in this world;
a stealer of water becomes a *cātaka* bird, while a stealer of grain becomes a mouse.
One who breaks a water conduit shall become a fish in the water;
indeed, a living being who commits acts of deception is born repeatedly as an owl.
One who eats after snatching it from another is reborn as a dog;
a living being who, having given his word, does not give, is born as a jackal in the forest.
One who constantly eats after committing theft is born as a village pig;
indeed, from insulting those worthy of worship, one obtains the body of a tortoise.
Indeed, one who treats all with contempt is born here as a caṇḍāla;
or he may become a debtor to another, or a bull, a horse, or a donkey. (14)
One who creates obstacles to sexual pleasure is born as a eunuch; one who eats the flesh of others is born as a cat;
and one who strikes another's property is indeed born as a partridge in the forest. (15)

Those who forcibly bring others under their control will indeed attain birth as women; those who forcibly commit sexual acts will suffer from diseases of the female and male organs, and so forth. (16)
Those who rob others of their homes and dwellings are born as wild animals;
and those who slaughter animals here are born as animals that are themselves slaughtered. (17)
Those who steal their master’s wealth become impoverished;
those who revile the learned become fools and childish. (18)
Indeed, those people who deceive living beings and act as their captors or killers are reborn as animals or birds confined in cages. (19)
A scorner of human beings is indeed born here with a distracted mind;
nourished by deceit, hypocrisy, and cruelty, he falls into the state of a gambler.
In this world, one who kills a human is born as a wielder of nooses and a betrayer of trust;
having become a killer of animals, he shall indeed become a goat for a hundred births.
One who eats fish will be born as a fish; one who eats all kinds of food will become a large fish.
One who steals the food, clothing, house, and so forth of others will become a tree in a desert wasteland.
One who steals sandalwood becomes deficient in the sense of smell;
one who listens to the censure of their guru, father, or those worthy of honor will indeed become deaf in this world.
One who strikes another's feet shall become lame; one who strikes with the hand shall have his hand cut off. One who causes suffering to women shall become a donkey belonging to a potter.
A woman who causes suffering to her husband shall likewise become a female donkey;
one who seizes the wealth of a laborer shall become a poor monkey. (25)

One who destroys living beings becomes a *godhā* (monitor lizard); one who kills small creatures in a wall becomes a *godhikā* (lizard). An impure person takes birth as a fly, and a wrathful person attains the state of a serpent.
One who is hateful toward village dogs shall attain birth as an ant;
one who lusts after what is forbidden shall become a castrated bull or a eunuch.
One who steals the food, grain, or wealth of others shall become a distressed dog;
those who consume the food and other belongings belonging to another shall attain the womb of a hen. (28)
One who destroys an undertaking is a ghūka; one who obstructs an undertaking is a jackal (śṛgālaka);
and one who steals vessels that have been served is a vṛkṣavāgulī.
A woman-stealer is a rākṣasa; a practitioner of spells is a piśāca;
a money-lender is a bhūta; and one with a cruel gaze is a śākinī.

One who is full of envy becomes a ḍākinī; one who performs malevolent rites becomes a piśācinī; a destroyer of the fetus becomes a courtesan; and one who desires her husband [to be unfaithful] becomes an unchaste woman. (31)
Even if she is not barren, she may here be childless;
however, by refusing to accept the gift [of intercourse] during her fertile season, she becomes entirely impotent.
Furthermore, that which cuts off others becomes the destroyer of itself;
those who bring about the destruction of the sleeping [state] are slain in the house of the slayer. (33)
Those who steal another's grain become those whose livelihood is not in their own fields;
those who destroy another's work are born from wombs of non-action.
One who steals oil becomes a consumer of oil, while a slanderer has a foul-smelling mouth.
One who steals grain has an extra limb; a slanderer has a putrid nose. ||35||
A killer of a Brahmin becomes a dog, a donkey, or a camel; in the end, he even becomes mute.
A thief of property becomes a worm or an insect, while one who causes the destruction of his teacher becomes an eater of grass.
One who steals gold suffers from consumption; one who steals cooked food has black teeth or deformed nails; one who steals food becomes unable to eat; and one who steals dyed cloth becomes mute. (37)
One who falsifies weights and measures shall become a *vaṭavāgulika* (a maker of deceptive small measures);
one who creates a mixture of counterfeit goods for sale shall become afflicted with labored breathing (*śvāsārta*). ||38||
One who deprives others of their lives will indeed suffer from the disease of consumption (kṣaya);
one who practices deceit in buying and selling will suffer from hemorrhoids;
and one who pours out water while still impure from food will suffer from urinary disorders and other such ailments.
In this world, a mendicant who takes the livelihood of others is treated with contempt.
One who is mutually intolerant and wicked becomes a Cāṇḍāla or an Āghāṭī; one who practices deceit and guile becomes a fisherman, a Śabara, or even a hunter. 41.
Even a weaver who is deceitful in the sale of cloth becomes a remover of impurity; an outcaste who cleans the filth from the squares where four roads meet becomes a purifier. (42)
One who prohibits bathing and purification becomes a washerman who cleans clothes;
and one who desires what is undesirable for others becomes a thief, being reborn as a crying cat. (43)
He shall be a provider of counterfeit medicines in a lonely forest;
he shall be a maker of fraudulent goods, and indeed a deceitful husband and father here.
He who, out of deceit, causes the mixing of gold, silver, and other precious substances,
shall be born from a mixture of castes and likewise become afflicted with oozing leprosy.
Those who cause harm to virgins shall be outcasts for their entire lives;
and a barber who performs the work of shaving [inappropriately] shall be a speaker of falsehood toward his master.
A maker of weapons is born as a leech;
those who eat the flesh of animals, birds, cattle, horses, and so forth, become vultures or scavengers that feed on excrement. (47)
Those who sell meat are born as lions, tigers, wolves, and hyenas;
those who sell their daughters are born as worms in the female genital tract;
and those who adulterate liquids are born as worms in excrement. (48)
Those who milk a source that has no basis become like lice on the head of a Māstika;
one who breaks the row becomes a mere filler of his own belly and suffers from intestinal disease. (49)
Dancers become those who cause distress to couples;
for indeed, those known as *vṛndalas* become those who separate people who are attached to sensual desires.
Those who abandon the pleasures of desire and find delight in empty forests become like deer;
and those men who possess delight and envy are born as frogs. (51)
One who commits treachery against virtuous men and women shall become mute and deaf among people.
For those who provide sustenance to others while remaining unsustained themselves, there arises the state of being a mouse of filth. ||52||
For those who kill animals for their milk, birth is in a waterless land;
for those who pierce the vital organs with the arrows of speech, birth is among porcupines and lizards. (53)
For those who commit the theft of flour, birth occurs among the rough bears;
for those who commit great theft, birth occurs among blind reptiles. (54)
One who betrays deities, sacred fords, and teachers, as well as one who reviles the teachings and causes distress to his family, shall become a "crow-lighter" in the forest.
One who subsists on wine and meat becomes a lion in the forest, or a king;
one who eats from nets, traps, and snares becomes a many-horned deer. (56)
One who is averse to bathing becomes a rhinoceros;
a stealer of flour becomes a bear; and one who eats in secret becomes a bat. (57)
Citrapicchā is chalakartrī; śilakī would be svatantriṇī.
Guptapibā is the house-lizard, and gavaya is guptabhojana. ||58||
Or just as, through the connection with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), diverse embodied beings are born repeatedly—ranging from eighty-four [thousand] types—as performers of various crafts. (59)
Those who treat the elderly with contempt are born as insects, trees, or those dwelling in grass;
they are born as buffaloes or bulls. (1.67.60)
Those who cause the destruction of married couples shall be miserable in birth after birth;
being excessively greedy for impure sense-objects, they shall always become worms dwelling in filth.
The Guptaghātas, Jhallādas, Pāśins, Śvapacas, and others [are the attendants of Yama].
One who destroys the senses becomes devoid of sense-faculties and suffers injury. (62)
Those who cause harm to others go with their bodies bent, constantly inflicting pain;
they are born as Tamasic Yavanas, Daityas, and Rākṣasas.
Women who kill their husbands are born as widows in birth after birth;
a woman who causes suffering to her mother-in-law is born as a lean donkey.
A female cat becomes one who hates her daughter-in-law; she suffers from leprosy and other such diseases.
A female dog becomes one who creates hatred toward her co-wife and suffers from mange.
The *pāśavī* leads one to partiality and the state of poverty;
the *ghūkī* becomes a destroyer of undertakings, while the *kābarī* brings about affliction. (66)
She who relishes flavors not offered as oblation becomes a vulture and a shrieking jackal;
she who behaves with deceit within the home becomes a hawk or a crane.
A black female crow becomes a rogue woman; likewise, a female jackal becomes a barber's wife.
A female snake becomes a hater, and she acts with malice toward her offspring. (68)
One who performs malevolent rites such as the destruction of gender-marks becomes a *ṣaṇḍhā*;
likewise, one who employs mantras for malevolent purposes becomes a *bhūtī* or a *piśācikā*. (69)
A *rākṣasī* is a killer of children, a destroyer of the fetus, and a slayer of the seed; a *yavanī* causes internal burning, while a *khasī* bestows suffering. (1.67.70)
Thus do beings become inhabitants of hell for many births;
again, through karma, one is born in a hundred thousand wombs.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Signs of Rebirth and the Recognition of Hell-beings," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the physical characteristics of people;
what kind of form, what kind of action, and what kind of qualities a person may possess. (1)
I shall explain that in brief for the sake of the world’s understanding:
the bodies of men, women, and gods are indeed all alike. (2)
Indeed, the state of difference in form is merely an indicator;
however, the state of difference among signs is the indicator of actions.
But for one devoid of wealth, the feet are shaped like winnowing baskets and veiny;
they are crooked, rough, and withered, and the nails, soles, and toes are pale.
The two feet of the destroyer of the lineage, which are calloused and stained with impurities,
shall become like wooden stakes at the feet of the slayer of a Brahmin.
In the hair-pores of a poor man there is only one hair each;
but for a king, a Vedic scholar, and likewise for those possessed of fortune and wisdom, there are two hairs each.
Indeed, those whose hair begins with the letter *trya* (the triad of *t*, *th*, and *d*) become destitute, partakers of suffering, and censured;
moreover, he whose hair is curled will surely die while away from home.
A person whose knees are fleshless shall possess good fortune;
one with sunken and small knees should always be understood as a person devoted to women. (8)
One with deformed knees will be poor; one with well-nourished knees will become a king;
one with large knees will be long-lived; but one with crooked knees will be lustful.
His feet have soft soles resembling the interior of a lotus;
his toes are closely joined with copper-colored nails, his heels are well-formed, and they are free from prominent veins. (1.68.10)
He whose [feet] are warm, elevated like the shell of a tortoise, and have hidden ankles shall become a king;
whereas that man whose penis is small shall indeed be devoid of offspring.
He who has a thick penis, even if he has offspring, will be devoid of wealth;
he whose penis is curved will be destitute of sons and riches.
He whose penis is bent downward will always suffer from poverty;
he whose penis is curved to the right is considered by people to be a father of sons.
If the penis is covered with large knots and veiny, one will have many sons; if the generative organ is concealed within a sheath, one will be a king and possess many sons. (14)
He will always have a long penis, a curved sheath, and be devoid of wealth;
he will be weak, have a single testicle, or have uneven testicles that are unstable. ||15||
A king is said to have symmetrical [shoulders], while one with drooping [shoulders] lives for a hundred years.
A man with a lion-like waist becomes a ruler, whereas a man with a monkey-like waist is destitute.
Those with snake-like bellies will be poor; those with thick sides will be wealthy. Those with even armpits will be rich in enjoyments, while those with sunken armpits will be devoid of wealth. (17)
Those with raised armpits become kings, while those with crooked or uneven armpits are dishonest.
One who has infrequent sexual intercourse has a short life, whereas one who has frequent sexual intercourse has a long life.
One with a broad navel shall be happy; one with a deeply sunken navel shall suffer misery.
A navel situated within folds of skin indeed causes the pain of colic.
A man with a right-turning whorl is wise, one with a left-turning whorl is self-controlled;
one with a long side-whorl will be long-lived, and one with a whorl above will be a lord of wealth.
A man with one line on his forehead shall live for a hundred years; one with two lines shall enjoy prosperity;
one with three lines shall be a lord of the earth or a teacher; and one with straight lines shall be happy.
One whose body hair curls to the right will be a great teacher of men;
one whose hair curls to the left or in the opposite direction will be a servant and a person of suffering.
People with fingers that are not protruding and are tapered become fortunate;
those with fingers that are protruding, uneven, long, and yellowish at the tips are poor men. (23)
The heart of kings is even, elevated, unshakable, fleshy, and broad; whereas that of base men is rough, hairy, and veined.
One with a level chest will be wealthy; one with a broad chest will be the lord of Lakṣmī;
one with an uneven chest will be destitute and shall meet death by the sword. (25)
One with uneven collarbones is poor; one with thick collarbones is a lord of wealth. One with a flat throat is destitute; one with a neck of veins and skin is happy. (26)
Śūra will have a buffalo’s neck; Śāstrānta will have the neck of a deer; the king Kambugrīva will have a long neck; and Lambakaṇṭha will be a glutton. ||27||
The kakṣāśvattha leaf is excellent, as is the fragrant magaromikā.
Otherwise, however, it is the cause of being devoid of wealth and of poverty. ||28||
The arms of a divine person are symmetrical, broad, well-knit, slightly curved at the shoulders, and fleshy; those of a king are likewise rounded and extend down to the knees. (29)
The hands of those who are destitute are hairy and short; the best hands are like the trunk of an elephant. Furthermore, the fingers of a lord of wealth are golden-colored. (1.68.30)
Furthermore, those [fingers] of the wise are slender, while those of servants are known to be flat;
those of the destitute have very thick fingers, and likewise, those of monkeys have hands resembling those of a monkey.
A person with a depressed palm will be a destroyer of paternal wealth;
one with a hidden wrist-joint (maṇibandha) bestows a kingdom, while one with a well-rounded wrist bestows wealth.
With hands and palms that are red like lac, soft, and reddish, one will be wealthy;
however, with those that are yellow and rough, one will always meet with death.
Those with nails like chaff are eunuchs; those with cracked mouths are destitute; and those with discolored or deformed nails are considered to be diviners for others. (34)
The gods are known by their copper-colored, rounded nails with raised centers;
a king has a big toe with a barley-corn mark, while one who has a son has full joints.
A man who provides a shelter for travelers shall have his hands marked with the yoke and the fish;
the thunderbolt is the mark of the wealthy, while the fish’s tail belongs to the learned. (36)
The conch, the parasol, the palanquin, the elephant, and the lotus belong to the sovereign;
the jar, the goad, the banner, and the lotus stalk belong to the lord of treasures.
A line resembling a drum [on the forehead] indicates one who is rich in cattle; a svastika mark indicates a lord of kings.
A wheel, a sword, a javelin, a bow, or lines resembling elephant tusks indicate a lord of kings. (38)
A line resembling a mortar is considered auspicious on the hand of a performer of sacrifices;
likewise, many circles and lines like a sacrificial altar belong to one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire. (39)
A line like a pond, a celestial river, or a triangle on the hand of a righteous person, and lines extending to the base of the thumb, bring happiness and indicate the birth of sons. (1.68.40)
The line that extends from the base of the little finger to the base of the forefinger is the "line of longevity"; if it is broken, there is danger from trees.
Those who are destitute will have many lines on their faces, while those who are impoverished will have thin chins;
however, one with fleshy and red-colored lips shall be wealthy. (42)
Those with lips that are like a bimba fruit, yet cracked, rough, uneven, and split, shall be devoid of wealth; teeth that are glossy and dense are auspicious.
Sharp teeth are excellent when even; a red and even tongue is auspicious.
It should be known that a smooth and long palate is favorable, whereas a white palate indicates the loss of wealth.
A tongue that is black, rough, and red-tipped is considered indicative of disease;
however, the mouth of a king is said to be gentle, symmetrical, smooth, and well-proportioned.
The opposite, however, leads to suffering, misfortune, and lack of worldly success:
for the wealthy, the face is round; for those without wealth, it is long. (46)
A fearful face belongs to an evildoer; a square face belongs to rogues;
a sunken face belongs to those without sons; and a short face belongs to the miserly. (47)
A thief possesses a full, lovely, smooth-bearded, auspicious, and soft beard;
it is compact, with uncracked tips, and is reddish in color. (48)
Kings with spike-like ears have short lifespans; those with hairy ears are long-lived; those with large ears are wealthy rulers; and those with small ears are miserly. (49)
One with sunken cheeks is indeed a seeker of enjoyments, while one with full cheeks is a counselor;
one with a parrot-like nose is said to be happy, and one with a parrot-like nose lives a very long life.
One with a nose like a well whose mouth is severed will have sexual intercourse with many women.
One with a long nose shall be fortunate; one with a crooked nose shall be a thief. ||51||
One with a flat nose will be cruel and likewise devoid of fortune;
however, a nose that has small nostrils, well-formed cavities, and is not crooked is considered [auspicious] for a king.
If the gaze is crooked to the right, it is cruel; indeed, a gaze crooked to the left bestows misfortune.
Those with eyes that are curved at the ends and resemble lotus petals are partakers of happiness.
The evil-souled Māra, with eyes like those of a cat, tawny as honey, [beheld him].
They were cruel, with squinting eyes, greenish eyes, and defiled by sin.
Those with squinting eyes are heroes; those with eyes like an elephant's are commanders of armies;
those with deep-set eyes are lords; and those with large eyes are ministers.
The wise possess eyes like blue lotuses; they are fortunate and have dark-hued eyes.
Those with eyes having black pupils would be uprooters [of the world]. ||56||
Those who are crooked-eyed will be sinful, destitute, and have dejected eyes.
One with long, closely-set eyebrows is wealthy; one with uneven eyebrows is poor. ||57||
Those with broad, high, and crescent-shaped eyebrows that are arched are rich in happiness;
one with broken eyebrows becomes destitute, and one with child-like eyebrows is poor. Those with very large foreheads or uneven foreheads likewise become impoverished.
People with a forehead resembling a half-moon are considered to be wealthy. ||59||
Teachers have fingers broad like oyster shells; evildoers have veined fingers;
and lords of men have prominent veins in the shape of swastikas.
Those with sunken foreheads deserve death, as do those who delight in cruel deeds; those with covered foreheads are miserly, while those with prominent ones are kings.
A smile that is steady is excellent; one with closed eyes brings misfortune;
a smile repeated many times is wicked; and one accompanied by pride becomes murderous.
Those who have three lines reaching the forehead shall live for a hundred years;
one with four lines shall be a king, and lives for ninety-five years.
If the lines are interrupted by nine crooked marks, the lifespan is half of that;
and if they reach the hairline, the man's lifespan will be eighty years.
With five, seven, six, fifty, and likewise many red [lines], as well as forty and thirty that reach up to the eyebrows. ||65||
With twenty teeth that are curved to the left, one's lifespan is short;
however, with heads shaped like umbrellas, one becomes a king, equal to Bāṇa, and wealthy.
The king had a head shaped like a jar, delighted in sinful deeds, was the cause of his father's death,
and possessed hair that was black, curled, glossy at the tips, and with unseparated ends.

The queen’s feet have soft soles adorned with the marks of a fish, an elephant-goad, and a banner; they bear the signs of a thunderbolt, a lotus, and a plough, and their ankles are well-concealed. (68)
The private organ is broad like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, excellent, and well-concealed; the penis is hidden, auspicious, fleshy, and circular at its tip. (69)
The navel is spiraled clockwise; the waist is adorned with three folds;
the lips are excellent and slightly reddish; and the face is fleshy and round. (1.68.70)
The hair of women that is glossy blue-black, soft, curled, and auspicious—whether it appears on the soles of the feet or on the palms of both hands—is likewise [a sign of excellence]. (71)
Horses, elephants, śrīvṛkṣa trees, sacrificial posts, barley, clubs, banners, chowries, garlands, mountains, earrings, and altars; ||72||
Those [lines] that appear as a conch, an umbrella, a lotus, fish, a svastika, an excellent chariot, a goad, and so forth, belong to goddesses; they are beloved by kings. (73)
The portions of Hari are the svastika, the bow, the trident-banner, and the fish;
and the line arising from the wrist that extends to the middle finger and the hand. (74)
That which is called an upward line may appear on the hand or the foot;
for both women and men, it leads to sovereignty and happiness. (75)
A woman bearing the marks of a man, and a man with the appearance of a woman—neither of these two brings about auspiciousness; rather, both act as causes of the opposite.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Display of the Physical Marks of the Divine Bodies of Nara and Nārī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||68||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, my beloved; I shall describe your characteristics to you.
Behold your navel, which is clockwise-rotating and endowed with profound depth.
Behold her navel with its three folds; behold her heart and breasts, free from hair;
behold her waist, endowed with all power, and see within it the firm, circular navel.
Look at the reddish-brown line below the navel of Svarṇabāṇa;
likewise, look at the mark of a sandal upon his left thigh.
Behold the line on her chest between the breasts;
observe the crown-like mark on her forehead and the dot upon her cheek.
Behold me, Viṣṇu, upon my chest in the form of four arms as a line;
O beloved, look also at the mark of the mace on my left arm.
O sinless one, behold the golden line upon the Vaijayantī necklace at her heart; and behold the elephant with its lotus in her right palm.
Behold the most auspicious mark of a conch on your right foot;
see the line at the base of your toes that resembles a celestial chariot.
Behold beneath the base of the little finger a boat marked by a fine line;
likewise, behold the lines of a conch and a mace, and the drawing of a crocodile.
Likewise, O beloved, observe the beautiful line of the peak in the middle;
see the line of the fish on the heel and the betel-creeper in the center.
Behold the mark of a barley grain at the base of your left thumb, delineated by a beautiful line;
and below that, behold indeed a great temple marked by a line.
Behold the parasol below that, joined with the upward line;
and behold the lotus line on the hood and the banner line. (11)
Behold the mark of a goad, the water-lily, and also the bilva fruit; observe the lines of a lotus on the ground and the lines of a jar. (12)
And behold the crescent moon on the second [tongue], the ten wheels, the golden line upon the hood, and the inscription of the *Tāntika* on the forehead. (13)
Behold the *bindu* on the chin, the *cakra* on the left breast, the lines of the hand on the right breast, and the beautiful, tawny-colored necklace around the neck. (14)
Behold indeed upon her hips a golden line like a bow,
and on the palm of her right hand a svastika, as well as a fish and a banner.
Behold the bow, the flute, the fish-marks, and the line of the jar;
behold the goad, the mandala, and the wheel upon the palm of his right hand. (16)
Behold the line of the rampart and the archway there as well;
behold the mark of the plough, O beloved, right there upon the coping stone.
Behold, Lakṣmī, the hidden parrot; likewise, behold the two lower lips that are slightly reddened.
Observe the upward line on the right hand, and likewise on the left. (18)
O my beloved, behold the upward-pointing lines on the soles of my feet;
upon my feet, there is the horse, the elephant, and the glorious great tree.
Behold the sacrificial post, the arrow, the barley grain, and the javelin in the lines;
and behold the mark of the rosary on the hand, as well as the lamp and the fly-whisk.
Behold the mountain and the earring; behold the altar with its line. Behold the face, eyes, eyebrows, forehead, lips, nose, and cheeks. (21)
Behold those radiant, fair-complexioned, and gold-beautiful ones; likewise, the goddesses, distinguished by their respective marks, are dear to the Blessed One. (22)
Indeed, women who possess devotion to me become embodiments of Lakṣmī;
by the power of my worship, I make them dwellings of Kamalā.
Those who dwell in the world of Brahmā, those who have made their abode on the earth of Goloka, those who have attained residence in Vaikuṇṭha, and those who have gone to Śvetadvīpa; ||24||
Abiding in the abode of nectar, situated in the center of the circle of fire, dwelling in the world of the sun, and established in the orb of the moon. ||25||

Those who dwell in Satyaloka, those born from the creation of Īśvara, those who have entered the progeny of the Pitṛs, and likewise those who are the wives of the Ṛṣis—[all these were brought there]. (26)
Then the goddesses, as well as the human women and those who are not goddesses but beloved by the nāgas and others—
all of them, having approached me with supreme devotion, became embodiments of prosperity (śrī).
O Mahālakṣmī, though I am Nārāyaṇa in form throughout many worlds, I do not delight them as I do you here in this abode.
Indeed, all those [other] Lakṣmīs arise through devotion of the mind;
however, those others who do not worship me do so because of their sinful karma.
They go to various forms of hells in this world and the next,
even after experiencing great sufferings during their birth in the realm of Yama.
Those women who belong to the city of Yama do not arise as givers of merit; rather, they come into existence for the sake of suffering after having experienced torments.
Those [births] characterized by even a trace of evil are declared to be nothing but givers of suffering;
listen, for I shall describe them to you briefly as the occasion arises. (32)
She whose little finger or ring finger does not touch the ground,
or whose forefinger extends beyond the thumb, is an unchaste woman.
A woman whose shanks are hairy, excessively fleshy, and covered with prominent veins, and whose private parts are sunken, small, and curved to the left, indeed brings suffering.
With a short neck she is destitute; with a long one, there is the destruction of the family;
and with a broad one, she becomes fierce—of this there is no doubt. (35)
If her eyes are squinting and tawny, and her cheeks are dark and trembling, and she smiles with hollows in them, she is certainly unchaste. (36)
A woman with a lock of hair hanging down upon her forehead kills her husband's younger brother;
one hanging on the abdomen kills the father-in-law; and one hanging on both buttocks kills the husband.
A woman who has hair on her upper lip is certainly not auspicious for her husband;
likewise, breasts with hair and uneven ears are inauspicious.
Teeth that are jagged and uneven lead to suffering;
those with blackish flesh and are long lead to theft and even to the death of the husband. (39)
With hands resembling flesh-eating creatures, like wolves, crows, and the like—veiny, uneven, and withered—those women become destitute of wealth. (1.69.40)
She who has a very prominent upper lip is harsh-spoken due to quarrels;
she with long ears, a harsh voice, and a beard is Kālikā on the foot. 41.
One with red eyes, a sharp chin, and a very small forehead is a killer;
one with many lines on the forehead, much body hair, and who speaks excessively is extremely fickle. ||42||
Having many social attachments, much sleep, great laziness, and excessive expenditure, he deliberates upon poverty and total destitution in every way. (43)
Therefore, one should always perform virtuous deeds and never unvirtuous ones;
from the merit produced by well-performed virtuous deeds, a body endowed with auspicious marks arises. (44)
One obtains excellent wealth, grain, friends, houses, gardens, and so forth;
yet time does not wait at all—what has been done by it, or what has not? (45)
A living being dies, is born, and thrives again and again;
yet that very process of death, birth, and growth is fashioned for the sake of liberation.
That [practice] should indeed be performed by oneself, or else by one's sons and family members;
one should act day and night in such a way that it may bring about auspiciousness for the living being. 47.
The earth provides a dwelling, water provides satisfaction, and the wind provides tranquility;
the body provides labor and food—why, then, should it not accomplish the highest good? (48)
Having repeatedly investigated, one finds that excellence exists everywhere;
and having likewise investigated, one finds that there is no excellence in dependence. (49)
Carrying out his own physical existence with whatever comes by chance, he should conduct the affairs of the world with a mind free from excessive attachment. (1.69.50)
O lotus-eyed one, he who does not constantly worship Nārāyaṇa as you do has neither happiness nor spiritual welfare; even liberation is far beyond his reach. 51.
One should worship me in the form of virtuous men and women through the total surrender of all things;
one should joyfully serve me in the form of the poor, guests, and the helpless. (52)
O Goddess, I wander in some places in the form of students, children, young women, the very elderly, teachers, and so forth; one should serve me in whatever form I may appear.
Remaining there, I shall personally bring about the supreme welfare;
indeed, I carry out initiation in order to always effect the welfare of my devotee.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marks of Lakṣmī and the Marks of Other Women," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, for without liberation, the journey to the next world is always miserable and brings only suffering, especially for one whose life has been earned through self-centered pursuits.

If one does not offer the appropriate rice-balls and other offerings even for the sake of the deceased, there will be an obstruction of their progress and an abundance of suffering shall befall them. (2)
Therefore, one who is about to depart upon the path of karma and is about to die should, while still alive, diligently perform meritorious deeds for the sake of one's own happiness. (3)
Whether a man or a woman, through the conjunction of body and senses, they naturally perform pleasure as merit and pain as demerit. || 4 ||
One should practice dharma for the sake of happiness, but indeed practice adharma for the sake of suffering;
since nothing has been done by oneself, what can a future [self] do? (5)
Nevertheless, the world is affectionate and people are likewise;
even a stranger sometimes acts out of affection.
When a living being indeed departs from the body for the next world,
then that body, deprived of the vital breaths, is designated as a corpse.
It quickly becomes untouchable, designated as worms, excrement, or ashes.
From the moment of the soul's departure at death, one should offer six funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in successive order.
At the place where death occurred, a funeral cake (piṇḍa) called "the corpse" (śava) is offered there;
by that, the earth and its presiding deity become satisfied.
If a traveler should be at the doorway, [an offering] is given by that name;
by that which is given, the presiding deities of the house and the site are satisfied.
At the crossroads, there is one named Khecara; by his name it is offered [as a sacrifice].
By that means, the multitude of spirits flees from there to avoid being harmed.
This offering, known as the *bhūta-bali*, is presented for the sake of those who dwell there:
the *piśācas*, *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, and others who reside in that place of rest. ||12||
For that body which is to be offered as an oblation, there are no factors that cause it to become unfit; rather, the practitioner offers a "preta" known as the *sādhaka* to it. (13)
Thus, by means of these five lumps, the corpse becomes fit for the oblation and the defects of the body are destroyed; thereafter, the fire should ignite the funeral pyre.
Having swept and smeared [the ground], and having scraped and removed [the debris] from the altar, and having sprinkled it and established the fire there according to the prescribed rule; ||15||
Having worshipped the deity known as Kravyāda thoroughly with flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
and having said, "Lead the deceased to heaven," one should perform the oblation of the body.
When half the body has thus been consumed, one should then offer oblations of clarified butter (ājya) to Yama,
Antaka, Mṛtyu, and Brahmā.
One oblation should indeed be offered into the mouth of Jātavedas, and likewise one into the mouth of the deceased;
thereafter, one should ignite the fire on the eastern side of the funeral pyre once again.
"This purifier blazes for the sake of the heavenly world, svāhā!
Having thus offered the oblation of clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds accompanied by the mantra, [he should proceed]. (19)
Then, it is said, the cremation must certainly be performed by the son;
he must weep bitterly thereafter, for in this way his happiness shall be secured.
Immediately after the cremation, having performed the rite of gathering the remains there,
one should indeed offer the *preta-piṇḍa* (funeral rice-ball) to pacify the suffering of the deceased.
Then, having performed a bath with their clothes on, the sons should offer water with sesame seeds upon a stone,
pronouncing the name and lineage, and they should also strike the stone with their palms.
People should say, "Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu!
and then, having gone to the right of his door, [they should apply] cow dung and white mustard seeds.
Having placed the god Varuṇa within his own dwelling and concealed him, one should eat neem leaves; having consumed clarified butter, one may go home.
One should not shed tears after offering the handful of water (añjali), because the deceased, being powerless, consumes whatever mucus and tears are consumed by the kinsmen. (25)
For three days, one should offer milk and water in an earthen vessel;
by looking toward a cremation ground, a crossroads, or one's own home, one is led away by the messengers of Yama.
For ten days, one should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at the grave day by day;
furthermore, handfuls of water should always be offered, intended for the deceased.
A son, a wife, a disciple, or a brother may indeed perform the rite;
however, half of the daily offered rice-ball (piṇḍa) bestows a body.
The third [day] he lives upon the messengers of Yama, and on the fourth;
after nine days and nights, the deceased attains completion.
When the body of a living being has been fully formed, hunger arises in the tenth month;
possessed by hunger, that embodied being stays upon the house.
Staying there, they then proceed along the path of Yama to the abode of Yama;
experiencing sufferings, they later lament when they obtain rebirth. //31//
Alas! While in good health, I did not do anything at all that bestows liberation;
I neither chanted the names of Hari nor listened to his stories. (32)

I have not performed the chanting of praises nor the singing of songs, nor have I practiced the remembrance of Hari; I have not performed His worship, nor the massaging of the feet of the virtuous. (33)
There is neither praise nor prostration performed with the body;
for that body is not mine, which has not been nourished by me to any great extent. (34)
Though it was protected, cherished, and served repeatedly and properly, it was abandoned by him in vain; thus his purpose was not accomplished. (35)
Having closed my eyes along with the senses, this body has been spent in vain;
the time available for attaining liberation was not made meaningful by me. (36)
The wife was favorable, the husband was dear, the sons and servants were compliant; yet even so, the self was deceived. (37)
I possessed abundant wealth and various kinds of objects for the purpose of giving;
yet, due to mere greed, I did not attain liberation. (38)
I did not perform service for virtuous men and women;
I am now reaping the fruit of my misdeeds—what indeed will happen now? (39)
Human birth is obtained through a great accumulation of merit;
yet I have not made it meaningful, for much else has been done instead.
Childhood was spent in play, youth was wasted in sexual pleasure, and old age has been cast away in anxiety; what can one who is powerless do at the time of death? (41)

This body, which possesses the splendor of the wish-fulfilling tree, the cow of plenty, and the wish-granting gem, has been exhausted in other pursuits; I have not accomplished my own true purpose. (4)
I am being excessively tormented by the servants of Yama; being dependent on another, what can I do?
Indeed, no gift was ever given by me, nor was any austerity ever practiced. (43)
No vow was ever observed, nor was an oblation offered into the mouth of the virtuous; no pilgrimage site was visited, nor were any ponds and such things ever caused to be constructed. ||44||
No field of merit has been cultivated anywhere; who will provide assistance?
No service has been rendered to others, nor have deeds for the sake of the next world been performed. (45)
The religious observances were not properly respected; what indeed could happen now?
Furthermore, service to my guru, as well as to my parents, was never performed by me at all. (46)
This female body is a source of great suffering, perpetually dependent on others and ever-impure;
yet, through devotion or service, it has certainly not been made meaningful by me. (47)
This human body is a great burden, inauspicious and carrying manifold cravings; yet, through neither devotion nor merit have I made it purposeful. (48)
Thus that preta of torment speaks, grieves, and weeps;
he is tormented and beaten by the messengers, and cries out again and again. (49)
Afflicted by suffering, he remembers the happiness derived from his wife, wealth, land, and home; he grieves deeply for his servants, friends, sons, grandsons, and family. (1.70.50)
Unable to proceed on the path, one is indeed dragged downward by messengers;
one merely laments piteously, "O beloved! O children and others! (51)
May they come together and release me from this unbearable heartache;
may my son, grandson, or kinsman perform meritorious deeds on my behalf. (52)
O my dear son, please perform the gift of a cow for my sake.
I shall cross the Vaitaraṇī; otherwise, my immersion there is certain.
I have not brought even a small amount of provisions for the journey named "merit";
neither austerity was practiced, nor oblation offered, nor mantra recited, nor gift given—whence, then, could it come? (54)
When one travels by a path that is hot, wet, or cold,
being fainting or terrified therein, one grieves only within the heart.
If some kinsman of mine were to offer a gift of clothing or the like, then this suffering would be destroyed; otherwise, it is indeed nothing but enjoyment [of the consequences]. (56)
The servants then say to him, "Where indeed is such merit of yours?
At that moment, crying out, "Alas, Fate!", he regains his composure for a brief instant.
If indeed I should obtain a human body once again, I shall certainly take recourse to the path that grants liberation; I swear this by oath. (58)

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Rituals for the Corpse, the Offering of Piṇḍas, Grief, and the Sorrow for the Departed Spirit," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 70 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having experienced the sufferings of the city of Yama, listen now to how those in hell emerge from hell and wander about. (1)
But those hungry ghosts, being uncertain as to what kind of birth they might obtain,
searched for their own family— among their wife, their son, and their kinsmen.
Or, having established themselves among kinsmen or dwelling within the household,
they roam about bodiless, being severely afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Sometimes and in certain places, they forcibly obstruct them, delude them,
cause them suffering, cause them to faint, and afflict them again and again.
"How is it that you have not indeed acted for my sake to secure our liberation?
Therefore, having become ghosts, we shall torment you most severely. (5)
Agitated by intense anger, they afflict them again and again;
likewise, those who obstruct that path block the gateways of the ancestors.
Like thieves on a road, they seize the portions belonging to their fathers in their own homes, upon floors defiled by the discharge of excrement and urine and other impurities.
Having stayed there, they observe whichever person might be diseased;
they afflict them with forms of fever and devour their food.
And they drink that blood, though only in minute and small quantities here and there;
remaining in places such as where food scraps are left, they constantly contemplate what is undesirable.
There they drink water mixed with the leftovers of their food;
they are always plotting deception against their family members, children, and others. (1.71.10)
Thus, those with such undesirable thoughts inflict suffering upon themselves;
a hungry ghost (preta) may afflict his own family, but he afflicts others through their vulnerabilities.
While living he was full of affection, but once dead, he indeed becomes wicked;
having found a flaw or impurity, he repeatedly causes suffering.
A hungry ghost (preta) shall torment that person who is devoid of all religious rites, who neglects the worship of the gods, and who eats impure food. 13.
For one there may be the loss of a son, while another does not obtain a son at all;
one may be devoid of progeny—indeed, in such cases, there is the fault of a *preta*.
The lineage perishes from the womb; that which has arisen is destroyed;
there is the loss of livestock and wealth, and enmity with one's kinsmen. (15)
The natural state undergoes transformation, as does strife among sons;
the sudden onset of misfortune—that affliction arises from the departed spirits. (16)
Indeed, madness, sleeplessness, indigestion, fever, belching, and abdominal pain—such suffering arises from the presence of a *preta*. (17)
A fondness for theft, domestic strife, poverty in wealth and grain, and the gradual decline of prosperity—this is the affliction arising from the Pretas. (18)
Even wealth that has been acquired slips from one's hand;
there will be loss of crops despite a period of plenty, and failure in one's undertakings. (19)
There will be the accusation of base deeds, fear from thieves, fire, and kings, as well as the onset of a great disease and affliction of one's own body. (1.71.20)
First she is a servant and later a wife, yet she becomes like a dog;
her mind is constantly intent on the ruin of the household, and that suffering arises from a ghost. (21)
Meditation devoid of mindfulness, action lacking mental focus, and daily quarreling among one's own kin—such suffering arises from the influence of a preta. (22)
For women, there may be the destruction of the embryo, and likewise the menses are not seen;
or even if the menses are seen, no fruit at all is seen. (23)
There is a gradual destruction of lives; there is constant strife over the teeth in the home; and in eating, there is a lack of satisfaction due to anger, agitation, and the like. (24)
Quarrels and even murderous acts arise from sons who are like the offspring of an enemy;
there is neither affection nor happiness, for that is the suffering born of the deceased.
One who does not obey the words of one's parents, nor serves one's own wife;
and a wife who does not look upon her husband as a deity—such suffering arises from the realm of the departed spirits.
Those who cause sudden death become afflicted *preta*s;
likewise, one who performs actions contrary to the law or performs rites devoid of the prescribed rules becomes a *preta*. (27)
At that time, due to association with the wicked, or because of the release of a bull [without proper rites],
or even due to the power of an evil death, his body remains undissolved.

O beloved, due to the omission of cremation rites and other ceremonies, and because of the fault of dying on a bed or similar surface, one is born as a preta through the affliction of hunger, thirst, burning heat, and death. (29)

Due to the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), one may become a preta in some place, devoid of speech and movement; once that state of being a preta has become firmly established, one should practice the liberation of the preta.
He who indeed thinks of the departed spirits after his own death shall himself attain the state of a preta;
in that family where there is the fault of pretas, no happiness is found. (31)
Intelligence, joy, pleasure, wisdom, and fortune—these five are destroyed;
when the third or fifth house from the male [ascendant] is afflicted, the cutting off of the lineage occurs.
In birth after birth, they become poor, destitute, and performers of evil deeds;
thus, as hungry ghosts, they torment themselves through their own cruel disposition. (33)
Tormented by hunger and thirst, the pretas shall enter their own homes;
having entered with bodies of wind, they shall find those born of their own lineage lying there. (34)
In dreams, they show themselves in their own forms as sons, wives, and so forth;
having become elephants, horses, or bulls, they appear with distorted faces. (35)
A cat, a woman, or a snake are repeatedly seen for a moment; or the bed is inverted, or one perceives oneself as being transformed. (36)
He who, having risen, looks about, is indeed tormented by a *preta*;
he is bound with fetters in a dream; this is caused by a *preta*, of this there is no doubt. (37)
If one begs for food in a dream, one is slain by many weapons;
or else one slays a person oneself—all this is shown by a preta.
Taking cooked food from one who is eating, he indeed flees;
or, afflicted by thirst, he forcibly drinks the water of himself or another. (39)
Mounting a bull in a dream, or fighting with bulls,
leaping up and traveling through the sky, or going to a sacred ford out of hunger.
One's own wife, one's kinsmen, one's son, one's husband, and one's teacher.
One may see even those who are living as dead; all that is shown by the departed spirits.
For the sake of the liberation of that deceased person who, overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, begs for water in a dream, one should have funeral cakes (piṇḍas) offered at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
As he departs from his home at night, he sees in a dream his sons, as well as his cattle,
fathers, brothers, and wives, due to the affliction of a *preta*.
For the sake of pacifying that [evil influence], one should perform libations at home, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or beneath a Bilva tree;
having honored black grains, one should give them to a master of the Vedas. 44.
For one who abandons all obstacles and undertakes the means to liberation, the fruit of that action is excellent: eternal satisfaction for the departed spirits.
The self alone shall be united with the highest good, and the deceased shall attain long-lasting satisfaction;
for those who are satisfied always desire the welfare of their own kinsmen. (46)
Otherwise, however, evil-minded people cause suffering to those born of their own lineage, through mere sight, conversation, activity, or even oppression. (47)
He does not attain a good rebirth; he is tormented by the curses of pretas;
he is childless and without cattle, as well as poor and diseased.
He shall be devoid of livelihood and wretched in birth after birth;
therefore, liberation for the deceased must always be effected through libations (tarpaṇa). 49.
Satisfied, they ward off the calamities arising from their own offspring;
later, when the time arrives, they attain liberation through their sons.
Wealth, prosperity, and success always bestow increase and growth upon one's kinsmen;
he who performs the auspicious Nārāyaṇa-bali rite dedicated to the ancestors [attains these]. (51)
By performing that [rite], obstacles are destroyed and one is not afflicted;
one is certainly liberated from the torments of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like. (52)
Having performed the Nārāyaṇabali rite, one should carry out the release of a bull and other such ceremonies;
thus, one shall attain freedom from all calamities and obtain every happiness. ||53||
In this world, there is no other supreme deity equal to one's father and mother;
the father, who brought about the birth of the body, is the manifest deity. (54)
The teacher who instructs one in what is beneficial is a visible deity;
therefore, the father, the teacher, the mother, the elders, and likewise the husband, are to be honored.
Body, wealth, wife, sons, and eternal worlds are obtained through his grace; who else is more worthy of worship than he? (56)
Because he protects his father from the hell named Put, he is therefore called "putra"; thus, one should deliver one's father.
If the father or mother of anyone should die of an untimely death,
one should perform the funeral rites (śrāddha) for the anniversary year, as well as religious duties, pilgrimages, marriage, and other such ceremonies.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Torments Caused by Pretas Dwelling on Impure Ground, the Signs in Dreams Caused by Pretas, and the Means for Their Cessation," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the ghosts born of untimely death— those who were heretics, those who died of greed, and likewise those who died without the purificatory rites.
Those who die from a caṇḍāla, water, a serpent, a curse, a tree, lightning,
or from fanged and horned animals, become pretas.
Those who died by hanging, those struck down by poison, weapons, and the like, as well as suicides and those killed by malevolent rites and similar acts; || 3 ||
Those who have died from great hardships or diseases, those killed by robbers, those struck down by cholera or fire, and those who have perished in landslides and similar calamities; || 4 ||

Those who died without performing the purificatory rites, those who were impure and subject to the stain of death, those whose funeral offerings were withheld, and those who died without having performed the rite of releasing a bull; || 5 ||

Those who die from falling off a mountain or from the collapse of a wall, or by traveling through the sky in this manner; or those who die while a woman is in her menses, or during sexual intercourse, or when the time for purification has arrived.

Those who have died in the intermediate space of the atmosphere, in a desolate region, or by means of a malignant thorn or similar cause, as well as those who have died during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) and so forth; || 7 ||
Those who have not obtained water when thirsty and those who have fallen under the power of an untimely death are indeed born as pretas; they wander upon the surface of the earth.

Those who seize cattle and livestock, those who plunder crops, those who destroy water sources and groves, those who obstruct the livelihoods of the gods, and those who disrupt the livelihoods of the distressed; || 9 ||
Those who destroy the act of giving, those who ruin meritorious deeds, and those who cause suffering to many, become hungry ghosts (pretas) due to their evil karma. ||1.72.10||
Those wicked ones who delight in harming others, having fallen under the sway of an evil death,
constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, attain the state of a preta.
Neither mother nor father is considered the cause at the beginning of birth as a preta or in other states.
Therefore, the state of being a preta arises from karma and from the intention (saṃkalpa) of Yama.
There indeed were some of deformed appearance, with hanging lips and distorted faces; some had large bodies and teeth, and others had crooked mouths.
They have the faces of serpents, the faces of cats, and various other faces;
whatever their names may be, they become hell-beings by virtue of the actions they have committed. (14)
A deceased person indeed possesses exactly such qualities at each respective time as correspond to the nature of the sin by which that human being attained the state of a preta. (15)
In that very manner, his hunger and thirst arise repeatedly;
yet, neither food nor even pure water can be obtained anywhere. (16)
But regarding pure food or water, there is no further requirement for ritual purification;
for pure food is purified by the Vasus, and pure water is purified by the Varuṇas. (17)
It was always guarded there, yet it was not even a portion for the hungry ghosts (pretas),
being filled with phlegm, urine, excrement, and various impure secretions.
Food that has been kept overnight as well as that which is left-over becomes the meal of the pretas;
the pretas always consume whatever is devoid of purity and is defiled. (19)
In whose house there is no purity nor any offering to the gods, but which is defiled by liquor and meat— in that house, the pretas consume the food.
Greed, anger, pride, laziness, sleep, sorrow, and fear; deceit, quarrel, hypocrisy, impurity, and the neglect of ritual bathing. (21)
The purification of the impurities of the elements and so forth is not like a cloth stained with dust and semen; nor is the wall made of saliva and phlegm, nor the tube filled with urine. (22)
In whichever house there are pretas, they indeed eat there; that food for the pretas constantly flows from his linga and bhaga. (23)
Death is always better for a living being than the state of a ghost should it ever occur—to one who dies with the food of an outcast still remaining in his stomach. (24)
Indeed, that man who falls under the power of an evil death is born as a *preta*;
he who seizes the property of the gods or the wealth of others is born as a *preta*. (25)
One who misappropriates the property of a guru or the property entrusted to another is born as a *preta*. So too is one who betrays trust, a deceiver, or a person who sells a maiden. (26)

One who seizes his brother's property, a slayer of people, a killer of cows, a killer of animals, an adulterer, a stealer of gold, a usurper of land, or one who speaks falsehood—such a person becomes a preta. ||27||
The man who abandons his mother, sister, wife, daughter-in-law, daughter, son, or father is born as a preta.

Those who are devoid of the conduct of the cultured, those who lack devotion to their parents, those who are addicted to liquor and meat, and those who perform such acts as the slaughter of animals; ||29||
Those who commit acts of malice against others, those who cause great terror, those who constantly seek out vulnerabilities, and those who bring about the destruction of others; || 1.72.30 ||
Those who are addicted to excessive sexual intercourse, who eat the flesh of the heart and other such things,
who are cruel, addicted to vices, wicked, and delight in performing forbidden acts— (31)
Furthermore, for others who are like them, there indeed occurs the exhaustion of their lifespan;
having abandoned their short-lived and wretched bodies, they become pretas. ||3||
With such a body, one should accomplish one's own welfare;
through meritorious action, one may achieve heaven or even liberation.
One experiences happiness or suffering due to the ripening of past karmas;
therefore, in this life, one should practice that which bestows happiness, namely, Dharma. (34)
Whether a man or a woman, even after having accomplished their own purpose on this earth, they should always strive for the sake of others; this is the supreme good that brings about liberation. (35)
One may indeed forget other things at will, but one must never forget liberation;
one may indeed forget other duties, but one must never forget dharma. (36)
One may forget other objects of enjoyment, but one must not forget the happiness of the Self;
one may forget artificial yoga, but one must not forget Hari who dwells within the heart. (37)
But he who abandons the Lord, the giver of happiness, and worships instead that which gives suffering, shall find suffering as his fruit; he attains no other good.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, the denizens of hell should be known to be of three kinds:
some reside in the city of Yama, while others have the form of pretas. (39)
But all other hell-beings are exceedingly miserable in every house,
for in their houses there is indeed no happiness due to the lack of the abundance of food and drink.
Because of their wives, sons, wealth, and grain, they are hell-beings right here before our eyes—those whose family is large, yet who are destitute in providing for its maintenance. (41)
Their clothes and food are never sufficient; they are hell-beings manifest in this world.
He who has more than one wife is a hell-being manifest in this world. (42)
He who commits adultery in his own home experiences hell visibly; likewise, one who is devoted to the wives of others, courtesans, and the like, experiences hell visibly. (43)
One who is counted among the company of ignoble women like a dog is a hell-being here in this very life;
and she whose husband is there with her like a bitch is also a hell-being in this very life. (44)
Those for whom you have created hatred and distress among their family members, who find neither sleep nor happiness, and whose love [is lost]—they are indeed manifest hell-beings. (45)
Where one's own kinsmen act as thieves, where one's own kinsmen act as murderers, and where one's own kinsmen act as deceivers—that indeed is hell manifest before one's eyes. (46)
Sons and others do not carry out one's commands, nor does a wife bestow true affection;
there is no family that grants honor—indeed, that is a hell manifest before one's eyes. 47.
One who always eats dry food, preceded by insults and the like, and looks upon others with eyes of hatred—he is a hell-being here in this very world. (48)
Torn garments, a house, a street, and a square;
honor treated as contempt—this is indeed hell manifest before one's eyes. (49)
Those who are always dependent on others, such as servants and messengers,
and those whose kinsmen behave like dogs— they are indeed hell-beings in this very life.

But that house which is a dwelling for the afflictions of mental and physical disease and their various conditions, a refuge for vulnerabilities, fierce rogues, and deceit, is a hell visible to the eye. (51)
A wife who bestows desires is by no means an adversary;
a husband who bestows pleasure is not one who strikes her—he is a hell-being here.
Those who are wounded by birth, afflicted by diseases of birth, tormented by the sufferings of birth, and burdened with afflictions from birth itself—they are indeed visible hell-beings. (53)
The body is indeed hell; because of dwelling therein, one is a denizen of hell. Saṃsāra is truly hell; because of dwelling therein, one is a denizen of hell. (54)
Indeed, one who performs what is beneficial with devotion is surely liberated from hell;
however, all those in hell remain there as long as they are not yet released. ||55||
Resorting to the gates of hell, of impurities, and of saliva—the union of the elements—he delights here; for he is truly a denizen of hell. (56)
Having emerged from the hells, he clings once more to the hells;
when fully developed, he is himself of the nature of hell—what indeed is more hellish than that? (57)
Insult is great suffering, but bondage is even greater than that;
dependence on others is a source of great terror, and one who possesses it is right here a denizen of hell. (58)
He who is attached to that which is called the hell of craving is considered a denizen of hell;
thus, this third hell exists here in every single house. (59)
Impurity, decay, and excess—these three defects are inherent;
whoever is bound by them shall indeed become like a denizen of hell.

These are the hungry ghosts (pretas): those who are alive yet dead as pretas in the abode of Yama, those who are invisible, and those who have the form of wind; these are the three types of departed spirits (paretakas). ||61||
All indeed are experiencers of suffering, and all likewise are givers of suffering;
all are devoid of devotion—what difference is there here among those who have passed away? (62)
Those three—the Yāmyas, the Vāyavyas, and the Mānavīyas—if they do not perform what is beneficial, then all three are equal to ghosts (pretas). ||63||
Therefore, that which brings about liberation must be accomplished with this human body.
Indeed, those who proceed toward liberation by means of that do not go to the state of a preta at all.
If his wife is a ḍākinī, or his husband is a source of terror to spirits,
or his sons are slayers of rākṣasas, then the preta flees from him.
The womb is a grinder, moistened by urine and semen; the body is like mud, and he who enjoys it is a denizen of hell.
Outcastes (śvapacas) who dwell outside the village are impure and baskets of faults;
what fault can be attributed to a fault? What can a ghost do there?
Just as one ghost should neither frighten nor torment another ghost, [so should one treat the deceased].
Likewise, what could one gain by harming a wicked person who is like a hungry ghost?
Indeed, having abandoned such a family, the deceased depart;
they dwell in sacred fords, in forests, or elsewhere, perpetually afflicted by suffering. (69)

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of Whose State of Being a Preta Occurs, the Dwelling, Food, and Other Matters of the Pretas, and the Threefold Nature of the Pretas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
