Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In all beings, at the beginning of every birth, happiness is ordained in varying degrees; however, in the human womb, the righteous soul becomes happy in every respect.
The merit and demerit of human beings arise from injunctions and prohibitions;
indeed, until five years from conception, one is not tainted by sin.
After five years, the embodied soul is tainted by half the sin;
after twelve years, the embodied soul is tainted by all the sins. (3)

According to the actual state of affairs and according to the degree of the taint of sin, for one who has died, the impurity (sūtaka) is understood here to be either greater or less than that [standard]. || 4 ||
For as many days as there are months until the miscarriage of the fetus, that period is considered *sūtaka* (impurity); during that time, no ritual action whatsoever should be performed by him. ||5||
If death occurs from birth until the performance of the *cūḍā* ceremony, one should cast the child into a pit;
however, milk should be offered according to one's ability for the sake of the child's satisfaction.
If death occurs before the tonsure ceremony at five years of age, one should then cremate the body;
for milk-based food should be provided, as that is the food of children.
In the event of the death of one who has completed five years,
the funeral rites must by all means be performed according to the prescribed rules in every respect.
One should perform the rites for the boy while he is still a child, providing him with food and clothing;
however, one should carry out these duties for the boy even if they are devoid of great sacrificial gifts (mahādāna).
Whether in childhood, youth, or old age, the body of embodied beings becomes a vessel [for death].
Indeed, the casting into the womb lasts for only two years of childhood.
After that, the cremation of the entire body is prescribed for everyone.
One is a *śiśu* (infant) until the eruption of teeth; one is a *bāla* (child) up to the appearance of the first hair.
Thereafter, the boy shall undergo the binding of the *mauñjī* [sacred girdle];
however, if death occurs after five years, it shall be without the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Likewise, without performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should indeed offer the sixteen *śrāddhas* on the eleventh day and cause the water-pot (*udakumbha*) to be given.

The offering of lamps, food, water, clothing, gold, and other such gifts, as well as the performance of funeral feasts, should be carried out as appropriate for the sake of bringing about the cessation of the state of being a preta. (14)
Upon seeing his son’s face, a father is liberated from his debt to his ancestors;
therefore, a legitimate son (aurasa-putra) should perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha.
Upon seeing a grandson, one is liberated from the three debts and attains heaven.
Those who are not biological sons, but are adopted, are considered to be of nine types. (16)
Indeed, the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha must be performed by those nine;
the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa for the father must be performed by the legitimate son (aurasa). ||17||
When the year is complete, one should perform the introduction of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-praveśana);
by performing the unification of the rice-balls at the end of the year, one attains the supreme goal.
When this has been done, the deceased spirit (preta) shall thereby become a member of the ancestral host (pitṛgaṇa).
A mendicant (bhikṣu) should not accept alms as long as the sapindikarana rite has not been performed.
One remains impure with respect to those of one's own lineage until the *piṇḍa* offerings have been merged;
this is because of the infinity of family customs and because of the exhaustion of men's lifespans. (1.73.20)
Because the body is unstable, one should perform the sapindikarana on the twelfth day,
or one should perform the sapindikarana in the third fortnight, or in six months, or in a year.
In the absence of a son, the wife should perform it; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother;
or else the brother, or the brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple. ||22||
Having performed the *sapiṇḍana* rite, one should thereafter perform the *abhyudaya* (prosperity) rite;
for all those who are childless, the daughter should perform the *sapiṇḍana*.
Or he may have the officiating priests (ṛtvij) perform it, or even the family priest (purohita);
he may also have the ancestral Śrāddha performed by his sons who have undergone the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā).
By that indeed the ancestors are satisfied, and likewise the satisfaction of the deceased occurs;
for the sake of the deceased’s attainment of happiness, everything is performed by the son.
A son may deliver one from hell, if liberation is not found;
for one without a son there is no destination, neither heaven nor anything else at all. (26)
The cremation must be performed by the son, and the grandson is indeed the giver of the fire;
with sesame seeds and darbha grass upon the ground, his mind shall be fixed there in Vaikuṇṭha. (27)
By placing the five jewels in the mouth, the life-force (jīva) flourishes;
the ground should be smeared with cow dung, and sesame seeds and darbha grass should be scattered there.
Upon that very [bed], the afflicted person placed burns away all their evil deeds;
there is no doubt that a bed of Darbha grass leads the afflicted one to heaven. (29)
Everywhere the earth is holy, for even those who are devoid of merit—Yātudhānas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas who follow cruel courses—are [there]. (1.73.30)
For when the sick man is released from being smeared [with the ashes], these base-born ones enter him:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śrī, and Agni himself. (3.1)
They abide within the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
Otherwise, he who dies will be tormented by the wind.
O Lakṣmī, these sesame seeds produced from my body are purifying; by their presence, the Asuras, Dānavas, and Daityas flee in terror. (33)
Darbha grasses are produced from body hair and sesame seeds from sweat; therefore, one should place them [there].
Brahmā resides at the root of the darbha, while Keśava resides in its middle. (34)
Śaṅkara resides at the tip of the darbha grass; the three gods are situated within the kuśa grass.
Viṣṇu, Ekādaśī, Gaṅgā, Tulasī, brahmins, and cows [are likewise present]. (35)
In this essence-less and difficult saṃsāra, these six lines bestow liberation;
they ward off the miserable state for one who is afflicted and has fallen into misfortune. (36)
Since the salty taste indeed originated from the body of Viṣṇu,
salt should certainly be given during the Prāṇāyāma, for it bestows the path to heaven.
Indeed, a gift should be given there; by that merit one is protected.
[One should give] sesame seeds, a cow, land, gold, cotton, and likewise salt.
Likewise, one should purify each of those [sins] by means of the seven grains or iron;
through the gift of gold, there is happiness and heaven, and through the gift of land, one becomes a king. (39)
By the gift of the seven grains, one attains grain and the servants of Yama are satisfied;
by the gift of iron, the messengers of Yama do not come to the house of the deceased.
The axe, the pestle, the staff, the sword, and likewise the dagger;
the noose, the whip, and the mallet—these indeed are the weapons held in the hands of Yama. 41.
The Kuriṇas, Sārvasūtrāpas, Śūṇḍas, Markas, Anurvaras, Śabalas, and Śyāmadūtas were gratified by the gift of iron. ||42||
Indeed, the gift of iron rescues one from the accumulation of sins;
moreover, the cow enables one to cross the Vaitaraṇī river and leads one to heaven and liberation.
Mahādeva repeatedly performed service to the cows even in Goloka,
while Śrī Hari indeed performs service to the cows at all times.
Cows are all forms of fortune; I dwell eternally within cows.
Through the gift of gold, one attains the world of the Sun, as well as the splendor of the Moon and Fire. 45.
The gift of salt likewise opens the gate to heaven;
the gift of sesame seeds destroys the great sins of a mortal. (46)
Furthermore, other gifts and material requisites should be given for the sake of the deceased’s attainment of happiness and liberation. ||47||
Seeing his father on the ground with eyes half-open and his breath faltering as it leaves its place, he is said to be one afflicted by the desire to give. (48)
At that time, whatever son causes all kinds of gifts to be given [with the words]:
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Kamalā! (49)
"O Vāsudeva, O Supreme Brahman, O Lord, O Śrī Rāma, O Lord of the Cowherds"—
in this manner, one should perform worship at the moment of the departure of the vital breaths.
"Śrī Hari is my refuge; O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, You are my goal.
Or one may mutter: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. (5.1)
One should give the patient the mantra of renunciation, as well as the mantras "Śrī Hari," "Śrī Kṛṣṇa," and also "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. ||52||
"Śrīman Nārāyaṇa," "O Lord Nārāyaṇa," as well as "Rāma-Kṛṣṇa," "Hari-Kṛṣṇa," "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa," and also "Om. ||53||
"O Nṛsiṃha! O Dattātreya! O Śrīśambhu! O Viṣṇu! Recite [my name]! "Victory to Govinda! O Gopāla! Victory to Mādhava!"—thus [he should say]. (54)
Viṣṇu is the mother, Viṣṇu is the father; Viṣṇu is one's own kin and kinsmen.
Viṣṇu is water, Viṣṇu is land; Viṣṇu is the earth, and the *kuśa* grass belongs to Viṣṇu. (55)
Viṣṇu is the Brahmin, the sesame seeds, the cows, the gold, and indeed the grain;
Viṣṇu is the giver and the receiver, as well as the leader and the one who causes [the gift] to reach its destination.
One should worship that very [deity] constantly and recite its name at the time of death;
for such a person, there is never an evil destiny, nor even the state of being a preta.
He by whom the peaceful ones have been seen at the time of death, bowed to, served, and propitiated—he indeed attains liberation swiftly; there is no doubt in this. ||58||

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Appropriate Sūtaka, Sapindikarana, and Other Rites, as well as the Giving of Sesame and the Imparting of Mantras to the Deceased," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||73||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: At the time of death, the gift of cows indeed yields the fruit of residence in heaven;
and those who give sandals travel mounted upon horses.
But by the gift of an umbrella, a preta shall wander happily in the shade;
likewise, by the gift of food, he shall wander happily, free from hunger. (2)
In the same way, by the gift of a lamp, one proceeds to happiness through illumination;
the lamp should be placed in the temple facing either the east or the north. (3)
One should offer a seat and a vessel, which bring benefit in the next world; one should offer water from a water-pot, thinking, "The thirsty one shall drink this water. (4)
On the eleventh day, flowers, a finger-ring, a vessel, and the gift of food should be given; thus the deceased goes to the highest state.
The gift of a water-pot, the gift of clothing, the gift of an elephant, horse, or chariot,
and likewise the gift of a buffalo— these should be given in the name of the deceased.
The gift of a bed with its bedding, as well as other gifts according to one's ability,
should be performed for the sake of attaining the satisfaction, happiness, and peace of the deceased.
When that self, mixed with the vital air, indeed departs from the body—
through the hair-pores above the waist as well as from the spheres of the sense organs— (8).
The vital breath (prāṇa) of the doer of merit goes upward, while that of another flows downward;
it consists of the ten sense organs, the four internal organs, and the five subtle elements.
Taking its subtle body along with merit and demerit, it goes wherever it may; there, in accordance with its karma, it is considered to take up a new body as its dwelling.
There are twenty-one lakhs of beings born from a womb; likewise, there are that many born from moisture, born from sprouts, and born from eggs. 11.
Thus, eighty-four hundred thousand types of birthplaces are recognized;
having gone to each of them, the preta suffers again and again in that same way. (12)
For one who does not worship Hari, there is dwelling again in the womb, birth and death again and again; indeed, for such a person, residence in the womb occurs repeatedly.
Since embryos are produced in women by means of the male seed, one should avoid the four nights of women during their fertile period. 14.
The embryo within the womb becomes impure during the course of seven nights; having passed the first week, it then enters into the even [periods]. 15.
The sixteen nights of the woman's fertile period are conducive to conception;
however, if the embryo is present on the fourteenth night, it remains there.
There, a virtuous son, a treasure-house of good qualities and fortune, shall be born;
for sons are born from women on even nights, while daughters are born on odd nights.
On the fifth day, for women there is a meal of *gaulma* (potherbs) and sweet foods;
for young women, there is a meal of pungent, sharp, and clarified butter (*sājya*) foods.
A woman, however, must strictly avoid exposure to the sun and should practice only cooling regimens;
on an auspicious day, she may enjoy betel, perfumes, and sandalwood paste.

Just as at the time of conception, when semen and blood are mixed, the son is endowed with the mental impressions of the man and the woman; so too is the son joined with their respective mental dispositions. (1.74.20)
Consciousness is eternally established in the seed-form of the semen;
indeed, when desire, the mind, and the semen attain a state of oneness, [then conception occurs]. ||21||
Then the man attains a state of fluidity within the womb of the woman;
if there is an excess of blood, a female is born, and if there is an excess of semen, a male is born. (22)
When the semen and blood are equal, the embryo attains the state of a eunuch.
Within one day and night it becomes a *kalala*, and a bubble (*budbuda*) after five days. (23)
On the tenth day it becomes a jujube fruit; on the twentieth day, it attains the state of solid flesh;
likewise, when the month is complete, it sustains the five elements.
In two months, the skin and flesh appear; likewise, the marrow and bones in three;
in the fourth month, the ankles and hair; and in the fifth, the ears and nose.
In the seventh [month], the throat, the secret parts, and so forth [are formed]; in the eighth, there is the completion of the limbs;
in the ninth, there is the desire to go outside; but in the tenth, one is born.
The fivefold [constituents] of earth are skin, bone, channels, hair, and flesh;
the fivefold [constituents] of water are saliva, urine, semen, marrow, and blood. ||27||
The fivefold group of fire consists of lustre, hunger, sleep, thirst, and laziness;
that of air consists of breath, movement, contraction, expansion, and the five [sensory] perceptions. 28.
Passion, hatred, fear, shame, and delusion are the five qualities born of wind; from space arise the qualities of sound, support, aperture, and depth. (29)
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Gāndhārī, Gajajihvikā, Pūṣā, Yaśā, Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī are the channels (nāḍīs). || 1.74.30 ||
The vital airs are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
and [the five subsidiary winds are] nāga, kūrma, kṛkala, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. ||3.1||
Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna in the anus, samāna in the region of the navel, udāna should be in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body. ||32||
The expansion of the *nāga* [vāyu] is considered to be yawning, while the contraction of the *kūrma* [vāyu] is [yawning].
The *śūla* [vāyu] causes the hunchbacked appearance (*kṛkalaja*), and the *devadatta* [vāyu] causes belching and so forth. (33)
Dhanañjaya [Arjuna] exists for the sake of expansion; even when dead, he resides in the third heaven.
Indeed, there are nine [orifices]: the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, anus, and genitals. (34)
The navel is the tenth, the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is remembered as the eleventh;
the womb-cavity in the secret place of a woman is the twelfth, and the breasts are the fourteenth.
Likewise, there are three crores and fifty million pores of the body;
thirty-two teeth are said to be present, as well as exactly twenty nails.
It is established that there are three hundred thousand hairs on the head and those located on the face;
however, the three [constituents] known as hair, blood, and flesh are derived from the mother. (37)
From the father come the sinews, bones, and marrow, as well as the sixfold sheaths;
the flesh is one thousand palas, and the blood is likewise one hundred palas.
Fat is ten palas, and marrow is twenty palas;
blood is said to be three palas, and semen likewise two kuḍavas. (39)
One *kuḍava* of blood, six of phlegm, and likewise half [a *kuḍava*] each of feces and urine;
the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*)—this is the internal instrument (*karaṇa*). (1.74.40)
All that, produced within the body, the embryo is expelled by the wind of birth and goes outside; indeed, being unconscious, it undergoes birth.
The entire form of the universe is situated within the body:
Satyaloka is the aperture of the head, and Tapoloka is the forehead. (42)
Janaloka is said to be the mouth, and Maharloka is declared to be the throat; one should know that Svarloka is in the heart, while Bhuvarloka is within the belly. 42.
The earthly realm (Bhūloka) is the region from the navel downward; Atala is situated at the hips; Vitala is said to be the private parts; and Sutala is at the roots of the thighs. 44.
The two thighs are considered Talātala and Mahātala; likewise, the two knees are Rasātala, the two shanks are Pātāla, and the feet are said to be Pātāla. (45)
In this context, urine is the salt-water ocean; milk is the milk-ocean;
phlegm resides as the wine-ocean; and marrow is the ghee-ocean. ||46||

The ocean of sweet taste is in the blood; the ocean of curds is in the [left] side; the ocean of sweet water is in the region of the belly; and the ocean of embryo-water is situated in the semen. ||47||
The Sun and Moon are in the two eyes, while Mars is said to be in the lips;
Mercury is to be known as being in the heart, and Jupiter is established in knowledge. (48)
Venus is in the semen, Saturn is in the navel, Rāhu is situated in the mouth, and Ketu is situated in the private parts; thus is the microcosmic body said to be the macrocosm.
Life-span, knowledge, wealth, fame, and even death—
these five are created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb.
With face turned downward and feet upward, he indeed emerges from the womb;
being protected by the one who brings about his birth, while he himself protects others who have taken refuge in him.
Protected by his sons, he eventually died; yet it was that very same person who, thereafter, would worship Hari constantly, without weariness, and at every moment with devotion.
Then liberation will surely occur, as well as heaven, the abode of all happiness, which is not intermingled with suffering and is not immediately swallowed up by it. (53)
And that happiness, brought about by longing, is the abode of the state of heaven;
he enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahmā.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Giving, the Time of Conception, the Formation of the Embryo, the Physical Sheaths, and the Unity with the Cosmic Egg," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The path to the city of Yama is eighty-six thousand yojanas in extent; for this reason, provisions for the journey are desired by all.
Even in Yamagrāma, food prepared by those born of their own lineage is accepted by them;
likewise for trees planted by someone, or reservoirs of water such as tanks and the like. || 2 ||
For by him who has prepared that path, they proceed with ease on the way to Yama;
he is not afflicted by frost or cold in the abode of Yama.
He who provides fuel attains happiness while performing his austerities;
those who perform sacrifices, festivals, and other rites become joyful there.
Satisfied, adorned, and endowed with perfumes and flowers, they go happily after the gift of land, fulfilled by all their desires. || 5 ||
By him who has given this earth, all of this— gold, land, pearls, and so forth, as well as garments, ornaments, and herds of cattle— has been given.
Whatever various condiments, foods, and edibles are offered according to the prescribed rite by sons to their father, that reaches him. || 7 ||
If one gives milk in an unbaked earthen vessel for three days, the deceased—
assuming a body of air— shall drink that milk while remaining in the sky.
Having completed the accumulation [of merit] on the fourth day, the touching of the Gaṅgā is prescribed;
however, during the first watch of the morning, one should offer the first handful of water.
One should cause a knot to be tied with two garments, one upper and one lower;
however, wearing only a single garment, one should offer a handful of sesame seeds together with darbha grass.
He should dwell in water for three days, and likewise in fire for three days;
he should dwell in the open air for three days, and one day in the presence of Vāsava.
Taking the form of wind, the wind indeed wanders; it enters even into a wall.
That *śrāddha* which is performed on the eleventh day is declared to be the general [or common] one.
Having performed the rites on the eleventh day, one should bathe again and become pure;
whoever performs them on the first day must complete them through the tenth day.
On the eleventh day after death, one should offer a rice-ball (piṇḍa) accompanied by mantras;
cooked food, sugar, cakes, and the like should be given to him.
A bed should be given as a gift; who will provide it afterwards?
A man remains a kinsman and a father only so long as he lives. (15)
Knowing this person to be a dead corpse, affection ceases in an instant;
for the self is indeed the friend of the self, and the self is also the enemy of the self.
Therefore, while alive, one should cause all of one's possessions to be given away with one's own hand.
For that reason, [one should provide] a wooden bedstead adorned with plaques of gold and other precious materials. (17)

It should be provided with a silk ball, a pillow, a mirror, and a hidden cord; it should be adorned with perfumes, garments, and excellent flowers, and accompanied by a fine fan and a nearby seat. || 18 ||
A covering cloth, the golden Lakṣmī seated upon Hari,
a vessel of ghee, betel leaf, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Saffron, a lamp, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, a vessel, sandals, seven kinds of grain, a water-pot, and a canopy.
In this way, by the gift of beds and other such things, the heavenly world becomes a giver of happiness;
for whatever was used by him in his house likewise [brought about this result].
Furthermore, whatever clothing, vessels, or ornaments may be attached to his body should be given; they shall remain present even in the abode of Indra and the realm of the Sun.

The woman who performs the rite for the nine ancestors, the sixteen-fold ancestral offering (śrāddha), the provision of a bed, and the annual memorial rites for her husband, shall attain prosperity in this world.
In the event of the death of a young woman, items such as her jewelry and other belongings should be given;
a bed, gems, garments, and so forth should be presented to the preceptor.
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many;
rather, they should be given to only one—the teacher alone. (25)
Whatever merit is gained during Vyatīpāta, as well as on the full moon day of Kārttika, at the solstices, on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses; || 26 ||
Whatever [merit] is found at Prayāga, Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, and Arbuda;
at the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean— || 17 ||
Through acts such as the gift of a bed, one shall obtain their respective fruits;
wherever that living being is born, there indeed he enjoys that fruit.
Upon the exhaustion of [his] karma, he is born on earth as a human being endowed with auspicious marks;
he is very wealthy, a knower of dharma, and an expert in all the scriptures. || 29 ||
Worthy of offerings to the gods and ancestors, he rejoices together with the Pitṛs,
having ascended a divine celestial chariot and being surrounded by Apsarases.
Highly honored by the gods, he goes to Vaikuṇṭha after death;
the father, satisfied by the Śrāddha, bestows sons who increase the lineage. (31)
Likewise, the grandfather (pitāmaha) who gave the gift of cattle is satisfied;
likewise, the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) who gave gold is satisfied.
The great-grandfather, being deceased, should offer abundant food;
however, one whose lineage has no further descendants should perform the Nārāyaṇabali.
He is liberated from all sins and is certainly freed from hell;
this applies to the five [nakṣatras] beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā and ending with Revatī.
In this case of the Pañcaka [death], cremation is not prescribed at all for one who has died;
instead, effigies are thrown near the corpse. (35)
Then, four effigies made of darbha grass, consecrated with the Ṛkṣa mantras, should be prepared; with these effigies, the cremation is to be performed.
That man who dies among the Pañcaka [asterisms] does not attain a [favorable] destination;
water is not offered there, for it shall always be inauspicious.
If one's own kinsmen are afflicted by suffering, the worldly journey [of funeral rites] must not be neglected;
after the five days have passed, everything must be performed according to the prescribed rules.
Otherwise, there would be grief for his sons and kinsmen;
indeed, there would be loss in his household if he were to die during the Pañcaka period.
Then, at the end of the period of impurity, the son should perform the most excellent rite for pacification;
he should offer sesame seeds, cows, gold, and clarified butter dedicated to him.
Food, sandals, an umbrella, a golden seal, two garments, and a sacrificial fee are also given, which destroy the sins of the deceased. ||41||
In a śrāddha for the pretas, one should avoid these eighteen items:
blessings, double-folded darbha grass, the word "svasti," and likewise the syllable Om. (42)

The fire-offering (agnīkaraṇa), the food remnants, the Vaiśvadeva portion of the Śrāddha, the scattering of grains, the utterance of "svadhā," the word "pitṛ" (father/ancestor), and the formal recitation—these [are the elements]. 43.
The invocation, the firebrand, the circumambulation as far as the boundary, the dismissal, the sesame oblation, and the full oblation—these are the ten and eight [rites]. 44.
While a deceased person remains within the village, one should avoid betel, tooth-sticks, eating, sexual intercourse, and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa). 45.
If anyone indeed meets death after practicing fasting,
having cast off the human body, he attains equality with Hari.
Therefore, fasting for men bestows the state of Vaikuṇṭha;
with a body remaining in its natural state, it is the very means of accomplishing liberation.
One who observes the vow of fasting shall dwell in the assembly of sages,
or among the Vairāja gods, or among the Īśas, or even in liberation.
Brahmā and the other gods are pleased with him; there are no torments of Yama for him.
In a human body, there are three hundred and sixty bones. (49)
Nourished by the water-jar, the water-pitcher is offered;
and upon a well-smeared portion of ground, cooked food is also offered.
In this manner, one should always act with the contemplation of Brahman;
for Nārāyaṇa himself, when remembered, grants liberation to such a person.

Before death, at the time of death, during the funeral procession, at the cremation of the corpse, and at the śrāddha ceremony—in all these instances, one should repeatedly utter the names Śrī Hari and Nārāyaṇa. (52)

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Miscellaneous Gifts, the Gift of a Bed, and Other Fivefold Gifts; the Post-mortem Rites, the Death of One Who Practices Fasting, and the Subsequent Destiny," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Śvetavyāsa said: Thus, O Suśikha, by the worship of Hari and the chanting of His names,
even King Hāṭakāṅga became one who delights in the essence of the sacred narratives.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I have indeed described much in this context; yet I shall speak even more for your benefit.
While still living, a person should take recourse to the path of liberation;
for I have prepared here very many means that bestow liberation. (3)
Liberation comes from knowledge; liberation from the destruction of karma; liberation through the force of dispassion;
liberation from sacred pilgrimage sites; liberation from the company of the virtuous; and liberation from dharma by taking refuge in a guru.
Liberation comes from desireless action; liberation comes from the path of renunciation.
Liberation comes from taking refuge in the virtuous dharma; liberation comes from relinquishment and service.
Liberation comes from the realization of one's own lack of agency, and even from congregational chanting.
Liberation comes through service to one's parents; liberation comes through service to one's husband;
liberation comes from the realization that Brahman is the Self of all; and liberation comes from the total surrender of everything.
Liberation comes from performing service for others, from bestowing happiness upon others,
from giving what is requested by others, and from bringing satisfaction to one's own self.
Liberation comes from the destruction of latent impressions; liberation comes from stainless awakening.
Even while all actions are being performed, the Self remains untainted; it is indeed liberated.
Free from the notions of "I" and "mine," likewise free from cold and heat, and devoid of the qualities of Brahma and Sattva—one is certainly liberated; of this there is no doubt.

Having abandoned the manifestation of being, consciousness, and bliss for that which is false, inert, and afflicted, he indeed considers himself bound; he who does not so consider himself is liberated.
The holy bathing-places of the Lord, the cities fashioned by Hari,
the rivers, the mountains, the sacred forests, and the temples— || 11 ||
The Śālagrāma stone, the Devaśilā, and the Bāṇa stones are divine forms;
so too are the Tulasī, sandalwood, Plakṣa, Dhātrī, Bimba, and Vaṭa trees.
Through planting, protecting, watering, bowing, touching, and chanting [their names], and by performing acts of creation and deliverance, they indeed destroy sins and bestow liberation. (13)

He who bathes in the mental sacred ford, which is a lake of knowledge with truth for its water and which removes the impurities of passion and hatred, shall attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
The Divine dwells everywhere if there is a pure disposition;
the Divine dwells nowhere if atheism shines forth.
Every morning, fishermen behold the Gaṅgā and other rivers;
everyone beholds the sun, yet one devoid of devotion does not partake in liberation.
By sacrificing one's life for the sake of one's father, mother, virtuous men, virtuous women, teachers, cows, gods, or the Dharma,
an individual shall certainly attain liberation.
Life through charity and enjoyment, and death on the battlefield or at a sacred pilgrimage site—these will certainly grant liberation, provided they are performed with dedication to the Divine. (18)
Death occurring in a field of merit, at a sacred ford, in the refuge of holy people, in a state of merit, or on an auspicious lunar day, shall grant liberation.
The giver of a daughter in marriage, the giver of the earth, and he who is the giver of fearlessness;
the builder of temples for the gods and the donor of dwellings—such a person partakes in liberation.
One who undertakes the restoration of dilapidated step-wells, wells, tanks, groves, gardens, and religious edifices becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
By giving a house equipped with all necessary articles, a cow together with its calf,
and a maiden endowed with all virtues, one indeed attains liberation.
If a virtuous and devoted wife, upon seeing her husband dead, produces fire from her own thumb and departs together with her husband, [she attains the highest state]. (23)
For thirty-five million years, he is honored in heaven.
If a devoted woman leads her husband to his abode, [she attains that supreme state]. ||24||
If her husband should be a perpetrator of great sins or a doer of evil deeds,
a woman who remains devoted to him destroys all her own transgressions.
He who is a constant giver of food, who always bestows knowledge, and who grants the eternal bliss of the Self—he indeed attains liberation. ||26||
He who bestows the gift of knowledge, he who performs the giving away of a daughter in marriage,
and he who provides the means of livelihood— verily, such a person shall attain liberation.
Through well-performed deeds one attains heaven; heaven is considered the ground for liberation.
Therefore, by abandoning trivial actions, one shall constantly partake in liberation. (28)
One should give gifts to the poor, and a daughter to one who has no lineage; one should provide righteous livelihood to the helpless, and one's own cherished objects to the virtuous. (29)
Meditation should be given to the guru; knowledge should be given to a worthy recipient seeking liberation;
wisdom should be given to a disciple of sattvic nature; and devotion should be given to one whose inner self is pure.

The net of delusion should be given to Māyā, one's entire being to the Supreme Self (Paramātman), liberation to one's own self (Svātman), and one's own self should be offered to the Supreme Self (Parātman). 2.1.
In this way, one attains liberation, and the donor shall obtain the fruit of his gift.
Therefore, everything should be given away, for it yields a result exceeding that of ten million sacrifices.
He who is the giver of all gifts and is a protector of nothing within himself should be understood as one liberated from objects; he is regarded as eternally liberated. ||33||
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the duty of a woman: what kind of gift is considered appropriate? Her maidenhood and virginity should be offered to her mother for the sake of the marriage fire. (34)
The body should be given to the Lord, the sense of "I" and "mine" to one's son,
beauty to old age, and the latent impressions (vāsanā) to death.
Affection for one's offspring and the binding of the bride and her maternal relatives;
the contemplation (bhāvanā) should be offered to Brahmā, and devotion (bhakti) should be offered to the Inner Self (antarātman). 36.
Liberation must be given to one's own self, and one's own self must be given to the Supreme Self;
thus, indeed, the gift of all one's possessions (sarvasvadāna) must be performed by those who desire liberation. ||37||
Without exchange, an object of priceless value is never obtained;
by means of the price of giving away all one's possessions, one may attain liberation, which is beyond price. ||38||
The self, however, is eternally pure; no further purification remains for it.
How could there be impurity for that which is pure, even by means of the impure body? (39)
Indeed, there is no vessel that is inherently impure; rather, it is the attached substance that causes impurity.
By removing the attached substance and such, the vessel is indeed pure.
The hand is indeed not impure; rather, it is the dirt that is called impurity. Because of the removal of dirt, the hand is considered to be pure. ||41||
If both the vessel and the hand are impure when joined together, then the vessel must be destroyed and the hand likewise cut off. ||42||
But they do not act in this way; rather, they expel impurity.
Thus the Self is always pure, considered to be like gold, fire, and space. (43)
Therefore, the impurities of passion and hatred should be removed by the fire of the intellect, through devotion, service, love, affection, endearment, and sincere disposition. (44)
The impurities are to be meditated upon and then destroyed; he is indeed the stainless Brahman.
Having himself become the form of Brahman, one should always worship the Supreme Brahman. 45.
Having attained the strength of Nārāyaṇa, one shall reach Nārāyaṇa himself;
for such a person, no further offering to Nārāyaṇa remains to be performed.
For one who lacks the strength of Nārāyaṇa, the Nārāyaṇa-bali must be performed for the sake of liberation; I shall describe its procedure to you. (47)

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Means for Liberation, the Gifts Given Without Desire that Grant Liberation, and the Offerings such as the Purification of One’s Own Self," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Out of affection for you, my dear, this knowledge that destroys worldly existence has been declared;
now I shall describe the Nārāyaṇa-bali for the sake of benefiting the world.
This rite is for the purpose of rescuing those who have perished through accidents and the like;
it should be performed at an auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha), in an auspicious field (kṣetra), or in a pure temple of the deity. || 2 ||
On the bank of a river, at the foot of a sacred tree, one should perform an offering to Nārāyaṇa,
dedicated to Viṣṇu, with mantras from the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
Facing the south, one should meditate upon the deceased as Viṣṇu, saying:
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, be the bringer of liberation to the deceased. (4)
The libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed in full, as well as the eleven śrāddhas;
one should offer water, rice, barley, wheat, and millet.
Food fit for oblation, auspicious hand-gestures (mudrās), an umbrella, a turban, and a garment;
milk, honey, grains, as well as clothing and sandals. || 6 ||
When the rice-balls are placed upon the ground, the libation (tarpaṇa) should then be offered with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth,
either into a conch or into a copper vessel.
First, having knelt upon the ground with his knees,
he should offer water for the sake of the deity and separately for each individual intended for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
"O divine waters, full of sweetness, you are prepared within this ball of food;
you are taken with a support—thus one should offer it at the second [offering]. (9)
O gods, go to the fourth ocean, and to the fifth.
"Agnir jyotiḥ" is on the sixth day; "ayāścāgne" on the seventh; "yamāya tvā" is to be known for the eighth; and likewise "yaj jāgrat" for the ninth.
Then, at the tenth [verse] with "phalinī," and at the eleventh with the piṇḍa,
one should perform the dismissal of the piṇḍas with the hymns beginning with "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ."
Having performed the Śrāddha for eleven deities, one should perform it on the following day;
one should invite the Brahmins, offer the Arghya water, and cause the gods to be present.
One should fashion Viṣṇu, who embodies everything, from copper; Rudra from iron; Yama from silver;
and Brahmā as a corpse from lead or from darbha grass.
Then, with the mantra beginning "āyātu," he should place the Sāmavedin [on the east],
and with the mantra "agne āyāhi," he should place Govinda on the west.
With the mantra beginning "Agnim īle," one should place Prajāpati in the eastern direction;
with the mantra beginning "Iṣe tvā," one should establish Yama in the south.
In the center of that mandala, a man made of darbha grass should be placed;
[representing] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Yama, and the deceased as the fifth.
Indeed, they should be placed individually in separate jars containing the five jewels;
likewise, garments, sacred threads, and ritual hand-gestures (mudrās) should each be placed separately.
There, one should indeed perform the recitation (japa) separately for the deities beginning with Brahmā;
one should then perform the five śrāddhas for the deities according to the prescribed rule.
Then one should offer a stream of water separately for each funeral cake (piṇḍa),
either in a conch shell, a copper vessel, or, if these are unavailable, even in an earthenware one.
Taking water with sesame seeds mixed with all medicinal herbs,
[he should offer] a seat, a seal-ring, an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot.
A vessel, grain fit for consumption, garments, and the eightfold position;
a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, together with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||22||
One should indeed give it there according to the prescribed rite to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa;
one should give land with its crops to a learned Brāhmaṇa who is a knower of the Ṛgveda.
One should give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Yajurveda, and one should give fine garments and a water-strainer to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Sāmaveda. (24)
One should offer sesame seeds and iron as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) dedicated to Yama;
then, an effigy (puttalaka) should be fashioned, provided with all medicinal herbs.
Having divided a portion of the stalks of the palāśa tree there,
he should spread out a black antelope skin and, with kuśa grass, fashion the form of a man.
The collection of bones is said to consist of three hundred and sixty joints;
having arranged them, one should bind them to the respective limbs with kuśa grass.
One should place forty [syllables] on the head and ten on the neck;
twenty are to be placed on the chest, and likewise twenty on the abdomen. (28)
One should give one hundred [blows] on both arms, twenty on the waist,
one hundred on both thighs, and thirty on both shanks.
One should assign four [bones] to the penis, six to the pair of testicles, and ten to the parts of the toes; in this manner, one should arrange the bones.
One should place a coconut at the location of the head and silver on the palate;
one should place the five jewels in the mouth and a plantain fruit on the tongue.
One should apply sand to the intestines and bāhlīka to the nose;
one should apply clay to the fat and likewise cow’s urine to the urine.
One should give sulphur for the bone-element, yellow orpiment and realgar for the flesh, and likewise barley-flour for the flesh, honey for the blood, and [the same] for the blood itself. (33)
He placed a mass of matted hair in the place of the head-hair, a deer-skin on the skin,
mercury in the place of semen, and gallstone in the excrement.
Likewise, he should apply red arsenic (manaḥśilā) to his body, sesame paste to his joints,
tāḍapatra leaves to his ears, and guñjā berries to his breasts.
One should offer a hundred-petaled lotus at the nose and a lotus at the navel-circle; one should place an eggplant on the testicles, and a wholesome leek on the penis.
One should indeed apply ghee to the navel, while tin is prescribed for the loincloth;
pearls are for the breasts, and an ointment of saffron is for the head.
With incense of camphor and agallochum, and with auspicious, fragrant garlands, one should place a silk thread around [the image's] waist and a piece of gold upon its heart. (38)

One should offer two golden ornaments for the hands representing supernatural power and prosperity, a cowrie shell for the eyes, vermilion at the corners of the eyes, and offerings such as betel nut. (39)
Having performed the worship of the *preta* as prescribed, accompanied by all medicinal herbs,
one should also offer the sacrificial vessels according to the ritual rules involving the sacred fire.
Having performed the purification of the deceased with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone, reciting the mantras "śanno devīḥ punantu mā," "imaṃ me varuṇa," and so forth; ||41||
Dedicated to Viṣṇu, one should give the gift of a cow— a great gift— as well as sesame seeds,
and one should present the Vaitaraṇī river adorned with all ornaments.
One should personally perform a Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha for the sake of the liberation of the deceased;
thereafter, one should effect the release of the deceased and meditate upon Hari there.
Having recollected, "You are Viṣṇu," one should likewise cremate the deceased in the fire.
Impurity (sūtaka) shall be observed for three days; however, for ten days, the offerings of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) must be maintained.
Indeed, everything should be performed for up to a year for the sake of the liberation of the deceased;
and the gift of gold, land, and a cow should be made for the attainment of final release. ||45||
A gift given at the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) bestows heaven for seven kalpas;
however, the gift of one's entire possessions to Hari results in infinite liberation.
The Vaitaraṇī river is twofold; one indeed flows along the path of Yama.
It is a hundred yojanas wide, but it is crossed by the gift of a cow.
Another latent impression, the Vaitaraṇī river itself, resides directly within the heart;
it is a hundred thousand yojanas long, and it is crossed only through knowledge and devotion. 48.

Therein, the first is foul-smelling and the second possesses the scent of existence (*bhāva*). The first has blood and pus-water as its current, while the other has the waters of passion and hatred; the first is filled with the mud of flesh, and the other with the mud of the [impure] elements (*dhātu*).
Filled with diamond-beaked porpoises, crocodiles, and diamond-cutters;
with saws, thorny plants, and living beings—such is that supreme realm of sense-objects where sinful mortals fall, wailing aloud. (1.77.50–51)
The gift of a milch cow saves one from pus and blood;
the gift of Hari, which produces nectar, saves one from the river of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The vital breaths should be understood as guests; they will not go along with the self.
They will dissolve right here; therefore, worship Hari, the giver of life. 53.
Sleep is death with breath; death is death without breath.
There is no trust at all in either for the sake of the soul's continued life.
One should strive today for the sake of liberation, before death occurs.
Death, having attained its synonym as liberation, has no other designation.
Who is the husband, or whose is the wife? Who is the son, or whose is the father?
These attachments arising from debts and worldly ties are what provide the river Vaitaraṇī.
Whatever effort one exerts after forming the notion "this is mine," all that effort-made thing remains far away once it is abandoned.
They do not leap with one who leaps; they do not honor him who honors them; they do not feel affection for one who feels affection. And yet, the ignorant person does not see this.
But people who are dry in their purpose praise one who possesses virtues, saying "Bravo! Bravo!
Having merely accomplished their own selfish ends, these harsh men depart far away; one should not follow after them. (59)
One should abandon everything else and always rely upon that friend who is meaningful in the beginning, likewise in the middle, and who possesses meaning even at the end. (1.77.60)
Whatever else remains to be done so that nothing whatsoever is left undone—that duty has all been performed; thus the friend will be liberated.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Nārāyaṇa Bali Rite," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. ||77||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"I have heard of the various destinies attained through karma, as well as the liberation of the deceased and the giving of gifts as proclaimed by the Lord. (1)
In this context, the world of Yama was also enlightened by the King of the Gods;
O Mādhava, I also wish to hear the story of Dhanvantari.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In former times, during the Satya and Tretā Yugas, everything was produced through the perfection of one's resolve; indeed, everything was obtained exactly as desired whenever one wished for it.
There was no incompleteness whatsoever in any object;
there was always contentment, always satisfaction, and the fruit of desire was ever-present.
Then the five elements transform according to his will;
whatever a person desires from those elements, he obtains it immediately.
When the Dvāpara age arrived, all the worlds became joyful, well-nourished, free from disease, and content in their own souls; thus did that transformation occur.
At that time, the power of the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) had somewhat perished,
and the efficacy of the thought-gems (cintāmaṇis) had reached a state where it was about to be destroyed.
When the sovereignty over the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) occasionally met with decline,
people then established their own ownership over the fields and forests.

In the hearts of people there arose thoughts concerning the acquisition of food and other necessities; through the distinction between "one's own" and "another's," there emerged anxieties, sorrows, desires, and mental afflictions. (9)
The lineages of unrighteousness quickly took up residence within the hearts of people;
meanwhile, the people, agitated by anxiety and other such states, began to wither away from their bodies.
At that time, indeed, there arose a need for strength-bestowing medicines in order to remove their pain and weakness. (11)
Indeed, at that time, there was an abundance of food for people, consisting of edible herbs, grains, fruits, and roots, as well as the successful cultivation of crops.
An expectation arose for the sake of the world's subsistence regarding the plants that sprout from the earth:
"What indeed is the medicinal herb consisting of edible fruits, grains, or leaves? (13)
"How is she to be well-nourished, and how is she to be employed for enjoyment?"—at that time, O Unborn One, there was no one who possessed such penetrating knowledge. || 14 ||
He again remembered his preceptor, Nārāyaṇa;
then the Lord, the all-pervading one who consists of all knowledge, arrived there.
He holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; he wears golden earrings, a golden crown, and is resplendent with a golden garland and the Kaustubha gem.
With a gentle smile and a radiant luster pervading his entire countenance,
he wore yellow garments and possessed a fame immediately extolled by the science of Ayurveda.
For he is filled with all flavors, honored as far as the Ocean of Milk,
and worshipped with the juices of vegetables by all the Guṇḍrās who bow down before him.
He is praised for his divine medicinal creepers, trees, grasses, roots, and so forth;
he has a bright face, a green complexion, and red lotus-like feet and hands.
Yoking himself with auspicious blessings, the compassionate Lord said to the Creator of the Universe:
"O Brahmā, how is it that I have been reminded by you in this Dvāpara age?"
Brahmā said: Then [I spoke] to the omnipresent God, the best of physicians:
"O Lord of Gods, I bow to You; I worship Your pair of lotus feet. 2.1.
Homage indeed to the one whose nature is that of an atom; homage, repeated homage, to the dyad.
Salutations to the triad; salutations again and again to the tetrad. ||22||
Salutations to you who take the form of the five subtle elements; salutations to you whose form is dust.
Salutations to you whose nature is fine particles; salutations to you whose essence is grit.
Salutations to you who have the nature of the pressing-stone; salutations to you, the crusher of the soma-juice globules.
Salutations to the seed enriched by the globules; salutations to the self that is the unmanifest sprout. 24.

Salutations to you whose nature is the leaf; salutations to you who take the form of the stalk and so forth; salutations to you who are the branches and twigs; salutations to you, the cause of the trunk and other parts. ||5||

Homage to the stalk and the flower; homage to that which is the essence of the juice and the fruit; homage to that which is the nature of the grain-particles; homage to that which is the essence of the ground flour and the liquid. ||26||
Homage to you who possess a form not born of cooking, and homage to you whose form is cooked;
homage to you whose forms consist of what is chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk. || 27 ||

Homage to the one whose nature is mixed; homage to the one in the form of medicinal herbs; homage to the one in the form of decoctions and the like; homage to the one in the form of powders and the like. ||28||
Salutations to you who are the measure of exhalation; salutations to the knower of ashes and other such things;
salutations to the bestower of life; salutations to the power of medicinal herbs.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Lord, for the sake of security, well-being, and renown; salutations to the enjoyer, the bestower of objects of enjoyment, and the inner controller of all. 1.78.30
O God of gods, you are the creator, the nourisher, and the protector of all bodies; yet in this age, the attainment of creative power by embodied beings comes to an end.
What is merely imagined does not arrive, does not present itself, and is not seen;
therefore, [one should offer] grain, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, which serve as the means for the ritual performance.
The grain, the root, as well as the stalk, grass, the crop, and that which holds milk—
sweet with the six flavors and unctuous— is indeed wholesome for all embodied beings.
Having sought out, purified, and blended great medicinal herbs,
you ought to provide food and medicine in order to awaken the worlds.
There is no one other than you who can awaken this emerging class of beings;
nor would there be anyone who, even if possessing knowledge, could be considered all-knowing in every respect. (35)
For him whose austerity consists of knowledge and who discerns cause and effect, everything— whether it be food to be eaten or drink to be drunk— is an elixir.
Whatever may be licked, massaged, smelled, or tasted, whatever may grant peace, and whatever may be savored without fail—you ought to perform all of that. (37)

Whatever is to be heated, whatever is to be boiled, whatever is to be parched, whatever is to be ground into powder, whatever is to be mixed, and whatever is of an essential nature—you ought to perform all that. ||38||
Thus entreated, Viṣṇu constructed his own hut upon the peak of Mount Meru, and the Lord made his residence therein.
Then, having performed the ritual invocation, the crops and medicinal herbs were offered to the celestial rishis, the sages, the ancestors, and likewise to the descendants of Manu and others.
Eagerly, those furrows took the form of crops and caused them to flourish;
from them, various kinds of food were produced in diverse regions. (41)
Those [plants] became the means of livelihood for agriculture, and numerous gardens were established;
nevertheless, by means of those forest herbs, this [sustenance] for living beings was still provided. ||42||
For the sake of attaining strength, the Blessed One indeed composed the Āyurveda; likewise, such medical applications were extensively formulated by Dhanvantari.
And on Mount Meru, halls for elixirs and other sciences were established with great renown,
wherein no medicinal knowledge pertaining to the three periods of time remained unknown.
"In this [age], there shall be no need for the mixing of medicinal herbs.
Thus did Hari speak in the first Caturyuga. 45.
He is himself the divine Dhanvantari, the Lord and protector of the universe;
yet, having entered the Kali age, the worlds have become exceedingly miserable. (46)
At that time, the Blessed One indeed desired to descend in person;
he appeared as Dhanvantari in a second form.
Born into a lineage of physicians, he became an eminent doctor in Kāśī;
listen now to that story, O Lakṣmī, in which family he was born. (48)

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Manifestation of the Primordial Dhanvantari of the Satya Yuga," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The sage Atri, the mind-born son of Brahmā, world-renowned,
performed difficult austerities with his arms raised high like a piece of wood.
Indeed, three thousand divine years passed as water consisting of the splendor of his asceticism flowed from his unblinking eyes.
Illuminating the ten directions with its beautiful milk-like luster, it flowed forth;
then, by the command of Vidhi, the ten directions received that embryo consisting of water.
Even though they poured it out, they were unable to sustain it;
therefore, that water became solidified into white-colored, cool, and beautiful snowballs.
Having indeed picked up that [discus] which had fallen upon the earth, the Lotus-born One placed it upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The sons of Brahmā— Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, and Vasiṣṭha, who were his mind-born offspring— offered praise.
Through the Ṛg verses, the Yajus formulas, the many Atharva-Āṅgirasa hymns,
and likewise through [other means], the splendor of Soma increased as he grew.
Moistening the three worlds and bestowing nourishment everywhere,
that white and cool radiance descended upon the earth.
Those herbs arose and attained nourishment through his splendor;
even Brahmā fashioned an auspicious chariot yoked with a thousand horses.
When he uttered, "He is indeed offered to Soma," the god became thus the nourisher of the world for all embodied beings.
Candra again performed penance for one hundred million lotuses;
indeed, the golden-hued Lakṣmīs sustain the world by their own power.
The all-pervading Soma bore them by his own splendor;
then Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, bestowed the kingdom upon him.
In all seeds, medicinal herbs, waters, brahmins, and nights—having obtained that great sovereignty, Soma, the lord of those who possess the Soma, [shone]. 13.
He performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, in which hundreds of thousands were given as sacrificial fees;
Hiraṇyagarbha was the Udgātṛ priest, and Brahmā attained the office of Brahman.
The Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa himself was present there as a member of the assembly,
surrounded by the primordial brahmin-sages headed by Sanatkumāra.
May Soma indeed bestow the three worlds upon the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in every way;
may Sinī, Kuhū, Vapu, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, and Vasu likewise [bestow them].
Fame, Splendor, and Fortune—these nine goddesses attended upon him;
having performed the final purificatory bath, he remained unperturbed, honored by all the gods and sages.
That supreme king of kings, having attained sovereign power, became arrogant and,
out of lust, abducted Bṛhaspati’s wife named Tārā.
Although he was entreated again by the gods and the celestial sages,
he did not at all release Tārā to Bṛhaspati.
Out of hatred for Bṛhaspati, Śukra seized the lunar disc belonging to the Asuras;
while Hara, surrounded by hosts of all beings, took the son of his preceptor out of affection.
Endowed with all divine qualities, Mahendra followed his preceptor;
by that means, Rudra also took up his own bow, Ājagava.
The destruction of the gods and asuras occurred, and a great slaughter of all took place;
and then, by fate, the Tuṣitas indeed appeared.
They went for refuge to Brahmā, the primordial god and grandfather;
then, having restrained Uśanas, Rudra, and the eldest Śaṅkara.
The Grandfather himself gave Tārā to Bṛhaspati;
and seeing that Tārā was pregnant, Bṛhaspati spoke to her.
Tārā cast this embryo of the moon outside;
she did not, however, release that boy, the greatest slayer of enemies.
Then Bṛhaspati himself performed the extraction of the fetus;
as soon as he was born, he possessed consciousness and was even more radiant than the gods. ||26||
He shone, possessing beauty like that of the supreme god of all gods;
seeing him, Bṛhaspati was filled with longing for his own new son.
"This one is mine," [Bṛhaspati] seized him; the son said, "I am not yours!
I am the son of the Moon; do not touch me, O Bṛhaspati! (28)
At that time, Brahmā entrusted his son to Soma;
the Moon-god gave the name Budha to that son. (29)
To Budha, by his wife Ilā, was born a son named Purūravas;
[the gods bestowed upon him] his beauty, virtues, generosity, character, splendor, and prowess. (1.79.30)
Having heard the great virtues being sung by Nārada in the abode of Indra, Urvaśī set her mind upon beholding Purūravas.
Mitra and Varuṇa were there as singers along with her;
however, Urvaśī’s mind was entirely attached to the human world.
Having learned this, Mitra and Varuṇa spoke to their beloved Urvaśī:
"O goddess, having abandoned us for the human world, your mind wanders toward wantonness. (33)
"Therefore, go down from that heaven and become united with a mortal man.
Thus, by the curse, Urvaśī immediately descended from heaven.
On the ground, she searched for Purūravas alone;
in the grove, she sang with a lute as sweet as the song of a cuckoo.
Then, seeing such a beautiful Urvaśī there, King Purūravas said to her, "Become my wife. (36)
She too was filled with desire there, and then she replied to him:
"Let it be so, O Great King, if you [will grant] my condition. (37)
"If you will do so, I shall dwell with you," said the king; "I shall do it," replied Urvashi. She then said, "These two rams are considered by me to be my sons. (38)
"As long as you protect me, O King, so long shall I dwell in your house;
you shall not be seen naked by me, O King, except at a moment [of your own] desire. (39)
"As long as you do not give me leavings, I shall dwell near you;
I will eat only ghee and I shall take delight with you."
Saying "So be it," the king accepted that excellent hand;
having placed her upon a celestial chariot, he [departed] from Himālaya toward Alakā.
In the Caitraratha forest on earth, in rivers and lakes, in the atmosphere, on Mount Meru, and even in the Mānasa lake. ||42||
On Mount Raivata, in the groves of lotuses and in the groves of kunda flowers, as well as on the banks of the Sarasvatī, he took delight, his passion further increased. (43)
For sixty-one years he delighted her as she took her pleasure;
she too, forgetting heaven, was filled with longing for him alone.
He did not consider even the delightful world of the gods to be pleasant without her.
Then, the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu, distressed by her absence, [lamented]. (45)
He went from the heavenly world to the earthly realm in an instant to bring her back;
for he had previously made a verbal agreement with King Purūravas regarding Urvaśī.
Having learned this, he joined with the Gandharvas and, in the middle of the night,
swiftly snatched away Urvashi’s lute from the vicinity of her bed.
"By whom was Urvashi's garment seized? Let this man be abandoned! When Pururavas heard that, he reflected while indeed naked. 48.
Thinking, "Let not the goddess behold me naked," he did not depart at that time;
instead, he carried off another ram, and Urvaśī then lamented.
"Alas! While I am helpless, my two young children are being seized by thieves.
I have no protector at all; to what man shall I go for refuge? (1.79.50)
Hearing those words, the king, overcome by indignation,
took up his sword and, though unclothed and naked, rushed toward him through the darkness.
"Who is this wicked one who carries off my ram? Whither do you go? Stay firm!
Stop, for taking my beloved ram, you shall not live! (52)
At that moment, a flash of lightning, intensely produced by the friction of the wind, appeared;
by its light, the goddess then beheld the king stripped of his garments.
Seeing that the time had come to an end, she departed from his house;
and Citraratha, the Gandharva, also went forth after releasing the two rams.
Taking the two rams with him, the king returned to his own bedchamber;
not seeing Urvaśī there, he wandered upon the ground like one mad.
Searching for Urvaśī on the earth, he reached Kurukṣetra, where there was a beautiful lake surrounded on all sides by lotuses. (56)
Seeing her sporting with four celestial nymphs, he said: "O wife, where have you come here, having indeed left me behind for the sake of bathing?"
"Come to my house, enter it, and take delight with me;
I could not live at all without you, my beloved—why have you come here? (28)
To him who was speaking thus, Urvaśī spoke the truth:
"O dear one, this assembly of kings is not for you to grasp with such persistence. (99)
"Because of you, I am pregnant and I take no pleasure at all;
may you come here within a year for the sake of obtaining a son."
"I shall indeed dwell with you for one night after the birth of my son.
Having been addressed thus, the king departed for his capital, lost in thought.
Urvaśī described her husband, the lord of the earth, who possessed excellent virtues:
"I have dwelt for a long time with this king, under the sway of desire. (62)
Upon hearing that, the friends of Urvaśī exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
and they all said, "We too shall take our pleasure with this king. (63)
Then, in that year, the king also went to the vicinity of the lake;
seeing Urvaśī together with her son, he experienced great joy.
She gave him that excellent son named Āyuṣ, so that she might spend that single night with him according to her desire. Indeed, she spent that night together with him.
She bore a fetus that would grant five sons, and she spoke to him again:
"O King, accept from the Gandharvas the boons that reside in your mind. (66)
Then, having seen the Gandharvas there as well, the king said to them:
"I possess a full treasury and have conquered the circle of my enemies. (67)
"I always choose to spend my time living with Urvaśī.
Having heard this, which would lead her to ascend to heaven, the Gandharvas [acted]. 68.
They gave the fire-vessel and the woman to the king and then said to the monarch:
"Dividing the fire into three parts, you should perform the sacrifice together with her."
By that act, you shall attain the world of Urvaśī; of this there is no doubt.
Then, taking the fire-vessel, the king [dwelt] in that forest with her.
Agni took his pleasure fully with a woman who was a cooking-pot, his mind being completely satisfied.
Then, the vessel that was in front of the woman took on the form of a cooking-pot. (71)
Realizing that it was in vain, the king indeed threw that vessel into the forest;
at that moment, the woman, glowing like fire, quickly vanished from sight.
And due to that insult, the bowl also became invisible;
the king, having fallen into despair, returned to his own palace. ||73||
But, driven by the force of passion, he thought repeatedly:
"Alas! A woman has gone; I have cast my vessel away in the forest. (74)
"Indeed, this vessel was entrusted to me by a Gandharva for the purpose of reaching the world of Urvaśī; I shall retrieve it. Having reflected thus, he went to the forest. (751)
Having gone there, he repeatedly performed acts of propitiation toward the fire-pot and the vessel;
meanwhile, that fire-pot rose up from that place in the form of a tree.
The fire was in the form of a woman made of *śamī* wood, and the vessel was a pot made of *pippala* wood;
having taken both the *śamī* and the *pippala*, the king returned home. (77)
Having gained their confidence, he thought: "These two are the bestowers of the boon of Urvaśī;
otherwise, these two might become women and cooking pots once again. (78)
Having deliberated thus in his palace, the king produced both together by friction;
he made the *śamī* wood the lower fire-drill (*araṇī*) and the *pippala* wood the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇī*).
From the friction of two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) measuring as many finger-breadths as there are syllables in the *gāyatrī* meter, that very triad of fires was produced. (1.79.80)
The king offered oblations into the three sacred fires in the sacrifice for the sake of obtaining Urvaśī;
Agni was pleased with the sacrifices and brought a celestial chariot from heaven.
By means of that very celestial vehicle, through the power of the merit of his sacrifice,
the king reached the world of Urvaśī and rejoiced with her.
Then, in the assembly hall of Indra, the king beheld a dance performed by celestial nymphs,
wherein Urvaśī danced repeatedly.
Then Urvaśī, filled with pride in her skill at dance and dramatic gesture, laughed at Purūravas in his presence and rejoiced exceedingly. (84)
The king attained a state of joy and laughed before his own [wife];
but Tumburu, the master of dance, having observed them both, indeed became enraged. (85)
In an assembly of countless gods, dancing is indeed a useless laughingstock;
therefore, let there be a swift separation between you two. (86)
Thus cursed, the two of them then went for refuge to Indra;
Indra, having shown compassion, spoke [to them] on Mount Gandhamādana on earth.
"Go to the mountain and bathe well at the sacred ford named Sādhyāmṛta; by that, your release from the curse will come to pass. (88)
"Your yoga shall always be perfectly accomplished. Having spoken thus to us both, those two then departed for heaven, traveling in their celestial chariots.
To them were born five sons of great strength;
Āyu was the eldest of all, and thus there were six excellent sons together.
In the world of the Gandharvas, there were known as Āyus, Dhīmat, Amāvasu, Viśvāyu, Śatāyu, and Gatāyu—the sons of Urvaśī. ||9.1||
They established their kingdoms at Prayāga and at Pratiṣṭhāna on the auspicious ground;
among them was the blessed Dhanvantari, whom I shall now describe. 92.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Lineage of Atri in the Kṛta Yuga of the First Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the birth of Soma from Atri, the birth of Budha from Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, the birth of Purūravas from him, and his six sons by the Apsaras Urvaśī, and so forth. ||79||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Āyu was the son of Purūravas, and he had five sons. Among them, the first was Nahuṣa, and the second was Kṣatravṛddha.
Raja was the third there, while the fourth was named Raṃbha;
the fifth was indeed Anena, and they were all equal to their father in prowess.
Kṣatravṛddha had one son named Suta;
Suta’s heirs were three sons who were supremely righteous.
Kāśya, Kuśa, and Gṛtsamada; Gṛtsamada’s son was Śunaka; his son was known as Śaunaka, and he indeed had sons. || 4 ||
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and auspicious Śūdras came into being;
for Kuśa’s son was Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and his son was Caranta.
The Śaunakas and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas were twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
Kāśya’s son was Kāśi; his son was Rāṣṭra, and from him came Dīrghatapas.
The Lord Dhanvantari, the son of Dīrghatapas, was the sovereign;
he is indeed the king of the city of Kāśī and the founder of Āyurveda.
The disease of that person perishes who remembers his name;
he is indeed the second Dhanvantari, the Supreme Lord himself.
But previously, when the ocean was being churned for the sake of the nectar of immortality, he who holds the earth appeared;
then he said to Nārāyaṇa, "O Lord, I am your son."
"O my father, grant me a portion and a place here in this world.
Śrī Hari spoke thus to his son Dhanvantari, who had arisen from the ocean.
The distribution of the sacrifice was indeed performed by the gods worthy of sacrifice,
and the ritual of the fire-oblation was established according to the rules in the Vedas by the great seers.
But it is not possible for you to perform the fire-oblation; indeed, you are exactly like that.
O Lord, you are my son born after me; O Master, you are truly the mantra of my name.
Therefore, at this time, you shall have no share in the sacrifice;
however, you will attain fame in that second birth.
The perfection endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) will belong to you while still in the womb;
by that very body, you shall certainly attain divinity.
The twice-born shall worship you with sacrificial offerings, clarified butter, and fragrances accompanied by the Caru mantras;
and then you, in turn, shall establish the science of Ayurveda once again.
For this matter was destined to happen; you were the first, born of the mind (Mānasa), Samudraja was indeed the second, and the King of Kāśī was the third.
Thus, indeed, there are three manifestations of Dhanvantari;
when the Dvāpara age arrived, he performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a son.
Dīrghatapas indeed beheld the Blessed Lord Hari before him—
serene-faced and tranquil, having arrived to grant him something.
The Blessed One said to Dīrghatapas, "Choose what you desire.
Then Dīrghatapas, with palms joined in reverence and full of humility, spoke.
"If you, O Blessed One, are pleased, then be my son, full of steadfastness. Having granted permission, saying "So be it," the Lord vanished.
O Lakṣmī, from his body arose Dhanvantari, who was Hari himself, the great king of Kāśī, the destroyer of all diseases. ||21||
The Lord who bears the mark of the bow is the protector of the world;
he is the nourisher of all things, as well as the giver of knowledge and the giver of liberation. || 22 ||
That god indeed composed the Āyurveda along with its medical practices;
having then divided it into eight parts, he imparted it to his disciples.
And Dhanvantari’s son was Ketumān, who was of great renown;
from Ketumān was born Bhīmaratha, also known by the name Divodāsa.
Divodāsa was a great devotee, equal to Viṣṇu in strength;
by him, devotion to Hari was increased among his progeny in every way. (25)
Although the Blessed Lord Śambhu resided on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves,
he found no happiness there without Kāśī, which was inhabited by King Divodāsa.
The Lord Śaṅkara is indeed in every way a devotee of Viṣṇu;
he worships Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, through meditative absorption.
Divodāsa, too, was likewise considered a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu;
yet Śaṅkara, having expelled that devotee, desired to dwell there himself.

Śrī Śvetavyāsa said: Having thus heard this discourse on the yoga of Śaṅkara’s teachings, which bestows tranquility, as well as the account of the devotee Divodāsa, Suśikha was then immediately [transformed].
Having heard this, the three-eyed Lord Śiva asked Lakṣmī about Divodāsa:
"How did he abandon Kāśī, and how did he come there from the mountain?"
O Mādhava, what was done by that king so that Divodāsa bypassed his own capital, Kāśī? I wish to hear this.
Having thus questioned her lord and husband, Lakṣmī, whose mind was one-pointed, addressed him as "Hāṭakāṅgada"; Nārāyaṇa then spoke to her.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Three Incarnations of Dhanvantari," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that sacred story which causes wonder among devotees;
Divodāsa was my devotee, and even more so was the King of Spirits himself.
My supreme devotee indeed remains on Mount Mandara;
by Mandara, a severe and most formidable penance has been performed.
Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, being truly highly pleased by the ascetic penance, said to Mount Mandara: "What indeed is it that you desire in your heart?"
"I am pleased, O Mahādeva; choose what you desire and I shall grant it.
Mandara said, "O Lord of Gods, I choose your own residence here."
By your dwelling here, my body shall become purified; having attained the status of a sacred ford (tīrtha), it will come to be honored by all. || 5 ||
All the celestial sages and seers have come for an audience with you;
they shall forever purify me by the offering of the water from your feet.
Having received this entreaty, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, dwelt on Mount Mandara; at that time, all the inhabitants of heaven likewise remained there.
Then the sages, the ascetics, and the attendants of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas—
all, taking refuge in Śambhu, made Mandara their dwelling place.
Those who were formerly in Kāśī— Skanda, Viṣṇu, Gaṇādhipa, Sūrya, the goddesses, and others as well— having abandoned Kāśī, went to the mountain.
When the hosts of gods had departed, the powerful Divodāsa ruled a kingdom free from strife, auspicious and filled with devotion to the Lord.
The king made Vārāṇasī his firm capital;
protecting his subjects with righteousness, he caused it to flourish through his devotion.
But those gods who resided in Kāśī, together with their hosts of Apsarases, though they were inhabitants of heaven,
Divodāsa expelled because they were devoid of self-restraint.
Those devoid of dharma, devoid of vows, and lacking self-restraint—
even other gods certainly must not dwell in my Kāśī.
"Those devoid of devotion to the Blessed One must especially not remain for even a moment," saying this, the king indeed drove out the gods and others.
Like the sun, he scorched the hearts and eyes of his enemies;
like the moon, he was pleasing to the hearts and eyes of his friends. 15.
Upon seeing that wielder of the bow, the hosts of enemies flee;
he is like another Dharmarāja, a discernor of righteousness and unrighteousness.
He was as powerful as Indra, like Varuṇa in casting the noose of his enemies, as wealthy as Kubera, and like Prāṇa in grasping all living beings. || 17 ||
He was indeed a king of kings, a conqueror of enemies like Rudra;
he was equal to Viśvadeva in beauty, and superior to Vasu in wealth. || 18 ||
Having assumed the form of the Aśvins, he was the delighter even of the Maruts;
he was a master of all sciences, skilled in song, and a bringer of joy to the world.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and dānavas served him;
the guhyakas and guptadāsas were his attendants and servants. (1.81.20)
His horses indeed learned the highest speed from Pavana,
and his elephants, being generous, taught others the art of giving.
In his assembly were those who understood him, and on the field of battle were those who fought for him;
yet no one anywhere ever conquered him through either scriptures or weapons.
In whose kingdom the subjects were indeed not objects of hatred and were full of happiness;
he alone was possessed of all arts, while all the people were abodes of art. (23)
In his kingdom, there was no one who had pierced the mountain of his lineage; he alone was the piercer of the mountain of his own lineage.
In his kingdom, there was no one subject to decay; even in heaven, the moon is subject to waning.
In that kingdom there was no obstruction; indeed, Diti had nine planets, for Hiraṇyagarbha alone was divine, and all of his [planets] were made of gold.
In heaven there is one seven-horsed [sun], while his people possess many steeds;
among the hosts of celestial nymphs in heaven, the Apsaras are always within his domain.
In Vaikuṇṭha he has but one Padmā, yet his lotus-pools number a hundred;
thus he never experienced sorrows, nor were there ever any afflictions for him anywhere.
May the entire earth be a giver of wealth, and may there be the destruction of wealth in every house;
thus, while the king brings happiness to his kingdom and subjects, may he live for eighty thousand years.
When autumn had almost passed, Śambhu then set his mind on residing in Vārāṇasī, desiring to effect a remedy.
The gods, having approached Bṛhaspati, held a consultation with him:
"May we be endowed with your splendor; indeed, you alone are the ones who bring about our misfortune."
Although that king honored the gods with sacrifices, nevertheless, human beings were not truly considered his friends. (3.1)
Although he has done us no wrong, nevertheless, the nature of the denizens of heaven is an intolerance for the excellence of others. (32)
