In the kingdom and palace of Divodāsa, there was not even the slightest accumulation of unrighteousness;
no one at all was able to bring about the defeat of this king.
In his realm, all men observe the vow of having only one wife,
and in his realm there exist women devoted to their husbands.
In that kingdom, there was no Brahmin ignorant of the Vedas, nor any Bāhuja (Kṣatriya) who was not a hero; likewise, there was no Vaiśya lacking diligence, and no Śūdra who did not perform service.
In his kingdom, there was no one who was a celibate student devoted to the vow of Brahman,
nor was there anyone who failed to show honor toward the state of the householder within that realm.
Nor were there forest-dwellers who lived by gleaning, nor those free from desire;
nor indeed were there those devoid of attachment who had set out upon the path of renunciation. ||37||
Likewise, others in his kingdom were also not traveling aimlessly on the road; on his land, there was no one who was childless, nor anyone lacking devotion, nor anyone destitute of wealth. (38)
They do not serve the aged, nor do they suffer untimely death; they are not prone to malice toward others.
They are neither flatterers nor loquacious chatterers, and they are certainly neither deceitful nor fraudulent. (39)
In his kingdom, there were no heretics, no jesters, no widows, and no liquor-sellers; everywhere, there was the practice of the Vedas, the scriptures, and so forth.
Everywhere the speech of the people is auspicious, and they abstain from liquor, meat, and the like;
there are no gamblers or pimps there, nor any debtors or thieves. (41)
Even the worship of the ancestors and the gods was never interrupted;
in that kingdom, there was no violation of vows, nor likewise any neglect of visiting sacred fords.
When there is constant affection between husband and wife, the family does not suffer affliction;
those worthy of honor are honored by those who offer salutations, and the supreme ones are worshipped by those who perform worship. (43)
But the wise are always honored there by the subjects;
and among the wise, those preeminent in austerity are honored by the ascetics, and those who have conquered their hunger by the practitioners of penance. 44.
By those who have conquered their inner selves, the knowers of Brahman whose wealth is knowledge,
all reality is perceived as having the form of Brahman.
Food offered to the gods is presented in the mouths of Brahmins, virtuous men, and virtuous women;
furthermore, it fills the waters of ponds, wells, and lakes.
The clouds rain in the northeast, and the earth is always covered with crops;
his subjects are always joyful, well-nourished, and pure, both [the king and his people]. (47)
Although the gods searched even slightly for a vulnerability in that kingdom, they found none;
then Bṛhaspati spoke to those gods.
Defeat will by no means occur unless there is a vulnerability; even one who is without a flaw can be overcome by employing the stratagem of sowing dissension. (49)
In that regard, even our own side possesses the wealth of happiness; nevertheless, those who hold other views would be helpful in the task of creating division. (1.81.50)
Having reached this conclusion and informed the gods who move within and without his mouth,
they all then paid homage to the god Agni.
Then Indra also said to Agni: "Establish yourself here in Kāśī;
remaining there in embodied form, you shall shine forth from that realm. (52)
Withdraw her quickly; in this way, victory shall be ours.
Otherwise, the officiating priests will be deprived of their forms, and sacrifices to the gods and ancestors will be abandoned. (53)
When that king is gone, the subjects will become destitute of wealth, seeing that the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) of the word "king" has vanished. (54)
The subjects there would become disaffected, the treasury and the army would be depleted, the king’s means of subsistence would also fail, and the three aims of life would naturally decline. (55)
Thus, Divodāsa will either perish from exhaustion or depart;
consequently, our residence here in Kāśī shall indeed be free from thorns.
Thinking thus in his heart, Agni, remembering what Indra had said, approached him, remaining entirely unmixed with any defects such as excessive heat. 57.
Then Mahādeva withdrew his own form from that spot,
along with the triad consisting of the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇa fires.
He also stole the digestive fire of the people living there; consequently, the subjects could not digest their food during the morning and midday rituals. ||59||
Then all those ritualists and cooks reflected upon that fierce fire: "What indeed can be done without fire? (1.81.60)
Having performed his midday rites, the king entered the kitchen;
he remained there until he had returned for the Vaiśvadeva offering and the meal.
Trembling, the female cooks informed him of his hunger-stricken state:
"O King, if you would grant an assurance of safety, [we shall tell you how to find food]. (62)
"Then we shall report the truth of what occurred.
Having been thus commanded by the king, the cooks spoke slowly.
O Lord, we do not know how the fire departed from the city;
once the fire has vanished, how could the vessels and other items come into existence? (64)
"Let us bring whatever has been cooked by the cooking of the sun";
meanwhile, the king understood that this was indeed the work of the gods.
Having understood this through the power of his asceticism and having reflected upon it, he then said:
"If the fire has gone out, there is no loss for me; indeed, it is only a loss for the gods."
Indeed, the kingdom was not obtained by me from them, but was obtained from my grandfather;
by my own power, I shall create wind, fire, water, and earth.
"Whatever is required here—whether it be light or anything else—I shall accomplish all that through consciousness; I have no need for the insentient. (68)
While he was reflecting thus, the people of the countryside arrived;
they were ushered inside by the doorkeeper to join in that very same cry. (69)
Having offered gifts as was appropriate, they sat upon seats of honor and then spoke of the extreme suffering caused by the fire procession.
Having heard that, the king, who brings happiness to all, said:
"O citizens, it was I myself who previously desired to perform this task. (71)
"Indeed, it would be better to remain indifferent so that no harm may come;
thus, O auspicious one, the fire has departed, and let my life-breath also depart quickly from here. (72)
Let the moon, the sun, Varuṇa, the earth, and even space depart from here;
through the power of the Lord’s yoga, I myself shall become fire.
In fourfold form as fire, I take up and digest that which [is consumed];
having myself become the vital breath (prāṇa), I shall sustain the embodied beings.
Becoming the great wind myself, I shall sustain the spheres;
and becoming the moon myself, I shall nourish the sprout that is the world.
Becoming the sun myself, I shall eternally scorch this earth;
becoming a cloud myself, I shall bring rain, and I shall also become Varuṇa.
I shall abide here in the form of water, and I shall also become the form of the earth;
I shall support the entire universe, and I shall become the form of space.
Having spoken thus and having consoled his own subjects, the king indeed became [the god] in that manner;
and having manifested in many forms, he carried out those various tasks.
Indeed, by means of the yoga obtained from the Blessed One, even he became many;
at that time, the king of the gods became Śalya in form.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara’s Residence on Mount Mandara after Receiving the Boon, the Devas’ Departure from Kāśī to that Place, the Praise of King Divodāsa’s Virtues, and the Formulation of a Plan to Expel Divodāsa from Kāśī," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. ||81||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Although Mahādeva was provided with every kind of comfort and utensil in his palace on Mount Mandara, he found no happiness due to the absence of Kāśī.
For him, pleasure became a source of dullness, and pleasure brought about only indolence;
even sandalwood paste for his body became like dust and fuel.
At that time, his bracelets became lotus stalks and his armlets became gravel;
the moon upon his forehead became a mere spark from the fire of separation.
To pacify the supreme agony of separation from Kāśī, he held the Gaṅgā within his matted locks; she was not abandoned, but was forcibly protected by him.
Nor was the Lord known by the gods to be like a fire of separation;
he remained as before, absorbed in meditation on Mount Mandara.
This indeed is the divine play of the Lord;
the Master, who is himself eight-formed (Aṣṭamūrti), heats the entire world with his own form.
The Hālāhala poison, though it has reached his throat, does not torment him;
rather, the ever-increasing heat of separation from Kāśī torments him.
Indeed, this garland born of cool moonstones worn upon her breast brings about the illusion of sun-stones, as if produced by the fresh heat of separation.

Although this [fire] brings the happiness of worldly pleasure arising from the emission of a sidelong glance, it surely reduces the ground of the mind to ashes; even that [fire], when scorched by the fire of passion, is consumed.
Even though he has rushed toward the path of the Vedas, he who bestows the happiness of his own devotees within—
his being scorched by the fire born of separation from him, despite his tranquility, is indeed a tragedy.
If the wind, having gathered the fragrant particles born from the beautiful Gaṅgā at Kāśī,
should touch me who am separated [from my beloved], then supreme happiness would arise for me.
Even if the dust raised by the streets of Kāśī were to be carried here by the blowing wind,
it would still be sufficient and powerful to forcibly ward off the suffering born of separation.
Having thus beheld Śaṅkara submerged in grief, Pārvatī,
after bowing to her husband-god, spoke these words that dispel inner distress.
O God, Great God, Lord and Sovereign of the worlds, O Śaṅkara, remover of the world's affliction, why do you burn with anguish in your heart? 14.
O Lord, I am Vāmā, whose very nature is the Left (Vāma), established here for Your worship; why do You cause me, who am intended to remove my own suffering, to suffer through You? 15.
O You whose forms consist of earth, water, fire, air, ether, moon, and sun;
You who are known through direct perception, inference, analogy, verbal testimony, presumption, tradition, and authoritative scripture. 16.
O master of all yoga, how can your separation from Kāśī overcome you, who possess the luminosity born of the practice of non-apprehension and the impossibility [of its loss]? 17.
O Inner Soul of all, O Omniscient One, who bears the form of Brahman like the sky;
Kāśī is at the tip of your trident—what cause for grief can there be for you because of that? (18)
Nevertheless, by the power of destiny, that divine city which bestows liberation does not admit any limitation caused by time, place, or substance.
Through union with You, there is no manifestation, no transformation, no destruction, no falsity, no dissolution, and no concealment, just as in the case of the light of a lamp. 1.82.20
O Lord, Kāśī—divine, endowed with divine hosts, possessing divine tirthas, purifying, and bestowing divine liberation—must by all means be visited. (21)
There is no happiness equal to Kāśī, no stability equal to Kāśī, and no peace equal to Kāśī; Kāśī is the bestower of all goals.

What is obtained as happiness? It is *kaṃ*. What is that *śaṃ* happiness attained from here? It is *śī*. Therefore, Kāśī is composed of happiness (*sukhamayī*); for this reason, she is to be resorted to by all. ||23||
Indeed, because of the residence of Brahmā, the refuge of Viṣṇu,
and the dwelling of Śambhu, Kāśī is the embodiment of the three gods.
Kā is said to be Sarasvatī, Ā is Lakṣmī herself, Ramā;
Śī is indeed the goddess Pārvatī—she is the embodiment of the triad of goddesses, Kāśī. (25)
Neither Mount Mandara nor the Himavat, nor gardens and forests— whether situated in the sky or upon the earth— bring happiness, just as [the sight of] the Kāśa grass does not.
Neither a god of action, nor Adharma, nor Yama, nor even one born in heaven is capable here of punishing the people residing in Kāśī. ||27||

Where there is the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no further rebirth after death; because of dwelling there, there is no stain of karma—O Lord, when indeed shall I behold that state? 28.
There are indeed many ancient cities and likewise numerous towns;
yet at every step, there are none that possess such prosperity as Kāśī. (29)
All stages established in truth do not become equal to Kāśī;
for just as it afflicts you, so too does the heat of Kāśī afflict me.
My birthplace is not like Kāśī, which removes all suffering;
for [Kāśī] is attained through austerities, sacrifices, fulfillment of vows, offerings, gifts, dharma, sacred observances, and the like. (3.1)
Liberation is not attained in that same way through yoga, Sāṃkhya, Vedānta, the ritual section of the Vedas, or the knowledge of the Self as by casting off the body in Kāśī. ||32||
Just as eternal liberation occurs through the falling away of the body in Kāśī, such a goal is not attained even by the study of the Vedas or by the observance of Brahmanical vows. ||33||
Neither in the world of truth (Satyaloka), nor in the world of Indra, nor even in the abode of the sages,
nor in Ātala and the other lower realms, is there happiness anywhere like that which is found in Kāśī.
By recollecting Kāśī even with the mind, one obtains the fruit of yogic practice;
indeed, for humans, the state of being born in Kāśī is always considered superior to that of the animal realm. (35)
"Then liberation would occur at death itself; what would be the fruit of the arising of knowledge?
Therefore, act in such a way that I may go to Kāśī and Ānandāraṇya. (36)
Śambhu said: "O Goddess of gods, you know my vow:
I consume only that substance which has never been tasted by another, and nothing else. (37)
Urged by Brahmā, Divodāsa ruled that city according to dharma;
how could one go there while another ruler was established? (38)
Just as Divodāsa abandoned the city of Kāśī and departed, so too should one act; having closed one's eyes to worldly concerns, dwelling there is indeed conducive to happiness. (39)
Obstacles arise for the unrighteous, but not for the righteous;
he who would create an obstacle for one established in dharma comes to ruin.
How can one endowed with dharma be eradicated from this place without a flaw?
Neither old age, nor great time, nor death, nor unappeasable diseases [can do so]. (4.1)
Neither obstacles, nor diseases, nor planetary spirits, nor piśācas, nor calamities, nor even elemental beings (bhūtas) can afflict one who practices the gathering of the Dharma. 42.
"Therefore, O Mistress, whom shall I send who might put him to flight?"—
as Śambhu was thinking thus, the circle of Yoginīs appeared before him.
When that wheel had arrived, Hara spoke these words:
"O Yoginīs, go quickly to where the most righteous king is."
"He who is known as Divodāsa rules Kāśī with righteousness;
act through your illusory power in such a way that he quickly abandons Kāśī. (45)
"Therefore, having renovated the auspicious city of Vārāṇasī, I shall reside right there; let everything be prepared quickly. (46)
Thus, accepting that command with their heads bowed, they departed full of eagerness, proclaiming, "We are most fortunate; we have been graced by the favor of the gods."
And having been dispatched for the sake of their mission to the glorious Ānandakānana, they flew from the valley of Mount Mandara and remained poised in the sky above Kāśī. 48.
They beheld a city rich with divine palaces, like another heaven;
with its banners, it seemed as if calling out to the travelers standing on the road. (49)
By means of great nets of white jewels, that pure blue sky is entirely whitened by streams of luster ascending toward heaven.
Then, even within the void itself, a manifold transformation of their own forms was performed by all of them; and they proceeded with diverse modes of knowledge. ||5.1||
Indeed, in various places throughout Kāśī, women appeared in diverse attire; beautiful yoginīs descended there for the sake of accomplishing their task. (52)

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Dispatching of the Circle of Yoginīs to Create Obstacles for Divodāsa Following Śambhu’s Intense Suffering Born of Separation from Kāśī in the Cave of Mount Mandara," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Behold, O Lakṣmī, how much hatred these women harbor; they assume many forms while striving for their own ends as long as those ends are not accomplished. (1)
Having abandoned her state as a Yoginī and concealed her divinity,
one became a female renunciant (saṃnyāsinī) and another a human ascetic woman (tapasvinī).
One became a *sairandhrī*, another likewise a female mendicant;
one was a garland-maker, and another became a barber’s wife.
One was an excellent physician, another was a skilled seller of scales;
one was a seller of vegetables, and another was a protector against snakes and other such creatures.
One was born as a dancer, another as a nurse and a servant; another became a singer, and yet another a player of musical instruments.
One became a keeper of keys, another a provider of magical mantras; one was skilled in weaving garlands, and another in the sale of oils and such.
One was an expert in the rules of gambling, another was the beloved of a cowherd; one was an actress, while yet another was a sweeper of streets and courtyards.
Her other occupations, such as dealing in honey and the like, seeking rags from the streets,
and being devoted to her children, resulted in her becoming a dog-cooker and a leather-worker’s wife.
There was a virtuous woman, a female cultivator, one who engaged in the business of selling milk,
another who lived at a sacred ford, a shaven-headed nun, and yet another who resided in a village temple.
One was an observer of marks and signs, another was skilled in writing and painting; one knew the mantras for subjugation, and another was a healer of fevers.

One was skilled in the application of collyrium and possessed the power of medicinal pills; another, by mixing various minerals and substances, was capable of creating protective coverings from cloth.
She is the deluder of men, possessing many forms; she is the speech that awakens the pillar-of-fire (agnistambha);
she bestows mantras for invisibility, the power of moving through the sky, the ability to assume other forms, and so forth.

She who knows the arts of eradication and attraction, who deludes the minds of the young, who bestows the desired object upon thought, who possesses knowledge of the luminous sciences, and who is the protector of cattle. (12)
One woman was a provider of tooth-sticks, another was a collector of cow dung and the like, while yet another Nāgarī woman was a seller of clay.
Having become female servants and maidservants,
those yoginīs entered every house and wandered about day and night.
Though they searched for even a slight opening or flaw for the purpose of creating obstacles, they found none;
thus, having returned to the bank of the Gaṅgā and gathered together, they were unsuccessful. (16)
"What should be done? Where should we go regarding Divodāsa and his subjects? Can some vulnerability of ours be found? How can we put ourselves far away? (17)
"Without having accomplished our task, we must not go back to our master," they deliberated,
and remaining there, they did not go to Mount Mandara.
"Who would remain in the presence of a master without having accomplished his task?
Even without the Lord, we shall indeed live here in Kāśī forever. (19)
The Lord, when enraged, may take away one's livelihood; Kāśī, however, takes away the fourfold aims of life.
Therefore, one should reside in Kāśī; one should certainly not go to Mandara.
Beginning from this point, the Yoginīs always remain in Kāśī;
having wandered through the cardinal and intermediate directions, they indeed return and stay there. (21)
Devoted to Nārāyaṇa, they bowed to Divodāsa and always considered it their supreme gain [to do so]. "Through the merit earned by serving Kāśī, even the Lord (Īśa) will come to us."
Without Kāśī, even there he would be miserable; therefore, he has come here. ||23||
Having thus resolved, the Yoginīs remained in the Forest of Śambhu’s Bliss,
constantly remembering that Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
I shall state their names; listen here, O Kamalālayā:
Gajāsyā, Siṃhavaktrā, Gṛdhrāsyā, and Kākatuṇḍikā. ||25||
She has the face of a camel, the neck of a horse or a donkey, the snout of a boar, and the face of a jackal;
she has eyes like an owl, makes a terrible sound, possesses the feathers of a peacock, and has the face of a sharabha.
Koṭarākṣī, Aṣṭavaktrā, Kubjā, Vikaṭānanā, Śuṣkodarī, Lalajjihvā, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, and Vānarānanā. ||27||
Ṛkṣākṣī, Kekarākṣī, Bṛhattuṇḍā, Surāpriyā, Kapālahastā, Raktākṣī, Śukī, Śyenī, and Kapotikā. ||28||
With noose in hand and staff in hand, she is Pracaṇḍā of fierce prowess;
she is the slayer of children, the destroyer with the noose, Kālī, and the drinker of blood. ||29||
She drinks fat, devours embryos, holds a corpse in her hand, and wears a garland of intestines;
she has hair like that of a bear, a vast belly, a serpent-like face, and the back of a ghost for a seat.
Dandaśūkadharā, Krauñcī, Mṛgaśṛṅgā, Vṛṣānanā, Phāṭitāsyā, Dhūmaśvāsā, Vyomapādā, and Ūrdhvadṛṣṭikā. (3.1)
Tāpinī, Śoṣiṇī, Schaghoṇā, Oṣṭhā, Koṭarī, as well as Vidyullolā, Balākāsyā, Mārjārī, and Kaṭapūtanā. ||32||
Aṭṭahāsī, Kāmākṣī, and Mṛgākṣī—
these are considered the sixty-four Yoginīs who are worshipped during the Navarātra festival.
They destroy the afflictions caused by malevolent spirits and protect the fetus, infants, and others;
neither ḍākinīs, nor śākinīs, nor kūṣmāṇḍas, nor rākṣasas [can harm them]. (34)
Whoever should recite these names will cause suffering to [their] enemies;
they grant victory in battle, in the royal court, or even in dispute. (35)
Through offerings of oblations, worship, and gifts, as well as the presentation of incense and lamps, the Yoginīs will quickly become pleased and grant one's heart's desires. (36)
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the best of men, observing a fast,
should perform an oblation with the names [of the deity] preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending in the dative case.
For each of these, a hundred and eight oblations are prescribed,
offered with guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter, in the measure of a small jujube fruit.
With a one-pointed mind and purified, having reflected in every way upon his own desired goal, a human being attains whatever accomplishment he may seek. ||39||
Even though the Lord had not yet arrived for a long time within the circle of Yoginīs,
he dispatched the Sun to ascertain the progress of Kāśī.
Śambhu said to Sūrya:
"O Ravi, let your residence be where there is no violation of dharma; act accordingly, O Divākara. (41)
O Bhāskara, for one who shows contempt toward a devotee established here on the path of Dharma, there shall be the destruction of all his possessions.
As long as the intellect remains firm in the Dharma and devotion toward Mādhava persists, so long there shall be no arising of obstacles; nevertheless, carry out your endeavors.
By the word of Śambhu, Ravi came to Kāśī like a mortal man;
he moved within and without Kāśī, among Divodāsa and the subjects.
He did not perceive even the slightest impairment in the flow of devotion to the Dharma;
wandering for a year like the sun, he became a guest and made a request of him.
Having subsequently attained everything, he assumed many forms:
he became a beggar, a generous donor, a wretched man, an astrologer, and even a master of mantras.
Sometimes he was an atheist, a rogue, one with matted hair, or a naked ascetic; a snake-charmer, a physician for poisons, a heretic, or even one who professes to speak of Brahman.
One who performs vows, one skilled in magic, a storyteller, one who carries a skull, a twice-born man, a man of knowledge, an alchemist, an astronomer, and one who knows excellent counsel. 48.
The virtuous one is indeed the nature of the dharma of renunciation, assuming the form of a female renunciant;
likewise are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, the Śūdra, the student, and the householder. (49)
Whether appearing as a forest-dweller, or in the form of a commoner, or even assuming the form of a caṇḍāla,
he wandered thus throughout Kāśī, yet he found no vulnerability anywhere.
For then, having accomplished his purpose, he did not wish to go back to Mandara out of fear of insult and because of the power of Divodāsa.
Having made his dwelling in Kāśī itself, with the inner core of his heart fixed in devotion, the destruction of the sin born of not making offerings shall come about through devotion. ||52||
For by one who protects the Dharma, everything is protected;
indeed, this very True Dharma arises from the practice of [residing in] Kāśī. (53)
Sons, friends, wives, fields, and wealth are obtained here in every birth; but Kashi alone is never obtained. (54)
"A devotee equal to Divodāsa is not to be found anywhere else;
therefore, having thus resolved, Divākara must dwell right here. (55)
Having manifested in twelve forms, he is established in the city of Kāśī as Lokārka,
Uttarārka, Sāmbāditya, and Khakholaka.
Drupadāditya, Mayūkhāditya, as well as the one named Aruṇa, Vṛddhārka, Keśavārka, Vimalārka, and the one named Yama. ||57||
Gaṅgāditya is established in Kāśī in twelve forms.
He constantly worships Śrī Hari in the company of Divodāsa.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Sixty-four Yoginīs assuming various forms to seek a vulnerability in Divodāsa, the Sun’s residence in Kāśī itself for that same purpose, and the Sun’s dwelling in Kāśī in twelve forms," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, whichever lord Mahādeva sends forth, he does not return; Hara became absorbed in anxiety.
The yoginīs have not yet arrived, nor has the sun yet risen;
if I am not to dwell in Kāśī, by what means shall my time pass? (2)
"I have burnt away my passion; let not passion torment me further.
Whom shall I send from here to seek news of Kāśī? (2)
Having reflected thus, Śiva spoke to the Creator with great respect: "The Yoginīs and the Sun have been dispatched by me. (4)
Even now they do not turn back from Kāśī, despite knowing its condition;
for the venom of separation from Kāśī does not afflict me as much as the poison [of their presence]. || 5 ||
"O Creator, ordain my task; go to Kāśī and strive there.
I must depart this very day, yet in accordance with righteousness."
"I cannot venture to transgress against King Divodāsa;
one must not dwell in another king's realm, nor should one eat what has been left over. (7)
"Go in safety; may your path be entirely auspicious in its outcome. Having received this command, Vidhi quickly departed for Kāśī through the air.
Seated upon his swan, he beheld the auspicious Ānandavāṭikā of Kāśī,
where the Gaṅgā, the trees, the people, and the palaces were eternally filled with bliss.
Those sense-faculties by which Kāśī is perceived truly exist as excellent;
for indeed, it is the choice grasses and grains that fall within Kāśī.
Today my life has become fruitful; oh, how great is my good fortune!
Today the tree that is my body has borne fruit, since I have beheld Kāśī.
I have created this entire creation, preceded by great skill;
however, Kāśī was fashioned in an entirely different manner by the Lord himself.
Thus, with a joyful mind, the Creator, assuming the guise of an aged brahmin,
descended from his swan to the earth and beheld Divodāsa.
Honored and duly respected by the king, the elderly brahmin sat upon a beautiful seat and bestowed blessings upon the monarch.
When there is real wealth, there is an increase in the treasury; in the interval between [births], there is an increase in happiness.
On the true path, there is an increase in progress; in the interval between those, there is an increase in coughing. 15.
The king said: "O venerable Brahmin, why do you speak with double meaning?
Where there is an increase in both righteousness and devotion, there true prosperity always resides. (16)
When there is no capital and when one is on an improper path, interest brings about fear;
when there is no capital, there is interest on a mere egg (a small amount), and when on an improper path, there is running away. 17.
Indeed, during the interval of the rains, no unhappiness shall befall the righteous;
however, for the unrighteous, unhappiness shall be equal [to that of the others] during that same interval. || 18 ||
In praise there would be an increase in light, but in the interval, it is otherwise, not so when defiled.
O old Brahmin, what do you desire? You are destitute of wealth and have gone upon a wrong path.
"What is this increase of hypocrisy in my heart? For a year I have been a partaker of suffering.
I am Divodāsa—do you wish for this? What do you desire? || 1.84.20 ||
"Do you wish for my escape from Kāśī? What do you desire? [he asked], whereupon the Brahmin spoke with deceitful words, assuming the false guise of a god on earth (a Brāhmaṇa). ||21||
In that regard, let there be a deceptive dharma; be one who possesses deceptive blessings.
Brahmā has declared here that "kūṭa" means deceit and the pretension of horns. 22.

Wherever there is a Brahmin of excellent speech, a god upon earth wearing the finest attire, and where the highest dharma prevails, there I shall be present, bestowing the most excellent blessings. (23)
If there is indeed deceit, it is certainly hypocrisy and nothing else;
where a Brahmin speaks with hypocrisy, he is a priest who wears the garb of hypocrisy.
There, the practice would be one of deceit, and he would be one who utters blessings with guile;
then the king spoke to that Brahmin Brahmā, whose nature was fraudulent.
If you are thus the very embodiment of Dharma, how can you engage in deceit?
In deceit, defeat is certain; one who takes a step toward deceit falls downward. (26)
"Come, O Brahmin! I shall offer you a welcome according to the practice of sincerity. Here is water for the feet, food, fruit, the water of the Ganges to drink, and an ornament. (27)
"Accept everything, O best of Brahmins; choose whatever dwells in your heart.
Brahmā said: "That has already been accepted through devotion; you shall increase in prosperity, O King. (28)
O King, you are victorious through your knowledge that awakens the truth and through your righteousness;
many kings have been seen who were performers of sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees.
They were learned in the Vedas, skilled in ethics, possessed of virtuous character, and had conquered their senses;
they were the very ground of forgiveness, compassion, profound depth, courtesy, and gentleness.
But among them, O King, you possess two or three qualities in particular:
your subjects alone are your family, and the Brahmins alone are your deity. (3.1)
Devotion and righteousness are your companions; you are the helper of ascetics.
These qualities are not seen in others; indeed, you are blessed and worthy of honor by the virtuous.
You are worthy of worship for your six virtues; you flourish through devotion and righteousness.
O righteous one, even the gods fear to commit any offense against you.
But I, O King, am a brahmin who has come here to perform sacrifices;
having found a devotee such as you, let my residence be here. (34)
Whatever else has been consecrated by mantra is indeed always far away; O King, let it remain far from here.
In this place, O King, are three holy sites (tīrthas): the Gaṅgā, the Earth, and that which is beyond the supreme. (35)
Where there is no exhaustion even at the dissolution of the world for deeds performed,
that wealth which was accumulated with effort should be employed in sacrifice.
To the Brahmin who remained thus silent, Divodāsa said:
"I am your servant in every way, O Hari, for you who desire to sacrifice."
"Take from my treasury the materials required for the sacrifice;
[namely] the sovereign, ministers, friends, treasury, kingdom, fortresses, and a good army. (38)
Appoint that which is necessary for your own purpose, but not even the slightest bit of it [for yourself];
rather, a king should delight his subjects with his sons, his wife, and his very body. (39)
The fire born from the distress of the subjects is more terrifying even than a thunderbolt;
while a thunderbolt may destroy only two or three, this heat destroys the kingdom, the lineage, and the body. (1.84.40)
With the dust from the feet of Brahmins, I always perform my ritual ablution;
I consider that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin to be superior to any sacrifice. (41)
Even today, there remains but one single aspiration for the sake of the Brahmins;
indeed, even one's own body becomes fruitful through its dedication to that end. (42)
Today my life has borne fruit; perform sacrifices with excellent gifts.
Worship the gods and know that assistance has been rendered by all available means. 43.
Having heard the king’s words, the Brahmin Brahmā gathered the necessary materials and performed ten horse-sacrifices on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
At that spot, having abandoned its former name Rudrasaras, that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) attained the renowned appellation Daśāśvamedha.
The Creator found no flaw whatsoever in his devotee Divodāsa;
what indeed could he have said upon going before Śambhu on Mount Mandara? (46)
Therefore, having installed the Daśāśvamedheśa Liṅga as well as the Brahmeśvara Liṅga and his own image, Vidhi dwelt right there.
Through the association of the virtuous, Divodāsa became a constant devotee of Hari;
[he attained] the worlds of Satya, Vairāja, Vaiṣṇava, and Śāmbhava.
That happiness which is called liberation indeed arises from serving Kāśī;
having bathed on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one shall be released from bondage. 49.

Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, libations to the ancestors, twilight prayers, worship of the gods, and ancestral rites— whatever is performed there becomes inexhaustible.
Having bathed on the Daśaharā day and worshipped the Liṅga, one shall obtain the merit of ten horse-sacrifices and shall not enter a womb again. ||51||
Brahmā remained in the form of a brāhmaṇa until the arrival of Śiva;
for Brahmā, Divodāsa constructed a hall of learning (brahmaśālā).
There, a most beautiful city of Brahmā was established by Ahalyā;
thus this land is eternally Brāhmī, bestowing the world of Brahmā. (53)
O beloved, what kind of great devotee was Divodāsa to me, such that even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were unable to repay his kindness? (54)

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Account of how Brahmā, sent by Śambhu from Mount Mandara, arrived in the form of a brāhmaṇa and bestowed blessings through deceptive verses during the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, and how, following their dialogue, he performed ten horse-sacrifices and settled in Kāśī."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Great Goddess Lakṣmī; while dwelling on Mount Mandara, Hara grieved there in many ways, thinking, "They have gone and do not return."
Why indeed do those Yoginīs—Sūrya and Vedhas—remain in Kāśī with their tasks unfinished and their vigor destroyed? Why do they not come? Whom shall I dispatch?
Thinking thus, the Lord of Devas summoned his attendants in great numbers and dispatched them, saying, "O, go quickly to Kāśī to dwell there."
Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahākāla, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Mahodara,
Nandiṣeṇa, Somanandin, Kāla, Piṅgala, and Kukkuṭa.
Kuṇḍodara, Mayūrākṣa, Bāṇa, Gokarṇa, Tāraka, Tilaparṇa, Sthūlakarṇa, Dṛmicaṇḍa, and Prabhāmaya. (5)
Sukeśa, Vindati, Chāga, Kapardin, Piṅgalākṣaka,
Vīrabhadra, Kirāta, Caturmukha, and Nikumbhaka— [these he saw].
Pañcākṣa, Bhārabhūta, Kṣemaka, and likewise Lāṅgalin;
Tryakṣa, Virādha, Sumukha, Āṣāḍhin, and Skanda as well. || 7 ||
Śaṅkara dispatched Mahāśākha, Viśākha, Śākha, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Naigameya.
These highly fortunate hosts are devoted to their master and firm in their vows;
having displayed various kinds of illusions, they are multiform and skillful.
With unblinking eyes, they stood waiting for a flaw in the king regarding his righteousness,
truthfulness, compassion, justice, and the protection of his subjects.

In matters of protection, the duty of giving, the duties of kingship, and what is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti; in the duties concerning the castes and stages of life, misfortunes, place, time, and so forth—(11)
In the performance of the five great sacrifices, the recitation of prayers, and the practice of serving and honoring devotees,
he never experienced any loss, deficiency, or flaw anywhere at all.
Having honored King Divodāsa,
who was incapable of being defeated, all the hosts, their own purposes unaccomplished, were deeply ashamed.
Having installed Mahādeva under their own respective names,
they dwelt continuously in Kāśī itself, freed from all distress.
They did not turn back from Mount Mandara until they had understood the greatness of Kāśī;
indeed, Vārāṇasī, which is more venerable than even heaven, must never be abandoned.
Nothing else is equal to the bliss obtained in the Ānanda garden;
here indeed is Kailāsa, and Vaikuṇṭha also exists here. (16)
Having abandoned emaciation, how should one act? One should remain dry and devoid of worldly flavor [in] Vārāṇasī, Kāśī, and also Ānandodyāna. || 17 ||
By whichever mouth this was proclaimed, there is no fear for him from Yama;
his body, measuring five krośas, is born from the three gods.
For those who have not accumulated merit, whose wealth and lifespan are exhausted,
and who are devoid of all other means, the city of Vārāṇasī is their refuge.

Those wise ones who dwell in Kāśī, having reached the certainty of the dissolution of the five elements, are to be known as liberated while living; they alone are indeed worthy of salutation and worship. 1.85.20.
In that Kāśī, a living being who has died is bowed to with great effort by Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others, who join their palms above their heads in salutation. || 21 ||
Where death is auspicious and where worldly splendor is but an ornament, where a loincloth is as fine silk—where can Kāśī be compared to? 22.
Having cast aside brothers, wife, son, field, home, and wealth—even accepting death—one must indeed dwell here [in this world]. (23)
Having thus reached their decision, they remained right there in Kāśī.
Then Śambhu [observed] those who had gone to Kāśī and remained there, yet had not returned.
Having ascertained the situation regarding the hosts, he dispatched Heramba, the elephant-faced one, saying:
"Go, my son; indeed, no one except you will be able to overcome this king."
Having devised a plan according to your intelligence, the proper time, and what is appropriate, drive out Divodāsa and bring Kāśī into your possession. (26)
Remaining there, strive together with your hosts for the sake of complete success;
ensure that we remain free from obstacles, and bring obstacles upon the king. (27)
Having received the command and prostrated with his head before Dhūrjaṭi,
Gaṇeśa set out swiftly for Kāśī for the sake of his father’s success.
Reflecting upon the means for Śambhu’s arrival at Kāśī, the Brāhmaṇa became a Vāḍava (crane),
wearing a thick girth and five limbs as his feathers, and indicating the omen.
Knowing the constellations and knowing the great circle of the luminaries, the venerable one entered the city and moved through the inner apartments, pointing out the directions with his staff.
Having carefully examined the lines on their hands, their omens, their fortunes, and the letters of their birth,
and having performed the calculations, he became well-disposed toward the citizens.
Having personally shown a dream to people during the night, he would go to their houses in the morning and tell them of their good and evil fortune. || 3.2 ||
Having had those questions resolved, he declared to them the dream-result:
"In a dream last night, while you were bathing in the water, you reached the bank. (33)
Sunk in the mud on the bank, you have been submerged again and again;
the fruit of this dream is evil—there shall be a blow for you in the water.
Having gone to the house of another as well, you indeed described your dream-vision;
thereafter, you saw in a dream one with a shaven head wearing a garment of kasha grass.
Either suffering equal to death or death itself shall be the result;
or if a solar eclipse is seen in a dream, death or a result equivalent to that shall occur.
The firm conviction was that two rainbows appeared at night, and that the sun himself had risen in the west to meet the moon. (37)
"You saw in a dream that one who was rising from the path of the sky was indeed cast down to the ground; the destruction of your kingdom will certainly come to pass. (38)
That two comets were seen fighting in the sky was also a dream-omen that brings about destruction, resulting in the ruin of the kingdom. (39)
When you saw yourself being led away to the south with your teeth shattered, that was the terrifying death of your family.
During the latter part of the night, you saw the breaking of the palace banner;
this is a great portent that will bring about the destruction of the kingdom and calamity among the subjects. (41)
This city which was seen flooded by the ocean will, within the space of two months, suffer a great destruction for its inhabitants. 42.
In a dream you traveled to the south by means of a monkey-vehicle;
therefore, your destruction or your departure from this city is certain. (43)
The woman who was seen by you weeping at night, naked, with disheveled hair, and moving through the sky—the fruit of that is the overturning of your kingdom. (44)
Since you have seen the pinnacle of the temple falling, the destruction of the kingdom will surely occur very soon, within just a few days. (45)
In that month, deer, jackals, and other animals are seen coming repeatedly around the city, howling; therefore, one should not cause agitation.
Owls, hawks, cranes, and vultures are flying all around the city, portending great suffering for its inhabitants. (47)
Taking up his mace, Hanuman struck him on the back; surely this was his destruction. The messengers of Yama were seen standing upon the backs of buffaloes.
They depart taking their offspring with them; the destruction of their progeny is certain.
Furthermore, the soldiers of a foreign kingdom come here and strike them down.
The fruit would be the destruction of Kāśī and the ruin of the worlds;
therefore, one must certainly go elsewhere within the course of a month.
"Indeed, staying here for more than two months will not bring happiness.
Thus he sent them away, speaking to many people of the subjects.
"Approximately half of the population has gone to other lands;
nevertheless, having observed the movement of the planets, he spoke to the people once again. (52)
Venus, Saturn, and Mars, situated in a single zodiac sign, are destroyers;
this comet, having pierced the circle of the Seven Sages in the sky— ||53||
It moves toward the western quarter and becomes the destroyer of Vaiśyas;
Saturn, having transcended its zodiacal sign, indeed proceeds in retrograde motion. (54)
Joined with Rāhu, Ketu, and Mars, it indeed causes great destruction; moreover, an earthquake occurring at evening will inevitably bring about ruin. (55)
A meteor moving from north to south across the sky, accompanied by thundering, and even one that remains stationary, portends nothing but destruction for her. (56)
Even though the sacred tree at the shrine of Catvara has been uprooted by the wind, it nonetheless portends a great slaughter of the people of Kāśī. (57)
At dawn, with the rising of the sun, if a crow cries out toward the east, there will be danger;
furthermore, two wild deer have entered the midst of Kāśī. (58)
Having diverted the gaze of the people, they departed as omens of the city's desolation;
for in autumn, mango and *śāla* flowers and fruit-sprouts are seen—methinks there is a great and untimely danger threatening this city. (59)
Having thus produced terror, Gaṇeśa, the twice-born,
indeed caused even the wealthy, the lords of the earth, and the heads of families to be driven away.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara’s Dispatching of the Forty-two Gaṇas and Gaṇeśa, and the Expulsion of the People from Kāśī by Means of Various Dreams, Direct Perceptions, Omens, and Portents," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which occurred in the past for the sake of inspiring confidence in women; having understood the situation through his meditative absorption, Gaṇeśa indeed entered the inner apartments.
Speaking only of matters already perceived, he became a source of trust for women;
whatever had previously occurred, he would recount it all. (2)
Having approached one [woman], he begot ninety-three sons;
among them, one was born from you, and having fallen from a horse, he died.
"By good fortune, this pregnant woman will give birth to an auspicious daughter;
whereas she was unfortunate until now, she has now become truly blessed. (4)
"She to whom this most beautiful pearl necklace was given by the king—she indeed is to be honored among the queens, for she is like you, O Queen, as if she were your very life. (5)
The king repeatedly considered this woman, who was the object of much affection;
however, he declared that two villages were to be granted to her as a favor.
Then the prince said to another queen: "If a son is born, I shall indeed grant you ten villages for your livelihood."
"Thus has it been promised by the king on his bed in your presence;
but then he spoke another word: 'If you, O good son, would be [so disposed]...'"
"I shall grant you half the kingdom," he said to Suputrā;
then, at a time of affection for another woman, the king spoke words intended for me.
"Give me that betel which you have preserved, and I shall grant you the three cities"—
thus did the Lord of the Gaṇas speak to him who had appeared before his very eyes.
He even spoke of his dreams to them, and thus he became an object of their trust; moreover, the queens describe his many virtues in his absence.
"Oh! There is indeed a certain venerable brahmin who discerns the truth;
he speaks of the past events exactly as they occurred, according to all authoritative means of knowledge. (12)

Free from greed, of virtuous conduct, contented, and perceiving the past and future; with a serene countenance, pure, and proficient in the scriptures, the Vedas, and the legal codes (Smṛtis). || 13 ||
Whatever he speaks by means of his light, all that proceeds as truth;
he is not like a speaker of dreams, for he is a direct speaker whose vision is before his eyes.
O Great King, Queen Līlāvatī herself, the consort of Divodāsa, spoke to the king: "The Brahmin is a treasure-house equal to Brahmā. (15)
Someone has arrived at Kāśī to be seen for the awakening of the planets;
what is his planetary period (daśā), what kind of dream did he have, what is the time, and what is the omen? || 16 ||
"He knows everything; therefore, whatever is to happen must indeed be asked of him.
Having heard this, the King then summoned the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Having arrived at the royal sage and received hospitality from him,
he sat down upon a seat and greeted him with blessings.
May there be security and well-being for you, as well as spiritual excellence and worldly prosperity; may dharma be auspicious for you, and may your dwelling be in the palace of Hari.
And having heard him, the king said to that brahmin: "O twice-born one, has well-guarded security been obtained? Where on earth is there peace that brings happiness? (20)
"May all that go to dissolution in *laṃ*; such is your heart's desire.
May there be welfare, prosperity, and auspiciousness for me and for the sake of Śivā. (21)
"May even that which is prosperity and auspiciousness become unrighteousness;
may the kingdom of Śiva be in my palace, and may liberation from Hari be mine. (22)
"O best of the twice-born, what do you desire from me regarding my destruction from this place?
Having learned of Divodāsa’s omniscience, he was struck with wonder. (23)
Having gathered those worthy of honor, Gaṇeśa returned to his own abode.
Then the king said to the queen, "This brahmin is a seer of the three periods of time."
The subjects flee to other lands; dreams appear terrifying;
a clamor is heard; and a state of being on the verge of imminent destruction prevails. (25)
Having summoned him in the morning, he should be clearly asked, "What will happen?
I believe that even Lord Śaṅkara has become adverse to me and is no longer a bringer of peace.
"Whatever is destined to be, that shall surely come to pass, even by the will of Nārāyaṇa.
Having summoned him in the morning and honored him, the king asked what was on his heart.
Having ruled this entire earth, I have enjoyed pleasures and prosperities;
indeed, the kingdom and its subjects were protected by me, free from sloth, as if they were my own life. (28)
My service to the twice-born has been performed completely; nothing remains for me to do.
Indeed, having observed the flight of my subjects and their wickedness even in sleep, [I am satisfied].
"Stupefied by the thought, 'What will happen?', I have come to see you; tell me the truth.
Gaṇeśa replied, "Kings, for the most part, are flatterers of the ears. (30)
People listen with delight to what is sweet, yet they punish the speaker of the bitter;
I, however, speak both the sweet and the bitter truth—let it be endured. (3.1)
Valiant, fortunate, heroic, renowned, meritorious, and highly intelligent—there is no one even among the lords of the thirty gods in heaven who is like you. ||32||
In wisdom you are equal to a preceptor, and in graciousness you are like the moon;
in splendor you are equal to the sun, and in majesty you are like fire. (32)
In strength you are equal to Vāyu, in splendor like Kubera;
you are a lord like Rudra, and in battle like Nirṛti.
In your noose you are Varuṇa, and in your staff you are Yama, the Lord of Justice;
through forbearance you are like the earth, and through your sense of propriety you are the Lord of Rivers.
In greatness you are indeed Himavat, and Śukra in the statesmanship of the king;
you are like Manu as a sovereign, and are considered a cloud that dispels the heat.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Those roaring Asuras, led by Śatakoṭi and accompanied by their powerful army, began to challenge the gods in battle.
They indeed fled from those gods who possessed great strength and prowess.
Assuming their own respective forms, they arrived by the thousands.
Some had made their own beds out of tigers, while others rode upon the backs of buffaloes.
Some were mounted on horses, while others stood upon the backs of elephants.
Likewise, some were mounted upon lions, while others had śarabhas as their vehicles.
Some were mounted upon vultures, and some were seated upon the backs of tigers.
Some have vehicles consisting of cranes, peacocks, swans, crows, and the like; others ride upon crocodiles, tortoises, camels, horses, donkeys, and jackals.
Thus, some have vehicles fashioned from cattle, while others have obtained mounts upon the backs of birds.
Likewise, there are those who sit upon the backs of creatures moving through water, space, and so forth. ||16||
Many foot soldiers, equipped with swords, spears, and double-edged blades in their hands, were stationed there upon chariots, mechanical engines, carts, and fire-vehicles.
With spears, nooses, iron clubs, tridents, and mallets in their hands, and bearing earth-missiles, daggers, swords, maces, discs, and arrows as weapons;
[they attacked] the celestial chariots, elephants, and likewise the chariots and horses. ||8||
There, the armies of the foot-soldiers, led by Bali, numbered in the tens of millions.
Then, competing with one another and roaring at each other,
the warriors stood firm, highly enraged, invincible, and eager for battle.
And they said: "One should never place trust in those of evil intent."
One should not place trust in those who have previously been one's enemies, even if they are now people seeking their own self-interest.
He who places his trust in an enemy shall carry the ocean of suffering upon his head;
for in former times, the gods were repeatedly befriended by the dānavas. (12)
Furthermore, it is they alone who have repeatedly practiced deceit;
nectar has not been given to us to drink, nor is even a small portion being granted. (13)
Therefore, their destruction must be accomplished through battle; from that, immortality [shall be attained].
And we shall enjoy the kingdom of heaven, won by us through our own battle. ||14||
They adorned the battlefield with banners, parasols, and flags,
as well as with yak-tail whisks, kettledrums, conchs, trumpets, and double-reed flutes.
In the same way, all the gods, headed by Indra, having gone to the battlefield and drunk the nectar, those illustrious ones donned their armor and mounted their mounts.
Endowed with their respective powers, they were fiercely intent upon the Daityas.
And Mahendra was mounted upon an elephant, while Sūrya was seated upon Uccaiḥśravas. ||17||
Just as the Moon is mounted upon a hare, so too Yama is seated upon a buffalo.
Nairṛta stands upon the back of a preta, and Varuṇa is situated upon a makara. ||18||
Pavana, however, was mounted upon a deer, and Śiva likewise was mounted upon a bull.
Kubera, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, as well as other powerful gods, [were present]. ||19||
Hundreds of thousands were situated in celestial chariots, and likewise, tens of millions were situated upon birds.
For there are tens of millions of Arbudas who stand as vehicles for cattle, deer, and other such animals. ||1.93.20||
All the gods, filled with their respective pride, were possessed by haste.
Enveloped by parasols and chowries, they were graced with the splendor of victory. ||21||
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu in the battle, the Daityas stood ready for combat;
all those Asuras there were formidable, as were the gods of terrifying prowess.
A terrible battle took place between them and the Daityas, Dānavas, and Nākis.
Extremely terrible, causing great destruction, and bringing fear to all living beings. ||23||
Raining down arrows, striking with weapons, and hurling missiles, it was terrifying;

Struck by javelins, spears, and iron arrows, some fell to the earth;
yet others, while being thus slaughtered, attained meditative absorption (samādhi) there.
Some were broken by *bhallas*, others fell down shattered by *nārācas*;
some were struck by *kṣuras* and others were crushed by *mudgaras*. ||26||
They were shattered by blows from weapons and mangled by the falling of arrows.
The army of the Daityas was shattered by the great Māras, and the gods rejoiced. ||27||
Making sounds from their conch shells, they signaled their victory.
Those mighty Dānavas, filled with indignation toward the gods, [prepared for battle]. ||28||
Bali and all the others rose up once more with great exertion.
Accompanied by many aerial chariots that resembled the sun, they were filled with haste. ||29||
A battle in pairs took place between those gods and the asuras.
Then Mahendra fought with the powerful lord of the Dānavas.
Yama was with Namuci, Nairṛta with Praghasa, Varuṇa with Kumbha, and Samīraṇa with Nikumbha. ||31||
Kubera was struck by Sudaṃṣṭra, while the remaining [demons] were struck by the remaining [gods].
Seeing Rāhu and Ketu approaching, the gods fled. ||32||
With his banner, he opened wide his mouth, which was like the sky, for the purpose of devouring the gods; then the gods fled in all directions.
Some remembered Hari, while others remembered Vināyaka with devotion.
Some [worship] Durgā, others Śambhu, and still others Brahmā and Amṛta.
Placing Rāhu at their head, the Daityas, intent on victory and exceedingly fierce, struck the gods with weapons, missiles, stones, and other such things.
Then the gods fled and the Daityas achieved victory;
at that time, Ketu first opened his own mouth wide to swallow Hari.
He became intent upon [seizing] the moon and likewise the sun as each approached him, thinking, "This one is immortal; he cannot be destroyed even by the thunderbolt."
Then Candra, running with palms joined in reverence, praised Mahādeva:
"O Śambhu, O God, protector of those who seek refuge, save me! (38)
Protect all the gods and likewise destroy the suffering caused by ill omens.
Thus entreated, Śambhu said to his sons, "Do not fear."
Indeed, as soon as the comet arrived there with the intent to devour the moon,
it was seized by Śambhu and strung upon his garlands of severed heads.
Ketū, having assumed two forms, departed from that place toward the heavens.
Then, placing Śambhu at their head, the gods set their minds on battle.
The Daityas were being struck by the gods with weapons, missiles, arrows, and lances.
Many fell there, wounded, broken, and mangled. ||42||
The dead Daityas turned the earth into a mire of flesh and blood.
There, rivers flow carrying the corpses of Dānavas, inspiring terror.
And the tops of standards, mechanical devices, banners, elephants, and horses.
And bottomless rivers of blood flow upon the field of battle. ||44||
Thus, in that most terrible encounter between the gods and the asuras,
The indignant son of Virocana struck the lord of the gods with his spear.
Having deceived that power, Indra instantly struck Bali with his thunderbolt.

And furthermore, with his thunderbolt, he struck down Vṛṣaparvan as well.
There too, he struck again and again with a hundred-edged vajra.

They were torn asunder by Yama, Vāyu, Varuṇa, and likewise Agni; by Nairṛta, Kubera, and even by Śambhu. ||49||
Having thus witnessed this carnage, the great asura Kālanemi—
seated upon a lion, clad in armor, fierce, and equipped with a trident— [advanced].

"What shall we all do now? How shall we conquer the Asuras?

"I am the very foundation of the gods; remain steadfast for the sake of a good death. (57)

He fought with Viṣṇu, who holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand and is accompanied by Garuḍa.
Then, by Garuḍa with his weapons—the beak, wings, claws, and so forth—
The Daityas were torn apart, mangled, and destroyed like lions. ||59||
Slain and shattered into pieces by Viṣṇu with his own discus,
the powerful Kālanemi struck Viṣṇu with his trident.
Grasping that trident effortlessly with his left hand,
