Then, having fainted and fallen, he rose and opened his eyes;
seizing his sword, he rushed toward Viṣṇu, but at that moment, by Viṣṇu—
Indeed, at that very moment, his head was severed by the discus.
But other Daityas were slain by the gods, destroyed, and brought to ruin. ||63||
The Daitya Kālanemi was slain, and the gods became truly free from thorns.
Viṣṇu had vanished from sight; thereupon Indra showed him compassion.
Hari restored to health those who were fallen, eunuchs, broken, terrified in heart, and those whose loincloths and topknots had been loosened.
Then Hari, accompanied by the host of gods, returned to the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa.
All the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras became joyful. ||66||
The celestial sages and the brahmin-sages said, "Let Indra be consecrated."
He himself was consecrated as Indra in Amarāvatī, accompanied by Śacī.
Then, O Lakṣmī, a supreme great festival took place in the world of the gods.
Conches, kettledrums, clay drums, large drums, lutes, and horns [resounded]. ||68||
Kettledrums, tabors, and trumpets resounded in every house in heaven.
And all the singers, as well as the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, sang. ||69||
Then the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and Ṛṣis offered praise, and the hosts of Apsarases danced; there was a festival at every spot.
Śukrācārya, the preceptor of the Daityas, having heard of his destruction, had gone to the Mānasottara mountain for the sake of penance; [the enemy], however, went to the field of battle. (71)
By means of the Saṃjīvanī lore, he restored the dead Daityas to life.
Just as those Asuras then arose when their sleep had passed away. ||7||
They all also went happily to Pātāla for the purpose of dwelling there.
By obtaining the drink of nectar, the gods indeed did not die.
The Blessed One restored the mounts and other things to life even by his mere will.
Thus, O Goddess, the churning of the ocean took place in ancient times.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "Description of the Battle between the Gods and Asuras Arising from the Division over the Drinking of Nectar, the Coronation of Indra, and Other Events," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Nārāyaṇa, tell me how, by whom, and when was the worship of Gaṇeśa first established, bypassing you indeed? (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this delightful narrative which bestows the realization of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s true nature;
he is indeed a partial incarnation (aṃśa) of Kṛṣṇacandra and likewise not born from a womb.
Mahālakṣmī herself, who is Māyā, became the daughter of Dakṣa.
And she, though Satī by name, [was consumed] by the censure of Śambhu on account of her being Dakṣa’s daughter.
Having cast off her body, Pārvatī was born from Himālaya through Menakā;
the Mountain joyfully gave that daughter to Śaṅkara.
Having taken her, Mahādeva went to a solitary forest.
While the two of them were always dwelling in a cottage suitable for the life of a householder, || 5 ||
For a period of a thousand years, there was indeed the pleasure of amorous dalliance;
for the gods, birth from a womb no longer occurred, nor did it happen for their sons.
Due to not obtaining a son, no happiness whatsoever arose for Pārvatī;
as day after day passed, her longing for a son increased.
The fruit of sexual union is pleasure, for indeed both [pleasure and offspring] may arise from it.
Without the fruit of a son, joy in old age becomes a source of suffering. || 8 ||
Pleasure devoid of a son leads only to future agitation.
Without offspring, by what means indeed should a woman pass the time? (9)
In dalliance with her husband, the passing of time becomes very brief.
In this world, the offspring of women born at any other time than that would be a sign of misfortune.
In his nurturing and protection, and in activities such as playing with toys and the like.
The time that passes for women is said to be heaven itself. ||11||
The first is the happiness of one's master; the second is heaven born of one's limbs;
the third is heaven produced by wealth and grain, which brings the joy of offspring.
The fourth, however, is heaven; the fifth is health, and the sixth is fame.
Indeed, these alone are the worldly pleasures that constitute the heavens. 13.
Thus, constantly filled with such thoughts, she took delight with her own husband;
Śambhu, perceiving her heart's intent, questioned that devoted wife.
"What do you always desire, my beloved? What dwells in your mind? What indeed are you contemplating during our dalliance? Speak, and I shall fulfill your wish. (15)
Pārvatī said: "O Lord of Gods, what is lacking for me in your presence?
For I have obtained one who is the creator and the bestower of everything upon all the worlds. (16)
Wherever the Blessed One dwells, there shall be abundant prosperity; there shall be no deficiency, nor any lack of peace, nor any loss of cherished objects. (17)
After the menstrual period, however, the husband is most dear to women, and after him, the son.
Although I have obtained a husband who is the lord of the three worlds, I have no son.
The desire for a son awakens in my heart at the sight of you;
O Lord of Gods, whenever I behold you, then and there [that longing arises]. (19)
A false resolve arises from delusion, through power, and by means of receiving the first honor.
"When will a son be born to me who is equal to a husband? ||1.94.20||
For beloved ones, separation from their beloved is said to be the first suffering.
If there is no delight in a beloved being, it is said to be the second kind of suffering. ||21||
And the third sorrow, exceeding all others, is childlessness.
Although I have obtained you, who are beloved by the three worlds, as my husband, I still have no son. ||22||
The life of a woman who is bereft of sons is meaningless;
[yet] merit performed in previous births through austerity, charity, recitation, and other such acts [remains]. (23)
Then a son shall be born who bestows happiness both in this world and the next;
a good son is a portion of his own father, granting him happiness equal to that of his father. (24)
But a bad son is a brand to his family, resulting only in mental anguish.
Therefore, people pray: "May I have a virtuous son. ||25||
The lord shall certainly take birth through a portion of himself in the womb of virtuous women.
A virtuous wife is like a mother and is always well-wishing. ||26||
"Unchaste, like an enemy, and constantly causing me torment—what remedy shall I employ? Tell me, O bestower of the fruit of sons! (27)
When the goddess Pārvatī had spoken thus, she then became silent.
Laughing, the god Śaṅkara enlightened Pārvatī.
Listen, Pārvatī, I shall speak; it will be for your welfare.
Indeed, for everyone, the accomplishment of their task arises through diligent effort. ||29||
I shall tell you the heart-pleasing method that bestows all accomplishments.
Having performed the worship of Hari, O fair-faced one, observe the vow.
For one year, you shall observe that vow known as the Puṇyaka-vrata.
This vow is a wish-fulfilling kalpa-tree that bestows happiness and grants sons. ||31||
That meritorious vow of Hari is the most excellent among all vows,
just as the Gaṅgā is the best of rivers and just as Hari is indeed the foremost among the gods.
Just as I am among the Vaiṣṇavas, so are you, O great virtuous lady, among goddesses.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the best among the social classes, so Puṣkara is the best among sacred fords. ||33||
Among flowers, the Pārijāta; and among leaves, the Tulasī leaf.
Among lunar days, Ekādaśī is the most excellent; among the days of the week, Sunday is the best.
Among months it is Mārgaśīrṣa; among all seasons it is spring; among years it is the year [of the Kṛta age]; and among the ages it is the Kṛta, the most excellent. (35)

Just as a wise man maintains no inner distance toward those worthy of worship, nor toward his mother or elders, nor does a wife maintain any inner distance toward those who act for her benefit or those she trusts; (36)
Just as jewels are among riches, and as a husband is among beloveds;
Just as a virtuous son is among kinsmen, so is the wish-fulfilling tree among trees. ||37||
Likewise, the vow dedicated to Hari is the most excellent among all vows and is meritorious.
Just as the mango fruit is the best among fruits, and Vṛndāvana is the best among forests. ||38||
Just as Śatarūpā is among women, and Urvaśī is among the Apsarases;
Just as Kamalā is among mothers, and the Sun is the best among those possessing splendor. ||39||
Among those who give delight he is the moon, and among the beautiful he is the god of love;
among the most excellent he is the Vedas, and among the perfected ones (siddhas) he is like Kapila.
Just as knowledge is supreme among glories, as a sovereign is supreme among pervasive rulers, as the eye is the best among limbs, so is truth the most excellent among meritorious deeds. (41)
Austerity is service to Śrī Hari; among products of the cow, ghee is supreme.
Among foods, the fire-god Agni considers nectar (amṛta) to be the most excellent, provided it is pure. ||42||
Just as gold among luminous things, sweet speech among pleasant things, Garuḍa among birds, and Airāvata among elephants; ||43||
Likewise, the vow of Hari is the most excellent among all vows and is meritorious.
Among the celestial sages, there is Nārada; and among the yogis, Sanaka and the others. ||44||
Among the Gandharvas he was like Citraratha, among the principles of reality like Consciousness, among poets like Śukra, and among those possessing forbearance like the Earth. (45)
Among gains, liberation is indeed the best; among prosperities, devotion is supreme;
as the virtuous man is among the pure, and as the syllable Om is among the castes. 46.
Among mantras, the mantra of Śrī Hari is supreme, just as the wish-fulfilling cow is among cows;
among the Vedas, the Sāmaveda is supreme, and among blades of grass, the kuśa is the best. (47)
Just as knowledge is among all forms of happiness, as Vāsuki is among serpents, as the letter *a* is among syllables, so is my father among those who wish one's welfare. (48)
As the lion is among quadrupeds, as Śālagrāma is among images, as intellect is among the sense organs, and as Hari is among those possessing power; 49.
Among perishable things, the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is the smallest; among givers, Dadhīci is the best.
Just as the Brahmāstra is foremost among weapons, and the Sudarśana among discuses; ||1.94.50||
Just as Kṛṣṇa is the essence of all things, so is the Puṇyaka among vows;
O Great Goddess, quickly perform this vow which bestows one's own desired object. 51.
Your son shall indeed become the most excellent of all through this very vow;
Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Lord and Sovereign of Goloka, is to be propitiated by means of vows.
When he is pleased, that giver of all things bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
by serving him, a person is released from bondage along with ten million ancestors.
Having delivered ten million persons, he attains happiness in Goloka.
[He should protect] his brothers, servants, companions, dependents, women, sons, and so forth. ||54||
A devotee of Kṛṣṇa, having been uplifted, goes happily to the abode of Hari.
Therefore, O Girijā, accept this supreme mantra-vow of Hari.
"Observe the vow and recite the mantra; success will soon be yours.
Having said this, he took water and bestowed the excellent mantra upon the goddess. (56)
Śambhu whispered the mantra into the ear of Girijā on his left;
Pārvatī, however, meditated upon that mantra being given in her heart as follows: ||57||
Oṃ, salutations to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, who assumes the form of a husband;
to the seed, to the one in the form of an embryo, to the one in the form of offspring, and to Śambhu. ||58||
Salutations to the one whose heart contains the seed of all intentions, and salutations to the bestower of sons;
salutations to the conqueror whose form is worthy of foremost worship—grant me a virtuous son! (59)
Grant me a son who is all-conquering and worthy of being honored above all.
O Kṛṣṇa, this meritorious vow is being performed for your pleasure.
May that [undertaking] be free from obstacles and fruitful; O giver of sons, be present in the form of my son.
Grant me a son equal to you who shall live for a long time; salutations, salutations! ||61||
O virtuous lady, having received this mantra from Haradatta,
Śambhu went with Pārvatī to the purifying bank of the Jāhnavī.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Bestowal of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, Accompanied by Many Illustrative Examples, Given by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī Who Desired a Son," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard what was to be done for the vow, Pārvatī, with a joyful mind,
again asked Śaṅkara about the entire procedure for the vow.
O Lord, that meritorious vow has been performed by me together with its prescribed observances.
In what manner should it be performed, and what materials are required therein? || 2 ||
Let it be considered that other fruits may also be given;
whatever object is required, provide and arrange that. (3)
He is considered the lord of women who observe vows, the bestower of all their goals.
The father always protects his daughter during her maidenhood. || 4 ||
The lord of the ascendant is the ruler in youth, whereas in old age, the sons and others are the rulers.
The father, having given his daughter, who was as dear to him as his own life, to a virtuous husband, became happy.
A husband, having entrusted his wife to his own sons, may indeed live in happiness.
Thus, a woman who possesses these three myriads is considered fortunate in this world.
One devoid of a single [of these] is mediocre; one lacking all of them is miserable.
One protected by these is fortunate; another, who merely relies on her husband, is censurable.
But my youth, which was fit for protecting my father, has passed away.
Moreover, youth suitable for protecting one's husband will soon pass away.
But without a son, who will provide protection for me in my old age?
Therefore, O Protector, grant me a son who will be the cause of my liberation. 9 ||
Indeed, in the presence of the Omniscient One, even erudition appears turbid.
I have nothing else to ask of you, O giver of sons, except for your great compassion.
Having heard this from Pārvatī, Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī.
Listen, O Goddess: through the Kṛṣṇa-vow, one's heart's desire shall become fruitful. ||11||
O beloved, the commencement of the vow on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is auspicious.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the vow shall reach its completion.
This meritorious vow, lasting for one year, brings satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa.
This must be performed according to the prescribed rite by a woman desiring a son.
Having fasted on the twelfth day, preceded by the consecration of the head.
Having performed purification of the body and purification of the garments, one should remember Hari at night.
Having risen from his bed during the Brahma-muhūrta, which follows sleep, he should remember Hari and perform purification, the cleaning of the teeth, bathing, and so forth. (15)
Having performed these acts and sipped water, he should offer the arghya-water to Hari and present two washed garments.
Then, having held [the vessel] and sat down, one should again perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) with sandalwood paste.
Having applied a drop or a sectarian mark made of saffron, one should meditate upon Hari;
having performed his daily and obligatory rites, he should choose an excellent family priest.
Having placed the water-pot according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions.
Having caused the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) prescribed by the Vedas to be performed, he should observe the vow.
Lord Hari himself is to be worshipped with the sixteen services:
invocation, the seat, water for the feet, and the respectful offering (arghya) thereafter. (19)

Likewise, the sipping of water (ācamana), the bath, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), as well as clothing, sandalwood paste, ornaments, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering (nivedana). || 1.95.20 ||
The sacred thread and betel leaf should also be offered with a spirit of devotion.
In that regard, one must not perform it deficiently, for that causes a loss of the fruit. ||21||
Gifts should be given according to one's capacity to Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu. Listen as I describe what specific attainment results from each particular gift. 22.
A flower of the Pārijāta tree should be offered for the sake of a beautiful form;
a white campaka flower should be offered for the sake of beauty.
A lotus should be given to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of the splendor of his face;
a mirror rich with jewels should be given for the sake of the brilliance of his eyes. (24)
Likewise, a blue lotus should be given for the sake of the beauty of the eyes;
a white chowrie, however, should be given for the sake of the beauty of the hair. (25)
A small box adorned with jewels should be given for the sake of enhancing the beauty of the nose.
When Bandhūka flowers are given, it causes one's own lips to become red. || 26 ||
Pearls should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the teeth;
jeweled mouthfuls should be given for the sake of the beauty of the cheeks. (27)
Likewise, jewel-nooses should be offered well for the sake of the chin.
And earrings adorned with jewels should be given as an offering for the sake of beautiful ears. (28)
Honey-wine and sugar-cane wine should be given for the sake of sweetness of voice.
Sweet nectar should be given for the sake of sweetness of speech. ||29||
A jewel-lamp should be given for the sake of the purity of vision;
water-vessels and the like should be given for the sake of strengthening one's power.
Lotus stalks should be given for the sake of strengthening the arms.
Red lotuses should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the hands. ||31||
Finger-rings should be given for the sake of the beauty of the fingers;
white gems should be given for the sake of the beauty of the nails. (32)
Likewise, jeweled necklaces should be given for the sake of the beauty of her chest;
and when they are ripe, auspicious fruits should be offered to him for the sake of the beauty of her breasts.
Likewise, a gold leaf should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the body.
A navel made of jewels was given for the sake of the beauty of the navel.
Two wheels inlaid with jewels should be given to one who has beautiful hips.
And pillars of plantain should be offered for the sake of the beauty of the hips. ||35||
Land-lotuses should be offered for the sake of the beauty of one's feet.
Golden fish should be given as gifts for the sake of removing fickleness of movement.
Golden swans and lordly elephants should be given as gifts for the sake of a good rebirth;
and a golden parasol should be given for the sake of the beauty of one's head. (37)
A *mālatī* flower should be offered for the sake of inducing gentle smiles and the like.
These priceless jewels should be given for the fulfillment of the vow and the attainment of happiness. ||38||
Pure crystal gems should be given for the sake of the tranquility of the mind.
Coral gems should be given for the increase of the beloved's passion. ||39||
Māṇikya gems should be given for the sake of the master’s good fortune,
as well as a pumpkin, a nine-colored object, a citron, and a bilva fruit.
These should be given to Harikṛṣṇa during worship for the sake of obtaining a son.
Precious gems should be given to the master for the increase of his wealth. ||41||
For the sake of increasing prosperity, one should have instrumental music played and cause Śrī Hari to be heard during the vow;
likewise, one should offer milk-rice, flour-cakes, clarified butter, sugar, and saffron.
These should be offered with devotion to Hari for the increase of his master’s enjoyments.
Flower garlands should be offered to Hari for the sake of increasing devotion. ||43||
Sweet-tasting food offerings should be given for the attainment of sweet foods; Tulasī leaves and flowers should be offered for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa. (44)
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, and the destitute for the increase of crops.
Offerings of handfuls of flowers and prostrations should be performed for the increase of devotion. ||45||
Remaining established in the vow, she should eat sacrificial food for six months, fruits and the like for five months, clarified butter for a fortnight, and milk for a fortnight.
One should maintain an unbroken lamp before Acyuta for the duration of a year.
One should always sit upon a seat of kusha grass and practice the vigil at midnight. ||47||
The holy life (brahmacarya) must always be observed for the sake of attaining the fruit of the vow.
But if there is an injury, an expiation must be performed: a fast and one hundred and eight recitations. ||48||
A vow of unbroken observance should be undertaken for the sake of attaining perfection;
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, that great festival should be celebrated. (49)
According to one's capacity, gold and silver coins should be given,
as well as three hundred and sixty garments, and an equal number of silver pieces.
There should be that many gold coins, and that many portions of food for the sages.
An oblation of sesame seeds should be performed three hundred and sixty times.
This is the daily duty, or it must certainly be performed at the end of the year.
The son shall be equal to Hari, a conqueror, and indeed worthy of the highest honor. ||52||
Through the power of this vow, beauty, supreme good fortune, sovereignty, abundant wealth, and the accomplishment of all desired goals arise for her. (53)
At the conclusion of the vow, she may enjoy her husband's bed, but not in the interval between vows;
during the year of the vow, a woman must never engage in sexual intercourse.
If one engages in sexual pleasure during the midst of a vow, the vow will be broken;
therefore, the failure to engage in intercourse during the fertile period (ṛtukāla) is here considered a fault, whereas [engaging at other times] is an ornament.
"O Maheśvarī, perform this single vow for one year;
O Pārvatī, let there be a son for me who is not born from a womb. (56)

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Annual Vow Named Puṇyaka for the Sake of a Son and the Description of the Gifts to be Given," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śvetavyāsa said: O Suśikha, Śaṅkara spoke of an ancient event concerning the Goddess of the Gods:
"Śatarūpā, the wife of Vaivasvata Manu, was indeed childless. (1)
He grieved that his birth, wealth, and even his sovereignty were fruitless;
for the opulent home of householders does not shine without a son. ||2||
The merit arising from austerity and charity performed in previous lives shall manifest for men as the sight of the faces of their daughters and sons. || 3 ||
Furthermore, the fruit resulting from a son is traditionally held to be deliverance from the hell named Punnāma.
Even those sages who possess nothing desire a good disciple in a most auspicious place.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself does not remain without a disciple.
For one without a wife, a disciple is indeed a son; for one with a wife, a son is wealth.
The sons of Menā and Śukā and others were born to those who were perpetually barren and widowed;
therefore, for one without a son, the life of an ascetic is better.
Kingdom, noble lineage, and prosperity are all meaningless without a son.
Men do not look upon the faces of those who have no sons at dawn.
One who has no son experiences shame when attempting to show his face.
Thus, tormented by grief, she then informed Brahmā.
Brahmā said: Listen, my child, to the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha;
from that time forward for a year, it is fit for this meritorious vow.
"Perform the vow exactly as instructed, and you shall obtain a son equal to Viṣṇu. At these words of Brahmā, she performed the vow according to the prescribed rite.
Devahūti, having performed her vows and received a boon from Nārāyaṇa, obtained two charming sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.
He obtained as his son Kapila, a perfected sage who was a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed the Arundhatī vow, she obtained a son named Śakti.
Śakti’s beloved wife, having performed a vow, obtained a son, Parāśara;
and Aditi, having performed a vow, obtained a son, Vāmana. ||13||
Śacī also, having observed this vow, indeed obtained a son, Jayanta;
and the wife of Uttānapāda, having performed this, obtained Dhruva as her son.
Anasūyā, having performed a vow, obtained the auspicious Candra as her son;
likewise, Bṛhaspati was indeed obtained by the wife of Aṅgiras through a vow.
Khyāti, having performed a vow for Bhṛgu, obtained Śukra as her auspicious son;
likewise, by the power of that vow, Nārāyaṇa himself became his son. (16)
Born in the house of Kambharā, he shall become your son.
Having spoken thus to the Queen of the Gods and having given her abundant wealth and many attendants. ||17||
Having explained the means of accomplishment, Śiva established himself in meditation, intent upon the worship of Hari and contemplating the ocean of the bliss of knowledge. ||18||
Then Pārvatī, having brought all the necessary materials for the sake of her vow,
chose the brahmin Sanatkumāra for the performance of the rite.
The lords of the gods arrived, having learned of the great festival of the vow;
Brahmā came with his wife, four-armed and accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Then, leaving his meditation, Śambhu came to the place of the vow.
Sanaka, Sananda, Kapila, and Sanātana; ||21||
Āsuri, Kratu, Haṃsa, Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, and Aruṇi.
Yati, Vaśiṣṭha, Sumati, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Bhṛgu. ||22||
Agastya, Atri, Aṅgiras, Durvāsas, Cyavana, Patnīvrata, Pracetas, Kaṇva, Marīci, and Kaśyapa; 23.
Gautama, Jaratkāru, Bṛhaspati, and Saubhari;
Utathya, Jamadagni, Jaigīṣavya, and Devala; ||24||
Saṃvarta, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Pāribhadra, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Lomaśa; ||25||
Gokarṇa, Mṛkaṇḍu, Puṣkara, and Pippalāyana.
Kautsa, Dvīta, Ekata, Trīta, Vatsa, and Lekhana. ||26||
Śaṅkha, Śaṅku, Āpiśali, Svayaṃprakāśa, and Āruṇi.
Dakṣa, Kaṇāda, Bālāgni, Aghamarṣaṇa, and Pāṇini. ||27||
Kātyāyana, Nārada, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa;
those who have taken the vow of Brahman, Mahāśveta, Vyāsa, and other great ṛṣis. ||28||
Gītā, Jayantī, Gāyatrī, Lakṣmī, Vidyā, Sarasvatī, Stuti, Ārādhanā, Pūjā, Bhakti, Nīrājanā, and Ramā. (29)
The Ekādaśīs, the Yoginīs, and also the Sāṃkhyayoginīs; likewise the Sādhvīs, the Vītarāgiṇīs, the Nyāsins, and the Siddhis. (1.96.30)
Mothers, rivers, cities, and likewise various other women.
They arrived there, eager for Pārvatī’s festival of vows. ||31||
Likewise, the guardians of the directions, the gods, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, and the kinnaras.
The Kimpuruṣas and Cāraṇas, as well as the mountains, possessed divine forms. ||32||
The Himalaya, filled with joy, was accompanied by his children and his wife.
He arrived with his retinue, bringing with him materials, jewels, and gems.
Having gathered all the gifts that were there for the vow, he departed.
Those were given to Pārvatī for the complete fulfillment of her vow.
The mountain Anantaratnaprabhava gave much to his daughter;
likewise, the Brahmins, Manus, Siddhas, Nāgas, and Vidyādharas [gave much]. (35)
The virtuous, mendicants, bards, genealogists, and panegyrists.
And there were Vidyādharī women, dancers, and likewise Apsarases who were dancers. ||36||
They came for the sake of pleasing Pārvatī, who was observing her vow.
Blessings were bestowed by them [the men] and by those [women]: "May you be blessed with sons. (37)
Welcome to all; may there be service, food, hospitality, and honor.
Honored by Śambhu, they were all pleased and bestowed auspicious blessings. ||38||

Skanda and Gaṇapati—these two sons bring happiness to their mother and father.
For the sake of their marriage ceremony, Śivā and Śambhu spoke together.
And how should the auspicious marriage of both sons be performed?
The six-faced one was overtaken by his army, and Gaṇeśa was abandoned by me out of affection. ||5||
An auspicious effort should be made for the sake of Gaṇeśa’s marriage;
likewise, Kārttikeya also desires to marry. (6)
This was the heartfelt intention of the Prajāpati Viśvarūpa regarding the giving away of his daughter.
"Two daughters must be given to two [suitors]; therefore, let it be so. (7)
"But it is best that two excellent daughters be given to Gaṇeśa.
Then, having summoned them at some point, they spoke thus. (8)
Listen with affection, my two good sons; I shall speak to you according to the truth.
You, the eldest, are always accompanied by a wife, whereas Gaṇeśa is devoid of a wife.
A rule has indeed been established for the happiness of your marriage:
both sons shall be equal, and no distinction shall be found between them.
Therefore, a wager was made between both sons:
"Whichever of you shall first return after traversing the entire earth [shall win]. (11)
For him alone should first be performed a marriage characterized by auspicious signs.
Having heard these words of his parents, the mighty Kārttikeya [acted].
Mounted upon his peacock vehicle, he departed swiftly from the temple.
For the purpose of circumambulating the earth with great speed. ||13||
Gaṇanātha, having reflected well, remained right there.
But my vehicle does not run at all on the earth. ||14||
Where am I, traveling by the path of the earth, compared to you who travel through the path of the sky?
What is to be done? Where is one to go, while still possessing this gross physical body? (15)
When one has gone only a single *krośa* ahead, one is unable to proceed further due to exhaustion;
how much more so after traversing the entire earth—is the hope for victory not a mere mockery? (16)
Having reflected thus, one should bathe and then enter the house.
Having prostrated before his parents, the Lord Gaṇeśa spoke to them.
The earth is my mother, heaven is my father, and the cow is said to be the universe;
the goddess Pārvatī is my mother, and the Lord Śaṅkara is my father. (18)
The vehicle for those two is a bull; this bull is the king of the Sudharma assembly hall.
The cow is the very form of the earth, my mother, who is the embodiment of Pīlā. (19)
Śaṅkara is my father; his body is considered to be the earth.
I must perform worship for these three in order to successfully accomplish my journey.
And here, for the sake of worshipping you both, a seat has likewise been prepared.
And remain here as my teachers; fulfill what is in your hearts. ||21||
Having heard those words of his, the two [of them] went to receive that worship.
The two of them took their seats, and Gaṇanāyaka honored them.
The son performed seven circumambulations around them with great reverence.
And seven prostrations were also performed; thereafter, [the offering] was presented.
Gaṇeśa said, "O mother, perform my marriage ceremony quickly."
The mother said: "O son, quickly perform a circumambulation of the earth."
Come before the prince; let this be the first marriage.
Gaṇeśa said: "O Mother, listen to my words."
I have traversed the earth seven times over again and again.
The mother said: "When, my son, was the earth traversed by you? (26)
Gaṇeśa said: "I have performed the circumambulation for both of you;
by that, indeed, the entire earth bounded by the oceans has been circumambulated by me. (27)
The Earth is his mother and the Sky is his father; both possess the very nature of Dharma.
Dharma is his vehicle, the bull, while the cow is the object of his desire. 28.
Having spoken thus, he performed a circumambulation of his father, the bull, and his mother;
by that act, a circumambulation of the entire earth was then accomplished.
The parents said: "We are delighted; well done, my son!
By this act, you have obtained the fruit of circumambulating the entire earth."
Through faith Dharma is attained; through faith Hari is attained;
through faith perfection is attained; through faith the fruit is attained. ||31||
The mother and father are the sacred site in the home, and the wife is always the Gaṅgā;
if one has no faith in them, everything done becomes useless. (32)
But he who, having performed the worship of the ancestors, proceeds with the departure rite (prakrānti), [is at fault].
Indeed, for him, the fruit born of traversing the earth is attained. ||33||

He who indeed departs for a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) after abandoning his parents at home shall not partake in the fruit of the pilgrimage; rather, he shall become a partaker in the fault of neglecting them.
In this matter, the lotus-feet of one's parents are a great sacred site for a son;
this proximate sacred site is easily accessible and a means for accomplishing dharma.
The husband is declared to be the sacred ford (tīrtha) for the wife, and likewise, both parents are the sacred ford for the son.
For a devoted wife, the holy fords are indeed her husband; they are truly her means of liberation.
If it is true that circumambulating the earth is always prescribed by the scriptures, then Gaṇeśa has told me so; for the scripture cannot be false. (37)
Devotion to one's father would be false, and all such devotion would be fruitless; likewise, devotion to one's mother and devotion to cows would be entirely fruitless. (38)
Therefore, I have performed the circumambulation of the earth here in every way;
let my auspicious marriage be prepared, for it must take place soon. (39)
Having heard these words of his, his parents were also pleased with him.
They both said, "O son, you are a knower of the scriptures; your intellect follows the path of the scriptures. (1.107.40)
No one is able to alter the boundaries of the scriptures; however, when an inaccessible task presents itself, faith born of the scriptures indeed prevails.
And it is likewise appropriate for one whose intellect is distinguished regarding suffering.
His suffering shall perish through the power of his intellect and wisdom. ||42||
He whose intellect is his strength—how can there be strength for one devoid of intellect?
A lion, intoxicated with pride, was cast into a well by a jackal. (43)
"O son, you have performed this circumambulation of the earth correctly; by treading upon the mother-cows, you have fulfilled the protection of Dharma. (44)
But Kārtika did not come; he ran away with great speed.
On the path ahead, he saw his younger brother going along, mounted upon a mouse.
Since Gaṇeśa performed a circumambulation of his parents, by the merit gained from that act, another form of Gaṇeśa [appeared]. 46.
Having become so, he indeed ran at the head with the speed of Kārttikeya.
But Kārttikeya, having seen that, then grieved most intensely. ||47||
"Aha! This mouse is so very small, while Gaṇeśa there is so large;
with what kind of speed does he run right ahead of me? (48)
By me with peacock feathers, or by Kaśyapa with the wind.
For all [the arrows] have been dropped; he was struck repeatedly for the sake of speed. ||49||
The peacock also, with all his might, now flies upward in that same manner.
Nevertheless, I truly do not encounter Gaṇeśa; who could possibly bypass him?
"Even in a dream, no crossing over or proceeding forward is seen;
therefore, I swear to you that I shall not perform this marriage nor any other. (51)
Having thought thus, he turned back and went to where his own home was;
having become calm and entered, he dispelled the fatigue with his army.
Then the parents exerted themselves for the sake of Gaṇeśa’s marriage.
And waiting for the path of Kārttikeya, they both set out.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Gaṇeśa’s Circumambulation of His Parents and Cows for the Sake of the Fruit of Circumambulating the Earth," within the account of the marriages of Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya, in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; Pārvatī, the mother of the world, being greatly delighted, performed many auspicious rites for the two daughters-in-law who were to become mine. || 1 ||
In the meantime, Prajāpati Viśvarūpa was there.
Having brought his two daughters, who were worthy of being given in marriage, he was indeed impelled by the prescribed rite.
One [daughter] should be given in marriage to Gaṇeśa, the ocean of virtues; the other should be given to Skanda, or else the opinion regarding the maiden is as follows. (3)
Seeing Skanda accompanied by his bride, the two did not choose him;
but seeing Gaṇeśa, the two maidens chose him for his beauty and excellent qualities.
Siddhi and Buddhi both became the two wives of Gaṇeśa.
Then a great festival for the wedding took place, causing exceeding joy.
The gods, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Guhyakas,
and others dwelling in the three worlds, being well-pleased, assembled for that wedding.
The words of the family priest, beginning with "May you two practice dharma together," became fruitful there at the wedding of Gaṇeśa.
Gaṇeśa indeed obtained supreme and constant happiness from those two;
for in this world, the state of being a rival enemy surely gives rise to suffering. || 8 ||
In this world, he whose fortune is shattered shall have two wives;
it is a settled certainty that a man with two wives is as good as half-dead.
Indeed, enemies do not slay him who has died with two wives,
for while one sleeps, the second indeed hates her with anger.
Another woman here performs service, while the first one becomes envious and angry.
For one with two wives, every single moment is considered a house of anger. ||11||
One regards the second as a blade of grass because of the attainment of sons,
yet the first indeed regards the second as a blade of grass because of the attainment of wealth.
One excellence of beauty does not cause the second to cease its festivities;
the second excellence of affection causes the first to be disparaged. 13.
In sleeping, eating, traveling, amorous play, wearing clothes, in gestures, expressions, pride, and in festivals—these two lead to hell. (14)
If, even there, they are with women of the crow species or the dog species,
then indeed those two shall go directly to the hell named Kumbhīpāka.
If both wives are present at the time of conception, then there shall be no suffering whatsoever; that house is considered worthy of the name "heaven."
Mutually assisting one another, equal in their experience of pleasure and pain, and bestowing gifts upon each other, they do not remain apart from one another. (17)
They did not differ from one another in their internal disposition, for they shared a single purpose and a single mind;
they assisted one another, being equal in their conduct, vows, and aspirations. (18)
In their offspring they share a single state, and likewise a single purpose;
there, the husband enjoys the bliss of heaven, delighted by those two.
Siddhi and Buddhi, both such as these, became the two wives of Śaṃda;
and after some time had passed for the high-souled Gaṇeśa, [the following occurred].
From Siddhi, the wife of Gaṇeśa, a son named Kṣema was born;
from Buddhi, a beautiful son named Lābha was born. (21)
Then the illustrious Nārada came to the wonderful abode of Skanda and said:
"I speak from no malice; this is neither untrue nor deceptive."
"Nothing else will ever be done for you as has been done by your parents;
having cast you out, they performed such a circumambulation while feigning indifference. (23)
Since Gaṇeśa performed his marriage with two women, that Gaṇeśa obtained two auspicious sons from those two wives. (24)
Only with the consent of his parents does he enjoy happiness continuously;
yet by you, through deceitful acts toward them, the earth has been traversed.
If even a mother or a father deceives their own son through deceitful means,
what can be said of other people regarding such deceitful conduct?
"Indeed, that deed was performed improperly by those two, your ancestors;
you too should reflect upon this here, for it is not considered auspicious in my mind. (27)
If a mother were to give poison, if a father were to sell [one], and if the king seizes all one's possessions—who else would be a protector? (28)
Who that is peaceful and wise would dwell in the house of such a father, by whom this deed born of partiality toward his own son was committed? (29)
"Thus has this policy been declared by me; do as you wish.
Having spoken thus, Nārada departed from there for Satyapura.
Then Skanda, overcome with grief and agitation, departed from his home;
having gone forth, he bowed to his parents, filled with wrath. ||3.1||
He went to Mount Krauñca, even though he was forbidden by his parents, thinking:
"If such deceit has been practiced toward me under the guise of affection," ||32||
The auspicious rites for Gaṇeśa were performed with ease;
however, I was then driven out from my home for the sake of a perilous journey. (33)
Indeed, I must not remain in this house for the rest of my life;
having mounted my own peacock and abandoned the army, I shall go to my father's home.
Devoted to Nārāyaṇa, he went to the great mountain Krauñca;
having become a supreme Vaiṣṇava, he worshipped Acyuta incessantly.
Having attained lordship, he thereafter embraced the state of a virtuous man;
remaining always established in the vow of Brahman, he conducts himself with the character of a saintly person.
He is worshipped on Mount Krauñca under the name Kārtikasvāmin;
on the full moon day of Kārtika, the gods, sages, and those possessing sacred bathing places always honor him.
The lords of sages went for the purpose of seeing the prince;
meanwhile, Umā fell into grief at being separated from Skanda.
The distressed woman said to Śaṅkara, "Go there with me.
For her sake, Śambhu himself went to the mountain by means of his own partial incarnation. 39.
That Śambhu, named Mallikārjuna, lived together with Satī;
Kārtika, having learned of that vow of his, became disillusioned and went elsewhere.
Indeed, having been entreated there by the gods and others,
Skanda, who maintains excellent conduct, remained for that long, staying at a distance of three yojanas.
Afflicted by affection for their son, Śiva and Pārvatī, being full of tenderness, indeed go on every lunar festival to behold Kumāra.
Indeed, on the day of the new moon, Śambhu himself goes there;
on the full moon, Pārvatī herself goes, accompanied by her army.
Thus, O beloved, the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa should be performed together with his two sons, Siddhi and Buddhi, as well as Kṣema and Lābha. (44)
This narrative is sinless, conducive to fame, and increases happiness; it bestows longevity, leads to heaven, is incomparable, and increases devotion to Śiva. 45.
O Mahālakṣmī, I have described to you the service to one's mother, which increases merit and is declared to bestow liberation. What else do you wish to hear? 46.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Account of how the Prajāpati Viśvarūpa bestowed his two daughters named Siddhi and Buddhi upon Śrī Gaṇeśa according to the marriage rite in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, followed by the birth of sons named Kṣema and Lābha, and the constant departure of Kārttikeya toward Mount Krauñca."
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, you have narrated this most wonderful account concerning Gaṇeśa as well as Kārttikeya.
"O Blessed One, I have a certain desire to know regarding this;
O Lord of the gods of gods, I ask you—having heard it, O Lord, please dispel that [doubt]."
That Kārttikeya should have gone far away, abandoning his parents, would be unsuitable in the world and could not even be possible according to the scriptures. (3)
Service to one's mother, father, and preceptor is auspicious and bestows liberation;
having abandoned such service and gone far away, the sin committed therein would arise.
Why was it that for Kārttikeya there did not likewise occur the fruit that the expiation of evil and sin would result in their destruction?
Service to one's mother brings liberation; the mother is considered to be of many kinds:
she who gives breast milk, she who carries the fetus, she who provides food, and she who is dear to her elders. (6)
The wife of a beloved deity, the wife of one's father, young maidens, a pregnant sister, the wife of a son, and a mother-in-law; || 7 ||
The mother’s mother, the father’s mother, and likewise the beloved sister of one’s uterine brother;
as well as the mother’s sister, the father’s sister, and the maternal aunt. (8)
The sixteen mothers ordained by the Vedas are remembered as belonging to all people;
they indeed should be honored, saluted, served, and praised by those who possess good sons.
Even their words of blessing protect one’s son from sin here;
he by whom service is rendered to them attains the eternal Brahman.
By serving them, one certainly becomes a fortunate son;
indeed, through their heartache, one's auspicious fortune is consumed by fire.
Merit perishes and excellent fortune abandons him and goes elsewhere;
how then could I, the sovereign of the world, be abandoned by Kārttikeya?
O Senāpati, how could you abandon your own dear wife who is devoted to her husband?
By abandoning a woman devoted to her husband, a man shall fall into hell. || 13 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, for everything was ordained by me in this manner from the very beginning;
by me was the cosmic egg created, containing the sacrifice, Śambhu, the Pitṛs, the Ṛṣis, and the gods.
In the first age, the Kṛtayuga, all Brāhmaṇas possessed the splendor of Brahman; for they were equal to the Supreme Self and their mere will brought about the fulfillment of all things.
In the Tretā age, their powers indeed became diminished due to the difference in time;
but in the Dvāpara age, they specifically fell into a state of lacking power.
Power has its root in austerity; it perishes when austerity declines.
Due to the decline of austerity among the subjects, they became devoid of power.
And just as their own power diminishes, so too does the power of the lineage of unrighteousness gradually increase. (18)
There, through unrighteousness, the subjects— possessed of falsehood, greed,
and pride— became givers of suffering to one another by the force of time.
Having seen this, Brahmā then remembered Śrī Hari, the supreme lord Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of finding a means to protect his progeny.
Established in the abode of Brahmā for the sake of protecting the world,
Hari, having perceived the intention of the Creator, arrived there instantly.
Then Brahmā, having bowed to and praised the Lord again and again, said:
"O Great King, ocean of compassion, you who uplift even the lowliest! (2)
Due to the division of the ages (yugas), people who were once devoted to austerity no longer practice it properly;
because of the absence of austerity, merit does not exist, and there can be no power that bestows happiness.
And due to their absence, O Lord, how am I to protect these human beings who are destitute of divine grace, burdened by suffering, yet devoted and seeking liberation? (24)
Even that which is fresh is burned along with the dry, though it be innocent;
O Blessed One, what means indeed shall I employ for its protection? (25)
O Supreme Lord, through the devotion, austerity, and yoga of Your devotees, all living beings certainly become truly happy; this is indeed certain. ||26||
If, due to the conjunction of time, devotees are indeed deprived of the means of austerity, then by what action are those living beings protected? ||27||
Therefore, devise a means for the sake of the happiness of living beings, by which devotees may always be happy throughout all the ages. (28)
Having heard this worship, which contains within it the protection of living beings performed by Vedhas, the glorious Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari, who is the Supreme Brahman, [spoke]. (29)
The Lord of Gods said to Brahmā: "O Lotus-born One, do not harbor anxiety;
the protection of the living beings within your cosmic egg who seek liberation is my task."
"I alone shall accomplish this; no one else could be such as I am.
Having reflected upon it myself, I shall do so for as long as the cosmic egg endures. (3.1)
For that long, however, protection must be provided by me, since my devotees are dear to me;
if I were to appoint another protector there, then he— || 32 ||
Dissolved by the force of time, one instead incurs suffering;
therefore, I am myself the manifest Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest.
Having indeed brought the imperishable Brahman together with the desire for progeny, I dwell here in this world; may that be the supreme welfare for all the worlds. (34)
Through my mere will, I shall take birth from Dharmadeva in a physical form; having accepted this, I shall become the essence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa here. (35)
"Practicing celibacy for as long as I live, established in the austerity of Brahman, I shall protect my subjects through austerity alone and serve the earth with devotion. (36)
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, and Nara is remembered as the Imperishable Brahman;
both are indeed rich in the vow of Brahman and have set their minds upon austerity. (37)
"I shall remain [in this state]"—this is the supreme means of protection;
for me, the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) is always dear, indeed most dear. (38)
I indeed always maintain that vow in the world of Brahmā,
and I maintain it right there in the divine Badarikāśrama.
Always established in austerity for the sake of protecting the lords,
he has come here as well and remains fixed in yoga upon a peak of the Himalayas.
Established in austerity, which consists of the restraint of all the senses, I shall protect my people by bestowing the merit of that austerity. 41.
"Do not worry, O lotus-seated one; the world is protected by austerity.
Indeed, various kinds of austerities exist for the sake of protection. (42)
That one should not smell anything else with the nose—this is called austerity;
even more distinguished than that is when one does not touch anything else with the skin. (45)
Furthermore, it is distinguished that nothing else should be seen with the eye;
furthermore, it is distinguished that nothing else should be heard with the ear. ||44||
Therefore, nothing else is truly superior to being tasted by the tongue;
likewise, nothing should be spoken by speech—penance is indeed said to be the highest.
With hands raised and one foot lifted, abstaining from food and established in austerity, the ascetic who has undertaken such hardship is said to be even greater than one who observes silence. 46.
Even better than that is one who is without water; even better than that is one whose ritual actions are not contrived;
even better than all those is one who is free from desire and possesses upward-directed vital energy.
The celibate student who has drawn up his vital energy is distinguished by the absence of sexual pleasure;
the restraint of the organ from all the senses is powerful austerity. (48)
The cessation of the tongue and the cessation of the mind, as well as the cessation of the element and the cessation of the skin—these four cessations are proclaimed. (49)
Indeed, these four types of restraint arise within the life of celibacy;
therefore, no other restraint is truly more difficult or powerful than this.

He who has fully observed the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) along with all its primary and secondary limbs is indeed the Supreme Brahman, Hari, in embodied form; there is no doubt in this matter. (51)
For one established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), no other duty remains to be performed;
the entire world is encircled by the golden thread of the beloved. 52.
He who is the two-armed Supreme Lord, detached from those [energies] and those [objects], saves the entire world here by the power of his celibacy. ||53||
I, the Lord composed of pure being, dwell within food;
I, the Lord who bestows supreme satisfaction, dwell within the digestive fire.
I, the Lord whose nature consists of passion and vigor, dwell within the elements;
by whomsoever protection is afforded to that [nature], protection is thereby afforded to me. (55)
One should never, under any circumstances, form a thought of sensual enjoyment;
nor should one ever listen to talk concerning the pursuit of sensual pleasures.
Since the mention of sensual enjoyment should not be uttered at all, one must never, under any circumstances, come into contact with sensual enjoyment. //57//
For the sake of sensual enjoyment, one must certainly not seek the sight of a woman;
for the sake of sensual enjoyment, one must certainly not engage in secret assignations.
One must never, under any circumstances, be intent upon the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
nor should one ever allow the emission of semen. (59)
Thus, this celibate life is indeed considered difficult for all;
it is difficult for living beings who have become coupled, and difficult for those who are not ascetics.
"Except for Nara and Nārāyaṇa, such celibacy does not exist elsewhere; therefore, assuming their form, I shall practice supreme austerity."
By means of that vow, I shall protect my entire progeny and my own body;
I shall deliver them from evil and bring them happiness in every respect.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Necessity for the Incarnation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, wherein it is shown that Nārāyaṇa told Brahmā that the descent as Nara and Nārāyaṇa was essential for the protection of his own progeny and for the practice of celibate austerity.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, having thus made this promise to Brahmā,
I immediately vanished from that place.
Established in the vow of celibacy within my supreme, imperishable abode,
I abide in every way just as I abide in the Badarī forest.
Then, having likewise resolved his intention at that hermitage on the edge of the divine abode of the Imperishable, he entered into Dharmadeva.
Together with the imperishable Brahman, he entered into my mother’s form through mere volition alone. || 4 ||
Those two boys, who were the very essence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, were manifested;
as soon as they were born, they were sixteen years of age, handsome, and capable of enchanting the god of love.
With all their limbs well-nourished and joyful, holding garlands and books in their lotus-like hands,
the two Supreme Lords were radiant and brilliant like ten million times ten million suns.
Their heads were adorned with matted locks resembling fine golden threads;
they wore only loincloths for covering, and possessed tree-shelters, rags, and water-pots.
Wearing the sacred thread, having fulfilled the vow of celibacy, and being ascetics,
you two appear like two female portions belonging to another man.
The left side of a person would be the locus of deficient power;
however, in me, Nārāyaṇa, there is not even the slightest deficiency of power in the left.
On both the left and the right, all powers are indeed equal;
in me, there exists no female aspect characterized by deficient power.
These two marks exist upon my chest, belonging indeed to my breasts;
in the absence of the mark of the breasts, there would be a deficiency in my form. (11)

There would not be completeness of all limbs; therefore, while the mark is preserved, in that man who is indeed my own form, breasts do not exist. Thus, in that man, there is an absence of even a trace of the state of being a woman.
The capacity of both sides has been demonstrated, yet there is no deficiency or excess in their respective powers.
The man without breasts is to be known as Bodhya, while I am Narāyaṇa with six breasts;
Lakṣmī is always to be protected by me, and therefore my breasts are indeed protected.
Since you possess the splendor of Lakṣmī in human form and are of excellent character, there is no need for me to have a wife who is the very embodiment of celibacy. || 15 ||
Therefore, this human form of mine is considered the supreme state of celibacy (brahmacarya);
two beings of such a form have been born, whose lotus-like arms reach down to their knees.
Having seen that their parents were truly well-disposed,
they performed the purificatory rites for the sake of complete purification and were commanded to engage in ascetic penance.
For at that time, those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, paid homage to us;
it was for the sake of service and not for the sake of penance, yet such service toward one's parents is indeed difficult to obtain.
Good sons must always conduct themselves properly in service;
for in this created world, a mother always protects her son well within her womb.
For that reason, the mother always endures great hardship;
there is suffering at the time of birth, and likewise suffering in the act of nurturing.
Day and night he attends to her, cleansing away her excrement and urine;
he constantly protects her as his own life and nourishes her with the drinking of breast milk. (21)
Carrying [the child] on her lap and at her waist, nourishing him even while she herself has not eaten,
fondling, pleasing, and serving— these are always performed by the mother alone.
Even by serving that mother from birth until death, a son can never truly be free from debt; what then could happen for one who does not serve her?
For a son who is devoid of service, the debt to his mothers does not cease;
therefore, service must be performed—this is what both of us approve of. (24)
A son who is devoid of service to his mother is not called a son;
he is indeed declared to be "no-son" (aputra), for he is merely a burden to his mother. (25)
Therefore, let us both always serve our parents;
for the son who does not serve them has a certain destination in hell. || 26 ||
Bound by the noose of Time, one may likewise become a preta;
furthermore, for the sake of repaying debts, one undergoes various births and torments. (27)
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
for one who remains indebted, there is no higher goal—neither heaven nor the state beyond rebirth. (28)
Having procreated a son for his ancestors, having discharged the debt to the gods through sacrificial rites,
and having cleared the debt to the sages through sacred knowledge, he should apply his mind to austerity.
Therefore, let us perform service; otherwise, we shall fall into a low state of existence. Parents who have grown old must be protected by their sons in every way. (1.110.30)
Younger brothers must be protected and sisters likewise must be guarded;
they should always be given in marriage after providing them with assistance derived from wealth.

One must provide for the maintenance of the family and exert effort in the acquisition of wealth; likewise, pleasure and pain should be borne equally by those kinsmen who remain in the household. (32)
Indeed, those two [parents] are considered worthy of service until they reach their residence in heaven;
for when the son becomes young, he will then protect us both.
"The two of us shall surely be happy"—such was the parents' expectation;
yet, having shattered it, he went to the forest as their son, for he was indeed a Rākṣasa. (34)
Indeed, he who does not acquire the masses of merit resulting from the benedictory words of his parents gains no fruit from the forest, but rather incurs sin. (35)
Even if he were established in heaven or in sovereign rule, he would be considered a denizen of hell;
therefore, we shall serve you both in every way.
By him who has served his mother, everything has been accomplished:
charity, sacrifice, austerity, fire-offerings, and even the study of the Vedas. (37)
By him the deities were worshipped, and likewise all forms of meditation were performed;
various austerities were practiced, and even the knowledge of Brahman was acquired. (38)
By him sovereignty was established and heaven was brought into his hand;
the state of supreme lordship was attained by him who served his mother. (39)
By him who has served his mother well, the ancestors have been gratified, the sages likewise honored, and guests have been worshipped. (1.110.40)
Indeed, all sacred fords, holy fields, and shrines have been visited by him who has served his mother; likewise, all acts of sacrifice and public works have been performed by him. (41)
There is no merit equal to service in the practice of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth;
there is no goddess equal to a mother, nor is there any Hari equal to a father. 42.
Even a fool who dies while being gazed upon by his parents shall attain heaven; who then would abandon those two gods? (43)
Indra, Sūrya, Śaśin, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, Śaṅkara, the Lotus-born (Brahmā),
Varuṇa, Agni, and likewise other gods are situated within the Father.
The son of Janaka daily obtains through perfect service an inexhaustible and excellent fruit that is ten million times greater than the fruit of worshipping the gods. 45.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sandhyā, Sāvitrī, and likewise Satī;
Gāyatrī, Rohiṇī, Saṃjñā, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. ||46||
And all those [goddesses] were honored by him who served his mother well; from the merit made by honoring them, ten million times that merit resides in the mother. (47)
All of them reside indeed within the form of the mother and not separately;
therefore, one should truly serve the mother and also attend upon the father.
"O Nara and Acyuta, knowing the greatness of serving our parents, we two shall remain here, taking up residence at the feet of our parents. (49)
But for a son who, though overcome by great sins, is devoted to the service of his father,
the messengers of Yama have no power over his eyes.
If, at the time of death, the eyes of the parents are joined with the eyes of a virtuous son, even then they shall attain a good rebirth.
At the time of death, if a virtuous son offers even a single drop of water from his mouth into [the deceased's] ear, by that alone the parents shall attain a happy rebirth. 52.
In whosever house there is a son, the ancestors are well-pleased;
however, the ancestors surely curse a family that is devoid of a son.
Not seeing anyone in their lineage who performs the ancestral rites (śrāddha), the great-grandfathers sigh hot breaths, tormented by the prospect of future hunger. (54)
And the sisters also heaved sighs, saying, "Because we have no brother, there is not even a brother among us who would give us this bodice. (55)
People say that one who is childless is not seen as auspicious; they say a daughter without a brother is unfortunate, and the world would say such a person is without lineage. (56)
A house devoid of sons is like a palace or a celestial chariot turned into a cremation ground;
likewise, all riches such as food, drink, and ornaments are useless when deprived of sons. (57)
They should be understood as being like the venom of a black snake; they do not lead to bliss—neither gods, nor sages, nor serpents, nor the species of egg-born nagas. (58)
Everyone desires virtuous sons; a birth without a son is useless.
Therefore, one should in every way strive to be a good son and a devoted servant. (59)
Therefore, we two shall always perform service to our parents;
therein the highest good is to be found, for service bestows liberation.
Having thus described the greatness of their parents,
Nara and Nārāyaṇa remained silent there, intent on the duty of service.
Filled with devotion for their father and resolved to serve their mother, Mūrti and Dharma were both pleased, having joined together in offering auspicious blessings. (62)

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Duty of Serving One’s Parents after Birth," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 110 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, then the god of dharma spoke to his two sons, who were firm in their resolve for service, regarding that supreme dharma than which nothing higher exists.
That dharma in which the immersion into all dharmas is established was first revealed by Hari within the Abode. || 2 ||

This Dharma, which brings about all that is most auspicious, which cannot be obstructed by debts, which bestows liberation, which was heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, which grants final release, and which is the supreme means—[this has been heard]. (3)
Dharma said: "Listen, my two most excellent sons; being righteous and devoted to your father, what you have spoken is truly beautiful."
The characteristic of a good son is the excellent service rendered to his parents;
now listen to that dharma, even superior to this, as spoken by Hari.
There is no dharma equal to the holy life (brahmacarya); indeed, there is none at all. All other dharmas do not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
He is celibacy, the dharma of Brahman; indeed, he is himself considered to be Brahman.
He is the form of Brahman, the embodiment of Brahman, the self of Brahman, and the bestower of the form of Brahman.
When Brahmā, the Lord of all, is pleased, everything becomes perpetually pleased;
before him, services, debts, and gifts are of only minor significance.
That which is said to be attainable through sacrifice is obtained by means of celibacy;
therefore, sacrifice is established in celibacy in every respect.
That which is attainable through sacrificial rites and charitable works, and that which is obtained through the practice of celibacy—
therefore, one should always remain firmly established in celibacy as the highest sacrifice.
That which is known as the form of Brahman is called brahmacarya;
it is superior to all dharmas, and through it liberation is attained. || 11 ||
Dharma is established in celibacy; austerity is established in celibacy. Those who are established in celibacy are considered to be established in the abode of Brahman.
Through yoga, perfection is born; through perfection, fame arises.
Fame and perfection come through austerity, and austerity comes through conduct toward Brahman.
The restraint of the senses, which is otherwise difficult to achieve, is accomplished through celibacy;
indeed, by means of celibacy and austerity, the world of Brahmā is attained.
For one who has entered the life of celibacy (brahmacarya), even the world of Brahmā grants all desires;
how much more so the worlds of the gods and others? For that [practice] is indeed the foundation of Brahman.
Whatever is to be attained through the *sattrāyaṇa* sacrifice is obtained through celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
in every respect, the *sattrāyaṇa* is firmly established within celibacy.
That which is to be attained through the vow of silence and that which is attained through celibacy—
in every respect, silence is firmly established within celibacy.
This state is attained through fasting and through the practice of celibacy;
one who stands in celibacy practices fasting in every respect. || 18 ||
That which is to be attained by going to the forest is obtained through celibacy;
even the very act of going to the forest is established upon celibacy.
That which is to be attained through the path of renunciation is obtained through celibacy;
renunciation regarding both the seen and the heard is established in celibacy.
That which is to be attained through non-violence and is gained through celibacy—that non-violence is universal; it is firmly established in celibacy. (21)
That which is to be attained through the vow of truth and is obtained through celibacy—that truth, therefore, is established in the threefold celibacy. || 22 ||
That which is to be attained through non-stealing and that which is obtained through celibacy—non-stealing, in its twofold form, is established in every respect within celibacy. || 23 ||
That which is attainable through non-possessiveness is attained through celibacy;
indeed, non-possessiveness itself is firmly established in celibacy. || 24 ||
That which is indeed attained through purity is obtained through celibacy;
purity is twofold, and through the yoga of Brahman, one becomes established in celibacy.
That which is obtained through contentment is obtained through celibacy;
contentment is entirely one's own and is established in celibacy. || 26 ||
Whatever various practices of austerity are fulfilled through celibacy, therefore the great section on austerity is completed within celibacy. (27)
That which is obtainable through the private recitation of the Vedas is obtained through celibacy;
the private recitation of the Vedas pervades everything and is established in celibacy. || 28 ||
The dedication to the Lord proceeds from celibacy;
therefore, dedication to the Lord is established in celibacy. || 29 ||
Postures such as Gorakṣa and others indeed bear fruit through celibacy;
therefore, one who is firmly established in posture becomes established in celibacy.
That which is attainable through breath control (prāṇāyāma) is attained through celibacy (brahmacarya). Breath control is fourfold and is established within celibacy. || 31 ||
The withdrawal of the senses bears fruit only when the vow of Brahman is maintained;
therefore, the restraint of the senses is indeed established in celibacy.
That which is to be obtained through meditation is obtained through celibacy;
meditation, which consists of one-pointed concentration, is established in celibacy. || 33 ||
Where concentration (dhāraṇā) is to be practiced, it is attained through celibacy (brahmacarya); therefore, all concentration is established upon celibacy. || 34 ||
Samādhi is that in which it must be practiced; it is accomplished through celibacy (brahmacarya). Therefore, whether twofold or fourfold, it is established upon celibacy. || 35 ||
That which is attained here through self-restraint, tranquility, forbearance, cessation, and so forth, is indeed obtained through celibacy; of this there is no doubt.

And that which arises from discernment, O All-pervading One, from inquiry, from practice, likewise from right action, from auspiciousness, from lack of despondency, and from lack of exultation; || 37 ||
All that is obtained through celibacy; of this there is no doubt—through knowledge, through dharma, through higher wisdom, and likewise through various forms of devotion.
Whatever may arise from the knowledge of reality and from the cessation of false cognition—all that is obtained through celibacy; there is no doubt in this matter. ||39||
One who is proficient in the Word-Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman;
through the expansion of the Word-Brahman here, one becomes established in the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).

The investigation of Brahman, as well as the paths of the *sad-bindu* (the six points) and *nāda* (the resonance), proceed from that Brahman; this is considered the fruit of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). 41.

The supernatural powers (siddhis) are: atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), extension (prāpti), heaviness (garimā), lightness (laghimā), as well as the power of will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitā), and mastery over all (sarvavaśitā). ||42||
The waters were delightful with the sounds of *tāra*, *sutāra*, *tārā*, and *tāra*;
and the *siddhis* also rejoiced, exulting in supreme joy. ||43||

Reasoning, oral instruction, study, and likewise the three types of destruction of suffering, the acquisition of friends, and the perfection of knowledge—these are the eight accomplishments (siddhis). ||44||
Hearing from afar, seeing from afar, taking [objects], moving through space, invisibility, and likewise all other supernatural powers (siddhis) are obtained through celibacy (brahmacarya). //45//
Whatever is attained through fasting, through purificatory baths, through enemas, and likewise through elephant-like physical exercises—
that is attained in every way through celibacy.

Whatever is obtained through the libations and the *śrāddha* for the ancestors, that is obtained through celibacy; through celibacy, one becomes firmly established in the *śrāddha* and other rites. (47)
But that which is propitiated through the birth of a son, through knowledge, and through the agnihotra sacrifice—
It is certain that he is propitiated by means of celibacy alone. ||48||
Whatever gain is obtained through the Śruti and the Smṛti, that gain is indeed attained through celibacy (brahmacarya);
for that very abode which is considered attainable through the worship of symbols (pratīkopāsana) is [attained] by it. 49.
That which is to be attained through celibacy is indeed attained without a doubt,
as well as that which is attained through service to one's mother, father, family, and the worlds.
That is obtained through the practice of celibacy; there is no doubt in this matter.
It is obtained by [serving] cows, Brahmins, gods, virtuous women, and likewise great souls.
That which is attainable through service to the virtuous is attained through celibacy;
those worlds belonging to a devoted wife are attained through celibacy.
That goal which belongs to those who are diligent in action, those who possess happiness,
and those who are most righteous is indeed attained through celibacy in a state even higher than that.
Whatever auspicious destination is attained by those of meritorious soul and by givers, the attainment of one who practices celibacy shall be even higher than that. (54)
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, vaināyakas, kūṣmāṇḍas, mātṛs, piśācas, pretas, and vetālas are terrified by celibacy. //55//
The ḍākinīs, śākinīs, śūlas, yoginīs, and tālikās likewise flee by the power of the celibate practitioner; of this there is no doubt. (56)
All human prosperities as well as the riches of the gods are indeed obtained through celibacy; they are firmly established in celibacy. (57)
The station of Indra, that of Varuṇa, that of Kubera, or indeed that of Soma; the station of Sūrya, that of Gaṇapati, that of Bhauma, that of heaven, and that of the ancestors.
The state of Vairāja, Aiśvara, Vārṣa, or Pārameṣṭhya is attained through celibacy; one is firmly established in the Brahman through celibacy.
The Āgneya, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Śāmbhava, Hiraṇmaya,
Prākṛta, Pauruṣa, and Mauktika [forms] are obtained through celibacy.
The indeterminate Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise the immortal realm,
as well as Kṣaira, Śvaita, and Bādrika, are attained through celibacy.
By the power of celibacy (brahmacarya), even the individual soul (jīva) attains the state of Śambhu—
that which is this Self (ātman), free from evil, devoid of sorrow, and exempt from death.
Free from hunger and thirst, and likewise free from old age, one whose desires are true and whose fruits are true indeed becomes so through the power of celibacy.
Having become equal to the Supreme Brahman and being permeated by that state of being in all things, one enjoys all desires through the power of celibacy (brahmacarya). ||64||
From the primordial nature up to the individual soul, the entire circle situated in the yoga of service becomes a servant at the feet and falls [at them] before the celibate student.
But for one who possesses the unshakable element, who is always devoted to celibacy,
and whose vital seed is drawn upward, the gods become his servants and attendants.
The eternal worlds always exist for the sake of the celibate student;
therefore, one should proceed by that path which the person who is a celibate student follows. 67.
Obstacles, malevolent spells, seizing spirits, demons, spears, and all inauspicious things—
every ill omen departs from afar through the majesty of Brahmā.
On whatever path the powerful celibate practitioner proceeds, the gods and other beings approach him nearby for the sake of welcoming him. (69)
The world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the lords of creatures,
and the Manus all approached that celibate student, who possessed the power of his vow of chastity.
The years, the seasons, the months, the days,
and the nights all come forward to welcome him who is radiant with his practice of celibacy.
The Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Vidyādharas, the Kinnaras and others, as well as the goddesses, all approach him who is radiant with the power of his celibacy. (72)
The sacred fires, those who perform the dakṣiṇā-homa, and the householders of the domestic hearth—
all approach the celibate student who is strengthened by his vow of chastity.
The Sādhyas, Kimpuruṣas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and others, as well as the Brāhmaṇas, approach the community of celibate students with joy. (74)
Millions of couples of men and women exist within the universe;
they attain purity by taking refuge at the feet of a celibate student. (75)
The celibate practitioner, being himself Brahman by the power of celibacy, is indeed capable of transforming the fundamental elements such as earth, water, and the rest. ||76||
A celibate practitioner is indeed capable of both protecting his own life and relinquishing it; in that matter, Time is certainly not the master.
Mahākāla went far away, as did Yama; who then were the followers of Yama?
[There remained] the Vālakhilyas, Sanaka and the others, the Siddhas, and likewise the lords of yoga. (78)
Haryaśva, Śabalāśva, Sādhu, and likewise Sādhvika—
by the power of their celibacy, they attained the state of Brahman.
Hanumān and Kārtikeya abide as celibate students (brahmacārins),
as do the illustrious and highly fortunate goddesses, such as Sarasvatī and the others.
"These women have indeed become celibate practitioners who have attained the state of Brahman;
therefore, my two sons, remain in celibacy and perform penance. (8.1)
By the power of celibacy, every debt is discharged;
there is no other austerity as difficult to practice as celibacy. (82)
Indeed, Brahman dwells directly within the body of the *brahmacārin*;
by worshipping the *brahmacārin*, the Supreme Brahman is worshipped. (83)
By feeding a celibate student, the Supreme Brahman is well-nourished;
by seeing a celibate student, the Supreme Brahman is revealed. ||84||
By touching a *brahmacārin*, one is considered to touch the Supreme Brahman;
by bowing to a *brahmacārin*, one bows to the Supreme Brahman. (85)
Service to a celibate student is considered the service of Brahman;
when a celibate student drinks water, it is Brahman who drinks that water. (86)
Dwelling in the presence of a celibate student is called dwelling in the abode of Brahman;
through the celibate student and the leader, one truly perceives Brahman itself. (87)
Indeed, with the nose of the celibate student (brahmacārin), one joyfully smells Brahman;
and indeed, with the tongue of the celibate student, one speaks of Brahman in every way. 88.
Through the tongue of the celibate student (brahmacārin), he tastes Brahman itself;
through the mouth of the celibate student, he always partakes of that which is supreme Brahman. 85.
The feet of Brahmā are the performers of the life of celibacy (brahmacarya), and his hands are born from the performance of that same discipline;
through the mental activity of one practicing celibacy, he perceives Brahman in every respect.
That which is enjoyed by one who has practiced the life of celibacy is considered the enjoyment of Brahman;
that which is the dwelling of one who has practiced the life of celibacy is always considered the abode of Brahman. (91)
The perpetual celibate, the lifelong student, and the temporary student—he is Hari himself;
by him the mother has been honored and likewise the father served.
