Whatever vow of celibacy has been protected by one who is of the nature of Brahman, and whatever has been performed as a student of sacred knowledge, all that is indeed performed by Brahman himself. //93//
Therefore, the dharma centered on Brahman is not taught apart from celibacy (brahmacarya);
for those who are indeed incarnations of Hari are themselves practitioners of celibacy. 94.
For those practicing celibacy, liberation is always held in the palm of their hand;
Nara and Nārāyaṇa remained steadfast in the practice of celibacy.
Having received this command from his parents, that man Nara-Hari bowed to and saluted Himavat, the mountain of snow, in order to perform austerities difficult to accomplish. (96)
They went there, to the peak always adorned with Badarī and other trees;
indeed, beneath the Badarī tree, those two performed austerities for the sake of the happiness of the world.
Likewise, this Kārttikeya also performs intense penance;
having undertaken the vow of a celibate student (brahmacārī), he worships Viṣṇu constantly.
Therefore, there is no capacity for even a trace of fault therein;
however, in the balance of celibacy, non-practice is considered to be of no consequence.

Indeed, that which is not service is not to be understood as service; rather, service is the very nature of austerity, for through the practice of celibacy and austerity, it delivers one's own two [parents].
That service rendered to one's mother and father is considered incomparable and beyond measure;
by performing it, the mother and father shall always remain well-pleased. (101)
Service rendered to him at all times is superior; no other service excels it.
Service performed by Kārtika consists of the vow and austerity of Brahman.
Pārvatī performed penance, and Śambhu certainly did so as well;
for it is well known both in the world and in the scriptures that penance ought to be practiced. (103)
O Lakṣmī, that penance consisting of the vow of celibacy bestows liberation; it does not bring about sin.
Mother Śivā was pleased, and Father Śambhu was gracious. (104)
Having attained the command of the army, the destruction of the demon Tāraka was accomplished;
thus, the word of his parents was fulfilled, which is the supreme service of obeying their command.
"And this unsurpassed arrangement of the Skandas was ordained by me alone.
Thus have I told you, Lakṣmī; what else do you wish to hear? 106.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Misfortunes of Kārttikeya and Others," preceded by a description of the greatness of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of my life, O Great Master!
You have stated that Mahādeva is in every respect the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas. || 1 ||
How indeed is one called a Vaiṣṇava? I am eager to hear that story.
O my dear one, tell me today: where and when did such a Vaiṣṇava first appear?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this divine narrative which brings about the state of a great Vaiṣṇava;
I shall relate in brief this story concerning Viṣṇu, which bestows liberation.
On earth there are mountains that provide dwellings for gods and others;
among them, the most beloved is the one that bestows coolness as well as liberation.
The Himalaya is ever peaceful; there lies the hermitage of Badarī.
Both the two persons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, reside there.
Among them, one was a white man and another was black in form;
the younger brother was said to be tawny, while the black one was Nārāyaṇa himself.
There, Nara and Nārāyaṇa appear respectively as two-armed and four-armed;
here the gods dwell, and there are the auspicious hermitages of the sages.
Where the divine Gaṅgā and the Alakanandā flow perpetually,
there Maheśa performed penance for one year.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, who grants fearlessness to his devotees, being well-pleased, said to Śambhu: "O Śaṅkara, choose a boon."
"O Lord, whatever you desire, I shall grant that very wish," Śambhu then said to Nārāyaṇa, the compassionate one.
"I shall accept them, O Lord, if you wish to grant them;
let two boons be given to me, O Janārdana, being well-pleased. (1)
May you always possess devotion; I shall become the king of devotees, renowned throughout all the worlds as Śiva, the great devotee.
"May the renown 'devotee of Viṣṇu' arise forever in the worlds and even throughout the entire universe, O Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World! (13)
Furthermore, those who will worship me, accept me, and take refuge in me—by your grace, I shall become the bestower of liberation upon them. (14)
"May liberation be certain for him to whom I am the giver of boons;
may I be a bestower of liberation to the devotee of Viṣṇu—grant me these two boons. (15)
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa himself spoke to Śambhu, the mine of virtues:
"O Śambhu, become my devotee; O source of liberation, be a giver [of it] for me."
Having thus obtained those boons, Śaṅkara then said to Hari:
"O Lord, grant me initiation, and I shall become a Vaiṣṇava."
One cannot be a devotee without being a Vaiṣṇava, nor can one who is not a Vaiṣṇava grant liberation.
Both worldly enjoyment and liberation are certain to result from that yoga once the state of being a Vaiṣṇava is attained.
"Therefore, one must become a Vaiṣṇava; grant me initiation and show me mercy.
Having heard this, the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa spoke to Śaṅkara.
O Śambhu, it is well-conceived that which you have intended for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds;
O Śambhu, accept first this auspicious jewel of a mantra.
"I am Brahmā, a devotee of Brahmā; recite this continuously.
This jewel of a mantra, by name, protects one who has come for refuge. (21)
The mantra "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa" bestows all fruits;
the mantra "Śrīman-Nārāyaṇa" accomplishes all goals. ||22||
The mantra "Svāminārāyaṇa" is remembered as the bestower of liberation;
the mantra "Naranārāyaṇa" is the bestower of the state of Brahman. ||23||
The mantra "Harinārāyaṇa" is the destroyer of suffering;
the mantra "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa" is the bestower of prosperity. ||24||
The mantra "Vāsudeva Nārāyaṇa" bestows sovereignty, while the mantra "Rāma Nārāyaṇa" is the destroyer of sins. (25)
Oṃ! This mantra of Śrī Nārāyaṇa bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; this mantra grants total surrender: "Śrī Hari is my refuge. (26)
Thus, this supreme group of ten mantras should be given to the devotees;
"Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya" is the king of mantras. (27)
O Śaṅkara, bestow upon these disciple-people the King of Mantras, the Jewel of Mantras, and the ten mantras— these twelve mantras indeed.
I am eternally and exceedingly pleased by the mere utterance of the mantra;
so too are all those who are entitled to the mantra—my devotees who seek liberation. (29)
Whether they be wise men, yogis, others, the dull-witted, women, or those who have taken refuge—all human beings endowed with devotion and faith are indeed qualified. || 1.112.30 ||
Among those authorized beings, such as the gods and others, who reside here within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
a mantra belonging to one of them should indeed be imparted for the sake of spiritual welfare.
Likewise, take up the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus in your arms;
and bear this mark of the heated seal, or indeed the mark of sandalwood paste. (32)
O Śambhu, take hold of my two arms, which bestow the form of Viṣṇu;
and indeed, accept this Gāyatrī consisting of twenty-five syllables.
"Oṃ, we know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva;
may that Brahman inspire us"—this mantra should be recited by you every day. (24)
Meditate upon me as having a beautiful form, either with two arms or four arms;
the two-armed form is that of Brahmā, established in the abode of Brahman.
The auspicious one, who sustains all incarnations, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman, has two hands—one holding a discus and the other bestowing fearlessness. (36)
Adorned with necklaces, earrings, garlands, bracelets, and a crown,
the Supreme Lord is clad in yellow garments, sixteen years of age, and gracious.
Meditate upon the form within your heart, four-armed, endowed with hands holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, together with Śrī seated upon his left lap. 38.
Then you shall worship me with the sixteen divine services (upacāras):
first the invocation (āvāhana) and the offering of a seat (svāsana), followed by water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya).
Likewise, the ritual sipping of water, the bath, the honey-mixture, as well as clothing,
sandalwood paste, ornaments, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering.
Give me a sacred thread and betel-leaf with a spirit of devotion;
give me fragrant arka-flowers, camphor, and pure fragrance, O sinless one. (41)
Perform circumambulations and prostrations like a staff;
offer praise and a handful of flowers, and likewise ask me for forgiveness. (42)
Cast me out from your exterior and establish me within yourself in your own heart;
[grant me] hearing, chanting, remembrance, and service at the feet. 43.
Perform worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender;
practice meditation, absorption, and oneness through these means of devotion.
O Śaṅkara, apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the tilaka upon your forehead;
likewise, apply the vertical mark and the tilaka upon your arms and your heart. (45)
In the center of that, make a moon-motif using fragrant sandalwood paste endowed with six filaments, or else use saffron.
Take this auspicious two-stringed Tulasī necklace upon your neck;
it should always be worn around the neck and never discarded at any time. (47)
"Accept this garland of *tulasī* consisting of one hundred and eight beads for the purpose of recitation, or one made of gems and other materials. (48)
I shall make your name end with "Īśvara," as Maheśvara;
you have been made the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) by Pālaka and Ramā. 49.
And by me, through my supreme fortune, you have been made the Supreme Lord;
for he who measures and worships "Paṃ" as Viṣṇu, "Raṃ" as Ramā, and "Ma" as myself [is truly devoted]. (1.112.50)
"You have been called the abode of sovereignty, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord;
O Śambhu, may all names ending in 'Īśvara' indeed belong to you. (51)
"Thus, O Lakṣmī, initiation was indeed bestowed by me upon Śrī Śaṅkara;
from that time forward, Śambhu has always worshipped me with undivided devotion. (52)
Having received initiation from Śambhu, he went indeed to Gandhamādana;
then, in his own abode, Kailāsa, he worships me day and night.
Whatever may be fit to be accepted— a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a bulb, or water—
Śaṅkara does not accept any of it without first offering it to me.
He applies the sectarian mark on his forehead, mutters my mantra with a rosary, and remains absorbed in meditation upon my form without any desire for worldly gain. (55)
Having thus observed the Vaiṣṇava devotion, Pārvatī said to Śaṅkara:
"Whose meditation, garlands, recitation of mantras, sectarian marks, and so forth [are these]? (56)
It is performed by the Lord of the World, who takes the form of the Supreme Lord;
for you yourself are indeed the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest. (57)
"Thus, for whom indeed is there meditation and recitation of the complete form?
Having heard this, Mahādeva spoke the essential truth to Pārvatī.

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Vaiṣṇava Initiation upon Śaṅkara by Nārāyaṇa at Badarikāśrama, along with the Demonstration of its Constituent Rituals and Accessories," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Pārvatī, the Great Lord Maheśvara, a devotee of Viṣṇu,
began to speak in order to dispel her desire to know.
Listen, O Satī, I shall speak: I worship Viṣṇu directly.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord. || 2 ||
He is always to be venerated, worshipped, and meditated upon;
indeed, I received initiation from him in the forest of Badarī.
"I meditate upon and worship that Supreme Lord eternally with devotion.
Pārvatī spoke thus to the Lord of Gods in detail, exactly as it was.
Make me hear all of this as well, if it is something I may grasp,
so that I too, by taking refuge in Govinda, may attain the highest good.
O Lord, why has that not been told to me even until now, nor anywhere else,
throughout all this time, apart from the worship of Śrī Hari?
All my days have been spent entirely in vain without Hari;
O God of gods, if I am indeed considered by you to be a worthy recipient.
Then, O Lord, initiate me as well, your devotee;
for the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the divine Guru is Janārdana.
The husband is declared to be one's own guru; everything is established in the husband.
Service to the husband is the supreme service; devotion to the husband is considered the highest devotion.
O Śaṅkara, the duty toward one's husband is the supreme dharma; grant that dharma [to me].
For if a husband is a Vaiṣṇava, yet his wife is not a Vaiṣṇavī, [then that dharma is lost].
Any service or devotion performed by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is entirely fruitless;
food prepared by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is impure and not purifying.
Indeed, the water from the hands of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is unfit to be drunk, for it is not purifying;
the entire house of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava is proclaimed to be a cremation ground. 1b.
"Lakṣmī departs from the house of one who is not a Vaiṣṇava in every way;
therefore, I shall practice the supreme, purifying Vaiṣṇava duty toward my master. (13)
"I desire to comprehend it; speak it in detail according to its true nature.
Having heard this verse from Pārvatī, Śambhu spoke to Maheśvarī:
Even until now you have not attained the state of being a fit vessel; therefore, I did not speak [to you].
Indeed, the state of being a fit vessel is attained through the merits of many births.
In this very life, the state of being a worthy vessel attains nourishment through listening to the narrative;
and by serving the virtuous, the self becomes eternal like heaven.
Through devotion to her husband and service to him, a woman’s soul shall attain strength;
for that person who is strong, fortunate, and a servant of the virtuous, [attains success]. || 17 ||
Its very activity becomes stainless, arising both internally and externally; and this stainlessness, O beloved, is in every way the seed of faith.
From that arises the desire to know, and by that, one possesses the qualification;
when such is the case, upon union with a guru, everything that is performed bears fruit.
But now all of that has arisen and been applied; it has arrived and come into being. Therefore, you are the most excellent vessel.
"O Great Goddess, you have been born today, and I am pleased;
oh, my dear wife, you desire the state of a Vaiṣṇavī!"
"What indeed could be a greater fortune for me than this?
O beloved, having heard your heart's desire, I am exceedingly pleased. (22)
"I shall indeed give you everything, since you have become Vaiṣṇavī;
O Goddess, from today until the very end, whatever is offered as food or drink [shall be yours]."
Having offered that to Viṣṇu, I indeed ate it afterwards;
what more can I say, O Goddess of the gods, for today I am filled with great bliss? 24.
"The rising of the sun for my gold has occurred in every way;
O dear friend, may you enjoy all the fruit of serving your husband. (25)
"May my entire household become Vaiṣṇava; may I be fortunate.
Today, O Goddess, during the bright fortnight of Kārttika, for the purification of the body—" (26)
On the tenth day, O beloved, observe a fast without food;
for the sake of purifying the body, take the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) here as well.
Construct a beautiful pavilion for the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
adorned with pillars of plantain trees and arches made of Aśoka leaves.
O illustrious lady, construct there a Sarvatobhadra mandala made of the seven grains, and place an auspicious jar within it.
Then, place eight new jars in the eight directions on the side;
wrap cloths around their necks and place five fresh sprouts upon their mouths.
Place eight coconuts, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī,
there within the central jar in a golden vessel with devotion.
Having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, then perform the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and have the worship of Lakṣmī along with Nārāyaṇa performed.
Present indeed the excellent sixteen types of offerings;
perform a vigil at night, and likewise perform your bath in the morning.
Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen types of offerings,
and likewise honor the one who has arrived there and is a knower of the rules for initiation.
Take refuge first in me as your teacher for the sake of attaining refuge in Hari;
for he gathers together the meanings of the scriptures and establishes you in right conduct. (25)
Because he himself practices [this] and certainly teaches the Veda, he knows the mantra of Viṣṇu and performs devotion to him in every way. || 36 ||
He who knows the knowledge of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa-sampradāya and delivers his own disciple—that teacher is considered a true Guru. (37)
A disciple who has full confidence in his words and is devoted to him should receive that jewel of a mantra on the eleventh day of the month of Kārtika.
"O Goddess, accept the conch, the discus, and the auspicious mudrā as part of the initiation;
having bathed them with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), worship the conch and the discus. (39)
Having established the fire according to the rite, one should offer clarified butter according to the injunction;
perform one hundred and eight oblations of ghee and milk-rice.
Then the Guru [should place] the heated conch and discus into the fire, and say:
"I am Śambhu, the Guru; indeed, with the discus and the lotus [conch], I [initiate you]. (41)
Having worshipped those two arms again, I mark them;
now perform the consecration upon the head with the water contained in the jar. 42.
Having put on a new garment, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with water;
then apply a tilaka mark on your forehead and an upright sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) adorned with a crescent moon.
With sandalwood and saffron, then receive my mantra:
"I am Brahmā, I am a devotee of Brahmā"—accept that from me three times. (44)
Therefore, O daughter of the mountain, worship me; bow down to me.
O Adrijā, take this tulasī necklace and wear it around your neck. (45)
O Daughter of the Mountain, accept this mantra: "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
And your names shall be Maheśvarī and Parameśvarī. 46.
Therefore, perform meditation upon that which is to be realized; likewise, always take up in your meditation the divine Śrī Hari as two-armed, and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. 47.
There is no deity higher than the Supreme Brahman Nārāyaṇa;
his very own other mantra is: "Śrī Hari is my refuge. (48)
"O Śivā, accept her today; you have become a venerable and true Vaiṣṇavī.
Practice devotion to Hari constantly, and perform service to my guru. (49)
Cause your branches of disciples and grand-disciples to flourish by bestowing the mantras;
for the abode of Lakṣmī has come to you, and that of Nārāyaṇa has come to me.
"We two shall always practice devotion to Nārāyaṇa;
we shall serve him so that liberation may become certain. (51)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Constituent Sections," in which Śambhu bestowed the Śrī-Vaiṣṇava initiation upon Pārvatī on Mount Kailāsa, within the first section of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā* concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to what was requested again by the goddess Vaiṣṇavī;
I shall relate it before Śambhu, for it is supremely worthy of being heard.
Pārvatī said: O Lord of Gods, O Mahādeva, O Sovereign of the Suras,
explain to me once again in detail devotion to Viṣṇu, which bestows liberation,
as well as the forms of Nārāyaṇa and the procedures for mantra and worship.

Out of affection for me, tell me in detail and without omission everything regarding His manifestations, qualities, and so forth; the means for attaining His abode; the nature of that abode; as well as its signs and majesty.
Thus questioned by the Great Goddess, Śambhu, the best among the devotees of Viṣṇu,
bowed to Nārāyaṇa Hari and spoke with supreme love:
"Well asked, O Great Goddess, you who desire the welfare of all living beings!"
O Maheśvarī, you who are endowed with excellent devotion, virtuous conduct, beauty, and qualities— I am well-pleased by your question; you are indeed blessed, O dear Vaiṣṇavī!
You have performed meritorious deeds and are a devotee of the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
And I shall describe to you, O Goddess, the supreme devotion to the Lord,
as well as the true nature of Nārāyaṇa and the ritual procedure for mantra-worship.
He alone is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord.
The Lord of all, the Great Lord of liberation, the Sovereign who transcends the imperishable.
The Supreme Person, the Best of Men, Śrī Hari himself—
the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Imperishable, the Transcendent beyond the Unmanifest.
Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of gods, Viṣṇu, the eternal; the Lord of lords, the Lord of the Great Māyā, the Witness, Sadāśiva. || 1.1 ||
The glorious Hiraṇyagarbha, Śrīyajña, Nārāyaṇa, and Nara;
the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Sovereign, Ananta, the one who rejoices in the Self, and the one who transcends all qualities. || 1-2 ||
He who is the knower of all eyes and all things, who dwells within the hearts of all as their controller;
the mine of virtues, of divine form, dark-hued, and captivating to the heart. 13.
He dwells eternally among his devotees and protects his own people,
together with Śeṣa, the Vedas, the Upavedas, and other deities headed by Bṛhaspati.
Indeed, it is not possible to fully describe the majesty of that God;
however, O beloved, listen as I describe to you separately the various aspects of his devotion. 15.
The form of Hari should always be meditated upon repeatedly within one's own self;
indeed, the marking with His discus and conch is considered the primary [practice]. (16)
The wearing of the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the formal adoption of their mantras, their worship, their recitation, meditation upon them, and the constant remembrance of their names;
the glorification of them, listening to them, saluting them, and honoring their feet. || 17 ||
And drinking the nectar of his feet, and eating the food offered by him. || 18 ||
Service to His devotees, the observance of the Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī vows,
the planting of Tulasī, and devotion— these indeed constitute the sixteen-fold path of devotion (bhakti).
Furthermore, there is the sweeping and smearing of his sacred temple.

Washing, fumigation, swinging, and likewise kindling; fanning, massaging, dyeing with colors, and applying collyrium; as well as perfuming and the offering of articles according to one's vow. || 1.114.20-21 ||
Laughing, conversing, and sleeping—these sixteen others are indeed varieties of devotion consisting of action performed for the sake of Hari. ||22||
Through these various forms of service, the bondage of worldly existence is destroyed for all the gods, the goddesses, and for me as well. (23)
Hari is to be worshipped eternally by the virtuous, by Brahmins, and especially by Vaiṣṇavas; one should indeed worship Him according to the prescribed rites. ||2||
Having indeed marked the roots of both arms with the conch, discus, mace,
and lotus according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the worship of Brahmā.
Having washed away his sins, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
worship performed by one who is devoid of the marks of the discus is fruitless.
A śrāddha meal eaten by one who is devoid of Viṣṇu’s discus is useless;
seeing such a non-Vaiṣṇava, the ancestors depart disappointed. (27)
Cows, land, gold, and other gifts should indeed be given to one whose arm is marked with the discus;
for what is given to one devoid of the discus, the asuras seize by force. ||28||
Those whose upper arms are marked with the heated discus go to the abode of Hari;
indeed, all holy places and sacrifices reside within devotees who bear the mark of the discus.
A Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the mark of the discus is considered a mere commoner;
one should not eat anything from him, even if he has performed a thousand sacrifices.
The discus of Nārāyaṇa alone is the destroyer of the wheel of saṃsāra;
whether heated or made of sandalwood, the discus should be worn for the successful accomplishment of one's actions. (3.1)
For the sake of accomplishing the Śrauta and Smārta rites and so forth, for the sake of the perfection of mantras,
for the sake of accomplishing the worship of Hari, and for the sake of attaining the status of a Vaiṣṇava.
For the attainment of knowledge, the discus should especially be worn;
one should avoid from afar a Brahmin who does not wear the discus.
Having placed him upon a vehicle, one should expel him from one's own city;
one should not even look upon a Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava in this world, as if he were a dog-eater (śvapāka).
O Supreme Goddess, it should be understood that a Brahmin should bear the Sudarśana on his right arm and the conch on his left. 35.
O lady of beautiful hips, the twice-born who bears Govinda’s weapons upon his body shall indeed attain that fourth abode of Viṣṇu, which is most exalted. (36)
The Ṛgveda verse beginning with "camūṣacchyenaḥ śakuno bibhrat" spoke thus;
however, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, a heated wheel was placed upon both his hands. (37)
The Agnihotra itself must be maintained, for it bestows liberation through Brahman;
the heated discus must be worn on the arm, and one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. (38)
One should maintain the *sudarśana* mark, which is also called the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*;
it consists of two lines, and he who knows this attains union with Brahman. (39)
One desiring union with Brahman should wear the heated discus upon the arm;
indeed, one devoted to Tatpuruṣa should wear the heated discus upon the arm.
O gods, by which arm, when brandished, you Pitṛs were struck down, and by which Sudarśana, the world of heaven was marked as attained through effort. ||41||
Indeed, men marked by him expand the creation of the world;
they should bear the heated discus on their arm and draw the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
By that [mark], it becomes double-lined, and there is no returning again.
That discus, consecrated by Viṣṇu as its deity, should be worn upon both arms.
Having placed the heated discus upon their arms, the gods go to Keśava;
the Brāhmaṇas wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with two lines, which grants lordship.

May those people bear day and night this Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu—which is a lowly thrower, a good slayer, which pierces even when struck in the middle, and which bestows much and possesses great splendor. ||45||
"‘Pavitram’ is Agni; it is the rim of the thousand-spoked wheel.
By means of that rim, the Brahmin whose body has been purified by heat shall indeed attain union with Brahman. (46)
He bears upon his body the wheel, heated by the power of the immeasurable Viṣṇu;
he goes to the celestial realm, shaking off all evils, just as the ascetics free from passion go forth. 47.
Marked by these signs of the one of vast strides, shall we indeed become fortunate in this world?
For those who go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, called the Imperishable, are marked by them in the highest realm. (48)

O Viṣṇu, indeed, for the sake of crossing the ocean of birth, the leaders of men place your two lotus-and-discus feet— the means of purification— upon the roots of their arms; others, the ancient ones, do likewise.
The marks of you have been bestowed upon my body. ||49||

That great-souled one who, having applied the upright *puṇḍra* and bearing the discus, constantly meditates upon the supreme Viṣṇu residing within the heart by means of the mantra with its proper accent.
That which is higher than the high, greater than the great. ||1.114.5 0||
If a person constantly wears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) as well as the discus, by that his inauspiciousness is destroyed and his auspiciousness increases. ||51||
The conch, discus, mace, and other [emblems], worn as ornaments bound by the sacred thread and so forth,
protect the great ascetic just as Viṣṇu’s own weapons protect him.
He whose body is always marked with the Sudarśana shall have Hari himself, endowed with Śrī, dwelling eternally within his person. 53.
Seeing one marked with the weapon of the discus, even Yama feels apprehension in his heart;
having offered salutation from afar, he indeed departs from that devotee of Viṣṇu.
One should mark all livestock, children, and household utensils with the conch and discus, and one should give them a Vaiṣṇava name. ||55||
One should mark [the body] with the conch and the discus, and indeed bestow a Vaiṣṇava name.
When both husband and wife perform the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras), they become true partners in dharma; it is not otherwise.
All Vaiṣṇava sages are marked with the Sudarśana;
by drinking the water from their feet, one is liberated from all sins.
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, who is attainable through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, a man who has applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark shall be liberated from all [bondages].
And here, by the snares of saṃsāra, he attains Viṣṇu. ||58||
Wearing the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and bearing the insignia of the discus,
he worshipped Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī with offerings such as the *arghya*, using the mantras of the *Puruṣasūkta*.
That great-souled one shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
For the sake of pleasing Him, for the sake of auspiciousness, for protection, and for the attainment of liberation,
a true devotee should always wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), which dispels fear.
Marked with the signs of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and bow,
and anointed with *tulasī* and sandalwood paste, one should perform the ritual worship of the twilight (*sandhyopāsana*).

Bathing, charity, chanting, fire-offerings, the twilight rituals, and the study of sacred texts—these, as well as fame and rites for the ancestors, are considered fruitless without the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*. (62)
One whose body is not heated does not enjoy that raw [state]; indeed, those who have been cooked [by the fire] attain it.
Carrying this, we shall make it long-lasting through our conduct.
Those whose bodies have been purified by this Viṣṇu shall cross the ocean of sins;
[they shall reach] the sacred foot of Hari and his Sudarśana discus, which is its rim.
Having made a long tilaka mark upon the forehead, they go to the supreme state;
those whose bodies have been heated by that [fire] go to the supreme imperishable.
O Agni, with that thousand-spoked [wheel] which destroys the material nature, which is the gate of Brahman and possesses great splendor,
and which is pure and radiant, purify us through that Brahman.
By that purifier with which the gods always purify themselves,
may those who are being purified cleanse me with its thousandfold stream.
That purifier belonging to Prajāpati is golden, with a hundred elevations;
through it, we who know Brahman purify the Brahman that has been purified.
The wheel of the breath (*prāṇacakra*) of the great-souled imperishable one is constant;
when the body is encompassed by that wheel, the state of supreme exaltation shall shine forth. (69)
The purifying rite of the Lord of Heaven is well-established on the right;
for him whose arm does not suffer, his ritual acts indeed bear fruit perfectly.
Those people who, according to the prescribed rite, carry the discus and the conch for the sake of enjoyment—
even if they are situated in opposition— they protect others and are dear to Hari.
Vaiṣṇavism is said to be twofold: external and internal;
the external consists of [bearing] the conch, the discus, and so forth, while the internal is protection by Hari.
In ancient times, the Vaiṣṇava practice consisted of marking the limbs with weapons such as the discus and always serving the glorious Nārāyaṇa within the heart with devotion. (73)
"In this way, by being endowed with these two, one becomes a Vaiṣṇava on this earth.
Thus, the greatness of the discus is manifold, nourishing the meaning of the Vedas. (74)
Therefore, O Great Goddess Pārvatī, that Sudarśana should be worn;
by means of it, both protection and liberation will certainly arise. (75)

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Sixteen Kinds of Devotion, the Heated Discus, the Puṇḍra, and so forth," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O beloved, Śambhu then spoke to his dear wife Pārvatī:
"O daughter of the snowy mountain, listen likewise to another greatness."
I shall now describe the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra); liberation is sought through its wearing.
It bestows the supreme world of Brahman upon man for the sake of final release.
And one should protect it from the Lord of the World; above that, the Puṇḍra is said [to be placed].
In the middle of the Puṇḍra is Lakṣmī, and the god Janārdana resides within the Puṇḍra.
He who has two marks upon the tip of his forehead attains imperishable liberation;
by the mere sight of him in the morning, the mountains of sin are consumed by fire.
He on whose body there is the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) has his abode in Nārāyaṇa;
for one who has the vertical mark upon the forehead, the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites shall accrue.
It shall also yield the fruit of all sacrifices, as well as the fruit of *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and public works);
it shall likewise yield the fruit of all gifts and the fruit of all yogas.
Upon seeing one whose forehead bears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one is indeed liberated from sins;
by offering salutation, one ascends to a celestial chariot and goes to the supreme abode of Brahmā.
Whosoever shall feed one who wears the ūrdhvapuṇḍra at a śrāddha ceremony,
his ancestors indeed remain satisfied and joyful for ten million kalpas.
For one who wears the vertical *urdhvapuṇḍra* mark, a funeral rite (*śrāddha*) performed by such a person yields the fruit of Gayā;
likewise, sacrifice, charity, recitation, hospitable treatment of guests, burnt offerings, and ascetic heat [attain their full merit].
The merit earned by one who has performed worship while wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is infinite;
any sacrifice or other rite performed by one devoid of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is in vain.
A body without the vertical *puṇḍra* becomes like a cremation ground;
for one who lacks the vertical *puṇḍra*, even the performance of the *sandhyā* and the recitation of Vedic hymns here [yields no merit].
The Rākṣasas indeed carry him away; he becomes personally tainted by his own fault.
One who goes without the vertical Puṇḍra-mark shall go to the inexhaustible realm of Yama due to his own sin.
Then, one should perform [the rite] with sandalwood paste rich in fragrance and stamens, or with white clay,
or with yellow or reddish-brown saffron.
That ornament for the forehead is indeed to be understood as fourfold:
the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the circular mark (puṇḍra), the broad band (paṭṭapuṇḍra), and the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍraka).
The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* shall consist of two lines, while the *puṇḍraka* consists of a single line;
the *paṭṭapuṇḍra* is broad like a cloth-strip, and the *tripuṇḍra* has three lines.
In rites for the gods, such as the worship of deities, a double-lined mark is prescribed;
however, for occasions such as royal consecration, the *tilaka* is remembered as being like a lamp.
For the sake of making the forehead appear non-empty, one should wear a cloth-band (paṭṭa) day and night;
however, during worship of Śṛṅgāra, Hāsa, Liṅga, and others, one should apply the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍraka).
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is indeed made with sandalwood paste, while the sectarian mark (tilaka) is considered to be made with saffron;
that called the "strip" (paṭṭa) is made with white clay, and the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍraka) is made with ashes.
Men who are devotees of Viṣṇu should indeed apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka);
for the Ekāntins, the Mahābhāgavatas, and the Sātvatas are always [so].
Above that, they form the shape of Hari’s feet with an intervening space;
in the center, it has a moon-like spot—that indeed is remembered as the temple of Śrī Hari.

The *kesara* [mark] should be straight, gentle, with beautiful lines, captivating, and very beautiful; it should have fine lines and, like that vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, be accompanied by a crescent moon.
It should be worn by men and women; it brings auspiciousness when seen, provided that within the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) there is a central crescent moon made of saffron.
In the center, Śrī Hari shines there, joined with Lakṣmī;
because there is no intervening space, he therefore departs together with Śrī Hari.
The earth from a dried-up pond is devoid of luster and without intervals [of moisture], whereas that of the pool named Vaikuṇṭha is possessed of luster and has intervals. (24)
Taking either white or reddish-brown earth, one should apply the vertical mark (puṇḍra).
One should then purify the earth by taking clay from a sacred bathing place or from the ground around a temple. || 25 ||
The earth from the root of a Tulasī plant is praised for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, as is the soil from the ground where Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s basil grew, and the earth from the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. (26)
The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* made from the earth of the banks of the Gomatī bestows the merit of sacred fords (*tīrtha*);
likewise, the ashes of the sacrificial fire and the clay from the fields of Hari (such as Mathurā) do so as well. (27)
Or even saffron, which is soft and purifying like a doe;
as well as bilva, pippala, tulasī, vaṭa, āmalakī, and udumbara trees.

The divine trees, the ground beneath them, the sacred earth fit for the application of *tilaka*, those situated on mountain peaks, those abiding by rivers, and those born within the waters of the ocean—[all these are pure]. (29)
Whether situated in an anthill, in a temple, in a sacred field, or within the depths of the earth;
whether sprinkled with the waters of the gods' ablutions, or found in the forest, carried there by rain.

The earth is the essence of all sacred fords (tīrthas), born from cities, forests, and other such places; it is the ground where the descent of Hari occurs and is the dwelling place of the Blessed One and the yogis.
And with that [earth], one should apply the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, which bestows excellent liberation:
the black [mark] grants peace, the red brings subjugation, and the white grants liberation.
Yellow is said to bestow prosperity, while grey destroys fortune;
likewise, a line that is broken, excessively thick, crooked, or not visible when viewed obliquely [is inauspicious].
Likewise, [the mind perceives] the intermediate space, whether subtle or with uneven intervals;
lines that are short or long, and lines that are thick or thin. ||34||
With its internal diameter touching the edges, with its base severed, likewise half or three-quarters hanging down, dried up, lusterless, and stretched out. (35)
A circular mark and an upward-pointing sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) are considered to cause harm;
[the latter] should indeed begin from the base of the nose and extend until it touches the eyebrows.
Two lines, each one finger-breadth in width, extend as far as the hairline; at the base of the nose, in the depressed area, they join like a second moon.
One should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), for that bestows the abode of Brahman;
one should place it on the forehead [for the sake of] the Supreme Brahman, and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa on the heart.
Having remembered Vāsudeva on the right arm and Nara and Nārāyaṇa on the left,
one should always perform [the rites] with substances that dissolve in Viṣṇu-water.
One should worship Nārāyaṇa on the chest, Govinda on the collarbone,
Viṣṇu on the right side, and Vāmana on the left side.
Having remembered Trivikrama at the neck, Dāmodara at the waist, Padmanābha on the back, and Vāsudeva upon the head; 41.
In this manner, the great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavata) should apply twelve marks:
on the forehead, the two arms, the nape of the neck, the throat, and the back. (42)
The measurement should be four finger-breadths on the sides and ten finger-breadths;
one should make it eight finger-breadths for the neck, the head, the belly, and the chest.
But for Śrī, it is with seed-syllables and includes the intermediate space, joined with saffron and camphor;
for Kṣatriyas, however, there are four [marks] on the forehead, the two arms, and the heart.
For Vaiśyas there are two [tattoos] on the forehead and heart; for Śūdra women, one on the forehead;
and for your devotees, O Girijā, it is like the leaf of the Aśvattha tree. 45.
For my devotees of Śambhu, it is like a lotus bud;
for those devoted to Gaṇeśa and others, it is like a bamboo leaf and so forth. (46)
Above that [mark] of Hari and the Bhāgavatas, there is a mark in the shape of Hari’s foot;
furthermore, a vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) in the form of a ray always bestows liberation. 47.
In the center is a drop of turmeric and saffron, the abode of Lakṣmī;
it is untouched by the two lines in the middle of the forehead, being as level as a grinding stone.
A mark made with turmeric, saffron, or a dot like the moon always bestows prosperity;
the dot and the vertical *puṇḍraka* should always be understood as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. (49)
Victory is always for him on whose forehead, heart, and arms [this mark] is present;
for one who is devoid of it, there is defeat both here and in the hereafter, immediately following.
Thus, O Gaurī, I have related to you this determination regarding the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and other signs, which was told to me by Nārāyaṇa and is entirely auspicious. (51)
Those devotees of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, the Goddess, the gods, and ascetics who are self-willed shall be regarded as playful jesters. (52)
But they, though men, will have faces resembling women's, will wear their hair in braided tresses, and will perform the duties of women's households. (53)
Those who wear clothing like women reveal their own female nature;
those who stand in male dress like women reveal their own male form. (54)

Deprived of their respective duties and so forth, they become destroyers of their own liberation; lacking the proper marks or possessing improper marks, they shall indeed go repeatedly to the hells. (55)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Urdhvapuṇḍra and Other Marks," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that thereafter Śambhu spoke to Pārvatī concerning the supreme majesty of the mantra— its seed-syllable and its full extent— for the sake of all goals.
Liberation or even any other goal is not accomplished by means of a mantra taught by one who is not a Vaiṣṇava; therefore, one should indeed take refuge in a Vaiṣṇava.
A mantra bestowed by a Vaiṣṇava Ācārya is indeed the accomplisher of all goals;
one should always make a Vaiṣṇava one’s guru, never one who is not a Vaiṣṇava.
Through the association with a Vaiṣṇava guru, human beings become purified;
for the Vaiṣṇava guru is declared to be the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa.
The divine Guru, equal to Nārāyaṇa, indeed delivers people;
the Guru is Nārāyaṇa himself, the bestower of mantras and likewise liberation.
He is certainly not inferior to Nārāyaṇa, and he is the giver of the bliss of Nārāyaṇa.
Equal to Nārāyaṇa in physical form, equal to Nārāyaṇa in virtue.
Equal to Nārāyaṇa in liberation and like Nārāyaṇa in bestowing the goal,
the excellent mantra should indeed be received from that preceptor who is the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas.
Even one who has studied a thousand branches of the Vedas, who is entitled to perform all sacrifices,
and who possesses birth as a Brahmin or other high caste, shall not be a guru if he is not a Vaiṣṇava.
Having taken refuge in the guru, the meaning of the mantra must indeed be correctly understood;
one should be marked with the signs of the conch and discus, and adorned with the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and the crescent moon mark (caṃdraka).
Wearing a garland of tulasī around his neck, the wise man should contemplate the meaning of the mantra;
the eight-syllable mantra is the ritual placement (nyāsa): "I am Brahman, I am a devotee of Brahman. (1.116.10)
Other Vaiṣṇava mantras as well, such as those dedicated to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and others—
the Nyāsa, the Mantra, and the form of the Mantra— are considered the supreme [teaching] of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Other Vaiṣṇava mantras are indeed deliverers for embodied beings;
once the purpose of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is fully understood, nothing further remains to be known.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, listen to the very meaning of this jewel of a mantra:
"I am Brahman, I am a devotee of Brahman; therein indeed are the four quarters. (13)
Because of its vastness and because of its nourishing nature, it is called the all-pervading Brahman.
That Brahman is indeed twofold: with form and without form.
In the abode of the Dharma, which possesses form and material manifestation,
the imperishable Brahmā resides as a servant, surrounded by his attendants.
At times my form is called Muktā, at times it is Śrīsvarūpaka;
at times it is in human form, and at times it is the lion-throne.
His duty is service to no other; it is service through devotion to her husband.
Such is the duty of service, which is the duty of Brahman, and likewise, he is the very embodiment of Brahman.
The second, however, is formless; it is called the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka).
It is described as the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma), that being the celestial abode of Śrī Hari.
Consisting of supreme splendor, peaceful, delightful, and bestowing the bliss of joy—that region of light is called the all-pervading abode. (19)
For the dwelling of the Supreme Brahman and for the abode of the liberated souls,
this divine ground exists as an eternally perpetual form.
That reality of Being-Consciousness-Bliss is indeed what is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa);
therein dwells the divine Hari himself, known as Puruṣottama. ||21||
It indeed dwells in that supreme abode called the Imperishable, which is the locus of bliss;
from that abode, there arises for it a nature characterized by stainlessness.
Pervading all the principles of Māyā, it is also untainted;
there is no staining by the attributes of Māyā, and for that reason it is proclaimed as "untainted" (alepi). ||23||
Thus, these two qualities are service and freedom from stain;
likewise, one who is both a servant and free from stain is said to be the meaning of the word "Brahman."
The word "I" (ahaṃśabda) conveys the Self as the possessor of a body; yet, when it has entered into a particular body, that conscious being is called "I. (25)
Indeed, such a Self, which is distinct from the body yet dependent upon it, characterized by name and form, and denoted by the word "I," is that which the seeker of liberation must realize. ||26||
"I am the Self within the bodies of both male and female, untainted and your servant"—let this be understood as the intended meaning of "I am Brahman. (27)

He who is the supreme lord in the state of devotion to Brahman, who is beyond the state of Brahman and the Supreme Brahman, who is the Supreme Self and the Transcendent Imperishable, is called Puruṣottama. ||28||
His devotion is indeed manifold, known as *pātivratya* (devotion to the Lord);
the devotee always takes refuge in Him, having surrendered and sought His protection. ||29||
Devotion, surrender, seeking refuge—these possess six forms: trust, choosing [the Lord], entrusting oneself, wretchedness, and firm resolve. (1.116.30)
And that following [of the Lord] should be understood; it is the sixfold refuge.
Wife, body, husband, and self—conducting oneself through the oneness of these two [husband and wife]. (3.1)
Devotion to one's husband is dharma; that devotion consists of serving her husband, as well as hearing of him, chanting his names, remembering him, and serving at his feet. ||32||
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender—such is devotion preceded by love; indeed, service is the service of one's master. (3.3)
"Whatever you may do after I have fallen at your feet, please do that for me"—this surrendering of everything is *prapatti*, the total offering of one's very life. (34)

I, who am the substratum of the word "I" and possess attributes such as being pervaded, dependent, and powerless—such an "I" performs service to my husband and lord, who is dearer to me than life itself. (35)
"I am performing [this]," thus I became the locus of service unimpeded by the three periods of time;
for the collective meaning is: "I am Brahman, I am a devotee of Brahman, born of mantra. (36)
I am a servant of Hari, whose nature is dependent on the pervasive [Lord], incapable [of independence], and so forth;
being untainted, I possess devotion such as listening to the stories of His wives' fidelity and other virtues.
The meaning expressed is: "I have become one whose dwelling is in the eternal state.
Having reflected upon this very meaning of the jewel of mantras again and again, [one should practice]. (38)
A devotee must by all means remain deeply immersed in the bliss of Brahman;
for there is no one other than Nārāyaṇa who bestows both happiness and liberation.
Therefore, having deposited and offered one's entire possession there from all sides, the name of Brahmā should be joined at the beginning of the mantra, fixed as "Oṃ. (1.116.40)
The three Vedas indeed consist of the syllables 'A', 'U', and 'M';
Viṣṇu himself is represented by the syllable 'A', and the one born from the ocean (Lakṣmī) is expressed by the syllable 'U'.
Through the syllable *ma*, those two are devoted; thus, they are indeed the three *om*s.
The syllable *a* is Vāsudeva, and the syllable *u* is the awakener of Śrī. (42)
With the syllable *m*, they are considered the servants of those two; thus, these three are regarded as *om*.
The letter *a* is the Supreme Brahman, while the letter *u* is said to be Brahman. (43)
By the syllable *ma*, he is known as their devotee, a servant through service;
his splendor is like that of the sun, and it is therefore eternally inseparable from him.
Lakṣmī is the body of Nārāyaṇa, the beautiful wife of Viṣṇu;
she is the eternal sovereign of the worlds, the mother who sustains the universe. 45.

I am considered to be the Self (Ātman), possessed of knowledge, having knowledge as its quality, the substratum of knowledge, subtle, residing in the heart, and the locus of the mass of consciousness and bliss. ||46||
He is considered a true devotee of the illustrious Hari who has become His remnant and His servant, having surrendered his sense of ownership to Hari and whose life is dependent upon Him. (47)
By the power of Nārāyaṇa, nothing would be unattainable for oneself;
for "nārāḥ" is indeed a collection of men, and they are themselves the Self. 48.
Because his abode (ayana) is therein, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa;
he is Śrī Hari, the all-pervading one within all sentient and insentient entities. (49)
Water born from *nara* is called *nāra*; because he moves (*ayana*) therein, he is Narāyaṇa.
He is said to be the refuge (*ayana*) for all *naras* (beings) who have entered into him at the time of dissolution. (1.116.5)
Therefore, the divine Nārāyaṇa is the agent of creation and destruction;
he in whom all is, from whom all comes, and who is all—Nārāyaṇa.
He whose eyes and feet are infinite, whose heads are infinite, and who is the Lord of nectar;
he is indeed Hiraṇyagarbha, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the past, the future, and the present.
Hari, who exists within the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśvara, and even the creation of the individual soul (jīva), stands pervading the three worlds with but a single foot. ||53||
He is the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable Brahman, Vāsudeva, the Golden One;
He is Vairāja, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Lords, Sacrifice, Savitṛ, and Śiva.
And he indeed stands pervading the earth, having touched it on all sides;
from him were born the Adityas and the Aditis, and all those who have two rows of teeth.
From him were born those who dwell in villages and forests, as well as the Sādhyas and the Ṛṣis;
likewise, from him came those with sacrificial threads and those without, and likewise the fires.
By him the enclosing fences were made; indeed, the entire world, from the nails to the crest of his hair, consists of these.
Likewise, the guardians of the directions and even the guardians of the Lokāloka mountain [are formed from them]. (57)
"Beings are born from that [source], and I am its devotee.
Having thoroughly understood this meaning, the servant attains perfection. ||58||
The world is always his food, his servant, and his very body;
one should take refuge in that embodied one who is to be worshipped and served. (59)
Now listen, O beautiful one, to another secret concerning the truth of mantras:
that which causes delusion is the mark, while compassion for all beings is the ocean.
Endowed with her, that Great Power is indeed declared to be Lakṣmī;
and Nārāyaṇa, joined with her, is the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī is said to be divine prosperity; he who possesses it is the Lord. He is called Śrīman Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of wealth through his grace. (62)
His own sovereignty is unimpeded, both sixfold and eightfold;
he possesses omniscience, eternal contentment, and a form that fulfills all desires. ||6.3||
Eternal bliss, the quality of being the controller—these six indeed exist there; likewise, freedom from sin, freedom from sorrow, and freedom from hunger. (64)
Likewise, freedom from hunger, freedom from thirst, freedom from decay, freedom from death, the power of true resolve, and the attainment of true desires—this is the group of eight qualities. (65)
Wherever that supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa himself is present as the master,
there the Lord Nārāyaṇa bestows celibacy upon the man.
For he is Hari-Nārāyaṇa, who removes the sufferings of his devotees;
and he is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who leads [them] away after drawing out Māyā.
He who dwells within, who plays, who is the inner controller, and who is the illuminator—
he indeed is Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who bestows the highest good.
For it is there that yogis delight; He indeed is Rāmanārāyaṇa.
That which is called "Oṃ" is the Supreme Brahman, and that which is called "Śrī" is the beloved of Hari. (69)
The multitude of men joined with those two; therein lay the inner controller-ship of Hari, as well as sovereignty, valor, glory, fortune, and wisdom.
And dispassion—these six indeed are proclaimed to be the designation of Bhaga.
To Vāsudeva, who possesses those [qualities], offer salutation and become most excellent. (7.1)
In whom reside knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor—he is the glorious Lord, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest. 72.
For the sake of self-restraint, I know and meditate upon Hari who dwells within;
may that all-pervading Lord impel me toward the task of liberation.
O Goddess, for one who worships Hari after knowing the meaning of the Gāyatrī mantra,
liberation has forever taken up residence within his very hand.
The glorious Hari is my refuge; my surrender is fully prepared for its purpose.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Various Mantras for Those Seeking Refuge Given by Vaiṣṇava Gurus," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Pārvatī spoke to Maheśvara, the Lord of Devas and foremost among Vaiṣṇavas:
"O Lord, tell me how the majesty of the form of Nārāyaṇa [is manifested]. (1)
Having drunk the nectar that bestows liberation, the mind is indeed never satiated;
how is it that even after such a long time, this has not been realized? (2)
This supreme, most worthy of being heard, the nectar of the nectar of the Supreme Brahman, must be heard by me eternally; indeed, it is ever-new with every hearing.
Then Śambhu spoke to the goddess Pārvatī, the Supreme Sovereign:
"Listen, O Goddess, for this narrative of mine is also centered upon Nārāyaṇa."
It shines with fresh sweetness, and the joy it brings increases;
I shall describe it as it is remembered, for though it is indeed beyond the reach of words.
The Supreme Brahman himself, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa,
the king of kings, eternally shines by his own power within that abode.
The Puruṣa has infinite heads, infinite eyes, and innumerable feet;
having pervaded the entire creation, he remained [standing] on a space no larger than a single hair.
He indeed shines everywhere, the Lord of Liberation, possessed of supreme prosperity;
there is no other superior to him, none equal, nor even one who shares in his inheritance.
In one-fourth of this world, all the creations of Jīva and Īśa exist;
however, one-third of this is the world of Brahmā, while the Brāhmaṇas indeed reside in the supreme ether beyond.
Neither hunger nor thirst arises there;
however, beneath that, the illusion based on hunger and thirst expands.
In his abode, indeed, are the supreme abodes;
he is the mind of the liberated ones, of the lords, and of the incarnations.
Holding himself within his own self, the divine, singular God shines forth;
thus, this one of vast form shines together with Brahman.
He is attended by hosts of attendants numbering infinite crores,
and likewise served by sovereign goddesses, glories, and powers.
He possessed a divine and auspicious form enriched with boundless celestial enjoyments; he was a youth of undecaying great courage, with limbs as delicate and soft as those of a tender infant.
His youth is the very embodiment of the full moonlight that gives birth to the world;
he is filled with inexhaustible love and the beauty of ten million Cupids. || 19 ||
For the sake of fulfilling the desires of Śrī, he established the realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
for the sake of bestowing happiness upon Rādhā, he remains as the dark-complexioned one in Goloka. 16.
The abode that bestows the bliss of liberation is considered to be the imperishable Brahman;
for the sake of enjoyment, there is Vaikuṇṭha in the supreme ether and the world of cows.
The entire universe was created threefold for the sake of divine play (*līlā*) and for the dwelling of devotees;
those manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) are the stages known as the enjoyment of happiness and divine play. (18)

There are three [powers] belonging to that very [Lord]; they constitute His threefold manifestation. The one called *līlā* is the entire creation, while the other two abodes exist for the sake of enjoyment.
For the sake of bestowing the bliss of liberation, Janārdana remains in his supreme abode when he withdraws his divine play, the great creation.
At that time, indeed, there exists an eternal state within the manifestation of enjoyment;
beyond even that is another state, consisting of the supreme form, which is great bliss.
Play, enjoyment, and bliss—these three are His very powers;
that supreme abode is three-footed, eternal, and the everlasting Lordship.
In the very peripheral regions of that [city], he has eternally established other abodes;
he has spread them everywhere for the sake of the enjoyment of service by his devotees. ||22||
He manifested the abode of nectar (Amṛtadhāma), the abode of Badarī, the unmanifest (Avyākṛta),
the abode of Lakṣmī, and the white abode (Śvetadhāma) for the sake of service and enjoyment.
And for the sake of penance, as well as for the purpose of protecting the world, he divided it into three parts; that [portion] was indeed eternal, while one part was non-eternal.
Acyuta, Vaikuṇṭha, and Gavāṃsthala, which are rich in the form of Brahman;
and Amṛta and Śrīpura, belonging respectively to Rādhikā and Śrī. ||26||
Indeed, these were created for the sport of the other wives of the Lord;
there, the Blessed Śrī Hari eternally maintains his youth.
This mother of the world, Lakṣmī and Rādhikā, is likewise eternal;
just as Viṣṇu is omnipresent, so too are Lakṣmī and Rādhikā.
She is Īśānī, the Great Goddess (Maheśvarī), the sovereign of the past and the future;
she is Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Rādhā, the inseparable consort of Viṣṇu.
She has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads, and faces on all sides; she is Nārāyaṇī, Kṛṣṇā, the consort of Viṣṇu, and the embodiment of the universe.
Mahāmāyā is the creator of the world, the performer of its emanation and reabsorption;
everything consisting of a mixture of the insentient and the sentient is situated within her side-glance.
She whose opening and closing of the eyes constitutes the world consisting of dissolution and emergence;
she who is eternally unborn, the left-hand portion [of Śiva], she is Mahālakṣmī, the supreme sovereign. (32)
Unmanifest yet possessing manifest form, she is established as all-pervading:
as *rasā* on earth, as *sudhā* in heaven, and as the meritorious [Ganga] in the abode of the ancestors.
In water there is cooking with sweet fire, and Lakṣmī in the form of wealth;
as well as beauty, splendor, good fortune, physical form, and loveliness.
Everything belonging to all women is united with her alone;
through her, [one attains] the state of Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and even Yama.
The solar, the Kaubera, the Āgneya, and the lunar [forms] were seen, all prosperous;
she is Mahāmāyā, Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Rādhikā, and the Beloved. ||26||
Kamalā, Śāradā, Padmā, Vidyā, Mā, Paramā, Ramā, Abdhiputrī, Satī, Śyāmā, Mahādevī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (357)
She is Nārāyaṇī, the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the consort of Viṣṇu, and Maheśvarī;
she is Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Śānti, Prabhā, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Rati. ||38||
Sāvitrī, Kaṃbharādevī, and Pārvatī—these sixteen names of hers should be recited every morning for the attainment of prosperity. (39)
May Nārāyaṇa bring to me Lakṣmī, who is golden-hued, tawny, composed of gold and silver, the daughter of the Moon, and made of pure gold.
O Nārāyaṇa, bring to me wealth, grain, cows, horses, vehicles, and male servants, as well as Lakṣmī who never departs.
May Kṛṣṇa bring to me that divine and radiant glory which is full of splendor, whose ramparts are of gold, and that fame which is celestial, majestic, and rooted in righteousness. 42.
May Nārāyaṇa bring to me Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of all, who is rich in fragrance, invincible, eternally nourished, and full of abundance. 43.
May Hari bring me the accomplishment of intentions, thoughts, and resolves;
I invoke here that Śrī who bestows gold, male servants, and female servants. 44.
For those by whom prosperity has been thus invoked, it shall never depart;
that Hari, the Supreme Person, is eternally attained upon his chest. 45.
Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of all, the Master of all, the mine of virtues;
he is omniscient, enriched with all powers, one whose desires are fulfilled, and who finds happiness in his own benevolence. 46.
I offer my service to that glorious ocean of compassion, who is affectionate toward those who have come for refuge and who is the sovereign wealth of both heaven and liberation. (47)
At all times, in every way, and in all states, I worship Him;
I indeed perform service for Him, for this entire world has become the servant of Hari. 48.
The glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa is the one to be served and attained, supreme even beyond the Imperishable;
he alone is mother, brother, father, son, and kinsman. (49)
He alone is the refuge, the support, the dwelling, the goal, and the ultimate end;
he is endowed with all divine qualities and is devoid of the qualities of Māyā.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa is the highest reality;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self, Nārāyaṇa is the highest. (51)
The meditator is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; meditation is supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard— ||52||
Pervading all that is within and without, Nārāyaṇa remains;
he, the Supreme Self, is established in the heart, in the midst of the individual soul.
In that supreme abode, Nārāyaṇa, joined with Śrī, resides;
by his power, by Śrī, who is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the Great Principle (mahat) was fashioned. ||54||
From that, Virāj arose—the earth and all living beings, both domestic and wild;
for from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, the social classes (varṇas) indeed came into being.
For from him were born the distinct classes of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; he is indeed the sacrifice (Makha).
He is the oblation to the gods and the ancestors, the priest, the enjoyer of the portions, and the sacrificial fuel. ||56||
The gods performed sacrifices to Nārāyaṇa, and those ritual acts were already present; indeed, supreme duties such as worship and other forms of devotion existed from the very beginning.
Those liberated in the past indeed attend upon the glory in the supreme abode;
those who practice devotion as His servants go to the station of Nārāyaṇa.
They indeed dwell eternally as perfected and liberated ones in the divine abode, in the supreme world beyond Māyā, having attained a state of similarity with Brahman. ||59||
Indeed, that abode of Hari is imperishable, having gone to which there is no return, unlike [the realms] of Māyā, Mahākāla, sinful karma, Yama, and the like.

Māyā, which consists of the universe, is eternal, composed of the three qualities (guṇas), and is indeed primordial nature (prakṛti); she is ignorance (avidyā), the yogic sleep (yoganidrā), and the eternal primary matter (pradhāna) and unmanifest (avyakta). 6.1.
She is the very nature of the shadow of the abode, whose essence is a mass of knowledge;
for she indeed makes the universe, which is as transient as a spider's thread, appear.
Enveloped by her, the entire world is covered by the splendor of Brahman.
The connection between Māyā and Brahman is said to be the limit of the Abode;
yet that [Abode], being all-pervasive, is limitless, though it is conventionally described as having limits.
Everything—contraction and expansion—is contained within the sphere of Māyā;
it remains hidden and yet manifests, while devotees go beyond it.
Then, having bathed at the boundary of the Brahma-lake—which consists of splendor, bliss, and consciousness—they attain the body of Brahman through the majesty of the supreme light. (65)
Then their forms are produced as embodiments of that very self in its own nature;
whether they be men or women, they go to the Imperishable through devotion. (66)
Bathing within the boundary of the Brahma-lake, the body itself becomes Brahman;
there is no other connection whatsoever to the splendor of external substances within the body. (67)
The Self, possessing excellent vision and conforming to the form of Hari, is perceived by itself;
there is neither yoga nor division, nor the appearance of the substances of a yogi.
He is the self whose form is the single reality of the Self, and he is Hari in his perfect embodied form;
Mahāmāyā, however, is Virajā, who leads those who go to Vaikuṇṭha.
Between Vaikuṇṭha and Māyā, she who is of the nature of the fluid of Nārāyaṇa is seen there, just as Śrī and the attendants appear after bathing therein.
In that way, male and female servants are produced eternally in Vikuṇṭha;
and that which is the supreme light, the sky, the imperishable, eternal Brahman—[is there]. (71)
That divine reality, known as Brahman, consists of truth, consciousness, and bliss;
it possesses a single hair-pore like ten million suns and fires, is undecaying, and is free from dissolution.

That which is devoid of dreams and the like, which brings cooling peace to the ocean of bliss, and which is the imperishable reality hidden in the Vedas—into that have millions of liberated ones entered. (73)
The ignorant do not know that; the wise sit there. That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu which the seers behold. (74)
Even the Vairājas do not behold that world, that state,
where the many-horned cows are ever-extending and always bestowing happiness.
That indeed is the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa, which brings happiness to the cows;
those who know it go to that realm which is effulgent like the sun and beyond all darkness.
There, indeed, dwell the liberated ones who are to be attained, beginningless from the past;
all the gods who have gone beyond the universe, being liberated, enjoy that bliss. ||77||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Glory of Nārāyaṇa and Nārāyaṇī, the Brahma-body, and Other Matters, Concerning the Manifestations and Pastimes of the Imperishable Abode of the Supreme Brahman," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Śambhu spoke to the Goddess: "O daughter of the mountain, listen; I shall describe to you in brief the manifestations of the splendors of Brahman."
The imperishable abode, the supreme Brahman, the eternal and highest ether, shines everywhere as a mass consisting of white light. || 2 ||
If all the stars that exist in the sky were to become suns, and the earth, well-prepared for creation, were to become made of divine glass; || 3 ||
And from their mutual union, whatever kind of splendor might arise,
such a dense and great splendor exists indeed in the Satya realm of the Creator.
The fiery [light] within the single throat-jewel of Vairāja is ten million times greater than that true piercing light; indeed, it exists even beyond that.
The splendor in the crest-jewel of Mahāviṣṇu is ten million times greater;
the splendor in the jewel of Vāsudeva is indeed ten million times greater than that.
And there are also infinite such jewels in the unmanifest realm,
as well as in Badarī, Amṛta, Śveta, Śrīpura, and Vikuṇṭha.
And having taken the splendors from Goloka,
one should fashion a mass (piṇḍaka) at the site of the areca nut, which is the abode known as the Imperishable Reality (tattvakṣara).
Indeed, one should attain absorption; what would that fullness be like?
It is like the splendor of the abode of the Imperishable and likewise of the liberated ones.
If the entire multitude should merge into a single hair of Śrī Hari,
then what would the great splendor be like there in the complete Hari?
Even it is not possible to infer that inaccessible, divine splendor; for I am indeed not its direct witness, but rather [know it] through meditative absorption (samādhi).
Through my extraordinary vision, I behold the Lord Śrī Hari, who resides in the abode known as Brahman within the cosmic egg, as one with my own self;
for by virtue of that proximity, even that which is beyond the supreme is perceived.
It is impossible to conceive, to reflect upon, or to understand this, for it is beyond the sphere of sensory perception.
How then, O beautiful one, can it be possible to describe him who possesses such infinite splendor and is an ocean of boundless virtues? (14)
He is a boundless great ocean of gentle smiles, beautiful in form and grace;
he is the singular moon whose steady light is the eye of the ten million liberated ones, who are like cakora birds.
The Lord, the supreme king of kings, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest,
shines upon the great lion-throne, appearing sixteen years of age.
His limbs were proportionate to his form, his face was radiant with a gentle smile,
and he wore ruby earrings as brilliant as millions upon millions of suns, moons, and fires.
His crown and earrings were bound with countless mani-jewels and gems;
he wore divine diamonds, excellent jewels, and necklaces of priceless gold.
He whose neck was radiant with the Kaustubha gem from the mine of fire, and who was encircled by the halo arising from the excellent rays spreading from his manifold splendors. || 19 ||
Resplendent with the center of his forehead shining with the brilliance of divine light,
his hair and beard were fashioned dark blue like a mass of clouds.
His eyebrows were like the curved ends of a bow fashioned by the God of Love alone;
his eyes were adorned with rows of lashes and possessed golden, subtle, and steady pupils.
Its eye-globes are like excellent divine white crystals with six facets; its lateral eyes possess the luster of fine red filaments. ||22||
In the center, there is a shimmering black pupil, made brilliant by the radiance of the form of the divine contact;
even there, the black pupil shines with the capacity for grasping the object.
His eyes, reaching as far as his ears, possess the luster of autumn lotus petals;
his ears have yellowish lobes that are as delicate as seven-fold bracelets.
His ears dripped with ichor like the fragrance of celestial flowers and full-blown campaka blossoms;
his cheeks were as soft as balls of cotton from a tree laden with ripe fruit.
His nose was curved and drooping like a sesame flower, tinged with a pale yellow;
his beard was adorned with lines resembling fine golden threads.
One whose upper lip has a curved line like the middle and tip of an archer’s bow, and whose lower lip is the very seat of desire, possessing a form like a river of love; ||27||
His two lips have the luster of red lotus petals;
his chin is well-formed, deep-set at the base of the jaw, and without protruding angles.
His teeth were as white as jasmine, sharp, with prominent tips, closely set, and firm;
his dental ridges were as brilliant as the seeds of a pomegranate, rich in red juice. ||2||
His nape was like a conch shell adorned with gold and excellent jewels; his neck was as thick as the base of Mount Meru and resembled the peak of the sky-supporting mountain.
His collarbones were positioned apart like the crescent moon at the end of an eon;
his well-nourished shoulders were raised high, bound by the strength of the flood of reality.
The hollows of his flanks and thighs were the constant seats for the meditations of yogis.
His arms were well-nourished and golden, possessing the form of the remaining coils [of Śeṣa];
his forearms were bright red and well-developed like pure gold;
his elbows were firm pegs, like the fixed pivot of the revolving wheel of the Pole Star. || 32-33 ||
His two hands are well-proportioned, gradually tapering, and full;
he wears beautiful golden chains, bracelets, and armlets.
His fingers were adorned with rings enriched with jewels, diamonds, and gems;
the circle of his true devotees was illuminated by the radiance of the shimmering beauty of his moon-like nails.
He was richly adorned with beautiful earrings, protected by armor made from the limbs of Akhamallas, and his shoulders were draped with upper garments beautified by golden borders. || 36 ||
His chest was beautifully marked with the Śrīvatsa and a divine, shining golden line;
his girdle was richly adorned with gold and gems, fashioned from twenty-seven strings.
The expanse of his three folds was like a sacrificial well, and his thighs were as radiant as the trunk of a gradually swelling elephant, rich with the wealth of desire. ||38||
His hips are broad and well-formed, worthy of the decorative patterns on the frontal globes of a majestic elephant;
his phallus is perfectly rounded, possessing the inexhaustible vigor of the eight supernatural powers. || 39 ||
He bestows the essence of the nectar of passion upon a multitude of young women;
his golden-colored belly shines with a line of golden body hair;
he is rich in the beauty of perfectly round [limbs], and his knees are firm and radiant.
His shanks are well-proportioned and firm at the back;
his ankles are hidden within, while the three joints of the wrists are clearly visible on the outside.
His body was inclined downward by the weight of his loosened ornaments, bending like the curved staff of a bow;
it was beautified by the moon-like luster of his golden, red-tinted nails. ||42||
With a body nourished and broad, protected by auspiciousness, and possessing a form most excellent among the excellent, Hari shines upon his throne within the great abode. 43.
Endowed with all sovereign powers, the capacity for action, knowledge, yoga, and so forth,
he sat upon a four-legged throne made of gold, exquisitely beautiful.
It stands with seven stairways, adorned with *kammānikā* creepers, and shines on its sides with *makha*, *malla*, *mahāgaddī*, and *pārśvatakkīya* [ornaments]. 45.
Above, a parasol was held, encircled by twenty ribs;
it was made of gold, soft, and a divine cloth was fixed upon the parasol.
A water-pot fashioned from gold, with a handle adorned with jewels and the like;
gems were set all around it, as well as golden bells.
On all sides, it is provided with seven divine, material jhallarikās; there should be two white chowries, as well as a fan and a mirror. (48)
Likewise, there are divine beings liberated and well-established in the dharma of service;
and there is the great liberated one [Śeṣa], adorned with a thousand hoods, who holds the parasol above him.
Assuming a massive form and spreading a canopy with his hoods, the great serpent Śeṣa,
resembling a mountain in stature, stands behind and serves Śrī Hari.
There, on the rear part of that lion-throne, there was a divine, great cloth made of golden threads, adorned with various colors and designs. ||51||
That which is the foremost lotus-shaped [structure], within which divine pillars stand,
and upon which there are indeed circles of pearls and gems.

And parrots, cranes, and Menakās, whose forms are truth, consciousness, and bliss, as well as trees, creepers, and other such beings, dwell there upon the pillars where excellent spots have been prepared. (53)
All conscious beings shine when they are devoted to the Supreme Brahman;
it is like a soft carpet upon a pedestal, beautiful with various artistic crafts.
Like an ocean of splendor, it was visible, resplendent with millions of jewels;
its infinite pearls were illuminated by the luster of moonstones that were his fingernails.
The lion-throne itself is the abode known as the Immutable (Akṣara), and nothing else;
there, within that form, exists a great, circular halo of supreme splendor.
He whose sides are pervaded by infinite cows of sweet, cool, and gentle luster;
he who possesses seven forms and seven grounds; he who is the surrounding enclosure—he too is liberated.
The splendor of Hari pervades all ten directions on every side of the great lion-throne;
it has no end, and those rays are like cows with many horns.
Where that lion-throne was, there indeed was a pavilion measuring one yojana;
therein were divine great pillars, imperishable and fashioned like plantain trees.
They were yellowish-green in color, with green leaves and auspicious green plantain trees;
they possessed a hundred pillars, were golden-hued, and were beautiful, draped in cloth coverings.
Their mechanical devices, variegated by the application of artistic skills, were of various kinds:
white elephants, sea-monsters, swans, and cranes. (61)
The peacock, the parrot, the white pigeon, the cakravāka, and the cātaka—all these indeed become liberated, possessing the very form of existence, consciousness, and bliss. ||62||
Accompanied by auspicious songs rendered with the sweetness of divine melodies,
they sing praises of his virtues in the Sanskrit language of that place.
Indeed, mandalas worth many millions of great pearls are established within the pavilion—on the ground, on the surface, in the middle, above, and in between. (64)
