Indeed, all those forms which were sustained by Hari throughout the various cycles of creation and dissolution have been established within this pavilion.
They shine in various forms, bearing the diverse marks of sovereignty, serving as causes for awakening to the deeds of his various births and incarnations. (66)
The divine manifestations, whose forms communicate the narrative,
all stand right there, at the center above the top of the pavilion.
The liberated ones dwelling there, having become mirrors for the sun, moon, and other luminaries,
indeed reside within those various pillars again and again.
In that [treatise], enriched by the citation of those authorities, the stars of liberated souls shine forth perfectly,
emitting cool radiance.
And there were gateways adorned with pearls, jewels, and diamonds,
which possessed the brilliance of glass and the splendor of many divine lamps and moons.
Above, below, as well as at the sides, in all the cardinal and intermediate directions,
radiant rays go forth from the pavilion, traveling along the path of the sky.
Such a pavilion or such a throne as that does not exist in other abodes; how can its wondrous splendor be described? (72)
Even divine splendor does not arise elsewhere; it cannot be described by me except for that palace atop the pavilion belonging to Śrī Hari. Listen to that, O beloved! (73)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Supreme Brahman Residing in the Imperishable Abode, His Lion Throne, and His Pavilion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Śambhu spoke again to the Goddess above the pavilion of Śrī Hari:
"Listen, O auspicious lady, to this palace which has never existed before and will never exist again."
It was one hundred thousand yojanas in width and one thousand yojanas in height;
it possessed a single row of a thousand pillars, and likewise, thousands of such rows.
In every direction, four auspicious *karmānika* pillars stand upright; in the center is a great smoke-pipe (*dhūmaka*), and likewise four in the cardinal directions. (3)
Indeed, four peaks shine at the four corners;
having certainly reached that Dhūmmaṭa, there are seven peaks.
There are three on the right and three on the left, while the greatest is in the middle;
where there is a pavilion at Kollā, beneath that is the lion-throne.
Upon the palace is a granary a thousand yojanas in height;
above the granary is a pinnacle measuring one thousand five hundred yojanas.
There stands a lotus-stone slab measuring five hundred yojanas;
there also exists a terrace-stone slab rising one hundred yojanas in height.
Above that, there are exactly one hundred divine golden jars;
above those, a single jar, which is considered the most important of them all.
Those [trees] were five hundred yojanas in height; beyond that, the flagstaff was a thousand yojanas in height, and the bamboo pole was likewise of such height.
There, the banner was five hundred yojanas long from its base to its tip;
it had seven colors and two tails, blazing as brilliantly as ten million suns.
These very beings, though liberated, assume forms for the sake of service; always liberated yet possessing bodies marked by signs, they remain thus engaged in service.
On the peak dwell the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, and indeed the Yoginīs reside in the cardinal directions; furthermore, there are lions and other man-lions who are indeed incarnations.
In those windows on the summit, pearl-eyed birds indeed dwell;
likewise, other figurines and other pearls dwell there together.
The *pāṭalikā* on the flagstaff is considered virtuous and liberated;
those who possess bells are also liberated, while others are divine attendants of Śrī Hari. (14)
Therein, the Great Lamp is the supreme lamp, and there is no other;
for that lamp is indeed greater than the great, being the most excellent of all.
Moreover, all the liberated ones indeed dwell upon the other peaks as well;
even the pinnacle atop the palace rises to a height of a thousand yojanas.
This divine great mansion, moving through the sky, is composed of light itself;
by the will of Śrī Hari, it moves in every direction according to his desire.
There, the celestial chariots of the sages, which travel at will, indeed wander about and perform circumambulations of the temple with devotion. (18)
The divine [waters] consist of cold and hot water, as well as eternal fire-pits;
they are impermanent, possess cool fragrances, are luminous, and have the form of milk. || 19 ||
Lamps with the power of true resolve, and utensils born of desire;
garments, food, ornaments, and the like, as well as drinks and vehicles, all born of desire.

The houses, the excellence of the dwellings, the male servants, and likewise the female servants—these are all divine beings with celestial forms, who are indeed liberated souls in embodied form. (21)
In the center of his own magnificent palace was a beautiful lion-throne;
on its sides, the residence of Dharmadeva and that of Bhakti were fixed.
On the left side, however, the residence of Mukti (Liberation) and Rati (Pleasure) is certain;
on the side of Dharma, the residence of Jñāna (Knowledge) and Virakti (Dispassion) is certain. (23)

The residence of liberation (mukti) is certain at the side of devotion (upāsti), and the residence of command (ājñā) is certain at the side of liberation. The residence of the desire for liberation (mumukṣā) is certain at the side of command, and the residence of surrender (prapatti) is certain at the side of the desire for liberation. ||24||
On the side of knowledge, there is a constant dwelling in discourse and conversation;
on the side of conversation, there is a constant dwelling in servitude and initiation.
Thus, I have described to you the residence below the seven peaks;
at Ghummaṭa, there is a circular circle of clans (gotramaṇḍala) in the clockwise direction.
Indeed, there are seven families of householders residing there;
in its circular gateway, that supreme knowledge is attained by which [liberation is reached]. (27)
The great circular golden divine rampart is thus described;
there, all around, shine the palaces inhabited by those liberated from time immemorial.
Their palaces are eternal, like conscious celestial chariots;
they move at will, travel as they desire, and are filled with every prosperity.
They are the abodes of all pleasant tastes—of food, drink, ointments, and offerings;
they are always radiant, divine, liberated, and possess the form of Śrī Hari.
They possess all powers according to their will and can manifest whatever they desire through their meditative cultivation;
O Pārvatī, listen with a steady mind as I shall declare their names to you. (31)
Gopāla who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta), Brahmā, the liberated Śuka, Śata, Suvrata, Niṣkula, Bhūmā, Vidhātṛ, and Vāsudeva. || 32 ||
Kṛṣṇa is eternal, inconceivable, and peaceful; he is renunciation, compassion, the supreme swan, dispassion, composed of consciousness, imperishable, and the Lord. (3)
He is self-luminous, solitary, dispassionate, and likewise conscious;
he is of the nature of consciousness, the person (nara), the venerable feet (śrīcaraṇa), and the purifier. || 34 ||
He is the steadfast one, the Great Being, Śiva, and the very foundation;
he is pure consciousness, the devotee of Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, and indeed devoid of qualities.
The Sage, the Lord of Auspiciousness, the Lord of Lords, indeed the Formless One, and the Immortal;
the Cowherd, the Holder of the Lotus, the White One, Vaikuṇṭha, and also the God.
Prakāśa, Prasāda, Sudharma, Sukhāśraya, Sukharūpa, Santopa, Jñāna, and Vijaya as well. || 37 ||
Badrika, Nivṛtta, Naya, Dhyāna, Śāntanu, Śama, Sukha, Mahāsukha, Acintya, Amogha, and Pramodaka. || 38 ||
Gavendra, Anubhava, Āditya, Acala, Viśvarūpaka, Prajña, Bodha, Vedānta, Mukunda, and Kṣema as well. || 3.9 ||
Puṇḍarīka, Vidhātṛ, Agrāhya, Śāśvata, Dhruva, Ameya, Pavitra, Sthaviṣṭha, and Ṛṣīkaka. ||1.119.40||
Prabhūta, Niyama, Yoga, Jagadīśa, Dayālaya, Sura, Dharma, Muni, Nara, Balabhadra, and Prakāśana. ||4 1 ||
Sidha, Sukhakara, Viśrāma, Keśava, Kapila, Svayaśodraṣṭṛ, Sajjana, and Sāṃkhya as well. ||42||
Bhāskara, Prabha, Ṛṣabha, as well as Saguṇa, Nirdvaṃdva, Nṛsiṃha, Videha, and Deva—thus [are they]. 43.
He is without support, full of trust, unchanging, and illuminating;
he is independent, without food, a being of pure essence, and is known as Lakṣmaṇa. 44.
Nirmoha, Bhūdhara, Bhadra, Mānada, Haṃsa, Pradyumna, Ānanda, Mañjula, and Pratoṣaṇa. ||45||
Bhajana, Nirmala, Śānta, Praśānta, Dhanya, then Savitā, Dharaṇa, Sujña, Satyeśa, and likewise Jyotiṣa. ||46||
Prabodha, Prabhu, Padma, and also Tāpasa;
Turīya, Svarūpa, Viveka, and likewise Vāmana. (47)
Nivāsa, Maṅgala, Akṣaya, Suvrata, Abheda, Turīya, Kṣemaka, and Dṛḍhavrata. ||48||
Nirviśeṣa, Vicāra, Jiṣṇu, Madhu, Vaiṣṇava, Avyaya, Muktiga, Varada, and likewise Saṃśita. ||49||
Vallabha, Suparṇa, Viśvadhra, and likewise Durlabha;
Dhana, Prasāda, Śyāma, and likewise Dahara.
Aiśvarya, Avadāta, Rādha, Dharmarūpaṇa, Vraja, Bhāgavata, Bāla, Upaśama, and Svastika. ||5 1 ||
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Śrīdhara, Amṛta, Yajña, Hiraṇyaka;
Īśāna, Prabhava, Pūta, Bhūgarbha, Prāṇada, and Praṇa. ||52||
He is the year, the auspicious one, the grateful one, and the lord of the gods;
he is the wise one, the bull, the wealth, the Sāman, the quality, the overseer, and the knower.
Loka, Vyūha, Sarvaga, Bhrājiṣṇu, Caraṇa, Sahiṣṇu, Catura, Anagha, Urjita, and Kāraṇa—thus [are the ten]. ||24||
Upendra, Dhṛta, Sattva, and also Sāttvata;
Utsāha, Viśruta, Anirdeśa, and Animeṣaṇa. (55)
Udāra, Subhūṣa, Anila, and likewise Vikrama; Satkāra, Saṃvṛta, Vṛtta, Viśiṣṭa, and Siddhimat. ||56||
Vardhana, Vivikta, Bṛhadrūpa, Pṛthuśravas, Aśoka, Sudāman, Sānukūla, and likewise Atula. ||57||
Ādideva, Śrīgarbha, Nirvāṇa, Bhājana, as well as Vyavasāya, Santoṣa, Virāma, and Nanda. ||58||
Sthira, Sudarśana, Viśāla, and Dakṣa; likewise Dharmayūpa, Ijya, Makha, Sūkṣma, and Pramāṇaka. ||59||
He is devoted to Brahman, affectionate, and of auspicious limbs; he is ancient, the unifier, the one who brings delight, the source of joy, and the most meritorious.
Durjaya, Kumuda, Sulabha, and Śuddha;
Yogīśa, Suvidya, Sākṣya, and likewise Dhanañjaya.
He is the indivisible one, the three worlds, the friend, the infinite, the golden one;
he is existence, being, sacrifice, and also the means of propitiation.
Vatsala, Vātsala, Susneha, Kuberajit, Soma, Alarka, Śūra, Mantra, Mañca, and Mūlajit. ||63||
The forehead mark, the earrings, the crown, the bracelets, the armlets, the finger-guards, the Kaustubha gem, the cloak, and likewise the tunic. (64)
Thus, those attendants, having taken refuge within the rampart,
always remain in the palatial mansions in that first enclosure.
And those who serve Hari dwell there as liberated beings from time immemorial;
they are also innumerable in the second enclosure.
They all possess forms identical to the [divine] form, and their lordship is equal to that of the form;
they all behold with equanimity the temple of Śrī Hari within their own hands. (67)
In that regard, there is no deficiency or excess among the excellent qualities such as sovereignty;
they exist exactly as intended, possessing eternal omniscience and vision. (68)
That first wall has an extent of ten million yojanas;
the second wall has an extent of one hundred thousand yojanas. (69)
The third wall, however, is one parārdha yojanas in extent;
there indeed dwell those liberated ones who have come from the worlds of the Īśvaras.
There is a rampart there, four times a parārdha multiplied by a parārdha yojanas in length; within it are the abodes of the liberated ones who have attained liberation.
Then, the fifth covering there is infinite;
therein are Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and also Amṛta, which are boundless.
Likewise, Avyākṛta, Śveta, and Badarikāśrama;
also Mātsyaloka, Kūrmaloka, and Vārāhaloka. (73)
I would abandon the abode of Kapila, as well as the home of Vāsudeva,
the station of Pārtha, the dwelling of Dattātreya, and Haṃsaka.
The abode of Nṛhari, as well as Vāmaneyaka belonging to Āryaman, the world of Paraśurāma, Yājña, and Sāketa as well. ||75||
The abode of Kaumāra, the abode of Hayagrīva, the abode of Nārada, the abodes of the kings of kings, and those which are the refuges of Vyāsa—[all these have been described]. (76)
There is indeed the abode of the Buddha, as well as other countless abodes;
for the incarnations are infinite, and the millions of universes are infinite. (77)
The emanations therein have infinite creations; their number cannot be calculated, and thus the number of those respective abodes is indeed neither one nor the other.
The number of the fifth enclosure is neither one nor many;
therein are forests, rivers, mountains, and infinite peaks. (79)
Gardens, monasteries, and grounds designated by syllables;
elements, mines, excavations, elevations, and peaks. (1.119.80)
All the celestial palaces themselves were the various classes of their respective attendants:
musicians, dancers, storytellers, and flute-players. (8.1)
Servants, sacrificial priests, chanters of the Sāmans, those engaged in strenuous efforts, artisans, and those who have attained the circles of liberation and non-liberation; ||82||
No one except Nārāyaṇa is able to count those who are beyond counting;
he too has declared that there is no numbering for the liberated souls within my abode. (83)
Likewise, there is no counting of the incarnations and their abodes;
so it is with the divine, imperishable abode, the manifestation, and the threefold path.
From that, by the playful power (*līlā*) of Śrī Hari, various abodes come into being;
thus, through the agency of Mahāmāyā, a creation arises consisting of millions of lords (*īśvara*).
There is no end, nor can any end be reached even in description;
how indeed could I complete a description by reaching its limit? (86)

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The General and Specific Enumeration of the Temple of Śrī Hari, its Appurtenances, its Enclosures, the Liberated Attendants (Pārṣadas), Their Incarnations, Abodes, and So Forth," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara, the friend of the world and the benefactor of the people,
spoke to Pārvatī concerning the description of Goloka.
Goloka is the abode of the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Hari, which is filled with infinite servants, maidservants, and all other opulences, splendors, and delights.
Listen, O Goddess of gods, for I have shown it to you in my meditative absorption:
on the far bank of the great river Virajā, there is a mountain surrounded by a wall.
Śataśṛṅga is fifty crores of yojanas in circumference;
its width at the top is one crore yojanas, and it extends for ten crores of yojanas [in total].
On its single peak is the Rāsa-maṇḍala, ten yojanas in extent;
beyond that is Vṛndāvana, and likewise thirty-two forests.
Beyond that is the imperishable banyan tree (Akṣayavaṭa), and from it proceed the creations of the cowherds, cowherdesses, and others;
above that, in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), is Goloka, and beyond that, the Imperishable (Akṣara).
That abode is indeed manifold, auspicious, and the remover of old age and death;
it is maintained by Brahmā and fashioned by the will of Hari.
It is impossible to describe it; nevertheless, I shall briefly describe it:
the two broad banks of the Virajā were seen by me through meditative absorption (samādhi).
Resembling pure crystal, they were very extensive and captivating;
they were endowed with mines of pearls, rubies, and the most excellent gems and jewels.
Adorned with rows of black, white, yellow, and red gems,
those two beautiful and well-lit coral-like [objects] were somewhere most enchanting.
Adorned with rows of mines of the finest and most priceless jewels, they possess mines of golden treasures of such extraordinary and great wonder that they are unlike anything else. ||11||
In some places, O beloved, they are mines of rubies and sapphires; and in other places, they are endowed with rows of emerald mines. (12)

In some places they have the appearance of syamantaka gems, and in others the appearance of rucakas; they possess the luster of priceless yellow gold and are endowed with mines of excellent gemstones.
In some places they are mines of jewels, in some places mines of the Kaustubha gem, and in others, auspicious mines of those gems that are beyond description. (14)
In certain places, there are two esteemed mountain plateaus with divine and most beautiful monasteries;
likewise, there is a lovely river named Virajā, beautifully adorned by its banks. 15.
It encircles Mount Śataśṛṅga, which is circular,
divine, made of gold, and blazing with the radiance of ten million suns.
And it was resplendent with long forests of pārijāta trees.
It was pervaded by various kalpa-trees and beautifully adorned with the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu.
Its height is ten million *yojanas*, and its width increases tenfold at each stage;
the length of the mountain range there is measured at fifty million *yojanas*. (18)
On its single peak, the circle of the Rāsa dance is shaped like a rampart;
it is ten yojanas in extent, circular in form, and most excellent.
The circle of the rāsa dance was perfumed by the fragrance of millions of gardens of various flowers,
and it was adorned with objects that stimulate desire and other such things.
Therein are tens of millions of jeweled pavilions, such as palaces and mansions, intended for pleasure.
The many stories were adorned with staircases and ladders. ||21||
They were beautifully adorned with golden jars of the seven precious gems and jeweled pillars;
upon those pillars were inlaid enchanting emeralds. (22)
The rubies are the color of vermilion, while the sapphires are radiant with light.
And there were various kinds of jewels and excellent varieties of gems. ||23||
Of that excellent pavilion, four gate-towers were likewise seen—divine, kissing the sky, and enriched with the beauty of their door-panels. (24)
There, from the very beginning, clusters of plantain trunks shone forth, joined with cords and knots and adorned with mango sprouts. 25.
In every place here, within the pavilion, ever-new splendor has been fashioned.
It was endowed with white grains, leafy networks, fruits, and sprouts of durvā grass. ||26||
Anointed with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
indeed millions of groups of cowherd girls take their delight here.
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments, they were resplendent with strings of gems.
Adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and jeweled anklets.
Their cheeks were resplendent with earrings made of jewels that dangled and snapped;
their hands and fingers shone, graced with beautiful jewel-encrusted rings. ||29||
Their toes were beautifully adorned with ornaments of jeweled anklets;
they were decorated with jewel-ornaments and radiant with crowns of excellent gems.
Their beautiful noses were adorned with ornaments of pearls from the lordly elephants,
and bright dots of vermilion were applied below their forelocks.
Having the luster of the color of yellow campaka flowers, anointed with liquid sandalwood paste, wearing yellow garments, and enchanting with lips like the bimba fruit; ||32||
Their lotus-faces were radiant with a luster arising from the full moon of autumn;
their eyes were as beautiful as the finest petals of a blossoming autumn lotus.
Intoxicated by the thick kajjala clinging to both their eyelids,
they were adorned with garments featuring clusters of blossoming mālatī garlands.
They possess a charming gait, slow and excellent like that of an elephant or a swan; they are endowed with the joining of curved brow-bends and gentle smiles. (35)
They were adorned with rows of teeth resembling the seeds of ripe pomegranates, and graced by prominent noses as beautiful as the beaks of the king of birds. ||36||
Bowed down by the weight of their golden breasts, which resembled the pair of temples of a lordly elephant, and bent low by the heavy burden of their firm, broad hips; ||37||
Their minds sporting with the pride of Kandarpa, they were overwhelmed by intoxication;
eager to behold the beauty of their full-moon faces in the mirror. ||38||
Their hearts and desires were intent on serving the feet of Rādhikā and Kṛṣṇa;
they were beautiful women, sixteen years of age, with the full bloom of youth as their only arrow. (39)
They dwell in a great, divine pavilion adorned with circles of lotuses;
there are hundreds of thousands of lakes of ritual action and tens of millions of flower gardens.
Indeed, they were filled with millions of lotuses possessing red, white, and pink lusters,
and their banks resounded with the humming of divine bees.
The pavilion was beautified by millions of bowers and leaf-huts containing flower-beds,
and it shone all around with the radiance of jewel-lamps.
Accompanied by articles of enjoyment, camphor, betel, and garments, and provided with white chowries, mirrors, and various flower garlands. ||43||
Furthermore, the Rāsa-maṇḍapa is beautiful for those who are worthy; beyond that, there exists a forest that is lovely, divinely wonderful, and possessed of manifold splendor. ||44||
There is a forest named Vṛndāvana, beloved by Rādhā and Mādhava;
it is supreme, consisting of desire-fulfilling trees, for the purpose of their play and pastimes. 45.
The conscious mind always shines with a gentle vibration, fragrant like a lotus grove, a lotus flower, musk, and other perfumes. (46)
It was enchanting with the warbling of cuckoos and fresh sprouts, and exceedingly lovely with the groves of kadamba trees for the sake of dalliance. 47.
It was made fragrant on all sides by bakula, kunda, mandāra, sandalwood, and golden campaka flowers— excellent blossoms of various sweet scents.
With oranges, jackfruit, mangoes, palmyra palms, wood-apples, and dates;
with rose-apples, jujubes, aguru, hog-plums, and fine pomegranates. ||49||
It was delightful, provided with *jambīra*, plantain, and coconut trees,
and [further] endowed with *śālmali*, *aśvattha*, *tintiḍī*, *nimba*, *pippalī*, and *sarjaka* trees.
It was crowded with various trees that always bore fruit and flowers,
and was filled with *mallikā*, *mālatī*, golden *ketakī*, and *mādhavī* vines.
It was adorned with fifty crores of beautiful bower-huts, resplendent with canopies of creepers such as *yūthikā* and *citrapuṣpī*.
There, tens of millions upon tens of millions of jewel-lamps and fragrant incenses are present;
winds mixed with perfumes for the body blow from all sides. (53)
In every place there were flower-beds anointed with fragrant *arka* and sandalwood, resounding with the humming of bees that had assumed divine forms and were adorned with pearls. (54)
In the beautiful Vṛndāvana, fifty crore gopīs, adorned with jewel ornaments, dwell by the command of Rādhikā.
There, on the inner ground, there are indeed thirty-two groves, known by names such as Kalpadru, Pārijāta, Kadamba, and so forth. (56)
There are circular forests consisting of various specific types of trees; beyond that is the place called Vṛndāraka, where the houses of the cowherds and cowherdesses are situated.
Indeed, cities dwell within the cow-pens of the cowherds and cowherdesses,
and there are thousands upon thousands of flower gardens.
Indeed, from the houses of each of the fifty crore gopīs, there are palatial mansions that are truly superior, and in beauty they are like those of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
All of them were twelve years of age, possessed forms equal to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, numbered in the hundreds of millions, and were the very embodiment of supreme beauty.
Indeed, innumerable gopīs and gopas dwell in Vṛndāraka upon ground made of jewels, diamonds, rubies, gems, gold, and other precious materials. (61)
In that divine and celestial realm, there are infinite prosperities;
from that time onward, Goloka has remained situated within the abode of Brahman.
Indeed, all around him were circles of cowherds and cowherdesses,
both in Vṛndāvana and likewise throughout Goloka.
Indeed, the Vasatis dwell in Vṛndāraka, which is circular;
and in the midst of those abodes of the Vṛndārakas is the supreme Goloka.
To the east, in the region of Vṛndāraka, there is indeed the Akṣayavaṭa tree;
it is five yojanas wide and ten yojanas high.
It possessed a thousand trunks and was endowed with tens of millions of branches;
it was rich with ripe red fruits and adorned with fresh sprouts.
Beneath that, there are jeweled railings with shadows cast by a dense canopy;
there, dark-complexioned cowherd boys take their delight. (67)
Wearing yellow garments, their minds were intent on the essence of play;
their beautiful forms possessed the fragrance of the finest sandalwood. ||68||
Those attendants, resplendent with beauty and youth equal to Kṛṣṇa’s,
richly adorned with all ornaments, enjoy themselves and sport.
Next to that, on the second side, is the one known as Bhāṇḍīravaṭa;
indeed, it is here that the union of Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā takes place.
There is a banyan tree five yojanas in width and twice that in height;
it is divine, with thousands of trunks and millions of branches and twigs. (71)
Beneath that, indeed, are the pleasure-pavilions of the young gopīs, consisting of golden altars inlaid with jewels. (72)
And all those cowherd girls, radiant with forms like that of Rādhā, were twelve years of age; they all sported and took delight together. ||73||
They constantly await Kṛṣṇa and come and go by the millions;
having obtained Kṛṣṇa, who is dearer to them than life itself, and having served him, they indeed depart.
Between those two banyan trees, however, is a charming royal road that leads far toward the great palace of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. (75)
On every side, however, were altars fashioned from rubies;
in some places they were constructed of sapphires, as well as with emeralds and diamonds.
In some places there were altars fashioned from rubies and crystal;
in other places on the sides were pavilions for rest and halls of righteousness.
In some places it was beautified by the liquid paste of sandalwood, musk, and saffron;
in other places it was adorned with parched grain, fruits, flowers, curd, durva grass, and betel nut.
It has golden campaka, mandāra, pārijāta, and other trees at its sides,
and it is resplendent with trees richly laden with fresh sprouts, flowers, and the like.
The groves of plantains shine, and the fruit-bearing trees shine;
the gargaryas, adorned with fine jewels, look most beautiful when placed upon their heads. (1.120.80)
For the purpose of fetching water, the golden jars placed upon the hips of the cowherd women shine brilliantly as they are filled with water. (8.1)
Anointed with vermilion and saffron, perfumed with fragrant scents, and adorned with floral ornaments, the cowherd women proceeded from there. ||82||
The young maidens proceed from one path to another in the form of streets,
toward their own delightful mansions with stairways made of jewels.
Wearing garments purified by fire and adorned with golden ornaments, they sleep upon flower-couches with white chowries and mirrors. 84.
By that path, the cowherds and cowherd girls go toward their own most beautiful mansions situated at the side, which are adorned with flower garlands and excellent archways.
They were surrounded by walls provided with sixteen gates, encompassed on all sides by moats, and guarded by gatekeepers. ||86||
Thus, that royal road, beautifully adorned on both sides,
enters the city gate and proceeds to the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, there are tens of millions of inhabitants dwelling within the walls;
the wall is circular in shape and extends for ten million yojanas. ||88||
This is the great divine Goloka, known as Mahāgoloka;
it is called Nijagoloka and also Rādhāgoloka.
The cowherds and cowherdesses know him by that name;
now, O Śivā, listen as I describe to you that preeminent Goloka.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of Goloka, Virajā, Śataśṛṅga, the Rāsa-maṇḍapa, Vṛndāvana, the Akṣaya-vaṭa, Bhāṇḍīra-vaṭa, the Royal Road, Vṛndāraka, and other sites," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, Mahādeva spoke auspiciously to Pārvatī regarding Goloka, which is surrounded by a wall and endowed with temples and other sites. || 1 ||
The extent of its wall is said to be ten million yojanas;
it is provided with four gates and is situated within celestial palaces in the sky. || 2 ||
Abounding with herds of cows protected by cowherds and provided with gatekeepers,
there were palaces inlaid with jewels and filled with many objects of enjoyment.
The fifty million gopīs who offered their entire being for the sake of Kṛṣṇa—
those beloved ones dwell there in the palaces of that place.
There, the hermitages of hundreds of millions of devoted cowherds abound with trees and creepers that provide every object of enjoyment and bestow happiness.
Beyond that, there are ten crores of hermitages belonging to the attendants, which are even more extensive and resplendent with jewels and gems.
All accomplishments are fulfilled, and not even the slightest deficiency exists;
there are maidens twelve years of age and youths sixteen years of age.
Beyond that, millions of other excellent attendants, assuming the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and residing in palaces, dwell there.
Because of their residence near Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there is not even the slightest deficiency in these dwellings; they are joined by palaces and by the gopīs who are pure devotees of Rādhikā.
Furthermore, there were thirty-two crores of other houses made of jewels, gems, and gold,
belonging to the gopīs who were devoted to Rādhā and to her maidservants.
There are indeed ten crores of various palaces,
divine, made of gold and fashioned with jewels, gems, and diamonds.
All the palaces within Goloka are granters of all desires;
they belong to those who have been purified by penance for a hundred lifetimes and are devoted to the service of Hari.
Those who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and who constantly chant "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa" go to the abode of Goloka and dwell within its ramparts.
Their dwellings were constructed from excellent gems, jewels, and rubies;
they were adorned with beds of flowers, flower garlands, and white chowries. || 14 ||
Richly adorned with the splendor of jeweled mirrors, they were beautified by emeralds;
their crests were filled with clusters of priceless jewel-pitchers. || 15 ||
The hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses were devoted, their divine bodies nourished by the accumulation of unfailing vigor, and adorned with fine garments and ornaments.
And tens of millions upon tens of millions dwell there, enjoying various kinds of nectar;
beyond that, in the midst of the great garden, is the supreme abode of the Rāseśvarī.
An hermitage exists, established through the memory of Rādhā, beautifully constructed for the foremost of the gopīs, the Goddess of gods. 18.
Belonging to Kṛṣṇa, who is dearer than life itself, it was captivating with its beautiful materials,
perfectly round in shape, and measured six gavyūtis in extent.
It was joined with a hundred pavilions, blazing with the luster of jewels,
and constructed as a magnificent edifice from heaps of priceless, choice gems.
It was beautifully adorned with moats that were deep and difficult to cross, surrounded by wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas), and interspersed with hundreds of flower gardens. || 21 ||
It was well-encircled by a rampart inlaid with jewels of great value,
and it was beautifully adorned with seven gates containing altars made of excellent gems.
There, a very large circular garden extends all around;
it is filled everywhere with trees and creepers. ||23||
In the middle of this inner garden, there is another enclosure wall;
it is surrounded on all sides and is likewise provided with sixteen gates.
Rising a thousand bows high, adorned with the pinnacle of a water-pot (kalaśa), it was beautiful, blazing with splendor, and graced by hundreds of celestial chariots (vimānas). ||25||
And all around that wall were hermitages numbering hundreds of palaces belonging to the cowherds and cowherd women, resembling the palace of Kṛṣṇa.
Within that enclosure was a garden endowed with divine fruits, possessed of divine flowers, and featuring beautiful basins of divine water. ||27||
To the south there exists a beautiful, divine lake;
on its bank stands the king’s palace, where dancers perform.
The instrumentalists and singers likewise sing the nectar-like songs of the daughters, which consist of beautiful melodies and are endowed with the virtues of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
And there, charming cowherd girls wearing various garments were seen in every place, longing for the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Some had mṛdaṅga drums in their hands, some likewise held vīṇās;
some held chowries in their hands, while others held cymbals.
Some held musical instruments in their hands, some were adorned with anklets,
and some made the pavilion resound with the ornaments of tinkling bells.
Some, holding water-pots in their hands and likewise upon their heads, being female leaders in male attire, danced there in many ways. (33)
Some assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa, while others assumed the form of Rādhā; some stood at a distance, and others were intent on embracing Kṛṣṇa. ||34||
Those cowherd women, though intent on their play, were also devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
near him, on the bank of the lake, there are excellent and magnificent mansions. (35)
Those houses of Rādhā’s friends are of beautiful appearance;
those thirty-three companions of Rādhā are in the full bloom of youth. (36)
In form, in virtue, in dress, in youth, in good fortune, and in age, they were the very equals of Rādhā. (37)
Listen, O Girijā, to the thirty-three principal names:
Candrakalā, Suśīlā, Yamunā, Mādhavī, and Rati. (38)
Kadambamālā, Sukuntī, Jāhnavī, Svayaṃprabhā, Padmamukhī, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Sumukhī, and Sudhā. (39)
Padmālayā, Pārijātā, Sugaurī, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Kālikā, Kamalā, Durgā, Bhāratī, and Sarasvatī.
Gaṅgāmbikā, Madhumatī, Campāparṇā, Sundarī, Kṛṣṇapriyā, Brahmasatī, Nandinī, and likewise Nandanā; ||41||
Indeed, their palaces were equal to the palace of Kṛṣṇa;
they were truly filled with jewels, minerals, objects of enjoyment, and golden pitchers.
Wherever there were maidens, cowherd girls, female friends, and cowherds who had dedicated their entire being to Kṛṣṇa, in every single house there— 42.
Assuming many forms, Kṛṣṇa dwells and delights with her—with each beloved and in every possible way. (44)
On the wall of Rādhākṛṣṇa’s palace there are sixteen gate-towers;
among them, the first gate-tower is made of jewels and gems. (45)
Joined by a pair of railings and featuring doors of vajra and jewels, there dwells the youthful Vīrabhānu as its gatekeeper. (46)
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with ornaments of gems, wearing yellow garments, his head radiant with a jeweled crown. ||47||
Indeed, under whose command there are two hundred and fifty thousand cowherds at the second gate, which is even more beautiful than that one; (48)
The gatekeeper is indeed the youth Candrabhānu, who is dark-complexioned, holding a golden staff, and seated upon a jeweled lion-throne. ||49||
At the third gate there, which was exceedingly radiant with jewels, five hundred thousand lords of cowherds remained under his command.
The gatekeeper is Sūryabhānu, a youth who holds a flute;
he has a staff of jewels in his hand and is adorned with golden jeweled earrings. ||51||
At the fourth gate, which was adorned with extraordinary ornaments, there were nine hundred thousand cowherds, dark and beautiful, who remained under his command.
Vasubhānu is the gatekeeper; Kiśora is the lord of Vraja, holding a jeweled staff and seated upon a throne of precious gems. ||53||
With lips like a ripe bimba fruit and adorned with every ornament,
he is one under whose command reside nine hundred thousand charming cowherds.
At the fifth gate, in a chamber variegated with wonderful diamond walls,
stands the gatekeeper Devabhānu, seated upon a beautiful lion-throne.
He has a crest of peacock feathers and beautiful earrings adorned with jewel garlands;
by his command, one million cowherds remain stationed [in service]. (56)
At the sixth gate-tower, adorned with diamond walls and doors, stands the gatekeeper Śukrabhānu, embellished with all ornaments. (57)
Under whose command ten hundred thousand cowherds are stationed at the seventh gate, which is exceptionally beautiful and distinct from the other six. (58)
The doorkeeper Ratnabhānu was the beloved youth of Śrī Hari;
adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste, he stood upon a lion-throne holding a fly-whisk.
Twelve hundred thousand cowherds abide under his command;
they are distinct even from those seven at the eighth gate.
The gatekeeper is Supārśva, beautifully adorned with a jeweled staff;
he is enriched by the splendor of jeweled earrings, and his lower lip is like the bandhujīva flower. ||61||
Under whose command there are always twelve hundred thousand cowherds at the ninth gate, which is rich with diamond-jewels and adorned with variegated garlands.
There is a doorkeeper named Subala, adorned with graceful forms and ornaments,
under whose command there are likewise twelve hundred thousand cowherds.
At the tenth beautiful gate, which is beyond description and supreme,
there is a gatekeeper named Sudāmā, as enchanting as Kṛṣṇa himself.
When the cowherds, numbering twenty lakhs, stood with staffs in hand at his command,
there was likewise an eleventh gate, most wonderful, beautiful, and marvelous.
The gatekeeper Śrīdāmā is seated upon a jeweled throne;
he wears yellow garments and is adorned with priceless ornaments and sandalwood paste. ||66||
Resplendent with earrings, bracelets, flower garlands, and a crown,
he is like a sovereign king of kings, for millions of cowherds abide by his command.
In the twelfth gateway, there were four altars made of priceless jewels,
enchanting with the beautiful murals on their walls of variegated and wonderful diamonds.
There, the doorkeepers were indeed gopīs, adorned with ornaments,
endowed with fresh youth, and graced by the weight of their braided hair.
Clad in yellow, red, and other colored garments, their hair braided with fragrant flowers,
they were adorned with ornaments of jewels, gold, and gems, and wore golden bracelets.
Their bodies were most beautifully adorned with armlets, anklets, and earrings;
they were bent low by the weight of their full hips and moved slowly under the burden of their buttocks.
One hundred gopīs, the most beloved and excellent of Hari, stand at the city gate; their attendants are ten million gopīs who are likewise dear to Hari. (72)
In the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth gate-towers, there are female doorkeepers who have reached the full bloom of youth. (73)
They are most excellent, captivating, delightful, supreme, blessed, and very beautiful;
they are dear to Rādhā, richly adorned, and auspicious with the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa. ||74||
Indeed, there are ten million times a hundred billion Gopikās who carry out their commands;
at the sixteenth gate, however, there are thirty-three principal Gopikās.
They have gatekeepers, whose form cannot be described;
they are neither Pārvatī, nor Lakṣmī, nor Urvaśī—how much less Rādhikā? (76)
Such were those women, adorned with jewel ornaments and in the full bloom of youth,
decorated with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and golden anklets.
Well-adorned at their waists with girdles of tinkling bells, they shone brightly upon the regions of their cheeks with the luster of jeweled earrings. ||78||
They were adorned with blossoming mālatī garlands, strings of jewels, necklaces, and the like; their face-maṇḍalas were graced by countenances worthy of the full autumnal moon.
Their breasts were radiant with garlands and necklaces of *pārijāta* flowers and other blossoms;
their lower lips were like ripe bimba fruits, and their lotus-like faces were smiling.
With rows of teeth as white as ripe pomegranate seeds and the finest kunda flowers, possessing the excellent complexion of golden campaka blossoms, they were slender-waisted with slim hips. (8.1)
Their noses were like golden sand interspersed with elephant pearls;
their nostrils were as slender as a parrot’s beak, and they possessed firm breasts.
With their minds attached to the feet of Kṛṣṇa, they bore the weight of full hips;
[they stood] before a gateway with long panels adorned with golden stars.
On the platform provided at the gateway stand those beloved of Hari;
the entire area within the gateway is adorned with jewels, gems, and other precious things. (84)
It was adorned on both its walls with emeralds and rubies, and made fragrant by garlands of *pārijāta* flowers. (85)
Within that [palace], there exists a great garden of flowers;
therein stands the magnificent mansion of Rādhā, which is indeed the very temple of Kṛṣṇa. (86)
Standing in the midst of the temples is the enchanting Śataśāla;
he is indeed reached through the seven desirable celestial palaces (vimānas) within the halls.
It was truly divine, constructed solely from the finest essences of jewels;
it was adorned with pillars made of various gems and jewels, set with diamonds. ||88||
It was resplendent with nets of garlands made from *pārijāta* flowers, and its walls were enchanting, fashioned with pearls, rubies, and diamonds. (89)
It was accompanied by white chowries, mirrors, and fans, as well as by water-pots;
it was provided with silk-thread knots and sprouts of *śrīkhaṇḍa* sandalwood.
And it was adorned with beautiful courtyards featuring clusters of jeweled pillars.
Combined with the liquid extracts of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. ||9 1 ||
It was resplendent with parched grain, white flowers, sprouts, fruits, and rice; and it shone with leaves, *dūrvā* grass, unhusked rice, parched grain flakes, water-jars, and necklaces.
Made fragrant by winds infused with various scents,
it was the foremost thing never before seen or heard, and that which is difficult to obtain even within the entire universe.
And the palace, adorned with various objects for the sake of Rādhikā, contained exquisite jeweled couches covered with fine garments. ||94||
Indeed, there were tens of millions of jewel-jars and jewel-bowls, adorned with various priceless and beautiful objects of that kind. (95)
It resounded with the sweet tones of various kinds of musical instruments,
and it was filled with the beautiful music of lutes and stringed instruments performed by the gopīs.
Enchanting with the sounds of musical instruments and the songs of female singers,
he was surrounded by throngs of cowherds who were equal to Kṛṣṇa himself.
He was resplendent amidst the many throngs of the gopīs, the friends of Rādhā, and he listened intently to the songs concerning the overflowing qualities of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. ||98||
Sweet song is heard, excellent dancing is seen, and supreme bliss is attained through the essence of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, O Daughter of the Mountain. (99)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Walls, Palaces, Gardens, Inner Apartments, Wall-Enclosures, Palaces, Gardens, Sixteen Gate-Towers, and Gatekeepers of Goloka," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 121 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved; then Śambhu spoke to his dear Satī regarding the excellent jewel-throne in the palace of Rādhikā-Kṛṣṇa.
It measured one hundred bows in circumference and was circular in shape,
adorned at its peaks and other parts with various golden jars.
Above that, extending like a seven-story palm tree, was a region pervaded by the brilliance of ten million suns, adorned with divine food, dolls, lovers, maidservants, and ornaments.
Wondrous, more beautiful than all radiant objects, you are the garment of splendor,
a mass of splendor, and the primordial mine of splendor.
That divine throne indeed moves through the sky at will;
it has lion-shaped legs, is variegated with creepers, and is attended by infinite cowherds and cowherdesses.
Cows, male calves, and female calves likewise, as well as devotees and beloved ones,
[are situated] upon the throne, on the stairs, on the pillar, at the door, and on the archway.
Musicians, dancers, and singers were stationed at the sides;
fashioned in the form of puppets, they all shone resplendently.
Peacocks, cranes, swans, cātakas, parrots, and mainas—these auspicious figurines are arranged in their respective places. (8)
Upon a divine throne, a mass of splendor, Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent—
the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the giver of boons, and the very cause of all givers of boons.
He is the bestower of all auspiciousness, the most auspicious among all auspicious things;
he is untainted and free from desire, the refuge of divine sovereignty and virtues.
He is eternal and possessed of form, the bearer of the manifestations of the arts;
he is the support of all, the form of all, the seed of all, and indeed beyond the reach of the senses. || 11 ||
He is both the body of the insentient and the sentient, possessing an independent and divine form;
He is the witness of all, the seer of all, the Lord who is existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 12 ||
He is the Lord of all, without beginning or end, the ordainer, the progenitor, and the father;
in every single pore of his skin resides an entire universe.
He who is born from a sixteenth part of that very same Great Viṣṇu is Kṛṣṇa,
whom those who know yoga meditate upon and serve, having attained the state of his servants.
A youth, most beautiful, the most desirable of lovely women;
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, wearing yellow garments, the excellent one. (15)
Two-armed, with a flute in his hand, smiling, and most enchanting;
with a crest of peacock feathers and adorned with garlands of jasmine. || 16 ||
He was anointed with the liquid essences of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron,
and adorned with ornaments made of the finest essence of priceless jewels.
He is radiant with a crown and diadem fashioned from priceless jewels;
the moon of his face eclipses the splendor of autumnal lotuses in full bloom.
He was resplendent with a lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit,
and enchanting with rows of teeth resembling the seeds of a ripe pomegranate.
Possessing a supreme joy through his beautiful smile, he enchants the minds of the three worlds;
with his two cheeks and temples, his shark-shaped earrings blaze forth.
He was adorned with lotus-like feet graced by anklets of excellent gems,
and he shone in priceless garments with the hue of fire-purified turmeric.
Adorned with excellent divine ornaments such as jewels and gold, he is enchanting with his bimba-fruit-like lips joined by a playful flute. ||22||
Full of serenity, he bestows grace upon his devotees;
his chest and arms shine with armor set with excellent jewel-beads. ||23||
Resplendent with the brilliant luster of the excellent jewels set in the Kaustubha gem, that youthful Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, shines forth. 24.
To His left stands His friend Rādhikā, whose limbs are beautiful;
she gazes at Her beloved with sidelong glances and a smile as He looks back at Her. (25)
She was adorned with a row of teeth that surpassed a string of pearls; her face was brightened by a gentle smile, and her eyes were like autumn lotuses. (26)
Her face was enchanting, radiating a brilliance that surpassed the full moon of autumn; her lower lip was beautiful, its luster enhanced by the abundance of *bandhujīva* flowers.
Her lotus-feet were resplendent with a pair of tinkling anklets,
and she was adorned by rows of teeth that eclipsed the luster of the finest jewels.
Clad in garments with the luster of saffron, adorned with red dye upon her feet, and her hips graced by a girdle of priceless, exquisite jewels. ||29||
Her garments were purified by fire and blazing with the brilliance of priceless gems; she was adorned with the finest of great jewels set amidst tinkling bells.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and anklets made of the seven precious gems,
she shone with radiant earrings fashioned from the finest essence of jewels upon her cheeks.
Her ears were adorned with ornaments of the finest jewels;
her nose-tip was graced by the beak of the king of birds and the pearls of the lord of elephants.
Adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers, she is graced by the weight of her curly tresses;
adorned upon the surface of her chest by a necklace of the finest *kaustubha* gems. (33)
Her garments were radiant with the glow of garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers,
and her fingers were adorned with clusters of jeweled rings.
She possesses the luster of molten gold, her body radiant with gold;
she is graceful with her hips and loins, and beautifully adorned with full breasts.
Adorned with beauty and decorated with all manner of ornaments,
her long eyes were like lotus petals, and she moved with the languid grace of one burdened by the weight of love.
She is the treasure-house of the desires of Kṛṣṇa, an ocean of all youthfulness, the ultimate limit of every form, white yet radiant with red. 37.
Her heart was captivated by Kṛṣṇa as his mind flowed forth with a stream of love;
she could not remain in her place for even a single moment without the touch of Kṛṣṇa. ||38||
"Without her beloved Kṛṣṇa, the beloved woman does not remain alone";
thinking thus, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, endowed with such splendor, set forth. (39)
There, upon a divine throne with the splendor of a sovereign of kings,
what indeed could be lacking in the union of the Blessed One and the Blessed Lady?
For the perfect Brahman and the perfect Brahmanī, what indeed could be incomplete? For even a moment spent in Goloka brings them true happiness. ||41||
On that very earth, they indeed pass through seven manvantaras;
for such a place is always a ground of exceedingly long-lasting bliss.
There were fragrant cows, wish-fulfilling cows, and dark-blue bulls;
as well as four-tusked elephants, white in color and adorned with ornaments of gold and other precious materials. ||42||
Horses sixty years of age, raining down intoxication,
traveling through the sky, with black ears, possessed of wings, and moving through the firmament.
Peacocks, garuḍas, swans, parrots, cranes, and peahens—various birds were there, as well as numerous trees and creepers. (49)

There were hundreds of palanquins carried by men, as well as vehicles drawn according to their own desire; these included those equipped with bells, those with sharp points, those protected by canopies, and those adorned with ornaments. 46.
Therein, the various mental impressions (smṛti) are the servants of air, water, and fire;
and the seasons are the servants of taste, smell, sound, form, and the other [objects of sense]. ||47||
Divine chariots that travel through the sky and such celestial opulences attend them in Goloka to provide for their desired enjoyments.
What indeed could be non-divine about the divine Kṛṣṇa at that time?
Kṛṣṇa is the divine Great King, and Queen Rādhikā is also divine. ||49||
The attendants, both male and female cowherds, are indeed stainless and divine;
all these palaces, situated upon the summit of the foundation, are truly celestial dwellings.
There, the divine-form chariot of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shone,
adorned with diamonds and the finest essence of precious gems.
He was adorned with a hundred thousand white chowries and ten thousand mirrors,
and embellished with fine saffron-colored robes purified by fire.
It was beautifully adorned with a thousand jars made of the seven precious gems and resplendent with clusters of garlands of *pārijāta* flowers. ||53||
Accompanied by the foremost of his attendants, he was auspicious and made of gold;
he was the very embodiment of splendor, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred suns.
In some places there, Kṛṣṇa remains in his chariot having become the four-armed Nārāyaṇa; indeed, he goes from one world to another world.
Then that man appeared, dark-complexioned, beautiful, and charming,
bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, and clothed in yellow garments.
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with a divine forest garland, he was anointed with the liquid paste of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron. ||57||
Four-armed, with a smiling countenance, he is intent on bestowing grace upon his devotees;
he is adorned with ornaments that are the very essence of the finest jewels and gems.
Always performing service to Mahālakṣmī, the Great Goddess, he possesses sovereign power and is praised by all the gods and goddesses. || 59 ||
And on a beautiful chariot to her left stands one of white complexion,
richly adorned with the splendor of jewel-ornaments and graced with yellow garments.
Her face is like the full moon of autumn, her eyes are like autumn lotuses,
her lips are like ripe bimba fruit, and with her smiling countenance, she is the bestower of desires.
Sarasvatī, whose hands hold a flute, a lute, and a book, who is eager to bestow grace upon her devotees,
is the presiding deity of knowledge and the very embodiment of wisdom.
On the right side, indeed, on Supārśva, she possesses a splendor equal to a hundred moons;
she has the luster of molten gold, is smiling, and is most enchanting.
Her beautiful cheeks were adorned with two earrings of excellent gems,
and she was decorated with priceless garments inlaid with jewels of incalculable value.
Adorned with armlets and bracelets made of priceless jewels, she was accompanied by the tinkling sound of anklets fashioned from the essence of excellent gems. ||65||
She was endowed with a waist and hips adorned with the tinkling of great jewel-bells,
and her chest was radiant with necklaces of flowers such as the pārijāta.
She is endowed with braided hair interwoven with garlands of full-blown mālatī flowers,
and she is graced by the orb of her face, which possesses a brilliance exceeding that of the autumnal moon.
Adorned with a tilaka of vermilion in the center of a drop of musk, her eyes are like autumn lotuses, beautifully embraced by dark collyrium. ||68||
Holding in her hand a great lotus rich with the beauty of a thousand petals,
she gazes upon Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, with sidelong glances.
Even while standing in the middle of the chariot, those three also move about;
furthermore, another excellent chariot was fashioned for him by Viśvakarman.
Fifty yojanas in height and four yojanas in width,
it was fashioned from the essence of gold and adorned with various jewels.
It is joined with the essence of the lord of jewels, endowed with garments as pure as fire, accompanied by white yak-tail whisks, adorned, and provided with a mirror. ||72||
It was adorned with a pinnacle-jar made of the essence of the seven precious gems and beautified by necklaces and garlands;
it was equipped with a thousand wheels, traveled at the speed of thought, and was enchanting to the mind.
Sudarśana possesses a splendor equal to the midday sun of summer;
he is brilliantly radiant with pearls, rubies, diamonds, and other precious gems.
Adorned with painted puppets, flower-lakes, and groves, and joined by women fit for dalliance, it shines with pleasure-pavilions. //75//
There, for the sake of serving Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Mahāmāyā also resides, adorned with ornaments of jewels and excellent, beautiful gold. (76)
Possessing great splendor and exceeding loveliness, resembling a treasury of majesty, she is endowed with a thousand arms and bears various weapons and other implements. ||77||
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, she stood for the sake of Krishna’s play,
adorned with beautiful golden and jeweled earrings resting upon her cheeks and temples.
She was charming with tinkling anklets fashioned from the finest essence of jewels,
and her waist was graced by a golden girdle set with excellent gems.
Adorned with golden bracelets, armlets, and chains set with jewels,
she was resplendent with rows of garlands made of Mandāra and Kalpa flowers.
With hips firm, a waist slender, and breasts full and shapely,
her face was like the full moon of autumn, radiant with a halo of splendor.
Her lotus-eyes were adorned with streaks of excellent black collyrium,
and her forehead was decorated with leaf-patterns fashioned from sandalwood and saffron paste.
She shone with beautiful teeth as white as pearls, pomegranate seeds, and jasmine; her hair was bound in a braid adorned with loose flowers, and she moved with a languid grace. 83.
Adorned with the beauty of a low-lying nose resembling the beaks of a parrot or a garuḍa, she wears a necklace of pearls from the ocean foam and from lions and other beasts. 84.

Other goddesses are also present for service, wearing bright garments and bodices, adorned with golden star-shaped ornaments and fine crescent moons, and having applied vertical tilakas upon their foreheads. (85)
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, and likewise the beloved Jāmbavatī;
Kālindī, Mitravindā, and another Satyabhāmā. (86)
Bhadrā and Lakṣmaṇā were indeed his two chief queens;
there was a great circle of sixteen thousand wives.
One who performs service to Kṛṣṇa indeed shines in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
there is no end to other [forms of service], for the entire world is under the control of Kṛṣṇa. (88)
Indeed, twenty-one crores of gopīs belong to Kṛṣṇa alone;
the others are not even counted, because all of them are like maidservants.
The thirty-three companions, as well as the eight noble ladies, and Rādhā indeed— these are the principal beloveds in Gokula.
Vasudeva and Devakī, Nanda and Yaśodā, as well as Uddhava, Sātyaki, Garga, Akrūra, and other Sātvatas. ||9.1||
Indeed, they dwell in Gokula, striking blows upon the grounds of its walls,
in its gardens, and within its great divine palaces.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever lacking in the enjoyment shared with Kṛṣṇa;
yet, for the sake of wandering about, there is a great chariot for the friends who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa. ||93||
It was four yojanas wide and five yojanas high;
it resembled pure crystal and was fashioned from the essence of jewels. ||94||
He was resplendent with a multitude of garlands made of unfading pārijāta flowers, and adorned with ornaments of precious gems and kaustubha jewels. ||95||
It was adorned with a jar of priceless jewels and graced by necklaces of diamonds; it was surrounded by thousands of millions of enchanting palaces. (96)
He possessed two thousand wheels and two thousand horses; he was clothed in fine garments and surrounded by ten million gopīs. ||97||
What else shall I describe of that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the glorious Hari—those delightful kitchens and dining halls? (98)
Bath-houses, fragrant chambers, and dressing rooms, as well as pleasure-houses for friends and assembly halls. ||99||
There were also halls for dancing and halls for social festivals,
as well as pleasure-pavilions and halls for recreation and delight.
The sleeping chambers, the beautiful moon-pavilions, and the thousand-storied mansions—
whatever such things exist here do not indeed exist in other abodes.
It was indeed created by Śrī Hari himself in the form of Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of happiness,
for the sake of granting happiness to his devotees, and especially to women.
The form assumed was indeed characterized by passion (rājasa) and possessed unfailing potency;
for what could possibly be said there that was deficient or even slightly inferior? 10.3.
"For that which is complete in every respect, what could possibly remain incomplete?
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you a small portion of the Goloka maṇḍala.
Even Kṛṣṇa himself is not able to describe in every way that which one shall hear or read concerning this Kṛṣṇa-Goloka.
Indeed, he shall obtain firm devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which is very difficult to attain,
as well as the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* and the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya*.
Right here [one attains] equality with Kṛṣṇa, perfection of speech, great fame,
a son, knowledge, poetic skill, and likewise unwavering prosperity.
A devoted, virtuous, well-behaved, and steadfast wife; progeny;
long-lasting fame; and at the end, a destination in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Jewel Throne of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā, Their Prosperity, the Four-Armed Form of Sarasvatī, the Form of Mahāmāyā as Mahālakṣmī, the Hundred Thousand Eight Noble Consorts of Rādhā, and Their Palaces," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard of the location of Goloka, Pārvatī was greatly delighted;
desiring to hear the divine narrative, she spoke to the excellent Śaṅkara.
O Creator of Ramā, I desire to hear about Vaikuṇṭha,
the divine abode which was indeed fashioned by Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of Śrī.
Having heard this, Mahādeva, the lord of disciplined yogis, remembered Hari;
meditating for a moment on Nārāyaṇa, he beheld the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
He described all of that in sequence with a spirit of devotion:
"Listen, O Vaiṣṇava wife; in this narration, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is truly relished. (4)
Without the nectar of devotion to Hari, other tastes are considered false;
indeed, the worlds of the three-quarter manifestation (tripādvibhūti) are truly innumerable.
All are composed of the abode of Brahman, resting in the bliss of Brahman-joy;
they are eternal, changeless, and entirely devoid of defects to be abandoned.
All were radiant with divine gold, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
and were served by the true essence of devotion to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
They are considered bestowers of perfect bliss through the singing of hymns and other acts for the Blessed One;
they are described in the Vedas, Śāstras, and other texts by the noble-formed liberated attendants. || 8 ||
They are presided over by divine women who are the very essence of knowledge and by Brahma-men,
and they are graced by lakes of the pure nectar of love and wisdom.
They were constantly nourished by the women known as the Śrutis, by the female attendants known as the Smṛtis,
and by the divine men known as the Śāstras.
Indeed, everything that is to be enjoyed and the highest object of enjoyment exists within the worlds of Brahmā;
there exists only consciousness, which arises from the reality of Brahman. || 11 ||
It is neither illusion nor insentient; it is neither suffering nor subject to destruction.
It is neither darkness nor arisen, neither perishable but eternal. 1.2.
Just as the existence of Goloka is within the limits of the Imperishable Brahman (Akṣara-brahman),
so too is the existence of Vaikuṇṭha within the limits of the Akṣara-dhāma.
On the far shore of Māyā is the great divine consort who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha;
she is indeed considered the perfect recipient of Nārāyaṇa’s love. 14.
Having immersed herself in the supreme bliss of devotion to Nārāyaṇa,
she forgot her own form and was indeed transformed into a liquid state.
Through union with Nārāyaṇa and by being dissolved in the essence of desire,
she [becomes] within the form of Nārāyaṇa, bringing forth streams of ten millionfold bliss.
She unites with Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, either through her own powers or through her essential forms;
she remains eternally dissolved in Him, reaching the pinnacle of bliss. 17.
Hari unites her with floods of bliss even within his own self;
therefore, she was born as the river Sarayū in Vikuṇṭha.
And on the further shore of Māyā, there is that divine, circular, and very great river;
it is filled with the essence of Brahman and flows with the stream of eternal bliss.
That river flows with golden fish and excellent silver sands;
it is covered with divine kāśa and kuśa grass, blazing as brightly as the splendor of the sun.
Captivating with the shimmering luster of jewels, diamonds, oyster shells, and the like,
she possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns through her union with divine rays.
Its steps were fashioned from excellent gems, diamonds, and other precious materials; it was adorned with countless descents suitable for vast bathing ceremonies.
It bestows the happiness of dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, bathing, and sporting;
it is beautifully adorned with two banks resembling pure crystal.
In some places it shines with variegated gems that are black, white, yellow, and red; in other places it is endowed with bright, gentle garments made of coral.
In some places it contains deposits of minerals such as silver and gold; in other places it is beautifully adorned with mines of sapphire and ruby.
In some places, it was made magnificent by excellent emerald fish;
in other places, it was adorned with grounds for recreation, bathing, and the like.
In some places it was delightful with lush grass and adorned with rows of forests; in other places, it provided rest for herds of wish-fulfilling cows.
With various divine boats, she was a sight for many to behold,
frequented by celestial birds such as divine garuḍas and swans.
Indeed, those living beings who are consecrated by its waters become eternally protected;
they are liberated and established in the world of Vaikuṇṭha, making their dwelling eternal.
On that beautiful bank there is indeed a forest called Kausala;
following the Sarayū river, it is also circular in shape.
It was composed of divine trees, including many excellent trees such as the *pārijāta*,
and it shone with vast forests of *kalpavṛkṣa* and *kalpavalī* trees that were as long as they were wide.
Its length is measured at two hundred thousand yojanas;
in some places there are kalpa-trees, and in others, indeed, pārijātaka trees.
In some places there are creepers with the flavor of Soma, in others mango trees that are full of juice; in some places there are Madhuka trees, and Jambu trees are found in countless numbers.
In some places there are *karmada* trees, and in others *ṭimburu* trees;
there are also groves of *śrīvṛkṣa* trees and *tilaka* trees that touch the sky. (34)
In some places there are varieties of nine-colored flowers and citrons;
in some places there are indeed plantains, and in some places pomegranate trees.
In some places there were grapevines, betel creepers, and bitter gourds;
in other places there were cinnamon trees, coconut palms, date palms, and wild jujubes.
In some places there were *setu*, *apuṣpīya*, and *rāmaphala* trees; in others, *badāma*, *badarī*, *sarja*, *pippalī*, *bakula*, and so forth. ||37||
In some places there were kesara trees, as well as kadamba, nīpa, and nimba;
there were jackfruit trees, campakas, aśoka trees, and sandalwood trees.
The śrīphala, śālmali, tāla, tintiḍī, and mādhavī trees;
the mallikā, mālatī, svarṇa, yūthikā, aśvattha, and kunda trees. ||39||
There are indeed various trees, all of which are united with Vaikuṇṭha;
in some places there are lakes, excellent wells, sprouts, and oblong ponds.
In some places there were various rivers carrying desirable waters of milk;
in some places were the peaks of mountains, and in others were the plateaus where forest-dwellers reside.
In some places there are houses built for the purpose of delightful recreation with celestial nymphs;
in that forest, there are infinite dwellings belonging to the forest-dwellers.
Through the grace of Nārāyaṇa, those living beings—be they beasts, birds, or reptiles—who have attained liberation in this kalpa and in other kalpas; ||43||
Released there in Kosala, they dwell eternally in that forest; indeed, by the will of Nārāyaṇa, they possess the power to assume any form at will.
Indeed, they travel through the atmosphere in some vehicle or celestial chariot.
In some places there are gods, in some liberated ones, and in some various noble lineages. ||45||
They truly exist and indeed abide there, satisfied by the drinking of fruits and other things;
they consist of divine enjoyments, the essence of drinks, and various kinds of fruits. (46)
For the sake of those residing in the forest known as Kausalyā, there are many beautiful groves of trees created by Viṣṇu in that forest. 47.
And auspicious jars made from *vaṭa*, *gundraka*, and *āmalakī* trees, as well as from *kiṃśuka*, *udumbara*, and *pippala* trees. (48)
Beautiful, golden-hued, and tawny creepers, clinging to the trees and forming canopies for the sake of the groves, shine forth. ||49||
There are pavilions with floors made of excellent gems, jewels, and diamonds,
featuring celestial litters for the purpose of ascending the noble paths of divine stairways.
Those indeed possess a thousand levels in the sky, with well-set flags;
they are endowed with sun-bowls and surrounded by various gardens. ||51||
Glass lamps, though enriched with pools of cold and hot water and adorned with circles of fire, are delightful only through their natural substance. ||52||
There, wish-fulfilling cows roam and graze;
likewise, there are divine dwellings for those who reside in the forests of Vaikuṇṭha. 53.
There were Lakṣmīs equal to Ramā, beautiful women in the full bloom of sixteen-year-old youth, well-formed, accompanied by their husbands, and joined by their own families. 54.
All those belonging to the lineage of Acyuta dwell there with devoted minds, their faces delightful with playful pastimes, and their couches adorned with beautiful coverlets. (55)
They indeed become fit for dwelling, fit for habitation, and fit for pleasure; they possess walls and palaces, and are provided with means for water and fire.
Equipped with fans and chowries, adorned with many mirrors, and decorated with food, clothing, conversation, dancing, and instrumental music. ||57||
There are palatial mansions and pavilions with the brilliant luster of jewel-lamps;
indeed, fragrant incenses are present there within the small chambers.
Cool breezes, moist with the essence of passion, blow forth, bestowing happiness;
for the sake of the pleasure of women, the forest is conscious and skillful. (59)
There are fifty crores of bowers, huts, and pavilions there;
having bathed in the Sarayū and become one whose body is liberated, one should then proceed from that place.
If he desires to dwell in that delightful forest of Kauśala, he takes up residence right there and rejoices like one who is liberated. (61)
Beyond this, at the front of the great protective enclosure, there is a divine,
excellent great wall extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
This [mountain] is circular in shape and rises to a height of one hundred thousand yojanas;
upon its summit are ten million magnificent, divine palaces.
All travel through the air in golden celestial chariots;
they are one hundred yojanas in height and one thousand yojanas in width.
Those palaces, traveling through the sky, are equal to celestial chariots;
all the men and women there are like those of Vaikuṇṭha and move according to their will.
There were young women and young men, twelve and sixteen years of age respectively,
richly adorned with the beauty of their braided hair and wearing garlands of flowers.
They were adorned with bracelets, armlets, neck-ornaments, chains, and crowns; they were further embellished with rings, the Kaustubha gem, and golden ornaments.
With the regions of their eyebrows arched with intense passion, carrying forth streams of love, they were full-bodied, white and reddish in hue, with limbs draped in golden garments. (68)
Always beautiful with forms like gold, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
and as cool as the autumn moon, they were like mines of all delights.
But they indeed become divided into fifty crores;
and those devotees, likewise, are eternal and number fifty crores.
Likewise, others also dwell there upon that circular rampart;
indeed, it has four gates situated in the four directions.
There, the attendants of the Blessed One indeed served as gatekeepers,
adorned with ornaments of jewels and radiant with crowns of excellent gems.
The four gates were guarded by all divine beings bearing celestial weapons, adorned with crowns and bracelets, and appearing as sixteen-year-old youths.
Thus, it is pervaded by the supreme fortress and is circular in shape;
at its center lies the divine, well-situated city known as Sāketa. (74)
That eternal place called Sāketadhāma is not confined to a single residence;
there are many gardens and countless groves therein. (75)
There are great rivers of the essence of Brahman, numerous mountain peaks,
countless fertile fields, as well as forests and groves.
For the pleasure and diversion of the Vaiṣṇavas,
and for the residence of their wives who possess young brides, dwellings were constructed there.
There are indeed hundreds of millions of villages along with their fortresses,
and hundreds of thousands of millions of diverse cities.
The villages of the city of Sāketa have grounds of precious gems and jewels; there are pavilions of jewels and excellent houses made of gems and diamonds. (79)
There were palaces made of pearls and rubies with walls of crystal,
as well as divine cows, calves, and auspicious heifers.
There were palaces and domes, as well as numerous spires;
indeed, there were countless moon-chambers and likewise resting terraces.
Local roads, royal highways, celestial chariots, and vehicles;
Garuḍas, swan-vehicles, bulls, elephants, and horses. ||82||
All kinds of various riches, and young women of the highest excellence, all twelve years of age and with the very first signs of youth beginning to appear. (83)
Divided into arbudas and sub-arbudas, those Vaiṣṇava goddesses dwell there;
they are radiant with the finest substances that stimulate desire and are masters of the art of love.
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments, they were resplendent with necklaces of gems;
they were decorated with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and various precious decorations. ||85||
Their cheeks were made radiant by six jeweled earrings and other ornaments;
the luster of their fingers shone forth as they wore golden rings inlaid with gems. ||86||
Adorned with ornaments of pearls, coral, silver, and gold, they bore beautiful crescent-moon marks on their foreheads made with red sandalwood, saffron, and other pigments. ||87||
Adorned with necklaces, strings of beads, and bracelets, they were beautified by armlets on their forearms and equipped with Bangiḍī ornaments and chains. ||88||
Their waists shone with girdles, and they wore small bells and anklets;
their faces were like the full moon of the fortnight, and their beautiful eyes were like lotus petals.
They wore fragrant flower garlands upon their coiffed hair,
and were endowed with slow, charming gait and arched creeper-like eyebrows that captivated the mind.
With firm, small, and excellent breasts, they were endowed with the grace of Nārāyaṇa;
they possessed the luster of yellow sandalwood and gold, and were clothed in yellow garments.
The women have beautiful teeth, melodious voices, and gentle natures; they are indeed objects of Hari’s affection.
They are of the same lineage as Ramā, and their heads are equal to those of Ramā.
All the figures have tilakas and are marked with the seven sacred signs; all the men are four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Adorned with the Kaustubha gem, garlands, ornaments, and other finery, they were white and pale,
eternal, sixteen years of age, and in the full bloom of youth.
Where the supernatural powers (siddhis) abide and wish-fulfilling trees stand in every house, there in Sāketa are the wish-granting gems (saṃkalpamaṇis), which are like those set free. 95.
And all divine prosperities—food, drink, and ointments;
bathing, giving, recreation, and so forth; as well as dancing, sporting, and instrumental music. (96)
All social festivals, assemblies, worship, honors, and rites of hospitality become divine, flowing like a stream from the vessel of nectar.
In that abode of Sāketa, for those who dwell there, there is nothing lacking— not even mountains of liquid juices, fragrant with the finest essences of fruits and flowers.
By the command of Mahālakṣmī, all of Sāketa was perfumed by her devotees;
it became worthy of being seen with divine vision, yet it could not be perceived by the eye of Māyā. 99.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Divine Sarayū, the Kausala Forest, the Residences therein, the Circular Fortresses within them, the Sāketa Region, the Gardens, and the Dwellings of the Vaiṣṇavas and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Śambhu spoke to Mahādevī regarding its description:
"In Sāketa, within that circular area, there is a royal highway."
It is one crore yojanas long and leads to the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
on its sides there are indeed infinite forests filled with wish-fulfilling trees.
There were also Dharma-halls, peace-halls, and resting grounds;
moreover, on both sides there were wells, ponds, and oblong lakes.
In some places there are white palatial mansions, and likewise in others there are excellent houses worthy of all honors for travelers.
All were made of jewels and gold, with golden pitchers for their peaks;
they possessed the essence of the finest nectar and were adorned with betel vines and other plants.
Indeed, on both sides there shine the palaces of the Vaiṣṇavas and Vaiṣṇavīs, complete with gardens and enjoyments, providing dwellings for excellent maidens.
With banners, arches, flags, couches, mirrors, and lamps; with gentle and soft implements, and an abundance of foods, drinks, and other offerings.
Indeed, those palaces, endowed with various means of enjoyment, shine forth;
there is not the slightest deficiency in their splendors compared to Vaikuṇṭha.
Starting from Sāketa, the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, the divine world,
exists situated in the intermediate space within the abode of Brahmā.
Indeed, all around that city dwell the inhabitants who are devotees of Viṣṇu; for they reside together in Sāketa within its circular enclosure.
In the midst of the dwellings of those who have made Sāketa their home is the supreme Vaikuṇṭha;
in the eastern part of that excellent Sāketa stands the Brahma-panasa tree.
Five yojanas in width and ten yojanas high,
it was adorned with a thousand trunks and possessed an extensive spread of ten million branches.
Abounding with ripe yellow fruits and adorned with green sprouts, it provides pleasant shade; beneath it are square altars. (13)
There indeed dwell and take delight the young boys of the devotees of Ramā and Viṣṇu;
they are equal in form to Nārāyaṇa, wearing yellow garments and possessing four arms.
Fragranced by the scent of sandalwood, musk, and other perfumes, and enriched with the beauty of all auspicious marks, they take delight and sport together. (15)
Next to it, on the side, stands a second *panasa* tree belonging to Lakṣmī;
it is five *yojanas* in extent and twice that in height. || 16 ||
Indeed, that is the place of rest for Ramā, who dwells there;
within its circular perimeter are altars made of the finest jewels and rubies.
And there were indeed pleasure gardens for the Vaiṣṇava maidens;
all those maidens were the abodes of beauty, form, and virtues equal to Lakṣmī’s. || 18 ||
Those twelve-year-old celestial maidens, radiant and beautiful, took their delight;
they waited upon Nārāyaṇa, going forth and returning again and again.
Having served Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Prāṇa, they indeed depart;
between those two *panasa* trees lies a captivating royal road.
