Beyond that, one approaches the palace of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
on both sides of it are jeweled platforms made of gems and rubies.
Divine mansions and palaces, adorned with the dwellings of Viṣṇu’s devotees,
as well as Vaiṣṇava maidens carrying vessels for worship, proceed there.
Carrying garlands, crests, and hand-ornaments made from the flowers of various gardens,
they indeed return there after having worshipped Nārāyaṇa.
Clad in garments of molten gold and possessing bodies of refined gold, their faces bewildered by ten million forms of desire, they serve Śrī Hari within the palace.
For those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha as well as those dwelling in Sāketa,
the path for entering and exiting is always crowded.
In some places along the side, there are indeed groves of mango trees.
In some places, it was beautifully adorned with gardens of fruits such as jackfruit and rambhā.
Adorned with flower gardens and the splendor of enchanting lakes,
he now enters the easternmost gate of the outer wall.
Everything within the enclosure wall is Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Hari;
within the enclosure wall, there are indeed millions of dwellings for the devotees.
The rampart is circular in shape and extends for ten million yojanas;
situated in the sky within the abode of Brahmā, it is called Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
The Vaiṣṇava people there indeed introduce themselves by the names "Nityavaikuṇṭha" and also "Paravaikuṇṭha."
Millions of celestial palaces (vimānas) abide upon the ramparts;
they proceed toward the abode of Brahmā and sport in Sāketa.
From within the cosmic eggs, they bring their own devotees to that abode.
All those attendants were servants at the foremost feet of Nārāyaṇa.
Divine beings dwell upon the ramparts and in the great palaces, within excellent storehouses filled with gems, jewels, rubies, diamonds, and the like.
In various places there, beautiful palaces exist, which are filled with many enjoyments and wealth, and which provide substances that grant great happiness. || 34 ||
There, within the walls and palaces, dwell Vaiṣṇava maidens who have offered the very essence of their lives to Nārāyaṇa, one after another.
Fifty crores in number dwell there the beloveds of Śrī Hari;
the hermitages are situated within that circular enclosure across seven levels.
There are divine crores of lotuses where those eternal attendants of Nārāyaṇa have made their abode; their splendor is only slightly less than that of Śrī Hari.
Indeed, hundreds of millions of the best of Vaiṣṇava devotees dwell there— those who are celestial gardens, mines of nectar, and natural reservoirs of bliss.
All were four-armed and sixteen years of age, like Nārāyaṇas;
all those maidens were twelve years old, like Kamalās.
Furthermore, at the end of that time, millions of other Sātvatas, who are great devotees and whose very forms are Hari, dwell in their constructed residences.
Furthermore, thirty-two crores of other handmaidens of the goddess Lakṣmī dwell there in the palatial mansions of the enclosure walls, appearing entirely green.
Having realized Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman, one attains transcendence of death;
his residence shall be there in the sphere of Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Through supreme devotion to Nārāyaṇa and likewise through service to Ramā,
they go to Mahāvaikuṇṭha itself, from which there is no return.
For their sake, those dwellings were constructed within the wall made of jewels,
possessing such opulences as flower-beds, flower-garlands, and food that was like nectar.
Adorned with umbrellas, fly-whisks, mirrors, and golden jars, their dwellings become richly beautified with garments and ornaments. (45)
Having attained bodies that are imperishable, unfailing in their potency, and full of joy and vigor, millions upon millions of Vaiṣṇavas dwell in their own celestial palaces. 46.
Indeed, there are eight great gate-towers on that rampart,
and fourteen levels of ground protected by gatekeepers.
The [mudrās] of Indra and Pāvaka, as well as those of Yama and Nairṛta;
likewise those of Varuṇa and Vāyu, and those of Soma and Īśāna. ||48||
This very office of gatekeeper has been eternally ordained for those gods;
indeed, all those gods who dwell there are devotees of Viṣṇu, eternal and liberated.
They are indeed the guardians of the gates, but not the protectors of heaven and the other realms;
namely Indra, Pāvaka, Yama, and likewise Nirṛti.
Varuṇa, Pavana, Kubera, and Īśa—
those who bear these names are the liberated ones dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha.
Under their command in Vaikuṇṭha are indeed hundreds of billions of Vaiṣṇavas;
all of them reside within the enclosure of each individual one.
This, however, is the seventh array; within that, moreover, is another consisting of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, bow Śārṅga, and plow.
The pestle and the eight weapons are his attendants (pārṣadas), each named after its respective weapon;
they are four-armed, embodied, and equipped with mantras, handheld weapons, and missiles.
Having arranged the sixth array, there are indeed [deities] in the eight directions in succession;
under the control of each one, there are indeed billions of Vaiṣṇavas.
Now, indeed, when the sixth [array] was stationed within the fifth array, there were the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the Atharvaveda. ||56||
Sāvitrī, Garuḍa, Dharma, and Makha— these eight attendants reside in Vaikuṇṭha,
embodied and possessing divine powers.
Indeed, crores upon crores of Vaiṣṇavas become subject to them;
then, they remain in the fourth manifestation (vyūha) with divine forms.
Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, Durga, Viṣvaksena, and Gaṇeśa—these are remembered as the divine liberated ones (divyamuktas). ||59||
Indeed, there are millions of Vaiṣṇavas who are under their control as well.
Now, in the third array, situated within the fourth [enclosure]— ||1.124.60||
Matsya (the Fish), Kacchapa (the Tortoise), Vārāha (the Boar), Narasiṃhaka (the Man-Lion), Vāmana (the Dwarf), Paraśurāma, Rāmacandra, and Kalki. ||61||
The Vaiṣṇavas are indeed portions of Nārāyaṇa’s divine manifestations;
likewise, there are tens of millions upon tens of millions of Vaiṣṇavas who are dependent upon him therein.
Then, in the second array, there were Prahlāda, Nārada,
Parāśara, Puṇḍarīka, and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Ambarīṣa, Dhruva, Vālmīki, and other great sages—
there are indeed millions of divine devotees who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha.
In the first arrangement, the temple of Vāsudeva is indeed in the east;
Lakṣmī dwells in the southeast, and the abode of Saṃkarṣaṇa is in the south.
Sārasvata is indeed in the southwest, Prādyumna likewise in the west;
Ratiloka is in the northwest, and Aniruddha’s realm is in the north.
In the northeast is Śāntiloka; thus is the first maṇḍala.
All these [worlds] are surrounded by billions of their own devotees, numbering as many as an arbuda and a pārārdhya. (67)
Others dwell in the great Vaikuṇṭha in the presence of Hari;
there is no deficiency in these divine manifestations nor in their palaces.
Of riches, of objects of enjoyment, of foods and drinks for pleasure, of young women, of fine garments, and of fragrant unguents and flowing liquids; ||69||
Of fragrant, beautiful, and pleasant-to-the-touch objects, of sounds reaching the path of hearing,
of visible divine enjoyments, and of gardens for those seeking the nectar of immortality.
Of sweet foods such as curd and milk, of beds, seats, and vehicles, of cold and hot condiments and the like, and of fans, mirrors, and lamps; ||71||
Of those who sported with their beloveds, who resided in palatial mansions, and who were adorned with collyrium, pigments, and flavorful delicacies; ||72||
Of the confectioners, the food-preparers, the attendants, as well as the female and male servants and the devoted Vaiṣṇavas who serve him well; ||73||
Of the female servants, of the beautiful worlds, of the trees, gardens, and forests abounding in fruits, flowers, and fine leaves, and of the honeyed ponds and rivers; 74.
And of material and divine objects— such as glass, woolen blankets, fine skins, mouth-fresheners and other articles, celestial chariots, and those who ride in them.
It was a place that provided dwellings for servants, for those of beautiful form, for the lovers of playful women, for things of delicate beauty, and for various objects.
Of musical instruments, Sāmans, and dances; of festive assemblies and celebrations;
likewise of thrones, grass mats, vessels, and arrows. ||77||
In beauty, virtue, capability, as well as in majesty and sovereignty,
there is indeed nothing inferior to Nārāyaṇa, nor is there anything inferior to Lakṣmī.
All the male devotees are equal to Nārāyaṇa, and the women are equal to Ramā;
indeed, in the residence of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, there is no inferiority to Nārāyaṇa.
Just as there is no difference between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, so too there is no distinction within himself;
there was no physical strength, no old age, no graying hair, nor any decline whatsoever.
There is no decline, nor even unattractiveness; there is no sorrow, so how could there be death?
Indeed, there is no loss of resolve; whatever one desires, that shall come to pass.
Everything is pervaded by the wish-fulfilling gem, with the tree of intention as its constant provision;
everything brings about imperishability, completely filled by the abode of Brahman.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Royal Road, the Brahma-panasa Tree, the Great Wall of Lakṣmī-panasa, the Palaces, the Gateways, and the Seven Enclosures in Mahāvaikuṇṭha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 124 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī concerning the description of Mahāvaikuṇṭha,
the abodes and creations of the imperishable Brahman situated within the Tripād-vibhūti.
Pure, tranquil, and perfectly peaceful, their essence is the bliss of Brahman;
they are eternal, changeless, and entirely devoid of anything to be abandoned. || 2 ||
Countless millions of golden lotuses, possessing the brilliance of the sun,
were filled with the true essence of devotion to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, wherever there are Sāttvatas who offer hymns of praise beginning with the word "Sāma," this supreme abode known as Mahāvaikuṇṭha exists right there. || 4 ||
The supreme good is called nirvāṇa, kaivalya, and mokṣa;
[those who have been] well-nourished by the enjoyment of the nectar at the feet of Nārāyaṇa [attain this]. || 5 ||
For indeed, high-souled and highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavas reside there;
and the female servants, the foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, are always devoted to the service of Hari.
That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, Vaikuṇṭha, that is the station of Hari;
it is filled with various regions and bestows the bliss of Brahman, which is existence and consciousness.
It was exquisitely adorned with rubies, sapphires, and many other jewels;
it was as radiant as ten million fires and was the great embodiment of all knowledge.
It was surrounded by many mandāra trees that produce fragrance and was joined by tens of millions of divine celestial chariots made of various jewels.
That world was vast, meritorious, pure, consisting of the self, and auspicious;
it was simultaneously illuminated by the radiance of thousands of millions of suns.
This realm of Viṣṇu is eternal; it is not dissolved at the end of Pradhāna.
It cannot even be seen by me or by the gods headed by Brahmā.
It was filled with wish-fulfilling trees, kalpa-trees, and nectar-creepers; it was auspicious, graced by long ponds with divine staircases and sweet water.
There, the maidens delight amidst lotuses that are golden-hued, ever unfading, and uniform in form; they sport there and wander about in celestial chariots.
He is endowed with millions of beautiful ornaments resembling blazing fire, and he is incessantly praised by Sāman chants like flocks of birds released [into the air]. || 14 ||
There was a dance pavilion there, adorned with fragrant substances,
surrounded by divine men and women who were less than sixteen years of age.
Richly adorned with the beauty of all the [major] marks and with divine, radiant ornaments,
he shone perfectly everywhere, completely filled with bliss.
There, dancing indeed occurs constantly with high-pitched notes and other melodies; by that, joy repeatedly arises for the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. (17)
Thus, in delightful regions, these women, who are dear to the Sātvatas, worship Nārāyaṇa together with their joyful husbands.
They always enjoy the happiness obtained through the grace of Nārāyaṇa;
they sing of the Lord’s divine play and his auspicious deeds. (19)
The women had eyes like lotuses and limbs as tender as the lotus;
endowed with divine garlands and garments, they were auspicious and resembled Padmā herself.
They stood together with their husbands, who were adorned with ornaments and bearing conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses, wearing garlands and yellow garments.
They serve Śrī Hari Nārāyaṇa and worship that divine one; for those who delight in one another, there is the blissful essence of devotion to Hari. 22.
It always increases and even becomes focused on the liquid;
thus is the inner mandala of the array pervaded by the dwelling. (23)
Within that mandala there exists a great enclosure wall, provided with four gates and equipped with lofty gate-towers. (24)
And there, even within that fortress, are celestial palaces and mansions;
at the eastern gate are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, and at the southern [gate] are Bhadra and Subhadraka.
In the west are Jaya and Vijaya; in the north are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ;
and [the others are] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanidra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—
these eight lords of the ramparts indeed reside at the secondary gates.
Within that enclosure were indeed the palace buildings, radiant like ten million fires and adorned with jewels. (28)
Indeed, they are filled with divine men and women who have attained full youth, and they stand situated within circular enclosures. (29)
The wall is circular in shape, measuring ten million yojanas;
it is seven-storied and stands in a circle all around within the great sky.
At the twelve gate-towers, the royal roads are well-supported;
within the enclosure wall there, they indeed lead to the royal palace.
O Durgā, surrounding the royal palace is the auspicious city;
for Ayodhyā is divine, blessed, and fashioned by Nārāyaṇa himself.
It was surrounded by rows of mansions containing suns made of infinite jewels,
and was filled with beautiful divine men and women who had reached the full bloom of youth.
It is endowed with divine rivers and streams, with fine cascades of the water of love;
it possesses divine food, drink, and clothing, and its means of accomplishment arise from mere volition.
It was adorned with countless divine palaces and Vaiṣṇava dwellings, and it was inhabited by great devotees of the Lord, Sāttvatas, and those who have offered themselves to Him. 35.
The men had the form of Nārāyaṇa with four arms, being excellent Vaiṣṇavas;
the women had forms identical to Lakṣmī, radiant with garlands and the Kaustubha jewel.
They were permeated with the fragrances of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron;
they resided in various flower gardens, celestial vehicles, mounts, and palaces. ||37||
At intervals there are numerous groves of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), as well as courtyards, moon-chambers, and pavilions excellent for rest. (38)
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, there exist divine palaces with a thousand floors;
standing beneath the shade of the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), those lotus-faced women reside there. (39)
Adorned with various flowers of divine fragrance and exquisite beauty,
they were seated upon smooth couches covered with auspicious spreads.
Resembling ten million moons, adorned with divine ornaments, they possessed beautiful golden eyebrows, smooth noses, and elegant faces. ||41||
There the Vaiṣṇavas, whose very forms are existence, consciousness, and bliss, take delight;
and the female devotees of Viṣṇu always serve Nārāyaṇa with devotion. 42.
In the divine city of Ayodhyā, there are indeed numerous temples dedicated to the goddesses who are Nārāyaṇīs and Vaiṣṇavīs. 43.
Moreover, the inner apartments themselves are indeed provided with walls, complete with gardens, and truly endowed with all means for achieving one's desires. (44)
In the eight directions there are eight lofty palaces with surrounding walls;
here, the eight Śaktis, who are the embodiments of Lakṣmī, are stationed all around. (45)
May Ramā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Padmā, Padmālayā, Śivā, Sudakṣiṇā, and Suśīlā grant me delight and the fulfillment of my desires. 46.
The conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, Śārṅga bow, and other weapons all assumed entirely new and unprecedented forms, filled with the fullness of youth.
In their own circular palaces, they were united with Nārāyaṇa;
they resembled molten gold and were adorned with all kinds of ornaments. 48.
They were adorned with rows of very glossy, dark blue, and curly locks of hair,
and they shone with divine flowers such as the mandāra and pārijāta.
Richly adorned with the beauty of jeweled crest-ornaments, their hair resembling a swarm of bees,
they were graced by ornaments such as armlets, bracelets, and necklaces.
With full breasts, those women belonging to Viṣṇu— indeed, the Nārāyaṇīs—
play incessantly with Hari, that ocean of infallible potency.
That Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is eternally captivating to the heart,
sports here within the inner apartments with those women as long as he remains free from physical blemish.
That Lord of Gods, resembling ten million moons and adorned with divine ornaments, finds manifold delight with the goddesses. ||53||
His face was adorned with a pair of beautiful golden eyebrows and a smooth, well-shaped nose;
he shone with two long, glossy cheeks of exquisite loveliness.
He is enriched with dark, curly hair; his eyes are like the petals of a red lotus;
and his hair is fashioned into a braid adorned with mandāra, ketakī, and jātī flowers.
His lips have the luster of smooth bimba fruits, his lotus-face is graced with a beautiful smile, and he is resplendent with rows of teeth that shine like priceless pearls. (56)
His limbs were smeared with yellow sandalwood paste and marked with a tilaka of musk;
he was graced by four divine arms with broad shoulders. ||57||
Adorned with hand-sprouts resembling hibiscus flowers, he was further graced by shimmering armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings. ||58||
He was graced by the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem upon his broad chest,
and adorned with divine necklaces of pearls that were richly beautiful.
He was draped in a garment as yellow as the moonlight of the rising sun,
and his lotus-like feet were resplendent, adorned with anklets of rubies.
He is resplendent with rows of nails resembling the stainless moon,
and his pair of lotus-feet are smooth, auspicious, and like red lotuses.
He was resplendent with a pair of arms adorned by the two conch-shells, Pāñcajanya and Rathaṅga,
and possessed a pair of beautiful lotus-feet as smooth as refined gold.
With them, the eternal Lord of Gods, Nārāyaṇa,
who assumes many forms and is endowed with glory, sports, being well-served by those many goddesses of fortune.
That king of kings shone as the refuge within his inner apartments;
their riches were equal to those of Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakṣmī.
Not even as much as an atom less than Nārāyaṇa exists, because they have Nārāyaṇa as their sole husband and Nārāyaṇa as their sole refuge. (65)
For they have Nārāyaṇa as their sole true life-breath, they are indeed of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
they possess sovereignty equal to that of Nārāyaṇa, and they are devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly immersed in Nārāyaṇa and making their own welfare the goal of Nārāyaṇa, they devote themselves to him with affectionate intimacy, laughter, playful gestures, and amorous sports.
Within the circle of these eight, beginning with Ramā, there is the contemplation of the massaging of their own limbs by the playful embrace of the bliss of love. 68.
The garden was vast and divine, with trees as cool as the moon;
there were trees of comfort, trees of sweetness, and likewise creepers of bliss.
The landing-stairs and bathing-pools have steps made of jewels and diamonds;
the regions are rich with cascades of nectar and filled with variegated flowers.
The sands are pearls, the grounds are gold, and the oceans are milk; the places are comfortable with soft carpets, and there are rows of most divine forests. ||71||
There are small celestial chariots as well as excellent paths;
there are water-spraying machines and beautiful swing-trees.
There are numerous groves with canopies formed of creepers, delightful places for reclining, and elevated grounds for resting. (73)
There are many places for pleasure, consisting of secret locations and grounds;
indeed, they arise according to the will of Nārāyaṇa, as required.
Invisibility and visibility, as well as luminosity and its opposite, transform according to that [subject] and by his will, as required. (75)
In the center of such a circular garden stands the temple of Nārāyaṇa,
possessing a hundred spires and exceedingly brilliant.
It consists of six hundred levels, is made of divine jewels, is vast,
measuring one hundred yojanas in extent, and is adorned with excellent archways.
It was filled with many palaces resembling houses and numerous dwellings,
featuring beautiful floors paved with gems, rubies, excellent jewels, and crystal.
It was beautifully adorned with windows shining with divine staircases, endowed with various domes, and displaying banners and flags. ||79||
With many golden pitchers, blazing with the luster of numerous moons,
and adorned on all sides by groups of divine female attendants, it was beautifully decorated.
This palace belongs in every respect to Nārāyaṇa as the inner apartment of Mahālakṣmī;
indeed, it is the principal inner apartment itself.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Inner Wall of the Mahāvaikuṇṭha, the Residences Within It, the Residence of Ayodhyā Within That, the Palace of the Eight Original Maidens, the Garden Within That, and the Palace of Mahālakṣmī in its Center along with Its Appurtenances," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. 125.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, Mahādeva described in its entirety that beautiful and independent inner apartment of Mahālakṣmī.
In the four directions, there are indeed staircases made of gold and jewels; and there are millions of small pillars and clusters that radiate the luster of gems.
On both sides of the ladder there are creepers adorned with fresh sprouts,
and likewise on both sides are creepers shining with jewel-like flowers.
And there were likewise thousands of decorative friezes,
fashioned from red and green gems, complete with mirrors and mother-of-pearl inlays.
The walls were fashioned with colorful mosaics made of powdered jewels,
and their sides were constructed of polished crystal.
The dry lands appear like water, and the waters likewise appear like dry lands; the small courtyards at the front seem like dry ground, repeatedly causing confusion among her friends.

Upon the pillars there are auspicious figures of goddesses, adorned with wings and holding excellent garlands; they appear as if they are flying upward, possessing beautiful youth equal to that of Lakṣmī.
Appearing as if they were calling out and as if they were showing honor, those conscious beings,
holding golden vessels in their hands, honored her with parched grain (lājā).
Clad in fine golden garments and possessing a golden luster, twelve-year-old Narasiṃhas,
assuming the form of Nṛhari, stand at the base of the pillar.
Gentle and with smiling faces, they are conscious beings like protectors;
indeed, dancers wearing but a single cloth dance amidst the *karmānikā* flowers. (1.126.10)
For the propitiation of Nārāyaṇa, the musicians, repeatedly withdrawing [the instruments] from within, took up various musical instruments. || 11 ||
At every spot above the gateways, bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists repeatedly played musical instruments for the sake of Hari’s pastimes, which culminate in his divine play.
The Vaiṣṇavas, bearing tilaka marks upon their foreheads, joyfully and repeatedly sing the praises of Hari and his wondrous deeds throughout his various incarnations.
The Vidyādharas, the Kinnaras, and the noble species of Kiṃpuruṣas always sing the virtuous deeds of Śrī Hari even before the creation [of the world].
In some places, twelve-year-old maidens indeed bring drinks mixed with cold, fragrant, and sweet substances for the satisfaction of Hari. || 15 ||
Elsewhere, all the maidens, the Ramās who are dear to Hari, cook one hundred and eight portions of food for the auspicious Lord Hari using fire.
In another place, however, amorous women prepare a bed for Him, while others, equipped with materials for bathing, do so for the sake of Śrī Hari. (17)
Some go to that husband taking excellent offerings;
the Gaurikas go taking fragrant substances and liquid materials.
Taking collyrium, fragrant unguents, rich oils, flowers with excellent juices, and fine substances for chewing betel, they go toward their beloved.
Fruits to be licked and sucked went toward Hari, along with objects that were visible, tangible, pleasant to hear, delicious to taste, and fragrant. (1.126.20)
Taking their husbands, the beautiful women go to delight them;
and the beloveds of the Lord, adorned with Kalki’s crown, go taking him along.
Clad in golden garments shimmering like lightning, with golden bodies and slender waists, they proceed for the sake of amorous play, adorned with the tinkling of small bells. ||2||
Indeed, at every spot along the main streets, divine moons appear;
in the courtyards and at the windows, cool suns truly blaze.
Conscious breezes, gentle, fragrant, and cool, blow forth;
subtle clouds rain down amidst the pleasure to alleviate the heat. (24)
In that dwelling, the divine sky shines forth in every direction;
there are instruments for seeing from afar and bands for hearing from a distance.
The foremost Siddhas, who perceive from afar, dwell in every house;
indeed, musicians play well-tuned instruments for the sake of awakening. (26)
In every place, in every palace, Hari exists in a thousandfold form;
delighting male and female servants, he rejoices in that very movement.
Bath-houses, sleeping-chambers, pleasure-pavilions, as well as pavilions for adornment and pavilions for worship; ||28||
Therein are houses for drinking, anointing, and sexual play, as well as pleasure gardens, gambling halls, and assembly places for recreation, commerce, and other such activities. ||29||
The places for cooking, the locations for weapons and the like, the destruction of missiles; the loss of gold, gems, pearls, jewels, rubies, and crystals. (1.126.30)
Wherein the Guptas are established, he stands above them all, endowed with many principal palatial mansions and temples. || 3.1 ||
Adorned on all sides by hosts of divine apsarases and women,
this preeminent royal palace has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again.
In the center was the royal pavilion of Nārāyaṇa itself,
a magnificent festival-hall made of jewels, auspicious, and adorned with a thousand pillars of rubies.
It was filled with divine Vaiṣṇavas and adorned with the chanting of the Sāman hymns;
in its center was a beautiful and auspicious lion-throne composed of all the gods.
He is established with feet consisting of sovereignty and dispassion born of the knowledge of Dharma,
and with knees in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas.
It is pervaded by the powers of faith, capacity, support, consciousness, and Śiva,
as well as by the sun, the moon, fire, lightning, and the nectar-rayed moon.
Kūrma, Śeṣa, Garuḍa, Haṃsa, the Vedic meters, and the mantras—these become the forms of the seats; in the center, however, is the lotus of Brahmā.
In the center is an eight-petaled lotus, and Sāvitrī resides upon its pericarp;
here Nārāyaṇa stands, well-joined with Mahālakṣmī.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, adorned with jewel ornaments, he was beautified by jeweled armlets, bracelets, and anklets. || 39 ||
Adorned on both cheeks with a pair of jeweled earrings,
wearing yellow garments, and decorated with a forest garland.
He is peaceful, the beloved of Sarasvatī, whose lotus feet are held by Lakṣmī; he possesses the grace of ten million Cupids, has a smiling face, and four arms. ||4 1 ||
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and radiant with a crown of supreme jewels,
he is the embodiment of supreme bliss, bestowing grace upon his devotees.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, he is a youth, a prince with smooth limbs and endowed with delicate features. (43)
Possessing the luster of a full-blown red lotus, with tender lotus-like hands and feet,
his eyes were like fully awakened white lotuses, and he was marked by a pair of beautiful, creeper-like eyebrows.
He had a well-formed nose, was endowed with beautiful cheeks, and possessed a most radiant lotus-face; he was adorned with teeth resembling pearls and was made lovely by his smiling lower lip.
Resembling the full moon at its peak, he possesses hair gathered into a braid,
graced by very glossy, dark blue, and curling locks.
Adorned with the Kaustubha gem, which resembles the thousand-rayed sun rising at dawn, he is resplendent with a conch-like neck graced by a necklace and a golden garland. ||47||
He is resplendent with high, thick shoulders resembling those of a lion,
and is graced by four hands that are rounded like fish and long.
He was adorned with finger-rings, bracelets, and chains,
and he shone with anklets variegated with various jewels upon his feet.
He is Acyuta, radiant with rows of nails resembling the moon accompanied by its light,
and a treasury of beauty, heroism, loveliness, nourishment, and other such qualities.
He is resplendent with his two upraised arms holding the conch and the discus,
and is beautifully adorned by his other two hands, which display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Seated upon her left lap is the goddess Mahālakṣmī, the Great Sovereign;
she is golden-hued, tawny, and adorned with garlands of gold and silver.
Endowed with divine marks, her body at the onset of youth, her limbs smeared with divine sandalwood paste, and her dark, curly hair. 52.
Richly adorned with the beauty of jeweled earrings, graced by divine strings of necklaces,
her beautiful hair was embellished with mandāra, ketakī, and jasmine flowers.
She possessed beautiful eyebrows, a beautiful nose, and lovely hips; her breasts were full and elevated, her face was like the full moon with a gentle smile, and she shone with earrings of the sun.
Golden-hued, adorned with golden ornaments, with four hands holding lotuses,
she is beautifully embellished with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings.
Her forehead is adorned with a golden thread, she holds two lotuses in her hands,
and she is graced by a golden citron held in her hand.
She is the gateway of fragrance, difficult to overcome, eternally nourished, and full of vitality;
she is the beautiful ornament of the ears, nose, and other limbs, and the auspicious mark and crescent moon of good fortune. 58.
She who offers a chowrie, uśīra-root, a handle, or moist betel-leaf to Viṣṇu rejoices indeed with Nārāyaṇa in the realm called Mahāvaikuṇṭha. (59)
Thus the Lord Nārāyaṇa rejoices in the eternal Vaikuṇṭha, in the supreme ether, together with Mahālakṣmī, who is ever-present and never departing.
On the right side are Dharmadeva, Nanda, and Sunanda;
as well as Śrutadeva, Jayanta, Vijaya, and Jaya.
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Puṣpadanta, Sāttvata,
Viśvaksena, Vainateya, Prabala, and Bala.
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa are always among his attendants;
they are divine Vaiṣṇava servants, ever-ready to perform the work of service. To the left, however, are Dharaṇī, Līlā, Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, and Kriyā.
And Yoga, Saguṇā, Prahvī, Jñānā, and likewise Satyeśanī. ||64||
Padmā, Jayā, Pāñcālī, Bhārgavī, Lalitā, Ramā, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Māṇikyā, Lakṣmī, and Mañjulā. ||65||
She is the essence of vigor, the mistress of wealth, the festival of lights, and the sovereign of the nectar of love;
she is the goddess, the best among gods, the mistress of the young, the radiant, and the auspicious one. (66)
Kāntā, Śāntā, Caturā, Haṃsāmṛtarasā, as well as Mūlikā, Kastūrikā, Sāvitrī, and Mauktikeśvarī. ||67||
Jayadā, Muktidā, Hemamālā, the excellent Godāvarī, Rambhā, Jāhnavī, Kāntīśvarī, and Lāṅgalikeśvarī. 68.
Nandā, Damayantī, Nirmalā, Ratnapuṣkarā, Maṇīśvarī, Rāliyantī, Campāvatī, and Dayā. (69)
Ramā, Jayeśvarī, Pāneśvarī, Savitā, Pramā,
Śānti, and Sukhakarī are the consorts of the Supreme Soul.
Taking up the requisites for worship, five hundred principal groups of divine apsarases, beloved by Hari, serve their lord and master. (71)
The women dwelling in the inner apartments possessed the splendor of ten million fires; all were equal in beauty, like goddesses of fortune, with faces resembling the cool-rayed moon.
They serve the Great King, the glorious Nārāyaṇa Hari,
who is that very Supreme Self abiding in the imperishable realm.
And assuming a form corresponding to his divine appearance, he descended in his own true nature;
Mahāmāyā praised him, saying, "O Great Lord, accept me. (74)
Then, having become Nārāyaṇa, he constructed an eternal abode named Mahāvaikuṇṭha at the edge of the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Having made his own left-born daughter Mahāmāyā into Mahālakṣmī,
Śrī Hari himself rejoices in the abode of Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
In other incarnations as well, wherever she was indeed taken along with Nārāyaṇa by him himself, those Ramās truly come into existence.
And they all worshipped Nārāyaṇa as their supreme husband;
he alone was the husband even of those millions of female servants.
Nārāyaṇa accepts service here in Vaikuṇṭha with devotion;
and those other beings who are great devotees (mahābhāgavatas) are also truly present here.
They dwell in the palaces of Hari and serve their beloved Lord Hari,
having indeed worshipped Nārāyaṇa with manifold devotion.
Having gone there, those who know the Self, established together with Viṣṇu, do not return; they eternally attain bliss equal to His.
For one who follows Nārāyaṇa, liberation alone bestows happiness;
one should constantly remember Viṣṇu, the Lord who grants eternal bliss. (81)
Merely by uttering his name, one shall attain the supreme state;
therefore, O Gaurī, one should always pray for the world of Nārāyaṇa.
One should worship the compassionate Lord with unswerving devotion;
He, the omniscient one, knowing [the devotee] as His own, certainly protects him in whatever way is appropriate. 84.
Having performed that vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), its mantra, its necklace, its rosary, devotion to Him, and His name, one indeed goes to Mahāvaikuṇṭha. ||85||
For the sake of Mahālakṣmī, this Great Vaikuṇṭha was created by Hari alone within the Imperishable (Akṣara); that indeed is this supreme abode.
The second [Vaikuṇṭha] was created by Viṣṇu, the son of Vairāja,
together with Lakṣmī for the purpose of dwelling beyond the Pole Star (Dhruva).
Beyond the fourteen worlds of truth,
upon the expanse of Vairāja at the edge of the watery covering, lies the second [world], Vaikuṇṭha, which is of the nature of light.
Furthermore, for the sake of the gods and others to attain their destination, for the sake of prayer, and for the sake of attaining union with that destination, it is also called Śvetadvīpa. (89)
The third realm created was Vaikuṇṭha, easily accessible for His own meeting;
even beyond that, He created a peaceful place for His own rest, which is accessible only to yogis.
The fourth [world], Vaikuṇṭha, situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk in the form of the one reclining upon Śeṣa, was created by Himself for the attainment of peace.
In that regard, O Goddess, the first is declared to be Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
now listen as I proclaim the second, which is situated within the enclosure of water. 92.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Service of Mahālakṣmī in Her Various Ramā-Forms Residing in the Great Palace, as Well as the Service of Nārāyaṇa Seated upon His Throne, His Pārṣadas, His Other Consorts, and Others," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Great Goddess Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara spoke to his beloved Satī concerning that second abode situated at the edge of the watery covering.
That abode of Viṣṇu, the son of Vairāja, is known as Vaikuṇṭha;
it is resplendent like ten million fires and is endowed with every object.
It was beautifully adorned with many fragrant kalpa-trees and endowed with tens of millions of celestial chariots made of excellent gems, jewels, and rubies.
Resembling Mahāvaikuṇṭha and surrounded by five lotuses extending for ten yojanas,
the great divine Devagaṅgā flows there in a circular course.
Possessing every splendor, radiant with divine milk-water,
it was fashioned from gold, jewels, gems, shells, rubies, and diamonds.
The descents and the riverbanks shine with rows of forests;
liberated lords endowed with manifold sovereignty reside there.
There were divine birds such as Garuḍas, swans, cranes, parrots, and peacocks,
as well as cuckoos and other sweet-voiced winged creatures.
There were beautiful Cātaka birds, peacocks, cranes, mynas, and others, as well as golden deer, great divine lions, and elephants. (8)
The horses of variegated hue, possessing great speed and considered capable of traveling through the sky, were his diverse mounts; and there were forests and groves as well.
Reptiles endowed with beautiful forms, divine beings numbering in the millions,
and Rohita fish as well as golden fish and others dwell there.
Those born of the lineages of tortoises, crocodiles,
and fish are indeed golden-hued, possess backs of jewels, and can assume any form at will.
In the world of living beings, in the worlds of the lords, and among those moving within the veils of existence,
there are those who are not overcome by the power of Śeṣa, Airāvata, and Nārāyaṇa.
Following the river is a circular forest situated within it,
named Devajayārāma, which measures one yojana in extent.
There, it was filled with mangoes, jackfruit, rose-apples, śrīphalas, oranges, jujubes, plantains, puṣpīs, grapes, dates, and figs.
With cardamom, betel nut, and cloves, and with various excellent trees of nectar;
with kunda, aśoka, sthalapadma, jātī, kamala, and campaka flowers. || 15 ||
With *ketaka* and *bakula* trees, and other fragrant flowering creepers; with *śāla*, *sarja*, *tāla*, *kadamba*, and *devadāru* trees. || 16 ||
With pippala, udumbara, vṛnda, khadira, kiṃśuka, and other trees;
with many species of grasses, trees, creepers, lotuses, and crops. || 17 ||
There was a great, magnificent forest named Devajayodyāna;
therein were pleasure groves, dwellings, bathing places, and grounds for sport.
There are palatial mansions for dwelling in good health and various sacred fields,
as well as delightful gardens bearing fruit for the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha.
Divine and auspicious things alone prevail there for those whose consciousness is under the control of the Lord;
within that forest, a great royal road is considered to exist.
He proceeds toward the Vaiṣṇava city of Devavatī;
there, on a circular, well-spread, radiant Vaiṣṇava altar of Hari, [the rite is performed].
Men and women, sixteen years of age and in the full bloom of youth, bow down;
the grove is circular in shape, and the area as well is circular. ||22||
Extending over ten million yojanas, there are indeed Vaiṣṇava regions,
as well as many various cities of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Indeed, those dwellings of the Vaiṣṇavas consist of every kind of prosperity,
[provided] with vehicles, mounts, carts, celestial chariots, Garuḍas, and so forth.
All those women, the devotees of Viṣṇu, travel through the sky;
there, within that residence, stands a seven-storied wall.
It is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, possessing four gates and eight gate-towers,
and is presided over by the most excellent Vaiṣṇava attendants and Vaiṣṇava women.
It was well-guarded by the gatekeepers, Caṇḍa and others, as well as by Kumuda and his companions;
it was adorned with rows of divine dwellings made of various jewels. ||27||
Within that region, however, is the city named Devavatī, extending for fifty-five thousand yojanas all around. (28)
It is circular and situated along the perimeter of the wall,
surrounded by millions of palaces rising a hundred yojanas high.
Adorned with divine men and women who had reached the prime of youth,
the men and women there were equal in beauty and were like the very image of Śrī Viṣṇu.
Adorned with divine garlands, garments, and excellent ornaments, and anointed with the finest sandalwood paste,
they were grounds for bathing, eating, reclining, strolling, and amorous play.
There were theaters for entertainment, halls for song and instrumental music,
areas for bathing, jesting, and ball games, and grounds for various pastimes.
There were areas for pleasure groves, gardens, rest-houses, and gambling halls;
and there were excellent cages for elephants, horses, cows, bulls, garuḍas, and swans.
In that place, there are thousands of dwellings for the Śramaṇas;
likewise, there are delightful halls for maidens and other halls for devotion. (34)
There were various kitchens for cooked food and beautiful sleeping quarters;
there were dressing rooms and palaces delightful with jewels. (35)
All the various royal highways and side streets become richly adorned with the beauty of diverse trees, and are provided with excellent water-jars and banners. (36)
The portions belonging to the assembly of gentle houses are each distinct;
and here, both women and men are adorned with all auspicious marks.
O Goddess of the Gods, those Vaiṣṇavas who mutter the mantra of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa rejoice there with the delightful joy of devotion. (38)
Having entered the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, they rejoice according to their heart's desire;
having gone there, they do not return, remaining forever in the company of Viṣṇu.
Those who possess the nature of Prakṛti go to Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
their path is uninterrupted, and they attain the auspicious union with Viṣṇu.
Those Sātvatas also enjoy happiness equal to that of Viṣṇu;
those men and women possess four arms, being no less than Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī.
Wherever the worlds of Hari are located, those people go there;
having gone, they do not return again to this cycle of existence, but proceed to that abode.
Just as Bharata, Śatrughna, and Lakṣmaṇa, along with Śeṣa and Śarada, have all gone to the world of Viṣṇu and become entirely divine in every respect. ||43||
If they should return to saṃsāra from their own desired world according to their wish,
there is indeed no movement or bondage for them caused by karma.
They depart just as they came to that supreme, eternal state;
for the Vaiṣṇavas, there is indeed no bondage of karma nor rebirth. 45.
Indeed, service to Viṣṇu is considered there to be liberation;
for servitude to Viṣṇu is eternal, and there is no other bondage whatsoever. (46)
Freed from all bonds, these mighty servants of Hari worship the Lord, that ocean of compassion, with unswerving devotion. 47.
Possessing all-knowing wisdom and virtues, he indeed protects his own people by chanting the glorious Nārāyaṇa mantra, which is supremely full of bliss. 48.
They attain the supreme Vaiṣṇava world, which grants all desires;
indeed, within this circular city of Devavatī.
This Vaiṣṇava palace, a white mansion adorned with a hundred peaks,
is indeed perceived in the sky as if it were a great celestial chariot.
There, the pillars were made of jewels, possessing the radiance of a thousand suns;
the walls and the foundations were composed of divine gems, and the ground was celestial.
Adorned with horns and other features fashioned from gold, diamonds, gems, and the like,
the precincts and the moon-chambers shine like the abode of Brahmā.
Endowed with all prosperity and possessed of every form and flavor, men and women there dwell, appearing as though they were less than sixteen years of age.
All of them are indeed Vaiṣṇavas, the most eminent attendants of that Hari;
and all the divine female attendants are auspicious and beloved by Hari.

There is no stage whatsoever that is inferior in its divine prosperities, such as food, drink, worship, objects of enjoyment, and things to be touched, for those whose fortunes are fully perfected by their desires. (55)
There, in the middle of the palace, was a divine and auspicious lion-throne;
its golden pedestal shone like a celestial chariot of flowers.
Upon an excellent throne of jeweled lions, within a mandala of an eight-petaled lotus presided over by the powers of the foundation and so forth, and richly adorned with various colored rays.
The divine, glorious Lord Hari, Nārāyaṇa, was stationed there, possessing a radiant luster equal to ten million rising suns at dawn. ||58||
His limbs were proportioned to his form, and he was most beautiful with ten million desires;
he was richly adorned with jewels and gold, and decorated with necklaces, garments, and other ornaments. ||59||
Worshipped by women devoted with love and served by celestial damsels,
and saluted by all Vaiṣṇavas, the Supreme Person shines resplendent.
And on his right side is the Mother of the World, golden-hued,
endowed with all auspicious marks, divine, and twelve years of age.
Adorned with garlands, ornaments, fine garments, and other auspicious substances,
she was most beautiful, her hands holding a lotus, a fan, and a chowrie.
Holding in her hands the drinking of nectar, a vessel of wealth, and a citron,
she always shines resplendent and performs service to Nārāyaṇa.
To the left is the goddess Pṛthivī, lovely and lotus-eyed,
adorned with ornaments, garments, perfumes, and the like, and embellished with amorous grace and other such qualities.
With her two upper hands joined together, she holds two beautiful and auspicious red lotuses;
with her other two hands, she holds a vessel of grain that bestows blessings.
Thus served on both sides by Pṛthvī and Lakṣmī, Hari,
the Lord of Gods, shines there, having performed worship beginning with Vimalā.
Vimalā, Sumati, Śyāmā, Suśīlā, and likewise Kuśalā;
Dīpāvalī, Jayantī, Ramā, and likewise Bhāgīrathī. ||67||
Sukhā, Kanakā, Vidyullatā, and Candrakalā— likewise,
he had hundreds of thousands of women adorned with all auspicious marks.
They served their beloved Hari, who stood in their midst as their lord,
adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, as well as great armlets and the Kaustubha gem.
He shone brilliantly with anklets, armlets, bracelets, crowns, and finger-rings,
and with the splendor of earrings, chains, and garlands.
The Supreme Lord, eternally served by the thirty [gods] residing there,
dwells in the city of Vaikuṇṭha in the Vairāja world, enjoying eternal bliss.
Thus, O Pārvatī, this world known as Vaikuṇṭha has been shown to you as the second; now I shall speak of the third—listen.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Second Vaikuṇṭha Above the Water-Sheath in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, containing the depiction of the Deva-Gaṅgā, the Devajaya Garden, the Royal Road, its splendors, the ramparts, the city of Devavatī, the Vaiṣṇava palaces, their opulence, the Vaiṣṇava devotees, male and female servants, the jewel-throne, Nārāyaṇa, His beloved consort, and so forth. || 127 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, then the god Śaṅkara, the husband of Pārvatī,
spoke to his wife concerning his third and most excellent manifestation (vyūha).
This third Vaikuṇṭha is called Śvetadvīpa;
it is the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, the ground of Śvetadvīpa.
For the sake of beholding the great-souled lords of yogis, Sanaka and the others—Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana—[he went]. (3)
Sanatkumāra, Sanatsujāta,
Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha were likewise the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
The eight Ṛbhus were yogins of pure being and great majesty,
who experienced the singular flavor of the bliss arising from the vision of the Blessed One.
Other sages, beginning with Tanu, indeed dwell there;
and Nara and Nārāyaṇa dwell in Śvetadvīpa.
The ascetics dwelling there are indeed devoid of food;
some subsist on fruits, while others subsist on air alone.
Some subsist on roots and water, while others feed on vapors;
still others take smoke as their food and consume the rays of the sun.
They subsisted on drinking the rays of the moon and were devoid of food and drink;
they wore garments made of śāla bark or dwelt naked as the directions.
Wearing the marks on their throats and bearing the mantras and mudrās,
they all worship and perform austerities for Nārāyaṇa Hari.
Detached from all enjoyments and free from passion and hatred, they subsist on food offered with devotion, perform acts of devotion, and take refuge in the true association of Kṛṣṇa. || 11 ||
Both men and women also purify their own impurities through austerity;
they are all meritorious and most meritorious, white in nature and renowned for their white deeds.
Those who are sattvic, free from anger, desire, and other such passions, and destined for liberation— those infinite Vaiṣṇava people indeed dwell there for the sake of austerity.
For the sake of appearing before them, Hari remains present for them upon a delightful seat resembling ten million moons, adorned with various jewels and excellent gems.
In the auspicious Śvetadvīpa, frequented by great practitioners of yoga,
Nārāyaṇa himself resides for the sake of being seen by yogins.
There are delightful gardens, vast forest lands, palaces like Mount Raivata, and rivers equal to the celestial Ganges. || 16 ||
And those grounds are considered to be filled with *pārijāta*, *āmra*, *kalpadru* trees, and *kalpavallī* creepers, abounding in fruits, flowers, roots, and leaves. || 17 ||
The rishis and sages of the fourteen worlds,
as well as other virtuous women and men, come and go for the sake of being seen.
There were many creeping vines with cooling properties, numerous sandalwood trees, lotuses blooming in lakes, and likewise land-lotuses and other such plants. (19)
The *kundabakula*, *śṛṅgāra*, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and others; the *tṛṇarāja*, *nāgaraṅga*, *nārikela*, fruit, and others. || 1.128.20 ||
Betel nut, cloves, mace, long pepper, cardamom, and so forth; jujube, plantain, rose-apple, mango, citron, and ginger. ||21||
In the forests all around, there were various reservoirs of water, as well as wells, oblong ponds, and cool mountain torrents. ||22||
In the midst of the island, and indeed throughout its borders, there are hot springs with sweet waters, well-sustained by forest herbs;
and here and there are hermitages belonging to liberated ascetics.
And there dwell the Sātvata sages together with their families.
They were devoted to the vision [of the Lord] and performed their duties; they sustained themselves on forest produce;
they were divine, like the moon, beautiful, gentle, and possessed of radiant forms. ||25||
They dwell in the White Abode; there is a beautiful city there known as Airāvatī, which should be understood as being crowded with many palaces. (26)
Overwhelmed by divine women and adorned with jeweled celestial chariots,
devoted men and women dwell there together with their families.
Indeed, all prosperities here arise from mere volition—celestial chariots, pleasure gardens, couches, and wealth. (28)
For indeed, various things exist even in the earth as they come together;
they are obtained through the power and manifestation of asceticism, just like the wish-fulfilling trees. ||29||
In terms of prosperity and opulence, there is indeed nothing inferior to Vaikuṇṭha;
even the sages residing in Satyaloka [are surpassed] by those on Airāvatī.
The deities dwelling in heaven, such as the Mahārājikas;
the sages situated on earth; and likewise others residing in sacred fields such as Mount Meru. ||3.1||
For those Daityas who went to Pātāla and were considered to be devoted in soul, there are indeed many palaces for them to dwell in. (32)
There are millions of lofty, circular celestial chariots resembling the rising sun,
as well as millions of aerial vehicles, sea-going ships, and watercraft.
There are hundreds of thousands of vehicles for traveling upon the surface of the ocean, and even millions of vehicles for traveling through mountains and forests. (34)
The royal highways, broad and expansive, with excellent elephants and horses as their vehicles, are always divine, most beautiful, and sprinkled with ichor. ||35||
In the center of such a city was indeed a great pavilion,
surrounded by divine gardens and constructed of jewels and gold.
It was perfumed with the fragrant scents of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, and was beautifully adorned with various flowered arches and canopies. ||37||
It was the dwelling place of divine apsarases, adorned with the chanting of Sāman hymns, and resounded with the sounds of dancing, singing, assemblies, festivals, and cries of victory. ||38||

Its ground was prepared with thousands of naturally provided halls for enjoyment, and its excellent terrain was intended for the purpose of worship through ninefold devotion and virtuous deeds. ||39||
With many locations provided with the requisites for the worship of Nārāyaṇa,
the house was made fit for drinking, eating, massaging, and anointing.
Having made his home for the purpose of accepting the service of the Vaiṣṇavas, he is in no way inferior to Vaikuṇṭha, even in its smallest aspects, nor is he lacking in material riches. ||41||
The celestial chariots of the gods come and go by means of the wind;
it is crowded with hosts of deities and resplendent with the king of kings.
In the center there is a lion-throne prepared for Nārāyaṇa;
and in the middle is a lotus, radiant as ten million suns and possessing the luster of the moon.
There, amidst soft *gaddīkas*, cotton, and other such soft materials, as well as golden-colored and tender things, Hari himself shines forth. (44)
Golden-hued, adorned with necklaces of gold, gems, and pearls, his hands were radiant, holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus as weapons. ||45||
Well-adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings, he shone with a pair of lotus-feet resplendent with gold. ||46||
He was adorned with very small nails, white like the full moon,
and possessed a most beautiful appearance with the form and youth of a sixteen-year-old.
Having applied the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and adorned its center with the beauty of fragrant sandalwood paste,
he was resplendent with his glossy, curly hair shimmering in a beautiful braid.
He was wrapped in fine garments with the luster of milk-foam and moonstones; his ears were adorned with earrings set with pearls, gems, diamonds, and other jewels. ||49||
Having assumed the auspicious lotus posture, he sits resplendent;
on the left lap of that Lord Nārāyaṇa is she of divine form.
Lakṣmī herself, twelve years of age, was her equal in beauty;
she shone, adorned with ornaments befitting every happiness. (5.1)
Possessing a form as beautiful as the filaments of a lotus, she was endowed with the vigor of youth;
she was perfected in all auspicious marks and was the abode of a multitude of virtues and moral conduct. ||52||
Clad in garments of golden silk, adorned with fragrant necklaces,
her hair was decorated with land-lotuses, jasmine, and excellent flowers.
Shining with four arms, adorned with armlets and bracelets,
resplendent with pearl necklaces, and wearing a crest made of mandāra flowers.
With a well-defined nose, teeth like jasmine buds, and ears adorned with shimmering earrings; her forehead marked with musk and her nose decorated with a fine pearl. (55)
Her well-formed breasts were like fine golden jars;
her divine body possessed a beautiful fragrance, and she was adorned with flower garlands and other ornaments. ||56||
She is beautiful and captivating, holding a lotus flower and other such items;
her hands carry a mirror, a citron, a golden lotus, a garment, and so forth.
Acting according to the will of her husband Nārāyaṇa,
she, the beloved of Śrī Hari, always shines upon the left half of his body.
Likewise, other Śaktis similar to her, who are worthy of Kṛṣṇa and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, shine forth in service. || 86 || 9 ||
The great goddess Īśāvāsya, Jāhnavī, Kamalā, Ramā,
Sāvitrī, as well as Śāntā, Kāntā, Brāhmī, and Sarojinī.
And likewise, the female attendants there were Wisdom, Intelligence, Fortitude, Forbearance, Faith, Retention, Tranquility, Learning, Discernment, and Memory. (61)
Vṛṣṭi, Vṛddhi, Mati, and the forest-dwelling Śrīs who perform service— indeed,
Nārāyaṇa has millions of wives other than these.
Ananta, Vainateya, Haṃsa, Karī, and the excellent Vaiṣṇavas—there are endless servants who are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. || 63 ||
The Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, the Viśvedevas, and the Kinnaras,
as well as the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas, were all devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Male and female servants dwell here in this abode of Śvetadvīpa,
within palaces, celestial chariots, houses, and cities.
Thus, in forests and groves, in domestic gardens and the sky,
on ramparts, in bowers, on riverbanks and at the shores of streams— 66.
Rich in eternal happiness, they sport, free from that which is to be abandoned and devoid of fruitlessness;
they are delighted by divine enjoyments obtained through the grace of Nārāyaṇa.
Those who mutter the mantras of Viṣṇu and are intent on the remembrance of Viṣṇu are equal to Nārāyaṇa in their form, qualities, appearance, age, and feet.
Those who observe the day of Hari attain that imperishable state;
the eternal world of Viṣṇu is attainable through unswerving devotion. (69)
Chanting, reciting the names, meditating, and the muttering of mantras dedicated to Hari;
as well as libations and the performance of fire-offerings for Viṣṇu—these grant the station of Viṣṇu.
The men and women there, seeking happiness that depends upon the bliss of devotion to Viṣṇu,
go to Mahāvaikuṇṭha at the time of their end.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Abundance of the Ṛṣis, Munis, Ascetics, Jewels among Men and Women, Gardens, Airāvata City, Pavilions, Thrones, Lakṣmī, Male and Female Servants, and so forth, in the Third Vaikuṇṭha known as Śvetadvīpa," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved; then Śambhu spoke auspiciously to Pārvatī concerning the fourth station, Vaikuṇṭha, situated in the Ocean of Milk.
For the protection of the inhabitants of heaven, the Supreme Lord,
the God who is eternally devoted to peace, [entered] the ocean of milk through sleep known as Yoga.
Hari himself, blue as a lotus, established in his own self,
resides within the inner chamber constructed for his divine dwelling.
In the vast Vaikuṇṭha, resplendent with the manifestations of the Fish and the Tortoise,
[all was established] by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa upon the surface of the earth in the Ocean of Milk.
When the ocean of milk was solidified by the Sudarśana discus,
the surfaces of the earth there became as white as milk.
There were four walls made of milk that had been boiled;
the divine canopy and the pavement were likewise fashioned from milk alone.
Walls, gate-towers, palaces, mansions, rows of forests, paths and byways, roads, and groves of trees and creepers—[all these appeared]. (7)
In this place there are jewels, ornaments, garments, and foods; as well as drinks, beds, vehicles, and mounts.
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, all things produced from milk—
lamps, jewels, and fruits born of milk— were present there.
Flower garlands, sandalwood, and other fragrant substances; collyrium and other articles of auspiciousness; and indeed those things produced from milk.
The pavilion, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas, was constructed of milk;
it was fashioned from milk-crystal, rubies, gems, jewels, and other precious materials.
White like the splendor of Brahman, divine like the manifestation of Brahman, it bestows the bliss and peace of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, like the world of Brahman. || 1-2 ||
There, by the will of Śrī Hari, many divine and magnificent mansions come into being for the sake of providing dwellings for His devotees. 13.
There is not the slightest thing here lacking as an object of enjoyment, an instrument, or a means;
yet, in the midst of that, the thousand-faced Śeṣa, the infinite one, is established.
White, soft, glossy, and warm, it was fit for a bed;
there, for the sake of Hari, a bed was prepared with the coils of her own body.
With a thousand hoods he formed a parasol for the sake of Hari,
and with his tail he created a staircase for Hari to ascend.
There, for the sake of Hari, lamps were made with the jewels from the hoods [of the serpent];
upon that couch of Ananta, the Lord of Kamalā lies.
Hari appeared as a fresh youth, dark-complexioned and wearing yellow garments;
his head was adorned with a crown and hair, and he was resplendent with necklaces and the Kaustubha gem.
He possesses the sacred thread, the sectarian mark (puṇḍra), the lotus, water, the earth, the discus, and weapons; he is accompanied by the mace and Garuḍa, and is resplendent with a forest garland.
His feet were once pressed by Lakṣmī;
he was adorned with bracelets and armlets, and his palms and soles were beautified like shimmering red lotuses.
Adorned with ornaments such as girdles, sandals, rings, and chains,
he was equipped with a sword, shield, bow, spear, iron arrows, and a mace.
He was worshipped with yellow sandalwood, saffron, and the finest musk,
and was adorned with flowers such as the kalpa, mandāra, bakula, and pārijāta.
He was resplendent with a well-proportioned, elevated nose, shoulders, knees, and forehead;
he possessed the beauty of toenails adorned with rows of tinkling bells.
His lips were as red as *aśoka* flowers; his face resembled the full moon; and he was captivating with a smile that shone with teeth like pearls. || 24 ||
Having reached the fullness of youth, he is the refuge for those seeking shelter;
yet he always lies down as if exhausted, as if at the end of a day's rest.
Having engaged in great battles with the Daityas, he lies down again and again;
his splendor is indeed equal [to theirs] in terms of beauty, character, virtues, and so forth. (26)
Possessing a beautiful form resembling gold and adorned with ornaments of refined gold,
she always remains there on the couch for the sake of service.
That large-eyed, deer-eyed young woman, slender-waisted, was endowed with beauty, grace, sweetness, splendor, and the virtues of good character. (28)
She was adorned at night with a bodice and a garment possessing the luster of milk-foam,
and her hair was embellished with Mandāra, Ketakī, and Jātī flowers.
Her hair was fragrant with oil, gathered into a flattened, needle-like topknot and braided;
she bore a tilaka mark made of musk and was beautifully adorned with strings of jewels.
She is adorned with ear-ornaments rich with various pearls and gems,
and she possesses a lower lip endowed with a red luster like that of a ripe bimba fruit or coral.
She is adorned with dark facial hair hanging from her waist and glossy locks of hair;
she possesses slightly elevated, firm, and full cheeks, hips, and breasts.
With her slightly raised, radiant, and soft cheeks,
she shines with four arms, flowing like a river of love.
With her two raised arms she held a pair of auspicious golden lotuses;
with her other two hands, she stood embracing her husband somewhere out of love.
The goddess Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, dwells in constant attendance there;
likewise do others of equal form, such as Narmadā and Tapatī. (35)
The Tuṅgabhadrā, the Kāverī, the Gaṅgā, the Godāvarī, as well as the Sindhu, the Phalgu, the Gaṇḍakī, the Tāmraparṇī, and the Sarasvatī. || 36 ||
The Karatoyā, the Karmanāśā, the Sābhramatī, and the Gomatī;
the Ojasvatī, the Bhadrāvatī, the Sarayū, and the Svarṇarakṣikā. ||37||
Indradyumna, Puṣkara, Nārāyaṇasaras, Aśvapaṭṭasara, and whatever other lakes there may be. (38)
And Lake Mānasa, Rāmasaras, Kṛṣṇasara, Matsyasara, as well as Śoṇa, Brahmaputra, and Gargara. ||39||
In this way, there were rivers and streams, lakes and oceans,
as well as the mountains Krauñca, Maināka, Himavat, Vindhya, Mandara, and Raivata.
The mountains, the goddess Earth, Varuṇa, and other devotees of Viṣṇu;
Mārkaṇḍeya, Bali, Bāṇa, Aśvatthāman, Hanumān, and Vṛtra. ||41||
Nimi, Bibhīṣaṇa, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Manu, as well as Satyavrata, Nanda, Gaya, and Tala; ||42||
These and other divine beings, beginning with the gods, who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa,
dwell there with celestial bodies in the pavilion of the Milk Ocean.
When the ocean of milk was churned, the Lord resided there in Vaikuṇṭha, while the Daityas were being slain and the gods, including Brahmā and Rudra, were being protected. ||44||
Being praised by Garuḍa, the Lord of Gods, resplendent and having slain the Daityas and Rākṣasas, returns here and remains. (45)
He lies upon the couch known as Śeṣa, attended by male and female servants;
thus, O Goddess Pārvatī, everything has been explained to you. 46.
When the functions of the senses become dulled, at that very moment Vaikuṇṭha is to be realized there by one who desires liberation. 47.
"You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are devoted to Puruṣottama;
thus you know the manifold majesty of the divine manifestations. (48)
O Goddess of gods, I worship that Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
for the sake of your liberation, I offer to you this practice of taking refuge. 49.

Accompanied by mantras, accompanied by the ocean [of ritual], with a sacred thread, and with the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra)—this is declared to be the "named" protection, by which liberation shall come to pass. (1.129.50)
Liberation does not arise from knowledge, meditation, austerity, yoga, sacrifice, renunciation, recitation,
or hearing [the scriptures] as it does from offering [all these] unto Him.
In that same way, O my beloved, accept the offering of yourself to me;
by that, liberation will certainly come to pass through the grace of Hari, the glory of Brahman. (52)
In this manner, Śambhu bestowed the Vaiṣṇava initiation upon his own wife;
from that time forward, she indeed constantly [worshipped] Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed worship and having made the offering, he takes food or water;
then those two, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, are indeed Vaiṣṇava devotees.
Devoted solely to my worship, surrendering their very selves for my sake, they are my attendants, my disciples, my very self, and dear to me. (55)
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"If those two gods are indeed Vaiṣṇavas who have surrendered their very selves to you, why does Śaṅkara wear the triple-ash mark and rudrākṣa beads? (56)
Thus this doubt has arisen in me; dispel it, O Truthful One! One who knows [the truth] would not abandon the state of Viṣṇu; there must be another cause.
Having heard this, Hari spoke to Lakṣmī regarding that narrative:
"How is it that Śaṅkara wears the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra) and other such external signs? (58)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Doubts Regarding the Wearing of the Tripuṇḍra and Other Marks by Śambhu and Long-Living Vaiṣṇava Devotees, Such as the Divine Enjoyments, the Couch of Śeṣa, the Mountains, Rivers, and Streams in the Fourth Vaikuṇṭha Abode within the Milk Ocean," in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, for exactly what you have asked of me was also asked by Pārvatī of Hara: "Why is this ash and so forth worn? (1)
Then Śambhu spoke to the Goddess a delightful ancient tale; listen to it, for it contains the cause [of all] and is enchanting even to the Asuras. || 2 ||
Pārvatī said: O Lord Śaṅkara, I ask you about a secret;
out of affection for me, explain it fully, for a great doubt exists within me. (3)
The wearing of skulls, ashes, skins, and bones is highly censured;
O Śambhu, for what reason do you wear that which is so despised? (4)
O Lord of Gods, O high-minded one, I ask you out of the fickleness natural to women; O Master, you should forgive me for this question, even though it is one that ought not to be asked.
Thus questioned by the Goddess in secret, away from people,
Hara spoke of that which was his own supreme secret and whatever he had practiced.
Listen, O Goddess; I shall proclaim that which is supreme, more secret than the secret.
Because it is not distinct from the body, I shall speak of it to you, O lady of excellent vows.
"You must not speak of this to anyone else among people in any way whatsoever.
Namuci and the other great Daityas were wicked beings during the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara."
When they were afflicted and broken by those who possessed great armies, great heroism, and great majesty, the gods led by Indra were overcome.
Having approached Viṣṇu, the gods chose him as their protector—
him who was invincible, a great hero, and one whose impurities had been cleansed by ascetic penance.
"O Keśava, you alone are worthy to conquer these great Daityas.
Having heard this from those gods who had fallen into fear, Hari [responded]. || 1 ||
Then, knowing them to be incapable of being slain, Hari said to Śaṅkara:
"O mighty-armed Rudra, you indeed [were created] for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods."
Practice some heretical conduct and perform a delusive dharma,
by which path the Daityas shall go, become weak, and fall into a low state.
May they be entirely devoid of strength and luster,
like those fallen from their own duties, outcastes, and as if dead.
May the gods, having conquered, become happy and free from all thorns;
may they [promote] the Dharma, the foremost of heresies, and the scriptures composed by heretics. 15.
Make them causes of delusion for the Daityas and preeminent adversaries of Viṣṇu;
likewise, make their emblems appear soiled, even though they have been fashioned [with care].
Just as all that belongs to those of a tamasic nature may become pleasing to you—through your instruction, through that scripture, and through the conduct fashioned by you. (17)
Those who are characterized by tamas will indeed perish by their very nature;
I, Viṣṇu, and likewise the gods [act] for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the Daityas.
"All that has been done by you; for a short time we shall give our full approval from the outside, having gained confidence through that. (19)
The Daityas will, with the conviction that it is truth, accept all that has been devised by him as heresy and a cause for sin; therefore, our victory shall be achieved.
Thus, in order to receive his command, Acyuta then spoke to Śambhu:
"O Lord, if I am to do this which has been spoken by you upon the surface of the earth..."
Therefore, O Lord, even my own destruction would be terrifying;
for it is not possible for me, who has taken refuge in you, to perform this deed.
"Moreover, your command must not be transgressed; this is indeed a great and more grievous sorrow.
Having been addressed thus, the God then comforted me once again.
Śambhu said: "There shall be no destruction for you, since I am your protector;
for the sake of the welfare of the gods, do as I say. (24)
"O Śambhu, act at my command; no harm shall come to you.
For although you are the agent, by my decree you shall remain unharmed as if you were not the agent. (25)
Constantly reciting my names and moving about according to my command, a person—even if he performs worldly activities—is not bound at all. (26)
Constantly remembering me in your heart, mutter the mantra dedicated to me:
"Oṃ haraye namaḥ. Practice this mantra as the Brahman. 27.
Worship me, who am attainable through devotion; perform the task requested by me.
My very command is the great dharma established by me for my devotee. (28)
Desire, anger, greed, deception, hypocrisy, cruelty, or even what is inauspicious or harmful—if spoken by me, that is indeed dharma. (29)
That which has been spoken by me is indeed said to be the Veda itself;
whether it be perceptible or imperceptible, what I have spoken is the Veda alone.
When I enjoin [someone] saying "Do it," then Dharma consists of that;
when I restrain them saying "Do not do it," then Dharma consists of desisting. (3.1)
Therefore, my command shall be Dharma, and its opposite shall be non-Dharma.
O Śambhu, perform [this] for me; I shall worship what you have done in age after age.
Therefore, the Daityas and those of the nature of darkness shall worship what has been performed by them;
for as I am, so indeed are you—the Lord who is eternally indestructible.
"Act quickly for my benefit; I shall destroy your obstacles.
O Śambhu, you shall have no devotion to any deity other than me. (34)
Worship me indeed with the mind alone for as long as there is need;
carry out my command out of love for me, and all this shall be auspicious for you. (35)
Having thus instructed me, O Goddess, she dismissed the hosts of Maruts;
and there I thought to myself: "How much of an entire kalpa is this? (36)
By which the Daityas would be deluded and rendered powerless at his feet;
therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the gods and for the purpose of destroying the Daityas.
Indeed, the wearing of skulls, skins, ashes, and bones has been performed by me;
indeed, the wearing of the triple-tilaka mark and rudrākṣa beads has been performed by me. ||38||
I ward off all those things from the outside, but not from within;
for having entered inside, O Goddess of Gods, [I ward off] the garland around the neck of Tulasī. (39)
I wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), as well as the Vaiṣṇava symbols and mudrās, in every way so that they remain secret and the Daityas do not know them.
O Nārāyaṇa, Hari, my eternal dharma is indeed mixed with heresy for the purpose of deceiving the Daityas. ||41||
He composed the *tāmasa* Tantras of the Śaivas and Pāśupatas; and having relied upon these very works of mine and having beheld me, [he did so]. ||42||
All those Daityas, characterized by tamas, turn their faces away from the Blessed One;
having smeared themselves with ashes and the like, they adorn themselves with flesh, blood, sandalwood, and other such things.
Enveloped by great and terrible darkness, fallen away from all dharmas, and possessed by desire and anger, they worshipped me alone. (44)
Having received boons from me, those who dwell in the realm of sense-objects—devoid of goodness and lacking in vigor—gradually go to a low state. 45.
Those who, being of a tamasic nature, accept my doctrine of wearing ashes and the like while being devoid of all [other] dharmas, indeed behold hell. 46.
All the Daityas are indeed characterized by tamas, as are others who hold that same view;
always defeated by the gods, the Daityas perish in every way. (47)
Thus, O Goddess, my conduct for the sake of the welfare of the gods has been censured;
yet, placing the command of Viṣṇu foremost, I have undertaken the wearing of ashes and bones. (48)
O Goddess, this external mark is for the purpose of deluding enemies;
yet within my inner heart, I constantly meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (49)
And indeed, I shall always enjoy that very name "Japan," which is a mine of the quality of eternal bliss— the absolute Brahman— along with you.
Then those devotees who do not abide in goodness (sattva) cast ashes and other such things upon me;
those who are characterized by darkness (tamas) know that ashes and the like are dear to Śambhu.
Those of such a nature consider even me, O Lord, to be tamasic;
they offer me tamasic things such as hemp, ganja, and the like. (52)
But I, O Goddess, am a Vaiṣṇava; I do not accept what has not been offered.
Therefore, I accept only that which is meritorious and pleasing to Viṣṇu, and nothing else. (53)
Do not fall into delusion, O Goddess; do not embrace that which is characterized by darkness (tamas).
Cultivate that which is characterized by goodness (sattva), O Goddess, for you are in every way a Vaiṣṇavī.
Indeed, nothing is taken by me without first offering it to Nārāyaṇa;
however, I have made a vow before Hari out of devotion. ||55||
Whatever object is to be enjoyed by the master must not become the property of the slave;
likewise, relying on this principle of dharma, one does not enjoy anything without having offered it. 56.
If one enjoys substances such as datura or saffron that are normally not to be enjoyed by the Master, it is done by His command; thus, there is no harm in the offering of oneself. (57)
Indeed, bodily purifications such as the wearing of ashes and bones are inauspicious;
yet even that purification becomes auspicious through the chanting of His name by His command. (58)

Thus has been fully explained to you, O Great Goddess, the practice of *dhāraṇā* such as the *tāmasī* and others, along with its underlying causes; having understood this, you shall not be deluded in this matter. (59)
That in which there is impurity, violence, killing, expulsion, and the like,
and where the mantras and worship are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), that indeed is tāmasa.

Therefore, O Great Goddess, that should never be grasped by those seeking liberation, because it is entirely characterized by darkness (tāmasa), ends in destruction, and indeed bestows suffering. ||61||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Narration of That Event by Order of Viṣṇu for the Purpose of Deluding the Asuras," in response to the question regarding the reason for Vaiṣṇava-Śambhu and Vaiṣṇavī-Pārvatī wearing ashes, bones, skull-bowls, and so forth, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: No one here in this world is able to know, in every respect, the true nature of the manifestations and the glories of Śrī Hari.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Who indeed were those Daityas, by whose strength did they flourish, and for what reason were they created and then slain by Viṣṇu? (2)
I desire to hear the sin-destroying narrative concerning Viṣṇu, which is purified by its connection to Him, and [the account] of the incarnations of Śrī Viṣṇu, the Supreme Soul. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe the eternal form of the Fish.
At the first creation, Brahmā produced the lords of progeny.
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Dakṣa, and Kardama;
as well as Pulastya, Pulaha, Aṅgiras, and Kratu.
There, the Blessed Marīci begot Kaśyapa;
and to Kaśyapa were born wives of various castes.
Aditi, Diti, Kadrū, and Vinatā likewise;
all the sons of Aditi were indeed the gods of auspicious appearance.
The sons of Diti were indeed the Daityas, the Tāmasa Asuras, and the Rākṣasas.
Once, while Diti was sitting with her husband during the summer heat, she fell asleep.
Having ascended the excellent celestial chariot, she arrived at the shore of the ocean;
there, together with Kaśyapa, she sat down upon the surface of the earth.
Due to the contact with the cool breeze mingled with the waters of the ocean,
the goddess, oppressed by the force of desire, longed for her own husband.
