She served her husband by massaging his feet and other such acts in a place endowed with very soft sand and adorned with the sight of trees, creepers, and the like. || 11 ||
On that pleasant bank, cooled by breezes moistened with droplets of cold water, she, overwhelmed with passion, performs her service.
When she bestows various kinds of pleasure upon her husband before the sun has set, at that very time aquatic creatures [are born]. (1.2)
And crocodiles, water-ghoṭas, tortoises, and aquatic creatures,
having gone to the shore, sit there for the sake of wind and for the sake of warmth.
Due to the conjunction with the evening sun, the sands on that shore shine like gold, as do the crocodiles and water-ghoṭakas there. (15)
During the time of Kaśyapa’s disciples, however, there arose a quarrel accompanied by strife;
the views of Diti and Kaśyapa became as opposed as those of the crocodile and the horse.

And at that very moment, the sprinkling of water upon the ground also became fruitful; for whatever the vision and whatever the intellect may be during the act of sprinkling, such indeed it becomes. (17)
Such a fetus is born with such a formation of its physical form;
by that, the body becomes like a crocodile and the head likewise like a horse.
Having attained the state of being formed within the womb, that child indeed remained there;
meanwhile, the couple, having ascended their own celestial chariot, set out for home.
Having come together and remembering that sea-monster Makara,
those aquatic creatures entered the water upon seeing the celestial chariot.
At the proper time, Diti gave birth to an embryo permeated by that [divine] nature;
its body was shaped like a sea-monster (makara), while its head resembled a horse.
This Hayagrīva, a sea-monster (makara), was well-consecrated by Kaśyapa;
though he was a dweller on land, he specifically became a dweller in the waters.
Brought by Kaśyapa and made to receive alms by his mother, the boy, capable of assuming any form at will, was there out of a desire to study the Vedas.
Assuming the form of a brahmin, he went to the Grandfather;
having prostrated before him and presented an offering of oceanic jewels, he set them down.
Assuming the form of a Brahmin, he deceitfully requested the knowledge of the Vedas;
Brahmā then questioned his parents regarding everything from his naming ceremony to his sacraments.
"I am the heir of Kaśyapa," he said to his great-grandfather;
and Brahmā likewise [spoke] to his own son Marīci.
Then he gave the Vedas to the son of Kaśyapa as his great-grandson;
having taken the Vedas, Hayagrīva went to the house of Kaśyapa.
His father Kaśyapa, being truly well-pleased upon seeing his son as a scholar, said: "O son, you must indeed teach others as well. (28)
Then Hayagrīva said: "O father, I will not teach;
the knowledge of the Vedas must never be given to anyone under any circumstances. (29)
The gods, strengthened by the Vedas, repeatedly oppose the asuras;
however, the Vedas must never be destroyed under any circumstances, nor should they ever be nourished [by worldly means]. (1.131.30)
O Father, since the Vedas, the sacrifices, and even the rituals of dharma proceed [from you], yet those sacrifices and acts of dharma are ultimately unreal. (3.1)
I have repeatedly observed injunctions and prohibitions in the Veda;
these two always bring about restraint, yet such restraint does not please me. (32)
All food, as well as drink, intoxicants, and objects of enjoyment may be used according to our desire; for us who are powerful, there shall be neither injunction nor prohibition. (33)
Therefore, I shall not teach others, nor shall I practice according to the prescribed rules;
I shall destroy the knowledge of the Vedas and utterly ruin those who recite them.
I shall afflict the people who follow the Vedic path, I shall slay those established in ritual sacrifices;
I shall perform the rites of the Karmakāṇḍa and shall not proceed otherwise than that.
Having heard his son speaking in this manner, Kaśyapa grieved for that state of being an asura, which was now his son's prerogative within his own abode.
One who is an atheist, a stealer of knowledge, a destroyer of Vedic learning, a thief of the Vedas, like a mere beast, and an adversary to the nourishment of the gods; ||37||

Considering him to be an unfit vessel for asceticism and learning— one who suffers from the fever of envy, who does not bestow future happiness, and who causes the loss of all one's possessions— Kaśyapa [reflected].
He caused Diti to be expelled from her home after taking leave of her in every way;
that Daitya Hayaśiras also assumed the form of a crocodile.
And he dwelt indeed in the great ocean, devouring those who lived in the waters;
having gone again and again to various mountain regions and sacrificial grounds.
He indeed destroyed the sacrifices and repeatedly subverted the duties of the Brahmins;
in the assembly of the twice-born, he even devoured the gods upon earth.
Assuming a divine and beautiful form, he went to heaven;
there he quickly carried off the wives, children, and homes of the gods.
Having destroyed the dwellings of the sages, he committed acts of violence against them;
thereupon, the celestial rishis went to Brahmā and petitioned him for his destruction.
Brahmā remembered Hari, the Lord of gods, the destroyer of the Daityas,
who reclines upon Śeṣa in a pavilion made of excellent jewels within the Ocean of Milk.
Then Nārāyaṇa, leaving Lakṣmī and seizing his discus, took up his mace, sword, and spear, and came forth for battle. ||45||
Where Brahmā was stationed on the shore of the Ocean of Milk,
there Viṣṇu himself beheld the goat assuming a form for battle.
Seated upon Garuḍa, the Lord spoke quickly to Prajāpati:
"O Brahmā, how indeed were you reminded? Speak quickly; I shall do it."
Brahmā said: Salutations to you, O Acyuta, who consists of the gods and the Vedas;
O rider of Garuḍa, the upholder, the creator of creation, nourishment, and destruction. 48.
You alone assume every form for the sake of protecting the world; indeed, you alone are the protector of the Brahmins, the Vedas, the sacrifices, the cows, the earth, and dharma. 49.
You alone, O Supreme Person, are the foundation of all dharmas;
you alone are the sacrifice, the knowledge, and the Vedas, for they have their origin in you.
The entire world has you as its support; the great ṛṣis are dependent upon you;
and we all, in our observance of prohibitions and injunctions, are dependent upon you. (5.1)
"By your command alone we shall guide people everywhere;
it is by adhering to this very path that you, O Supreme Person, conduct yourself. (5.2)
Impelled by you alone, people engage in both good and evil deeds;
the boundaries established by you must be preserved, for it is certain that dharma belongs to us. (5.3)
Having studied the Vedas from his teacher, he should then teach them to young pupils;
he should promote the duties established therein—this is the eternal command of the Supreme Lord.
Transgressing that boundary, the Mākarāsura Kāśyapa,
who has the face of a horse, transforms at will, causing suffering to the gods.
O Daitya, having carried away the Vedas, he has entered the great ocean;
for this entire universe has the Vedas as its foundation, and through the Vedas comes the refinement of dharma.
From performing what is shown by the Vedas, all satisfaction arises;
therefore, having struck down the demon who destroys the sacred rites—the nihilist—[one attains this]. (57)
"Therefore, O Keśava, you alone ought to bring back the Vedas.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord, [responded].
He said, "O Brahmin, grant me peace; let Garuḍa remain here.
I shall go to the ocean, assuming a form suitable for traveling by water."
Having bowed to the sages, Nārāyaṇa himself became a fish;
he was a devourer of even the great timiṅgilas, possessing a sharp snout and being truly unprecedented.
In another moment, his body became like the Himalaya mountain;
entering the water, he devoured sea-monsters that resembled its peaks.
The ocean was agitated by him, and the earth trembled repeatedly;
then the clouds fell from the sky and the planets were thrown into turmoil.
The gods and great sages, having arrived there, praised Hari;
Nārāyaṇa, meanwhile, entered the depths of the ocean on all sides.
Having searched for the great Daitya, he seized him by the throat after climbing upon him;
then that Asura, becoming a master of great illusion, indeed became invisible.
Assuming the form of a fisherman, equipped with a net in his hands and becoming as large as the Himalayas, he desired to seize the fish.
Nārāyaṇa, too, assuming a fierce form resembling the great fire of universal destruction, struck the fisherman with his mace.
Then, casting off that form of a fisherman, he became a great mountain, the summit, base, and other parts of which could not be found anywhere. (67)
Having made his back as firm as a thunderbolt, he lay down asleep, resting upon the surface.
Indeed, by Nārāyaṇa, power was hurled with such great velocity. ||68||
Having reached the far shore and shattered that back which was like a diamond,
the Daitya then assumed the form of a fish and stood in another place.
"Thinking, 'I shall not kill him, considering him my own creation born of my own species,' or else, having deceived him, I shall kill him again. (1.131.70)
Having deceived Hari there, he was struck again with his tail;
he fled into the midst of the water in order to enter the mud.
Having climbed onto that seat, the Lord Hari seized him by the throat once more; tearing him open with the tip of his beak, he struck him down.

Having completely withdrawn all the Vedas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs, which reside within his heart and consist of the nature of knowledge belonging to that Self, he caused them to become concealed.
Having led him up from the ocean by means of her power and meditative concentration,
she cast that demonic soul into the darkness of ignorance.
Having cast [the world] into the realm of Yama, Hari came to the shore of the ocean;
and then, beholding his fish-form, which was like the snowy mountain, [he remained there]. (75)
The celestial sages and seers there were rendered motionless by wonder;
having displayed that form for a moment, he became a tiny fish.
Then Nārāyaṇa, the god in human form, the auspicious Sudarśana,
the destroyer of the waters, appeared with a gentle appearance, praised by all.
The omnipresent Lord gave all the Vedas to that Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
indeed, he offered to Brahmā his entire knowledge consisting of the Vedas.
Having offered all blessings and accepted the worship performed by him,
he mounted his Garuḍa vehicle and vanished into the ocean of milk.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the account of the Fish Incarnation during the first Dvāpara age has been told;
now hear the second account concerning the Fish.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Account of the Birth of the Daitya Hayagrīva as a Son of Kaśyapa, His Theft of the Knowledge of the Vedas, and the Destruction of that [Daitya] by means of the Fish Incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, Including the Annihilation of the Daityas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Mahālakṣmī, whenever it becomes evening for the Creator (Brahmā), at that very time,
during the eternal dissolution, the ten worlds beginning with Svar and the rest [are withdrawn].
Just as in a previous creation they went to dissolution reaching down to the depths of Pātāla,
so too at the time of dissolution do they go to their end for the sake of preserving the seed.
Hari indeed assumes the form of a fish that moves within the waters;
first, there shall be a drought for a hundred years at the end of Brahmā’s day.
Due to the absence of rain and because of severe famine, embodied beings go to their destruction;
all water dries up, and plants perish.
By the heat of the sun, the earth becomes entirely parched;
then, in due course, the seeds become as if roasted.
Roots and tubers perish, and the multitude of living beings perishes;
for a hundred years, the land is scorched by heat, deprived of rain, in due succession.
Consequently, the oceans indeed dry up on all sides;
then, the entire multitude of living beings dwelling therein perishes in every way.
Twelve blazing and fierce suns scorch everything completely;
by that means, within a hundred years, this earth, along with its mountains and subterranean realms, [will be consumed].
Indeed, everything from the netherworld up to heaven is entirely consumed by fire and reduced to ashes; all living beings have perished.
Then, accompanied by their subtle bodies, they go to Maharloka;
and in Maharloka, they all remain, sustained by rays of merit.
Then the clouds rain continuously for a hundred years,
until everything as far as the tenth world becomes entirely filled with water.
Indeed, water reaching up to heaven fills that place during the dissolution;
thus it remains from the evening until the morning. 12.
This destruction of the ten worlds is called the daily dissolution;
again, at dawn, Brahmā himself creates the ten levels of the earth.
Having created [the worlds] from heaven down to the netherworld (pātāla), he brings forth creation;
recollecting each preceding stage, he fashioned them exactly as they were before.
Furthermore, when evening arrives, there occurs once again that dissolution;
at that time of dissolution, O God, Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari, [manifests].
For the sake of protecting all the seeds of virtue, that ocean of compassion himself assumes the form of a fish at the conclusion of the dissolution of the Vedas.
Having arrived, he protects that which is worthy of protection out of the power of his compassion;
indeed, at the end of the day, in the evening, Brahmā rises for the sake of the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā). || 17 ||
Taking his own water-pot, he went toward Puṣkara;
having bathed and filled the water-pot with water, he sat down upon the bank. || 18 ||
While he was taking water from his water-pot for the purpose of sipping,
he then beheld a very small fish upon the palm of his hand.
As small as a barley seed or like a tiny insect,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) casts handful after handful of water into the ocean;
at that very moment, [the body] becomes the size of a span, leaps up, and falls upon the shore.
He said to me, "O Grandfather of the gods, protect me within your water-pot."
The Unborn One continued to do so until [the water] no longer reached his water-pot.
Then Timitiminga said to him, "O Lord, this is not sufficient for me."
"My body is growing rapidly; therefore, throw me into the well. Having been told this, he was indeed thrown into the well by Brahmā, yet he continued to grow.
He was not fit to be measured in the well; thereupon he said to the Creator:
"O Father, this well is not sufficient for me; cast me into a lake! (24)
Having been lifted from the well by Brahmā and placed upon the Puṣkara lake,
this body of Puṣkara instantly became great in size.
He too could not fit within the lotus; he spoke again to the Grandfather:
"The lotus has become too small for me; O Creator, cast me into the ocean. (26)
Then Brahmā, having led him away, cast him down into the ocean and said: "Who are you that are here? Tell me; you are performing a marvel for me. (27)
Having grown large in the ocean, the fish then said to the Grandfather:
"I am Nārāyaṇa himself, for the purpose of protecting the world. (28)
Therefore, you have assumed the form of a fish this evening;
by this, the ten worlds, parched by heat, are considered to be swiftly submerged in water. (29)
Therefore, let this man take the primary seeds contained within the four caskets and board the ship; thus shall the fourteenth Manu be established.
Even a ship a hundred million yojanas long, with a deep foundation, firm and consisting of a hundred decks, must be filled with seeds ready to sprout. (3.1)
The sages, the ascetics, as well as the gods; cattle, elephants, vehicles, and mounts; the various classes of plants and seeds; the goddess Earth; and the Brahmins. (32)
Furthermore, whatever you have used this morning that may serve as seed, take all of that, place it in a boat, and set it aside.
Having established Manu in truth there, you indeed go to your own Satyaloka; then I shall [bind] Nāda with a chain.
Having bound me to its horn, it will wander through the great waters during droughts,
under the heat of the sun, and during rains that last for a hundred years.
And he brought a boat to the treasury of the waters of the great Pātāla, saying,
"I shall protect all of them until the end of the dissolution at nightfall."
"I shall nourish them with my divine power until morning;
do not grieve, O Brahmin, for I shall give you wealth again at dawn. (37)
"Then he will indeed perform that very creation of the ten worlds.
Having been thus commanded, Brahmā then spoke to the fourteenth Manu.
Having entrusted the seeds along with the seeds of the gods and sages,
he presented the boat to the Fish, who was Keśava.
Brahmā, however, went to the world of truth, and night indeed set in at that time,
during the twilight hour at the end of a thousand yugas, when the age was coming to its close.
A drought that lasted for a hundred years occurred constantly;
then the sun, becoming a seven-horsed chariot, rose up as the blazing fire.
Those seven rays of his drank up the water from the great ocean;
then, by their heat, the earth was scorched.
The entire earth, with its mountains, rivers, and oceans, became devoid of moisture;
indeed, it turned into a single mass of flame by means of his sharp, blazing rays. 43.
Then that terrible fire Saṃvartaka swept away the worlds;
having burnt all the netherworlds (pātālas), it indeed consumed the heavens above.
Then, terrible Saṃvartaka clouds, shaped like herds of elephants and adorned with flashes of lightning, rose up indeed in the sky.
Blue, white, collyrium-colored, smoke-colored, and yellow clouds—
terrible in form and making terrible sounds— filled [the sky] with showers.
They extinguished that entire most terrible and inauspicious fire;
and when the fire was extinguished, the vault of the sky remained filled with water for a hundred years.
Thus, when the world was enveloped by water and the entire universe had become a single ocean,
nothing at all could be discerned then, for want of water.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, the Lord makes night;
the Blessed One, as the Fish Incarnation, protects the boat in every way.
During a hundred years of terrible famine, amidst the great fire of time,
that Lord protects the boat by the power of his own nectar.
And he protects [the world] during the night, amidst the waters of the single ocean of darkness;
then, when the end of the night has arrived, the Lord of Creatures awakens.
He fashioned the various ten worlds according to their respective inhabitants;
indeed, in this manner he brought about their dissolution at every evening.
He always performs creation again at every dawn;
this is called the daily dissolution of the ten worlds.
Thus, at the end of a hundred years, the cosmic egg together with Brahmā perishes;
that is declared to be the other [type of] dissolution, known as the occasional (naimittika).
Then, from that primordial illusion (mūlamāyā) as well, the twenty-four forms dissolve; at that time, one should understand that the great dissolution of nature (prākṛtapralaya) has occurred. ||55||
When liberation occurs for the individual soul through the perfect union with the Lord and through devotion from the heart, that is to be understood as absolute dissolution (ātyantika-laya). ||56||
During that night of dissolution, however, there is no protection because of the absence of creation;
furthermore, since there is no necessity for the protection of the Manus, [the Lord does not descend]. (57)
Therefore, during the night of the Manvantaras, no creation occurs;
for the final Manu who has been proclaimed, as well as the seed-sages (ṛṣis), [remain].
For those situated upon the great ship, who were well-ensconced in the state of sleep,
death did not exist by the power of the will of Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa.
They live until the end of the age because they remain as the seed of creation;
indeed, all those who are long-lived do so through their devotion to Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa.
Having created the world again at dawn, Brahmā himself then indeed causes those [beings] to dissolve back into that very creation; it is never otherwise.
"In this way, thousands of my incarnations in the form of fish are born;
O Lakṣmī, I know them all according to their respective purposes. (6.2)
Thus, at the commencement of creation, that great Asura Hiraṇyākṣa, who was the son of Diti, established his abode upon the mud.
Like a sovereign emperor, he enjoys the great earth situated within the waters;
him indeed I shall destroy, having been born from the nostril of Brahmā.
Assuming the form of a boar, I shall lead that asura to the abode of Yama;

"I shall not let those waters rise further, and I shall establish them in a very stable state;

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Assumption of the Fish Incarnation by Brahmā at the Time of the Daily Dissolution in the Evening of the Kṛta Yuga for the Purpose of Protecting the Seed-vessel, and the Assumption of the Boar Form for the Purpose of Recovering the Earth Seized by Hiraṇyākṣa," in the First Section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: How was Hiraṇyākṣa born, and how did he seize the earth? And when did the Lord again become a boar for the sake of his destruction? || 1 ||
"Thus, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, tell this divine story of Viṣṇu which bestows the essence of all relationships; I am never satiated by hearing such tales."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī; Diti, the wife of Kaśyapa who was authorized [to rule], performed severe penance for the sake of easily obtaining a son.
At first, she mourned her dead son for many days;
repeatedly remembering Hayagrīva, she became emaciated.
He does not eat choice foods, nor does he desire drinks and the like;
indeed, he never rejoices in worldly attachments.
Whenever that beautiful woman beheld the face of Kaśyapa,
streams of tears indeed fell from her eyes out of grief.
Whether exiled, driven out, estranged, or even separated;
whether renounced or deceased in the other world—a son causes his mother to burn with grief.
Having heard that Hayagrīva had indeed been driven out from his house and was dead, he grieved in many ways; for such is the nature of affection for a son.
She set her mind upon destroying Viṣṇu, the destroyer of her son;
she strove in many ways to obtain a remedy for the loss of her child. || 9 ||
"May my two sons become powerful enough to destroy Viṣṇu,
so that I may obtain manifold retribution for the eldest horse-faced one."
"Without the perfection of ascetic penances, my heart's desire will surely not be fulfilled.
Having reflected thus, that goddess performed penance for a hundred years.
Subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, she remained thus for fifty years;
likewise, for twenty-five years, she subsisted only on water.
Furthermore, for fifteen years she subsisted on vapors alone;
likewise, for ten years that goddess remained without any food at all.
Through her penance, she propitiated Brahmā again and again;
the fortunate woman saw no other and touched nothing else in any way.
She never performs any other decoration, remaining always established in austerity;
she constantly sleeps upon the bare ground and does not desire the massaging of her limbs.
Oṃ, salutations to you, O Brahmā; salutations to the Lord of creatures.
Grant me offspring, grant me offspring, endowed with prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu. || 16 ||
Thus, she performed the recitation of mantras daily according to the prescribed rule;
indeed, she spent a hundred years in penance entirely free from obstacles.
Reduced to skin and bone, she performed the great worship;
reciting the prescribed mantra, she indeed performed one million fire-oblations.
Then Brahmā, having approached, spoke to that ascetic bride:
"O Goddess, what can be obtained by you? Speak, and I shall give it; do not practice penance."
"Choose quickly what you desire; I shall fulfill it through the power of my asceticism.
There is nothing here that cannot be granted to you by me; choose swiftly."
Having bowed to the Creator who had spoken thus, she, feeling bashful, said to Mānasa:
"Welcome; I shall perform the hospitable rites for my venerable father-in-law."
Having bowed at the feet of my great-grandfather, I salute my venerable ancestor;
I ask for forgiveness if there should be any lack of discipline on my part.
If the elders who extend the lineage do not show favor, then the members of that lineage will surely suffer; where else could they go for supreme refuge? (23)
If the elders of former times, being capable, had not fulfilled the desires of their descendants, then who else would there be to deliver those descendants? (24)
"Therefore, having made my resolve before my venerable grandfather, I shall remain thus established in austerity until I attain the complete fulfillment of my desire. (25)
I choose two powerful sons, possessing the heroism and prowess of Viṣṇu, by whom my intended service to my eldest son may be accomplished. (26)
Brahmā said, "So be it; let Nārāyaṇa do that.
You shall have two virtuous sons whose prowess will be equal to Viṣṇu's. (27)
Neither Viṣṇu nor one devoted to Viṣṇu possesses prowess equal to Viṣṇu;
nowhere, at any time, does anyone else possess prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu.
"Therefore, having gone to Vaikuṇṭha, I shall pray to Nārāyaṇa. Having thus granted his blessing to Diti, Brahmā vanished from sight.
Then, with great speed, he quickly went to Mahāvaikuṇṭha,
where the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, the protector of devotees, resides.
The king of kings, who brings welfare to all, shone resplendent;
having bowed, praised, and sat upon his seat, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
O Friend of the distressed, O Ocean of Compassion, You are the one who effects the liberation of the world;
O Ever-Undecaying One, You are always capable of granting the fruit of Diti’s penance.
They have requested two sons equal to Nārāyaṇa in prowess;
O Mādhava, you yourself must deliberate upon granting them to them. (33)
"Act in such a way that her two sons may indeed become as dear to her as her own;
then Nārāyaṇa [spoke] to his elder brother, the Creator. (34)
He reflected in his heart on how to make those words bear fruit:
"By creating some pretext, I shall fulfill this desire. (35)
For what purpose I have come to this earth, and under what pretext I shall perform the playful deeds of men; [36]
And the Geyas shall meet with him, and by that they will attain liberation;
therefore, for this purpose, let it be a source of happiness for my devotees.
"Let them both become my devotees, equal to me, and possessing prowess no less than mine;
let these two be the true sons of Diti, having caused them to commit acts of hostility toward me. (38)
"Thinking, 'The fruit of my penance must be bestowed, and thus my purpose shall be fulfilled,' Hari himself [considered] the misconduct of his two attendants. (39)
The two gatekeepers named Jaya and Vijaya, at their own will, allowed [the four] to enter;
they sent Sanandana and the other three to behold Him.
And while the news of Viṣṇu was still being conveyed by the Creator,
the sons of Brahmā, possessing the swiftness of their own volition, arrived.
Sanātana, Sanaka, and Sanandana as the third—these, along with others such as Sanatkumāra, came to behold Viṣṇu. (42)
Sanatkumāra and Turya—all of them possessed the luster of Brahman;
they were the mind-born sons of Brahmā, omniscient and embodiments of knowledge.
Treating detachment as if it were a blade of grass, these sky-clad ones live their lives;
gentle and appearing like five-year-old children, they are indeed embodiments of Brahman.
Indeed, those defects residing in the bodies of men and women do not exist in them;
for, except for the Blessed One, their activities do not wander toward anything else. ||4||
Those in whom no vision arises anywhere except for the vision of Brahman, and into whose hearts nothing else enters even for a moment except the form of Hari; ||46||
Chanting His names, they come along the royal highway;
many Vaiṣṇavas dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha follow after them.
And they praise those fools, saying: "Oh, look at these Vaiṣṇavas! They are equal to Kṛṣṇa in appearance, with their moon-like faces and gentle smiles. (48)
Golden-hued, equal to the sun, and beautiful with a halo of splendor; their limbs were enchanting and well-developed, and they were as soft as land-lotuses. ||49||
Possessing not overly long, golden-hued, and glossy side-locks of hair, they captivated the minds of people with the radiance emerging from their foreheads. 1.133.50.
With steady gazes from eyes like the petals of autumn lotuses, they enter deeply into the heart;
with lips as red as fresh sprouts, they steal away the mind.
All of them bore the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark, wore flower-earrings as ornaments,
held garlands of worship in their hands, and shone with the brilliance of millions upon millions of suns.
With the sacred thread draped over their left shoulders and girdles of muñja grass at their waists,
their limbs were proportioned to their forms, and the palms of their hands possessed a golden luster.
Wearing a garland of *tulasī* on their necks and hands as a mark of divine lordship, the residence of Svarṇarekhā and Mahālakṣmī is seen upon their chests. (54)
They were equal to Nārāyaṇa in beauty, similar to Kṛṣṇa in physical form, like Śambhu in whiteness and in meditation, and equal to Brahmā in their bodies. (55)
In devotion they are equal to Lakṣmī; who could these people be?
Let the Vaiṣṇavas behold these marks of a Great Being. (26)
"By the power of our good fortune, we behold these divine beings";
thus [they spoke] to those Vaiṣṇavas residing in the second Vaikuṇṭha. (57)
They praise and behold them, yet they find no satiety in seeing them—all those who come forth naked, appearing in the form of children. (58)
He arrived at the gatehouse where the two gatekeepers, Jaya and Vijaya, were guarding the door; they both rose up with their staffs in hand. (59)
They did not depart until they had asked; then the two attendants holding staffs said, "Who are these naked ones going there? How can they enter the inner apartments?"
"Let them stay, let them not go at all, let those who have gone return!"— thus,
possessed by impudence, they repeatedly forbade them.
Nevertheless, those whose minds are fixed on Brahman proceed regardless;
do not the yogis see what the door is, or who the gatekeepers are? (62)
For those who see no fault whatsoever other than the reality of the Self, what injunction or prohibition could there be for them? What indeed would be a restraint? (63)
"Do not go! Do not proceed! Who are these deaf ones?
O stiff ones, you who look like maidens, who are you, burdened as you are by your buttocks? (64)
"Where indeed are these unknown ones going? O Jaya, go and turn them back!
Who are these sons of she-asses, and why are these sons of a female dog? (65)
Those who have come here, let these people bind them;
let them strike them with stones and tie them up with trees.
Shameless and unstained by worldly ties, they are indeed seen departing without a second thought.
O deer, do you have parents? Or how could you face death? (67)
Naked and without possessions, for whom do you wander in search?
Your mothers are not here; run quickly away from this place! 68.
"If these do not turn back, place a staff at the region of the anus. When Vijaya spoke thus, Jaya then replied: (69)
Having turned back and stood still, they heard everything that was inauspicious; they did not go forward, nor did they offer any reply. (1.133.70)
Jaya, having gone there, struck them gently on their backs with his own cane;
he pressed upon the middle of their hips with a staff. ||7 1 ||
Having given her a slap on the cheek, she struck him on the head;
then, seizing their lingas, she threatened them, saying, "Cut these off! (72)
Having thus rebuked and insulted them,
and having seized all four by their forearms, he bound them with a single creeper-cord and did not let them out.
Having thrown dust upon their backs, he caused them to place it on their faces;
thus were Jaya and Vijaya deluded by their own lack of discipline.
Thinking them to be children, they committed offenses such as insults;
meanwhile, Ramā, Jayā, and other friends were eager for recreation.
Then, having gone out through that city gate, they saw those familiar ones who had assumed the forms of Viṣṇu— these four Nārāyaṇas.
Having fallen at their feet, they performed prostrations as an act of worship;
likewise, they shook off the dust [from their bodies] and were released from their bonds.
They repeatedly kissed their feet and wiped them clean, exclaiming, "Alas!
By what wicked person has such torment been inflicted upon our lords? (78)
Whose hands and feet have been broken, and whose fortune has utterly shattered? Or indeed, whose food from this place has truly come to its end? (79)
Whose water has been lost that the hot-rayed sun has arisen? Or whose line of merit has been severed today, falling to the earth? (1.133.8)
But by whom has the disparagement of such holy men been committed?
They shall have no dwelling here; let them not even know it. (8.1)
Indeed, as long as Nārāyaṇa himself does not know [of this], so long shall the status of the one who treats him with contempt remain here; but after that, it truly does not exist.
Seeing them thus lamenting and weeping again and again, Lalitā went and informed Nārāyaṇa. ||83||
As soon as the Lord of the Gods heard this, he rose from his lion throne and, with his feet uncovered, ran swiftly from his own seat for a long time.
Just as Śrī Hari himself arrived there at the city gate,
so too did his wives by the hundreds of thousands and the Vaiṣṇavas by the millions.
They gathered there on the ground and prostrated before Sanaka and the others;
Śrī Hari, in turn, bowed down like a staff before those four sages.
"What was done, and by whom? he asked Avamānaka, "by whom this insult was committed against virtuous men such as yourself? (87)
He does not deserve to dwell in my gateway, nor even in Vaikuṇṭha, if his feet and hands have committed offenses against me. 88.
I would rather cut out my own eyes or sever my tongue than harm her;
I shall surely abandon my own Fortune, for she is a doer of wrong. (89)
Free from the touch of worldly winds and with minds untouched by defilement,
even children sport for the welfare of those who seek a home.
Even those who appear childish are indeed not childish; they are considered fathers regarding liberation and other goals.
For they wander about as purifiers of sinners and as fires for the world. 9.1
Having shown compassion toward me, please forgive my offenses;
come into the inner palace and accept the service of your servant.
Having thus entreated them, Nārāyaṇa placed the dust from their feet upon his head; and having taken them with him, he arrived at the city gate.
Then Nārāyaṇa indeed beheld his two attendants, Jaya and Vijaya, bereft of their splendor, with dejected faces and trembling. 94.
Then those children said: "In this abode of Hari, which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), entirely pure, peaceful, bliss-giving, and the ground of liberation. (95)
In this changeless, profoundly serene, divine abode of Hari, such gatekeepers as these are not suitable; they are givers of suffering and destroyers of liberation.
Possessing defilements and likewise enraged, speaking vulgar words and stubborn, they are devoid of the conduct of the disciplined and act like Asuras. ||97||
Since they were indeed fit only to resort to the womb of Asuras, they were not fit to resort to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which consists of pure being. 98.
"These two cruel ones are certainly not fit for the feet of Śrī Hari, since you two, fallen from your station, have entered the sinful, demoniac womb. (99)
Then, as they were falling from their place due to the power of the curse,
with eyes full of tears, they both entreated the brahmins for forgiveness.
Having bowed down by the will of Nārāyaṇa, the compassionate sages and children spoke to them regarding that triple birth as it truly was. || 101 ||
"Thereafter, having abandoned this state of being asuras, you two shall attain completion;
we shall indeed return to the status of gatekeepers once more—of this there is no doubt. (102)
Thus cursed, the two sons of Diti fell from their own abode in the world of Viṣṇu;
they were born as two great Daityas of immense strength.
And in Vaikuṇṭha, at their station, Hari appointed Aja and Ajaya as gatekeepers until his own arrival.
With hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of male and female servants, gardens, groves, and the like,
he provided hospitality, worship, food, and vehicles for his feet.
Various forms of service, such as drinking, massaging, and providing beds and other comforts,
were rendered to the four brothers, Sanaka and the others, who were devoted to Śaṃbhu.
Having properly performed the act of seeing and having bestowed her own vision,
and having brought and offered merit, she has come to this world of truth.
Accompanied by the Creator (Brahmā), they indeed went to their own paternal abode;
from there, they then went to Meru to see Kaśyapa.
Having bestowed blessings upon their two sons, who were like Hari himself,
they departed for the divine abode of Hari, Śvetadvīpa, the eternal seat.
Then Jaya and Vijaya, having adopted an asuric disposition, were born; Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger.
For a hundred years we remained within the womb and did not undergo birth;
for if birth were to occur, we would surely experience suffering. || 11.1 ||
Thinking that birth itself was not to be accepted, they did not depart;
however, Nārada then arrived there and enlightened them both.
"By the very act of taking up these births, at the end of three lifetimes you shall both regain your own Vaiṣṇava abode and become my attendants."
Having thus instructed him, he then likewise commanded the mantra;
having made him hear "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa," he then gave his command.
Out of a spirit of hatred, you two shall indeed worship Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
and in your second birth, you shall likewise worship Sītā and Rāma.
In your third birth, you both shall worship Kṛṣṇa and Nara;

Having spoken thus, the divine Nārada departed for his own three worlds;
meanwhile, the two demoniac attendants, while wandering, indeed obtained birth.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Account of the Births of Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa, Beginning with the Departure of Sanaka and Others for Vaikuṇṭha by the Impulse of Hari and Their Subsequent Dismissal by Jaya and Vijaya, Resulting in the Curse of Attaining Asura-nature for Three Births," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes the penance performed by Brahmā for the sake of sons for Diti, the granting of blessings by Brahmā, his journey to Vaikuṇṭha, his prayer to Viṣṇu there, the narration of the boon granted by Brahmā for obtaining a son equal to Nārāyaṇa, and the subsequent departure of Sanaka and others to Vaikuṇṭha under the direction of Hari, their being insulted by Jaya and Vijaya, and the resulting curse.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Those two sons of Kaśyapa were born with great strength; they possessed a complexion like the color of gold and were arrogant due to their immense heroism and power.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder brother, and Hiraṇyākṣa was his younger brother;
his body became immeasurable in size, and his eyebrows were like mountains.
He indeed travels upon the great waters, he travels in the sphere of the wind;
he goes again and again in his journey through the intermediate space and in the heavens.
He wanders through the sky like a planet, goes to the netherworld like Śeṣa,
reaches Mount Meru like a bird, and moves through the atmosphere like Vainateya.
Indeed, he goes beyond the eight enclosures like Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot;
possessing a massive body and golden eyes, he takes no account of anyone at all.
Just as he desires, so he causes it to grow within his body, like the spreading of a tree;
whenever he goes to another world for the sake of recreation, at that time— || 6 ||
He indeed began to worry about his own birth-house there, thinking:
"If someone were to take away my golden house, then what would happen? (7)
"I shall become supportless," he thought, and then, reflecting further, he turned back;
for his own palace had been caused to be built by Hiraṇyākṣa through Viśvakarman.
On the region of the Meru’s slopes and in the intermediate space, at a uniform distance of one thousand yojanas above the earth, [there is the world]. || 9 ||
The circumference of that house was indeed ten thousand yojanas,
and its height was likewise made to be one thousand yojanas.
Whatever prosperities belonged to Indra, Sūrya, Soma, Varuṇa,
and the wise Bṛhaspati, they all came to belong to him.
Whatever is new, gentle, or beautiful in the mind should indeed come within the range of his vision; even for the great, that shall come to pass.
Having forcibly brought those [treasures] together, he indeed enjoyed them in his home free from all obstacles;
thus his prosperous house was like another Meru on earth.
Having thus abandoned his prosperous home, he goes to the grounds of the monastery;
then he indeed experiences anxiety, for there is fear of an enemy from another.
Therefore, at one time, he grew perfectly great like Mount Meru;
having extended his thousand arms, he uprooted this earth.
Having separated Meru’s palace from the earth— including its continents and mountains—
and having led both of them far away from Meru, he entered the great waters.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose at the destruction of the earth; thirteen worlds remained here, and indeed the destruction of others would have occurred as well. (17)
The entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, along with all living beings, was seized and held fast by the great Daitya.
Brought down like a myrobalan fruit from the hand, he was cast into the great waters below;
then all the hosts of gods, afflicted by fear, cried out.
They went for refuge to the Lord Nārāyaṇa-Hari;
having reached the shore of the Ocean of Milk, they praised him at great length.
Crying out, "Protect! Save! O Hari! Preserve us! they fell at his feet upon the ground;
crying out, "Protect! Save! O Hari! Preserve us! they fell with their heads at his lotus-like feet.
Having heard this, the god Nārāyaṇa arrived on his bird-vehicle and,
having perceived the great marvel, inspired confidence in them all.
Janārdana, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, possessing a universal form,
assumed the body of a boar and stood there accompanied by the gods;
he whose body was without beginning, middle, or end, possessed great tusks and mighty arms.
Uttering a great cry of "Hā! Hā!
and making his body hair bristle, Hari—who has hands, feet, and eyes on all sides and who consists of all sacrifices—became dark-hued like a rain cloud, resembling Mount Meru in stature.
With his face in the form of a boar and his body consisting of Nārāyaṇa,
the Lord— bearing the conch, discus, mace, sword, spear, shield, and other weapons—
went swiftly through the sky downward, deeper and deeper, toward the great waters.
As he moved along, the great wind became agitated and bewildered;
even the houses, supported by it, were dragged behind him.
When the god entered the great waters, the asura,
though overwhelmed by fear and impelled by haste, remained intent on battle.
Then, having placed the earth within his belly, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa assumed a body like Mount Meru and seized a mace resembling the Himālaya mountain.
Having whirled him around, the great Daitya fought the Lord of the Universe;
a mace-duel ensued for a hundred years, involving many transformations and leading to destruction.
Then that Hari, in the form of a boar, became as large as Mount Meru;
and his tusk grew long, as hard as a thunderbolt or even harder than a thunderbolt.
Five himālayas thick and ten himādris long,
the tip of his tusk was exceedingly sharp, measuring a hundred gavyūtis.
Then Hari, the Supreme Lord, manifesting the power of his Vairāja body,
tore that great Daitya apart with his tusk.
At that moment of death, the Daitya let out a terrifying and great roar,
causing fear among the inhabitants of Vairāja, who belong to the external creation.
Bringing joy to the gods and instilling fear in the Daityas and others,
a festival occurred at every place throughout the beginning of the entire creation.
With his great limbs crushed, that lowest of the sons of Diti died;
he saw the earth fallen there, as well as the golden palace.
Having lifted [the earth] with his fangs, the Lord of Gods indeed came to the surface of the world;
and having firmly fixed the earth so that it remained attached as it was on Mount Meru, he established it there. (36)
In that very manner, he, appearing in visible form, went indeed to his own home;
there, on the shore of the ocean of milk, [he beheld] the Great Hari in the form of a boar.
Having seen him, the deities, bowed with devotion, praised him with reverence:
"Salutations to the Great Boar, whose form is the embodiment of perfect sacrifice; salutations! (38)
Salutations to the one whose very form is Mount Meru; salutations again and again to the slayer of the Daityas. Salutations to the one with great fangs; salutations to the upholder of the earth.
Salutations again and again to You, whose form embodies the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and all their branches;
salutations to the one with a thousand arms, salutations to the one whose nature is the universe.
Salutations to You, whose nature is creation and sustenance, who are the very form of time;
salutations again and again to You who assume ever-new forms and who abide everywhere. 41.
Salutations to the Lord of Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and Kaṃbharā;
salutations to Him whose nature is peace, salutations to the Inner Controller of all. ||42||
Having praised him thus, she, along with the gods, sages, seers, and the Earth,
performed the worship of Hari in his Boar incarnation with garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
Being worshipped by those gods, he granted them their desired boon:
"Whenever there is need for the gods and the sages who are of my own essence," ||44||
"Whenever you are reminded of me, I shall then provide protection from calamity.
Having spoken thus, [he was honored] by the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and great sages.
While being sung and praised, he vanished right there;
thus do the incarnations as the Boar appear in every Kalpa and within those intervals.
"When a great task involving water arises for me, all this—the glory and other attributes of the Varāha—is recounted. 47.
O Lakṣmī, my dear, listen as I describe the man-lion form assumed for the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was more powerful even than Hiraṇyākṣa. (48)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Hiraṇyākṣa by the Boar-form [Viṣṇu] in the Great Waters," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning Hiraṇyākṣa who had brought the earth along with his celestial aerial chariot.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Mahālakṣmī; having heard that his own brother had been slain, Hiraṇyakaśipu was consumed with grief, blazing with rage.
Biting his lip with his teeth,
slapping his thighs, and grinding his blood-red eyes which were ablaze with the fire of anger, he sighed.
Roaring, gazing at the subterranean cavity and the smoky sky,
he was terrifying and exceedingly cruel, shaking the earth with his feet.
With his brow knit into a frown difficult to behold and beads of sweat upon his forehead,
he was as agitated as a cloud of frost, rising like an ocean of wrath.
Then, seizing a long sword in his hand, he rose from that seat;
raising the sword high into the air, he roared swiftly like a thundercloud.
Awakening the assembly of the Daityas and making the earth devoid of its luster and power—
if anyone indeed thinks thus, he truly eats only a mouthful of grass.
The Daityas are indeed devoid of vigor, nor does the earth possess vigor;
yet those who are breathless are dead even while still breathing, though they have not undergone physical death.
I do not count Mahāviṣṇu, nor even the Grandfather (Brahmā) of Mahāviṣṇu;
for who indeed is Viṣṇu, wandering about in the form of a beast? || 8 ||
If Viṣṇu, proud of his own strength, thinks in his mind,
"I am the slayer of the foremost of the Daityas," then he truly eats only grass.
Indeed, not all the Daityas have died so that Viṣṇu might be happy;
for if he were to be happy while a Daitya still exists, that Daitya would simply consume his fodder.
When Viṣṇu exists, the Daitya does not; when the Daitya exists, Mādhava does not.
Viṣṇu may live or die, the Daitya may live or die, and Hari may live or die.
While both are alive, the kingdom of the earth cannot be free of thorns, whether by means of force, wealth, vehicles, or weapons. (12)
If there is any deficiency in my army, my knowledge, my weapons, or my mantras,
I shall perform severe and formidable penance by which Viṣṇu became Hari.
I shall indeed perform even more intense austerity than that,
so that I may swallow as many as ten million Viṣṇus in a single mouthful.
"I shall even make Mahākāla my morsel; who is this Eḍaka?
This Viṣṇu, worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas, is merely a sheep in comparison to me. (15)
It goes far from the race of Daityas and enters the abode of waters within;
therefore, the Daityas indeed become fully prepared, weapons in hand.
"We shall pay homage to my high-souled brother with the abundant blood from his body pierced by my weapons. (17)
Free from distress, I shall satisfy my brother, who is fond of blood:
O Namuci, O hundred-armed one, O two-headed one, O three-eyed Śambara! (18)
O Śatāra! O Sahasrāra! O Puloman! O Samilvala! O Pramedya! O Mahādhūmra! O Devāri! O Gajāsura! (19)
O birds, O crows and owls, listen to me further:
all of you go to the earth in the forms of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others.
Repeatedly destroy the Brahmins who perform sacrifices through austerity;
for the strength of Viṣṇu is always increased by the sacrifices of the Brahmins.
Through sacrifices, the gods who dwell in heaven always attain nourishment;
and the ancestors also always become satisfied by sacrifice. (22)
The sages, the seers, and even Viṣṇu who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha—
all of them indeed attain nourishment again and again through their shares of the sacrifice.
Through sacrifice Indra sends rain and the clouds become ready for the downpour;
the Brahmins are fulfilled by sacrificial fees, for sacrifice is indeed the root of life.
Through the destruction of the Brahmins, the sacrifices are indeed destroyed;
when sacrifices are destroyed, whence can there be rain, and whence can there be sustenance for the gods? (25)
With the destruction of the gods who subsist on sacrifices, we shall be happy;
thus, by the power of their asceticism, the great seers have flourished.
Therefore, let them take women with them and effect the destruction of their ascetic powers; for by means of suitable counterparts, even altered forms are brought to accomplishment.
Therefore, let the wives of the Daityas become Brāhmaṇīs in various places;
likewise, let the Daityas become Brāhmaṇas and servants of the sages. (28)
Having constructed huts in the great forest, let them indeed dwell there—those who perform the Agnihotra falsely and who display sacrifices falsely. (29)
Let those forest-dwellers become proponents of false doctrines;
and let them, having entered among them under the guise of the Brahminical dharma, do so through deception.
"Let them kill, let them devour, let them destroy at every opportunity wherever there are twice-born ones, sacrifices, cows, dharma, and virtuous rites! (31)
Go to those various places, set them ablaze, and tear them asunder; here, with your weapons raised, make a solemn vow before the assembly.
"All the Daityas must always unite and act as one; indeed, they must constantly strive for the destruction of the Brahmins and their sacrifices. (32)
In this matter, those who do not join together should be known as the strengtheners of the gods;
they must be slain by the hosts of Daityas, otherwise they become killers of their mother.
Having heard this, and having uttered, "May victory indeed belong to Hiraṇyākṣa," those Daityas raised their weapon-bearing hands.
Having departed for another land at his word, they made a vow;
they wrought havoc among the brahmins and set the cities on fire. (36)
Some broke down cities, others set fire to those seeking refuge;
they shattered the arrangements of sacrifices and wrought great carnage.
At that time, O Lakṣmī, the gods and the brahmins moved about unobserved upon the earth;
meanwhile, the great demon Hiraṇyakaśipu [ruled] over his own [subjects].
Having thus instructed him, he departed alone for Mount Mandara;
renouncing all enjoyments, he went solitary into the lonely forest.
He performed a most terrible penance for a thousand divine years,
subsisting on air alone, taking no food, and standing balanced on his big toe.
Upon Rudra, the great Daitya uttered, "Obeisance to Rudra";
and when a full thousand years had passed, [he emerged] from the head of that high-souled one.
The terrifying smoke, rising up and ascending into the sky, increased until it pervaded the realm of Brahmā; it was a great radiance, intensely scorching.
It was as if it were a forest fire, or perhaps the submarine fire of Vāḍava, accompanied by garlands of flames from either fire or the sun. ||43||
Likewise, a smoke-colored fire arose, reaching the farthest reaches of the sky;
by that fire, indeed, all ten directions blazed on every side.
Scorched by that [heat], the gods of heaven then went to the world of Brahmā and informed Brahmā of the Daitya’s unbearable asceticism. (45)
O Lord, quickly extinguish the fire arising from that;
otherwise, that great Daitya will seek the state of Vairāja.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are as mere blades of grass in his presence;
yet, by the power of his resolve, he desires to conquer them through asceticism.
Having destroyed the gods and others, I shall create a new creation consisting of Daityas—Daitya-formed and favorable to myself—by means of my own splendor. 48.

Having brought Mahākāla under my control, I shall create beings who are no longer subject to death; what is the use of vainly seeking the station of Viṣṇu and other such realms for those already swallowed by Time?
Having adopted such persistence, he performs difficult penance;
therefore, act according to what is right and quickly save the gods and the others.
Then, having led the gods along with Brahmā, he went toward Rudra;
and having led Śaṅkara along with him, he caused [the matter] to be heard by Rudra.
They all went to the valley of Mount Mandara where that king of the Daityas was;
from the sky, they looked all around for the spot where the great asura lay.
Although he was searched for in many ways, he was not seen clearly anywhere;
nevertheless, in a desolate and parched wilderness, from the top of an anthill, [he appeared]. (53)
With its mass of rising flames and smoke mingled as it rose from the churning-sticks,
the king of the Daityas was seen and inferred by all to have come into being here.
Just as they were descending toward the region of Jvālāmālin, they saw there a great mound of earth rising from the ground. ||55||
It was frequented by ants and covered with trees, grasses, and reeds at their summits;
it was filled with great dry stalks like a mountain with its beautiful peaks. ||56||
He was concealed by various anthills rich with tiny peaks;
hidden away, his life hung on by dried flesh, blood, and bones.
There, he was beheld by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin through his meditative concentration;
even Brahmā was immersed in wonder, while the others were then shaken with awe.
"Aha! This is the very pinnacle of asceticism," they cried, their hearts overflowing with emotion.
Then Brahmā, smiling, spoke to his great-grandson Kāśyapa.
Arise, my son, arise! Success in your asceticism has been attained.
This Rudra, Mahādeva, has come here to grant you a boon.
Kaśyapa is your progenitor, and his progenitor likewise;
Marīci has also arrived, whose brothers are most excellent.
They have arrived for your sake, pleased by your asceticism;
these bestowers of boons have come—choose whatever you desire.
Behold your own strength and the intensity of your austerity;
moreover, neither has anyone else done such a thing in my presence, nor will they do so.
And he shall hold his life-breaths for a hundred years within a heap of bones without water;
who else indeed could maintain [this] thus? Choose a boon as you desire.
When, despite being awakened again and again, he indeed does not go outside,
his body merges into the earth and his self merges into Śaṅkara.
Who listens? Who remains awake? One who has entered a meditative absorption resembling a corpse;
whose joints of dry wood-like bones have become as rigid as wood. (66)
When the lord of the Daityas, who was like a stone, did not tremble even slightly,
then Brahmā [took] the auspicious water from his own water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Placing [the water] in his hand, he consecrated it with mantras that grant life;
having thus empowered it, he sprinkled it upon that very anthill.
A youth equal to the sun in beauty, well-nourished like a god in heaven.
With limbs and body like a diamond, he arose with a complexion the color of gold. ||69||
Having shaken off from his body the dust of trees, pillars, ants, and clay,
and having beheld the gods, including Brahmā, Rudra, Kaśyapa, and others, he bowed down to them.
Delighted, Rudra, with eyes full of tears, offered them hospitality; then he said to the Daitya: "What is pleasing to your mind? (71)
"For the sake of which you have performed these austerities, choose boons; I shall grant them.
Having heard this, and having seen the giver of boons, he bowed down and spoke with a faltering voice: ||| 72 ||
Salutations to the one who transcends all beings, salutations to the inner controller of all;
salutations to you, the Brahman, the source of bliss, the bestower of the fruits of austerity. ||73||
Homage be to Janaka and to the venerable Kaśyapa;
likewise homage to Marīci, and repeated homage to all the ṛṣis. ||74||
May you all always be bestowers of auspiciousness upon me, if a boon is to be granted to me and I am considered by you to be a worthy recipient. (79)
Of the gods, asuras, and humans; of the gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
and of the beasts, birds, wild animals, and the great-souled siddhas.
Of the yakṣas and vidyādharas, of those born from sprouts, of the kinnaras,
of the kiṃpuruṣas, of all diseases, and of those who employ spells, weapons, missiles, and mechanical devices.

And let there be invulnerability for me against all those who have been granted curses—neither from within nor from without, neither by day nor by night, and neither by the conscious nor by the insentient. (78)
"Neither on earth nor in the sky shall there be death for me as long as the world endures; moreover, in battle I shall have no rival, and I shall be the sole offspring among all embodied beings. (79)
"May my sovereignty over all the world-protectors remain unimpaired;
may there be no destruction of my power derived from austerity and yoga. (1.135.80)
"May these boons, which are desired by me, be granted to me by my ancestors.
Then, at the command of Brahmā, Rudra spoke to his ascetic disciple: (8.1)
And these disciples are excellent, though always difficult for those subject to birth to find;
nevertheless, we bestow them today—for who is an eternal being in this creation? (82)
Having thus granted these boons, Rudra, Brahmā, and the others returned to their abodes;
Hiraṇyakaśipu also withdrew from the place of his ascetic penance.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how Rudra, Brahmā, and others, having assembled, granted immortality from the Creator’s creation to Hiraṇyakaśipu," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. In this chapter, Hiraṇyakaśipu, filled with wrath, incites the Daityas for the purpose of destroying the sacrifices and rites of the Brahmins, and departs for Mount Mandara to perform penance; meanwhile, Rudra, Brahmā, and the other gods arrive and bestow upon him the boon of immortality from the Creator’s creation.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, with one-pointed mind, to that story of how your enemy Hiraṇyakaśipu obtained such boons.
Remembering the destruction of his brother, he indeed harbors hatred toward Mādhava;
having gone again and again to all directions and likewise conquered the oceans.
Having abandoned the place of Brahmā, he brought under his control all the continents, as well as the sub-continents and the earth together with the netherworlds (pātāla).
The Manus, the Ṛṣis, the lords of the ancestors, the gods and demons, the lords of the day (the suns),
as well as the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and human beings.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, bhūtas, piśācas, uragas, kinnaras,
kimpuruṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, vetālas, and vināyakas— || 5 ||
And the Sādhyas, the Maruts, the Viśvedevas, as well as the reptiles,
the Nāgas who dwell in the waters, and the lords residing in the three worlds.
Having conquered and brought others under his control, he then became the conqueror of all (Viśvajit);
likewise, the gods acted as world-protectors, and there were palaces and prosperities.
All the celestial gardens, the ocean-born jewels, and even the abode of Mahendra as far as the dwellings of the world-protectors. || 8 ||
The chariots of all the planets, the gods, and ever-new goddesses—all were brought under his control; the Daityas were stationed everywhere by him.
The preeminent splendor of the fourteen worlds has been rendered as his own;
there are great divine palaces, excellent mansions, and supreme abodes.
There, the stairs were made of coral, the walls of divine crystal,
the terraces of great emeralds, and the rows of pillars of lapis lazuli.
There were celestial canopies of divine cloth, seats of ruby,
highly precious palaces, and brilliantly illuminated gabled chambers.
His couches were like the foam of milk, adorned with pearls and gems;
his enjoyments consisted of food, drink, and pleasures, and he had sixteen playful women.
Golden-hued and richly fragrant, those deer-eyed women were skilled in understanding gestures;
their dwellings resounded with the tinkling of golden girdles and anklets.
Their lotus-like faces were reflected in mirrors inlaid with excellent gems;
they possessed beautiful teeth, slender waists, and eyes as long as lotus petals. (15)

The celestial women possess bodies shimmering with the wonder of golden hue; they are born from sources of short space within firm knots at their tips, middles, and ends, sustained by the sovereign freedom of the powers of contraction, expansion, and so forth. || 16 ||
Because the palaces where the Daityas sport and always take delight were brought under his control by him, all those [palaces] remained within his own jurisdiction. || 17 ||
His footstool is worshipped by all the gods; he possesses great strength.
And he shines upon the throne of Mahendra, resplendent and honored with divine offerings by all the lords of the celestial realms. || 18 ||
He was highly praised by the foremost Gandharvas Viśvāvasu, Tumburu, and others, and he was honored with hymns of praise by Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Munis, Vidyādharas, and Apsarases.
Like another Nārāyaṇa, he shines as the sole sovereign of the world in sacrifices, in acts of charity, and in the performance of rites for the sacred fire.
Thus he himself enjoyed the portions offered with devotion by the officiating priests;
his earth was the "Vasumatī" (possessor of wealth), and his land was the "Medinī," which yielded crops even without being ploughed.
Heaven rained down objects of desire; the wind blew with soothing calm; and the ocean and the rivers offered up jewels and their waters.
The seven continents and the oceans serve and exalt him;
likewise do the mountains, trees, forests, gardens, the seasons, and the sky.
With their respective retinues, they constantly performed service for him;
Agni became his cook, and Vāyu indeed became the house-sweeper.
The earth became his bed, the water became his water-vessel, and the clouds became the providers of fans that manifested coolness. (25)
Candra, the bestower of coolness, remained ever present to dispel the fatigue of her amorous play;
Kubera was his bearer of ornaments, and Sarasvatī was her singer.
Indra became the provider of drinks, and Yama became the lord of the necklaces;
all the oceans became jars of water containing milk and desirable liquids.
The sun itself became the jewel within his crown,
and the netherworlds (pātālas) then became the footstool for that Daitya.
The Apsarases shall always be her handmaidens, and the goddesses her foot-massagers;
the rivers shall provide for her bathing rites, and the forests shall yield her fruit.

What deficiency can there be for a servant who has performed his devotions, even if he has fallen from his station, when he has always been dear to you and has obtained your favor through ascetic penance?
For me, his devotee, there shall indeed be nothing lacking here in the way of enjoyments;
whatever he desires, I shall grant him even more than that.
Power, the intoxication of wealth, youth, and lack of discernment—each one leads to misfortune; how much more so where all four are present? (32)
Therefore, one should always and in every way cultivate a state of being untainted;
such a person indeed attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation, while another falls downward.
To the very extent that a fool indulges in the mountains of sense-objects, to that same extent he becomes greedy, set ablaze by the snares of delusion. || 34 ||
Enjoying at will the objects of the senses belonging to a sovereign of the whole earth, that great fool was not satisfied; on the contrary, he went astray. (35)
That man of darkness agitates the world-protectors with fierce punishments;
he does not protect his subjects, but incites the Daityas on his side.
Thus, as the one who increased the faction of the Daityas and destroyed the faction of the gods,
he passed an arbuda of years in this very manner.
Then the world-protectors, the seers, the sages, and the brahmins, having attained supreme suffering and being distressed, felt as if their protection had vanished.
The gods, the ancestors, and others who were beset by states of suffering—all of them went for refuge to the Imperishable One on the shore of the Ocean of Milk. (39)
Salutations to the one who is worthy of refuge, whose nature is peace; salutations again and again to you, the abode of sorrow, in whom Lakṣmī dwells as a portion of the Daityas.
Salutation to Hari, the protector who grants the state of asceticism and renunciation;
salutation to the one whose dwelling is the cycle of rebirth, whose very self is that cycle. ||41||
For a long time you have granted the status of a universal monarch to the Daitya who was devoted to you;
now it is fitting that you grant it to those who have slain the Daityas.
Out of compassion, you ought also to grant what is desired, such as wine and other things; O Viṣṇu, perform a reversal, for the unbearable time has passed. (43)
Having thus prayed, all the gods remained on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk;
some were well-established in meditative absorption (samādhi), while others were intent upon the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña).
Having received a boon from Nārāyaṇa as well as his word for protection,
and having made the resolution, "We shall depart from there," [they set out].
They remembered Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the great lord Nārāyaṇa;
at that moment, an incorporeal voice known as the sound of space spoke.
"O leading gods and others, your purpose shall be accomplished;
a fortunate future will certainly come about for your sake. (47)
For all [beings], there is subsequently a commitment (samaya) regarding the arising and the setting of Kālacakra; it does not exist at all otherwise. (48)
The wheel produced by merit and demerit, which binds all beings to their actions, turns according to the law; this [wheel] exists and has been set in motion for him. (49)
Indeed, the merit of Hiraṇyakaśipu was truly greater;
it shone forth so brightly that even his destruction was difficult to achieve.

Wickedness, the disparagement of those worthy of worship, unrighteousness, and likewise the violation of one's wife's vows, surely cause the destruction of one's lifespan and swiftly bring about the destruction of merit. (51)
Blinded indeed by the intoxication of fortune, he acts excessively;
when his time is full, I shall bring about his destruction—let them behold the arrival of that time. (52)
Hostility toward the twice-born, gods, cows, virtuous women, holy men, and those who practice dharma brings about swift destruction; this is especially true for one who is devoted to me. (53)
Therefore, his days have for all intents and purposes almost come to an end;
I shall certainly employ a means for this, so you all go back to your own place. (54)
Having spoken thus, that voice ceased; then the gods and others, remembering Śrī Hari in that direction and bowing down again like a staff, [prostrated themselves]. (55)
They all returned to their own abodes and considered the Daitya slain;
Hari, observing Prahlāda, resolved upon the destruction of the Daitya.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s Hatred toward the Gods, Sages, and Others; His Great Power; and the Worship of Viṣṇu Performed by the Gods and Others for the Purpose of His Destruction," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī who bestows auspicious marks,
indeed performs total self-surrender for the sake of the welfare of the gods.
The daughter of Uttānapāda, a maiden named Kalyāṇī,
became the wife of Hiraṇyakaśipu and gave birth to four sons.
Prahlāda, Saṃhlāda, Āhlāda, and Hlāda—these were they;
among them, the first was my devotee and possessed great splendor.
Having entirely abandoned all other pursuits, he devoted himself to the service of great souls;
he was devoted to Brahmanas, endowed with virtuous conduct, and his mind was fixed upon the practice of truth.
He is indeed as dear to the hearts of all people as their own self;
he conducts himself like a servant in the service of the feet of the great.
He is the gentle remover of the suffering of the distressed, a devoted servant of Mādhava,
and from birth he was indeed enriched with learning, devotion, lordly power, and prosperity.
He is devoted to his guru and to the cows and Brahmins, and is free from vices and the like;
he understands the principles regarding the body as being impermanent, impure, and full of suffering.
He was not attached [to anything], being free from the effects of illusion such as envy and the like;
nor did he feel even the slightest delight in childish playthings.
For him, play is with the form of Hari; Hari himself is his friend—[that person] who is devoted to Hṛṣīkeśa even while dwelling in the womb.
In all circumstances and in all actions, through the deeds of mind, speech, and body,
he knows no one other than Viṣṇu, the eternal Nārāyaṇa.
His mind was naturally inclined toward Vāsudeva, Hari Kṛṣṇa, in whom all the great qualities of the Sātvatas are eternally established.
He is deeply asleep toward the world, yet he remains awake toward Śrī Hari;
sleeping, breathing, rising, moving, turning over on his side,
floating, seeing when hungry, tasting, smelling, speaking, and touching.
Drinking, rinsing, eating, meeting others, and reflecting slightly—[these are all done]. || 13 ||
Having no other occupation, protecting his devotion to Hari, and chanting "Hare, Hare," he meditates upon, remembers, and contemplates the Lord at every moment. (14)
In some places, remembering Hari out of love, he sheds tears;
in other places, beholding the divine Lord situated within his heart, he laughs.
In some places he himself sings the names of Hari with exceeding love;
in some places, his very soul filled with love, he dances; and in some places, he melts away in devotion toward Hari.
In some places, touched by the divine form, he becomes dissolved and attains a state of insensibility;
thus, immersed in the essence of Brahman, he dwells perfectly within Nārāyaṇa.
For him there is neither hunger nor thirst, neither adornment nor grooming of the body;
neither the acquisition of garments and such, nor anything else dwells in his mind. (18)
Hari is in her eyes, Kṛṣṇa is in her mouth, and Hari alone is in her tongue;
whether externally or internally in whatever she does, Hari was her refuge.
Having been initiated at the proper time, that wise youth lived in the house of his preceptor;
his preceptor was the family priest Kāvya, who is worshipped by the Asuras.
That Kāvya Śukra had two sons who were masters of the scriptures:
the first was Ṣaṇḍa and the other was Amarka; to them the king entrusted his adopted son.
They taught him the subjects to be studied, which consist of the Asura doctrines, as well as the Sāmaveda and other such texts; he grasped what was to be grasped and nothing else. ||2||
Many divine and non-divine great vidyās were all recited; he heard everything spoken by his guru and repeated it back in due order. ||23||
He correctly grasps with devotion that [knowledge] by which liberation occurs, and he inwardly abandons any other knowledge based on false attachments. (24)
Having studied all the Vedas and various treatises,
at a certain time, the son of the Daitya [went] together with his preceptor.
Having approached his father, he prostrated himself at his feet;
the father, in turn, embraced with both arms that son of auspicious mind.
Placing him upon his lap, his father Hiraṇyakaśipu asked:
"Prahlāda, you have been residing in the house of your preceptor for a long time. (27)
"Tell me properly that excellent instruction which was learned from your guru.
Prahlāda, having bowed down, being filled with joy, spoke those words.
Having abandoned the great net of the household, the man who knows the Self should worship by means of the Self, embracing the garland of the Self which rests upon the bed of the heart.
He who is the illustrious Supreme Lord, moving through all objects of knowledge—that alone is the all-pervading, virtuous reality; any other object is devoid of purpose.
Having heard his sons' words, which were filled with a current of devotion to Viṣṇu,
the Daitya laughed and spoke to his preceptors regarding the instruction of his sons.
With a childish intellect, like a clean garment, she was placed by his side; how did this distinction enter his mind when it was created by the wing of Viṣṇu? (32)
O Venerable Ones, instruct him in such a way that his immature intellect is not shattered by the truth, so that he may never speak thus again.
Then his teachers, having brought him to their own home, questioned him with conciliatory words: "By whom was this meaning of Viṣṇu taught to you?"
This goal bestows happiness upon the faction of the Daityas; abandon it!
For how could this goal, which consists of Viṣṇu, come to you either from yourself or from another? (35)
Prahlāda, the soul of all, said: "Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the inner self of all, commands: 'Worship Nārāyaṇa always. (36)
The Guru said: "The Nārāyaṇa spoken of by you is your father;
there is no other Nārāyaṇa whatsoever. Devote yourself to him and be happy. (37)
The disciple said: "O Guru, it is true that through devotion to Nārāyaṇa, devotees indeed become equal to Nārāyaṇa; yet my father was not like this. (38)
Because he dwelt among a multitude of men, even my father was Nārāyaṇa;
however, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the lord of the imperishable, is not subject to the consumption of time.
There is a great difference between those two, like that between a moth and a sun-fly;
I falsely regard the firefly, my father, as the sun.
O Guru, I know Nārāyaṇa to be the truth that reveals the Self;
nevertheless, I regard him as my father, indeed as my father alone. (41)
"Because of your hatred for Nārāyaṇa, you do not show me much respect;
nevertheless, my teacher said, 'You must carry out your father's command.'"
"Always carry out your father's worship, service, attendance, and commands.
Having been thus instructed, Prahlāda returned home in the evening.
Embraced by his father and seated upon his lap with affection, he was asked gently: "My son, what have you studied here today?"
"Speak; having heard it, I shall become happy and learn the lore appropriate for our lineage.
Prahlāda, having bowed to his father, said: "I shall speak that which has been studied. (45)
You are indeed Nārāyaṇa; it is not false, but according to the truth, you are Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the true one served by the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. 46.
I worship Him; may you also, my father, worship Him.

[The ninefold devotion consists of: hearing of Viṣṇu, chanting His names, remembering Him, serving His feet, worshipping Him, bowing to Him, serving as His servant, being His friend, and self-surrender. ||47||
Teaching in nine ways is supreme; everything else is mere mockery.
One should practice studying in nine ways; what is the use of any other mockery? (48)
Having heard this most devoted speech, the lord of the Daityas then became enraged and said to his preceptor: "What is this that you have been taught? (49)
"O evil-minded one, for what purpose did you speak words praising Hari to my son—a deed most unbecoming of our family? (1.137.50)
O son of the preceptor, what indeed is this training in the faction of the enemy? You are a secret partisan of Viṣṇu, wearing a deceptive guise.
The time for even those who are deceitful yet called virtuous is not far off;
punishment shall fall together upon the son of the preceptor’s son. (52)
Then the teacher’s son said: "It was not taught by me in such a manner; rather, his intellect is innate—do not bring us into disrepute. (53)
Nevertheless, the lord of the Daityas said: "This has not been studied by you from a teacher;
tell me, O child, how exactly this was studied, as is fitting."
Prahlāda said: "O Lord of the Daityas, my intellect has been granted by Kṛṣṇa;
otherwise, how could it have been so, unless my body were sprinkled with even a tiny particle of the dust of Kṛṣṇa's devotees? (55)
Without association with the virtuous and service to the holy, such an intellect as this would not exist;
yet, by the grace of the God of gods, the Lord Hari, I have been instructed. (56)
No other teacher speaks for me; that very Hari is the impeller.
He exists everywhere as the hearer, the thinker, the speaker, and the seer.
"Lord Hari alone is the imperishable teacher and the master who bestows intelligence.
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu, filled with rage, spoke to his son.
