"I alone am the Lord in the world, considered the sovereign of the three realms;
worship me alone as Govinda, and abandon that enemy, Acyuta. (59)
Or else, worship the god Śaṅkara, Rudra, the Lord and Teacher of the worlds,
the presiding deity of the gods, the auspicious one who bestows all sovereignty.
Prahlāda said: "The gods have fallen into this delusion of Māyā;
even the Rākṣasas think, 'We alone are the lords.'"
Śaṅkara himself is a devotee of Viṣṇu and stands at the forefront of the Vaiṣṇavas;
how is it that this demon does not know this, and why has he fallen into such delusion?
"O Father, you do not recognize this because your mind is obscured by the pride of intoxication;
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate reality, Nārāyaṇa is supreme. (63)
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation. He is the eternal goal of the entire world, the supreme Lord.
Vāsudeva, the eternal, is the sustainer and the ordainer of the world;
he alone is the Universal Person here, and the entire universe depends upon him for its life.
He possesses a golden body and eyes resembling lotuses;
by him alone were Brahmā and Īśa created, and they abide under his command.
Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun rises;
out of fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on.
In the beginning, there was only the one divine Lord Hari, the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
neither Brahmā nor Īśāna existed, nor did the moon or the sun. (68)
Neither heaven and earth, nor the stars, nor the dwellers of the sky—only the wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. ||69||
Having abandoned that Śrī Hari, why should one worship the father Śiva,
whom the hosts of deities beginning with Brahmā, Īśa, and Śakra worship?
That which the high-souled yogis, such as Sanaka and others, meditate upon;
by even a half-glance from the side of whose eye Lakṣmī gladdens the inhabitants of heaven.
By the mere chanting of whose name Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Varuṇa, Yama, Soma, and the Lord of Wealth attain eternal liberation. (72)
To Him, the Lord of Śrī, the God of gods, the infinite Puruṣottama, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, who bestows the bliss of eternal joy; ||73||
I shall worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Hari, the Protector;
thus, with great ease, I shall attain that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable and supreme master, abiding in consciousness;
the eternal Hari, Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond the universe and yet the universe itself. (75)
Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe and the supreme refuge, should always be known;
Nārāyaṇa is the form of the highest light, whose very essence is Nārāyaṇa. ||76||
Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard, Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without. (77)
I salute the Supreme Brahman, the Truth, the Cosmic Order (Ṛta), the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, Nārāyaṇa of exalted conduct, whose very nature is the universe. ||78||
Having thus heard his son’s words, Hiraṇyakaśipu was then possessed by great anger, and the whites of his eyes became bloodshot.
Overwhelmed with rage, he cast his devoted son from his own lap onto the surface of the earth and, looking around at the Daityas, spoke thus: || 1.137.80 ||
"By my command, let them strike down Prahlāda—who stands on the wrong path and is intent on worshipping the enemy—with terrifying volleys of weapons. (8.1)
Let this lowest of men, who has abandoned his own kinsmen and friends, be put to death immediately—
he who worships the feet of Viṣṇu like a servant while being the slayer of his paternal uncle.
A limb that is diseased and beyond the scope of medical treatment must indeed be amputated;
even another person who brings about a multitude of benefits should be resorted to, like a bitter medicine or the like. (83)
It is said that Hari alone is the protector;
indeed, by his power, may I behold today itself the protection of Hari, which shall make my birth fruitful.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Death Sentence and Other Orders Motivated by Hatred, Resulting from the Manifestation of Divine Knowledge in Prahlāda, the Son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, Who Had Mastered All Sciences," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, the Rākṣasas—trident-bearing, with sharp fangs, terrifying mouths, and copper-colored beards and hair—[attacked] my devotee. || 1 ||
Uttering terrifying cries such as "Cut!
and "Pierce!", they surrounded him and struck him with spears, javelins, and pikes.
O auspicious lady, there, by virtue of his constant remembrance of Hari, Prahlāda’s body became as hard as a diamond;
indeed, the blows dealt there were rendered fruitless.
Having reached and touched that body, the great weapons of the Rākṣasas were shattered and fell upon the earth like the withered petals of a lotus.
The Daityas were not at all able to pierce even that very slight part of his body;
the warriors stood near the king of the Daityas, struck with wonder and with their faces cast down.
Against another who is devoted to the Lord—the inexpressible Brahman, the Self of all—whose mind is disciplined through great devotion, whose weapon could possibly be effective? (6)
When his efforts proved fruitless and he saw that son remained unscarred,
Hiraṇyakaśipu was then struck with the utmost astonishment.
Blinded in his heart by great sorrows and as if swooning with rage,
he devised means for his destruction through malevolent spells and acts of casting him down.
Through illusions, suppressions, fasting, and throat-binding,
Śrī Hari protected him everywhere like a mother.
Even though this was done without obstacle, the Daitya remained apprehensive:
"Will he die or will he not die? Shall I kill him, or what shall I do? (1.138.10)
Nevertheless, the enemy must be destroyed as long as one's power of intellect remains;
then he commanded the biting serpents of great venom.
"Let them devour Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the others," he said;
thus commanded, those serpents, fierce with their potent venom, then set about it.
With flaming mouths and great terror,
those whose weapons were poison devoured that mighty one, the servant of the one whose banner is Garuḍa, having bitten him.
The wind-eating serpents became fangless and rendered venomless,
their vital organs and limbs severed by Garuḍa as he was impelled by Viṣṇu.
They fled quickly from that place, no longer looking back;
vomiting blood, broken, and dead, they became nothing at all. || 15 ||
Seeing even the great serpents and his sons rendered fruitless, he,
filled with great rage, commanded the world-elephants who cannot be turned back.
Intoxicated with pride and exceedingly furious, elephants surrounded him and struck him with their massive tusks; yet he possessed a body as firm as a diamond.
Under the influence of my mercy, not even a single hair on his body was harmed;
on the contrary, the tusks of the elephants were severed at their roots and fell to the ground.
Deprived of their tusks, the elephants fled in great distress;
yet, even upon seeing such a marvel, Camatkāra did not desist.
"Oh, the illusion of Hari, O fair-browed one, causes even the lowest of the low to fall!
Having seen his son severed by the great serpents, he [fell] in rage. (1.138.20)
When the great fire was kindled, she cast her own son into it;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the village, the hamlet, and the kingdom.
Even though he was the god Agni, he did not burn that devotee who was dear to Hari reclining upon the waters;
rather, the fire remained extinguished, like the moon.
Nevertheless, the fool did not realize that his protector was present;
later, he administered a most terrible poison in his food and drink.
Even though it was placed within a collection of garments, the poison did not touch him;
by the power of Nārāyaṇa, the poison became nectar.
Then, seeing his son unharmed as before,
he caused a much larger pit to be dug there in the earth for him.
Having cast in great boulders, he filled the earth level;
thus was Prahlāda severely tormented by Nārāyaṇa in the royal palace.
Seeing him arrived there, seated upon a great lion-throne like a god and yet still alive, the Asura was overcome with fear.
"This one of mine is indeed Māraka," the king of the Daityas declared with certainty;
"O Rākṣasas, lift him up and cast him quickly into the ocean! ||28||
All of them did exactly as instructed; having previously arrived at their homes, they saw him thus on the Himalaya mountain and then cast him into a great fire.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa protected him from the cold of the snow, yet they did not allow him to reach the palace of the Daitya;
he was seen by the Rākṣasas.
There are indeed means for death, yet they do not bear fruit in this case;
what is to be done, where is one to go, so that death may no longer exist for me? (3.1)
A boon was obtained by me for my own sake; has it now borne fruit here?
Both father and son are equally praiseworthy, yet they are indeed Vaishnavas who bestow relief from suffering. (32)
"If it is destined, it shall come to pass; is this death of mine not already ordained?
Nevertheless, I shall make my resolve; for what power does even a blade of grass possess against devotion? (33)
Having reflected thus, he spoke to his son: "It was said by you before me that [Viṣṇu] is designated as 'Viṣṇu' because of his pervading all beings. (34)
Show me the direct perception of its existence everywhere;
for that God who is omnipresent is indeed the Supreme Lord. (35)
His [qualities] consist of sovereignty, power, splendor, knowledge, heroism, and strength; as well as beauty, prosperity, majesty, virtuous attributes, and noble conduct. (36)
Having seen Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, correctly from that [distance], I then thought:
"If he is superior to me, having conquered me by means of his strength and heroism. (37)
May she obtain sovereignty here, and never by any other means; for there is no one among the gods in this world who is my equal. (38)
"By the boon granted by Rudra, I am indeed unslayable and invincible.
Hearing these words of his father, Prahlāda then laughed aloud.
He related in every way the power of Hari and the Daitya,
[describing] him who is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest.
Because he moves among men and not among non-men, he is called Nārāyaṇa;
because he dwells within all beings, he is indeed Vāsudeva. (41)
Viṣṇu is the nourisher of the entire world because he enters into it;
indeed, there is nothing in this world, whether stationary or moving, that exists without him.
In the midst of all consciousness and unconsciousness, its very form exists;
its pervasion extends three-quarters in the supreme abode, while its quarter-pervasion is that of Māyā.
Thus, this Lord, who holds the discus and mace in his hands, is visible in every way to those possessed of devotion;
he is not seen by those with evil qualities such as anger, envy, and pride.
Pervading all beings—among gods, animals, humans, and even stationary things—it abides within all, whether they be small or great. (45)
Even as Prahlāda was speaking thus, at that very moment,
the left eye, lip, shoulder, and other parts of Hiraṇyakaśipu throbbed.
A crow cried out repeatedly upon the king’s flagstaff;
then, the flagpole broke and fell down of its own accord as it slipped.
His heart trembled as he recognized those ill omens,
for Dhūmraketu and Śakali were indeed seen in the path of the sky.
A black goat-cart was seen traveling toward the southern direction;
his own wife, wearing a single red garment, was seen for a moment embracing him. (49)
For a moment, he saw his own head separated from his body and held in his own hand;
then, during the day, he saw Śukra in heaven and the quarters of the sky filled with dust.
"Upon seeing him, I perceived that death would surely come from this conflict. Then he recognized him as someone whose splendor had somewhat faded and who was looking downward.
Śaṇḍa and Marka, the two sons of Śukra, said, "For the sake of consolation, O Indra among kings, do not grieve; for you alone are the conqueror of the world. (5.2)
"We two shall instruct him so that he may follow the family tradition;
having bound him with Varuṇa’s nooses, we shall keep him guarded in our own home. (53)
"When youth has reached its maturity, your intellect will become well-informed.
Having accepted these words, indeed cast away your grief. (54)
He entrusted his son to them for the study of royal duties and other sciences,
for instruction in the duties of household life, and for the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
The two sons of the Guru also instructed those worthy ones in the aforementioned duties as was appropriate,
but he did not take them into his own circle.
That by which dualities arise does not lead to liberation; having understood this, summon suitable youths at the time of the void. (57)
He taught the doctrines known as liberation, which transcend all worldly existence;
and those children, being pure of soul, received them like most delicious nectar that bestows liberation.
They respectfully accepted those pure dharmas that bestow the bliss of the Self.
To them, he said: "O pure children, Viṣṇu dwells everywhere. (59)
And he dwells especially within those children whose souls are pure;
Keśava accepts with devotion everything that is offered by children with reverence.
Among all things that can be sought, liberation is the foremost object of pursuit;
therefore, with this transient human birth, one should seek that alone. (61)
This self, indeed, having been born many times in the wombs of gods, asuras, and others,
returns again and again by way of the path of sensual enjoyment and luxury.
Liberation does not come by way of the path to liberation; it is difficult to find anywhere.
Sensual pleasure is found everywhere, for it flows from one's own nature. (63)
In that endeavor, one's own life would indeed pass away in vain;
however, the lotus feet of Śrī Hari are the cause of well-being and security. 64.
As long as the body has not perished, the wise man should accomplish his own welfare;
for a person's lifespan is ten million years, a hundred thousand years, or a hundred years.
Whether for a thousand years, a hundred years, or even twenty years,
half of that time is spent in sleep, and a tenth part in childhood play.
A tenth part is taken away by learning, a tenth part is taken away by old age, and a tenth part remains in the pursuit of sensual objects or in the acquisition of wealth. (67)
O friend, if its expenditure were for one's own sake, then nothing would have been done for the sake of liberation; in that case, nothing at all would have been accomplished. (68)
If anything whatsoever is done for the sake of liberation, then everything has been accomplished;
having reflected thus, O fools, you should always perform the means to liberation.
The Lord himself, residing within the heart of all like a pearl in a necklace, is to be realized;
yet for householders, there is attachment to women, attachment to sons, and attachment to friends. (1.138.70)
Affection for brothers, sisters, and daughters is a bond like a shackle;
having highly esteemed the objects of sexual pleasure and worldly gain, one becomes attached to this world.

Though afflicted by the threefold suffering— due to the hardships of maintaining a family, the toil of acquiring sense-objects, and the defilement of their pursuit— he indeed does not abandon his effort.
One who covets material wealth, who steals material wealth, and whose desires are unappeased perishes;
even if he possesses knowledge, he does not attain liberation but enters into death. //73//
One who has fallen into the shackles of desire is like a pet deer and is not liberated;
therefore, O fools, abandoning falsehood, worship Hari with devotion. (74)
The Lord rejoices instantly and bestows upon him a son who is his own joy,
amidst the gross, subtle, and abundant elements, as well as within the senses and the vital breaths.
Even within Māyā, whether in its modified or unmodified state, Mādhava alone is sought; indeed, he is both immanent and transcendent.
He is both the nature of the visible and the nature of the seer; he is indeed the pervaded and the pervader, possessing limbs such as feet, arms, belly, and face, all full of bliss.
Keśava, the soul of all beings including the gods and demons, dwells within the heart;
the Lord speaks within the heart: "This is the right, this is the truth, this is beneficial, this must be done. (78)
He alone is truly himself who says that what is false and deceptive must be abandoned;
he who says "no" to what is untrue and says "yes" to what is true. (79)
Abandoning the demonic nature, conduct yourselves with that spirit of friendship by which Mādhava is pleased; worship Acyuta.
Dharma and the other virtues are Hari alone; the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) are Hari;
the means of accomplishment are Hari alone; all branches of knowledge and the arts are Hari. (8.1)

The surrender of one's entire self to Viṣṇu, which results in the fruit of all that ought to be done, is declared to be the pure-minded devotion toward Hari, toward the servants and maidservants of Hari, and toward his devotees. (82)
The bathing in the dust of their feet is the great essence that bestows liberation;
this was indeed taught to me by the god Nārada while I was still in the womb. (83)
Hari and His devotees are to be served, because everything else grants further birth;
for while others bestow illusion and egoism, the virtuous grant liberation from Hari.
Having heard this, the sons of the Daityas asked him: "When did Nārada, while still in the womb, attain that inconceivable awakening by taking hold of the [right] moment? (85)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Futility of the Means Employed by Hiraṇyakaśipu to Kill Prahlāda, the Instruction Given by his Guru, and the Instruction on Daitya Children Given by Prahlāda," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Prahlāda spoke to those sons of the Daityas who were devoted to knowledge:
"While my father was performing austerities on Mount Mandara, smoke arose. (1)
Covered by anthills, bamboo, wood, and other debris, the Daityas became hopeless;
thinking that the foremost leader of the Daityas was dead, they were filled with grief.
Then, perceiving them to be powerless, the gods resolved to fight;
the Daityas, struck by the celestial armies, fled in every direction.
Abandoning their wives, sons, daughters, sisters, fathers, families, wealth, grain, and belongings, they fled.
The gods, endowed with all their might, plundered the assembly of the Daityas;
having seized the royal palace, they carried off my auspicious mother.
When Indra was leading him toward heaven, Nārada met him on the way and said to him: "Where are you taking me so quickly? (6)
"You are unworthy to take away Satī; release her, for she is indeed innocent.
Indra then said, "In her womb lies the child of a Daitya."
Therefore, she must indeed be protected until her delivery, for she is irresistible;
once her purpose is fulfilled, she should be abandoned, as I have no further need for her.
Nārada said to Indra: "That great embryo is indeed Vaiṣṇava;
he is a devotee of the gods, Viṣṇu, and the cows, and a servant of the Brāhmaṇas and Sāttvatas."
Whatever fear you have, do not doubt it; abandon it.
At that time, Indra accepted what Narada had said and left her.
Having paid his respects, the great lord Nārada also departed for heaven;
taking my mother with him, he went toward his own hermitage.
"O child, having been consoled by these words of encouragement, you must dwell here happily until your husband returns from his ascetic penance."
Having thus obtained a virtuous refuge, she dwelt there truthfully and without fear;
with supreme devotion, she constantly attended upon the sage with joy.
The compassionate sage bestowed upon her the knowledge that grants liberation;
all of that was firmly acquired by me even while remaining in the womb.
It dissolved into my mother and became firmly established within me;
I remember it all with firm impressions, exactly as it was told.
For you who delight in knowledge, O fools, there is nothing else that brings about the highest welfare, for that [knowledge] is indeed to be grasped through faith. (16)
I shall speak something of that knowledge, having extracted its essence from all sources; may it, instantly reflected in a heart as clear as a mirror, become the bestower of liberation. (17)
One should listen with a mind directed exactly as it is, so that through simplicity there may be gain for women and children; thus one should hear the essence for oneself. (18)
In accordance with past karma, the radiant and extremely subtle self enters the father's seed; thus the semen is infused into the womb.
That object composed of the elements is *vīrya* (potency), while the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
it is atomic, luminous, eternal, the knower, and essentially a mass of knowledge. || 1.139.20 ||
Then, vitality conjoined with the individual soul becomes associated with passion (rajas);
through passion, vitality, and the soul, all creation and consciousness come into being.
This body—whether it be a male, a female, or a neuter—would thus be composed of six sheaths, existing in all three ways. (22)
From the father come the sinews, bones, marrow, flesh, hair, and blood;
these are the six sheaths situated in the body, and the Self is firmly established within these six. (23)
In the gross body of a child, the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—indeed exist, as do the five objects of the senses. (24)
The gross [element] consists of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound;
it is indeed perceived respectively by the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears. (25)

The organs of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the external ones; their functions are, respectively, speaking, grasping, moving, excreting waste, and discharging urine. Furthermore, one should understand that the mind (manas), the intellect (citta), and the ego-sense (ahaṃmati) are the internal faculties. (26)

That which is called the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is considered to be the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti). Indeed, its state of equilibrium, endowed with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, is the cause;
that very same nature, when in a state of disequilibrium, is the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the embodiment of the principles (tattva). ||27||
Those transformations of *māyā* which are subject to destruction are considered such;
the Self (*ātman*), however, is non-illusory and pure, and its destruction never occurs. (28)
The body, however, is born later; it grows through abundant food, undergoes transformation, wanes, perishes, and is false. (29)
And the Self exists there everywhere; therefore, it truly is.
The body and so forth are indeed insentient, whereas the Self is purely conscious. 1.139.30
The body and so forth are indeed of the nature of suffering, whereas the Self is always composed of bliss; He is called Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda), neither a Daitya nor a Dānava.
The self is neither a god nor an asura; it is neither female nor male;
it is neither neuter, nor possessed of passion, nor devoid of hatred—it is indeed pure. (32)
But the ignorant person, being devoid of sublation, indeed possesses at times a sattvic disposition, at times a rajasic disposition, and at times a tamasic disposition.
I consider *sattva* to be the producer of happiness, while *rajas* would be the producer of passion;
*tamas* is declared to be the producer of affliction. Therefore, one should cultivate the quality of *sattva*. ||34||
Even the acquisition of a virtuous nature is considered beneficial for oneself;
however, if it is harmful, even that is abandoned, provided it grants liberation. (35)
When Nārāyaṇa is established within one's own self, that sattvic intellect will indeed always be conducive to gain and even bestow liberation.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep occur in the body and so forth, never in the Self; grossness, subtlety, and causality reside in the body and so forth, never in the Self. (37)
Sin and merit, both together, as well as birth, growth, and death, and the state of being a god, a demon, or a human—all these reside in the body and so forth, never in the Self. (38)
What is called "home" is not truly a home; it is said that the body is the home.
Since that [body] is momentary and fragile, one should thereby strive for liberation. ||39||
For the Self is indeed unattached everywhere; yet if it were to become attached to people, attachment toward a pure lineage or caste would give rise to pride. (1.139.40)
Therefore, hatred would arise toward that which is contrary to those respective [views] and possesses the true meaning;
and if the self is enveloped by the egoism of "I am a Daitya," [then aversion follows].
At that time, there will certainly be hatred toward the god Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, due to that hatred for Nārāyaṇa, there will be a falling away from the path to liberation.

Therefore, we are pure as long as we are not subject to the fragmentation of the intellect; as long as words that follow our own positions have been acquired, one may thereby establish liberation. (43)
One should seek the twenty-fifth principle among the twenty-four principles;
having sought one's own self, one should then offer it into the twenty-sixth.
This saṃsāra, consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā), persists only so long as the thorough discrimination between the Self and that which is not the Self has not been made here. (45)
Having understood the network of principles—whether peaceful, terrible, or deluded—and having fully realized that supreme Self which is higher than the highest, one should take refuge in it. 46.
Neither mother, nor father, nor son, nor sister, nor kinsmen shall be companions in the next world; only Hari shall be the giver of assistance. (47)
And although it exists everywhere within all beings, that [Self] is not perceived by the embodied soul without the perfection of the means. 48.
The means for attaining the Lord are as follows: service to the guru, as well as loving devotion, constant attendance, and the offering of all that one has obtained. ||49||
Association with virtuous men and women, the supreme worship of Viṣṇu,
listening to His stories, chanting His names, and the description of His qualities.
Meditation upon His form, intense vision, remembrance, and so forth;
the perception of Him in all beings, and the worship of Him by devotees—[these constitute the path]. (51)
Everything is surrendered there, and all delight is also found therein;
all activities consist of that alone, and therefore nothing other than that is perceived.
Whether in meditation, in concentration, or even in meditative absorption, he is absorbed in that;
likewise, whether awake, dreaming, or even in deep sleep, he is absorbed in that. (53)
Whether in active engagement or in withdrawal, in all states he is absorbed in that—whether laughing, weeping, singing, dancing, crying out, or sleeping. (54)
Whether it be anointing with unguents, rolling on the ground, drinking, eating, sexual union, walking, sitting, seeking, or even seeing, touching, or hearing [the Lord]. (55)
Sneezing, reflection, discernment, as well as sitting, pondering, and absorption in that [state], accompanied by joy, horripilation, tears, and a faltering voice. (56)
Then Hari may indeed be perceived here through the yoga of devotion;
for that purpose, one must certainly engage in reflection after hearing His stories. 57.
By contemplating that form, one's impurity is washed away;
thus, with a stainless soul, one is purified in every way, both within oneself and elsewhere.
One should behold Nārāyaṇa and indeed worship that Imperishable One;
the wise person should attain the eternal reality and abandon whatever is impermanent. (59)
By means of a steadfast self, one must indeed attain the steadfast Hari;
for He is everywhere the nourisher, the giver of happiness, and likewise the giver of liberation.
Excessive pleasure should be abandoned, and that which is perishable should certainly be abandoned;
that which is impure should always be abandoned, while that which is free from such defects should be accepted. (61)
That [liberation] is obtained from Nārāyaṇa alone and never from anyone else;
therefore, Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon and he alone is to be worshipped within one's own self. 62.
The entire world, acquired through the defects of what is seen and what is heard, is composed of illusion;
that which is empty of it is the abode of bliss, and therefore one becomes Nārāyaṇa.
O children, through devotion to Him, eternal bliss must be attained by us,
wherein there is no impermanent happiness found in sons, wives, houses, and the like.

Whether it be wealth, sovereignty, ministers, elephants, horses, people, and so forth, or a palace, a circle of friends, or even that which is trifling yet considered eternal—[in all these, one should remain detached]. (65)
In an instant, that which appears auspicious may perish along with the body;
in a moment it yields misfortune, appearing as prosperity, and thus it cuts away all suffering.
What indeed is the eternal self-interest of the self here? Let that be examined: [is it] in the body, in the collection of bodily parts, or even in whatever object is dear? (67)
That [state] belongs to Viṣṇu because it is his abode; for Hari is the beloved self of all.
Wherever a living being goes—whether a Daitya, a Yakṣa, or an Asura—[he attains that state].
Whether a god, a human, a gandharva, or even a rākṣasa, one who worships the Lord Nārāyaṇa shall possess well-being; there is no [well-being] apart from Him.

Neither vows, charity, nor the practice of austerities; neither great learning, nor physical beauty, nor ritual worship, nor purity, nor even the pursuit of noble goals, serve to please Mukunda. (1.139.70)
The cause is stainless devotion, which shines within a soul moistened by contemplation;
may children thus cultivate such supreme devotion toward Hari. (71)
By this devotion which has always been practiced by me, I behold Keśava—
the sages, the ancestors, the gods, the ascetics, and likewise human beings.
The Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Daityas, Yakṣas, and those who are Kimpuruṣas;
as well as the Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and Siddha-puruṣas. ||73||
The Vidyādharas, Piśācas, or whatever other Bhūtas, Pretas, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vaināyakas, and Bhairavas [there may be]. ||74||
Vetālas, Gaṇas, the followers of Yama, Nāgas, reptiles, birds, wild animals, aquatic creatures, land-dwellers, and those who take refuge in the wind; ||75||
And those planets situated in the atmosphere, both stationary and moving;
children, the elderly, women, Śūdras, those of mixed castes, and those of sinful birth. ||76||
Having abandoned evil, they have attained liberation by taking refuge in the glorious Nārāyaṇa;
therefore, we too [should do so] here in this human birth which is so difficult to obtain. (77)
"Lord Hari alone is to be worshipped directly; everything else is a mere mockery"—this instruction was received by me from Nārada while I was still in the womb. (78)
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Kamalā; O Lord of Pārvatī, O Lord of Mukta, O Lord of Prabheśa—salutations to you! ||79||
"Acting thus, I conduct myself here; you all should do exactly so.
Having heard this, all the boys grasped it precisely as it was; yet in the schoolroom, they did not grasp even a tiny bit of what they were taught by their teacher. (1.139.80)

Then the teacher’s son, distressed and terrified, reported everything to the king: "The children have indeed fallen onto a wrong path. Upon hearing this, he trembled with intense rage at what his own sons had done.
The Daitya father set his mind upon bringing about the death of his son;
having summoned Prahlāda, he reviled him with harsh words.
Looking askance with an evil eye out of anger, he spoke to his son, a devotee of the Lord worthy of upholding the lineage, who was otherwise peaceful. (83)
O you of lowest intellect, who have taken refuge in the distinctions of various sciences, you do not yourself practice the training, yet you lead others onto the wrong path. (84)
O evil-minded one, as if fearless, you do not heed my command, the ruler of the worlds; I shall send you to the abode of Yama.
"O lowest of men, disregarding my words, upon whose strength do you rely that you remain so arrogant before the king of the fourteen worlds? (86)
Having heard that, Prahlāda said: "Whatever power your father possesses, I also possess that same power—by which power the world is made strong. (87)
That power by which Brahmā, Rudra, and all others shine as kings of kings through their own vigor, splendor, and strength—that power belongs eternally to us both. (88)
Abandoning the state of hatred, O father, place that meditation within your mind;
for he who contemplates it with a humble disposition considers it as worthy of worship. 89.
One should uplift oneself by that much alone, and never otherwise;
for even conquerors of the quarters are overcome by delusion, anger, and the swift force of hunger.
"O Father, do not go into their power, for they have already fallen under its sway;
the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Upholder of the Earth, must not thus cast himself down. (91)
With devotion, you should cause him to ascend to the supreme abode, the realm of Hari;
O father, why do you instead accumulate sin, which brings about total destruction? 92.
Having heard this spoken by his own son, Hiraṇyakaśipu, at that time,
being on the verge of death and unable to endure the fire of unbearable agony, [acted].
He said to his son: "Your death has clearly arrived here;
you boast in the wrong place, O wicked one! Where is your Supreme Lord? (94)
If there is no other lord besides me, then he would protect you;
and if he exists everywhere, he must be omnipresent. (95)
"Show that Viṣṇu to the pillar; otherwise, you deserve death. Having spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas suddenly seized his sword.
As he proceeded to kill his son, the pillar split in two;
a terrifying sound arose from the pillar, pervading the sky in all directions.
With that great sound, which shattered the ears of the Daityas and seemed to split the very interior of the sky with its roar of universal destruction, [the world was filled]. 98.
Then all the Daityas fell to the ground and thought, "The three worlds are destroyed, or else the dissolution has come upon us. (99)
Then, from the pillar, the immensely powerful Mahāgiri emerged,
assuming the form of a man-lion (Nṛsiṃha), and let out terrible roars.
Blazing with the fury of the radiance of many millions of suns and fires,
he had the appearance of a lion in his face, while his body was human in form.

The omnipresent Lord had a face made terrifying by his fangs, with the tip of his tongue quivering in its length; the ends of his hair were wreathed in flames, and his eyes were like glowing, heated brands.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and adorned with celestial ornaments,
the Man-Lion stood there to destroy the Daityas and Dānavas.
Upon seeing that form never seen before, the great Asura Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Daitya, fell with his limbs trembling, and others swooned.
Then Prahlāda, beholding Hari who resembled a man-lion,
paid homage to Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, with shouts of victory.
At that time, the devotee beheld the worlds within the Man-Lion;
listen, O Lakṣmī, for I shall describe exactly what was shown.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Time of Prahlāda’s Receiving Instruction from Nārada while in the Womb, the Dispute with Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Striking with the Sword as a Child’s Lesson, and the Manifestation of Nṛsiṃha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Prahlāda and the other Daityas could not discern at all what that object was;
from where or by whom did this great sound arise, which caused the world to shatter?
It was seen that the sound had a source, yet neither its form nor its originator could be perceived; having heard that unprecedented roar, the gods were not terrified.
Making true that which was spoken by Prahlāda and declared by Brahmā, this Hari Kṛṣṇa became Nṛhari (the Man-Lion). || 3 ||
Immediately from his body there issued forth a very great splendor that pervaded everything as far as the world of Brahmā;
and gradually that splendor dissolved within the assembly hall.
Then, within that pillar, he beheld a being of great ferocity;
"This is neither a deer nor a human—what is this, resembling a lion among men? (5)
As soon as the Daityas and the lord of the Daityas clearly beheld Nṛhari—
terrifying, with a lolling tongue and wide, blood-red eyes— [they were struck with fear].
His face flashes like the sun, his mouth yawns like that of a lion,
and his filaments are golden lightning-vines shimmering with great splendor.
With formidable fangs and the fierce fire of his wrath manifest in his furrowed brows,
with ears stiffly erect and a wide-gaping mouth and nose, he was endowed with every artistic perfection.
With hair like the rays of the moon and great, extremely sharp claws as weapons,
that being grew large-bodied and possessed of great strength.
That divine palace, equal to Mount Mandara,
vanished into the divine Nārāyaṇa, the lion among men, whose form was unprecedentedly fashioned.
Prahlāda indeed beheld within his limbs the worlds,
the oceans, the continents, as well as the gods, gandharvas, and humans.
He indeed beheld thousands of egg-born beings upon the tip of his mane,
and he saw the abodes of the sun, the moon, and other luminaries within his eyes.
In his two ears are the twin gods Aśvins, as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions;
on his forehead are Brahmā and Rudra, and in his nose are the sky and the wind.
He placed Indra and Agni at the corners of his mouth, Sarasvatī upon his tongue, and lions, tigers, śarabhas, and great serpents upon his fangs. (14)
He beheld Mount Meru upon the throat of the Supreme Self, the Himalayas and other mountains upon His shoulders, and gods, animals, and humans upon His arms.
He saw the intermediate space in his navel and the earth in his feet;
all medicinal herbs in his body hairs and trees in the rows of his nails.
In his exhalation, he beheld the four Vedas with their limbs and sub-limbs,
as well as the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and Maruts.
And [he saw] the Apsarases, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as the worlds of the Āpālās, together with their furnishings and inhabitants.
Then Prahlāda beheld him upon his limbs; he saw that gentle one, whose chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and who was adorned with a forest garland.
Having beheld the meaning of all the Upaniṣads as embodied in the conch, discus, mace, sword, Śārṅga bow, and other weapons, he prostrated himself like a staff.
With his limbs drenched by tears of joy, he stood at the side in meditation;
meanwhile, Hiraṇyakaśipu was brought under the power of death by his own rage.
"Who indeed is this slayer of mine? I shall kill him and conquer him!
Raising his sword to fight, he then rushed toward that Man-lion.
All the gods, sages, and living beings born from the creation of Brahmā came to witness that battle of Śrī Hari. ||23||
Then all the hosts of Daityas, possessed of great strength and immense speed, with their weapons ready, struck Hari; they fell into the fire like moths.
By the fire arising from the mane of Nṛhari, all the thousands of weapons and the Dānavas themselves were completely reduced to ashes in an instant. (25)
Furthermore, other rākṣasas, daityas, dānavas,
and asuras who fell upon him to engage in battle— Hari struck them down in two ways.
Keśava destroyed some with his fierce fangs, some with his extremely sharp claws, and others with his most terrible weapons. ||97||
Having left Prahlāda along with his followers, and after the host of Rākṣasas had been reduced to ashes and the Daitya army destroyed, he resembled the crest of the fire of cosmic destruction.
As soon as Hiraṇyakaśipu raised his sword with the intent to slay the Man-lion, the Lord seized him.
Severing the sword, the Lord of Gods released that enemy;
meanwhile, the Lord of Daityas took up his mace and performed circular maneuvers.
Even as the mace was brought down,
Hari seized a great shield and sword from within it and indeed rushed toward the Daitya in a circular motion.
And he led him to the door of the house, where, having leaped into the midst, the demon—displaying great strength—assailed him, throwing his hands and other limbs about. ||3||
Then the Lord of the Gods, seizing the Asura with one hand as he fell repeatedly to the ground, cast him down.
Having brought him to the brink of death with blows from his feet and placing him upon his lap,
he tore him apart with sharp, dense claws that resembled thunderbolts.
The sin committed by reviling Viṣṇu, as well as that born of enmity toward a Vaiṣṇava, was then reduced to ashes merely by the touch of Nṛhari. (35)
That Great Lion tore through the mass of bones in the chest of the lord of the Daityas,
splitting his body into a hundred pieces with his sharp claws.
Having pulled out his long intestines and hung them around his neck,
that lordly king of the Daityas, being pure in soul, beheld the face of Hari directly before him.
Having attained his goal, he abandoned his life-breaths with death already within the grasp of Hari;
for him there was no death in the sky nor on the earth, neither within nor without, nor by any creatures born of creation. (38)
Hari himself could not make it real with either dry or moist elements;
therefore, assuming a form that was not yet created and establishing the space as his abode, he [proceeded]. 39.
Placing him on his lap in the evening, he struck him with his claws in the middle of the doorway;
for that which Hari knows how to do, no one else knows how to do in such a manner.
Then, with weapons in hand and raising their arms, the Daityas surrounded Nṛhari on all sides to slay him, who had become like a *kiṃśuka* tree due to the blood of the lord of the Daityas. ||41||
Then he rushed toward them and struck them with his heels, claws, and the tips of his forearms;
and he let out a roar that split the very shells of the cosmic eggs.
Pervaded by loud laughter in the world of Brahmā and throughout the celestial abodes,
clouds fell from the sky and the planets trembled from their positions on the firmament.
The oceans were agitated and the elephants of the quarters cried out;
the sky seemed to whirl, the celestial chariots became motionless, and the earth trembled. (44)
The mountains rose up, the sky and the quarters did not shine;
and then, in that palace which was empty of Daityas but rich with devotees, [they beheld] Nṛhari.
Filled with great joy, the goddesses indeed rained down flowers;
at that time, the celestial sages and seers, stationed in divine chariots, [honored] Hari.
And they beheld musical instruments such as kettledrums and the like;
then the Apsarases played them with great affection and likewise danced.
The Gandharvas performed songs, the celestial women sang auspicious hymns, and the inhabitants of the cosmic egg, having arrived there, praised Nṛhari. 48.
Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Girīśa, the Pitṛs, Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and Cāraṇas;
the Prajāpatis, Manus, Vidyādharas, and Mahoragas. ||49||
Yakṣas, kiṃnaras, vetālas, hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, kimpuruṣas, sādhyadevas, and the Viśvedevas who perform sacrifices; ||1.140.50||
The earthly gods (bhūdevas), his attendants (pārṣadas)—Nanda, Sunanda, Kumuda, and others—praised that Narasiṃha, whose gaze was terrifying to behold. ||5 1 ||
Homage to you who are the imperishable one whose form transcends syllables and who dwells within them;
homage to you who are worshipped by the liberated, and homage to you whose self is the cosmic manifestation.
Salutations to you who are the form of primordial nature, to you who are the Pradhāna-Puruṣa;
salutations to you whose very essence is Mahākāla, to you whose form is the Infinite (Bhūman). ||23||
Salutations to you whose essential nature is inconceivable, who possess infinite forms, who bring destruction to those devoid of devotion, and who provide protection to your devotees. ||54||
Salutations likewise to you, the destroyer of the Daityas who grants boons in accordance with [desire], the soul of all, Karāla, and Vikarāla. 55.
Salutations again and again to you, the giver of sacrificial portions and the protector;
salutations again and again to that one who awakens the gods within the heart and is their savior. 56.
Salutations to you who have set out upon the path of austerity, who are accessible to the sages;
salutations to you who bestow faith and satisfaction here, and who grant [the fruits] in the world beyond. ||57||

Salutations again and again to you, whose soul is dharma, who have expanded the path of yoga, who are the abode of spiritual powers and prosperity, and who are preeminent through the strength of austerity. ||58||
Salutations to the praise and the object of praise, to the knowledge and the auspicious sovereign;
repeated salutations to the bestower of jewels, to justice, and to the upholder of ethics. ||59||
Salutations to the protector of humanity, the bestower of the status of Prajāpati, whose very self is the play and song of actors, dancers, and singers.

Salutations to You, the bestower of the state of being a vehicle; to You, the giver of service and honor; to You, the one who assigns tasks as laborers; salutations to You, the Lord of the Universe. ||61||
Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, to Kṛṣṇa, to Śrī Hari, the protector of the Vaiṣṇavas and the wearer of many forms.
Salutations to Hari, who is eternally of a peaceful nature yet now appears terrifying, whose true form is never forgotten, and who is wondrous.
Thus they praised from the sky, yet none came near him;
for who, being alive, would fall into the mouth of fierce Death, save for one seeking glory? (64)
Fearing him, they sought to propitiate the blazing, all-facing Goddess, the sovereign Mistress and the nourisher of the worlds. 65.
Having meditated upon the auspicious Nārāyaṇī—the golden-hued, tawny one who destroys all calamities, whose limbs are eternally and irreproachably beautiful—[one attains the goal]. (66)
While reciting the Śrīsūkta, they indeed paid homage to the Supreme Goddess;
and as she was being meditated upon, that goddess then manifested right there.
Four-armed and large-eyed, she is adorned with all ornaments and the like;
she is clothed in fine silk garments and is auspiciously graced with the Kaustubha gem and flower garlands.
Then, seeing me, the wife of the God of gods and the mother of the worlds, the deities spoke with palms joined in reverence: "Make Śrī Hari well-pleased."
Having been addressed thus, Lakṣmī suddenly prostrated herself from afar before her beloved husband Hari, and having paid homage, she said to him, "Be gracious."
Nevertheless, the anger of that glorious Hari did not subside even slightly;
because she had never been seen before, she did not approach his presence.
Then they sent their devotee, the child Prahlāda, who is composed of Brahman;
he went quickly and then fell at his feet.
Seeing that child who was to be protected, the compassionate Śrī Hari then bowed down like a staff before the Lord, smiling with palms joined in reverence.
Raising him up, he placed his hand of reassurance upon his head again and again;
he embraced him, holding him to his heart, and pressed his own feet against his chest.
Meanwhile, Śrī also went to the Lord of Gods and stood there after bowing;
then the ocean of compassion took the Goddess upon his lap and embraced her.
Then Mahāhari gazed upon them with a look moistened by the nectar of compassion;
meanwhile, they were loudly praising him and bowing down, crying out, "Victory! Victory! (76).
Thus, for those who were satisfied with what they had seen, there arose a joyful agitation;
then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with rapture, [rejoiced]. (77)
Having bowed to the Lord, the Master of the World, they spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Lord of the World, we are not able to behold that most wonderful splendor of yours. (78)
We are not even able to behold your exceedingly fierce and new form;
O Lord, how could we possibly remain in your presence? (79)
Though entreated by the gods, that exceedingly terrifying and fierce splendor did not subside; and Prahlāda [beheld] that form of the Lord.
Having meditated upon Nṛsiṃha in his heart, he, with a concentrated mind, praised Hari:
"Obeisance to the God of gods, whose form is dissolved in pure being. (8.1)

Salutations to Him who possesses that form from which even Brahmā and the other gods are struck with fear, and who is endowed with a noble lineage, physical beauty, asceticism, sacred learning, strength, and other such qualities. (82)
Homage again and again to you, who are satisfied by prosperity and eloquence;
even a Brahmin who is averse to your feet, though endowed with restraints and observances, [is not favored]. (83)
Salutations to you who eat even the smallest portion; salutations again and again to you who are satisfied with what is humble and devoid of honor, yet gladdened by devotion. ||84||
Salutations to you, Hari, who bestows the happiness of those who rely on the path of devotion;
salutations again to the giver of protection, sovereign power, prosperity, and true bliss. ||85||
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, desiring the vision of peace, praise you, the Supreme Self whose form is peace; therefore, act accordingly.
O Lord of Gods, I do not fear the cruel form of Nṛsiṃha;
I fear desire, anger, and the like—therefore, grant me protection from them. (87)
That protection from the Asuras was indeed performed for the sake of protecting the body;
that is not my true protection. Therefore, grant me my protection. (88)
O Lord of the Universe, since one is indeed bound by the unborn nature of afflictions, karma, and its maturation, grant protection; for that alone would be true protection. (89)
The desires for sons, wife, wealth, power, and the like are never fulfilled, O Lord of Heaven; protect me from them.
The splendors of the lord of the Daityas were seen by me, yet they do not protect;
the sovereign powers were seen by me, yet indeed these do not preserve at all.
Moreover, even the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) of the gods do not provide protection;
you, however, become manifold in form for the sake of protecting your devotees. (92)
O Soul of the Universe, you uplift all; likewise, grant me deliverance.
For sovereignty is said to be a bondage, a great evil, and the most wretched of sins. (93)

Whatever obstacle arises in serving the virtuous due to defects such as pride and the like, or when, out of wretchedness, they resort to asceticism while still afflicted by desires—[all these are obstacles]. (94)
The sin lies in forgetting you after having obtained enjoyments;
therefore, [one should not be attached] to wife, children, wealth, and so forth, which are merely the presiding deities of those things. (95)
O Lord, grant me yoga; grant it at Your lotus feet.
Grant me yoga among the servants of Your servants. 96.
These gods desire to behold your gentle form during the day;
therefore, O Mādhava, show us your gentle and bliss-bestowing form.
Thus entreated, the Blessed One withdrew that most terrifying energy,
which had been filled with wrath, and became pleasant to behold.
Resembling ten million autumnal moons, with eyes like white lotuses, he possesses a mass of manes composed of nectar and a radiance like ten million flashes of lightning. ||99||
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, rings, and other ornaments made of the seven precious gems,
he shone with his two uplifted arms grasping the conch and the discus.
He is beautifully adorned with his two hands granting boons and fearlessness, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and he is embellished with a forest garland. 101.
At that time, the Man-lion (Nṛkesarin) shone, adorned with earrings, necklaces, girdles, jewels, and gold, and was joined by Śrī, who stood upon his left side.
Upon seeing that Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha, the gods along with the great sages sprinkled him with tears of joy and offered continuous salutations.
They offered divine flowers and other articles of worship to the Lord of the Self;
having consecrated the Eternal One with jeweled jars filled with nectar, they performed the rite.
Having worshipped Janārdana with garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, delightful incenses, and divine offerings and lamps.
They praised him with divine and excellent hymns and bowed down again and again; having bestowed his desired blessings upon all who had fallen at his feet, he [departed].
He made Prahlāda the imperishable king of all the Daityas;
then the Lord, being pleased, again urged him to request a boon.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Clear Manifestation of Nṛsiṃha, the Pervasion of His Splendor, the Tearing Apart of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Hymns Offered by the Gods and Others, the Prayer of Prahlāda, the Gentle Appearance, and the Hymn of Lakṣmī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, that Lord Nṛsiṃha, indeed for the purpose of testing his devotee and to forcibly grant boons to his own devotee, spoke thus.
"Accept the sovereignty over the earth as far as the oceans and be happy;
accept the earth consisting of the seven continents and be happy. (2)
O best among devotees, accept sovereignty over the seven netherworlds,
or likewise rule a kingdom consisting of the seven heavens and the station of Dhruva.
Accept this new kingdom and the entire universe, O beloved;
whatever you desire, O devotee, I shall grant that happiness to you.
Vehicles, women, female and male servants, elephants, horses, divine celestial chariots, and the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 5 ||
The station of piercing, the station of Śiva, the station of Viṣṇu, and the station of Virāṭ—I shall grant you a truly new one; take it if it pleases you.
Indeed, there is not even the slightest calculation of the cosmic eggs before me;
they exist in my teaching as truly innumerable.
The worlds, the guardians of the worlds, as well as the protectors of the cosmic egg,
and indeed the countless Brahmās, Viṣṇus, and Maheśas, are all under my control.
Likewise, I offer you this independent abode—whether it be that of Īśa, Vairāja, or Vaiṣṇava; O sir, take whichever you desire.
Thus, even while wandering about, he remained free from desire for worldly objects;
he never begged Janārdana for anything other than the feet of Hari.
"Whatever you wish to give, O Govinda, let that remain yours alone; I have no desire for it.
I am not one who solicits for his own destruction, nor do I desire what is already lost and base. (1.1)
This [Self] is indestructible and eternal; how could I seek that which ends in destruction?
That entire kingdom is artificial; indeed, the uncreated is never attained through the created.
One who has not acted is never released by means of performed action;
for eternal liberation is obtained through the self alone by taking refuge. 13.
In this context, it refers either to Prakṛti-Puruṣa or Pradhāna-Puruṣa,
or likewise to Vairāja, Mahāviṣṇu, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā.
The worlds, kingdoms, powers, and prosperous abodes of Rudra, the world-protectors, the gods, and likewise the hooded serpents [were attained]. 15.
All those that are called "natural" (prākṛta) consist of rajas and tamas; even those that are sāttvika are said to be secondary, for they are indeed hells.
Except for the supreme abode, the Imperishable, those material realms are indeed hells;
I have no desire for any place whatsoever there, save for the station of Hari.
Therefore, O Lord, always grant me Your lotus feet within my heart;
grant me constant service to You, as well as service to Your devotees. (18)
Always grant me delight in the virtuous; grant me a dwelling in Your abode;
grant me love for You as its object, and always grant me single-minded devotion to You alone. 19.
Grant me that supreme, eternal bliss produced by my own self within you alone;
I do not desire any other bliss here or hereafter, for it is impermanent and subject to decay.

Whenever, wherever, for whomsoever, from whatever cause, for whatever purpose, by whatever means, or toward whomever I may act—whatever that may be—it is truly yours alone, for it is for your sake. (21)
May everything related to you be offered to Kṛṣṇa by me forever; may my body, senses, mind, intellect, and vital breaths never be satisfied [with anything else]. 22.
May there be eternal satisfaction in You; O Lord, grant that to me, I choose it. Bestow upon me a constant delight in You, and tear apart everything else other than You. 23.
"Grant me liberation; grant me service to the virtuous, O bestower of refuge!
Having thus entreated him, Prahlāda, the foremost among the wise, fell silent. (24)
The Blessed One said: "I give that food to him who does not desire it;
I do not give it to him who desires it—such is my way of turning. (25)
"By my command, accept this kingdom which belonged to your father;
by my direction, you shall not undergo any bondage therein. (26)
Without offering it to me, one must never consume even a real object;
always remember me during action, whether in the body or in the mind.
"You are a child, yet you possess the wisdom of the aged; you are devoted like one who is eternally liberated. Therefore, indeed, accept this kingdom comprising the seven netherworlds."
I do not truly accept that person who worships me with ulterior motives; however, the devotee who worships me without such motives attains the highest honor in my presence.

I am the master; seeing a devotee who is free from desire, yet seeing another devotee who possesses desire, I go far away and certainly not near him; however, toward one who is desireless, I approach in every way.
Therefore, enjoy that sovereignty over the Daityas for the duration of a Manvantara, while listening to and narrating my stories which bestow liberation. (31)
Entrusting all actions to me, rule the kingdom free from thorns;
indeed, by constantly contemplating me, practice the state of actionlessness itself.
Exhaust what has already been done by means of enjoyment, and whatever is new, exhaust that by means of dedication alone; thus bring about a future in which there is nothing to be enjoyed.
"When the body dissolves in due time, you shall attain me with immediate glory.
Prahlāda said, "O Lord of Gods, grant me this boon: the purification of my father. (34)
That compassionate one committed an offense against you by means of his censure;
indeed, he has also committed an offense against me, who am your devotee. (35)
"May he be instantly purified from this sin by taking refuge in Your grace;
I choose nothing else, O Lord—salutations be unto You! (36)
Hari said: "Twenty-one of your ancestors have been delivered by you, the foremost of devotees; what further praise is there for this? (37)
Wherever there are virtuous people who are tranquil and possess equal vision, that land—though its inhabitants may follow the customs of barbarians—is truly inhabited by humans. (38)
They are purified here through the yoga of devotion to one such as you; of this there is no doubt.
Perform the funeral rites for your father, and he shall go to his rightful destination.
Furthermore, O sinless one, in the third birth of mine as Kṛṣṇa, when Rāma is born in the world of truth, there shall be a Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa.
The asura Śiśupāla will become [my manifestation]; from that, he shall attain liberation.
Those two who were my attendants Prahlāda, Jaya, and Vijaya—[they too shall be so] (41).
Due to an offense against Sanaka and the others, two brothers were born:
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger brother after him.
Those very two shall become Rāvaṇa, the elder, and his younger brother Kumbhakarṇa;
those same two shall also become Dantavakra and Śiśupāla.
Then, liberated from that curse, those two shall attain the side of my attendants through their devotion to me, which consists of the narrative of my births.
The worlds shall sing of your deeds and thereby attain liberation;
and through devotion to you, the steadfastness of devotees in their devotion shall increase. (45)
Thus pleased, the Lord of Lakṣmī granted him his desired boons;
thereafter, the Lord of All, who is affectionate toward His devotees, [departed] together with the hosts of gods.
Having consoled his devoted devotee Prahlāda and having had him consecrated by the foremost of the gods, he made Prahlāda the imperishable king of all the Daityas.
Having bestowed unfailing devotion in the form of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya), Hari, the man-lion, was praised by the hosts of gods. 48.
Scattered by showers of flowers, he went to the forest of lions;
there, he engaged in battle with Śambhu, who had assumed the form of a śarabha. 49.
Having abandoned one another, the lion and the Narasimha rock became invisible; Śambhu, however, remained as the Lord of the Śarabha.
And they shall both endure for as long as creation itself shall persist;
thereafter, all the hosts of gods returned each to their own respective abodes. ||51||
Furthermore, with delighted minds, they partook of their sacrificial portions;
meanwhile, Prahlāda ruled the kingdom according to the Vaiṣṇava dharma.
Having worshipped Hari through many sacrifices, gifts, and other rites,
he will thereafter go to the eternal abode of Hari, which is accessible only to yogis.
Those people who hear this account of Prahlāda’s life shall all be liberated from sin and go to the abode of Śrī Hari. (54)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described to you the majesty of Hari as Nṛsiṃha;
his descendants, who have lion-like heads, dwell in the Raivata forest.
Alternatively, O beloved, I shall describe to you the form of Vāmana; listen.
On the divine mountain Raivata, Hari himself came as Vāmana.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Granting of Boons to Prahlāda by Nṛhari, His Consecration in the Kingdom of His Father, and the Disappearance of Nṛsiṃha in the Forest," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved, I shall relate to you clearly and exactly as it happened everything for which the form of Śrī Hari as Vāmana appeared.
In the western region of Saurāṣṭra is the great mountain Raivata,
where hosts of gods dwell and hundreds of thousands of Siddhas reside.
The yoginīs also dwell constantly at the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Prahlāda had a son known as Virocana. || 3 ||
His son was the mighty-armed and powerful King Bali;
by him many excellent sacrifices were performed upon various lands.
A single sacrifice was performed there on the plateau of the Raivata mountain,
where the Lord Vāmana himself came and requested [the earth] from Bali.
O Mahālakṣmī, I shall relate that supreme, divine, purifying, and liberation-bestowing discourse; for there is no satiety in the nectar of such stories.
Where there is the Dāmodara Tīrtha as well as the Nārāyaṇa-hrada, what is the use of many other holy places? By bathing in those two, one is fully liberated.
To the north of Siṃhāraṇya, at the site of Vyāghrāraṇya,
near Somanātha, stands the great mountain Udayānta.
On the very side of that mountain which is called Kṛtasmara, and which has been turned to ash by the submarine fire (Vāḍavānala), there is known the mountain named Revatā;
this is a fragment of the Kaustubha jewel of Śrī Hari that has attained a massive form.
The Manu named Raivata resides there as the inner self (adhyātma);
this very divine Mount Raivataka is situated within the heart of Kṛṣṇa,
like a pair of golden bells upon the neck of a great elephant.
Likewise, on the evening of the full moon, the moon and the sun both rest upon it;
its height reaches as far as heaven, while its base is situated within the atmosphere.
The perfected ones (siddhas), such as Dattātreya and others, indeed dwell upon its peak;
all the deities dwell within the hollows of its peaks.
On the slopes of the mountain dwell the venerable Arhat Nātha, Gautama, and others—those illustrious sages who are truly perfected yogins. (13)
On the broad slopes of the mountain dwell the Gandharvas, as well as the Kinnaras, the gentle Vidyādharas, and the Kiṃpuruṣas. (14)
On the knee-region of the mountain dwell the Yoginīs, beloved of Śaṅkara,
as well as the goddesses, the Kṛttikās, the Ābhīrīs, and the virtuous women.
On the lower part of the mountain are indeed herds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu),
as well as gods and divine elephants, white and possessing four excellent tusks.
Lions, tigers, and divine beings who are the kinsmen of Narasiṃha dwell there, moving through the sky, celestial and radiant as the sun. (17)
At the site of Raivata’s feet dwell the auspicious cowherd girls, beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
though they are divine, they indeed wander about in human form.
The great cave of Mucukunda, which extends into the netherworld (pātāla),
contains the beautiful mansion of Rādhā, situated upon the golden Rakṣā river.
Indeed, the capital city of kings such as Rukmāṅgada is situated there,
and the miraculous deeds of the brahmin named Patnīvratā take place.
There were wild mango groves and forests of *kṣīrikā* trees,
as well as slopes of *karmada*, *ṭimburu*, and *jāmbū* trees.
And there were forests of golden plantains with fruits as large as watermelons,
as well as plateaus of sugarcane with roots like lumps of sugar.
In the great region called Boriyā, the goddesses bathe and dwell;
and in the region of the Nārāyaṇa lake, the yoginīs roam.
The divine rivers, carrying logs through the forest, wander at the sacred bathing place; here,
forests of pārijāta flowers, kunda blossoms,
and kalpa trees exist, their fragrance extending for a hundred yojanas.
The wind, having carried [fragrance] from all sides, makes the grounds fragrant;
it turns the hot pits of fire into cool reservoirs of water in some places. || 25 ||
The rivers, possessing the luster of gold and silver, with their flow of pure water,
carry waters that are full of lakes and rich with the essence of medicinal herbs.
By drinking those waters, men become gods and goddesses;
even earthly kings and their queens partake of those waters and medicinal herbs.
Always sixteen years of age, ever joyful and well-nourished, surpassing desire and radiant, they sport with moon-like faces, causing one to wander through heaven. (28)
Nowhere was there a scarcity of fruits such as the nine-colored jackfruit, nor of dates, bilva fruits, and coconuts which are like nectar. (29)
Indeed, there are clusters of *āmalaka* and *triphalā*,
as well as *guṃdraka*, *iṅgudī*, and the pods, leaves, fruits, and bark [of these].
And the forests of trees such as the bamboo, the *mālā*, the *bilva* and *tinduka* shrubs, as well as the *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *sarja*, and *tilaka*.
There are forests of tulasī plants here, as well as branches of devadāru trees,
and likewise creepers of grapes, betel vines, and bitter herbs.
Indeed, Mālatī, Mallikā, Śvetā, Jīvantī, and Svarṇavallī creepers shine here, resplendent with an abundance of fruits, flowers, and leaves.
In every place, even on dry land, streams of water flow forth;
likewise, there are goldsmiths, copper-workers, and those who fashion ornaments for the body.
There are also creepers that destroy hunger and thirst, and there are trees as well;
divine ponds exist there, and by bathing in them, one becomes invisible.
Likewise, there are pits with golden water; iron becomes gold from that water.
Leaves and grasses indeed exist there, and a severed body is perfectly sutured.
The Rakta-ghaṭṭa certainly exists, as does the Saṃjīvanī;
there are likewise water-pools where, by bathing, a woman becomes a man. (37)
Whether one is born as a man or a woman, from that point on there is movement toward the mountain;
it is not otherwise, for such is the power observed on Mount Raivata. (38)
By bathing in a certain pool, wings for flying arise;
by bathing again, one surely returns to the human state as it was before.
By the gift of a boat, women become goddesses;
by the gift of a linga, men are born with perfected wombs.
In some cases, through the application of medicinal herbs, a person may take on the form of a lion;
having hunted deer and other animals, they become a human being once again. (41)
On that mountain there are small pools whose waters consist of the objects of desire;
indeed, whatever form one desires while bathing here arises for them.
Furthermore, all the inhabitants there enjoy nothing less than the pleasures of heaven. (42)
Indeed, there are various forests that fulfill all desires;
they are always laden with fruit and possessed of leaves, flowers, and the like.
In their midst, clouds that grant rain dwell perpetually upon the hips. (43)
And the lightning always bestows its brilliance upon it slowly at night;
the stars remain steady there for a while, dwelling as it dispels fatigue. (44)
There were silver mines and gold mines mixed with various minerals;
there were mines of diamonds, rubies, crystal, gems, and coral. (45)
Divine elixirs that reach down to the very roots of Pātāla exist here on Mount Raivata and are obtained by those who possess merit. (46)
The celestial nymphs of heaven come here to bathe and depart; indeed,
hundreds of thousands and millions of gods, humans, and virtuous people—
both men and women— perform the great circumambulation during the month of Kārttika.
Both the Gaṇas and the Gaṇikās are purified by the gift of their bodies;
there is the Parī-sarovara for the purpose of bathing for the Parīs, and likewise the Indrasarovara for the purpose of bathing for the Devīs. ||48||
There, Rohasarovara exists for the purpose of bathing for the gods;
Dātṛsarovara is in the valley for the purpose of bathing for donors;
and Vīrasarovara is in the valley for the purpose of bathing for the ancestors. ||49||
The excellent Satīsarovara exists there for the purpose of bathing for virtuous women,
as does the Bhaveśvara-taḍāga, which is a rasāyana of all medicinal herbs;
thus, divine lakes exist upon that mountain.
There, rivers flow out on all sides with inexhaustible waters;
standing upon Mount Raivata, they all behold the earth in every direction—the oceans, mountains, countries, villages, worlds, and regions. (51)
When there arises a desire to go to heaven with one's physical body, then,
having gone to the peak of Mount Raivata, one attains perfection through bathing.
Having reached it, one should proceed from there; one will not fall back as long as there is no latent impression (vāsanā).
Indeed, by merely bathing at Gaumukhī, by immersion in the water of the *kamaṇḍalu*, and by drinking a drop of water from Dattātreya, people become perfected beings (*siddha*). 53.
Having found rest upon its peak, the planets proceed toward other directions;
and the celestial chariots of the dwellers of heaven, having rested there, likewise depart.
From that peak, people indeed proceed along the paths leading to Brahmā, Īśa, Viṣṇu, and likewise to Mokṣa and Īśvara, as well as to Yama and to heaven.
When a person reaches the place named Bhīravajapa, he falls into that very forest; yet even there, heaven exists for him.
There is certainly not even the slightest deficiency compared to heaven;
indeed, many sacred fords of the gods exist there.
The deities, sages, seers, celestial beings, ancestors, and likewise yogis, come to perform circumambulation of Mount Raivata. (58)
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and those of divine origin, as well as the gods in the form of holy men, traverse all around him. (59)
And goddesses in the forms of virtuous women wander upon that mountain;
so too do Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Rāmacandra, Dattātreya, and Nṛhari.
Kapila, Vāmana, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, as well as Nārada, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Kumāra, and even Buddha. ||61||
All the manifestations such as Sanandana and others, as well as Brahmā and the rest,
[arose] on the full moon day of Kārttika, known as Prabodhinī, for as long as it lasted.
May the gods, the sacred fords, the purifiers, the holy fields, and the abodes;
all the mountains, rivers, oceans, and likewise the lands, protect us.
They come and dwell here on Mount Raivata at every spot;
they dwell upon every leaf in order to perform circumambulation.
Whoever has performed the circumambulation of Mount Raivata at that time has indeed performed the circumambulation of the entire earth along with its sacred sites.
At that time, those humans who circumambulate Mount Raivata are not to be regarded as mere men; rather, they are to be seen as tens of millions of gods.
By obtaining the dust of their feet, millions of births are liberated—whether they be boys, youths, elders, men, or even women at that time. (67)
Those purifiers who have taken refuge in Hari circumambulate Raivata:
the virtuous man, the virtuous woman, the male renunciant, the female renunciant, and the dispassionate one.
Whether they are Vaiṣṇavas, Śāṅkarīs, or Goddesses; or whether they are Vaiṣṇavas, Śāṅkaras, or even followers of Gaṇapati—those who walk the path to liberation are indeed deities.
To them indeed one should give food, a gift, clothing, or whatever else belongs to oneself.
All of that should indeed be given; in service, it shall become a bestower of heaven.
Whatever object may be in one's possession should be given away in every way to that person before whom it lies;
the virtuous and the holy should be gratified even with body, speech, and mind. (71)
To the one who offers everything to him, Nārāyaṇa Hari himself indeed gives back his own entire self to that devotee who is of the nature of Brahman.
Those who die at the supreme holy site of Dāmodara, wherever that may be,
indeed dwell in the abode of Hari and never fall again into worldly existence.
The first gift is the offering of oneself; the second is the offering of wealth; the third is the offering of fields and so forth; and the fourth is the offering of one's own [body]. (74)
All this is the fruit born of circumambulating that mountain;
there, sins are consumed by fire and do not arise at all.

Whatever merit has been performed—whether called "benefiting others," whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, whether pertaining to the body, the senses, or the heart—that leads to liberation. (76)
The nature of Brahman may conquer, but the nature of the body will defeat it;
one who is free from doubt shall be liberated, while the one whose soul is full of doubt perishes.
Therefore, O Mahālakṣmī, that Raivataka mountain peak is exceedingly pleasing to me as well; there I dwell as Dāmodara. (78)
I indeed dwell as Trivikrama in the temple at Rukmadurga;
I also dwell in the middle of the city in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
On dry land, on a tree, in a flower, in a leaf, at the root, in dust, on a mountain, in rivers, on the surface of the earth, in a well, in a pond, in a forest, and in water— ||1.142.80||
In the water-lily, the lotus, the night-blooming lily, and the land-lotus;
in stone, a cavity in the earth, an anthill, a tree, and a shrub. ||8.1||
Wherever Raivata exists, there I dwell everywhere;
I am indeed the Raivata mountain, and I am Raivata—there is no difference between us.
My ornament, my body, Raivata, the supreme purifier—for those dwelling in Saurāṣṭra, even the Yamas do not behold their home. (83)
Indeed, after performing austerities, the Kṣatriya Ānarta obtained a portion of the jewel from Kṛṣṇa at Goloka; that very portion has been established here. (84)
Saurāṣṭra is renowned as a place where those residing there have no fear from any quarter; how much less, then, can there be any fear for those who have gone to this divine mountain? (85)
Wherein indeed there are minerals that are red, white, blue, and likewise pale;
there are stones shaped like elephants, and others made of gold and silver. (86)
Others are shaped like chickpeas, while the sands extend as far as the *gokṣura* plant; there are also divine trees, creepers, shrubs, and *santāna* trees.
All gold—whether root, flower, fruit, or leaf—is composed of light;
the sinful soul does not see it, but one liberated from sin sees it. 88.
That mountain is constantly served by those seeking minerals and other resources;
furthermore, people of all castes and stages of life wander there and dwell there. (89)
There were many birds there: cranes dwelling in the sky, cuckoos, cātaka birds, peacocks, swans, and likewise mayūrakas.
Garudas, vultures, pigeons, far-sighted ones, ruddy geese, cocks, partridges, and those of divine species; ||91||
All auspicious words are always propitious and bringers of welfare;
likewise, deer, lordly monkeys, tigers, and lions [are so]. (92)
Bears, elephants, divine horses, and likewise the Sāttvatas—
by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), they do not behave wickedly at all.
Even beasts, birds, and reptiles, when they meet their death in due time,
all ascend celestial chariots and go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth fall by the wind into the golden protective water—indeed, all of that attains liberation. (95)
The wife of Hari, known as Suvarṇā, always exists in the form of a river for the service of Dāmodara through the flow of her love. 96.
That river Suvarṇarakṣā, joined with golden sands, shines as if it were made entirely of gold, and it turns others into gold as well. (97)
There, the Naga king Vāsuki, having split the earth to bathe, arrived by way of that very opening at its base. 98.
And Indra, having returned from heaven and performed abundant sacrifices, took away the merit for the sake of liberation and went to the painless heaven. 99.
Furthermore, those people who perform a fast for even a single day shall,
by the power of Śrī Hari, attain the abode of Hari.
Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Sukarṣaṇa,
as well as other lords numbering hundreds, lakhs, and crores, indeed dwell there.
Their beloveds, with faces like the beautiful moon—fair-complexioned and dark-complexioned, yet all possessing firm waists—play eternally before Dāmodara. (102)
There were women with shapely hips and beautiful hair, with fine noses and long eyes;
they had graceful ankles, lovely eyebrows, well-formed waists, and full breasts.
With beautiful faces, lovely shanks, and likewise excellent feet, limbs, and bellies,
they sport and laugh upon that mountain named Raivata.
There is the Revatī-kuṇḍa there; having bathed there, whatever woman gives gifts such as gold will become possessed of sons and fortunate. (105)
In the month of Kārtika, women who speak in various regional dialects keep vigil before Dāmodara, repeatedly performing songs and dances.
Having become Ramās and Lakṣmīs, they go to the abode of Śrī Hari;
that abode of Hari is beautiful, lovely, and consists of five stones.
Or, having constructed a divine pinnacle endowed with many forms, one transcends all desires and attains the Supreme Brahman. || 108 ||
