One should place a five-colored banner atop the house of Dāmodara;
for as many years as there are threads [in the banner], one goes to the divine realm of Viṣṇu.
In the form of Dāmodara, Vāmana shines here;
his auspicious field, Vastrāpatha, measures six gavyūtis.
From the ascent of the mountain up to Vāmanasthalī in the west,
the intervening ground of Vastrapatha is six gavyūtis in length.
King Gaya, a devotee of Hari, arrived there once;
that Vaiṣṇava performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu together with his subjects.
Having bestowed many gifts and having offered oblations into the sacrificial fire,
he performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu here in the vicinity of Mount Raivata.
At that sacrifice, some drank smoke with their faces turned downwards;
others subsisted on dry leaves, and still others lived on fruits.
Other twice-born ones were eaters of roots, while others subsisted on air;
some were practitioners of the five-fire austerity, and some remained seated in water.
Some chant the divine Gāyatrī, others chant Sarasvatī;
some chant the Sūktas, and others chant the twelve-syllable mantra.
Likewise, some recite the eight-syllable mantra, while others chant "Hari"; they observe eating once a day, eating only at night, eating unasked food, or fasting.
Having performed such meritorious deeds before Dāmodara,
they became fulfilled in that great sacrifice dedicated to Viṣṇu.
King Gaya shone together with as many sages and others as were present,
and thousands upon thousands of celestial chariots arrived.
There, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras arrived together with the attendants of Viṣṇu to lead [him] to Vaikuṇṭha. (1.142.12)
Then the subjects, headed by the sages, ascended into celestial chariots;
along with them, that king, together with his wife, [ascended] with all his kinsmen.
Having ascended to a celestial chariot, he went to the stainless world of Viṣṇu;
there, in that sacred field, Vāmana begged Bali for alms.
Such a supreme field has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again,
where liberation arises simply by residing there, and nothing further remains to be done.
In that place there are many sacred sites (tīrthas); I shall describe them, for a location becomes powerful by virtue of a powerful person.
O Lotus-born one, the sacred fords (tīrthas) come there for the sake of their own purification;
having first mentioned them, I shall thereafter describe Trivikrama.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Wondrous Majesty and Prosperity of Dāmodara, the Vāmana named Pratāpadeva, and Others Residing on Raivatācala; the Divine Abode of Kārtika; the Circumambulation; and Sacrifices Performed by Gaya," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, he who undertakes a pilgrimage there at Vastrāpatha on the full moon day of Kārttika becomes liberated once that holy place has been visited.
In Dāmodara, the auspicious river named Svarṇarakṣā is proclaimed;
there is the Brahmakuṇḍa holy site as well as the Śiva known as Brahmeśvara. || 2 ||
Kālamegha is proclaimed, as well as Bhava and Dāmodara;
Kālikā is situated two gavyūtis distant upon the mountain peak.
Indreśvara is in the direction of the wind (the northwest), and Mṛgīkuṇḍa is near Bhava; Sāraṇika was the sacred ford in the Kṛta age, and Hemamāraka in the Tretā age.
To the west lies the field called Unnabhīla, extending for a distance of one yojana;
there are many sacred fords (tīrthas) there, as well as sixteen sites of the Siddhas.
There is the Sūryakuṇḍa holy site, as well as Gaṅgeśa and Maṅgala;
and the great god Siddheśvara is located one gavyūti to the west of the city.
At Indreśvara is Cakratīrtha; Hāṭakeśa is to the west;
there is the great goddess Yakṣeśvarī, and beyond that is a mountain.
Somaliṅga is the middle [region], where there are numerous sacred fords (tīrthas);
there is the footprint of Gajendra, and right there is the well of nectar (rasakūpikā).
There are a hundred sacrificial pits there, and Ambikā is upon the peak;
likewise Pradyumna, Sāmba, and Gorakṣaka as well.
Gaṇeśa, Hanumān, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Mādhava also dwell in the midst of the forest; and the forests are named after each of them respectively.
Bhava arrived there, and I shall relate this story:
once, upon the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, in the presence of Śiva.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods arrived there swiftly;
Viṣṇu then spoke to Śambhu, who had granted boons to the Daityas.

He proceeds step by step, prostrating himself on the ground like a staff,

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Causes for the Abodes of Various Tīrthas, Bhava-Īśvara, Dāmodara, Svayaṃbhū, Trivikrama, Vāsiṣṭha, Svarṇarakṣa, and Others in Vastrāpatha during the Raivata Manvantara," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
For the sake of uplifting the world, I dwell in this excellent holy place;
yet I reside everywhere as well, for the sake of being the inner controller.
I am always present in every form for the purpose of accepting service; I dwell in each respective place here for the sake of affection toward my devotees.
Sometimes due to the insistence of devotees, or else because of my own resolve,
and sometimes out of the necessity of some task, I dwell in various places.
In the western region of Bhārata, as far as the edge of the ocean,
there exists no other divine holy site equal to Raivataka Mountain.
In that very place, in the southern forest, is the abode of Somanātha;
in the northern Golden City is the abode of Anādikṛṣṇa.
To the east, at Kuṅkumavāpī, is the abode of Gopālakṛṣṇa; to the west, at Vāmanasthalī, is my own abode as Trivikrama.
Thus, I dwell everywhere in that region, at every spot;
indeed, in the great capital city, there is the abode of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
In every corner [of the earth], I dwell for the sake of uplifting the people;
at the end of the age, my palaces revolve here and there.
Just as worn-out things are dissolved and new ones are produced, so too do I come into being again for the sake of my devotees. || 9 ||
There is no end to my divine abodes according to the divisions of the ages;
those very lands and regions shall exist, and I too am indeed that same one.
Due to the excellence of the priest's austerity, through the power of the devotee's devotion,

Kaśyapa indeed performed most formidable austerities on the riverbank,

Having drunk the water of the Ūrjayantī there for a thousand years in a secluded place where Vāmanasthalī is situated, he did so for the sake of obtaining a son.
There, Hari himself was propitiated by that Kaśyapa along with Aditi;
he was chosen as their son, and thus I became Vāmana.
I shall tell you the reason for that which dwells in my mind; listen, Lakṣmī.
Having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Lord himself became Nṛsiṃha.
He gave the three worlds to Indra and the nether regions (atala) and so forth to Prahlāda;

His son was the mighty-armed Bali, the best among the Sātvatas;

Having conquered the world-protectors and the guardians of the quarters on all sides,

Bali, possessing great strength, ruled the earth under a single umbrella;

Fragrant flowers and succulent fruits; trees bearing fruit upon their very trunks; and honey in every blossom. (22)

The Vaishnava people constantly worship Hrishikesha;

He enjoyed sovereignty over the three worlds, acting with pride in his strength;

Freed from the sufferings of poverty and death, they live long lives; for in that place, even at night, there is light like that of jewel-lamps as if it were day. (27)

The gods were gratified by the sacrifice; henceforth there shall be no mutual warfare, nor even strife among those with rival wives, nor among beasts and birds. (29)
When the entire world, both stationary and moving, had attained a state of loving-kindness,
Nārada no longer saw any war in the three worlds.
At that moment, a great pain arose within his belly;
what was the use of satiating offerings, ritual bathing, recitation, or burnt oblations?
That is a bath where elephants fight with the clashing of their tusks;
that is a twilight when the earth is made pale-red by the blood of headless trunks.
Where the flesh-eaters are satiated—that is my preferred libation;
where kṣatriyas are slain in battle by the flood of weapons of kṣatriyas—that is my worship. (33)
That man, where the best of men are offered as oblations and slain—without such a battle, the three worlds appear empty to me day after day. (34)
"I shall do so, yet a conflict with Indra will arise.

"What Bṛhaspati tells you must not be spoken by me to you;

And having beheld the mango grove, the powerful river, the land of lush foliage, and all the pleasure found in the shade of trees by water and on land; 11.9.
Bali dwelt there and caused sacrificial pits to be constructed;
that region of Bali’s excavations became renowned as Balimakhya.
Having had that ground consecrated and a sacrificial pavilion constructed,
he commenced a great twelve-day sacrifice accompanied by all the prescribed priestly fees.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārāyaṇa’s Residence at a Holy Place, the Praise of Bali’s Virtues, Nārada’s Departure for Indra, the Counsel for Bali’s Fall, the Austerities of Kaśyapa and Aditya in Saurāṣṭra, the Attainment of Boons from Nārāyaṇa, the Birth of Vāmana, Bali’s Conquest of the Quarters, and the Commencement of Bali’s Sacrifice in Saurāṣṭra," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, Vāmana also wandered over the earth visiting holy places;
he first went to the sacred field of Hari-Hara and from there to the city.
Having reached Kapilāśrama, he went to Brahmaputrānada;
then, having seen Kāmākṣī of Kāmarūpa as well as Paśupati.
Having reached Kedāreśvara, he went to Badarikāśrama;
having reached Hanumat-tīrtha, he proceeded to Mount Kailāsa.
From there he went to Haridvāra, and after that to Kurukṣetra;
then he proceeded to Yāmuna, Vṛndāvana, and Gokula as well.
Then, having gone to the city of Ayodhyā and to the Sarayū and Prayāga,
he went to Gayā and the Godāvarī, and thereafter proceeded to the Kāverī.
Having gone to Kāñcī, Kṛṣṇā, Tāmraparṇī, and Kumārikā, as well as Setubandha, Janārdana, and the Malaya mountain; || 6 ||
Having reached Aruṇācala, Padmākṣetra, Varāhaka, Bhūtapurī, and then Siṃhāraṇya, and thereafter the Narmadā; || 7 ||
Then the Tāpī, followed by Siddhapada, and then the lake named Puṣkara;
then the Sindhu, the Nārāyaṇa lake, and then Suvarṇadvārikā.
While Vāmana was bathing at the confluence of the Gomatī with the ocean,
the sages also arrived there for the purpose of bathing.
Gautama, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa,
Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, and Nārada beheld the Supreme Lord.
Having recognized Vāmana by his characteristic marks as the Supreme Lord, they bowed down to him;
and Hari said to them all, "Go to the abode of Bali."
"Let the sages go there and perform the great sacrifice;
I shall come there myself and accomplish that offering."
Having been addressed thus, all the sages departed for the sacrificial pavilion;
the great twelve-day sacrifice, accompanied by all the ritual fees, was then commenced.
All the sages were invited by Śukra to the sacrificial rites;
a Brāhmaṇa devoted to his wife also arrived at the sacrificial ceremony.
Sages, ancestors, gods, seers, yakṣas, rākṣasas, daityas, dānavas, nāgas, serpents, and the various species of uragas; || 15 ||
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, vaināyakas, and kinnaras; likewise sūtas, māgadhas, bards, and cāraṇas. || 16 ||
Gandharvas, dancers, actors, flatterers, those who dwell outside the home, kushmandas, and vetalas—these are impure, even though they belong to pure castes. (17)
The heavens, the planets, and the comets; the principles (tattvas) and the powers (śaktis);
the supernatural attainments (siddhis), the circle of Yoginīs, and likewise the virtuous women and the virtuous men. || 18 ||
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, as well as the servant castes;
rivers and mountains, sacred fields and pilgrimage sites, and the oceans. (19)
The lakes and forests, these birds and whatever else there is that is divine and possesses a meritorious form—[all these were created]. || 1.145.20 ||
Bali, the ruler of the three worlds, had those palaces located on the fourteenth level constructed within his own kingdom.
By the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions, they arrived from all sides upon the earth, in heaven, on mountains,
in the oceans, and in forest regions— everywhere, O Nūpurā.
For the sake of all, palaces equal to royal residences were constructed;
for those dwelling in the waters, there were cities with celestial chariots in the sky.
In the layer of wind, there are palaces and dwellings situated within the clouds;
likewise, on mountains, in forests, among trees, upon the earth, and within the interior of the earth.
And in whatever way the suitability for their bodies was found in a place,
in that very way the king constructed dwellings for them.
Then Viśvakarman, Maya, the artisans, and the craftsmen, as well as all the sixty-four arts, the sciences of craftsmanship, and beautiful forms [appeared]. (26)
Likewise, cities and villages appeared in embodied form; as did causes and effects, the seasons, months, and years. ||27||
The fires, all the Maruts, the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds, as well as the personified principles, the elements, and the objects of the senses. ||28||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as their attendants and millions of servants—the Vaiṣṇavas, the devotees of Śiva, and likewise other celestial Sāttvatas—[were there]. ||29||
Summoned there to the sacrifice were both auspicious and inauspicious birds,
as well as wish-fulfilling animals and birds such as Garuḍa and others.
Nectars and milks were milked out, as well as various kinds of food in every way;
there were many varieties of drinks and mountains of edibles and solid foods. (3.1)
And there were various flavors—intoxicating liquors and meats, both dry and moist—as well as abundant foods from the sky-dwellers that were rich and unctuous. (32)
Rice, barley, wheat, chickpeas, unbroken grains, sesame seeds, javarikā, and mung beans— these foods and sacrificial offerings were in great abundance.
Neither seen nor even heard of are those [trees] upon the fourteen levels whose fruits, leaves, and so forth are excellent foods for them. (34)
In this [assembly], there were those born from the ocean and those born from fire, produced from the most excellent materials;
as well as rows of vessels, garments, ornaments, and the like, along with vehicles and mounts.
There were millions of electric lamps and numerous water-machines;
thousands of wells, ponds, clothed mansions, and kitchens. (36)
There, cooks and sacrificial priests were appointed by the hundreds of thousands as officiating ministers (ṛtvij);
likewise, there were reciters, worshippers, and Vedic singers. ||37||
And there were crores of Sādhyas, as well as other Viśvedevas, learned men, the preceptors of the gods, and likewise the preceptors of the Daityas. (38)
Then the goddesses— the rivers beginning with Gaṅgā, as well as Śāradā and Sarasvatī— were engaged in various tasks and auxiliary parts of the sacrifice.
The Sāvitrī and other such verses, as well as those distinguished by song and fame,
along with the Ṛgvedic hymns, the Vedas, and the Śāstras, all become manifest in embodied form.
In that regard, what deficiency could there possibly be where King Bali, the protector of the three worlds and a great devotee of the Lord, was the performer of the sacrifice? (41)
At that time, during that great sacrifice, everything there was indeed dwarf-sized, except for him by whose will the fourteen worlds always rain down as he desires.
Kāma, Vasanta, and Bāṇa, as well as Rati, came together;
likewise, the passionate ones, the passions, the musical scales (grāmas), and the modulations (mūrchanās) arrived. ||43||
The Manvantaras, the lineages of Dharma, those endowed with excellent qualities and so forth, the Vasus, the Nidhis, the Rudras, the Directions, and the Āditya deities; ||44||
The moon and the constellations, villages, towns, market-towns, and hamlets;
as well as medicinal herbs, those born in water, those born on land, and likewise those born from roots. 45.
Amṛtavallikās, Nāgavallīs, and Jīvavallikās;
those who know the terrestrial sphere (bhūgola), those who know the celestial sphere (khagola), as well as astrologers and mathematicians. ||46||

Likewise, all the auspicious moments (muhūrtas) and astrological conjunctions (yogas) that had assembled there, as well as wrestlers, actors of many forms, theatrical performances, and jesters. ||47||
There were numerous divine displays, including frequent fire-works, delightful animal combats, and athletic contests of men. (48)
Explanations and storytellers, renunciants, ascetics, and holy men; students of sacred knowledge, the Bālakhilyas, and likewise those who practice upward-directed conduct (ūrdhvaśīlin). ||49||
Whatever reality exists in the world, all of it was gathered there;
the world was honored by Bali with great respect and a warm welcome.
Then that entire Siṃhāraṇya became filled with living beings and gods; the atmosphere, the waters, and the land were completely crowded with guests.
Or rather, it appeared there like a newly formed cosmic egg;
indeed, an assembly such as this has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again.
The sacrificial pavilion for that sacrifice was one hundred *gavyūtis* in extent,
stretching from Svarṇadvārikā as far as Someśvara.
From the abode of sea-monsters (the ocean) as far as the Kuṅkumavāpikā, that ground shines with its pavilions like a newly created heaven. (54)
The sacrificial pit was made one yojana in extent and shaped like a lotus;
from the forests were brought the Pippala, Apāmārga, Udumbara, and Kiṃśuka trees.
Other mountains of sacrificial wood were prepared for the fuel,
as well as mountains of ghee, coconut, plantain, grape, and other fruits.
There were mountains of sesame, rice, barley, and grain, as well as mountains of flowers, leaves, roots, branches, blossoms, and seeds. (57)
Abundant offerings of sugar, milk-preparations, and various types of milk-rice were being poured into the fire,
while the resonant sounds of the Vedas reached the heavens.
Food remains from sacrifices are always consumed, and indeed, sweet drinks pleasing to the sacrifice are drunk. (59)
The coming and going of the lords of the gods also takes place there in that pavilion in an uninterrupted stream.
The triad of sages known as Ekata, Dvita,
and Trita produces ninefold wealth through the mantras of their respective deities and others.
The sun shines there in a second form, and likewise the moon; there is indeed no distinction between day and night.
This Vāmana, the all-pervading Śrī Hari himself, partakes of streams of ghee that cannot be interrupted, poured before the fire. 63.
In this way, auspicious fire-rituals are constantly accomplished;
what more need be said there, for even Śeṣa has attained exhaustion? (64)
Even the spectators grew weary; what need is there to mention the painters?
For one endowed with devotion to the Blessed One, everything is prosperous—of this there is no doubt. (65)
Indeed, by the power of his devotion to the Lord, Bali’s infinite riches were ever-present for the performance of fire-sacrifices,
as well as for food, drink, and the offering of water to guests.
There is no end to the giving of gold, even for one who is infinite;
let it be given, let it be given, and likewise, let it be enjoyed, let it be enjoyed.
"Drink! Drink! "Bring it! Bring it! likewise;
"Welcome! Welcome to you!"—this pentad does not cease here. (68)
The sound of the Vedas, the sound of songs, the sound of the names of Hari, the sound of musical instruments, and the sound of his glory—this pentad does not cease here. (69)
Extremely delighted, Bali gave gifts at the sacrifice amounting to a parārdha:
crores of gold pieces, diamonds, and silver coins.
There were ten million quintillion gifts of cows, a hundred billion times ten million gifts of garments,
and ten million times a hundred billion lotuses worth of ornaments, silver coins, and seals.
Of parasols, sandals and the like, and of bowls, there were ten million;
likewise of vehicles, mounts, elephants, and horses.
He gave away gifts of chariots and maidens by the tens of millions, billions, and trillions, like Viṣṇu himself, a second Kṛṣṇa in person. (73)
At that time, the Vasus were the primary ones in this matter of giving gifts;
Lakṣmī, Ramā, and Mahālakṣmī were the primary ones in the bestowing of gold and other riches. (74)
When the primary gift is made, heaven and earth are the recipients for the bestowing of jewels, food, and so forth;
therein, Mount Meru is the most eminent recipient for the bestowing of vessels, cattle, and the like.
The oceans, Kubera, the Himalayas and other mountains, the great forests, Viśvakarman, Maya, and other inhabitants of heaven [were also present]. (76)
In the giving of vehicles, mounts, and the like, such as the splendor of jewel ornaments, they were all made the foremost; indeed, they gave away their very everything.
An announcement resounded in all directions throughout the fourteen worlds:
"Bali, the lord of the three worlds, is bestowing gifts by the millions at his sacrifice. (78)
Abundant food is served to everyone from golden vessels;
yet a learned Brāhmaṇa guest is honored even with one's entire possessions. (79)
The subjects dwelling in all the worlds came there to that sacrifice, [saying]:
"Let them go; let them accept the gifts; let them enjoy the food."
Behold what kind of sacrifice this is, such as has never occurred before nor will ever occur again, renowned in the land of Saurāṣṭra in the vicinity of Mount Raivata. ||81||
The field is known as Vastrāpatha; there indeed is this Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
To the south-west of that is the great sacrifice of Bali. ||82||
Having heard this supreme proclamation, the great lord Vāmana, though omniscient, acted as if he were not; thinking, "If I go thus, I shall obtain [the kingdom]. (83)
Acting thus, the Brāhmaṇa, a master of the four Vedas, arrived at Mount Raivata on his pilgrimage, his activities unknown to the people. (84)
He had a large belly, short arms, short feet, and a massive head;
he possessed a large jaw, a thick neck, and thick shanks, and was exceedingly lazy. ||85||
With his topknot tied, wearing a cloth, an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot, he arrived at Vastrāpatha on the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā. (86)
Vāmana reflected upon Somanātha, the Lord of Bhava,
as well as Dāmodara, Dattātreya, and Mount Raivataka.
"Having seen [it], I shall then go indeed to Bali's sacrificial ground.
Having resolved thus, he went to Someśvara and beheld Śambhu.
Somanātha Mahādeva spoke to Viṣṇu Vāmana:
"O Viṣṇu, you have succeeded in every way; the accomplishment of your purpose shall come to pass. (89)
Having bowed to him, he went to where Hara, the Lord of Bhava, resides;
he arrived at that divine and beautiful forest on Mount Raivataka.
There were various kinds of trees with long branches laden with fruit—
banyans, udumbaras, bilvas, sarjas, arjunas, and kadambakas.
Palāśa, aśvattha, jambu, dhava and other trees of the vāruṇa class; śamī, kaṅkola, nimba, bījapūra, and pomegranates. ||9 1 ||
Badarīs, bakas, pūgas, śivās, kamala-śalyakas, hintālas, śirīṣas, bījakas, vaṃśas, and khādiras; ||13||
Ajamodā, nikumbha, iṅgudi, karīraka, dhāmārgava, kurabaka, karañja, and punarnavā; ||94||
Aṅkola trees, pāribhadra trees, kambalyas, as well as panasa trees, utpalas, haridrās, gaṇḍīras, and vāyasī trees; ||95||
Tamāla trees, mangoes, date palms, karamardakas, sevatīs, śālmalīs, śālas, madhūkas, and bibhītakas; ||96||
Harītakīs, Kandarālās, Vaṭas, Aṭarūṣakas, Vikaṅkatas, Kapitthas, Rohiṇīs, Vetras, and Pāṭalas. ||97||
Madanas, nirguṇḍīs, plantains, śiṃśapās and other such trees, as well as cardamom, cloves, lavalī, sarala, and aguru trees. (98)
Then Vāmana beheld śrīkhaṇḍa and karavīra trees, as well as most excellent kalpavṛkṣas—shady trees worshipped by the gods. (99)
Seeing trees whose shadows were not obstructed at either sunrise or sunset, and having bathed in a pond, he went to the foot of the mountain.
While he was drinking the water from the pond and desiring rest, five guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) arrived to see him. || 101 ||
One named Ekapāda always dwells on the slope of the mountain;
the second, named Giridāruṇa, resides on the mountain.
On the summit of Mount Ūrjayanta is Meghanāda, the third;
on the beautiful peak of Bhavānī is Siṃhanāda, the fourth. (103)
Kālamegha also dwells on the bank of the river Svarṇarakṣā;
having obtained a vision of Vāmana, they returned to their own abodes.
Beginning from the eleventh day until the full moon day—
that is the excellent Bhīṣmapañcaka in the month of Kārtika, for it bestows liberation.
One should perform circumambulation, as well as the protection rite with gold;
furthermore, one must by all means behold Dāmodara and Bhaveśa.
Then the Lord Nṛsiṃha arrived to see Vāmana;
having offered praise and stood before him, Vāmana then spoke to that Nṛhari.
"You must remain here in front of Dāmodara at my command;
you must always provide protection for all those dwelling in this sacred place. (108)
"One must always remain in the presence of the God for as long as fourteen Indras [reign].
Saying "So be it," he indeed performs the protection of that sacred ford (tīrtha).
Then indeed, the god Vāmana, that Hari, went to the peak situated in the sky to see Bhavānī, the mother of Skanda.
Having beheld that Mother Bhavānī, he stood with his arms raised,
gazing upon the entire earth, which has the western ocean for its garment.
Then Acyuta himself went to the peak of Gorakṣa;
thereafter, on the third peak, he beheld Dattātreya.
Having flown up, one should go to Aśvapaṭṭasara in the east;
having reached Kukumavāpī, one beholds Kaṃbharā and Gopāla.
Having performed his ablutions at Patnīvratatīrtha, he flew up to Raivata;
from there he went to Maṇipura, and then to the city of Vāmana.
In that city of the Asuras, Vāmana would go from house to house among the Brahmins, always seeking auspicious alms.
At delightful crossroads and in temples of the gods,
he sat surrounded by people, shaking his thick staff.
He shakes his thick head and dances with the playful movements of a child;
at times he moves on short legs and sings most enchantingly.
All the sons of the Daityas, as well as those of the Brāhmaṇas, studied the four Vedas adorned with dense clusters of clouds.
Day and night, people go about Vāmana with playful jests;
men come to behold his wondrous dwarf-form.
Led by many youths, Vāmana was brought to the sacrificial pavilion where King Bali,
the performer of the sacrifice and giver of gifts, was present.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Vāmana’s Pilgrimage in the First Section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, the Gathering of Fourteen Hundred Million Beings including Bhavānī and others at Bali’s Sacrifice, the Sacrificial Pavilion, the Fire-pit, the Homa, and the Gifts; Vāmana’s Journey to Mount Raivata, His Stay at Vāmanapura, and His Return to Bali at the Sacrificial Pavilion," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to my wondrous account of the vision of Vāmana;
having seen him, who is distinct from all others, curiosity arose within me.
A great clamor arose; someone short in stature arrived, equal to Viṣṇu in form and splendor, yet assuming a disguise in his body.
Standing there reciting the Vedas together with many Brahmins, he was announced to the Daitya by the Daitya youths who had entered [the assembly]. || 3 ||
"This dwarf Brāhmaṇa has indeed come to witness the sacrifice.
Delighted, Bali spoke these words: "This is truly the dawning of my good fortune!"
The desireless dwarf god does not ask for anything at all;
"I shall honor the lord of brahmins and I shall give him whatever he desires. (5)
Viṣṇu himself has arrived as a guest; one should give to him whatever he desires.
One recipient is composed of the Vedas, while another recipient is composed of austerity.
The worthy recipient, having arrived, will take away the sacrificial offering;
while the sacrifice is underway, the priestly fee must be given by me.
"This sacrifice of mine is indeed the very last, fulfilling a thousand [offerings].
Whatever I possess here must be given to beggars without hesitation. (8)
A hundred sacrifices are considered necessary for the attainment of Indra’s station;
the attainment of the station of Brahmā (Pārameṣṭhī) occurs through a thousand sacrifices.
Therefore, let this great sacrifice not suffer from the confusion of the syllable "na";
indeed, one must give, one must give, one must give by all means whatsoever.
The word "no" should never be spoken regarding one's body, wife, children, or possessions.
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my life is fruitful. (1.1)
Having seated him upon a seat of flowers according to the prescribed rite,
and having prostrated and paid homage, he spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
O best of Brahmins, having worshipped you, what pleasing service may I perform for you? For what purpose, O most excellent of the twice-born, have you come here with me in mind? (13)
"I shall grant that to you quickly; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas!
Thus addressed, Hrasva, with a joyful heart, spoke to the lord of the earth.
"O Lord of the Daityas, grant me the ground for my sacrificial fire-pit;
you ought to give me land measured by three strides. (15)
Of all gifts indeed, the gift of land is the most excellent;
he who gives land, O King, to a Brahmin who possesses nothing else.
Or even if he possesses only as much land as the size of a thumb, he shall become a lord of the earth;
for in this world, there exists no nourishment equal to the gift of land.
He who accepts land and he who bestows land—both of them are performers of meritorious deeds, destined for the heavenly realm. (18)
Therefore, O Great King, grant me a piece of land measuring three paces;
O Lord of the Earth, do not hesitate to give even this small amount of ground.
"O King, it shall indeed be known as 'The Bestowal of the Three Worlds'";
thereupon, with a joyful heart, the lord of the earth replied, "So be it."
He then resolved to perform the gift of the earth according to the prescribed rites;
at that moment, his preceptor Śukra restrained Bali.
"O King, let some other gift indeed be given; let not the earth be given. But listen to something else, O King: an improper act is being committed by you. (22)
Outside, those twice-born who are poor, blind, miserable, and so forth— those who are deaf, dwarfs, hunchbacks, maimed, diseased, or harsh— should be honored.
Those who are like lumps of sugar do not deserve worship near the sacrificial pit;
rather, Vāmana should be worshipped outside with gold, silver, and garments. (24)
The birth of four types of people is in vain, and sixteen kinds of gifts are likewise fruitless:
the birth of those without sons is in vain, and the birth of those who are unrighteous is indeed in vain. (25)
The birth of those who subsist on the food of others is in vain; the wife of another is born in vain.
A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin, as well as to one who is unmarried or fallen, is likewise useless. (26)
In the case of a Brahmin who neglects the twilight prayers, one who is crooked, a thief, one who causes displeasure to the guru, or one who is averse to his father and mother; 27.
To one who is a mere nominal Brahmin, to an ungrateful person, to a seller of the Vedas, likewise to a beggar in one's own village, to one conquered by women, and to the husband of a Vṛṣalī; ||28||
"To one who seizes serpents, to a slanderer, and in sixteen other cases, gifts are in vain.
In the midst of this, Bali said: "O Teacher, you should not speak thus."
Whoever studies the Vedas is, in my view, equal to Viṣṇu;
no delay should be made when a learned Vedic scholar arrives at one's home.
With rising from one's seat, with words of welcome, and by washing the feet, a householder should provide food according to his ability. 3.11.
When Vāmana departs unhonored from the sacrificial pavilion, then this sacrifice, with all its possessions given as sacrificial fees, goes to ruin. ||32||
Therefore, [know] this twice-born one who is disguised as a dwarf, yet possessing the form of Viṣṇu,
his body radiant, tawny, and resembling the sun.
"I shall indeed grant him whatever he desires; what does he not wish for?
I am blessed, for in my sacrifice a twice-born man equal to Viṣṇu has arrived."
Having done this, he indeed offered him the sixteen types of service;
he quickly presented him with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and the cow.
Having smelled the *madhuparka* offering, the cow was saluted by [Vāmana] with a low bow;
and Vāmana, having offered salutations to the sacrifice and all those present at the sacrifice, [proceeded]. (36)
"I have come as a petitioner; speak, O Bali!
O Lord of Daityas, grant me a place to dwell, and give me three paces of my beloved land. (37)
"Having constructed a divine cottage, I shall teach my disciples.
"The three steps have been given to you; accept them," Vāmana said. (38)
"Give it not," said Śukra; "this is the eternal Viṣṇu.
Then Bali said to Śukra: "What recipient could there be greater than this? (39)
Having placed the sacrificial grass (darbha) along with grains of rice in his right hand, Bali performed the ritual;
however, the Guru did not carry out the formal application, nor did he pour water into the hand.
The members of the assembly, the Hotṛ priests, the sages, as well as the Brahmins, the gods, the worlds, and the Daityas who were his kinsmen, were all struck with wonder. ||41||
When it is said, "It has been given, it has been received," why does one not let go of the water?
Water is offered into the hand for the sake of Vāmana for the attainment of auspiciousness. (42)
That gift which is given only in words but not followed by action casts the giver into hell and destroys his family. (43)
Uśanas said to the lord of the Daityas: "This Vāmana is Hari;
he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, and this Hari has been entreated by the gods. (44)
By some stroke of fate, I have come here to see you;
having bypassed the entire earth, I have arrived here specifically to find you. (45)
Whether it be unpleasant or even pleasant, I do not know what he will do;
therefore, O King, the earth must not be given to that great-souled one. 46.
"O King, accept some other matter from my words.
Then, laughing, that king spoke to his preceptor with composure: [47]
I know that through the power of destiny and likewise by the grace of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice shall reach completion;
it will indeed become complete through the twice-born.
I am Indra, I am the twice-born, I am Viṣṇu, and the sacrificial substance has the Sun as its deity;
so how could it not be given by me, saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased"? (49)
Having spoken thus, Bali gave water into the hand of Vāmana.
"Hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ! O King, what is this being done? It is not at all appropriate."
Having uttered this, Śukra then stood outside the pavilion, saying:
"For the pleasure of Vāsudeva, every meritorious act has been performed by me. (51)
Today I am blessed, for Viṣṇu himself has come here;
today my life and great happiness must indeed be offered to him. (52)
Therefore, having married her and having devotedly washed his feet with reverence, I shall certainly bestow even the three worlds upon him. (53)
The nectar of his feet was indeed placed upon his mouth and on the head by Bali;
with a joyful heart, he (Bali) gave him the gift of wealth.
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose," he said then after giving the earth:
"O best of Brahmins, take this earth as you desire. (55)
Moreover, if you desire sovereignty, gold, diamonds and the like, various kinds of jewels, and hundreds of male and female slaves; ||56||
I give you divine wealth and other riches, palaces and mansions, as well as means of accomplishment and celestial chariots, if you so desire.
"O Lord of Gods, I, the king's wife, and whatever belongs to me—my sons, grandsons, and so forth—I give it all for your sake, whatever I may possess. (58)

Even the Supreme Person is not attained through austerities performed over infinite births; if He is obtained through His grace, what need have I for the worship of my wife and other such duties? (59)
Having uttered this, the devoted Bali fell at the feet of Vāmana;
Vāmana said, "O lord of devotees, everything is contained within three steps."
O King, I am pleased by your devotion;
today, while you look on, I shall measure out the earth with a single step in your presence.
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord abandoned that form of a young brahmin student and grew exceedingly as Vāmana, assuming a four-armed form.
Seeing Hari increasing in size, the Brahmins, sages,
and gods praised the Lord Janārdana, who had appeared in the sky.
Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O bestower of grace upon devotees!
Victory to the short one! Victory to the long one! Victory to the mendicant Vāmana! 64.
Victory to You, the bestower of divine grace; victory to You, who are accessible to Your devotee!
Victory to the Sacrifice, victory to the Oblation, victory to Agni, and victory to Acyuta! 65.
Victory to you, the seeker of victory, the giver, and the leader; victory to you whose form creates the universe!
Victory to you, O Fish; salutations to you! Victory to you, O Tortoise, the upholder of the earth! 66.
Victory to you who assume the form of the Boar! Salutations be to you, O Nṛsiṃha!
Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! Victory to you, O glorious Nārāyaṇa! Salutations be to you! 67.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd of Yaśodā; salutations again and again.
Salutations to you who are known as the husband of his wife, the Lord of Lakṣmī. ||68||
That which has been described in many ways in the scriptures but was never seen before is now being witnessed by those dwelling upon the fourteen worlds through a mere fragment of grace.
Having seen that great Vairāja form of yours, we are thrilled and delivered;
even those yogis such as Sanaka and the others praise Janārdana.
When Kṛṣṇa had ascended to the midpoint of the sky before the city of Bali,
they all stood with their faces turned upward, gazing at him as he went toward heaven.
The parasol, the staff, the deerskin, the water-pot, and the sandals—all these that were before Hari increased along with him. (72)
Having first appeared in the form of a parasol, Hari subsequently ascended upward;
the sun shines like a crest-jewel upon the head of Hari. (73)
Thereupon it grew again and appeared like a tilaka mark upon his forehead;
yet Hari continued to grow, until he became like the sun encircled by its halo.
Because Hari rose so high, he became the sun;
and having gone before him, Mahendra placed a forest garland around his neck. (75)
The earth trembles under his weight, and the host of planets dwelling in heaven shall go to destruction; those Daityas, filled with fear, behold Vāmana.
Nevertheless, Kṛṣṇa expanded; the sun-like Lord rested upon his navel-lotus, which was fifty crores of yojanas wide, encompassing the earth with its oceans and mountains.
Madhusūdana grasped with a single foot the entire world, including its oceans and continents, along with its gods, asuras, and humans.
O lotus-born one, having stepped across the entire earth, that foot became extended for an additional hundred yojanas. ||79||
The Eternal One granted divine vision to that lord of the Daityas;
and having beheld that universal form of the Lord, Bali, the sovereign of the Daityas, [was struck with wonder].
Having seen the Lord, having prostrated before him, and having praised him with hymns of praise, he attained incomparable joy, his eyes overflowing with tears of bliss.
With a voice faltering and a heart overflowing with joy, he said:
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose by beholding you, the Supreme Lord. (82)
"O Supreme Lord, you yourself take this triple world!
Then Viṣṇu, the Lord of All, [took] the second step, which is unfailing. 83.
The Infallible One extended his foot upward as far as the world of Brahmā;
yet, O lady of auspicious countenance, the foot of the Infallible One was not fully contained [within it]. (84)
Hurled with great force by Hari, he was carried to the summit of the cosmic egg;
the cosmic egg became shattered by the strike of his big toe.
When this [subterranean realm] was breached, the external waters of the three worlds entered it;
then the Gaṅgā, originating from the foot of Viṣṇu, flowed forth from that place.

The Grandfather (Brahmā), having recognized the foot of Hari as marked with the signs of the discus, lotus, and so forth, took up his water-pot and then [purified it] with the waters from that [foot].
He repeatedly washed the lotus feet of Śrī Hari;
by the power of Kṛṣṇa, that water became truly inexhaustible. ||88||
That auspicious water fell upon the peak of Mount Meru as a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), indeed flowing in the four directions for the sake of purifying the world. 89.
In the east she is celebrated as Sītā; in the south, she is known as Śālaka-nandā; in the west, she is called Cakṣuḥ; and in the north, she is considered to be named Bhadrā. (1.146.90)
And there, at that time, the Ālakanandā also became threefold by name:
in the upper region she is called Mandākinī, and in the middle she is celebrated as Gaṅgā.
When she reached Pātāla, she was considered Bhogavatī;
when she went to heaven, she is called Svardhunī; and when she reached the earth (Gā), she is Gaṅgā. ||92||
Having gone to the netherworld (pātāla), she became known by the name Tripathagā;
she was served, worshipped, beheld, touched, drunk, and plunged into.
Having kindled [the fire], it bestows liberation upon the embodied being by burning away all sins;
O lady of auspicious countenance, having seen her flowing from the center of Meru. (94)
Who could hold back her as she falls with streams of extreme velocity?
For the earth, seeing the force of that great torrent, is terrified of being torn asunder. (95)
She requested Śambhu to bear her within his matted locks;
for the sake of purifying himself, Śambhu bore her upon his head.
She remained with her matted locks for a thousand divine years;
then King Bhagīratha and Gautama, of great asceticism, [arrived]. (97)
Having propitiated Śambhu through ascetic penance, he requested Gaṅgā for the sake of [his son];
she was then granted by Śambhu to those two for the benefit of all the worlds. (98)
Brought by Gautama, she is celebrated as Gautamī;
and having come [down] with Bhagīratha, she is called Bhāgīrathī. (99)
Being drunk by Jahnu and then made manifest again by Jānu, she is celebrated as the Jāhnavī; indeed, this purifying river flows all the way to the ocean.
Having rescued the sixty thousand sons of Sagara who had been burnt in the hermitage of Kapila, he descended into the ocean.
Having grown in this manner, Viṣṇu seized two feet;
there was no space for a third, as the entire universe had been taken up.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Vāmana’s Entrance into the Sacrificial Ground, His Begging for Land, the Granting of Three Paces of Land Despite Śukra’s Prohibition, the Growth of Vāmana, and the Emergence of the Gaṅgā from the Egg-Shell with the Second Pace," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
At that time, a great and supreme dejection came upon the asuras. O Rame, he strode across the earth with a single step.
By the second [verse], the seven heavens [are attained]; for the sake of the third, nothing remains [to be taught].
Now, Brahmā, Marīci and others, and the yogins such as Sananda and others— || 2 ||
The Vedas and Upavedas, the Niyamas and Yamas, the Purāṇas and Saṃhitās, the ascetics, the sages, and the celibate students who have sublimated their vital energy; || 3 ||
They worshipped that foot of the illustrious Vāmana, which had been trodden upon by Truth,
with water, flowers, sandalwood, and divine-scented ointments.
With fragrant incense and lamps, with parched grain, unbroken rice, fruits, and the like;
with hymns of praise and shouts of "Victory!", and with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums.
With dances, instrumental music, and songs imbued with that same power,
they celebrated the great festival of this Vijaya.
But the Asuras, burning within their hearts, could not endure this at all—
the deceitful Vāmana and his false stride.
"Since falling on the side of the gods results only in death, this is our instruction.
Thus did the Daityas, Asuras, and Dānavas take up their weapons.
Armed with weapons in their hands, fierce and devoted solely to their own interests,
they fled in indignation, unwilling to obey King Bali.
Against them, Viṣṇu’s attendants stood with weapons and missiles in their hands:
Bala, Nanda, Sunanda, Prabala, and Kumuda.
Viśvaksena, Kumudākṣa, Garuḍa, and likewise Sāttvata; Jayanta, Śrutadeva, Puṣpadanta, and others as well. (11)
All those [demons], possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, slaughtered the Asura army;
Bali, however, restrained the Daityas, the foremost among the Dānavas.
"Do not fight; turn back! Time does not grant us our purpose—that god who once brought prosperity to us has now become the adversary of the dwellers of heaven."
That very same Blessed One has now turned against us;
therefore, having met with defeat, we must now abide by his teaching.
"But when the time arrives, we shall conquer through the power of Hari.
Having heard these words of Bali, the Daityas entered the netherworld (Rasātala).
Then, there Garuḍa bound Bali with the nooses of Varuṇa;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the entire universe, in place after place.
Vāmana said to him, who was bound, deprived of his kingdom, and abandoned by fortune:
"Three steps were granted; one remains there. (17)
Your kingdom has been seized by two; provide a third [share].
For one who fails to give what has been promised, residence in hell is certain. (18)
"Enjoy for some years the fruit of your deception: hell.
Thus treated with hostility, the devotee spoke to the Lord, indeed seeking to please him. (19)
My word shall not be false, for the sake of showing you favor; my body has been surrendered for the sake of the third step. (1.147.20)
Indeed, your noose and my foot would lead to the cessation of existence;
for you are a praiseworthy teacher, whose state remains beyond the perception of those with demonic natures.
O Lord, my grandfather was indeed protected by you;
likewise, Prahlāda here too has been well-guarded from the noose of worldly existence.
The noose fashioned by your hand is not a snare, but rather a means to liberation;
it is a kingdom, heavenly bliss, a kinsman, life, and even death itself—your teacher. ||23||
Liberation and bondage—whatever exists—all that you alone are for me;
I know no other who bestows either happiness, bondage, or liberation. (24)
Then, rising from his seat, Prahlāda said to Keśava:
"Delusion had taken hold of him regarding the state bestowed by you; it has now been destroyed by you."
That very grace has arisen; who other than you could liberate her?
Sandhyāvalī, the wife of Bali, spoke with palms joined in reverence to Mādhava: 26. Sandhyāvalī, the wife of Bali, spoke with palms joined in reverence to Mādhava.
"By you it was given, by you it was enjoyed, and likewise by you it was offered;
everything is merely your play, O fool—such is the grandeur of your lordship. (27)
Brahmā said: O Lord, release this devotee of the Sāttvata lineage, Bali, who has surrendered himself and who rejoices even while in bondage.
All his property has been taken away and he has even been subjected to imprisonment;
furthermore, his very body has been surrendered by him—thus, he does not deserve punishment.
Vāmana said: "If, through my illusory power (māyā), there is still the sense of 'I' and 'mine' regarding my devotee—even toward what is harmful such as a kingdom—then what grace indeed have I shown?"
If one is not deluded by birth, occupation, age, form, learning, power, wealth, and the like— this indeed is my grace upon you.
If he should become deluded, I shall surely destroy that delusion by force; even then, if my mind remains firm, he has indeed conquered the unconquerable.
"What kind of devotee is this of mine? He has now been tested by me—deprived of his wealth, fallen from his position, bound, and humiliated. (33)
Although forbidden by my guru, he did not abandon the truth for my sake;
yet, when asked for his entire property under a pretext, I took it from him by force. (34)
Nevertheless, my noble-mindedness does not abandon its state of servitude to me;
therefore, I do not forsake him who is intent upon my propitiation. (35)
I grant him the auspicious and prosperous world of Rasātala,
which belongs to all the Dānavas, the Nāgas, and even the aquatic creatures.
"I shall make you king Bali until the dissolution of all beings;
and during the Sāvarṇi Manvantara, you shall again become Indra. (37)
Whatever I favor in a person, all that I shake off;
having destroyed pride and delusion, I make him prosperous once again.
Then Bali said to the Lord:
"O Protector, such as I have obtained, the like cannot be found by anyone else; what more can I say of my great good fortune?"
"Only my head remains here for the sake of your third step;
place your foot there, and everything shall be obtained by me."
Hari, filled with compassion, placed his own foot upon his head;
having taken the third step, his heart's desire was completely fulfilled.
Having forcibly brought Bali down to the netherworld (rasātala) by means of his weight,
he installed him there in the kingdom, surrounded by his kinsmen.
Balīśa said to Vāmana: "O Blessed One, upon your lotus-soft soles, my hair-pins are indeed impaled, causing me great pain. (43)
Where is the body of the Daitya, and where is the lotus-foot of Hari?
Since pain has arisen in my foot, O Lord, grant me forgiveness. (44)
Thinking thus, Bali licked that foot with his tongue;
out of love, he repeatedly kissed the tender sole, which bestows liberation. (45)
Since all this that has been obtained is already established within that [Reality], how could there not be the licking of it, which grants the drinking of the nectar of bliss? (46)
Hari said: "Enough of this, O Balarāma! I am pleased with your devotion;
hear what you desire, for there is nothing that I cannot give to you. (47)
Bali said: "May this auspicious foot, which washes away the sins of the Daityas, always dwell in my house for the sake of perpetual worship. (48)
O Lord of Śrī, create a well for me; grant me constant protection.
May I never again fall into the state of a demon; O Master, make me Your attendant. (49)
Hari then said, "Standing at the gate, I shall provide protection;
and my Sudarśana discus shall protect the kingdom."
I do not remain without Bali, nor does Bali have a standing without me;
I stand here at your city gate to grant you my sight.
My discus shall destroy those wicked ones who transgress your command;
I, for my part, shall always protect you, along with your family and retinue.
"You shall behold me always present within your own home;
indeed, by the power of my grace, your demonic nature shall perish."
Rule over Rāsātala as your kingdom; your grandfather is in Sutala.
Prahlāda, my devotee, is in Pātāla, and Hāṭakeśvara is in Hāṭaka. (54)
Śambhu is my devotee, and I dwell here and there;
taking up my mace, Govinda dwells in the palace of Bali.
The Lord Vāmana, having assumed that very form,
dwells forever in the palace of Bali for the sake of protection.
Having accepted the worlds from Bali in the guise of a young brahmin,
Vāmana [bestowed them] upon Mahendra, who was adorned with a crown, necklaces, and a tilaka.
Having performed the auspicious rites of honor, he bestowed upon him sovereignty over the three worlds;
thereafter, the gods along with the gandharvas and the sages of great luster [congratulated him]. (58)
The fourteen classes of celestial beings honored the imperishable Indra;
then the final oblation of the sacrifice was performed, augmented by auspicious fruits.
There, Viṣṇu, acting as a performer of meritorious works through the hand of Indra,
spoke to Śukra regarding the flaw in the ritual and its proper sequence.
Since you, as the preceptor, must indeed avoid partiality, Śukra said to Hari: "In this matter, you are considered the witness of the action."
Whence could there be any inequality in that ritual action where the Lord of Sacrifice is worshipped, even if there be a defect in the mantra, the tantra, the place, the time, or the materials? (5)
Everything that has arisen shall indeed be without flaw through your direct presence;
having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the purificatory bath (avabhṛthasnāna) in the ocean.
Having performed [the rites] at the great sacred field of Somanātha, all those sacrificers,
sent by Viṣṇu, departed for their respective abodes.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, you have attained the great sovereignty over the three worlds;
likewise, Prajāpati Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara [have attained it]. (65)
Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and other eminent ones—the celestial sages, ancestors, and kings—for the sake of pleasing Kaśyapa and Aditi, and for the peace of all the worlds. (66)
The guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds indeed made Vāmana their lord, as did the sages, the ascetics, the gods, and the mountains. (67)
Of the worlds, of the world-protectors, of the dharmas, of glories, of splendors, of vows, of the duties of giving, of sacrifices, and of meritorious deeds; ||68||
He appointed Upendra as the lord for the sake of all prosperity— of auspiciousness, of splendors, and likewise of heaven and liberation.
Then everyone rejoiced after bowing down to Vāmana;
they returned to their respective capitals, while Indra [took] his younger brother Vāmana [with him].
Having led Acyuta to his own palace by way of the path of the gods, he honored him;
and having obtained sovereignty over the three worlds, he was protected by the arms of Upendra.
Mahendra rejoiced and the gods became happy, sheltered by Vāmana; thus were the gods, including Indra, well protected in ancient times by Śrī Viṣṇu.
Supreme joy arose among the gods on account of Vāmana; Vāmana set his mind upon Vāmanasthalī as his dwelling place.
In ancient times, it was here that Vāmana repeatedly requested alms;
because of the subjugation of Bali, that city was indeed destroyed by the Daityas. (74)
The Daityas likewise brought the entire city to prosperity in Rasātala;
then the blessed Lord questioned that Brāhmaṇa Garga.
Tell me, in which place should I establish the Vaiṣṇava city, where there shall be both happiness for men and liberation from the bondage of worldly existence? (76)
To the west of Raivata in Vastrāpatha is Vāmanasthalī;
a city was constructed there by Viśvakarman and placed at the disposal of the Brahmins. ||77||
In former times, her kingdom was governed by a Brahmin devoted to his wife; though it had been held by his lineage for generations, at the end of the age it passed into the hands of another.
On Mount Raivata, three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) also reside;
namely Bhadrā, Madhumatī, Urjasvatī, and Svarṇasurakṣikā. (79)
Indeed, all the wives of the Blessed One exist in the form of rivers;
by remembering their names, by bathing in them, and by giving gifts there, one is liberated.
In every kalpa, great sacrifices are performed by Bali;
sometimes on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain, and sometimes on the earth at Puṣkara.
In one instance on Mount Raivata, and in another on the bank of the Narmadā;
and in another kalpa, this Vāmana [appeared] on the bank of the Narmadā at the abode of Bali.
Having gone to the sacrifice and bound Bali, he will indeed seize the three worlds;
in this way, thousands of forms as Vāmana truly come into being.
In every kalpa and in every set of four ages, the Vāmanas are indeed remembered as distinct;
there is no end to my incarnations, of which only a mere indication is proclaimed by me.
All this regarding the majesty of Vāmana has been told to you, O beloved.
Speak, Lakṣmī, what further meritorious and heart-pleasing account do you wish to hear? (85)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Bali’s Bondage with the Noose, the Granting of the Kingdom of Rasātala, Vāmana’s Residence in Bali’s House, the Bestowal of the Three Worlds upon Indra, the Concluding Bath, and the Founding of the City named Vāmanasthalī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
What is the nature and how is the milk-vow (payovrata) and the vow for non-widowhood (avaidhavyavrata) to be performed,
by which there may be the attainment of sons and constant union with one's husband?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: It was first proclaimed by Brahmā to the high-souled Kaśyapa;
he then related it to his wife named Aditi.
Aditi indeed became the mother of sons such as Hiraṇyākṣa;
that vow, which gratifies Keśava, must be performed for twelve days.
This vow is proclaimed for the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
beginning from the first day (pratipad) until the thirteenth day of the bright half.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, and perform ablutions three times a day;
one should speak the truth, abandon enjoyments, and renounce all various types of passionate pleasures.
One should always abandon malice and violence, and perform the worship of Hari with dance, instrumental music, song, hymns of praise, and recitations of benedictions.
With the sixteen types of offerings, with sacred discourses, and likewise with acts of worship,
one should always feed five Brahmins according to one's capacity.
At the commencement, on the new moon day, one should smear the house with cow-dung and earth from after midday, and thus bring it to a state of purity.
Having personally washed her clothes and other items, a woman should perform purification;
at evening time, the observer of the vow should bathe after smearing herself with pure clay.
She should bring earth from a field or from the very source of a stream;
while taking the earth, the bride should recite the mantra in her own language.
O Goddess, you were raised up by Śrī Varāha in the form of the Earth;
I raise myself up—salutations to you—destroy my sin.
Having recited this, one should then collect the clay at home;
having bathed, one should worship Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the night.
At the beginning of the night, one should worship Hari with the sixteen types of offerings and make this formal resolve:
"From tomorrow onwards, I shall observe the milk-vow."
May that [vow] of mine for the sake of obtaining a son be fulfilled through your grace;
during that twelve-day vow, one must observe restraints such as celibacy and the like.
"I shall always protect and feed at least two Brahmins;
for twelve days, I shall perform worship for you with sixteen kinds of offerings. (16)
One should daily worship Śrī Hari with a spirit of devotion in an image, on a sacrificial mound, in the sun, in water, in fire, in the guru, or in the husband. || 16 ||
And one should offer praise in speech, auspicious and composed of meaningful words:
"Obeisance to you, the Blessed One; obeisance again and again to the Supreme Person. (17)
Salutations to Vāsudeva, who has made his abode within all things; salutations again and again to the Witness, the unmanifest, the subtle, and the manifest Person. ||18||
Salutations to the twenty-four principles, the cause of transformation;
salutations to the two-headed one, the three-footed, the four-horned, the bearer of the thread. 19.
Salutations to the seven-cubit one, to Kratu, to the one whose self consists of the three Vedas;
salutations again and again to Mahādeva, to Rudra, to the Bull.
Salutation to the Lord of living beings, who is empowered by knowledge;
salutation to the one whose treasury is gold, salutation to the self that is the vital breath of the world. ||21||
Salutations to you who possess the sovereignty of perfected yoga, and salutations to you, the performer of yoga;
salutations to the primordial god of all, and salutations to you who abide in the self.
Salutations to you, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the sage Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the glorious one whose body is dark like a blue lotus. 23.
Salutations to you, O Keśava, O Ananta; salutations to you who are clothed in yellow garments.
You are the giver of boons, the most excellent, the Lord who grants the desires of all people. 24.
The dust of your feet, when worshipped, truly bestows liberation;
the gods follow after you, and Śrī stands at your feet.
"I yearn for the fragrance of Your compassion; O Blessed One, may You be gracious to me.
Having thus praised Kṛṣṇa, the Teacher of the World, one should invoke Him. 26.

One should cause water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and a seat to be given to Hari; then, having rubbed [the image] with good oil, arka leaves, and so forth, one should offer the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should offer a bath with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar, and then cause a bath and consecration with pure water to be performed. ||28||
Having performed the wiping with a cloth, one should offer auspicious garments;
one should worship the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), the Kaustubha gem, and the essence of oil (tailasāra) and Arka.
One should worship the Lord with saffron, *abīra*, colored powders (*gulāla*), and unbroken grains (*akṣata*);
one should offer sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
One should wear ornaments, weapons, a crown, and so forth, as well as forehead marks and the like;
one should offer water for the feet, water for the face, and an arghya offering, and likewise place betel leaf in the mouth.
One should offer fruit, one should offer water, and one should perform prostrations like a staff;
one should circumambulate, give a sacrificial fee, and present the guest-offering (arghya). ||32||
"I shall perform your worship for twelve days; give me back my son. Having recited "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times, he should offer milk-porridge or something else.
One should offer oblations filled with ghee and sugar while reciting the vidyā-mantra. ||34||
Having offered milk-porridge, sweetmeats, or any other food,
one should give it to the devotees in small portions out of a spirit of grace.
One should drink [the water] oneself for the sake of one's sons, and praise the Lord with hymns; then, having placed that water upon one's head, one should dismiss the deity. ||36||
There, he should feed two excellent Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa);
then, permitted by them, the observer of the vow and the performer of the rite should indeed eat.
At the beginning of the night, having performed the concluding rites, the observer of the vow should then sleep on the ground;
he should sleep at night as a celibate student on the first day when dawn has broken.

Having bathed according to the rules during the Brāhma-muhūrta and having performed the prescribed rites, one should daily worship [the deity] in the morning after having likewise bathed him according to the injunctions. ||29||
Until the completion of the vow, one should eat only a single meal for the sake of the god Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa; it should consist of milk-preparations and nothing else.
He should spend the day with devotion and the night in recitation and sleep;
he should constantly offer oblations into the fire and also feed Brāhmaṇas.
Thus one should perform this daily for twelve days while observing the milk-vow;
accompanied by the worship of Hari, one should observe this vow of subsisting solely on milk.

The worship of Hari, fire-offerings, ritual adoration, and the feeding of holy men should be performed starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the thirteenth day of the bright half. 43.
Devoted to Kṛṣṇa, both the husband and the wife should perform the bathing and other rites for Śrī Hari on the morning of the thirteenth lunar day.
One should have everything performed according to the rules by Brāhmaṇas who are experts in the ritual procedure;
one should perform the great worship and must not practice stinginess regarding wealth. 45.
Having cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the fire of the milk-boiling rite for one desiring oblations,
he should worship Kṛṣṇa with that boiled offering into the mouth of the fire.
One should offer an oblation (naivedya) to Nārāyaṇa, which bestows great satisfaction;
one should greatly gratify the preceptor, who is learned in the Vedas and endowed with knowledge. 47.
One should also satisfy the officiating priests with gifts such as cows, ornaments, and garments;
and one should feed them with many kinds of sweet foods, sacrificial fees, and other offerings.

One should joyfully feed other Brahmins, as well as virtuous men and women; and one should offer gifts to the Brahmin, the teacher, the preceptor, and the virtuous man and woman, according to their merit. 49.
And he should give excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), as well as to others who have arrived;
he should also gratify those who have come as guests and even the outcaste dog-cookers (aśvapāka).
By giving food, water, and other necessities to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others, one should consider that they are satisfied and thereby Viṣṇu is satisfied. (51)

Having given cows, horses, ants, and so forth, one should eat together with one's kinsmen, while proclaiming names, recounting the stories of Kṛṣṇa, offering hymns of praise, and reciting prayers. (52)
One should spend the remainder of the day in the supreme service of the Person;
this is declared by me to you as the milk-vow (payovrata). ||53||
In the preparation of milk-porridge, rice or wild millet (nīvāra) are considered auspicious.
One should not consume a diet of vegetables, for one who eats vegetables becomes dark-complexioned.
And he should eat milk-porridge; by that, offspring radiant with strength will be born.
Afterwards, at the final oblation of the vow, he himself [should approach] on even nights.
The wife, however, should lie down with him; thus a powerful son shall be born.
She should approach her wife on even nights; a daughter shall be born who bestows success.
O Lakṣmī, this auspicious vow, the essence of austerity, bestows sons;
it must be performed by both husband and wife together in order to yield its fruit. (57)
Otherwise, it would not indeed yield fruit; rather, its result would be uncertain.
O beloved, listen as I also describe the vow of non-widowhood (avaidhavya-vrata). ||58||
The daughter of Mount Raivata, Raivatī, dwells eternally on Mount Raivatācala to the west of Dāmodara. (59)
There indeed lies the Raivatī-kuṇḍa, which destroys all sins;
it ensures that women do not suffer widowhood and likewise serves as the cause for progeny.
That water bestows good fortune upon all women;
by bathing there, a woman shall become endowed with many sons and wealth. (61)
She shall not suffer widowhood; her good fortune shall be incomparable.
Having bathed, fruits, saffron, and kajjala should be offered.
The Gaurī-thread should be given, as well as betel-leaf and flowers;
a yellow garment should be offered, and likewise a bodice and a staff.
Having placed fruits in bamboo vessels, as well as sweet foods,
together with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), for the virtuous and faithful women.
Having bathed in the morning, one should then behold Raivatī;
furthermore, her worship must be performed with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
One should perform this praise for the sake of obtaining a son and also for the sake of avoiding widowhood;
O ever-compassionate Goddess Raivati, show me your grace! (66)
"May I always remain free from widowhood, likewise possessed of sons and grandsons, and may I be endowed with wealth and grain; O auspicious one, grant me my desire. (67)
Having thus offered praise and prostrated, and having beheld Dāmodara during the fifteen-day period of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, [he remained there].
One should always go to one's own home; there, food consisting of milk-rice, as well as sweetmeats, side dishes, and likewise items cooked in ghee, should be eaten.
She may dwell together with her husband, for that is not forbidden;
likewise, she need not observe fasts, nor does she require any other form of worship.
The observer of the vow performs the ritual bathing of the sacrificial pit during the viewing of the Raivata hymn;
he also gives gifts such as the aforementioned fruits and beholds Dāmodara. (7.1)
This vow, which increases good fortune when performed every morning for fifteen days, has thus been shown to you as that which brings about the state of non-widowhood. (72)
"Then, O Mahālakṣmī, what else do you wish to hear from me?
Lakṣmī said: "O ocean of mercy, [tell me] of the holy fords on Mount Raivata. (73)
And tell me what other beings dwell by their side;
how powerful they are, O Keśava—I wish to hear this. (74)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Milk-Vow that Grants Sons and the Vow for Non-Widowhood," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe to you the holy places situated on Mount Raivata, which are endowed with the fruit of pilgrimage and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I shall also describe to you those sacred fords (tīrthas) of Vastrāpatha that were established by him, which bestow both heaven and liberation. || 2 ||
In the former Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Bhoja in Kānyakubja;
having approached him from the forest, a forest-guardian spoke this to him.
"O King, a wonder has been seen by me as I was wandering in the forest just now;
I saw a woman with the face of a deer who had joined a herd of deer. (4)
Then that King of the Bhojas said to his commander-in-chief:
"We must go this very moment to where that young woman resides."
Let the cavalry and infantry go forth and surround the forest and the mountain;
for that woman, wearing the guise of a female, is indeed a doe who must be brought under control.
The Bhoja king surrounded the mountain with his infantry;
however, the monkey-faced goddess, leaping about, was held back by the army.
The king brought the female deer from Kānyakubja;
upon seeing her, a sense of wonder arose among everyone in the royal palace.
The king bathed her with divine perfumes and ointments;
then, in a secluded and solitary place, the king spoke to her as she was beautifully adorned.
"Who are you? Whose daughter are you? And for what reason, O deer-faced one, do you not speak even when questioned?"—though thus asked, she neither ate nor drank. (1.149.10)
Then Bhoja, having paid due homage to the astrologers, the experts in mantras, the physicians, and the tantrikas, spoke: "Behold, O twice-born ones! (11)
How indeed does she have the body of a woman, and how is her face like that of a deer? How will she come to have a human voice and countenance? (12)
The Brahmins said: "In Kurukṣetra, there is a brahmin named Sārasvata;
he knows the matter exactly as it happened, and he will tell it."
Bhoja approached that brahmin who was performing such penance;
having paid his respects, as Bhoja sat down, that twice-born one spoke to him.
"Let us go where that woman is; she herself will tell us.
Having said this, the brahmin Sārasvata went to where the woman was.
Having smeared the ground and arranged a svastika, having placed a water-filled jar and having set out the fire-rite (agnikārya). || 16 ||
Having placed Indra, the gods, and the guardians of the quarters within the ritual pitcher (kalaśa),
and having offered oblations into the fire and prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), he performed the worship of the planets.
He himself performed the consecration and consecrated that woman;
by means of divine vision, she then spoke of many of her previous births.
O Bhoja, in the seventh previous birth, you were a king in the Kaliṅga country together with me; I was the queen born in Vaṅga. (19)
You are evil-minded, of improper conduct, and devoid of compassion and righteousness; you are a destroyer of cows, the earth, Brahmins, gurus, the Vedas, the gods, and the scriptures.
Having conspired with the subjects, you, the oppressor of the world, were slain;
taking my dead husband, I entered the fire and died along with him. (21)
If a wife, taking her deceased husband with her, enters the fire, both of them are indeed honored in heaven until the dissolution of all beings. 22.
Then, in the land of Mālava, you became a Brahmin who was an atheist;
I, however, became your devoted wife, a Brāhmaṇī.
When you abandoned the gold and wealth you had earned and met with death, I did not die along with you out of greed; rather, I died at a later time. (24)
"You were indeed a white serpent, and I was a brahmin maiden; I was married to another brahmin, and you bit him. (25)
"I have become a widow, and you, the serpent, have been killed by people;
having bestowed widowhood upon me, both the brahmin and the serpent are dead. (26)
Having died, you were then born as a crocodile in the Godāvarī; at that time, I too came together with people to visit the holy site of Bhīmeśvara. ||27||
While I had entered the water to bathe, I was indeed seized by a crocodile;
the crocodile was then struck down by the people with blows from spears and other weapons. (28)
At that time, I met my death by the fangs of sea-monsters;
you were then born as a hunter, and I became a Śabarī in the forest. (29)
Those for whom death comes from fire, water, a serpent, an elephant, a lion, or even a horse; or from anger, or from boils—they are destined for hell.
The killer of one's own self, the killer of an embryo, the killer of a woman, the killer of a Brahmin, the false witness, the seller of a maiden, and the one who utters a false accusation; || 31 ||
He who sells a Vedic sacrifice, he who drinks liquor, the Brahmin who betrays the king, the thief of gold, and he who destroys the livelihood of those who follow the path of Brahman; || 32 ||
The cow-killer, the one who misappropriates a deposit, and he who violates the boundary of a village—
all these go to hell, as does the woman who deceives her husband.
Having died from disease as a Śabarī, I was then born as a female curlew in the forest;
once, out of desire, I became intent on sporting with a male curlew. (34)
At that moment, the hunter struck down the crane with an arrow;
and the crane then cursed him: "Become cruel in the great forest! (35)
Deprived of women, you shall become a tiger-like being and suffer again and again;
thereafter, you became a tiger on Mount Raivata.
Having died by the power of fate, Krauñcī became a deer on Mount Raivata;
to the west of Bhaveśvara, however, was the water of the Svarṇarakṣā river.
I had come there to drink water when I was seen by a lion;
out of fear of him, I leaped up and fell upon the opposite bank. (38)
Just then, the lion leaped up and fell forcefully before me;
meanwhile, I turned around and prepared to leap as well. || 39 ||
My head was caught between two kīcaka reeds standing in the water at my side;
while swimming between the two kīcakas, it became like a noose.
My body was in the midst of the water, while my head was caught within a bamboo thicket;
seized by a lion at the neck, it was torn away by his fangs. (41)
Just as the lion was dragging my body out from the midst of the water,
I slipped away on foot by means of a clump of *śaivala* grass and fell back into the water.
Because the water was bottomless and thick with moss on all sides, that lion was unable to emerge; he met his death.
A lion that had died in the Svarṇarakṣā water became King Bhoja;
by the power of that sacred site (tīrtha), his status as a king was brought about. 44.
For this is my seventh birth as a king, well-known as Bhoja; my head hangs upon the lineage, while my body remains submerged in the water. (45)
There, my body was shattered in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, but my face did not fall; the skin and flesh remained fixed upon the head. (46)
Consequently, I was born from the womb of a doe in human form;
however, because my face as a deer did not fall into the water when I was born, [I have this mark]. (47)
I am not the daughter of Hariṇa, but rather the daughter of the noble sage Uddālaka;
once, when I had come to bathe for the protection of my gold, [the king seized me]. (48)
At that time, the yoginīs arrived at that very place to bathe;
then, the sage was repeatedly tested there by the yoginīs. (49)
"What kind of brahmacārī is this— is he firm or not?"— saying this,
she seized him by the neck with her arms and embraced him again and again.
They sported in many ways, yet the sage did not undergo any change of state.
Then, at that time, there was a certain yoginī named Kāmadāhā.
Having entered within the body of Uddālaka by the power of his yogic strength,
Kama became terrified and fled from the body of the sage.
Otherwise, that Yoginī situated within would cause burning;
due to the arousal of Kāmadeva by the heat of the Yoginī, [the practitioner] would be consumed. (53)
And due to the force of the onset of youth, as well as from his playthings and the like,
although he was paralyzed at that time, he fell into the water by the force of his momentum.
Along with the current, the mineral element went to the Nārāyaṇa lake;
there, a certain doe drank the water mixed with that mineral.
By the force of my past karma, my residence was within her womb;
thus I, Mṛgānanā, was born as the daughter of the sage Uddālaka. (56)
"I have been raised by the yoginīs, for I am the daughter of the yoginīs;
I am a yoginī with the face of a deer, both divine and likewise human. (57)
"O King, my seventh birth likewise exists for you;
indeed, this sage Sārasvata knows it through the power of yoga.
Having previously entered the fire and died along with you, [I shall do so] again in the seventh [birth]."
"May my husband not exist without you; this is what I have requested at the point of death. (59)
Then, O Indra among kings, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky:
"This king is a man of evil deeds; he is violent, cruel, and exceedingly greedy."
One who is not proficient in the Vedas and Shastras, devoid of compassion and righteousness, lustful, arrogant, highly wrathful, and abandoned by truth and right conduct— (61)
That evil-minded one knows neither the gods, nor his guru, nor the Brahmins;
he honors neither the virtuous men nor the virtuous women, being excessively arrogant.
One who speaks untruth, one of wicked soul, a destroyer of the dharma of sacrifice, a consumer of raw flesh, a reviler of Viṣṇu, and a robber of livelihoods— [these are the ones who must be avoided].
One who visits a prostitute is deprived of the merit of bathing, giving, and religious rites; having attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, how great indeed is his sin? (64)
Such a sinner as he cannot even be counted;
