for although you are a virtuous woman, you have indeed been burnt by him.
Therefore, for seven births you shall be joined with him;
however, due to his great sins, heaven shall not be his.
Having first experienced the fruit of his evil deeds, he will later possess a kingdom;
and for him, this eighth birth shall be a birth among the gods.
"Then, having become human, you shall afterwards go to heaven.
Having said this, she ceased speaking; I remember everything through the power of yoga.
I even have a skull-bowl kept upon a bamboo pole;
if someone goes to Vastrāpatha and offers up their head, [I shall accept it]. (69)
"O King, in the waters of Svarṇarakṣā, my face shall become human;
though I am one with a human face, I appear to others as having the face of a deer. (1.149.70)
"Moreover, this face of mine, shaped like a deer's, is obscured by the shadow of my sins.
Having heard this, the Bhoja king [sent] the doorkeeper to that place.
Sent by him, he saw that the deer's head, impaled upon a bamboo pole, was lying upon the waters of the Svarṇarekhā in the great forest. (72)
When she was seized and cast into the waters of the Svarṇarekhā,
her auspicious face, which resembled the moon, appeared within the palace of King Bhoja.
It became human and divine, with eyes as beautiful as lotus petals,
exceedingly handsome, with long hair, long ears, and auspicious teeth.

With a neck like a conch shell, the fragrance of a lotus, and endowed with all the auspicious marks—neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a Kinnara woman [possesses such beauty]. (75)
Just as that beautiful woman had then been born with the nature of a sacred ford (tīrtha),
so was that beautiful woman married by Bhojarāja.
That queen Bhojasundarī, renowned as Mṛgānanā—whence did she come to become the chief queen by the wise King Bhoja? (77)
The most excellent of countries, the most excellent of mountains;
the supreme of sacred fields, the supreme of forests. (78)
The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Revā, and Svarṇarekhā reside within its waters;
there dwell Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and all the gods beginning with Rudra. (79)
Nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas are established in this field;
having bathed in the rivers that protect Svarṇa and in the lake of Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, having bathed at the Mṛgītīrtha and in the pool named Dāmodara,
and likewise having bathed in the Revatīkuṇḍa, one shall attain heaven and liberation.
The holy Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, and Svarṇarūpiṇī have come and stand upon the river; golden leaves are seen there. (82)
The Sarasvatī shines with golden forms, the Gaṅgā with silver leaves, and the Yamunā with copper leaves within the waters of the rivers. 8.3.
Thus, that river named Suvarṇarakṣā, endowed with golden streaks and bestowing liberation, flows upon the Raivata mountain.
A slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a destroyer of an embryo, and one who violates the teacher’s bed—
by bathing in the waters of Svarṇarekhā, such a person is liberated from all sins.
And even those such as insects and moths that die in the waters of Svarṇarekhā, as well as trees, creepers, shrubs, and bushes—they too attain the supreme goal. (86)
Having praised the Brahmin Sārasvata, Bhoja spoke these words:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Sūrya, Indra, Agni, and the hosts of Maruts—" [87]
O Lord, gratified by your celibacy and austerity,
[we have come] with you and also with me for the sake of a journey to Mount Raivata.
If there is compassion, then you must go, and I shall have my purpose fulfilled.
What is to be taken? What is to be eaten? What is to be given? And what is not to be given? (89)
Fasting at sacred fords, ritual bathing, the sequence of procedures for twilight baths,
worship, sleep, and recitation— explain all of this concisely regarding the night.
Thus questioned by the king, the son of Sarasvatī explained that procedure;
the brahmin recounted the entire fruit of the gift and so forth exactly as it is.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Svarṇarakṣā River through the Account of Seven Births of King Bhoja and His Wife Mṛgānanā in the Former Kṛta Yuga," within the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; thereafter the great sage, the Brahmin Sārasvata, spoke to him regarding the power of the pilgrimage to Mount Raivata in Saurāṣṭra.
When one must go to Mount Raivataka in the land of Saurāṣṭra, then,
having observed the strength of Jupiter and performed the libation for the Sun, [one should depart].
Having placed another [calculation] on the left and the back, and having observed the purity of the day,
one should examine the Moon, the Ascendant, and the planets as being powerful from the perspective of the birth sign.
Having perceived an auspicious omen, people should indeed set out;
[the asterisms] Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are well-adorned for this purpose.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Puṣya, Mūla, and Hasta are always auspicious for the giving away of a daughter, for journeys, and for rites such as consecrations.
Venus and the Moon, situated in the birth sign or in the second house, bestow auspicious results;
as do Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and the Moon in the third house.
Mars, Saturn, the Moon, and the Sun [are situated] in the fourth house; Mercury is excellent in the fourth;
Venus and Jupiter are in the fifth, joined with the Moon and Ketu. (7)
Mars, the Sun, and Mercury are excellent in the sixth house; Jupiter and the Moon in the seventh;
Venus and Mercury in the eighth; and Jupiter situated in the ninth is auspicious. (8)
The Sun, Saturn, and the Moon are in the tenth house; all the planets are in the eleventh house;
and Mercury as well as Venus shall be in the twelfth house, bestowing happiness.
The crocodile is best with the lion; the ram is most excellent with the virgin;
the fish is [best] with Libra; and the crab with Aquarius. (1.150.10)
A Bull with an Archer, and a Scorpio with a Gemini—this is the "Six-Eight" configuration which leads to affection; of this there is no doubt. (1.1)
Mercury is known as gentle, Jupiter as swift, Venus as mild, the Sun as steady,
Saturn as cruel, Mars as fierce, and the Moon as even-tempered.
Kṣatriyas desiring victory should set out under swift [nakṣatras], enter [the battle] under mild and fixed [nakṣatras], and fight under harsh and fierce [nakṣatras]. (13)
The consecration of a king and the fire-ritual are recommended on a Monday; one should also undertake the construction of houses and other such works when the Moon is in Libra or Libra’s degree.
Command of armies, heroic combat, and the practice of weapons are prescribed for Mars; while the accomplishment of tasks, counsel, and military expeditions are prescribed for Mercury. (15)

Recitation, worship of the gods, clothing and ornaments for the guru, the giving away of a daughter in marriage, and mounting an elephant—these are the auspicious times for women during the period of Venus. (16)
Establishing a deity, entering a house, and tethering an elephant are auspicious under Saturn; the Moon, situated in the seventh house or in any of the upacaya houses, is auspicious in all matters.
In the bright fortnight, the moon on the second, fifth, and likewise the ninth day,
being worshipped by people, is regarded like a spiritual preceptor.
If [the Moon] is situated in the birth sign, it brings satisfaction; in the second, there is no peace;
in the third, royal honor; and in the fourth, the arrival of quarrels. (19)
By the fifth lunar day, there will indeed be the acquisition of a woman;
by the sixth, the arrival of wealth and grain; and by the seventh, pleasure and honor.
In the eighth house, there is danger to life; in the ninth, the accumulation of wealth;
in the tenth, the accomplishment of one's purpose; and in the eleventh, certain victory.
With the twelfth lunar day, which is the Moon, death itself occurs; of this there is no doubt. The first day of the dark fortnight is excellent when conjoined with the son of the Moon (Mercury). 22.
The third [lunar day] is auspicious with the son of the Earth (Mars), the fourth with Saturn;
the fifth would be auspicious with Jupiter, and the sixth with Mars and Venus. (23)
The seventh [tithi] is auspicious with Mercury, the eighth with Mars and the Sun, the ninth with Monday, and the tenth is auspicious on Thursday. (24)
On the eleventh day, Jupiter is pure; on the twelfth, Mercury again;
on the thirteenth, Venus and Mars; and on the fourteenth, Saturn is most excellent. (25)
The full moon day and the new moon day are most auspicious when Jupiter is present;
likewise, the Sun in Mūla, the Moon in Śravaṇa, and Mars in the latter Bhādrapada are excellent. (26)
Budha is in Kṛttikā, Guru in Punarvasu, Śukra in Pūrvaphalgunī, and Śanaiścara in Svāti. (27)
These are the "Amṛta-yogas," which accomplish all undertakings:
when the Sun is in Hasta, Jupiter in Puṣya, and Mercury in Anurādhā, they are auspicious. (28)
Rohiṇī is most excellent on Saturday; the Moon-day (Monday) is indeed auspicious with the Moon (Monday).
Revatī is most excellent on Friday; Aśvinī is auspicious on Tuesday. (29)
Indeed, among these, the applications of yoga are destroyers of all defects and bestowers of success in one's undertakings; therefore, one should commence one's work therein.
Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Revatī, Mūla, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Hasta, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā—these are said to be most auspicious for setting out on a journey. (31)
The Yoginīs also must be awakened; they cause extreme suffering when encountered face-to-face.
Brahmāṇī is stationed in the east on the first lunar day (pratipad).
Māheśvarī is in the north on the second and tenth lunar days;
Vārāhī is situated in the south on the fifth and thirteenth lunar days.
On the sixth and the fourteenth [lunar days], Indrāṇī is situated in the west;
on the seventh and the full moon day, Cāmuṇḍā is in the region of the wind (the northwest).
On the eighth lunar day conjoined with the new moon, she is within the range of Mahālakṣmīśa;
on the eleventh and the third, she is Vaiṣṇavī in the southeast corner.
On the twelfth and the fourth lunar days, as well as in the southwest, one should not engage in going or other such activities in the presence of the Yoginīs. (36)
The fourth, the sixth, the eighth, and likewise the ninth;
the new moon day, the full moon day, the twelfth, and the fourteenth. ||37||
The Sun burns the twelfth lunar day, and the Moon burns the eleventh;
Mars burns the tenth, and Mercury burns the ninth. (38)
The Jīva [Saturn] burns the eighth lunar day; Bhārgava [Venus] would burn the seventh;
the Son of the Sun [Mars] would burn the sixth. Indeed, there is no [inauspiciousness] regarding journeys and other such activities on these days.
One should avoid setting out on a journey from afar on the ninth lunar day, as well as on the fourteenth and eighth days, and on Wednesday.
The sixth lunar day [is auspicious] in Aries and Cancer; the eighth in Virgo and Gemini;
the fourth in Taurus and Aquarius; and the twelfth in Capricorn and Libra. (41)
The tenth lunar day in Scorpio and Leo, and the fourteenth in Sagittarius and Pisces—these are "burnt" (inauspicious) days; indeed, living human beings should not travel on them.
The three stars of Viśākhā are presided over by Āditya; the three stars of Pūrvāṣāḍhā by Śaśin; the third star of Dhaniṣṭhā by Bhauma; and the three stars of Revatī by Budha.
On a Thursday, one should avoid the triad beginning with Rohiṇī; likewise on a Friday, the triad beginning with Puṣya;
and on a Saturday, the triad of Uttarā-phalgunī.
This is the yoga of portents; it brings about death, disease, and so forth.
Five ghaṭikās are proclaimed for Viṣkambha, and seven for Śūla. ||45||
Six [muhūrtas] in Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, nine in Vyāghāta and Vajra;
and day by day in Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti. (46)
These are indeed joined with death; one should avoid all ritual actions during them.
So too are Viśākhā, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Ārdrā, and Bharaṇī. (47)
The asterisms Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, and Citrā bring death on a journey;
therefore, having carefully considered this, one's departure shall become a source of happiness. (48)
A full water-pot, a brahmin, a courtesan, white grains, a mirror,
curd, clarified butter, honey, parched grain, flowers, dūrvā grass, and white unbroken rice.
A bull, a lordly elephant, a horse, a blazing fire, gold,
wool, and various kinds of ripe fruits.
A woman with sons, a lamp, an excellent jewel, a pearl, a garland of flowers, fresh meat, and sandalwood. (5.1)
Indeed, these auspicious objects are seen ahead:
a Brahmin, a maiden, a corpse, a cow, a conch shell, a drum, the earth,
a flute, women, and a full water-pot— these are auspicious when seen during a journey.
On the left side, the camel, donkey, mongoose, water-pot, and corpse of Śiva are auspicious. ||23||
The royal swan, the peacock, the wagtail, the parrot, the cuckoo, the pigeon, the śaṅkhacilla bird, and the cakravāka are auspicious. (54)
A black antelope, a fragrant cow, yaks, white chowries, and a cow with her calf— these auspicious items, used as banners, are placed on the right.
Cotton, medicinal herbs, oils, cooked food, charcoal, and snakes;
a woman with disheveled hair, red garlands, and a naked person—these are seen as inauspicious at the beginning of the day. (56)
In the southeast it causes hiccup; in the south it is considered to bring grief;
in the southwest it causes agitation; and in the west it bestows sweet food. (57)
In the northwest it is said to bestow wealth; in the north, it causes strife;
and in the northeast, it grants death—one should thus understand the auspicious and inauspicious results. (58)
One should always go to a sacred ford (tīrtha); indeed, all months are auspicious, and all lunar days (tithis) are excellent for bathing, giving gifts, worship, and other such rites.
Departure for a pilgrimage to sacred fords in the springtime is said to be the best;
having restrained one's senses, become pure, bathed, and conquered the organs of perception. || 1.150.60 ||
Those people who, having abandoned elephants, horses, and chariots, travel on foot,
go to the abode of Kṛṣṇa by means of a celestial vehicle drawn by swans.
Whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for, or by subsisting on alms-food, or on water, or by subsisting on fruit; ||62||
By means of fasting, rigorous penance, or subsisting on a diet of vegetables, people perform pilgrimages; for them, there are eternal worlds.
Or else, fanned and honored by hosts of goddesses, he goes to heaven;
traveling on foot without shoes, the performer of the journey proceeds to the solar orb.
Having abandoned mother, father, country, brothers, kinsmen, and relatives, as well as village, land, and home, and having practiced restraint of the senses; |||65||
For that person who, having received the Vaiṣṇava initiation, goes to Raivata,
there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the power of Dāmodara.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Auspicious and Inauspicious Planets, Constellations, Days, Yoginīs, Omens, and so forth, at the Beginning of the Pilgrimage Departure," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Sārasvata spoke to the king, the bull among the Bhojas: "There is delicious, delightful food and various auspicious drinks. (1)
Vessels worthy of worship, flowers, ritual implements,
garments fit for giving, and fragrant sandalwood.
That person who places various lotuses adorned with gold, silver, and other ornaments upon his shoulder and proceeds on foot; || 3 ||
And having offered these at the front of the horse, one shall obtain inexhaustible merit:
water from the Gaṅgā, honey, clarified butter, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Carrying guggulu resin, bilva leaves, and likewise dhattūra flowers upon his shoulder, he worshipped the God while walking on foot.
One who goes to Bhavanātha should likewise report [his arrival] upon seeing him;
having bathed in the Svarṇanadī, he should worship Dāmodara.
Completely liberated from all bonds, he shall indeed attain Kailāsa;
he becomes a liberated Gaṇa for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts.
Whether with wife, friends, sons, brothers, virtuous people, kinsmen, or other well-wishers, he who goes [to the deity] while remembering the god [attains his goal]. || 8 ||
Accompanied by that maṇḍala, he goes to heaven,
having fashioned the auspicious form of the deity as well-established and seated upon a chariot, like the primordial sun.
He worshipped her with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, as well as with saffron,
various flowers, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
With songs, dances, instrumental music, laughter, and various types of graceful movements,
[they offered] the earth, gold, cows, water, food, and garments.
Offering pleasing words at Tṛṇendhana, he proceeds to Raivata;
then, having gone to Dāmodara and likewise to Bhaveśvara, he worships them.
In the lake at Svarṇavatī or in the pool fashioned by Raivata,
he bathes, recites prayers, worships Govinda, and gives food in abundance.
In that place, the person who bestows gifts and even his entire possessions is seized by the hand of a celestial nymph in the Nandana grove.

Having gone there and performed the bath, twilight prayers, worship, and other rites at the sacred ford according to the words of the Brahmins, he enjoys auspicious pleasures as long as the moon and stars endure.
Then, with faith, one should employ darbha grass, sesame seeds, and sacrificial food (haviṣya),
as well as agastya, bhṛṅgarāja, and auspicious hundred-petaled flowers.
Camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, saffron, and a leaf of tulasī—when these are offered at a sacred ford with a formal resolve by mortals, that merit becomes infinite. || 17 ||
One should indeed offer balls of food the size of bilva fruits at sacred sites,
along with betel leaves, fruits, offerings, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water.
Within the month, during the bright fortnight, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
under the Gajacchāyā yoga, on the thirteenth lunar day, or when wealth has been obtained— on these occasions, O best of the twice-born.
One should perform the Śrāddha rite at home for the sake of liberation from the debt to the ancestors;
however, it is a hundred times more meritorious when performed by a river that flows to the ocean.
Then, [the merit] is infinitely greater at a temple in the presence of a deity,
at the holy sites of Prabhāsa and Puṣkara, and at Gayā, the place where the funeral cakes are offered.
Furthermore, one should perform the śrāddha at Prayāga, at the Gomatī, at Bhāva, at Dāmodara, at the Narmadā, at Tapatī, and at Trivikrama.
And likewise at the Svarṇarakṣā river, at the Nārāyaṇa lake,
at the Ojasvatī and the Bhadrā, as well as on the bank of the Śatrujit.
If a person performs a śrāddha ceremony at the edge of the Vāmanasthala Kuṇḍa, his ancestors, liberated from all sins, attain the supreme goal. (24)
Having attained the supreme continuity and enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
the performer of ancestral rites ascends a divine celestial chariot and goes to liberation.

In sacrifices such as the birth-rite (jātakarman) and others, in marriage, in domestic rites, at the commencement of the installation of a deity, and in works such as the digging of wells and tanks; ||26||
All the deities are satisfied and the ancestors of men rejoice;
when the Vṛddhi-śrāddha is performed at home, every auspiciousness arises.
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, pride, and the like; deceit, envy, backbiting, lack of discernment, and lack of reflection. (28)
Egoism, arbitrariness, fickleness, and greed; the exertion for unjust means, negligence, and malicious violence. (29)
Laziness, procrastination, and consorting with another's wife—
these faults must always be abandoned by a person who travels to sacred fords.
He shall indeed be an ornament to the land, the region, and the city;
being illustrious, learned, and of noble birth, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.

Bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, libations to the ancestors, ancestral rites, and worship of the deity—all these become effective for one who has abandoned all faults. (32)
Rising again and again, one should bathe and likewise worship Hari and Hara;
one should speak the truth, act for the benefit of others, and give gifts according to one's ability.
Fear of slandering others, avoidance of the wives of others, not adopting the faults of heretics, and the joyful service of the virtuous; ||34||
One should not harbor even in one's mind anything unpleasant toward one's father, mother, or teacher;
a householder should give medicine and vegetables to those who ask for them.
On the eleventh, fifteenth, fourteenth, and eighth lunar days; on the new moon day, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the sun's passage into a new sign, and during eclipses; || 36 ||
On the day of Vaidhṛti, on the anniversary of the death of one's father or mother, on an auspicious day,
or on the first day of a Yuga or Manvantara, a great festival should be celebrated at home.
One should go on pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha), where merit becomes a hundredfold;
one must conquer the senses and avoid liquor and gambling. (38)
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, worship of the gods, honoring the twice-born, and the worship of virtuous men and women must be performed, for they bestow inexhaustible merit. (39)
Even a single cow, adorned with garments and ornaments, yielding milk, provided with a cloth, young, accompanied by her calf, should be given to a virtuous twice-born man.

Excellent food and fine delicacies should be given to the virtuous man, and garments, ornaments, and other articles to the virtuous woman; such things should be given so that there may indeed be mutual satisfaction.
One who gives a single cow is liberated from all sins, even if he has been most wicked throughout seven births and the lowest of men in this present life. (4.2)
When he is led bound along the path of Yama by the servants of death, then the cow approaches and protects him as her own son. (43)
Having conquered those messengers from afar by a mere utterance of "Hum," the cow takes her donor and indeed goes to the abode of Hari.
The bull is said to be Dharma; at a sacred ford, the gift of a bull should be performed. Dharma protects and leads the donor to heaven. ||45||

Even a mere morsel of alms should be given at a holy place by those living as householders; likewise, food prepared in vessels such as jars or leaves, along with an umbrella, sandals, and a water-pot.
By giving a ring and garments, a man goes to heaven;
likewise by giving drink to one afflicted by fatigue and thirst, and food to one afflicted by hunger. (47)
Clothing should be given to one who is naked; such goddesses lead him to heaven. Food should be constantly given according to one's ability, drenched in ghee. (48)
There is great suffering from hunger in the world; food is considered its medicine.
Through that, it attains peace, and therefore the gift of food is supreme. 49.
Food, clothing, fruit, water, buttermilk, vegetables, ghee, honey, leaves, flowers, as well as sandals, a patched garment, a staff, and a water-pot.
An umbrella, an alms-bowl, as well as knowledge, a book, and the worship of the gods; a maiden, a kusha-grass mat, seeds, medicinal herbs, and houses. (51)
The jewel, the field, the sacrificial vessel, the yoga-band, and the sandals;
the black antelope skin, the gift of wisdom, and the narrative discourse on the teaching of Dharma. ||52||
Having gone to a sacred ford (tīrtha), much should be given by him, so that great spiritual merit may arise;
having brought about the destruction of all sins, the donor goes to the abode of Hari.
Whatever fruit may accrue to men from sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, or from the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā, that same fruit shall be obtained upon seeing Dāmodara on this earth.
On the eleventh day, having performed his ablutions, he should be intent on the worship of the deity;
having bathed with sacred water and having consecrated the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having worshipped with water mixed with saffron, agallochum, sandalwood, and camphor,
he should then worship with fragrant lotuses.
One should thoroughly fumigate the garment and the sacred thread with many bright jasmine flowers and tulasī leaves, and likewise burn incense.
One should offer a lamp with ghee, or even with oil in the absence of ghee;
one should also offer various kinds of food offerings, as well as fruit and betel leaf.
One should perform worship of the temple with the offering of banners and so forth;
then one should give a cow along with its calf, which carries one across the ocean of worldly existence.

Then, having performed a circumambulation accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments, as well as the recitation of the Vedas and Purāṇas, and with commentaries and divine narratives; || 1.151.60 ||
One should perform a vigil before the deity on grounds illuminated by lamps,
[constructing] seven mountains made of the seven grains and provided with lamps.
One should provide fruits, betel, and cooked food as offerings to learned, Vedic-scholarly, peaceful Brahmins, as well as to virtuous men. (62)
The Vaiṣṇava narrative should indeed be heard by virtuous women and householders;
likewise, the vigil (jāgaraṇa) should be performed by those free from passion, hatred, and other such afflictions.
Having kept a vigil at night, when the solar orb has risen,
one should perform the morning twilight ritual after bathing, and then carry out the midday rites.

Having gratified the gods, the ancestors, and human beings according to the prescribed rites, and having performed the ritual bath for the ancestors, one should give gifts according to one's capacity. ||65||
Having worshipped the Lord Dāmodara with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
one should then again perform a bath in the waters of the Raivatī-kuṇḍa.
One should indeed behold the image of Rādhā and others in the waters of the Golden River (Svarṇadī),
and from there proceed to the Arohaṇa step-well of Hanumān.
One should indeed perform the ritual viewing and drink water;
then once again, one should undertake the ascent of the mountain, or else proceed toward the city.
And having arranged for the spectacle of the three-striding leap, he provided various gifts, including food and all other necessities in every way. (69)
Having given and performed [the rite], the performer of the pilgrimage (tīrthakāraka) should depart for his own abode.
Thus has been described to you the supreme pilgrimage-rite that bestows liberation. ||1.151.70||
Having heard this, King Bhoja also went to Mount Raivata;
having performed auspicious rites, he beheld the principal holy fords.
Lord Dāmodara, Svarṇarakṣā, Mṛgānanāsthalī,
Ambā in the form of Dattātreya, and likewise Nārāyaṇahrada.
Having beheld Raivatācala, as well as Gaṅgā, Gomukhikā, the temple of Trivikrama-raṇacchoḍa, and Vāmanasthalī; ||73||
Balermakhasthalī, Bhadrā, as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā,
Ojasvatī, Somanātha, and likewise Suvarṇadvārikā.
Having thus established various sacred fords (tīrthas), and having given land, cows, gold, silver, and other gems as well as ornaments, [he attained his goal]. (75)
Having given garments and food to Brahmins, as well as to virtuous men and women, and to the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others, these gifts should be bestowed abundantly. (76)
The lord of men arrived at his kingdom of Kanyakubja, which was free from strife;
together with his queen, he celebrated a great festival for the journey.
At that time, by the power of his merit, King Bhoja’s vision indeed became divine;
he beheld Vaikuṇṭha as well as Kailāsa, along with Hari and Hara together with their attendants.
Then he beheld a magnificent, divine celestial chariot that grants liberation;
there, he with his wife, possessing a divine form, was established by the attendants.
"Having become liberated by the power of Hari, he went directly to Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O beloved Ramā, the wonder of Raivata has been told to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Rules for Holy Places, Charitable Gifts, and Other Duties," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 151 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lotus-born One, I shall declare the observances (niyamas) and restraints (yamas) to be maintained at the sacred ford;
the observance of these niyamas and yamas shall be fruitful.
He who has conquered desire and anger, who is free from greed, delusion, and the like,
and who is faithful, a believer in the hereafter, and pure— he shall partake in the fruit of the sacred ford.
He whose hands, feet, belly, tongue, mind, and genitals are indeed restrained truly attains the fruit of the sacred fords.
Truthful in speech, firm in his vows, tranquil, and viewing all beings as himself,
one who has attained purity through austerity and knowledge enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords.
At a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should indeed observe a fast, undergo a haircut, perform the Śrāddha rite with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka),
feed virtuous men and women, and give gifts with sincere devotion.
For women whose husbands are living, shaving is never prescribed;
nor should anyone ever perform an examination of the foods to be eaten.
And there, the primary duty toward the local deities must be performed with ornaments,
garments, substances, vessels, fruits, and offerings of food.
But one who is unable [to perform these] should offer salutations, as well as sweeping and other such tasks,
and service consisting of attending upon the feet of the virtuous, which bestows grace.
For him by whom virtuous people have been served through his body, mind,
and material possessions, there shall arise the fruit of all great worship and the fruit of visiting all sacred fords.
He by whom the virtuous have been gratified through the means of surrendering all his possessions obtains the fruit of every gift; for the virtuous one is indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever rite is performed at sacred fords (puṇyatīrtha) or at a confluence of rivers,
it becomes multiplied a thousandfold and yields infinite fruit.
Whatever is performed at a sacred site, even if it be very little, increases through the power of that site;
merit constantly increases, while sin is always dissolved.
Among living beings who have made [the place] a sacred ford (tīrtha), not even a trace of sin exists;
because it enables people to cross over [to liberation], it is therefore called a tīrtha. || 13 ||
Whatever a virtuous person performs at a sacred ford (tīrtha), all that becomes a bestower of merit;
indeed, those who bear bodies should dwell at a sacred ford according to the prescribed rules.
A seeker of the sacred ford (tīrthakṛt) should indeed cultivate purity of mind and service toward the virtuous;
[he should avoid] the greedy, the slanderous, the cruel, and the deceitful.
Neither for the impure, nor for the thief, nor for the nihilist, nor for the deceitful, nor for the slanderer, nor for the malevolent, shall there ever be the fruit of the sacred ford.
The mind does not become pure by merely discarding physical impurities;
rather, the mind becomes pure by abandoning the perception of faults. || 17 ||
Attachment and aversion are of the nature of impurity; by abandoning them, one becomes stainless.
Whether by women or by men, divine splendor is indeed to be beheld at the sacred ford.
Through a divine state, one's own inner divinity increases day by day;
the Lord should be held within the divine internal organ in the circle of sacred pilgrimage sites.
He indeed shall deliver the devoted one who is stainless and a vessel of merit:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from possessiveness. || 1.152.20 ||
Purity, austerity, contentment, self-study, devotion to Hari, chanting, worship, beholding the Deity, listening to His teachings, and prostration. ||21||
These acts must be performed especially so that the full fruit of the sacred ford (tīrtha) may be attained.
One must not give way to anger at a sacred ford, for it indeed consumes one's merit.
At a sacred ford, one must never eat the food of another, nor ever drink the water belonging to another.
And one should not accept gifts, for they indeed rob away the power of one's asceticism.
With sweetmeat balls, pearls, delightful kasāras, and ghṛtapūrakas;
with saṃyāvas, milk puddings, cakes, śaṣkulis, khājakas, and so forth. ||24||
With side dishes such as *parpikā* and *piṇḍaka*, with split pulses (*dvidala*) and the like, and with curds, milk, buttermilk, and juices as sweet as sandalwood milk; ||25||
The virtuous brahmins and their wives, as well as the poor and children, were to be gratified with other well-prepared foods, including those fit for eating and licking, seasoned with ghee and sugar.
By that, the ancestors shall be satisfied, and his merit shall be infinite.
One who desires the fruit of the sacred ford should both eat from it and cause others to eat.
One who desires happiness should never make a pilgrimage site barren;
for the conscious pilgrimage site is considered superior to the inert pilgrimage site. (28)
The peaceful, the virtuous, the yogis, the ascetics, and the celibate students—all these are sacred sites of consciousness; in attaining them, there is great merit.
During the Cāturmāsya period, service to sacred fords (tīrthas) is especially enjoined;
at that auspicious time, when penance and restraints are observed, the fruit shall indeed be infinite.
For those who perform these excellent Cāturmāsya vows—which require little effort, yield abundant fruit, and bestow the fortune of a son—their reward is inexhaustible. (31)
Having touched a cow, having bowed to a Brāhmaṇa, and having fully honored virtuous deities, an ascetic, a tranquil mendicant, one learned in the Vedas, and a celibate student; |||32||
[He should honor] his mother and father, his sister, her husband, his daughter's husband, his nephew, his grandson, as well as friends, relatives, and kinsmen. ||33||
Virtuous women, faithful wives, and maidens; poor, blind, and wretched people;
children, the elderly, and the sick; cows, guests, and the helpless. ||34||
By feeding hungry and weary mendicants, travelers, and those dwelling at sacred fords, householders are liberated from their sins. (35)
A king, an elephant, a horse, a mongoose, a virtuous woman, a bull, a mountain, a mirror, a milky tree, one who gives food, and likewise virtuous people—[these are auspicious sights]. (36)
Holy places consisting of water and land, temples, and divine images—these purify merely by being seen for one established in the Cāturmāsya vow. (37)
Having heard the discourse on the Vedic dharma, having seen men intent on liberation,
and having remembered Lakṣmī, Hari, Śambhu, Śivā, and Gaṅgā, the celestial river— 38.
Having kept a vigil for Viṣṇu and having given gifts according to one's ability—
betel, flowers, a lamp, food offerings, and Tulasī leaves— (39)
By performing song, dance, and instrumental music in the temple of the gods,
one attains great prosperity as well as the fruit of heaven and the granting of liberation.
The one-pointed concentration of the senses and the mind is the highest austerity;
that one-pointedness toward Vāsudeva should be practiced by people through meditation and other means. (41)
During the four-month retreat, the sages and seers, having conquered the swift flow of the tongue’s taste for flavors,
perform austerities to obtain the fruit of pilgrimage.
Subsisting on fruits, drinking milk, or eating only once a day;
or else, abstaining from leafy vegetables, consuming only leafy greens, or eating sesame seeds. (43)
Consuming curd, renouncing ghee, eating only a single meal, or even subsisting on a mere measure of mung beans, black gram, and so forth—this is indeed the vow. ||44||
Sleeping on the ground, bathing in water, and the avoidance of oil massage and similar luxuries;
devotion, worship, the use of garlands, the chanting of mantras, and the glorification of Śrī Hari. (45)
Constantly listening to sacred discourses, beholding one's chosen deity, serving holy men at a sacred ford, and observing vows that bestow great merit. (46)
Brahmins and virtuous persons are to be honored and fed with excellent flavors;
the constant worship of Kṛṣṇa with the most excellent sixteen types of service is the vow.

The constant worship of the virtuous, or alternatively, the supreme vow of fire-offerings (homa), as well as the renunciation of ghee, sugarcane products, salt, and so forth, is considered a vow (vrata). 48.
That vow consists of consuming only what has been offered to the Blessed One;
by such an action, both the virtuous and the Blessed One are likewise satisfied. (49)
They should be pleased; therefore, that vow which grants liberation must be performed as the most excellent.
Service to one's mother, father, and guru is the supreme among all vows. (1.152.50)
Service to her husband is the vow of a wife; pleasing her husband is the vow of a devoted wife. Service to the guru is the vow of a disciple; pleasing the guru is the vow of a disciple. (5.1)
On Mount Raivata, the Kārttika vow must especially be observed,
as well as at Vaṭatāla, in the sacred field of Hari-Hara, and at Kapilāśrama.
Alternatively, the vow known as fasting for a month, or the Cāndra-kālika vow, or the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should be performed;
auspicious penance begins from the full moon day. ||53||
On the full moon day of Āśvina, there are indeed fifteen morsels;
on the first day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, there are fourteen mouthfuls.

Day by day, following the sequence of the lunar dates, there is indeed a reduction of the morsels; on the new moon (amāvāsyā) there should be a fast, and on the first day (pratipad) there is only one morsel.

Two mouthfuls [are consumed] on the second lunar day, and in this manner, until the full moon, the increase of mouthfuls should be performed according to the increase of the lunar days; and that vow should be observed accordingly.
A mouthful that goes down below the throat with a single effort—neither less nor more—is always considered appropriate for the purpose of the vow. (57)

Or whatever other penance and vow is proclaimed by the founders of other sects—such as standing in water during the day from sunrise until sunset, which constitutes the *jalakṛcchra*—[is surpassed by this]. (58)
On the tenth day, one should collect cow urine, cow dung, ghee, milk, and curd;
on the eleventh day, there is a fast—this indeed is the Hari-kṛcchra vow.
From the seventh day onwards, one should respectively take water, milk, curd, and ghee;
on the eleventh day there is a fast—this is the Paitāmaha Kṛcchra.
Drinking milk for three days and fasting for three days following the sixth [day] is declared to be the Māhendrakṛcchra; it should be performed especially at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
For three days one should eat rice and other grains starting from the third day;
for the next three days, barley and so forth; and then there is fasting for three days—this indeed is the Vaiṣṇava Kṛcchra.
Drinking milk for five days, eating curd for five days,
and fasting on the eleventh day is called the Bhāskara-kṛcchra.
From the fifth day onwards, one should eat in sequence: beans, barley, vegetables, curd, milk, ghee, and water on the eleventh day; this is called the *ṛṣikṛcchra*.
Milk well-boiled with the leaves of *palāśa*, *bilva*, *darbha*, lotus, and *udumbara* should be drunk on the first lunar day; one should observe a fast on the sixth day.
This vow, known as the Āgneya-kṛcchra, has thus been described;
from the seventh day onward, one subsists on milk, bilva fruits, lotuses, and lotus stalks.
Fasting on the eleventh day is declared to be the Lakṣmī-kṛcchra;
eating only leaves for eleven days constitutes the Parṇa-kṛcchra.
Eating in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, and eating food obtained unasked for three days, and fasting for three days—this is declared to be the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra. ||68||
By twelve days of fasting, the Pārāka-kṛcchra is declared;
by consuming only fruit, the Phala-kṛcchra is proclaimed.
By the consumption of water alone, that is called the *jalakṛcchra*; likewise, by the consumption of leaves alone, it is called the *dalakṛcchra*. (1.152.70)
By the taking of flowers alone, the Puṣpakṛcchra is proclaimed;
by the taking of seeds alone, that is called the Bījakṛcchra. ||71||
By taking a mere sesame seed, by taking a chickpea,
or by taking roasted rice grains, that specific *kṛcchra* penance is said to be performed.
The Pakvakṛcchra, the Āmakṛcchra, the Saktukṛcchra, and the Audanavrata—
these Kṛcchras should be performed according to the prescribed rule during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
When accompanied by devotion to the Blessed One in every way, these [rites] grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; otherwise, they are considered to grant only heaven.
If fainting occurs during the performance of a *kṛcchra* penance, one should then have the patient drink cow’s milk;
likewise, water, roots, fruits, milk, leaves, flowers, clarified butter, and curd [may be given]. (75)
Buttermilk, oil, sugar and the like, forest grains, vegetables, and sea products; camphor, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, neem, black pepper, and medicinal herbs. (76)
Ginger, which is a substance that cleanses the mouth, as well as its decoction—
these twenty-four principles indeed do not destroy one's vows.
Alternatively, there is unasked-for alms, or even the eating of uncooked food;
the renunciation of vegetables, the renunciation of fruits, the renunciation of savory flavors, and the avoidance of cooked rice. (78)

The renunciation of salt, the renunciation of products of the cow, and the renunciation of sugarcane products—these vows are indeed well-spoken, bringing about both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (7–9)
These duties should be performed at sacred fords during the rainy season, or else in the month of Kārtika:
the gift of food, the gift of water, the gift of clothing, and providing assistance.
The gift of a vehicle, the gift of land, the gift of a daughter, the offering of cows, the gift of gold, the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of a lamp, and the offering of a house. ||81||
Thus, one who desires further rewards must give everything that is required for oneself;
this worship of Rāmā and Āmodara is called a vow (vrata). ||82||
One should worship Hari with a hundred thousand flowers of the ketakī, jāti, and agasti, as well as with lotuses, water-lilies, and tulasī leaves.
At every leaf and every flower, one shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
with his body anointed with the juice of dhātrī fruits and having well-eaten dhātrī fruits as food, [he attains this]. (84)
With his body adorned with *dhātrī* fruits and taking refuge in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree, one who has duly worshipped Dāmodara shall go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa. (85)
A sky-lamp should be offered in a temple at the onset of night;
and cooked foods should always be presented to the deity by the wealthy. (86)
In the month of Kārtika, a person should receive the initiation of the great Bhāgavata and wear around his neck a garland made of tulasī, offered at the feet of Hari. (87)
That individual is surely liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra;
by even a single vow during the month of Kārttika, one obtains the fruit of the Cāturmāsya observance. ||88||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Restraints (Yamas), Observances (Niyamas), Gifts, Austerities (Kṛcchras), Vows, and so forth to be Observed," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: To the northwest of Vastrāpatha is a divine lake;
to the western side of that is a forest of dense trees.
There, in the center, was a linga made of clay within a bilva tree;
at that place, a certain hunter arrived during the springtime in search of water.
Having arrived and stationed himself beneath the Pippala tree,
he rested for a moment at its foot and then went to drink water.
At that moment, he then beheld two men, one dark and one pale,
wearing yellow garments and skins, with beautiful hair and well-formed matted locks.
Wearing the Kaustubha gem and a shaven head, holding a discus and a trident in their hands,
they wear garlands of Vṛndā and Rudrākṣa beads, and possess two eyes like lotuses and three eyes respectively.
Their foreheads were adorned with the moon-like tilaka mark and served by the virtuous Padmā;
they were joined by Garuḍa and Vāsuki, and their necks possessed the beautiful luster of the conch and the sapphire.
Divine, appearing as the bringers of the end of nourishment, they strive for the cessation of life;
overcome by passion and darkness, they cling to the path of the sky.
As soon as the hunter saw them heading toward the Bilva forest, they both vanished from sight, having entered into the linga and the rock respectively.
The white one vanished at the linga, while the black one went into the rock;
then the hunter, filled with wonder, went to that spot.
Then, having seen a clay liṅga and a stone image of Viṣṇu there, the hunter abandoned his drinking of water.
Remaining well-established right there, the two gods contemplated with devotion;
hungry and thirsty, they remained in that very state until evening.
When this event occurred at evening on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
In that secluded place, those two gods remembered [him] again and again.
The hunter, repeatedly worshipping these two—Śiva and Viṣṇu—brought bilva leaves and lotuses from the lake and offered them to them. (13)
Thereafter, having taken water, they were bathed and honored with flowers;
by that much of the night, those two, dark-blue and pale-white, were saluted.
From that very [tree], two men of divine form emerged; they spoke to that hunter because, in this forest region, [he had acted thus]. (15)
Since you came today and offered a bilva leaf and a lotus, by the power of this worship, your sins have likewise been burnt away. (16)
O God, by worshipping Śivarātri, you shall become a hunter and dwell in heaven until the dissolution of all beings, possessing a divine body. (17)
"By virtue of the observance of Śivarātri, by keeping vigil on Śivarātri, and by dwelling beneath a Pippala tree, you shall become a devotee of Viṣṇu. (18)
Having thus granted the boon, Hari and Hara vanished;
at that moment, a celestial chariot of beautiful golden hue and moon-like luster appeared there.
He descended from the path of the sky into a place beautifully adorned by Apsarases,
endowed with every prosperity, and inhabited by male and female servants.
Then the goddesses said to that meritorious hunter:
"Come, O beloved, to the beautiful heaven; we have been prepared as your wives. (21)
You have become a perfected deity through the worship of Śiva and Viṣṇu,
having performed a vigil on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, when the moon was present.
"Therefore, all this is now obtained; ascend it and take hold!
Thus did those celestial women address the hunter as if he were their beloved.
Having fashioned this celestial chariot and placed him upon it, they departed for heaven, the city of Hari.
And Indra, beholding him then, was utterly amazed.
Then the hunter was asked, "By what merit did you obtain this? He replied, "It was by virtue of [attending] Śivarātri that I had the vision of those two. (25)
The one possessing a divine form [related] all that—the vow, the worship, and how it had occurred.
Then, when the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha arrived again, ||26||
O Goddess Lakṣmī, on that day Indra arrived upon the surface of the earth,
having bowed down to Bhava and Mādhava along with countless gods and goddesses.
He worshipped according to the prescribed rites and completed his vow.
What is the use of many gifts given? What is the use of vows? What is the use of worshipping the gods? (28)
What is the use of sacrifices, what use of austerities, and likewise what use of celibacy?
What is the use of offering funeral cakes at Gayā or dying at Prayāga? (29)
What is the use of going to Someśvara, to Sarasvatī, or to the lunar festival;
what would be gained by going to Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu? (1.153.30)
What would be gained by the gift of gold equal to a balance-scale or by the recitation of the Vedas?
What need is there for the ritual release of a bull, by which all sins are destroyed? (31)

What indeed does the gift of a cow accomplish? What does the gift of sesame seeds accomplish? And what kind of fruit is obtained during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the transits of the sun? ||32||
Whatever fruit is obtained when a vigil is performed on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, one attains that inexhaustible fruit; even Mahendra attained such a fruit.
Having worshipped Vāmana, Trivikrama, Dāmodara, and Bhaveśvara according to the scriptures, and having likewise performed the vow, Hari [is pleased].
Having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake and sipped water from the mouth of a cow,
Vāsava paid homage to Ambā, Nātha, and Dattātreya.
Having gone toward the north, he indeed found rest for a moment;
there, the Linga known as Indreśvara was installed by the mountain-dwelling god.
Worshipped by Vāsava and likewise bathed by the goddesses,
Bhava, the Lord of Gods, came directly within the range of Indra’s vision.
Likewise, the four-armed Lord Viṣṇu was seen there;
Viṣṇu, the four-armed one, had been installed by Indra upon that spot. (38)
Having been honored, fed, consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājana), and saluted, Viṣṇu said to Indra: "In another birth, you shall become Brahmā. (39)
"Having indeed ruled over another Brahmāṇḍa, attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Having obtained this boon from Indra, he installed Hara and Hari.
The Lord of the Gods went to heaven; he goes there every year for one who observes the Śivarātri vow while residing at Vastrāpatha. ||41||
He was bathing in the Nārāyaṇa lake, serving Dāmodara, a true devotee of Bhaveśvara, and a worshiper of Trivikrama. ||42||
Excellent women arrive to lead away the bridegroom and to perform the rites;
from Indra’s abode, they come to see the bridegroom and choose one another.
"May this divine husband of mine, equal to Śambhu and Nārāyaṇa, be yours;
for he, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), is my husband and not yours."
Trees, insects, moths, as well as beasts and birds—these die and, having become equal to Viṣṇu, they indeed go to heaven. ||45||
Then, at Vastrāpatha, those goddesses take various men as their husbands;
having obtained a husband who is like the god Śambhu and possesses the form of Viṣṇu.
They laugh, sing, dance, and proclaim his fame;
they utter cries of victory and lead that god to a comfortable bed. Even in the Nandana grove, the goddesses question that god.
Tell me, by what power has your lordship become divine? ||48||
Then that god indeed speaks by the power of Vastrāpatha:
"The gods become divine; that holy site (tīrtha) bestows even liberation. (49)
When Maheśvara arrived, having mounted Airāvata,
that king of elephants stood upon the summit of Mount Ūrjayanta.
For a specific reason, that elephant placed its foot upon the head of the mountain;
pressed down by it, the excellent mountain discharged pure water. (51)
"The water produced from the elephant's foot shall indeed always remain stable.
Thus it was ordained by the Lord of the Gods for the benefit of those seeking the sacred ford. 52.
Furthermore, in the northern quarter,
there is a Liṅga established by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), known as Dhanadeśvara, which is a sacred site that bestows happiness.
Likewise, the goddess Pārvatī, the wielder of the trident, shines there;
and in the south-western corner of Bhava is the Gaṇa known as Hairambha.
Yameśvara was established by Yama, while Bāṇa exists [there];
likewise, Citragupteśvara was established by Citragupta. ||55||
Prajāpati established Kedāreśa on the high peak of Mount Raivata to the west,
and likewise Niminātha Śiva.
On the southern side of Bhava, Nṛsiṃha and Śrī Hari were likewise installed by Śrī Vāmana; they are especially worthy of worship. (57)
Having attained a human birth and having recognized Hara as well as Hari,
those seeking liberation should observe Śivarātri and Vāmanadvādaśī.
It is declared to be the bestower of merit and happiness, and the granter of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
this annual vow should be observed by people for twelve years. (59)
The life of men is fickle; therefore, one's duty is to perform monthly rites.
Every month, one should observe the vow of Śivarātri and the vow of Dvādaśī.
If an obstacle arises in the middle, or even by the turn of fate, there shall be no violation of the vow; that which was undertaken is considered completed.
On the fourteenth and twelfth days of the dark fortnight, having performed his daily rites,
he should undertake the vow and its observances and bathe in a river or an auspicious lake.
Anointing with oil should not be performed, nor should activities associated with the night be undertaken;
one should practice visiting sacred fords and serving holy men, which brings about happiness. 63.
Devotion to the deity should be practiced by those dedicated to celibacy;
having gone before the deity at night, the seven mountain offerings should be performed. (64)
Honored with cooked food, fruit, betel, flowers, incense, and other offerings, a lamp of ghee should be prepared for the purpose of destroying sins. ||65||
Whether by day, at night, or during the twilight, a lamp should be offered according to one's capacity;
a divine lamp should be prepared, for its fruit is considered great.
The gods are entirely satisfied by even a slight manifestation [of devotion];
therefore, one should keep a vigil at night accompanied by song and instrumental music.
The narrative of Śivarātri and the vow of Vāmanadvādaśī should be heard, and songs of devotion should be performed by the circles of devotees.
Gifts should be given at night during the vow and likewise while keeping the vigil;
furthermore, one should bathe at dawn and worship both Hari and Hara.
The virtuous are to be honored with food, clothing, and other necessities;
householders must provide food for those who practice austerities.
Twelve, eight, four, or six guests are especially worthy of being fed;
however, even a single knower of Brahman, or a celibate student (brahmacārī), is highly honored.
One who is honored in one's home with devotion is equal to thousands [of others];
on the preceding day, one should personally eat food that is free from pungent and salty seasonings.
Likewise, food must be given to one's sons, friends, and wife;
in this manner, the Śivarātri vow on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be performed.
Vāmana himself shall be pleased, and Śiva shall be repeatedly gratified;
at the conclusion of the vow, an auspicious black cow together with her calf should be given as a gift.
Divine [images], adorned with garments and ornaments and beautified by bells, horns, and so forth,
should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru and to the Brahmins according to one's capacity.
Having distributed food to the ascetics, one should likewise ask for their forgiveness;
for the devotee who acts in this manner, no sin remains. (76)
Having become pure and meritorious, having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures, and having obtained an excellent lineage as well as worldly peace, [he attains liberation]. ||77||
Mounted upon a celestial chariot and surrounded by divine women, he is led to the world of the Lord amidst the sounds of singing and musical instruments. (78)
In the month of Bhādra, during the bright fortnight, on the twelfth lunar day under the asterism named Śravaṇa, at the time of midday on a Wednesday, Vāmana was born from Aditi. (79)
On the eleventh and twelfth days, subsisting on fruit is prescribed;
one should observe a fast on the eleventh day, or indeed take only a single meal at night on the twelfth.
At that time, for the sake of worship, one should fashion an image of Vāmana made of gold.
Short, with matted hair, and equipped with a parasol, a staff, and a water-pot. ||81||

Then, one should duly worship Vāmana with flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, along with the sixteen excellent services (upacāras), while he is adorned with yellow garments and ornaments.
In the Sarvatobhadra mandala, one should worship him at midday with whatever offerings are available, and with devotion, using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth. //83//
One should worship Aditi, Kaśyapa, and Indra along with his family;
one should offer auspicious food offerings consisting of sweet delicacies such as ghee and sugar-candies.
One should cause the deeds of the Vāmana incarnation to be sung;
and on the thirteenth day, one should satisfy many hungry people with sweet foods.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, at the dead of night,
Mahādeva appeared between Viṣṇu and Brahmā as the radiant form of Śrī Hari.
He became the very essence of the Śiva-liṅga, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns;
indeed, that third Mahādeva remained invisible within the liṅga. ||87||
Indeed, at the time of creation, this world arose from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
on the fourteenth day, one should offer variegated garments to Mahādeva.
One should wear a fine, variegated garment and ornaments of gold, and with affection, one should worship Maheśvara along with his family. 89.
One should cause the Rudrasūkta to be recited, preceded by an ablution;
at midnight, one should worship Śambhu with leaves, milk, and fruits from the *Bhaṅgā* plant.
One should worship with jasmine, kunda flowers, golden flowers, and oleanders, as well as with sixteen kinds of substances and other offerings.
One should offer various kinds of food offerings according to the requirements of place and time;
and at that time, one should have the hymns of the *Ekātmapaṭala* sung by the two, namely Dhara and Rudra.
One should bestow various other gifts and abundant jewels according to the prescribed rites;
on the second day, one should perform a most magnificent festival of feasting.
In this manner, one should observe the vow of both Hari and Hara on Mount Raivata;
and in the months of Kārttika and Māgha, one should perform the pilgrimage that bestows liberation. For such a person, residence on Kailāsa, in the realm of Viṣṇu, and final liberation are certain.
Whether a man or even a woman, one shall attain liberation through this vow. ||95||
By that [means], a passionate woman becomes Ramā or Pārvatī;
by that same means, a dispassionate woman surely attains liberation in the divine abode. //96//

During the month of Māgha, all people, observing their vows, should perform circumambulation clockwise for the sake of nourishment; likewise, worship, charity, and the observance of vows should be performed at Raivatācala. (97)
By him, the circumambulation of the earth must be performed;
it shall constitute the worship of thirty-three crores of gods. ||98||
Those seeking liberation must not let the two barren months of Kārttika and Māgha pass in vain;
for if these are barren, one should understand that the entire human birth has become utterly barren. 99.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Hunter’s Vision of Hari and Hara, the Installation of Indra-Īśvara and Viṣṇu, the Sacred Sites of Gajapada, Dhaneśvara, Triśūlinī, Yameśvara, Citragupteśvara, and Nṛsiṃha, and the Greatness of the Vows on Vāmana-dvādaśī and Śivarātri," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, on the Raivata mountain which abounds in clusters of jewels and possesses divine luster, Mount Mandara arrived, interspersed with golden stones.
Having entered into that divine, radiant [jewel] in its gross form and remaining there in union with it, the light of the gem is no longer visible.
Likewise, Kumudādri arrived there at Mount Raivataka;
having entered within it, he exists in a massive form upon that Raivata mountain.
Listen indeed to that divine narrative originating in the former Kṛta Yuga.
Formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, all the mountains were made winged.
Flying up with their massive bodies, they were about to fall down at will;
Brahmā restrained them so that Meru, Mandara, and Kailāsa remained firm. ||9||
But when others, though restrained, did not remain stationary,
their wings were then cut off by Indra with his own thunderbolt.
On the southern peak of Meru, however, is a mountain named Kumuda;
it is divine, winged, golden, and abounding in the splendor of celestial gardens.
The entire region was prosperous, exceedingly beautiful, and like Vaikuṇṭha itself;
thereupon, the divine city of Viṣṇu was established by Viṣṇu.
And in the midst of that, O Viṣṇu, is a great palace accompanied by Ramā;
on the peak of Meru known as Mandara is the beautiful city of Śiva.
And there, in a golden assembly hall, Bhavānī always rejoices;
and there is also the city of Brahmā, with its palaces and excellent citizens.
On its peak at Aruṇācala, which is rich with jewels, diamonds, and gems,
those three gods reside where they hold counsel together.
In the lotus grove of Viṣṇu, there were golden creepers;
the flowers were also tawny and golden, as was their fragrance.
In that city, fragrant floral scents are constantly wafted by a gentle breeze,
and even the trees are richly endowed with fragrant leaves and clusters of blossoms.
The winds carried fragrances indeed from every palace;
once, the Blessed Lord Rudra arrived at Kumuda.
Seeing Hara arrived at his home, he was worshipped by Viṣṇu;
Gaurī was worshipped by Lakṣmī, and she was indeed honored with great joy.
While those two were seated on a single seat consulting with one another,
at that very moment, Kumuda and the mountain Mandara also arrived there.
Having truly assumed human form, they both arrived for the purpose of service;
there Śambhu spoke to Hari, saying, "Since Bali is indeed powerful."
O Hari, having assumed the form of Vāmana on Mount Raivataka, you must by all means lead [the demon Bali] from the earth to Sutala.
I too must go there to Mount Raivata;
having caused Bali to dwell in Sutala by means of a stratagem.
"Furthermore, we shall return here once our task for the gods is accomplished.
Mādhava said "Om" to him, and then those two mountains [departed] with joy.
Kumuda and Mandara pray before Hari and Hara:
"We two shall go together to that place where Hari and Hara abide. (2.1)
Having received the boon, "So be it," those two lords of the earth,
Hari and Hara, together with their wives, vanished and went toward the Creator.
On the peak of Aruṇācala is the city of Prajāpati; there, having indeed held a consultation for the purpose of providing a dwelling place in Sutala for Bali, [he established it]. ||23||
The two of them returned again to their respective cities and to their respective mountains;
and when the time had arrived, Viṣṇu indeed became Vāmana.
And Śaṅkara also went to the sacrifice of Bali;
at that time, Kumuda and Mandara went to the Raivata region in Saurāṣṭra.
Flying through the atmosphere with their wings spread,
those two drew along many other clusters of stars with great speed.
Then they both arrived at Mount Raivata, situated on the banks of the river Svarṇarekhā; having personally learned of that injustice toward them, the Lord of the Gods himself [appeared].
And taking up his own vajra for the purpose of destroying the wings,
he mounted an excellent celestial chariot and went to where those two mountains were.
As long as he hurled the thunderbolt, those two mountains repeatedly spoke with palms joined in reverence to the gods Hara and Acyuta for their protection. (29)
Then Indra, with the thunderbolt in his hand, was instantly paralyzed; meanwhile, Hara and Acyuta said to him, "Do not kill these two mountains! (1.154.30)
Indra sought those two for the sake of releasing Stambhana; he chose Kumuda and Mandara as the means for his deliverance.
Having granted the boon, saying "So be it," Mahendra then halted his pillar and restrained Mount Kumuda on Mount Mandara and Mount Mandara on Mount Raivata.
On the Taijasa mountain, Hari and Hara have eternally established themselves;
this very Mandara belongs to Ambā, while Kumuda is on all sides.
Having attained the form of a lotus through the division of twelve petals, these two mountains are seen within the radiant gem. (34)
On the Raivata mountain, within the Taijasa principle, those two—Viṣṇu as Dāmodara and Śiva as Bhava—established themselves.
There, Viṣṇu as Dāmodara and Śiva as Śambhu took up their residence.
Having brought Brahmā to Aruṇācala, he indeed arrived there;
he established Aruṇācala on the eastern side of Mandara.
There, Brahmā made his own dwelling and resided in the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
wherein he maintained that reservoir of water in the Mandara pool.
Jātakaṃmaṇḍalukuṇḍa is a sacred ford that bestows imperishable merit;
it is there on the first peak of Aruṇādri that Brahmā indeed resided.
That place became the holy site known as Brahmakuṭī, which bestows liberation;
and on the second Aruṇādri resides the great lord Dattātreya.
Indeed, he performed severe penance at that sacred ford which bestows liberation;
thus Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva reside there, taking refuge in Revatī.
When the dissolution arrives, O beloved, those three mountains— Mandara, Kumuda, and Aruṇādri— will go to Merau along with Prakṣiṇa.
They will indeed go to the Sapakṣa [heaven] and will remain there;
in those three [abodes], there are three classes of gods and thirty-three crores [of them]. (42)
The gods dwell there as well; this secret has been told, O beloved:
by the movement of Raivata, the circumambulation of Meru was accomplished. (43)
By performing worship of Raivata, the worship of Meru is accomplished;
by beholding Raivata, the beholding of Meru is accomplished. ||44||
Those who perform a circumambulation of Mount Raivata, which is thirty krośas in extent, have effectively performed the circumambulation of Meru and of the entire earth in this world. (45)
By those who have performed a circumambulation of Mandara and Aruṇa, a circumambulation has been performed of the two worlds named Satya and Kailāsa. (46)
Whoever has performed the circumambulation of the twelve mountains of Kumuda, by him the circumambulation of Vaikuṇṭha has been accomplished. 47.
When the three gods arrived there to dwell, Nara and Nārāyaṇa went to that forest known as Boriyā. ||48||
From the bowl of Brahmā’s water-pot, the Gaṅgā, protected by Jāmbavī,
falls downward onto the earth at the hermitage of Badarikāśrama, which is known as Bori.
The two ascetics, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by all the sages, remain invisible to ordinary people, yet they are seen by those who possess great merit. (1.154.50)
To the south of Mount Mandara, at the source of the Gaṅgā, those two always dwell;
to the north of Mandara, there are indeed mango groves.
He has arrived from the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, situated beyond the enclosure of waters;
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and the Lord of Sītā have come together with mango groves.
The self is indeed liberated, eternal, and always endowed with fruit;
it is the abode of those from Sāketa, possessing well-formed leaves and branches.
And there is the Sughaṭṭa forest, which is called Sītāvana;
likewise, there are Lakṣmaṇavana, Rāmavana, and Kīśavana.
The forest ground of Sītāpaṭī is divine, equal to the abode [of the gods];
there indeed the sun does not shine, nor does the moon or the stars shine. (55)
Where even the lightnings do not shine, how then could fire shine there?
Such was that place, endowed with great and divine streams of water.
There is a divine and vast forest, endowed with mines of gold, silver, red chalk, and other minerals in the earth, which provides comfort in all seasons. (57)
There, in that eternal forest of Sāketa, the Sarayū flows with its own springs, even as it carries forth cascades of divided waters. ||58||
Hanumān resides there in that forest for the purpose of protection;
this great sacred site (tīrtha) is said to be supreme, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 59.
And in the eastern Raivata region, near Aruṇācala,
the Indradyumna lake is situated there, having come into existence.
Having heard that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and Sītā and Rāma had arrived, [he went forth].
In the city of Puruṣottama, the Lord himself, Jagannātha,
having brought the mountain named Nīla as well as the banyan tree born from the ocean, [established his presence].
Having arrived here for a dwelling, they surely stayed previously in the eastern direction,
where there are trees bearing ṭīmburu fruits, as well as jambu, āmalaka, and karmada trees.
Indeed, there are forests where there are many mango trees, rāvaṇa trees, jujube trees, and amṛta trees, as well as numerous sītā fruits.
Where the water is like milk, the fruits are as sweet as nectar,
and happiness is equal to that of heaven— there, on the peak of Mount Eraivata, lies the eastern region.
Where there is black earth mixed with the essence of gold, and various minerals exist over an area of twenty *krośas*. ||66||
Then, to the east, is the auspicious field of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
the delightful Ciñcāṅgūḍīvana forest, and the beautiful Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The river that has conquered its enemies is called Saumyā; this region is known as Kambharākṣetra, where Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is worshipped under the name Kambharā-Gopāla.
He is worshipped and honored by gods, by those who honor the gods (brahmins), and likewise by humans;
even there, the lineage of that brahmin devoted to his wife remains established. (69)
Two krośas further to the north of Kuṅkumavāpikā, there exists a sacred field, beautiful and endowed with forests and other such features. (1.154.70)
In the field of Laṅkācatuṣṭakī, where Sarasvatī is protected, she flows forth clearly, endowed with most divine waters. (71)
When the goddess Sarasvatī, the great river, having taken up the submarine fire from the Himālaya, proceeded toward the western ocean; 72.
Then, having gone from Mount Arbuda to the perfected field of Śrīnagara, and likewise to Virāṭanagara, he reached the fortress of Sāraṅga. ||73||
Having reached Unmattagaṅgā, Bhogā, and Bhadrā,
and having reached the sacred field of Laṅkācatuṣka, she arrived at Jayanta.
Having gone to the Ghaṭṭa known as Bhadreśvara-Nṛsiṃha,
she then went northward to Skandapura and the city of Kālīvaṭa.
Having reached Prakāśa from Ājyā, she went to Suvarṣādvārikā;
then, on the southern side, on the mountain named Barāṭa.
Having reached Bilveśa, the bestower of joy, she arrived at Navanītādri;
having reached Vāmanasthala, she came to Umāvastrāpatha.
Having circumambulated Mount Raivata and Mount Kṛtasmara,
and having ignited the sacrificial pit, he went to the Pippala tree situated in the east.
Having reached Ekatarṣisthala, she then arrived at Somanātha;
thereafter, she reached the auspicious and secret Prayāga in Vyāghrāraṇya.
Having gone to the divine land of Siṃhāraṇya, she entered the four oceans;
then, having cast off the Vāḍava fire, she [reappeared] again on Mount Raivata.
The goddess Sarasvatī is eternally established in every location; the goddess resides in every sacred pool (kuṇḍa) for the sake of the welfare of all people. 8.1.
On Mount Raivata, there were monkeys renowned by the name of Hanumān;
likewise, there were Sītā-maṭha, Hanumān-maṭha, and Santama-maṭha.
The great goddess Vyāghreśvarī resides on the mountain named Māhiṣa;
[there are also] the Śrīrāmapādukā-tīrtha, Bilveśa, and Hāṭakeśvara. (83)
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, there are other holy places on Mount Raivata which are indeed stars for living beings, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By whomsoever holy places have been visited or their waters drunk—even if done in some casual manner, or for one's own sake, or even with indifference—[by him the goal is attained]. (85)
Whether they have bathed in those waters or merely worn their dust and mud, through the destruction of their sins, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be theirs. (86)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Mountains Kumuda, Mandara, Aruṇa, Nīla, and Others, as Well as the Tīrthas Badrikā, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Sītā-Rāma, Jagannātha, Sarasvatī, and the Rest, upon the Taijasa Raivata Mountain within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, how Mahālakṣmī, who dwells in the supreme Vaikuṇṭha,
came together with Nārāyaṇa to Mount Raivata.
When Bali was indeed bound by Hari here on Mount Raivata,
Bali’s wife remembered the Supreme Goddess within the pavilion.

Then, while residing in the abode of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, he [Viṣṇu], with a humble disposition, [meditated upon] Mahālakṣmī who was present within his heart, using hymns for the sake of releasing Bali from his bonds.
Sandhyāvalī, with palms joined in reverence, bowed to her and spoke from her heart:
"Salutations to the Mother, Mahālakṣmī! Protect my husband, who is devoted to you."
Salutations to you who are known as Prakṛti; salutations again and again to you, the Root.
Salutations to you, the destroyer and the mere essence of Brahman; salutations again and again to you, the creator within the womb.
Whether they be dwarfs or tall, those Nārāyaṇas are in your mouth;
Mahākāla and the others are also your morsels—salutations to you!
The Saṃkarṣaṇas, the Rudras, and the Yamas are all within your mouth;
they are all chewed by your single fang. Obeisance again and again to you, the Great One!
Vāsudeva, Bhūman, and the Nārāyaṇa-puruṣas were struck by your creeper-like arms; salutations again and again to you of great power!
From you Lakṣmī was born; Mahāviṣṇu is born from your lap;
and the cosmic eggs reside within your pores—protect us! Salutations again and again to Lakṣmī.
The great fires, those submarine fires (*vāḍavānala*), are hidden within your sweat; and those blessed ones are within your womb—may salutation protect you, O Caṇḍalakṣmī!
O Caṇḍī, at your yawn there are dissolutions; Time trembles, and the great cosmic eggs are ground to powder upon the back of your lap; salutations be to you! 1.1.11.
Protect, protect my husband, O Great Illusion, O Supreme Goddess!
Caṇḍī, Taṇḍī, Mahāmuṇḍī, Ghaṇḍī, Ḍiṇḍikā, and the others—[protect him]. (12)
Kālī, Karālī, Prajvālī, Lihālī, Raktilā, and the others—these are your powers; [with] that drop of blood, protect [him] and quickly bring him back to life! 13.
Protect me quickly, otherwise I shall cut off your throat and offer you as a sacrifice!
If I am to become a widow, then you must first become a widow! 14.
"If I am deprived of my kingdom, you must remain without Vaikuṇṭha;
if the king is insulted, you too shall be insulted. (15)
"If there should be an obstacle to your sacrifice, let it likewise be so for my sacrifice of wine!
Thus spoke Caṇḍavegā, even as she was rushing toward the members of the assembly.
"Do not, do not!"—thus did the gods then restrain that woman;
at that moment, Mahālakṣmī, the wife of the Great Lord, arrived there.
Having consoled the queen, she fell at her feet with bowed head and said:
"O Lord, do not do this; O Master, do not utterly destroy one who is devoted to you."
Then Vāmana said: "I shall certainly not kill him, nor shall I deprive him of his kingdom; rather, I will make him my excellent servant. (19)
"O beloved, let Sandhyāvalī remain with the gods and possess great good fortune;
O beloved, let this Daitya rule the kingdom of the Daityas in Sutala."
"If I must abandon Vaikuṇṭha, I shall dwell in the house of Bali;
O Mahālakṣmī, you shall remain with me as my queen and perform service for me."

Having given the kingdom of the gods to the gods and the kingdom of the Daityas to those two powerful ones, and having thus laid it down, you must depart; in this way, there will be welfare for Sandhyāvalī. (22)
Then that Mahālakṣmī was worshipped by the foremost Daityas, and the Mother, the protector of all prosperity, was worshipped by the gods. (23)
Together with Vāmana, she too was requested by them on Mount Raivata;
Mahālakṣmī was made to dwell there for the sake of all prosperity.
To the west of Raivata, on that very height, Mahāmāyā Mahālakṣmī is eternally established, the one who protects life.
She was saluted and honored with flowers, saffron, unbroken grains, and sandalwood;
with vermilion, bilva fruits, garments, cloths, oil, and fragrant perfumes. ||26||
Likewise, with auspicious articles of good fortune, various kinds of pure foods, and ornaments such as bracelets, armlets, earrings, necklaces, and so forth. ||27||
With various kinds of garments such as bodices and shawls, and with auspicious threads, earrings, and other ornaments, [he should worship] with devotion. (28)
On the day of the festival of lights, that Mahālakṣmī is always gracious;
she casts away misfortune, inauspiciousness, and calamity. (29)
It bestows a virtuous kingdom, a beloved son, and likewise wealth;
for the purpose of worshiping Mahālakṣmī, an image with four arms should be fashioned.
She was made of gold, possessed of a beautiful form, charming, and sixteen years of age;
she held a jar of lotus-nectar in one hand and likewise a vessel for worship in the other.
With her right and left hands, she displays the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) and giving (*varadamudrā*) respectively;
one should worship her with the sixteen secondary articles of service. (32)
Having offered the food offering (naivedya), fruit, and betel leaf, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
various foods and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should also be given.
Gifts consisting of jewels, diamonds, gems, and gold;
as well as garments of fine silk, woolen blankets, and likewise cows. (34)
By the power of Mahālakṣmī, his merit shall become inexhaustible;
having enjoyed manifold pleasures, he shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha at the end.
Maidens up to twelve years of age, who are embodiments of Lakṣmī, should be worshipped like Lakṣmī herself with gifts of clothing, food, and wealth. (36)
Likewise, they were provided with food, adorned with ornaments and articles of decoration,
and served various delicious flavors such as sweet cooked foods, milk-rice (pāyasa), and other excellent delicacies.
Likewise, virtuous women who are detached and established in Sāṃkhya and Yoga should be honored;
various gifts that bring about desired results should be given to them. (38)
Indeed, when wealth exists there, women with children and husbands, as well as widows, the destitute, those seeking refuge, and the protectorless [all find support]. (39)
They are to be fed, honored, and given sacrificial fees;
they must be constantly respected, for when they are satisfied, prosperity itself is satisfied. (1.155.40)
When Mahālakṣmī is pleased, all prosperity increases;
nothing whatsoever remains deficient, and whatever one desires shall be attained.
