When fully worshipped, she drives away all misfortune from the home;
O Lakṣmī, hear here the story concerning the churning of the ocean.
I shall now relate, in this context, that story which bestows happiness—the tale of the garland of *pārijāta* flowers given by Durvāsas. (43)
Indra struck the head of the elephant with his hand;
seeing that it had been reduced to a state of being like a foot-stool, the sage cursed the lord of heaven.
"May the fortune of you who treat me with contempt perish!"— with these words,
Lakṣmī vanished in an instant, and the jewels fell into the ocean.
To extract that [nectar], the ocean of milk was churned by the gods and demons;
at that time, Mount Mandara was held upon his back by Hari in the form of a tortoise.
From that churning, the great poison Kālakūṭa arose;
the Lord drank it all, and they churned it once again.
While that [ocean] was being churned by me and the gods, O Lotus-born One, the goddess Jyeṣṭhā emerged, clothed in red garlands and garments. 48.
That elder sister of yours is Alakṣmī; she is unattractive even in her body—resembling a Kirātī in form and a fisherwoman in her face.
Her ears were like those of a lizard, her nose resembled a tube,
her eyes were like those of a female buffalo, and her head was like that of a Rākṣasī.
On the forehead it resembles the point of a sword; on the cheeks it is like soot;
on the teeth it resembles the tip of a spear; and on the lips it is like a camel.
She resembles an elephant in her neck, a donkey in her voice, a *varbura* tree in her hand, and an anthill in her two breasts. (52)
Her belly is like a granary, her back like a stone slab, her waist like an oil-press, and her feet resemble the trunks of date-palm trees. (53)
The appearance of a leech on the fingers, a resemblance to the back of a tortoise on the nails, and the quality of a frog on the tongue—yet, by nature, she is like a female dog. (54)
She is like a poor woman in her graciousness, like a skeleton in her laughter;
she resembles a leather-worker in her clothing and a Caṇḍāla woman in her dwelling. (55)
In the case of parching and crushing, it resembles an empty well dug in dry land;
in cohabitation, it resembles a bhāṇḍī flower; and in marriage, it resembles alkaline soil.

Seeing her there, amidst the conversation, with a state of despondency due to the likeness of the battlefield and yet possessing an abundance of prosperity, the gods, dānavas, and humans were struck with awe.
They reflected: "Who is this woman, adorned with every inauspicious thing?
Is she the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), the Great Plague (Mahāmārī), or perhaps the Hunger at the End of the World (Pralayakṣudh)? (58)
Holding a garland of shells in her hand, she desires a husband;
she wanders here and there as long as she seeks a husband. (59)
Seeing her, all the gods and asuras fled far away, unwilling [to look], saying, "She is not for us; go! Do not let her go to another! || 1.155.60 ||
When the garland of choice was not accepted by anyone, she, becoming despondent, said: "Let a dwelling be given to me anywhere where I may stay. (61)
"I have been born, yet I am purposeless; what should I do?"—thus did the hosts of gods and asuras quickly speak to that goddess at that time.
"To those in whose house quarreling constantly breaks out, we grant that place; dwell there, possessed of misfortune. (63)

In whose house there is the worship of skulls and bones for the purpose of malevolent magic, where harsh speech prevails, and where there is the practice of incantations and rituals for killing; ||64||
Untruthfulness, violence, gambling, drinking, hunting, intoxication, neglecting one's mother and father, and the disparagement of one's teacher. ||65||
The sighs of women and children, the distress of a householder’s kinsmen, where there is infidelity, and where there is a breach in the row [of diners]; ||6||
Dwell in their house, bestowing suffering and poverty, where indeed there are the breaths of cows and other living beings that have fallen under your power. 67.
And where the protection of those who depend on him is not carried out according to policy.
And likewise between mother-in-law and father-in-law, husband and wife, and two sons. ||68||
Where there is mutual discord between father and son, between brothers, between mother and daughter, or between two sisters, stay away from that place; for there is loss.

Wherever there is a housewife in the household, there is a tendency toward expenditure through theft among the circle of family members, and each person acts as if they possess their own private property.
Even one's own home is regarded as belonging to another by those who consider their own kin as such;
laziness in performing one's duties and dependence on others for one's livelihood [are further signs of this]. (71)
Where the words of the elders are not honored at all, and where bathing, worship of the deity, and the recitation of mantras do not exist; ||72||
Stay where there are no human or divine festivals, nor those occurring annually; stay where there is greed and the expenditure of unrighteousness—there, remain happy. (73)
Where there is the harming of living beings, where there is the censuring of the virtuous, where there is hostility toward dharma and atheism—there, O you who delight in strife, you shall dwell. (74)
Where there is no hospitality for guests, where purity is not found, where filthiness prevails, and likewise where there is a lack of effort; ||75||
In which moment after moment there is anger, where there is thirst for sense objects, where there is gluttony as well as lust, and where there is addiction that knows no bounds. (76)
The unjust oppression of male and female slaves and laborers, as well as the mistreatment of cattle, birds, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, and other animals. ||77||
One should dwell there where there is no trust in one's household members, and where neither the Śrāddha rite nor the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) takes place. (78)

Where the ritual utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* are not found, and where indeed neither the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), nor the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) exists; //79//
Falsehood regarding one's wife, children, house, masters, ministers, or servants;
where there is deceit toward another, or where there is the consumption of forbidden food—[in all such cases, it becomes a sin]. (1.155.80)

Where there is non-protection of those who ought to be protected, likewise the non-nourishment of those who ought to be nourished, and where there is non-punishment of those who deserve punishment—there one should make one's dwelling. (8.1)
Dwell always in the house of those who seize the livelihood of gods, brahmins, and cows, and in the house of those who cause suffering to the helpless, the wretched, and the blind. (82)
Dwell in the house of one who harbors malice toward virtuous men, women, ascetics, yogis, and the detached, or in the house of those who prohibit the practice of charity and dharma. 83.
Dwell in the house of one who steals bodies, steals thoughts, and steals the heart; of one who acquires wealth through injustice and who employs false scales.
Let a permanent residence be established in the house of one who gives false testimony;
dwell forever in the home of one who insults the learned. (85)
In those fourteen worlds where there is injustice and lack of discernment, and where the honoring of those worthy of honor is transgressed—there let your dwelling be ordained. (86)
When merchandise is mixed with fraud, when business is accompanied by deceit, and when conduct is directed by hypocrisy, one should always make one's dwelling elsewhere. (87)
Where the king sides with righteousness while the subjects consume through violence, there the kingdom would be one that consumes its own heart; in such a place, you should always dwell. (88)
Where the wealth [offered] for the sale of a maiden is digested in the belly, and where the practice of selling women prevails—there shall always be your dwelling. (89)
Where there is no virtuous conduct or religious observance, and no pure heart, even the recitation of sacred verses proceeds from deceit; indeed, your dwelling is always in hypocrisy.
He whose day passes impelled by passion and hatred, and where there exists a lineage of unrighteousness—dwell always in that place. (91)
[One should not trust] an ungrateful person, a deceiver, a gambler, an assailant, an arsonist, a poisoner, or likewise a murderer who acts unjustly. ||92||
Let a permanent residence be ordained for one who stands outside the Dharma in the house of a person who reveals what is hidden by others, as well as in the house of a wicked person. (93)
Dwell always in the house of one who does not give food, clothing, or shelter;
dwell in the house of the slanderer, the sower of discord, and the creator of suffering. (94)
In the kingdom, in the realm, as well as in the wilderness, in gardens, and in forests; in the pleasure grove, in the fields of cultivation, on the mountain, on dry land, and in the water. (95)
In trees, crops, and likewise in seeds, gems, gold, liquids, and battle;
in combat, in festivals, in divine or human matters, whether on land or in water—96.
At a sacred ford, in eating, in legal proceedings, in buying and likewise in selling, in knowledge, in the arts, in craftsmanship, and in the seasonal rain. ||97||
Wherever there is a ruler who is deceitful, fraudulent, a gambler, a thief, and violent; wherever he is wicked, unjust, and a great sinner—there you shall always dwell. (98)
What is the use of much that you have said? For wherever there is violence, falsehood, as well as theft, sexual misconduct, greed, impurity, craving, and censure; 99.
"May you always have your dwelling there, where Lakṣmī herself does not dwell.
Having spoken thus, the gods gave her to the seer Uddālaka.
Then he again sent away Alakṣmī along with her husband;
thereafter, they all, being well-composed, performed the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Then the goddess Vāruṇī, of auspicious countenance, was born;
thereafter, Ananta, the king of serpents, took that beautiful-eyed woman as his own.
Then the goddess Gāruḍī was born, endowed with auspicious marks; adorned with every excellence, she became the wife of Vainateya.
Then divine throngs of Apsarases and Gandharvas of great prowess were born, endowed with beauty and devoted to sweet singing.
From that [ocean] were born Airāvata, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas,
Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, Surabhi, and the cow who grants all desires.
The thousand-eyed one, honored by all, seized them all;
then, at the time of dawn on the twelfth day, when the sun had risen.
While the great ocean was being churned, Śrī Mahālakṣmī arose;
from that [churning] came the moon, and from that was born Tulasī, who is beloved by Hari.
Lakṣmī chose Keśava along with Tulasī;
thereupon, the Blessed One spoke to all the great sages.
The Ekādaśī is immensely meritorious and the destroyer of all calamities;
therefore, the Dvādaśī is always meritorious and dear to me.
From this day forward, those people who, having fasted on the eleventh day,
remain endowed with supreme faith at sunrise on the twelfth day—
Those who worship me with devotion, together with Tulasī and Śrī, are all liberated from bondage and attain my state. || 11.1 ||
And those who do not worship me, Puruṣottama, on the twelfth day—
those sinners my insurmountable Māyā binds with worldly objects.
She incessantly casts those who are atheistic and averse to me back into the cycle of worldly existence;
for it was from the ocean that Lakṣmī herself was born on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
From that time forward, the sages, the gods led by Brahmā,
the Siddhas, humans, yogins, and the best of munis [have acted].
Placing the command of Viṣṇu before them and endowed with supreme devotion,
they fasted on the Ekādaśī day and likewise worshipped Janārdana with devotion.
On the twelfth day, they worshipped me as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
for that day is yours, and it is indeed my day as well.
It is called Harivāsara, and it is also called Lakṣmīvāsara; because of the eternal union of the divine couple, what else do you wish to hear? 1.17

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Mahālakṣmī’s Arrival at Raivatācala in the Kṛta-yuga lineage of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; Her Worship and Giving; the Emergence of Alakṣmī during the Churning of the Ocean, Her Form, and Her Abodes; and the Manifestation of Lakṣmī and Tulasī, along with the Greatness of Dvādaśī," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, I desire to hear the procedure for the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī),
and how all the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites are to be performed."
O my beloved, describe to me the power of her merit;
indeed, the power of my own vow must be heard by me in every respect.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the vow for your birthday;
by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of your vow, I shall always be well-pleased.
Ekādaśī was born from my limbs as my wife;
likewise, you are my wife, born from my left side.
Furthermore, since you were born from the ocean, you are then called Abdhijā;
on Mount Aruṇa you are named Padmā, and as the daughter of Bhṛgu, you are Bhārgavī.
You, Kambharā, were born from love; Suvarṇikā was born from a mine;
and Ramā, though giving birth again and again, dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.
My wife is eternally divine; wherever I am, you are indeed there.
You abide in every house, yet you never remain without me.
When, while in the supreme abode as the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, I willed a second form from myself for the sake of delight.
Then, by my will, you became my invisible attendant stationed on my left side,
equal to me in all respects except for the six attributes such as my own form.
In beauty, virtue, sovereignty, happiness, enjoyment, and luxury, there is no deficiency in the state of being female; however, the deficiency lies in the state of being male.
That alone is the deficiency of this woman, and no other deficiency belongs to me;
for there are the powers of my eleven sense organs. (11)
Having combined together, you were indeed born as my twelfth [daughter];
since you are the embodiment of my wives, you alone are to be understood as Dvādaśī.
Your manifestation took the form of the twelfth;
therefore, you are called Dvādaśī, my wife, my consort. (13)
"O limb of mine, because you cause Hari to dwell [within me] and protect him, you are Harivāsara;
you, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), are my wife, appearing in the form of my very day."
My form, my dwelling, and my delight are always in you;
therefore, you alone are considered Hari’s day, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). || 15 ||
This secret, indeed, has been told by me to you in confidence;
furthermore, on the twelfth day during the churning of the ocean...
Since you were indeed born at dawn, your twelfth day (dvādaśī) has consequently become renowned everywhere as your birth-jayanti.
And at whatever time and in whatever place there is the manifestation of me, Hari Nārāyaṇa, and also of you, Lakṣmī, at that time he shall become powerful.
By the power of Hari, even the appointed time becomes powerful and bestows merit;
for indeed, when my birth and your birth both take place here together.
In each of those places, great festivities should be held with gifts and feasts, as well as with songs, instrumental music, and dances, and with worship, hymns of praise, and devotion. || 1.156.20 ||
When the Ekādaśī day has arrived, men who fast here on this day,
being liberated from all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Then the full merit of the Ekādaśī vow shall be attained;
thereafter, on the Dvādaśī day, one should perform the worship of us two and then break the fast. ||22||
Sin accumulated over seven lifetimes, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly,
goes to dissolution in an instant through the worship of us on the twelfth lunar day.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of the fast on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī). 24.
The twelfth day bestows merit, grants wealth, fulfills all desires, and grants liberation to all people, wherein both you and I are worshipped. (25)
And that goddess Ekādaśī is the great strength of my senses; the vow requested by her is indeed entirely without food.
In that regard, food must certainly not be eaten, for sin resides in food;
there exists nothing whatsoever that protects one from sin equal to Ekādaśī.
O beloved, whatever sin has been committed through the eleven sense organs, all of that shall go to dissolution by fasting on the Ekādaśī day. ||28||
My wife Ekādaśī is also called my day;
by fasting on that day, I shall be pleased with her again and again. (29)
Having offered me a food offering on the twelfth lunar day, one should break the fast;
by that, I am always satisfied and indeed become pleased.
"When I am satisfied, the world is satisfied; may there be the fruit of universal satisfaction.
O my beloved, the Saṃhitās proclaim this again and again.
On the eleventh day, when the day of Hari has arrived, one must not eat—
this always applies, O beloved, to all castes and stages of life, as well as to women and children.
The fast on the eleventh day must certainly be observed under all circumstances;
even if a śrāddha for one's mother or father falls on the eleventh day, which is their anniversary of death.
That [offering] should be given on the twelfth day, never on the day of fasting;
for the Vaiṣṇava ancestors do not eat the śrāddha on the eleventh day.
One should avoid with great effort that [eleventh day] which is mixed with the tenth;
it should be mixed with the twelfth at the time of dawn. (35)
Having abandoned that twelfth day, one should perform the pure [observance] without hesitation;
then, on the thirteenth day, having quickly performed the morning bath and other rites, [one should proceed]. 36.
If even a single digit of the thirteenth lunar day occurs at sunrise, then [the fast] indeed belongs to the portion of the twelfth day prior to that sunrise. (37)
The breaking of the fast must indeed be performed, but not during the "dregs" (pala) of the thirteenth day;
the fast is observed on the twelfth day, and the breaking of the fast likewise on the twelfth day alone. (38)
Remaining awake during the middle of the night—that indeed is that vow.
It is called Harivāsara; it is the most excellent of all and is dear to me. (39)
He who, having abandoned this vow, should practice another vow, is like one who,
having cast aside a great kingdom held in his own hand, begs for alms.
Where the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) lasts for even a single digit (kalā) while the sun has already risen on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī),
the observer of the vow should abandon all other Ekādaśīs and fast on that very one.
If the rising of the sun occurs during the thirteenth digit (kalā) [of the lunar day], then the twelfth day itself is considered pure for the vow on the preceding day. ||42||
On the tenth day, he should eat only once, abstaining from sexual intercourse at night;
sleeping on the ground in the morning, he should be anointed with the fruit of the dhātrī tree.
One should bathe, perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and offer worship to me;
fasting on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the evening, one should worship me.
One should worship with devotion at night using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, ornaments, and food, as well as through recitations, hymns of praise, and prostrations. 45.
And one should worship Lakṣmī at night with articles and substances that bring good fortune;
there, one should have one's hair dressed and wear a garland of flowers. (46)
Then one should braid the hair into a lock and fashion it into a *kabarī*;
thereafter, one should apply vermilion, scented oil, and other substances to the hair on the head.

One should apply sandalwood, saffron, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth upon the forehead, and provide a beautiful chain, a cord, or a golden ornament; one should also fashion a splendid crescent moon mark.
She should also wear earrings and beautiful nose-ornaments;
she should apply collyrium to her eyes and perform the coloring of her lips. 49.
One should place decorative leaf-patterns on the cheeks, fine tilaka-marks on the temples,
golden ornaments on the neck, and wear beautiful flower garlands.
One should place bracelets on the arms and jeweled rings on the forearms;
one should wear finger-rings and a saffron-colored bodice.
One should wear around the neck a silken garment with golden threads at its borders, a sacred thread (brahmasūtra), a kaustubha gem,
a necklace of full-blown leaves, and a golden fillet.
Upon her waist she should wear a golden girdle, a saffron-colored sash, and a tinkling belt;
upon her feet, golden anklets joined with small bells and jingling ornaments.
One should offer silver sparks and worship with lac upon the plate;
one should wear rings on the fingers and indeed foot-ornaments on the feet.
One should, out of great respect, perfume the soft leather sandals made of gold and silver with the fragrant scent of *gandhasāra*.
One should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika) for Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa with five wicks, circumambulate them, prostrate like a staff, and offer salutations, hymns, and praises.
One should then offer the food offering (naivedya) consisting of sugar, ghee, fruits, and so forth;
thereafter, one should present drinking water, water for rinsing the mouth, and betel leaf.
One should give a comfortable bed, such as one with soft pillows and the like; a white cotton sheet, a variegated rug, a royal mattress, or a pillow of peacock feathers. (58)
One should scatter flower petals upon the bed,
provide a breeze with a fan, and perform the massaging of the feet.
And by the command of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, one should perform the massaging of their limbs;
having caused those two deities to sleep, one should [bathe them] in the morning with fragrant waters.
Having awakened them, one should bathe the two deities with devotion, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth; one should wipe them with a cloth and have them wear new garments.
Having gratified the ancestors and the deities with water mixed with *tulasī*,
one should worship Janārdana, the Lord of the worlds, together with Lakṣmī.
With tender tulasī leaves, with lotuses and land-lotuses (sthalapadma), and with fragrant unbroken grains and flowers that bring about good fortune and auspiciousness; ||63||
Then, with water, ritual implements, ornaments, and jewels,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) there with one hundred and eight lamps.
One should properly present a garland made of lotuses to those two, and offer incense, a lamp, food offerings, and betel leaf. (65)
Divine milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by sugar, along with saffron, combined with fine nutmeg, and made fragrant with the powder of cardamom. ||66||
Pūrikās, polikās, various vegetables, and many kinds of cooked foods; likewise, buttermilk, curd, milk, soup, broth, and boiled rice. ||67||
One should offer parpaṭas, cakes, and numerous kinds of sour gruel (āranāla),
as well as fruits, water, a small amount for cleansing the mouth, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having performed circumambulation, prostration, and the request for forgiveness, one should indeed choose a boon that is desired and bestows happiness following the worship. (69)
Wealth, grain, health, clothing, and indeed vehicles;
conveyances, vessels, ornaments, as well as fields and excellent gardens.
Cows, buffaloes, bulls, and so forth; likewise, the happiness of husband and wife; offspring; long life; and the unimpeded accomplishment of one's tasks—[may these be attained]. (71)
Prosperity, great beings, sovereignty, a home, a kingdom, family, the wealth of happiness, heaven, and whatever else is desired—[all these he bestows]. (72)
May you grant all the wealth of happiness and good fortune from both deities;
release [us] from affliction, calamity, suffering, distress, and anxiety.
May widowhood and childlessness never befall me at any time;
may my family, consisting of sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth, be happy. (74)
Likewise, with devotion, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) into the fire one hundred and eight times,
accompanied by the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Śrīsūkta*.
One should offer oblations verse by verse with devotion, feed the Brahmins and the virtuous,
and having personally fed one's own dependents, one should then eat the food oneself.
He should spend the auspicious day listening to the Saṃhitā and other scriptures; remaining celibate and sleeping on the ground, he should likewise avoid censure and similar faults.
One should keep a vigil at night; thus one should perform the Dvādaśikā vow.
The Blessed One, being pleased, will certainly grant all desired objects.
In the house of one who observes the vow of Harivāsara, the eight Vasus indeed dwell in heaven by virtue of the boon granted by Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī. (79)
Āma, Bhava, Soma, Dhara, Nala, Anila, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are indeed the eight Vasus who dwell there. (1.156.8)

At whatever sacred ford there is worship of you, wherever there is veneration of you in a home, wherever there is remembrance of you in the forest, and wherever there is the telling of your name by the ocean; 81.
Dwell everywhere in that world where your fame exists;
wherever you and I have mental meditation during the hour of Brahma. 82.
There, practice the remembrance of my name and devotion; dwell there with me where, in the morning, the assembly of children remains serene and happy. (83)
Dwell there with me where one neither cries out nor reviles;
dwell where there is no distress for husband and wife in the morning. (84)
Dwell there in purity where, at dawn, there is the purification of the body through bathing, washing, and so forth, as well as the purification of the bed and the purification of the garments. 85.
Through sprinkling with water, sweeping, and smearing the house with cow-dung, and by means of decorative lines and the svastika symbol, may there be auspiciousness for you dwelling therein. (86)
Wherever the lamp and the fire on the hearth shine in the morning, there dwell curds, milk, ghee, sweets, and cooked food. (87)
Reside always wherever you find flour-based foods, meals of roasted barley flour, well-cooked rice and the like, or morning offerings of wheat cakes and similar delicacies. (88)
In the morning, the water from wells, ponds, and other sources that has been brought and placed within the house—reside always in those two water-pitchers and in the water used for worship. (89)
Dwell where there is always morning bathing, meditation, worship of the gods and others, honoring those worthy of honor, and respect for the elderly. (1.156.90)
O Lakṣmī, dwell forever in that place where the courtyard, the cow-pen, and so forth are swept clean every morning, and where purification from stale food and the like is maintained. 9.1.
Dwell in that place where there is the sight of Brahmins at dawn, as well as of the virtuous, of chaste women devoted to Hari, and of one's parents. 92.
Dwell there at dawn, beholding the learned, the gurus, virtuous women endowed with merit, the gods, and the cows. (93)
There is merit in the moon-like mark on the forehead and likewise in the collyrium of the eyes;
dwell in that mouth where there is flower and fragrant substance. (94)

The Agnihotra sacrifice, the Gāyatrī, the worship of Viṣṭnu, the adoration of Śiva, the worship of the gods in the morning, and the offering of oblations—dwell there [in that state] where these exist. (95)
Cleaning the teeth with wood and purification with earth, water, and so forth;
bathing, auspicious ornaments, and the like—dwell always wherever these may be found. (96)
The drinking of milk and so forth by infants, the nursing by calves and the like, and the consumption of grass, water, and so forth by animals—dwell there always in that state. (97)
Where there is protection for birds such as parrots and for dogs and the like, and where there is honor and water, dwell there always. (98)
Do not dwell where there is no fear for the riding of bulls, horses, elephants, or camels, nor where there is no terror from other animals. 99.
The various types of plants, such as those growing from the soil—like the trees and creepers in domestic gardens—obtain water and food; therefore, you must always dwell there.
Dwell forever in that house where grains of flour and the like are obtained from householders by insects, ants, and other such creatures. (101)
O my beloved, may you two reside in that village where cattle are not needlessly beaten by people, and which belongs to those who are compassionate. (10.2)
Dwell where guests who have arrived, mendicants, and visitors alike are satisfied with food, water, and kind words. 103.
Dwell where food is not for one's own sake, but is the remains of offerings made for the sake of others; where there is no breach of the row, and where there is no pursuit of self-interest.
Dwell there where there are ancestral rites, vows, and festivals, where there is righteous dancing and singing,
and where there are social gatherings and feasts for kinsmen performed for the sake of others.
Dwell where there is devotion to the virtuous, contentment, a disposition toward generosity, honor for the great, and compassion for the wretched. (106)
One should dwell where there is a righteous livelihood for many, providing food, clothing, water, and shelter, bringing contentment to those destitute beings. (107)
Dwell there in that house where the virtuous, the celibate students, and the helpless find great satisfaction through service, even at the cost of their entire possessions. 108.
Dwell in that place where there is no deceit, no affliction, no trickery, no dishonesty, and no cruelty, but only perfect peace. (109)
Where there is no greed, anger, great agitation, envy, unrighteous conduct, jealousy, malice, or hypocrisy— there you should dwell.
Thirst, censure, slander, malice, intoxication, arrogance, and the exposing of others' faults—these do not exist there; dwell in that place.
The food of those who act unjustly, the food of beggars, the food of others, as well as the food of sinners and the food of the wicked—none of these is digested; dwell within that [stomach]. 112.
Dwell always where activity is conducted according to justice, where buying and selling are righteous, and where there is never deceit regarding weights, measures, acquisition, or giving.
Dwell not where there is deceit regarding the old and the new, nor in mixing them together; where there is guile in the giving of one's word, yet no such guile in the giving of one's heart.

Where the expenditure of wealth is for the sake of helping others, for the merit of religious offerings, for the purpose of sacrifice, or for the welfare of the nation— dwell there for the sake of others.
O Lakṣmī, dwell in happiness where there is no killing of animals, birds, or living beings dependent on others, and where no fear exists. (116)
Dwell forever at the food-distribution hall for children, young girls, virtuous women, the righteous, the wretched, the helpless, and the poor.
Dwell always in a pond, a well, a tank, and the like; in a river, a lake, on the ground, in a dug-out pit, a natural spring, or even in an open water-shed.
Dwell there among those who have noble masters—the mountains, forests, and fields that possess grain, gardens, and groves. (119)
Dwell always where there are sacrifices of charity, sacrifices of ritual action, and sacrifices of yoga; where there are sacrifices of devotion and sacrifices of knowledge.
Where there are indeed sacrifices to the elements, sacrifices to Brahman, sacrifices to the gods, sacrifices of Vedic study, and devotion and service—there you should always dwell. 1.21.
Dwell where there are no vices—neither liquor, meat, theft, unjust indulgence with women, and other such useless addictions. (122)
One who is wicked in thought, wicked in heart, and wicked in speech and action—whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another—does not truly dwell there. 123.
Dwell always where there is devotion to one's husband as a duty, where there is fidelity to the vow of a wife, where there is virtuous conduct, trustworthiness, and gratitude. (1.24)
Through policy alone comes the performance of action; through policy, the bestowal of wealth;
and through policy, the protection of subjects. Dwell always among those who possess such policy.
Dwell happily where there is no withering of the subjects, nor the wailing of women, nor the oppression of the miserable.
Dwell always within the home of those who honor women, those who assist others, and those whose efforts have borne fruit— this is what should be meditated upon.
Dwell always in the kingdom of those kings who protect their subjects like their own sons, who sacrifice even their own lives, and who are righteous and devoted. 128.
Enemies, violent men, thieves, the arrogant,
the greedy, deceivers, rogues, scoundrels, and heretics do not dwell constantly in that kingdom.
The sovereign, the ministers, the princes, the queens, the counselors, the domestic chaplains, the commanders of the army, and the forest guards—none among them were wicked; dwell there.
The prison warden, the superintendent of justice, the wall-guards, and the gatekeepers of the inner apartments—do not dwell there with those who are wicked. (131)
Merchants, artisans, craftsmen, laborers, those well-versed in the scriptures, and judges—those who dwell there are not wicked; do not reside among them. (132)
Neither among the stages of life nor the social classes, neither among women nor men, nor in villages nor in forests—therein you shall find no wickedness; dwell there. (133)
Among servants, among groups of spies, among disciples, and among dependents—
as well as toward teachers and kings— one should not perceive wickedness when dwelling among them.
Whether in the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, in the ground, in a hole, in heaven, or in the atmosphere;
whether in truth, in a season, or in a womb—there is no wickedness there with which you dwell. 135.
In food, in drink, likewise in what is to be drunk, in ornaments, in cooking, in fire, in wind, in form, in taste, and in smell—do not dwell there in wickedness. (136)
Dwell where there is no wickedness of mind, no wickedness of leaders, no deception of the people, no wickedness of kings, no wickedness of teachers, and no wickedness of women. (137)
Dwell wherever there is no wickedness in you, no wickedness toward me among deceivers,
and no wickedness of livelihood among atheists.
Whatever fruit is found in offerings to the deity, and whatever gain is obtained through service to the deity— may you always dwell there, utilizing it in every respect.
What is the use of much detail? I shall speak in brief:
where there is Dharma and Bhakti, there I myself, Nārāyaṇa, am also present.

"Wherever there are virtuous ones and the lineage of the Dharma, there let your dwelling always be. Thus has the abundance of your abodes been described out of a desire for you to reside [there]. (141)
I must dwell wherever there is assistance rendered to others, according to my heart's desire; wherever there is the eating of forbidden food and the drinking of forbidden drink. (142)
Where there is no performance of improper acts and where there is no falling away from right conduct—there, indeed, is the Age of Truth; dwell there with me.
Among both lords and living beings, the lineage of Dharma is dear to me;
one should always make one's dwelling there, just as on Mount Raivataka.
Where there is evening worship of the gods, where there are discourses, recitations, and festivals,
and where living beings find rest— there your residence shall always be.
O Lakṣmī, by my command, you should always make your dwelling wherever there is great honor for the virtuous who belong to the lineage of the Immortal.
May you always dwell where there is constant observance of the duties prescribed by the Vedas, the Shastras, and other traditions, and where there is no atheism regarding divine rites. 147.
O beloved, you must by all means dwell wherever people remain active from dawn until evening. (148)

Wherein not even the slightest sense of another's ownership exists regarding one's own property, there one should always remain established in that ownership; what need is there for much speaking, O fair-faced one? (149)
Your devotees are humans, gods, Daityas, Nāgas, as well as Īśvaras;
they include Ṛṣis, Munis, and non-gods—all those who dwell within creation.
They are constantly devoted to your worship, ever desiring the arrival of you,
and they have made every effort for your sake, even offering up their own lives for you.
Out of devotion to you, they endure hardships even in a foreign land;
for your sake, they abandon their own kin and go elsewhere to desolate places. (152)
Whether you attain [your goal] or not, death will surely come;
having seen their asceticism there, you may dwell if it pleases you. (153)
O beloved, dwell always in each respective house corresponding to their particular effort; dwell as required in the hands of those who perform those various tasks.
"Go wherever you wish, O blessed lady, but return again to my house;
indeed, no other house is eternal, nor should one dwell there without me. (155)
"O sinless one, a charming home has been prepared for you by me;
O beloved, take my heart with you and dwell wherever you please. (156)
Dwell everywhere as you please; do not touch that lord of the planet.
O beloved, my devotion to my husband must be protected by you in every way.
"Wherever you may dwell, there is my state as the inner controller;
I am all-pervading everywhere, O beloved, and I reside [there]. (158)
Therefore, worship me alone everywhere through the vow of devotion to your husband;
in this way, not the slightest portion of your dharma as a devoted wife shall be lost.
Wherever you have your dwelling in a house, there my residence is upon his forehead;
you are the clothing and ornaments, while I am the splendor upon his brow.
In that house where your eldest sister Alakṣmī dwells, both of you should indeed take up residence together, even if it is only for half of that house.
Indeed, not all [houses] possess prosperity, nor likewise are all devoid of prosperity;
in one house, prosperity exists in one half, while in the other half, misfortune resides.

In a single place such as one's own home, some things are slightly deficient and cause suffering, while others are excellent and bestow happiness; yet for everyone, nothing therein is universally supreme. (163)
O sinless one, you must live with such a person in the house, enduring everything with peace, even while misfortune dwells there together with you.
"You must remain in one corner, while my elder sister Alakṣmī remains in the other; no quarrel should ever be made between us. (165)
The relative strength or weakness [of the planets] must be observed according to the lines of destiny (bhāgyarekhā);
it is the teaching that the place should be given to the strong by one who is weak. 166.
The principle that "it exists everywhere" is intended solely for the sake of happiness;
however, I shall now describe to you other sacred sites on Mount Raivata.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Causes for the Twelfth Day being Hari-vāsara, the Ritual Worship of Lakṣmī, its Fruit, and the Abodes of Lakṣmī," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"It has been mentioned as 'Revatī-kuṇḍa'; who indeed was that Revatī?
Let my curiosity regarding her be appeased first, and then tell me about the holy sites."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that narrative concerning the Satya Yuga,
which describes how Revatī was born and how the Kuṇḍa Tīrtha came to be known by her name.
She who was the daughter of Dakṣa and is indeed the wife of the Moon exists in the form of a lunar mansion; as Revatī, she shines in the sky.
From Sūrya, born from the nose of Saṃjñā, was produced a son named Raivata;
O Goddess, he is the fifth Manu, renowned by the name Raivata.
For he who, by his inner nature, resided within the Raivata mountain as if endowed with life, was the son of the Manu named Raivata; he is called Kṛtavāk Manu.
O King, when the birth of a son occurred in the house of Kṛtavāk, the lunar mansion at that time was named Revatī; that became his birth-star (janmarkṣa).
He celebrated the festival of his son's birth and performed the postnatal rites, such as the *jātakarman* and others;
he bestowed various kinds of gifts upon the Brahmins alone.
Likewise, the king performed other rites appropriate for the occasion;
indeed, at the time of his son's birth, the king suffered from a great fever.
Even in his dream, he saw himself performing the act of pulling a cart;
his left limb throbbed, and a crow cawed upon his head.
From the treasury, golden coins go forth, yet for the gods they become scorpions;
the jackal howls facing him, and the dog barks directly at his face.
The crown fell from his head, the staff fell from his hand,
and the eloquent man fell from the stairs of the palace, rolling upon the ground.
Thus, when the son was born, there occurred these ill omens;
from the very moment he was born,
that king was afflicted by a chronic disease, and his mother became a leper.
The king, distressed, fell into reflection, wondering, "What is this? || 1.3 ||
A son who is foolish and unfortunate indeed brings suffering to his father;
especially one who goes astray becomes a source of misery upon misery.
For human beings, childlessness is better than having a bad son;
for it does not lead to the benefit of friends, nor to the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Indeed, day after day, a wicked son brings about the ruin of his mother and father;
ultimately, that evil son meets his own destruction here in this world.
Better is it not to perform the marriage ceremony, better is it not to approach one's wife during her fertile season;
better for a woman is barrenness, and better is the destruction of the embryo. (17)
Better is a child who dies at birth, or better still is the death of an infant; even exile is better—indeed, a wicked son is considered not better than these.
Grief for the deceased lasts only as long as there is memory of them;
however, for foolish and wicked sons, grief and torment arise at every step.
Though unfulfilled, joyless, and overwhelmed by suffering and grief,
he brings delight to the hearts of his parents, yet constant joy to his enemies.
But an evil son brings about premature old age for his father;
it leads neither to heaven nor to hell, and is not even for his own benefit. (21)
A good son understands the heart of his parents day by day;
blessed are those sons who are honored by the entire world.
Fie upon the birth, fie upon the kingdom, and fie upon the wealth of those who do not help others, who are not peaceful, and who do not follow after virtuous deeds—even if they have sons! ||23||
Thus, by the conduct of his exceedingly wicked son,
he whose speech was stilled and whose mind was consumed with grief questioned the aged Garga.
In former times, the Vedas were studied by me according to the prescribed rule and with firm vows; having duly completed my studies, I then took a wife.
Every dharma was perfectly upheld; indeed, my mind never turned toward unrighteousness.
This son was begotten for the sake of a son—how could he be such as this? (26)
Is this wicked and evil hunter, who brings us such sorrow, born through his own fault or through the fault of my mother? (27)

He is a perpetrator of violence, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and one who always causes suffering and poverty; he is a constant despiser of his parents and one who has abandoned the duty of service. ||28||
Indeed, after his birth, Fortune departs from the house;
at the sight of his face in the morning, even the Kali age inevitably arises.
His food turns to ruin, and the day passes as a foul day.
And then, at that time, my wife became afflicted with leprosy.
I have become constantly afflicted by the disease of fever,
and those others whom I must support are likewise falling into ruin.
Whatever task I perform here does not become fruitful at all;
even if it were to succeed, a twofold loss would instead ensue. ||32||
Therefore, O brahmin-sage, reflect upon what the cause here might be;
I shall effect a pacification for it if you tell me how I may obtain happiness. (33)
Garga said: "This son of yours was born under the constellation Revatī at an inauspicious time; therefore, he indeed causes you sorrow. (34)
Revatī is almost past, for it is said that the time is indeed unfavorable;
whatever birth occurs at the end of Revatī will bring all suffering. (35)

There is no fault on the part of the son, nor indeed on the part of the mother, nor is there any corruption on your part; rather, it is because of your own misconduct that your birth occurred at the end of the Revatī asterism.
The junction between Revatī and Aśvinī, as well as that between Āśleṣā and Maghā,
and also that between Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, is declared to be a Gaṇḍānta, which brings about fear.
Men, women, and horses born under the three *gaṇḍa* [nakṣatras] do not remain in the home for long; even if they do remain, they bring fear. (38)
Thus addressed by Garga, Kṛtavarman then became enraged and said, "The birth of my son occurred at the end of the asterism Revatī. (39)
"Does Revatī not know that the Brahmin will curse me? Therefore, let Revatī fall from the sky, burning with fire. (1.157.40)
When these words had been thus spoken, while all the world looked on with minds filled with wonder, it fell down as far as Revatī.
By the power of the Lord's will, an exceedingly brilliant fragment fell on all sides upon Mount Kumuda, reaching as far as Revatī. ||42||
That mountain is indeed proclaimed by the name Khaṇḍa-Ūrjjayanta;
it fell upon the peak Kumuda and was thus stilled upon Kumuda.
Suddenly illuminating the forest caves and waterfalls,
the mountain shone forth, as if forming a friendship with the white water-lily.
The Revatī-khaṇḍa, indeed, always resided in Kumuda while bestowing vigor;
for that reason, he is called Kumuda Raivataka. (45)
Those two remained together with one another until the dissolution of all beings;
and from that fragment of the mountain, Kumuda, the Raivataka mountain became renowned.
Ūrjayanta is fire-colored; Kumuda is moon-colored;
and from the mixture of these two, Raivatācala is the color of red ochre.
Furthermore, there is indeed the Revatī-khaṇḍa within Kumuda;
at some point, that Jvālāmukhī will surely become Raivata.
Indeed, Mandara and Aruṇa, through their conjunction with the Revatī-khaṇḍa,
will at some time become the two Jvālāmukhas during the dissolution.
Ūrjayanta, Kumuda, Mandara, Aruṇācala, and Kṛtasmara—these five, together with Raivatācala, [are the six]. 1.157.50.
The very great, divine Mount Raivata, which has the luster of gold, exists;
that mountain Raivataka subsequently gave birth to a daughter. (51)
Revatī, the auspicious sister of the one named Khaṭvāṅga, possesses a luster like that of Revatī and a face resembling that of Revatī. 52.
There, on that mountain, it was told by the eminent brahmin named Pramucu, who lived like a father while performing austerities.
The sage Pramucha named his daughter Revatī after his own father; Raivata, for his part, called that daughter by the name Revatī.
And she remains there, having established her abode in a mountain cave;
that place is full of splendor and is the refuge of the waters of all sacred fords.
The flow of the Gaṅgā’s waters, as well as the water of the Yamunā and the water of the Sarasvatī— these three are present there in those pits.
That pit situated at the mouth of the cave is called Revatīkuṇḍa;
it was in that very cave that the young girl was raised by the great ṛṣi.
She attained youth there on Mount Raivataka;
and seeing her endowed with such youth, that sage Pramuca—
In solitude, he reflected, "Who shall become her husband?
Having offered oblation after oblation, that best of the twice-born questioned the fire-god, his preceptor.
"Be gracious to me and tell me: who will become her husband? Is there a suitor worthy of her, or is there no one at all? (1.157.60)
Then, rising from the sacrificial fire-pit in person as the embodied consumer of oblations, he himself said:
"Listen to my words; who shall become her husband?"
Born in the lineage of Priyavrata, possessed of great strength and prowess,
he was the son of Vikramaśīla, born from the womb of Kālindī.
"A lord of the earth named Durdama shall indeed become her husband.
In the meantime, that lord of the earth, Durdama, arrived there.
Under the pretext of hunting, he saw that cave there;
having seen the maiden by the turn of fate, that Durmada spoke to her.
"O beloved, where is your father? Shall I have a sight of him or not?
There, situated in the fire-sanctuary, the sage heard those words.
Having reflected, "Who is this person who addresses me as 'dear one'?
he went outside and beheld the king.
Seeing his future son-in-law Durdama, he rejoiced;
and he said to his disciple Gautama, "Offer him the auspicious guest-offering (arghya) and other honors."
"By the turn of fate, this son-in-law shall become my wife and my son.
Then the great sage, the brahmin, having accepted the guest-offering (arghya), [approached] him as he sat upon his seat.
Pramuca said: "O Indra among kings, is all well in your city? Is there prosperity in your treasury, your army, your friends, and among your servants and ministers? (69)
I offer you a welcome here, for by the turn of fate you have returned from your journey;
is all well with yourself, in whom everything is established?
"O King, your wife is well; tell me everything as it truly is.
Durmada replied, "By your grace, O Pramuca, let her always be mine. (71)
The kingdom and the wives—Subhadrā, whose sins are pacified, as well as the daughter of the Kāverī—are especially intent on seeing you, O virtuous one. (72)
Surāmā, Jānujātā, Kadambā of noble offspring, Vipāṭhā, and Nandinī—these other wives of mine have always been skillful. (73)
Pramuca said: "O Durdama, you have said 'Priye' (O dear one);
that disciple of mine, Revatī, is indeed called 'Priyā' (the dear one) by you. (74)
That shall not be otherwise; your word cannot be in vain.
Accept this auspicious maiden as your wife by my command. (75)
By these and other such words, the king was persuaded by his wife;
likewise, the Brahmin prepared to perform the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites. (76)
Then Revatī said: "O Sage, listen to something from me:
let my marriage with Durdama indeed take place under the asterism of Revatī. (77)
"Without the conjunction of Revatī and the Bear (Ursa Major), my auspicious moment will be fruitless.
Then the sage said to his disciple, "There is no moon conjoined with Revatī. (78)
"Today the moon is situated in another constellation; therefore, as you say, I shall do so. The maiden said: 'By means of my ascetic power, I shall make the moon joined with Revatī. (79)
"So be it; may you be blessed," Pramuca said to his daughter, "I shall place both of you in the path of the moon for the sake of the constellation Revatī."
Then, by the power of his asceticism, the great sage joined the constellation Revatī with the Moon, and subsequently performed the marriage ceremony.
The sage said to his son-in-law: "What wedding gift shall I give you?
Even that which is difficult to obtain I shall give, for I possess great ascetic merit. (82)
Then the king said to the brahmin: "Listen indeed to these difficult words:
Saṃjñā, the wife of the Sun, was in the form of a mare. (83)
Then, through the conjunction of her horse-form with the Sun, Raivata was born from her nose; he is the Adhyātma here on Mount Kumuda.
There, invisible, he dwells having come to the constellation Revatī;
this maiden is indeed that Revatī who has been born as my wife. (85)
O sage, through my yoga, that son Raivata was born again from her; I myself was born into the lineage of Svāyambhuva Manu.
"By your grace, I choose as my son one who shall be the lord of a Manvantara; having indeed obtained birth [as such], he shall thereafter become the ruler of a Manvantara. (87)
"I choose that he alone shall become the fifth Manu. "So be it," the sage replied, "he shall indeed become the Manu. (88)
Revatī, having bathed in the Revatī-kuṇḍa, will grant him a son;
that son, being a portion of Manu, shall indeed become Manu himself. (89)
Born from a portion of Revata, he shall be known as Raivata;
and he who is called Parvata shall always exist in two forms under the name of Manu.
Having thus obtained the boon, the king bathed in the waters of the Revatī;
Revatī likewise bathed, and through that union, she gave birth to a son.
He was born as Manu, and the name Raivata was given to him;
thus, a son shall be born in the house of whoever bathes in the Revatī-kuṇḍa.
He shall indeed become fortunate, a possessor of a kingdom, wise, and renowned for his fame;
and those women who bathe [there] shall be freed from suffering and poverty. (93)
"They shall obtain a son of fiery nature, honored by all the worlds.
Thus has this sacred site, joined with the Revatī-kuṇḍa, been described to you. 94.
Then, through her ascetic penance, Revatī propitiated Vāmana Hari;
Dāmodara, being pleased, spoke to Revatī.
"Let your union with the Moon be restored as it was before;
choose another boon that dwells in your mind, for I am pleased. (96)
Revatī said: "O my Lord, here indeed at the mouth of the cave, there is a pool joined by the river Svarṇarekhā where I have bathed. (97)
For those who shall bathe there, let their mountains of sin be destroyed;
may they go to heaven, may they go happily, and may they obtain sons. 98.
Furthermore, when the churning of the ocean took place,
from that which was being churned, the Pārijāta and other trees emerged.
Then, having arisen there, she became the tree Āmardaka;
because she was born during the crushing (*āmarda*) of all the gods, she is known as Āmardakī.
It was offered by Hari to the Moon as he was departing for heaven;
then, out of great affection, the Moon gave it to me while in the sky.
The tree situated in that grove, belonging to the Raivata-khaṇḍa, fell while remaining within that grove,
when it fell upon the Kumuda lake due to the curse of Kṛtavāk.
That divine tree, rich with fragrant flowers and the abode of Lakṣmī, has indeed come together with me on Mount Raivata. (103)
The Goddess Lakṣmī resides upon this tree and is served by the best of the gods;
this Vaiṣṇava tree is worshipped by all the deities, beginning with Brahmā.

O beloved, those who shall perform the ritual procession of this tree on the day of Hari— on the eleventh or the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna— [shall attain the highest goal].
Their sons and grandsons shall be even more endowed with virtues;
in the end, they will dwell in the city of Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt. (106)
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna,
and having bathed, one should worship the goddess Ekādaśī in an image on a mountain or in a forest with auspicious flowers; at night, people should observe a vigil.
One should perform her circumambulation one hundred and eight times with fruits.
One should consume the fruit of that [observance] as food; two water-pots filled with water should be given;
a lamp provided with ghee should be placed at the entrance together with a *śrīphala* fruit.
Likewise, food fit for oblation, as well as betel-leaf, fruits, and so forth, should be given;
and likewise, a vigil should be observed by those intent on listening to sacred narratives.
Human beings are liberated from the grave sins arising from their actions;
at the end of their bodies, all those men are honored in the abode of Hari.
Then the goddess Revatī, having spoken these words as she arrived, said with supreme affection: "May fever and leprosy be destroyed! (1.12)
"May your son be endowed with excellent virtues; I shall indeed return to heaven.
However, by means of a portion of myself, I shall remain here at the Revatī-tīrtha until the end of the kalpa."
Having spoken thus, she departed for heaven and united with the Moon;
that sacred ford (tīrtha) became known by the name Revatīkuṇḍa.
Now, indeed, Marīci was the son of Brahmā; his son was Kaśyapa;
his son was Vivasvat, and his son is called Śaryāti.
He was known as Ānarta, by whom, after performing austerities at the western ocean, a portion [of the land] was brought from Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Goloka.
This very fragment of the jewel was brought from what is called Saurāṣṭra;
it is divine, the foremost mountain, and the source of Ānarta’s excellent lineage.
Having obtained a portion of that [merit], he was then given the name Raivata;
that Raivata arrived at the golden river for the purpose of a pilgrimage. || 118 ||
Having made this vow for the sake of a son, Raivata was bathed in the waters of the Revatī; then he said, "O brahmin-sage, may my son indeed be equal to you."
"So be it," said the brahmin-sage; then, having made his departure, Raivata went to Kuśasthalī, the city of his father Ānarta.
Then Ānartanirmitā went to his house;
there, the brahmin-sage Kṛtavāk became present through a portion of himself in the form of a son.
And Revatī heard that her father-in-law had indeed passed away;
he was the excellent son of Ānarta and the noble son of Raivata.
Then, out of affection, Revatī also arrived;
and to the noble son Revata, there was born one named Kakudmin.
And in the house of Kakudmin, the maiden Revatī was born as a partial incarnation; and seeing her endowed with beauty, virtue, and youth, she was fit to be sought in marriage.
When he did not find even one beloved as beautiful as Revatī,
he then went to Satyaloka to ask for a boon.
Accompanied by Revatī, King Kakudmin went to the assembly hall of the Creator, where there was a performance of Gandharva music interspersed with dance.
The king proceeded into the assembly hall frequented by tens of millions of gods;
having stood there for a moment without finding an opportunity, he then approached Brahmā.
Having paid homage with humility, he declared his intention:
"O Brahmin, there are indeed many kings upon this earth."
Suvarṇāṅgada, Bhūpāla, Maruttvān, Rukmabarhiṣ, Ikṣvāku, Indrasena, and others were likewise universal emperors (cakravartins). || 129 ||
"To whom should this maiden be given by me? Speak, and I shall do that which you say.
Having heard that, Brahmā then laughed and said to him: ||| 1.157.1 ||| 30 ||
"Alas, O King! They have indeed died, their lifespans equal to yours;
there are no longer even the names or lineages of their sons and their descendants. (13.1)
In the world of truth (satyaloka), in a single moment of time, twenty-one cycles of four ages pass;
this is the great time (mahākāla) of the earth, during which those who have been taken into one's heart perish.
When you return again after half a moment has passed,
then the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age will come into being there.
At the conclusion of that [period], this jewel of a daughter must be given by you to Balabhadra, who exists at the end of that time and is the form of the final incarnation.
Having gone quickly, Kakudmin will give his jewel of a daughter to Balayogin exactly as agreed, and he himself will go to the forest for asceticism.
Furthermore, that Revatī will establish a sacred ford on Mount Raivata;
then, upon her husband's destruction, she will certainly go to Goloka.
Thus, that Revatī is celebrated as the former wife of Hari;
she remains once more as the daughter of Dakṣa, existing in the form of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
Furthermore, that daughter of Raivataka remained in a mountain cave;
she was again proclaimed as the daughter of Kakudmin and the wife of Bala.
She shall always dwell there on Mount Raivata in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha);
for even from a single manifestation, her births and deeds are manifold.
Indeed, divine deeds occur simultaneously;
I know them all. What else do you wish to hear?
In this way, it should be understood that even in another aeon, their manifestations will occur in exactly the same manner, just like your own manifest nature. (141)

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, [is described] the cause for the earth’s descent during the Revatī-nakṣatra-khaṇḍa; the birth of Revatī on Raivatācala—which consists of five mountains; her union with the moon in the constellation Revatī; her marriage to Durdama; the birth of Revata again upon Revatī; the greatness of the Revatī-kuṇḍa; the greatness of the Āmardaka tree; and the birth of Revatī in the house of Kakudmin, named Kṛtavāca, who was the son of Revata and grandson of Ānarta.
The one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Arrival at the Assembly and the Marriage with Balabhadra," etc.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved Lakṣmī; likewise, the two gods Nārāyaṇa and [Lakṣmī] always dwell on Mount Raivata, and they are to be beheld during the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
Having seen Dāmodara there and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, one obtains the fruit of a pilgrimage to the city of Puruṣottama. || 2 ||
Having seen the Blessed One in the month of Māgha, one is not born again in existence,
whether at Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Kuśasthalī, or Janārdana.

Whatever fruit [is obtained] by seeing Dāmodara and Ramā for even half a moment, that indeed belongs to one who has died at Vastrāpatha; for such a person, there is neither the state of a ghost nor hell.
They are the most blessed even among the blessed, the true deities even among the gods—
those whose death occurs at Vastrāpatha and whose minds are fixed on Hari, the Lord.
There, the gift of a cow should be performed, as well as the feeding of Brahmins;
and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be made, which provides satisfaction until the end of the kalpa.
Dāmodara, Bhava, Svarṇarekhā, and likewise Brahmeśvara;
Brahmakuṇḍa, Kālamegha, and likewise Nārāyaṇahrada.
Kālikendreśvara, Mṛgīkuṇḍa, Unnabila, as well as Maṅgala, the Siddhas, Siddheśvara, and Revatī.
Revatīkuṇḍa is said to be the Cakra garden and its vicinity;
by thus remembering these and other sacred fords (tīrthas), one shall destroy sin.
Blessed is Dāmodarakuṇḍa, which always grants liberation to the deceased;
even for a doer of evil, it shall deliver him if his bones fall therein.
Wherever ashes have fallen, they always liberate the embodied soul;
even a mere drop of water that has fallen into the mouth [brings the same result].
It truly burns away the sins committed in other births;
for the fruit of a śrāddha performed on its bank and of gifts given there is indeed limitless.
A śrāddha ceremony must certainly be performed there, as it bestows liberation;
blessed is the Nārāyaṇahrada where the śrāddha is so highly praised.
Indeed, I shall proclaim to you the fruit of the śrāddha for each respective lunar day:
by honoring the ancestors on the first day (pratipad), one obtains beloved ones in a good household.
When the Śrāddha is performed on the second lunar day, radiant daughters are born;
when it is performed on the third lunar day, auspicious horses are born.
If the Śrāddha is performed on the fourth day, goats and sheep will be found in the house;
if the Śrāddha is performed on the fifth day, sons endowed with lordly power are born.
When the śrāddha is performed on the sixth lunar day, all [the ancestors] become free from disease and endowed with splendor;
indeed, when the śrāddha is performed on the seventh lunar day, there shall surely be the attainment of success in agriculture.
If a śrāddha is performed on the eighth day, one shall obtain profit in trade;
if a śrāddha is performed on the ninth day, there will be many single-hoofed animals.
When the Śrāddha is performed on the tenth day, there is an abundance of cattle, buffaloes, and the like;
when the Śrāddha is performed on the eleventh day, there is an abundance of garments, vessels, and the like.
Sons endowed with spiritual luster and great power are born;
moreover, when the Śrāddha is performed on the twelfth lunar day, there is abundant wealth such as gold and other riches.
If the Śrāddha is performed on the thirteenth day, one becomes highly honored as the best among kinsmen;
if the Śrāddha is performed on the fourteenth day, one shall be victorious in battle.
If a śrāddha is performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one shall attain all desires;
if a śrāddha is performed on the full moon day (pūrṇimā), one shall become prosperous in many ways. ||22||
In the dark fortnight, from the tenth day onwards—excluding the fourteenth—the lunar days are commended for rites such as the śrāddha; other days are not so.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight, so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for a śrāddha ceremony. ||24||
O beloved, the ancestors are properly gratified by a śrāddha offering consisting of sesame seeds, rice, barley, mung beans, water, as well as roots and fruits.
In all śrāddha rites, sesame seeds are traditionally considered the most important;
likewise, there should be many kinds of sweet foods, along with cow’s ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Water, roots, fruits, products of the cow, and excellent food fit for drinking—whatever is mixed with honey at a śrāddha ceremony grants infinite satisfaction. (27)
O beloved, listen as I describe the results of performing a śrāddha under the various lunar mansions:
one desiring offspring should perform it under Rohiṇī, and one desiring splendor under Mṛgaśiras.
One who performs cruel deeds [should act] under Ārdrā; one desiring wealth under Punarvasu;
likewise, one desiring nourishment under Puṣya; and one desiring a son under Āśleṣā. (29)
One desiring preeminence among kinsmen should perform it under Maghā; one desiring good fortune under Phālgunī;
one seeking offspring under the Uttarās; and one desiring success in undertakings under Hasta.
A man desiring good sons should always perform the śrāddha under Citrā, one desiring success in trade under Svātī, and one desiring sovereignty under Anurādhā. (3.1)
One who desires many sons should perform a *śrāddha* under Viśākhā;
one who desires sovereignty under Jyeṣṭhā; and one who desires health under Mūla.
One desiring fame should perform the śrāddha during the Pūrvāṣāḍhās;
during the Uttarāṣāḍhās, however, one who desires freedom from sorrow should perform it. (33)

One desiring to become a physician should perform the śrāddha under Abhijit; one desiring a good rebirth under Śravaṇa; and one desiring sovereignty under Dhaniṣṭhā, according to the prescribed rule. (34)
One who desires success as a physician should perform a śrāddha under Śatabhiṣaj;
one who desires goats and sheep should perform a śrāddha under Pūrvabhādrapadā. || 35 ||
One who desires a wife should set out under Uttarā; one desiring wealth under Revatī;
one intending to acquire horses under Aśvinī; and one desiring long life under Bharaṇī. ||36||
One should perform the śrāddha rite on Mount Revatādrī in the vicinity of Dāmodara,
as well as at the Nārāyaṇa-hrada and likewise at the Dāmodara-kuṇḍa.

But those who offer sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya) to those who have fallen away from the Dharma and are devoid of good conduct— for them, that offering perishes after death.
Those who have bathed after completing their studies, the Vedas, and their vows; those devoted to virtuous conduct;
those who serve their mother and father; and likewise those devoted to truth and righteousness. (39)
They were consecrated at holy pilgrimage sites and likewise performed the final purificatory bath;
they were free from anger, patient, capable, and had conquered their senses.
Those ascetics who know the dharma of liberation, who possess knowledge of yoga, and who are likewise firm in their vows—
those disciplined ones who constantly cause people to hear this history.

Those who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas), those with true knowledge of the scriptures and philosophical systems, those learned in the Dharmaśāstras and Purāṇas, as well as virtuous women and holy men. ||42||
Those who belong to the lineage of the Immovable (Acyuta-gotra), they are all indeed purifiers of the assembly;
one should invite all those who are intent on the welfare of all beings to the śrāddha ceremonies. 43.
While those [ancestors] are indeed eating, the Pitṛs eat there;
for the so-called Pitṛs are those created by the Self-existent One. (44)
The lineage of the ancestors consists of seven groups, as previously observed by the Self-born;
and the Viśvedevas have Agni as their mouth—these I shall declare by name. (45)
Bala, Dhṛti, Vipāpman, Puṇyakṛt, Pāvana, Pārṣṇi, Kṣema, Samūha, and likewise Divyasānu; ||46||
Vivasvān, Vīryavān, Hrīmān, Kīrtimān, and Kṛta;
Jitātmā, Munivarya, Dīptaromā, and Bhayaṃkara. ||47||
Anukarmā, Pratīta, Pradātā, Atyaṃśumān, Śailābha, Paramakrodhin, Dhīroṣṇī, and likewise Bhūpati; ||48||
Sraja, Vajrin, and Varī, as well as the eternal Viśvedevas;
and by name, Vidyudvarcas, Somavarcas, and Sūryaśrī. ||49||
Somapa, Sūrya, Sāvitrī, Dattātman, Puṇḍarīyaka, Uṣṇīnābha, Nabhoda, Viśvāyu, and Dīpti. || 1.158.50 ||
Camūhara, Sureśa, Vyomāri, Śaṅkara, Bhava, Īśa, Kartṛ, Kṛti, Dakṣa, Bhuvana, and Divyakarmakṛt. ||51||
Gaṇita, Pañcavīrya, Āditya, Raśmivān, Saptakṛt, Somavarcas, Viśvakṛt, and also Kavi. ||52||
The Protector, the Good Protector, the Grandson, and the Lord—these illustrious ones have been celebrated as those whose sphere of activity is the course of Time. ||53||
The Grandfather (Brahmā), Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Pulaha;
Aṅgiras, Kratu, and the great Ṛṣi Kaśyapa. ||54||
These ancestors, the ancient ones, are remembered as great lords of yoga;
they are the eighty-eight thousand great sages known as the Bālakhilyas.
Others are remembered as the ancestors (pitṛs) belonging to various lineages and branches;
they are the Agniṣvāttas, the Barhiṣads, the Ājyapas, and likewise the Somapas. (56)
This host is fourfold, and they are your ancestors as well;
created by Brahmā, they are the divine ancestors (devapitṛs) who possess long life.
The Śravaṇas, the Pretakas, the Yāmyas, the Nārakas, and the Pitṛs are the Sāṃvatsaras; the Āgneyas and those Pitṛs who have attained birth [are also included]. (58)
Then those other progenitors of lineages, having died, went to the world of Brahmā;
they are to be known as the Pitṛs of Īśvara who desire their shares. ||59||
These eat from six vessels and attain satisfaction;
for them, food, sacrificial oblation, refined fruit, water, and milk-rice [are provided]. (1.158.60)
Various offerings should indeed be given; when satisfied, they protect the descendants of the lineage.
One should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to Dāmodara on the bank of the Svarṇarekhā river.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather;
the mother, the grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother. ||62||
To my maternal grandfather, his father, and the great-grandfather and others—
may this pinda offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible.
For those in my family who have died and for whom no destination is known,
I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa) for their deliverance.
For those who have passed away among my circle of kinsmen and for those whose destination is unknown,
I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
To all those who have not yet grown teeth, and those who were aborted in the womb—
for their deliverance, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who have been consumed by fire, to those who have perished from cold,
and to others who have perished without fire— to them I offer this rice-ball.
To those killed by lightning or thieves, those who died in forest fires,
and those killed by predatory tigers— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).

To those killed by fanged beasts, horned animals, clawed creatures, venomous serpents, weapons, or nooses, and to those who committed suicide or were killed by hunger— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those who have perished from thirst or hunger in the forest, in the wilderness, or on the road,
and to those [afflicted] by spirits, ghosts, and demons— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
For the sake of uplifting those who dwell in Raurava, in Tāmisra, and in Kālasūtra, I offer this rice-ball (piṇḍa).
For the sake of liberating those who have gone to the world of hungry ghosts, existing in various states of torment, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
Having fallen into miserable states of existence and being struck down by curses and the like, I offer this *piṇḍa* for the sake of their deliverance. (73)
I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the sake of uplifting those who have fallen under the power of Yama’s messengers in all the hells.
To those who have entered the womb of animals, and to the birds, insects, and reptiles,
and even to those situated in the womb of trees— to them I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who wander through thousands of different births by means of their own karma, and for whom a human birth is difficult to obtain—to them I give this offering. (76)
To the ancestors and kinsmen dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth, and to those who died without having received the sacramental rites— to them I offer this rice-ball.
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas,
may they all forever attain satisfaction through this rice-ball offering.
To those who have no kinsmen, to those who are kinsmen, and likewise to those who are kinsmen from other births—
to them this funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered by me shall indeed reach as an inexhaustible offering.
Those who have died in the paternal lineage, those who have died in the maternal lineage, and those other kinsmen of teachers, fathers-in-law, and relatives who have passed away; ||| 1.158.80 ||

Those in my family for whom the funeral cakes have been cut off, those who are deprived of sons and wives, those whose sacred rites have fallen into neglect, those who are blind from birth, and those who are lame; ||8|| 1 ||
May the pinda offered by me reach those in my family who were deformed or born from unripened wombs, whether known or unknown; may it remain inexhaustible for them. (82)
To those who belong to my paternal lineage up to Brahmā, and those born in my maternal lineage, and those born in both families—to them I offer this rice-ball (piṇḍa). ||83||
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas, may they all attain satisfaction through these barley-meal offerings mixed with sesame seeds. (84)
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, whatever exists, moving or unmoving—may all attain complete satisfaction through this rice-ball offered by me. (85)
I perform my bath in the Dāmodara pool for the purification of the self, for the attainment of the worlds of the Sun and other realms, and for the liberation of the deceased. (86)
Having bathed, one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the gods and others according to the prescribed rule:
"From Brahmā down to a blade of grass—the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans. (87)

May the Vairājas, those established on the path of Brahman, and others who have gone to the worlds of merit—all the ancestors, including mothers, maternal grandfathers, and so forth—be satisfied. (88)
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather, whose forms are now presided over by the sacrificial fire, attain satisfaction today. (89)
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
abiding within the bodies of these brahmins, attain satisfaction today.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through these rice-balls offered by me upon the earth. (91)
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this devotion which has been uttered by me. (92)
May the maternal grandfather attain satisfaction; may his father attain satisfaction.
May the Viśvedevas attain satisfaction; may the Lord Hari attain satisfaction. (93)
When a *yati* (ascetic) eats at one's *śrāddha*, Hari himself eats there;
when Hari eats at one's *śrāddha*, he eats the three worlds.
Vaiṣṇava saints should especially be fed at a śrāddha ceremony;
indeed, virtuous women should also be fed, for this brings about inexhaustible merit and satisfaction.
If one, knowing that ascetics are residing in the village, disregards them and feeds other twice-born men instead, that offering to the ancestors goes to the Rākṣasas. (96)
When a renunciant who is a devotee of Hari eats at a śrāddha ceremony, then that śrāddha becomes complete, even without the full ritual requirements of a śrāddha. (97)
Satiated with food, milk, ghee, honey, and sugarcane products, even all the hosts of ancestors attain inexhaustible satisfaction. (98)
One should offer faultless milk-rice, cooked grain, and grains of the sages (nīvāra) produced from the ocean to all the ancestors; by this, they are always satisfied. 99.
Milk, curd, ghee, and fresh butter from cows are indeed purifying;
however, the ghee of buffaloes is considered superior, though their milk is not so described.
The maternal grandfather, the daughter’s son, the sister’s son, the maternal uncle, the mother’s sister’s son, his son, and likewise the maternal uncle’s son; ||| 10.1 ||
The son-in-law, the father-in-law, the wife’s brother, and his son;
the officiating priest, the preceptor, the sub-teacher, the teacher, and likewise the Vedic scholar (śrotriya). || 102 ||

Those who are firm in their vows, virtuous men and women—these are indeed purifiers at śrāddha ceremonies; they know the dharma appropriate for each age and are protectors of learning, conduct, and other virtues. (103)
The time known as Kutupa, a Nepalese blanket,
silver, Darbha grass, sesame seeds, and a daughter's son— these are purifiers at a Śrāddha ceremony.
The day is always known to consist of fifteen muhūrtas;
among these, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called Kutupa.
Agastya, bhṛṅgarāja, tulasī, śatapatrikā,
campaka, and tila flowers— these six are beloved by the ancestors.
When a conflict arises between the lack of a recipient and the lack of material goods, only a mere morsel (piṇḍa) should be given;
when the day for the Śrāddha has arrived, one should perform the Śrāddha according to one's capacity.
One should offer a water-pot, or even a plantain fruit, or give grass to a cow; one should not let a day pass by in vain.
The Śrāddha, which has been prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas to be performed sequentially on the eleventh day,
should also be performed on the twelfth day, because the ancestors are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
Having performed the *śrāddha*, one should fast after smelling that which has been partaken by the ancestors.
A guest who arrives at the time of the *śrāddha* must be fed; this constitutes the completion of the *śrāddha*.
Free from disease, unimpaired, a consumer of food, long-lived, possessed of sons and grandsons,
wealthy, and an enjoyer of riches— the performer of the śrāddha ceremony prospers.
