Vahni said to him, "Certainly; it shall be as you desire.
Death shall come to you by her upon whom your heart is fixed."
Having been addressed in this manner, Rambhā then went to see the yakṣa named Mālavaṭa in the cattle-pen of Mālavaṭa.
Elephants, buffaloes, horses, cows, goats, and sheep were there in great numbers; she set her heart upon a buffalo.
Desiring him, she approached the lord of the Daityas when she was three years old;
and he too, having become a buffalo, engaged in sexual union with her, being full of strength.
Taking that queen who was pregnant, he went to his own home;
there in Pātāla, he, a doer of forbidden acts, was abandoned by the Dānavas.
Having again led the queen to the yakṣa named Mālavaṭa, he returned to his dwelling; there the queen gave birth to a son.
Having obtained his son, a bright buffalo capable of assuming any form at will and possessed of great strength, Rambha indeed rejoiced again and again.
Then another buffalo, seeing that very same buffalo-cow in her season, desired her; she then spoke of this to Rambha. || 16 ||
Then a most terrible battle took place between Rambha and the buffalo;
at that time, he was struck in the heart with its two sharp horns.
With his heart pierced through, Raṃbha fell down and died;
thereafter, the queen went for refuge to the Yakṣas.
And that [place] was guarded by Yakṣas; having warded off another buffalo, the Yakṣas such as Mālavaṭa and others then [beheld] that Raṃbha who had died.
They placed her upon the funeral pyre, and she ascended it there;
then, from the midst of the fire, a man fierce and terrifying arose.
Then, sword in hand, he drove the yakṣas away from that place;
he slaughtered the buffaloes and nurtured his son with sincere devotion. ||21||
He became the son of Rambha, known by the name Raktabīja;
he was indeed possessed of great strength, invincible, and could always assume any form at will.
In his youth, he fought with the gods as well as other guardians of the worlds;
the guardians of the quarters, the world-protectors, and the planets were all conquered by him in battle.
Then, having brought Aja to Śaṅkara, the gods went to Janārdana and reported the activities of Mahiṣa and Raktabīja.
O Lord, the kingdoms of the Aśvins, the Sun, and the Moon; of Water, Wind, Fire, and Brahmā;
and of Kubera, Indra, and the other gods, have indeed been assailed.
"O Lord, we gods have been cast out from our abode and now dwell upon the earth;
this would not have happened if Viṣṇu or Śambhu had provided us with protection. (26)
As we were being dragged away by him toward the netherworld (rasātala),
the Blessed One, upon hearing this, felt an unbearable anger there.
At that time, a great radiance indeed issued forth from the mouths of the Lord Śambhu and likewise from Brahmā, as well as from the gods beginning with Indra. ||28||
That goddess who, having slain Madhu and Kaiṭabha, indeed became the embodiment of the strength of all the senses; from her, that very splendor emerged. || 29 ||
All of that was as solid as a mountain, most difficult to withstand,
and filled with splendor within the hermitage of the great seer Kātyāyana.
From that was born the large-eyed Kātyāyanī Maheśvarī;
the splendor of Śambhu became her face, and the splendor of Vahni became his three eyes.
His hair became the splendor of Yama, and his arms became the splendor of Hari;
eighteen arms were thus produced.
The pair of breasts and the chest were formed from the splendor of Soma; the thighs, shanks, and hips were formed by the splendor of Indra; and the waist was formed by the splendor of the Moon.
The pair of feet became the splendor of Brahman, tender and reddish;
the fingers [became] by the splendor of the Sun, and the teeth by the splendor of Prajāpati.
Her nose was born from the splendor of the Yakṣas, her ears from the splendor of Vāyu;
and her brow became the splendor of the Sādhyas—was it perhaps the bow of Kāma?
Thus, having combined the splendors of the gods there, she was born as Sundarī,
known by the name Kātyāyanī, for the purpose of destroying Mahiṣa.
Then Śambhu gave him the trident, Hari gave him the discus,
the Lord of Waters gave him the conch, and Hutāśana gave him the spear.
Vāyu gave him a bow and swift, inexhaustible arrows;
the Sun-god gave him a thunderbolt and a bell; and likewise, Yama gave him a staff.
Kubera gave her a mace, Brahmā gave a water-pot,
Kāla gave her a rosary of beads, and he also gave her a sword and a shield.
Soma gave a necklace and a chowrie, the Ocean gave a radiant garland,
and Himālaya gave a lion as a vehicle to Śrī.
Viśvakarman gave him an axe and two crescent-shaped earrings,
while Citraratha gave him a crest-jewel and a drinking vessel.
The serpent Śeṣa gave him a necklace of snakes, the Seasons gave him a garland of unfading flowers, and the gods gave him all kinds of weapons and ornaments.
Then the Goddess became exceedingly pleased and indeed let out a loud laugh;
honored with blessings by all the gods, she went to the Vindhya mountain.
Dwelling upon the high peak, she remained captivating to the heart;
and Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the two messengers of Mahiṣāsura, beheld her.
Having gone to the buffalo, they said: "How can you lie there unconcerned when a maiden beautiful in all her limbs has arrived; please accept her. (45)
What is the luster of the moon-like face? The hair resembles dark clouds. Are there three fires and three eyes? Is there a conch-shell mark situated upon the neck? (46)
Her breasts were well-rounded with depressed nipples, resembling jars;
her eighteen arms were plump, auspicious, and equipped with weapons. (47)
Her belly was marked by three folds, her waist was devoid of hair, and her shanks and thighs—vessels of beauty—were as radiant as gold. (48)
With beautiful and auspicious palms and soles resembling land-lotuses, and eyes like lotus petals, she was the vessel of all beauty. (49)
Accept that maiden, beautiful as a celestial nymph, as your wife;
without her, this divine form of yours does not shine at all.
"Without her, O Lord, even your sovereignty—or even the sovereignty of Indra—is in vain;
go to the Vindhya mountain, behold it, and do what you deem appropriate."
Indeed, when good or evil has been committed by men, it surely follows after them;
yet, by my own good fortune, this jewel of a maiden has appeared for my sake. (52)
And having thus deliberated, he likewise [confronted] Muṇḍa, Namara, Bāṣkala, Caṇḍa, Viśālanetra, Kapila, and Vikṣura. ||53||
That king of the Daityas commanded Ugrāyudha and Raktabīja:
"Let the great Asuras, having prepared themselves, proceed toward the Vindhya mountain. (54)
Then, having arrived and encamped their army on the Vindhya mountains, they remained there;
at that time, Dundubhi, the son of Maya, spoke to the Goddess.
"O Kumārī, I am indeed the messenger of Raṃbha’s son, Mahiṣa;
listen to the command of my lord and master, and then do as you wish. (56)
Dundubhi said: "O maiden, choose me by all means;
the immortals are my servants, having been conquered by me. (57)
The worlds up to the realm of Brahmā have been brought under my control, as have the guardians of the world;
I am Indra, I am Rudra, I am the Sun, and I am the Moon. (58)
"I am Lokeśa, O Great King; worship me, the Lord of the World.
You are a preeminent jewel among women; indeed, worship me, who am worthy of you. (59)
Having heard the words of the messenger, the queen then said:
"It is certain that in my family there exists a custom known as *śulka*. (1.163.60)
"If he were to give me that buffalo, I would accept him as my husband today.
Dundubhi said, "Tell me, what kind of bride-price (śulka) is that?"
"For your sake, my master would even give his own head; what then [could stop him]?
Then the Goddess said, "He who shall conquer me in battle shall win the maiden as his bride-price."
"Report to him that he alone shall be her husband.
Having heard this, Dundubhi arrived and spoke as follows: ||63||
The buffalo-demon Mahiṣa, possessed of great splendor and the leader of all the Daityas,
having heard this, arrived at Mount Vindhya and stood there, surrounding it.
There, the commander-in-chief of the Daityas was known by the name Cikṣura;
he was a leader at the head of the army, accompanied by a fourfold force.
Other Daityas and Dānavas, accompanied by their respective armies and dispatched by Mahiṣāsura, arrived there for the sake of battle.
Then, for the sake of assisting the Goddess, Sūrya, Candra, and others—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Indra, Varuṇa, and the rest— arrived there.
Then, on the Vindhya mountain, the fierce and truly terrifying armies of the gods and the Daityas were arrayed against one another.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Mahiṣāsura, the Son of the Asura Rambha, and the Subsequent Account of the Birth of Kātyāyanī who Destroyed Him," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, then the commencement of their battle took place;
all the soldiers, fully equipped and with weapons raised, rushed forward.
And then Mahisha beheld the Goddess, blazing like fire,
possessing the splendor of the causal sun, and making the bowstring resound.
She stood there, having agitated the entire army, her crown scraping the sky,
pervading all directions with her thousand arms.
Having resolved to conquer, the Daitya was bewildered in many ways;
a terrible battle then commenced between the gods and the enemies of the gods.
The space between the quarters became pervaded by various weapons and missiles discharged in many ways;
Kṣura, the general of Mahiṣāsura’s army, fought with the immortals.
Udagra fought with the gods using sixty thousand chariots,
while Mahāhanu fought with ten million [chariots].
Then Asiloman fought with fifty million [demons],
and Bāṣkala fought there with six hundred thousand times ten thousand.
There, the cat fought against tens of millions of chariots, which moved through the sky and were equipped with countless elephants, horses, and chariots as their means of transport.
There were also tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of other Daityas and Dānavas there,
with horses, elephants, chariots, vehicles, weapons, missiles, and likewise foot soldiers.
Those asuras fought in battle with the gods and the goddesses using javelins, slings, clubs, and swords.
With maces, spears, swords, axes, and sharp-edged missiles, the gods fought the Dānavas according to the rise of their respective intelligence and strength. || 11 ||
Then the Dānavas repeatedly hurled weapons at the goddess in order to slay her;
she effortlessly severed them with her own weapons.
With swift hands, Caṇḍikā quickly discharged weapons and missiles upon the army of the asuras and struck down that host of asuras.
The Goddess cut down the scattered and assembled hosts of Daityas and Dānavas almost entirely, just as a farmer cuts down crops.
Then other Dānavas, by means of the Saṃjīvanī lore, rose up even though they had been cut down, and fought with him. || 15 ||
The gods destroyed them with showers of arrows and volleys of weapons;
then the Goddess, drawing her bow, struck the host of Dānavas.
With floods of arrows and divine, sharp weapons, he cut the army into many pieces;
some he struck with a mace, some with a sharp sword, and others with javelins.
With a noose, and likewise with spears, javelins,
clubs, and discuses, the goddess Maheśvarī struck down some of them right there.
Striking some with thunderbolts and others with clubs,
the goddess fought in battle and heaved many sighs.
Then all those lords of the Gaṇas, born from the breath of the Goddess,
fought with missiles and weapons and struck down the Daityas and Dānavas.
They rejoiced and sounded kettledrums and trumpets;
they blew conchs and beat mṛdaṅgas and bherīs upon the field of battle.
And then the lion, enraged and repeatedly shaking his mane,
being as formidable as Mahākāla, began to destroy the Dānavas.
Some Dānavas were indeed split in two by swords and tridents;
others, their chests pierced, were cut down by arrows and battle-axes. ||23||
Struck down by the mace, they fell and lay upon the earth;
some of the asuras, struck by clubs, vomited blood.
Millions of soldiers there gave up their lives by means of arrows;
others fell with their arms severed and their necks cut off by discuses.
Some, split in the middle by swords, lie in two parts;
others, split into half-parts, sleep upon the earth. (26)
Others, severed at the waist, fell upon the ground in two parts;
some were headless trunks with only one eye, arm, or foot, cut into two pieces.
Headless trunks fell there, rising again and again;
others, with swords, scimitars, and spears in their hands, fought and danced. || 28 ||
Others, intoxicated with pride, fled and abandoned the battle;
considering her to be the formidable Kālarātri, they scattered in all directions. (29)
The earth became impassable due to those who had fallen while advancing in battle;
in that interval, great rivers flowed forth with waters of blood.
Thus, a great destruction of the asuras occurred on earth at that time, [caused] by elephants, horses, donkeys, camels, and buffaloes upon the field of battle. (31)
Seeing his own army being slaughtered, the commander Cikshura then drew his firm bow and rained down a net of arrows.
Then the goddess repeatedly cut his arrows with her own shafts;
he then took up sixteen other arrows with golden feathers.
He struck the four horses with four arrows;
having killed the charioteer with one, he cut down the standard with another.
With one [arrow] he severed the bow, and with mallets he shattered the chariot;
thus, his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed... (35)
Taking up his sword and shield, he rushed forward with speed;
but Maheśvarī cut down both the sword and the shield with four arrows.
Then he seized a trident and rushed again toward Ambikā;
thereupon, that king of the Daityas hurled it at Bhadrakālī.
Taking up another sword, he struck at the arm of Śaṅkara’s consort;
the sword broke into two pieces, while the trident shattered into a hundred fragments.
The spear hurled by the goddess tore into his own chest;
she then severed his feet, hands, and head with her excellent sword.
Thus the commander Cikshura fell, divided into six parts;
and seeing the general slain, Namuci, who stood at the head of the army, [advanced].
And having approached with speed, he released a spear at the goddess;
however, she reduced that spear to ashes as soon as it was struck by her "Hum" sound.
In the battle, the Daitya seized a trident and hurled it at the lion;
the Goddess, however, shattered that as well with arrows possessing razor-sharp edges.
Then the lion, springing up, seized Namara by the throat with his sharp-edged fangs as he remained between the frontal globes of the elephant.
Having cast the lifeless one from the shoulder of the elephant, he was presented to the goddesses;
then, seizing Namara with his right hand, he whirled him about above his head.
Then she made a sound like a drum together with loud laughter;
from that laughter, various spirits with deformed bodies emerged.

Some had the faces of tigers, others the faces of wolves; some had the faces of horses, and others the faces of buffaloes; some had the faces of boars, others the faces of cocks; some had the faces of rats, and others the faces of goats.
With various faces, eyes, and feet, and endowed with various weapons,
some sing, others laugh, and others play, all mingled together.
Others there were playing instruments, while others were praising Maheśvarī;
she, together with the bhūtas, destroyed whatever remnant of the Dānava army remained.
Then that great asura Ugrāsya rushed forward with speed,
along with Bāṣkala, Uddhata, and another named Biḍālanayana.
Durdhara and Durmukha fought with great speed;
however, in the battle, they were struck down by the Goddess with stones, trees, and other weapons.
And with blows from his teeth and fists, Bāṣkala was also struck down;
then, with the falling of her mace, the Goddess crushed the arrogant one to pieces.
With a bhindipāla weapon and likewise with arrows, he crushed Biḍāla; and with a mace, he completely shattered Durdhara, Durmukha, and Karālaka.
The Supreme Goddess struck Tāmra, Andhaka, Ugravīrya, and Mahāhanu—
those who possessed three eyes and wielded tridents.
When the army had thus been destroyed, Mahiṣa, the king of the Daityas,
then assumed his buffalo form and terrified those Gaṇas.
Some he struck with blows from his snout, others with the throwing of his claws,
some with slaps of his tail, and others with the goring of his horns.
Having struck down many Pramathas— some with speed, others with his roar, some by whirling about, and others with the fire from his eyes and his hissing breaths.
At that very moment, that asura of great heroism, who tore up the surface of the earth with his razor-sharp claws, rushed forward out of anger and strength to slay the lion.
With his two horns, he hurled high mountains and let out a roar;
by the force of his whirling and striking, the earth there was shattered. ||58||
From the blow of his tail, the ocean overflowed its shores and inundated the world;
and by the striking of his horns, tail, and ears, the clouds were shattered and went to their destruction.
Struck by his breaths, the mountains fell from the path of the sky;
indeed, that mighty one then produced the suspicion that the very universe was being destroyed.
Thus, that enemy displayed the entirety of his strength;
then the Goddess indeed bound his body with a noose.
Then, in an instant, she abandoned that buffalo form once again;
at that moment, the Goddess became a lioness as she was about to sever the head.
He appeared as a man with a sword in his hand;
at the very moment the goddess pierced him with arrows, he likewise [pierced her].
Bearing a sword and shield, the elephant became like a mountain;
with its trunk, it dragged that lion and roared.
Maheśvarī severed that trunk with her very sword;
meanwhile, that Daitya, having assumed the form of a buffalo, rushed toward Caṇḍikā.
Then Caṇḍikā hurled mountains with her two horns,
and she pulverized them with her mace, iron clubs, and javelins.
Drinking wine, she became enraged with blood-red eyes;
intoxicated by the pride of her own strength and vigor, she spoke to the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Roar, roar for a moment, O Daitya, while I drink the honey;
once you have been slain by me right here, the gods will quickly roar.
Roar, roar for a moment, O you who stand in fear, as long as you do not release your excrement;
once you have been slain by me right here, the Dānavas will quickly perish.
Having spoken thus, he forcefully hurled a trident at his heart;
by the power of its impact against the bones of the Daitya’s chest, the trident shattered.
Then he hurled a spear, but it fell to the earth with its point blunted;
then a discus was launched, but it too fell down with its edge dulled.
Then that mace, too, having been hurled, fell to the ground split in two;
likewise, both the noose and the staff, when thrown, were shattered.
The vajra struck him there in the throat, and he then fell into a state of wretchedness.
Thereupon, the Great Goddess, filled with rage, leapt upon the great asura.
Mounted upon his back, the Daitya then leaped forward;
she, however, crushed him with her feet and rendered him devoid of strength.
He pierced his throat with a spear, and a man emerged holding a sword;
he was none other than that preeminent asura, the great demon who had become the son of Mahiṣa.
As soon as he had stepped out, [the other] struck him with a sharp-edged sword;
then, seizing him by the hair in rage, he cut off his head with a blade.
Then the remaining Daitya army, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", was mostly destroyed by the Pramathas; it entered into the netherworld (Pātāla).
The gods attained great joy and praised that Caṇḍikā;
the Gandharvas sang her glory and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Indeed, musical instruments were played and sounds of victory arose;
the gods said, "O Great Goddess, there is truly no limit to your greatness."
He thought, "May I become many"—that desire is You, the Supreme Goddess; that [desire] is celebrated as the beauty within the form of Hari. (1.164.8)
You are propitiation, as well as devotion and liberation;
you are the Supreme Goddess, Nārāyaṇī, Mahālakṣmī, Brahmāṇī, and Maheśvarī. ||8 1 ||
You are Mahāmāyā, whose nature consists of the three guṇas; you are Prakṛti, the sovereign mistress of all actions; you are Ramā, Vairājñī, Lakṣmī, and Śrī in the home of the virtuous. 82.
You are misfortune in the house of the meritless, and you are the intellect within the sky of the heart;
you are faith, you are modesty, you are fear, and you are the Svāhā-call in the performance of sacrifice.
You are *svadhā* for the sake of the ancestors; you are knowledge for supreme liberation.
You are Speech, you are Gāyatrī, you are Sāvitrī, and you are composed of the three Vedas.
You are conduct, intelligence, Durgā, and Gaṅgā, the bestower of prosperity;
you are the power within all the senses—to her, and to you, salutations again and again. (85)
Protect us always, O Mother, from weapons and missiles in all directions;
O Goddess, forever slay the asuras who constantly create obstacles for the gods.
Having thus offered praise, she was honored with divine flowers, anointed with fragrant unguents, and worshipped with incense, lamps, food offerings, ornaments, garments, and other such gifts. (87)
Prasannā said, "Choose the gods and whatever you desire.
The gods said, "Remembered by us, do indeed destroy the great calamities. (88)
O goddess with a face like a lotus, be gracious to us for the increase of wealth, property, prosperity, power, sons, wives, and all such excellences. 8–9.
Having said "So be it," and having repeatedly encouraged all the gods,
and having declared, "I shall prevail for the sake of the immortals," he entered among those gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Army of Mahiṣāsura and the Army of the Gods, the Destruction of the Asura Army by the Goddess, the Slaying of Mahiṣāsura, and the Praise Offered by the Devas," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved; I shall tell you once more of her origin from the beginning, for the sake of destroying Śumbha, Niśumbha, and their followers. Listen.
Born from the Vairāja in the lotus, Brahmā remained without a creation;
accompanied by the lotus, he wondered, "What should be done by me here for the sake of creation? (2)
Then, at that moment, there arose in him the recollection of his previous birth; [he thought:
"Without a seed, there is no arising; therefore, I shall offer the seed. (3)
Prajāpati offered the semen situated within his own body as an oblation into the fire;
formerly, the two Brahmās had likewise offered their semen into the fire out of a desire for progeny.
The eight sages were born from Vahni; hear their names:
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (5)
Atri and Vasiṣṭha—these eight were the sons of Brahmā;
they were resplendent, endowed with physical forms and their own respective powers and virtues.
When the semen was offered into the fire, it united with the flame;
then that Prajāpati gave him the name "Bhṛgu," saying, "You are Bhṛgu."
Requested by Śiva and granted by Brahmā out of a desire for a son, Vāruṇa was born from Varuṇa, Śaiva from Śiva, Āgneya from Agni, and Bhṛgu from Brahmā.
And the Lord offered his own second seed into the coals;
from those coals, O Aṅgiras, the limbs were then gathered together, and thus Aṅgiras was born.
For Āṅgirasa was named after Agni; he was the second son of Brahmā.
When Śukra was killed six times, six sons were born again.
From Marīci was born Marīci, who was the third;
since he was born from the sacrificial oblation (homa) during the ritual (kratu), he is this fourth one, Ṛtu.
But he who was saved by Viṣṇu and became his fifth son, Atri,
is this one known as Pulastya, who is adorned upon his body with hair-like pores.
From his long hair was born Pulaha, who is considered the seventh;
from that [hair] was produced Agni Vasu, who is called the self-controlled Vasiṣṭha.
For these were the first sons of Brahmā, endowed with seeds and human form; all were lords of progeny, and all were likewise practitioners of austerity.
Among them, there were ten sons of Atharvan, the son of Aṅgiras;
they were born of Surūpā and were named Ādhāryu and Āyu.
Danu, Dakṣa, Dama, Prāṇa, Haviṣyān, and likewise Haviṣṇu;
as well as Ṛta and Satya—among these, this Dakṣa is to be understood as the father of Satī. (16)
Dakṣa, desiring to create various offspring through sexual union,
took Asiknī, the daughter of the Prajāpati named Vīraṇa, as his wife.
Twenty-four daughters were born to him;
thirteen, beginning with Śraddhā, were given by Dakṣa to Dharma.
Faith, Fortune, Conduct, Contentment, Nourishment, Intelligence, as well as Action, Wisdom, Modesty, Wealth, Peace, Success, and Fame—these are the thirteen. (19)
From them, eleven younger daughters of beautiful eyes remained:
Khyāti, Satī, Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and likewise Kṣamā.
Sannati, Anurūpā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā;
Bhṛgu, Bhava, Marīci, and the sage Aṅgiras as well. (21)
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, Vasiṣṭha,
Agni, and the Pitṛs— these are, in order, the sons-in-law of Dakṣa.
And due to the power of a previous curse, as well as the force of Brahmā’s command, for the purpose of producing a son for the sake of destroying Tāraka and the others. ||23||
And because that which is to be is inevitable, she came to exist in the house of Dakṣa.
Listen, O beloved, to how the former curse upon the Goddess occurred.
For the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura, Kātyāyanī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), was created by all the gods; she destroyed that preeminent among asuras.
When she again became invisible and vanished among the gods,
she was then protected by Rudra at the tip of his trident.
Known by the name Satī, she was always protected by Rudra at the tip of his trident;
throughout thousands of future births, she shall never be separated from Śiva. (27)
When that asura named Māhiṣa was struck down by her, his wife, renowned as Kuṇḍhī, remained devoted to her husband. ||28||
And having lamented repeatedly before the Goddess with a heart distressed by suffering,
he cursed her so that she would be deprived of children and other kin, and be deeply afflicted by the loss of her husband.
I am burning in the fire of the funeral pyre, and you likewise are suffering;
you suffer because of the death of your husband and because of the pain of being childless.
"You shall burn in the fire of time; become dull-witted and miserable!"—thus was the curse then pronounced upon the queen, the consort of Mahisha.
The goddess Kātyāyanī, though virtuous, had her face withered for a moment.
Seeing this, Brahmā and the others then said to the goddess, "O lady of auspicious countenance! (32)
"Do not grieve; your husband shall never die.
We gods shall strengthen Hara with auspicious blessings."
However, a sorrow equal to death will befall your husband;
for the wise consider the loss of honor for the great to be death itself. (34)
By means of the sign of Kāmadeva, through the power of future worship, and by means of the appearance of the *liṅga* when desire arose in Śaṅkara. (35)
Indeed, when Śambhu, having raised his phallus, shall go among the assembly of the sages' wives naked, performing his willful acts as he pleases; (36)
Then, however, the Brahmins there—sages who were knowers of the mantras and free from impurity—beheld Hara naked, full of lust, with his phallus raised up. ||37||
With a blade of darbha grass and by means of mantras, they will cause the linga to fall from its base; they will repeatedly show it contempt.
"The destruction of virility is the destruction of the organ; this is proclaimed as the destruction of the man himself.
Śaṅkara will indeed undergo this suffering, which is truly equal to death. (39)
Then the gods on earth shall install the Liṅga upon you as its pedestal;
they shall worship that Bāṇa, and it will attain renown throughout the world.
Then Hara will become renowned as the Jyotirliṅga;
taking the cut-off linga, they shall join it back into its place. ||41||
"Furthermore, that person will become worthy of you once again when he possesses his [original] marks.
This has occurred merely as a sign; do not grieve. (42)
In this state which is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, how could there be any occasion for grief?
Listen further, O Goddess: Dakṣa will perform a sacrifice.
"He will not grant a place for Śaṅkara at that sacrifice;
thus shall this loss of honor come to Śambhu from Dakṣa. (44)
On account of that, at that time, there shall be a blazing in the fire for you;
you will be childless, sorrowful, and face the fruits of curses and the like. (45)
"You, O dull-witted Kālī, shall be burnt; you will become Śailaputrī (the Daughter of the Mountain), and there your marriage with Śaṅkara will take place once again. (46)
"Do not grieve thus; what is to be will not be otherwise.
Therefore, go to the house of Dakṣa and become the daughter of Dakṣa. (47)
The Dānavas, headed by the Asura Tāraka and possessed of great strength, shall indeed be born in accordance with the granting of boons to them. (48)
For the sake of producing a son, become the daughter of Dakṣa;
there, by means of Rudra, a son Kārttikeya shall be born to you. (49)
"Since the destruction of the Asuras shall also come about through that means,
go, O Goddess, to the house of Dakṣa and become the daughter of Dakṣa."
Having thus received this command, the goddess appeared from the command of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, as the daughter of the Lord of Creatures. (51)
By the command of Brahmā, Dakṣa gave that Satī to Rudra;
and Rudra, the wielder of the trident, accepted Dākṣī as his very own.
Born from a mass of splendor for the sake of the gods who were oppressed by the Daityas,
the Goddess, having destroyed the hosts of Daityas, became the daughter of Dakṣa.
Thereupon, that virtuous goddess Satī, having abandoned her body through yoga due to the reproach of her husband, shall become Pārvatī.
Listen, Lakṣmī: thousands of sons were born in the house of Dakṣa;
they were all true brothers, whose sins had been washed away by their austerities. (55)
And one hundred and ten thousand [beings], through the instruction of Nārada,
went to the abode of Brahmā, a realm characterized by non-return.
When the Haryaśvas had been released, there were others known as the Śabalāśvas;
five thousand and five hundred sons were indeed born to them as well.
Through the instruction of Nārada, they certainly attained the state of liberation;
though joined with creation by their father, they were sent forth into the world by Nārada. (58)
Then Dakṣa, becoming very angry, cursed Nārada:
"O Brāhmaṇa Nārada, go to destruction; dwell within the womb! (59)
Then Dakṣa indeed made an agreement with Kaśyapa, saying:
"May Nārada become your son through my daughter."
Then Nārada also cursed Dakṣa, the son of Aṅgiras, saying:
"Just as I am the son of Brahmā, so shall you become a descendant of Kaśyapa through my curse. (6.1)
And at that time, you shall become a human king from this point forward—the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of the Pracetasas. (62)
O Dakṣa, you shall take Māriṣā, the daughter of a tree, as your wife;
from her, sixty daughters, beginning with Śraddhā, will be born to you. (63)
Ten of them will belong to Bhaviṣya; you shall bestow [the others] for the sake of the Dharma: twenty-seven to Śaśin and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
You shall bestow four upon Tārkṣya for the sake of another form;
and you shall bestow two each upon Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Kṛśāśva.
Thus, when the time arrived according to the curse, Prajāpati Dakṣa gave thirteen of his daughters to Kaśyapa.
Therefore, that sage Nārada was born again through the power of a curse;
thus, although he was originally Brāhma, Nārada was indeed born here as a descendant of Kaśyapa.
Thus Dakṣa, the son of Aṅgiras, was born as the son of Pracetas;
it was in his house that Mahāmāyā took birth for such a duration.
At that very time, two exceedingly powerful Daityas named Niśumbha and Śumbha, who brought suffering to the worlds, came into existence.
Kaśyapa had a wife named Danu, who was the daughter of Dakṣa;
from her were born three sons of great strength and prowess.
The eldest was known as Śumbha, and another asura was Niśumbha;
the third was named Namuci, who always caused suffering to the gods.
To slay Namuci, the giver of suffering, Indra took up his thunderbolt;
out of fear, Namuci then entered the chariot of the Sun.
Even though struck by the sun, he did not come out from the chariot;
and being repeatedly cast down and beaten by the sun with his foot-rod, [he remained there]. (73)
Nevertheless, even though he was outside, he did not come forth at that time out of fear of Indra’s thunderbolt;
perceiving him as one who had sought refuge, the Sun protected him from Vāsava.
Then he made an agreement with Ravi and Vāsava:
"I shall certainly not remain on earth, nor ever in heaven."
"I shall dwell in the netherworld; let me be released by the gift of my life.
Thereupon he was released by the Lord of the Gods, and then he chose a boon as follows: ||76||
"O Lord of the Gods, grant me the boon of invincibility against weapons and missiles.
Having received this boon, the Dānava said, "So be it," and Indra replied, "Let it be so. (77)
Realizing that he was invulnerable to his own [weapons], that Dānava abandoned the chariot of the Sun with his handheld arms and missiles and quickly entered the ocean. ||78||
Even as he was sinking into the ocean, the lord of the Dānavas saw the excellent foam of the sea; seizing it, he stood within the water.
Having filled his mouth, nose, ears, and other orifices, he remained within the water;
then Śakra hurled his thunderbolt at him, even though he was invisible.
Struck by the foam-bodied Vajra, he fell down and died;
with his nostrils obstructed by the foam-bodied Vajra, he indeed perished.
Then his two heroic brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha, filled with rage,
made a supreme effort and arrived for the purpose of destroying the goddess.
The gods also went forth for battle, relying upon Indra;
a most tumultuous war ensued, and the deities were conquered and overcome. (83)
The vanguard troops, along with their forces and vehicles, were conquered by the two Daityas;
moreover, Indra’s elephant was seized, and my buffalo was taken away. (84)
When the jeweled parasol of the Lord of Waters was seized, the mace of Hari was taken;
and the treasures, such as Śaṅkha and Padma, were forcibly seized from Kubera.
The three worlds have been brought under his control, and his own sovereignty has been secured;
the guardians of the quarters and the world-protectors have for the most part been subdued.
Having returned to the earth, most kings were brought under their control;
there, having encountered those two while they were ruling on the banks of the Revā, [the others likewise submitted]. (87)
They both asked the one named Raktabīja, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am a Daitya, the minister of Mahiṣa, known as Raktabīja. (88)
Out of fear of the Goddess, I rule here in secret;
Mahiṣa has two ministers named Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
"Your two mighty arms remain submerged in the water out of fear of the Goddess;
such is our situation, which you both must also understand. (1.165.90)
Thus questioned from behind, Śumbha and Niśumbha both spoke to him:
"I am Śumbha, the elder; this one is Niśumbha, the younger."
The two sons of Danu, born of Kaśyapa, conquered the gods and others, and they also defeated other great protectors who had come to the earth. || 92 ||
While they were thus conversing on the bank of the Narmadā,
the two Dānavas, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, emerged from their dwelling in the water.
Those five Dānavas, having come together as mutual allies,
assembled for the sake of avenging their enmity toward Mahiṣa and Namuci.
Having made this counsel for the sake of victory, those truthful ones said,
"We shall marry that virtuous woman, who is like a jewel."
Having thus addressed Satī, they went to the Vindhya mountain to search for her;
she was not seen there, so they departed for the Himalayas.
Seeing the virtuous Pārvatī going there to bathe, they said, "Choose us! and Pārvatī then spoke to them.
"I am the goddess Vindhyācalī, and I have come here for the sake of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
You must not speak thus; let them go from this excellent tīrtha just as they came. (98)
"My residence is on the Vindhya mountain; there, what dwells in my heart must be spoken.
Having performed my ablutions at a sacred ford, I shall depart; you indeed should go there. (99)
Having thus dispatched the Daityas, Śumbha and the others, Pārvatī proceeded forward to the celestial Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing.
Then, having assembled there in great numbers, the lords of the gods first praised the Goddess for the sake of dispelling their own suffering.
"A boon was indeed granted to us by you, that when remembered in times of distress, you would surely destroy our suffering; now that time of distress has arrived. (102)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Eight Great Sages from the Creator through his own Vīrya-homa in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Cause of the Goddess Satī’s Birth in the House of Dakṣa Āṅgirasa; the Cause of the Birth of Dakṣa Prācetasa; the Cause of the Birth of Nārada from Brahmā and Nārada from Kaśyapa; the Sons and Daughters of Dakṣa; the Birth of the Sons of Danu such as Śumbha and Niśumbha; the Defeat of the Gods; and the Prayer of the Goddess. || 165 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, having meditated upon Maheśvarī, the gods offered praise on the bank of the Gaṅgā; listen as I relate it to you. || 1 ||
Homage to the Mother, the Great Mother; repeated homage to you, the Progenitress! Homage to Māyā, the Great Māyā; repeated homage to you, the Illusion! || 2 ||
Salutations again and again to you, O Brahmanī, O Akṣarāṇī, O Muktānī;
salutations again and again to Vāsudevī, to Prakṛti, and to Pradhānā. || 3 ||
Salutations again and again to Bhūmi, Kālī, Mahākālī, and Mahālakṣmī;
salutations again and again to you, Hiraṇyā, Sugarbha, and Vairājī. || 4 ||
Salutations again and again to you, Golokī, who are most excellent and possess the most beautiful form;
salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī, Kṛṣṇā, and Vaikuṇṭhā. || 5 ||
Salutations again and again to Śvetā, Badarī, and Mārtaṇḍā;
salutations again and again to Pāvanī, Pavamānā, and Avyākṛtī. || 6 ||
Salutations again and again to you who are Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and Raudrī;
salutations again and again to you who are Dhātrī, Gaurī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Jyotsnā.
Salutations again and again to you, the chaste one, the sacrificial offering, the heroic power;
salutations again and again to you, the great one, the conceited one, and the intention. || 8 ||
Salutations again and again to her who is consciousness, activity, manifestation, and dissolution;
salutations again and again to her who is heaven, the world of truth (Satyaloka), and the guardian of the worlds.
Salutations again and again to Ramā, to Jayā, and to Vijayā;
salutations again and again to you, Rādhā, the accomplisher of all, Lakṣmī.
Salutations again and again to you, Nairṛtī, who brings about the attainment of happiness;
salutations again and again to you, Saumyā, the very essence of the seed-syllables, the goddess Rati. || 11 ||

To that Goddess who, as the illusory power of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇumāyā), is established among all beings—to her belongs the ritual placement (nyāsa), to her belongs the salutation; obeisance, obeisance to her, obeisance again and again! || 12 ||
That which exists as volition in the form of intellect, and that which exists in the form of sleep;
that which exists in the form of shadow, in the form of hunger, and in the form of power. || 13 ||
Thirst is said to be patience and compassion; salutations again and again to her who is each of these!
She is likewise modesty, peace, faith, splendor, conduct, and mindfulness. (14)
Salutations again and again to you who are called Contentment and Nourishment;
salutations to you, the Goddess, the Mother, the Sustainer and the Ordainer. || 15 ||
A great calamity is occurring for the Asuras;
O you who remain within and look upon them again and again, salutations, salutations to you! (16)
Thus being praised, that Pārvatī, the supreme goddess,
arrived there by way of her bathing place at the spot where the gods were offering their hymns of praise.
Then, being pleased, she who had been saluted by the gods spoke to those deities:
"Having extracted from my body this beautiful one, who is like a treasure-chest," (18)
I give myself for the protection of the gods; let the gods accept me!
Let them accept my form, which is beautiful and endowed with divine splendor. (19)
The gods, having taken the maiden Kauśikī, went to the Vindhya mountain;
and then Kauśikī became established within the goddess of the Vindhya mountain.
Then the gods made an effort for the sake of destroying the asuras;
that body of Pārvatī, which consisted of the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, became the form of their treasury. 21.
Having become black in complexion, she was known by the name Kālī or Kālikā.
Following the words of the Goddess, the Daityas went to the Vindhya mountain.
They held consultations with messengers regarding a wife for him here;
they dispatched Sugrīva as a messenger toward the Vindhya mountains.
The messenger said: "O Great Goddess, I have been sent by Śumbha;
Śumbha is the great king, the sole sovereign and lord of the three worlds. (24)
Listen to what that king, whose mind is enamored of you, has said:
"I have conquered the fourteen worlds together with the guardians of the quarters. (25)
Whatever kingdoms in the three worlds have been brought under my control,
and whatever jewels exist in the three worlds, they are now in my house.
Airāvata and other elephants are in my palace; Uccaiḥśravas and other horses also reside in my palace. (27)
The Kalpavṛkṣa and Pārijāta trees perfume my home, as do the swan-drawn celestial chariots of the gods, Gandharvas, and Nāgas. (28)
Indeed, treasures such as the Mahāpadma and others exist in my house; likewise, the jewels of the ocean, as well as parasols, fly-whisks, and garlands. ||29||
There were various wonderful chariots made of the finest jewels,
as well as diverse excellent elixirs that bestow eternal youth and nourishment.
Thus, male and female servants, and manifold ornaments of desire—all are under my control through sovereign power; such are the supernatural accomplishments (siddhis) present in my home.
Mountains, rivers, the seven oceans, forests, deities, abundant celestial bodies, and my servants are all present in my house. (32)
The queens have thousands of attendants according to their desire;
I shall indeed make them all your servants if you become mine. (33)
"You are a jewel among women of renowned beauty, and we are the ones who enjoy such jewels; therefore, O Goddess, accept either me or my younger brother, for you are the most excellent of gems. (34)
"I shall make you my chief queen; come into my possession.
And why, O Goddess, do you not accept me, a jewel among men? (35)
Thus addressed, she, with a deep inner smile, spoke to him:
"What has been said by Śumbha, the conqueror of the three worlds, is indeed true. (36)
However, there is a family tradition passed down through our lineage of goddesses:
whoever conquers a maiden in battle, she shall become his beloved. (37)
Then let that famous one of such auspicious nature come;
or let Niśumbha himself come to the field of battle and conquer me.
"Why does he not take the hand of such a maiden as this in marriage here so soon?
Then the messenger said to the goddess, "Do not be thus arrogant in this matter."
"The proud kings of the fourteen worlds have been conquered by him;
therefore, go with me, preceded by a grand welcome. (1.166.40)
"Do not go, lest you suffer the humiliation born of having your hair pulled.
The Goddess said: "You speak with true respect indeed. (4.1)
But the ancestral dharma of the Goddess's lineage can never be otherwise.
Therefore, explain that to Śumbha so that he may act accordingly.
The messenger, having bowed, went to Śumbha and related it in detail.
Having heard this, the highly arrogant one became enraged and spoke to Dhūmrākṣa, who was standing before him in salutation.
Go quickly with your army and, after first dragging her by the hair,
bring that wicked woman here and slaughter her guards.
Having heard those words, Dhūmrākṣa, accompanied by sixty thousand dānavas,
went quickly to the one who dwells on the Vindhya mountain.
She said, "Come, accept an auspicious husband in a straightforward manner; otherwise, I shall certainly take you away by force. Do as you wish. (46)
Then the goddess said to the Daitya: "Without battle, I have no stake;
you are powerful and endowed with strength, so do as you wish. (47)
Hearing this, he, unable to endure it, arrived there with the intent to seize [her] by force;
however, right there, he was reduced to ashes by the Goddess through the fire of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Then the army, greatly enraged and having arrived for the purpose of destroying the goddesses,
rained down arrows, weapons, missiles, spears, and battle-axes.
They covered the goddess with a rain of arrows like a mass of straw;
then, by the command of the goddess, the lion let out a roar.
Then, from the thundering spray and droplets of foam, thousands of other lions were born, possessing manes and tufts of hair, with claws and fangs as their weapons.
Strong, endowed with youth, and possessing the power to fly through the sky,
they descended upon the sixty-thousand-strong army of Dhūmranetra.
Then, they struck some of the asuras with blows of their hands, others with their fangs,
some with their tails and claws, and others by trampling them.
They tore open the bellies and heads of some,
drank their blood, and devoured their entrails in great quantities.
The entire army was destroyed by them, and the ground shone red with blood;
hearing this, Śumbha became enraged, his lips quivering with anger.
And he said to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, "Go at once;
having seized her by the hair and bound her, bring that doe here. (56)
"If you have any doubt regarding my life-force, let that gentle doe be killed;
let the lions also be slain, and then provide me with proof. (57)
Thus commanded, the Daityas, headed by Caṇḍa, equipped with weapons and accompanied by the fourfold army, set out toward the Vindhya mountain.
And from a distance, O Goddess, they said to her: "Come quickly!
Come, O Kauśikī, choose Śumbha as your auspicious husband!"
"If we do not carry her away by force while she is overwhelmed by the pulling of her hair,"—
at that point, Kauśikī directed a fierce wrath toward those enemies.
Beholding Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, she knit her brows into a three-pronged frown;
then, overwhelmed by extreme rage, her face became terrifying.
From the knitting of her eyebrows, which was dark and black with a mixture of wrath,
Mahākālī emerged, a yoginī bearing weapons.
Holding a sword in her hand, she is beautified by a khaṭvāṅga in her grasp; she is adorned with a sword, a noose, a goad, a mace, a bell, and a mallet. || 63 ||
Clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she has wide-open eyes, a lolling tongue, protruding fangs, and a cavernous mouth.
Armed with weapons, that Mahākālī struck down the enemies of the gods;
she severed some with her sword and other asuras with her khaṭvāṅga staff.
In that battle, she destroyed horses, elephants, chariots, maces, and foot-soldiers; then, assuming a form as massive as a mountain, she held back those who had come to the fray.
Having cast camels, elephants, along with horses, chariots, and infantry into her own mouth, Kauśikī, as Mahākālī, devours the army.
He seized some by their shaven heads, some by their waists, and some by their feet;
he deprived the soldiers of his army of their lives on all sides.
Ruru fled from the army toward a cave in the Vindhya mountains;
Kālī pursued that great asura in order to overpower him.
The goddess struck him violently on the head with the tip of her khaṭvāṅga;
his head became matted and he died at that very moment.
Having cut away the hair from the corpse of Ruru, that goddess Kālī bound her own hair with it; she shone exceedingly like a *kiṃśuka* tree in bloom.
Having separated and plucked out a single matted lock, he cast it upon the ground at dawn;
it then became a girl, dark in complexion with a body that was half-white.
Kālī said to that maiden, "Bring Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa here;
I myself will slay them both. She then rushed toward those two.
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa also fled toward the south out of fear;
Caṇḍamārī, for her part, mounted a very swift donkey.
When those two Daityas had departed, she followed after them in anger;
on the way, she saw a buffalo named Pauṇḍra belonging to Yama.
Having torn out its horn, it pursued the Dānavas with speed;
then Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, abandoning the earth, took refuge in the sky.
Then the Naga Karkotaka, while going along, came within the sight of the Goddess;
likewise, she saw Garuda and took his feathers.
Having thus seized Karkoṭaka, they rushed at the two of them with great speed;
they were assailed, crushed, and bound by Karkoṭaka’s own cords.
Having brought them into her presence, she presented them to Kālī;
then both Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were rendered headless by the Goddess.
There, upon the straps of Ruru deer skin, the heads of the Asuras were indeed fastened with variegated feathers of Tārkṣya by Kṛṣṇā.
Having fashioned an incomparable garland, he offered it to Caṇḍikā;
then he also offered her that gurgling lute made from the skin of a Ruru deer.
Having fashioned another garland from the feathers of Tārkṣya,
Kālī placed it upon her own head in her braided hair and was satisfied;
she then drank the abundant blood of the Dānavas until she was no longer thirsty.
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were slain by the Goddess and made into ornaments for her head.
Because the heads of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others were placed upon her crest,
she thereafter became known by the name Cāmuṇḍā due to that association with them.
Then Cāmuṇḍā, Kālī, and Kauśikī—these three having united—wrought great destruction upon the Daityas. 85.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise of Pārvatī by the Gods on Kailāsa in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; Kauśikī, born from the body of Pārvatī, goes to the Vindhya mountain; the arrival of the messenger Sugrīva sent by Śumbha; the destruction of Dhūmrākṣa; the manifestation of Kālī; and the account of her being named Cāmuṇḍā due to the destruction of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, Śumbha himself, desiring to fight, approached and said to the Daitya Raktabīja: "Slay these women who are like she-asses."
Then Raktabīja, accompanied by an army of three hundred million,
was joined by Kātyāyanī, Kauśikī, Kālī, and Cāmuṇḍā.
The heroic great asura Raktabīja arrived to fight, and at that time, the sounds of battle-instruments pervaded all directions. || 3 ||
Then those four goddesses let out great roars;
from the regions of their mouths, millions of Brahmāṇīs emerged.
And they became three-eyed goddesses of Maheśvarī, bearing tridents; they were fierce, adorned with great serpent-bracelets, and likewise possessed of earrings. || 5 ||
There, millions of Kaumāryas appeared, adorned with peacock feathers;
there, millions of Śaktis appeared, mounted upon peacocks.
From her two arms, crores of Vaiṣṇavīs arose mounted upon Garuḍas;
from her back, crores of Vārāhīs were born with Śeṣa as their vehicle.
Indeed, crores of Nakhinīs and Nārasiṃhīs were born from the heart;
their great roars are capable of destroying the cosmic egg.
Upon hearing that they had become equal [to the gods], Śaṅkara indeed arrived;
Śivā also came with him, having seen the effort made by the Daityas.
Then Śivā said to Śambhu: "O Śaṅkara, go to the Daitya and say to Śumbha and Niśumbha: 'If you wish to live... (1.167.10)
Therefore, go and take him from the seventh netherworld;
let Vāsava regain heaven, and let the gods be free from their affliction.
Then that goddess was born from him by the name Śivadūtī;
and they all, having heard the words of the messenger, were filled with pride.
They rushed toward the place where Kātyāyanī, Kālī, and Kauśikī were,
[striking] with hooks, spears, arrows, javelins, and bhūśuṇḍi missiles.
They showered Kātyāyanī with spears, iron clubs, javelins, tridents, and axes; she, however, swiftly cut them all to pieces.
With sharp-edged arrows and great shafts resembling winged birds, he struck down the mighty asuras who were intoxicated with battle. || 15 ||
Raṇacaṇḍī, indeed Cāmuṇḍā, slew ten thousand dānavas;
Kātyāyanī, as Mahāmārī, struck them down with tridents.
Kauśikī, Brāhmī, Kumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī likewise [appeared], with skull-topped staffs, water-nooses, spears, and thunderbolts. || 17 ||
Stationed in their heroic deeds, they struck down tens of millions of dānavas;
Caṇḍī slew them with thunderbolts, while Vārāhī struck them with her snouts and discuses.
Nārasiṃhī struck the asura soldiers with her fangs and claws, Śivadūtī with fire, and Kālī likewise with her swords.
Thus, being struck there by the hosts of goddesses,
those Dānavas and Asuras fell down, having indeed abandoned their lives.
Then others, out of fear, went for refuge to Raktabīja; thereupon Raktabīja approached the circle of Mothers with excellent missiles.
In his fury, he struck them in many ways and entered the middle floor;
then all the Mothers struck him with sharp weapons.
As many drops of blood as fall upon the earth from Raktabīja’s blood, so many Raktabījas are born.
Then, indeed, from the body of Raktabīja, armies emerged;
at that time, Kātyāyanī said to Kālī, "Devour the Dānava! (24)
By means of which the rapid emergence of the army of Raktabīja would be blocked—Mahākālī quickly cast that Raktabīja into her mouth. (25)
Then Carmamuṇḍā, becoming as large as a mountain at the mouth of the cave,
cast down and devoured the armies born of Raktabīja.
Then other Dānavas cried out, "Alas, brother! Alas, father!
and with their bodies and limbs cut in half, they went to Niśumbha for refuge.
Niśumbha, suddenly seizing his sword, desired to kill her;
however, being deluded by the Goddess's true form, he was paralyzed for a moment.
The Goddess said: "O Niśumbha, you wish to conquer me through delusion.
Go, O Daitya; you have already been conquered by me; being infatuated, you shall not defeat me. (29)
Then, O Goddess, the Daitya said to her, whose body was so delicate:
"How can she be slain by me? Therefore, I shall not kill this beautiful woman."
I am certainly unable to conquer you in battle without the discharge of weapons;
however, if weapons were discharged, your destruction would occur and my purpose would not be fulfilled. (31)
Thus, out of a sense of what ought to be done, I have maintained this state of bewilderment;
for there is no gain for me in the falling of the weapon, nor indeed even in its not falling. (32)
Therefore, O beautiful one, what gain is there for you in death?
Turn your mind away from battle; become my wife and grant me enjoyment.
Having heard this, the goddess laughed and said to the Dānava Niśumbha:
"O hero, I have not been conquered in battle; I shall not become the wife of anyone. (34)
Whether it be your death or my own death, even fleeing from battle is worse than death itself. (35)
Even in that case, a man who turns back from battle out of pride for women is considered by women to be a worthless eunuch.
Those lowest of men indeed seek to conquer a woman through battle;
women are never to be conquered by war, nor has it ever been heard that they were wives [won] in such a manner anywhere. (37)
Whatever woman does not desire to become the wife of a certain man, she alone desires a destructive battle with that man. (38)
In battle, however, there is destruction for only one; she shall not fall into the hands of a weakling.
If she should fall into the hands of a man by force, she will certainly bring about his destruction. (39)
Neither a friend nor an enemy resides within his mind;
yet you must quickly make him free from fear so that he may truly abide in my heart.
"Since you desire me as your wife, therefore conquer me in battle;
for I shall never become the wife of a eunuch or a fool. (41)
Thus addressed, the Dānava, his eyes copper-red with rage, brandished his sword and hurled it with great speed; but she cut that [sword] down with her own blade.
Just as the Daitya hurled his mace,
Kālikā severed both his arms right at the shoulders with a razor-edged arrow.
Like a branch severed from its trunk, the Daitya was separated from his head;
and upon the destruction of Niśumbha, Caṇḍa and the others raised a tumultuous shout of joy.
"Victory, O Goddess! the gods exclaimed, and they released a rain of flowers;
the sound of musical instruments resounded, proclaiming their victory. (45)
Then, ill omens befell his brother Śuṃbha;
having entered the camp at night, a jackal howled with a harsh sound.
Crows remain in the camp, crying out day and night;
black, fierce, and terrifying serpents slither through the dwellings. (47)
Crows, vultures, and cranes wandered and circled above the camp;
and fetuses were aborted in women, cows, and does. (48)
There is no ghee in the milk, nor is oil found in the sesame seeds;
yet the people there fight one another within their own camp. 49.
Dark-complexioned, with long hair and blind eyes,
she went weeping toward the abode of the lord of the Dānavas, unrecognized as she went.
Then, a certain ascetic covered in ashes, filled with anger, or perhaps some silent, naked mendicant, was seen wandering about in the camp. (51)
Having sounded the hand-drum, he utters the syllable *hūṃ* while naked;
he causes untimely clouds to release water and produces the flash of lightning. ||5 2||
Hailstones fell from the clouds and thunder roared repeatedly;
an earthquake occurred, and a conflagration of the quarters also arose. (5.3)
At night, packs of dogs stood before him howling with their mouths upturned;
by day, owls shrieked, and a comet appeared in the sky.
There the solar disc is seen surrounded by a wheel;
headless trunks are seen in the sky, and the moon does not shine.
Then the stars were seen in the sky during the day by the Dānavas;
likewise, the various classes of beings were seen as embryos within the Dānava women.
Then the horses neighed and the elephants, though well-fed, dropped their tails;
and the ministers were seen in the camp to be despondent in spirit. || 57 ||
The fire blazes in the hearth, yet no fierce wind blows;
banners flare within the armies, and the sky becomes grey with dust. (58)
In a dream, Śumbha’s heart became agitated;
on the field of battle, he saw his own head severed from his trunk. (59)
Seated upon a ram-drawn vehicle, he proceeds toward the southern direction;
and a certain naked female demon performs an oil massage for him.
Clad in red garments, she strives to embrace him;
she indeed offers wine for him to drink and likewise bestows kisses. (61)
Having shaved his head, he then wailed and went toward the south;
the camp was seen fallen and destroyed by tigers.
The naked Śumbha was seen to have matted his own body, crushed it,
drunk his own blood, and likewise tasted it.
"Śumbha’s wife cast her own body onto the funeral pyre and was seen there"—thus did the dream of the Daitya Śumbha appear, whether in sleep or while awake, in every respect. (64)
The signs of destruction were visible, and for that reason he indeed fell into a state of dejection; meanwhile, he heard of the death of Niśumbha and the crushing of his army.
There he wept in many ways and fainted again and again;
yet even so, [he was overcome] by a state of darkness and by passion rooted in desire.
He regained his composure once more and, intent on avenging his enmity,
mounted a great elephant and advanced with a spear in hand.
Meanwhile, the guest, out of anger, came to slay Kauśikī in battle;
indeed, the war-drums and kettledrums were sounded again and again.
Then eighty-four armies of the Kambūyas marched forth,
and fifty clans of Asuras also set out at that time.
Then another hundred families of the Dhūmras departed,
as well as ten million clans of the Kālakas, the Daurhṛtas, and the Mauryas.
Beholding Karīṣṭha, who was exceedingly radiant and had arrived at the field of battle with eight arms and great weapons, the gods sounded their conch shells.
Then Ambikā caused her bow to twang, rang her bell,
and filled the quarters with the sounds of battle.
But the lion let out a roar after the great rutting elephant had been forced to retreat;
there, thousands of lions filled the vault of heaven with their roars.
They filled [the space] with an exceedingly fierce echoing resonance;
thousands of goddesses arrived there upon the field of battle. 74.
By the command of the Great Goddess, all the queens were also fierce in battle—
those goddesses who were the handmaidens of Brahmā and those who were the handmaidens of Indra and Bala.
Likewise, there were crores of female servants of Varuṇa and Yama, as well as male and female servants of Kubera and Īśāna. ||76||

There were tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of female servants of Agni, as well as female servants of Nirṛti; there were ten million female servants of Vāyu, and female servants of the guardians of the directions.
Equal to the world-protectors, possessing the most excellent female servants, and having exerted themselves with their armies,
they were skilled in the weapons and missiles of war, numbering in the hundreds of millions and tens of billions.
Adorned with infinite divine vehicles such as weapons and chariots, they are renowned jewels within the fourteen worlds. (79)
The wives of the army, who understand the nature of war and battle, have assembled;
the destruction of all the Asuras is now certain.
Otherwise, happiness for tens of millions of gods would never be possible;
it is only by staking their heads as a wager that such happiness is obtained.
Wearing armor and helmets, they were resplendent in their military attire;
though women, they possessed the full strength of youth and moved with great power.
With all the components of war fully prepared, they arrived at the field of battle;
there, on the battlefield, Mahendra caused the nectar to be drunk by them all.
It is the nourisher, the life-giver, the extractor of arrows, the bestower of rest, the remover of fainting, and the stopper of blood. (84)
Then the Aśvinīkumāras brought various medicinal herbs that serve to join together the severed fragments of bodies split in two. (85)
Then, by means of the movement of the vital breaths, the essences were instantly drawn there;
they were foods that were nectar and drinks that were like nectar. (86)
In that battle, they were protected within their camps by the gods and others; for the purpose of guarding the army of women, the gods provided a ninth [division]. 87.
In that battle, victory shall be certain, and not even a single hair of anyone on the side of the Goddess shall be lost; indeed, there shall be no death or injury to any of her followers.
Thus, all this has been accumulated by those skilled in action who know how to act;
even by Śumbha, protection was arranged in his presence accordingly. (89)
Then, a great sound indicative of the commencement of battle was produced by the asuras in the path of the sky, from their war-trumpets and kettledrums.
Then a most intense battle took place between the armies of the Goddess and Śumbha;
at that time, goddesses numbering in the hundreds of millions struck down the asuras.
Ten million billion trillion asuras destroyed the forest consisting of the Goddess;
and the drums of ten million asuras cried out: "Listen, O asuras! (92)
For the sake of destroying the lineages of the Daityas and Dānavas, the host of women has arrived at the battlefield; wage war, you snatchers of life! (93)
Let them not look at my back, nor let them make the heavens their battlefield;
thinking "this is a woman," let them not abandon me on the field of battle. (94)
Today the earth shall surely become either filled with asuras or filled with gods;
let there be the existence of only one of these two, not both sides together. (95)
"Let the gods live, or let the asuras live alone;
indeed, a creation consisting of a mixture of gods and asuras is not what is intended now. (96)
Let the gods be widowed, or let the daughters of the Danavas become widows;
whatever may happen, let it happen—do not flee! (97)
Let the fierce ones slay, destroy, and strike them down;
let the restless ones overpower, crush, and grind them to dust! 98.
Thus did the drums of the Dānavas resound upon the field of battle,
while the conchs of the goddesses then proclaimed their presence upon the field of battle.
Let them devour, let them feast upon, and let them destroy the Dānavas;
let them tear asunder, let them overwhelm, and let them slay those who cause delusion.
The Asuras terrify the gods at every moment in every way; let them terrify, let them diminish, let them devour them in my presence! || 10.1 ||
All the gods have arrived to assist you;
let them not leave you with only five feet remaining, but let them destroy and cause [the enemy] to perish. 102.
Thus, at that time, thunderous roars from the sky arose, bestowing awakening;
sounds produced by kettledrums and conchs were heard, impelled by Time.
"For those who die in battle, there is heaven; for those who survive, there is lordship over the earth;
but for those who retreat, there is indeed nothing at all. Therefore, one must certainly die here."
Thus did the battle-cries awaken the warriors and their commanders;
meanwhile, the blows were dealt and the weapons were brought down.
With sharp arrows, shafts, and iron bolts, they struck down the foremost warriors;
with razor-headed arrows, crescent-shaped blades, and spears, they struck one another.
By Kātyāyanī, Kauśikī, Kālī, and likewise Cāmuṇḍā,
the army of the Dānavas was covered with arrows in the sky.
The army and the host of goddesses in the sky were covered by arrows— Kambukas, Kālakas, Dhaumras, Kālakeyas, and Daurhṛtas.
They cut down volleys of arrows with their own arrows and struck others likewise;
there, the quivers of those possessing inexhaustible shafts reached a state of depletion.
When the arrows of the Daityas and the goddesses were destroyed, set ablaze, shattered, and broken by the strikes of their tridents, they fell from the bows.
And hundreds of thousands of slain Daityas lie prostrate upon the surface of the earth—
some with severed feet, some with severed hands, and others with severed necks and chests.
And hundreds of thousands of goddesses fainted there upon the field of battle;
their mounts were destroyed, and the elephants and other creatures were broken or dead.
There, lions, buffaloes, peacocks, and camels died in battle;
they were brought back to life again by the gods and the Daityas through the essence of their vital breaths and mantras.
Then [they struck] with swords and crescent-headed arrows, tridents and bhūśuṇḍi spears,
iron clubs and maces, as well as with darts and lances.
Then, with swords, spears, sharp scimitars, and battle-axes,
there occurred a mutual combat that caused mutual destruction.
There they are cut from their bodies, likewise split from their chests;
they are severed from their waists and likewise hacked from their hands.
There they die by the throat and likewise are cast down by the thighs;
being dragged again and again, they are slain, and being embraced repeatedly, they are tormented.
Seizing them foot by foot, they tore them asunder in the fray;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, for no one could discern who it was or what it was.
At the very moment the body arrived, it split in two;
such indeed was the battle of blinding speed, burdened with a tumultuous clash.
At that time, millions upon millions of soldiers in the army were slain;
the earth was drenched in blood and strewn with the corpses of gods and demons.
The path through the forest of the body is pervaded by hundreds of rivers of blood;
it is filled with mountains-like teeth and bodies, and is strewn with the corpses of donkeys, camels, and other creatures.
Covered with countless dead corpses visible even in the winter season, those who had fallen there, half-dead, cried out "Drink! Drink!
And headless trunks (kabandhas), rising up again and again upon the ground, were there without clothes.
They flee even while armed, and then fall again upon the ground. || 123 ||
At that time, no one there was able to provide assistance to anyone—not even the millions of delicate goddesses or the demons in the prime of their youth. (124)
In battle, those who possess the form of gold, when dead, shine like the moon;
even when crushed and destroyed in combat, that is indeed the work of Mahākāla.
A great terror also arose in the hearts of the spectators;
then, indeed, Brahmā informed Vibhāvarī of what had occurred there.
"And you, O beloved, employ the weapon of sleep at that time, for it is appropriate then;
for during the night, the presiding deity of the mantra of sleep is in charge."
Having joined the weapon to the tip of an arrow and released it at that time between the two armies,
the hosts of both the goddesses and the dānavas were overcome by sleep.
Those [beings] that were born indeed find rest in every way during deep sleep;
then, at that time, the Daityas rained down upon the army of the Goddesses.
They prepared the nectar and the life-giving herbs;
they also brought forth the goddesses, the lions, the vehicles, and all those things that possess consciousness.
All of them were indeed restored to life by a rain of nectar;
and at that time, we also revived the Daityas with mantras.
And with the *saṃjīvanī*, the *sandhinī*, the *viśalyā*, the *virāmā*, the *mūrchānāśikā*, the *raktarodhinī*, and with life-giving juices; || 132 ||
Just as the army that had been treated was restored to life and made free from disease, it then became entirely healthy, as if having risen from sleep. (133)
In that manner, the great army of the goddesses once again became ready; likewise, the army of the Daityas also became ready once more.
Commanded by Brahmā, Vibhāvarī then brought the weapon of sleep (nidrāstra) upon her own army; thus, both armies became comfortable.
Then Brahmā said to Śambhu, the destroyer of the Dānavas:
"The battle must be fought with weapons alone; let Caṇḍikā and the others engage in combat."
Having brandished the weapon with wrath and visualized the enemies, one should employ it;
let this mantra of Kālakavala be given by you to the goddesses.
Oṃ! O Death, from death, O Great Death, remain firm together with your own death! Oṃ! O Death, from death, O Great Death, remain well-concealed within your own death! || 138 ||
Thus, having first uttered the syllable *phuṭ*, whatever weapon there may be, such as arrows and the like, one should hurl it into the body of the enemy; having died, he shall not live again.
Even with many medicines, mantras, and medical treatments,
he does not live again due to the power of Death, Mahākāla.
Then, by the command of Brahmā, the Rudra named Mahākāla taught the mantra for devouring Time (Kālakavala) to the goddesses.
In a mere moment, he became perfected through the majesty of Mahākāla;
and by the will of Brahmā, he remained there established in embodied form.
Terrible, the death of Death itself, devouring the armed asuras,
he was seen by the goddesses as he rose up, consuming all living beings.
In that very instant, he assumed various forms among the goddesses;
well-established upon their tongues, he became intent upon his task.
This activity of Brahmā and Rudra was not understood by the Daityas;
they rose up, considering themselves immortal, and engaged in battle. || 145 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Anantadevī from the Blood-Seed Daitya in the Battle with Raktabīja, the Destruction of Mūlaraktabīja, the Slaying of Niśumbha, the Ill Omens for Śumbha, the Ascent of the Dānavas, the Arrival of the Goddess’s Army from the Fourteen Worlds, the Appearance of Sañjīvanī and Others, the Tumultuous Battle with Musical Instruments and Weapons, the Great Destruction, the Sleep-Inducing Weapon Discharged by Vibhāvarī, the Revival of the Army, and the Goddesses’ Acquisition of the Kālakavala Mantra," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛtayuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen further, O Mahālakṣmī, regarding how one becomes fearless even toward death;
then a battle between the two armies commenced, leading once more to rebirth.
Brahmā knows, Śambhu knows, and the goddesses know that the destruction of tens of millions of Daityas brought about by Time has indeed arrived. || 2 ||
Then, by the command of Śumbha, eighty-four crores of Kambus fought with missiles and weapons, as well as with mountains and forest trees.
The Asuras fought with showers of stones, showers of fire, and arrows;
then the goddesses, in their forms as Vārāhīs, waged battle against them.
With missiles, weapons, showers of stones, mountains, tusks, trees, showers of fire, and arrows charged with mantras that make them like the jaws of Time (Kāla). || 5 ||
Then the Nārasiṃhas likewise fought to assist them,
using their claws, fierce fangs, tails, hands, and leaps.
They fought repeatedly with enchanted foam from their mouths as if with weapons;
they were characterized by weapons, missiles, boulders, trees, arrows, foam, and other such things.
Struck by the mantra of Time, the Daityas did not rise again though they were dead;
yet fifty crores of families of Asuras remained standing in the battle.
Likewise, the guardians of the quarters and Indrāṇīs by the hundreds of millions and tens of millions fought with weapons empowered by mantras called Kāla.
Those Asuras were destroyed and dead; they did not rise again in that battle.
Then there arrived hundreds of millions of families of Dhaumras, as numerous as the petals of a lotus.
Those who met their death by weapons consecrated with the mantras of Time fought against the goddesses Mahāmārī, Caṇḍikā, and the others.
Furthermore, they do not even breathe; they are dead and have departed in every way—those Kālakeyas and Kālakas, Daityas numbering in the tens of millions and hundreds of billions.
Rising up there with their armies for the sake of devouring the goddesses,
crores of Kuṇḍalinīs armed with tridents fought with them.
Overpowered by time and fate, they did not wake from their slumber;
the Mauryas, full of malice and transgressing all bounds, waged war.
At that time, tens of millions of their clans were destroyed by hundreds of thousands of lions;
though they rose up again by means of medicinal herbs, they were slain once more by young maidens.
Those destroyed by weapons consecrated with the Kālakavala mantra do not even breathe;
then there were other Daityas, Śambaras, as well as those from the sea and the mountains. (16)
The inhabitants of Pātāla, others from the surface of the earth, Nāgas, and those dwelling in trees, all overcome by old age,
were utterly bewildered upon merely beholding the forms of the goddesses, yet they engaged in battle.
The Śaktis, who are the messengers of Śiva, struck them with enchanted weapons;
once dead, they do not return, for having gone, they have attained ultimate liberation.
There were crores and billions of asuras, tens of millions of daityas,
padmas of dānavas, and scattered śaṅkus.
Slain, gone, dead, and lost, they were deceived by name and form; their blood became a sea, rising up from the rivers of their life-blood.
Even now it does not dry up, nor does it appear discolored;
this great battle in the sky has arisen in the northwestern direction. (21)
The earth and the ground will become a sea of blood, and the land will be drenched in gore.
Then, the demon Śumbha [will appear] on the Vindhya mountain, which has increased in height toward the sky.
Standing upon the peak touched by Rāhu and Ketu, he beheld the crushing;
the great earth was pervaded in every direction by slaughtered armies.
"Such a universal war between goddesses and dānavas, who fight fiercely in the paths of the sky, shall never happen again. (24)
And that Śumbha, possessing a range of vision extending for a hundred thousand yojanas from the peak of the Vindhya mountains,
then desired to burn Kailāsa and Badarikāśrama with his weapon.
From the peak of the Vindhya mountain, the lightning-weapon was hurled upon Hara;
from it, millions of fires and thunderclaps were produced.
Desiring to consume both Meru and Mandara, they descended to the earth;
from the path of the sky, they blazed forth toward Kailāsa and the abode of Badrikā.
Then, the copper weapon released by Maheśānī there drew that lightning toward itself and entered the world of Atala.
Then the armies of the goddesses in the sky to the north of the Vindhya mountains took a moment's rest, while the fire-missile was discharged against them.
He set ablaze the planets, the gods, and the piśācas who have the wind as their support;
he fell upon the two worlds, heaven and earth, roaring like Śambhu.
On Kailāsa and at Badarī, he set forth many fires;
and then, having been seen by the goddess Vāruṇī, who destroys the fire-missiles, [he was restrained].
The cold-mountain weapon, consisting of stones from a shower of cold rain, was discharged;
by that shower of snow and cold rain, masses of rocks fell.
Even the fire-weapon was pacified by showers of snow and masses of ice;
from that time on, the great Golden Mountain became the Great Snowy Mountain.
Then, for their destruction, he discharged the weapon of suppression (nirodhāstra);
and at that time, the goddess Vāyavyā brought about their destruction by obstructing their breath.
The wind-weapon was swiftly discharged, and the weapon of suppression was indeed destroyed;
then the king of the Daityas performed a fire-oblation with the mantras of the Rākṣasas.
Rākṣasas, resembling mountains, arose by the millions;
with weapons and missiles in their hands, they fell from the sky upon the army of the Goddess. || 36 ||
This forest, spread across by these [trees] like masses of clouds during the rainy season, has been crushed by the showers that are the army of the goddesses. 37.
Seeing them, the goddesses created others who were Nairṛtas;
these Nairṛtas, having been produced from the weapon of Nirṛti, began devouring the Rākṣasas.
Just as the timiṅgila fish devour the timi fish, so did he [consume] them;
then Śumbha released another, many-hungry preta-missile.
At that very moment, armies of pretas arose by the millions;
