Śiva went to his own abode, Kailāsa, and found peace.
When the time of the heat had passed and the arrival of the clouds occurred, Satī then said to Śambhu: "Listen to my words, O beloved. (17)
This is the season of dense gathering; clouds rain constantly.
Pleasant winds blow, shaking [everything] with great velocity. (18)
Everywhere the ground was saturated and thick with mud, offering no firm footing;
the trees and creepers were broken and completely drenched, filled with water.
The thundering of clouds and the play of lightning arise;
moreover, the sun and the moon are not seen in the sky when shrouded by clouds.
Great trees, struck by the wind, fall to the ground causing terror;
so too do tigers, lions, and extremely cruel, venomous creatures. (21)
They wander in desolate forests, beset by cold, heat, wind, and fire;
these and other obstacles, which cause suffering, persist at all times. (22)
Therefore, you should now build a house for the purpose of dwelling somewhere, wherein there may be shade, comfortable beds, and the abundance of food and drink. (23)
Furthermore, they would always be capable of being protected by conventional rules (sāmayika) if there were no building for people to obtain a place of rest. (24)
At that time, what profit is there for a forest-dweller in carrying wood?
Even birds such as the ruddy goose and the pigeon would find themselves without shelter. (25)
When the time arrives, ants, mice, and other creatures build their homes in the hollows of trees, and they also construct subterranean dwellings.
Therefore, the protection of offspring, which is an integral part of the duties of the householder's stage, should indeed take place at home—secure, firm, and providing comfort in all seasons. (27)
The dwellings of my other sisters are indeed vast, divine, and possessed of countless riches; yet for me, there is no house.
In the first [dream], there was the emptiness of the house; in the ocean of saṃsāra, this is suffering. In the second, there was the lack of grain; in the third, the absence of wealth. (29)
The fourth is childlessness, the fifth is considered impurity;
the sixth is friendship with the diseased, and the seventh is [association with] those who do not give and so forth.
And eighthly, there is the affliction of lions, bulls, and serpents within the home.
Since I possess these eightfold miseries, what use has a yogi for the life of a householder?
One may be a yogi but not an enjoyer, yet one may be an enjoyer while possessing the state of a yogi;
therefore, let the fruit of yoga be applied toward the destruction of the eightfold suffering.
Behold, in the forest, a forest fire indeed arises here in many ways.
And crops grow densely upon its surface.
Dark, silver, red, and white varieties of grass grow there,
sprouting thickly upon the ground of the seating area.
Uneven ground, thorns, and crooked terrain are to be avoided as they cause great suffering;
they are terrifying during sleep or sexual union at midnight. (35)
Fierce sounds were heard, causing extreme suffering through the destruction of their work;
at midday there was intense heat, and the downpours of rain were likewise distressing. (36)
Behold my feet, where a permanent hut of sharp thorns has formed; what kind of thorns are found there? (37)
Behold the misfortune of the water droplets from the clouds upon my body; having fallen, they merely cover my body, causing the suffering of cold. (3.8)
In this time of adversity, the crows and the cakora birds are building nests as their homes; how will you find peace without them? (39)
"Great fear arises in my heart today, born from the clouds;
therefore, strive for the sake of the palace, do not delay at my word. (1.173.40)
A wife must be guarded, one must dwell in the forest, and pleasure—not food—must be savored;
all of this leads to our ruin and does not produce happiness. ||4 1||
O Śaṅkara, whether on Kailāsa, or on the Himālaya, or on the banks of the Gaṅgā, or anywhere else upon the earth, construct a dwelling fit for habitation.
May guests who have arrived become peaceful in this hermitage;
act in such a way that it abounds in wealth, grain, and prosperity according to their needs. 43.
Having heard what Satī had spoken and considering it meaningful in his mind,
Śambhu then spoke to the Goddess, repeatedly delighting her heart.
"Tell me, O Goddess, where the clouds never go at all;
there I would have a palace built, if it pleases you, O Śivā. (45)
If it pleases you, I shall cause clouds to move as far as the slopes of this mountain, or on a peak such as Meru. (46)
Likewise, O Goddess, on the slopes of Kailāsa the clouds generally move even during the rainy season; would that please you? (47)
Clouds generally move across the peaks and slopes of Aruṇācala, but they never go beyond that point. 48.
On Mount Raivata in Saurāṣṭra, which possesses peaks like heaven and is endowed with excellent luster,
the clouds remain settled upon its slopes and do not move upward.
Since clouds do not even go to the peaks of Śiva on the Himālayas,
where there is the coolness born of the moon, I shall instead build a palace that pleases me.
"Since these lords of mountains were seen by you in a previous birth,
tell me quickly which among them your heart's desire may rest upon."
If you have a desire for that place where the wives of the Siddhas indeed dwell upon the lofty golden peaks, I shall construct a great temple there.
If you have a desire for that place where the goddesses dwell with delight upon the Golden Peak (Svarṇaśṛṅga), I shall construct for you a palace made of gold.
On Mount Āruṇa, Maṇikuṭṭa, Lokāloka, or Raivata,
there are daughters of the Nāgas, daughters of the mountains, Kinnarīs, and daughters of the Phaṇis.
"Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Vidyādharīs frequent wherever you take pleasure; I shall make your home like unto heaven. (61)
All of them will constantly perform service for you, O beloved, always with mutual approval, with shared vehicles, and with shared play and other such activities. (56)
Beholding this incomparable form and beautiful face of yours,
they will cast aside their own bodies and become your handmaidens.
Or else, Menā, endowed with many forms and qualities, is in the Himalayas;
there she will bring you joy of mind through her excellent service. (58)
The daughters of the mountains always go to the golden peaks for the sake of instruction;
therein lies the beautiful summit named Śiva, if it pleases you. (59)
O beloved, why do you wish to dwell there, which is always filled with the sounds of cuckoos and throngs of birds, and where the splendor of spring prevails?
It was endowed with various lotus ponds, crowded with countless lotuses,
and provided with wish-fulfilling trees, nectar-creepers, and the celestial cow Kamadhenu.
The region was free from herds of wild beasts, well-frequented by ascetics and holy men,
and adorned with crystal, celestial diamonds, and silver.
It was frequented by mind-born swans, horses, and celestial elephants,
and adorned with golden nets of jewels, as well as lotuses in bud and full bloom.
It was beautifully adorned with lovely flowers such as blue lotuses,
and likewise with saffron, all kinds of perfumes, and shimmering scented waters.
It was beautifully adorned with young grassy lawns and tall bamboo trees,
and with aged peacocks dancing and bees and other insects humming.
It was filled with cranes and cuckoos warbling sweetly,
and it resounded daily with the constant singing of those [birds].
"O beloved, do you wish to dwell always accompanied by these ladies who kindle the fire of passion, and joined by ever-new companions? (67)
Or rather, on the excellent peak of Meru, which is its very essence and most auspicious,
I shall construct a supreme palace for you to sport there with your companions, adorned by throngs of Apsarases— this is what you desire.
Śacī will constantly perform service and provide assistance to you. || 69 ||
Of the Lord of Waters, of Kubera, of Īśāna, and of Yama;
of Agni, of the deity Nairṛta, of Māruta, or of the Supreme One.
On the peak of Meru, the lofty abode of the gods, adorned with cities and frequented by hosts of long-limbed celestial nymphs such as Śacī, Raṃbhā, and Menakā; (71)
If you wish to dwell there, I shall construct a great abode for you;
or else, [I shall build it] on Kailāsa, the king of mountains, which is my eternal refuge.
You desire a beautiful dwelling in the vicinity of Kubera’s city, moistened by droplets of Ganges water and radiant like the full moon. (7.3)
Adorned by the daughters of Brahmā in its caves, on its ridges, and in its valleys,
it was a place where various wild animals dwelt and which was surrounded by hundreds of lotus ponds.
Then, you should especially create for us such a place as is adorned with the jewels of the qualities of real entities and is favorable to both of us. (75)
"Tell me quickly where you have a desire to dwell for a long time;
I shall indeed fill that house for you with an abundance of gold, jewels, and gems. (76)
Satī said: "I desire to dwell forever on the Himālaya mountain with Śambhu;
therefore, O bestower of desired boons, establish your residence there without delay. (77)
Having heard this, Śambhu always took Satī and went to a lofty peak,
which was adorned with lakes and forests and frequented by hosts of Siddha women.
It was covered with various flowers, variegated in many ways by diverse jewels; it was inaccessible to birds and consisted entirely of crystal clouds.
It was endowed with lush meadows covered by showers of various flowers,
and it resounded with the humming of bees upon the tips of the branches of blossoming trees.
It was filled with blossoming lotuses and clusters of blue water-lilies, and frequented by celestial cranes, swans, parrots, and ducks. (8.1)
It was frequented by horse-faced Siddhas and Apsarases.
It was frequented by Vidyādharīs, goddesses, and Kinnarīs. ||8 2 ||
He was accompanied by housewives, mountain-dwelling women, and maidens,
amidst the sounds of lutes, harps, stringed instruments, mṛdaṅgas, and paṭaha drums.
It was beautified by the festive performances of dancing apsarases,
completely surrounded by fragrant ponds named Devikā,
and adorned with beautiful groves of flowering flowering creepers.
In the vicinity of the city of Himālaya, near the city of Kubera. ||85||
Having gone joyfully with Dākṣāyaṇī to the beautiful Śivaśṛṅga, which has vast peaks and is as enchanting as heaven, Hara [remained there].
Having constructed a palace named Kailāsa, he took delight for a long time in that new city of Kailāsa, which possessed high walls and great halls. (87)
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he caused a noble city to be built, named Kailāsa, wherein the palaces shone resplendently. (88)
There are firm and delightful places for beds, as well as bathing areas, with walls inlaid with gold, gems, and jewels. (89)
There were pools of cold and warm water, as well as ponds of sweet water;
there were delightful kitchens and auspicious fire-sanctuaries.
There were places for the preservation of provisions such as hard and soft foods, as well as excellent grounds for amorous pastimes and pavilions for laughter and diversion. (91)
There are secret palaces for the sake of amorous gestures, emotional expressions, and dalliance, as well as very large houses for the residence of guests. (92)
There are sleeping chambers rich with couches for resting from sleep, and excellent upper stories with balconies shining with swings, hammocks, and the like.
Gaming tables for dice and other games, assembly halls and pavilions, quadrangles, water-jars, and watchtowers exist everywhere. (94)
There are gardens and private groves, as well as houses, vehicles, and electric lamps; there are also sound-machines and sight-machines.
Indeed, garments of many varieties were made by the hundreds of thousands;
there were vessels of gold and silver, and ornaments of gems and refined gold.
There were various chambers and inner apartments, secured by doors and kept hidden;
there were wind-fans and mechanical devices, as well as rooms for music and song according to one's desire.
There were paths for entertainment and marketplaces with many sights, as well as excellent and noble houses inhabited by tens of millions, hundreds of thousands, and tens of thousands.
Gardens, monasteries, and auspicious royal capitals were established,
wherein there exist divine nectars of immortality as well as the essence of Brahman.
Indeed, it is a place where there are truly excellent drinks and other stimulants for desire,
and which is a ground of medicinal creepers that produce the nourishment of fresh youth.
There were dwellings for the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, as well as auspicious laboratories for elixirs (rasa), and vehicles consisting of bulls, lions, Garuḍas, elephants, and horses. 101.
Maidens' schools were indeed established and commissioned;
such was that new Kailāsa, the best of cities. || 102 ||
This most excellent [palace] was caused to be built by Śambhu through Viśvakarman;
in its presence, the palaces of the world-protectors then became insignificant.
Beholding her own city, which possessed a hundredfold prosperity compared to the house of Dakṣa,
Satī looked upon it again and again and rejoiced repeatedly.
Whatever object is conceived, each of those is present there;
nothing is lacking, from Brahmā and Viṣṇu down to the gods and others.
The virtuous Śiva and Pārvatī are served by the supreme splendor of the king of kings;
they shine with the parasols and chowries of the lord of the sovereign of kings. (106)
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he went at times to another region;
and having wandered through the sky over Meru and other peaks, as well as in the heavenly realms and elsewhere, || 107 ||
Having gone again and again to ever-new Kailāsas and returned, the virtuous couple enjoyed themselves;
thus did they emulate the bliss of the householder’s life.
Thus Śrī Śaṅkara always beheld the happiness of Satī, and Śrī Śambhu likewise beheld everywhere the happiness of Satī. 10.9
Thus, through their mutual association, Satī and Śiva caused the tree of passion to grow by watering it with the waters of their affection.
Once, while staying there, Satī, her face filled with wonder, questioned Śambhu;
she had attained a state of dispassion, yet remained content through the enjoyment of happiness. (111)
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, show compassion toward me!
You are the supreme one, free from the qualities (aguṇa), who has attained identity with the Supreme Brahman.
"I am blessed, for I have become dear to you, and you have been born as my lord and husband.
O Lord of Gods, I wish to know the reality by which one may cross over worldly existence. (113)
Having heard that which, when performed, causes the embodied soul to necessarily attain the supreme state, Śiva spoke here concerning that which is for the sake of Satī’s knowledge.
Listen, O beloved, I shall declare that reality by which one becomes liberated:
know that the supreme reality is always Hari Nārāyaṇa. 1.15
His realization is difficult to attain, O beloved, and those who know it are rare;
I am a servant of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman.
Devotion to Nārāyaṇa bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess, you were remembered in a previous birth in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Having gone there, you indeed became a Vaiṣṇava, and thus you were made a Vaiṣṇavī;
and from Goloka, I too am a Vaiṣṇava, and shall become a Vaiṣṇava once again.
And you must always maintain devotion to Viṣṇu and devotion to Brahman within my house,
toward this Nārāyaṇa who dwells in the abode of Brahman in every respect.
Mindfulness, consciousness itself, propitiation, and worship at all times; reflection, devotion, and loving service—all these are one and the same. (1.173.12)
Indeed, through her alone is Nārāyaṇa attained, and not by anyone else;
she, whose nature is his grace, is proclaimed here as ninefold.
O Goddess, [these are] always hearing, chanting, remembering,
and serving Śrī Hari, as well as servitude, worship, and salutation.
Friendship, self-surrender, and those nine limbs— by means of these, one should constantly honor Hari with one's body and other possessions through the recitation of His stories.
That drinking of its meaning with steadfastness is called "hearing" (śravaṇa);
having heard it, one must perform reflection upon that meaning, for that indeed bestows the fruit.
Constantly reflecting in one's heart upon the births and deeds of Śrī Hari,
and reciting them with great affection— this is called kīrtana.
Having realized that the glorious Hari is all-pervading, he is remembered by him with his mind at all times and in all places; that is declared to be remembrance (smaraṇa).
In every way, whether waking or dreaming, that service which consists of attending to one's own most beloved objects is declared to be *sevana*. (127)

Service that is always performed with a favorable disposition, through the enjoyment of the nectar of the heart, and in a manner pleasing to Hari—that indeed is declared to be true servitude (dāsya). || 128 ||
The worship of the Supreme Self consists of the offering of the sixteen articles, beginning with water for the feet, according to the prescribed rule and in accordance with prosperity at all times.
That which consists of the recitation of the name and meditation, performed through both mind and speech,
as well as prostration like a staff while touching the ground with eight limbs— that indeed is *vandanā*.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious act Śrī Hari performs for me, trusting that all of it is for my welfare—this is called friendship. (131)
Having made everything, including the body and so forth, an offering to Him for His pleasure, one’s own state of emptiness is for the sake of sustenance; this is self-surrender to Hari.
The nine limbs of devotion to Hari bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
they are exceedingly dear to me and are the generators of true discernment. (133)
O my beloved, there are many ancillary practices for devotion to Him, such as the service of Tulasī and the sweeping of the temple. (1.34)
The protection of the temple and other such duties should be gathered together through reflection;
thus, O beloved, devotion to Hari, complete with all its limbs and sub-limbs, is the most excellent of all. 135.
The mother of wisdom and dispassion, the handmaid of liberation, shines forth;
in the three worlds, there is no path as conducive to happiness as devotion. (136)
For a person possessing devotion, Śrī Hari is a helper;
the essence of devotion is that very reality which leads to the attainment of the Supreme Reality. 1.37
Furthermore, that devotion is twofold: with attributes (saguṇā) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇā).
All that which is performed with a desire for a fruit is described as being with attributes. || 138 ||
That very same devotion, when devoid of desire for fruits, is called "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇā).
Furthermore, that devotion is twofold: the ritualistic (vaidhī) and likewise the spontaneous (svābhāvikī). (139)

That which is performed by force according to the rules is considered "prescribed" (vaidhī), while that which is performed by command is likewise [prescribed]. That which is performed by its very nature is regarded as "natural" (svābhāvikī).
And that devotion is further twofold: the higher (parā) and likewise the lower (aparā).
The higher has the form of Hari, who is the goal; the lower has the form of the means. || 141 ||
The *naiṣṭhikī* [devotion] is of two kinds, ultimate and non-ultimate; the ultimate is considered to be sixfold:
trust, choosing, renunciation, wretchedness, and firm resolve. (142)
The avoidance of opposition accompanied by conformity;
this sixfold devotion is considered to be of one kind for those who have reached the ultimate goal, and of another kind for those who have not.
Devotion performed solely for one's own sake is proclaimed as non-final;
furthermore, that [devotion] is considered to be of two kinds—enjoined and unenjoined—and the enjoined is further regarded as twofold.
Furthermore, non-recognition (anājñā) is said to be undetermined; it is again threefold—middling, superior, and inferior—and therein it becomes manifold through various degrees of intensity.
Nowhere else does equality with the chanting of Hari’s name exist;
for one who departs while uttering the Brahman signifying "Hari" and remembering Hari as he leaves the body,
he attains the supreme goal.
The world is pleased by devotion, and Hari indeed is pleased by devotion.
Listen, O Goddess, to what occurred in a former kalpa regarding Nārāyaṇa: for sixty thousand yugas, I performed a most difficult penance.
Then Nārāyaṇa himself became visible to my sight—
a youth with exceedingly beautiful limbs, dark and handsome.
With limbs proportionate to his form and exceedingly serene and charming—
having seen Hari in such a state, my eyes truly found no satisfaction.
Beholding it, I became devoid of blinking and was not satisfied even for a long time.
Then the Blessed One said to me: "O Śambhu, why are you not at all satisfied? (151)
"I am going to my own abode; choose a boon as you desire.
I am pleased by your devotion and your asceticism; do not delay."
Then, O beloved, hear from me what I requested of Nārāyaṇa:
"Whatever shall be for your enjoyment, let that not be for my enjoyment beforehand. (15.3)
O Lord, I consider the entirety of Your grace to be my object of enjoyment;
may I always possess Your service as well as the state of having offered myself to You.
May every other form of devotion as well be directed toward you alone, so that it may grant me liberation;
and may matted hair remain eternally upon my head, truly awakening me to ascetic discipline.
May the ashes from my funeral pyre indeed awaken dispassion within my body;
may I possess equanimity toward sandalwood paste and mud, and toward a clod of earth and a sovereign jewel.
O Lord, let there never be ornaments such as crowns worn by me;
instead, O Hari, let serpents who are enemies of Garuḍa be worn by me.
My vehicle is indeed a bull, offered to Kṛṣṇa from Goloka;
likewise, flowers such as the pārijāta and fragrant substances such as sandalwood. (158)
"May that which is suitable for you be mine; may I never have a share in anything else. May my constant delight be in the *dhattūra* flower and in the wearing of *bilva* leaves. (159)
May my delight be in scentless flowers through the state of detachment;
may there be no passion for clothing or ornaments, but rather for the skins of elephants and tigers.
May there never be any delight for me in celestial beds or divine enjoyments;
may my dwelling always be in the cremation ground, and never among the crowds of people anywhere.
In this cremation ground, free from obstacles, may your meditation always be mine;
O Śrī Hari, may your knowledge be eternal and the destroyer of the three qualities (guṇas). || 162 ||
May my trident take the form of dispassion, and my ash the form of detachment;
may my bull be the form of dharma, and my devotion toward you the state of being a yogi.
And this necklace around your neck was fashioned from the heads of those hostile to devotion; these garlands of ornaments were made from unsuitable rudrākṣa fruits.
"Let there be no enjoyment for you from trees such as the *vṛnda* for my sake;
let not Goddess Lakṣmī be mine, but rather let Alakṣmī indeed be mine. (165)
May whatever sweet drink belongs to Hari never be mine;
may I always have poison, dhattūra, ganja, bhaṅga, and the like. (166)
Thus, everything was requested by me at the time of my ascetic penance,
and Hari granted that boon for my welfare.
For the sake of instructing the devotees, it manifested the devotion of a servant;
yet by His command, it was concealed for the purpose of deluding the asuras. (168)
Therefore, if you exist, I shall grant you a livelihood from Hari, and not otherwise.
Listen now to another excellent story, filled with the grace of Hari. (169)
Once Sanatkumāra went to Vaikuṇṭha;
there the sage beheld Hari Nārāyaṇa having finished his meal.
Having prostrated with devotion, he praised Him with secret hymns;
being pleased, the Lord who is affectionate toward His devotees granted him a boon. 171.
There, he himself ate a small portion; as for the remainder that was kept, he guarded it carefully so that it would be difficult even for his kinsmen to obtain for their own consumption. (172)
For that reason as well, that sage gave some [food] to me while I was staying at the hermitage of Siddha; and all of that was eaten by me with reverence.
Having partaken of the rare grace of Hari, I performed a dance;
with all my limbs covered in horripilation, I became filled with joy and tears in my eyes. (174)

Then, with devotion, I sang the praises of the qualities of Śrī Hari in a beautiful voice, maintaining the proper rhythm and measure, and remaining single-mindedly focused on the various musical modes (rāgas). 175.
The hand-drum fell from my hand, as did the horn and the tiger skin;
then, having fallen down myself, I wept and even lost consciousness. (176)
The form of Śrī Hari is exceedingly lovely and heart-stealing; being overwhelmed by it, I meditate upon it within my heart for that very duration. (177)
In that interval, O beautiful lady, you, Durgā, arrived there with joy;
and as for me, O beautiful lady, I remained standing after rising from my swoon. || 178 ||
The very cause that brings about such a swoon there has indeed been asked by me;
however, I have told you only that which results from my favor. (179)
"O Goddess, having perceived that you were angry, you then said to me:
'You are the nourisher and protector of the worlds, and especially so of me.'"
If you, who are the speaker of the four Vedas and the bestower of all prosperity, practice such wicked policy, who will protect the Dharma? (181)
"I am always to be protected by you, nourished, devoted, and a servant;
yet, due to the fault of my past actions, I have been deprived of partaking in the grace of Hari. (182)
Some things are purified by gold, some are purified by air, and some by washing alone; but everything is purified by offering it to Viṣṇu. (183)
"All deities, ancestors, and guests should be worshipped with food offered to Viṣṇu; this is the settled conclusion in the Vedas. (184)
That which is not offered is unfit to be eaten, whereas the offering (naivedya) is indeed fit to be eaten;
he who eats thus with devotion shall become a foremost attendant (pārṣada).
The nectar of all things, which is the essence of what is desired and very difficult to obtain, does not equal even a sixteenth part of the food offered to Viṣṇu. (186)
Alas! That nectar which destroys untimely death merely serves to delude the foolish;
yet the food offering (naivedya) of Hari alone makes one equal to Hari himself. 187.
He who, through the company of the virtuous, partakes of that food offering by chance,
obtains the fruit of ascetic penance for sixty thousand years.
He who, being a devotee, always eats with devotion after first offering to Hari, should be known as a sanctifier of the assembly; he is equal to the splendor of Hari himself.
"I am not the author of the Vedas; what power do I have to speak them?
Having performed penance for a very long time, you, O Lord, were obtained by me."
"O Lord, how have I been deceived by you through the grace of Viṣṇu?
Having spoken thus, you, O Durgā, broke into tears. (191)
Then, out of supreme love, I respectfully placed you upon my chest and, wiping the tears from your eyes with my hand, awakened you again and again.
Then, being fully satisfied, you said to me, "I shall become your husband; otherwise, O Hari, I will cast off this body without having offered it as an oblation. (193)
I constantly bear this body that increases your good fortune;
but how can I carry a physical form devoid of such fortune?
The unprecedented food offering to Hari, which removes birth, death, and old age, was not indeed given to me; behold, therefore, I am casting off my body. (195)
Having spoken thus, O Great Goddess, you prepared to cast off your body;
then indeed you were praised by me: "O Great Goddess, remain firm! (196)
O beautiful one, you ought to forgive my entire transgression;
show compassion toward me, your servant who has been won over by your ascetic power. 197.
"It is the will of Śrī Hari himself; I am not even capable of granting it.
Upon hearing this intention of Śrī Hari, Durgā became satisfied.
Then he went quickly to the river of gold for the purpose of bathing;
having bathed and worshipped with devotion, he then prepared cooked food.
When she then offered me the food-offering (naivedya), I, Nārāyaṇa,
went there, ate everything myself, and gave her whatever she desired.
And she returned to Vaikuṇṭha, O Lakṣmī,
having given that very grace to her husband, and whatever remained of it, Durgā consumed.
Thus, Śiva and Aśiva are indeed devotees from a previous birth who were Vaiṣṇavas;
they always remain immersed in that form [of Viṣṇu] as supreme yogins.
I do not dwell in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor upon your chest; I am forever bound by the noose of devotion within the heart of Sadāśiva.
By this son of mine, the five-faced Śaṅkara, constantly sings my song which is established by its own inherent power; therefore, I abide within his heart.

There, being struck down by the powerful Ṛbhus, twenty thousand of the groups of virtuous women died on the spot, while the remainder fled. || 17 ||
At that time, one hundred thousand soldiers of Dakṣa’s side went to the abode of Yama;
meanwhile, those venerable persons—the pure Viṣṇu and the brahminical sages—remained.
Thinking that they must not be killed, the gods on earth were likewise not slain;
at that time, those sages, the gods led by Śakra, and the hosts of Maruts [remained].
The Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the world-protectors, and the planets remained silent,
stationed upon their respective celestial chariots in the path of the sky.
Anxious and repeatedly praying for the absence of obstacles were the sons-in-law of Dakṣa,
the daughters of Dakṣa, and the members of Dakṣa’s family.
The sacrificial ground, protected with great effort by the hosts of Viṣṇu and the Brahman-sages,
was then purified by the removal of the corpses.
Furthermore, because Dakṣa had seized [the sacrifice], everyone remained stationed on the sacrificial ground;
then, with the desire to complete the sacrifice, the rite of oblation (homa) quickly took place. ||23||
In the meantime, a voice from the sky spoke there:
"O Dakṣa, O you of wicked conduct, O hypocrite, O great villain! (24)
"What is this that you, fool, have done which will bring about your own ruin?
Dadhīci has departed after pronouncing a curse upon your sacrifice; you did not realize it. (25)
He did not honor his eldest daughter when she arrived at his home, though she was worthy;
being devoid of knowledge, he did not worship Śiva and Pārvatī out of pride. ||26||
He did not worship her thinking of her as a daughter;
he did not propitiate that virtuous woman who bestows all auspicious fortune. ||27||
You have not worshipped the Goddess who bestows auspiciousness upon her devotees;
you have not bowed to and gratified the Śakti who removes all fears. ||28||
He did not propitiate with love the Goddess who is bowed down by him and who grants his heart's desires;
nor did he meditate upon and worship the Sovereign who bestows fame and prosperity. (29)
He did not nourish the Dhātrī, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he did not hold in his heart her who protects, sustains, and destroys.
He did not lead the mother of all creation to peace, nor did he offer a portion of Śambhu to the consort of Śambhu at the sacrifice. ||31||
For the perfected ones perform austerities, and virtuous women desire a vision of it;
likewise, yogis engage in yogic practices out of a longing to behold it. (32)
He did not show due honor to those two, the fathers of the entire world;
for this very reason, the destruction of this sacrifice will certainly come to pass. (33)
Since you have been treated with such hospitality and honor, how could it not result in your welfare?
Your misfortune has been transferred to me, and all calamities have likewise passed to you. (34)
"Thinking, 'May I attain auspiciousness without having worshipped Śivā and Śambhu'—has this pride come upon you? Your pride shall perish this very day. (35)
"Turning away from Śaṅkara, who among these gods would be your helper in this matter? I do not see anyone at all—
whether they be the gods or others— who might now be your allies."
Surely they shall meet their destruction by fire like moths;
let your head be ablaze, and let the sacrificial offerings also burn;
let those who assist you enter into and be consumed by this inauspiciousness. (37–38)
"Let the gods and their own retinues depart from this sacrificial ground;
in a moment, the destruction of those who remain here shall come to pass. (39)
"Let the children, the elders, the women, and others depart from the sacrificial ground;
O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, let the two luminaries also depart from the site of the sacrifice."
"Otherwise, your destruction will surely occur in the next moment.
Having thus addressed them all, the celestial voice indeed ceased. 41.

Those who had gone to the sacrificial ground did not depart, for their future was destroyed by fate; even though they were filled with grief, they remained there solely for the sake of completing the sacrifice.
They quickly perform the oblation, and the sacrificial rite proceeds.
Then the divine Śrī Nārada quickly [departed] immediately after the cremation of Satī.
He went to Kailāsa to recount the entire account of Satī to Hara; having gone into the presence of Śambhu and bowed to Hara, he spoke with breathless urgency.
Displaying suffering and manifesting grief and dejection, he likewise aroused intense compassion and made known his fear. (49)
Shedding tears from his eyes and trembling, he said to Śaṅkara:
"It is observed that there can be no sublation of one who is free from illusion by means of illusion."
Even if everything were to perish, what concern would a yogi have in this regard? Nothing of yours shall diminish, nor indeed shall anything increase.
Because you are immutable and perfect, how could there be decrease or increase in you?
Today, your sovereignty has indeed been assailed by Dakṣa through his very position.
For one to whom honor and dishonor, as well as blame and praise, are equal, and for whom loss and gain are not reckoned—what indeed can the sound of a drum do before such a person? 49.
Even when his own destruction is imminent, he does not tremble at all;
why then has he vainly accumulated that burden born of power and treasure? He possesses no wealth of pride, nor any sorrow caused by contempt.
He related everything before her, just as the story had been told before the queen.
Before one who is free from pride, the excellent woman who possesses pride is blessed; indeed, she who is proud before the prideless is a virtuous wife.
O Sage, it is heard that she either sleeps or perhaps does not; do you even have ears, or do you not?
For, upon hearing your censure, that virtuous woman has treated her own life as a blade of grass.
Having heard this, Śambhu then became like another Mahākāla;
Rudra grew exceedingly fierce, inflamed by the fire of great wrath.
There, Vikarālānana quickly said to Nārada: "Hum! Hum! Hum! What happened there? He has treated his own life as a mere blade of grass! (55)
"O Nārada, what do you say? Satī has abandoned her life!
Shouting "ḍūm̐h ḍūm̐h ḍūm̐h ḍūm̐h ḍūm̐h ḍamāk ḍaṃ ḍūm̐h," Śaṅkara sounded his ḍamaru drum; 56.
agitating his matted locks, he struck the surface of the earth with force in his wrath.
From that collision, a great smoky vapor arose, digging into the earth. ||57||
From the midst of that, however, there arose a mountain characterized by the emergence of great flames;
from that mountain was then born Girideva, who causes trembling in Time and Death.
Manifest in the form of an image, he was as terrifying as Rudra himself;
Vīrabhadra was another Rudra, possessing the prowess of the hundred Rudras. ||59||
In his hand was then a mace equal to Mount Mandara,
a spear as long as the Vindhya range, and a club like Mount Raivata.
When his eyes were opened wide, they were like the sun and the moon;
his lolling tongue was like the blazing flame-mouthed goddess Jvālāmukhī.
His chest shone like Mount Arbuda;
seizing it quickly by the middle with his big toe and his toes, he [pulled it].
Having uprooted a peak of the Himalaya mountain and held it in his matted hair like Śiva, he bowed to Śambhu and then said: "What service may I perform for you?"
By Your command, I shall make the entire universe, with all its moving and non-moving beings, into a single morsel;
I shall drink up all the oceans with a single handful. 64.
Having exchanged the netherworlds, I shall lead them downward even if they are above;
and here I shall bring the world-protectors, including Indra, seizing them by their hair.
Having bound Time and Death, I shall indeed bring them into your presence;
in the battle between the Daityas and Dānavas, I shall slay the powerful one.
Behold, from my falling at your feet the circle of the earth trembles;
yet with my two arms, I shall forcibly crush all the mountains to dust.
What is the use of much speaking? Grant me your command; there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Know that, having relied on the power of your feet, today my thought has been fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, Vīrabhadra, with his thousand uplifted arms,
stood in the presence of Śambhu and placed the dust of His feet upon his head.
Just then, the hosts of attendants arrived there weeping from the sacrifice and said,
"O God, O Mahādeva, protect us who have come to you for refuge!"
O Lord, listen with respectful interest to the detailed account of Satī;
for Dakṣa, out of pride, showed her disrespect.
He gave you a portion from us and presented it to the gods;
however, upon hearing this, Satī became enraged and spoke harsh words loudly at the sacrifice.
Having censured his father many times, he consumed his own body in a sacrifice;
at that time, forty thousand Gaṇas perished in the ritual.
Out of shame, they engaged in a fierce battle and were slain in the sacrifice;
at that time, our own factions and the Gaṇas became the destroyers of the sacrifice.
In the sacrifice, they were slain by the Ṛbhus produced through the *bhṛgu-homa*;
others, who were the slayers of Lakṣa, were killed by the Gaṇas of Dakṣa.
Nevertheless, Dakṣa and the celestial sages who support his faction are performing the sacrifice, having first purified the sacrificial ground.
They do not grieve for Satī, nor do they even remember Śambhu;
laughing at the destruction of Satī, they show their teeth toward you. (77)
O Satī, at that sacrifice, Dakṣa and all those wicked ones, being exceedingly arrogant, especially insulted you.
"Indeed, for the sake of reviving these lost hosts, grant us the mantra that turns ashes into life; grant us the nectar-dew! (79)
In that regard, grant me the great power of the Mahālaya so that I may destroy and obstruct those others, Bhṛgu and the rest, whom they are about to produce.
That mantra known as Kālakavala was given by Brahmā to Śambhu;
it was then given by Śambhu to the wise Vīrabhadra.
Having brandished his weapon in wrath upon seeing the enemies, he should employ it;
for this mantra of the "Maw of Time" should indeed be bestowed even upon others. (82)
Oṃ! O Death, O Mortality, O Great Death, remain steadfast together with your own death! Oṃ! O Death, O Mortality, O Great Death, remain well-established together with your own death! ||83||
Thus, having first uttered the syllable *phuṭ*, whatever weapon there may be, such as arrows and the like, one should hurl it at the body of the enemy; having died, he shall not live again.
At that time, Vīrabhadra was instructed by Śaṅkara himself, and he was likewise empowered there by the command of Śaṅkara. (85)
Then, having smeared ashes upon his body and performed ten thousand fire-oblations in that fire,
he performed one hundred thousand recitations right there with ten thousand golden-bodied beings.
Having accomplished the mantra of Time and having dissolved his bodies, Vīrabhadra, the great destroyer, became once again a single being. ||87||
He became ready to depart, requesting permission from the Earth;
and Hara likewise [learned] from Nārada that Satī’s body had been reduced to ashes.
Having heard from the assemblies his own censure and the extreme arrogance of Dakṣa, he cast his matted locks upon the ground for the sake of the destruction of Dakṣa and everyone else. (89)
In his rage he struck out forcefully;
in his fury he swept it away, shaking it in every direction.
From the power known as Mahālayā, through the striking of his matted locks, the Jvara spirits were born; and from the rubbing [of them], those called Kālikā arose. (9.1)
By the shaking [of his body], hosts of spirits were born by the hundreds of billions; by the clapping of hands, millions of spirits that cause great terror were produced. (92)
There, ten million and even a hundred million goddesses reside; they carry weapons, possess eight excellent hands, and are proud of their fresh youth. (93)
Of most terrifying appearance, weary from the labor of battle, these thirteen crores of cruel fevers have taken embodied form. (94)
Armed with weapons, they bring about the end of destruction; they never return to their enemies;
these great Caṇḍīs, such as Kālikā and others, dance upon the field of battle. (95)
The Mahākālīs, terrifying and rich with weapons, mantras, and wisdom, are all present in numbers of a parārdha and even multiples of a parārdha. 96.
Equipped with weapons, armor, missiles, and other gear, they were experts in warfare;
blazing forth, they quickly sought out Hara, illuminating the ten directions.
Beholding the gateway of Śambhu’s command, they indeed prepared themselves with haste;
meanwhile, a new, countless army appeared right there on Kailāsa. 98.
Vīrabhadra said to Hara: "Command me quickly, O Lord;
O Śambhu, the oceans are to be dried up by me in just half a moment. (99)
In that place, I could grind down mountains in half a moment;
in an instant, I could reduce the cosmic egg or even the gods to ashes.
All the worlds have fallen into ruin; tell me, what must be done by me?
I bow to you, O Mahādeva; once again, I bow to you.
A throbbing has also arisen in my left limbs, which portends victory;
moreover, an unprecedented surge of joy and enthusiasm has been born within me.
"O Śambhu, send me quickly; tell me what must be done at once.
Then Śambhu, whose eyes were copper-red, spoke to Vīrabhadra.
Out of pride, Dakṣa is hastily performing a sacrifice in opposition to me;
therefore, having reduced that sacrifice, along with its assembly and its attendants, to ashes— || 104 ||
"Return once more to Kailāsa; go quickly and make haste!
Whether they be gods opposed to me, or Gandharvas, or other sages," ||| 105 ||
Whether they be sages, Brahmins, or whoever else has gathered there,
reduce even them to ashes instantly and with great haste this very day.
If Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Mahendra, or even Yama should take the side of Dakṣa, reduce them indeed to ashes!
O Bhadraka, reduce to ashes those who, disregarding the opinion of Dadhīci, remain at the sacrifice as partisans of Dakṣa.
"Though awakened by a voice from the sky, they still do not go outside;
O auspicious one, reduce those who are hostile toward my sacrifice to ashes!"
O Bhadraka, reduce to ashes those who obtained wealth at Dakṣa’s sacrifice and who proclaimed the superiority of Dakṣa— those who were consumed by the wrath of Satī and Śambhu.
And even those who have gone over to the side of Dakṣa, having perceived the fear of death, should become your followers for a moment; reduce them as well to ashes.
Whether they be gods or sons of gods, Manus or sons of Manu, Brahmās or sons of Brahmā, or even their grandsons who are indeed wicked; || 11.2 ||
"Reduce to ashes all those who oppose Satī and Śambhu, along with their wives and sons; afterwards, drink the water. (113)
Thus addressed, Vīrabhadra became repeatedly possessed by passion;
likewise, Pracaṇḍaka became possessed by Rudra and possessed by Time.
Invisible and invincible even to the creator Nārāyaṇa,
there arose a terrifying onset of dissolution, an onset of fear.
Then, from his head, oceans of the fire of time emerged;
having bowed to Śaṅkara, he set forth, setting the cosmic egg ablaze.
Nārada also, having clearly perceived Kali, went before the sacrifice and spoke to Viṣṇu, Śakra, Brahmā, and likewise to the gods.
Vīrabhadra is approaching; there will be a terrifying destruction.
Therefore, let them depart from here and not behold the abode of Yama.
This time is not merely a destroyer of family and kinship;
therefore, those of sound intellect must flee from the onrush of dissolution.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu, Yama, Veda, Mahendra, the Brahmins,
and others who despised the faction of Dakṣa departed from that sacrifice.
Accompanied by their wives and their retinues, stationed upon their respective celestial chariots,
they traveled by way of the sky, proceeding further and further away.
Then Bhrigu, having discerned through his sacrificial rites the armies and the many millions of hosts belonging to the Rbhus, Śṛṅgins, Dharās, Ambhas, and others, [acted accordingly].
Nine parārdhas were created from his right side;
they were equipped with weapons and fires, assuming forms at will, both beautiful and deformed.
Skilled only in combat and devoid of counsel, they were not truly alive;
the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas stood ready on the earth and in the sky.
The sacrificial rite proceeds; only its completion remains. Since the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is to take place at midday, one must act with haste.
Then the priests performed the sacrificial rites with haste;
however, [this was prevented] by the curse of Satī and the words of Dadhīci.
"The sacrifice will certainly not be completed,
since Vīrabhadra has already arrived before midday with an army consisting of many millions upon millions."
From a distance of a hundred yojanas, the sound of the army was heard approaching;
from a distance of ten yojanas behind, a mountain of dust was seen rising.
Within that destruction, the fierce and terrifying hosts of Śaṅkara, resembling mountains and possessing bodies as vast as mountains, were seen as warriors.
They descended and alighted upon the armies of the Ṛbhus in the sky,
upon the armies of the Śṛṅbhus on the earth, and also upon the terrestrial forces.
Then Śambhu dispatched another hundred crores of great hosts of attendants following Vīrabhadra, who had been produced from his own breath.
The sky was completely covered by them as they moved to the sides and behind;
indeed, the peaks of the mountains were uprooted by some of them.
Some indeed uprooted mountains from their very foundations to their peaks;
others, having torn up *śāla* trees, departed taking them with them. || 133 ||
All the attendants of the Destroyer of Time (Kāla) possess the form of Rudra;
they are tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of lions, tigers, crocodiles, and elephants.
Taking up millions of vehicles and mounts,
the armies went there, and as they departed, a rain of flowers fell.
Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Īśānī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Muṇḍamardinī [also went].
Accompanied by these nine Durgās— namely Bhadrakālī, Bhadrā, Kauśikī, and Vaiṣṇavī—
the terrible Mahākālī went with great haste for the destruction of Dakṣa. || 136-137 ||
Ḍākinīs, śākinīs, hosts of bhūtas, pramathas, and guhyakas; kūṣmāṇḍas, parpaṭas, caṭakas, and brahmarākṣasas. || 138 ||
The Bhairavas, Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, and Vināyakas—those heroes who were the destroyers of Dakṣa’s sacrifice—emerged in haste. (139)
In the same way, the circle of Yoginīs, accompanied by the sixty-four Gaṇas and joined by ten million Vetālinīs, suddenly emerged in a state of wrath.
And Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, approached with ten crores;
likewise, Kekarākṣa with ten, and Vikṛta with eight.
Viśākha has four [teeth], Pāriyātrika has nine;
Sarvāṅka is heroic with six, and likewise Vikṛtānana.
Jvālakeśa [is accompanied] by twelve crores, Jīmūta by seven;
Dudrubha by eight crores, and Kapālīśa by five.
Saṃdāraka would go with six koṭis of koṭis;
Viṣṭambha, the best of the hosts, would go with sixty-four koṭis.
Śaṃnāda and Pippala would travel with ten billion [attendants],
while Āveśāna and Candratāpana each traveled with eight.
Mahāveśa went with a thousand [attendants], Gaṇapa likewise with ten million;
Kuṇḍī went with twelve crores, and Parvataka also set forth.
Kāla, Kālaka, and likewise the Gaṇa Mahākāla,
with a hundred crores [of followers], set out toward the destruction of the sacrifice.
Agnikṛt by a hundred million, and Agnimukha by ten million; Ādityamūrdhā by ten million, and likewise Ghanāvaha by ten million. (148)
Sannāha with a hundred koṭis, Kumuda with a koṭi, and Amogha and Kokila, the lords of the hosts, each with ten million koṭis. || 149 ||
Kāṣṭhāgūḍha, Sukeśī, Vṛṣabha, and the lord of the Gaṇas, Sumantraka, likewise departed for the sacrifice. (1.176.150)
Kākapādodara and Santānaka were accompanied by sixty crores [of followers],
while Mahābala and Puṃgava were likewise accompanied by nine crores.
Madhupiṅga and Pūrṇabhadra went forth with ninety crores [of followers];
so too did Virūpākṣa, Tālaketu, Ṣaḍāsya, and Pañcavaktraka. || 152 ||
Saṃvartaka, Kulīśa, Daityānta, Lokāntaka, Bhṛṅgīriṭi, Śṛṅgiriṭi, Aśani, and Bhālaka. || 153 ||
Accompanied by sixty-four [thousand], they each went to the sacrifice;
there were thousands of crores of beings and three crores of dog-herds.
It fell through the path of the sky onto the sacrificial grounds of Dakṣa;
and by it, the kettledrums, conchs, tabors, and even the gomukhas [were shattered]. 155.
Various kinds of horns resounded indeed at the festival of battle;
and there occurred the throbbing of the right and left eyes, as well as the arms and thighs. 156.
At midday there was an earthquake; Dakṣa beheld the stars, the quarters were shrouded in darkness, and the sun became devoid of luster. || 157 ||
Surrounded by seven halos and inspiring terror,
the stars fell and thunder roared out of season.
At that time, the movement of the stars became crooked and turned downward;
and a vulture, having touched the head of Dakṣa, departed carrying away the cloth covering his head.
Jackals howled and harsh winds blew at that time;
there was a shower of meteors, a rain of dust, and a falling of white scorpions.
Swarms of locusts as numerous as bubbles within bubbles were seen in the sky above the sacrifice,
and the sacrificial pavilion of Dakṣa was carried upward by the winds.
Those worthy of sacrifice vomited blood and became trembling; then there was a rain of blood, a burning of the quarters, and the directions were shrouded in darkness. || 162 ||
Those present at Dakṣa’s sacrifice beheld such portents;
they fell to the ground in a swoon, crying out, "Alas! We are destroyed! and lamented thus.
In the meantime, a voice from the sky spoke to them:
"Fie on you, Dakṣa! Fie on you gods and others! Irresistible suffering has arrived."
Meanwhile, Śambhu’s armies entered the sacrificial courtyard;
then Dakṣa, overcome with fear, went for refuge to Hari.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle of Satī with the Attendants, the Celestial Voice to Dakṣa, Nārada’s Return to Kailāsa, the Birth of Vīrabhadra from Śambhu’s Matted Locks, the Arrival of the Remaining Gaṇas at Kailāsa, the Creation of the Army of Kālikā, Jvara, Gaṇas, Bhūtas, Siṃhas, and Others, Their Dispatch to the Sacrifice, Nārada’s Return to the Sacrifice, and the Inauspicious Omens for Dakṣa and the Others," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then Dakṣa, agitated by fear, remembered Viṣṇu within the lotus-born [Brahmā]:
"O God of gods, O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World! (1)
Protection must be afforded to me, to the sacrifice, and to the people;
let there be no destruction of the sacrifice, for you, O Acyuta, are the very soul of the sacrifice.
Then his prayer was heard by Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
mounting upon Haṃsa and Garuḍa, they returned once more from their own abodes.
With his mind agitated by fear, he fell at their feet;
then Viṣṇu, having raised up Dakṣa whose heart was melting with distress, [spoke].
He said: "O Dakṣa, listen to these words which are beneficial in every way;
for you, not knowing the truth, have indeed shown contempt. (5)
Everything done with contempt for the Lord becomes fruitless;
it is not merely useless, but brings misfortune at every step.
Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped, and he who is worthy of worship is not worshipped, there three things surely arise: poverty, death, and fear.
A great danger has arisen from Mahādeva because he was treated with disrespect;
indeed, Lord Śaṅkara is a Vaiṣṇava who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, an offense has been committed by you against a devotee of Nārāyaṇa;
for the Lord is truly not capable of providing protection to one who offends his devotee. (9)
Go for refuge to Śiva; he indeed will provide protection.
I am subject to the will of my devotees, and I am sorrowful due to the destruction of Satī.
"May you receive the fruit of your cruel deed; what will happen?
Hearing those words, Dakṣa became pale-faced.
And he said to Śrī Hari: "O Kṛṣṇa, by your power this commencement of the sacrifice has been made, as a witness to our deeds for the sake of the perfection of Vedic dharma."
Therefore, O Lord, protection must be provided for this sacrifice of mine; for there is no one capable of protecting the sacrifice and us except you. (13)
Viṣṇu said: "I must certainly provide protection for the sacrifice;
my entire vow is well known: the preservation of dharma."
The boundary of the Vedic dharma must always be protected by me, as well as the sacrifice of the three deities and other great-souled ones. (15)
There is a share for the Suras and others, and the Veda declares it not otherwise;
yet you have committed a transgression against that rule by performing a sacrifice out of pride.
Speak, O skillful one: how could the stake of dharma be abandoned by me?
Why were Satī and Śiva not invited by you previously to the sacrifice? (17)
How indeed has the boundary of sacrifice been transgressed by one who knows?
O evil-minded one, do you not see what is action and what is inaction? 18.
This sacrifice is empty because it lacks the Lord; it will not yield fruit.
Relying solely on mere knowledge and relying on pride, the officiating priests [have failed]. (19)
Having abandoned the Lord and remaining fixed in action alone,
they are indeed bound by the fetters consisting of karma throughout many births.
Those who show contempt for the Lord are cooked in the hells;
however, on one side, the army of the brother named Śiva has arrived. (21)
And elsewhere, the lineage flows through the sons and grandsons of Dakṣa and others;
all these kinsmen are indeed gods, yet they constitute but a single family.
Tell me now, where should the Sudarśana discus be released—against householders, servants, or in every way against great-souled ones? (23)
"Your destruction is imminent here due to the fault of insulting Śiva;
Destruction has been summoned by my intellect, and the ruin of your home is at hand. (24)
"This Vīrabhadra, the lord of Rudra’s hosts and the crusher of enemies, has indeed come for the purpose of destroying everyone; of this there is no doubt. (25)
While Govinda was speaking thus, the army then arrived;
the gods and others indeed beheld it surrounding the sacrificial ground.
Then Indra, laughing at Rudra and the attendant Vīrabhadra,
took his thunderbolt in hand and prepared the host of gods for battle.
Indra is mounted upon his own elephant; Anala himself is mounted upon a goat;
Yama is mounted upon a buffalo; Nirṛti has a corpse as his vehicle. ||28||
Varuṇa, mounted upon a sea-monster, and likewise Anila, mounted upon a deer,
as well as Kubera, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, fought together with the attendants of Śaṅkara.
Likewise, other valiant warriors— the gods, yakṣas, cāraṇas, and guhyakas—
mounted their respective vehicles and fought.
Then there was a great battle between the gods and the hosts;
conchs, kettledrums, and large drums resounded.
The ḍiṇḍimas, paṭahas, raṇa-śṛṅgas, and gomukhas resounded;
with sharp tomara-spears and nārāca-arrows, the gods struck down many of the Gaṇas.
The hosts of Śambhu, including Indra and the other world-protectors, were utterly defeated;
they were then conquered by the armies born from Bhṛgu’s mantras and fled.
