Then Menā said to the virtuous man, "O holy one, what dear thing do you desire? (5)
"I shall give you exactly as you wish; speak clearly and I will grant it. Then Śambhu said to Menā, "If you say 'I give'... (6)
"I have already attained it, saying 'I attain'; I shall attain it when the opportunity arises.
Mother, I will return then; give alms to me, who am alone. (7)
Then Menā, beholding that wonder, fell at his feet and said:
"I shall certainly give [her] to you, provided she is worthy for your sake."
Śambhu said: "So be it, Mother;
see for yourself how I wander in the great forest without her, without my beloved Śivā."
"In your house, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, will take birth;
for my sake, she shall become alms, and I, Śaṅkara, have arrived."
Upon hearing this, Menā became exceedingly joyful within her heart;
Śambhu, having been fed and honored, departed according to his will.
From that time forth, Menā remembered her future daughter and Śambhu as her son-in-law, and she rejoiced within the sky of her heart.
Due to the power of devotion from a previous birth, her devotion to Śiva increased;
having meditated upon Śivā, she thought, "O daughter of the ocean, she will become the mother of Śiva."
Lakṣmī said:
"O Śrī Hari, tell me who that Menakā was, the mother of Śivā.
Hari replied: "Listen, Lakṣmī; I shall tell you in brief. (14)
Sixty daughters of Dakṣa, the son of Vedhas, are celebrated;
he performed their marriage with suitors such as Kaśyapa and others.
Among them, he gave a daughter named Svadhā to the Pitṛs;
she had three fortunate sons who were endowed with righteousness.
Jyeṣṭhā, Madhyā, Kaniṣṭhā, Menā, Dhanyā, and Kalāvatī—
these three were born from the mind of their father, for they were indeed not born from a womb.
Those yoginīs, whose movements are unimpeded and who can assume any form at will,
were three sisters who at one time went to a sacred ford out of a desire for pilgrimage.
They went to Śvetadvīpa, the world of Viṣṇu, for the purpose of seeing him;
having ascended a divine, auspicious celestial chariot that moves at will, they departed.
Having descended from their celestial chariot, they offered praise and prostration to Viṣṇu;
by his command, they stood on Śveta, where a great and well-ordered assembly was formed.
Then, in that assembly, the five-year-old sons of Brahmā, headed by Sanaka, arrived; having offered praise and bowed to Hari, they remained there.
At Viṣṇu’s word, Sanaka and the others remained in the assembly;
then the assembly rose, offering a welcome to the sages.
At that time, the assembly of goddesses, satīs, and yoginīs also rose up;
however, the three sisters remained behind, failing to rise due to delusion.
Since those three are situated in the middle and at the back of the yoginīs,
those in the rear do not see them, nor do those in the front see them likewise.

Since those who are established in the state of the assembly do not perceive even these three, how much less could they perceive what must be done after rising? For it is because they have realized this that they do not rise.
This very illusion, consisting of indolence and deluding through negligence,
having come into being, they indeed fell under its sway and did not perform the fitting honor.
Although the wise, being virtuous, are indeed not subject to the power of anger, they are nevertheless impelled by the force of future wrathful radiance. (27)
Seeing their immediate action, even the peaceful Sanatkumāra, the lord of yogis and liberated soul, issued a curse as a punitive rod.
"You three sisters are certainly the daughters of a father, yet you are devoid of refined conduct, lacking both rising from your seats and bowing. (29)
May those filled with the deeds of petty men be far from heaven;
let human women come forth and receive the fruit of their own actions.
Having heard those three [verses], those virtuous women fell at the feet of the sage and said:
"O Sage, ocean of compassion, be gracious in every way! (3.1)
The disposition of virtuous beings such as yourself truly exists within our hearts; however, due to negligence, we failed to perform acts of hospitality such as bowing and rising to greet you. (32)
O Sage, show us favor by granting the fruit of our own deed;
O Brahmin, at your very word, may we again attain the path to heaven.
Having shown compassion there, the sage, with a pleased mind, spoke:
"I shall indeed effect the removal of the curse; a great task will come to pass. (34)
And for your sake, there shall be a source of happiness where an embrace with Hari occurs;
[therein] Menā shall be the elder wife of Himavat, who is a partial incarnation (aṃśa) of Hari.
This maiden shall become your wife; she will be born as Pārvatī.
By bestowing her upon Śambhu, you will indeed attain supreme happiness.
At the beginning, through the auspicious blessings of Śiva and Śivā, you shall attain liberation and Kailāsa;
in the middle, you were the fortunate daughter-in-law of Janaka, the beloved wife of Daśaratha. (37)
Let your daughter Mahālakṣmī become Sītā;
by bestowing her upon Rāma, you shall indeed attain supreme happiness. (38)
"Before Sītārāma, by his grace, you shall attain Vaikuṇṭha;
and Kalāvatī, the younger sister, [shall remain] in the house of the Vṛṣabhānu clan. (39)
"Let this maiden become your wife; Rādhikā shall be born to you.
By bestowing her upon Kṛṣṇa, you will attain supreme happiness. (1.179.40)
And by the grace of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, you shall attain Goloka;
for when the suffering of those who perform good deeds has passed, happiness that was once difficult to obtain shall prevail. (41)
All of you, daughters of my father, are always enjoyers of celestial delights; by taking hold of this very purpose, you shall become attainers of liberation. 42.
Afterwards, Sanatkumāra and the others departed from the assembly for their own abodes;
then Menā and the other two women went to the dwellings of their fathers.
Then once, having bathed at Kurukṣetra, Indra and the other gods were there in the month of Āṣāḍha under the Mṛgaśīrṣa asterism; for that was indeed the day of the moon's disappearance.

Indra and the other gods respectfully offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the ancestors in that [tīrtha], consisting of sesame seeds, honey, well-cooked food, sweets, and sacrificial oblations (haviṣya). ||45||
Then the Pitṛs, being pleased and fully satiated, said to the gods, "Choose what we shall bestow. The gods then spoke to the Pitṛs.
"Listen all to our words, O fathers, with delighted minds;
if you desire to accomplish the work of the gods, that must be done immediately and exactly as we say. (47)
Remember what was chosen by the maidens in Śvetadvīpa;
remember that curse of Sanatkumāra and consider what is appropriate.
Having married with great affection that eldest daughter of yours named Menā, who brings auspiciousness, to the mountain king known as Himavat; ||49||
May all beings be happy and find gain at every step;
may there be the destruction of suffering for you and for the immortals.
Having heard the words of the gods and remembering the curse that occurred in the past, the ancestors said, "So be it," and gave Menā to Himavat.
The divine Himādri mountain, possessed of great splendor and abundant prosperity, exists in the world in two forms, distinguished as mobile and immobile. ||52||
Having deeply penetrated the eastern and western oceans, he stands firm and steady;
he is the most formidable ordainer of frost, frequented by gods, sages, and perfected beings.
Austerity quickly bestows perfection and is purifying for the great-souled;
indeed, it alone takes on a divine form, beautiful and lovely in every limb. (54)

And Śailarāja, a great devotee who is a portion of Viṣṇu and possessed of a beautiful form, he himself [acted] for the sake of the stability of his own lineage and for the purpose of increasing righteousness. (55)
Desirous of performing his own marriage and wishing for the welfare of his father and the gods, he then took Menā’s hand according to the rites of marriage. (56)
There was a great festival at that most auspicious wedding;
even Indra and the other gods, the sages, the seers, and the mountains were present.
They arrived there for the wedding and praised the Himalaya;
they caused a festival to be celebrated and gave gifts in abundance.
Filled with great joy, the gods, having praised the divine ancestors and received honor and worship, returned to their respective abodes.
Having obtained Menā as his young bride, Himavat became full of joy according to the duties of domestic life;
he took delight there, following his desires as he pleased.
Then, at that time, while Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, was on the Himavat mountain together with Śambhu, Menakā approached her.
"Having taken up residence in my house, my daughter is indeed considered virtuous"; thus perceiving her to be equal to his own daughter, he served her with the dignity of a mother.
Thus constantly meditating, Menakā served Satī;
and Satī, having cast off her body at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, remembered her mother.
Having resolved in her heart, "May I become his daughter," Satī, when the time arrived, out of affection became the daughter of Menakā. (64)
Having performed penance, Pārvatī again obtained Śiva as her husband.
To Menā, three daughters were born, endowed with beauty and virtue. (65)
Rāgiṇī, Kuṭilā, and Kālī are the three maidens in their respective order;
she [the first] has red limbs, red eyes, and is adorned with red garments.
O beloved, the eldest daughter of Menā, named Rāgiṇī, was born;
she possessed auspicious limbs, lotus-petal eyes, and dark, curly hair. (67)
The middle one is named Kuṭilā, wearing white garlands and garments;
she resembles a mass of blue collyrium and has eyes like blue lotuses. 68.
Kālī, the daughter of Menakā, was the youngest and peerless in beauty;
and the fourth son became renowned as Sunābha. (69)
O beloved, those three daughters were born six years ago;
as they went forth to perform penance, the gods beheld those auspicious maidens.
Then, by all the Divākaras and the Vasus,
that ascetic maiden named Rāgavatī was led to heaven by the gods.
Created by Brahmā for the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura, she possessed a beautiful form and was endowed with the glow of twilight, appearing in the very form of the time of twilight.
Pratīcchukī always remains in the sky in the portion of Kṛttikā;
Kuṭilā, possessing the luster of the moon, was led to the world of Brahmā by the gods. 73.
Brahmā said: "This daughter was intended for the destruction of Mahiṣa;
indeed, she is seen to be truly incapable of bearing the fiery energy of Śarva."
Therefore, let this river, which has always made its abode in the world of Brahmā within Truth and consists of water, remain in my house, overflowing with its waters. (75)
When it was thus understood that the two daughters had departed, Menā,
perceiving her third daughter to be ascetic, restrained Menā from her penance.
"O daughter, perform penance"—thus she obtained the name Umā.
This has been told in brief; what more do you wish to hear? (77)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, Śambhu indicates to Menā the purpose of Satī’s birth; Menā, Dhanyā, and Kalāvatī—the three daughters of the Pitṛs—went to Śvetadvīpa. There, they received a curse from Sanatkumāra and were subsequently born as the wives of Himagiri, Sīradhvaja-Janaka, and the Vaiśya Vṛṣabhānu. Their daughters were, in order, Śivā, Sītā, and Rādhā. Furthermore, Menā had three daughters: Sandhyārāgiṇī, Kuṭilā-Brahmanadī, and Kālī.
The one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Sunābha’s Son."
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Supreme Lord, tell me the divine story of Kālī’s birth;
tell me also the story of how Kālī again became Gaurī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī; having abandoned her body, Satī then became unmanifest. She remained hidden and invisible within the regions of the Himālayas.
Having reached Kailāsa and prostrated at that auspicious place, the gods then remembered, bowed down to, and praised Satī.
O Goddess, you are indeed both; you are Gāyatrī, the Supreme Sovereign, worshipped by the sages of Brahmā and honored by powerful kings and rulers.
You are the earth, worshipped as "Bhūḥ" by the Vaiśyas and as "Śivā" by the Śūdras; you are the unshakeable forbearance of sages and the compassion of those who observe self-restraint.
You are the mass of great expedients for those who spread the principles of policy;
you are the cultivation of wealth, and you are the desire cherished in the hearts of living beings.
You are the liberation of all beings; you are the intellect of all embodied souls.
Thus, you are the passion of those with impassioned hearts, and you are the joy within the hearts of the embodied.
You are the fame of those who are truthful; you are the peace of those of evil deeds;
you are the delusion of all beings; you are the goal of those who perform sacrifices.
You are the great shore of the ocean; you are the grace of the playful;
you are the origin of all things; and you are the stability of the world-protectors.
You are the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), dwelling throughout the entire circle of the worlds;
you are the dark night (Vibhāvarī) who bestows the bliss of embracing the neck of your beloved.
O Ambikā, you are the protector of the helpless; grant us your vision!
O Goddess, you are worshipped in the world through many diverse forms.
O Durgā, ever beloved of Śiva, we bow to you, O Maheśvarī—
the auspicious Power, the purifier, the nourisher, whose form is the Great Unmanifest.
We bow with devotion to you, the pure one who is devoted to Brahman;
we bow to you, who are well-pleased by both inner knowledge and higher knowledge. 1.3.
You are the radiance residing in the sun and the moonlight united with the moon;
you nourish all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—we bow to you. 14.
You are Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas; you are Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī. You are the livelihood of all the worlds, and you are the triple Veda (Trayī) whose form is Dharma.
You are sleep in all beings; you alone are hunger and satisfaction.
You are the prosperity of those who perform meritorious deeds, and likewise, the misfortune of the sinful. (16)
You are the peace of all the worlds; you are the sustainer who nourishes life.
You are the melody of the Sāmaveda; you are the knot of the Yajurveda and the sacrificial oblation.
She is the measure of the Ṛgveda and the supreme goal of the Atharvaveda;
she is the power of all the gods and the one who effects deliverance from suffering. (18)
O Śivā, O Rudrāṇī, O Sannidrā, O Caṇḍā, O Kātyāyanī, O Satī, O Kauśikī, O Caṇḍikā, O Kālī, O Nārāyaṇī—salutations be unto you! (19)
O Pārvatī, beloved of austerity, who are ever visible, salutations again and again to you!
Be gracious, O Goddess of gods, and grant me your vision, O lady of excellent vows.
"O Great Goddess, receive the state of being Menā’s daughter; salutations be unto you!
Thus was the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, praised by the gods. (21)
The Mother of the World appeared before the gods;
there arose a mass of bliss for all the inhabitants of heaven.
Again the gods bowed down and praised her especially:
"O Śivā, O Śarvāṇī, O auspicious one, O Ambikā, hear our petition. (23)
O Maheśvarī, although the daughter of Dakṣa was born for the sake of the gods' mission,
that mission of the gods was not fully accomplished.
O Great Goddess, fulfill the desire of the gods;
by doing so, the words of Sanatkumāra shall become fruitful. (25)
Having been the daughter of Menakā, may you become the wife of Rudra once again;
may all beings be happy, and may suffering perish entirely.
Having heard this, Śarvāṇī said: "I am pleased, there is no doubt;
I shall become the daughter of Menā. Let Hara obtain his own happiness. (27)
"Go all of you to your own abodes; I always remember Śaṅkara, who, for my sake, remains in great suffering while wearing this disguise. (28)
Distraught by separation, the Lord has with great affection fashioned a garland from my bones;
he constantly wears the ashes of my funeral pyre upon his body. (29)
Therefore, for the sake of pleasing Rudra, I shall descend;
my devotees, having performed most difficult penance, shall become dear to Śambhu.
"I shall accomplish the task for the gods; go now to your own home, truly.
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished and went to the abode of Himavat.
The gods, having bowed in that direction, returned each to their own abode;
Himavat and Menakā both performed supreme penance.
With hearts full of devotion, they worshipped Śivā,
and they constantly gave gifts to the Brahmins for the sake of pleasing her.
Beginning from the month of Caitra, for twenty-seven days,
Menakā, desiring a daughter, worshipped Śivā.
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, on the ninth lunar day one should offer oblations consisting of sweetmeats,
flour-cakes, milk-rice, perfumes, and flowers.
Having fashioned an image of earth at Oṣadhiprastha on the Gaṅgā,
he worshipped Umā with offerings of various articles and other such honors.
Taking no food, or subsisting on water, or occasionally on air,
Menakā spent twenty-seven days in her vow.
When her vow was completed, the Supreme Goddess appeared;
she beheld Menā, who was filled with contentment and seated in the midst of a circle of splendor.
Having become manifest before her, she, being well-pleased, said to Menā: "Choose a boon, O great virtuous lady, whatever dwells in your heart. (39)
"I am pleased with your austerities, vows, and meditations; I shall grant you [your desire].
And having seen her, Menakā bowed down to that virtuous woman and spoke.
I bow to the Great Goddess, the bestower of all desires and goals;
I ever bow to the perfected one, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self. 4.1
I bow always to her who is eternal bliss, appearing in the form of the intellect of a woman;
I bow to her who is rich in compassion—grant me my desire. 42.
O Nārāyaṇī, salutations to you, the Śakti who acts for the welfare of women, who bestows the bliss of Brahman, and who fulfills the desires of your devotees. 43.
Thus praised, she said to Menā, "Choose what you desire.
Menā then replied to the Goddess, "If I am worthy of a boon... (44)
"O Mother of the World, may I first have one hundred sons;
thereafter, three more sons, and one son endowed with excellent qualities. (45)
Among those three daughters, my youngest daughter shall be the object of my affection;
may you always be my source of happiness. (46)
"O wife of Rudra, become Bhavānī and likewise perform divine play in my presence.
Having heard that, the Goddess said to Menakā, "So be it. (47)
Having spoken thus, the beloved of Hara quickly vanished;
then Menā reported the granting of the boon to her husband. (48)
Having heard this, the Himalaya mountain was delighted and praised his beloved;
and in the course of time, their dear sexual union proceeded.
He became an embryo within Menā and grew day by day; Menā gave birth to her son Maināka, who was auspicious and endowed with all virtues.
Then, in due course, she gave birth to other sons who were all equal [to him],
and subsequently, by the grace of Satī, she gave birth to two daughters.

Then Menā, the virtuous wife of the mountain, conceived a child in her womb— a daughter who was dearer to the mountain than his own body, and who would become the supreme refuge for all beings dwelling in the world.
Menā shone forth even more brilliantly, adorned by a circle of splendor,
due to her beloved’s affection, the joy of her heart, and the wealth she had acquired for herself.
The mountain performed the appropriate rites for the elevation of his learning;
then, at the proper time, he, full of confidence, beheld Menā on the verge of childbirth.
When the ninth month had passed and the tenth was fully reached,
at the passing of midnight, Menā’s body began to feel as if pierced by a spear.
In the spring season, during the month of Madhu, on the ninth lunar day under the asterism Mṛgaśiras,
at the auspicious hour of Brāhma-muhūrta, she gave birth to a beautiful daughter.
A divine goddess was born, like Lakṣmī from the ocean;
Menā’s house became pervaded on all sides by her splendor.
Then it was a most auspicious time; the moon, planets, and stars were serene, the sky attained clarity, and light shone in all directions. (58)
The earth, abounding in auspiciousness and containing sacred fords, villages, and oceans,
truly saw lotuses bloom in its lakes, rivers, and ponds.
Pleasant, cool, and fragrant breezes blew,
and a rain of flowers fell, preceded by a shower of water.
The fires, though previously extinguished, blazed up; the clouds thundered at that time;
all the virtuous rejoiced, and the best of the Gandharvas sang.
The women of the Vidyādharas and hosts of Apsaras danced in the sky;
then, a great festival took place for the gods and others in the vault of heaven.
At that moment, the goddess Satī, the power of Brahmā and Śivā,
appeared before Menā in her own form.
She emerged from that womb like Śrī Lakṣmī from the ocean;
she was born as the beloved of Śiva, like Gaṅgā from the lunar orb.
There, in the city of Himavat, all suffering came to an end;
all the inhabitants of every world became happy.
At that time, even for the denizens of hell, happiness became equal to that of heaven;
indeed, the hearts of even cruel beings became truly gentle.
The luminaries also became exceedingly radiant with splendor, and the herbs dwelling in the forests were endowed with fruits of excellent flavor. (67)
And the great mountains, beginning with Meru, having taken on embodied forms,
arrived at that great festival with their hands extended toward the divine.
The oceans and the rivers gathered from all sides,
as did the sages, the tranquil ascetics, and all the gods, headed by Viṣṇu.
They arrived full of happiness and with affection beheld the Mother of the World; they praised that auspicious Mother Śivā, who had assumed a physical form for the sake of Śiva.
O Mother of the World, O Great Goddess, we bow to you at all times;
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, perform that which brings auspiciousness to the gods. (71)
"The desire of Menā has been fulfilled, and that of Śiva as well.
Having thus scattered handfuls of flowers, the gods returned to their own abodes. (72)
At that time, the Himālaya mountain became the one to be served, approached, and sought as a refuge by all beings, both mobile and immobile, throughout the world; it was the best of mountains.
But having seen her, who possessed a divine form, a youthful appearance, and a golden luster—
though dark in stature, she was radiant as the petals of a blue lotus.
Extremely delighted, Menā approached Mṛḍānī and offered this praise:
"O Mother of the World, O Mother who has acted for me, you have shown great compassion toward me. (75)
"O daughter, you who have appeared in my home, remain forever steadfast;
I bow to you, overwhelmed by a heart full of affection. (76)
Thus, with eyes full of tears of joy, she drank in her daughter;
at that moment, the goddess became manifest, bearing eight divine arms.
With her limbs fully developed and possessing the beauty of youth, she was twelve years older than sixteen. (78)
Richly adorned with the splendor of golden ornaments, she was exceedingly radiant in her divine garments;
her face was full of smiles, and her eyes were filled with gentle love. (79)
Adorned with the splendor of the prosperity of a king of kings,
the divine Śivayogī, having assumed a physical form, graciously granted her a vision.
The Goddess said to her mother: "O Mother, let there be repeated salutations to you;
for you previously propitiated me with devotion in order to grant a boon. (8–1)
"Since you have come to me for the sake of your daughter after making a request, I, the Supreme Goddess, said 'Om' and vanished from sight. (82)
Though I am a divine being and the wife of Śiva, I have been born as your daughter in your house; O Mother, by my grace, be favorable toward me. (83)
Indeed, this divine form has been assumed by me so that you may remember me;
otherwise, in your mortal state, you would have ignorance regarding me. (84)
"O my parents, by always contemplating me with the divine disposition of a daughter, you two have gone to my supreme state. (85)
I shall perform the work of the gods by enacting a wondrous sport upon the earth;
I shall become the wife of Śambhu and I shall deliver the virtuous.
Having spoken thus, that great goddess, possessing great splendor, became a daughter and wept there, adopting the ways of the world.
Hearing that beautiful weeping, all the women living in the house rejoiced with excitement; filled with joy, they went to Menā’s house. ||88||
And Himācala, the mountain king, also gave jewels, garments, and wealth as a reward to the one who announced the birth of his daughter. (89)
Upon seeing the maiden of divine form, the onlookers were then struck with wonder;
likewise, there was a great festival, and musical instruments resounded profusely.
Auspicious songs were sung and excellent women danced;
Himācala gave gifts to the Brahmins and performed the birth-rite (jātakarman). ||9 1||
Having caused [the rites] to be performed, he went outside and gave wealth to the monks;
and on the eleventh day, he gave his daughter the name Kālī.
That Kālī grew daily like the digit of the moon in its bright fortnight;
people called her by the name appropriate to her lineage, Pārvatī.
In her childhood, while in the midst of her female companions, she took delight again and again on the sandy banks of the Gaṅgā with artificial balls fashioned as sons.
At that time, with a restrained mind, she studied the science of the true guru;
constantly intent on meditation upon Śambhu, she indeed became devoted to asceticism. 95.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise Offered by the Gods to Satī while she was invisible on the Himavat Mountain during the Kṛta Yuga lineage in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Granting of Boons for Satī’s Birth to Menā and Himādri; the Austerities of Menā; the Conception of Kālī in Menā’s Womb; the Divine Vision of Her Birth; the Great Festival," and so forth, in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga. || 180 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once the divine Nārada went to the home of Himagiri;
the mountain performed worship for the celestial sage with great devotion.
He cast his own daughter at the feet of Nārada for the sake of purification and said,
"O best of divine sages, tell me the fortune of my daughter."
Having seen her hand and especially all her limbs, Nārada said, "O Mountain, this maiden increases the joy of her parents. (3)
This great virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, will bring extreme happiness to her lord;
she will become highly honored like a great divine queen. (4)
If there is a line at the middle joint of the thumb, she becomes a mistress (īśvarī);
if the hand has lines of an elephant, a banner, a lotus, and a trident, she is a sovereign lady (īśvarī).
She who has a great mark on her hand will become a queen;
she who has the mark of the moon on her forehead will become the wife of Yama, the Lord.
If there is the mark of a svastika on her hand, she will be victorious in her undertakings;
if her eyes reach as far as her ears, she is a certain Brāhmī, a supreme sovereign lady.
And within his heart, O Mountain, Śambhu indeed exists in the form of a white mark,
from which the Great Goddess Śakti shall surely arise.
On her abdomen, a line below the navel shall be worshipped as the Goddess;
on her foot, there shall be a betel vine, and she will certainly become the wife of a lord of gods.
Indeed, a single, distinct line exists above the thumb, and likewise a line exists on the forehead corresponding to it. (1.181.10)
O Śaila, hear the fruit of those two: it may come to pass, or it may not.
He will be a renouncer, naked, devoid of virtues, and abandoned by his mother and father.
Hearing that her husband would be one who lacks desire and wears inauspicious attire,
Menā and Himālaya experienced grief for a moment.
Having regained their former memory of Śiva, they both attained supreme happiness;
but Pārvatī, hearing those words, rejoiced greatly in her heart again and again.
The lines of destiny, the writing of Brahmā, never prove false anywhere;
Śambhu is such a bridegroom, and there is no other husband like him.
Thinking thus, the daughter of the mountain remembered Hara day and night;
meanwhile, Nārada, having received honors, was proceeding toward the abode of Śiva.
He reminded the lord of mountains of what had been said by Hara regarding Satī:
"O Satī, O beloved daughter of Dakṣa, I do not choose any other woman but you."
"I shall not take her as a wife; I tell you this truth.
Having thus reminded the Mountain of the words of Śarva, Nārada spoke. (17)
The lion-throne of your daughter shall rest upon the thigh of Śambhu;
having obtained the seat upon Śambhu’s thigh, she shall become the Great Queen.
Having spoken thus, the celestial sage Nārada departed for the world of Brahmā;
meanwhile, the parents constantly delighted their young daughter.
As Girijā grew, her youth becoming such that she was fit for marriage,
Indra then remembered Nārada once again.
That sage quickly reached the abode of Mahendra;
Indra, rising up, honored Nārada with water for his feet and other offerings.
Having learned that both he himself and Nārada were well,
Mahendra, being asked, "How was I remembered?", spoke to Nārada.
The young daughter of the mountain has been born; she must be united with Śambhu.
Therefore, an effort must be made quickly, and everything should be arranged accordingly.
Having heard this, Nārada went quickly to the abode of Śailaka,
assuming the form of an aged Brahmin and holding a lotus leaf in his hand.
Then the Brahmin sat down upon a beautiful seat offered by the mountain;
having accepted the hospitality provided by the mountain, he spoke in a gentle voice.
"O King of Mountains, is all well here with your asceticism at all times?
The mountain replied, "Out of compassion for the very aged, all is well with me. (26)
"But tell me the result of this: has my daughter become marriageable?
At that moment, Menā, followed by her daughter, approached the Brahmin.
Menā and the daughter of the mountain paid homage at the feet of the brahmin;
and beholding his daughter, the brahmin-sage honored her with blessings. (28)
With a face full of wonder and beholding her fortune, he spoke these words:
"O blessed lady, no husband has been born for you, for you are devoid of the auspicious marks. (29)
With palms turned upward and feet utterly wandering, one should understand that even one's own shadow [is not one's own]; what else indeed remains to be said here?
Having heard this, Himālaya fell into a state of confusion and, submerged in grief,
forgot what had been previously told by Nārada and spoke to the Brahmin.
The lines of karma are extremely difficult to traverse, yet they inevitably yield their fruits;
they follow one through successive births among the various species of living beings. (32)
Without women, the creation of living beings would never come into being;
yet the female species is by its very nature pitiable and subject to wretchedness.
Reflecting that there might be contempt for them, the Creator declared that a daughter is equal to ten sons as the field for the continuation of the lineage. (34)
An unfortunate and wretched maiden always causes sorrow to her father; yet she is even more so when she is deprived of a husband, sons, wealth, and good fortune. (25)
And you have spoken only of the faults of my daughter in every respect;
alas, great sorrow has arisen for me today upon hearing this from your own mouth! (36)
"Moreover, O Brahmin, even if she might attain some measure of good fortune in her old age, you must still speak [the truth]; therefore, wipe away for me the suffering born of my sin. (37)
Women were indeed created by Brahmā for the happiness of men;
their birth becomes meaningful through the attainment of a husband, otherwise it is fruitless. (38)
Women who rescue their paternal lineages in both this world and the next are indeed proclaimed here as those who have attained a true husband and are thus "rescuers. ||39||

A good husband is difficult for women to find; indeed, even a husband devoid of virtues is obtained only through merit, for even a husband who is utterly dull-witted cannot be attained by a woman without her own religious merits.
Even without means, the true Dharma brings the joy of obtaining a son;
wealth, livelihood, and fortune are established in a woman through her husband. (41)
Though he be penniless, foul-mouthed, foolish, and devoid of all auspicious marks, the husband alone is always considered the supreme fortune of a woman. (42)
Whatever woman, out of stinginess, hatred, or envy, or by her very nature, destroys the pleasure and happiness of another, the fruit of that action is the loss of her husband. (43)
She who hates sensual pleasure, creates obstacles for [others'] desires, and censures those who find happiness in desire, shall not obtain a husband. (44)
Even though she is married, she does not give the gift of love to her husband;
for a lover who does not grant pleasure finds it difficult indeed to obtain a wife. 45.
The fruit of those who have accumulated much merit—such as sensual pleasures and the like—is always granted to humans; it does not come to pass for sinners. (46)
Even beasts and birds, when attached to sensual desire, are separated from it;
for her, the pleasure of desire does not arise as the pleasure of a husband. (47)
For those women who, out of a desire for dharma, treated men with contempt as if they were blades of grass,
even birth in a noble family was rendered as insignificant as grass by the attainment of a husband.
For those who lack the pleasure of sensual desire, there is the state of being consumed by the fire of desire;
indeed, in this world, that is a constant, clinging suffering, like a heated iron statue.
Giving that is free from the obstacles of desire is indeed no ordinary gift; for through such giving, one always attains the merit of being a lord of the virtuous. (1.181.50)
For her in whom great merit from the gift of desire has been accumulated, this human birth alone becomes a constant granter of desires. //51//
Pigeons, sparrows, and other such birds are constantly lustful among winged creatures;
this should be understood as the fruit of the gift of desire previously bestowed, and not otherwise. (52)
The desire for cattle, such as cows and buffaloes, is indeed rare;
likewise, the fruit of a desire not previously granted is small. ||5 3||
Indeed, even in trees, fruits arise through the union with men;
likewise, even in creepers, there is the union with flowers, yet no fruit is seen at all.
All that is indeed the fruit of what was given, whether intentionally or unintentionally;
what kind of deed could my daughter have performed in a previous life? (55)
O Brahmin, that no husband has been born for her, as stated by you, is an incomparable misfortune and a vessel for countless sufferings. (56)
Moreover, you have described this [earth] as always having her hands outstretched;
for the state of having hands outstretched can only belong to those who are begging for alms. (57)
"You two have called her feet, which grant good fortune and the rise of auspiciousness, 'givers of poverty' and 'deviant' because of their beautiful luster. (58)
Even in that regard, a better hope than this does not appear to me at all;
however, O Brahmin, I shall cause you to hear what was previously spoken by Nārada.
"May her husband be one who is generous yet naked, devoid of virtues, abandoned by his mother and father, free from desire, and dressed in inauspicious attire. (1.181.60)
Therefore, O sinless one, tell me what truth is to be grasped by me here in this wandering;
if you know it, O Lord, my sorrow shall come to an end. (6.1)
Nārada, whose soul was that of an aged brahmin, spoke to the deeply distressed mountain:
"Since this sorrow of yours arises from delusion at a time when there ought to be great joy. (62)
Listen, O Śaila: her husband was not born; he is the unborn Sadāśiva.
He is eternal, perpetual, the immovable Sthāṇu, unshakable, and ancient.
The bodies of others are born from karma, but his is not so, for he is unborn;
listen indeed, as he is distinguished by being devoid of these characteristics.
Lakṣaṇa is said to be the physical mark produced by karma;
it reveals one's lifespan, wealth, fortune, excellence, and death. (65)
But this Maheśvarī is of the nature of Brahman and is devoid of karma;
she possesses no body produced by karma, nor does she possess any [physical] characteristic. Thus [it is said]. (66)
Indeed, her divine marks are innate;
listen now to how her palms are turned upward, for one whose palms are turned upward is always a granter of boons.
And the hand of this Great Goddess will certainly belong to him in every way; she shall become the bestower of boons upon gods, asuras, sages, and living beings.
Listen also to her feet: they are clear and faultless;
her feet resemble lotuses, are translucent, and shine with bright nails. (69)
Indeed, the luster of the jewels in the crowns of the bowing gods and asuras, moving about in great abundance on all sides, entered into those two. (1.181.70)
Such are the feet of both you and her, served by good fortune;
O Mountain, tell me, what thing could possibly be lacking for the wife of Śiva? (71)
As for what was said previously, that her husband will be a renunciant—Śiva is certainly always devoid of passion and is therefore considered a renunciant. (72)
Though naked, he is devoid of illusion; though lacking the garment of illusion, he is devoid of qualities, for he is free from the three qualities of illusion. ||73||
For one whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, there is neither mother nor father;
it is eternally fitting that Śiva is devoid of mother and father. (74)
Free from desire—that craving which binds through longing—he is devoid of that thirst.
He is the inauspicious, tamasic state that brings about both creation and dissolution. ||75||
And he was indeed maintained here in the form of a disguise for the sake of his purpose;
for that fierce, destructive guise is called an inauspicious dress. (76)
Indeed, even in the world, Śaṅkara possesses what is known as an inauspicious appearance: the wearing of funeral ashes, matted locks, a tiger skin, and bones. (77)
That Śambhu, the Lord Hara, who is the supreme Brahman and an incarnation of the Self, shall, through the rising of your good fortune, become the husband of this daughter of yours. (78)
In this regard, listen with affection to the means by which you shall obtain happiness;
therein, one should examine the auspicious or inauspicious characteristics of Śambhu. (79)
The objects of awakening are indeed bestowers of happiness, for Hara is the very embodiment of bliss; in this regard, the sun, fire, and the Gaṅgā serve as illustrative examples.
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, you too must give your daughter to Śiva;
that Hara, being swift in his grace, will accept your daughter.
"Your daughter should perform penance so that she may obtain Śiva through her asceticism;
even though he is capable [of obtaining her otherwise], he will come under the sway of your daughter in every way. (82)
By the power of your asceticism, even one with poor handwriting shall become a fine scribe;
moreover, your daughter, a beloved of Śiva, will certainly become your wife.
Through her excellent service, she will bring Śambhu’s mind under her control;
he too, having abandoned this daughter of yours, will not marry any other woman.
The affection between these two is not matched by that of any other beings past or future;
indeed, through their union, many great tasks of the gods shall be accomplished.
The duties to be performed are well-known; therefore, give her to Hara.
Indeed, by means of this maiden, Śambhu shall become Ardhanārīśvara. ||86||
Moreover, by means of the marriage rite and by properly propitiating Hara through ascetic penance, your daughter shall attain such renown. (87)
Having cast off her dark form, she will become fair-complexioned;
thus, by the name Gaurī, she shall become Vidyudgaurī. ||88||
Likewise, she has many other names as well;
listen, for I shall tell them to you exactly as they will be. (89)
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī.
Bagalāmukhī, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā, as well as Caṇḍī, Bhairavī, and Saiṃhī—these indeed are her names. (9.1)
"You must never form the intention to give this to anyone else;
and this [teaching] of the gods is to be kept in secret and must not be revealed anywhere. (92)
Then Śaila said to the elderly brāhmaṇa, "Listen to my words:
Śiva is always absorbed in meditation and is beyond the reach even of the gods. (93)
Having abandoned all attachment, free from passion, always devoted to the yoga of meditation, and with his inner self offered to Brahman—how can such a person be won over? (94)
How can the supreme Brahman—devoid of qualities, changeless, free from affliction, effortless, and imperishable—be something to be accomplished? (956)
How can he, within whom the entire universe resides and who perceives nothing external, be accomplished through the ascetic penance of this daughter? (96)
Having heard that, the Brahmin said: "You should certainly not worry;
even though the God of gods is free from desire, he has become possessed of longing for your daughter."
Through austerity, it must certainly come to pass; therefore, nothing is impossible.
Kālī herself will surely attain Hara, the Great Time (Mahākāla). 98.
"I am going, O Lord of Mountains; perform the marriage ceremony.
Having said this, the Brahmin rose and set his mind on departing.
Then Śaila, concealing his form as an elderly brahmin, joyfully offered him excellent hospitality; indeed, that protector of the earth (bhūsura) performed such honors for him.
The celestial sage Nārada, assuming his own form and traveling through the path of the sky, called out "Nārāyaṇa! with love while those two were looking on.
He quickly departed from Menā and Śaila toward the city of Indra;
Menā and Śaila were filled with great wonder upon seeing Nārada.
It was certain that this daughter, the wife of Śambhu, was always fortunate;
that maiden was filled with joy, as were her parents. (103)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Arrival at the Home of Himagiri in the Form of an Old Brāhmaṇa within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Book of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning Pārvatī’s statement that Aaguṇa would become her husband through lines [drawn by her], Himālaya’s anxiety, the clarification of the meanings of words such as *Aaguṇa*, the determination that she would become the wife of Śiva, and Nārada’s departure for Mahendra’s city via the path of the sky after abandoning his form as an old Brāhmaṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O beloved, after a short time, Menā, overcome by delusion, spoke to the lord of mountains, Hema, with her mind bowed down in devotion. (1)
A daughter should not be given to a poor man; she should be given to one who possesses wealth. Perform the marriage of your daughter with a handsome groom indeed. || 2 ||
"My daughter, dearer to me than life, is delicate and fortunate;
she has been nurtured with various enjoyments and the abundance of happiness and prosperity. (3)
Therefore, her marriage also, in a home consisting of every prosperity,
is joined with a bridegroom born of a noble family and endowed with auspicious marks.
"Act in such a way that she may become happy upon obtaining an excellent husband.
Having heard this, the Lord of Mountains spoke to Menā in order to dispel her apprehension.
"Abandon this delusion, my dear wife; she must indeed be given to Śaṅkara.
If you have true conviction in this, then I shall give her; otherwise, I will not."
If you have affection for your daughter, instruct her with respect:
she should perform penance directed toward Śiva; for through penance, Śiva is attained.
And Hara, becoming pleased, will take Kālī’s hand in marriage;
for indeed, all happiness, wealth, prosperity, and so forth, reside in Śaṅkara.
All inauspicious things always become auspicious in Śivā;
and all kinds of happiness always abide in Śivā.
In Śambhu resides unbroken vigor; in Śambhu resides lordship over the gods and goddesses;
in Śambhu resides the state of being worshipful for all people; and in Śambhu resides the causality of all beings and embodied souls.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space, as well as the sun, the moon, and other luminaries, are always His bodies. (1.1)
All prosperity is indeed contained within the very body of that Śambhu;
for the sake of Śiva’s daughter, assign her to penance, so that it may be auspicious.
Upon hearing of the penance and seeing her daughter so tender, Menā was instantly pained;
for a moment, she was unable to instruct her daughter.
Then Pārvatī, having understood [the situation], spoke to her mother at that time:
"O Mother, listen; during the hour of Brahmā (brāhmamuhūrta), I saw a dream."
The ascetic Brahmin, being well-pleased, spoke in order to perform penance for Śaṅkara; having thus instructed him, he placed a beautiful crescent moon upon his forehead.
Placing both hands upon my head and holding me to his own chest,
he bestowed his blessing and departed, possessing a beautiful form like Śaṅkara.
"Therefore, remembering that Person in my heart, I shall perform penance.
Having heard this, she went to relate the very matter of her dream.
Then even the lord of mountains spoke to his own dream:
"Listen, O Mena; today in my dream a person performing austerities has arrived. (1.8)
Having assumed the form described by Nārada, he zealously set out to perform penance on the outskirts of the city; there, I led my daughter.
"By his physical marks, I certainly recognized that this was Śaṅkara;
therefore, I instructed Pārvatī in the service of that ascetic. (1.182.20)
And when he did not accept that boy despite my having entreated him, I engaged in many debates with him using the insights of Vedānta. || 21 ||
In some manner or other, he then took the girl for his enjoyment;
and she, Pārvatī, served him out of love—this was witnessed by me.
Then the time arrived that was near and destined to yield fruit;
he [Śiva] resolved to instruct Pārvatī in asceticism for the sake of her long-term success.
Upon hearing this, Menā became joyful and instructed Pārvatī;
she too, constantly meditating on Śambhu, remained steadfast in her ascetic penance.
At the mealtime, the goddess takes a single portion of food;
like a yoginī, she performs her bath three times a day and worships Śaṅkara. (25)
One should repeat the thousand names of Mālikā while following the name of Śambhu;
sitting in the svastika posture with eyes closed, one should perform meditation. 26.
In the morning and evening, one should perform the *ārātrika* rite for Śaṅkara,
offer prayers, recite hymns of praise, and then remain awake for a short while.

She performed her penance in this manner: sleeping on the ground covered with grass, wearing garments of bark, observing silence, remaining out of sight from her side, and practicing austerity. ||28||
Śaṅkara himself knows that Satī performs penance;
wandering about in solitude, he indeed performed extraordinary wonders.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Śambhu, in the guise of an ascetic, appeared in a dream to Satī and Himālaya during the penance of Satī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: What kinds of wonders did Śaṅkara perform then,
while wandering happily upon the earth performing penance without Satī?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Śaṅkara, although there were many great devotees of mine who were performers of wonders, I shall indeed tell you of two or three of them.
After the time of Satī’s cremation, following Pārvatī’s marriage,
Śaṅkara was once tormented by the fire of separation from Satī.
Having observed silence on Mount Kailāsa, distressed by the separation from his beloved,
he remembered his dear wife and the virtues that increased their love.
He described it in many ways, demonstrating the worldly course of existence,
having abandoned the way of household life through the force of his dispassion.
Clad only in the directions (naked), he wandered through the land, the forests, and the wild tracts;
yet, pained by the sorrow of separation from his virtuous wife, he found no peace anywhere.
Having restrained his mind on Kailāsa, Hara entered into meditative absorption;
and then, many years passed while he remained in that samādhi.
The Brahma-fire intensely scorched the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and the forehead;
by the heat of his ascetic yoga, drops of perspiration appeared upon his brow.
Having become gross, he fell upon the earth, infused with the essence of austerity;
on that earth, there indeed appeared a child of a blood-red complexion.
Four-armed, ruddy, beautiful, possessing extraordinary luster, and auspicious,
he then wept in the very presence of that Śambhu.
Knowing that Śambhu was absorbed in meditative concentration, the goddess Vasundharā manifested right there,
assuming the form of a fresh and beautiful woman.
The Earth placed the child on her lap and suckled him with her breast;
out of affection, she kissed his face and played with her son.
Śambhu, the Lord residing within, perceived all of this through his meditative absorption.
He suddenly rose there from that meditative absorption and laughed at her.
Being pleased, he said to the Earth: "O beloved Dharaṇī, you are blessed!
Out of affection, you have protected this son of mine who was born from you. (14)
This boy, born from the drops produced by my sweat, shall be known in the world by your name and shall possess the virtues of a donor of land and other such qualities. || 15 ||
"This son of the Earth, Maṅgala, shall become a bringer of auspiciousness; he will also be a bestower of happiness upon me. Accept this son of yours."
Then, having worshipped Śiva and received his words of blessing, Bhūmi took that child and departed for her own abode together with her sons. || 17 ||
Taking her son with her, that woman always dwelt in Kāśī in another form; meanwhile, the son reached the prime of youth.
And he knew his father to be the god Śambhu, constantly remembering him;
in Kāśī, at the form of Mahādeva, he always served Śaṅkara.
And seeing his young son, the father said: "Today I am pleased by your service; choose something, and I shall grant you whatever you desire. (1.183.20)
The son said: "I have obtained everything; I have attained complete satisfaction.
There is nothing that could possibly equal the satisfaction of my father. (2.1)
Among all things to be obtained and enjoyed, the favor of one's father is the most excellent;
if that is attained by sons, everything is attained. (22)
The fruit of serving one's father is said to be heaven and liberation from which there is no return, as well as the destruction of all obstacles and the bestower of all prosperity. ||23||
Sovereignies over the sun, moon, and so forth, or earthly realms situated below; likewise, positions of supreme lordship and the fruit of propitiating the ancestors. (24)
"Your service must always be performed; I have no other desire," he said, and falling at the feet of Hara due to the absence of any ailment in his heart, [he remained there]. (25)
Śambhu, placing his hands upon the head of Bhauma, said to that good son:
"I shall establish you within my home; become the planet named Maṅgala."
"Until the heavens endure in this creation, so shall you indeed exist.
Having received this blessing, he bowed to Śambhu and Vasundharā. (27)
He quickly went to the divine world, which is superior and more excellent than the world of Śukra;
there he obtained a great kingdom known as Bhaumagolaka. || 28 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the origin and characteristics of Bhauma, as well as the life of Śaṅkara during the period of his separation from Satī. (29)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Planet Maṅgala from a Drop of Sweat on the Forehead of Śaṅkara," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Henceforth, O beloved, listen with affection to the life of Hanumān;
O auspicious one, it is the account of Rudra as it occurred in the first age.
Then, having witnessed the conduct of Brahmā toward Mohinī,
the bodily constituents of Śambhu fell down, just as those of the Creator did.
Once, Śambhu, accompanied by Vidhūtrā, was on the Himavat mountain in autumn,
listening to the warbling of cuckoos amidst a landscape whitened by moonlight.
In that place pervaded by fragrant breezes, resounded by peacocks,
and filled with cool groves, he remembered Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
"Alas! I have no beloved; what indeed will be my fate?
How can the autumn season be passed without my friend? (5)
For gods, lords, and all who possess vital breath, the appointed time of death— which arises from the nature of the Supreme Brahman— is inevitably a destroyer.
Although I am free from desire, nevertheless, due to the influence of my body and by means of a temporary impulse,
I remember Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go without my virtuous companion?
Without her, the cold afflicts me, and even the god of love torments me today."
At the beginning of the Brahma-muhūrta, Hara became immersed in anxious thought;
rising again and again, he remained there, remembering Satī intensely.
Afflicted by the fever of desire, he sat and remained there;
having taken refuge at the mango tree, he sat down, free from all longing.
Then, having understood this, the virtuous Goddess of the gods, the daughter of Himālaya,
having attained the power of yoga, assumed a second form.
Then, having arrived there in the sky, a beloved voice from the ether spoke:
"O Brahmā, you have been brought forth by Kṛṣṇa, the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. (12)
You are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman; go now to the abode of Goloka, where your infinite companions reside, and sport there as you please.
Why do you grieve here in this forest region in vain like one who is wretched?
There, Kṛṣṇa will be your protector; he will destroy your sorrow.
Having spoken thus, he then ceased and remained silent upon that tree;
Śaṅkara, too, having heard that, became startled within his heart.
Having reflected thus in his mind many times, he rose from that spot and departed by way of the sky to the eternal abode of Goloka.
And Satī, though beloved of Śambhu, remained invisible while staying upon the mango tree;
yet, step by step, she went to Goloka, the eternal abode.
As long as she remains a maiden, she does not desire Śaṅkara;
once her marriage has been performed, she always desires Śaṅkara.
Having resolved thus, she went to the realm of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of her husband’s peace;
having gone to Goloka, Śambhu prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (19)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, offered a welcome to Śambhu;
however, when he asked about his purpose, Śaṅkara did not speak.
Then the lotus-eyed goddess Satī became ashamed;
she entered into Hari Kṛṣṇa, who brings joy to Śaṅkara.
Having understood the heart of Hara, she who was established in Kṛṣṇa spoke:
"O Śambhu, you are always dear to me; why have you not brought back Satī? (22)
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, he shed tears from his eyes;
then, slowly regaining his composure, he spoke concerning the destruction of Satī.
Having reported his own misfortune which was also a source of sorrow,
Kṛṣṇa then spoke comforting words that grant happiness to Śambhu.
"You have arisen from my own form, O Satī; you are born from my very being.
You are my son, O Lord of Gods; welcome here, and may all be auspicious."
Whatever belongs to me in Goloka, all that is indeed yours as well; therefore, dwell in Goloka as you please and sport there according to your desire.
"Many female and male servants shall indeed perform service worthy of you;
O Śambhu, enjoy happiness always, whatever dwells in your mind. (27)
Then Śambhu said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Lord, I too am your devotee;
O Hari, that which is to be enjoyed by you has always been chosen by me as not to be enjoyed by me."
Therefore, O Mādhava, I shall not wander about in this form;
if you have compassion for your disciple, I shall indeed become a bull here. (29)
"I shall dwell in the midst of cows; indeed, I shall sport among the cows.
Grant me this command, O Lord; have mercy upon me, O Master. (1.184.30)
"As long as the Lord's command remains, so long indeed shall I stay here;
afterwards, I shall go once more to my excellent home on Mount Himavat."
"So be it," said Kṛṣṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, to him.
Then, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, Śambhu instantly became a young calf.
And the cows, seeing that most beautiful and excellent calf, licked him with their tongues and served him again and again. ||33||
Yawning and running about, they, immersed in touch, served those cows; and seeing them, the goddess Satī, through her yogic concentration, [perceived their state].
And by the power of Satī’s entrance, all those cows who serve the bull Hara entered Śaṅkara, the bull. (35)
They served him in many ways with love so that Śambhu might be happy;
as he thus sported among the cows, Vṛṣaśaṅkara became fully satisfied. ||36||
An eternal satisfaction arose such that the bull no longer desired the cow;
then, O Mādhava, Satī emerged from the body of the cow.
Having entered, he said to Hara: "O Lord of Satī, go to the Himālaya mountain.
Then Śambhu, abandoning his form as a bull, became Śaṅkara.

A yogi must never place his trust in women;

Knowledge indeed accomplishes its own task and shakes off the tasks of others;

Upon seeing a handsome man, she bestows her entire being upon him;

Therefore, friendship should certainly not be maintained by me now that I am aware of this;
go to that delightful place which produces delusion, for I am no longer your companion.

Māyā-Mohinī indeed slithered from that place toward Satyaloka;

But in another moment, the delusion of Mohinī was then contracted;

Satī, however, having emerged from the body of Śarva and remained outside,

then Śambhu said to her, "I have no need for you."
"Go to Brahmā, O Goddess of the Gods, if you have business there.

That essence, having been rubbed with cloth for the sake of protection upon the Brahma-seat, produced a hundred thousand grains all around the lion-throne. ||84||

And those were indeed declared by the Creator to be the milk produced from the lake of Brahmā;
then this god Śaṅkara, closing his eyes, entered into self-restraint.

Mohinī, who enchants the minds of the three worlds, spoke:
"O virtuous one, understand my words; they shall bring happiness to you, O seeker of desire. (1.184.90)

For a clever woman and a clever man, a new union is difficult to obtain; [so too are] the pair of breasts, my thighs, and the beautiful lotus-face. 92.
Who would not rejoice in happiness upon seeing [her] with her playful knitting of the brows?
The essence of pleasure is the delight in women, which even sages long for. (92)
The enjoyment of pleasure with one who appreciates it is sufficient and exceedingly rare;

Having heard those words, Śambhu spoke this beneficial and truthful speech to her:

Truth is the duty appropriate for the family of ascetic Brahmins;
sexual union with one's own wife at the proper time is praised as dharma.

A woman who is desirable and present before one must be accepted by householders, not by ascetics;

He who abandons his own wife and takes another's woman suffers a loss of fame, wealth, and longevity; for him there is no well-being either in this world or the next. (101)
Of what use is the excellence of a woman or universal sovereignty to an ascetic? And what need have you for me, who am both dispassionate and intoxicated [with the spirit of renunciation]? 10.2
"Go, O beautiful one, to one who is well-dressed, handsome, well-nourished, and young. Hearing this abandonment, she spoke with humility: ||| 10 3 ||
With the beautiful hue of a lovely campaka flower, as handsome as Kandarpa himself, he was well-built and highly esteemed by women due to the power of his asceticism. 104.
Without you, whom else shall I go to? Or who is there that is dearer than you? Where could a woman like me go, afflicted by love, after abandoning you? (105)
"O Lord of Yogis, quickly accept me, who am utterly consumed by the fire of passion;
otherwise, I shall utter a curse, or else take me at once."
The vital breaths are burnt, the mind is burnt, and now my very self is being consumed; bring about the state of extinction through drinking the nectar of fresh erotic sentiment. 107.
If a woman, afflicted by the suffering within her own heart, pronounces a curse upon someone, neither the Creator nor Śaṅkara is able to nullify that curse. 108.
Behold me, possessed of supreme luster, yet consumed by the fires of passion— my fresh essence having burst forth, yet remaining unscarred and inviolate by anyone.
She wears a dot of vermilion along with a dot of musk;
she possesses the beautiful hue of a campaka flower and is eternally fixed in the bloom of youth.
She possessed a pair of broad hips and full buttocks and breasts;
her face stole the splendor of the moon’s rays during the autumnal full moon.
Clad in fine garments and adorned with jewel ornaments,
she was capable of enchanting everyone at will by her mere playful side-glances.
Desiring one such as you, who moves with the gait of a lordly elephant in rut,
her entire body covered in horripilation, she was on the verge of fainting.
"Take me quickly, for my throat, lips, and palate are parched"—
thus did Mohinī delude Śarva with these words.
Śiva did not fall into delusion, nor did he ever abandon his meditation; meanwhile, Rambhā, an apsarā, arrived there and spoke.
Listen, O girl, to the mantra for attracting young yogis, if your mind has the desire to take pleasure with a young man. (116)
With Kāmadeva as your ally, accomplish your own desired task;
this Brahmā will grant your wish along with the necessary means upon your request.
If you have no passion for me here, seek out another youth;
either by assuming an unprecedented disguise or by employing the god of love as before. (118)
Go there yourself with him and delude him, O Mohinī, for he is the foremost among those who have conquered their senses and is the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa himself. (119)
"Without the companion of desire, who is capable of conquering the Lord?
O enchantress, go to Kāma, who has made his dwelling right here at this side."
"The compassionate Lord of women will become an immediate ally.
Having been told this, Mohinī went there to the abode of Smara.
Kāma too, seeing Mohinī, became deluded and fell into agitation;
Kāma suddenly stumbled and for a moment became like one who is inert.
Due to that [union], two sons were born, Śṛṅgāraka and Vasantaka, who were endowed with enchanting and peerless beauty and were vessels of all loveliness. (123)
In an instant, two sons were born who, with the bursting forth of their youth, provided assistance to Kāma; indeed, Kāma himself, for the sake of Mohinī, brought them along.
Having been requested for the sake of assistance, he arrived where Śaṅkara was;
there he beheld Hara, the yogi, established in self-restraint and appearing as Mohinī.
Standing before him, she began to delude that very man;
for a moment she danced beautifully with graceful limbs, and for a moment she sang.
The song concerning Satī, which deludes the minds of devotees—
having heard that desired song of hers, the Teacher of the worlds [was moved].
With all his limbs covered in horripilation, he opened his eyes and gazed;
overcome by desire, Hara became infatuated with her, his eyes filled with tears.
Seeing the charming five-faced one, the enchanting goddess, her mind filled with joy,
playfully assumed there a state of being equal in measure to his own artistic skill.
He displayed his own limbs preceded by a smile and a contraction of the eyebrows;
for what shame can there be in this world for one whose consciousness is struck down by desire?
Nevertheless, the steadfast Śaṅkara, closing his eyes there,
desisted from the path of yoga and did not look at Mohinī.
But that enchanting woman indeed ascended into the heart of Śambhu;
she, the deluder, was perceived within his inner faculty even during meditation.
Then Mohinī, for a moment, incited that Kāma who stands outside—
the foremost of all the senses and the mental portion of Viṣṇu.
The seed-syllable of passion, possessing five arrows, eternally presided over by women,
accompanied by fragrant breezes, and impelled by the intoxication of amorous elegance.
Then Kāmadeva also, having prepared himself at the will of Hari,
stood himself in the sky and fixed an arrow to his bowstring.
He discharged a great weapon, purified by mantras, at Śaṅkara;
and Śambhu became agitated, filled with desire by that kāma-weapon.
He gazed for a moment again and again at the face of Mohinī,
which was smiling, possessed of curved eyes, and showering forth the essence of passion.
In the meantime, Kāma, who was well-versed in the conventions of time and skilled in the application of yoga,
manifested himself and discharged his five arrows at Śaṅkara.
The first is Sammohana, the second is Sampravega, the third is Unmattavīrya, and the fourth is Jvalajvara. 1.39.
Having dispatched the fifth, Cetanahara, along the path of the sky,

O Hari, having himself gone there along with the bees, the fragrant breeze,
and the male cuckoo, the latter uttered its sweet cry in his presence.
A six-legged bee, standing before her, hummed softly over her beautiful and delicate form; O beloved, a fragrant breeze blew constantly, gentle and exceedingly cool.
There Madhu himself wandered about constantly in a state of joy,

With his entire body covered in horripilation, Śaṅkara, the lord of yogis,

With her mind struck by the arrows of love, the woman with the curved eyes spoke;
for by a mere gesture, the minds of women instantly become intoxicated. (145)
He who, having drawn [the woman] toward himself, effects enjoyment, is considered the best;

But that man who performs amorous adornment afterwards, having been repeatedly entreated by a woman afflicted with desire, is indeed middling. (147)
Having forcibly seized and defiled [her], that man is considered the lowest.
Alas, that eunuch was not a man, for he was not stained by her in secret.
Arise, O Lord of the worlds! O helmsman, bring to the further shore those submerged in the terrible, impassable, and fearsome ocean of passion. 149.
Quickly purchase me, your servant whose mind is constantly fixed on you, in birth after birth, as the price for pleasure with this priceless jewel.
Having spoken thus, the enchanting woman, overwhelmed by passion, approached Śambhu nearby and, smiling, drew his hand toward her.
And as Śambhu also rose up, desiring to embrace her,
Satī then said to Kṛṣṇa, "Lead him to the region of the Himavat."
The Lord of Mohinī, having taken her hand, desires to go to a secluded spot;
as he moves forward, Śaṅkara follows behind him.
In another moment, Mohinī led him to the region of the Himalayas;
there Hari [the Lord] approached Hara, who was rendered motionless by passion and yet remained untainted, possessing only a slight taint.
In the vicinity of Kailāsa, which was endowed with various trees and creepers, pervaded by a cool breeze rich in gentle fragrance, and exceedingly refreshing; (155)
In a charming bower of trees whose branches were adorned with beautiful flowers,

"Take this seed of Śaṅkara and go to Kaiśarī, the daughter of Añjana.

On the fourteenth lunar day, when the sun was in Aries and in conjunction with the Citrā asterism,

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [is described]: on the Himalayas, the remembrance of Satī by the widowed Śaṅkara; the journey to Goloka by means of a celestial voice; the wandering in the form of a bull; the prayer of Kṛṣṇa to bring Śambhu to the Himālaya mountains; the arrival of Śambhu at Satyaloka together with Kṛṣṇa in the form of Mohinī; and the birth of cities from the seed of Brahmā, who faltered upon seeing Mohinī, as well as from the seed of Kāmadeva, who also faltered.
