Menā did not accept it, but rather became distressed in mind;
then Pārvatī, joining her palms, spoke to her own mother.
"What benefit is there for me from this unfortunate body without a husband?
How can that Śambhu, who grants happiness, be obtained as my husband forever? (1.186.20)
Through austerities one’s desired goal is attained; indeed, nothing is unattainable for one who practices austerity.
Yet, while the means exist, people in vain endure misfortune.
"O Mother, tomorrow morning I shall go to perform austerities in order to attain Maheśvara;
grant me permission today to depart for the penance grove."
Menā said: "O Śivā, what have you gained by your previous penance?
On the contrary, having become sorrowful, you have obtained birth here in my house. (23)
"O Pārvatī, perform penance in our house today; do not go outside.
All the gods and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell in our house forever. (24)
"O daughter, you must not act with impetuosity, nor should you go anywhere outside;
for your body is delicate, while asceticism is great and harsh. (25)
"My daughter, you must not go; that is not at all fitting for women," her mother thus forbade her, and from then on she was known by the name Umā.
"I shall either accomplish Śambhu as my husband or I shall cast down his body;
grant me permission for penance, otherwise Pārvatī does not exist here. (27)
Seeing such intense persistence, she then gave her command;
having bowed to her mother and father, she went forth together with her two friends.
Having abandoned all objects of enjoyment and various garments, and having quickly donned bark-cloths and tied on a girdle of muñja grass. (29)
Having cast aside her necklace and donned the beautiful skin of a deer,
the daughter of the mountain set out for the plateau where the Gaṅgā descends.
Where, in former times, Śambhu remained and performed austerities for the sake of truth;
beholding that plateau of the Snowy Mountain to be devoid of Hara— ||3.1||
"Alas, Hari!"—recalling this for a moment there, she became overwhelmed with grief;
"this very peak of Gaurī has attained the name 'Śikhara'. (32)
The meritorious descent of the Gaṅgā is adorned with various minerals,
pervaded by divine flowering creepers, and its trees resound with the humming of bees.
The divine, cool waterfall was frequented by beasts and birds, and it was made fragrant by water-born and land-born lotuses in full bloom. (34)
It possessed deep caverns within its interior and was filled with divine abodes;
it shone with the green luster of wish-fulfilling trees, creepers, vines, grasses, and shrubs.
Abounding with flowers, buds, fruits, and filaments of every season,
Pārvatī, the virtuous one, was initiated there for the sake of religious observance.
Having consecrated the ground and personally constructed an altar there, Pārvatī planted and nourished with water the most excellent trees. (37)
Having bathed three times a day and subsisting on dry leaves, she began a great penance,
restraining all her senses along with the internal mind.
Having withdrawn their mode of existence into their own self, which is of the nature of Śiva,
they remained stationed there like a blazing fire burning all around them day and night during the summer.
Having done so, she stood in their midst and performed the penance of the five fires,
while inwardly chanting the five-syllabled mantra of Hara at all times.
During the rains, she maintained a firm posture upon stone slabs amidst the downpour;
in the cold, she constantly remained in the midst of water, devoted to the fire of Śiva.
Amidst gale-force winds, intense heat, and frosty nights,
she performed austerities while meditating in her heart upon Śiva, her future husband.
First, she subsisted on fruits, and secondly, on a diet of leaves.
And with a single leaf, she passed a third thousand [years]. ||43||
Then, having even abandoned leaves, Aparṇā remained engaged in austerity;
standing on one foot and subsisting only on air, she meditated upon Śaṅkara.
Three thousand years passed for Kālī in the penance grove,
where Hara had performed austerities for sixty thousand years.
Having calculated that suffering is threefold— pertaining to the present, the past, and the future—
that virtuous woman remained for a moment in the place of Hara and reflected.
O Mahādeva, established as I am in my vows, do you not know me now?
If I am devoted to you with my whole being, then be gracious to me, O Lord. (47)
If this mantra was performed out of devotion, then be gracious to me, O Lord;
if you know that I am yours, then be gracious to me, O Lord. (48)
"O Lord, if I am to be accepted by you, then be gracious to me, O Master," thus praying day after day, the virtuous woman remained engaged in ascetic penance. (49)
There, by the power of Pārvatī’s asceticism,
even naturally antagonistic creatures did not harm one another.
And there all the trees, as well as the grasses and the meadows, the various flowers, and the tender leaves [were present]. (51)
"Beings are always born"—thus was that forest, resembling Mount Kailāsa, produced through the power of her asceticism; it remained forever in the form of a perfected realm. ||52||
While Pārvatī was thus performing her penance for five thousand years, the Mountain approached and spoke to her. (53)
"Daughter, Hara, who reduced Kama to ashes because he abandoned you, his excellent servant, has departed in anger; being devoid of virtue, he will not return."
"O daughter, you have fallen into vain delusion; the Lord does not desire you. Therefore arise and come quickly to your own home, O Pārvatī. (55)
In this very manner, she was addressed by Menā, as well as by Meru, Sahya, Mandara, Maināka, and the mountain Krauñca. (56)
Despite her brothers, sisters, and others [trying to dissuade her], she did not abandon her asceticism, thinking:
"Either I shall win Hara, or I shall cast down my own body. (57)
I have but one vow: how shall my lord not come?
It is fortunate that Smara was burnt by him; he departed, abandoning me, devoid of merit.
"If I am truly devoted to him, I shall bring her back through the power of my asceticism;
all of you may go, for I will not go to his house. (59)
"Having brought my lord Śambhu, I shall return to his home";
having said this, the sweet-spoken Girijā became silent.
Having recognized the firm resolve of Mahāsattvā, they all returned to their own abodes, praising her and bestowing blessings with great wonder. (6.1)
Accompanied by her friends, Satī performed severe penance;
by that, the entire three worlds, including all moving and unmoving beings, became scorched.
Then the gods and asuras, the siddhas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and cāraṇas;
the guhyakas, sages, sādhyas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas—[all came together].
The Asuras, humans, Prajāpatis, and likewise the Guardians of the World,
having encountered the most painful heat, did not know its cause.
Then, having gone there, they questioned the Creator regarding the cause of the asceticism;
Brahmā, too, having understood that the heat was produced by Pārvatī’s penance, [spoke].
Accompanied by the hosts of gods, he went to Hari to inform him of that;
having praised and bowed down to Him who was sporting in the Ocean of Milk, [he spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, he said: "Save us, save us who have come to you for refuge!
We are scorched by the heat of our wife's devotion; O Teacher of the World, grant us peace! (67)
Having heard this, Hari said to them all, "Let us go toward Śaṅkara;
let us request him for the sake of Satī’s hand in marriage, and from that we shall find happiness. (68)
Having thus deliberated together, the gods and others went to behold the asceticism of Satī;
they bowed to her, the sustainer of the world, and then proceeded toward Hara.
They beheld Śaṅkara seated comfortably, serene, and affectionate toward his devotees; having bowed to him as he sat upon his yogic mat, they offered praise.

Salutations, salutations again and again to the destroyer of suffering and the bestower of peace; salutations, salutations again and again to the perfect grantor of the fruits of Pārvatī’s austerities. ||7 1||
If you, being free from passion, do not accept Pārvatī,
then she will consume this entire world of moving and non-moving beings with her ascetic power.
Furthermore, through her marriage, the purpose of the gods will be accomplished.
"Therefore, having granted her this word, quickly undertake the obstruction of her penance.
Having heard this, Śambhu said to them: "A great task has been accomplished by me;
Kāma has been burnt. Let [the others] remain celibate, free from desire."
"Let them indeed be endowed with supreme bliss and free from transformation.
In the possession of Satī, she will restore Kāma to life once more.
From desire (kāma), there arise anger, delusion, the loss of memory, and so forth."
May all those gods who bestow suffering and torment always abandon them. ||76||
If a woman has been married, she is known as a great fetter;
there are many evil associations, but association with women is greater than those. (77)
One is released from all bonds, yet one is not released from the bond of women;
indeed, even for a yogin, desires increase through association with women.
If one desires the liberation of Brahman, one should cast far away the snare of women;
for a man, a woman is like a white-coated *indravāruṇī* gourd.
For the sake of a woman, even a man, as well as white-powdered *indravāruṇī*, should be understood as mutual poison; nevertheless, such is your word.
"I shall protect it for the sake of removing the calamities of the gods;
you all go to your respective abodes and remain there forever free from fear. (8-1)
"I shall go for the sake of the peace resulting from the penance of Satī and for the benefit [of all].
Having heard this and bowed down, all the gods then departed for their respective homes.
Then Śaṅkara remembered the seven sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others;
with serene countenances, the seven sages arrived quickly. 8.3.
Having bowed down, they all sat down, highly honored by Śambhu; and they were told from his side: "She is performing penance with an unbroken mind. (84)
Having abandoned all desires, she is intensely longing to obtain me as her husband;
go there and put the firmness of your love to the test. (85)
Thus commanded, they all went to where that virtuous lady was performing her penance;
having bowed to the daughter of the mountain, they asked, "For what purpose are you performing this austerity? (86)
"Speak, O Goddess; we shall do exactly as you wish.
Having bowed to the sages, Satī spoke according to the procedure described by Nārada. (87)
"May Rudra be my husband"—having thus resolved, she remained steadfast in asceticism;
may Lord Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, fulfill that hope of hers. (88)
Having heard this, the sages laughed and spoke these deceptive and false words:
"How can Nārada, who is fond of strife, a creator of distress, and untrustworthy, [be our messenger]? (89)
In every way, he is one who acts with deceit and incites others to affliction;
you know the sons of Dakṣa, and for that reason they have been cast out by you.
Do you not know that the wicked Citraketu was made to relinquish his kingdom? Do you not know that he caused Prahlāda to be alienated from Hiraṇyakaśipu? (9.1)
Indeed, as soon as Nārada’s science of wickedness fell even slightly upon his ear, he abandoned his own home and became miserable, just as you have. (92)
Nārada is foul-souled, yet he possesses a body that shines brilliantly on the outside;
we, who dwell with him, know him especially well. (93)
They praise the crane as virtuous because he does not eat fish at all;
one who lives with another may come to know the character of that companion through shared living. (94)
Moreover, you who have remained steadfast in austerity have indeed placed your trust in his words;
you have been deceived, O Great Goddess—go home and abandon your penance.
But he for whose sake you undergo suffering is indifferent toward you; he is ever aloof, shameless, inauspicious, homeless, and of low birth. (96)
Born of spirits, ghosts, and demons, naked and wearing a wretched disguise—you have been deceived by that spear-bearer, the foremost of rogues. (97)
Having granted the boon, he departed five thousand years ago and has not returned;
what kind of affectionate person is he? He is merely a deceiver of you. (98)
Reflect upon this, O Goddess of Gods: having first married Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, he did not even provide for her protection; what then will he do? (99)
He is indeed so full of anger that he will not fulfill his promise;
rather, that deceiver will again find fault with you and abandon you.
How will you live, having burnt the god of love who grants happiness, by one who has no compassion in his heart and does not even look upon a young maiden? 101.
O maiden, honoring my words, go home;
for the favor of one whose mind is unstable is like a flower in the sky.
A beauty such as you would shine in every way in the house of Viṣṇu;
all virtues reside in you, and great virtues reside in Viṣṇu. (10.3)
His house was vast, prosperous, and divine— the most excellent Vaikuṇṭha—
frequented by millions of male and female servants and adorned with celestial chariots and gardens.
"O beautiful one, worship that Lord of Lakṣmī, or Lord of Ramā, or Lord of Rādhā;
through him we shall arrange your marriage—abandon Śaṅkara! (105)
In the fourteenth year, the marriage of a maiden is said to be appropriate;
at that suitable time, service was rendered by you and the request was made accordingly.
Nevertheless, he did not take Svaratā’s hand in marriage;
five thousand years passed thereafter.
Nevertheless, that fool does not accept it at all; you are even worse than he.
Therefore, abandon your obstinacy and become happy through Viṣṇu.
There can be no satisfaction for the thirsty from the water of a mirage in the desert;
however, O daughter, there are two kinds of happiness for embodied beings in this world. (109)
The union of body with body brings supreme bliss to the mind,
just as a maiden’s body is indeed tender, beautiful, and auspicious.
Likewise, if the body of the youth were to exist, there would indeed be bodily pleasure for both husband and wife; otherwise, there can be no bodily pleasure. (111)
By nature he was naked, terrifying, adorned with bones and a bellows,
carrying a skull-bowl, a beggar, unclothed, with deformed eyes, and of unstable conduct.
He has the appearance of one intoxicated or insane; he is a collection of loathsome things; he is embodied misfortune itself, attended by a host of spirits.
How can he—who carries human fat and bones, who is terrifying with the hissing of snakes, and who dwells in the cremation ground like a dog-cooker—be desired by you, my daughter? 1.14
Hari exists as the sustainer of the world, the enjoyer of sacrifice, and the subduer of Pāka;
he is the god of gods, the blazing one, the wind, and the vital breath of embodied beings.
Kubera, Candra, Sūrya, Varuṇa, and other gods—
those beings enjoy their desires at will, assume forms at will, and possess the power to fulfill every desire.
Why do you not wish to attain even one of these?
That labor for the sake of attaining Śiva is like a tree that bears no fruit.
Therefore, come, my daughter; remaining at home, be happy. Choose another husband, O auspicious one; what has been done will bear fruit somewhere.
Having heard this and more in detail, Pārvatī laughed and said:
"Although what you have spoken is logical, I consider it to be according to your own understanding."
For that [practice] is indeed intended for one who is weak, lacking faith, and not firm.
By birth I am a daughter of the mountains, firm, powerful, and steadfast.
Whether Hara meets me or not— though he be steadfast, invincible, and stubborn—
I shall not abandon this gentle austerity which is innate to us.
I shall obtain him and choose him; otherwise, I will remain without fuel.
For the forest, austerity, and hardship are innate to one born of the mountain race.
All of that is indeed as I desire; you ought not to restrain me.
Nārada’s words are wholesome and perfectly suited to my nature. (123)
The mountain-dwelling goddess will certainly be won by this forest-dweller;
victory is always with those who are steadfast in the words of their gurus. 124.
For those who do not reach the goal, there is only suffering here and in the hereafter, never any peace.
Know this: to whom does space belong? To whom does fire belong? To whom does the wind belong? (125)
To whom does Indra belong, to whom Varuṇa, and to whom do the sun and moon serve as guides?
For such is surely the mindset of those corrupted by insanity and other such afflictions. (126)
Indeed, they consider even desirable objects to be contrary;
for they regard what is contrary as if it were slight and trivial, yet they consider it to be excellent.
I dwell in an empty house or do not go elsewhere;
for Viṣṇu, the abode of virtues, the wandering one, and the perfectly prosperous, is always present there.
He indeed displays worldly sovereignty to men;
but Śambhu is devoid of qualities, changeless, and free from pride and the like.
The Avadhūta is the supreme Haṃsa, the supreme bliss, the supreme Lord;
for those smeared by Māyā there is a desire for ornaments and such, but not for Brahman.
O brahmins, if that Śiva does not perform my marriage,
then even though I am auspicious, I shall always remain inauspicious, being forever unwedded.
I do not possess craving for sensual pleasures, nor do I perform austerity for the sake of desire;
rather, I perform austerity for that very purpose for which you perform it.
If Śarva accepts my hand, there will be happiness for both of us;
if he does not accept my hand, then the happiness of that virtuous woman will be even greater.
Now the Pure One is being realized; beyond that, I shall realize the Supreme.
Whether it merges here or not, it will certainly merge in liberation.
Whatever I do, I do only after reflection, for there is neither loss nor gain;
why then should I desire another husband? Indeed, I have no longing for sensual pleasure.
I beg forgiveness for my excessive speech; may you accept my service and unite me with auspicious blessings, just as a swan meets another swan.
By your words of blessing, Mārkaṇḍeya has become long-lived;
and by your grace, the outcaste has become the sage Arundhatī.
By your grace, Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brahmarṣi;
likewise, by even a fraction of your grace, Śailī shall become Śarvāṇī. (138)
Having spoken thus, she bowed to them and honored them with divine objects;
then, remembering Śiva, she who was devoted to the eternal path of Śaivism fell silent.
"May it be auspicious for you, O sages! May your heart's desire be fulfilled!
May the fruit of your asceticism be realized swiftly; may there be a meeting with Śambhu!"
May our marriage take place quickly; may there be great honor for us;
may we become carriers of people; and may everything be most auspicious. (141)
Having thus properly honored Śivā with these blessings, they departed for Hara—
those who were well-disposed toward the task of the gods, ever hopeful, and discerning.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatī’s Grief, Nārada’s Instruction, and the Prohibition of Her Austerities; nevertheless, Gaurī remains on Mount Gaurīśṛṅga performing penance for five thousand years, and though her penance was forbidden by the mountain-sages, she persists, and is finally joined with blessings by the Seven Sages," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O beloved, the sages, being unperturbed, spoke to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods,
after Pārvatī had indeed made her life depend upon him for the sake of Śaṅkara.
Fearless, without support, free from hope, and without possessions;
devoid of qualities and without effort, she blazes until the dissolution of all beings.
Either Śambhu’s austerity born of the nature of the mountain might meet with success, or it might not;
both [worldly] happiness might be attained, but the bliss born of liberation would not be attained thereby.
"There is indeed great happiness; asceticism is never in vain.
I shall either accomplish auspiciousness or cast off this body. (4)
"Either I shall marry Śambhu, or I shall remain forever a maiden;
or else I shall lead a life of celibacy and take up the state of renunciation."
"I shall die; I shall go to the state of final liberation, to Brahman and Śaṅkara.
Having thus made this resolution, that virtuous woman performed penance.
Then, whatever was to be done there, indeed what ought to be performed by the Lord—
Having thus reported the event and received permission, they went to their own homes.
Then Śaṅkara, desiring to test the asceticism of the Goddess,
assumed the form of an excellent matted-haired ascetic, being intent on that examination.
The twice-born elder, adorned with various marks and carrying a staff and an umbrella,
went to that peak, blazing all around with splendor.
Wearing a deer-skin, with a girdle of muñja grass, carrying a water-pot,
and possessing a sacred thread, he was a great elder, aged and his body smeared with ashes.
Seeing the mendicant approaching, having wandered from hermitage to hermitage and arrived at Kālī’s hermitage, she rose up and bowed to him.
Approaching him with affection, the virtuous woman fell at his feet and honored him with all the articles used for the hospitable reception of guests.
The virtuous woman asked that celibate student about his welfare:
"O Brahmin, from where have you come, and in what place is your hermitage? (13)
"To which direction will you go? Please take rest right here.
The mendicant said, "O female ascetic, I am coming here from various sacred fords (tīrthas)."
My residence was in Vārāṇasī; I shall go to the site of Pṛthūdaka.
I have bathed at Prayāga, at Kubjāmra, and at Caṇḍikeśvara.
From the assembly of kinsmen at Kurukṣetra, Haridvāra, and Kanakhala,
and from Kedāra and Badarīkuṇḍa, I have come here to your hermitage.
Having performed the ritual at this sacred ford, I shall go to Pṛthūdaka;
for I am an ascetic who travels according to my own will and bestows happiness upon others.
Skilled in the journey of renunciation, the destroyer of the suffering of ascetics, free from the pairs of opposites, desirous of liberation, and a worshiper of the gods, I am such. 18.
"I am old and am emaciating my body through asceticism as is fitting;
whatever I ask of you, you ought to explain that to me. (19)
"For what purpose, O auspicious lady, do you, established in the first stage of life, perform such fierce asceticism that brings about the experience of suffering? (1.187.20)
Who are you, whose daughter are you, and for what purpose do you perform this difficult penance in the lonely forest—a penance hard even for sages to accomplish? (21)
"You are neither a child nor an old woman; you appear beautiful as a young woman.
Being mature, why indeed do you perform such severe penance without a husband? (22)
In middle age, women enjoy amorous pleasures together with their husbands; thus, times spent engaged in excellent enjoyments pass away while youth remains firm.
"O auspicious lady, are you the companion of some ascetic?
That ascetic does not support you; O goddess, he has gone elsewhere. (24)
Tell me, in whose family were you born? Who is your father, and what is your station?
You are a vessel of great good fortune; how is it that you take delight in asceticism? (25)
Are you Lakṣmī, born from the Vedas? Are you Ramā? Or are you Sarasvatī?
I believe that you too are endowed with beauty, people, sovereignty, and prosperity.
Why, then, have you cast aside these ornaments and taken up matted locks?
Having abandoned the fine silk garment, why indeed have you donned bark cloth? (27)
"Tell me, for whom, for what purpose, and who is she? I am worthy [to hear it].
Having heard this, Pārvatī, the daughter of Himavat, spoke to the best of brahmins.
"I perform penance for the sake of Śaṅkara; may I find Śaṅkara as my husband. Formerly, I was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, composed of yoga. (29)
With my body consumed by fire, I have today become a daughter of the mountains;
I remained here engaged in service to Śambhu as he was performing penance.
Having reduced me to ashes and having destroyed the god of love, he departed;
I, however, came here for the sake of penance, yet failed to attain Śaṅkara.
At the end of my ascetic penance, while intending to enter the fire, I saw you standing there for a moment;
go now, for I shall enter the fire, seeking auspiciousness in another birth.
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī indeed entered the fire before him;
at that very moment, the fire became cool like sandalwood paste.
Then, after a moment, the twice-born one rose from the fire and, laughing, questioned her as she was flying up into the sky along the path of the atmosphere.
Oh, the great majesty of your extreme asceticism prevails, by the power of which even the fire did not burn you, remaining perfectly cool! (35)
"Speak, O Goddess, according to the truth; I shall fulfill your heart's desire. What boon do you wish for, O fair-browed one? You must not hide even the slightest thing. (36)
But since all power resides in you, what is the use of your asceticism?
Having obtained a jewel in your hand, why do you seek worthless glass? (37)
How has such beauty of form been rendered futile?
Having abandoned ornaments, garments, flowers, and precious objects, you have donned bark-cloth. (38)
"Having abandoned my home, I have obtained this forest for my dwelling, which is always a source of suffering.
Tell me, O Goddess, how there might be happiness for me; I shall do what is beneficial for you. (3.9)
Having heard this, Ambikā urged her friend Vijayā to speak;
Vijayā said, "This daughter of the aged Brahmin belongs to the Himavat mountain."
By name she is Pārvatī Kālī; she desires Śaṅkara as her husband.
This friend of mine is still a maiden, for she has not been married by anyone. (41)
Five thousand years have indeed passed while she was performing penance;
nevertheless, because she is the daughter of a god, she appears as though only sixteen years old.
Indeed, there is no diminution in the stature of the gods born of noble lineage due to their years;
though they have a lifespan of ten million years, their form remains that of sixteen-year-olds.
It is forever perfectly stable, subject neither to old age nor grey hair;
it has abandoned Mahendra and the other gods, and even Vishnu and Brahma.
Pārvatī, however, desires to obtain Śaṅkara as her husband;
by her, these trees have been planted, now flourishing with an abundance of fruits and flowers. (45)
They are always held in her heart as worthy of worship for Śaṅkara;
having offered everything in dedication, she remains forever engaged in austerity.
"She may come, or she may not come; yet she is indeed dedicated to Śarva.
Thus have I described to you the mental resolve of Pārvatī. (47)
The matted-haired ascetic also spoke with a laugh: "I do not trust what has been said by a friend;
if it is the truth, then let him speak for himself, for there would otherwise be no cause for laughter. (48)
Pārvatī, knowing in her mind that the person was related to Śambhu, spoke with a gracious heart to her friend: "What you have said is exactly so. (49)
In thought, in word, and in deed, Śaṅkara was indeed chosen by me;
yet I knew Śambhu to be difficult to attain, while regarding him as easily attained.
I shall perform penance until the end of my life, for such is my conviction;
though He may not meet me externally, He has indeed met me within.
"Oh! What great fortune is mine to behold the Seven Sages, and to see the venerable Brahmin Devasvāmin, who is filled with auspiciousness! (52)
I have reached this place in the terrible forest, and even there, upon the mountain peak;
thus has the tree of my desire attained its seasonal bloom.
Whether that indifferent Lord knows or does not know, I know that I have been impelled by the Compassionate One through a mere fragment of His grace. (54)
"A Brahmin was his mouth; he speaks as a learned priest (vipra), therefore it is his mouth.
Indeed, I know only that he speaks, for Śaṅkara remains hidden within you. (55)
And let my salutation be offered to him, joining my head to his feet, just as I bow with my head joined to your two feet. (16)
Having heard that, the Brahmin said: "Listen, O maiden beloved of Hara!
O fair-browed one, O lady of excellent vows, you speak everything appropriately and in a fitting manner. (57)
I know Mahādeva; listen attentively.
At times Hara is naked, and at other times he wears the skins of tigers and elephants.
The bull-bannered god was smeared with ashes, his appearance made strange by his mass of matted hair;
he held a skull-bowl and bones in his hands, with serpents coiled around his limbs.
He is one who consumes poison, who eats what is unfit to be eaten, and who is indeed three-eyed;

Ten cubits in height, served by hosts of spirits, he is described as soiled, unhappy,

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen with great pleasure, O Lakṣmī, to what happened immediately thereafter.
Having heard of Pārvatī’s arrival, Himācala, accompanied by Menā, [acted]. || 1 ||
Having prepared excellent vehicles, he set forth, overwhelmed with joy,
accompanied by the family priest, the citizens, his friends, and the young maidens.
Likewise, other relatives and brothers, overwhelmed with joy,
went toward that female ascetic while uttering cries of victory.
Having placed auspicious water-pots upon the leveled royal road,
which was beautified with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, fruits, and branches, [he proceeded].
It was crowded with domestic priests, Brahmins, and sages, as well as Brahmanical seers;
it resounded with the voices of women, dancers, and singers.
It was filled with vehicles and mounts such as lordly elephants, horses, and great swans,

It was made white by the radiance of hundreds of thousands of lamps and rendered beautiful by throngs of Brahmins uttering auspicious sounds.
Amidst the pervasive sounds of various musical instruments, marked by signs of welcome,

In the meantime, Durgā approached the vicinity of the city gate;

Extremely serene, with tearful eyes and minds overwhelmed with joy, they ran forward upon seeing their daughter; the virtuous woman saluted them with her head.
Placing their daughter upon their chests, the two of them bestowed auspicious blessings;
the women, headed by the brothers' wives, gave her firm embraces.
"By his asceticism, he has accomplished the salvation of his lineage; we have been purified," they said, praising her thus, and they bowed to her and honored her with flowers and sandalwood paste.
The gods of the sky showered flowers, bowed down, and offered praises;

Then the Brahmins, the family priest, her friends, and other women ushered Satī into the house with great honor.

He bestowed gifts of gold upon virtuous brahmins and bards;

When the singing of various musical pieces had commenced, O beloved, the elders, sisters, brothers, kinsmen, and citizens gathered together in the pavilion.
