"The medicine is wholesome for the patient, yet it causes discomfort," saying this and having received his meal, the brahmin Hara departed. (69)
Menā said to her husband: "O Lord, I have heard of Śambhu’s conduct;
such a person I will not give my daughter to, nor shall she be cast into a pit."
If you do not believe my words, I shall die without a doubt;
I will either leave my home immediately or consume poison. (71)
"Having bound my daughter around my neck, I shall go to the dense forest;
I will drown in the great ocean, for I will not give my daughter to him. (72)
Śaila thought, "That [proposal] is not suitable; my daughter must not be given to one devoid of qualities.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? For my daughter is indeed persistent. (73)
"I am to be wedded by Śaṅkara alone, and not by anyone else;
otherwise, I shall either die or live as a forest-dweller. (74)
And as for what is destined to happen, let it be; I have no desire for it. Let her go according to her fate, indeed, to be given to Śaṅkara. (75)
Thus Menā and the Mountain attained an attitude of indifference toward Hara;
perceiving that their desire had been fulfilled, the gods and others were indeed filled with joy.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Welcome of Pārvatī upon Her Return from Austerity, Śambhu’s Dancing in the Pavilion in the Guise of a Performer, Pārvatī’s Petition which was not accepted by Menā and the Mountain [Himavat], Śambhu’s Arrival Again in the Guise of a Vaiṣṇava, the Censure that [the boon] was not granted to Śiva, and the Manifestation of Menā and the Mountain," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O lotus-eyed one, Rudra, established on Kailāsa, remembered the seven sages who are oceans of knowledge, together with Arundhatī.
And they all gathered at Kailāsa, which is the refuge of Śaṅkara;
seeing that they had arrived, Śaṅkara rose up and honored them.
Then he said, "Be seated" upon soft, golden-colored cushions; and then [addressed them]:
"O son of Varuṇa, O son of Gādhi, O Gautama, listen! (3)
O Bharadvāja, listen; and you, O Aṅgiras, listen as well.
You, O most excellent ones, go toward Himādri, the king of mountains.
Let the Lord of Mountains, Himavat, be entreated on my behalf for Pārvatī;
according to the principles of the Vedas, those two have become desirous of giving their daughter.
"Indeed, at the instigation of the gods, I have committed this act of reviling.
Upon hearing that, the two of them became utterly despondent and exceedingly wretched.
Since the Seven Sages did not wish to give their daughter to me at that time,
they paid their respects and quickly departed for the Himalayas.
Śambhu said to Arundhatī: "O beautiful one, go to the mountain;
for housewives indeed know the way to accomplish the good works of other housewives."
Thus commanded by the Seven Sages, Arundhatī departed with them,
having gone to the city of Himavat situated at Oṣadhiprastha.
In that manner, Sunābha and the others entered, as did the host of mountain-dwelling women,
along with Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and other attendants preceding them.
The Himalaya mountain,
rising up and taking an excellent offering (arghya), [presented] the delightful, vast, and gold-bright realm of Himavat.
He went to the gate himself and worshipped the supreme lords;
having brought them into the assembly hall, he offered them seats upon which they took their places.
Realizing the fruitfulness of his birth, he, beautiful with a smile, spoke:
"Is this a rain from a cloudless sky, or is it a flowerless fruit? (13)
Your auspicious arrival is beyond reasoning and inconceivable;
I am blessed and purified, since you have graced my courtyard.
Having purified themselves from association with the wicked, these compassionate ones, whose desires are fulfilled, wander upon the earth for the sake of others. 15.
I believe you have come for the accomplishment of some task;
I have been commanded—let that which is worthy of a servant be told.
Aṅgiras spoke to the lord of mountains: "We have indeed been sent here by the three-eyed Śiva; hear what we must request. (1.7)
"This Kālī, your daughter, who is the most beautiful among all women—Pinākin himself seeks her as his own daughter. (18)
Therefore, quickly purify yourself and offer this maiden to Śaṅkara;
for that task of the gods has been pending for a very long time.
This effort must be undertaken for the sake of rescuing the world;
indeed, he alone is a blessed father whose daughter has Hara as her husband.
By the power of austerity, one attains the Lord of the lords of the gods;
may all the lords of the gods of gods bow down to Pārvatī and Hara.
"We are the suitors and Śarva is the giver of the boon; you too are Umā, the bride and mother of the entire world. Do that which is for your own welfare. (22)
Having heard those words of Ānanda, Himādri summoned his own kinsmen—
the foremost of mountains, such as Meru and others— from all directions.
They also arrived and sat upon golden thrones:
Udaya, Hemakūṭa, Ramyaka, and Mandara.
Uddālaka, Vāruṇa, Varāha, Garuḍāsana, Śuktimān, Vegasānu, Dṛḍhaśṛṅga, and Raivata. || 25 ||
Citrakūṭa, Trikūṭa, Śṛṅgavān, and other mountains were there;
then Girīśa himself summoned his wife Menā.
Then Himālaya, addressing them all with a melodious voice, said:
"These sons of the Ṛṣis are indeed supplicants for my daughter today. (27)
"I have indeed informed you all regarding this maiden for the sake of Maheśvara;
therefore, as my kinsmen, you yourselves must speak according to what is right. (28)
Having heard this, Meru and the others said, "It is entirely appropriate;
the sages are the petitioners, and Śaṅkara himself is the suitor. (29)
"O Mountain, let Kālīya be given; for he is our desired son-in-law.
Having heard these words of his kinsmen, the Himavat mountain [acted].
Having bowed to the ṛṣis and joined his palms, the King of Mountains spoke this:
"O highly fortunate Seven Sages, that which has been uttered by you—"
"For that has indeed been accepted by me and by my wife in every respect;
now, however, a certain brahmin, a follower of the Vaiṣṇava dharma, has arrived. (32)
"Śiva is a mine of misery; he will not give her away," she said.
"Neither does Rudra desire the marriage of his daughter, nor do I. (33)
A daughter should indeed be given to one who brings happiness, not to a miserable beggar;
therefore, I beg for your forbearance, so that my daughter may not fall into suffering.
Having spoken thus, that king of mountains became entirely silent;
Menakā, however, went into the interior of the house and slept motionless.
The sages sent Menakā back toward Arundhatī;
upon merely seeing Arundhatī, Menakā bowed and spoke.
"Oh! What merit is this of ours today, we of meritorious birth, that the wife of Vasiṣṭha, devoted to her husband, has arrived here! (37)
"For what purpose have you come, O Goddess? Tell it to me, your servant.
Having heard this, Arundhatī said: "My dear, listen to the reason for which I have come. (38)
Listen, O Menā; let there be success for your birth, my friend!
Give Pārvatī to Śiva, for he is none other than Brahman himself. (39)
There is no end to his prosperity; by whom have you been led astray in vain?
She who is the wife of an unfortunate man shall be bound to a wild ox.
She who is the wife of one possessing all fortune shall be honored by all;
yet Śaṅkara is exceedingly generous only so long as there is no daughter-in-law in his house. (41)
In that state of total renunciation (avadhūta), he shall construct the supreme city of Vaikuṇṭha at that very spot in the forest where your daughter’s feet were touched.
In that place there are great riches; even Śiva is possessed of wealth.
By whom has she not been encouraged? Do not grieve; remain steadfast. (43)
"You are worthy of worship by one who is worshipped by the world; become my eternal mother-in-law.
Having said this and taking her with him, he departed toward the Seven Sages.
Then the Seven Sages also spoke to the Lord of Mountains for his own benefit:
"Give Pārvatī to Śiva; become the father-in-law of the Destroyer. (45)
"By the request of Brahmā, Śambhu will accept your daughter.
The Mountain replied, "I do not perceive the royal splendor of Śambhu. (46)
If a father gives his daughter to an unsuitable suitor, whether for the sake of some power or position, or for the sake of kinsmen and relatives; (47)
Driven by lust, delusion, fear, or greed, he is ruined and shall go to hell;
the maiden, too, being distressed, will then cast a curse that lasts for her entire life.
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Lord of Mountains, speech is considered to be of three kinds:
the first is entirely harmful; the second, however, ends in happiness. (49)
Having reflected well, one should indeed grasp the third [alternative], which is the happiness of the beginning and the end;
for that which is currently pleasant to hear may later prove to be unreal and harmful.
The enemy of good intellect says that which is never beneficial at all—something that causes displeasure at first, but brings happiness in the end. (51)
For a compassionate kinsman who is devoted to righteousness certainly awakens [one] through the mere hearing [of the teaching], which is like nectar and brings happiness at all times. (52)
The best speech is said to be that which has truth as its essence and brings about benefit;
such a householder gives his own daughter to one who possesses royal wealth and power. (53)
By giving his daughter to one who is suffering, a father becomes a slayer of his own daughter;
for who knows that Śaṅkara is suffering, he whose servant is Kubera? (54)
Indeed, by the mere play of a frown, he is capable of creating and destroying the universe;
he who is called the Supreme Brahman is indeed Śaṅkara himself. (55)
And his threefold form consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
Brahmā is the creator in Satyaloka, while Viṣṇu is the nourisher in Vikuṇṭha.
On Kailāsa, Hara is the destroyer, and the manifestations of Brahman are in full splendor;
the Prakṛti of Brahman is threefold: Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī.
This Pārvatī, the wife of Hara, was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, in birth after birth; when she was consumed by fire, Śaṅkara wears her ashes.
Therefore, by your own will, give your daughter to Nityavara;
or else, she herself shall go to her beloved’s place when she is given away.
Having gone to your daughter’s place of asceticism and having comforted Pārvatī,
he assumed the guise of a mendicant and there begged from you for Pārvatī.
Having been sent forth by him, we have even brought Arundhatī along;
indeed, we are instructing you—give Pārvatī to Rudra.
That marriage will indeed take place here by the power of destiny;
Śaṅkara himself granted this boon to Pārvatī while she was performing penance.
The promise made by a lord does not turn out otherwise for one who acts contrary to it;
for once one has given a single thing, O Lord of Mountains, all prosperity must indeed be protected.
O Lord of Mountains, by taking even a single [stone], all one's prosperity shall be destroyed;
by giving Pārvatī, however, the Destroyer will reduce everything to ashes.
What need is there for much? Give your daughter to Śaṅkara; happiness will ensue.
Whether today or at the end of the year, this girl must be given away.
Having understood this, give your daughter Pārvatī to the supreme recipient, or to someone else distinguished, or specifically to the Lord Śiva.
"O King of Mountains, abandon Kuruṣa along with your wife Menā.
Then Menā said to them all: "Regarding that which has been spoken by Śaṅkara concerning Pārvatī..."
A son named Sena shall be born, and he will slay Tāraka;
she, being worthy, should be given to Śambhu, who is likewise worthy, for the sake of attaining happiness.
Then her father, the mountain, spoke to his daughter, who was distressed at hearing this:
"Daughter, you have been given by me, as well as by Menā, to Śarva."
Kālī, the consort of Śambhu, joyfully praised the sages;
then Arundhatī, having consoled Kālī, bestowed blessings upon her.
Then the Seven Sages said: "O King of Mountains, listen to this auspicious and meritorious lunar day, which is endowed with the excellence of the *jāmitra* yoga. (7.1)
When seven days have passed, at a rare and exceedingly auspicious moment, when the lord of the ascendant is situated in the ascendant and the moon is joined with its own son; ||72||
When the moon was in conjunction with Rohiṇī in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, pure and free from all defects, on a Monday. ||73||
When Jupiter is conjoined with all true planets and free from the view of false planets, it bestows virtuous offspring and grants good fortune to the husband. (74)
"O Parvata, having given your daughter to Śarva, become one who has fulfilled his duty;
on that lunar day, Hara shall take her hand according to the sacred mantras."
And other mountains also said, "O mountain, act accordingly.
Then Menā, out of affection, addressed Pārvatī as "Śivānī."
Having fed the sages, Arundhatī, and the mountain, he himself ate;
and having adorned Pārvatī, he seated her upon the lap of the sage.
"It has been decided that this portion must be given to Śaṅkara;
Śaṅkara is the beggar, Brahmā is himself the giver, and Himālaya is [the host]. (78)
"And this alms-food of Pārvatī is of the nature of Brahman; what could be more excellent than this?
Then the great sages bestowed auspicious blessings upon her. (79)
Having touched her there with your hand, may it be well with you;
may good fortune always be yours, unbroken and radiant. (1.189.8)
Having spoken thus and having given flowers along with fruits to Himācala, all the sages then established their trust [in him]. (8.1)
Arundhatī tempted Menakā with the virtues of Śambhu;
she wiped away the mountain’s beard with turmeric and saffron. (82)
Having performed the worldly customs, the most excellent auspicious rite,
they then fixed an auspicious moment on the fourth day.
Rejoicing with one another, they went into the presence of Śiva and said, "Everything has become fruitful; by him, your daughter was given through the granting of his word."
O Hara, go forth for marriage to the auspicious abode of Himācala;
marry Pārvatī according to the prescribed rites. 85.
Śiva said: "Marriage has never been practiced nor observed by me before;
the entire ritual, from its commencement to its conclusion, must be performed by the great sages. (86)
The sages replied to Viṣṇu, the Creator (Brahmā) along with his assembly,
Indra, the hosts of seers, the yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, and kinnaras.
Bring the Vidyādharas, the gods, the Sādhyas, the deities led by Indra, the hosts of Maruts, the throngs of Apsarases, and the assemblies of the Brahma-sarasas.

All of them are well-versed in worldly affairs, accompanied by their wives, and established in the duties of householders; they will successfully accomplish your task exactly as it ought to be done, without any impairment.
Having spoken thus, the sages bowed and departed, taking with them the honors [bestowed upon them].
Śambhu said: "You must come with great respect to my wedding."

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Seven Sages Sent by Śiva to the Abode of Himālaya, the Summoning of the Mountains, the Consultation for the Bestowal of Pārvatī’s Hand in Marriage, the Bestowal of the Hand, and the Determination of the Auspicious Day," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, Himagiri,
having invited Meru and the others through his own priest Garga, had the marriage horoscope (lagnapatrikā) written.
The brahmin sent that letter along with all the necessary materials to Śiva;
having applied the *tilaka* mark, he delivered it to Śaṅkara.
Then, having been greatly honored, the twice-born one returned to the mountain;
the mountain invited his kinsmen and others residing in all directions.
He caused a collection of various excellent foods and other provisions to be prepared—
materials of diverse kinds suitable for the performance of the wedding ceremony.
He offered many, many mountains of rice, chickpeas, flattened grains (pṛthuka), wheat,
barley, pulses, and so forth.
Mountains of jaggery, of sugar, and of various salts; mountains of sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas), of fried cakes (śaṣkulis), and of fried pastries (khājakas).
Mountains with hundreds of holes and the like made of garments and clarified butter,
as well as heaps of pearls and mountains of parched grain.
Great heaps of *pūrīs*, *polikās*, and *bharjikās*,
as well as various kinds of *phullavaṭīs*, *parpaṭas*, and *śṛṅgas*.
And there were peaks of svastika-shaped sweets mixed with sugar and long pepper,
as well as [peaks] of milk, clarified butter, curds, and honeyed water.
He likewise constructed long ponds of nectar, sugarcane juice, and fermented liquors,
as well as reservoirs for various flowing drinks.
He caused anthills to be made from the finest essence of milk and fresh butter,
as well as mountains of various cooked foods.
There are many substances that cause fermentation, such as vegetable leaves and the like, as well as mustard seeds, radish sprouts, fermented gruel, sour gruel, and so forth. (12)
Priceless golden garments, grass mats, and lion-thrones; as well as large canopies, including those with cotton down and silk brocade.
Various kinds of precious gems, gold, and silver; many types of bowls, vehicles, and mounts. || 14 ||
Having gathered these and other such fragrant items,
Śaila began to perform auspicious rites on that day of auspiciousness.
Then the wives of the mountain had Pārvatī undergo the purificatory rites according to the prescribed rules;
they adorned her and sang songs for her.
The women of the city, filled with joy, performed auspicious rites with blessings, ornaments, and auspicious substances, following the traditional customs of the world.
Delighted by the arrival of his kinsmen, Śaila too, with festive spirit and with his whole being, performed the most auspicious rites of welcome according to tradition.
Then the divine mountain, the abode of the gods, arrived there in embodied form,
bringing great jewels and priceless articles.
Accompanied by an assembly resplendent with single diamonds, excellent gems, and jewels;
possessing noble lineage and bringing gifts, Mount Mandara arrived.
Accompanied by his family adorned with ornaments, he arrived from the western mountain (Asta-giri) along with his kinsmen, bearing golden decorations, jewels, and gems.
And from the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayādri), filled with great joy,
the Mountain of Malaya arrived, accompanied by a retinue of jewels.
Dardura, possessing divine splendor, arrived with his wife and others;
Niṣadha came forth accompanied by his retinue and his attendants.
Saśrīputra, Hiraṇyādi, and Gandhamādana arrived; the very wealthy Karavīra and Mahendra also came.
Accompanied by his sons, wives, male and female servants, and kinsmen, Pāriyātra, a mine of jewels and gems, arrived there. (25)
Krauñca arrived accompanied by his servants, retinue, and offerings;
Puruṣottamaśaila also came, bringing gifts and other such things.
Mount Nīla arrived with his retinue and offerings;
there, Mount Raivata also arrived, accompanied by his wives, sons, and others. (27)
Urala, accompanied by his army, as well as Vindhya in like manner,
arrived there together with many jewels, utensils, and other provisions.
Trikūṭa, Citrakūṭa, Veṅkaṭa, the auspicious Śrīgiri,
Gokāmukha, and Nāradādri arrived with those who had taken refuge in them and others.
Kālañjara with his retinue, Kailāsa of divine form,
and whatever other mountains exist upon the earth or are situated within the islands.
Those who dwell in the oceans, in the atmosphere, among the planets, and even those on the mountains,
were invited by Himādri along with their wives, sons, grandsons, and others.
Together with male and female slaves, servants, armies, retinues, and householders, and with excellent gems, jewels, diamonds, gold, silver, and other such objects. || 32 ||
With ornaments, garments, celestial chariots, and various priceless gifts, they arrived with great joy, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and [Umā]."
Gharghara, Śoṇabhadra, and the great river Brahmaputra—other rivers as well arrived, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā. || 34 ||
The Godāvarī, the Yamunā, the Triveṇī, and the Sarasvatī, adorned with divine ornaments, arrived for the marriage of Śiva and [Pārvatī]. || 35 ||
Mahāmodā, Narmadā, Gaṅgā, and Rudrakanyakā—these divine women arrived with great joy for the wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī. || 36 ||
The Sindhutapati, the Kāverī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, the river Mahī, the Ojasvatī, the Svarṇarekhā, the Bhadrā, and likewise the Sābhramatī. || 37 ||
The Śatrujit, Gomatī, Bhogavatī, Gaṇḍakī, Tāmraparṇī, the divine rivers, and other auspicious streams; || 38 ||
They were crowded with sons, daughters, retinues, and family members,
and were accompanied by the necessary materials for offering ornaments, jewels, and gifts.
Divine, possessing the forms of goddesses, beautiful, and radiant as gold,
they were all embodiments of loveliness, each graced with a beauty exceeding that of sixteen-year-old maidens.
Greatly delighted, they gathered together, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā," at Mahākālavana, the forest known as Sundara, the Madhuvana grove. 4.1.
They proceeded with reverence to Vṛndāvana and other forests,
as well as Siṃhāraṇya, Dharmāraṇya, and Naimiṣa.
They also respectfully visited other prosperous forests,
as well as Kurukṣetra, Bhṛgukṣetra, Brahmakṣetra, and others.
Thinking with love, "The wedding of Śiva and Pārvatī is taking place," the cities such as Svarṇapūrī and other divine cities arrived, well-adorned and moving by means of aerial chariots.
The worlds assembled, thinking, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā," bringing golden and silver ornaments as well as divine garments. (45)
All fragrant substances and so forth that are fit for rubbing, as well as unfading fruits and flowers, and excellent gems, jewels, and diamonds— 46.
And there were many diverse vessels and numerous seats, as well as excellent vehicles, mounts, and great celestial chariots. ||47||
He saw divine necklaces of pearls, divine articles of luxury,
various ornaments, and garments of exquisite appearance.
Having gathered divine [beings] resplendent like the sun, blazing with boundless beauty, as wedding gifts for Śiva and Pārvatī, they departed. (49)
Then, with all of them having arrived from every direction, that divine city on the snowy mountain became crowded and endowed with great splendor.
The gate-towers were adorned with banners, flags, canopies, and arches, as well as with water-pots, cloths, garlands of *kalī* flowers, plantain trees, and auspicious *svastika* symbols. (5.1)
The royal highways, crossroads, streets, palaces, and pleasure gardens were adorned with colorful garlands and decorated with lamps and musical instruments. (52)
And the portions of the park grounds, refined by the supernatural powers of sweeping and sprinkling, scented and adorned, were indeed like heaven itself. (53)
Well-shaded pavilions were constructed to ward off the heat of the sun, and drinking halls, dining halls, and resting areas were established. (54)
There were assemblies of actors, dancers, musicians, wrestlers, and wandering performers;
there were expositions, entertainments, games, spectacles, and storytelling. (55)
Various acts that bring joy and serve the needs of guests were performed;
for what indeed could be lacking where one's father-in-law is a mountain? (56)
He whose son-in-law will be Lord Śaṅkara, and in whose house the Mother of the World, Mahāmāyā, shall become the daughter-in-law. (57)
Just as heaven is divine, or Vaikuṇṭha,
or even the world of Brahmā, so indeed does that city shine.
With great joy, devotion, faith, and respect, Himālaya honored those who had arrived according to their respective status. (59)
In all the delightful palaces, which possessed gardens with water features and swings, and which shone with constant swings, couches, pavilions, seats, and various articles; 1.190.60.
He assigned separate dwellings within the forms of their own celestial chariots,
and at that time, he employed hundreds of thousands of male and female servants for their service.
And that king of mountains, the mountain, completely gratified them with various desirable collections of gifts and objects of enjoyment.
In his own city, in his own courtyard, he had an auspicious arrangement made;
indeed, at every gate, auspicious items such as the Rambhā plant were placed.
Rambhā fashioned a courtyard provided with pillars,
featuring archways made of mango leaves firmly fastened to silk-woven pillars.
It was provided with garlands of *mālatī* flowers, pearl necklaces, and *kāṅgarikā* ornaments, and was adorned in the four directions with highly auspicious substances and other items. (65)
Placing Garga at the forefront, the Mountain,
with joy, then performed every most excellent rite for the sake of his daughter, as was fitting for the auspicious occasion.
The goddess Earth, having arrived, gave the ground for the purpose of the pavilion;
that earth, situated in the intermediate space, then shone like the sky.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he had him construct a pavilion made of gold,
exceedingly vast, and beautiful with its altars and other features.
In the foothills of the Himalayas, it extended for many yojanas; endowed with manifold wonders, it was like heaven situated in the sky. 69.
All that is stationary and all that is moving are mutually similar,
creating a delusion for the observer, yet they are interspersed with the attendants of Haṃsa.
Then, the mobile was surpassed by the immobile in beauty,
and the immobile was likewise surpassed by the mobile through its superior splendor.
The earth was conquered by water, and the water was conquered by land;
there, one could not truly discern what was land and what was water. ||72||
At the gate, on the side of the Karmānikā tree, there were in some places artificial lions;
in other places there were cranes and swans, and in others there were elephants. (73)
In some places there were peacocks, parrots, mynas, and sarikas;
and in other places there were cuckoos, all artificial yet appearing as if they were conscious beings.
In some places, women—both real and artificial—are dancing with men upon elevated platforms; they enchant the spectators as they gaze upon them. (75)
In some uppermost parts, there stood divine, artificial apsarases, adorned with flower garlands and endowed with wings, seated upon lotuses.
At the tops of the stairs and gate-towers, the door-keepers stand equipped with bows, bearing weapons, accompanied by shouts of defiance, and likewise provided with *bhūśuṇḍī* firearms.
The inexhaustible vessels of ghee remain there, stationary yet appearing as if moving;
Mahālakṣmī stands at the door, and above her is a beautiful artificial image.
Sprinkled from both sides by elephants with water-pots and lotuses, the slender Sarasvatī played a lute while singing. 79.
In each of the four [gates], there were artificial elephants adorned with golden ornaments, as well as horses, decorated horsemen, elephant-drivers, and so forth. (1.190.80)
Chariots, splendid with their draft animals led by their riders, as well as numerous vehicles such as Garuḍas and swans, [were seen]. (8.1)
There were palaces and celestial chariots, both artificial and beyond comparison with anything man-made; and in his assembly hall was an artificial grove containing rows of trees.
Artificial actors, actresses, and dancers of many forms were present, and circles of Apsarases, Rāsas, and singers were formed.
Thus, for the sake of causing delusion, much was also created within the pavilion:
[the forms] of sages, ṛṣis, gods, rivers, and likewise mountains. (84)
Furthermore, artificial rows of forms for the rivers and forests were all created by Viśvakarman, which indeed produce the illusion of movement.
Viśvakarman created those various artificial [images] which were already there, as well as others that would arrive, and those situated in the pavilion and on the ground. ||86||
Janavāha and Śaṅkara, dressed in excellent attire upon a bull, were fashioned as artificial images by Viśvakarman for the pleasure of Śambhu. ||87||
Likewise, at the great gate, O Bho, a large Nandi made of crystal was fashioned;
and above the Nandi, in the sky, there is a great support for the hump.
A magnificent, artificial celestial chariot named Puṣpaka was fashioned, enriched with jewels and adorned with excellent parasols, chowries, mirrors, leaf-patterns, and arched gateways.
It was perfumed by celestial lamps and stars, radiant as the moon,
and adorned with garlands of plantain leaves, flowers, and fruits.

On the left side, two golden-colored elephants were fashioned, accompanied by their female mates; they have four tusks, are sixty years of age, are full of ichor, and possess the luster of mountains. (91)
Likewise, two artificial horses, sun-colored and adorned, were fashioned,
as well as other gatekeepers, men bearing golden staffs.
Artificial and smiling Lokapālas were fashioned;
all the gods, together with their goddesses, were made along with their families. (93)
The secondary gods, the Guhyakas, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras;
the Ṛṣis and the Pitṛs, as well as the Manavas who are of artificial origin. ||94||
Those whose selves are not disciplined appear as if they were sentient beings;
[just as] Viṣṇu is joined with Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa is joined with Ramā. 95.
Likewise, Brahmā accompanied by Vāṇī, as well as Garuḍa and Haṃsa, along with their respective attendants and families in every respect. (96)
The Vedas, Sanaka and the others, and the reciters with books in their hands—
all these were created as artificial beings by the pleased Viśvakarman.
Indra, seated upon Airāvata and accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, as well as the other world-protectors such as Dhanada and the rest, [were present]. (98)
And artificial ones were indeed fashioned there by Viśvakarmā;
O Lakṣmī, what is the use of much speaking? For whoever belongs to either of the two sides [shall be victorious]. 99.
The assembly has arrived, and furthermore, the great multitude will arrive;
they all, both men and women, were fashioned by Viśvakarman.
"Created as if unmade for the sake of wonder for those two"—referring here to the platforms in this pavilion, and above them, the grass mats and wooden planks. (10.1)
The auspicious regions were made to resemble milk, crystal, and mirrors;
the delightful plains were like the moon, green, and covered with lush grass.
There, artificial and painted [images] might deceive those whose minds are deluded;
however, for the purpose of providing a dwelling for the Self-born (Brahmā), there is an artificial [palace] born of Satyaloka.
A palace, the Sudharmā assembly hall, and a wonderful artificial pavilion were constructed for the purpose of providing a residence for Viṣṇu; thus Vaikuṇṭha became possessed of great opulence.
Created by Viśvakarman, that divine city, filled with celestial wonders,
shone forth like the artificial city of Indra situated in heaven.
Likewise, for the sake of providing dwellings for the guardians of the other directions and for those equal to the world-protectors, Viśvakarman constructed their cities.
There, for their respective dwellings in the sky, artificial mansions— greatly divine and wonderful— were constructed as residences.
In an instant, by the one of great intellect, Viśvakarman,
rows of palaces were fashioned and artificial royal ramparts were constructed.
Likewise, he fashioned the divine Kailāsa, a brilliantly radiant abode for the high-souled Śaṅkara, consisting of every kind of prosperity.
There was Badarikāśrama, and the White Ocean of Milk;
there Goloka was depicted, fashioned as an artificial representation using liquid substances.
Such auspicious structures were fashioned by Viśvakarman with the desire that Śiva, Hari, and all the others might be pleased. || 11.1 ||
Everything was joyfully prepared, adorned, and executed by the Lord of Snow Mountains for the further enhancement of the splendor of his daughter's wedding. (11.2)
Having thus made all preparations and increased the worldly festivities for the occasion,
Himācala joyfully awaited the arrival of Śambhu.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Himālaya’s Commissioning of Heaps of Cooked Food, Jewels, and Utensils, as well as Auspicious Rites; the Arrival of Invited Mountains, Rivers, Tīrthas, Forests, Gods, and Goddesses; and the Beauty of the City and Pavilions Constructed by Viśvakarman," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall tell you what Śambhu did;
having received the auspicious letter, the Lord remained on Kailāsa.
Having had it read, he composed a letter and accepted it according to the prescribed rites; having honored the bearer of the letter, he sent him away with due respect.
Śaṅkara invited the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, saying:
"May all of you come with enthusiasm, accompanied by your wives, sons, grandsons, and others."
"Those who do not come here to this festival of my wedding must not be considered as one's own kin, regardless of who those great men may be. (4)
He dispatched Nārada to the fourteen worlds;
having invited them all with due honor, the sage returned to Śaṅkara.
Then, for the sake of honoring his guests, Śambhu created another divine city, a new Kailāsa.
Where there were hundreds of thousands of palaces and likewise tens of millions of houses,
as well as thousands of gardens and hundreds of groves.
There were also ponds and long oblong lakes, celestial palaces and pavilions,
kitchens for juices, kitchens for cooked food, halls for dancing, and pleasure gardens.
There were dining halls, halls of delight, incomparable exhibition halls,
drinking saloons, bathing halls, sacrificial pits, and assembly houses for storytelling.
Divine pavilions were constructed, and everything was arranged as if it were heaven itself;
there was nothing lacking compared to the world of Brahmā, Vaikuṇṭha, or even Nāka.
Those who travel with people and those residing within the cosmic egg arrived, having been invited,
along with their families, retinues, male and female servants, and friends.
First, however, Mahāviṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī and his attendants, arrived with all his retinue after having composed amorous gestures. || 1 ||
Likewise, the Creator of the Universe arrived, taking all his own kinsmen along with him,
accompanied by groups of male and female servants, and adorned on all sides.
The Vairājas, the Brahma-sages, Vāsudeva and the others, as well as the incarnations of Hari and the Rudras by the millions. || 14 ||
Yama and the other ancestors, the solar and lunar hosts, as well as the world-protectors, the sages, and the guardians of the directions, each with distinct forms; || 15 ||
Adorned with ornaments and full of grace, they were provided with all their belongings,
accompanied by their wives, sons, daughters, kinsmen, and the rest of their families.
The wedding of Śiva and Śivā took place at Śiva-Kailāsa;
their parents, the heavens, all the yakṣas, and even the rākṣasas arrived there.
Bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, as well as arbuda-koṭis of gaṇas;
likewise kūṣmāṇḍas, bhairavas, vaitālas, and fires. || 18 ||
Vidyut, Mahākāla, Jarā, Mṛtyu, and Mahālaya; the Dhūmra nights, as well as the goddesses Caṇḍikā and the other Mothers (Mātṛs). || 19 ||
Likewise, fevers, diseases, comets, and other planets,
as well as various calamities, arrived there for the wedding of Śiva and [Pārvatī].
The Kiṃpuruṣas, the Māgadhas, the Sūtas, and the Bandins, as well as the Cāraṇas dwelling on earth—all of whom belong to divine and human lineages—[approached]. || 21 ||
The immobile and the mobile, the oceans, rivers, streams, and so forth;
the asuras, dānavas, and daityas, as well as those born of Kadru who are devotees of Śiva.
At that time, there were nāgas, sarpas, garuḍas, and others belonging to the faction of Śiva, as well as gods and goddesses numbering in the hundreds of millions.

Together with their wives, sons, and families, the earth and the other elements are forms of Śiva—full of energy, accompanied by their retinues, adorned with ornaments, and possessed of their vehicles. (24)
Great yogis such as Durvāsas and others, as well as yoginīs,
virtuous women, and the most excellent avadhūtas and avadhūtīs, arrived there at that time.
The female celibates arrived, and likewise the goddesses Durgās came; all the Śaktis also arrived, for it was the wedding of Śiva and Śivā.
Śambhu himself performed various forms of hospitality for those who had arrived;
during the great festival, the troupe of female dancers performed beautiful dances.
To conduct the bridegroom’s procession on Kailāsa, the great deities (mahīmānakāḥ) stayed there,
considering it their own duty, and rendered excellent assistance.
All the Mothers indeed fashioned the Gīṣṭakāmarda for Śambhu,
and they performed the supreme rite of adorning Śiva according to what was appropriate.
At that time, during the rite of Śiva’s adornment, excellent musical instruments were played;
the great lords partook of food, and the celestial women danced.
The attendants decorating the vehicles separately,
while the queens adorn their limbs with unguents and fragrant liquids.
Then, in every pavilion, those of great energy set forth—
the lords of the Gaṇas and the Kārtikas who had arisen in the previous creation.
Hundreds of thousands arrived from the Vairāja realm seeking auspiciousness, acting as assistants for the army in the service of their eternal father. (33)
Listen, O beloved, to what Śiva’s attire was like at that time;
his natural appearance then became his mode of adornment. (34)
In that naturally matted mane, the lightnings and thunders remained cool, while the masses of hair stood forth brilliantly radiant.
Then Gaṅgā herself, in the form of water, mingled with the rays of Brahmā and created a halo of light all around that abode consisting of splendor.
From Goloka, the divine golden crown, accompanied by matted locks and joined with the *kalpa* tree, was offered by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and shines upon his head. (37)
There hangs a string of garlands made of *pārījātaka* flowers;
on the forehead of the second [goddess], the full moon serves as her tilaka mark. 38.
The third eye on the forehead is peaceful, wide awake, and exceedingly brilliant;
then, with that light upon the forehead, it takes the form of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Then the two serpents Vāsuki and Kārkoṭaka, assuming forms at will,
became the earrings of Śambhu, radiant and inlaid with precious gems.
Vāsuki was upon his neck, and a beautiful golden necklace was seen around it; at that time, two golden bracelets became the Vāsukī snakes upon his arms.
Then the rudrākṣas on Śambhu’s wrists became golden bracelets set with jewels, assuming whatever forms they desired. ||42||
The beads of his rosary were made of crystal, while his auspicious rings were made of fire-born [coral];
and at that time, the ashes of the funeral pyre became the collyrium for his eyes.
That ash on the face of Śambhu indeed became a liquid born of milk,
while the white ointment-powder upon his body turned into ash.
Then his bark garment became an excellent golden tunic,
and the elephant hide became a fine upper robe for the sovereign.
And then Mekhalā became a divine waistband of gold, enriched with twenty-seven cords and bound with excellent jewels and diamonds. (46)
Then the drops of snow became worthy offerings of sandalwood for Śambhu;
and the poison residing in his throat then indeed became the Kaustubha gem.
A tiger skin was upon his hips, and he wore a yellow silk garment;
he held a trident and a most radiant golden sword.
His auspicious staff was made of gold,
and his wooden sandals were very soft, adorned with golden ornaments.
"O Pādarakṣikā, you who possess divine beauty, you have become very affectionate toward me;
yet at that time, even his betel, though most fragrant, became bitter. (1.191.50)
At that time, Gṛñja became his supreme stimulating pill;
and then Kanaka became his armlets and anklets. || 51 ||
Indeed, the garland of severed heads became for him a great necklace of priceless jewels;
and that skull then became his most excellent and beautiful crest-ornament.
Having opened [the door], there appeared a white celestial chariot (vimānaka) there,
accompanied by a thousand white elephants, horses, bulls, vehicles, and so forth.
Mounted upon his elephant, the thousand-eyed Indra, together with Indrāṇī, held a wide, dry-clothed umbrella for the Lord.
Then the Yamunā, the best of rivers, being situated upon the tortoise,
shone as she held a white yak-tail fan by his side.
Sarasvatī, mounted upon her elephant, took up a second [lotus];
the six seasons offered handfuls of flowers to Hari.
And the Vahnis, having taken up lamps, stood on all sides;
and the Ocean stood there, holding a vessel of ointment.
Such a beautiful form, capable of assuming any shape at will, was then assumed;
yet everything is transformed within the Lord, whose supreme self is beyond transformation.
By the will of the Lord, those who were of cruel form then became of suitable form;
by the will of Śrī Śaṅkara, they became adorned with ornaments worthy of choosing a boon.
When the traveling party had been thus prepared, those on Śaṅkara’s side approached and said, "O Lord, proceed together with us."
Then Viṣṇu said to Śambhu: "Today, indeed, you ought to perform the rite for Pārvatī’s own marriage here, according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras."
Have the erection of the pavilion and the Nāndīmukha rite performed;
for Brahmā is indeed authorized there in rites appropriate for prosperity.
Urged by Brahmā, the sages performed the rite according to the rules:
Kaśyapa, Atri, Gautama, Kaṇva, and Bṛhaspati the preceptor.
Vasiṣṭha, Bhāguri, Śakti, Agastya, Cyavana, Garga, Śilāda, Akṛtaśrama, Aruṇa, and Parāśara; ||64||
Jamadagni, Śilāpāka, Mārkaṇḍeya, Akṛtavraṇa, Bharadvāja, Dadhīci, Upamanyu, and likewise Kuśika. ||65||

Pippalāda, Kautsa, and Śvetavyāsa along with his disciples— all of whom had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) and performed rituals according to the injunctions declared in the Vedas— [66]
Hundreds of thousands of sages named Maṅgala arrived there;
having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony, they provided protection for Śambhu.
In accordance with the rites prescribed in the Vedas, they performed various auspicious ceremonies using the hymns of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the worship of the planets for Śambhu.
They performed the worship of the gods stationed in the mandala for the pacification of obstacles;
then Śiva, being pleased, bowed down to the best of the twice-born.
Having placed the Brahmins, the gods, and others before him, Hara emerged from Kailāsa; having prepared himself, he went outside and stood there.
Then songs, instrumental music, and beautiful dances arose, and a great festival took place;
and other hosts of attendants also departed, with the exception of those guarding Kailāsa.
And Śaṅkhakarṇa approached with a very prosperous retinue of ten million;
likewise, Kekarākṣa with ten crores, and Vikṛta with eight crores.
Viśākha has four crores, Pārijāta has nine crores,
and both Sarvāntaka and Vikṛtānana have sixty crores each.
Dundubha was accompanied by eighty million [attendants], Kapāla by fifty million;
both Kanduka and Kundaka were joined by groups numbering one hundred million times ten million.
Sandāraka is endowed with six [crores], Viṣṭambhaka is joined with eight crores; Pippala and Sanāda are each joined with a thousand crores.
Likewise, the Gaṇa Āveśana went with eight koṭis, and Mahākeśa went accompanied by a thousand koṭis, as did Candratāpana.
Kuṇḍa and Parvata, together with twelve crores [of attendants],
as well as Kāla, Kālaka, Agni, and Mahākāla, are the lords of the Gaṇas.
Śatakoṭi is joined by hosts numbering one hundred koṭis; Agnimukha is likewise with one koṭi; Ādityamūrdhā is with one koṭi, and Ghanāvaha is also with one koṭi. ||78||
Sannāha, Kumuda, Amogha, Kokila,
and the leaders of the hosts departed with a hundred crores, while Sumantra went with ten billion.
Kākapādodara with sixty crores, and likewise Santānaka;
Mahābala, who is honey-tawny, is joined by nine crores.
Nīla and Pūrṇabhadra were accompanied by ninety crores;
Caturvaktra was with seven crores, and Karaṇa was joined by twenty crores.
Yajvākṣa, Śatamanyu, and another named Meghamanyu,
along with Ahiromaka, departed accompanied by nine hundred million [followers].
Kāṣṭhāgūṣṭa, accompanied by the sixty-four Gaṇanāyakas, Virūpākṣa, Sukeśa, Vṛṣabha, and Sanātana. ||83||
Saṃvartaka, Lakulīśa, Cañcvāsya, and Ṣaḍānana;
Saṃvartaka, Tālaketu, Nakulīśa, and then Caitraka. ||84||
Lokāntaka, Dīptātman, Bhṛṅgi, Daityāntaka, Riṭi, Devapriya, Aśani, and Bhānuka—these are the Gaṇas. (85)
Accompanied by hosts numbering sixty-four crores, they went forth for the wedding festivities;
adorned with ornaments and dressed in auspicious attire, it was the marriage of Śiva and Śivā. (86)
A thousand bhūtas went forth with three crores of pramathas;
Vīrabhadra went with sixty-four [crores], and the hair-born ones with three crores.
Then Bhairava also departed, accompanied by two thousand others, ten million times ten million, and groups of ten million times ten million.
They have many arms and are beautiful in form; they wear crowns of matted hair, have the moon upon their foreheads, possess three eyes, have blue throats, and carry tridents. ||89||
Adorned with the splendor of rudrākṣas and sacred ash, these great lords possess divine forms,
decorated with necklaces, armlets, earrings, crowns, and other ornaments.
Some, served by the powers such as *aṇimā* and others, moved through the sky, the earth, and heaven; and who were those that traveled through the seven heavens and the seven netherworlds? ||9.1||
Then all the gods, with serene minds and assuming forms at will, became gentle and proceeded to that great festival. 92.
Not everyone felt joy at the thought of the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī;
for Caṇḍī, the sister of Rudra, was adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Mounted upon the vehicle of the deceased, with a golden pitcher upon her head, she was beautiful, filled with joy, and carrying a jar full of water. (94)
Filled with curiosity, she came there to that great festival;
accompanied by ten million hosts of spirits, she arrived proclaiming victory.
Followed by eleven crores of Rudras who had gone to her rear, the great roar of their hand-drums (ḍamaru) then pervaded the three worlds. (96)
The world was filled with the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, and drums;
behind the hosts [of Gaṇas] were the gods, followed by the Siddhas and the great Ṛṣis. 97.
Then the world-protectors followed after him, and in their midst was Hari, together with Garuḍa,
accompanied by Lakṣmī and his auspicious attendants adorned with their own ornaments.
Accompanied by crores and billions of Vaiṣṇava servants belonging to the classes of Abja and Abjaja, and by Lakṣmīs, Ramās, and Kamalās, he departed. (99)

Then Brahmā, together with those who possessed knowledge of the Vedas, Shastras, Samhitas, and Agamas, with the Vairajas established in celibacy, and with the Siddhas beginning with Sanaka; ||| 1.191.100 ||
Adorned by the Prajāpatis, his sons such as Sāvitrī and Pramada, as well as by the Ṛṣis and Munis, he proceeded along.
And with celestial chariots drawn by swans and well-adorned vehicles,
Indra then arrived with his army, seated upon Airāvata.
Adorned and successful, he shone accompanied by various hosts of gods;
and then the sages, the Brahmins, the Sādhyas, and likewise the virtuous ones [gathered].
The renouncers, forest-dwellers, and Vaiṣṇavas all went forth with joy,
invited and delighted by the thought that it was the wedding of Śiva and Śivā.
Then the yogins, ascetics, those free from passion, those who take refuge in Śiva, and the renunciants went forth, saying, "This is the wedding of Śiva and Śivā. || 105 ||

Countless crores of male attendants (gaṇas) and female attendants (gaṇikās), as well as crores upon crores of those who lead to Śiva—the female servants of the Gaṇas and the wives of the Gaṇas—departed. || 106 ||
Adorned with ornaments, dress, and the like, and beautified by every kind of decoration, all those [goddesses] residing on Kailāsa were present for the wedding of Śiva and [Pārvatī]. || 107 ||
Then they joyfully went to crores of maṇḍalas of yoginīs and to hundreds of millions of groups of female renunciants.

For the sake of which all the stages of life (āśramas) exist, for the sake of which the social classes (varṇas) are honored, and for the sake of which the sacred traditions (sampradāyas) endure— that is the marriage of Śiva and Śivā.
Then the ḍākinīs, śākinīs, vetālinīs, and the Mothers (mātṛs), as well as the bhairavīs, yātudhānīs, and kinnarīs, all departed.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, Hūhū, Parvata, and others—the Gandharvas and Kinnaras—went forth joyfully, blowing their musical instruments. || 111 ||
Surrounded by ten million maidens, adorned with the beauty of love,
and encouraged by the songs of the goddesses, Śaṅkara then proceeded from there.
Mounted upon a celestial chariot drawn by bulls as brilliant as pure crystal,
he was respectfully honored by the Brahma-lakes in the sky with their retinues.
Strengthened by showers of flowers and shouts of victory, Śaṅkara departed;
Hara went forth for the purpose of taking the hand of the daughter of the Himālaya mountain.
Nārada was sent ahead toward the abode of Himavat;
he departed swiftly to announce the arrival of the bridegroom’s procession. 115.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Śaṅkara Received the Marriage Proposal, How the Inhabitants of the Fourteen Worlds Were Invited and Arrived, the Auspicious Rites such as the Preparation of Śiva’s Wedding Attire, the Installation of the Pavilion, the Nāndī Ceremony, and the Organization of the Procession for the Bridegroom, and the First Dispatching of Nārada," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Listen, Lakṣmī; having gone there, Nārada was struck with wonder upon seeing that marvelous creation fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Deluded by these artificial things, Nārada said to the king:
"The bridegroom's procession has already arrived; what else is there here?"
Śaila replied: "O divine sage, abandon this artificial astonishment;
this visible circle of gods and others was created by Viśvakarman. (3)
Having been fed, honored, and entreated to come to Śambhu,
Nārada went quickly and spoke to Śambhu and the gods and others.
And the Himālaya mountain awaits her arrival,
for that excellent army is coming there both to cause delusion and for the sake of great wonder.
Therein lies an illusion fashioned from variegated colors, wherein the three worlds are contained;
all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahendra, are beautifully depicted there.
Artificial things, through their variegated forms, leave nothing behind; for that which is perceived as active is indeed conscious, whereas the insentient is not.
Having heard this, the bridegroom and others became anxious to see him;
by the command of Śiva, the bridal procession set forth.
The army of Hara arrived at the city of Hemādri;
having heard this, Hemādri dispatched other mountains.
Having gathered the necessary provisions himself and accompanied by the brahmins and his army, Śaila went forth to hold a conversation with the Lord.
Then, seeing the great army of the lords of mountains and that even greater force of the Śaivas,
those belonging to both sides were struck with supreme wonder.
The eastern and western oceans met together,
the golden mountains, and the brahmins and others bowed down repeatedly to Śaṅkara, the bestower of boons.
Seated upon his bull-vehicle, with a most serene countenance and beautifully adorned,
he illuminates the quarters of space with the sublime luster of his divine limbs.
It was filled with jewels and served by the lords of the gods with parasols and chowries;
it had Hari situated on its left and Brahmā situated on its right.
Then, having honored the excellent Mahendra, who was seated upon his back accompanied by hosts of gods, with necklaces and other ornaments as well as drinks and other refreshments; 15.
Having settled the bridegroom’s party in rest-houses by the command of Śiva, the Himālaya mountain went to the sacrificial altar according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having been summoned to perform the excellent rites, those lords, including Īśvara and the others, set out; with Īśa at their head, they proceeded to the abode of the King of Mountains.
At that moment, Menā, longing for the sight of Śiva,
approached the moon-chamber, placing Nārada by her side.
Śiva, desiring to manifest his own creative power,
spoke to Brahmā and Viṣṇu as they had gone separately toward the sacrificial post.
Having made the army compact and strong, we shall go to Sudarśanā;
seeing the beautiful army stationed there, Menā rejoiced.
And at the first mountain gate were the beautiful Gandharvas, radiant,
richly adorned with divine ornaments and garments, auspicious, and accompanied by their vehicles.
Playing musical instruments and accompanied by the singing of apsarases, they then entered, adorned with banners and victory scrolls.
Then, seeing the Lord of Wealth, she said, "This is Śiva.
Nārada replied, "This is not he; for these are indeed the servants of Śiva. (23)
Then, seeing the lord of the yakṣa army named Maṇigrīva, who was enriched with double the splendor, she said, "This is Rudra."
Nārada said: "This is not he; for these others are also servants of Śiva.
Then Anala, situated in the midst of an army enriched with twice the splendor, [appeared].
"He has indeed been seen coming; this is Śiva's master," she said.
Nārada replied, "This is not he; for this is the fire from Śiva's eye. (26)
Then Yama arrived, possessing twice the splendor of him [Kubera], and seeing him accompanied by his own army, Menā said, "This is Śiva. || 27 ||
Nārada said, "This is not he; this Yama is the son of the Sun.
Then, seeing Nirṛti approaching accompanied by his own army, she [spoke].
"This one, who is twice as magnificent in beauty as Yama and is the great lord of the Puṇyajanas," Śiva said to Menā; Nārada replied, "No. (29)
Then, seeing Varuṇa approaching, endowed with double the splendor and situated in the midst of his army, she said: "Is this indeed Rudra?"
Nārada said: "This is not he; Vāyu has arrived.
Then, seeing him in the midst of the army, possessing twice that splendor, [he spoke again].
Menā said, "This is Rudra; it is not Nārada at all.
Then the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) arrived, endowed with twice that splendor.
Seeing him standing in the midst of the army, Menā said, "This is indeed Śiva," but Nārada said, "This is not he; this is the lord of the Guhyakas."
Then, Īśāna arrived, surrounded by his own army;
seeing him endowed with twice the splendor, Menakā said: ||| 14 ||
"This is Rudra," Nārada said to her; "this is not Śaṅkara.

"Everything has become a means of purification for me, leading to the eternal increase of my glory.
Having spoken thus, he bowed with palms joined in reverence, preceded by respectful honor. || 146 ||
He invited Hara, together with Viṣṇu, the gods, and others. Then, commanded by Hara, the gods bowed to Himālaya.
The sages and seers, who were well-versed in the conventions of propriety, replied:
"O King, your fame is now equal to that of Viṣṇu throughout the three worlds."
Indeed, there shall be no one more meritorious than you;
for at your door stand the Blessed Lords, the masters, and tens of millions of gods.
Even though uninvited, they came of their own accord to the wedding of Śambhu;
the charming Janavāsa was established, and the customary practice was duly honored.
Honor, the provision of all necessary materials, meals, drinks, male and female servants, and those who are constantly engaged in service; 151.
O Mountain, everything unprecedented, indescribable, and exhaustive has been honored; it has been made complete by you and your kinsmen. 152.
Thus there arose this supreme praise of the mountain’s wing, following upon the ritual bathing, twilight prayers, silent recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and libations. (153)
For the sake of a meal, he affectionately brought Hara along with his bride;
then, having washed the feet of Śambhu as well as those of the Blessed Ones, [he served them].
Having shown due respect to all those who had come as spectators,
he seated them in long pavilions arranged in excellent rows.
With various divine foods, many kinds of sweet and most delicious items—eatables, chewables, lickables, suckables, bitter ones, and flowing drinks. || 156 ||
He gratified Śaṅkara, along with his bride and the people; and according to the custom of worldly conduct, the women of the city partook of the meal.
Laughing with soft voices, they made the bearers of the bridegroom’s party hear their insults; and while smiling, they uttered many abusive words.
Having eaten and sipped water according to the rules, those followers of Śiva took leave of the mountain and dwelt comfortably on the second and third days.
When the fourth day arrived, the fourth-day rite was performed according to the rules for the sake of purification,
by which the festival was prevented from being interrupted.
On the fifth day, the gods spoke to the mountain for the sake of the procession.
Having heard that, the mountain said: "O gods, please show me mercy. (161)
"Let all of this remain with you for however many days," having said this, he made them stay with great respect for many days indeed.
Every day there was always divine food, ever fresh and new, as well as ever-new drinks and complete service. (163)
Every day he causes dances, songs, instrumental music, festivals, abundant gifts, and vocal performances to be held. 16.4.
Every day there was wrestling, every day dancing by actors and dancers,
every day divine drama, and the sacrificial rites were performed constantly.
Every day there were the songs of wandering minstrels and constant expositions,
as well as the charming amorous gestures of women every single day.
For the sake of the happiness of those possessing great majesty, [the mountain] was fashioned by the mountain-dweller;
nothing was lacking, nor did any affliction arise.
In this manner, many days passed as they resided there;
then Śaṅkara himself, having determined the course of action, requested permission for the journey.
The Mountain, being well-pleased, gave the command for their departure;
all became ready, and Menā spoke auspicious words to Śivā.
"Having shown compassion, you will protect my daughter in every way;
O Āśutoṣa, you will forgive the hundreds of faults of your daughter-in-law."
If this wealth of yours is sentient, let it not be treated like an insentient object;
like the body itself, it must always be protected and never punished as if it were something devoid of purpose.
For your sake, through mind, speech, action, and much austerity, I have endured great hardship; now that you have attained the fruit [of my efforts], protect me, your handmaid who has come to you.
If she should remember me, or if she should wish to see me, then bring her here;
by that sight of you both, I too shall find great happiness. (173)
And you must constantly provide news of your conduct through messengers;
may you both be happy and well, for I shall always remember you. (174)
Listen, daughter, to these beneficial words that will bring you prosperity in the state of a wife:
in this world, a woman devoted to her husband is always honored after attaining victory.
There is no duty equal to devotion to one's husband that bestows all goals upon a woman;
she serves her husband with her whole being, in every way, and at all times. (176)
Having enjoyed all pleasures here with her husband, she shall attain an auspicious state in the end;
she is a purifier of all worlds, worthy of worship, and especially blessed. (177)
She should eat when her beloved husband has eaten; she should remain standing while her husband remains standing;
she should sleep when her husband sleeps, and she should always wake up first. 178.
In every way, one should act for the benefit [of the master] with sincerity and without deceit; one must certainly not present oneself to the master without being properly adorned. 179.
When her husband has gone abroad on business, she should be devoid of all adornment;
even if reviled, she should not revile in return, and even if struck, she should remain gracious.
If he should say, "I shall strike you," she should say, "O Master, have mercy!
and, being thus summoned, she should go to his side, leaving behind her household duties. (181)
One should not stay for long, nor stand at the doorway, nor indeed remain in another's house; one should never reveal the secrets of the household to anyone else whatsoever.
One should prepare the requisites for worship and service even if not explicitly mentioned; furthermore, one should remain waiting for the opportunity to perform such service. 183.
She should not utter her husband's name, nor should she reveal the secrets of the household;
she should never go on a pilgrimage to sacred sites without her husband’s permission.
She should never go to social gatherings or similar events without her husband;
the water from her husband’s feet is considered a sacred ford (tīrtha), the best of all sacred fords.
One should eat food through the husband's favor, considering it a great favor;
and one should not eat without having shared it with the gods, the ancestors, and guests. (186)
Among the circles of attendants, the cattle, and the community of mendicants,
she was restrained in her household utensils, skillful, joyful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
One should perform the vow by the husband's command; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.
[This applies even if he is] seated comfortably, at ease, or enjoying himself according to his own will. (188)
Even for her own internal affairs, she should never rouse her husband;
while her husband is asleep, she should never disturb his sleep. (189)
Whether he be impotent, in a wretched state, diseased, or even old;
whether he be destitute or afflicted by sorrow—one must never disregard one's husband alone.
A woman in her courses must not show her own face for three nights, nor should she let anyone hear her voice, until she becomes pure through bathing. 191.
Having bathed, she should look at the face of her own husband and never that of another;
but when her husband is far away, she should look upon the sun while remembering him.
She should also keep the articles of auspiciousness, such as turmeric and saffron.
Sindūra, collyrium, red lac, and fragrant oil. (193)
A water-pot, betel-leaf, as well as an auspicious thread, a loom, a shuttle, a necklace, ear-flowers, and earrings; 1.94.
A bracelet, a vamgiḍī, a ring, as well as a girdle, a chain, a jhāṃjharī, and likewise a hair-ornament for dressing the hair; || 195 ||
A wife desiring her husband's long life should never keep a datyūha bird at a distance;
nor should she cultivate friendship with a gadfly that destroys the summer heat.
She should not listen to the censure of her husband; she should never bathe naked;
and except at the time of sexual intercourse, she should never behave shamelessly.
One should not take up a seat upon a mortar, nor on a water-jar, nor on the sacrificial grass, nor on a pestle; nor on a grinding stone, nor on a broom, nor on the threshold.
A woman of love should be present wherever her husband finds pleasure;
she should rejoice when he rejoices, be dejected when he is dejected, and be dear to him when he is dear to her. (199)

Devoted to her husband’s welfare and remaining constant in both prosperity and adversity, she should maintain her composure and never allow her face to show any sign of agitation; she should always be cheerful.
Even if she is hidden by oil or other such means, she should not cause her husband distress;
at the time of her husband's meal, she should never reveal her own agitation. 201.
"Whether from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or even Śiva, Nārāyaṇa is the superior Lord.
To this she should give a reply with humility, and not out of anger. (202)
One should not resort to a high seat, nor should one speak what causes agitation;
one should certainly not utter slander, nor should one ever engage in quarreling. (203)
One should not laugh nor speak loudly in the presence of gurus;
seeing someone approaching from outside, one should likewise rise with a smile. (204)
The husband should always be gratified with water, food, betel, clothing, a seat, and the massaging of his feet and limbs, as well as with words that dispel fatigue and weariness.
The father gives but little, and the brother likewise gives but little;
one should propitiate the master, who is the giver of no small amount. || 206 ||
The husband is a god, the husband is the guru, and the husband is the bestower of both worlds;
the husband is dharma, the husband is the sacred ford, and the husband is the vow—for a wife, the husband is considered everything. 2.07
Without her husband, a woman is considered impure and equal to a corpse;
blessed indeed are the mother, father, and husband in whose home there dwells a devoted wife.
Three generations of ancestors on each side—of the father, the mother, and the husband—ascend to heaven through the merit of a devoted wife; otherwise, they cause them to fall.
The dust from the feet of a devoted wife is as purifying as the feet of a holy sage;
by the dust of her feet, the sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire are purified.
Even waters are purified; she is considered superior even to the Gaṅgā.
By the sight of a devoted wife, one obtains the fruit born from beholding a holy person.
A woman who treats her husband with contempt shall become a female jackal or a dog;
a woman who abandons her husband shall become an owl that dwells in trees. || 212 ||
She who strikes her husband will become a tigress or a cat;
she who displays anger in her eyes will become squint-eyed. (213)
Without her husband, she who eats sweets becomes like a gluttonous sow;
but she who speaks ill of her husband becomes mute among people for a lifetime. (214)
She who is envious of her co-wife shall become unfortunate and diseased;
she who out of desire does not look upon her husband shall become one-eyed and deformed.
Furthermore, she is the very root of domestic happiness and dharma;
the devoted wife is the foundation for rites such as those performed for the gods, ancestors, and guests.
In every house there are women proud of their beauty and charm;
they devour men by casting them into misery, for they are indeed like ogresses.
And [there were] the devoted wives Sāvitrī, Lopāmudrā, Arundhatī, Śāṇḍilyā, Śatarūpā, Anasūyā, Lakṣmī, Svadhā, and Satī. || 218 ||
Saṃjñā, Sumati, Śraddhā, Menā, and the devoted wife Svāhā—by the very power of their devotion to their husbands, they all attained the state of being honored by all. (219)
They are of four kinds: superior, middling, inferior, and most inferior.
Among these three states, the superior woman is devoted solely to her husband and is never devoted to another.
In a dream, she does not touch another with her body; she is the middle one (madhyamā).
In the waking state, she does not touch another with her body; she is the youngest (kaniṣṭhikā).
She who touches no one else and commits no transgression out of fear of her husband or fear of the world is considered a *sātīkaṇṭhikā*.
She who brings about the praise of others is called *vyabhicāriṇī*;
you are the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World, and Śiva himself is your manifest husband. 223.
By remembering you, women shall become devoted to their husbands;
however, what was previously stated has been said according to worldly custom.
Having thus instructed her, saying, "O dear daughter, as you depart,
you must return at the proper time," he embraced his daughter.
Then, for the sake of preserving some semblance of decorum, she wept slightly;
and Śivā too, out of maternal affection, wept with a faltering voice.
Then the entire family wept, overwhelmed with affection, as did those on both sides whose hearts were bound by love. || 227 ||
At the time of his departure, the men, women, gods, goddesses, and likewise the celestial nymphs, all became tearful-eyed.
Then the Mountain brought a palanquin for the sake of Pārvatī,
and there the wives of the brahmins helped Śivā ascend it.
The father, the mother, the twice-born, and all others bestowed their blessings;
they also gave the Mahārājñī customary gifts and dowries such as jewels and other valuables.
Śivā, having bowed to all her gurus, as well as her father and mother,
and having saluted the twice-born and the family priest, said, "I am going," and then departed from there.
The Himalayas and others went to Śambhu and offered their praises;
likewise, all those who were in the great pavilion and the people who carried them did so as well.
Embracing one another and bowing down, they greeted each other repeatedly;
uttering "Victory!", they departed toward their respective cities.
The noble ladies and the couples, having performed the pilgrimage, returned home;
likewise, the devotees of Śiva and others then set out on their pilgrimages.
The Mountain went with them as far as the border to see them off;
and all, praising the wedding, returned to their respective homes.
Having taken leave of the Himalaya mountains, they went home;
then Śiva, together with everyone, reached his own city and [consoled] the people.
And with affection, he fed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and all the others who had come for his wedding. (237)
Having offered appropriate worship, Śaṅkara propitiated them;
and those gods and others, having taken their leave, departed for their own abodes.
O beloved, this divine marriage of Brahmā and Brāhmī has been described;
by reading or hearing it, this [account] destroys sins and fulfills one's desires. (239)
It bestows long life, wealth, liberation, and even worldly enjoyment;
it pacifies obstacles and diseases, and is in every way a refuge of auspiciousness.
It brings great fame, leads to heaven, bestows progeny and lineage, and is the supreme granter of desires;
it should be recited everywhere during the festivals of Śiva, especially so.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this account been told—the auspicious narrative of the wedding—for the benefit of all householders. (242)
It is worthy of instruction for both girls and boys, and for both sides alike; it is in every way a great destroyer of sorrow and a bestower of happiness.
And it was exactly thus at your marriage, O Lakṣmī, in the past;
speak if you have the inclination—what else do you wish to hear? (244)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [described are]: the worship of the family deity by Pārvatī; the investiture with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); the ornaments and other items sent by Śiva; the arrival at the pavilion and other sites; the offering of *madhuparka* and other honors; the ritual of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) including the names and lineages; the giving of gifts; the circumambulation of the fire; the birth of Brahmā and the other *Vālakhilyas*; the conduct on the altar and worldly customs; the restoration of desire through the request for pleasure involving suggestive gestures (*vyaṅgya*) and the like; the honoring with food and other services; the duties of a devoted wife (*pativratā-dharma*); and the conduct of the husband and wife, and others.
The one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Journey to Kailāsa," etc.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
The daughter of the mountain Himavat was Kālī by complexion;
however, at the time of her marriage, she indeed assumed a form according to her desire.
Having assumed a fair complexion, she became like Kālī once again;
O Keśava, tell me that story—how did Gaurī become permanently fair? 2.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the form dear to those who perform the duties of a householder—a form resembling gold or like that of a land-lotus and the like. (3)
Whether resembling the moonlight or, on the other hand, like a flash of lightning,
every form of Kālī was perfectly fashioned according to its appropriate place.
The natural color of the father's lineage was indeed blue;
Śambhu and Śivā sported on their own Kailāsa with exceeding passion. || 5 ||
Śiva, addressing Śivā as "Kālī" in a playful spirit,
laughed in many ways while repeatedly uttering the word "Kālī."
In whose house the wife is blue-colored and the offspring are blue,
the family becomes black because of those blue children.
As soon as I saw her, the delusion that she was Kālī vanished and became dissolved;
there would be no radiance in the women of one's household or kinsmen [without her]. (8)
No respect whatsoever can prevail over one who dwells in the household; what can I do? According to my fate, Nīlamohinī has been obtained by me.
"If there is no objection on your part, I shall take another Gaurī;
I shall fix an auspicious moment for her marriage with the daughter of the Lord of Rain."
"Speak, O Goddess Mahākālī; give me counsel in this matter.
Thus addressed, the Great Goddess immediately became broken-hearted.
She replied: "If you have no love for my caste, why were I kept right here for all this long time?
If I am not dear to you, why was it not told to me before?"
And if the days pass with me because of my lack of delight, [then what will become of you]? (1.3)
And those who are mindless depart; why was this not told by me before?
What purpose do I have here in staying within the abode of the mindless? 1.4
If you are living in discontent, how indeed can you find delight with me?
For one who is a lord and capable, it is not impossible to acquire women. (15)
How is it that, by this much alone, she who resembles a *campaka* flower has not been brought [to me];
or rather, for one liberated and delighting in the self, pleasure is not a means to happiness? (16)
"I know that for this very reason, you previously reduced even Smara to ashes;
I believe you have been engaged in my ascetic penance for five thousand years."
For this very reason, when you had come together, it was then forbidden by me in many ways;
yet the marriage was performed by you by force, even though I was indifferent.
Let that indeed have happened; it could not possibly have been otherwise.
Even though she was gentle in all her limbs, she did not bring satisfaction to her husband.
"Though she possesses many virtues, this wife of mine remains useless while living in the household; that her worthlessness has been revealed today is indeed a good fortune. (1.195.20)
And I shall exert such effort that I may become fair-complexioned, for a woman is created as the locus of all the happiness belonging to her husband. (2.1)
In that regard, if there is no satisfaction therein, what delight is there then in being a husband? For in this act of creation, the woman's portion is exactly half of the husband's.
If she is not dear to her husband, then of what use is she? For even if she is a married woman, if she does not bring satisfaction to her husband, what purpose does she serve? (23)
There is no satisfaction from another, nor does one find contentment within oneself;
what fruit is there in that? Therefore, I shall become Gaurī, the daughter of Kāla.
Therefore, there is no bright complexion that does not exist for the sake of pleasing Śiva;
I shall abandon this [darkness] through austerity and attain a fair complexion. (25)
Or rather, having cast off this body, I shall obtain a new one through birth—one that is fairer than fair, like the pointing out of the first finger. (26)
Having spoken thus, Kālī suddenly rose and said in a faltering voice:
"O Śambhu, I beg your permission; I have a desire to go forth for penance. (27)
Upon hearing this, Śambhu became stunned; a loss of humor arose within him.
Even a jest does not cause destruction, yet it must never be uttered by one who possesses knowledge.
Thinking, "May there be separation from Pārvatī for me," Śambhu bowed to Satī and said, "O beloved, how have you been provoked to anger by my joking words? (29)
Without you, where is my delight? And you are the ground of my delight when I exist; like the two eternal gods Pārvatī and Parameśvara, we are eternally devoted to one another.
For their delight is eternal, owing to the nature of inseparability;
do not harbor agitation at my words, nor feel distress, O beautiful lady. (31)
Our state of passion, however, is eternal and not artificial;
it is for the delight of ordinary people that it has been produced as something artificial. (32)
Desiring me and thinking that I was of the same status as other goddesses, he came even by force to overpower me;
he has been reduced to ashes by me. (33)
It was not because he considered me to be Kālī that I reduced him to ashes;
rather, he was restored to life by me for your sake through Mahākāla.
I am Mahākāla and you are Kālī; we are certainly not incompatible. Indeed, this eternal form suitable for the two of us was fashioned by Kṛṣṇa.
"Do not grieve, O Great Goddess; do not set your mind upon the purpose of penance, for you have already performed penance for five thousand years in the past."
In that matter, her steadfastness toward me was tested;
subsequently, she was married by me so that she might always attain identity with me.
The lineage of Mahākāla also indeed gives rise to Mahākālī; you should not think in that regard that the lineage of Kālī would be dark. (38)
You are the first in Goloka, the second in Sadāśiva;
you are Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, as the third, and Pārvatī to me as the fourth.
"You go, you are she, you are the most excellent; O Kṛṣṇā, do not bring me distress.
I am one, and you are my second; by me, Kālī has been wedded. (1.195.40)
"There is no room for a second Gaurī; this is merely a jest. Since I am your beloved, O dear one, you should not feel anger over this jest. (41)
Then it was said, "Kālī is bitter yet beneficial to hear; she is sweet, and she has never been married to another before, nor will she ever be so hereafter. (42)
And having heard this, Pārvatī said: "I have heard many such flattering words before, but never such great flattery as this which destroys the cycle of worldly existence."
If a wife who is disliked by her husband does not indeed renounce her life, she, censured by her husband, is always utterly despised by the world. (44)
Surely there must be a great deal of resentment toward me in your heart;
otherwise, that [anger] would never have been present even in a word spoken in jest. (45)
Just as blackness is being driven away by all [the gods] and likewise by you,
so too must the blackness of my body be washed away by the fires of austerity.
Having separated the body of Kālī, I shall slay the great asuras;
having made my own portion Gaurī, I shall forever serve Hara.
Your will exists within you; Kālī, consisting of wrath, may arise.
But Gaurī, who is characterized by goodness (sattva) and performs service, shall always dwell upon my lap. 48.
