"I shall do so, O Lord; let your resolve be fulfilled.
By propitiating Brahmā through asceticism, I shall soon become Gaurī. (49)
"In the past, having propitiated Brahmā and become Satī, I wedded Hara;
likewise, having propitiated Brahmā, may I become Gaurī, and then you shall wed me."
Having spoken thus and circumambulated her husband,
the devoted wife went to that very peak of Pārvatī where she had previously performed her penance.
And having gone to that very place to perform penance, she, Nīlalohitā,
saw her parents, bowed to them, and then informed them of what had occurred.
Having assumed the dress of an ascetic woman, bathed, and made a formal resolve on that day,
she fashioned an image of Brahmā and worshipped it with excellent fruits and other offerings.
On that peak, aiming for the fruit [of her goal], she performed penance to attain a fair complexion.
Then, after a long time had passed, a tiger arrived.
Hungry, he stands nearby for the purpose of devouring Pārvatī;
as soon as he approaches her vicinity, he becomes motionless like a painting. (55)
Thus, as if performing a ritual service out of a desire for food,
she cast a compassionate glance toward him that was favorable to the Goddess.
"Since protection from other wicked and fierce creatures occurs for me when I am in the form of a lion, she has cast a compassionate glance upon me by her very nature. (57)
By a mere trace of her compassion, the tiger’s hunger subsided;
the stiffness of his limbs vanished, and he recognized the virtuous goddess.
The innate wickedness [of the demons] was then utterly destroyed;
having become Devaka, he became a restrainer of evil beings.
Brahmā, pleased by the goddess’s ascetic penance, arrived there;
and then Brahmā was duly honored by the goddess with the offering of arghya.
The Creator of the Universe spoke to her as if unaware of the purpose of her asceticism:
"What is to be accomplished by your penance? Hara has already been won through your austerity. (61)
Or perhaps this playful role of an ascetic woman is appropriate for virtuous ladies;
yet it is a marvel that you remain engaged in penance while separated from Śambhu.
Pārvatī said: "O Brahman, first the great virtuous lady Vairājī was born from Kṛṣṇa; at that time, you became my son in the past."
From that, Sadāśiva came into being, and I too then became Sadāśivā;
at that time you were my elder brother, and from your forehead [I] was born.
When he was Rudra, then I was Rudrāṇī and you were my father-in-law;
Himālaya was your son, and therefore you are my grandfather.
For this reason, O Grandfather, the quarrel of Gopī and Kali was made public here;
moreover, when the time for sleep arrived, Śambhu repeatedly said to me, "Kālī."
"Therefore, having cast off this blackness residing in my body, I desire to become fair-complexioned; grant me the fruit of my penance accordingly. (67)
Brahmā said, "So be it," and at that very moment the goddess Kālī,
casting off her dark sheath, was indeed born with a fair sheath.
The maiden Kausuki, whose nature was a dark sheath and who was named Kali,
went toward the Vindhya mountain for the destruction of Shumbha and Nishumbha.
A divine girl was born, fair-complexioned, fresh, and golden-hued like a campaka flower; she spoke to Brahmā, the creator of the universe.
"This divine lion, the protector, has become mine through my service;
O Lord of the Gaṇas, let him be granted to me as my vehicle. (71)
"So be it," Brahmā then replied, and he gave him that very lion;
he was made a lord of the Gaṇas by the Goddess under the name Somanandin.
Requested by Brahmā, Gaurī then desisted from her ascetic penance;
having bowed to her parents and the trees, she went to where Maheśvara was.
Just as she rose after bowing down, the Supreme Lord took her by both arms, embraced her, placed her upon his lap, and kissed her.
A great festival was held for her on account of the transformation of her body;
then Gaurī spoke many stories concerning the power of asceticism.
"By austerity, what indeed is not attained? Everything is established in austerity.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, it should be practiced; what more do you wish to hear? (76)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how Pārvatī became sorrowful due to Śaṅkara’s joking remark ‘Kālī,’ performed penance, and became Gaurī, while the lion, having become a devourer, became Somanandī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, there is that radiance of Brahmā."
Then Śarva was born, and he indeed became Sadāśiva.
I have heard from your mouth that this radiance is the Brahman-liṅga;
for that formless Brahman is indeed manifested in the form of Bāṇa. || 2 ||
Is it that very Śivaliṅga, or is it another one worshipped by the world? Cut through this doubt of mine by making me understand the true account of what occurred. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this divine story, which is wonderful, destructive of sins, celestial, filled with the marvels of the gods, and not destined for anyone else. 4.
For even sages who possess wives become performers of austerity when endowed with self-restraint, being solely devoted to meditation upon Brahman.
Nevertheless, due to the state of desire and in some cases by the force of bondage,
having resorted to worldly convention and not yet attained the state of Brahman— || 6 ||
And due to their ignorance, they became unaware of the gods;
for in former times, there were sages of rigid vows in the Dāruvana forest.
And they were not freed from anger; they were merely of deluded intellect, even though all those sages viewed pieces of wood and clods of earth as equal.
Furthermore, while studying the Veda and performing the rites for the establishment of the sacred fires,
they lived as householders according to the bodily mode of life.
At the time of Pārvatī’s ascetic penance, Śiva too, though without a second,
lived like an ascetic, having renounced all his own possessions.
Having neither hide nor a loincloth, nor any other means of support,
he indeed wanders about naked, protecting himself for the sake of concealment.
Wearing a garland of flowers around his neck, a youth beautiful in every limb wandered from forest to forest and through the hermitages of sages, carrying an alms-bowl.
Having said, "Give alms," he departed from there in haste for the hermitages;
meanwhile, the best of the twice-born had gone to the forest during the day to fetch sacrificial fuel.
In the excellent hermitages nearby, the wives of the sages were there alone;
they, the women of those who discourse on Brahman, beheld him as he had arrived at the hermitage.
Some became agitated and struck with wonder, while others were seized by fear;
some were bewildered there, yet others arrived, longing for a sight [of him].
The women said to one another, "Come, let us see the mendicant;
by seeing him and worshipping him, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are obtained. (16)
Having said "to one another," they took roots, fruits, and other such things; likewise, others embraced one another, while yet others held each other's hands.
Due to their mutual contact, the wives of the sages became deeply agitated; those women of the hermits said to that god, "Accept alms. (18)
He too, extending his alms-bowl toward the women, said:
"Give alms; may it be well with you; may you be possessed of wealth and sons. (19)
Having given alms, those fickle women laughed much and asked, "Who is this by whom such a vow of nakedness has been undertaken? (1.196.20)
"You are indeed a pleasing ascetic; speak, if you so desire," Śaṅkara said, smiling, "I have a secret vow."
Thinking that there would be no fruit in making [this] public, they did not ask;
thus addressed, those wives of Brahmā replied, "Come to our home."
Having uttered this, they then indeed grasped him with their bud-like hands;
some at his neck, some on his back, and some on the region of his belly.
Some [placed them] on the knees and the hips, as well as on the matted locks and the sides;
some on the feet, and others on the nose and the ears.
Thus, surrounding the lord of the monks on all sides,
those wives of the twice-born captivated him, each drawing him toward herself.
In the meantime, O brahmins, having taken their sacrificial fuel, they went to their own homes; there, this marvel was observed by them.
Seeing that which was contrary [to their expectations], they became instantly filled with rage:
"Who is this? Of what sort is he? This intoxicated man who causes such agitation among women! (27)
"Who are you? From where have you come? Why do you not wear clothes?"—though thus questioned, that Avadhūta, naked as the directions, did not say anything at all. (28)
On the contrary, by not listening to that [instruction], he displayed fickleness toward the *liṅga* and manifested the power of desire there, like a negligent yogi. || 29 ||
Perceiving his agitation and knowing him to be truly intoxicated, the gods of the earth saw that the sign of his transformation was like a sprout and struck him with blades of darbha grass.
They struck him excessively with wood, stones, and slabs of earth;
and with that blade of darbha grass, together with the mantra, they struck him from the very root.
The linga fell to the earth, its testicles severed;
when he was struck with a splinter, it broke into twelve fragments.
But when the Liṅga had been cast down from there, the Lord vanished;
then grief arose among those sages of purified souls.
Everyone is agitated; we do not know Śaṅkara.
Who is this yogi? How has he arrived? For what purpose has the ascetic himself come? (34)
As they were all speaking thus, they considered themselves to have committed a sin;
then all those fragments of the linga flew up into the sky.
Wherever each fragment went, there it then consumed whatever it encountered before it like fire; then, leaping up again, it moved forward.
Wherever and whomever he goes, he burns them in every way;
even the fragments that have gone to the netherworld (pātāla) and those who have likewise gone to heaven (svarga).
They went everywhere upon the earth, flying up and falling down;
they scorched the entire universe and did not remain steady anywhere at all. (38)
The worlds became agitated and those sages were exceedingly distressed;
none among the gods, asuras, sages, or humans found any peace. (39)
Deprived of the means for pacification, they went to Brahmā for refuge;
having gone there, they all then bowed to and praised Vidhi.
At the time of dissolution, however, they remained with their faces cast down out of shame;
they then related all that had occurred to Brahmā, the creator.
Having understood that deed of Śaṅkara, Brahmā spoke these words:
"Alas! These Brahmins are always angry; they do not know the ultimate truth. (42)
Those of deluded intellect do not know the Dharma or any ritual action;
those who realize the true nature of Brahman are proclaimed as Brāhmaṇas. ||43||
In Brahman there is no desire, nor is there any transformation or anger from any source;
indeed, the attributes of the body do not exist in the presiding witness of the body according to the ultimate truth. (44)
The twice-born truly know that the self and its attributes do not reside in the body;
whereas those who are devoid of this knowledge are possessed by the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body. (45)
Depending upon the body, they become angry and then cause others to be slain; furthermore, relying on the distinction between "another's" and "one's own," they act with malice. ||46||
Thereafter, indeed, by the power of their karma, they experience the states of heaven and hell;
therefore, the wise person should purify that mind through the cultivation of knowledge, yoga, and the self. 47.
When that [intellect] is purified, the inner self, being itself changeless, is not afflicted by the afflictions of the body nor by the auspicious and inauspicious qualities of the body. ||48||
And that being so, the possession [of the body] would not be rooted in desire, anger, and the like; and in the absence of those, such misfortune would not arise. (49)
"Sirs, you who dwell in this hermitage are overcome by anger and desire;
yet, in the hermitage of the wise, being overcome by anger and desire is in vain. (1.196.50)
In reality, there is no body of women that bears the name "woman," nor is there a body of men that bears the name "man. (51)
In both cases, however, there always exists the embodied self (śārīrātman) which bears the designation "man" (nara).
That body which is to be enjoyed by man is proclaimed as "woman" (nārī). //52//
A body, whether possessing a beard or lacking one, is called "woman.
Enjoyment belongs only to this very body, and not to any other body whatsoever. (53)
The pleasure and pain of another's body are not experienced by one's own self;
indeed, the pleasure and pain of one's own body are experienced by one's own self. (54)
Therefore, who is this woman and to whom does she belong? Who is this man and to whom does he belong? Where has all desire been laid to rest, and where is this delusion consisting of women? (55)
Where is such terrible anger, by which you do not even know yourselves?
For one who is angry, whatever he sacrifices, gives, or even mutters [is in vain]. //56//
Even if he performs an oblation, he does not obtain its fruit; he is a performer of vain acts.
And you, O twice-born ones, being knowers [of dharma], are indeed performing a censurable deed. (57)
In that case, those who are ignorant would act; what wonder is there to be inferred therein?
For whom could well-being arise, or how could it come to be, by opposing Śiva? (58)
One should not neglect a guest who arrives at the time of midday;
for such a person takes away one's own merit and gives them their own demerit. (59)
If even the Lord who dwells beyond the two abodes must be sent forth, how much more so when Śaṃkara is present?
As long as the Liṅga does not become stable, there will surely be no welfare for the worlds.
"You must act in such a way that health may be restored here.
Having heard this, the sages said, "O Brahmin, instruct us in the truth. (61)
Brahmā said: "Having propitiated Hara, we shall attain happiness;
let us go for refuge to the god Śiva on Kailāsa, the abode of Śiva. (62)
They went there together and beheld Śaṅkara standing there; then the gods began to praise the Formless One (Aliṅga). 63.
Salutations to you who are without marks, whose form is the great flame of fire;
salutations to the sky-clad one, the unchanging, the supreme creator.

Salutations to You, whose divine play is radiant; salutations to You, whose nature is forgiveness. Salutations to You, whose true form is peace; salutations to You, who possess a formidable manifestation. 65.
"O Mahādeva, forgive our offenses here; salutations be unto you!
O Lord, O God, please withdraw your own fallen liṅga. (66)
Consisting of fire and assuming twelve forms, it burns the three worlds;
O Mahādeva, have mercy, for the universe is composed of your divine play.
Thus praised and pleased, Śaṅkara then spoke with joy:
"O twice-born ones, perform worship for him against whom the offense was committed. (68)
Then there will be peace, and the linga shall remain fixed in its place;
I shall indeed become possessed of a linga in such a way that my supreme delight may be attained.
"O gods of the earth, you shall then obtain the happiness you desire; for so it is with the gods, the ṛṣis, the munis, the brahmins, and likewise the asuras. (1.196.70)
"Having gathered together, let them perform worship of my *liṅga* with the sixteen services (*upacāras*);
then these twelve shall indeed become pacified. (71)
These are fragments of my linga, and never otherwise;
wherever they fall, whether at Kurukṣetra or elsewhere, [there shall be my presence]. (72)
Let the twice-born establish them in their respective seats of origin (yoni-pīṭha).
First, you all should go together to Kurukṣetra. ||73||
Having bathed there in that lake, perform the worship of one [of them];
through his pacification, the others will become pacified fires. (74)
"O highly fortunate ones, wherever fragments of the *liṅga* have fallen, there let them perform worship; therefore, go without delay. (75)
"Having propitiated my wife Satī Sthirāyanā from a previous birth, let them transform her into the form of a womb and establish her there. (76)
Having established one water-pot and fashioned an excellent eight-petaled lotus, let them fill it with water from sacred fords and with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass.
Then, let them consecrate that pitcher with Vedic mantras;
having worshipped that pitcher, [let there be] an ablution with its water.
"Let them perform sprinkling with the Śatarudrīya mantras and also bring peace; Bāṇa will attain peace within the womb-shaped [image]. (79)
Having thus established a fragment of a *liṅga* before the *liṅga*,
let them invoke me with fragrant sandalwood, as well as with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Let them satisfy the Supreme Lord with offerings of food and other forms of worship, as well as with prostrations, hymns of praise, dances, songs, and circumambulations. 81.
Then, having performed the rite for well-being, let them proclaim, "Victory!
"O Lord, grant all peace; be gracious in every way. (8.2)
"Be peaceful, O Mahādeva, and always grant us protection.
O Brahmins, act accordingly; let them depart without delay. (8.3)
Having been addressed thus, those twice-born ones, gods, and others bowed to Maheśvara and, with tranquil minds, arrived at the shore of the lake in Kurukṣetra. (84)
There, the goddess Satī, having been propitiated by the gods (bhūsurāḥ) and being remembered, immediately appeared in her divine form for the sake of Śaṅkara. ||85||
Then that divine source, in the form of a vulva, was worshipped by the Brāhmaṇas;
there, the tip of the Liṅga was likewise established by the Brāhmaṇas with mantras.
Having thoroughly cleansed all stains, such as blood and the like, and having leveled the ground by means of treading and other methods,
one should worship it with the sixteen types of offerings using Vedic mantras and [invocations] beginning with "O God" (surādi).
There, the tip of the Liṅga was worshipped with devotion using various offerings;
and Mahādeva, being well-pleased, indeed appeared there in embodied form.
Then Hara, golden-hued, exceedingly radiant, encircled by rays of light, with a gracious countenance and tranquil, spoke to them all. (89)
"O Brāhmaṇas, that deed called malice committed by you has been pacified;
and wherever you all are, there everything is likewise at peace."
But this Linga-tip of mine, which has been worshipped by Satī and established within the womb,
shall attain fame by the name Hāṭakeśa.
And let that [liṅga] dwell in Pātāla under the name Hāṭakeśvara;
and here, let Brahmā, the creator of the universe, then [install] a liṅga made of stone.
Having installed the primordial liṅga, Brahmā himself then worshipped it; thus, it attained renown by the name Sthāṇvīśvara.
Therefore, know that after some time, it shall indeed attain fame by the name Nāgeśvara, having resorted to the Dārukā forest. 94.
Then, when the fragments had fallen, the gods went there and purified them, having established them as seats of the womb (yonipīṭhas). || 95 ||
And in each of those places, those fragments, having received worship with devotion,
became invisible of their own accord and were joined together in due order.
The tip of the *liṅga* also, having risen from the netherworld (*pātāla*),
came together and then attained union with its proper place.
Thus, having attained fullness, that conscious Liṅga then reached the testicles of Śiva and remained fixed in its proper place. ||98||
Just as it was joined together by Śiva of wondrous deeds, so too could Brahmā, or Śaṅkara, or Viṣṇu, or even Śakra do likewise. (99)
For no one else possesses this power regarding killing, binding, or movement;
rather, this wonder has been performed for the sake of honoring all.
Then, indeed, on the dark fortnight of Caitra, the fall of the linga occurred;
on that day, twelve lingas worthy of worship appeared.
In the month of Caitra, on the thirteenth day, through the conjunction of a divine lunar mansion,
and on that most meritorious and auspicious day marked by the union of Venus, the Sun, and the Moon.
The Sthāṇu-liṅga was established by Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds,
and has been worshipped by sages and hosts of gods for eternal years.
Thus, those twelve *liṅgas* are indeed the *jyotirliṅgas*;
for they are the great *liṅgas* consisting of light belonging to Śaṅkara.
Wherever there is the presence of sacrificial portions (khaṇḍas) possessing the nature of consciousness,
and where worship and consecration have been performed— that alone is Śaṅkara.
Those very [deities] exist manifestly; Śaṅkara himself shines forth in embodied form as the Great Brahman, eternally in the nature of light. 106.
I shall now describe those very jyotirliṅgas; listen, O beloved:
Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra and Mallikārjuna on Śrīśaila. (107)
One should worship Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, Oṃkāreśvara at Oṃkāra,
Kedāra on the back of the Himalayas, and Bhīmaśaṅkara at Ḍākinī.
And at Vārāṇasī, he beheld Viśveśa; Tryambaka on the bank of the Gomatī;
Vaidyanātha on the cremation ground; and Nāgeśa in the Dāruka forest.
At Setubandha one should visit Rāmeśa, and at Śivālaya, Ghuśmeśa;
the food offering (naivedya) of these should be received and eaten with great care.
O beloved, listen as I describe here those various liṅgas which were repeatedly re-established by devotees at those respective locations when they had fallen into decay. || 111 ||
In Saurāṣṭra, however, is Somanātha, who brings an end to the suffering of the Moon;
the God established by Candra became manifest and then entered into a state of absorption.
O Dear One, through worship, Someśa—an incarnation of Śiva who exists in the form of a Liṅga—is the destroyer of diseases such as consumption and leprosy. (113)
The second incarnation of Śaṅkara is indeed known as Mallikārjuna; it is said to be established on Śrīgiri in the form of a Liṅga.
When Kārttikeya, out of anger at Gaṇeśa’s marriage, departed after making a vow to observe the celibate student's discipline (brahmacarya), [the gods were distressed]. || 15 ||
There, Śaṅkara, filled with grief due to the separation from his son, departed;
that second Hara himself remained there in the form of a Liṅga.
In the city of Ujjayinī, Śaṅkara himself, assuming a physical form, went there as the deity named Mahākāla for the protection of a Vedic Brahmin.
Then Hara, by a mere *huṃkāra*, quickly reduced to ashes the demon named Dūṣaṇa, who was a destroyer of the Vedic dharma.
This very one named Mahākāla is established here in the form of a liṅga;
Śambhu, having been entreated by the gods, exists in the nature of a jyotirliṅga.
Then Śaṅkara himself, meditated upon by the Vindhya mountain, manifested there in embodied form as the fourth Jyotirliṅga installed by Brahmā.
Śambhu is established there under the name Oṃkāreśvara;
Hara himself is present in person on Mount Kedāra in the Himālaya range.
Known by the name Kedāreśvara, the fifth divine being remains there by the will of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, embodied in the form of Bāṇa.
Now begins the sixth and most excellent incarnation as the Śiva-jyotir-liṅga: Hara [manifested] to King Sudakṣiṇa, the sovereign of Kāmarūpa.
Having slain the terrible Asura, he indeed became Bhīmeśvara;
he himself remains present within the Ḍākinī in the form of a Jyotirliṅga.
He who, having come from Mount Mandara, resides personally in Kāśī as the very embodiment of light— that Viśveśvara of Kāśī is the seventh.
Then, through the praise of Gautama, Hara himself manifested on the bank of the Godāvarī as the eighth [form], known by the name Tryambakeśvara.
Then, through the praise of Rāvaṇa, Hara himself appeared upon the cremation ground as the Lord of Vaidyanātha, established as pure light.
Then Hara himself slew the tenth Rākṣasa, known as Dāruka,
and protected his devotee, the Vaiśya named Supriya.
Śambhu, accompanied by Ambikā, remained there assuming the form of a jyotirliṅga;
then followed the eleventh, installed by Rāmāditya.
He himself, in the form of Rāmeśvara and consisting of a jyotirliṅga,
Śambhu shines forth, bestowing the boon of victory upon his devotees.
Propitiated by the devotee Ghuṣma,
Hara himself went forth for the protection of Ghuṣmā’s son, who had indeed been slain by Sudehya.
Thence, he shines forth in the form of the Ghūṣmeśvara Jyotirliṅga.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the twelve forms of Hara have been described to you. (132)
Having seen, worshipped, meditated upon, or even heard of them, a person is liberated from all sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 133 ||
Thus, having taken hold of these signs, the jyotirliṅgas came into being;
then, in the course of time, due to the contraction of the sacred sites and the distinction between the ages (yugas), [they appeared].
Others will establish [the teachings] through the work of restoring what has decayed, according to the distinctions between different ages; what else do you wish to hear? 1.35

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Falling of the Liṅga with a Blade of Darbha Grass and the Twelve Jyotir-liṅgas for the Naked Śaṅkara Who Went to Dāruvana for Alms," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Blessed One, O Lord, tell me about the worship of the Ācārya, the worship of Vyāsa, and the worship of the Guru,
which constitute the nature of daily worship.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
One should worship the preceptor Vyāsa, as well as the Guru, according to the rules and with devotion;
having brought the vessel for worship along with the ritual offerings, one should go before the Guru.
One should first pay homage by touching the feet with the head,
and then perform the consecration of the big toe of the right foot with water.
Then, one should place there in the vessel flowers, saffron, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
one should offer sandalwood paste and smear it there with a drop [of liquid].
Afterwards, one should smear that sandalwood paste on the forehead with an upward line;
in the center, one should fashion an auspicious crescent moon mark made of saffron along with unbroken grains of rice.
One should place upon his head a highly valuable and radiant turban-band (paṭṭaka),
excellent, long, and richly colored, set with rows of golden stars.
Likewise, one should give a silk scarf, a woolen garment, and a fine bodice; as well as an upper garment with gold thread and two types of woven cloths.
One should give a lower garment, a bathing cloth, and likewise a new upper garment; and one should also give a beautiful, soft ball with a concealed cord.
One should also give a couch, a mattress, pieces of cloth, and a coverlet;
one should likewise give soft leaf-covers and even a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Likewise, one should provide a shoulder-strap and an excellent seat;
one should also give two cotton side-cushions as well as a cotton cloth.
Likewise, there are two small pots and two small baskets;
also, the vessel for sipping water (ācamanī), the oblation vessel (homapātra), the worship vessel (pūjāpātra), and the triple-mouthed vessel (tribhāṇaka).
A round vessel, as well as a drinking vessel, an excellent water-pot,
a betel-box with an umbrella, and two very soft sandals.
One should indeed give sandals, a staff, and an excellent waist-band, all fashioned from various metals and materials. (13)
There were golden ornaments for the ears, as well as auspicious ornaments for the neck;
ornaments for the hands, ornaments for the waist, and ornaments for the feet in every respect.
One should give chains, bracelets, garlands, rings, excellent necklaces, and a golden girdle, along with the finest fragrant substances.
One should indeed offer musk, camphor, various fragrant oils, and scented body-pastes with great devotion.
A vehicle, a celestial chariot, a carriage, a mount, and a cow that yields milk;
likewise, male and female servants, as well as wealth, especially gold and silver. || 17 ||
And one should give various kinds of fine food, grain,
pulses and the like, as well as prepared items such as vessels, cumin and the like, and sour condiments.
One should offer sugarcane products, fresh butter, ghee, and various kinds of food directly to the venerable guru, who is the yogi Nārāyaṇa himself.
To the Brahmin, the giver of knowledge, the bestower of mantras, and the compassionate one—to that venerable Guru, one should offer whatever is dear to one's own heart. (1.197.20)
Having thus performed everything, he then again placed near his side various kinds of fruits, both dried and fresh.
He who indeed gives the gift of liberation to the venerable Guru, having bowed at his feet, [should address him] as "Vīra" and also as "Gulāla. (22)
One should offer the sacred tulasī leaf and various kinds of flowers,
and perform the washing of the two holy feet with milk.
One should also perform the ceremonial bathing of the Guru with milk according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, having bathed him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water.
Having bathed repeatedly with a substance that removes impurities, one should massage the major limbs to eliminate fatigue. (25)
One should cleanse the body with garments and then offer fragrant scents;
one should put on clothes, ornaments, and wear fine decorations. ||26||
With sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, garlands, collyrium, fragrant powders for the head, golden necklaces, jewels, diamonds, and so forth, he [worshipped] with devotion. (27)
One should worship with incense, lamps, and various auspicious food offerings;
one should worship and feed [the deity] comfortably with sweet, pleasing, and most delicious foods.
One should offer fragrant water for drinking and excellent betel leaf; likewise, one should offer pleasant fruit and perform the waving of lights (ārātrika). ||29||
Then one should offer excellent hymns of praise like a staff, prostrations, an apology for any faults,
circumambulation with palms joined in reverence, and the offering of handfuls of flowers.
Having received the blessings spoken by the guru and accepted the gift of grace,
and having taken leave of him, one should go home together with the recipient of the gift of grace.
Having bestowed that very grace upon his own kinsmen, he should always meditate on the Guru in the morning and worship him in the proper sequence. ||32||
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru is the manifest Supreme Brahman, the giver of liberation, for he is indeed the purifier.
There is no substance equal to the guru; there is no deity higher than the guru;
there is no liberation other than through the guru; there is no merit greater than that of the guru. (34)
Within the body of the Guru, Hari, the Supreme Brahman, shines eternally;
the Imperishable Brahman is in his head, and Vāsudeva is upon his forehead.
The Sun and Moon are in the two eyes, and the Aśvinīkumāras are in the nose;
Nārāyaṇa, the sacrifice, is in the mouth, and the circle of the Vedas is on the tongue.
Sarasvatī resides in the speech of the guru, Viṣṇu himself dwells in the heart,
and the Lord Vaiśvānara always abides in the stomach.
In her hand is a lotus, and Kamalā Mahālakṣmī resides in her mind;
the Vasus dwell in her feet, as do the purifying sacred fords (tīrthas).
The principles (tattvas) exist as deities within all the sense organs, and the goddesses reside in the pores of the skin;
she is the form of the Guru, the embodiment of merit, the embodiment of mantra, and the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī). 39.
Heaven, truth, and Vaikuṇṭha are all established within the form of the Guru;
the eternal, unconditioned bliss of Brahman resides in the Guru.
One who knows Brahman is Ānanda; he alone is the Guru and no other.
The syllable *ga* refers to rays and knowledge, while the syllable *ra* refers to substance and giving. (41)

The Guru is said to be one who possesses the substance of light himself through the gift of knowledge; the syllable *ga* signifies the realization of mantra, while the syllable *ra* likewise signifies the act of bestowing it. (42)
The Guru, who is Lord Hari himself, is the locus of the power to bestow the mantras;
food given to the Guru shall produce the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||43||
Giving garments and other gifts to the guru bestows the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
worshiping the guru is the worship of Hari, for the guru is considered the fruit of yoga. (44)
The Guru is the vow, the Guru is the sacrifice, and the Guru alone is meditative absorption;
the Guru is declared to be the oral tradition, and the Guru is considered to be direct realization. ||45||
When the guru is pleased, there shall be the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), tranquility (śama),
and indeed all the means of practice (sādhanas) are truly accomplished when the guru is satisfied.
At birth, the parents are declared to be the gurus; the one who performs the naming ceremony is the guru;
the mother is the instructor of speech, and the sister is the instructor of practical duties. 47.
The best of gurus is one who bestows the sacred thread, teaches the scriptures, imparts mantras, grants knowledge, and bestows liberation. ||48||
Immersed in beginningless ignorance, this self wanders through the various wombs;
therefore, by constantly bestowing knowledge, one should utterly destroy its ignorance. (49)
Having brought about the destruction of latent impressions and karmas,
he then certainly shows the path of enjoyment through the propitiation of Hari.
This very Guru, who bestows everything, leads one to the state of liberation;
he is the remover of suffering and the giver of happiness—who else could be a greater Guru than him? (5.1)
The power of the Guru, which is of the nature of knowledge, having entered the self of the disciple,
the Guru brings about liberation through his own direct experience.
Initiation, possessing the power of knowledge, enters the body of the disciple and leads him to liberation through the bestowal [of grace], purification, and the power of the Guru. (53)
A disciple deserves grace in accordance with initiation and instruction; however, in the absence of initiation and instruction, there is no attainment of knowledge, nor liberation. (54)
Therefore, through this purificatory rite called initiation and through the acquisition of knowledge called instruction,
the disciple shall always attain purity gradually by means of the Guru.
Because he is to be instructed, because of the reason for reverence toward the teacher, and because it is the practice of the cultured, the disciple should observe reverence toward the teacher. (56)
He who is the Guru is declared to be Hari; he who is Hari is remembered as the Guru. The Guru is Kṛṣṇa himself, abiding as the very essence of knowledge and instruction. (57)
As is Kṛṣṇa, so is knowledge; as is knowledge, so is the guru. The fruit of worshiping Kṛṣṇa, knowledge, and the guru is equal.
This Guru is the embodiment of all gods and consists of all mantras;
the disciple, with every effort, should bear the Guru’s command upon his head. (59)
If one who seeks the highest good does not transgress the teacher’s command even in thought, that disciple who obeys the teacher’s command attains the perfection of knowledge. (1.197.60)
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, one should carry out the word of the guru;
by the guru’s command, one should perform other duties as if offering oneself.
One should perform all actions in the presence [of the teacher] and with the permission of the guru;
in the house of the guru or in his presence, one should not sit as one pleases.
Since the Guru is the manifest God himself, his house is a temple of the Divine;
just as gold here sheds its impurity through contact with fire.
Just as ghee situated near fire melts quickly, and just as dry wood is consumed when the fire blazes; ||64||
In the very same way, through contact with a Guru, a human being casts off impurity;
all sin dissolves away and latent tendencies are utterly consumed by fire. (65)
One should not provoke the anger of the guru through thought, deed, or speech;
for by his anger, one's lifespan, prosperity, knowledge, and virtuous deeds are consumed. (66)
For those who harbor anger toward him, their sacrifices become fruitless;
indeed, even their restraints and observances likewise turn out to be fruitless.
One should never speak anything contrary that pierces the vital points of the guru;
for if a disciple speaks thus out of great arrogance, he indeed goes to a downward state. 68.
One should not practice misconduct in thought, deed, or speech;
one should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru, whether commanded or not. (69)
Whether in the presence or in the absence of the guru, one should act for the guru's pleasure;
setting aside one's own affairs on all sides, one should attend to the guru's business. (1.197.70)
The reality that generates consciousness, intermingled with supreme bliss—he who has realized this here in the world is the very one who bestows liberation in this world. (7.1)
A boat carries that which is supported by it; can a stone carry another stone?
How can there be awakening for one devoid of Brahman, and how indeed can there be self-mastery? (72)
United here with the reality of Brahman, the liberated one liberates all beings;
his intellect, satisfied by that experience, has reached the pinnacle of bliss. (73)
By the mere sight of him, supreme bliss arises;
by the act of serving him, the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) is certainly accomplished. ||74||
For that embodied being, everything becomes accomplished through the desire to serve him;
he alone, full of bliss, is to be served by those seeking liberation.

Because knowledge is the realization of the Self and the attainment of Brahman, yet liberation is not [attained thereby]; nor is bliss even reached—therefore, that state is not to be realized while remaining under a teacher. (76)
One should always serve with devotion the brothers and sons of the guru who bestow awakening and gather disciples through devotion; one should constantly propitiate the guru.
One should satisfy him who bestows fearlessness upon all and whose mind is overcome with compassion, through manifold devotion and worship consisting of the offering of one's very self.
The disciple should propitiate [the guru] until he becomes pleased;
when the guru is pleased, the disciple's sins are immediately destroyed. (79)
Therefore, [give] wealth, jewels, fields, and houses; ornaments, garments, and vehicles, beds, and seats. (1.197.8) 0.
One should give these to the guru with devotion according to one's means; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires one's own welfare. 81.
He alone is the father, the mother, the husband, the kinsman, the wealth, the happiness, the companion, and the friend; therefore, one should offer everything to him. 82.
Those who do not fall into despondency even when reviled or beaten—those who are non-violent, compassionate, and whose minds are intent upon liberation; ||| 83 ||
Free from pride, wise, having abandoned rivalry, speaking kindly,
upright, gentle, pure, humble, and steady-minded— (84)
Such auspicious women and men, composed of eternal existence, as well as female and male disciples, should take refuge in a true guru. 85.
Those disciples who, being fully committed, perform service for their teacher—there is no fault in them for lacking independence, because they act for the sake of another. (86)
What need is there for much speaking here? Whoever has taken refuge in a Guru and has set out upon the path of Brahman will surely become a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. (87)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Guru-Worship and Other Matters," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 197 ||
Śrī Lakṣmī said: "I have heard that in ancient times Kāma was born from the form of Nārāyaṇa;
at that time, his residence among the lords was purely mental."
Furthermore, O Supreme Puruṣa of the Purāṇas, tell me according to the truth: when was this [teaching] revealed by the Creator at the time of creation?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having fully propitiated Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
created all those subjects, beginning with the gods, asuras, and humans.
Having created the lords of creatures, the most excellent of gods headed by Dakṣa,
he then created his mind-born daughter Sandhyā, who was beautiful in form and engaged in silent recitation.
Having seen her—who was exceedingly beautiful, possessed of lovely eyebrows, capable of deluding the minds of sages, worthy of a man, and endowed with every excellence—(he was struck). || 5 ||
At that time, all mental states consisted of beautiful women; may such women, who are the very locus of the qualities of passion, be auspicious.
May there always be for those couples the power that increases affection and takes the form of mutual attraction. (7)
Having thus understood their intentions, the Creator himself mentally resolved, "So be it," and fashioned a man of that very kind.
At that moment, a handsome man of golden complexion, broad-chested and with a fine nose, appeared there from the mind of Brahmā.
With well-rounded thighs, hips, and shanks, with dark, curved tips to his manes, with joined eyebrows, restless, and with a face possessing the splendor of the full moon. || 1.198.10 ||
With a very firm and broad chest, adorned with hair like a swarm of bees, he was handsome, cloud-colored, stout, and dressed in fine blue garments. || 11 ||
With his hands, eyes, face, feet, and trunk reddened,
possessing a slender waist and beautiful tusks, he has the scent of a rutting elephant.

With eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus, his mouth perfumed with betel; possessing a neck like a conch shell, he whose banner bears the fish, tall in stature, and having the makara as his vehicle. || 13 ||
Arrogant, bearing the five flower-weapons and adorned with a flowery bow,
the handsome youth caused his two eyes to roll by casting a sidelong glance.
Flickering with his two beautiful eyes and steeped in the sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), upon seeing him, all the sons of Brahmā, headed by Dakṣa, [were captivated]. (15)
Attaining the highest eagerness, their minds drawn by wonder,
the hearts of them all quickly became agitated.
There was no fortitude at all among those whose minds were agitated by desire;
then Kama himself, having bowed to Brahma, spoke in haste.
"What shall I do? O Brahmin, I am your servant; employ me in some task.
For a wise man should employ a servant according to his qualities and appearance. (18)
Having heard this, Brahmā spoke to his son Kāma, the bestower of pleasure:
"With this form of yours and with your five flower-arrows..."
Deluding both men and women, create the eternal creation;
all beings shall possess vital breath and consciousness, as shall I, Viṣṇu, and others.
"We shall remain under your control and act as your providers of sustenance;
having entered into the minds of people and assuming an invisible form. (21)
Becoming a great bestower of happiness, perform the eternal creation;
for the minds of living beings, longing for pleasure, shall become the target of your arrows.
"Let it be so; your place has been established, but the essence born of the body is [the soul].
Let your sense organ be the garden, and may you there be the one who produces intoxication. (23)
Thus has that great deed of yours been told, which set in motion the creation, and how our minds were stirred by it; now, therefore, [listen] to yours.
He is called Manmatha because of his power over the mind; he is also known as Kāma because of mutual desire;
and he is renowned as Manobhava because he is born from the mind. (25)
Because you cause intoxication, you shall be Madana; because you are the pride of all, Kandarpa; and your renown shall be Puṣpabāṇa and Rati-pati. || 26 ||
Among the gods, there shall indeed be no one equal to you in pervasive power;
therefore, let all places belong to you, the all-pervading one.
"O sinless one, your weapons have always been described as the Enthraller, the Delighter, the Bewilderer, the Witherer, and the Slayer. (28)
"Accompanied by them, you shall indeed achieve victory over all created beings.
Having received this benediction in the presence of Sandhyā, he [departed]. (29)
To test his proficiency, he discharged arrows at the Creator;
in this manner, he repeatedly fixed his bow with shafts.
Assuming the *ālīḍha* stance and drawing his bow with great effort, he formed it into a circle; fragrant winds began to blow. || 31 ||
The Enchanter deluded all the mental sages;
gazing at Sandhyā,
they were filled with the force of transformation, their passion increased and their senses inflamed.
Having seen the twilight, forty-nine states arose from the body.
That which was intended by Brahmā through desire was made manifest and rendered possible;
then, from the body of Brahmā, the bodily elements and water fell at that time.
The groups of ancestors known as the Agniṣvāttas were born; they are remembered as Pitṛs, blue-colored ascetics who have made the house of saṃsāra empty.
The Agniṣvātta purifiers consist of sixty-four thousand,
and likewise there are eighty-six thousand others known as the Barhiṣads.
Then, from the body of Dakṣa, the bodily fluids fell upon the earth;
from that was born an excellent woman, endowed with all auspicious qualities.
She possessed gentle limbs and a slender waist, with fine golden hair;
her body was soft, her teeth were beautiful, and she blazed with a circle of splendor.
Her limbs were lovely with a golden luster, her body possessed the brilliance of the moon,
she was twelve years of age, named Rati, and most enchanting.
She was filled with the essence of desire and a true mine of all beauty;
she was then [the daughter] of Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, and Aṅgiras.
And the seed of those whose senses were unrestrained fell upon the ground;
from it were born the hosts of Pitṛs, namely the Somapās and the Ājyapās.
Likewise, the Sukālins and the Haviṣmants were the Kavyavāhakas;
from Kratu were born the Somapas, who were the Ūrdhvakālins of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage. 42.
From Pulastya were born the Ājyapas, and from the sons of Aṅgiras came the Haviṣmats;
this entire host of ancestors became known as Kavyavāṭ in every respect.
Having become the mother of the ancestors (Pitṛs), Sandhyā became intent upon that goal. Then Dakṣa spoke to Kāma regarding her, who was endowed with excellent form and qualities.
"Accept this daughter of mine as your wife, for she is worthy of you in her virtues.
Having said this, he gave her to him—she who was born from the sweat upon his body. (45)
Having married her, named Rati, who sought him as her husband,
Smara too rejoiced exceedingly with that excellent Rati.
Beholding the pair of her eyebrows, he forgot his own bow;
seeing the movement of her side-glances, he forgot the discharge of his arrows.
Having smelled his fragrant breath, she forgot the breeze from Mount Sumeru;
having beheld her beloved’s face with its beautiful eyes, she forgot the moon. (48)
Beholding her two breasts, which resembled golden lotus buds and were adorned with a pair of nipples, he remembered a pair of stars.
Seeing the garland hanging down between her two firm, plump, and elevated breasts as far as her navel, he remembered the moonlight.
Having beheld her pair of eyes, he forgot the twanging of his bowstring, which was like the humming of bees; having beheld them, he forgot the lotus petals [that adorned it]. (5.1)
Beholding her slender belly, she remembered the golden altar;
beholding her two thighs, she remembered a pair of plantain trees. (52)
And beholding the reddish hue at the heels, the foreparts, and the edges of his feet,
he remembered his friend named Anurāga, who was stationed at those very feet.
Her pair of hands was red, with nails resembling *kiṃśuka* flowers, and was captivating due to her rounded fingers that tapered to fine tips. (54)
Having seen her pair of arms, which were as long as a pair of lotus stalks and resembled the coils of the excellent jewels on the serpent-arms of Hari, he remembered them. 55.
Seeing her soft, glossy, and coral-hued [complexion], Kāma indeed rejoiced;
her enchanting mass of hair resembled a dark blue cloud. (56)
Resembling the tail-hair of a yak-cow, the life-sustainer of Smara shines forth;
such is this wheel-lotus, provided with fragments of lotus-stalks. (57)
She was the abode of all loveliness, possessing beauty in every limb,
adorned with twelve ornaments, and endowed with the sixteen modes of amorous grace.
Beholding that enchanting Rati, Kāma seized her with eager longing;
there, Brahmā duly performed their marriage ceremony.
Then a great festival took place there, proceeding with happiness;
Dakṣa was exceedingly pleased, and his daughter Rati rejoiced.
Having attained exceedingly great pleasure, Kāma shone resplendently together with her;
and beholding her again and again, he took hold of her upon his heart.
She who was formerly Sandhyā, the daughter of Brahmā born from his mind,
having performed austerities and cast off her body, has been born as Arundhatī.
Having become the daughter of Medhātithi, she chose Vasiṣṭha as her husband;
on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river, she performed penance for four yugas.
Then, as soon as he was born, Brahmā granted him the boon he had requested, saying, "So be it," and that the god of love (Smara) should enter him.
From that day forward, Smara entered into twelve more beings;
she too, having thus withdrawn her asceticism, went into the sky.
"And she dwells in the circle of the Seven Sages as the companion of Vasiṣṭha;
thus, O Lakṣmī, this story of Kāma has been told to you once more. (66)
At the beginning of the Kalpa, she was born as the daughter of a Cāṇḍāla and was exceedingly virtuous. During a twelve-year drought, the sages, seeking food, [approached her].
Then, having been entrusted by her father, they arrived together for the sake of alms;
along with that alms-food, [she went] to Vasiṣṭha, the purifier.
She was removed from the midst of the cows, purified, and wedded;
she alone is the goddess Arundhatī, devoted solely to her husband.
Thus everything has been told to you exactly as it is;
regarding the different types of kalpas and the different modes of creation, what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Birth of Sandhyā, Pitṛs, Kāma, Rati, and Arundhatī," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the creation of living beings.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, during the churning of the ocean, you assumed the form of Mohinī for the purpose of deluding the Daityas; having seen you then, Śaṅkara— || 1 ||
"How did even the Lord of Māyā, who is devoid of qualities, fall into the delusion of Māyā? O Lord, sever this doubt of mine and tell me that story."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to all this exactly as it is, without any doubt:
I am Nārāyaṇa in person, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest.
Though I am devoid of qualities, I always become the source of divine attributes;
by my will, the entire universe arises from my qualityless form.
That which has arisen is endowed with qualities, being mixed with the qualities of sattva and the rest;
I am the impeller and the instigator of both Prakṛti and its qualities.
Just as, wherever, and whatever kind of task arises,
I myself accomplish all of that by assuming such a form.
"Resorting to the entry into another [body], I shall accomplish my purpose as one who seeks virtue;
Śaṅkara is my devotee, forever untainted by Māyā. (7)
He is not agitated by the qualities of illusion, nor is he stained by illusion;
nevertheless, for the sake of instructing others, I have displayed this delusion.
Both virtuous women and virtuous men who have taken refuge in the vow of renunciation,
having utterly conquered delusion, indeed become divine beings.
Nevertheless, if through the force of the senses yoga should occasionally fail and delusion should arise, they might become performers of vulgar acts.
Even Śaṅkara, the king of yogis, attained the delusion of Māyā through his devotion;
therefore, those who desire liberation must break free from the senses and so forth.
Heedfulness must always be guarded; heedlessness is said to be death.
Heedlessness is indeed delusion, born from the pursuit of men and women. 1.2.
"Those devoted to Him must never, under any circumstances, partake of intoxicants derived from the body.
This was shown by me to Śaṅkara for the purpose of providing this counter-instruction. 13.
Furthermore, for the sake of attaining gold and for the purpose of bestowing the auspicious mineral (mercury), I have performed this rite with its proper cause within the womb of this Vasumatī.
Listen to that very account of mine exactly as it occurred; because of the unity of these two, this story is considered to bring about liberation through its hearing. (15)
Having assumed the form of a woman and deluded the Dānavas, Viṣṇu caused the gods to drink the Soma; having heard this, Śaṅkara himself [acted]. 16.
He desired to see that form and arrived there with great haste; then, having understood Śaṅkara’s intention, Hari assumed the form of Mohinī.
Having caused the gods to drink the nectar, she departed from where Hara was,
appearing as a sixteen-year-old woman filled with the fullness of all desires.
Adorned with a braid of hair and richly decorated with shimmering leaf-patterns,
she was captivating with a face resembling the full moon of autumn.
With two frowns upon her forehead that pierce the heart of those who rely on the arrows of desire,
she is adorned with flower-ornaments that are red, yellow, and pure white.
Her excellent hair-braid was fashioned into a cluster of land-lotuses,
and she was adorned with leaf-patterns of saffron mixed with fragrant sandalwood.
Her beautiful eyes, with corners moistened by dark, shimmering collyrium, reminded one of the secret cave of the bodiless God of Love, filled with a subtle radiance in their center.
Her earrings were adorned with fine gems, jewels, gold, and diamonds; she was further endowed with necklaces of shimmering, exquisite, and finest pearls hanging down.
Her cheeks were like golden moons adorned with beautiful diamonds;
her nose was like a jewel, its bridge like a slender golden star.
Her pair of lips, like ripe bimba fruits, called to mind the act of kissing;
her chin was adorned with a shimmering golden mark set amidst jewels.
Adorned with the excellent Kaustubha gem, which possesses a luster equal to the rising sun,
her chest is beautified by golden necklaces and the two breasts.

With a neck like a conch shell and a golden necklace around her throat, her beautiful arms were like the core of a plantain tree; the luster of her fingernails was like the moon, and the radiance of her fingers was like excellent red sprouts.
She was adorned with golden rings, armlets, beautiful bracelets, and *vaṅgīḍīs*;
her two feet shone with anklets, girdles, waist-bands, and toe-rings.
Adorned with golden anklets accompanied by tinkling bells, she was joined with a girdle of various and wonderful golden beads in red and other colors. || 29 ||
Her garment was a beautiful cloak with edges adorned with golden stars;
she wore a bodice that resembled a fresh panel of dyed cloth.
Holding in her hand a garment possessing the splendor of the moon and lightning,
she plays again and again with an excellent leaping ball.
Moving gracefully through a tree-thicket rich with the beauty of flowers and sprouts,
she was possessed of a slight tremor and the swaying motion of her breasts and hips.
Her face became visible as her veil was partially displaced,
and her long eyes were restless with amorous gestures, expressions, and playful charms.
Placing her hand upon her breasts, she pressed the bodice excessively;
at times, seizing her braid, she adjusted her lower garment.
Playing with a ball, she who causes extreme infatuation of the mind goes along, repeatedly lifting her garment, her face often breaking into smiles. (35)
Having tucked up her lower garment so as to reveal her uncovered thighs,
she would slink away under some pretext and creep toward wherever Śaṅkara was located.
Beholding her, who was thus entirely focused on him, with his own one-pointed mind, Śambhu became stupefied; his soul was overwhelmed and his inner being was struck down.
Through the loss of his conscious awareness and memory, he became deprived of light;
he was mounted solely upon the radiance of the state of desire, becoming entirely absorbed in that mental construction.
Then she became deprived of her excellent shawl, which had been carried away by the waves of the wind;
meanwhile, her girdle loosened and fell to the ground with a jingling sound.
Situated within the space of consciousness, like a flash of lightning amidst the clouds,
it is intensely radiant with great light, possessing the luster of gold, campaka flowers, and the sun.
Beholding her, Śaṅkara set his mind upon becoming deeply attached;
the wind carried away his garments, and she carried away Śaṅkara.
Then, filled with shame, she moved from tree to tree;
meanwhile, his senses became hardened by the force of passion, and he was overflowing with virility.
Having followed him with great persistence and seized his hair, he drew that body near,
lifted it up, and embraced it with both arms.
She was forcibly embraced and kissed again and again;
though unwilling, she freed herself from his embrace. (44)
She fled toward a thicket of trees, and Hara followed her;
due to the intensity of the force of his semen, it was discharged as he ran.
Wherever she did not run, there the semen of him who pursued her fell upon the earth; from that, mines of gold were produced.
Mohinī moves swiftly ahead by way of the sky;
the deluded Maheśvara, driven by the force of desire, runs after her.
On the ground, in forests, on mountains and the like, by rivers, and in the woods—
wherever Mahādeva ran, there the mineral element likewise fell.
And in each of those places, through contact with that [fluid], the earth indeed became made of silver, following the oozing of the entire substance of Śaṅkara. ||49||
Lassitude arose, and then awakening occurred once more:
"Who indeed is this enchanting form? Who am I? And where am I going? (1.199.50)
"How have I incurred this stain? How has there been a transformation in one who is unchanging? Such a form could not exist without the Creator of the World. (5.1)
What illusion could there be for one who is free from illusion, by whom illusion has been brought under control?
Is this not indeed the Vaiṣṇavī Māyā that has made such an effort, saying, "Come to me"? (52)
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded by his very illusion;
if I am drawn by him, then there is indeed nothing wonderful for me.
Joined with that very [power], I always delight with Śivā;
impelled by that very [power], I sport according to her will.
Having reflected thus, his face rejoiced and did not fall into dejection;
and the Blessed One also, considering that devotee to be a true knower (pramātṛ), [bestowed grace upon him].
Assuming the form of a female seducer, she said: "Who are you, and why have you been rendered inert?
Where has your virtuous courage gone, as if you were devoid of strength without yoga? (56)
By whom has such a state been brought upon you, even though you are capable? Come, come; let us enjoy ourselves together in the secluded groves of the lonely forest. (57)
Thinking, "You shall never again obtain such a woman with an uninjured waist," Kṛṣṇa himself, Nārāyaṇa, kissed him.
But Hara, his vital energy shattered and his penis overcome by flaccidity, lacked the enthusiasm to take delight with her there. ||59||
There he spoke to Mohinī, saying, "Nowhere except for Nārāyaṇa..."
No one else at all is able to rob the yogis of the steadfastness of their minds.
Salutation to that Blessed One who assumes forms through his illusory power;
salutation to the divine Kṛṣṇa, to Nārāyaṇa, to Viṣṇu. ||6 1||
Salutations to you, whose own nature is enchantment and who are of the form of delusion;
in you, Nārāyaṇa, the highest beyond the high, there is no sorrow for me here.
Nevertheless, O Lord of the gods of gods, protect me from the delusion of Māyā;
for this delusion, which arises as latent desire (*vāsanā*), is the cause of bondage for all worlds.
Your yoga is considered to be both delusive in nature and liberating in nature, yet devoid of qualities;
this form of yours is supreme, a vessel for exceeding beauty. (64)
"For that [gift] bestows liberation alone, and not bondage for myself or anyone else;
therefore, what has indeed been done by you is truly my supreme gain. (65)
Even while dwelling with Pārvatī, I shall always remember you, the enchanting one;
thus, I will become obsessed and shall surely incur a loss of virtue.
Having heard this, the Lord, the husband of Kamalā, who knows the heart of Śambhu,
withdrew his female form and in an instant became four-armed.
Laughing, the Soul of All embraced Hara with his heart and said:
"O Śaṅkara, you, my devotee, have conquered the illusion created by me."
Neither by knowledge, nor by fortitude, nor even by supreme devotion can anyone other than you cross over this Māyā in the form of a woman.
This creation of entities, like a delusive deception, is a mere form of a rope called "bondage"; it does not touch those who have taken refuge in Me.
She is the deluder of non-devotees, yet the bestower of enjoyment and liberation upon devotees;
having entered into union with me, she is always devoid of qualities for her devotees.
Mahāmāyā, Mahālakṣmī, Kamalā, Rādhikā, Ramā, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and Pārvatī do not bestow bondage at all. (72)
Rukmiṇī, Kambharā, Brāhmī, the devoted Jānakī, Mohinī, and Tulasī—these bestow liberation, not bondage. (73)
Prabhā, Māṇikī, Jayā, and Lalitā do not bestow bondage;
all of them, being of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, are traditionally held to grant liberation through yoga.
Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Campā, Haimī, Dayā, Ramā, as well as Puṣpā, Muktā, the goddess Śāntā, Godāvarī, and Manu. (75)
Ojasvatī, Jīvā, and Maṅgalā were those excellent female companions;
they were divine embodiments of those virtuous yoginīs. (76)
Therefore, those who have directly realized Kṛṣṇa as their mark and wear His garments are purifying and bestowers of liberation;
they are indeed the Yoginīs of Sāṃkhya and likewise the female renunciants (saṃnyāsinīs) here.
Those who are dispassionate, who possess my form, and who are female ascetics granting liberation—
all of them are indeed my powers (śaktis), and being of my nature, they are beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).
Whosoever has attained union with them, those living beings are eternally devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
they are pure while living here and are indeed liberated—of this there is no doubt. (79)
Just as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are endowed with yoga in those [energies],
so too are Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others eternally liberated and eternally the supreme lords.
"Furthermore, O Śambhu, those whose lives are objects of compassion are eternally liberated lords;
thus has this unsurpassed majesty of mine been told to you. (8.1)
Those whose vision is clouded by defects do not correctly understand this; nor do those who are attached to my own nature, nor those who grasp at awakening from me. (82)
