He is the master, the doer, the destroyer, the teacher, the nourisher, and the protector;
he is the chosen deity and the one to be worshipped—for there is no guru higher than the master.
I am a maiden born of a noble family, carefully protected by my beloved;
I am the wife of Upabarhaṇa and the daughter of Citraratha.
O Hari, O Mādhava, the wife of the Gandharva king is ever devoted to her husband;
you alone are capable of bringing all things under your control.
Bring Time, Yama, and Death into my presence.
Having heard Mālāvatī’s words, the Blessed One, the mine of compassion, [spoke].
Having summoned them to the assembly, he showed them directly;
there, Mṛtyukanyā was seen by Mālāvatī as she arrived.
Dark-complexioned, of terrible form, clad in red garments, and inspiring great fear,
she likewise stands with six arms on the left side of her husband named Kāla.
Smiling yet possessing a cruel forehead, she was accompanied by sixty-four sons;
and Kāla was seen by Mālatī—six-faced, hideous, and roaring.
He has twenty-four eyes, sixteen arms, and is fierce;
he has six feet, is black in color, wears red garments, and is terrifying. ||79||
Thus Mālāvatī beheld those terrifying hosts of diseases—children, the aged, the very elderly, and youths who were utterly deformed. (1.201.80)
There he beheld Yama, black in color and of a cruel form.
Having seen him previously, Mālāvatī questioned the teacher of Dharma. ||8 1 ||
"O Dharmarāja, why do you take my beloved away at an untimely hour?
Yama replied, "No one on earth dies before their time has come. (82)
O virtuous lady, without the command of the Lord, I do not move even a falsehood;
I am Time, the Daughter of Death, and the diseases—all are servants of the Lord.
Just as one's lifespan is determined by destiny at the time of conception, so too does the Daughter of Death approach the embodied being; O Mālikā, listen with respect! (84)
"Though I was created here long ago by the Creator of the Universe for this very task, I am not able to abandon a living being whose death has arrived. (85)
And if Satī were capable of reducing the world to ashes, then I myself would have been reduced to ashes; I shall not kill embodied beings. (86)
Impelled by Time, I and my sons, the diseases, perform our task as commanded; there is no fault whatsoever on our part in this matter. (87)
Then Mālāvatī spoke at that time to the one born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa:
"O Lord, how can you carry off my beloved while I am still alive? (88)
Kāla said: "Listen, Mālāvatī, to everything done by Hari:
who am I, who is Yama, who is the daughter of Death, and likewise the mental agonies? (8–9)
We wander constantly as the executors of Kṛṣṇa’s commands;
we are all his creatures, as are Māyā, Brahmā, and the others.
The Vairāja Ṛṣis, the gods, humans, and all living beings—out of fear of whom the wind blows and out of fear of whom the sun shines. (91)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—the creator, the protector, and the destroyer—exist out of fear of him; and Yama, the witness of actions, and Dharma likewise abide through his fear.
Out of fear of whom the zodiac signs and the planets revolve in their proper order,
and by whose command even the lords of the quarters and the guardians of the directions carry out their duties.
Out of fear of whom the seasons move among trees and other plants, bestowing flowers;
the clouds rain down, and likewise the earth grants wealth.
The support of all, endowed with forbearance, she protects everyone like a mother;
she is considered Māyā, the mother of all, who fulfills [desires] out of fear of her. 95.
He whose limit no one knows, who is omniscient, and who dwells within the heart—of Him I am the sixteenth part; He is Time, the maker of the end of time.
Therefore, by meditating upon that Acyuta, who is the death of Death and the bestower of desires,
this Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, will grant you a husband.
"He who has impelled us all is the giver of all prosperity";
having said this, Kāla ceased speaking, and Hari then spoke to her.
Time has been seen, Yama has been seen, and likewise the Daughter of Death and mental agonies have been seen by you quickly, O virtuous lady; tell me, what is in your heart?
Mālāvatī said: "Just as a disease that is difficult to ward off might not recur, you ought to tell me here the entire means for that."

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Death of Nārada—who was essentially the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa—and the Lamentation of His Wives, as well as Their Petition to Brahmā and the Other Gods for the Husband’s Return to Life," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the words of Mālāvatī, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, spoke to Mālāvatī: "O Māle, listen; I shall speak to you exactly as it is."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, the pacifier of all diseases,
that Lord created the four Vedas as the source of auspiciousness.
Having seen the Vedas known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan, and having reflected upon their meaning, Prajāpati composed the Āyurveda.
Having composed that fifth Veda, the Lord gave it to Bhāskara;
then Bhāskara himself composed the Bhāskarasaṃhitā.
Bhāskara, however, gave that [work] to his own disciples; and thereafter they composed other compendiums (saṃhitās) concerning the practice of treating diseases. || 9 ||
Dhanvantari, the King of Kāśī and son of Divodāsa, who was himself the son of the Aśvins, indeed composed this *Cikitsātattvavijñāna*.
Nakula, Sahadeva, Arka, Cyavana, Janaka, Budha,
Jābāla, Jājali, Paila, Karatha, and Agastya as well.
All these sixteen physicians are destroyers of disease;
yet, in the matter of treating one's own body, one's very self alone shall be the physician.
Then diseases do not approach, and those already present perish.
Listen, O virtuous one: how health is to be protected with vigilance.
Eye-water, physical exercise, massaging the soles of the feet with oil,
and oil applied to the ears and the head destroy old age and disease.
He who wanders about in the spring, maintains a small fire,
and enjoys the company of young women at the proper time— old age does not approach him.
Old age does not approach him who practices bathing in cold water in the morning, uses sandalwood paste, and does not go out into the wind during the summer heat.
In the rainy season, he does not bathe in hot water nor indulge in thick rainwater;
by taking wholesome food at the proper time, old age does not approach him. (13)
In winter, he does not endure excessive cold and takes baths after digging [a pond];
he eats fresh and warm food, and thus old age does not approach him. (14)
Old age does not approach him who consumes fresh meat, new grain, young women, milk-based foods, and ghee. (15)
He eats excellent food when hungry, drinks water when thirsty, and daily consumes betel-leaf, as well as fresh butter and molasses. (16)
Curd and *haiyaṅgavīna* (fresh butter) do not undergo decay;
for those who constantly engage in physical exercise, old age flees far away.
Old age, together with its siblings, approaches with great joy one who indulges in an elderly woman, dried meat, the morning sun, and fresh curd.
The sixty-four daughters of Mṛtyukanyā are diseases, and Old Age is their son;
and Old Age, together with his brothers, wanders perpetually upon the surface of the earth. (19)
Old age swiftly devours those who consume curd at night, those who have sexual intercourse with an elderly woman or one in her menses, and those who engage in excessive sexual activity.
When hunger is burning intensely and food is not obtained,
bile arises in living beings within the maṇipūraka cakra.
Having eaten the fruit of the palmyra or the bilva tree and drinking water at that very moment, that indeed becomes bile which is supremely fatal to life instantly. (22)
He who consumes hot water on his head during the month of Bhādrapada, eats bitter food, and partakes again of unwholesome things, in him pitta (bile) is produced. ||23||
Barley flour mixed with sugar and combined with cold water,
chickpeas, and all products of the cow, excluding curd and buttermilk.
Ripe *bilva* and *tāla* fruits, as well as all kinds of alms-food, fresh ginger, mung bean soup, and sesame paste with sugar—these are permitted. (25)
Bathing immediately after a meal causes a depletion of bile and is detrimental to strength and nourishment, unless one is suffering from thirst and drinks water. (26)
Stale food, buttermilk, ripe plantain fruit, curd, rainwater, water with sugar, and the watering of turbid water; 27.
Coconut water, radish, as well as the karkaṭī fruit, and bathing after digging [a well] during the rainy season—all that causes phlegm (śleṣman). || 28 ||
Its birth occurs at the *brahmarandhra*, and it destroys great virility.
[The remedy consists of] *marīca*, *pippalī*, dried ginger, fresh ginger, *jīvaka*, and honey. (29)
Indeed, the substances known as "service to fire" (vahnisevā) immediately remove phlegm, bestow strength and nourishment, and destroy diseases. (1.202.30)
"O beautiful one, tell me by what fault has your beloved died?
Having heard this, Mālāvatī said, "My husband died through yoga."
"Now, O Janārdana, give back my beloved life!
Having bowed down before you along with our master, we women shall go to our own home. (32)
Having heard this, Janārdana went quickly indeed to the assembly of the gods;
there he spoke to the wife of Upabarhaṇa and to the daughter of Citraratha. || 3ā ||
Together with her sisters, she requested the gift of life for her own master;
though she desired to curse all the gods, she was dissuaded by me for the sake of peace.
Then Brahmā, as well as Viṣṇu and Nārada Upabarhaṇa, spoke to him regarding what the certain performance of this task should be.
He gave up his life-breaths through yoga, yet due to my very curse,
his stay upon the earth shall endure for a period spanning a hundred thousand yugas.
"Then, having entered the womb of a Śūdra, he shall become my son once again;
O Supreme Lord, a small portion of this remaining time still exists for him. (37)
His lifespan at present is indeed only one thousand years;
however, by the grace of Viṣṇu himself, I shall grant him the gift of life.
"I shall certainly act in such a way that this curse does not come to pass.
The word *viṣi* signifies pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the particle *nu* denotes 'everywhere' (*sarvatra*). (3.9)
"May that all-pervading Viṣṇu indeed grant life," they said,
and having spoken thus, they went to where the bride Mālāvatī was.
Brahmā poured the water from his water-pot onto the body of the corpse;
he restored the movement of its mind and made its form beautiful.
Śiva gave him knowledge; thereafter Dharma gave him righteousness;
Agni gave him the digestive fire, and Vāyu then gave him the vital breath.
Then the Sun granted him vision, Vāṇī bestowed speech,
Lakṣmī gave him beauty, and the Lord of Śacī granted him ritual action.
Nevertheless, the corpse did not rise; Viṣṇu then granted him life.
He attained a distinguished awakening, yet he did not rise without a witness.
Then Mālāvatī, overcome with grief, bowed to Mādhava:
"Without you, I have no husband; you alone are my husband in every way. (45)
In the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), you who are the life-force of all living beings, restore my husband to life;
for Hari indeed established his presence there through his own powers.
Then the Gandharva rose, took up his lute and two garments,
and bowed down to the assembly of gods and to Viṣṇu, who stood before him.
There the kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell at that time;
all the gods bestowed supreme blessings upon the couple.
Then he, named Upabarhaṇa, danced and sang;
indeed, by the grace of the gods, he regained his life before them. ||49||
She went once again to the city of the Gandharvas along with her wives;
at that time, the queens [received] ten million jewels and hundreds of thousands of cattle as wealth.
They gave gifts to the Brahmins and fed many of them;
they also respectfully performed various kinds of great festivals.
They conducted various searches for their own husbands and performed service and worship for their lord as was appropriate for the occasion. (52)
Together with him, they took great delight for a very long time;
by that same mantra, all of them obtained the Gandharva as their husband. (53)
O Mistress of Kamalā, listen now to that sixteen-syllable mantra, as well as the hymn and the armor (kavaca), which were bestowed by Vasiṣṭha. (54)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of the Rāsa-maṇḍala, svāhā!
Know this sixteen-syllable mantra to be a wish-fulfilling tree. (55)
After that, Kṛṣṇa gave it to the Lord in Goloka;
likewise, in ancient times, Kṛṣṇa gave it to Brahmā at Puṣkara. ||56||
And Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, gave this armor to Kumāra; Hari himself [gave it] to this armor which purifies the entire universe.
The seer is Gāyatrī, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is I, the Blessed Lord Hari;
its application is always considered to be for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (58)
By reciting [this mantra] three hundred thousand times, one shall become the bestower of all siddhis.
May the Praṇava protect my head, and may "namo rāmeśvarāya" protect it as well. (59)
May the forehead protect me; salutations to the Lord of Rādhā for the pair of eyes.
May Kṛṣṇa protect the pair of ears, and may Śrī Hari likewise protect the sense of smell.
The tongue is protected by *vahnijāyā* (svāhā), and "to Kṛṣṇa, obeisance from all sides" (*kṛṣṇāya sarvato namaḥ*),
as well as "to Śrīkṛṣṇa, svāhā" (*śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā*)— may this six-syllabled mantra protect the wood.
"Hrīṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ" protects the face; "klīṃ" and "pūrva" protect the two arms;
"namo gopāṅganeśāya" protects the shoulders; may the eight-syllable mantra protect [the rest]. 6.2.
Salutation to the two rows of teeth and the pair of lips; salutation to the Lord of the Gopīs.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Sovereign of the Rāsa-maṇḍala, svāhā!
May Hari, the sixteen-syllabled mantra whose essence is the sacred formula, protect the region of the chest;
may "Oṃ Śrīkṛṣṇāya Svāhā" always protect the pair of ears. 64.
With "Oṃ viṣṇave svāhā," may the cheeks be protected on all sides;
with "Oṃ haraye namaḥ," may the back and feet be protected forever.
Oṃ, svāhā to the bearer of Govardhana; may he protect my entire body.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect me in the east, and Mādhava protect me in the southeast.
May the Lord of the Gopīs protect me in the south; may the Son of Nanda protect me in the southwest;
may Govinda protect me in the west; and may the Lord of Rādhikā protect me in the northwest. ||67||
May the Lord of the Rasa dance protect me in the north; may Acyuta himself protect me in the northeast.
May Hari Nārāyaṇa himself protect me constantly from all sides. (68)
Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste,
and having bathed and bowed down to him, the wise person should wear the armor (kavaca).
By the grace of the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), a man shall become liberated while living; if he possesses the perfected armor, O beloved, he becomes Viṣṇu himself. (1.202.70)
From the recitation of this, great merit arises, equal to the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites;
one without a son obtains a son, and one without a wife obtains a virtuous wife.
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one seeking wealth shall attain wealth;
one who has lost his kingdom shall regain his kingdom; and one desiring success shall achieve it. (72)
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one who is bound is released from bondage.
Having attained devotion to Hari, one finally reaches the imperishable abode.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world and having established a fame that is very difficult to attain,
he becomes a foremost attendant and goes to the abode of Goloka.
Thus the preeminent Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa enjoyed himself with those wives with devotion for the remainder of his lifespan.
And he performed various kinds of excellent sacrifices together with his sons;
then, in the course of time, Upabarhaṇa gave up his life due to a Brahmin’s curse.
By the power of a curse, he was born from the womb of a *vṛṣalī* through the seed of a Brahmin;
meanwhile, the virtuous Mālāvatī gave up her life in the sacrificial fire-pit.
And other women as well, having attained the dharma of widowhood, remained steadfast;
such was she for King Sañjaya, born of the lineage of Manu. 78.
Born of his wife as one who remembers her past lives, she thought, "He shall be my husband. I was always a celestial maiden belonging to the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa.
In the region of Kānyakubja, there was indeed a king named Drumila;
his wife was Kalāvatī, who was barren yet devoted to her husband.
Due to her husband's fault, she was barren; nevertheless, at her husband's command during her fertile season, she approached the sage Kāśyapa Nārada in the formidable forest.
He went indeed to that second Nārada, who was born as the son of Kaśyapa due to the curse of Dakṣa. ||82||
Meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
she stood before the sage in beautiful attire at the conclusion of her meditation.
And Nārada saw before him Sundarī, whose youth was eternal, golden-hued, adorned with gold ornaments, moon-faced, and lotus-eyed. (84)
And seeing her, who had arrived at the king's desire for a son and was adorned with amorous grace, the sage asked that queen: "Who are you? To whom do you belong? Tell me. (85)
Then Kalāvatī, having remembered Hari, spoke to Nārada:
"I am the wife of Drumila; by my husband's command, I am a cowherd woman. (86)
"Desiring a son, I have come into your presence; show me mercy! Bestow your seed upon my womb; for a woman who has approached you must not be neglected. (87)
"For the more powerful, there is no fault, just as fire consumes everything;
thus spoke the righteous Nārada, a Brahmin practicing dharma. (88)
The Brahmin who, weak in knowledge, takes a Śūdra woman as his wife, falls to a lower status by birth; he is no longer eligible for the rites of the twice-born. (89)
A twice-born man who approaches a Śūdra woman shall be deprived of his right to perform ancestral rites (śrāddha), sacrifices, the touching of ritual stones, and the worship of the gods. (1.202.90)
If one's chosen deity does not accept the food offering nor that water, that brahmin takes birth in the womb of a śūdra as the fruit of that [action]. 9.1.
"You have said that for those of great power there is no fault in it, and that it is indeed nectar.
I am giving you the seed from afar; take it if you have the capacity. (92)
By holding [the seed] within the womb through one's power, no fault exists at that time; "I am not having sexual union"—if this thought occurs, there would be no fault in the union. (93)
Having been addressed thus, that wife of a Śūdra, devoted to her husband, then remembered her own lord and became absorbed in meditation. (94)
Having completely dissolved his gross body, [the Lord] entered through the subtle body by means of yoga; and at that moment, Nārada likewise [entered]. ||95||
Through the power of her entry, she did not perceive her own body—endowed with desire and composed of the elements—as distinct from her gross body, as if it were a dream. (96)
The sage's semen fell there upon a bed of *sarja* leaves;
the Śūdra woman quickly picked it up, drank it, and protected the embryo within her. (97)
Having bowed to the sage, she was delighted, having accomplished her purpose without attachment;
and the sage too became joyful, having achieved his goal without the fault of attachment.
Having gone into the presence of her husband, she related the entire account;
Drumila, too, became pleased and spoke these words that brought happiness to his beloved. (99)
"That which was indeed the seed of the Vaiṣṇava Nārada within your womb—that very child shall become a Vaiṣṇava; he is truly a portion of Nārada."

In the womb of which a Vaiṣṇava is born, or by whose heroic power [it is conceived], a hundred and a hundred generations of men from both [the father's and the mother's lineages] go to Vaikuṇṭha. || 10.1 ||
And those two, by means of a divine Viṣṇu-chariot resplendent with jewels,
went to the city of Vaikuṇṭha, which removes birth, death, and old age.
Having spoken thus, that king of cowherds bathed, performed the libations,
worshipped his chosen deity, and gave wealth to the Brahmins.
With joy, he gave to the Brahmins thousands of elephants, horses, chariots, cows, swans, male servants, and female servants, as well as vessels, ornaments, garments, and jewels.
Seeing his wife pregnant with a son and remembering Hari in his heart,
he recognized the auspicious thread of his lineage and thereafter attained detachment.
He went to the sacred field of Badarī and, through the practice of yoga, gave up his life-breaths;
he was carried away by the messengers of Hari in a celestial chariot to Vaikuṇṭha.
There he attained the service of Hari and became a servant of Hari;
meanwhile, in another year, the goddess Kalāvatī was protected by the Brahmins.
She gave birth to an auspicious son who possessed the luster of molten gold,
who excelled Kāmadeva in beauty, and who blazed with the splendor of Brahman.
His feet were marked with lotuses and wheels; his lotus-like hands held a bow and a banner; he had a golden tilaka upon his forehead, and his chest was adorned with the mark of a garland.
Having recognized her as the form of Viṣṇu, all the people rejoiced;
the Brāhmaṇas nurtured that queen along with her son, just as they would their own daughter.
Accompanied by her son, she served the twice-born like a maidservant of the brahmins;
that boy grew there like the moon in the bright fortnight. || 111 ||

Endowed with knowledge and remembering his previous mantras at all times, he was one who remembered his past births; at the moment of his birth, water mixed with human remains indeed rained down upon the earth.
Because he was given a *nāra* at the time of his birth, he is remembered as Nārada;
and because he gives *nāra*, which is knowledge, to children, he is called Nārada.
Through the power of Nārada’s own vigor, he became Nārada;
furthermore, because he gave his throat to men for singing, he was also called Nārada.
He who bestows quickly (aram) is indeed called Nārāyaṇa;
because he bestows quickly through the gift of Nārāyaṇa, he is likewise proclaimed as Nārada.
Those who possess teeth (rada) are not "arada" (without teeth), for they are endowed with old age;
he who has neither teeth nor old age is the long-lived Nārada.
In the course of time, that boy gradually reached the age of five years;
he constantly sang the qualities and other attributes of Kṛṣṇa’s glorious deeds.
Singing the verses of Kṛṣṇa and offering oblations of dust,
he fashioned an image out of dust and worshipped the Lord with dust.
The mother calls her infant son for his morning meal, but he gives this reply: "I am worshipping Hari. (119)
The five-year-old children, the Brāhmaṇas, and your friends—the four beginning with Sanaka—have taken them away in secret. || 1.202.120 ||
Those eminent sages duly bestowed upon him the initiation of Hari’s name-mantra; they accepted the roots, fruits, and other offerings given by the boy.
The four of them consumed the remainder of that [food], and the child ate it as well;
then the fourth sage gave him the mantra of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, this son of a Śūdra woman, through his association with the Brāhmaṇas, ate the auspicious food and drink from the vessels of the sages like a servant. || 123 ||
Day by day, the boy Gopikā became completely purified in the house of the Brahmin;
all his impurities were consumed away by eating the food provided through the grace of the Ṛṣi.
The food-remnants of the virtuous bring grace to the inner self;
they shake off great sin and purify the mind.
It brings about consciousness, increases the state of self and sentient beings, purifies faith, and accomplishes service. || 1.26 ||
It inspires true love, increases steadfast devotion,
impels one toward His form, and sends one to the imperishable state.
Having partaken of the palatable food, including leaf-plates and boiled rice, offered by the sages and brahmins, Nārada indeed attained a divine state.
Once, while traveling on a path at night with her infant son, that mother died,
bitten by a serpent, even as her mind was instantly fixed on the remembrance of Hari.
That virtuous woman immediately went to Vaikuṇṭha, accompanied by the attendants of Viṣṇu,
indeed by means of Viṣṇu’s vehicle fashioned from excellent jewels.
Having performed the funeral rites for him, the child remained on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
having bathed there, he chanted the mantra of Hari given by the Brahmin.
On the shore, amidst the trees, he indeed stood near the root of an *aśvattha* tree;
having assumed a yogic posture, he remained there and meditated upon the form of Hari.
Remembering Śrī Hari, he recited the twenty-two-syllable mantra:
*Oṃ śrīṃ namo bhagavate rāsamaṇḍaleśvarāya*. (133)
He muttered the mantra "Śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā," O Kalpadruma,
and performed a most enchanting meditation upon the Lord Kṛṣṇa.
He meditated upon Govinda, who is as beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud,
whose eyes are like autumnal lotuses, and whose face is as auspicious as the autumnal moon.
Resplendent with lips like a ripe bimba fruit, adorned with teeth as white as kunda flowers, smiling, with a flute in hand, and more beautiful than ten million gods of love. || 136 ||
He shines with the luster of ten million moons, pervaded by full and youthful beauty;
he has three bends in his body, two arms, wears yellow garments, and is adorned with the Kaustubha gem.
Adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and golden anklets,
his ears were graced by jeweled earrings, and his cheeks were beautified by their radiant glow.
He has a crest of peacock feathers, a chest enriched with jeweled garlands,
arms reaching down to his knees, and he beautifully wears a forest garland.
His body was moistened with sandalwood paste and other unguents; intent upon bestowing grace upon his devotees, he was joyfully gazed upon in play by the sidelong-eyed gopīs.
He was accompanied by Gopikā, who appeared to be less than fifteen years of age;
he was the most excellent one, adorned and served by Rādhā, Ramā, and Mahālakṣmī. 141.
The divine Nārada meditated upon Hari, the youthful beloved of the cowherd girls, who is untainted and beyond all qualities—the Supreme Self, the infallible Acyuta. (142)
For a thousand divine years he remained without food, his belly emaciated;
yet, perfected in yoga through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, he possessed the power to sustain his life.
Through the power of mantra-yoga, he beheld a boy residing in the divine realm,
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Kṛṣṇa, who was in the bloom of youth, beautifully dressed as a cowherd, clad in yellow garments, and well-served by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses. || 145 ||
Having seen him with two arms, a flute in his hand, anointed with musk and sandalwood paste,
and possessing a peaceful countenance, the son of the cowherd woman became tranquil.
And having vanished, he did not see that form again;
not seeing the dark-complexioned beauty, he wept at the foot of the Aśvattha tree.
And a voice from the sky arose, speaking words that were beneficial, true, and concise:
"The form which was shown but once shall not be seen by you again now. (148)

Even for those whose passions have been ripened, it is difficult to perceive [this state] while they remain in this body; however, when dissolution into this body has occurred and the divine form has been attained, [it becomes manifest]. 149.
"You shall see again Govinda, the Lord Hari, who dwells in Goloka.
Having heard this, he ceased speaking; in due time, he cast off that body.
Remembering Kṛṣṇa, Nārada departed for the divine abode known as Goloka-dhāma, freed from the curse; then the kettledrums resounded.
Then a rain of flowers fell as he dissolved into the body of Brahmā;
and once again, the son of Brahmā, the Brahmin Nārada, was born.
O Lotus-born One, for liberated beings and for devotees, there is no birth, death, old age, or disease, nor do they experience manifestation or disappearance at their own will. 153.
Furthermore, when another yuga had passed and during the creation of the Creator,
he [Nārada] was born from the throat of the Ordainer named Nārada.
And there is the one renowned as Nārada, the lord of sages and the mind-born son [of Brahmā];
this Nārada is said to be the mind-born son of Hari, being the very form of Kṛṣṇa. (155)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [are described] the means for destroying diseases according to the methods of Āyurveda and other sciences, following the prayer of Mālāvatī.
