Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Brahmā, the supreme preceptor and progenitor of all who are worthy of worship, directed Nārada to perform the work of creation. || 1 ||
The teacher of knowledge and the teacher of mantra are both superior to one's father;
I am your giver of birth, your giver of knowledge, and your giver of mantra. (2)
And by my command and out of love for me, take the wives of the Kurus;
for a disciple who obeys his guru’s command, or a son, shall deliver his ancestors.
He always attains security, both mundane and eternal;
he is a wise man, he is a man of knowledge, he is secure, and he is meritorious. (4)
The wise man who is disciplined, fortunate, and entitled to the heavenly realm—
he who carries out the word of his guru, for him there is well-being at every step.
Indeed, the householder stage of life is meritorious, for it provides refuge for all stages of life;
a home enriched by sons, grandsons, and a wife is the fruit of austerity.
The ancestors come to the householder’s home at the time of the festival, the deities at the time of worship, and the sages at the time of alms-seeking.
Those in the householder stage of life perform their constant and occasional duties;
having enjoyed every happiness here, they go to heaven, which is great bliss.
The householder who possesses wealth and enjoys fame, virtue, bliss, and so forth, is happy;
he is liberated while living, and upon death, he is liberated in the hereafter—of this there is no doubt.
Even for one who has died, if his body exists through fame, he truly lives;
even for one who is alive, if his body does not exist through fame, he is indeed always dead.
Thus, knowledge is to be obtained, as well as fame and devotion to Mādhava;
auspicious wives, fortune, heaven, and sons and other blessings are to be obtained.
Merit is to be gained, as well as health; indeed, eternal happiness is to be gained.
Likewise, the highest [happiness] pertaining both to this world and the next is to be gained.
One should always perform one's duties as an enjoyer through attachment like a householder, yet remain like an ascetic; for Nārāyaṇa indeed told me that there is truly no bondage at all.
Having heard this, Nārada said: "One proceeds toward that which is desired;
for me, there is neither the quality of being a means to what is desired nor the absence of connection with what is undesired. (14)
How indeed could I proceed toward a noble woman, given the absence of any cause for bondage and because of the opposition to this object in my previous births?
Having died due to your curse, I became the Gandharva Śūdraka; now, having been released from that curse by the passage of time, I am here—for indeed, enmity leads not to happiness.
He is the guru, the father, the kinsman, the son, the master, and the protector—
he who awakens one to devotion to Śrī Nārāyaṇa and causes that firm devotion to be practiced.
It is appropriate for a father to turn away a fool who persists on an evil path;
how could he instead lead him onto the path of a wife, which obstructs the true path? (18)
The grasping for a wife is a great snare that leads only to suffering;
it is an obstacle to austerity, heaven, liberation while living, and the great liberation. (19)
Women are divided into three types: the virtuous, the self-interested, and the antagonistic.
The virtuous woman, regarding her duty as her primary concern, serves her husband and always bestows happiness.
Devoted to her own duty, that virtuous woman remains indeed equal in joy and sorrow;
yet, for the sake of accomplishing her own purpose, she attends upon her husband.
She serves her beloved for the sake of enjoyment and not otherwise, for she is indeed self-interested;
[she desires] clothing, ornaments, sexual pleasure, affectionate food, wealth, and so forth. (22)
As long as she is provided for by her husband, she serves him solely for her own interest;
however, through a spirit of deceit, she may serve her husband or another man.
Whether for herself or for another, she by whom all men capable of granting desires were envisioned as being without respect [for her]. (24)
But she, abiding in contradictory attributes, was a paradox:
her heart was like the edge of a razor, yet her face was a festival for the autumn lotus. (25)
Every word of a woman is considered sweet as nectar when it serves her own interest;
however, in her anger she is like poison, and in her trust she is destructive. (26)
One's intention would be exceedingly hidden; one would always be like a thief in action;
likewise, there would be lack of discipline, pursuit of self-interest, recklessness, deceit, and falsehood. (27)
Illusion, deceit, and impurity—these eight are born of his own nature;
they are the eight qualities of the Puruṣa, eternally the God of Desire who carries away even the most powerful.
Food is always double [the usual amount], and harshness is fourfold;
moreover, anger and violence there indeed possess sixfold intensity. (29)
Affection for one's own interest is indeed tenfold, while that for others is sixteenfold greater;
such being the case when a woman’s body is seized by defects, O Grandfather, what reliance can there be?
What kind of sport can there be for one with a pure body in that which is called a pit of excrement and urine?
In such enjoyment, there is a loss of vigor; in friendship, there is the destruction of fame and the depletion of wealth.
Excessive indulgence leads to the wasting away of the body; in quarreling, there is the destruction of pride;
in misplaced trust, total ruin; and in captivity, the obstruction of liberation.
Only loss is ordained by her; what gain is there in grasping for a woman?
As long as one possesses wealth and youth, she is one's own; otherwise, she is not.
She gazes upon her husband—aged, destitute, and likewise afflicted by disease—as one who is disagreeable;
yet, out of fear of public censure, she gives him food only sparingly, like that given to a dog.
O Omniscient One, you know everything; grant me this boon now. I pray for devotion to Kṛṣṇa, for which I have performed supreme austerity. (35)
Having bowed down, praised, and entreated him, and having performed a circumambulation and asked for his forgiveness,
Brahmā grieved for a moment upon seeing his son departing.
If you go to perform austerities, what is that to me in my worldly affairs?
[And who are] Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana? (37)
Turya, Sanatkumāra, the other Sanatsujāta, Yati, Haṃsi, Āruṇi, Voḍhu, and likewise Pañcaśikha. ||38||

Your sons have departed for asceticism; what use have I for the activities of worldly existence? Others are undiscriminating and incurable; what use have I for the activities of worldly existence? (39)
The wise desire that which has the characteristic of impelling as its meaning, or as Dharma;
a Brahmin, having donned the sacrificial thread and having studied the Vedas according to his ability, [should act accordingly]. (1.203.40)
Having completed that, he thereafter gives the teacher's fee;
then he should marry a virtuous woman, born of a noble family and well-disciplined. ||41||
A woman is not said to be bondage; rather, latent impression (vāsanā) is considered bondage.
A person free from latent impressions attains liberation even if joined with a virtuous wife.
The faults attributed to women do not exist when they have a virtuous husband;
if the husband should go astray, what fault then can be imputed to the woman? (43)
When there is a husband, the faults of a wife become virtues;
her virtues and faults are dependent upon the husband, and as is the husband, so is the virtuous wife.
There is no fault in the case of maidens; as is the seed, so is the fruit.
But the field is pure in every respect; as is the soil, so is the sprout.
Women were indeed created for the sake of men’s attainment of happiness;
they endure all abuse and remain submissive at all times. (46)
Having personally embraced suffering, they bring happiness to their virtuous lord;
they are the means for a man scorched by the threefold affliction to find a place of rest. 47.
I created this jewel among women; you should not find fault with her.
That maiden was indeed given away by her father to another, having abandoned everything.
She moves about free from suffering like a cow; do not revile her, O Nārada, for she is always dependent on others, seeking refuge elsewhere like a maidservant or a slave-girl. (4.9)
O Nārada, do not censure her who remains engaged in service having abandoned pride;
for where there is a mine of rubies, how could a glass trinket be born there?
Therefore, my child, all women born from a portion of Kamalā are givers of happiness;
even a virtuous wife serves and praises her husband, even if he is devoid of merit.
A virtuous man, guided by the eye of dharma, should take a maiden born of a noble lineage;
having begotten sons upon her, he should retire to the forest for asceticism in his old age.
"O son, you have studied the Veda with me; now give me my teacher’s fee. Do this very thing here: take a wife."
"O child, you [must marry] Malati, a girl of noble birth who was your former wife,
the daughter of Srinjaya of Manu's lineage, who is now devoted to ascetic penance."
"Accept her as your wife and perform the marriage ceremony, my son;
remain in the house of a Vaiṣṇava and always practice devotion to Hari."
First Brahman, then a woman, then dwelling in the forest;
for him who has Hari within and without, O son, what is the use of asceticism? (5–6)
O son, what is the use of penance for one who has neither Hari within nor without?
Having obtained a woman, protect Hari; for Hari resides within the woman.
Sons should be understood as being made by Hari, since they are the protectors from hell;
therefore, Hari is to be served even through austerity, for service is indeed the supreme austerity. (58)
"Liberation is obtained through austerity and service; that is their fruit.
My child, by my very word, remain at home and worship Hari. (59)
The grace of the father must be obtained, and the debt to the father must be repaid;
that is accomplished by taking a wife, so indeed, take a wife.
The pleasure of a wife, the pleasure of sensual desire, and the great pleasure of physical touch—of all these, the sight of a son is the most blissful; therefore, become a householder.
A wife has her purpose in her son; indeed, she is dearer than all else.
A son is dearer than a hundred wives, and there is nothing dearer than a son.
One should seek victory from everyone, but defeat from a son or a disciple;
for a son is one's own self and a kinsman—one should entrust the true essence of the Self to him.
Having heard this, Nārada said, even though he knew it himself: "O Father, why do you urge me toward this world which is like a bubble on the water? (64)
Having abandoned service to Hari, may my human birth not be fruitless;
for whose wife am I, whose son, whose husband, and whose kin? (65)
The entire web of actions performed is a bond consisting of volition;
he who indeed releases one from that is the father, the teacher, and the friend.
But he who bestows bondage upon these [beings] with a mind intent on binding, and who causes them to fall away from liberation—that enemy is the one who joins them to saṃsāra. (67)
However, the fourth word of the father, which ought to have been accepted by one seeking liberation, was not accepted by you three times; consequently, you have obtained its fruit: affliction. (68)
"In my first mental son, your command was not obeyed;
because of that, my death occurred, and from that I became Mārīca. (69)
Again from Mṛti came Gandharva, and from that Mṛti came the one born of Śūdra;
then from that Mṛti I became this Brāhma, the fourth in this lineage.
Therefore, whether it was appropriate or inappropriate, your command has been borne upon my head;
O Brahmin, be gracious to me so that I may be forever happy.
"O Blessed One, at first I shall go to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
having heard the story of Nārāyaṇa, I will take a wife. (72)
"O Father, just as I may always remain intent upon the practice of giving, so should you grant me your blessings, lest my liberation be obstructed. (73)
"Grant me the mantra of Kṛṣṇa along with its meaning and a description of His qualities.
Then Brahmā spoke to his beloved son, the repository of all knowledge.
One should never take up the mantra of a husband nor the mantra of a father;
Maheśvara is your guru from before—go toward him.
Having heard this and bowed to his father, the sage went to the world of Śiva,
which was endowed with every prosperity like a second Vaikuṇṭha.
It was adorned with crores, padmas, arbudas, and lakhs of hosts and supreme attendants,
as well as with formidable and terrifying sacred sites and wish-fulfilling trees.
He beheld Śiva standing in the midst of his attendants in that divine assembly—
three-eyed, five-faced, adorned by the Gaṅgā, and crowned with the moon.
He has a golden beak and a mass of matted hair, chanting the name of Hari with his rosary;
he is blue-throated, wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and is worshipped by yogīs, siddhas, and others. (79)
Having gone before Him who is gracious, the bestower of peace, dear to His devotees, and the supreme Vaiṣṇava,
he bowed down, offered praise, and sang while strumming the three-stringed lute.
And Śaṅkara gave him a suitable seat and the honors due to him;
he inquired after his arrival and worthy objects of meditation, and performed the rites of hospitality.
The sage made his formal presentation, including the arrival of the meaning of the mantra;
having heard it, Śambhu became pleased and said "Om" to Nārada.
Maheśvara duly bestowed upon Nārada the hymn to Hari, the armor, the mantra "Obeisance to Śrī Hari," as well as meditation and knowledge. (83)
Nārada said to the Lord of Gods, "O Master, tell me my daily duties.
Thereupon, Śambhu explained to him the duties of a brāhmaṇa.
In brief, O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe to you all those eternal practices of right conduct which bestow happiness both in this world and the next. (85)

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Instruction to Nārada for the Purpose of Creation in the First Kṛtayuga-Santāna of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; Nārada’s Acceptance of That through the Gate of Knowledge, and His Journey to Kailāsa for the Sake of the Meaning of the Vaiṣṇava Guru-Mantra."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Śambhu spoke to the divine sage Nārada: "Listen to the daily ritual (āhnika).
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should meditate upon the Guru on the forehead."
One should meditate on Hari at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and worship Kṛṣṇa in the heart— He who has a gracious countenance, is peaceful, radiant, and captivating.
The deity, the mantra, the ritual of worship, and the recitation are bestowed by the Guru;
the disciple is purified by the Guru; therefore, the Guru is superior to the deity. (3)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the god Maheśvara; the Guru is Prakṛti, Īśa, and the others; the Guru is the Moon, Fire, and the Sun.
The teacher is Vāyu and Varuṇa; the teacher is mother, father, and friend;
the teacher alone is the Supreme Brahman; there is nothing more worthy of worship than the teacher.
When one's chosen deity is angry, the preceptor is capable of providing protection;
but when the preceptor is angry, not even all the gods are capable of providing protection.
For him whose guru is truly pleased, there is victory at every step;
for him whose guru is angry, total ruin is ordained.
The deity does not destroy the evil arising from failing to serve the guru for one who worships the deity alone without first honoring the guru.
The Guru is capable of removing the sin born from failing to worship the gods;
therefore, the Guru is considered more worthy of worship than even one's chosen deity.
Having meditated upon and remembered the Guru, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, as well as virtuous people,
one should go to a suitable place for the evacuation of feces and urine.
A water source, a temple, a tree, a path, a cow-pen, an auspicious spot, a house, fire, a crossroads, moist grain, an anthill, and a cave—(these are the places where one should not dig). 11.
Having avoided such places as gardens, groves of *darbha* grass, fruit trees, cremation grounds, and playgrounds, one should always discard impurities and the like.
One should apply one application of clay to the penis and four applications to the left hand;
this is proclaimed as the purification for urination when using both hands.
After sexual intercourse, one should perform purification twice as much;
one application on the penis, three on the anus, and ten on the left hand.
Seven [applications] of both [hands] should be given; by three on the feet, one is purified.
This indeed is the common rule for the cleansing of excrement for everyone. (15)
Purification performed with substances such as water or clay that removes odor and stains is indeed true purification; otherwise, it is certainly not purification at all.
One should avoid impure earth that contains living organisms or has been trampled;
having performed purification with water, one should then wash one's own face. 17.
One should clean the teeth with a tooth-stick and rinse them with water.
A tooth-cleansing stick should contain milky sap and possess thorns. (18)

One should take water eight finger-breadths higher than the mouth, using the half-finger-width of the tongue for the wiping; then one should perform the water-bath while remembering the God, the Guru, and Hari.
To Ravi, Viṣṇu, Hara, Lakṣmī, Satī, and the gods beginning with Brahmā,
[he offered oblations] at a river, a stream, a pond, a sacred bathing place, a well, or the ocean.
Having first made this resolve, one should smear clay upon the body [with the mantra]:
"O Vasundharā, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu! (2.1)
O Earth, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me;
you were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms. ||2||
Climbing upon my limbs, release me from all sin;
O highly fortunate one, bestow merit upon me and grant me permission to bathe. (23)
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Narmadā, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! (24)
Nalinī, Nandinī, Sītā, Mālinī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Gaṅgā born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, Māṇakī, and Gaṇḍakī. ||25||
Padmāvatī, Bhogavatī, Svarṇarekhā, Kauśikī, Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Śubhagā, Viśvakāyā, and Śivāmṛtā. ||26||
Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, as well as Lokaprasādhinī, Kṣemā, Kaṃbharā, Śāntā, Śāntidā, Gomatī, and Satī. (27)
Sāvitrī, Tulasī, Durgā, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rādhā—who is dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life—Lopāmudrā, Rati, and Diti. ||28||
The wise man should also remember Ahalyā, Aditi, Saṃjñā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Arundhatī, Śatarūpā, Devahūti, and others. 29.
Having bathed with water and put on two suitable cotton garments,
the wise man should apply a *tilaka* mark with both water and sandalwood paste.
At the base of the two arms, on the forehead, at the region of the throat, and on the chest—
one should apply an auspicious, circular mark made of saffron (kuṅkuma) in their center.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and taken his seat, he should then perform the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā);
thereafter, he should perform the worship of the deities by means of the sixteen preparatory rites (sādhana).
The worship of Hari is highly recommended at Śālagrāma, on a gem, through a mantra, in an image, in water, on dry land, upon the back of a cow, and before a guru or a brahmin.
A seat, clothing, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, flowers, sandalwood paste, incense, a lamp, and excellent food offerings. (34)
Fragrant oil, ornaments, betel, water, fruit, the waving of lamps (ārārtika), and so forth should be offered; this is the sixteen-fold worship of the Self.
Then there is bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as the consecration bath (abhiṣeka-snāna);
furthermore, garments, sandalwood paste and the like, flowers, and ornaments.
A seat, a lamp, incense, and an offering of food; likewise, drinking water, betel, the waving of lights (ārātrika), and circumambulation. || 37 ||
The offering of hymns of praise and the handful of flowers— these sixteen services should always be offered with devotion to Hari during the performance of worship.
First, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and after that the breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then the assignment of the limbs and sub-limbs (aṅgapratyaṅganyāsa), and after that the assignment of the mantras (mantranyāsa). || 39 ||
Then, having performed the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), one should designate the arghya vessel;
having drawn a triangular maṇḍala, one should worship Kūrma there.
Having filled the conch with water, one should likewise place it upon the tortoise;
then, having performed the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrtha-āvāhana*) into the water, one should purify the ritual materials.
One should worship the bell and worship the conch, as well as the water-pot;
one should worship the Śālagrāma stone, and thereafter indeed worship Hari.
Having worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings, one should dismiss the deities;
likewise, one should perform the sacrifice to the gods and the ancestral rite (śrāddha) according to one's means.
One should perform the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña) according to one's ability during the honoring of guests;
one should salute the elders and always pay homage to the sun and other deities.
Having fed those who are to be supported, the householder should always eat;
sacrificial food (haviṣya) is always recommended for Brāhmaṇas and householders alike. 45.
That which remains as the leavings of Nārāyaṇa is desirable, while that which has not been offered is unfit to be eaten;
he who constantly eats the food offering (naivedya) of Śrī Viṣṇu is indeed a Vaiṣṇava. 46.
Food, water, fruit, flowers, and leaves offered to Śrī Hari may be eaten or drunk; however, anything other than that is not to be drunk and is not to be eaten. Thus it is said. (47)
That which is corrupted by its species, corrupted by its appearance, corrupted by its form, corrupted by its qualities, or corrupted by its transformation—that indeed must not be eaten. (48)
During the observances, food must certainly not be eaten; it should not be eaten before the worship [of the deity].
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness [are the five yamas]. (49)
For these restraints (yamas) must be observed; they bestow happiness and even liberation.
Purity, contentment, austerity, study, and the worship of Kṛṣṇa also grant liberation. (1.204.50)
One should never, under any circumstances, engage in the censure of anyone by anyone else;
for even the truth, if it causes pain to others, should not be spoken, as it brings suffering. //5.1//
For dharma is that purpose characterized by impulsion, and not that which is purposeless;
one should not be ungrateful, nor should one ever practice deceit.
Furthermore, one should acquire wealth that is legally tradable and acquired according to the rules;
one should exert effort according to one's strength toward riches, grain, and the means of livelihood. (53)
One should never seize another's property under false accusations;
one should exert oneself during the day and perform the evening twilight prayers, recitations, and so forth.
Having visited the temple of Hari and performed hymns of praise, congregational chanting, and other such acts,
householders should go to sleep after reciting the mantra for income and expenditure.
Women must be protected in every way and gratified with material things;
one should not become agitated, nor should one ever experience distress.
Those seeking liberation must indeed engage in the investigation of the self and the non-self;
the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, resides within all embodied beings. (57)
He is both the witness and the bestower of the fruits of bodily actions;
Viṣṇu himself, as the five vital breaths, is to be gratified with excellent food offerings. (468)
The mind, as Brahmā, is to be gratified with bliss, delight, and the like;
Indra and Rudra, representing the sense organs, are to be gratified with wholesome objects. (59)
Māyā, whose nature is consciousness, is to be gratified by means of hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices;
the Self, the witness, who is itself Brahman, is to be satisfied through the offerings until they are fully presented.
The Supreme Brahman, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, eternally resides within all conscious beings;
indeed, those conscious selves are dependent upon Him, though they possess distinct karmic dispositions.
Living beings, endowed with the fruits of their karma, subsist through functions within insentient matter;
the insentient exist for the sake of others and are joined with the Supreme Being so that they may attain the state of being objects of experience.
And volitions are indeed joined with true objects for the sake of obtaining enjoyments;
Māyā, consisting of the three guṇas and being insentient, then became the principle of Mahat.
From that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born; from it, the deities of the senses [arose].
From the subtle elements, the gross elements emerged. (64)
Their physical body is obtained by the conscious self through its own past actions;
its destruction occurs through knowledge and action, while its lack of bondage is achieved through dispassion.
O one who has attained preeminence through Dharma, the merit of providing a vehicle at the abode of Hari with devotion should not even be considered [as one's own],
for it is indeed the Blessed One who acts.
The self is the embodied being, yet it is not the agent; Hari himself is the agent and the sustainer.
By their very nature, Prakṛti is bound and liberated, but the conscious spirit is not.
The body is born from the aggregates of the elements, but there is no birth of the self;
the body perishes through its states, but there is no disintegration of the self.
That which is of the same class is always experienced by a body of the same class;
for the body is indeed experienced by the body, since it possesses enjoyment.

The gross [body] is the support of enjoyment, while the subtle assumes various forms; within [the mind], there arises the thought: "This has been obtained," "This has been experienced," and "I am happy."

This notion arises with respect to the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) produced by egoism (ahaṃkāra), and not with respect to the Self (ātman). That it occurs elsewhere than in itself is surely a delusion. 7.1.
The world of transmigration (saṃsāra), accompanied by the latent impressions produced by it, is indeed called "delusion" (bhrama).
When delusion ceases, the house [of the body] ceases; this is truly the cessation of transmigration.
When there is the existence of delusion, there is the existence of a house and likewise the notion of a wife;
where is the house, and where is the wife? All of this is said to be mere mental impression (vāsanā).
In the absence of that [Self], where is the house, where is the wife, and where are the sons and so forth?
Even the body does not exist; what then can be said of those who are well-yoked in yoga with it? (74)
Therefore, the self is a devotee of the Supreme Brahman, a ray of Hari;
it is devoid of the qualities of māyā and is not tainted by time.
There is no staining even by karma, for therein there is no intrinsic nature;
what bondage indeed can there be for consciousness, which is devoid of qualities and whose very form is bliss? (76)
The Lord indeed performs everything; it must certainly be understood in this very way.
The farmer sows the seed, and the farmer waters it. (77)
The farmer guards the food, and the farmer also gives it;
the cultivator reaps the grain, and the cultivator also eats it. (78)
The ordinary farmer produces the entire crop, yet he does not produce it at all;
but Kṛṣṇa, the great farmer, produces the seed itself. (79)
Mādhava bestows birth when the seed resides within the womb;
indeed, Keśava protects one in childhood, youth, and old age.
Kṛṣṇa alone indeed bestows food, water, and clothing;
Kṛṣṇa impels death, and Mādhava leads one to dissolution.
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the witness, performs everything; indeed, I do nothing at all.
Thus, having surrendered everything to Kṛṣṇa, that [offering] is for the sake of liberation from bondage. (82)
Indeed, worship of Kṛṣṇa, propitiation of Mādhava, devotion, service, and whatever else there may be—all that belongs to the Lord of Kamalā. (8.3)
That indeed must be surrendered in every way, as well as the liberation of the living being here;
for the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, is the all-pervading inner controller everywhere. (84)
Endowed with all divine qualities, he resides in Goloka, the supreme imperishable realm, as well as in Vaikuṇṭha, Śvetadvīpa, Badarī, Amṛta, and Ākāśa. ||85||
He is indeed Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Naravāsa, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Rādhā, the Sovereign of Light, and the Master of Māṇikya. ||86||
He is the Lord of Lakṣmī, the husband of Kambharā, and Śrī Hari himself;
he is the Lord of Sītā, the master of Satī, and indeed the Lord of Pārvatī. (87)
Kṛṣṇa himself is the Lord of all; Śrī Kṛṣṇa is eternally possessed of form. He is the supreme Vyūha, the Vibhava, the Antaryāmin, and indeed the Mūrti itself. (88)
The Blessed Lord Hari exists in six forms:
as his own essential nature, as formless, as with form, as the Infinite (bhūman), and even as possessing a beautiful form.
Though invisible, he is clearly visible to those endowed with such eyes; for he is the object of meditation for yogis and the bond of love for devotees. (1.204.90)
For women, it consists of the husband; for the distressed, it consists of their wretchedness.
Though invisible to the physical eye, it is indeed visible through divine vision. (91)
Yogis constantly meditate upon that Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest, whose form is supreme bliss, and who is the cause of all causes. ||92||
Just as a potter indeed fashions a jar from clay, so too does the Supreme Brahman fashion creation in every way through primordial nature (prakṛti). ||93||
That supreme Brahman is eternal, and Prakṛti is indeed considered eternal;
that Prakṛti is the power (śakti) of Brahman, the body in the form of a seed.
Brahman, endowed with the power of primordial nature (prakṛti) and possessed of splendor, indeed exists eternally;
and he in whom that splendor resides is truly the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). ||95||
Without a cause, how or from where could an effect exist?
Indeed, its great effect, which is light, could not exist without the Puruṣa.
The Vaiṣṇavas meditate in every way upon that most charming, divine form of the Supreme Soul, which is graced by pearls and other ornaments. ||97||
The Lord, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, in the bloom of youth, with beautiful eyes radiant with the splendor of the midday sun in autumn; 98.
His face possesses a radiance exceeding that of ten million full moons of the autumnal new-moon festival;
he delights the god of love with the playful grace of the beauty of ten million Cupids. (99)
Hari, whose every limb was full and overflowing with the sweetness of beauty,
smiling, holding a flute in his hand, and wearing yellow garments.
His entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, he was resplendent with the Kaustubha gem,
and he was adorned from his knees upward with a garland of jasmine and a forest garland.
He stands with his three-fold bent posture, adorned with jewels, gems, and the like;
he has a crest of peacock feathers and is radiant with a crown of diamonds.
Resplendent with jeweled armlets, bracelets,
and jeweled anklets, he was beautifully adorned on the cheeks by a pair of jeweled earrings.
[He saw her] with teeth like pearls, lips like ripe bimba fruit, and a nose like a parrot's beak;
she was attended with respect by women endowed with stable youth and accompanied by smiles. (104)
He was gazed upon by the gopīs, as well as by Ramā, Rādhā, Jayā, and the others—
the beloved of his devotees, the lord of his devotees, and the one who bestows grace upon his devotees.
The Lord of the Rasa dance, full of divine relish, well-served by the great liberated ones,
the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the eternal Blessed One.
The Vaiṣṇavas indeed meditate here upon Hari and Lakṣmī in such a form;
yet that very Lord, the Master, is two-armed in Ādi-Goloka.
Attended by cowherd companions dressed as cowherds, the most perfect and glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhikā, [shone forth]. 108.
The inner self of all is directly perceptible everywhere through the state of devotion;
the word *kṛṣi* signifies "all," and the syllable *na* denotes the "Self.
Thus, Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed to be the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all.
The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies "all," and the letter *na* denotes "the beginning. || 1.204.110 ||
The all-pervading primordial person is himself proclaimed to be Kṛṣṇa;
the word *kṛṣi* signifies "earth" (or "root"), and *ṇa* signifies "bliss. (111)
The ground of bliss is the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa; this is certain in every respect.
"Kṛṣi" means the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and "na" means leading to one's own abode.
Because He bestows liberation upon the pure [soul], He is Himself proclaimed as Kṛṣṇa.
*Kṛṣi* means cultivation, *karṣaṇa* means drawing forth; *na* means leading, and it is divine and imperishable. (113)
Having led him to his own abode, he becomes Kṛṣṇa himself in person;
that very Lord, by his portion, is four-armed in Vaikuṇṭha.
Attended by four-armed attendants, he is the Lord of Kamalā;
that very Viṣṇu, the Lord of Ramā himself, is the protector who bestows the fruit [of his grace]. (115)
He alone is the four-armed Lord of the daughter of the ocean in the world of Śveta;
he alone is Hari himself, reclining upon Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk.
He alone, abiding in the imperishable, is the cause of all forms;
he is indeed the Supreme Brahman, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord. || 117 ||
"All this has been told to you; indeed, he must be meditated upon by you.
Having spoken thus, Nārada praised Śambhu as he was ceasing [his speech]. || 118 ||
O Nārada, having attained knowledge and mastered all the mantras and other sciences,
he prostrated before the divine Śaṅkara and departed for the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Daily Duties, the Worship of Nārāyaṇa, the Knowledge of Reality, Permissible and Forbidden Foods, and the Supreme Brahman, as Narrated by Śaṅkara to Nārada" in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this most enchanting account concerning the Badarī forest.
Śrī Nārada went to that excellent hermitage and beheld it.
It was adorned with divine trees, lovely creepers, and great forest monarchs,
and resounded with the cries of cātakas, menakās, kīras, and male cuckoos.
It was surrounded by śarabhas, lions, tigers, elephants, and cows;
and due to the union of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, it was entirely free from the fear of violence.
It was adorned with hermitages of three crores of Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Munis, and Gandharvas,
and was endowed with forests of Kalpa-candana, Tulasī, and Pārijāta trees.
Divine, endowed with all classes of divine sentient and insentient beings,
bestowing peace, that great forest was inaccessible to those with the stature of ordinary mortals.
Where Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the two blessed sages who protect the world,
shine like excellent kings, there dwell other innumerable sages as well.
In the midst of the sages, at the base of a banyan tree, in a charming assembly hall fragrant with the breeze from the royal trees in the shade of the Badarī grove.
He beheld those two blessed ones seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
chanting the supreme Brahman, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Seeing those two, the supreme teachers of yogis, he prostrated himself;
they rose, embraced him, and bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
They both inquired after his welfare and performed the rites of hospitality;
they respectfully seated him upon a jeweled lion-throne.
Dwelling upon a delightful seat and freed from the fatigue of the journey,
he spoke to those two best of sages, the eternal lords.
Having studied all the Vedas so that they became meaningful to my father,
and having obtained knowledge and mantras from Śaṅkara on Kailāsa, I [departed].
"O Blessed Ones, I have come to obtain special knowledge and the supreme compassion of the Lord; I pay homage to you, who deliver one from saṃsāra. (13)
Having spoken thus, Nārada sang a hymn of praise with his own lute, in a beautiful meter, with a melodious voice, accompanied by graceful dancing and a perfect rhythm.
Victory, victory to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the hand-guard of Rādhā’s lover!
Victory to the virtuous one, the Lord of the Siddhas, the triple-striding one, the deliverer from battle, the small one!
We praise you, the supreme Brahman, the destroyer of the seizing demon, the giver of liberation from battle;
victory to you, O Satī, Lord of the Siddhas, O you who possess the three strides, the giver of liberation from battle! 15.

Victory, victory! You are the reality that transcends the conceptualizations of existence, non-existence, and that which is other than both; you are the movement of the Vedic revelation "That Thou Art," the tree named Aśvattha with its roots turned upward, and the support that dispels both consciousness and unconsciousness.
I praise you, the support of both consciousness and unconsciousness, the friction-point of both the individual and the collective;
the tree known as the Aśvattha, whose roots point upward, the support of both consciousness and unconsciousness. 1.6.

Victory, victory to you, O Sustainer of the Universe, O Soul of the Universe! The Vedas have provided a thorough exposition within their own selves regarding the world’s transformation, its middle state of persistence, and its final dissolution—all of which have you as their substratum.
The Vedas declare that You, whose feet crush all evils, are the ultimate locus of the universe;
they declare that You abide as the central support within the transformation of the world.

Victory, victory to the Lord of the three worlds! O virtuous Lord of the three, son of Vṛṣa, you who sustain the three principles (tattvas), whose service is performed by the Goddess stationed at your side, heart, and limbs.
We choose him whose service is performed [by his devotees], who removes ignorance through his wisdom, and whose service is performed by the Goddess stationed at his side, heart, and lap. 18.
Victory, victory to You, who are to be known through the Vedas, meters, and limbs [of the Veda], and who are the fruit of the fruits of the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*);
victory to You, the enjoyer and the invoker; victory to You, the sacrificial offering whose nature is delighting in Your own Self!
We worship the one who delights in his own self, whom the sages, Janaka, and the women serve;
victory to the enjoyer, victory to the offerer! O oblation, victory to the one whose nature is delighting in his own self! 1.9
Victory, victory to you, the nourisher of the qualities of lifelong devotion! Victory, O ascetic, refuge of the compassionate!
Victory, O right-hand one; victory, O left-hand one; victory, O dual-natured one who removes the intellect of the worldly-minded!
We bow to the remover of the vulgar mind, who grants a noble destination with his own feet;
victory to the right, victory to the left—O you who are of dual nature, the remover of the vulgar mind! 1.205.20
Having thus offered praise and prostrated like a staff, his body covered with horripilation and his eyes clouded with tears, he bowed down again and again. ||21||
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa was exceedingly pleased and said to Nārada:
"O best of Gandharvas, having today heard this song accompanied by dance—" (22)
I am pleased with this supreme music, which possesses rhythm, melody, a moist heart, and is pregnant with emotion; become here the bridge between the two shores.
May you be one who promotes devotion to me; may you be a constant performer of my worship.
May you become an ocean of all knowledge and virtues, endowed with eternal and stable youth. 24.
By this very body, become one whose body is liberated and imperishable;
for you there is no death, no disease, no old age, and no transmigration.
Just as I am, so are you; O Mānasa, always remain in my own form, and though you are a devotee, become the Lord himself.
Having received this blessing, he himself became an incarnation of Brahmā;
indeed, by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, he became a partial manifestation (kalāṃśa). ||27||
Nārāyaṇa, having touched his head with his hand, spoke again:
"O great sage, you have truly been accepted by me today as dear to my heart."
May that same perfect omniscience which exists in me be present in you as well, without cessation;
and compose for me the Pañcarātra scripture that bestows devotion. (29)
Worship Him whom Viṣṇu, Śiva, the Creator of the Universe, Śeṣa, Gaṇapati, the gods, the Manus, the sages, and the lords worship. 1.205.30.
Worship him whom Lakṣmī, Śivā, Sāvitrī, Ramā, Ṛddhi, Siddhi, Devikā, Mānavī, and Īśvarī worship. 3.1.
Worship him whom the Gaṅgā, Gomatī, Revā, Gaṇḍakī, Sarasvatī,
Yamunā, and Svarṇarekhā all revere.
Worship him whom Pārvatī, Prabhā, Amṛtā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Dīpotsavī, and Rādhā likewise worship. (33)
To cross the ocean of saṃsāra, to leap over the forest fire of worldly existence,
and to protect yourself from the serpent of the world, indeed take up the service of Hari.
Having crossed the forest of birth and seeking to cross over the mountain of death,
as you proceed toward the region of the Abode, take refuge in the celestial chariot of Kṛṣṇa.
Worship that Kṛṣṇa, upon whose body hair all the worlds reside, who held Govardhana on the tip of his tooth, and who held the earth on the end of his finger. 36.
O Nārada, worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who moves through all the scriptures and from whom these Vedas have issued forth, and in whose mouth they reside. 37.
Time, illusion, evil karma, and the attendants of Yama—those lords exist only through a portion of His power; therefore, worship that Kṛṣṇa at all times. (38)
Worship Him whom Bhū, Sītā, Bhārgavī, Padmā, Gopī, Vṛndā, Kubjikā, Śabarī, and Piṅgalā—the goddesses—worship. (39)
Worship in every way that Hari, of whom Virāṭ is but a fraction, the Manus are fractions, and the sages are fractions of fractions of fractions. 1.205.40.

The earth rests upon the thousand-headed Śeṣa, he upon the tortoise, and he upon the waters; those waters rest upon his splendor, that splendor upon his great splendor, and that great splendor rests upon Hari—worship Hari, who is their support. 41.

Those who abide in the abodes, those who abide in the celestial spheres of the worlds, those established in yoga, and those established in Brahman—even they do not reach the further shore of one who is established in his own self; therefore, worship Hari, the boundless. 42.
Worship that infinite Hari, whose liberated souls are innumerable, whose maidservants are of endless count, and whose revelations and creations are infinite. 43.
Worship that Nārāyaṇa, of whom Śrī, Lakṣmī, Dhiḥ, Brāhmī, Sādhu, and Māyā are but single portions of his form, acting as his powers (śaktis). 44.
Nārāyaṇī is the power (śakti) of Hari; women have been created as her portions.
O child, having married a wife, you should enjoy Nārāyaṇī as your bride.
"Obey my command and your father's command; accept your wife, who is the very embodiment of authority.
Thus, as a protector of dharma, may you be honored and victorious. (46)
He who indeed pleases his own wife with garments, ornaments, and articles—Nārāyaṇī, being pleased with him, delivers him just as Kṛṣṇa does. ||47||
Lakṣmī is the power (śakti) of Nārāyaṇa; she indeed exists in the form of women.
By insulting women, she becomes utterly defeated. ||48||
By her being dishonored, a man becomes dishonored;
being dishonored by her, that unfortunate man finds no happiness anywhere.
By him who worships the divine woman, who bestows all that is desired,
she shall become a virtuous mother of sons and a granter of all auspiciousness.
That primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) is one, having the nature of the perfect Brahman;
yet she indeed possesses six forms, and she should be worshipped by those seeking auspiciousness. (51)
Indeed, that Rādhikā alone is the beloved who is the very life-breath of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the second is Lakṣmī, the bestower of prosperity, who is the life-breath of Nārāyaṇa. (52)
The third is Sarasvatī, the goddess who presides over speech;
the fourth is Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, whose life-breath is Brahman.
And Satī Pārvatī, the fifth [daughter], whose form is the very life-breath of Śaṅkara, was married; she is indeed the bride of every embodied being. (54)
This sixth [letter] is to be understood as having the form of the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and as bestowing the lineage;
becoming a lord of yogis like a second Kṛṣṇa, one should serve her. (55)
"Let there be no bondage for you therein; I have assumed my own form [there].
O Nārada, always maintain this knowledge which has been granted by me. (56)
And Nārada, having received the command of Hari, prostrated himself; out of love, he performed a circumambulation and fell like a staff upon the ground. ||57||
Having meditated upon that Nārāyaṇa, he went there together with Nara to perform sacred rites at the holy fords (tīrthas), even though he was already liberated.
Previously, he bathed in the cold water of the Cālakanandā;
at that moment, his body became divine like that of Nārāyaṇa.
At that time, it was uncontradicted in terms of space, time, and substance;
it was pure consciousness, the substratum of all powers, like the body of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Journey to Badarikāśrama, His Vision of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, His Hymn of Praise through Song, His Attainment of Divinity, the Instruction on Devotion, and the Command to Perform Marriage," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, tell me briefly which sacred fords (tīrthas) were established by the sage in that hermitage, and how they are purifying.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having bathed in the Gaṅgā and assumed a divine form,
Nārada went first to Badarī, which is the descent of the imperishable Brahman.
Having bowed, praised, and worshipped her, and likewise having performed a circumambulation,
he ate a leaf and a jujube fruit as a token of her grace.
Having meditated internally upon that form— smooth, thornless, divine, green, covered with sprouts, possessed of flowers and fruits, and beautiful.
Then the sage went to the purifying Vahnitīrtha;
there he drank the water and heard that narrative from the mouth of a man.
In ancient times, an assembly of sages belonging to the Ūrdhvasrotas lineage gathered at Prayāga, the sacred ground where the Gaṅgā and Yamunā meet.
There, at the horse sacrifice, the consumer of oblations (Agni) began to question those whose minds were stained by the sin arising from devouring all kinds of forbidden food.
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, how may my liberation from sin be achieved?
Vyāsa then said to Vahni, "Go to Badarī for refuge."
Having bathed there in the waters of the Gaṅgā where the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, the destroyer of the sins of his devotees, resides, and having performed circumambulation of Hari; || 9 ||
By prostrating oneself like a staff, the destruction of all faults occurs;
thereafter, Agni reached Badarī and likewise bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having gone to Nara-Nārāyaṇa and bowed down, he offered praise;
and [he praised] Agni as Pāvaka, Ātmapāvaka, and Brahmapāvaka.
I bow down to the purifier of Māyā, the purifier of sacred fords, the Lord who bestows the meritorious fruits of the penances of the sages and grants liberation. 12.
I praise the Guru, who bestows knowledge, who bestows dharma, who bestows yoga, the ascetic Hari, the giver of happiness, who is clothed in bark garments, and who possesses the eightfold power. 13.
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa said, "O Pāvaka, choose a boon.
Agni replied, "O Hari, I am a consumer of all things; that is a great defect. (14)
"How indeed may the destruction of defects occur, for fear arising from defects is most difficult to overcome?
Nārāyaṇa then replied: "It is by the sight of this sacred field. (15)
"By my grace, let there be no sin for living beings;
and from this day forward, O Agni, since you have bathed here, let this be known as Agnitīrtha."
It shall become renowned upon the earth as the remover of the sin of eating all things;
and by my power, let your residence there always be established through a portion of yourself.
Then, having bathed in that sacred ford, Nārada, the purifier of the world,
went with devotion to perform the rites at the five Śilā-pañca-tīrthas.
The Nāradī, Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Gāruḍī, and the one renowned as Mārkaṇḍeyī—these stones are supremely purifying. (19)
And the sage Nārada, who was himself Brahmā in his first birth,
performed most rigorous penance for the sake of beholding Mahāviṣṇu.
For sixty thousand years he subsisted on air alone upon a stone slab; while he remained there living under a tree, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa, [approached him].
Having granted him his vision, he said: "O sage, why do you suffer?
Tell me what you desire; you have become pure through your asceticism."
Nārada, the compassionate one, said: "Who are you in this forest?
Merely by the sight of you, my mind attains serenity. (23)
At that moment, Nārāyaṇa appeared there, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
clad in yellow garments, he wore the Kaustubha gem, a forest garland, and a sacred thread.
His chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa, he possessed a golden line upon his lotus-like form, and,
possessing a beautiful smile, he was being served by his attendants such as Sunanda and others.
He revealed his own form to the ascetic Nārada;
seeing him, [Nārada] rose up suddenly and, with palms joined in reverence, paid homage.
He praised the Supreme Self, the Lord who is an ocean of compassion, the Sovereign of the worlds, who exists as the witness and who shows favor to his devotees. (27)
I bow to the compassionate, divine ascetic; be gracious, O Purifier, who has undertaken austerity for the protection and welfare of the world of the virtuous. (28)
O giver of the fruits of austerity, be gracious, you who possess a form of pure being; you whose graceful charm possesses the loveliness of ten million Cupids, yet you are free from desire.

O Lord of Gods, you are a celibate student; be gracious, O All-pervading One, whose word is truth! You are the wish-fulfilling tree for those who take refuge in you, and the remover of suffering for the distressed.

There, even those non-Buddhist practitioners see those of divine form;
though they are defiled, they become purified and partakers of liberation.
Having bathed at the Vasudhārā Tīrtha, Nārada then proceeded to the Pañcadhārā Tīrtha located in the south-western direction.
Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, Gayā, and Naimiṣa—these five sacred fords [purify] sinners from the taint of their sins. (82)
Having heard the reason for Brahmā’s arrival and remembering Badarikāśrama, they went to the Creator of the Universe for the sake of purification. 83.
He said, "Go quickly to Hari’s Badarikāśrama, where by the mere act of entering, merit shall arise that destroys all sin. (84)
Then, having bowed down, they all went to Badarikāśrama;
by merely entering there, their sins were completely destroyed.
Then, assuming two forms, they remain in a liquid state;
even when returned to their own places, they abide in their respective forms.
Having bathed in them and bowed to Hari, a person who observes five fasts shall enjoy many pleasures in this world and attain the same realm as Hari (sālokya). ||87||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Vainateya Stone, the Gāruḍī Stone, the Five-faced Gaṅgā, the Nārasiṃhī Stone, Brahma-tīrtha, Sarasvatī-tīrtha, the Dravadhārendrapada-tīrtha, Mānasodbheda, Vasudhārā, the Pañcadhārā-tīrtha, and others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; from there Nārada went to Somakuṇḍaka, the place where in ancient times the Lord Soma performed penance.
But Soma, the son of Atri, [attained] great and divine heavenly bliss.
Having heard from the Gandharvas more than once the cause for obtaining his father, [he departed].
And he asked again: "O Father, tell me how I may become the supreme lord of the planets, constellations, stars, and medicinal herbs. (3)
"Tell me likewise the means for its accomplishment. Having heard this, Atri spoke to him three times: "Everything is attained through austerity; likewise, by propitiating Hari."
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever difficult for the virtuous to attain in either world;
for there exists such a supreme sacred site as Badarikāśrama.
Having heard this, Soma went to Badarī and performed the worship of Viṣṇu,
preceded by the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra.
Devoted to the Blessed One, he performed most rigorous austerities for eighty-eight thousand years, bathing daily at the three sessions of the day.
Śrī Hari, being pleased by that austerity,
arrived and said to Soma again and again, "Choose a boon."
Then Soma, having prostrated himself like a staff before Hari there while laughing, said:
"I am the lord of the planets, constellations, stars, and medicinal herbs."
"By your grace, may I also become one among all the twice-born.
Hari said, "You do not possess such austerity; choose something else."
Soma did not indeed request any other boon, but practiced penance once more;
after thirty thousand years, the Blessed One then appeared.
"Choose a boon," Soma said; and having heard this, Hari likewise chose a boon and vanished, while Soma then spoke again.
He performed most rigorous penance for forty thousand years;
thereupon Hari, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, was pleased with him.
He appeared and said, "Choose a boon as a gift.
Soma said, "If you are pleased, then grant me that boon. (14)
O Lord of the World, grant to me sovereignty over the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars; likewise, over the medicinal herbs, the brahmins, and the night. (15)
The Blessed One said: "Soma, which you have requested, is indeed difficult to obtain;
nevertheless, I grant it to you today—become a king of such a kind."
Then all the inhabitants of heaven assembled in the Badarī forest and,
with great reverence, duly consecrated Soma as their king.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot and become the Moon (Niśākara), the king departed for heaven; and that sacred bathing place became renowned as Somakuṇḍa.
By the mere sight [of it], they become free from defects and go to the world of Soma;
or by touching it or bathing there, they go to the world of Viṣṇu. (19)
For them there is no returning again, even in hundreds of millions of eons;
by remaining for three nights reciting the mantra, one attains perfection.
Having then established Somatīrtha, the venerable sage Nārada departed;
he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites at Dvādaśādityatīrtha.
The sons of Kaśyapa and Aditi, having performed most rigorous penance, attained the status of Ādityas; indeed, that sacred ford is a destroyer of sins.
Indeed, by bathing according to the prescribed rite on Sundays, on the seventh lunar day (saptamī), or during a solar transit (saṃkrānti),
a person effects the destruction of the sins acquired over seven lifetimes.
But he who performs the Pārāka-Kṛcchra vow according to the prescribed rule, having enjoyed happiness in the world of the Sun, proceeds to the world of Viṣṇu. ||24||

Having bathed and drunk [the water], one is liberated from great diseases; there is no doubt about this. Then, having performed his ablutions at that holy site, he went to Catuḥsrotas, the best of sacred fords.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa exist here in their substantial forms; they reside respectively in the directions starting from the east, serving as the means for the liberation of living beings. (26)
They exist here in this supreme field in accordance with the command of Hari;
they do not meet in any other field, for such a thing is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Those of a sattvic nature, who have acquired merits through the service of Nārāyaṇa, behold those personified goals of human endeavor here.
At the Pumartha-tīrtha, Brahmā and the other gods, as well as sages and ascetics, come on sacred festival days, purified, to bathe for the sake of its renown. (29)
Having performed his rites at that holy ford, the venerable Nārada went to the sacred site named Satyapada, which was adorned with a triangular pool.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, established in the triangle and composed in meditation, perform penance along with the sages for the gratification of the worlds. ||3 1 ||
On the eleventh day, Hari himself, the purifier, comes there,
along with sages, seers, gods, and others whose wealth is their austerity.
Devoted to the worship of Hari, they come to this pool to bathe,
performing the chanting, austerity, praise, meditation, salutation, and worship of Hari.
For those who perform this accumulation of merit by bathing, observing a fast, and worshipping the Lord Hari, it is impossible to describe the full extent of their store of virtue. || 34 ||
Having become liberated while living (jīvanmukta) here, one then becomes liberated in Brahman;
having bathed and reached Satyaloka, one thereafter proceeds to the state of final liberation (mokṣapada). || 35 ||
There, at midday on the day of Hari, the divine song of the Gandharvas and Apsarases is indeed heard by those devoted to their vows of truth.
By the majesty of his splendor, sins such as the *pātaka*s were dissolved;
having performed the rites for the sacred ford, he went to the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa. (37)
There, two kinds of water are seen—the preeminent among all sacred fords (tīrtha), and supremely pure: namely, the white and the non-white. (38)
Having bathed there and worshipped Hari, one is liberated from sin;
for having performed the ritual of the sacred ford there, it is indeed the most excellent Urvaśī-tīrtha.
He went to the peak that is the abode of Nārāyaṇa, where there flows pure water,
rich in coolness, where the king of sages, Nārada, resides.
And he questioned the man regarding his history, and the man indeed spoke:
"Mūrti was the wife of Dharma; from them were born Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (41)
Two sons were born: the Lord Hari, who dwells in the imperishable abode, was called Nara, and Nārāyaṇa was Hari himself. (42)
And those two, having remained on two mountains to perform penance,
constantly practiced severe austerity by the command of their parents.
"These two are for the sake of protecting the subjects and likewise for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
Indra, terrified by their ascetic power and apprehensive of the loss of his kingdom, [acted]. (44)
He dispatched Kāma along with his retinue to the side of Vasanta,
as well as Harṣa, Preman, the arrows, the bow, and the Apsarases.
The breeze was rich with fragrance, cool, and delightful;
mingled with droplets from the clouds, it was the auspicious hour of night. (46)
The moonlight was white, as were the cuckoos and the cātaka birds;
likewise, there were peacocks, singers, dancers, and musicians. (47)
Thus, when all have assembled, the ritual means will not be deficient;
likewise, by the command of Indra, they all united with Kāma. (48)
They went to where the sage Sanatkumāra was performing austerities as Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
there the moon remained, spreading its moonlight for the first time. 49.
The entire surface became tranquil, as if washed white;
even the night, through its radiance of clear darkness, seemed to have shed its passionate impetuosity.
And there, the Rājasa Samaya also spread forth;
assuming the conceptualization of passion (rajas), it repeatedly became an inspirer. ||5.1||
The cuckoos dwelling in the world of the gods, as well as the peacocks and peahens,
began to coo slowly with sweet sounds and cries of *kekā*.
The mango trees, awakening desire, shine with flowers and blossoms;
spring has assumed the form of fragrant flowers upon the trees and creepers. (53)
Then a breeze arose, rich with fragrance, gentle and cool;
and all the singers, dancers, and instrumentalists performed in harmony.
While they were engaged in singing, dancing, and instrumental music infused with passion, Harṣa and Prema then entered into Nara and Nārāyaṇa. 55.
With his bow, the Mind-born [God of Love] discharged arrows such as the "Deluder" (mohana),
and a divine host of Apsarases who displayed gestures, expressions, and amorous charms.
Then, assuming the form of a fifteen-year-old, he performed a bewildering display of various movements of his limbs.
And with devotion, she massaged the feet of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
going to their sides again and again, she kissed them many times. (58)
Likewise, Kāma discharged his arrows at her cheeks, hands, and thighs;
thereafter, he indeed became exhausted.
Even amidst all manner of disturbances, Nara and Nārāyaṇa remained with their eyes fixed and motionless, as if established in ascetic meditation alone.
Not wavering even slightly, they remained thus absorbed in meditation;
at that time, the assembly of Kāmadeva became fruitless.
When they were unable to bring about the destruction of his asceticism, they all departed dejected; becoming restless, they spoke to Mahendra.
Indeed, our army does not exert even the slightest prowess there,
for everything that has been done and undertaken has become fruitless, just as the tortoise [failed] according to the command of Hari.
And Indra, having heard them all, went to that place and brought them there;
he then caused them to perform the practice of love once again.
They became fruitless while remaining in perfect meditative absorption before the presence of Hari;
then Nārāyaṇa himself, rising from his meditation, spoke to those who had assembled.
"For what purpose have you come? Please accept hospitality.
Having said this, he gave them fruits and roots in great abundance.
Then Nārāyaṇa said to Nara: "Behold the circle of Indra;
this great Indra is conceiving pride in his mind because of the celestial nymphs."
Nowhere else are there such deluding celestial nymphs;
yet he, utterly infatuated, does not recognize even a fraction of my sovereign power.
All these were created by me alone, and they are absorbed back into me;
I alone nourish these beautiful forms, yet he does not know this at all.
Therefore, go and bring mango blossoms without delay;
once you have them, crush them here in my presence with your left leg.
When Nara had done this, a most radiant woman was born there;
she who was born from his thigh was Urvaśī, who became enamored even of the twelve Adityas.
When the dark Apsarases, whose limbs were perfectly proportioned to their forms, appeared before him, they became lusterless; even Kama was shattered by his pride.
Indra became dejected in countenance upon seeing Urvaśī restored to youth,
she whose touch had indeed made her more beautiful than the finest flower in the three worlds.
"A jewel among women has been born; who is capable of deluding her?
Thinking thus, he went to Nārāyaṇa in order to request forgiveness. (74)
Falling quickly at his feet, he cried, "Save me from my transgression! and, becoming overwhelmed, he spoke like a man who has committed an offense.
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "Your task has been accomplished by you;
I do not take your offense into account. Go to heaven and be happy. (76)
I practice austerity for the sake of the happiness of the worlds, not out of craving, nor for the sake of your kingdom, nor for any other sovereignty. (77)
I have no thirst for kingship, nor do I have any longing for your kingdom;
for my eternal kingdom is Vaikuṇṭha, which comprises all that is conscious and unconscious.
"This universe was created by me; I am certainly not deluded regarding it, even though you, considering me an ordinary man, sought to delude this ascetic. (79)
All my exertion was indeed in vain regarding me, Nārāyaṇa;
for Indra, having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, was deluded by the power of Urvaśī.
He again entreated her for that beautiful object created by Māyā, saying,
"O Blessed One, such a jewel is an obstacle even to ascetics."
And it appears to me that she is worthy of heaven; you have no need for her.
Therefore, O Lord, grant her to me; I am your servant and I beg this of you. (82)
"I shall certainly not commit any further offense against you in the performance of my ascetic penance.
Having heard this from Nārāyaṇa, he granted him the beautiful Urvaśī.
Delighted, he too went to heaven along with his retinue for Indra,
where Urvaśī was born from the crushing of the thigh of Purūravas.
In that place is the Urvaśīkuṇḍa Tīrtha, endowed with water;
having bathed there according to the prescribed rite and fasted for two nights, [one attains the fruit]. ||85||
Having worshipped Hari there, a man shall become Nārāyaṇa;
and for one who possesses desires, a goddess resembling Urvaśī shall appear in heaven.
Having reached Urvaśīkuṇḍa, a person whose desires are powerful may attain the world of Urvaśī merely by bathing there with devotion. (87)
The Blessed One, the embodiment of austerity, always remains there in the vicinity of the Urvaśī-kuṇḍa, inspiring the welfare of all living beings. 88.
Insects, moths, and birds laugh at the deities in heaven;
we are endowed with both worldly enjoyment and liberation, while you are merely givers of liberation. (89)
Having reached Urvaśīkuṇḍa, a person should dwell there for one day;
indeed, on the southern side of Urvaśī are the weapons of the Lord of the Universe.
By seeing them, one shall not suffer from the fear of weapons;
there are many sacred fords on the mountain inhabited by Nārāyaṇa. (91)
I know all of them, and no other ordinary person indeed knows them;
whoever should hear this with devotion or cause it to be heard while composed in mind—||92||
Whether one recites it oneself or causes others to recite it, one shall obtain the fruit of each respective sacred ford;
having shaken off all sins, one shall attain the same world as Hari (sālokya). ||93||

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "Description of Somakuṇḍa-tīrtha, Āditya-tīrtha, Catuḥpuruṣārtha-tīrtha, Urvaśī-samutpatti-tīrtha, and others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, how Nārada subsequently went to the auspicious place known as Meru,
a sacred site situated to the south of Brahmakuṇḍa.
That mountain Meru, the abode of men, was established here by Hari when the Blessed One made his auspicious residence in Viśālā.
Then, leaving Mount Meru itself, the gods, great sages, and Siddhas, along with the Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas, were eager for a vision of Hari.
They arrived full of eagerness to dwell forever in Viśālā, having set aside their attachment to that [former] abode upon obtaining the vision of the Blessed One. || 4 ||
Deprived of the gods and others, Meru fell into grief;
becoming distressed, he went to Nārāyaṇa for the purpose of making a request.
He said: "O Blessed One, all of them are eager for a vision of you;
they have come here, leaving me behind, without their auspicious dwelling."
"It is not fitting for me to dwell there; indeed, I must certainly not stay.
I, too, desire to dwell here at your feet. (7)
And the Blessed One then said: "This will certainly not lead to your welfare;
for it is held that the stability of the fourteen worlds depends upon your stability."
Therefore, by my command, the gods and others must indeed remain there;
and they must also remain right here in their second forms.
"You too must always remain here in my hermitage in this second form of yours, for through this you shall obtain the merit of serving me."
Having thus received the command, they assumed a second form and arrived from all sides upon the peaks of Mount Meru in a subtle state.
Indeed, those golden forms were grasped by Hari with his own hand and established there for the sake of all dwellings.
Having beheld all the peaks which were golden in form, they were filled with joy;
gracious and satisfied, they praised the compassionate Lord Nārāyaṇa.
The compassionate Lord, the God of the gods, brought the peaks of Mount Meru for the sake of the happiness of the Day-makers; to him we offer our salutations. (14)
May that Lord Śrī Narāyaṇa, the abode of compassion, who bestows manifold fruits even upon those with little devotion or scanty mercy, be pleased. || 15 ||
Ever compassionate, Kṛṣṇa, that ocean of mercy, bestows instruction upon us like a father; may he protect us even from calamities. 16.
May the Blessed One, the protector of devotees, who grants the heart's desires of the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Ṛṣis, always protect us here. (17)
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, said to them, "Choose a boon. The gods replied, "May those people who behold the peaks of Mount Meru [attain this]."
By your grace, let their residence indeed be upon Mount Meru;
you must not abandon this place, nor should Mount Meru ever be abandoned.
"And for those who have obtained residence with me, let their dissolution be in you at the end of their enjoyment.
Having spoken thus, "So be it," Hari vanished right there.
From that time forward, the gods and others [resided] at the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
sometimes on Mount Meru, sometimes in heaven, and sometimes indeed on Mount Raivata.
Where Nārāyaṇa and Nara dwell free from fear;
having thus established the Meru-tīrtha, Nārada departed from there.
Hari himself went to Meru, a gentle sacred site presided over by the world-protectors and endowed with lakes; there he beheld the deities.
Then the sages, the ascetics, the world-protectors, the gods, and others, having seen him, said to the world-protectors: "Indeed, you yourselves are kings."
Dwelling in the hermitage of the sages and others is not suitable for you;
please come to the place prepared by me, which is appropriate for you. (25)
"And let them dwell right there, relying upon my presence.
Thus were the world-protectors brought from the central region of Mount Meru.
For their benefit, he established [shrines] and constructed a great reservoir;
moreover, having struck the earth with his staff, he created a pleasure-pool.
The world-protectors, the Gandharvas, and the gods, accompanied by thousands of celestial nymphs, wander about, offer their approval, and sing praises at all times. (28)
Indeed, he created forests delightful with the fragrance of flowers,
and the Blessed One brought supreme joy to everyone.
On the twelfth lunar day and on the full moon day, he comes of his own accord for immersion;
at midday, a supreme radiance is seen within the water.
The fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas) is obtained right there;
the Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī ford bestows rewards both in this world and the next.
And by offering a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) here at Puṣkara on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one obtains eight times the fruit that is obtained from Gayā.
Having performed sacrifice, charity, and austerity, a person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose;
he enjoys imperishable fruit and thereafter attains liberation. ||33||
This indeed exists hidden in the midst of the Badarī-tīrtha;
those who have generated abundant merit behold it, and no others.
Having thus established the Daṇḍodaka Tīrtha, Nārada departed for the supreme Tīrtha at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Mānasodbheda.
The fruit of performing penance at Prayāga for thirty thousand years is obtained by one who performs an ablution at the Mānasodbheda Tīrtha.
To the south of Saṅgama is the auspicious abode of Dharma,
where the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa took birth in embodied form.
Wherein Dharma has four feet— truth, sacrifice, austerity,
and likewise charity— the fruit of that which is practiced there indeed becomes inexhaustible.
Then, in the southern quarter, is the holy site named Urvaśīsaṃgama;
following that is the Kūrmoddhāra tīrtha, which brings purity to the soul through bathing.
Beyond that is the holy ford of Brahmāvarta, for it bestows the world of Brahmā;
indeed, there are many such sacred fords within the forest of Badarī.
Through seeing, remembering, bathing, drinking, sipping water, and likewise through sprinkling,
these [sacred waters] destroy sins and grant liberation through yoga.
Having visited all the sacred fords, Nārada returned once more to the primordial hermitage of Nara, having stayed there after hearing [the account] from the mouth of Nara. 42.

With a mind focused solely on peace and with his afflictions dispelled, he heard of the majesty of the sacred field known as Badarī, the domain of Hari, which is difficult to attain even within the three worlds. (43)
By remembering it, even his most terrible sins are destroyed;
the merit acquired at another sacred site becomes equal to that of Badarī through mere remembrance. 44.
Whatever fruit is obtained from a thousand horse-sacrifices and from subsisting on air, that same fruit is attained at Badarī in a single moment within this sacred field. 45.
In the Kṛta age it is known by the name Muktipradā; in Tretā, it is Yogasiddhidā; in Dvāpara, it is Viśālā by name; and in the Kali age, it is indeed Badaryāśrama.
Just as she is the bestower of liberation and the giver of success in yoga in every way, so too is Viśālā [the bestower] through the destruction of this body composed of the elements. 47.
Indeed, because of its connection with the Badarī tree, that place is called Badarikāśrama;
one may abandon all other holy sites at the time of the end of a Yuga.
Indeed, Hari Nārāyaṇa never leaves Badarī;
for sixty thousand years, he remains there through yoga, and the fruit which is obtained at Kāśī [in that time] is attained here. 49.
But at Badarī, that same fruit is obtained in a single day;
for there indeed exist the distinguished halls of the gods, the holy fords, and the sages.
And likewise, the Śālā of knowledge is considered vast and meaningful;
that vast [Śālā] is beginninglessly established, just as the Vedas are the body of Hari. //5.1//
Except for liberation through death according to the ordinances of one's own dharma, liberation stands within the grasp of men simply by the sight of Badarī. (52)
Then, having conquered both merit and demerit and beheld Narayana, the Lord of Badari,
a person indeed attains liberation here without any effort.
In all ages, the Blessed Lord, having reached Badarī, which is auspicious and resembles Vaikuṇṭha itself, dwells there in person.
Without knowledge, without yoga, and without the exertion of wandering to sacred fords, a living being attains the state of absolute liberation in a single lifetime. //55//
He by whom Hari has been worshipped throughout thousands of previous births shall go to see Badarī, having gone to which one does not grieve.
By uttering "Badarī, Badarī" even incidentally, one becomes a partaker of liberation;
having beheld the vast Badarī, whence can there be fear of death for a man? (57)
The earth, together with its mountains and forests, was circumambulated ten times by Hari on the ground at Badarī, at every single step.
The merit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and of a hundred vājapeya sacrifices is indeed equal to the merit found at every single step in circumambulating Lord Hari.
Whatever food has attained a divine state that the Blessed One eats at Badarī,
that should be consumed by all for the purification of their being, without hesitation.
The immortals become intent on consuming the food offerings made to Hari;
yet, in childhood, youth, or old age, they have committed sins that end only with life. (6.1)
Having eaten what has been offered to Viṣṇu at Badarī, one returns there;
by eating the food offering (naivedya) here, one attains the same world as Hari (sālokya).
He who has the form of Hari in his heart, His name in his mouth, the food offering in his stomach,
and the water from His feet along with the remains of His floral offerings upon his head— he is Acyuta himself.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by the nectar of [his] feet;
what is the use of gifts, austerities, pilgrimages, observances, or arduous efforts? (64)
If even a mere drop from Viṣṇu’s feet and so forth at Badarī should touch one, it indeed yields the fruit of a great gift made at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse. ||65||
In Badarī, by merely taking a single morsel of food, one gains more merit than the fruit of the Cāturmāsya vow;
and from the nectar of the feet [of the Lord] in Badarī, one obtains the merit of hearing the Vedānta.
Even for those who are dull-witted, liberation is held in the palm of their hand merely by seeing the sacred ground of Badarī, where they have received the Vaiṣṇava initiation.
Whoever should constantly hear this, cause it to be heard, or teach it, or should read it, being liberated from sin, attains the abode of Viṣṇu. ||68||
The king attains victory; he who desires a son obtains a son;
he who desires a daughter obtains a daughter; and the maiden finds a virtuous husband. (69)
One seeking wealth obtains wealth; it destroys disease, mental anguish, and poverty, and it eliminates misfortune, untimely death, malefic planetary influences, bad dreams, and the like.
Having heard [the account], having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and having partaken of the prasāda,
that Nārada departed for the true world of Brahmā for the sake of the wedding.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Meru Tīrtha, Daṇḍa Puṣkariṇī, Mānasa Udbheda, the Birthplace of Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the Arrival of Urvaśī, the Rescue of Kūrma, Brahmāvarta, and Other Tīrthas, as Well as the Grace of Those Sacred Fields and the Nectar of Their Feet," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Mahālakṣmī; the devoted worshipper of Hari, Nārada, went to his own abode, for Brahmā was greatly pleased. (1)
Having performed his pilgrimage and arrived there, he summoned the gods and others and began a fitting celebration for Nārada.
Nārāyaṇa himself, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, and also the Lord of Ramā (Śrī), as well as Śiva and the other world-protectors and sages, all assembled there. || 3 ||
Then that divine assembly of Brahmā shone like the abode of Brahmā itself;
there, in the presence of the virtuous who were listening, Brahmā addressed his son Nārada.
In the presence of Śaṅkara, the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa, who was the husband of fifty women, spoke these righteous and excellent words to Nārada.
In another birth you were [her husband], but now you are the son of Brahmā;
and among them, one virtuous woman, Mālāvatī, [worshipped] Śaṅkara through austerity.
Having propitiated him, she obtained her desired boon and Nārada as her husband;
she is that daughter of Sṛñjaya who was the sister of Svarṇaṣṭhīvī.
"Obey the command of Śaṅkara:
'Marry her,' for she is the most beautiful among beauties and is devoted solely to her husband."
