O Nārada, marry her who is desirable due to the boon of Hara, whose youth is eternally firm, and who was inscribed by the Creator upon her forehead.
Just as you previously stated regarding the pilgrimage, so too has the fortune of marriage been attained; by whom can that which was ordained in the past be warded off?
An action that has been performed is not exhausted even by hundreds of millions of eons;
whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been done must necessarily be experienced.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Nārada, who was then observing his father’s command, showed humility and bowed down to all the deities.
This Veda, commanded by my father, is always maintained by me;
furthermore, by your grace, there shall be no bondage for me therein.
"I choose this boon: may my mind be devoted to the Blessed One.
"Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, and Śiva shall grant it so," they said. (14)
Having bowed down to the gods, Nārada departed for the abode of Sṛñjaya;
there he beheld the beautiful and divine daughter of Sṛñjaya and was captivated by her. 15.
Having mentally accepted that auspicious lady, who was ascetic, highly fortunate, and devoted to the vow of Viṣṇu, Nārada spoke to her.
"O fool, do you know me, yet you do not know your own elder sister, the most excellent of Gandharva women, renowned as Mālavatī? (17)
Having heard this and having seen Nārada, Mālāvatī fainted,
recognizing him as her very husband from her previous birth.
She quickly fell at his feet and kissed him for the sake of choosing him; Nārada, standing before her father, also made a request for her.
And having understood Mālāvatī’s intention, Śrī Sṛñjaya himself gave his own daughter to Nārada by means of the formal gift of words.
Having partaken of the *tilaka* food and having offered a garment and a cloth,
Nārada bowed to his father-in-law, and likewise inquired after his mother-in-law and his beloved wife.
He went to the beautiful assembly hall of Brahmā, which was inhabited by all the gods;
having bowed to his father, he, being tranquil, spoke to him the entirety of the truth.
Hearing the auspicious words regarding the gift, Brahmā, with a joyful countenance,
summoned all the lords and celebrated a magnificent festival.
Having summoned the sages, seers, ancestors, gods, daityas, dānavas, and all the offspring of Kaśyapa, he performed an auspicious rite.
Sṛñjaya sent a letter with a messenger-brahmin;
Brahmā, having accepted it, caused his son to perform the customary rites of the world.
There, the Creator of the Universe indeed caused the auspicious moment for the marriage to be proclaimed and had various kinds of foods prepared.
The Creator of the Universe caused to be prepared in their entirety gifts, vehicles, utensils, drinks, foods, and various articles for distribution.
At an auspicious moment, Brahmā himself [was accompanied] by crores upon crores of lotuses and arbudas, as well as by gods, demons, and multitudes of people, each joined with their respective women.
Accompanied by jeweled vehicles, he arranged a magnificent procession,
placing his son at the front and a highly resplendent army of people behind him.
Accompanied by Śambhu and Acyuta, he took with him Mahīmāna, who was joined by Arbuda, Koṭikoṭi, and Arbuda, and went to the palace of Sṛñjaya.
Sṛñjaya went forth with his kinsmen and relatives to honor [the bridegroom],
and he stationed the bridegroom's army for a moment in his own garden.
Having provided him with water to drink, rest, and a meal,
and having adorned him in the evening, he led him toward the pavilion.
And for the sake of the maiden, Brahmā indeed sent many beautiful garments and ornaments, each suited to her.
Having performed worship at the gate according to the conduct of the learned, Sṛñjaya then observed the worldly custom and honored the excellent Nārada.
And near the principal fire-altar, he stationed the bridegroom;
he then had the maiden, richly adorned with ornaments, brought there.
There, by the Brāhmaṇas, the Munis, the Saptarṣis, and the gods on earth,
auspicious mantras were recited and the purification of the body was performed.
Having tied the knot of the garment and offered the bridegroom’s garland,
the King of Sṛñjaya himself placed the maiden’s hand into the hand of the bridegroom.
Then the sounds of the Vedas arose and musical instruments were likewise played;
then the bride, taking a morsel of food, placed it into the mouth of Nārada.
Nārada also placed a propitious morsel of food into the mouth of the new bride;
then, having circumambulated the fire, he performed the rite of oblation.
Having performed the highest traditional rites and having given abundant gifts,
he then brought all the wedding ceremonies to completion.
The personal property of the bride and the honorarium for the groom were given;
then, after all the people had performed the rites, they partook of the meal.
Having slept through the assembly, they beheld the auspicious sounding of instruments at dawn, along with the dancing and singing of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Many gifts and all kinds of food were given by Sṛñjaya; guests were honored with hospitality. ||43||
Having given his entire possession as a sacrificial fee, including jewels, pearls, and the like,
he joined his palms in reverence and offered this plea for exemption.
And King Śṛñjaya, having affectionately bestowed his daughter upon him, sent Vāhinī away with humility and great joy. (45)
Then Śṛñjaya and his wife could not endure that sorrow born of separation from their daughter; they wept for a moment. || 46 ||
The daughter also wept out of affection, mingled with the pain of separation; having prostrated before her parents, the girl likewise wept for her mother.
Embracing him and summoning his fortitude, the Creator joyfully ascended the chariot,
taking with him that son along with his wife.
Honoring worldly custom, he went happily to the world of Brahmā,
[passing through] the ṛṣis, munis, gods, ancestors, siddhas, and humans.
He fed the Brahmins during the auspicious rite along with its constituent parts;
he caused gifts to be distributed and had the drums beaten.
And Nārada, the best of sages, caused all the great beings— the gods and the asuras— to subsist by means of his own work, Likhita.
And upon that most delightful bed of flowers, anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste, he took delight together with Ramā; he perceived neither day nor night.
Once, while Nārada was stationed there at the foot of the banyan tree,
a naked man arrived, blazing with the splendor of Brahman.
The venerable Sanatkumāra was a child of five years;
he had not yet received the topknot ceremony nor been initiated, and he was devoid of Vedic study and the twilight devotions.
Then, chanting the mantra of Kṛṣṇa together with his three brothers, he, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas and the teacher of teachers among the wise, [remained there]. (55)
Nārada saw from afar that sage Nārāyaṇa, whose very sight bestows liberation, and his brother, the best among the virtuous.
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, he offered an excellent seat;
there, the boy spoke to the auspicious Nārada with a smile.
"O brother, what are you doing? Is all well, O husband of a young woman? The love between man and woman increases ever anew through the impulse of desire. (58)
It is considered a bolt on the path of knowledge, an obstruction to the path of devotion, an impediment to the path of liberation, and a constant bestower of bondage. (59)

Having abandoned the nectar of Nārāyaṇa, he instead consumes the poison of the nectar born of sense-objects; being excessively attached to worldly objects, he eats like one who is utterly deluded, thinking it to be true.
Having fallen under the sway of illusion and delusion, one abandons nectar and consumes poison;
you, however, are a devotee, a knower of the Self, and are eternally liberated while living.
"Go forth for asceticism, O brother, leaving behind your illusory wife;
while Nārāyaṇa remains upon the earth, worship him always through austerity. (62)
"Accept my mantra, the two syllables 'Kṛṣṇa';
I give you that mantra which I myself received from Nārāyaṇa. (63)
Having spoken thus, he bestowed the mantra and likewise gave auspicious blessings;
then he departed for Goloka to behold the eternal Lord.
Nārada constantly recites the two-syllabled mantra with a rosary,
[seeking] unwavering devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which cuts asunder the bonds of past karma.
Having enjoyed his wife— who was a knower of the Self through the practice of yoga combined with dispassion—
for two hundred thousand years, as well as sons and daughters, [he departed].
Having procreated a hundred thousand Gandharvas and a hundred thousand Gandharva maidens,
he established all his offspring in the world of the Gandharvas according to his power.
Having made all [beings] Vaiṣṇavas and directed devotion toward Mādhava, and having made his wife free from passion and directed her toward devotion as well; ||68||
Having instructed his sons in that skill, the sage departed;
he set his mind upon performing austerities on the bank of the Kṛtamālā river.
There he beheld Śambhu, the eternal primordial preceptor;
and having seen him, Nārada bowed his head in salutation to his guru, Śiva.
Śiva said: "Having seen you, I am indeed pleased;
for embodied beings, the very day on which they behold their devotees is a truly auspicious day."
For this is the supreme gain for devotees: when they have union [with Him]. He who has seen a Vaiṣṇava has indeed bathed in all sacred fords.
In Goloka, the mantra consisting of only two syllables, "Kṛṣṇa," was indeed granted by Kṛṣṇa; it was obtained by me, as well as by Dharma and Brahmā.
Then Dharma gave it, together with its meaning, to Nārāyaṇa;
Brahmā gave it to Sanatkumāra, and by him, indeed, it was given to you. (74)
By the mere reception of the mantra, a person becomes Nārāyaṇa;
its preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is said to consist of five hundred thousand recitations. ||75||
And the Vaiṣṇava should meditate upon the meditation that burns away evil—the dark form of Kṛṣṇa, possessing the charming body of a youth and a complexion like a rain cloud. (76)
Clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, and more beautiful than ten million gods of love,
he was adorned with ornaments and the like inlaid with priceless jewels.
His entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, he was resplendent with the Kaustubha gem,
his crest was adorned with peacock feathers, and he was beautified by a necklace of jewels.
I worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa at all times—He whose face shines with a gracious smile, who is the vessel of beauty, and who bestows grace upon His devotees. 79.
Having thus reminded him, Śambhu then vanished from sight;
Nārada, for his part, remembered Hari and performed most rigorous penance.
Having attained Nārāyaṇa through devotion and having assumed a divine body, he became one whose nature is eternally liberated, with an unimpeded path to Goloka and other realms. ||8 1 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the marriage of Nārada;
by hearing which one may become dispassionate—what else do you wish to hear? (82)

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Arrival at the Assembly of Brahmā, the Proposal for Marriage by Brahmā, Nārada’s Bridal Procession for the Hand of Sṛñjaya’s Daughter Mālāvatī, the Auspicious Time, and His Departure to the Kṛtamālā River to perform austerities after producing one hundred thousand sons and one hundred thousand daughters following two hundred thousand years," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
The fires indeed have Brahmā as their mouth; they are portions of Brahmā and deities of sacrifice.
When and from what were they produced? O Lord, relate that story to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The cause of fire, which possesses the quality of heat and is of the nature of an effect,
is that conscious deity Vahni, the mind-born son of Brahmā.
That deity presiding over fire was born from him with the exclamation "svāhā";
he had three sons: Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci. || 3 ||
The solar fire is indeed pure; those originating from lightning are considered to be purifying (pāvaka).
In the Śrāddha rite, the fire is Pavamāna, and his son is Kavyavāhana.
Pāvaka had a son named Saharakṣas;
likewise, Śuci’s son was Havyavāha, who provides food for the gods.
Kavyavāha is the [offspring] of the Pitṛs, and Saharakṣas of the Asuras;
their sons and grandsons number forty-nine.
The son of Vaidyuta was Brahmaudana, whose son was named Bharata;
his son was Vaiśvānaravahni, and his son was indeed Kāvya, the essence of the waters.
From the churning of the Puṣkara ocean, Atharvāgni was born;
his son was Dadhyañca, who indeed resides in the circle of fire as Bodhya.
Atharvan is said to be Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras is the son of Atharvaṇ;
therefore, the fire of the world is declared to be both Bhārgava and Āṅgirasa.
Pavamāna was to be churned out and was also known by the name Gārhapatya;
he had two sons, Śaṃsya and Śukra, according to their names.
The Āhavanīya fire, which is the carrier of oblations and consists of ritual action, is to be praised;
likewise, the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires are considered the two sons of that praiseworthy Agni.
The praiseworthy one, however, desired sixteen excellent women from the rivers:
Kāverī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Narmadā, and likewise Yamunā.
The Godāvarī, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Irāvatī, the Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, the Śatadrū, and likewise the Sarayū. || 13 ||
Sītā, Sarasvatī, Hrādinī, and Pāvanī—
those fires which were produced from them are indeed proclaimed as the Dhiṣṇyas.
Ṛtu was the Pravāhaṇa Agnīdhra; the Samrāḍ Agnis were Kṛśānuka and the eight Tvaṣṭṛs, as well as Nabhas by name, who was the Parṣan. || 15 ||
Vasu, Havyasūrya, Viśvāyu as the fifth, Ṛtudhāman, Ajaikapād, and Ahirbudhnya—these are remembered [as the Vasus]. || 16 ||
For the sons of Śaṃsya are to be honored, and their sons are to be entertained;
there should be eight such entertainers: Śānti, Pracetas, and Satyaka. (17)
Viśvadeva, Avakṣu, Acchāvāka, Uśīraka, and Vyaratni—these are to be known [as the deities] according to the transition between the pressings (savana) in the sacrifice. || 18 ||
The purifier is the embryo of the waters, and his Avabhṛtha bath is the fire residing in the heart;
the son of that digestive fire is Wrath, and his is the terrible Saṃvartaka.
In the ocean is that [fire] called Vaḍava; his son is Saharakṣaka;
his son is Kṣāma; and his son is Kravyāda—these are the fires born of the lineage of Pāvaka.
The fire of the Araṇi sticks belonging to Śuci is called Āyu;
his son was Mahimā, and his son is considered to be Śāva.
Savana was his son, and Adbhuta is said to have been his son as well;
Vivici was the son of Adbhuta, and Arka is said to have been his son.
The fires are Arkasyānīkavān, Vāsṛja, Rakṣohā, Pitṛkṛt, Surabhi, and Rukmavān. ||23||
In all the Manvantaras, there arise the Jātavedases;
they are all remembered as the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) and are endowed with light.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, these fires have been described to you by their principal names; all of them always bestow fruits through oblations and other rites, and bring about the perfection of mantras. 25.
Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Vahni," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Supreme Lord, I desire to hear about the creation at the end of the Dvāpara age and at the beginning [of the Kali age], pertaining to Kaśyapa and to sexual union; tell it to me."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O descendant of Kaśyapa; I shall tell you about them in due order.
Dakṣa gave his own daughters, fourteen in number, to Kaśyapa.
They were given away according to the marriage rites; hear their names from me:
Aditi became the mother of the gods, and Diti likewise the mother of the Daityas.
Kadru became the mother of serpents, and Vinata likewise the progenitor of birds;
Surabhi was the mother of cows and the mother of all livestock as well.
Saramā was the progenitor of beings such as dogs; Sū was the mother of quadrupeds; Danu was the mother of the Dānavas; and Timi was the progenitor of the host of aquatic creatures.
Tāmrā is the mother of hawks and vultures; Muni is the progenitor of the Apsarases; and Krodhavaśā is the mother of serpents, biters, and other wrathful beings.
Ilā was the mother of trees, Surasā the mother of the Yātudhānas, and Ariṣṭā the mother of the Gandharvas; from their progeny this world is composed.
Indra, the twelve Ādityas, and the gods beginning with Upendra are likewise declared to be the sons of Aditi, possessed of great strength and prowess.
Jayanta, the son of Indra, was born of his wife Śacī;
from Sūrya were born Śanaiścara and Yama, and likewise Yamunā from Saṃjñā; and from the seed of Upendra, Maṅgala was born upon the Earth.
Beholding the form of Upendra, Vasundharā, afflicted by desire,
assumed the guise of a beautiful woman and approached his bed.
Upendra, having understood her mind, manifested amorous passion;
and she was unable to restrain that which had arisen as the infusion of his seed.
The prince, the son of Nārāyaṇa himself, fell upon a leaf of coral, equal in splendor to the sun. 12.
That auspicious one, named Maṅgala, was established among the planets by Hari. Then from Diti were born Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.
A daughter, Siṃhikā, was born, and her son was Saihikeya;
she, Siṃhikā, was Nirṛti, and by him Rāhu was born as a Nairṛta.
In his boar incarnation, the youthful Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in the midst of the waters;
and Prahlāda, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, was the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas.
Virocana was his son, and his son was Bali himself; Bāṇa was the son of Bali—a great yogi—thus is the lineage of Diti proclaimed.
Then there were the serpents born of Kadrū: Kālīya, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya, Takṣaka, and Padma as well. || 17 ||
Airāvata, Mahāpadma, Śaṅku, and likewise Śaṅkha;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Saṃvaraṇa, Durdharṣa, and likewise Durjaya. (18)
Durmukha, Bala, Gokṣa, Gokārmuka,
and Virūpa— these are the foremost among all the serpent lineages.
The maiden was indeed Jaratkārvī, and Jaratkāru was her husband;
their son was Āstīka, whose virtues and prowess were equal to those of Viṣṇu.
By the mere mention of their names, there shall certainly be no fear of nāgas. Now, [the sons] of Danu were Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Nirāmaya.
Mahāviśva, Gaveṣṭhin, Dundubhi, Aṅgirāvṛta, Marīci, Akṣaka, Mahāgārgya, and Ajāmukha. ||22||
Śila, Vāmana, Vikṣobhya, and likewise Suhṛda;
Suketu, Suvīrya, Indrajit, and Viśvajit as well. (23)
Suravimardana, Ekacakra, and Tāraka;
Mahābala, Suvāha, Puloman, and Pravīṇaka. ||24||
Vaiśvānara, Mahāśiras, Svarbhānu, Muṇḍaka, Vṛṣaparvan, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūkṣma, and Tāpina; ||25||
Ūrṇanābha, Mahāgiri, Aśiloman, Sukeśaka, Sada, Balaka, Kumbhanābha, and Mahodara. ||26||
Pramodāha, Vyomamūrdhan, Kupatha, Hayamastaka, Asura, Virūpākṣa, Śatamāyu, and Śambara. ||27||
Śarabha and Śalabha are proclaimed as the sons of Danu;
their progeny, consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth, is beyond counting and infinite.
Then, these sons of Vipracitti were born from Siṃhikā:
the powerful Śatagāla, Nyāsa, and another, Śāmba.
Ilvala, Namuci, Vātāpi, the blood-sacrificing Dasrājaka, Harakalpa, Kālanābha, Bhauma, and likewise Naraka.
And these sons of Siṃhikā, numbering ten thousand, including Rāhu,
shall indeed become enemies of the gods, born through the succession of their lineage.
Citrasena, Ugrasena, Ūrṇāyu, Anagha, as well as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Puloman, and Sūryavarcas. ||32||
Simultaneously [there were] Tṛṇapāt, Kāliṃdīti, Citraratha, Bhramiśiras, Parjanya, Kali, and likewise Nārada. ||33||
Thus these divine Gandharvas belonging to Mauneya have been fully described;
likewise Miśrakeśī, Āśī, Parṇinī, and Alambuṣā.
Māricī, Putrikā, Vidyudvāṇī, Tilottamā, Adrikā, Lakṣaṇā, and the goddess Rambhā, who is enchanting. ||35||
Suvarā, Subāhvī, Pūrṇitā, and Pratiṣṭhitā; Puṇḍarīkā, Sugandhā, Sudantā, and likewise Surasā. ||36||
Hemā, Śāradvatī, Suvṛttā, Kamalā, Subhujā, Haṃsapādā, and likewise the worldly apsarases. ||37||
For these Gandharvas and Apsarases are proclaimed as belonging to Mauneya;
they are remembered as the four Apsarases who were the daughters of Suyaśas. (38)
Lauheyī, Bharatā, Kṛśāṅgī, and Viśālikā—by Viśāla, sons were begotten upon them as follows. (39)
The Lauheyas, the Bharateyas, the Kṛśāṅgeyas, and the Viśālajas;
and two daughters of beautiful eyes, Śivā and Sumanā.
By those two, together with Viśravas, the Vidyādharas were produced;
and by that very Vikrānta, the Kinnaras were also produced.
Samudrasena, Kālinda, Mahānetra, Mahābala, Suvarṇaghoṣa, Sugrīva, and the heroic Mahāghoṣa. ||42||
In this manner, the hosts of Kinnaras with horse-like faces, as well as those with human faces, were produced by Śāṃśapāyana. ||43||
Hariṣeṇa, Suṣeṇa, and the heroic Vāriṣeṇa;
Rudradatta and Indradatta; and Candradruma and Mahādruma. ||44||
Bindu, Bindusāra, and the Kinnaras of the lunar lineage;
and Lauheyā’s daughter, who bore the name Suravindā. (45)
From her were born the Bhūtas, the Āveśakas, the Niveśakas, the Sutāras, the Kālabhavanās, the Nirdeśakas, and the Videśakas. ||46||
Those who dwell in trees move through the sky as far as the treetops;
by means of the Paiśāca marriage, he whose vehicle is the Buddha [attained] a woman with beautiful teeth.
O Piśācikās, those two indeed gave birth to two daughters, Brahmadhanā and Jantudhanā; from them, millions of Piśācas [were born]. (48)
And Rākṣasas were also born there by the millions, tens of millions, and hundreds of billions;
likewise, Kratusthalī, the mother of Yakṣas, is considered to be the auspicious Apsaras.
The Yakṣa Rajatanābha is the grandfather of the Guhyakas;
twenty-four of them are considered meritorious and are known as the Puṇyajanas.
These Puṇyajanas are known as the offspring of Maṇibhadra;
thus, these Yakṣas and Guhyakas are the sons of the excellent Maṇi.
And those Rākṣasas, capable of changing their form at will, were born from Khaśā;
and from the Rākṣasī Vikacā, the Piśācas were born by Nairṛti.
The Pūtanas were produced by them and are considered to be destroyers of children;
from Krodhā, twelve daughters were born, produced from her own self.
Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Haribhadrā, Irāvatī, Bhūtā, Kapiśā, Daṃṣṭrā, Niśā, and likewise Tiryā. (54)
Śvetā, Svarā, and Surasā are likewise renowned as his daughters; from Mṛgī were born the Hariṇas, the other deer, and the hares.
The nyaṅkavas, the śarabhas, and those who are rurus and pṛṣatas;
the kings of beasts, the mṛgamandas, and likewise the gavayas and others. ||56||
Buffaloes, camels, and boars, as well as rhinoceroses and white-faced wild asses, were the sons of Hari; likewise, the golāṅgulas and hyenas were his offspring. (57)
Monkeys, kinnaras, tigers, and kimpuruṣas were likewise born;
the son of Irāvatī was Gaja, who is known as Airāvata. (58)
Some had two tusks, some four, and others eight;
his sons, grandsons, and descendants likewise became elephants in infinite numbers. (59)
Now, all those sons of Bhūti were indeed *ūrdhvaretas* (celibate ascetics);
they were all devotees of Bhava and were devoid of wives and sons.
Kuṣmāṇḍī gave birth to sixteen sons who were Kapiśas, and from the Kapiśas, she bore pairs of flesh-eating Piśācakas.
Chagala and Chagalī, Vakra and Vakramukhī, Sūci and Sūcīmukhī, as well as Kumbhī and Kumbhapātraka. ||62||
Vajradaṃṣṭra, Dundubhi, Upacāra, Apacārikā, Ulūkhalī, Ulūkhala, Anaka, and also Arka. (63)
Kukhaṇḍikā and Kukhaṇḍaka, Pāṃśu and likewise Pāṃśumatī;
Pāṇipātra and Pāṇipātrī, as well as Nipuṇā and Nipuṇa. ||64||
Nitunda and Nitundī, Praskanda and Skandikā,
as well as Chalāda and Uccheṣaṇā— these are the hosts who belong to the lineage of Ananta.
The hosts of Kuṣmāṇḍas are known to have the faces of goats and the faces of cranes;
they have hair on all their limbs, are called Vṛtta, and likewise possess fangs and claws.
The animals, the man-eaters, and the Piśācas are indeed downward-facing;
the Ṛṣayas, the fish, the mother, the circular, and likewise the inverted [are also mentioned].
Listen now to the offspring of those daughters who followed after them:
the Sahasradantas, the Makaras, the Pāṭhinas, and the Timirohitās.
These were declared to be the hosts of Mena; the crocodiles and the porpoises produced the tortoises, the circular ones, and the *śaṅkhalas*.
She indeed gave birth to various transformations of frogs,
as well as deer-skins, shells, pearls, and cowries.
Likewise, the descendants of Svedā, born from the transformed products of Śaṅkha, multiplied by the millions upon millions of their lineage.
Those born from water, those born from men and bears, those born from animals, and likewise those born from sentient beings;
those born from earth and water, and those produced through the conjunction of the rains. ||72||
Likewise, [beings] arise from dry modifications such as cow dung and the like,
and similarly, those produced from mud and the like do not originate from the heat of the sun.
The offspring of Kāśyapī were both those born from a womb and those not born from a womb;
the offspring of Saramā were the dog, the boar, and likewise the jackal. (74)
Śyāma, Śabala, Arjuna, and likewise Harita;
Kṛṣṇa, Dhūmrāruṇa, Tūla, Alābu, and Kadruka. (75)
Surasa gave birth to one hundred sons, who were the immortals Śiro, Mṛta,
Sarpān, Takṣaka, Mūrdhanya, Nāgān, and Vāsukiśobhana.
From Tāmrā, by the son of Pulaha, were born Śyenī, Bhāsī, Śukī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Krauñcī; and from Aruṇa, Śyenī was born.
And he begot Sampāti and Jaṭāyu, the best of birds;
and from Jaṭāyu were born sons such as Kāka, Gṛdhra, and Karṇin.
Śukī gave birth to many sons, the Garuḍas;
the extent of these devourers of serpents was fourteen thousand.
The Bhāsas, owls, crows, and cocks are known as the sons of Bhāsī; so too are peacocks, sparrows, pigeons, quails, and partridges. || 1.212.80 ||
From Vārdhīṇasa was born Krauñcī; from her came the hawks, ospreys, cranes, and herons.
Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, the beautiful woman, gave birth to the swans and the ruddy geese.
And by her were born the cakravāka birds, the anantaka birds, and three daughters of Ilā: Latā, Vallī, and Vīrudh.
[He saw] creepers and trees that were leafless and stood upon the sandy banks;
likewise, he saw flowering and fruit-bearing trees situated in gardens.
Then Vallī gave birth to shrubs, trees with fibrous bark, grasses and the like, creepers, and leafy vegetables such as radishes. ||84||
And for these very beings, when there is a deficiency in place and time, deformity arises through various differences in form and action. (85)
If there is a difference in the field, the form of the seed will undergo a state of confusion;
and if there is a difference in the seed, the form of the embryo will turn into another form. (86)
When many combinations of creepers, climbing plants, and shrubs are possible, they indeed become diverse; for there is no end to them.
And when trees, shrubs, and plants undergo a transformation through a distinct process of combination, there arises therein a variety of forms belonging to many different species.
Indeed, through the intermixture of gods, sages, and humans, as well as of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and the wrathful ones, other beings arise with diverse forms. (89)
The various forms of embodied beings—whether composed of earth, water, or fire—are indeed distinguished according to their respective modifications. || 1.212.90 ||

O Lotus-born One, how many creations, how many other creations, how many different worlds, and how many intervals between dissolutions have occurred? What has transpired therein? I am unable to traverse this. (9.1)
In brief, I have described the well-known creation of the Kāśyapī;
even though the expansion of creation exists, there is no purpose in describing it here. (92)
For this time is indeed limitless, and there is no end to creation;
I have told you what is most essential—what else do you wish to hear? 93.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offspring of Kaśyapa Belonging to the Fourteen Worlds," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. This chapter details the progeny of Diti, Aditi, Kadrū, Vinatā, Surabhi, Saramā, Danu, Tāmrā, Muni, Krodhā, Ilā, Surasā, and Ariṣṭā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Lord, I desire to hear the purifying lineage of the sages;
therefore, relate it to me in brief, for upon hearing it, the heart becomes purified. (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Kaśyapa, desiring a lineage, performed supreme austerity;
he thought, "May I have two sons who will be the founders of my lineage."
Asita and Vatsāra also became possessed of the form of Brahman;
and Vatsāra had two sons, Nidhruva and Raibhya.
From Raibhya were born the sages known as the Raibhyas, who possessed great fame;
and from Nidhruva were born the Sumedhas and the Kuṇḍapāyins.
From Asita, upon Ekaparṇā, was born the most devoted to Brahman;
these three—Nidhruvas, Śāṇḍilas, and Raibhyas—are indeed Kāśyapas. || 5 ||
The sons of Devala were the renowned Varas and likewise the Ṛṣis; the sons of Mānasa were the Riṣyantas, and his [son] was known as Dama.
From Dama, the great seer Tṛṇabindu was born;
Tṛṇabindu’s daughter was Iḍaviḍā, who became the beloved wife of Pulastya.
From him was born Viśravas, whose wife was Devavarṇinī;
she is considered the daughter of Bṛhaspati, who possesses great fame.
In her, Vaiśravaṇa was born as Kubera, who was indeed ugly;
and Atri had three sons: Datta, Durvāsas, and Candra.
From Kaśyapa were born Nārada, Parvata, and likewise Arundhatī;
and from Arundhatī, the auspicious Śakti was born as the son of Vasiṣṭha.
From Pulastya were born Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and Vibhīṣaṇa;
from his lineage the Rākṣasas were born, as well as Brāhmaṇas who were learned in the Vedas.
Khyāti bore to Bhṛgu two sons named Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, as well as one daughter, Śrī; she was the eldest and became the wife of Nārāyaṇa.
O virtuous lady, my two sons are Balotsāha and Nārāyaṇīya; Niyaṃti is considered the wife of Dhātṛ, and Āyati is the wife of Vidhātṛ.
Their two sons were the eternal Pāṇḍu and Mṛkaṇḍu, born in due order;
and from Mṛkaṇḍu, through Manasvinī, Mārkaṇḍeya was born.
To him was born a son named Vedaśiras from his wife Mūrdhanī;
his entire lineage became renowned as the Mārkaṇḍeyas.
From Pāṇḍu and Puṇḍarīkā was born Dyutimān Sṛjamānaka;
their sons and grandsons are celebrated as the Bhārgavas. || 16 ||
Marīci’s wife, Saṃbhūti, gave birth to Pūrṇamāsa, as well as a quartet of daughters: Kuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Tviṣā, and Apaciti.
Pūrṇamāsa begot Viraja and Parvasan through Sarasvatī; Sudhāman was the son of Viraja, and his son was named Vairāja.
Then Gaurīputra became Sudharmā, the guardian of the world;
and Parvata [became] Yajñavāma Kāśyapa on every auspicious day.
Āṅgirasa gave birth to four daughters through Smṛti: the maidens Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati. (1.213.20)
Bharata begot two sons, Agni and Kīrtimant, both world-renowned. From Agni, Parjanya was born of Sahatī.
Hiraṇyaroman was born as a son from Parjanya by Mārīcī;
Kṣamā, however, gave birth to sons for the patriarch Pulaha.
Kardama, Ambarīṣa, and Sahiṣṇu—these three were born;
and from Vasiṣṭha’s wife Ūrjā, many Vāsiṣṭhas were born.
Among the Vāsiṣṭhas, the Kāśyapas, as well as the Bhṛgus, Aṅgirases, and Atris—in these five lineages, the exponents of the Veda are born. (24)
The Vālakhilyas were the sons of Kratu; Śukra was the son of Bhṛgu;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, Varūtrī, Śaṇḍa, and Amarka were the sons of Kavi.
And Devayānī, the daughter of Śukra, was born of Yajñā.
The great Triśiras Viśvarūpa was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ. || 26 ||
A son was born to Yaśodharā, the younger brother of Viśvakarman; he became Cyavana, the son of Pracetas, and from him the Cyāvaneyas are considered to have descended.
Bhārgava had two sons, Ātmavān and Dadhīca;
and from the thigh of Ātmavān, Aurva was born.
Jamadagni was born to Ṛcīka by Satyavatī;
Parśurāma was born to Jamadagni by Reṇukā. || 29 ||
The heirs of Atharvan were Bṛhaspati, Dhiṣṇuka,
Saṃvarta, Vicitti, Utathya, and Vāmadevaka.
Utathya and Śaradvat—these are considered the descendants of Atharvan.
Bharadvāja was the son of Bṛhaspati, and Bhāradvāja was his son. || 31 ||
Marīci’s two sons were indeed Ariṣṭanemi and Kaśyapa;
Soma’s son was Budha, and Budha’s son was Purūravas.
From him [Sudhanvan] was born Amāvasu; from him, Bhīma; from him, Kāñcana;
from him, Suhotra; from him, Jahnu; and from Jahnu came the Jāhnavī (the Gaṅgā).
Jahnu’s wife was Kāverī; Suhotraka was born of her. His son was Ajaka, and his son, in turn, is said to have been Balākāśva.
The son of that Kuśa was Kuśika, named Gādhi;
his son, Viśvāmitra, became a Brahmarṣi in ancient times.
The son of Viśvāmitra was known as Devarāta;
indeed, many Kauśika sages, rich in asceticism, were born.
Viśvāmitra, Māndhātṛ, Saṃskṛti, and Kapi;
from Kapi came Purukutsa, Satya, Anṛhvan, and Anṛthu. (37)
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa and Ajamīḍha, as well as Bhāga, Kākṣīva, Śijaya, and other great chariot-warriors likewise. || 38 ||
Rathītara, Runda, Viṣṇuvṛddha, and other kings—
these are remembered as being endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas, yet they attained the state of sages through their ascetic penance.
From Purūravas came Āyu; his son was named Suta-hotra.
His son was Gṛtsamada; his son was Śunaka; and his son was Śaunaka. (1.213.40)
Śala was the son of Suhotra; his son was Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, a treasury of asceticism. Kāśa was the son of Suhotra, and Dīrghatapas was his son.
The wise and powerful Dhanvantari was the excellent son of Dīrghatapas;
Ketumān was the son of Dhanvantari, and Divodāsa was his son.
His son was Pratardana; his sons were Garga and Vatsaka.
Vatsa’s son was Alarka, and Sannati was his offspring.
In his lineage was Gārgya, and Vatsya was the ṛṣi of Vatsa;
likewise, these became great ṛṣis who were both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. ||44||
For Marutta was a king, as were the great seer Sātvata and others;
likewise, Nahuṣa, Yayāti, and the rest were indeed righteous kings. ||45||
Dīrghatamas was indeed born to Mamatā by Ūśija;
Dīrghatamas begot a son upon Sudeṣṇā, the wife of Bali.
He became Kakṣīvān, and his sons were in the thousands;
Medhātithi was born in the lineage of Atri, as were the Kāṇṭhāyana brahmins.
Bharadvāja was born as the son of Vṛhaspati by Mamata;
in his lineage was born the preeminent sage named Trayyāruṇi. (48)
The son of Bṛhatkṣatra was the sage named Suhotra;
in his lineage was born the great sage named Medhātithi. 49.
Paurava became a follower of the Kauthuma branch of the Sāmaveda;
Mudgala was the son of Ṛkṣa, and the descendants of Maudgalya were born from him.
From Ahalyā was born Śatānanda, and his son was Suvrata; from Cyavana came Uparicara Vasu, and his son was Kuśāgraka.
The son of Kuśāgra was named Ṛṣabha; his sons were the Ārṣabhas.
These are declared to be the Brahman-Kṣatriya ṛṣis, the purifiers of the world. (52)
Other sages who are knowers of the Vedas also appear on earth, as do ascetics; by them indeed is the world protected.
Some are devoted to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), some likewise to Brahman;
others are devoted to yoga, and others still are devoted solely to austerity (tapas). ||54||
Likewise, others who are intent on spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) and devoted to worship and other such practices—those meritorious ones indeed bestow the highest welfare. ||55||
For these great sages are indeed my own portions;
they have been described to you, O Mahālakṣmī. What else do you wish to hear? 56.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Genealogies and Lineages of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Ṛṣi Sages," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Mādhava, I wish to hear in brief about the Kalpas and the Manus;
likewise, I wish to hear about the characteristics of Dvāpara and Kali.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the fourteen Manus born day by day;
one thousand kalpas are produced in a single year of Brahmā.
One thousand sets of four ages constitute a *kalpa*;
this *kalpa* should be understood as being the same in all *kalpas*.
The first Kalpa is indeed celebrated as Vārāha at the beginning of the world;
the second is the Bhuva-kalpa, and the third is called Tapa. || 4 ||
The fourth is to be known as Bhava, and the fifth is called Raṃbha;
likewise, the sixth is the Ṛtukalpa, while the seventh is remembered as Kratu.
The eighth was Vahni, the ninth Havyavāhana;
the tenth Kalpa was Sāvitra, and the eleventh is remembered as Bhāva.
Uśika is there as the twelfth, Kuśika as the thirteenth,
and Gandharva as the fourteenth, where indeed the musical note Gāndhāra resides.
O beloved, the fifteenth kalpa should be known as Ṛṣabha;
the sixteenth kalpa is Ṣaḍja, wherein the sages are the Ṣaḍjanas.
Śiśira, Vasanta, Nidāgha, Varṣa,
as well as Śarad and Hemanta— these were the mental sons of Brahmā.
Then the seventeenth Kalpa is remembered as Mārjālīya;
after that, the eighteenth is called the Kalpa named Madhyama.
Then the nineteenth kalpa was named Vairāgya,
wherein Vairāja Manu, the son of Brahmā, indeed came into being.
Then the twentieth eon is proclaimed as Niṣāda;
O beloved, the twenty-first eon should be known as the fifth.
The five vital breaths were the mind-born sons of Brahmā; Svara became the twenty-second Kalpa, which is to be known as Meghavāhana.
The twenty-third kalpa is to be known as Cintaka;
the twenty-fourth is indeed called the Ākuti kalpa.
The twenty-fifth kalpa is proclaimed as Vijñāti;
thereafter, the twenty-sixth kalpa is designated as Manas. ||15||
The twenty-seventh kalpa is indeed called Bhāva;
the twenty-eighth kalpa is designated as Bṛhat. || 16 ||
The twenty-ninth eon is to be known as Śvetalohita;
thereafter, the thirtieth eon is proclaimed by the name Rakta. || 17 ||
The thirty-first kalpa is known as Pītavāsas;
the thirty-second kalpa is indeed named Sitakalpa.
The thirty-third aeon is indeed named Kṛṣṇakalpa;
the thirty-fourth aeon is named Viśvarūpa.
Thus, these [sacrifices] are described by the names of the worlds, as well as by the names of the seasons,
by the names of the sacrifices, and likewise by the names of the fires.
[He spoke] by the names of the vowels, as well as by the names of the vital breaths (prāṇas),
likewise by the names of intentions (ākūtis), and also by the names of Śambhu and Viṣṇu.
These thirty-four kalpas have been declared, and by association with them,
there are likewise seven other kalpas according to the names of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
Furthermore, there are eight other kalpas designated by the names of the eight Vasus, and likewise others consisting of nine kalpas due to the conjunction with the nine planets. (23)
There are eight kalpas for the eight guardians of the directions, and likewise eight others; furthermore, one kalpa is considered to be the personal kalpa of Brahmā. (24)
There are likewise three kalpas for the gods of the three qualities (guṇas), and eleven kalpas for the eleven Rudras. || 25 ||
There are fourteen kalpas named after the fourteen Manus,
and likewise there are fourteen kalpas named after the fourteen great Indras.
There are as many [deities] by the names of the twenty-seven lunar mansions,
and likewise as many by the names of the forty-nine winds.
There are likewise other kalpas known by the name Caturviṃśatyavatāra, and there are forty-nine Vahni-kalpas, equal in number to those [preceding]. (28)
By the names of the four feet of Dharma, those [Manus] are likewise four;
and by the names of the three branches of knowledge (vidyās), there are likewise three Kalpas.
Thus, at the time of the onset of creation, whosoever had previously attained yoga, and whosoever had previously established a connection with the path of Brahmā’s recollection; || 1.214.30 ||
The kalpas are considered to be the days of Brahmā, each named after its respective [deity];
indeed, one thousand kalpas constitute a year of Brahmā.
All these [periods] of Brahmā likewise revolve again within another year;
thus they rotate throughout his lifespan of one hundred years.
In this creation, the kalpas of Brahmā proceed by way of a continuous flow of play;
indeed, these very same things are born again and again, for there is no fixed rule that they do not exist [again].
There are also other aeons named after women:
those called Lakṣmī-kalpas, as well as Ramā-kalpas, Padmā-kalpas, and Śrī-kalpas.
The Śivā-kalpas, the Yoginī-kalpas which are the progenitors of virtuous beings, as well as the Śacī-kalpas, the Kālī-kalpas, and the Śakti-days; 35.
Likewise, there are others called Vidyā-kalpas, as well as the Ādya-avyakta-dinas; there are also Īśvara-kalpas and others known as Deva-kalpas. (36)

There are also the Kalpas of the Goddesses, the Kalpas of the Apsarases, and the days of devotion; likewise, there are the Kalpas of the Principles (tattvas) and even the Kalpas of primordial activities.
That which is seen by the Creator at dawn as the primary and supreme [state], by that name indeed were those Kalpas ordained by Brahmā. (38)
In each kalpa, there are fourteen Indras and fourteen Manus; indeed, one Manu enjoys sovereignty for a long time, specifically for seventy-one [yugas].
A cycle of four ages (caturyuga) is said to consist of four such sets of four; the gods know a caturyuga to be twelve thousand years.
A thousand cycles of four yugas pass in a day of Brahmā;
likewise, a thousand cycles of four yugas pass in a night of Brahmā.
Two thousand four-sided [palaces] belong to Brahmā day and night;
by this sequence, the Creator indeed lives for a hundred years. 42.
Then, indeed, one day of Vairāja is thus calculated;
by this sequence, Vairāja lives for a hundred years.
That [period] is indeed reckoned as a single day of Mahāviṣṇu;
by this sequence, Mahāviṣṇu lives for a hundred years.
That which is calculated as a single day for the Pradhāna-Puruṣa, by this sequence, one lives for a hundred years of the Pradhāna. ||45||
A single day of that primordial Puruṣa is thus conceived;
the creation of that Puruṣa and Prakṛti proceeds for a hundred years. ||46||
From that, the great dissolution occurs, and absolute absorption is attained;
thereafter exists the world of liberation of Brahmā, together with the Supreme Lord. ||47||
When that much time had passed, he looked again in that same way:
"May I become manifold," for the sake of creation, according to the sequence of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
In every eon, there is likewise the manifestation of the Manus;
and likewise, there is the manifestation of the cosmic eggs and the worlds. (49)
O beloved, listen as I recount by name the fourteen Manus;
in this Vārāha Kalpa, the first Manu was named Kratu.
Svāyambhuva Manu is declared to be the very son of Brahmā;
Svārociṣa was indeed the second Manu, and he was the son of Agni.
The third Manu was indeed Auttama, the son of Priyavrata;
and the fourth Manu was Tāmasa, the brother of Uttama.
Raivata, the brother of Tāmasa, is declared the fifth Manu;
and the sixth Manu is indeed named Cākṣuṣa, the son of Cakṣuṣa. ||53||
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and likewise Raivata—these four Manūs are considered to belong to the lineage of Priyavrata. (54)
In the lineage of Uttānapāda, Cākṣuṣa is called the Manu.
Kaśyapa’s sons by Aditi are known as the twelve Ādityas.
Therein, the son of Vivasvat is known as Śrāddhadeva;
he is this very Vaivasvata Manu, who is called the seventh Manu. (56)
In Chāyā was born Sūryaputra, the eighth Manu;
the ninth Manu is Dakṣasāvarṇi, who was born from Varuṇa.
The tenth Manu is Brahmasāvarṇi, the son of Upaśloka;
indeed, Dharmasāvarṇi is declared to be the eleventh Manu. (58)
Rudrasāvarṇi by name shall be the twelfth Manu;
the thirteenth Manu will be Devasāvarṇi, the son of Sunṛtā.
The heir of Satyasahasa is indeed Vedasāvarṇi;
he is called Manu Indrasāvarṇi, the fourteenth.
O beloved, these fourteen indeed occur in every kalpa;
a kalpa is measured by these [yugas] and consists of a cycle of a thousand yugas.
And his night is of equal duration to a thousand cycles of yugas;
here, the word "yuga" should indeed be understood as referring to a cycle of four yugas.
In this way, during other kalpas, there will likewise be fourteen other Manus and fourteen other Indras, each distinct from the others.
And there are other sages, seven by seven, of such a kind;
and there are others who become guardians of the quarters and protectors of the worlds, performing similar deeds.
Other Vedavyāsas appear in every cycle of four yugas;
there are twenty-four incarnations of Hari for each such set of four.
The portions, the descents, the parts, and the sub-parts are indeed infinite for the sake of the practitioner;
and there are likewise incarnations for the purpose of the world's welfare.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Many Kalpas and the Fourteen Manus," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to all the characteristics of the Kali age at the end of Dvāpara;
when the first Dvāpara arrived, creation arose from the *yugala* (the divine couple).
When that [state] born of the dharma of pairing—arising from the union of man and woman—began there, as did the vices produced by desire. || 2 ||
Secretive action, thievery, anger, selfishness, as well as violence, falsehood, theft, loss of virility, and possessiveness. (3)

Impurity consists of thirst, enjoyment, exertion, excessive greed, and such things as the egoism and possessiveness directed toward the body, its objects, and the conscious and unconscious realms. (4)
They proceed with each individual, increasing the flow of their own respective objects;
from that, embodied beings are born as those of no merit or little merit. (5)
The mind becomes turbid, the intellect becomes perverted, evil intentions arise, and one proceeds upon an evil path. (6)
Gambling, drinking, women, and the slaughterhouse are indeed the seats of unrighteousness;
likewise are gold, falsehood, lust, intoxication, enmity, and passion.
Indeed, there will be exactly five conditions for the afflictions caused by the influence of the Kali age:
all people will consist mostly of barbarians (mlecchas) and will likewise be devoted to unrighteousness and falsehood.
They were slayers of women, children, cows, and Brahmins; they coveted the wives and wealth of others;
they rose and set for little purpose; they gave meager gifts and possessed fierce tempers.
Lacking in ritual action, they are unrefined, possessing little strength and short lifespans;
pervaded by passion and ignorance, they are mostly barbarians who are masters of wealth.
The lords of those regions and the people themselves were devoted to that character and conduct;
their virtue was truth, compassion, forbearance, purity, longevity, mindfulness, and strength. (11)
As the increasing power of the Kali age spreads day by day,
all forms of excellence find their source of prosperity in wealth alone.
In the establishment of justice and law, wealth is the cause and becomes the power;
in the union of husband and wife, mutual affection is the cause, or else wealth, or even the object of desire.
In the state of being a Brahmin, the *sūtraka* is the mark; in shaving, *vijaya* is considered auspicious.
In scholarship, there should be *vitaṇḍā*; in the practice of renunciation, poverty is [the sign].
The hypocrite should appear as a great saint; at the wedding, there should be mutual consent between the two;
outwardly, there should be a display of wonder, bathing, false splendor, and adornment. (15)
The sacred ford may be far away, the hair on the head is but an ornament,
filling one's belly is merit, and truthfulness is indeed invincible.
Skillfulness in accomplishing one's own tasks, the pursuit of fame, and the practice of giving—
these consist of two hundred, one hundred, fifty, and twenty-five [units] respectively.

When the life span of beings has dwindled to the end of fifteen years, it is then the final [age]; this occurs for those who indulge in theft, falsehood, senseless violence, sexual misconduct, and so forth. (18)
In the Kali age, young women remain unmarried and wear very little clothing;
likewise, men and women touch everyone and seize all that belongs to others.
All castes are mostly barbarians, and cows are mostly goats;
hermitages consist mostly of wives, and kinsmen consist mostly of wealth.
Herbs consist mostly of grass; trees are reachable only by those who are tall;
clouds bring rain for but a moment; and houses are devoid of substance. 21.
In the Kṛta age, there was truth, compassion, charity, and austerity, but those do not exist in the Kali age;
[in that age] people are contented, compassionate, friendly, peaceful, self-controlled, and patient.
In the Kṛta age, all people indeed delighted in the Self and were equal-minded;
in the Tretā age, however, the portions of Dharma’s feet diminish by one-quarter.
The feet of unrighteousness—falsehood, violence, and craving—as well as strife, enter there; and people engage in these by their very nature. (24)
However, in the Tretā-yuga, people are devoted to austerity, they are neither excessively violent nor licentious,
and they are primarily intent upon virtue, wealth, and desire.
Even those of the highest caste, when their conduct is corrupted, are born as outcasts;
in the Dvāpara age, austerity, truth, compassion, and charity diminish by half.
In the Kali age, even a bull— though it be the best of its kind— is destroyed by violence, thirst, falsehood, hatred, censure, envy, and threats, as well as by unrighteousness and evil qualities.
They are merciless, hostile, greedy, full of craving, and devourers of all; they are of evil conduct and are ever eager for the indulgence of drinking and sensual enjoyment.
All creatures indeed come to possess the use of the tongue and the genitals;
they also develop deceit, falsehood, sleep, laziness, hatred, and despondency. (29)
In the Kali age, among people there is daily sorrow, delusion, fear, and wretchedness;
they are destitute of wealth, addicted to wasteful expenditure, drinkers of intoxicants, and possessed of false views.
Men and women are everywhere intent on their own self-interest and rooted in desire;
the lands are filled with bandits, and the Vedas have been ruined by heretics.
Then kings will devour their subjects, people will be satisfied only with their genitals and bellies,
those wearing saffron robes will be devoid of vows, and householders will become mendicants.
Austerity is for the sake of gaining deceit; even a deposit is for the purpose of seizing wealth.
Men are dwarfs, gluttons, have many children, and have many wives.
Women, too, speak sweetly like female cranes, yet they are naked even while clothed;
they are deceitful in their dealings and petty, stained by love for the path of the unrighteous. (34)
They abandon a husband who is destitute, and even leave behind their families;
forsaking fathers, brothers, and friends, they go away to one who satisfies their desires. (35)
All accept gifts, and all are indeed priests;
all possess authority over mantras, even the barbarians who pride themselves on being Brahmins. (36)
And the deceitful instruct their disciples who are likewise endowed with deceit;
for deceitful disciples naturally resort to a deceitful teacher. (37)
Those who act contrary to dharma speak words of dharma among those who follow unrighteousness;
yet toward those who abide in their own duty, they constantly harbor hatred, censure, and envy. (38)
Deprived of food, wealth, and clothing, and lacking even a home or sustenance, people indeed die prematurely in the terrible Kali age when death has not yet arrived. (39)

In the Kali age, there will be droughts, excessive enemies, and people afflicted by severe diseases; indeed, for the sake of achieving even their meager goals, men will become destroyers of one another.
In the Kali age, wicked sons do not protect their aged parents;
nor do wicked husbands protect their virtuous wives. (41)
In the Kali age, women protect their sensual pleasures according to their desire;
they seek out men who provide wealth and grant them sexual gratification. (42)
In the Kali age, people undergo suffering like cats for the sake of a single cowrie shell, and they even sacrifice their very lives for the sake of falsehood. (43)

These teachers, gurus, and preeminent men, whose minds are pervaded by heresy, strike down even their own kinsmen for the sake of their own meager interests, thereby destroying their true welfare. 44.
In the Kali age, people indeed find neither happiness, nor liberation, nor peace;
seized by time, they quickly undergo destruction, being constantly agitated.
Men of little faith, untruthful, highly wrathful, and unrighteous are born indeed when they are mixed with Yavanas. ||46||
In the Kali age, men—corrupted by the evils of the age—enjoy themselves by killing women, by slaughtering children, and by slaying one another. 47.
O Brahmins, all these kings— whether of exalted lineages or those who have risen only to fall— are indeed to be fed by outcasts, just like dog-cookers.
Deprived of virtue, pleasure, and wealth, and following the conduct of barbarians in every respect, the people will then meet their destruction, possessed by nihilism. (49)
In that Kali age, when the assembly of men is small and women are many,
[beings] will fall away bit by bit in terms of lifespan, physical form, strength, and sacred learning.
Afflicted by barbarians, the barbarians themselves repeatedly go to their destruction;
with their wealth ruined, they suffer greatly from diseases and are devastated by drought and other calamities.
The forest-dwellers will become destitute and deprived of their livelihoods;
cities, villages, and other settlements will be destroyed, and people will lose their mutual affection.
Those who resort to intermixture, being humpbacked and dwelling by rivers and mountains,
are born like fishermen in the forest, subsisting on fish.
At that time, they subsisted on deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey,
hyenas, honey, vegetables, fruits, roots, and small creatures.
They wear rags, various leaves, bark garments, and deerskins;
they wear only a loincloth, having resorted to a life dependent on animal products.
Residing by rivers, they tend goats, sheep, donkeys, and camels;
they have many offspring, lack food, and are devoid of purity and proper conduct.

Then those Brahmins, who have become Śūdras in essence and who perform rites such as the employment of mantras for malevolent purposes, adopt even the most base and unrighteous practices followed by the beasts. (57)

In the household, women are the chief counselors and brothers-in-law are the primary authorities; the marital union is subject to sale, and there is a state of mindlessness leading to separation. (58)

In the Kali age, the sacred fords have been oppressed by Yavanas, the gods have been insulted by Cāṇḍālas, and the noble lineages have been destroyed by Mlecchas, all reduced to a single uniform state.
There is no yogi, nor any perfected one (siddha), nor any wise man contemplating Brahman;
there is no one at all free from dullness—behold, Lakṣmī, the power of the Kali age!
In the Kali age, countries will always be destitute of food, the twice-born will be sellers of stories, and women will always be sellers of their pleasure.
But all things devoid of essence—fraudulent, wicked, and base—are like demons of sin; they are indeed like mere husks, lacking even a grain of substance and devoid of sprouts. (62)
The story is heard by all, yet it is not protected by anyone;
in the Kali age, during the auspiciousness of Śrāvaṇa, the essence of the story shall vanish.

In the Kali age, when the welfare of those who frequent sacred fords has declined, people may bathe at holy sites, dwell there, and observe vows, yet the essence of their discourse will have vanished.
In the Kali age, which is auspicious for ascetics, the essence of austerity shall depart from those whose minds are agitated by desire, anger, fear, greed, and thirst.
Due to the lack of mastery over the mind, greed, hypocrisy, and resorting to heretical doctrines,
the essence of meditation shall vanish in the Kali age, even when auspiciousness arises from meditation.
Thus, at every stage, the very essence of things dissolves away;
for by the force of the age, all that [decays], and no one is to be blamed.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Observation of the Arising of the Nature, Qualities, and Defects of the Kali Age," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*. || 215 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: When five thousand years of the Kali age have passed, the foremost of sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, shall depart from the surface of the earth for the abode of Śrī Hari.
The Śālagrāma is the form of Hari, and Jagannātha is a deity;
after a short time has passed, they shall go over to the side of Hari.
Initiations, divine mantras, ritual injunctions, ancestral rites, and libations,
as well as all sattvic actions, shall go to the abode of Hari.
The worship of Hari, as well as the chanting of His names and qualities—even that of Hara—all forms of knowledge of reality shall go to the abode of Hari. 4.
In the Kali age, there are no observers of vows, asceticism, fasting, or hospitable rites toward village deities; nor are there those who regard birth-impurity and similar conditions as obstacles.
In the Kali age, great men are indeed said to be killers of those possessed by cruel egoism; there is no mutual division among men, nor among women.
Throughout the entire land, women— both those under the control of men and unchaste women alike— in both their homes and in the forest,
constantly strike their paramours as well as their husbands with threats and reproaches.
In the Kali age, the mistress of the house becomes the wife, while the husband becomes inferior even to his servants; and daughters-in-law become equal to maidservants and slaves.
In the Kali age, the creators [of one's lineage], the powerful kinsmen related by birth, and the mother-in-law and father-in-law are the primary authorities in the household.
There is not even conversation with those connected by learning; for one's own kinsmen and others are regarded as strangers. (1.216.10)

In the Kali age, those who preach the doctrine of the body and its worldly concerns study the sciences of the Mlecchas; though claiming to be superior, they are devoid of essence and become servants to the Shudras.
In the Kali age, Brahmins will be devoid of the sacred thread and lacking in protection; they will be engaged in agriculture, bereft of dharma, and will perform the work of barbarians.
Trees devoid of fruit, women devoid of offspring, cows devoid of milk, and milk devoid of ghee; (13)
Husbands and wives will be devoid of love, householders will be bereft of happiness, kings will be lacking in virtue, and the subjects will be oppressed by taxes. || 14 ||
Rivers, streams, ponds, wells, and lakes may be devoid of water;
among hundreds of thousands, some fortunate person might encounter [the truth], or perhaps not at all.
In the Kali age, men, women, and children are born base, deformed in appearance, addicted to evil news, and following contemptible paths.
In the Kali age, there will indeed be neither cities nor villages for long; people will dwell among trees and in pits, subsisting on leaves like rabbits.
In the Kali age, forests indeed arise within the lands of villages and cities; likewise, rivers, ponds, crops, fields, and wildernesses [appear everywhere]. 18.
Wealth is not seen anywhere in one who has resorted to the conduct of a beast;
there is trust in truth placed in a rogue, and the esteem of merit is found in a sinner. (19)

In the Kali age, those who are undisciplined are considered disciplined; the lecherous are counted as those who have conquered their senses; and harlots are indeed reckoned as virtuous women worthy of honor.
There were paramours who observed the vow of Brahman, and lifelong celibates who took on all female forms;
there were ascetics who concealed their sins, revilers who considered themselves truthful.
In the Kali age, those who are killers become compassionate, thieves become adorned with virtue, and beggars become deceivers. (22)

Those who serve the lowly, those who serve the great, those who delight others with stories of hatred, those who provide laughter, the dull-witted, and the hunters—these indeed are to be honored in the Kali Yuga. (23)
In the Kali age, even at fifteen years of age, people are afflicted by disease and old age, their hair turns grey prematurely, and they become like the very aged.
A young woman of five years who has reached puberty and possesses sons, a woman who gives birth at the end of six months, and one who has reached old age at twelve—[these are the results]. ||5||
For the most part, many were barren women, those who had suffered miscarriages, and those with deformed offspring;
they were all sellers of daughters and sellers of sons. (26)
They were intent on procuring paramours for their mothers, wives, and daughters-in-law;
they lived by procuring paramours for their daughters and sisters. (Verse 7)
Those who sell the names of Hari, those who give gifts for the sake of fame, and those who steal the livelihood of a deity, the livelihood of a brāhmaṇa, or the livelihood of a guru; ||28||
Those who enjoy their daughter-in-law, mother-in-law, daughter, co-wife, or sister, as well as those who enjoy the wife of a brother—these are practitioners of forbidden sexual intercourse. (29)
In the Kali age, men abandon their place of birth and wander about;
in the Kali age, there is no certainty regarding wives or husbands.
In the Kali age, all those who are false-speakers— whether they be officials over subjects, goods, or villages— become thieves and gain power.
In the Kali age, people are indeed killers of men, likewise killers of the weak, killers of their gurus, and killers of the Dharma.
In the Kali age, they engage in the trade of lac, metals, juices, and salt, and they employ their sons and wives [in such work]. (33)
A prostitute, a usurer’s wife, a courtesan, a woman in her menses, and widows indeed prevail as beggars in the kitchen. (34)
There is no certainty regarding foods, nor is there any certainty regarding wombs; there is no certainty regarding gender signs, and for children, it is all the more so. (35)
At the end of that Kali age, trees will be only a cubit in height, human beings will be the measure of a span, and animals will be half a span in size.
There shall be the slaughter of the virtuous, of elders, and of ascetics;
there will be constant fear of drought and the ruin of countries. (37)
In the Kali age, men and women alike will all perish simultaneously through the heat of poison, death by fire, or destruction by fiery meteors.
In the Kali age, the downfall of subjects occurs due to ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, evil deeds, improper traditional practices, and the ritual faults of Brahmins. (39)
Violence, deceit, envy, anger, malice, and intolerance toward men—
these fierce qualities of worldly people, as well as passion and greed, will prevail in the Tiṣya age.
In the Kali age, there are disturbances, conflicts, and afflictions among every person; and for all those of the lowest birth, there are social ties formed through sleeping and eating together. (4.1)
In the Kali age, lifespan, intelligence, strength, physical form, and lineage perish; moreover, there will be female sorceresses, bringers of pestilence, and women skilled in mantras. (42)
When the terrible Kali age has set in, there will be an increase in the power of beasts of prey, a decline of cattle, and the destruction of the sacred traditions.
At that time, the god will rain down variegated things, and people will have variegated offspring;
merchants will use false measures, and those of evil character will take on the appearance of hunters.
The world is full of many beggars who offer no return for favors;
their minds are ruined, they are reckless, and they have long hair and the dress of women. (45)
In the Kali age, there will indeed arise thieves of grain, thieves of clothing, even thieves of thieves, and plunderers of those who themselves plunder.
Insects, mice, and snakes attack human beings after they have committed the killing of women, children, or cattle, or having killed one another. 47.
In the Kali age, having destroyed their own lineage, people seek happiness through unrighteousness, fear, and lack of ethical conduct;
indeed, those in the Kali age are characterized by tamas.
In the Tretā age, dharma lasts for four months; in the Dvāpara, it lasts for one month;
and for atheists and the weak, in the Kali age, it lasts for only a single day.

In the Kali age, there is always the neglect of initiation, the neglect of Vedic study, the neglect of purificatory rites and sacrifices, and the neglect of the impurity caused by menstruation and birth.
In the Kali age, the purification of cooked and uncooked food, the cleansing of the mouth with gargles, and the rites for purifying corpses and cremation grounds shall perish. (51)
At that time, temples and the images of the great ones shall be worshipped;
however, in the Kali age, the sacrificial feasts for the benefit of others will perish.
In the Kali age, the distinctions between virtuous wives and widows, between householders and those living at home, and between those who observe honor and those who do not, shall perish.

In the Kali age, the discernment between those deserving of punishment and those not, the channels for distinguishing between what is to be protected and what is not, and the discernment between what is to be cultivated and what is not, will all perish.
At that time in the Kali age, women, cows, and maidens will be as strong as oxen; even women and outcasts will occupy the seats of kings in the courts of justice.
In that Kali age, the entire empire of the outcaste dog-cookers (śvapaca) arises;
indeed, in the Kali age, there is always the kingdom of the shaveling, the kingdom of the youth, and the kingdom of self-interest.
In the Kali age, there shall be the kingdom of Bali, the kingdom of the rogue, and the kingdom of the naked;
that which is seen as truth and anything else is indeed considered invalid in the Kali age. (57)
In the Kali age, equality of wealth, equality of mansions, and equality of inheritance occur swiftly;
in the Kali age, there is equality among people, equality in actions, and equality with the naked.
In the Kali age, O Guhyaka, there is equality with women, equality with men, and equality with the elderly; there is equality in action, equality in armor, and equality in suffering. (59)
In that Kali age, there will be equality of faces, equality of hair, and equality of breasts; there will be equality of nakedness, equality of thighs, and equality of embryos.

In that Kali age, there will be a similarity between oil, ghee, fat, and clarified butter, as well as between water and [other liquids]; likewise, there will be a similarity between milk, curd, *haiyaṅgavīna* (fresh butter), and so forth.
In the Kali age, sugarcane, tubers, fruits, roots, sugar, molasses, and other such sweets, as well as sweet, salty, pungent, and bitter tastes, will all become equal [in quality]. (62)
In the Kali age, equality in speech, equality in action, equality in form, and equality in dress prevail; there is equality among gods, humans, yakṣas, serpents, and nāgas. (63)

In that Kali age, there will be equality regarding festivals, grief, passion, vehicles, seats, and social status; likewise, there will be equality of mind among children, youths, the elderly, and heroes.
In the Kali age, there is equality in the loss of one's own interests, those of others, friends, and enemies; there is equality in decline, equality in expenditure, and equality in hunger.
At that time in the Kali age, there will be equality of the seasons, equality of the years, and equality of nights and days; likewise, there will be equality between the states of sleep and waking.
At that time, it was considered equal to a couch, a bedstead, a cushion, a granary, and a water-jar; likewise, it was regarded as being like a fortress, a rampart, a gate-tower, and a courtyard. (67)
In the Kali age, there is an equality between living in forests, gardens, wildernesses, hamlets, and villages; and for humans, cattle, birds, and the like, there is a sameness with insects. (68)

In the Kali age, those who engage in mere chatter and cavil regarding commands, instructions, and ritual procedures are equal [to the ignorant]; likewise, there is an equality of failure in establishing valid reasons and restrictive rules. (69)
In the Kali age, Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī share the same condition as widows;
and in the Kali age, the learned who follow their own spiritual paths share the same condition as eunuchs.
In the Tiṣya age, indeed, there is a similarity between rains and the sky, a similarity between crops and time,
and a similarity between the earth and the back of a tortoise.
In the Kali age, there is indeed equality among faces through their grasping, equality among hearts through the similarity of their throbbing, and equality among loves through their conflict. //72//
In the Tiṣya age, the equilibrium of the senses indeed arises from righteous deeds;
however, in the Kali age, there is no similarity of signs other than the presence of faith.
When the Kṛta Yuga arrives once again, the world will become alive once more;
through the yoga of Hari, it will likewise become blissful, endowed with the power of Brahman.
"This ritual manual, consisting of all prosperity and endowed with the qualities of the actions of all dharmas, has thus been told to you. What else do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteen chapter, titled "The Specific Description of the Characteristics of the Kali Age," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Blessed One, I wish to hear about that Bhūmikā who was brought here by the power of her own penance as the queen of King Narta in the first Dvāpara age.
O Lord, tell me the great majesty of that sacred site, along with its history, where the illustrious Lord Kṛṣṇa has eternally established his own abode.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the most terrible Kali age, which is frequented by many heretics, I shall describe a great sacred ford for the sake of crossing over; listen to me.
It stands situated on the shore of the western ocean;
it is that city known as Kuśasthalī, which was built by King Kuśa.
Even before that, the ground brought by the King of Ānarta was the very city of Ānarta; it existed prior to all others.
Where the Gomatī flows, joined by the ocean,
that city is proclaimed as Dvārāvatī, known by the name of Ānarta.
There dwells Hari, the soul of the universe, who eternally bestows liberation;
he is endowed with sixteen digits and joined with twelve forms.
That Dvārakā is indeed blessed, for there the four-armed Kṛṣṇa resides;
having gone there, people shall attain liberation in age after age.
Ānarta was indeed a great devotee; he became the son of Śaryāti.
When the kingdom was being divided by his father, he did not accept a share for himself.
Likewise, the devoted dancer instructed his father:
"This human body of mine is indeed intended solely for liberation."
This tree of the eon (kalpabhūruha), so difficult to find, must not be destroyed while I still hold the kingdom;
for it is by me alone that liberation, which is like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), is to be attained here.
Having heard what was said by my father at that time— "I do not consider you worthy,
nor does a son who fails to rule a kingdom please me in my lineage"— [he spoke].
"Accept a share of the kingdom, or else go to another land.
Having heard this from his father, Ānarta bowed and departed for the western region.
On the shore of the salt ocean, where the ground was covered with sand,
he performed austerities for a long time, worshipping Hari by the name of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Kṛṣṇa, being pleased, approached him in the presence of his devotees and said to Ānarta: "O my devotee, what is in your mind? (15)
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; I shall grant whatever you desire.
Having prostrated himself like a staff, he said: "O Lord, lead me to Goloka. (16)
I have no thirst whatsoever, nor do I possess any latent impression of a physical body;
I have no regard for asceticism except for the service of your feet.
Laughing, the Blessed One said: "Listen, O devotee, to that which is for your benefit:
though exiled by your father, you perform penance for my sake. (18)
"I shall give you a great kingdom that has passed entirely under my father's control;
come with me, and I shall grant you a divine portion of the earth."
Having done this, Śrī Kṛṣṇa took her with him and went to the abode of Goloka, having divided a divine portion from his own Goloka.
"Having offered him to Ānarta, take this auspicious jewel;
go to the divine world, to that place on earth where you performed your austerities."
"Therefore, place this fragment of the jewel on a beautiful shore of the ocean;
this very region shall indeed become your independent kingdom."
Having thus fulfilled that hope and led him to a portion of Goloka,
Anarta returned to the coastal region on the shore of the western ocean.
There, as soon as the jewel was released, it expanded to a vast size;
it became a supreme, divine terrestrial expanse, one hundred yojanas in width.
A new earth was born and that became a divine kingdom;
then, because Kṛṣṇa remembered Ānarta, it was thereafter called the city of Ānartapura.
Just as the capital city had been fashioned as directed by Kṛṣṇa,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived there at the time of worship and spoke to him.
"Since I must dwell here at the conclusion of the Dvāpara age, therefore,
establish a preeminent and delightful city that shall remain under my protection."
By Ānarta as well, that auspicious and divine city, possessing the splendor of the abode of Goloka, was established according to the path described by Kṛṣṇa. 28.
Thus, this stage, characterized by serene faith and frequented by celestial dancers, is this very region of Surāṣṭra, consisting of sacred fords, which bestows liberation. (29)
Listen, Lakṣmī; thereafter, after some time, that city was repeatedly destroyed by the waters of the ocean through floods of water.
When, at the end of the Dvāpara age, Kṛṣṇa set his mind upon going there,
there was no village, nor city, nor even a pleasant spot to be found.
Afterwards, Kṛṣṇa himself, joined by his brother Saṃkarṣaṇa, bowed to his parents; then Hari called Garuḍa to mind.
Staying at the foot of a banyan tree in Madhupurī, he remembered the ocean;
he remembered Viśvakarman and assumed the guise of a king.
Casting off his cowherd attire, he called to mind the eternal discus;
and Sudarśana arrived, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
And he bore that Sudarśana, which was equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor, the destroyer of all enemies, and the infallible weapon among weapons.
Placing the jewel-vehicle at the forefront, Garuḍa also arrived;
Viśvakarman, along with his artisans, went to the vicinity of the ocean. (36)
Seeing them and being shaken, the ocean approached and bowed down;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said, "O Ocean, ten yojanas of your land [shall be mine]."
"Give me a portion of Goloka for the sake of my city;
let the ocean quickly make that much of the earth devoid of water. (38)
That divine ground of Goloka shone forth as if it were another;
she spoke to Viśvakarman himself, saying, "Fashion this earthly terrain."
"O Kāra, build for me a city that is beautiful in the three worlds,
delightful, highly divine, and desirable to women."
And the desired [abode] for my devotees is the supreme realm resembling Goloka, the crown of all heavens, which is my own dwelling place. (41)
O Garuḍa, remain day and night in the presence of Viśvakarman for the sake of the materials, until he constructs my city. (42)
"And remain by my side day and night, O Sudarśana.
Having thus commanded him, Kṛṣṇa himself departed for Mathurā.
Every evening, Viśvakarman always approaches Kṛṣṇa; he reports what has been accomplished and also considers what is new to be done. (44)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke to Viśvakarman regarding the process of construction:
"A most enchanting city extending for ten yojanas. (45)
With rubies, emeralds, and exceedingly deep blue sapphires; with topazes, coral, and pale-green stones; and with syamantaka gems. ||46||
Also with fragrant substances, gālima, as well as sun-stones (sūryakānta) and the like, moonstones (candrakānta), and excellent gold-bearing suhīraka gems. ||47||
And with crystals that are greenish-yellow, dark-blue, and white-faced; with yellow substances like *gorocanā*, and those having the form of pomegranate seeds. ||48||
With corals, lotus seeds, and blue lotus-colored pigments; with dark substances like collyrium, and with clear, radiant jewels. (49)
With white [garments] shining like the color of campaka flowers, resembling molten gold,
of great value and many virtues, and beautiful with reddish-yellow hues.
With the most precious and excellent true gems, jewels, and diamonds,
according to the prescribed rite, as was appropriate, wherever it was required, and whatever was desired.
"Perform now the divine rite for my sixteen thousand women, and also for the one hundred and eight wives of others. (52)
The camp had excellent moats, was encircled by high walls,
possessed twelve halls, and was beautifully adorned with a lion-gate.
It was beautifully adorned with door-panels and other features finely painted in three colors and more,
and it was made exceedingly beautiful by circular gardens containing the trees of the gods.
The well-characterized water-wheel, the lunar piercing, the solar abode, the knowledge of the stellar wheel, the knowledge of the elements, and the wheel of the seasons. ||55||
The assembly hall, the sacrificial hall, the terrestrial hall, and the celestial hall;
the hall for the instruction of machines and the hall for hearing from afar.
It should have a large hall visible from afar and be equipped with lightning chambers and the like;
there should be knowledge of the seasons, knowledge of the planets, and likewise knowledge of the winds. ||57||
The discernment of the ground-covering and the knowledge of portents—all that, you must arrange there in that city on a suitable site. (58)
Construct delightful hermitages for the Yadus, as well as houses for the servants,
and residences, gardens, and pleasure groves for the laborers.
"Build a beautiful residence for King Ugrasena, a palace that surpasses all others, leading to heaven, and entirely auspicious."
Likewise, cause to be built for my father Vasudeva a divine and spacious hermitage, the foremost of its kind, endowed with all forms of supernatural powers and worldly renown.
Viśvakarman spoke to Hari with the desire to inquire about the excellence of trees:
"Which trees are praised, and likewise which ones are prohibited? (62)
O Teacher of the World, tell me who are the givers of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness; and for whom is the camp assigned, bringing either happiness or unhappiness? (63)
O Lord, tell me in which direction water is auspicious and in which it is inauspicious;
