and in which direction does a planted tree indeed bestow good fortune? (64)
"O Lord, tell me the dimensions of the houses and the courtyards;
and in which direction, O doer of good, are the grove of trees and the flower garden? (65)
O Lord, tell me the measurements of the ramparts, the moats, and the gates, as well as the dimensions of the dwellings and the palaces.
O Lord, tell me which wood of which tree is auspicious for a house, and of which trees it would be inauspicious; please explain that to me, O Lord. (67)
Then Kṛṣṇa said to the carpenter: "Listen, and having performed meditation, [know that] a coconut tree in a hermitage shall bestow wealth upon householders. (68)
To the northeast of the camp, in the east, stands the tree that bestows sons;
everywhere, this beautiful king of trees brings about auspiciousness. (69)
The mango tree in the east shall be the bestower of prosperity upon men;
the bilva, the jackfruit, and the jujube are considered to grant happiness at all times.
In the east they bestow progeny, in the south they bestow wealth, and everywhere they bestow prosperity; from them the householder prospers. (71)
The Jambū tree, the pomegranate, the plantain, the āmrātaka, and the bandhūpṛṣṭha are in the east; and those [trees] that give friends are in the south.
Likewise, on the south it is Suvāka; on the west, it bestows happiness and joy;
and wherever it is situated along the side of the house, it grants wealth and sons. (73)
The Campaka tree at the side of the house, however, bestows auspiciousness everywhere;
in the northeast (īśāna), it likewise grants happiness and brings about gold and other riches.
The bottle gourd, the pumpkin, the cucumber, along with the *kiṃśuka*, the date palm, and the watermelon—these are the auspicious plants in the camp. (75)
The vāstūka, kārabilva, and vārtāka bring happiness;
likewise, the creeper-fruit that grows by the side of the house bestows well-being. (76)
Likewise, fruit-bearing trees and flowering trees always bestow auspiciousness;
similarly, fruiting creepers and flowering creepers likewise bestow auspiciousness.
In every way, the trees, creepers, grasses, and the flowers, fruits, and fragrances produced therein are indeed auspicious, truly bestowing sons, wealth, and prosperity. (78)
Those which have variegated colored leaves and beautiful flowers, as well as those gentle stems, become sources of happiness. (79)
Listen now to those that are praised, those that are declared, and those that are forbidden:
wild trees are forbidden, as are those devoid of fruit and flowers.
In a house, a palace, a garden, a city, or likewise at a gate, wild forest trees are useless; they are prohibited and not considered auspicious. 81.
Where vultures, herons, and crows dwell, and where those bhūtas and piśācas reside, being excluded and devoid of fragrance. (82)
The banyan tree is always forbidden within a camp as it brings fear of thieves; however, when seen in cities or on open ground, it bestows merit. (83)
A silk-cotton tree (śālmali) is not recommended in a camp, a city, or a village;
it is always considered a source of misery for rulers. (84)
It is not prohibited in a village or a city, nor on the outskirts;
however, it is strictly forbidden in a place of learning, as it constantly causes suffering. ||85||
The Tintidī tree causes the loss of wealth and brings about the destruction of the subjects;
it is strictly forbidden in a camp, while in a city its presence is only slightly restricted. 86.
The perfected one is not prohibited anywhere, whether in villages or cities;
however, the wise man should always avoid a place of learning where [the practice] is forbidden. 87.
Both the date palm and the *gahu* tree are indeed forbidden within a camp;
they are also forbidden in a village or a city, but not on ground outside [the settlement]. (88)
Indeed, trees such as those of chickpeas and other grains that bring auspiciousness should be planted all around—in villages or cities, in military camps or even in houses. (89)
Sugarcane stalks constantly bring about auspiciousness and increase prosperity;
the Aśoka, the Śirīṣa, and the Kadamba likewise bestow auspiciousness.
Turmeric should be understood as bestowing auspiciousness, and likewise, fresh ginger is auspicious;
chebulic myrobalans are auspicious, and emblic myrobalans grant prosperity. ||9 1 ||
The bone of elephants brings auspiciousness; the bone of horses brings happiness;
so too do the bones of monkeys, humans, donkeys, and even cattle. 95.
The bones of cocks, jackals, cats, mongooses, and pigs are inauspicious;
however, [the bone] of a boar is auspicious when located in the bladder.
In the northeast, as well as in the east, west, and north, the water of the camp is auspicious; elsewhere, it is indeed inauspicious. ||94||

One should not construct a temple on a low-lying site, nor on one that is uneven or irregular; for if a house or palace is built on a quadrangular site that is irregular, it causes the destruction of the wealth of its inhabitants. (95)
A house or city that is devoid of length and likewise devoid of the triad is empty; such an empty place bestows emptiness upon men. (96)
On a plateau, a doorway that is two cubits wide and three cubits long is auspicious for both the enclosure wall and the house. 97.
In the central region, nothing should be made that is either deficient or excessive;
a square camp with a moon-shaped opening brings auspiciousness. (98)
The camp that brings misfortune, causes the sun’s division, and bestows no auspiciousness; the courtyard that brings misfortune, causes the sun’s division, and bestows no auspiciousness. (99)
Within the camp, the auspicious Tulasī was always planted;
she bestows wealth and progeny, as well as righteousness and liberation.
Mālatī, yūthikā, kunda, mādhava, and likewise ketakī; nāga-campaka, mallikā, dhattūra, and bakula are auspicious. || 101 ||
Śubhadā and Aparājitā are their [two] gardens that bestow wealth; Śubhada and Sukhada are likewise located in the east and the south.
A householder should not construct a house higher than sixteen cubits;
a wall higher than twenty cubits does not bestow auspiciousness.
One should not allow an oil-presser, a goldsmith seeking to purchase diamonds and the like, or a carpenter to reside within the village grounds or in the center of the village.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a virtuous Śūdra, an astrologer, and auspicious men— such as a Bhadra, a physician, and a florist— one should station near the camp.
A moat for drinking water around the rampart is recommended to be one hundred cubits [in width];
however, around the encampments, ten cubits is recommended.
A secret gate with a moat, provided with a signal, is highly recommended;
so too are *tintiḍī*, *śālmali*, *hintāla*, and *sindhuvāraka* trees.
Nimba, Udumbara, Dhattūra, Eraṇḍa, and Vaṭa trees are likewise inauspicious and givers of suffering; therefore, one should not plant them within the camp. 108.
The king should always avoid a tree that has a thunderbolt on its trunk;
for such a tree would destroy his sons, wife, and wealth, and therefore he should not establish it there.
Having received this command from Hari, Viśvakarmā slept at the site of the banyan tree on the shore of the ocean,
and in a dream he beheld Dvārakā.
Beholding Viśvakarman sleeping— by whom Dvārikā was built— the gods, who had easily accomplished their task, laughed.
Just as she had been clearly manifested in a dream during the night,
the artisan, having awakened in the morning, beheld the auspicious city of Dvārakā.
Buddha saw that city of Pūrṇā, which Viśvakarmā had built in shame,
exactly as Śrī Kṛṣṇa had described it, extending ten yojanas in width.
Having conquered the cities of Brahmā and the other gods, he shone with preeminence;
and by his splendors, he adorned the second heaven, which was strewn with heaps of jewels.
In the meantime, O Lakṣmī, the lords of the fourteen worlds arrived at Dvārāvatī as early as morning to behold it. (115)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Construction of Dvārakā, Complete with Auspicious and Inauspicious Trees, Creepers, and Other Features, in Saurāṣṭra—which consists of the Goloka-khaṇḍa brought by Ānarta, the son of Śaryāti—within the Greatness of Dvārakā, in the first section on the Succession of the Kṛta Yuga" of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 2.17 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then Brahmā, together with his wife, went to behold the city,
as did Bhava accompanied by Bhavānī, Ananta, Dharma, and Bhāskara.
Agni, Kubera, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Yama;
the eleven Rudras, Candra, Mahendra, and likewise the Vasus. || 2 ||
Then the Ādityas, Kinnaras, Daityas, and Gandharvas arrived;
and Kṛṣṇa, seated at the foot of the banyan tree, was saluted by those staying in their celestial chariots.
Praised by them, they beheld Dvārakā, delightful and exceedingly enchanting,
resplendent with rows of pearls, rubies, diamonds, and other precious gems.
It was square on all sides, ten yojanas in extent,
and well-surrounded by seven moats that were very deep.
It was endowed with nine enclosures and pleasure-lakes for water-sports,
filled with various aquatic lotuses, white water-lilies, and red lotuses.
It was adorned on all sides with *sarvatobhadra* trees and flowering gardens,
and it was made fragrant by the winds carrying the scent of blossoming flowers.
It was adorned with sandalwood trees and tulasī plants,
and made fragrant by gentle, cool breezes carrying sweet scents.
It was graced by groves of coconut trees and exceedingly beautified by betel-nut trees;
it was also adorned with guvāka trees numbering more than a hundred thousand.
Beyond that, it was beautifully adorned with mango trees possessing fourfold qualities,
and it was illuminated all around by as many breadfruit trees.
Likewise, it was filled with palm trees, as well as *aśvattha*, *badarī*, and other species;
with *vaṭa* trees, *āmrātaka*, *bilva*, *jambū*, *kadamba*, and *vaṃśaka* trees.
With *śālmali*, *tintiḍī*, and *nāraṅga* trees; with *jambīra*, *dāḍima*, *campaka*, *bakula*, *nāgeśvara*, *arjuna*, and *kharjūra* trees. || 12 ||
With sugarcane, golden trees, harītakī and dhātrī plants,
with moon-like [flowers], śāla, priyāla, hintāla, and cool saptaparṇa trees.
It was completely covered on all sides by creepers, adorned with golden domes,
and endowed with nine hundred thousand beautiful palaces and lovely, lofty mansions.
Adorned with pearls and rubies fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems,
her temple features golden pitchers made of rubies and diamonds.
It possessed stairs, door-panels, and walls fashioned from jewels;
its pillars were made of emeralds and its excellent floors of white crystal.
It possessed variegated, diverse, and very fine garments, yak-tail whisks, and mirrors; its courtyards were paved with rubies, and it contained excellent white mansions.
It was provided with streets and lanes filled with sapphire gems,
and it was beautified by royal highways whose centers and other parts were inlaid with jewels.
Blazing with the brilliance of jewels like the midday sun in summer,
it possessed rows of great palaces and other structures endowed with hundreds of thousands of windows.
Having thus beheld the elephant stables, the horse stables, and the aviaries for swans and garuḍas, all the assembled gods marveled at the beautiful city of Dvārakā.
The region of Ānarta shone upon its hundred-yojana expanse;
joined with Dvārakā, it appeared as if doubled in size.
Then Kṛṣṇa called to mind Vasudeva and Devakī,
Ugrasena and the Yādavas, and the Pāṇḍavas along with their mothers.
Nanda, Yaśodā, the cowherds, the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the sages—all arrived when remembered, crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (23).
By the power of Kṛṣṇa, those divine ones—Vidyādharīs, Kinnarīs, dancers, and singers—possessing the splendor of divine movement through the sky, [became his attendants]. (24)
Singers, musicians, bards, astrologers, and mendicants;
kings residing in many lands, physicians, and brahmins. ||25||
Renunciants, ascetics, forest-dwellers, and celibate students,
as well as the Avadhūtas, Siddhas, and sages, all arrived there.
Sananda, Sanaka, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra,
Sanatsujāta, Voḍhṛ, Pañcaśikha, and likewise Āsuri.
Hundreds of thousands of people who observed the vow of celibacy arrived there;
and Durvāsas also came, accompanied by ten thousand disciples.
The Lord himself, devoted to his wife and possessing the form of Mahābrahmā,
arrived at the abode of Kṛṣṇa accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples.
Kaśyapa was accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples, Vālmīki by a thousand,
Gautama by a hundred thousand disciples, and Bṛhaspati by ten million gods.
Śukra also had ten million disciples, Bharadvāja had one hundred thousand, Aṅgiras had ten thousand disciples, and Vasiṣṭha likewise had ten thousand disciples.
Pracetas had a hundred disciples, Pulastya was joined by a thousand,
Agastya had ten thousand disciples, and Pulaha was joined by a thousand.
Kratu with a hundred disciples, Atri, and Bhṛgu as his follower,
as well as Marīci with a thousand disciples, arrived there.
Śatānanda was followed by five hundred disciples, as was Pāṇini;
and Vibhāṇḍaka’s son, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, was accompanied by a thousand pupils.
Kātyāyana and Yājñavalkya likewise departed with a thousand [attendants];
Vyāsa went with a thousand disciples, and Garga with more than a hundred disciples.
Gālava with a hundred, Saubhari with twenty people, Lomaśa with ten lakhs, and Mārkaṇḍeya with three lakhs. (36)
Sāndīpani and Devala, along with hundreds upon hundreds of their own disciples,
as well as Boḍu and Pañcaśikha, were accompanied by sixty disciples and their further pupils.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa went with a great multitude of ascetics;
likewise Viśvāmitra and Vatsa went with thousands of disciples. (38)
Jaratkāru, Āstīka, Paraśurāma, Dakṣaka, Saṃvarta, Jaimini, and Paila, along with their own followers, [were there]. (39)
Upamanyu, Śukadeva, Kaca, Gauramukha, as well as Lālāyana and others, and also Aśvatthāman and Droṇa.
Kṛpa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and other deities of the age,
along with the two most divine ones named Kambharā and Gopāla, arrived accompanied by their disciples.
The Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the Yakṣas are to be propitiated in the rite of house-construction;
as are the Cāraṇas, the Pitṛs, the Rudras, the Mātṛkās, and the guardians of the directions. (42)
Those whose bodies were composed of the four minerals, as well as those dwelling in the netherworlds and other realms,
along with the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, all arrived at the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
The Vasus, the treasures (Nidhis), the other seven sages (Saptarṣis),
the Prajāpatis, the Manus, and the Vālakhilyas were all present before him.
The six seasons, beginning with spring, arise from the families of Dharma and Adharma;
the Apsarases begin with Kāmā, while the Parya and Devī goddesses are the handmaidens. 45.
Virtuous male ascetics, female ascetics, detached nuns, and indeed female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga may come; for Kṛṣṇa indeed constructs their dwelling.
Likewise, there are the Avadhūtīs, the Caṇḍīs, Durgā, Māyā, Ramā, and others;
the Lakṣmīs, Jayā, Vijayā, and so forth; the Sakhīs, and the Māṇikya-kanyakās. ||47||
Prabhā, Pārvatī, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī; the gopīs, the gopas residing in Goloka, as well as the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. ||48||
Then maidens and youths, as well as female ascetics, Śaktis, Smṛddhis, and the personified forms of Siddhis, arrived there. 49.
The principles, the Vedic scriptures, various auspicious sciences, the qualities, sovereign power, and capacity—both those bound and those liberated—all came forth. ||1.218.50||
The four stages of life, the social classes, the wretched, and helpless beings, as well as the worlds and the non-worlds, all came together because Kṛṣṇa was preparing a dwelling place.
Listen, Lakṣmī: where all the holy fords and the lords of the lords of holy fords have assembled—that land is beyond description; what more need I say? (52)
Dvārakā, the supreme among all sacred fords (tīrtha), is the most excellent and bestows great merit;
by the mere act of entering it, birth and death are destroyed. (53)
Charity, faith, and worship of the gods bestow fruits of infinite merit; it is the very embodiment of all sacred fords—what sacred ford is superior to Dvārakā? (54)
The great king Ugrasena always resided within his own abode in the midst of Dvārakā, which was superior even to the palace of Mahendra, by the command of Kṛṣṇa. (55)
He beheld the gate guarded by thousands of doorkeepers,
as well as the interior of the camp extending from those six gates.
He [built] hundreds of temples resplendent with jewels and fruits,
as well as ten thousand rutting lordly elephants and ten thousand horses.
The bull among kings also beheld ten thousand camels, ten thousand chariots, and fifty thousand charioteers. ||58||
Within that beautiful place, he beheld the divine assembly hall named Sudharmā, where hosts of gods and sages were seated, and which was furnished with golden lion-thrones.
Adorned with pure white garments and radiant with the brilliance of jewels,
he entered the beautiful assembly hall and heard the resonant sound of conch shells.
Hearing the sound of kettledrums and the chanting of the sages,
Hari and Balarāma entered the assembly hall where Ugrasena was arriving.
Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Śeṣa— the preeminent among the gods—
as well as all the deities, sages, and human beings, rose up.
The lord of kings sat upon a beautiful, jeweled throne.
And Ugrasena [acted] according to the command of the gods, of Hari, and of Garga.
There, Nārada performed the consecration of the king with a pitcher filled with water from the seven sacred fords (tīrthas), using Vedic mantras.
To him, the high-souled Varuṇa gave a pair of garments,
as well as garlands of pārijāta flowers, sandalwood, and jeweled ornaments.
Baladeva gave him a jeweled parasol and other gifts individually;
Brahmā gave him a water-pot, and Maheśvara gave him a trident.
Pārvatī offered a jewel necklace and a crown; Kṛṣṇa himself [offered] golden ornaments, the lords of kings, the subjects, and various gifts. || 617 ||
The other fourteen inhabitants of the world also gave him wedding gifts;
Vasudeva, however, gave him two white chowries.
Nanda gave the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), Yaśodā gave a garland of jewels, and Akrūra, out of devotion and by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, held the parasol.
On a beautiful jeweled throne, the king beheld a mirror and heard the auspicious words of the bhaṭṭas, mendicants, and learned brahmins.
The gods, sages, and twice-born brahmins bestowed auspicious blessings upon him;
he gave jewels by the millions to the brahmins and mendicants.
Mādhava bestowed gifts in abundance— clothing, food, drink, and golden vessels— upon all who were worthy recipients of charity.
Hari Kṛṣṇa, the source of all auspiciousness, performed the Vāstuyajña sacrifice and fed everyone foods that were indeed pleasing to their taste.
In the assembly, the inhabitants of the world bowed down to Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva and said:
"O Blessed One, Dvārakā is beautiful and exceedingly enchanting. (74)
Protected by your arms, this city is purifying and the destroyer of sins;
indeed, no other city such as this exists here within the entire universe.
Those [powers] of ours which belong to the earth have indeed been forgotten through lack of vision.
No such supreme, divine place as this is seen anywhere else. ||76||
Thus was that city of Dvārakā praised by the gods;
then Kṛṣṇa proceeded to give them gifts.
Then the gods beginning with Brahmā, the lords, the guardians of the world,
the sages, the ascetics, the goddesses, and all those belonging to the divine races— ||78||
The oceans, divine rivers, mountains, sacred lands, forests, abodes, cities, groves, and streams; ||79||
Lakes and ponds, mountain peaks and caves,
temples as well as excavated and non-excavated reservoirs— these are the most purifying places.
Having bowed to Hari in embodied form, they earnestly prayed:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, may your auspicious blessings be upon us. (8.1)
All gifts bestow prosperity and liberation; no gift excels them.
Therefore, O Lord, we request these gifts from you, if it pleases you. (82)
We shall always remain here in this state of yours with divine forms;
through your yoga, great bliss will surely be ours forever. (83)
O Lord Śrī Hari, we shall become purifiers for those who touch the multitude of holy places that constitute Your praise; therefore, O Master, protect us always in Dvārakā. 84.
"Have mercy, O Lord of Compassion! We shall dwell here at your feet;
for elsewhere, even the most sinful among us must wash away their sins. (85)
Having given [these things], they all depart, while we remain shrouded in sin;
we shall fall at your feet and wash them indeed. (86)
And we shall become purifiers in your station;
therefore, O Lord, grant us an eternal dwelling here in this city of yours. (87)
"Wherever there is a boundary here in the forest, or on the shore, or outside, or all around and at our sides—we shall always dwell happily. (88)
We shall behold you and indeed drink your nectar;
we shall carry upon our heads that which has been purified by the washing of your feet. (89)
"By [serving] your feet, we shall attain the meaningfulness of our births in this world.
Hearing this request, Hari then spoke to all those lords.
"May all dwell happily in Dvārakā, each according to their station;
this Nārada, my devotee, will show you the sacred sites."
Those places shall become sacred forsthanas (tīrthas) by your names;
in each of those locations, I must remain together with you perpetually.
Having thus received the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
all the deities and holy fords resided upon the soil of Ānarta.
To the east, it extends as far as the city boundary; to the south, to Mount Raivata;
and to the north, up to the lake named Nārāyaṇa—such is the earth, which is dear to the Lord.
At every step, everything became filled with sacred fords and deities.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having summoned all those who had taken up residence there, spoke to them.
Having performed worship with devotion, he fed him excellent flavors,
choice foods fit for noble sages, and drinkable water.
He performed worship for all the sages according to their respective merits,
offering precious gems, coral, gold, and supreme wealth.
He joyfully gave pearls, rubies, diamonds, and other gems to those who had arrived,
as well as a jewel among elephants, a jewel among cows, and captivating horses.
He gave many seats, bowls, ornaments, and likewise jewels; he also gave grains, crops, and many garments.
Mādhava Keśava caused vehicles, draft animals, celestial chariots, and all the furnishings suitable for a household to be provided.
He caused kettledrums to be sounded and had auspicious rites performed;
he fed everyone and provided lodging for all on every side.
Then, having summoned the sacred fords (tīrthas), the Blessed One spoke according to the truth: "When the Kali age has arrived, human beings will become sinful."
This divine city of Dvārakā has been established by me upon the earth as the abode of all holy fords (tīrthas), for the sake of their deliverance. 103.
Those people here, whether in water or on land, who are blackened by the impurities of the Kali age,
shall go to my abode if they perform the rites of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
It removes birth, death, old age, and disease; it is supremely joy-inducing;
it dispels grief and anguish; and it cuts away the very root of karma.
Meditating again and again upon me, Hari, the Supreme Brahman residing in Dvārakā, may they attain devotion and go to the supreme state. 106.
When Kali arrives, which cuts away the very root of dharma,
there is no restraint for men and women, nor is there any restriction regarding castes.
For the Brahmin, the twilight prayers and other rites will cease to exist; the mark of the sacred thread, the sacrificial cord, and the sectarian tilaka—everything else will be lost.
Devoted to sexual intercourse by day and abstaining from righteous deeds,
men and women will become thieves in every household.
There shall be the total abandonment of sacrifices, vows, and austerities;
and the husband shall always remain under the control of a woman who acts according to her own will. (1.218.110)
A woman who has become the mistress of the household may beat or revile her husband;
and in the Kali age, all women are intent upon serving paramours.
Her affection for her lover will be equal to that she has for a hundred sons;
she will give food to her husband with the same anger as she would to a servant. (11.2)
Smiling, she looks upon her lover with a glance full of nectar out of desire;
she looks upon her husband with a glance like poison and a cruel look out of anger.
She constantly showed respect toward her paramour of that sort, yet she perpetually struck her husband with the palm of her hand. || 1.14 ||
And with faith and devotion, she gave sweet food to her paramour;
always dressed elegantly, she was constantly intent upon serving her lover.
In the Kali age, the vital breaths are the kinsman and the refuge, and the self is the paramour of women;
the service of guests has vanished, and the service of Viṣṇu has been utterly lost.
In the Kali age, the worship of the ancestors and the gods will be abandoned;
in the Kali age, men will be those who harbor hatred toward Viṣṇu and his devotees.
At that time, people will become graspers of false doctrines;
they will [reject] the Śālagrāma stone, Tulasī, Kuśa grass, and likewise the water of the Gaṅgā.
A deceitful man devoted to the customs of the Mlecchas shall not touch it;
for after five thousand years of the Kali age, my worship shall indeed perish.
After four thousand years, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī,
as well as sacred fords and devotees of Viṣṇu, shall perish from the surface of the earth.
At the end of this [age], in the Kali yuga, all will be intermingled with one another;
they will become of a single caste—outcastes (cāṇḍālas)—powerful and deceitful.
Service to one's parents, service to the guru, service to gods and brahmins, and likewise service to guests, is avoided by all people. (122)
The earth would be devoid of crops, the world would be without rain, likewise trees would be without fruit, and rivers would be without water. (1223)
A Brāhmaṇa devoid of the Vedas, a king devoid of strength, all people devoid of their caste, and likewise kings who are Mlecchas—[these are all equal]. (124)
A son may strike his father like a servant, and likewise a disciple may strike his teacher; a wife may strike her husband, and a householder may strike his wife like a greedy cock.
When the Dharma has fallen into decline,
then in the Kali Yuga, people will harbor false conceptions in their hearts.
The connection will become ever newer and newer solely for one's own sake; those who thrive on the Kali age will become the most excellent gurus and deceivers. (127)
In the Kali age, the wicked— those who are lower than the lowest and engaged in base deeds— will certainly not cross over [the ocean of worldly existence] without devotion to Hari.
For the sake of their upliftment, Dvārakā is the purifier of all;
it is a ground consisting of all sacred fords (tīrthas), capable of delivering even the Kāleyas.
Where not even a trace of the Kali age exists, such a place has been established upon the earth;
there, bathing, beholding, observing vows, worship, and offering prayers [yield great fruit].
People who, out of devotion, perform worship, offer water for drinking, bathe with dust, and chant praises, shall go to the supreme state.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of Divine Dvārakā, the Arrival and Worship of Countless Gods, Sages, and Others by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, His Dwelling There, and the Majesty of the Forest Endowed with the Greatness of That Tīrtha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Mahālakṣmī; for that Dvārakā, the abode of the Blessed Lord, is composed of all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas). What more need be said regarding its particular excellence?
Nevertheless, I shall describe some of the sacred fords (tīrthas) as they are;
among them, one should indeed go first to the preeminent Gomatī, which takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
By the mere sight of whom one is liberated from all sins;
by the mere touch of whom there is the destruction of inauspiciousness and evils. || 3 ||
One should bow to the water of the Gomatī, which fulfills all desires and is meritorious;
indeed, the water of the Gomatī bestows both ultimate welfare and a favorable rebirth.

In ancient times, when the world had become a single ocean and all moving and stationary beings had perished, Brahmā was born from the lotus of his navel; from him indeed were born Sanaka and the others.
Having been brought forth and commanded for the very purpose of the work of creation,
they departed for asceticism, disregarding those words.
Then, taking the western direction along the shore of the lord of rivers and streams,
they desired to behold Hari, whose very nature consists of radiant splendor.
Fixing their minds in concentration, they performed severe penance;
after many thousands of years, the Blessed One himself became pleased.
He hurled his own discus, Sudarśana;
having pierced the earth and drawn up the water, the Sudarśana was composed of pure light.
It emerged from within, resembling the sun, with a thousand spokes, difficult to approach,
the slayer of Daityas and Dānavas, and the eternal protector of devotees.
Seeing the wheel, the sons of Brahmā were filled with wonder;
then a voice from the sky spoke to those youths.
O Brahmins, O perfected yogis, Nārāyaṇa himself, Hari,
being pleased by your asceticism, will manifest directly and swiftly.
For the sake of that Arhat, this water appeared;
quickly offer the arghya with this pure water.
This weapon, which is pervaded by splendor, is the Sudarśana;
it belongs to Śrī Hari, the Lord of the World. Therefore, offer him this arghya.
Having heard that, Sanaka and the others praised Sudarśana:
"Salutations to you whose nature is light; salutations to you, the weapon of Brahmā. (15)
Salutations to you who protect your devotees; salutations to you, the weapon of Viṣṇu.
Salutations again and again to you, the thousand-rayed sun, whose aim is never missed.
Having thus praised and paid obeisance, they worshipped him with unbroken grains, flowers, leaves, water, and hymns, bowing down again and again. || 17 ||
Hari, Brahmā, and Vasiṣṭha arrived at that place;
delighted by the penance of their sons, they then granted them their vision.
Gangā, though residing in Satyaloka, arrived there in bodily form;
then Brahmā said to Gaṅgā, "Vasiṣṭha is my little son."
Follow to the edge of the ocean; having become water, dwell within the waters, where the Sudarśana gate is located and from which merit has arisen here.
There, let your abode always be at that sacred ford which destroys all sins;
O daughter, become forever meritorious through the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
"Because you shall always abide in the waters arising from the Sudarśana [lake], which are the foremost of the rays of the cows, you shall indeed have the auspicious name Gomatī.
Following Vasiṣṭha, become a daughter in the form of a river."
"Be like the daughter of Vasiṣṭha, who was as a father to her son."
Having said "So be it" to them, she set out in the form of water;
Vasiṣṭha went ahead, and the Gaṅgā followed behind him.
Seeing her proceeding toward the western ocean, all men, gods, and millions of holy places paid homage to that most meritorious one. (25)
Following Vasiṣṭha, she set out for the abode of Varuṇa;
the illustrious lady strewed that river with flowers.
Filled with wonder, the gods and the other beings worshipped him with divine garlands, fragrant perfumes, incense, and unbroken grains of rice. || 27 ||
By the mere sight of this, human beings shall attain liberation;
how much more so, then, by performing ablutions, giving gifts, and other rites, that they go to the abode of Hari? (28)
Having spoken thus and offered the guest-water (arghya), they praised Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
who was clothed in yellow silk and adorned with a forest garland.
Richly perfumed with divine fragrances, adorned with divine golden armlets,
equipped with divine ornaments and weapons, and wearing earrings in the shape of sea-monsters.
He has a blazing crown and diadem, his chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa, his four arms hang down, and his hands bestow fearlessness upon his devotees. || 31 ||
To Him who is dark as a rain-cloud, whose face is serene, and whose lotus-feet are served by Lakṣmī,
they bowed down again and again, and having bowed, they praised Him repeatedly.
Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, with a gracious mind and supreme affection, spoke to the twice-born,
the gods, and likewise to Kumāraka.
"May you all remain here, untouched by my *māyā*;
being wise and liberated, you shall indeed dwell here as purifiers."
"Indeed, this Gomati has been brought by me for your sake; it has attained the preeminence over all the sacred fords (tīrthas), including yours. (35)
I was also propitiated here by the princes who were seekers of liberation;
therefore, this supreme sacred ford named Gomati is the bestower of liberation.
O brahmins, for the sake of favoring you, I first displayed the Sudarśana discus by piercing through the earth and likewise the waters.
Having pierced through the divine, radiant [obstruction], it has arrived before me;
known as Cakratīrtha, it shall manifest within the Gomatī.
My residence shall also certainly be here, and yours as well in every way;
indeed, there will always be an eternal dwelling at Cakratīrtha.
For those people and others who bathe at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean,
and for those who have bathed at Cakratīrtha, liberation is held within their grasp.
Indeed, all holy places of pilgrimage reside in the Gomati and the ocean;
indeed, all the gods and sages reside at their confluence. 41.
Then Sanaka and the others, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), bathed, and drunk water,
washed the feet of Hari and then placed that water upon their heads.
There, Gomatī was worshipped by all the gods as well as by the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds; likewise, her meritorious water was drunk.
The water held upon her head washed the feet of Hari;
she, Gomatī, having become a maiden, then took the water in a jar.
Having prostrated at the feet of Hari, she held the water upon her head;
having prepared the arghya for Śrī Hari, she offered it along with a handful of water.
Having scattered flowers there, the great sages beginning with Sanaka, as well as the gods and the seers, entered the abode of Varuṇa.
Whichever holy fords and ancient forests arrived there,
they all took up residence in that place, established as the very forms of sacred fords.
Thus, through the power of Śrī Hari, that auspicious Gomatī became composed of all sacred fords (tīrthas), bringing great prosperity, purifying, and bestowing liberation. 48.
And Hari vanished from the sight of all the holy fords;
all the gods and others, having bowed toward that direction, returned to their own abodes. ||49||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that Gomatī became the ocean-going Gaṅgā,
the best of rivers, who removes all sins through her union with Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the History and Greatness of Gomatī-tīrtha and Cakra-tīrtha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 219 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having gone to the bank of the Gomatī and prostrated before her like a staff,
he washed his hands and feet with water while holding kuśa grass in his hand.
Facing east, one should offer unbroken grains, fruit, and curd, as well as the arghya water, saying:
"O Gomatī, for the sake of purification from all sins, I offer this arghya."
"O Goddess worshipped by the three worlds, O Gomati, take away my sin!
Having recited this and obtained the earth [clay], one should remember Viṣṇu and indeed utter [the following].
O Vasundharā, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu!
You were lifted up by the boar-like Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.
O Earth, take away my sin that has been accumulated by me in the past;
when the sin is destroyed by you, one is liberated from all sins.
Having thus taken earth, one should perform a bath in river water;
the merit that is obtained at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse is attained thereby.
By performing the ritual bath according to the rules in the Gomatī river in the presence of Kṛṣṇa,
one should, endowed with devotion, offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
By the offering of water from the Gomatī, they attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having invited Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas, one should perform the Śrāddha for the ancestors.
And one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of gold, silver, garments, and so forth;
[and a cow] endowed with horns of gold and adorned with silver hooves.
Having worshipped it with garments, ornaments, and decorations, one should give away that cow— which has a tail of jewels, milk, a copper-colored back, and is accompanied by its calf.
One should give the seven grains, saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me.
[The practices include] the Gomatī, bathing in cow-dust, the gift of a cow, and gopicandana.
And the sight of Gopīśa—these five things beginning with the letter 'ga' are difficult to obtain.
Indeed, by performing a śrāddha at the Gomatī, the deceased ancestors truly become liberated.
Those in hell, the immobile beings, and even the winds that have attained the state of insects—
all of them attain liberation through the performance of *śrāddha* and the giving of gifts at the Gomatī.
The fruit of the horse sacrifice, of bathing at Prayāga,
and of daily offerings to the consumer of oblations (Agni) is obtained from the waters of the Gomatī.
Indeed, the ancestors born of three lineages go to the world of Viṣṇu, [freeing themselves] from that which was committed through speech, mind, and action over many thousands of births. (15)
Indeed, sin goes to dissolution by the mere sight of the Gomatī;
for one who bathes in the Gomatī during the month of Kārtika, Lord Hari becomes gracious and bestows prosperity.
When the full month of Kārtika has arrived and it is Wednesday,
one should bathe Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with the water of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
One should anoint [the deity] with sandalwood paste mixed with musk and saffron, and worship Hari with garlands of flowers, fruits, lamps, and incense. 18.

One should offer a beautiful food-offering (naivedya), saying, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me," and should perform a vigil with songs, instrumental music, sacred narratives, hymns of praise, and dance.
At the end of the month of Kārtika, one should perform a bath at the confluence of the Gomatī with the ocean;
by worshipping the Lord of Ramā (Viṣṇu), the vow shall reach completion.
For one who performs the Māgha bath in the Gomatī, Hari becomes pleased along with Śrī; there, He also bestows liberation. ||21||
Sesame seeds, gold, silver, and sweetmeats mixed with jaggery,
as well as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), should also be given to a Brāhmaṇa on the bank of the river.
An oblation (homa) with sesame seeds, clarified butter, grains, and fruits is also approved; at the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise offer fine red garments, a bodice, and a turban.
One should also give sandals, as well as sweet food and a meal cooked with oil or cooked with ghee, saying: "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me. (24)
He obtains the fruit of all gifts as well as the fruit of all sacred fords;
he attains all desires and the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
And in this regard, people indeed obtain [the fruit] by bathing in the Gomatī during the month of Māgha;
one should conclude the month of Māgha on the full moon day (Māghī) at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean.
By the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, everything deficient shall attain completeness;
the sin of those who steal the property of Brahmins or the gods is destroyed by bathing. ||27||
The sin of betraying a friend or killing a teacher is destroyed by touching [it];
by seeing it, one attains a station higher than the realms of Brahmā and Rudra. (28)
Whatever fruit a person obtains by granting fearlessness to those who are afraid, that same fruit one attains from the confluence of the waters of the Gomatī. ||29||
The person who drinks the water of the Gomatī becomes one who has fulfilled all his duties;
and he who drinks even a mouthful of it is indeed released from the three debts.
Devotees who serve the Gomatī reside in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
they wear forest garlands, possess four arms, and are anointed with divine perfumes. (31)
Men, being of the very nature of Viṣṇu, and women, being of the very nature of Lakṣmī,
go to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is characterized by the absence of rebirth.
And having performed [the rites] at Gomatītīrtha, one should indeed go to Cakratīrtha,
where stones marked with the discus are seen in every way.
Even a stone held around the neck sends the man who wears it to Goloka,
by the power of the Lord marked with the discus.
Even he upon whose bones fall here attains the supreme goal;
this Cakratīrtha, which bestows liberation, is superior even to Prayāga. (35)
Wherever the branding with the discus is obtained, by remaining there for six months,
a person, having shaken off all sins, goes to the abode of Hari.
Having gone to Cakratīrtha and washed his feet and hands,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should then prostrate himself like a staff before Kṛṣṇa.
Having taken the five jewels, leaves, flowers, as well as unbroken grains (akṣata),
perfume, fruit, gold, sandalwood, and also the water-offering (arghya).
Having gazed upon the ocean, one should indeed offer it to Viṣṇu in the form of the discus, saying:
"Obeisance to you who are the very form of Viṣṇu; obeisance to you, the Discus of Viṣṇu. (39)
Accept this water offering given by me; be the granter of all desires.
You are born from fire, you are the body of sacrifice, you are the strength of Viṣṇu, and you are the giver of liberation.
O Ocean, you who bear Viṣṇu’s discus and are eternally endowed with Cakratīrtha;
O Wielder of the Discus, I perform my ablution here in this sacred ford—grant me liberation! 41.
Having placed earth upon his head and bathed, he then worshipped Hari,
gratifying the gods, the ancestors, men, and the attendants of Hari.
O Kṛṣṇa, by merely bathing at Cakratīrtha according to the prescribed rites after having offered the Arghya, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. 43.
At Cakratīrtha, the Viśvedevas are satisfied by the gift of gold, the ancestors by the gift of silver, and they are also fully gratified by the offering of food. (44)
Clothing and ornaments should be given to the poor and the wretched;
the gift of a chariot is declared to be preeminent, along with its horses, equipment, and abundance.
Horses, stallions, and especially carriages should be given as gifts;
furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be bestowed for the sake of pleasing the Lord of the World. 46.
The ancestors born in the three lineages— whether as ghosts, insects, or denizens of hell—
all attain liberation through the power of Cakratīrtha.

In the case of a *śrāddha* ceremony, the fruit of Gayā should be understood; in bathing, the attainment of the state of a sacrificer is held to result; in libations (*tarpaṇa*), the merit arising from a lunar festival (*somaparva*); and in giving gifts, that which exceeds [the merit of] a solar eclipse. 48.
The fruit shall be obtained; men should take up the wheel-mark on their arms.
The sin produced by [evil] thoughts, words, and deeds is destroyed through bathing. 49.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have certainly described to you Cakratīrtha as well;
people who perform their rites at this sacred site shall become pure and attain union with Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals and Fruits of Gomatī-tīrtha and Cakratīrtha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thereafter, O Mahālakṣmī, one should go to the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean;
it is declared to be the Gate of Liberation in the Kali age, without a doubt.
Whatever fruit is obtained at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, or at the meeting of the Sindhu and the ocean,
that same fruit is attained here at the confluence of the Gomatī and the sea.
Sin is destroyed by bathing; one should indeed offer the arghya according to the prescribed rite, holding kusha grass and likewise a coconut fruit in both hands.
Having offered salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, one should present the *argha* offering, saying:
"O King of Holy Waters (*tīrtharāja*), obeisance to you; protect me from the ocean of worldly existence."
"O Ratnākara, accept this water-offering (arghya) along with Gomatī; salutations to you.
Having offered the arghya, tied his topknot, and meditated upon the One who reclines upon the waters, [he continued].
One should perform the bath facing the east and then offer libations to the ancestors;
having likewise performed the ancestral Śrāddha, one should give an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should give gold and two garments, as well as a tunic and a turban;
and one should give great gifts if one desires one's own welfare.
Having said, "May Viṣṇu himself, Hari, along with Lakṣmī, be pleased with me," one should give various gifts and meals.
And one should perform the tulāpuruṣa gift at the confluence of the ocean;
having become a king of the seven islands, that man goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
He who would weigh himself against gold, silver, and the like, or against garments, saffron, camphor, sugar, fruits, and flavorful juices; || 1.221.10 ||
Having enjoyed pleasures and happiness in heaven, he, honored by the gods, attains liberation;
[for] the gift of gold, the Vājapeya sacrifice, and bathing in the waters of the Gomatī are equal. (11)

One who performs the gift of a daughter in marriage, the gift of land, and the gift of knowledge according to the prescribed rites at the confluence of the Gomatī shall indeed attain the state of Brahman.
Having indeed bestowed a cow made of gold, a cow made of ghee, and a cow made of sesame seeds,
and having given a cow made of cloth and so forth or a cow made of sugar, one goes to the supreme state.
On the principal lunar days marking the beginning of the Yugas, during the Pañcakas and the Aṣṭakas, as well as on the Vaidhṛti, Vyatīpāta, and the occasion known as Gajacchāyā; || 14 ||
Likewise, having bathed in the ocean on the sixth, eleventh, eighth, and twelfth lunar days, or during a śrāddha or a virtuous vow, as well as at the Gomatī and Cakratīrtha; || 15 ||
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean, one shall attain the state of Brahmā;
on the day of the new moon, a śrāddha ceremony should be performed at the junction of the Gomatī.
A person may obtain in a single day the merit that is earned by performing the ancestral rites (śrāddha) during the fortnight,
even if that rite is devoid of faith, devoid of mantras, or performed for unworthy recipients.
A śrāddha for the ancestors that is deficient in material offerings, deficient in timing, or devoid of one-pointedness of mind, becomes complete when performed at the ocean.
One shall dwell in the ocean of that [state] by offering rice-balls at Gayā or by casting bones at Prayāga, and likewise by bathing in the Gomatī, Kamalā, and Candrabhāgā rivers. (19)
By offering a *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), eternal merit is attained;
this is so for a man observing vows who desires to perform ablutions at all sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*).
One should indeed perform a bath with devotion at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean;
[thereby] a woman who is childless, whose children have died, who has given birth only to daughters, or whose children are miscarried, [shall obtain her desire].
A woman is liberated from her defects at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean;
likewise, by performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), giving gifts, offering libations to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa), and beholding the waters [there]. (22)
Vows, ritual bathing, merit, recitation, fire-offerings, and glorification at the confluence of the Gomati and the ocean produce eternal satisfaction and merit. (23)

Those on the mother's side, those on the father's side, as well as those on the sister's side; those on the daughter's side, those on the mother-in-law's side, and likewise those on the father-in-law's side. ||24||
Those belonging to the side of the father’s sister, as well as those on the side of the daughter-in-law, those on the side of the co-wife, and even those on the side of the female guardian; ||25||

Those belonging to the side of the brother’s wife, those belonging to the side of the sister, daughter, and so forth, as well as those belonging to the side of the father, brother, son’s wife, and other relatives—[all these are to be avoided]. (26)

Those who are friends, kinsmen, or servants, as well as those who maintain a relationship with them; those who have gone to other births, those in the hells, and those dwelling within the womb of the earth—[may they all be liberated]. (27)
All of them, when remembered at the confluence of the Gomatī and the ocean during a śrāddha ceremony, and when remembered while bathing or giving gifts, attain eternal satisfaction. ||28||
They are liberated from all sins and attain liberation, without a doubt,
by worshipping Vāmana on the occasion of Śrāvaṇa-dvādaśī.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gomatī, one attains the supreme world,
becoming clad in yellow garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
Bearing four arms and adorned with a garland of forest flowers, he was served by celestial women and had a celestial chariot as his vehicle. ||31||
A person who worships Śrī Hari, being praised by the ṛṣis,
becomes purified at the confluence of the Gomatī and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed in the ocean of the Gomatī, one should proceed to the seven Prakuṇḍas.
Worshipped by all, Kṛṣṇa, who is Hari, manifested himself.
Having seen Hari together with Lakṣmī, the great sages headed by Sanaka dug seven sacrificial pits filled with water and sprinkled the goddess Indirā.
Therefore, these lakes of Lakṣmī become the lakes of Rukmiṇī in the Kali age;
and because they were resorted to by Bhṛgu, they are remembered as Bhṛgutīrtha.
There, having washed his feet and likewise sipped water (ācamana), he should then take up kusha grass,
face the east, and receive the arghya offering with unbroken rice grains and other materials.
Raising both hands above the head with fruits and other offerings,
one must indeed present the *argha* here in the lake named Rukmiṇī.
Then, having meditated upon the sacred fords, the ancestors, and the deities, one should perform the ritual bath,
satisfying the gods, humans, and ancestors with a disposition of devotion to Hari.
Having invited the Brahmins, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony with devotion, offering sacrificial fees, silver, gold, fruit, sweet food, and clothing. (39)
One should also give food to the couple, as well as ornaments and the like,
an excellent sari, a bodice, a waist-belt, a cloth, and so forth.
Having worshipped the rows of ancestors and other women and young maidens,
one should give gifts while saying, "May Rukmiṇī be pleased."
Prosperity always dwells in his house, of this there is no doubt;
he attains all abundance, and Lakṣmī is pleased with him. 42.
One should offer gifts separately at each of these seven lakes;
all that becomes inexhaustible and bestows happiness in the world of Lakṣmī. ||43||
Misfortune perishes for him upon whom Fortune is gracious;
likewise his cattle, children, house, garden, fields, mansion, and granary [prosper]. (44)
Those toward whom Lakṣmī is pleased become constantly preeminent;
for her who is satisfied with someone, there is an increase of gold and other riches. (45)
One obtains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
at the seven lakes, providing food for women with one's own hands is excellent. (46)
Giving and worship, as well as honor, ornaments and the like, decoration, vehicles, carriages, and bodily requisites and so forth—[these are for the sake of the Lord]. (47)
One should indeed offer [the gifts] individually, saying, "May Lakṣmī be pleased with me.
For him, Lakṣmī dwells forever in the house; of this there is no doubt. (48)
He shall not be of low fortune, nor shall he be a beggar;
he who bathes in the Rukmiṇī-hrada becomes the foremost among all. (49)
There shall be no returning; the man goes to Vaikuṇṭha, and together with his wife, four-armed, he enjoys eternal bliss.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Gomatī-Sāgara Confluence Tīrtha and the Lakṣmī-Saptahrada Tīrtha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Thereafter, one should go to the great holy site that grants liberation to Kṛkalāsa, renowned as Nṛgatīrtha; for there was once a king named Nṛga.
Hundreds of thousands of kings were under his command;
he was constantly devoted to his teachers and intent upon the worship of the gods.
He constantly gave great gifts by the thousands,
and he always bestowed a thousand cows upon the Brahmins.
Having devoutly washed their feet and likewise offered a pair of linen garments,
and having worshipped them with sandalwood paste and flowers, he gave a cow to each brahmin.
He gave sacrificial fees and wealth, and indeed grass for the sake of the cows;
having offered betel, he said, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me."
As he gave gifts and likewise performed sacrifices, as he enjoyed pleasures and likewise worshipped Śrī Hari; || 6 ||
As he protected the earth according to dharma, time passed filled with happiness.
Once, [he visited] the brahmin Gautama, who was always free from possessions.
Having summoned him and honored him, the king gave him a cow,
adorned with golden horns and silver hooves.
Having led the cow along with her calf— she who was well-fed, beautiful, and bound by a rope— to a body of water, Gautama went to his own home.
Taking water to give it to drink, the Brahmin went out from his house.
Seeing a camel on the road, she became terrified and snatched [the vessel] from her hand.
Having run, that cow went to the vast herd of royal cattle;
Gautama, searching for her, did not find the cow and returned to his own home.
On the second day, King Nṛga again summoned the Brahmins and,
according to the prescribed rites, bestowed many gifts of cows.
Having honored and hospitably entertained him with devotion through garments, ornaments, and food,
that King Nṛga gave that cow to Somaśarman according to the prescribed rites.
Having taken that cow, he departed from the royal palace;
Gautama, too, while searching for her, beheld that very same cow.
He spoke to Somaśarman as he was following behind him:
"Having carried off this woman of mine, why do you flee like a bandit? (15)
Upon hearing that he himself was a bandit, Somaka was struck with amazement;
having received [the gift] from the king, he said to him, "Today, by virtue of this gift, I am no longer a bandit."
"I have ownership over the cow here; I shall lead the cow to my own home.
Gautama replied, "O King, this cow was indeed delivered to me by you yesterday."
"O Soma, when I give away my cows, ownership over them belongs to me alone and not to you; how then can you take them while Gautama is still alive? (18)
Thus disputing, the two brahmins approached the king’s gate, engaging in a terrible quarrel while addressing the gatekeepers with affection.
Seeing the two brahmins at the gate, Nṛga bowed and honored them again;
that best of kings then requested them to pacify the quarrel.
For each single cow, I shall provide one hundred thousand gold coins as collateral,
and I also give a thousand cows as security for the debt.
"O twice-born ones, let one accept this single cow given by me, while the other accepts a thousand cows and a thousand gold rings. ||2 2||
And Gautama and Soma, being full of pride, spoke thus; out of a fit of impetuosity, they both said, "We two shall take the earth, not the thousand [cows]. (13)
Gautama said, "I indeed take this cow as my own"; and Soma said, "I indeed take this cow as being under my control. (24)
I do not accept a thousand cows nor a thousand pieces of gold;
indeed, I have no need for even a thousand such things as my own cattle.
Though entreated by the king many times, awakened [to reason], and even honored,
their minds were agitated by anger, and they fasted for three nights.
Then, having been treated with contempt by the king, the two foolish Brahmins were told: "O Brahmins, go to your own homes; you are fools, devoid of luster, and unworthy recipients. (27)
When an unfavorable occasion arises, that wise man should indeed prepare his path;
for when one must be humble and the other is angry. (28)
Pride must be abandoned and obstinacy must be abandoned when there is no other recourse;
yet that is not being done, O Brahmins—what can I do in the face of such equality? (29)
"But in this matter, you two shall both become defiled regarding a single object;
therefore, O fierce twice-born ones, go to him and do as you please."
Thus addressed, the two Brahmins, being capable in their dealings with the king, then spoke these words in anger to the monarch.
"Since you treat us with contempt and do not grant us what is right, you shall therefore become a lizard; of this there is no doubt. (3.2)
Having thus cursed them, O King, both brahmins then abandoned the cow and prepared to go to their own homes, filled with sorrow.
Nṛga, having approached the gate and prostrated himself like a staff, made this petition: "O twice-born ones, your words are never in vain. (34)
"Having shown compassion toward me, please quickly grant an end to this curse.
To that, Somaśarman then replied: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, Hari himself [will appear]. (15)
Having arrived at Dvārakā, Vāsudeva— that very Kṛṣṇa— will grant you liberation and lead you to Goloka.
Having spoken thus, those two brahmins then departed for their own abodes;
King Nṛga, too, succumbed to the law of time due to that curse.
Having reached the palace of the King of Dharma, he was questioned regarding his karma to be experienced: "First you shall experience merit or sin; speak quickly! (38)
"You possess infinite merit, yet there is sin born from the transgression regarding the cow.
Having heard this, Nṛga replied, "Indeed, my evil deed was very small."
By the permission of Yama, this great lizard came into being;
for thousands of years, he has remained situated within this well and pond.
He became one who remembers his past lives and subsisted on grains of food and forest herbs;
once, he was being dragged here and there by the Yadu boys.
He played with them, remembering Lord Hari and considering it to be the time of his own liberation;
however, when he became weary due to his heavy body, [he stopped]. (42)
Having fallen upon the earth in a swoon, he did not move;
indeed, he remained there by means of yoga, having made his body exceedingly grosser than the gross.
Though pulled by many boys, he did not move;
having attained extreme bulk, he grew larger moment by moment. (44)
Seeing him, some children were startled and filled with fear;
they reported it to Kṛṣṇa, who, having recognized that animal, [approached].
Having arrived, he then touched Nṛga with his hand;
liberated from the bond of the curse, King Nṛga became divine.
Then, his body like that of a god, with palms joined in devotion,
he praised the Supreme Lord, the giver of liberation, the most excellent Kṛṣṇa.
O Blessed One, my karma is fully exhausted; nothing else remains.
I have placed my auspicious refuge in you; O Acyuta, grant me liberation. 48.
Then Kṛṣṇa said to him: "O King, by my power of yoga, go to the worlds of the merit-makers and enjoy unsurpassed pleasures. (49)
"You shall attain my abode, characterized by the absence of rebirth.
And Nṛga said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Hari, if you are pleased with me..."
"Let this pit become a merit-bestowing holy site (tīrtha) in my name;
whoever bathes here and performs the libation (tarpaṇa) for the ancestors," ||51||
By your grace, may the ancestors go to your abode;
and those who perform the pilgrimage here shall indeed be partakers of liberation.
Having said "So be it" to the king, Kṛṣṇa then departed;
the king went by means of a divine chariot to the home of those who perform sacrifices.
That which is indeed the second Vaikuṇṭha, called the station of Vairāja—
starting from that time, Nṛgakūpa became the most excellent of holy places on earth.
One should offer the *argha* oblation to Nṛga Kṛṣṇa, bathe, and drink the water;
one should gratify the ancestors, the gods, and human beings, and perform the *śrāddha* rite.
One should also give a golden sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and various kinds of gifts;
one obtains inexhaustible fruit and, in the end, indeed the supreme goal.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Nṛga’s Birth as a Chameleon Due to the Mismatch in the Gift of Cows, His Liberation Effected by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the Nṛga-kūpa Tīrtha," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thereafter, O Mahālakṣmī, one should go to the holy ford (tīrtha) originating from Viṣṇu’s foot,
where the Gaṅgā arose, she who takes refuge at Viṣṇu’s feet.
Once, Durvāsas arrived for the purpose of a pilgrimage;
hearing of this, the Blessed One, accompanied by Ramā, rose up suddenly.
The Lord went toward Durvāsas for the sake of performing the rites of hospitality;
he whose wife was not at home and who had no worthy recipient to visit [was not to be honored].
"The gods and the ancestors do not accept his water offerings"—
thinking thus, Śrī and Kṛṣṇa departed, filled with joy.
Having mounted his chariot, Śrī Kṛṣṇa went together with Rukmiṇī;
on the shore of the ocean, he bathed and, blazing with splendor, relieved his fatigue.
Having bowed with devotion, the Blessed One likewise inquired after his well-being;
the sage said: "O Kṛṣṇa, is it well with you? Where is your dwelling now?"
"How many wives and how much wealth do you have? Is all always well with you?
Kṛṣṇa replied, "By your blessings, indeed, all is well with me. (7)
By your very sight, my lineage has been especially purified;
furthermore, ten yojanas of land were granted to me by the Ocean.
On a stretch of land ten yojanas in extent, a city made of gold was caused to be built by me; there, nine hundred thousand palaces were caused to be constructed.
"By your grace, I dwell there joyfully and without fear.
Having heard that, Durvāsas said, "Tell me your number—
how many queens you have, as well as your sons and your attendants."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, there are sixteen thousand one hundred and eight wives in my home.
For each one, I have ten sons and one daughter as offspring."
"I have fifty-six kinsmen and likewise attendants;
this is my chief wife, Rukmiṇī, who is known as Ramā.
You are worthy of worship by sages; please come to my home."
"Having placed my feet upon your head, I shall thereafter attain purification.
Durvāsas said: "O Kṛṣṇa, I am always forbearing;
yet at any moment I may become enraged. Why do you lead me away, O Keśava? (14-15)
"Lead me if you will do my bidding along with your wife;
if you desire to take me, then carry both your wife and me in the chariot."
Upon hearing this, Kṛṣṇa, together with Rukmiṇī, was then filled with joy;
saying, "I am purified," he quickly became the leader of the chariot.
Then that best of sages, having united Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, stood upon the chariot, took hold of the reins, and said, "Go! Go! || 18 ||
Being honored by the gods with flowers, O Kṛṣṇa, He proceeded;
while the chariot was being drawn by those two, Rukmiṇī became thirsty.
She said to her beloved, "Give me water; thirst afflicts me now.
Hearing that, Kṛṣṇa struck the Earth with his foot-lace.
Then the earth split open, and from it the cool Gaṅgā emerged;
auspicious in form, with fragrant white waters, she shone forth. 21.
Without having asked the sage for permission, Rukmiṇī drank the water of the Gaṅgā;
seeing this, the Ṛṣi became enraged and immediately cursed the supreme lady.
"Since you drank the water without asking me, you shall therefore experience the fruit of that act:
the pain of separation from Kṛṣṇa," he said as he descended from his chariot.
Having crossed over, his eyes bloodshot with rage, he stood right upon the ground;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Ramā, praised him with humility.
"O best of sages, may your words come true in every way:
let Rukmiṇī, separated from me, take the form of water here in this forest. (25)
May she remain forever together with Gaṅgā, in the form of Gaṅgā herself,
at the place where the water, having burst through the earth, became manifest.
May that water be the eternal Rukmiṇī-rūpa-tīrtha;
may Rukmiṇī’s residence always remain right here in this grove within the temple. (27)
"And may liberation also come to the followers of other paths through the grace of Ramā.
Then, at the onset of night, Durvāsas spoke to Kṛṣṇa in the morning.
"May there be eternal union with Rukmiṇī for you; I grant you this favor.
Having spoken thus, the sage, the son of Atri, then departed from that place.
Rukmiṇī was established there in that preeminent palace-garden;
she was also established in a second form as the embodiment of water.
That sacred ford, consisting of water, is indeed remembered as the water from Viṣṇu’s feet;
in its primary form, it is always engaged in the service of Kṛṣṇa’s queen.
"May he always remain in the palace"—thus Durvāsas also bestowed his favor; having received that boon and having gone there, he obtained worship.
From this place, Kṛṣṇa went to Kailāsa itself, while Rukmiṇī went to her home; and the water from the foot of Kṛṣṇa became threefold in form.
There, in the palace situated in the garden, she exists as a second form;
and the third is the Great Queen, who is eternally united with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, that very Rukmiṇī-tīrtha, which is the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet, became the Gaṅgā herself—auspicious, bestowing liberation upon those who bathe there. (35)
It likewise bestows inexhaustible merit upon the performer of the śrāddha for his ancestors, grants them eternal satisfaction, and bestows the abode of Goloka.
Whoever performs charity, fire-offerings, recitation, meditation, worship,
or the offering of water (argha) at that place, all of that becomes the bestower of inexhaustible merit.
Where Kṛṣṇa himself, endowed with splendor, dwells forever—what indeed could be lacking there for those residing at a sacred ford compared to Goloka? (38)
Even from visiting other holy places (tīrthas), no fruit is obtained that is inferior to that of Goloka.
One should offer various kinds of food and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) of gold and silver.
Gifts should be given according to the prescribed rules to the distressed, the blind, and the miserable;
sandals should be bestowed, as well as a water-jar together with a cloth.
Curd-rice and various kinds of grains should be offered,
as well as red cloth, a skirt, a bodice, and a waist-cloth.
Ornaments and articles of adornment should be presented to Rukmiṇī;
one should worship a pair of Brahmins with the thought, "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me. (42)
When the *tīrtha* has been thus established there, the ancestors born of the three lineages go to the world of Hari, satisfied; and Lord Hari, being pleased, is accompanied by Śrī.
Having constantly enjoyed sensual pleasures here and the splendors of heaven and other realms,
those purified by the Rukmiṇī-tīrtha finally go to the abode of Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha—consisting of the water of the Gaṅgā issued from the blow of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s foot for the purpose of quenching the thirst of Rukmiṇī while she was occupied with the task of pulling Durvāsas’s chariot, and the threefold nature of Rukmiṇī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Thence one should go to the most divine Gopītaḍāga-tīrtha,
where the first meeting with the gopīs indeed took place by Kṛṣṇa.
At that place, through giving, bathing, recitation, ancestral offerings, and worship, a human being indeed attains liberation. || 2 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, residing in Dvārakā, dispatched Uddhava— the foremost among devotees—
to Gokula for the sake of the gopīs and his friends.
Seeing Uddhava arrive— skilled in doing what was pleasing to the cowherds and in speaking his own words— the inhabitants of Gokula were filled with longing.
They honored Uddhava with garments, ornaments, and food;
and when he had eaten and rested, Yaśodā, who was deeply affectionate toward her son, [honored him].
Nanda inquired after his health and asked about the welfare of Hari:
"Is Kṛṣṇa dwelling in happiness? And is Rāma prospering in well-being? (6)
Does someone remember Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the dear people here?
Will Śrī Kṛṣṇa come and deliver us from our suffering?
"O Uddhava, is the family of Kṛṣṇa also living in great happiness?
Having asked this, they both became filled with tears of affection.
Then Uddhava, with sweet messages from Kṛṣṇa drenched in affection, revived both those two and the people residing in Gokula.
Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the women of the household offer salutations to their parents;
they inquire after their well-being and remain in good health.
Kṛṣṇa will quickly come to Gokula along with Rāma;
he will provide all happiness and will accomplish what is beneficial for you.
Thus, having comforted them with these messages from Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
Uddhava slept peacefully in a secluded place to dispel his fatigue.
Then, seeing the chariot blazing like the sun, the gopīs were struck with wonder and exclaimed, "Whose is this? Who has come here? and they approached it.
Having come together, all those women of Vraja,
emaciated by grief, asked him in private for the message from Kṛṣṇa.
Is Kṛṣṇa well? Why has he not come here?
Having taken hold of our very lives, why has he gone and not returned? (15)
Remembering this, the gopīs, overwhelmed by grief and delusion, wept as they gazed upon the servant of Kṛṣṇa, being themselves captivated by love for Kṛṣṇa. (16)
Uddhava comforted them with words that brought solace,
for Kṛṣṇa too had remembered you again and again, day and night.
Afflicted by the god of love and distressed as he brooded upon you, he remained thus;
meanwhile, the gopīs became agitated and spoke many words in various ways.
Having seized us mercilessly and then abandoned us, he has gone and does not return; who could be dear to that slayer of Pūtanā? 19.
Wherever one goes, there one finds a new beloved;
for one who is surrounded by city women, we have no further need.
"What should be done? Where should we go? How will the Lord be found?
Lamenting with such words and remembering Him, they wept for Hari.
Seeing their exclusive devotion, Uddhava then said:
"The birth, life, youth, and wealth of all these women have become fruitful. (22)
"Those women who possess unwavering devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they say, 'Do not lead us there where our beloved of life resides. (23)
Knowing their resolve to be firm, Uddhava said "So be it" to them; then all of them went with Uddhava, desiring a sight of Kṛṣṇa.
Singing the songs of Kṛṣṇa, they went toward Dvārakā;
indeed, the fatigue of the journey did not touch them because their minds were united with Kṛṣṇa.
When they reached the bank of the pond dug by Maya,
Uddhava prostrated and said, "O cowherd women, please stay here."
"I shall go to inform him; Kṛṣṇa will provide what is beneficial.
Having said this, Uddhava went toward Kṛṣṇa and spoke to him.
"The cowherd girls are standing on the bank of the lake; do as you wish.
Kṛṣṇa then quickly went to the pond by means of a human vehicle.
He saw him approaching, in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa), radiant and adorned,
with a blazing crown, diadem, necklace, and crocodile-shaped earrings.
He bore the Śrīvatsa mark, possessed mighty arms, was finely clothed in yellow garments, and was accompanied by a parasol, beautiful whisks, and a golden staff.
And seeing their beloved, they embraced him from all sides—
on his hand, his back, his breast, his cheek, his neck, his head, and his face.

In the mouth, the eyes, the chin, the shoulders, the chest, the thighs, the sides, the hips, the shanks, the feet, the front [of the body], the lower garment, the upper garment, and likewise in the belly; || 32 ||
Having touched and embraced Kṛṣṇa again and again, they, overwhelmed with love, kissed their beloved;
and having gazed upon their beloved for a long time, they fainted and wept profusely. || 33 ||
"Alas, O Lord! O Beloved! O Master! O Enchanting Lord of Vraja!
We have all been abandoned by you; why are you angry with us, O one whose heart is now arid? (34)
O Janārdana, O Kṛṣṇa, you who abandon father and mother and abandon those who are devoted— having been forsaken by us, we have not been looked upon by you again.
How can your separation be endured, and how shall we pass these days, O Remover of Suffering, deprived of our Lord? Do as you wish.
The Blessed One, who knows the inner state of beings, having heard them, instructed them:
"Indeed, there is never any separation from you for me. (37)
"I am the inner self of all, especially yours; know that my yoga is always present with you in the form of a husband. (38)
Desire is happiness, eternal bliss; from me everything proceeds.
Knowing this, O great virtuous ladies, do not grieve in vain. (3.9)
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa and embracing him again and again, they,
being exceedingly comforted, abandoned the torment born of their long separation.
"Today our birth has become fruitful; today our eyes have become fruitful, for we behold you, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa! Thus they spoke repeatedly. (41)
Kṛṣṇa said to them all, "I shall have a pond constructed here;
it will certainly become famous by the name Gopī-taḍāga."
"Since the vision of me has occurred here, I have fulfilled their desires;
let the gopīs now indeed perform their bath together with me. (43)
Having done this, Hari then bathed together with the gopīs;
there, the gopīs were fed with sweet foods, cakes, and other delicacies.
Having thus sported in the water, Kṛṣṇa would always return to his palace;
Hari, the bestower of happiness, delighted them all with love.
Having bathed in the lake on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, he shall offer libations to the ancestors; for them, there will be eternal satisfaction.
Likewise, he who gives a gift while intending me and keeping the ancestors in mind, attains the eternal realm of Viṣṇu together with his ancestors. ||47||
The *argha* offering should be given, and likewise the *śrāddha* rite should be performed; sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should be bestowed.
Auspicious milk-rice (*pāyasa*), ghee, and sugar should be served as food. 48.
Garments, an umbrella, a woolen blanket, a sārī, a bodice, and a water-pot—these should be given as gifts here at the pond, O ladies, while remembering me. (49)
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain, they shall enjoy many pleasures here, and at the end, attain the imperishable state.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Holy Site through the Meeting of the Gopīs of Gokula with Kṛṣṇa at the Gopī-taḍāka," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the vicinity of Lake Māyā, he created another lake;
that great holy site (tīrtha), O Lotus-born one, is indeed known as Gopī-saras.
It was frequented by the women of the Yadu clan as well as by the Yadu youths;
and for the sake of the cowherd girls, Kṛṣṇa caused this auspicious place to be constructed.
"O Gopīs, you must address me with the word 'Gopracāra' (Cow-pasturer) as my name,
and first of all, as 'Gopīśvara' (Lord of the Gopīs)."
It shall become famous in the world as Gopītaḍāga;
having offered the arghya according to the prescribed rite, the wise man should perform his bath.
One should give a cow along with its calf, adorned with garments and ornaments,
accompanied by the prescribed sacrificial fee, to a Brahmin who maintains a family.
In this regard, the fruit of the gift of the earth is indeed obtained through the gift of a cow;
moreover, by merely bathing, a person truly obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
As many steps as a person takes toward the Gopikā lake,
for that many generations their family rejoices in heaven and in the abode of Hari.
Those who go to the lake as singers of Kṛṣṇa’s glories shall have no further dwelling here within a mother’s womb.
That person who performs the pilgrimage at the Gopīsarastīra-tīrtha attains all desires and shall reach the world of Viṣṇu.
One should perform the śrāddha ceremony and especially offer libations to the ancestors;
furthermore, one should give betel leaf, collyrium, gold, and clothing as gifts.
One should give garments, ornaments, and wealth to the couple;
and to the maidens, one should provide food, clothing, ornaments, wealth, and so forth. (11)
By that, the Gopīs shall always be pleased, bestowing prosperity and good fortune;
and cows, bulls, elephants, horses, and maidens should be given as gifts. (12)
Whatever the world desires, he shall grant that, and it shall meet with fulfillment again;
indeed, this lake shall remain as long as the worlds exist.
And the cowherd women, dwelling in the city of Dvārakā, meditated upon the supreme Kṛṣṇa with the feeling of him being their husband or else with the feeling of him being Brahman.
Constantly serving him, they then became truly fulfilled;
having offered salutations at Kṛṣṇa’s command and having served Kṛṣṇa with contentment. || 15 ||
Accompanied by Uddhava, she went to Gokula, her own auspicious home;
there Kṛṣṇa established that most excellent tīrtha on earth for the sake of the gopīs.
The dust from the bodies of the gopīs was divine, as were the divine pollen and the tawny [honey];
likewise, the water was divine, as were the divine trees and creepers situated upon the banks.
The divine abodes of that [Goloka], including the sentient beings such as cattle and birds, are indeed celestial;
for they are truly the presiding authorities of the realm of Goloka.

A person whose limbs are smeared with gopīcandana, who bears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) made from the dust of the gopīs, and whose mouth contains particles of the gopī-clay, becomes liberated. || 19 ||
O Lotus-born One, upon seeing anyone whose forehead is marked with a dot of gopīcandana, even the messengers of Yama flee far away.
The gods always behold the Vaiṣṇava tilaka made of gopīcandana; by its constant presence in the morning, all sins go to dissolution.
