then the great, divine attendants of Hari arrived.
And they said: "O King of Tīrthas, this auspicious Mahārājñī Dvārakā is indeed worthy of being served; therefore, may you all remain here always according to your own will. (88)
Then, having circumambulated Dvārakā and prostrated before it, the deities of the sacred fields and holy fords took up residence there. (89)
O beloved, fifty crores of holy places (tīrthas) are situated to the north,
while rivers with sixty crores of holy places are located in the eastern direction.
In the southern direction, sacred fords, mountains, forests, and lakes are situated together with their own retinues numbering nine hundred and ninety million. ||9.1||
The seven oceans and others are situated in the western direction;
and in all the intermediate directions, there is no counting of the sacred fords (tīrthas). ||92||
A hundred crore of sacred fords dwell at the confluence of the ocean;
Vārāṇasī is in the northeast, while Avantī is situated in the eastern direction. 93.
In the southeast is Kuṃkumavāpī, while Kāñcī is in the south;
Māyā is situated in the southwest, and Ayodhyā is located in the west. (94)
In the northwest is Kurukṣetra, and likewise Harikṣetra in the north;
thus the first enclosure is protected by sacred fords, fields, and other such sites. (95)

The second was [attended] by the lords of creatures (prajeśvara), the third by the leaders of the gods (devanāyaka), the fourth by the multitudes of sages and perfected beings (ṛṣisiddhaugha), and the fifth by the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
The sixth [obscuration] is by means of the Tīrthas, and the seventh by Kāśī and other such places;
the eighth is by the chief sacred fields (kṣetra) and so forth, and the ninth by the hermitages (āśrama) and so forth. ||97||
Those with divine vision indeed behold those ten [sacred sites] beginning with Meru;
thus say the divine attendants and other purifying holy places. 98.
They took up residence with their own second forms;
having received leave from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of the Gomatī, they departed.
Having performed their ablutions at the holy ford, all the attendants of the deities of the sacred sites departed;
they return every year when Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Mass Gathering and Residence at the Dvārakā Tīrtha by All the Tīrthas, Devas, and Pārṣadas, along with the Godāvarī, while Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo," within the *Dvārakā-māhātmya* of the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Mahālakṣmī, especially when Jupiter is situated in the zodiac sign of Leo,
the heaps of sins of those who visit the holy places of Dvārakā are consumed by fire.
Those men who make a pilgrimage to Dvārakā every year attain liberation by touching the dust of their feet.
I shall first relate that which was asked of Vasiṣṭha by Dilīpa:
"The sin committed in another's field perishes through the service of sacred fords (tīrthas). (3)
It is said that the sins committed at sacred fords and fields possess the nature of an adamantine coating;
since such sin is like an adamantine coating, there is no liberation from it anywhere, or is there?
"O Sage, tell me of that field where the growth of sin does not occur.
Having heard this, Vasiṣṭha, possessing divine vision, spoke to the king: || 5 ||
A certain ascetic named Māyānanda, a triple-staffed mendicant residing in Kāśī,
was indeed infatuated with a beautiful young woman of the Matanga caste.
Drawn by a kingly disposition and intoxicated by liquor and meat,
he, his mind deluded, indulged in such food out of pride for sensual desires.
Bearing the status of a Cāṇḍāla, he committed theft at night out of greed;
his sins increased through his constant association with a Mātaṅga woman.
In Kāśī, by the power of time, he died and became a wild wolf;
thereafter, he became a tiger, a monkey, a dog, a jackal, and a boar.
That sin, which had not perished even after thousands of births, was then destroyed upon a saline wasteland;
by the power of Kāśikā, he became a Rākṣasa in a solitary place who remembered his former births.
Wandering through forests and mountains, the Rākṣasa reached the Vindhya mountain;
there, his liberation from that sinful birth occurred as a matter of wonder.
Having performed the great pilgrimage at Dvārāvatī and beheld Kṛṣṇa,
he bathed in the waters of the Gomatī and drank the nectar-like water of Kṛṣṇa.
A certain Brahmin residing in Gayā, while traveling home,
stopped for a moment on the road at a sturdy tree-stump on the Vindhya mountain in order to rest.
There the Rākṣasa beheld that Brahmin, who bore a vertical tilaka, was a devotee wearing a garland of tulasī, and was purified by the waters of the Gomatī.
By the mere sight of him, the mass of his sins, which was as hard as adamant and destined to yield future suffering, was reduced to ashes in an instant.
By the manifestation of his merit, he recognized Kṛṣṇa as a traveler;
then, approaching him face-to-face, he saw Kṛṣṇa, the traveler from Dvārakā.
Having bowed to him and praised him, he said: "By the sight of you today, the mass of my sins, as firm as adamant, has been burnt; I am liberated in every way."
Then the traveler went to his own home, and the Rākṣasa,
having realized the great power of the sacred ford, arrived at Dvārakā.
Having cast off his own body in the Gomatī, he attained the station of Viṣṇu;
indeed, sins do not sprout again from her, by the mere sight of one who is intent on her pilgrimage.
What fruit, indeed, can be described when one is directly in union with Dvārāvatī?
It is the great burner of sins, even those as stubborn as adamantine cement. ||1.232.20||
The supreme field born of Goloka, the foremost among all fields, is indeed the field of Dvārakā, established on earth by Kṛṣṇa. (21)
Having heard this, Dilīpa also went to Dvārakā for the sake of visiting the sacred sites;
and having seen Kṛṣṇa and the Gomatī river, he attained supreme perfection.
In Dvārakā, both men and women remained four-armed.
They indeed reside in Goloka, and the dwellers of heaven behold them. ||23||
Even insects, moths, and the like, as well as insentient stationary beings, having reached their residence in Dvārakā, become divine forms of Goloka. ||24||
For those residing in Dvāravatī, the goal [of liberation] is difficult to attain even for those of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas).
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, recited as prayer, given as charity, performed as ritual bathing, or practiced as austerity in Dvārakā [becomes infinitely fruitful]. 25.
O Lakṣmī, everything in the presence of Kṛṣṇa is indeed infinitely multiplied by ten millionfold;
all men and women residing in Dvārakā possess four arms.
In Dvārakā, indeed, no sin takes root due to the power of Hari;
even the most meritorious dust of that city brings liberation to the wicked. (27)
Beginning from Kuśāvarta and extending as far as the ocean, the Gomatī flows there when Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo. (28)
A bath [at these places] shall yield fruit greater than sixty-two baths in the Godāvarī;
likewise for Dvārakā, the Gomatī, the Gopī-saras, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself. (29)
But those who remember [it] every day, even if they reside a thousand yojanas away,
are also partakers of the full fruit of the Dvārāvatī-tīrtha.

One who betrays a friend, a killer of a brother, a slayer of a cow, one who is devoted to another's wife, a killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of an embryo, a killer of a Brahmin, and one who violates the bed of his teacher; |||3 1||
They are liberated from all sins by the sight of Kṛṣṇa at Dvārakā, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, on the Jayantī, and on the day of Viṣṇu. ||32||
Especially during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra,
as well as on the full moon, the new moon, the eleventh day (ekādaśī), and at the confluence of rivers.
On the twelfth lunar day, at the beginning of each fortnight, as well as under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa,
Puṣya, and Punarvasu, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and on the day of the sun's turning point (dinakṣaya).
Beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa at Dvārāvatī on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, bestows infinite merit. (35)
In that [city], there were sacrificial sessions, water-stations, palatial mansions, temples, monasteries,
as well as dwellings for ascetics and holy men, halls for virtuous women, and shrines.

He should construct ponds, wells, and tanks, restore dilapidated works for the livelihood of others, perform the consecration of an image of Viṣṇu, and likewise provide royal enjoyments and other such comforts.
Having caused [this] to be made and having enjoyed the pleasures existing in heaven, a man or a woman shall attain the enjoyments of Vairāja and Vaikuṇṭha, reaching equality with Kṛṣṇa. ||38||
Whoever installs an image made of wood or stone in Dvāravatī shall attain universal sovereignty and reach equality with Śrī Viṣṇu himself. (39)
Those who have gone to the Dvārakā tīrtha rescue one hundred and one generations of their lineage,
as well as seven generations of their kin, through the power of Kṛṣṇa.
For every single step taken toward the city of Dvārāvatī, embodied beings in the Kali age obtain the merit of thousands of sacrifices. ||41||
Even a stone marked with the discus-sign, by whomsoever seen, brings about liberation;
so too do Sudarśana and the single-discus [form], as well as both Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
With three [qualities] he is Acyuta, and with four he is Indra, Janārdana;
with five he is Vāsudeva, and with six he is indeed Pradyumna.
He is Baladeva with seven [senses], Puruṣottama with eight;
he is the Soul of All with nine wheels, and the Lord of Ten with ten wheels. ||44||
With eleven [forms] he is Mahāviṣṇu, but with twelve he is the Self who bestows liberation;
beyond that, he is Ananta, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||45||
Those who perform the rite of releasing a bull on the full moon day of Vaiśākha or Kārtika—having abandoned their state as piśācas in Dvārakā, their ancestors were liberated. (46)
Thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of family lineages dwell in that state of Viṣṇu by virtue of beholding Kṛṣṇa on the Trispṛśā day.
Whether established in good deeds or established in forbidden acts, they go to the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
what indeed is the use of bathing in the sixty-seven holy places, O my beloved? (48)
If, having obtained a human body, one does not go to Dvārakā, the divine people residing in Dvārakā grieve for that person as one whose birth was in vain. 49.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you in every way the majesty of my sacred field;
by hearing which, liberation is considered to be held within one's grasp.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Visiting Dvārakā, Which Is Like Indestructible Cement in Destroying Sin, for Māyānandayati Residing in Kāśī," within the section on the Greatness of Dvārakā, in the first part concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī Kamalā!
From hearing the description of the earth of Dvārakā, great joy arises within me.
O Lord, today you, the compassionate one, have fulfilled my purpose;
now, tell me the greatness and the true nature of the Trispṛśā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe to you the greatness of Trispṛśā, for there is no other vow equal to it in bestowing both fruit and liberation.
Having heard of that fruit by which one is released from the bondage of karma, one attains liberation through the instruction of the vow; because of the vow, Mādhava rejoices.
Therefore, I shall declare to you that which fulfills all intentions—
that very vow by which Kṛṣṇa was indeed worshipped before his eyes.
The one who proclaims the name of Trispṛśā partakes in the merit of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
[that merit] cannot be attained through the Vedas, nor through ancient legends, nor through sacrifices, nor by multitudes of holy pilgrimage sites.
O Lotus-born One, even if one has worshipped other deities and performed countless hardships, liberation will not be attained if the Trispṛśā has not been observed.
Being thus questioned by Brahmā,
I then spoke this great path for the sake of crossing over the multitude of people afflicted by the objects of the senses.
It is said that the Trispṛśā vow alone is the path that grants liberation; there is no other way.
For those whose senses are like intoxicated horses, stability cannot be achieved without austerity.
"For I have declared that Ekādaśī is attained through the triple touch of austerity; yet those who are immersed in the forest of sense-objects will perform the vow [only nominally]. (1.233.10)
Then, for those who observe the Trispṛśā vow, there shall be eternal liberation;
this bestower of liberation should be performed by the most excellent among the virtuous.
When that [tithi] occurs by conjunction during the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
it bestows the merit of ten thousand Soma sacrifices and grants liberation in the hereafter;
it is the mighty destroyer of the great sin of ten million killings.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are [cleansed] by resorting to the Trispṛśā vow.
They go to immediate dissolution; what need is there to mention other sins?
This does not happen at Prayāga, nor at Puṣkara, nor at Badarī, nor in the region of Kāśī.
Neither at the Gomatī nor at the Revā, nor at Raivata nor at Indradyumna; neither at Kuṅkumavāpī nor at Kedāra, nor at Rāmeśvara nor at Mathurā. (15)
O Mahālakṣmī, liberation will occur even if the Trispṛśā [vow] has not been performed, provided one abandons life at Prayāga, Kāśī, or likewise at Kuśapura. || 16 ||
The eternal liberation that is considered to result from bathing in the Gomatī river arises at home through fasting on the Trispṛśā day. || 17 ||
It is said to grant liberation especially to women and Śūdras who lack knowledge;
it always bestows higher realization, is meritorious, purifying, and grants the supreme goal.
She is the mother of all that is auspicious, the immediate bestower of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
she is the very life-force for those devoted to Viṣṇu, and especially for women. (19)
She is the purifier and the meritorious mother of all, like the Mother of the Vedas;
she is as purifying as Lakṣmī and a protector equal to Rati.

Bestowing the fruits of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as superior fruits and all-encompassing results, she is joined by hundreds of millions of sacred fords; [one should go] to the Jāhnavī with the desire to bathe.
He goes to the Gomatī to be in the presence of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of purification;
thousands of millions of holy places reside on the banks of the Gomatī.
She too performs the Trispṛśā vow for the purification of her sins—[sins such as] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the slaughter of a cow, or the murder of a woman. (23)
Seizing the property of a Brahmin or a deity, beating one's mother or father, treachery toward a guru, enmity toward a preceptor, and the eating of forbidden food; 24.
Indeed, approaching those who should not be approached, violence, and constant reviling of the virtuous, as well as other cruel deeds and whatever other sins there may be—[these he performed]. (25)
That most purifying Trispṛśā indeed dispels misfortune;
it is superior even to Sarasvatī and is highly honored by hundreds of millions of sacred fords.

She who excels ten million sacrifices, who excels in the merit of fire-offerings and gifts, who is more meritorious than ten million recitations, and likewise who excels in the goals of human endeavor; |||27|||
Excelling both Sāṃkhya and Yoga and honored as the pinnacle of self-knowledge, the Trispṛśā vow should indeed be performed; it bestows liberation.
When the Ekādaśī is conjoined with the Sun, followed by Dvādaśī,
and Trayodaśī remains at the end of the night, that is indeed the Trispṛśā Ekādaśī.
If the tenth lunar day persists at the time of dawn, prior to sunrise,
that is called *daśamī-vedha*.
O my beloved, I cannot tolerate the defect arising from the piercing of the tenth lunar day.
Indeed, that [Ekādaśī] which is joined with the overlapping of the tenth day (daśamī-vedha) should never be observed at all.
Just as a husband is defiled by the fault of his wife being in her menses, even so, the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) pierced by the tenth day (Daśamī) bestows defilement. //32//
When the tenth, eleventh, and auspicious (twelfth) lunar days occur on a single day, that is also called Trispṛśā; it belongs to the Asuras and must be avoided with great effort.
He by whom the Ekādaśī vow is observed mixed with the tenth day has consumed the Hālāhala poison; he has committed sin, and that vow is not truly performed.
The merit accumulated over ten million births is exhausted within one's own continuum;
his family falls from heaven, and he himself goes indeed to the Raurava hell. (35)
Therefore, that day of mine joined with the tenth [lunar day] must indeed be avoided;
when there is an increase [of the lunar day], one that is pierced should be abandoned, and that joined with the twelfth should be observed. (36)

The Creator has ordained that for one who observes the vow on the tenth day when it is pierced by the eleventh (Mohinī), a great sin is incurred; therefore, this must be understood as a grave transgression.
Likewise, whether there is an increase or a decrease [in lunar days], or when a doubt has arisen, my beloved Dvādaśī must always be observed by my command. (38)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the true procedure for the Trispṛśā vow;
[it may be made] with a pala, or half a pala, or even half of that, O Padmaja. (39)
A golden image of me should be fashioned according to my wealth;
there should be a copper vessel filled with sesame seeds, and a jar provided with jewels, water, and other offerings.
Likewise, provided with leaves, flowers, white cloth, camphor, and other such items,
[the deity] should be installed upon a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala made of grain.
O my beloved, that golden image should be placed in a jar or a vessel;
Lakṣmī should be placed at my side, and then one should perform the worship. ||42||
One should offer the invocation, the seat, water for the feet, and the respectful offering;
then one should offer water for sipping and a bath with water.
One should perform a bath with milk, a bath with curd, and thereafter a bath with ghee;
then one should offer a bath with sugar and a bath with honey.
One should perform the consecration with sacred waters and wipe [the image] with cloths;
likewise, one should provide it with a washed garment, a fine cloth, a protective bodice, and a tunic.
One should likewise offer an upper garment, a lower cloth, and a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), as well as an auspicious thread, a kaustubha gem, and a garland. 46.
She should attend to her hair, apply oil, flowers, and the like,
arrange her braid, and likewise scent and tie her topknot.
One should apply collyrium to the eyes and a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) with a crescent moon on the forehead;
one should worship with sandalwood paste mixed with musk and enriched with camphor. 48.
One should place the *nāsānatthī* on the chin, the *ṭibakī* on the cheeks,
the *kuṇḍale* on the ears, and likewise the *airana* and *śṛṅkhalā* as ear-ornaments.
One should apply vermilion and saffron as a coloring agent for the lips;
one should offer garlands of Tulasī and beautiful clusters of flowers.
One should give necklaces of gold, gems, and pearls, as well as chains, bracelets, rings, girdles, and beautiful anklets enriched with small bells.
One should offer sandals, socks, and staffs with their tassels intact;
likewise, one should present a crown, floral crests, and ear-ornaments.
I shall offer a fan and sandals, well-adorned and worthy of a king, as well as garlands of *tulasī*, to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (53)
A person should offer red powder, blood from a hero, unbroken grains, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings to Śrī Viṣṇu. (54)
One should indeed offer pleasing food offerings, many kinds of sweet delicacies, very sweet fruits, and cool water. (55)
One should offer fragrant, desirable drinking water that bestows peace;
one should give betel-leaf enriched with many ingredients for the purification of the mouth. (56)
And one should indeed offer a golden ring as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Keśava;
whatever else is required there for the worship, that too one should present.
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite with nine wicks illuminated by five lamps;
thereafter, one should repeatedly wipe the image with a white cloth three times. (58)
Then, one should perform the "whirling of the conch" over the tip of the face;
thereafter, with a sincere disposition, one should pour water from the head down onto the wet garment.
One should offer praise like a staff, circumambulating again and again;
one should perform many prostrations and likewise offer a request for forgiveness.
Having scattered a handful of flowers, one should pray to the Supreme Lord;
closing the eyes, one should meditate upon His form while standing before Him. (6.1)
One should worship the feet for Dāmodara and the knees for Mādhava;
the private parts for Kāmasvarūpa and the waist for Vāmanamūrti.
One should worship the navel with "Salutation to Padmanābha," the belly to "the Cause of the Universe," the heart to "the Embodiment of Knowledge," and the throat to "the Dweller in Vaikuṇṭha."
To the thousand-armed one, [I offer] the arms; to the one whose form is yoga, the eyes;
to the thousand-headed one, the head; and likewise to the Lord, the entire body. (64)
I meditate indeed upon your form both in its manifold aspects and as a whole within my heart;
O Great King, you who are attainable through meditation, you swiftly destroy my sin. (65)
When remembered, you take away sins, bad dreams, and evil thoughts; you remove ill omens, fear of Yama, and the suffering born of miserable rebirths.
And furthermore, protect me from whatever may arise— whether pertaining to the body, this world, or the next— and from every offense that brings about suffering.
O Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, may there always be devotion unto You;
grant me service at Your feet and lead me indeed to Vaikuṇṭha. (68)
For me, at the Trispṛśā festival, Dhātṛ himself, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord,
and you alone— Hari, Mādhava— shall grant me liberation.
Having thus offered praise, one should then perform a dance accompanied by song and instrumental music— melodious and beautiful to behold— in the presence of the God.
Thus, having worshipped the Lord Kṛṣṇa in the morning according to the prescribed rite, [one should worship] the golden image which is the form of Ekādaśī and the form of Lakṣmī.
Then, having offered salutations, one should proceed to the assembly of the virtuous for discourse;
likewise, by means of chanting, devotion, worship, and recitation. (72)
One should spend the day entirely through hearing, remembering, serving, worshipping, or by means of perfect salutation.

Whether capable or incapable, one should perform the vow—whether abstaining from food entirely, subsisting on water, eating only at night, or eating but once a day—which bestows the fruit of the fulfillment of one's own desired goals. (74)
At the time of midday, one should offer betel-leaf, food, and fruit;
likewise, one should provide water, as well as a bed with a frame, a pillow, and a bolster.
In the evening, one should again offer water and perform the ārātrika ceremony according to the prescribed rules;
one should also perform worship with devotion using the varieties of the sixteen articles.
Having thus honored the Guru, one should keep vigil during the night,
accompanied by singing, dancing, ritual performance, and hymn-singing.
Then, at the end of the night, having offered arghya to Hari according to the prescribed rite and performed the rituals such as bathing, one should feed virtuous Brahmins with excellent food.
One should feed virtuous women and children, and bestow gifts and sacrificial fees;
and thus, either on the portion of the twelfth day or on the thirteenth day.
For the sake of breaking the fast, one should indeed eat with devotion,
having prepared the Sarvatobhadra mandala, as well as the water-pot and the image of Hari.
One should perform the dismissal according to the prescribed rite and shall attain the fruit of liberation;
by hearing this narration of the Trispṛśā vow, one obtains its fruit. ||81||
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices are truly performed by him who has observed the Trispṛśā fast.
One who performs the Trispṛśā vow certainly saves one hundred and eight generations of their family, including their mothers, fathers, and maternal uncles, in every way.
Endowed with all these merits, the observer of the Trispṛśā vow is honored in the world of Viṣṇu and partakes in the fruit of ten million sacred fords and ten million holy sites.
Men and women of all castes attain liberation by observing that vow;
it was first established by Brahmā and later established by the great seers.
This [rite] should always be performed by devotees, both those with desires and those free from desire;
it yields that same fruit which would be obtained by bathing in the Gaṅgā for ten million years. (86)
The true merit of one who observes the Trispṛśā vow shall be even greater than that;
it is equal to the fruit obtained at Kurukṣetra during ten million solar eclipses.
Whatever merit is gained there by the daily gift of hundreds of loads of gold, that same merit born of the gift of ten million cows accrues to one who observes the Trispṛśā vow. (88)
Thousands of millions of sins and hundreds of millions of killings are destroyed by the fast of the Ekādaśī, specifically when it is a Trispṛśā.
Whoever proclaims this vow shall also obtain its fruit;
for the Trispṛśā, which is difficult to find in the world, is not easily attained by human beings.
Even those ancestors who, having performed unknown deeds, have fallen into the state of hungry ghosts (pretas)—
a person born of noble family, by performing the *trispṛśā* rite, shall deliver them from their downward descent.
What need is there to say more in this regard? The Trispṛśā bestows liberation;
it grants prosperity in this world and indeed bestows final emancipation in the next. 92.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruits, Worship, and Other Rites of the Trispṛśā Ekādaśī Vow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the narrative concerning the origin of Ekādaśī,
which arose in the former Kṛta Yuga and was brought forth by Nārāyaṇa.
In that Satya Yuga, there was born in the Tālajaṅgha lineage a great,
most wonderful, and exceedingly fierce Asura named Nāḍījaṅgha.
He had two sons; the elder was Murajaṅgha, who struck terror into the gods.
Having performed austerities for a thousand years, he attained supreme strength.
Even Indra was conquered by him, and all the gods were defeated;
the gods were expelled from heaven and wandered upon the surface of the earth.
Terrified and deprived of their composure, they went where Purandara was;
Purandara, too, filled with grief, went where Janārdana was.
Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and other lords of the gods likewise went and praised the illustrious Nārāyaṇa as he lay within the waters.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge,
the crusher of the Dānavas, Daityas, and Asuras.
You are always the refuge for the afflicted and the destroyer of suffering for those seeking shelter;
O ocean of compassion, protect us from the Daitya who has increased his strength.
You are the refuge, you are the supreme bliss, and the ultimate resort for devotees;
you are the mother, the protector, and the master; you are the father, the guardian, and the Lord.
You are indeed the cause that is rightly expressed as origin and creation;
you alone are the fulfiller therein, and you alone are Hara, the possessor of form.
You alone are the deity who effects dissolution and the provider of food;
you are Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra; you are Agni and you are Om.
Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa are indeed you alone;
you alone are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, as well as millions of gods.
You alone are the sun and the moon; you are space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
From you proceeds the intermediate creation as well; you alone are Puruṣottama.
You are the giver of boons, the protector, and the one who withdraws those boons;
everything, both the stationary and the moving, is indeed established in you. 14.
Whenever the preeminent gods are defeated by Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas and become miserable, they then go to you for refuge.
"We have all fallen from heaven and are oppressed by the Dānavas and others;
we wander through the forest regions, O Lord, desiring protection. (16)
"O Lord, protect us in every way from the Dānava named Mura.
Hearing this, Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, questioned them.
"What kind of Dānava is he? What is his name, what is his strength, and what is his condition?
O lords of the gods, tell me everything, so that having heard it, I may contemplate his destruction. (18)
Then Indra spoke to the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa:
"He is born in the lineage of Brahmā; he has become a Danuja from Kaśyapa. (19)
Tālajaṅgha was exceedingly cruel; his son was Nāḍīprajaṅghaka, who was a great sinner, and he had a son as well.
Known by the name Murajaṅgha, he performed a severe penance for a thousand years, during which time he remained without food.
Standing on the big toe of his foot, he performed penance for a hundred years;
lying in water for a hundred years, he practiced formidable austerity;
subsisting on air for a hundred years, and gazing at the sun for a hundred years.
Having performed most terrible austerities for a hundred years while subsisting on tears, [he attained his goal].
Having practiced ascetic penance for five hundred years in meditative absorption,
an anthill covered with glass shards grew over his body there.
Enveloped by trees and creepers, he indeed became like a mountain peak;
then a most terrible smoke issued forth and ascended to heaven.
From his head arose a great fire by which the sky then blazed, as did the earth and the worlds beginning with Satyaloka; and the gods and human beings trembled in fear.
They all went for refuge to Brahmā, the Great-Grandfather;
they told him of their failure to protect their own kin and of the ocean of misery.
"Who is this fire? How has it arisen? Alas, it consumes everything! Protect, protect us, O Lord of Creatures; bring peace, O Master of the World! (28)
Having heard those words, Brahmā, together with the gods, set out to search for him;
following the trail of smoke from the fire, he went to the base where he was situated on the earth.
Seeing the trees and other things there, the Creator of the world then became bewildered:
"Alas! Not a single ascetic person is to be seen here at all."
"How and why must he be sought by me here?"—
having thus reflected, Brahmā indeed sat down upon the surface of the earth.
Then Viṣṇu indeed repeatedly sounded the great conch shell;
yet even so, O gods, Mura did not awaken there at that time.
All remained there with their hopes destroyed and their inner desires withered;
then Viṣṇu established himself there in meditative absorption and self-restraint.
And he entered there into the body of the demon Mura,
which was like dry wood— a mere mass of dried-out channels, flesh, and bones.
Having made his body both with flesh and with action, the Unborn One caused it to overflow;
when he then sprinkled it again on the head with water from his water-pot, [the body was restored].
Then, when the body of the demon Muradānava had reached the state of sprouting leaves, his eyes were opened; having seen the gods, that demon [arose]. (36)
Having bowed, he said: "How have you come with the desire to destroy my penance?
Go far away; I have no business at all with the gods. (37)
Then Brahmā said to the Daitya: "We have been pleased by your asceticism and have arrived to grant you a boon; speak, O son, according to your desire. (38)
Mura said: "Death shall not come to me by any means through your creation, nor even through Viṣṇu or Hara; therefore, grant this to me. (39)
Having granted the boon, saying "So be it," Brahmā and the others then departed;
Mura also, rising up delighted, went to his own abode.
He protected according to the law his beautiful ancestral capital, Candrāvatī, which was inhabited by Dānavas.
The gods were conquered by him and expelled from heaven;
having seized Indra’s station, the Dānava was made the new Indra.
Having established his own place of fire, another fire was created outside;
and two others, the sun and the moon, were fashioned along with the planets and constellations.
Other Dānavas born of his own lineage were made the guardians of the directions;
indeed, having conquered the gods, Mura appointed others as the world-protectors.
The hosts of gods were cast into prison and bound in fetters;
another world of the gods was created and adorned by the Dānavas. (46)
But everything else he has previously done has indeed been overturned; O Lord, abandon him before he arrives for the sake of Lakṣmī. 46.
The longer the Lord delays, the greater the loss at every moment;
therefore, rising quickly, set your mind upon his destruction. (47)
Having heard these words of Indra, Hari himself, whose vehicle is the serpent Śeṣa,
arose and resolved to destroy Mura.
Hari, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, as well as the gods and great sages, went to that city of Candrāvatī where the great Asura was located. (49)
Then Hari, standing outside near the vicinity, blew his conch;
hearing that sound which signaled the commencement of battle, he came out from the city.
Accompanied by his army, the hero Mura, assuming many forms, waged a fierce battle for the sake of giving in combat with millions of missiles and weapons.
By means of mantras, the powers of illusion, sorcery, and millions of forms,
he waged a terrible battle that caused the destruction of the gods.
The gods, whose very nature consists of forms, were wounded, slain, and destroyed;
they were broken, fainted, perished, and among the brahmins, they were deprived of consciousness. ||53||
Being struck by hundreds of thousands of countless weapons by those preeminent asuras,
all the gods fled in the ten directions.
Seeing Viṣṇu, Mura said to him, "Stay! Stay!
Mukunda hurled a heavy mace, but Mura shattered it.
With his own mace, he swiftly hurled the formidable discus;
by the power of the boon, the discus was shattered against Mura.
Viṣṇu, overcome with wonder and his eyes bloodshot with rage,
took up a second discus and hurled it at the millions of soldiers.
The foremost of the Dānavas and Daityas had their heads severed;
some fell down dead, while others fainted and became lifeless.
There, having attained its true meaning through the distinctions of Daityas and others, that battlefield became the earth itself—the slumbering forest of the Dānavas. (99)
Indeed, nowhere was the surface left empty without a headless trunk;
then Muru fell into great distress due to the destruction of his army.
Then, wandering alone, he fought with weapons against Viṣṇu;
by that enemy, the foremost of Viṣṇu’s weapons were destroyed.
Then all the divine weapons were again seized;
at that time, Viṣṇu became deprived of his missiles and weapons.
The hosts of Daityas rejoiced, and the great Dānavas exulted; the gods indeed fell into despondency, and the Asuras were filled with hope for their survival.
Then, realizing that Viṣṇu was indeed unarmed, Mura engaged in a fierce hand-to-hand combat with Viṣṇu through his strategic skill.
By means of his illusory power, the demon Mura assailed the arm of Viṣṇu;
he bound the arm, and indeed, the [other] arms became paralyzed.
The four gods who were there also became distressed; crying out piteously, "Alas! Alas!", they were terrified and their hopes were shattered.
At that time, Muru was completely victorious in the slaughter of the gods;
having conquered those born in Satyaloka, he ruled a splendid kingdom. ||67||
Then Muru became the sovereign of the fourteen worlds;
terrified, Viṣṇu went to Badarikāśrama on the snowy mountain.
In the Himalayas, there exists a very great cave named Siṃhavatī, measuring four yojanas in length and breadth. (69)
Having gone to that city which had but a single gate, the Great Lord,
desiring the welfare of the worlds, showed fear to those who were asleep.
While searching for Dānavatsa there in that cave,
he eventually discovered Viṣṇu fast asleep and entered the interior of the cavern.
Seeing Śrī Hari asleep, the lord of the Dānavas said to him:
"Aho! O you who are worshipped by the three worlds, why do you take refuge in this cave? (72)
"Do you not provide protection for those who have taken refuge in you during times of distress?
Arise, O Viṣṇu, may it be well with you; arise and engage in battle! (73)
Is the sleeping of jackals like you natural?
Either I shall send you to the abode of Yama, or else you must take refuge with me. (74)
Always perform service for me, or grant me Vaikuṇṭha itself;
or else, O Viṣṇu, engage in battle—do not practice deceit at this time.
While Muru was speaking thus, Hari, while he was still asleep, reflected within himself for the sake of his destruction.
He indeed called upon Mahālakṣmī for the sake of the destroyer of the Dānavas,
remembering the boon granted by Brahmā to the ancestor of Mura.

And thinking, "May there be no destruction caused by the piercing [of the vital points] during creation," he [bestowed] power consisting of a portion of Lakṣmī, which is composed of his own eleven senses. (78)
Hari indeed manifested that divine nature of austerity;
and it became embodied there in the form of a most beautiful maiden.
The maiden was radiant with excessive splendors, resembling gold,
and cooled by a mass of light pervaded by the brilliance of the moon.
Possessing a form perfectly suited to every aspect, she was exceedingly beautiful in the likeness of Hari;
she was equipped with divine weapons, and her two breasts were newly emerged and lovely. (8.1)

She was somewhat overcome by a form beyond that of the bodiless god of love; her sight was enchanting, and she was beautiful with garments and locks of hair adorned as if with the very substances of good fortune.
Her long eyes reached to her ears, as if pervaded by the brilliance of lightning;
she was possessed of great power, like the enchantress Mohinī incarnate.
Richly adorned with the splendor of golden ornaments, her breath was fragrant;
she possessed a melodious voice, and her lotus-face was serene with every grace. (84)
The soles of her feet and her toes possess the luster of campaka flowers;
she is delicate and possesses delicate limbs, abiding in all-encompassing beauty. (85)
Captivating the eyes, enchanting the mind, and utterly ravishing the soul, she appeared with a most beautiful form and broke into laughter. (86)
There, Mura beheld her shining in the midst of that splendor;
and Mura, falling into a state of delusion, proceeded to embrace her.
The maiden said: "O great Daitya, you are wise and you are righteous;
yet, without the performance of a marriage rite, I cannot consent to being yours. (88)
"Having conquered me, take her now, O Dānava; this is my stake.
Having defeated me in battle, take this high-minded woman as your slave. (89)
Having heard her cry and forgetting Viṣṇu himself, Muru prepared for the course of battle, equipped with weapons, missiles, and other gear.
When the great Asura engaged in the battle with the maiden,
his head was indeed severed from the region of the neck and reduced to ashes.
His body was pulverized by the club with its protruding knobs;
Mura was slain, and his warriors were likewise killed by it.
Hearing the great clamor and abandoning his sleep, Viṣṇu awoke;
seeing Mura dead, he was filled with wonder. ||93||
"Aha! By this maiden indeed has the mighty asura been slain—he whom I could not previously conquer; he has truly been conquered and killed by her. (94)
This indeed is Mahālakṣmī, the Great Power, the Great Illusion;
she is capable of destroying suffering and acts for the welfare of the gods. 95.
Every favor has indeed been rendered both to the gods and to me;
the wicked Dānava, who struck terror into the gods and Asuras, has been slain. ||96||
Having thus attained a state of clarity, he then questioned the maiden:
"Who are you? How was the Daitya slain? What is it that dwells in your mind? (97)
The maiden said to Hari: "I am considered Ekādaśī of Viṣṇu;
I am the destroyer of all enemies and the annihilator of all sins. (98)
I am composed of all splendor and bestow all human goals;
I have arisen from your body and am born from the power of your senses.
"O Lord, I am your daughter, joined with your consciousness;
a Daitya has come here to kill my father while he is fast asleep."

And the power of consciousness (cic-chakti), beholding the demon, became for you elevenfold, consisting of the splendor of the eleven senses, including the emergent ego (ahaṃkāra) and the rest. || 10.1 ||
Therefore, O Hari, I have arisen under the name Ekādaśī to bestow all merit and for the destruction of the demon, O Mādhava.
"The great Daitya, who caused suffering to the gods, has been destroyed by me.
Having heard these words of her son, Hari spoke to that daughter.
"Choose a boon, O auspicious lady; a great task has been accomplished for me.
I am pleased, and may you be blessed; I shall grant you everything that is in your heart. (104)
O Goddess, there is nothing that cannot be given by you; the gods have been well protected by you.
Dharma has been firmly established, and the divine vow has been observed.
The path of virtue has been constantly established by you for the sake of all people;
therefore, indeed, everything belonging to yourself must be given for your sake.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, Ekādaśī spoke as follows.
I am indeed named Ekādaśī, the presiding deity whose essence is the vow.
That day of the eleventh lunar tithi is considered by me to be my own day;
whether it be the bright or the dark fortnight, that divine day is indeed a sacred vow for me.
This day is of great merit and purifying; it is the most meritorious among all meritorious acts.
Therefore, my day should be observed through vows, fasting, and keeping vigil.
The objects of the senses, which are their nourishment, must be avoided with great effort;
for he who observes a fast here on my day is truly a man.
One undoubtedly attains merit equal to that of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) by means of eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, or by [offering] fruit. || 111 ||
One may even perform the vow with water alone; such a person shall go to the abode of Mādhava.
One should keep a vigil at night and perform the worship of Hari. (11.2)
One should cause my worship to be performed with flowers, incense, lamps, and various excellent articles; indeed, one should then carry out the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Thus, one who performs this vow shall go to your imperishable abode;
he shall not undergo residence in a womb and shall become entirely free from sin.
On my day, may purity always arise among my devotees;
may devotion toward the Lord increase, as well as faith in my vow.
"May hunger not afflict my devotees, those observing vows, and women;
such are the boons that should be granted to me, O Lord. (1.16)
O Hari, these must be given to me; likewise, O Lord, hear another thing from me:
Hari is my father, Hari is my mother, and Hari is always my kinsman as well.
Hari is the sustainer, Hari is the creator, Hari himself is the nourisher and the destroyer;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, through these various forms, be my husband forever.
"May I become your wife in twenty-six forms; act accordingly so that the fault of my lack of sacramental rites may be destroyed through marriage."
"Devoted eternally to my husband, I shall serve you, my beloved lord;
grant me this boon, O Master, and cause my good fortune to increase."
Having heard this, Hari said: "O auspicious lady, let that which you desire be fulfilled;
let your vow be meritorious, and let your forms also be perfected."
May I become your husband through various forms; be the bestower of prosperity, and be in every way the granter of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Purified by the vow of Ekādaśī, may they go to my Vaiṣṇava abode;
having obtained the true fruit in this world, may they attain liberation at the end.
"Thus, O my beloved, I bestow these boons upon you.
Having said "Om," Ekādaśī herself indeed became manifold. (124)
Then Hari, by means of twenty-six forms of his own body,
duly assumed at that time the form of the eleven wives.
Having dissolved her form as a daughter, she exists in the form of wives for twelve months and two additional days of the year.
When combined, these are considered to be twenty-six Ekādaśīs;
for an Ekādaśī is defined as a full day and night (ahorātra), even if it includes a single ghaṭikā of the tenth day.
That lunar day (tithi) should indeed be avoided; rather, the auspicious twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast.
For the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is complete [in duration], while the twelfth day is increasing [in length]. || 128 ||
On the thirteenth day, however, breaking the fast yields a hundredfold merit;
thus, if a person performs this vow, they shall partake of its fruits and become a partaker of liberation.
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor even Puṣkara,
nor even the sacred field of Viṣṇu is equal to the day of Hari.
Having thus offered praise and taken his wife with him,
Hari departed for the royal capital called Candrāvatī, which was indeed built by Mura.
There, Hari liberated the gods who were bound in fetters;
having made heaven his own, the Lord departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this supreme majesty of the vow of Trispṛśā Ekādaśī; what else do you wish to hear? 133.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Ekādaśī on Account of the Battle with the Dānava Mura, the Vow, and the Granting of Boons," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||234||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Hari, tell me of the vows for the twenty-six Ekādaśīs;
how they are to be performed according to the rules, and how the deity is to be worshipped in each case.
What are the names, the lords, the fruits, and the rituals of all the Ekādaśīs? Describe them individually.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to their story, which is purifying and likewise bestows liberation;
it is my divine Yoga-māyā, which grants Vaikuṇṭha and other realms.
Likewise, hear from me concerning Unmīlanī and Pakṣavardhinī;
and with focused mind, understand from me the fruit of keeping vigil.
Indeed, Ekādaśī lasts for a full day and night; if it extends for even one ghaṭikā at dawn, it should be known as Unmīlanī, and it is exceedingly dear to Hari.
Whatever sacred fords and whatever holy places exist in the three worlds, as well as penance, the Vedas, and sacrifices— all these are not worth even a ten-millionth part of it.
They are indeed never anywhere equal to Unmīlanī;
nothing has ever been, nor will there ever be, anything equal to Unmīlanī.
Neither Kāśī, nor Gayā, nor Prayāga, nor the land of the Kurus;
neither the Puṣkara lake, nor Nārāyaṇa, nor the Himavat mountain.
Neither Mount Raivata, nor the Vindhya, Malaya, or even Meru; nor Kuṅkumavāpī, Naimiṣa, Kālakṣetra, or the forest.
Neither the Candrabhāgā nor the Kāverī, nor the Sarayū nor the Gomatī; neither the Godāvarī nor the Narmadā, nor the Svarṇalekhā nor the Vedikā.
Neither the Tāpī, nor the Bhadrā, nor the Sindhu, nor the Candanā; neither the Śatruñjitā, nor the Ojasvatī, nor the Vipāśā, nor the Gaṇḍakī.
Neither the Śoṇa nor the Tuṅgabhadrā, nor even the Sarasvatī, nor indeed any other sacred fords (tīrtha) are truly equal to Unmīlanī.
There is no merit equal to that of the Non-mīlanī day, nor is there any god superior to Śrī Hari;
this is so for those who, having reached the Unmīlanī day, have performed the worship of Hari.
Having shaken off their mass of sins, they go to the imperishable abode when the auspicious lunar day of Ekādaśī unfolds within that month. || 14 ||
One should fashion a golden image of Hari according to the name of the month and worship it with supreme faith, devotion, and many excellent offerings.
The pitcher should be filled with purified water, endowed with the five jewels,
joined with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, and adorned with garlands and cloth.
One should place a coconut or other fruit in the central mandala;
having established the image here in the one known as Sarvatobhadra, one should worship it.
A vessel filled with wheat and endowed with various jewels, combined with diverse fragrances and scented with the aroma of jasmine; || 18 ||
One should place it near a banyan tree together with *jātī* flowers;
furthermore, the vessel should be filled with white-eyed rice grains.
One should place [the image] beside the pitcher and worship Hari repeatedly;
one should also present a pair of garments along with an upper cloth and a sacred thread.
One should also give sandals, an umbrella, a cooking pot, a water-pot,
vessels filled with the seven types of grain, and sesame seeds in abundance.
One should give silver and gold, as well as cotton and milk-rice; likewise, one should give signet rings, finger-rings, and beautiful cows.
One should also give ornaments and various vessels,
as well as a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, a copper-colored back, and accompanied by a calf.
Then one should give to the preceptor a cow that yields milk from a bronze vessel and has a tail adorned with jewels;
one should also give a bed together with a couch, provided with a ball and its necessary furnishings.
One should offer incense, a lamp, food offerings, fruits, leaves, and so forth,
as well as various Tulasī leaves and lotus flowers.
Then, during the worship, one should offer various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to Hari;
furthermore, one should contemplate the form of Śrī Hari, especially limb by limb.
One should meditate upon the feet with the name of the month, the knees with the name of Viṣṇu,
the private parts with the name of Śrīśa, and the hips with the name of Kṛṣṇa.
One should remember the navel by the name "Brahman," the stomach by the name "Viśva," the heart by the name "Jñātṛ," and the throat by the term signifying "Vaikuṇṭhavāsin."

A wise person should meditate upon the forehead with the name of the Guru, the head with the name of the Supreme Brahman, and likewise all the limbs with the name of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).
Having performed meditation, one should indeed worship the weapons, ornaments, garments, and decorations, and with devotion, one should offer the arghya and other offerings.
Having placed a fruit upon a conch shell, provided with scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
and having wrapped it with a thread, one should offer the arghya with devotion.
In this manner, one should worship Hari with these sixteen excellent offerings;
and having bowed to Hari, one should pray: "Lift me up from the great ocean! (32)
Indeed, some small amount of merit has been performed by me for the sake of my deliverance;
nevertheless, you are my master, so deliver me from the great ocean.
By means of the Unmilini vow, rescue my ancestors here—
those who have fallen into base births, those who are sinful, and likewise those who have met with untimely death.
Lift up all other pretas, both those of the past and those yet to come, from the great ocean; O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Mādhava, grant them supreme liberation! 35.
"Grant me, who am afflicted, eternal devotion to your form;
thus [worship] with incenses, lamps, food offerings, and water-offerings. (36)
One should fully satisfy Śrī Hari with hymns of praise, lustration rites, and dances;
likewise, by the gifting of garments, the gifting of cows, meals, and service. (37)
A devotee should please the guru in such a way that he attains satisfaction;
for when the guru is pleased, one should act accordingly, as the fruit is great.
Since the Guru was created by the Creator for the sake of delivering the worlds, one should therefore always satisfy the Guru with the offering of all one's possessions and other services. (39)
Worship of the Guru must be performed, for the Guru is Lord Hari, the bestower of liberation;
he is indeed the one who releases one from what is harmful and always shows one what is truly beneficial.
By the gift of knowledge, one should destroy ignorance and become a bestower of happiness;
one should sever the beginningless bondage and bestow eternal bliss. ||41||
One should always take refuge in that Guru, Hari, who is skilled in the knowledge of Dharma and its purpose;
one should serve him at all times with devotion and should not practice deceit regarding wealth. 42.
The grace of the guru must be obtained so that the vow may become complete;
having performed his ablutions on the twelfth lunar day, the devotee should worship Hari. (43)
Afterwards, he should feed his guru and many Brahmins;
having fed virtuous men and women, he himself should perform the breaking of the fast.
One who observes the vow should pass their time with stories of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, there is no gift equal to the gift of knowledge. (45)
Knowledge should always be imparted constantly through the recitation of scriptures and other means;
Viṣṇu should be presented as the giver of that knowledge, and the donor shall attain liberation. 46.
Thus, he who performs the Unmīlanī Ekādaśī vow certainly dwells in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of infinite kalpas. ||47||
O Lakṣmī, this very Vaiṣṇava vow has been proclaimed to you;
by hearing which, all sinners attain liberation at that very moment. (48)
The performer of the Unmīlanī vow is glorified in the heavenly world;
both the gods and the ancestors shall attain a divine state. (49)
A seeker of knowledge obtains auspicious knowledge that brings about all prosperity,
through the vow of Ekādaśī, the worship of Viṣṇu, and the adoration of the Vaiṣṇavas.
The excellent service of virtuous men and women—these four are difficult to obtain.
By hearing this, one may be liberated from the bondage of birth and death throughout one's life. 51.
Neither Viṣṇu nor his devotees should ever be treated with hostility;
having honored them and fed them, one should then partake of one's own meal. ||52||
A Śālagrāma stone should be worshipped, especially by a Vaiṣṇava;
one should also offer incense, the waving of lights (ārātrika), and conch-water to Viṣṇu.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) to Viṣṇu and then also to the Vaiṣṇavas;
thereafter, the observer of the Ekādaśī vow should partake of his meal.
One should offer a lamp, likewise perform singing and daily prostration;
and, overflowing with love, one should perform worship with Śyāmā sprouts. (55)
When worship is performed with *dūrvā* grass, the merit is equal to the gift of the earth;
moreover, worship with the dark sprouts of *dūrvā* is exceedingly dear [to the deity]. (56)
In this world, there is nothing more auspicious than the sprouts of dūrvā grass;
one who desires union with Viṣṇu should perform worship with them. (57)
One should worship Hari with dūrvā grass, barley, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
performing the worship according to the rules at dawn on every twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of each fortnight.
This auspicious Viṣṇu-vow, which bestows liberation, happiness, and long life, has been proclaimed as the granter of prosperity for the Vaiṣṇavas. (59)
It bestows happiness upon householders and grants liberation to ascetics;
it pacifies all diseases and the like, and purifies the three bodies.
The great Unmīlanī vow, free from the overlap of the tenth day, should be performed along with a night vigil; it is supreme and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with a hundred thousand *tulasī* leaves;
likewise, one should apply the mark of *gopīcandana*, the crescent moon, the *tilaka*, and the vertical *puṇḍra*.
One should wear it for the sake of worship, for by its mere sight it bestows liberation;
one should also wear the Vaiṣṇava weapon and armor, which destroy all suffering.

A killer of a Brahmin, a stealer of gold, a drinker of intoxicants, an eater of meat, one who has sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, a great sinner, and a speaker of slander and falsehood; ||64||
They attain liberation from sin by wearing the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark, as well as by wearing a garland of *dhātrī* fruits and a garland of *tulasī* around the neck. (65)

A Vaiṣṇava devotee should indeed wear the stone discus from Dvārakā and [the stone] from the Gaṇḍakī river, which are the very forms of the initiation for worship and other rites, as well as Viṣṇu himself.

One should worship Tulasī daily; it yields the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Indeed, a day of Viṣṇu that possesses an astrological conjunction (sa-vaidha) must certainly not be observed as a fast.
The king in whose kingdom a day of slaughter prevails is defiled by that sin and shall become a denizen of hell. ||68||
Having abandoned all other types of piercing rituals and observed the fast on the day of Hari,
there shall be the liberation of ten million members of one's lineage, and one shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu.
If fifty-five ghaṭikās remain from the rising of the tenth [lunar day], that eleventh day is the next day; it is called a "pierced" (viddha) Ekādaśī.

If even a single ghaṭikā of the tenth day (daśamī) exists during the day and night of Ekādaśī, that lunar day (tithi) must certainly not be observed for fasting; rather, the vow of Dvādaśī is prescribed.
When two Ekādaśīs occur, the later one is to be observed, not the earlier;
when two Dvādaśīs occur, the earlier Dvādaśī is indeed to be observed.
When the eleventh day (ekādaśī) has ended, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) for the sake of the vow;
likewise, when the tenth day (daśamī) has ended, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day for the sake of the vow.
When the tenth day occurs as a pair [with the eleventh], one should fast on that Ekādaśī;
likewise, when the waning of the twelfth day occurs, one should fast on the Ekādaśī.
Knowing this, one should perform the vow; Hari becomes pleased.
The performer of the vow goes to the abode of Hari by the will of Śrī Hari. (75)
And on the twelfth day, that single ghaṭikā of Ekādaśī which occurs at dawn, after the break of the Aruṇodaya, belongs to the time of the day's manifestation. ||76||
Likewise, it awakens for the purpose of opening the eyes of human beings;
therefore, O beloved, it has been called by me "Unmīlanī" (The Opener).
She who unites the upward-facing Brahma-Vaikuntha, the supreme abode, as well as the imperishable Goloka, is described by me as Sonmīlanī. (78)
She who, through the practice of her vows, unites with the supreme Brahman above—the dark Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Hari—is called Unmīlanī. (79)
She who, having pierced through ignorance— which is the form of sin— and fear and death,
unites one with the upper world and light, is indeed meaningful.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual Worship and Observance of the Ekādaśī Vrata Named Unmīlanī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the Ekādaśī named Pakṣavardhinikā, which is exceedingly dear to me; by means of it, one may attain liberation.
The Ekādaśī that is complete yet joined with the contamination (vedha) of Daśamī, and that Ekādaśī which is joined with the contamination of Ekādaśī and occurs at sunrise on the Dvādaśī; || 2 ||

In this sequence, the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the full moon (pūrṇimā) are complete when sixty nāḍīs elapse at the moment preceding the sun's [next] rising; the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) is likewise of that same duration.
Starting from Ekādaśī and ending with the day of Pratipad,
when the duration of the day consists of a full sixty nāḍikās.
Then that Ekādaśī is to be known by the name Pakṣavardhinī;
that Dvādaśī should be observed as a fast, and the vow should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
O Mahālakṣmī, that Pakṣavardhinī [vow] would be equal to ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
by performing it, one obtains infinite fruit.
When Viṣṇu is worshipped and honored, the fruit of Vaikuṇṭha is attained;
I shall now describe that worship by which Keśava is pleased.
One should construct a Sarvatobhadra mandala with the seven types of grain;
in its center, one should place a new golden jar filled with water.
And there should be a copper vessel, or else one adorned with the five types of sprouts,
joined with the five jewels, and wrapped in a white cloth.
Having honored him with sandalwood paste and encircled him with flower garlands,
one should place there a large vessel made of copper, filled with wheat.
One should properly prepare a coconut along with fruit and delicious food;
one should have an image of Kṛṣṇa made of gold, bearing the name of the current month.
One should likewise bathe Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the prescribed rite;
then one should perform the consecration with waters from sacred fords and apply [the unguents].
With saffron, unbroken grains of rice, musk, sandalwood, and camphor, [he should offer] a pair of garments, a sacred thread, the Kaustubha gem, and ornaments. (13)
Ornaments such as flower garlands and the like should be presented, as well as bracelets, armlets, crowns, chains, waist-bands, and finger-rings. (14)
A lion-throne should be offered, together with an umbrella and sandals;
and highly potent fragrant substances should be given with sincere devotion. (15)
And there, Lakṣmī should be established, adorned with all ornaments,
and embellished with all the substances of auspiciousness and every kind of decoration.
Ekādaśī herself, in her own form, is to be worshipped by the side of Hari;
one should worship Śrī Hari there, seated upon a water-pot.
One should meditate upon Padmanābha; there, one should contemplate his feet.
Having contemplated him as the embodiment of the universe, one should then remember his knees. (18)
Having recollected Him who is attainable through knowledge, one should meditate upon the thighs there;
and having remembered Hari, the bestower of knowledge, one should also meditate upon the hips.
Having remembered Viśvanātha Hari, one should meditate upon the belly;
having remembered Śrīdhara Śrīhari, one should meditate upon the heart of Hari.
Having recollected Hari, who bears the Kaustubha gem, one should properly contemplate His throat;
having recollected Him, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, one should properly contemplate His arms.
Having recollected Hari as the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa), one should then contemplate the forehead;
having meditated upon Hari as possessing all forms, one should properly contemplate the head. 22.
One should meditate upon all the weapons and all the limbs as being named Kṛṣṇa;
having thus meditated, one should then offer the arghya with a coconut.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Keśava, lift me up from the ocean of saṃsāra! O Lord, accept this worship and the water offering; O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, salutations be unto You! 24.
The sixteen varieties of offerings should be presented to the Supreme Self;
one should offer various kinds of food oblations and give cool water. (25)
One should devoutly offer betel-leaf that is very fragrant and made of excellent ingredients;
and one should also devoutly light a lamp with either ghee or oil. ||26||
One should perform the night-rite, prostrations, circumambulation, and hymns of praise;
one should request forgiveness and offer a handful of flowers. (27)

Having performed the auspicious worship of Hari, one should likewise carry out the worship of the Guru by offering sandalwood paste and other substances, as well as garments, ornaments, and so forth. (28)
One should cause to be offered robes, turbans, necklaces, and other such items, as well as fragrant substances and the like;
likewise, one should present sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), food, grain, and so forth, as well as ritual hand-gestures (mudrās). ||29||
Having offered food and betel leaf, one should satisfy the preceptor;
according to one's wealth and according to one's ability, the festival should be celebrated most excellently.
In the evening as well, worship should likewise be performed with a spirit of devotion;
thereafter, one should keep a vigil accompanied by song and dance.
One should worship the goddess named Pakṣavardhinī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa with the syllable *śrīṃ*, accompanied by ancient narrative tales and filled with laughter and joy.
One who hears its greatness shall obtain the fruit of the vow;
it is equal to the merit found in the practice of the five fires and in ten million sacred fords (tīrthas). || 33 ||
A person attains that fruit through keeping a vigil for Viṣṇu;
when a fast is observed there, the destruction of ten million killings occurs.
This must be performed especially by Vaiṣṇavas who are practitioners of the yoga of knowledge;
neither sacred fords, nor forest hermitages, nor holy mountains [are as effective]. (35)

Just as the waxing fortnight enables people to cross over [the ocean of existence], so too, on this day, there is an increase of merit, just as the digits of the moon increase during its bright fortnight. (36)
Just as darkness is destroyed at sunrise, so too is ignorance destroyed by this [knowledge]; it increases the side of liberation, just as it increases the waxing fortnight of the moon. //37//
She bestows the digit of liberation and nourishes the sixteen digits and beyond;
she is ever equal to Kāśī in granting liberation and likewise similar to Dvārakā. (38)
Equal to Kuṅkumavāpikā, she bestows whatever is desired;
indeed, she always increases the side of liberation for her devotees. (39)
Knowledge, righteousness, and likewise devotion increase in every way;
one should not make any distinction between them as being either white or black. (1.236.40)
It delivers the performer [of the vow], as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants;
the twelfth day, when observed on both [sides of the month], delivers the one who observes the vow. 41.
Dwelling in Vārāṇasī for sixty thousand years, or performing sacrifices and giving gifts at Kurukṣetra during a thousand lunar festivals; |||42||

During the excellent yogas such as Vidhṛti and others, a hundred times more than the highest of the high gifts of a hundred thousand was performed at Kurukṣetra as a gift of the sun, the moon, and the planets. ||43||
The fruit that one always enjoys by giving a thousand Soma sacrifices at Prabhāsa is equal to the fruit of feeding a hundred thousand ascetics at home.
The fruit of drinking the water of Kedāra, which results in the non-appearance of rebirth, does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī day. 45.
The fruit of giving a thousand cows is indeed said to be multiplied a thousandfold;
the fruit of honoring the virtuous is ten times greater than that. (46)
Furthermore, the merit from worshipping one established in Brahman is ten times greater than that;
likewise for one who gives land for the sake of the gods, and for one who gives a daughter in marriage. (47)
Ten times greater than even that is the merit in being purified by the final ablution of a sacrifice;
indeed, for one who observes the Ekādaśī vow, the fruit shall be infinite.
Whatever merit is found in fasting, half of that is obtained by eating only at night;
half of the merit of eating at night is obtained by eating once a day, or by subsisting on fruit.
Whatever merit one obtains by eating once a day, by eating only at night, by fasting, or by consuming fruit—
that same merit is obtained when a vigil is kept at night.
The measure of merit for fasting on Ekādaśī is not known; listen as I proclaim the greatness of each individual fast. (51)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual Worship and Observance of the Pakṣavardhinī Ekādaśī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, the great sleep (mahānidrā) causes the destruction of merit;
it must be avoided by all means during the night of the vow, and even during the day.
The state of sleep is most terrible, characterized by darkness, and it clouds the mind;
having the non-perception of objects as its support, it brings about indolence.
She is the creator of defects such as those occurring in dreams and the obstructer of devotion and service;
this occurs occasionally when the rajas quality has become predominant due to an abundance of faults.
She who causes the breaking of the vow of celibacy,
who brings about seminal emission, and who destroys the vow, would become like one whose vigor is as swift as the wind.
Therefore, one must by all means remain awake throughout the night for the sake of the vow;
for when there is an abundance of food and drink, the bodily constituents generally [become disturbed].

They become nourished through that practice; however, if there is an involuntary depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), fasting becomes useless, especially in the event of breaking the vow of celibacy.
Therefore, at that time, eating fruits and so forth is considered to be the concise rule;
people should always avoid solid food on the day of the vow. (7)
Sleep, however, must be avoided by all means; it destroys the conduct of the virtuous, causes the depletion of merit, is the receptacle of all defects, and is characterized by extreme darkness.
Indeed, [the senses] must be conquered with effort by the devotee observing the vow;
one should diligently perform the vigil (jāgaraṇa) which nourishes the observance. 9.
On the eleventh day, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with love at night,
a person should join together with Vaiṣṇavas and perform the vigil during the vow.

Through singing, instrumental music, dancing, and so forth; through the recitation of the Saṃhitās and the like; through conversation consisting of the glory of the Blessed One; and through service as well. (11)
The devotee should keep a vigil for the sake of the success of the vow,
offering incense, lamps, food offerings, flowers, perfumes, and ointments.
One should devotedly offer and perform the fruit, the guest-offering (arghya), faith, ornaments, the sentiment of love, and the entire vow free from sleep. || 13 ||
Completely purified of all sins, he becomes an attendant of Hari;
when the vow of keeping vigil has arrived, the Vaiṣṇavas are indeed filled with enthusiasm.
Fasting, they should observe the vow and keep a vigil accompanied by the *tāṇḍava* dance;
they should indeed perform that vow known as Viṣṇu’s and chant the recitation of His names.
Those who, having meditated upon Śrī Hari with their minds, repeatedly utter His name, are indeed the most blessed in the world; they are my saviors and my personal attendants (pārṣadas). 16.
During exhalation and inhalation, the name of Hari is fourfold in merit;
chanting the name for one watch (three hours) yields fruit a hundred million times greater.
Devotion to the Name during the four watches of the night is considered to yield immeasurable fruit; likewise, keeping vigil for even half a moment in the presence of the Image [of the Lord]. (18)
The fruit of that would be unsurpassed, multiplied by millions upon millions of billions;
one should perform a dance before Kṛṣṇa, full of wonder and overflowing with love. (19)
One should perform circumambulation with enthusiasm and free from negligence, laziness, and the like, while offering salutations again and again.
One should likewise perform the *ārārtrika* offering again and again at every watch of the night,
beholding the form moment by moment with a heart full of tenderness.
One should clap one's hands; thus the vigil (jāgara) should take place.
He who performs the vigil during the vow should do so endowed with many such virtues. ||22||
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, nor should one harbor greed during worship.
He who performs [worship] in this manner with devotion is not born again on earth. ||23||
Indeed, by performing the vigil, the observer of the vow is absorbed into Viṣṇu;
one should not deceive oneself with atheism regarding the vow. (24)
However, one who mocks another during the vigil of the Nārāyaṇa-vrata is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years. (25)
And that Brahmin who, though a knower of the Vedas, acts as a buffoon in dance, becomes tainted with fault here; indeed, he is lower than a Cāṇḍāla. ||26||
Whether for a moment or even for a watch of the night, he who remains awake engaged in dancing with devotion shall attain the fruit of the fourfold aims of life.
A Vedic priest who reviles one while awake goes to hell together with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Those who are bitten by the serpent of atheism indeed sleep during their vow;
deluded by illusion, they certainly do not keep watch.
They are ruined, there is no doubt; for they have fallen away from liberation.
Devoid of eyes and devoid of knowledge, they are indeed bereft of the goals of human life.
When the night has passed and the morning has arrived, one should cause the story of Hari to be proclaimed;
one should repeatedly cause various divine and wondrous accounts of Hari to be heard.
In the absence of a reciter, one should have that [text] recited by someone else in private;
one should perform singing and dancing, as well as laughter and other such expressions born from union with Hari.
During the festival, one should cause the play of Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the rāsa dance, to be sung;
[it is equal to] a thousand horse-sacrifices and ten thousand vājapeya sacrifices.
If the vigil is performed during the vow, the merit shall be multiplied ten millionfold;
without the vigil during the vow, there would be a loss of the merit of the vow. (34)
Those belonging to the father's side, the mother's side, and likewise the wife's side—hundreds of them are indeed uplifted when the vow of keeping vigil is performed. (35)
If the night or day of the fast is pierced by sleep, that vow is pierced; such a vow is indeed an asuric vow.
But its fruit will consist of demonic nature and take the form of a curse;
Viṣṇu does not come there, and even having arrived, he departs.
Having cast a curse upon the place where he had fallen asleep, Hari departs;
but when the place has been kept awake, even though Lakṣmī is present, Hari indeed remains.
When seen, he comes into their presence and dances himself among his devotees; having entered into those most devoted followers filled with love, he rejoices exceedingly. ||39||
For as many nights as one performs vows and keeps a vigil in the presence of Hari,
for that many yugas is the performer of the vow honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the house of one who is constantly sleepy on the day of the Ekādaśī vow and other such observances, the Asuras, Rākṣasas, and the followers of Yama—who cause undesirable things—dance. 41.
On the day of Hari’s vow, one should perform singing, recitation, and chanting;
otherwise, like a mute at the time of departure, one shall suffer from dumbness for seven births. (42)
He who does not perform a dance before Hari out of excessive shame should be known to suffer lameness both in this life and in his next birth. 43.
For one who performs singing, dancing, japa, and keeping vigil, my supreme Vaiṣṇava abode has been fashioned by me for their residence. (44)
And whoever causes others who are devoted to other deities to keep a vigil on the day of Hari shall dwell in my abode as one of my foremost attendants, remaining there without blinking.
He who, on the day of Hari, engages one prone to sleep in a state of wakefulness shall dwell for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha, accompanied by ten million ancestors.
He who gives his counsel regarding the vigil on the day of Kṛṣṇa’s vow shall indeed dwell in Śvetadvīpa for sixty thousand years.
Whatever sin has been committed by you through the fault of desire, whether in this birth or another, all of it goes to destruction during the night vigil for Śrī Hari. 48.

Those who perform a night vigil (prajāgara) in the presence of Hari as well as in the presence of a Śālagrāma stone shall obtain the fruit of having performed rites at ten million sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
Otherwise, indeed, all that is well-done is destroyed by sleep;
even by mere censure, the vow is destroyed—how then could its fruit be realized?
Human goals, prosperities, sons, fame, wealth, and the like,
as well as eternal worlds in heaven, are obtained through this vow of the vigil.
Without keeping a vigil for Viṣṇu, there can be no favor from Him;
indeed, the eternal realm is never attained even through ten thousand sacrifices. (52)
When the vow and the vigil have been performed, the eternal abode is attained;
for one who goes for the sake of the vigil, there shall be the fruit born of a horse-sacrifice at every step. (53)
With the dust of his feet still clinging to them, he remains awake for a thousand divine years in Vaikuṇṭha, in the highest heaven.
On the night of the vow, one should go to the temple of Hari for the sake of keeping watch;
for as many ages as there are grains of dust clinging to one's feet, one shall dwell in the abode of Hari.
Likewise, on the night of the eleventh and twelfth lunar days,
one should diligently perform the ritual vigil (prajāgara) for the sake of shaking off the ignorance of the individual soul.
It is considered to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior; among these, the superior vigilance must indeed be practiced. (57)
A vigil accompanied by storytelling, singing, and especially dancing, and characterized by the sattvic emotional states (sāttvikabhāva), is considered the most excellent. ||58||

Accompanied by music from the Gandharvas and Harikīrti and others, joined with rhythmic beats (tāla) and so forth, and enriched with the splendor of lamps, incense, and other offerings—such a vigil is considered the most excellent. (59)
Accompanied by a state of devotion and joined with the chanting of the Name,
this supreme vigil is considered to be the source of purity and contentment.
Accompanied by festivities such as public entertainments and spirited celebrations,
and provided with offerings of food, fruits, drinks, and the like, there was an excellent night vigil.
Where there is the offering of lamps to Hari, where there is the circumambulation of Hari,
and where there is the recitation of the Rāśi-yoga before Hari— that indeed is the supreme vigil (jāgara).
Where there is indeed knowledge of the scriptures, service to the guru, and service to the deity;
where there is remembrance [of the Lord], service at His feet, and keeping vigil—that is truly the highest state. (63)
Where all beings reside in Hari, and where the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas dwell—
