that vigil (jāgara) indeed must be performed during both the bright and dark fortnights.
"Nor by vows, gifts, austerities, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and so forth; nor by any other meritorious deeds, if one does not keep a vigil during the vow. (65)
Whether in exile, in a forest, in a field, in a wilderness, or even in another village;
in a garden, in an assembly, by a river, on a mountain, or in battle. ||66||
He who keeps me awake during times of exhaustion, or while I am dependent on others on the great highway—he is exceedingly dear to me in my vow. (67)
Whether one is a devotee of anyone else or even my own devotee, on the day of the vow, one should by all means abandon sleep; thus one shall attain the fruit.
Whether one is a devotee of Śiva, the Sun, Śakti, or Gaṇeśa,
or even a devotee of my own manifestations, one should observe the vigil during the vow.
One who is prone to sleep should be known as a beast; he is merely one who delights in the objects of the senses.
He has done me an injury, for he did not keep the vigil during our vow.
He who indulges in sleep and food, which are the nourishment of the senses, shall repeatedly fall into the womb of an animal at every moment during my vow. (7.1)
By him the ancestors have been slain and the slaughter of the gods has been committed;
by him the line of merit has been struck down and her good fortune has been destroyed. (72)
By that excessively proud man, prosperity was turned into a vessel for calamities,
since he did not observe the vigil and the vow on the day of Hari.
Playing the *satālī* drum and playing the *gālava* instrument, dancing, singing, and displaying various wonders, one should indeed perform the vigil (*jāgara*). //74//
Delighting the Vaiṣṇava people by reminding them of the Lord's deeds, he displayed his own body hairs bristling with joy and filled with love. (75)
Producing delightful conversations, manifesting sweet emotions, revealing suggestive gestures that are powerful and perceptible, and discerning the meanings of the hymns; ||76||
Thus performing the vow and manifesting love while keeping vigil,
in every single moment his merit shall be equal to that of Naimiṣa.
For him, there is the fruit of ten million sacred fords, the great fruit of ten million sacrifices,
the fruit of ten million heavens, and indeed the great fruit of ten million acts of charity.
With a peaceful mind, one should offer incense, lamps, and the *nīrājana* ceremony; by likewise keeping a vigil at night, one shall become the sovereign of the seven continents. (79)
Great sins and even more heinous sins, equal indeed to the killing of ten million people,
truly go to destruction piece by piece when one correctly observes the vow of the night vigil.
On one side are all merits, and on the other side is the vigil kept during the vow; the great merit of the vigil is distinguished as superior to all other merits. ||8 1||
Kāśī, Dvāravatī, Raivatācala, Somapāṭṭaṇa, Arbuda, Aruṇa, Mandara, and the Himaparvata mountain. ||82||
The Sahya mountain, Navala-kṣa, Vindhya, Droṇācala, as well as Mahākālavana, Vṛndāvana, and Avantikā. ||83||
Puṣkara, Prayāga, Revā, Svarṇā, Yamunā (the sister of Yama), Gayā, Gokula, Godāvarī, Gaṅgā, and Bhadrikā; ||84||
The Gaṇḍakī, the Tāmraparṇī, the Brahmaputra and other rivers; Kukkuṭavāpikā, Māyā, Kāñcī, and Śrīpuruṣottamā. 85.
Even if all those [other rites] are performed according to the rules of their respective traditions,
they do not yield such fruit as that which is obtained from the vow of the day of Hari.
Since the merit derived from being awake [in this practice] surpasses all other merit, [therefore] sacred fords, mountains, rivers, oceans, and forests [are not its equal]. (87)
The forests, the sacred shrines, the continents, and likewise the earth;
the principles of reality, the gods, the seers, the sages, the ancestors, and the fires. ||88||
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Nāgas, Cāraṇas, and those born of Brahmā’s creation;
the Vaimānikas, the Vairājas, and the lords who possess the conceit of being Time (Kāla). ||89||
Whosoever are called saviors, they are all sustainers of the world;
indeed, on the night-vigil of Ekādaśī, they all assemble from every direction.
Therefore, there is no doubt that the gods themselves are the ones who keep watch;
one should satisfy the gods assembled there with gracious favors.
The pleasing and excellent food offering must be guarded with great care;
it should be consumed by one seeking the merit of the vow on the twelfth day at the time of breaking the fast. 92.
Having bathed at the time of dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta and having worshipped Hari, one should dedicate the fast, the vigil, and the vow as well. ||93||
One should offer everything to Hari—the vow as well as its fruit—and pray:
"O Śrī Hari, may you be gracious to me in every way through this vow. (94)
Having recited this, one should offer water upon the ground in the presence of Hari, saying:
"Be, in every way, the giver of knowledge, the giver of liberation, and the giver of happiness to your devotees."
Having spoken thus and then bowed down, the observer of the vow should indeed feed the Vaiṣṇavas;
thereafter, he should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) before them as circumstances permit.
One should give a gift, including a maṇḍala known as Sarvatobhadra;
one should also give to the preceptor a water-pot and other items, along with grain and an image.
If on the morning [of the following day] even a small portion of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) does not remain,
then one should by all means perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) during the night, while it is still the twelfth day.
In that case, there is no fault regarding the night; there is no prohibition against breaking the fast.
Bathing at night and breaking the fast there do not bring about any defect. 99.
One should perform the ritual action during the first and last watches of that night as if it were day;
provided that even a very small portion of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) remains on the day of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
At the time of dawn, one should perform two rites, as well as those for the morning and midday;
he by whom the twelfth day is thus completed attains indeed infinite fruit.
Thus, by one who has performed this vow, everything shall be accomplished;
having observed the vow on the twelfth day and having completed the day of Hari.
Many divine Vaiṣṇavas have indeed gone to the abode of Viṣṇu;
there is no god equal to Hari, and no lunar day equal to the twelfth (Dvādaśī).
There is no vow equal to the Ekādaśī, for these three together bestow liberation;
and through union with Hari, all that becomes complete and eternal.
Hari makes himself beloved to his devotees;
he who performs vows, keeps vigils, and offers worship becomes beloved to Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Ekādaśī Vow, the Vigil, and Other Practices," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; once Mahādeva approached me and inquired about the greatness arising from each Ekādaśī.
I have also recounted to him the greatness of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī),
hearing which all the sages attained their fruit and went to heaven.
I shall declare that to you, which bestows the fruit of ten million heavens;
the Ekādaśī is always considered most excellent when conjoined with a lunar mansion (ṛkṣa).
Jayā, Vijayā, and Jayantī are the most excellent among my [manifestations];
when the Punarvasu asterism occurs on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, [these names are applied].
She is to be known by the name Jayā; it is the most excellent lunar day for the purpose of the vow.
And when the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, [it is especially so].
That is proclaimed as Vijayā, yielding a thousandfold fruit;
and when the Rohiṇī asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, then [it is especially so].
That lunar day named Jayantī is the destroyer of all sins;
it shall annihilate the sin committed over seven lifetimes, whether dry or moist.
Whenever the Puṣya asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
that lunar day should be known as highly meritorious and the most excellent of all.
Indeed, for one who performs the gift of a prastha of sesame seeds for a year,
the fruit of whoever observes a fast on this [day] is even greater.
Through the practice of this vow, Hari himself becomes pleased;
he appears before one's very eyes, and the fruit that bestows liberation shall be attained.
By fasting on the day joined with the Puṣya asterism, one shall obtain liberation as well as the supreme state from the sins committed through speech, mind, and body over seven lifetimes.
Through this vow, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand Ekādaśīs;
bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, and worship of the deity [all bear fruit].
And whatever is performed in this [rite] yields inexhaustible fruit and bestows liberation,
as was indeed done by King Svarṇāṅgada for a brahmin devoted to his wife.
In the former Kṛtayuga, with the desire for the attainment of liberation, [the sages] asked:
"What is the fruit of fasting, eating only at night, and eating only once a day? (14)
For those whose senses have turned away from sense-objects, dwelling in the divine form or in the world— this indeed is the fast that bestows fruit.
Whether devoid of water or accompanied by water, it is indeed called a fast;
whether it bears fruit or is joined with the drinking of milk, it is likewise declared to be so. (16)
On the tenth day, however, having observed a single meal, one should perform the vow;
or likewise on the tenth day, having eaten only at night, one should indeed perform the vow.
When the sun has grown dim in the eighth part of the day, that meal is called "nakta";
"nakta" does not mean eating at night.
For a person engaged in religious observances, eating at night (nakta) is indeed permitted on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), provided that the stars are visible at night. || 19 ||
Since there is no one to restrain him, that person may act as he pleases;
however, having taken a single meal at midday, he should observe his vow.
This regard for food is for the sake of one who is weak and lacking strength;
therefore, at the time of dawn on the eleventh day, the person observing the vow [should act].
One should undertake the discipline of turning away from sense objects,
and worship Hari in the morning with the sixteen auspicious articles.
And one should pray to Hari: "May my vow be fulfilled;
may there be no obstacle for me therein, nor any loss of faith. (23)
In that vow, one should not engage at all in worldly affairs;
however, one should perform what is necessary, provided it does not contradict the injunctions of the vow. (24)
Milk, water, fruit, root, leaf, vegetable, juice, as well as medicinal herbs, the word of the guru, and the word of Brahman—these must be consumed even against one's will. (25)
Indeed, these eleven are known as non-vow-breakers;
furthermore, it should be understood that for one who is incapable, even eating food does not break the vow.
At midday as well, one should perform a bath in water and worship Hari;
bathing in a well is inferior, while that in a large oblong pond is indeed middling.
Bathing in a pond or a river is indeed considered excellent;
bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in a great river, or in the ocean, is the most excellent of all. 28.
Indeed, for one who is unable [to bathe in a river], bathing at home is certainly prescribed even for the wealthy;
O Earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu! (29)
O Earth, I smear you upon my body; grant me forgiveness!
Remove all my sins and now perform meritorious deeds for me.
Having spoken thus, a person, observing silence and remembering the name of Kṛṣṇa, should apply clay to his body for the sake of purification in auspicious water.
Likewise, the observer of the vow should bathe and have an offering of food (naivedya) presented there to Hari;
he should also offer water and pass the time with sacred narratives.
The observer of the vow should pass the entire day with devotion to the Blessed One, and likewise the night with reverence using articles imbued with great significance. 33.
One should perform the worship of the God of gods and keep a vigil at night;
whether it be the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, one should conduct it in this manner according to the prescribed rite.
One should not spend the day of Ekādaśī fruitlessly, devoid of the vow;
for to the one who thus performs the rite of the vow, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari himself [is pleased]. 35.
He becomes pleased and leads that person to his own abode;
he bestows the eternal fruit, which is the nature of perfect bliss.
Indeed, the merit of one who bestows gifts on four hundred thousand *saṃkrānti* days is not equal to even a single fraction of that of fasting on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*).
Whatever fruit is obtained at Prabhāsa, in the land of the Kurus, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, that fruit is surpassed by one who observes the fast on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī).
Having drunk the water at Kedāra, rebirth no longer exists;
likewise, for one who possesses the merit of Ekādaśī, rebirth does not exist. (39)
The merit in this vow would be greater than that of sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha;
it is equal to the merit of maintaining a thousand ascetics in one's home every day for a year.
And he enjoys the most excellent fruit of that fasting on Ekādaśī;
a merit greater than a thousand cows arises, exceeding even a hundredfold. ||41||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa dwell within one who has observed the Ekādaśī vow; such a practitioner becomes Keśava himself, the very embodiment of the gods, within his own body. 42.
There is no end to the merit of service rendered to the Lord of Rukmiṇī;
nor is there any measure of the merit of the Ekādaśī vow. (43)
By means of fasting, one indeed attains the full merit; by eating only at night, half of that;
and by eating only once a day, half of that again—such is the merit produced in this vow. (44)
Holy places, charities, and religious observances roar only so long as a living being does not fast for the day beloved by Hari. 45.
There is no thousandfold great sacrifice equal to Ekādaśī, nor a thousandfold great gift, nor even a hundredfold great heaven. ||46||
She arises from the merit of Ekādaśī and is indeed considered for the sake of liberation;
born in the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, she is dear to me.
And because it has arisen from the [previous] name, that eleventh day is considered its "origin" (utpatti);
the observer of the vow should perform its origin, its injunction, and its worship. (48)
She too is proclaimed as Abhayā; he who possesses auspicious marks is to be worshipped.
Kṛṣṇa [should be worshipped] with sesame flowers, and jaggery-rice is the food offering. 49.
The fruit of the [offering] shoulder should be given to one worthy of honor, and the gift of a bull is likewise esteemed;
in the same way, a golden ring should be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Kṛṣṇa.
The rite for the festival of the vow must indeed be performed there according to the prescribed rule;
at dawn, Nārāyaṇa is as if under the power of sleep in his cave.
On the Himalayan mountain, one should construct a cave in the Himācala range, as if reached by means of Siṃhavatī; within it, Śrī Hari himself resides.
One should understand that he is asleep; Muradānava must be slain.
Likewise, Ekādaśī is divine, appearing in the form of a maiden born of gold.
She should be depicted as equipped with weapons and likewise displaying the act of combat; furthermore, the destruction of Mura and the waking nature of Nārāyaṇa [should be shown]. (54)
And there, in that cave, the worship of those two and of Hari on the eleventh day should be performed with the sixteen articles.
In this [rite], a mandala named Sarvatobhadra should be constructed using seven kinds of grain; and in its center, [an image] made of gold or copper should be placed.
A water-pot, adorned with five precious gems, cloth, and sprouts, and provided with fruit, should be placed there; likewise, a vessel containing sesame seeds should be set down. (57)
In that case, the [image] should be set up; indeed, two forms should be installed according to the mantra.
The auspicious worship should be performed according to the rules, following the previously mentioned procedure. (58)
A comfortable bed should be prepared along with a couch that bestows ease;
the vow must be observed day and night, and a vigil must also be kept.
And worship of Hari should be performed there directly at night;
in the morning, one should perform the ritual bath, worship, the gift of a cow, and the gift of land.
A gift of gold should be given according to one's ability to the preceptor or to a Brahmin;
thereafter, the formal dismissal should be performed, and one should undertake the breaking of the fast.
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, children, Brahmins, and the poor;
and one should perform the gift of an image to the guru with devotion.
Furthermore, an extensive distribution should indeed be performed according to one's wealth and according to one's power;
namely, the gift of a kingdom, the gift of a village, the gift of a field, and the offering of a house.
The gift of a maiden, the gift of a beast, the giving of jewels and gems; the gift of an elephant, the gift of a horse, and the gift of vehicles and mounts. ||64||
The gift of food, the gift of clothing, and the bestowing of knowledge and learning—
whatever capacity a donor may possess, such is always considered the true nature of giving.
Neither the wealthy man nor the king should practice stinginess regarding wealth;
they should instead give fruits, wood, sesame seeds, or other such gifts.
Even by one who is destitute, service arising from the body must be performed;
likewise, service should be rendered through speech, through the mind, or with both hands. 67.
Sweeping, smearing [the floor], fetching water, and massaging the feet—these should be performed in the temple like a servant for the sake of attaining infinite fruits and other rewards. (68)
The Blessed One is pleased by service performed with devotion;
listen to the auspicious account therein, which can deliver one even by being heard. (69)
Formerly, in the third kalpa of the Creator, there was a king born in the desert region named Maruddhanvan, who was devoted solely to his own self-interest.
At the end of the eon, in the Kali age, the king became excessively addicted to sensual objects; and due to the defects arising from desire and greed, the subjects likewise became such as he was.
When the subjects abound in faults, the king is tainted by that fault;
and due to the king's sin, rain indeed does not fall in its proper season.
Thus, when the rain was obstructed, all the subjects were tormented; they seized from one another their own clothing, food, and all other necessities in every way. (73)
Everything is carried away by force, and no justice is found therein;
just as the season passes away without rain, so it is with that time.
Having oppressed the subjects, that king drags away wealth and food;
the monarch forcibly takes away women and cattle—indeed, all of it.
In a land defiled by the evils of violence, falsehood, theft, force, and the like, the destruction of the subjects occurred, and even the king stood on the verge of ruin. (76)
He repeatedly committed many kinds of exceedingly great sins;
consequently, for a period of seven years, no rain fell at all.

Because the king’s wife was devoid of sons and afflicted by the onset of disease, she became face-to-face with death; likewise, when his son also became face-to-face with death, [he was overcome]. (78)
That king reviled me, saying: "O Supreme Self, lift me up!
Only great sins have been committed by me, and no merit has been earned. (79)
I have obtained great suffering as the fruit [of my actions], and destruction itself has been placed upon my head;
O Mādhava, beyond this, I am truly unable to do anything more.
"Deliver me from this great suffering, from the loss of life caused by hunger!
Thus, meditating on Hari, he cried out with lamentation. (8.1)
At that moment, a voice from the sky said: "O King, do not weep;
sins are consumed by repentance as well as by the remembrance of me."
"Take this water produced by the rain, as well as leaves and other such things;
eat them, for your lives will be preserved, and may you be happy. (83)
Therefore, on the third day from now, my beloved lunar day Ekādaśī arrives; perform its vow. (84)
Rain will fall everywhere throughout your kingdom, bringing happiness; furthermore, the subjects in your realm will again be intent upon their own well-being. (85)
The land shall abound in wealth and grain as the fruit of that;
and those subjects shall also obtain [these benefits] if they observe the Ekādaśī vow.
Having spoken thus, the king, the queen, and likewise their son ceased;
they then observed a waterless vow, and from that great merit arose.
When the vow was completed, a great rain fell and the land became rich with crops;
thereafter, the people found their dwelling, and the queen attained freedom from disease.
His son was also born with great fortune; he entrusted his own burden to him.
In that year, indeed, the Ekādaśīs were observed by everyone throughout the entire year.
At that moment, two celestial chariots arrived through the path of the sky,
occupied by the denizens of the heavens for the sake of the queen and the king respectively.
The celestial messengers said to them: "Come here together;
for the merit arising from your vows is indeed equal to a thousand [residences in] heaven."
Indeed, that [world] exists for a duration of a thousand yugas as an object of experience;
by virtue of his merit, he becomes the god named Marut in the fourth kalpa. (92)
"O lord of the earth, you shall become [a king] together with your wife; indeed, take up your residence in heaven.
Having been addressed thus, that lord of the earth, together with his wife, abandoned his body.
In another kalpa, he went again and again to that place which bestows heaven;
having become a god, he enjoyed various pleasures with great devotion.
Having become a great devotee of the Lord, Svarṇāṅgada served Hari like an exceedingly humble servant and attained the abode that is free from all veils.
Then, on the eleventh day of the waxing fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the vow should be performed with great effort; it leads from heaven to heaven and bestows liberation.
Thus, by means of the Ekādaśikā vow of origination, there shall always be the attainment of sovereignty, sons, and wealth, as well as health in every respect. ||97||
Every desired object shall be attained and even liberation shall result from it;
therefore, that great vow should be performed by both those with desires and those free from desires. 98.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Ekādaśī Vow in the Dark Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, its Ritual Procedure, and the Attainment of its Fruits," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
I bow to the Lord of the gods of gods, who bestows happiness upon all living beings; the inner controller who is to be worshipped, and the granter of the fruits of all desires. (1)
I ask, O Blessed Viṣṇu, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds—for the destruction of the sins of the sinful and for the prosperity of those with desires. (2)
In the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, what is the name of the auspicious Ekādaśī?
What is its fruit, what is its ritual procedure, who is its presiding deity, and who is its sovereign Lord? (3)
"O Lord, explain that to me in detail according to its true meaning.
Hearing this, the illustrious Hari, the Lord who acts for the benefit of his devotees, spoke.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the vow of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa;
by merely hearing of it, the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice shall be obtained.
On the tenth day, one should eat only at night, sleep on the ground during the night,
remain celibate, and abandon faults such as anger.
On the eleventh day, during the muhūrta known as Brāhma,
one should remain awake and remember Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara, the Lord and Master who bestows liberation.

She is the remover of all sins, the bestower of liberation, and the one designated by the name "Liberation"; she is proclaimed as "Mokṣadā" (the Giver of Liberation) by Kṛṣṇa according to his own desire.
On Mount Raivata, she was accepted by him in the form of Dāmodara;
therefore, the Lord Dāmodara is to be worshipped together with her.
In the morning, one should remember Hari Dāmodara, the beloved who grants liberation;
one should then form the resolve: "Today, by me, this vow must be performed for the sake of liberation."
For the sake of prosperity or for every desire,
the householder, having performed purification such as ritual cleansing and having bathed at a sacred bathing place (sutīrtha), [should proceed].
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should prepare the materials for the worship of Hari;
one should have a Sarvatobhadra mandala constructed using the seven types of grain.
One should place a vessel made of gold or copper in the center,
filled with the five types of sprouts, garments, and so forth, as well as the five jewels and fruits.
O noble one, one should place there the vessel containing sesame seeds and clarified butter, or a cooking pot;
and therein, the golden image of Dāmodara and Mokṣaprada.
One should install and worship [the deity] according to the prescribed rite with the sixteen types of offerings,
using Tulasī blossoms and auspicious incense, lamps, and other such items.
One should worship Keśava along with Śrī using garlands of Mālatī flowers;
the water offering (arghya) should consist of a fruit, specifically a citron, and likewise, sweetmeat balls (modakas) should be offered as the food offering (naivedya). || 16 ||
The seven grains should be given for the attainment of special fruits:
barley, wheat, grains, sesame, and likewise millet. (17)
Śyāmāka and cīnaka—these indeed are the seven grains;
they should be given according to one's capacity, for they are in every way the most excellent for giving.
Then she should pray to her husband and to Keśava along with Śrī:
"By me this vow has been performed for the sake of attaining you, O giver of liberation. (19)
O Keśava, worship has indeed been performed by me according to my ability;
be pleased, O Lord of Gods, and become the bestower of all prosperity.
"O Lord, grant me liberation; O Savior from the ocean of saṃsāra!
Having thus offered praise, he presented the food offering, fruit, and water. ||21||
One should then offer betel-leaf and fragrant substances, perform a prostration,
conduct the waving of lights (ārātrika), and recite salutations and hymns of praise.
One should perform a circumambulation and prostrate like a staff, and offer a handful of flowers, [reciting]: "Whatever sins there may be, committed knowingly or unknowingly... (23)
"O Lord of Gods, may [all obstacles] go to dissolution through this worship, vow, and other rites of yours.
Having uttered this and bowed once more, one should then perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana). ||24||
At midday, one should cause sweet food to be offered to the deity;
in the evening, at the onset of night, one should perform worship with the sixteen excellent articles.
Then one should cause a vigil to be performed and have it celebrated by devotees;
likewise, on the twelfth day, having bathed in the morning and worshipped Keśava.
He should bestow gifts and cause various kinds of donations to be given.
And one should give many articles and so forth, as well as food and other provisions, to the preceptor. ||27||
Thus, one who performs this vow shall possess the power of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he shall be a savior of his ancestors, who were afflicted by the suffering of hundreds of generations.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this ancient tale concerning the bestowal of the fruit that grants liberation:
all the ancestors who had fallen into lower births attained salvation. (29)
In the city of Campā, there was a great king named Vaiśvānara;
later, he attained the state of a great Vaiṣṇava and became a savior of his ancestors.
That king protected all his subjects as if they were his own sons,
and many Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas resided in that city.

They were proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted to virtuous deeds and the like, prosperous, endowed with great wealth, and their subjects were likewise blessed with abundance and prosperity.
Indeed, for King Vaiśvānara, the years were full of happiness and perfectly equal,
even though he possessed a mass of merit and the austerity performed in the past.
Having obtained a vast and prosperous kingdom, the king was always possessed by the intoxication of sovereignty;
due to his nihilistic views, he performed neither religious vows nor acts of charity. (34)
He did not perform ancestral rites at all, nor did he give gifts of food, water, and so forth;
nor did he ever cause any meritorious deed to be performed.
No new merit is produced; because of that, the ancestors are distressed.
Deprived of food and water, they have descended from the world of the ancestors. (36)
Seeing their own kinsman as king, yet performing sacrificial rites such as the *śrāddha* improperly, they became exceedingly sorrowful, suffering from hot breaths and extreme weakness. (37)
Having fallen into hell due to the king's sins, such as his nihilism, they came together at night and appeared before him in a dream. (38)
Weeping and gasping, afflicted and likewise emaciated, their throats excessively parched by thirst, they were powerless and deprived of strength. (39)
Deprived of luster, with parched veins and darkened faces,
they cried out, being exceedingly poor and miserable like beggars.
Speaking to one another of their truly unbearable sufferings, they said:
"Alas! Even though he was born of our own lineage, that atheist remains established in the kingdom. (41)
He performs no ancestral rites, nor does even Vaiśvānara offer water at the proper time, not even for a moment during the fortnight of the ancestors.
He does not give food at all, nor does he give water;
he does not perform the libation at all, nor does he cause it to be performed. (43)
Tormented by that suffering, we have always been miserable;
we have all gone to a downward state and likewise fallen into hell.
"This king has become an atheist; what is the use of such a wicked son?
Better indeed is childlessness, or better still is having a son who is a believer. (45)
Even the path to liberation is better than having a bad son;
for others will certainly not give [what is needed], and a son does not even give it himself.
How, why, and from where could even a small amount of food or water be obtained?
If this person were to give us balls of rice, we would be endowed with happiness. (47)
Having spoken thus, they all vanished; the king was filled with wonder and, at dawn, related that account born of his dream to the twice-born ones.
In a dream, I saw my own fathers cast into hell, and they said: "O son, deliver us who have fallen to a low state. (49)
Seeing them speaking thus, sighing, weeping, and wailing, and remembering them, even happiness does not come to me.
Today my prosperous kingdom, as well as my queen, elephants, and horses, do not appear to grant me any happiness; even food does not please me. (51)
The sin against my son burns within me constantly; I find no pleasure in it.
What shall I do? My heart is tormented by the fire born from my father.
O best of the twice-born, where shall I go for their very salvation?
Let that austerity and vow be declared by which my ancestors may be liberated. (53)
Whether it be yoga, sacrifice, or some other great festival such as a gift-giving ceremony, or whatever else—be it great or small—that may be called a means of deliverance. (54)
If the parents suffer in a terrible hell while their son is living fit and capable, what then is the fruit of that son? (55)
In this matter, their very deliverance must be desired by me in every way;
let not the twice-born feel any hesitation, for I speak the truth. (56)
Having heard the king’s excellent words, the twice-born were then greatly delighted; those brahmins spoke to him regarding that effort for his father’s welfare which was centered upon the brahmins.
"O King, among us here is this great sage Jaigīṣavya, who is indeed capable; he understands the past and the future, for he is a master of supreme yoga.
Having perceived everything through his divine vision in meditative absorption, he [will inform you]. (58)
How will the virtuous ancestors who have gone to the lower realms quickly inform [you]? (59)
Then, having been thus entreated and having meditated upon his ancestors for a moment, the great sage Jaigīṣavya spoke there to that king.
O King, it is not merely your own nihilism that is the cause;
rather, your father's nihilism is also a cause. ||61||
Listen; I shall tell you the truth—do not be angry, but seek peace.
I know all the former deeds of your ancestors.
I shall tell you about your father; listen and be attentive.
When he was ruling the kingdom, due to his atheistic disposition, ||63||
He seized the livelihood that had been granted to your predecessor by the King;
likewise, he did not take the slightest account of the law of the scriptures.
Having attained the intoxication of sovereignty, he has turned toward unchaste women;
now, having gone to another village, he is being detained by an unchaste woman.
Even during her fertile season, you did not go to your mother's house;
nor was the righteous *ṛtudāna* given by you to your mother. (66)
Thus, having repeatedly delayed, he became heavily defiled by sin;
likewise, at the time for the ancestral rites, the śrāddha was not performed by that violator of dharma.
By the power of that evil, having caused his own ancestors to fall and having made them dwell in hell, he was filled with a state of nihilism.
Having performed the final seasonal sacrifice for you and for your mother,
he met his death in due time and fell even into hell.
Together with his ancestors, he fell into hell due to his own sin;
likewise, there was the giving of one's wife during her fertile season and sexual intercourse with an unchaste woman.
Atheism toward the ancestors and likewise the failure to perform śrāddha and other rites are the causes for the fall of the ancestors from the world of heaven and its great bliss. (71)
These very ones have fallen here and long for deliverance from their son;
yet you, though born as a son, are indeed the offspring of an atheist through the rite of impregnation.
The conduct toward a son at the time of his consecration is exactly as it was toward you, for you were born of an atheist and an unrighteous man. (73)
Therefore, you have become an atheist and do not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) at all;
O father, you were a usurper of the gods' sustenance, and this is the retribution for that. (74)
There is no atonement even for hundreds of millions of eons;
the livelihood of the gods, bestowed by kings of old, must never be taken away. (75)
Because of that sin, there is no end to suffering in hell,
even for one who has merely touched the dust of the feet of those who live by the service of the gods.
"Whoever has fallen upon this [spot] shall remain a denizen of hell for seven kalpas"—this was said previously by a Caṇḍālī woman as she walked before Mahendra. (77)
Once, a certain low-caste woman was in the cremation ground,
standing above a hearth constructed from the breast-bones of a village pig.
Holding a human skull as a cooking vessel, he places dog meat therein,
pours liquor over it, and cooks it with the fire of a funeral pyre.
Just as Mahendra emerged from that side,
the cooking vessel was quickly covered with a pair of sandals.
Then Indra, feeling apprehensive, questioned that very clever woman: "O lady with the head of a man, where is the dog's meat cooked in liquor here by the fire of the funeral pyre? (8.1)
"How is it that all this, which is indeed impure, is covered by skin?
Then that Cāṇḍālī replied: "Listen, O King of the Gods! (82)
Those who seize or cause to be seized the livelihood of the gods, the twice-born, or cows—out of fear of the dust from their feet, this [earth] has indeed been covered with hide. (83)
If you were such a person, then my cooked food would become impure;
it would not be fit for me to eat, as it would be defiled by the sin that destroys one's livelihood.
Indra asked, "How can a woman commit such a great sin?
The Cāṇḍālī replied, "Listen to my words according to the truth. (85)
The gods are indeed called the fathers, and likewise the deities are the mothers;
the gods are the givers of rain, and the gods are always the protectors. (86)
All the deities are the providers of security and well-being for the worlds;
indeed, one who destroys another's livelihood and occupation is called a slayer of life itself.
Without a livelihood there is no life; without a livelihood one becomes as if dead.
Therefore, one who seizes the livelihood of a deity is likewise a slayer of his father and a slayer of his mother.

The slayer of a cow and the slayer of a Brahmin is indeed a destroyer of the gods, a destroyer of dharma, a destroyer of the self, and a destroyer of heaven; he is a destroyer of rain and a destroyer of the world. (89)
He becomes a destroyer of gods, a destroyer of rain, and indeed a destroyer of all;
even the dust from his feet is a stain that produces great sin.
If that [food] has fallen upon dog-meat, it is not to be eaten by me, for it is indeed impure;
therefore, I have covered that vessel with a hide. (9.1)
If you are the giver and the performer for those who live like gods, then let this flesh here be purified by the dust of your feet. ||92||
"I have no fear regarding my clothing; go, O venerable one, as you please.
Even Indra, in his own assembly, [is attended] by celestial sages, ancestors, and humans.
And it was said regarding Śobhitā: "May you not become destroyers of one's livelihood.
Nowhere has an expiation ever been prescribed for one who severs a livelihood. (94)
From that time forward, the granting of livelihoods has been praised throughout the three worlds;
therefore, O King, there is indeed no other deed for you that so effectively delivers your ancestors.
By means of which their deliverance may occur even without a connection to Hari, a true connection with Hari arises through the observance of the vow alone. (96)
O Hari, by its power, this vow bestows liberation and grants liberation;
it is declared to be the refuge for those who have no other resort and the atonement for even the most heinous sinners. 97.
"Let all [the offerings] be made without water, and let the fruit be given to the ancestors;
through the merits of the vow generated by Ekādaśī, which bestows liberation, there shall be final release. (98)
Thinking, "It shall come to pass," he took all of that, honored it, and having respectfully treated the virtuous Brahmins, he announced his departure for home. ||99||
Then, when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa had arrived, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight,
the king observed a fast and performed the worship of Hari according to the prescribed rites.
Having prepared the *sarvatobhadraka* mandala, he worshipped Lord Hari on the eleventh day according to the prescribed rites and gave away abundant gifts.
He remained awake throughout the night, and likewise performed his morning ablutions and other rites;
having thus completed this meritorious act, he also offered oblations to the ancestors.
King Vaiśvānara then performed the breaking of the fast according to the prescribed rites;
by the merit of that Ekādaśī which bestows liberation, his ancestors were then [liberated].
Together with their father, they all quickly attained liberation;
and when the merit was bestowed upon the ancestors, they became gods traveling in celestial chariots.
They rained down a shower of flowers and spoke these holy words:
"May there be well-being, may there be well-being for you! We, the gods, have assembled here as your sons."
"By the gift of merit from Ekādaśī, your ancestors have been delivered; they have all attained liberation. Thus indeed did those ancestors speak to you. (106)
We have attained liberation; may it be well with you, my son.
Be happy always, and be a bestower of happiness upon all embodied beings.
Be a performer of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), a performer of sacrifices, and a worshiper of the gods; O sinless one, always be a servant of your mother and father. (108)
May you be long-lived and possessed of faith; be devoted to your wife, a provider of sustenance for the gods, and a worshiper of the Brahmins.
May you always serve the virtuous, protect the vows of the holy women, and constantly guard cows and the earth; O son, may you be prosperous at all times.
Having thus joined with such blessings, the ancestors and the gods praised the power of the merit of the vow which bestows liberation.
They departed for their respective destinations, repeatedly pronouncing blessings of well-being;
and the king also, through the power of Mokṣadā, was liberated from his sins.

He was born as a great devotee of the Lord, together with his family, always steadfast in faith; he constantly performed sacrifices and offerings, and was a worshiper of Brahmins and holy men. || 11.3 ||
He was a performer of divine worship, righteous, and free from faults;
his son was the great and virtuous Hutabhuk, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having bestowed the kingdom upon his son, he attained supreme liberation;
and Agni, whose nature is divine, remains within the bellies of all living beings.
Having indeed become a great Vaiṣṇava, he abides in the form of fire;
the sovereignty of the vow that grants liberation should be understood as bestowing the nature of that deity.
O Lakṣmī, for one who thus observes the auspicious Mokṣa Ekādaśī,
their sins are destroyed, and upon death, they shall attain liberation.
There is nothing superior to this for destroying the sins of the vajra; nor has there ever been anything that bestows liberation like the power of Nārāyaṇa. || 1.18 ||
There is no counting its merit; indeed, this vow is dear to me.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, it bestows liberation and is very dear to me.
Through both reciting and hearing it, she bestows a fruit equal to that of a religious vow;
she grants sons and prosperity, bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is my beloved.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of King Vaiśvānara and the Liberation of His Ancestors, etc., in the Ritual for the Mokṣada-Ekādaśī Vow on the Bright Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
What is the name of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, and what is its ritual procedure?
What is its fruit, who is the presiding Lakṣmī, and which deity is worshipped? Please tell me. (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the vow of the Ekādaśī of the month of Pauṣa;
I am pleased in every way by the vow of Ekādaśī.
Indeed, that [lunar day] of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa is named Saphalā;
on that day, one should worship the Lord and Master Nārāyaṇa, known as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
One should worship the one joined with Sunandā’s husband, endowed with meditative visualization;
for the worship, sage-flowers are used, and in the food offering, there are jaggery-laddus.
In this context, the offering of the *arghya* with the *amṛta-phala* fruit and the gift of gold are recommended;
likewise, the tenth and eleventh days should be observed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
And the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) must be performed according to the stated method;
indeed, it should be done in the morning on the day of the vow within the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Having placed the jar before Hari, the observer of the vow [should worship] with various fruits— namely,
coconuts, areca nuts, and citrons.
With jambīras and pomegranates, as well as auspicious dhātrī fruits, with cloves and jujubes, and especially with mangoes. || 8 ||
Wherever the attainment of a particular fruit may occur, one should worship with those very fruits;
one should perform the great worship with the sixteen secondary articles and so forth.
One should especially perform the offering of lamps during the Saphalā festival;
likewise, the gift of grain, the gift of clothing, the gift of gold, and the donation of cows.
One should perform a night vigil together with assembled Vaiṣṇavas;
for even he who performs the vigil for but a moment of the night [attains great merit].
The fruit of this is superior to that of sacrifices and equal to the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords;
it shall be a fruit even greater than the fruit of austerities performed for a thousand years.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of King Māhiṣmata of old.
Born in the Satya Yuga, they became successful through their reliance on vows. || 13 ||
On the bank of the Narmadā, in a forested region where the terrain is mostly mountainous,
lies the auspicious city of Māhiṣmatī in the middle of the southern part of Bhārata.
The kingdom of King Māhiṣmata became exceedingly great;
he had five gentle sons, all of whom were princes.
They were Dhīmān, Śrīmān, Dhṛtimān, Kīrtimān, and Śaktimān;
among them, Dhīmān was indeed the eldest, yet he became devoted to sin.
Having attained youth, he drank wine and other intoxicants, ate meat, frequented courtesans, and excessively violated the wives of others. || 17 ||
And by employing his own men to commit robbery by force in foreign kingdoms, he became a man of sinful, exceedingly wicked, corrupt, and most base conduct. (18)
Cultivating these vices— gambling, drinking, hunting, women, and meat—
he indeed squandered his father's wealth.
Through evil deeds, his jewels, gold, and other riches were exhausted;
consequently, he became hungry, filthy, and a reviler of the Vedas.
Asabha was a reviler of the Brahmins and of the dharma of the virtuous;
he became especially a reviler of the Vaiṣṇavas and the gods. (21)
For he constantly causes calamity for the subjects in every way, like a piśāca; therefore, the one named Lumbhaka has been summoned by the king. (22)
Indeed, Lumbhaka was abandoned by his father and all his kinsmen, and he was driven out from the kingdom by the subjects through beatings and other such means. ||23||
Wherever that miser goes, he meets with contempt;
he finds no happiness, and no one shows him respect. (24)
Deprived of wealth and having lost his vitality, he was even cast out by the courtesan;
wandering among the trees of the forest, he himself was afflicted by hunger and thirst. (25)
He endured that most terrible and formidable suffering, which was indeed the very nature of his asceticism;
thereafter, he repeatedly felt remorse for the actions he had performed for his own sake.
I have been abandoned by my kinsmen, my father, and my subjects, as well as by my courtesan;
I have been expelled from the kingdom and despised by everyone. (27)
In this matter, dwelling in the forest is better than an enmity that does not subside;
indeed, I slay my enemies only for the sake of bringing that enmity to an end.
I shall utterly destroy my father’s entire city; I shall demolish the palaces and seize the wealth and other possessions. (29)
This supreme wealth must be taken away very gradually;
one must dwell in a hidden forest so that I do not fall into his hands.
Having thus formed an evil intent, he dwelt in a dreadful, dense forest,
constantly delighting in the slaughter of living beings and being cruel through theft, violence, and other such acts.
And dwelling there at night, he would go into the city and, having slain many people with weapons, [seize] abundant wealth, grain, and clothing.
He used to lead [people] into the great forest, devouring them and rejoicing repeatedly;
by that man of sinful conduct, the entire city was plundered.
Great terror prevailed continuously among the people, as merchants and common folk were suddenly and forcibly robbed of their wealth. (34)
In some places he acted deviously, even killing those who were still alive;
once, he entered the house of the king’s minister.
By him much wealth was taken away, as well as food was eaten;
likewise, women were enjoyed and children were beaten. (36)
His house was set ablaze and a great calamity was wrought;
meanwhile, the king’s soldiers, who were like night-stalkers, arrived there. ||37||
Seized, bound in fetters, and held by his hands with reins,
he said to them, "I am indeed the son of King Māhiṣmata."
"I alone must be released here; otherwise, there will be no happiness for you.
I shall take away your lives and destroy you with my weapons. (39)
"I shall surely bring about the destruction of you who desire wealth, wives, and homes;
a king's son must never be detained by those who seek their own pleasure. (1.240.40)
Neither a serpent nor a brahmin nor a kṣatriya should ever be provoked;
for they indeed bring about the fruit of destruction, whereas protectors are always to be bowed down to. 41.
Having heard this, he was released by them and went back into the forest;
there he remained, constantly eating meat and consuming the fruits of trees.
He sustains his life by means of roots and the like;
likewise, living in the forest, he maintains his livelihood even through theft.
In that forest, there was an ancient and deserted abode of Viṣṇu, located at the base of an Aśvattha tree, its walls having crumbled away. (44)
There, with this broken image of Viṣṇu, the altar had its gates destroyed, its halls destroyed, its shade destroyed, and was left without support. 45.
It was accepted for the sake of a dwelling, and here rest is obtained;
even the holy fig tree is ancient, with its many-year-old trunk and gnarled branches. (46)
Indeed, by virtue of its divine nature and through the yoga of Viṣṇu, this tree exists;
for, due to the residence there of the Lumbhaka and the majesty of the goddess’s abode. (47)
But the Buddhist, having become sattvic in nature, reflected deeply:
"Alas! I have committed many sins for which there is no atonement. (48)
Moreover, I must not commit violence that takes the life of living beings;
instead, taking refuge at the Pippala tree, I shall sustain myself by eating roots and other such things. (49)
And Viṣṇu himself dwells here in this form upon the Pippala tree; he will bring about my welfare and will burn away my sin.
Having thus resolved his mind, even during the cold season,
he passed the night with great hardship on the ground, taking refuge at the base of a tree trunk.
Just then, other forest-dwelling thieves arrived there during the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa and plundered Lumbhaka’s clothes and other belongings.
On the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, at the very break of dawn, he gathered some fruits and somehow managed to eat them; thus the day passed.
But at night, an unexpected cold fell, thick with frost, such that there was no protection even by means of heating with fire. ||54||
Thus, he indeed became a victim of the cold current;
stripped of clothing, with rolling eyes and a closing mouth, he became senseless. (55)
The pleasure of sleep was destroyed, and he became like one whose life-breath had departed;
his mouth, teeth, and tongue were pressed together, and his hands and feet were paralyzed. (56)
Then he was born like a corpse, tormented by cold;
yet his life-breaths had not departed, for he remained devoid of movement. (57)
Even though he was born at dawn on a fruitful Ekādaśī, he nevertheless remembered Viṣṇu, his protector, again and again within himself.
Even at the rising of the sun, he, chilled and drenched, did not regain consciousness;
only when the sun had reached the meridian did that Lumbhaka regain his senses.
Looking here and there, he indeed rose up from that state;
having bowed to Viṣṇu, the tree, and the sun, he went into the forest, stumbling with his feet.
Moving slowly like one with a lame leg, emaciated by hunger and devoid of strength, he gathered excellent fruits even while his limbs were trembling. (6.1)
"Having reflected that these must first be offered to Viṣṇu and only then taken by me," he approached, placed them at the foot of a tree, and [sat down]. (62)
While the extremely weak Luṃbaka remained beneath the tree, the sun set; at that time, he indeed lamented in great distress. (63)
Shedding tears, what state will be mine?
The cold oppresses me completely, and there will be no protection from leaves.
There was no thick bark garment or the like to ward off the cold; there was neither a cave nor even a mat of grass to be found here. ||65||
"Nevertheless, I shall sleep here, making my bed upon this heap of grass.
Having thought thus, he was eager to gather grass nearby. (66)
Having placed the fruits near the image of Viṣṇu, one should recite:
"May Hari, the Lord of Śrī, be pleased with these fruits. (67)
Then he went very close for the purpose of fetching grass;
however, having lost his strength, he remained near the altar. (68)
He fell into a swoon once more, remembering Nārāyaṇa;
then, rising after a moment, he took some *pippala* grass.
As soon as he himself came and sat upon the base of the pillar,
fainting occurred once more, and then he regained consciousness.
Remembering Viṣṇu, that thief found no restful sleep;
he passed the night thinking only, "In the morning I shall eat fruits. (7.1)
Thus, having arrived there helplessly and being unaware that it was the day of his vow, he observed the fast and kept the night vigil, though afflicted by the cold. (72)
Keśava considered the worship with those fruits to be his offering of food,
and Viṣṇu likewise considered the keeping of the night vigil for that evil-minded man.
Viṣṇu, who is compassionate and affectionate toward the distressed, considered the vow of Saphalā as well as the penance born from her own refuge to be complete; thus, he attained a state of grace.
He made the fortune of Lumbhaka abundant in merit, eternal, and auspicious;
indeed, that Lumbhaka had undertaken this very vow quite spontaneously.
Then, on the morning of the twelfth day, having eaten fruits before Hari,
he offered praise to the Lord for protection from the cycle of worldly existence.
Until the rising of the sun, Viṣṇu appeared before him in his four-armed form as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Richly endowed with the beauty of divine limbs, adorned with divine ornaments, and graced by the splendor of a divine countenance bright with smiles and playful gestures; ||78||
Touching that *lumbha* with his right hand, he said over her head:
"O devotee, you shall obtain a kingdom through the power of Saphalā. (79)
"Go to your own city; there your father has met his end.
Other sons will contend with one another for the consecration."
Mutually opposed and deprived of the crown of sovereignty, they did not obtain the kingdom, being unauthorized by both the ministers and the subjects. ||81||
Your subjects await your arrival for the increase of their fortune;
this time has come again for you through the arising of the fruit of Ekādaśī.
By those very same things by which one was previously struck down and humiliated through the force of time, one is now desired; oh, how great is the power of time! (83)
Great suffering arises from the loss of fortune, whereas happiness occurs when fortune rises;
the rise of fortune is produced by [auspicious] conduct and the like, and that indeed must be practiced. (84)
"Therefore, go to your own kingdom and take possession of it; do not delay.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished right there.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu at the Pippala tree, Lumbhaka indeed obtained splendor;
possessing a divine form and nature, he returned to his own city. ||86||
Honored by the ministers and the leaders of the people, and greeted with cries of welcome,
the Vaiṣṇava was then adorned with the splendor of divine ornaments.
Having become [the king], he obtained the royal consecration inherited through his ancestral lineage by the grace of Hari and by means of the fruitful observance of his vow.
By the dawning of his fortune, that king obtained a kingdom free from thorns;
he made that auspicious kingdom prosperous through the performance of duties such as protecting and guarding the subjects. (89)
Having ruled that kingdom for a hundred years and likewise propitiated Hari,
he received the blessing of his subjects and [installed] his son named Mānajit.
Having consecrated [his son] in the kingdom, he departed for the forest where [the sage] formerly resided;
and having propitiated Viṣṇu there, he constructed a temple for Viṣṇu. (91)
Having installed an image of Hari and served it daily in that manner,
one should exhaust the latent tendencies within by means of austerity and the equilibrium of yoga.
He went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa by means of a brilliantly radiant celestial chariot,
while the attendants of Hari held him there in that chariot.
They went to the divine abode of Hari, reaching which one no longer grieves;
in that very realm known as Goloka, King Lumbhaka indeed resided.
He who performs this supreme vow in this world in such a manner constantly serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa, being honored by his personal attendants. 95.
Having attained happiness in this world, one who dies shall obtain liberation;
blessed are those men in the world who perform their vows with success.
But for those by whom this vow has been performed with true devotion, their birth is fruitful, and their wealth and other possessions are likewise fruitful. (97)
The Saphala-ekādaśī bestows the fruit in the form of royal fortune and grants liberation; therefore, it should be observed by those who desire both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (98)
By reciting it, by hearing it, and likewise by performing the vow, a human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 99 ||
The observer of the vow obtains sons, grandsons, wealth, prosperity, fortune, and even sovereignty;
as well as knowledge, nourishment, health, and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Fruitful Ekādaśī Vow in the Dark Half of Pauṣa and the Narrative of the Attainment of the Kingdom by the Prince Lumbhaka, the Son of King Pāpi," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you, the ancient Supreme Person!
[Tell me of] that auspicious vow which grants liberation to living beings and bestows its fruit.
By hearing this, indeed, the heaps of sins are set ablaze;
it is the auspicious Ekādaśī that occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
Please tell me out of grace: what is its name, what is the procedure, which deity is worshipped there, and what is considered the fruit thereof? (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved, for the sake of the welfare and benefit of the worlds, I shall describe that Ekādaśī known as Putradā, which occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
This [vow], which removes all sins, should be performed with effort by devotees;
it is called Sānandā, and it bestows the joy of sons.
Nārāyaṇa, together with Padmā, is the presiding deity here;
he is the one to be worshipped, the god who bestows all perfections and fulfills the desire for a son.
He should worship with guggulu flowers and other seasonal blossoms,
and he should offer powdered sweets as a food offering (naivedya) to the Supreme Self.
One should offer the arghya water, pomegranate fruit, and other fruits as well;
likewise, a jar filled with ghee should be offered to the Lord of Śrī Padmā.
Furthermore, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given, especially in the form of gold;
on the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat only at night and sleep upon the ground.
On the eleventh lunar day, having risen during the Brahma-hour, one should remember Hari;
having bathed and gathered the articles for worship, one should worship Hari.
Having placed [the deity] in a worthy vessel, one should bathe the Lord of the gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) or with water, and then clothe him in garments and ornaments.
One should smear it with substances, perfumes, and the like, and beautify it with flower garlands;
one should worship it with the full array of incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and flowers.
One should offer food offerings such as sweet delicacies and drinks such as water;
one should propitiate [the deity] with the waving of lights, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and so forth. || 13 ||
For the sake of the vow, she should pray again and again to the god Nārāyaṇa:
"O Giver of Sons, I am performing this vow; may it reach completion. (14)
Having thus made this request, one should then prepare an auspicious mandala;
indeed, the Sarvatobhadra mandala should be constructed there, and a water-pot (ghaṭa) should be placed within it.
On a raised platform, one should place a vessel filled with auspicious sesame seeds along with sprouts and other offerings; upon that, the image of Hari should likewise be placed.
Having established [the image], one should worship the Lord with sixteen articles;
then, one should offer the waving of lights (ārātrika) and a handful of flowers. || 17 ||
One should pray for the attainment of the fruit and likewise cause gifts to be given;
at midday as well, one should offer worship, food offerings, and so forth. || 18 ||
Furthermore, after evening, one should perform a distinguished worship,
and likewise observe a vigil on the twelfth day in that same manner.

The observer of the vow should perform worship and the gift of material objects; thereafter, he should feed the people, the twice-born, the virtuous, and the virtuous women, and then himself partake of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
One should indeed complete the vow, and the fruit—liberation and so forth—shall come to pass;
for that person who performs this very vow with devotion shall obtain sons and wealth. (21)
Through the grace of Śrī Hari, the observer of the vow shall obtain auspicious sons, daughters, elephants, cattle, horses, grain, fields, and so forth, and shall also attain liberation.
In this regard, listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall relate to you a narrative that bestows the fruit of sons and daughters, grants the attainment of one's own prosperity, and provides supreme happiness. (23)
In a former age, in the city named Bhadrāvatī in Saurāṣṭra, there was a king named Ketumān, and his queen was named Cumpā.
And although the king had reached extreme old age, no son was born to him; therefore, being childless, the monarch grieved day after day. (25)
Time passed, yet he had no hope even for his own wife to bear a son;
they both contemplated performing acts of charity and worship that would grant them a son. (26)
And whatever various [deeds] have been performed, just as they were shown by the brahmins, so too has that manifold auspicious work been proclaimed and accomplished in many ways by many. ||27||
Then the king obtained no son at all to continue his lineage;
he thought, "What shall I do? Where shall I go? Old age is seen before me. (28)
In some way, even at the final hour, let there be the attainment of a son.
Having thus resolved, the king should again employ skillful means. ||29||
She approaches virtuous people who are renowned in many places and endowed with power, and she accepts their blessings;
yet those blessings become fruitless.
Suketumān found no happiness in his kingdom nor in his realm;
he remained constantly and exceedingly distressed, as if with a virtuous wife who was always absent.
Furthermore, whatever water and other offerings are given by those two, whether out of anxiety or grief,
all the ancestors partake of them while they are still lukewarm during the śrāddha rite.
"Ketumān has died; we see no one born in our lineage for our funeral libations. What can we do? Who will offer us satisfaction? (33)
Thus, all the ancestors go forth in this way, suffering and devoid of happiness;
nor do their kinsmen, friends, ministers, or counselors [follow them]. (34)
Friends, subjects, male servants, female servants, prosperities, and elephants—
even in a dream— bring only suffering to this king.
The mind of that sonless man is perpetually unsettled and tormented by despair; this is true both here in this world and even for a king there in the next. (36)
For a wealthy ruler of a kingdom, there is indeed no fruit of birth;
for one without a son, the house, the wife, and prosperity appear as mere emptiness. (37)
Without a son, one is not released from the debt owed to the ancestors, the gods, and the sages;
by obtaining a legitimate son, one attains freedom from that debt to the fathers and the deities.
In this world one gains fame, and in the next world an auspicious rebirth;
therefore, a person should produce a son through a son. (39)
But for those who perform meritorious deeds, a son is born who always bestows happiness;
he is the increaser of longevity, health, prosperity, wealth, and grain. (1.241.40)
Without the grace of Hari and likewise without merit, the birth of a son indeed does not occur;
nor is there attainment of the worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds without a son. (41)
A son is declared to be great wealth; indeed, a son is called prosperity.
A son is said to be one's home, and even a son is celebrated in the worlds as a true kinsman. (42)
Without learning there is no social connection, nor without that is there the status of a householder;
without that there is no fame in the world, and without that there is no expenditure of one's own voice. 43.
Day and night, the king himself reflects and finds no peace;
yet if I bring about my own destruction, through that self-slaughter there will be an exceedingly miserable rebirth. (44)
In this world, even fasting leads to cries of "Alas! and miserable rebirths;
therefore, having reflected thus day and night, what should be done by me? (45)
Thinking that the emaciation of the body through austerity was better, he, with a steady mind,
mounted his horse at night and went alone into the forest.
Neither his subjects nor his wife and household knew [of him];
they were filled with anxiety, wondering, "Where has this great king gone? (47)
Overwhelmed by anxiety and extreme suffering, they set out indeed in search of him;
seeing the tracks left by the horse's hooves, they proceeded through the forest, looking again and again. 48.
When the hoof-prints of the horses were not seen upon the ground in a place of very thick grass, then they [turned] toward their own city.
Grief and anxiety came upon them, and they dispatched their dependents into the forest to search for him; yet even by them, the king was not found.
From one forest to another, and from that even to a more dense forest, the king entered further and further into regions frequented by lions and elephants. (51)
By the power of fortune, the king was not slain by any of the hunters;
nor did even the horse meet its death, for it lived on through the turn of fate. (52)
Beholding forest trees—banyans, wood-apples, kadambas, jackfruit, mangoes, dates, peepals, and golden champakas. (193)
Likewise, he beheld palm trees, sarja trees, tamāla trees, sūtilaka trees, banyan trees, bakula trees, saptaparṇa trees, and tamarind trees. (54)
Iṅgudī trees, badarīs, jambūs, and karamardakas; bamboo, aśokas, plantains, nāryaṅgas, and coconuts. ||55||
Beholding lions, deer, and birds, as well as fires, swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, bakas, yaks, cows, and hares, he went through the formidable forest.
And tigers, bears, jackals, horned deer, and porcupines;
elephants, gayals, wild buffaloes, and likewise serpents. ||57||
Beholding embodied beings such as he had never seen before, filled with wonder,
he heard the cries of owls, jackals, bears, deer, and other animals.
Eating wild flowers and fruits, the king proceeded;
then, becoming thirsty with his throat and neck parched, he reflected. (59)
Following the cries of the birds, he searched for a reservoir of water;
there he beheld a beautiful lake of divine water, naturally formed.
It is renowned as Aśvapaṭṭa, situated to the east of Mount Raivata;
it is adorned with fish, crocodiles, and other aquatic creatures, and filled with lotuses.
Upon seeing it adorned with swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, and anala-birds, he experienced supreme bliss.
The king, eager to drink water, departed in haste;
at that moment, his auspicious right eye, hand, and chest throbbed.
In the water, he beheld the divine gods who were performing their ablutions;
having gone there, he dismounted from his horse and, moving forward, bowed down to them.
He bowed down individually to those gods in the form of sages,
who were chanting the prayers of Śrī Hari and whose bodies were emaciated by their vows.
With palms joined in reverence, he became choked with emotion and prostrated himself like a staff;
then, bathed by their blessings, the king questioned those gods.
"Who are you, sirs, who have come here to bathe in this waterless, desolate wilderness where no human being dwells? (67)
Let them speak here according to the truth, so that there may be welfare for me as well;
for the sight of the virtuous is indeed considered to be for the destruction of the suffering of those who suffer. (68)
Thus questioned, those gods spoke to him whose fortune was now favorable:
"O King, we are the Viśvedevas, gods who dwell in heaven. (69)
The sages themselves arrived for the purpose of bathing during the Putradā vow;
today is indeed the Ekādaśī known by the name Putradā.
"We have come from Mount Raivata to bathe here at this sacred ford;
having bathed, we shall go to heaven, for today there is indeed a great vow. (71)
"How have you come to this desolate and dense forest?
Having heard of it, the king was exceedingly delighted, even though he was suffering from hunger and thirst. (72)
Considering the water to be pleasant to himself, he did not drink it at all;
rather, he regarded his vow as naturally resulting in the attainment of the fruit of a son. (73)
The king said to those sages: "Indeed, being childless, I have performed many meritorious deeds out of a desire for a son; nevertheless, I have not obtained a son. (74)
Then, my limbs overwhelmed with grief, I arrived here for the sake of penance;
out of compassion for you, I shall perform penance here for the sake of a son. (75)
Then the sages said, "O King, because of your vow to grant a son, this merit that brings about the attainment of a son has arisen for you; do not perform further penance. (76)
One should keep a vigil at night and, having worshipped Keśava in the morning,
perform the breaking of the fast with water as well as with leaves, flowers, and other offerings.
"By means of these, you shall have a son who will become a lord of men;
thus it shall be through the power of destiny and likewise by the performance of this vow. (78)
Having received the blessings of the gods, he returned home;
in due time the queen conceived, and a most fortunate son was born. (79)
That lord of men became a long-lived protector of his subjects;
and because of him, Saurāṣṭra was known by the name Kaṅka, as if it were made of saffron (kuṅkuma).
His kingdom became renowned and his lineage indeed became devoted to Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, the Putrada Ekādaśī vow should be observed.
And for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, this has been told by me to you;
those people here who shall perform this auspicious vow, O daughter, [shall obtain their desires].
Having obtained sons in this world, they shall indeed go to heaven after death;
[they obtain] wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and even long life. (83)
By performing this vow, people will certainly obtain a beautiful wife, a gentle husband, fertile fields, and the greatest prosperity. (84)
O Lakṣmī, from the recitation, hearing, and likewise the remembrance of this, there shall arise the fruit of obtaining a son as well as the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (85)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of King Ketumān’s Son Obtained through the Greatness of the Pauṣa Śukla Ekādaśī Vrata," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Mahāviṣṇu, O Hari, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Master! Having bestowed your supreme grace, please speak [of the rites] during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
What is the name of Ekādaśī, and who is its presiding lord? What is the ritual procedure, what is the fruit, and what are the specific gifts that should be given? (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved, the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha is known as Ṣaṭtilā;
its presiding deity is Vāsudeva together with his consort Śrī.
He should be worshipped with land-lotuses and tender water-lilies; as for the food offering, there should be *ghṛtapūra* cakes, and the respectful gift (*arghya*) should consist of grapes.
Woolen garments, blankets, and the like should be given with devotion;
as well as food prepared with fenugreek, beans, sweetmeats, and meals consisting of black-gram cakes.
Other substances that provide nourishment and cooling garments should likewise be given during acts such as worship and offerings.
Pulastya previously told Dālbhya that the Tila-deyā is proclaimed as the destroyer of all sins; its vow bestows happiness.
Those humans who, though endowed with youth, are emaciated by the suffering of poverty and commit sins for the sake of a livelihood, being indeed powerless; (8)
The killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a child, the killing of a woman, the slaughter of cows and so forth, as well as violence, the theft of another's property, and vices; || 9 ||
Non-attachment to one's own wife, the destruction of another's prosperity, forcibly inflicting suffering, reviling gurus, and falsehoods; 1.242.10.
Livelihood through wicked deeds, the selling of daughters, mixing undesirable substances into flavors, treachery, and deception; || 11 ||
Whatever such evils as these arise among men from passion, this vow is the means for their destruction.
The form of the Tiladaikādaśī, which burns away all sins,
is a powerful vow performed during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
One should purify the inner self of a living being and likewise wash away their sins;
there is no other vow such as this that so swiftly cleanses a creature.
One who observes the Māgha vow should eat only one meal on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, and thereafter should sleep upon the bare ground at night. || 15 ||
On the eleventh lunar day known as Brāhma, one should remain celibate;
having risen during that hour, one should remember Nārāyaṇa within the heart.
One should likewise take up the names of the most excellent, virtuous, and devoted Sātvatas,
and perform the worship of Hari’s names for even a moment.
Having struck the cymbals and repeatedly called to mind the Form, [he said]:
"O Hari, O Rāma, O Dark as a Rain-cloud, O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, O Master! (18)
"I am yours forever; O bestower of liberation, abide in me, your devotee.
Having thus praised [the deity], one should then go outside for the purpose of purification.
Having performed purification with earth and water, one should perform gargles;
then the observer of the vow should thoroughly rub the body with sesame powder.
Then, chanting the names of Hari, one should bathe with water mixed with sesame seeds;
one should also perform an oblation of sesame seeds and likewise drink water mixed with sesame seeds.

One should perform the gift of sesame seeds and practice the consumption of sesame; one should bathe with sesame, rub oneself with sesame, offer oblations of sesame, and drink water infused with sesame. (22)
The giver of sesame and the eater of sesame—these six types of sesame destroy sin;
for as long as the shoots of sesame grow, and as long as there are branches and sesame seeds, [so long does the merit endure].
For so many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world;
black sesame seeds are considered excellent for bathing, giving, and worship. (24)
Having bathed, the observer of the vow should worship Vāsudeva, joined by Śrī, with sixteen new articles at the very dawn of day.
And while offering a handful of flowers, one should pray: "O Lord, I shall perform the *śaṭtilā-vrata*; may it be free from obstacles and grant me its fruit. (26)
By even a single drop of your grace, may my vows be brought to completion;
indeed, may lust, anger, ego, greed, malice, and the like never be mine.
Having thus entreated the guru, bowed to him, and likewise remembered Śrī Hari,
the observer of the vow should have the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala prepared in the morning.
In the center of that, one should place an excellent vessel made of gold or copper, filled with water containing five types of sprouts, excellent gems, and other auspicious substances. ||29||
One should place it there, wrap it with cloth and also with thread, and then worship it; thereafter, one should place upon it black sesame seeds.
One should place a cooking vessel there and install a golden image of Vāsudeva, accompanied by his beloved Śrī and sixty thousand sesame seeds.
One should bathe her with ablutions using the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
and one should provide her with garments, ornaments, and other decorations.
With colored powders, saffron, fermented rice-gruel, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and garlands;
with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel leaves, and fine fruits. ||33||
With *kūṣmāṇḍa*, coconut, *amṛta*, and *bījapūraka* fruits, and with circumambulations, prostrations like a staff, salutations, hymns of praise, and so forth. ||34||
One should worship Śrī Vāsudeva and seek forgiveness again and again;
one should offer the food oblation for him to eat and present sweet water to drink.
One should offer betel leaf prepared with camphor, fragrance, cardamom, cinnamon, and cloves.
A couch with its accessories, as well as a mirror and a fan. ||36||
One should devoutly offer a yak-tail whisk and clusters of flowers;
then, having performed the lustration ceremony nine times, one should bow down to Keśava.
One should perform one's own worldly affairs in such a way that they do not indeed cause an obstacle to the vow;
at midday, one should offer to Hari sweet, auspicious, and excellent food.
One should offer water, fruit, a betel-roll for cleansing the mouth, fragrant essence, richly scented land-lotus, and arka-water. (39)
In the evening as well, the observer of the vow should properly perform the worship of Hari;
he should conduct all the rites such as the waving of lamps (ārātrika) and also provide the meal.
Ten days prior [to the festival], the observer of the vow himself bathes;
then that observer of the vow collects cow dung that has not fallen upon the ground.
Having scattered sesame seeds, one should have cotton balls made,
numbering one hundred and eight, until they become dry.
