Then, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, under the asterism of Mūla or Ārdrā,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) at night while reciting the names of Hari three times.
One should keep a vigil at night and have the verses of Viṣṇupadī sung;
having risen early on the twelfth day and bathed, one should perform worship.
One should offer gifts consisting of sixteen kinds of objects to the venerable Guru: a water-pot, a golden image, and coins made of gold and silver. (45)
May Hari be pleased with me as I offer sesame seeds, a bed, garments, grains, and juices, along with an umbrella, sandals, and bowls. (46)
A black cow and a vessel filled with sesame seeds should be given;
the offering here is said to be presented to the preceptor or to a Brahmin who maintains a family.
In heaven and other realms, food, drink, and so forth are obtained through the gift of sesame seeds;
even in liberation, eternal satisfaction arises for one who partakes in emancipation. (48)

If all that was to be done has been performed, yet the gift of food and the offering of sesame seeds have not been made, then in the hereafter everything will be met with; however, from that [failure], food itself will never be obtained.
Sesame, rice, and other such items should be given; indeed, everything should be given—whatever is required here, including women, sons, houses, and gardens.
Gardens, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, goats, and the like; as well as vehicles, celestial chariots, and household utensils. ||51||
In this world, the means for great loss are the pursuit of dharma, wealth, desire, and so forth, as well as golden ornaments, foods, and various kinds of drinks. (52)
On the attainment of Ekādaśī, various objects of sight, things to be enjoyed, pleasant things to be heard, and diverse gifts should be given. (53)
Those merits shall indeed be obtained hereafter multiplied a hundred thousandfold;
therefore, one who observes the Ekādaśī should especially give these gifts. (54)
Listen now to a hair-raising story concerning this matter from the east:
long ago, in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a virtuous Brāhmaṇa woman named Kapilā.
That maiden was possessed of knowledge, devoted to the life of celibacy, endowed with self-knowledge, and always delighted in the worship of the gods. (56)
Abounding in the desire for fruits such as heaven, she remained without possessions;
her body was indeed emaciated by fasts and virtuous vows.
Whatever is acquired— such as houses and the like through learning, knowledge,
and so forth— all that is offered as a gift to a worthy recipient at an auspicious time.
Likewise, [it is given] to the gods, to Brahmins, to young maidens, and to the virtuous.
Bestowing houses upon virtuous women established in Brahman,
that great chaste lady, providing various other articles of utility,
always remains engaged in the worship of the gods with a desire for happiness.
Pervaded by excessive craving and great delusion due to her very nature as a woman,
she practices self-knowledge yet does not abandon her desire for pleasure;
knowing that food is easily obtained, she does not give food to a mendicant.
The virtuous were not satisfied, nor were the children fed;
indeed, everything else was given away, but not even a grain of food was given. Not even a single alms-offering was given to a mendicant, due solely to a trace of ignorance. (62–63)
Once, a profound thought occurred to me regarding that devotee of mine, whose intellect was pure; for her body, through various difficult vows, had undoubtedly been purified,
and Lord Hari had been worshipped by her repeatedly with many offerings.
The world of Viṣṇu is indeed honored through the physical mortification of this reality.
Everything auspicious has been performed with desire by means of this practice of desire;
for her sake there is heaven, but not for her here at any time.
Indeed, no gift of food was made by you, having disregarded its priceless value;
consequently, no food will be available for her in the heavenly worlds.
Through the gift of food, one indeed attains edible nectar in heaven;
for that which is given is obtained there by which supreme satisfaction comes to pass. (68)
Therefore, for the sake of the happiness of my own devotee, I must by all means beg for food there in the form of a mendicant. (69)
"She will give me food; she shall obtain the fruit of that in heaven.
O Lakṣmī, having reflected thus, I have come to the world of mortals.
In the form of the venerable Kapila, I went to that house for the sake of alms;
I requested alms, saying, "Lady, give me alms. (71)
At midday, she became occupied with the worship of my image;
then, perceiving an obstacle to the worship, she abandoned the fruit of her alms. (72)
And due to the force of my anger, at that time I did not say anything at all;
yet once more I said to her, "O beautiful one, give me alms. (73)
Due to the grace of worship, the clay from there—along with the tulasī—was taken and, being naturally moistened by water, formed into the shape of a funeral cake (piṇḍa). ||74||
Then, out of great anger, she threw a lump of clay into my copper vessel; not even a tiny bit of food was given by her. (75)
I begged for food in her name, yet she did not give it to me;
moreover, by giving me insults and the like, she drove me out. (76)
I have gone to my own Vaikuṇṭha; that female ascetic died in due course of time, having attained [this state] through the power of her celibacy and her gifts of houses and other such acts.
Having become a goddess, she went to heaven, honored by the goddesses in the celestial realm;
she obtained the fruit of giving a lump of clay and attained an auspicious home.
He beheld a divine house, filled with every prosperity yet devoid of heaps of grain; no food whatsoever was to be seen. (79)
Having departed from that house, she came to my palace;
indeed, she went to that second Vaikuṇṭha of mine which exists upon the waters.
Through the power of her celibacy, that Kapilā was like the sun;
yet, possessed by anger, she said to me: "Why is there no food in my house? (8.1)
A magnificent palace devoid of food was obtained by me in the divine Triviṣṭapa, where there is no nectar whatsoever, and neither solid food nor drink exists. (82)
"How am I to live in this great heaven, the abode of enjoyments?
Therefore, O Lord Mahāviṣṇu, grant food to me, your devotee. (83)
"Otherwise, I shall not remain in this house which is like a cremation ground. And I told her then: 'Food has never been given by you to him. (84)
It was not offered by me to Brahmins, nor to the virtuous, nor even to chaste women; rather, it was for the sake of alms that a lump of clay was requested from you and offered by you. (85)
Or is it not remembered, O virtuous lady? That fruit is not obtained from mere food;
what is performed and given in the land of action, its fruit is obtained in heaven. (86)
"Since food was indeed not offered by you, how could you attain heaven?
Nevertheless, you are my devotee and must always be favored by me. (87)
"From the gift of this earth, may alms-food be the fruit for you; indeed, may even this earth always become food in the form of grain, so that you may eat the fruit of immortality. (88)
By you, through various vows, rigorous penances, and numerous fasts, as well as through worship, I have been honored; the fruit of that is this nectar in your home. (89)
"O beloved, let my house never be empty of you;
go to heaven, for those filled with curiosity long to see you anew."
The goddesses who perform the Ṣaṭtilā vow will arrive;
you must not open the door, but remain out of sight. (9.1)
If they are insistent on seeing you, then those goddesses should be told: "If you desire to see him, [then wait]. (92)
"Give me the merit of six sesame seeds performed by you in the past;
I shall open the door so that you may see me, the beloved of Hari. (93)
The merit arising from that Ṣaṭtilaikādaśī, which had been bestowed by them, was then opened; consequently, the beloved of Hari was seen by them.
Neither among the goddesses, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Asuras, nor the Pannagas, nor among any others in heaven, was there a divine being such as Kapilā. (95)
O Mahālakṣmī, through her union with Hari, she became your equal in heaven;
endowed with beauty and splendor, she is a Vaiṣṇavī and my beloved. (96)
By the acquisition of six sesame seeds, a palace filled with the nectar of food appeared instantly; indeed, nothing greater than this occurred elsewhere at that time. (97)
The mansion was fully furnished, obtained through the merit of six sesame seeds;
it was filled with wealth, grain, fine garments, and the like, as well as gold, silver, and other riches. (98)
And she was enjoyed by that Kapilā until the end of the kalpa; thereafter, at the time of the eternal dissolution, Kapilā entered my abode. 99.
There, my beloved, in the form of Ramā, became four-armed;
she, your friend, attends upon me with extreme devotion due to her service to me.

Therefore, whatever has been performed by those who have directly undertaken this supreme vow of the six sesame seeds—what is there that they do not obtain? Everything shall be attained by them in every way. (101)
By my yoga, the observer of the *tiladā* vow shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth, nor should greed ever be entertained.
O noble lady, every kind of gift that ought to be given shall be obtained once it has been bestowed;
according to one's own wealth, one should cause sesame seeds and grains to be given.
He who gives clothing, food, vehicles, conveyances, houses, water,
and necessary implements in this life obtains freedom from disease in the next world.
Through fasting on the Ṣaṭtilā day, a devotee shall not fall into poverty, nor suffering, nor misfortune, nor emptiness, nor shall he suffer division. 105.
Therefore, one should undertake the vow and the gift of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rule;
thus one is liberated from sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation.
O Dear One, whoever should hear this, or cause it to be heard, or recite it,
shall obtain the merit arising from the Ṣaṭtilā vow.
Nothing inauspicious that causes obstruction remains here or in the next world;
the Brahmin shall attain merit, and the Kṣatriya shall attain victory.
A Vaiśya shall attain abundance of wealth, and another shall enjoy supreme happiness;
one who seeks dharma attains dharma, and one who seeks desire obtains a woman.
One seeking wealth obtains wealth; one seeking a son shall rejoice in a virtuous son; and one obtains vast fame as well as preeminence among kinsmen. (1.242.11)
Having obtained unshakable prosperity, he shall attain the highest good;
his fear is destroyed, and he gains splendor and valor.
A woman who has fulfilled the vow of the six sesame seeds shall delight her beloved husband and obtain sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, and unbroken good fortune.
Having obtained sensual pleasure here, she rejoices as a goddess in heaven;
and having become Ramā, the consort of Viṣṇu, she delights upon the couches of Hari.
And then in Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, she eternally enjoys the pleasures of youth with her own husband, Kṛṣṇa-Hari.
There is no other vow equal to that of Ṣaṭtilā which bestows such happiness;
it was performed by Padmā in the past, and you, O Lakṣmī, are indeed she for me.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Māgha-Kṛṣṇa-Ṣaṭtila-Ekādaśī Vow, and How through the Merit of that Vow Kapilā Nārī Attained the Status of a Goddess and the State of Ramā," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O ocean of mercy, O bringer of liberation to the world!
Out of your grace, please tell me about the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha.
What is the procedure, what is the presiding deity here, and what is the fruit of this vow?
Furthermore, please describe the concluding rite (udyāpana) which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the observer of the vow.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; on the bright fortnight of Māgha, there is a day named Jayā, which bestows great merit, destroys sins, grants liberation, fulfills desires, and bestows happiness.
The auspicious Ekādaśī is declared to be observed by one who has taken a vow;
it destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin and eliminates states such as being a Piśāca.
It bestows all prosperity upon kings, grants victory in battle, confers triumph in heaven, and secures victory in worldly affairs. || 5 ||
In whatever task it is performed, that [mantra] is considered to yield the fruit of victory;
its fruit is declared to grant victory to those traveling through the three worlds.
For this reason, O Lakṣmī, she should be worshipped with great effort by oneself on the tenth day, either by eating only one meal or by eating only at night.
While maintaining the journey of the body, one should sleep on the ground at night;
and having risen in the morning during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should remember Śrī Hari.
Having performed purification, bathing, and other such rites, one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana);
then, having recited the Gāyatrī mantra, one should perform the worship of Hari.
The Lord Mādhava, her husband, should be fully worshipped together with Nityā;
first, one should bathe him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with consecrated waters.
One should bathe Kṛṣṇa with the waters of pure sacred fords and smear him with liquid unguents;
one should anoint him with excellent fragrant oils, sandalwood paste, and the like.
Furthermore, one should bathe [the deity] with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) and offer garments,
a crown, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings.
One should likewise wear all kinds of ornaments made of chains, girdles, gems, diamonds, and so forth, as well as divine ones. (13)
One should worship the Lord with powdered rice, unbroken grains, saffron, and Abīra;
likewise, one should worship Him with incense, lamps, and Bakula flowers.
With other lotuses and land-lotuses blooming at that very time, along with ornaments, necklaces, beautiful leaves, and clusters of *tulasī* blossoms; || 19 ||
Then one should worship Śrī Hari with sandalwood and fragrant substances;
as for the food offering (naivedya), there should be sweet foods and bījapūra fruits.
Maṇḍakas, laḍḍukas made from mung beans, and pearls of fine rice, along with milk-porridge mixed with fragrant spices, should be offered to Hari. (17)
Pomegranate, the seven-colored fruit, and likewise coconut;
grapes and plantains should also be offered. (18)
Then the nightly lamp-offering (ārātrika) should be performed, followed by circumambulations and other rites;
having offered a handful of flowers and requested forgiveness, one should then indeed pray for the fulfillment of the vow.
"O Kṛṣṇa, today I indeed perform the auspicious vow of the Ekādaśī named Jayā, for the sake of attaining Your supreme grace. (1.243.20)
"May this vow of mine be fully accomplished; please show me your compassion here.
Having thus prayed and then bowed to Mādhava, the God of gods, [he spoke].
Adorned with the seven grains, the observer of the vow should cause a mandala to be made;
in its center, he should place a golden pitcher or a copper one.
In that [pitcher], which is beautified by five sprouts, jewels, water, cloth, and so forth,
one should place a vessel of sesame seeds together with fruit.
There, one should worship a water-pot and likewise invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as a golden image of Mādhava fashioned together with Jayā.
One should likewise install her together with her eternal consort;
one should worship her through the sequence beginning with invocation and likewise bathe her.
One should likewise adorn [the deity] and offer flowers, food, and so forth;
one should worship with great devotion using the sixteen secondary articles and other offerings.
Then, having offered water for drinking, one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) of Mādhava;
there, one should offer betel-leaf and ask for forgiveness for any transgressions. ||27||
For the sake of the vow, one should pray, "May my vow be fulfilled," and one should perform the worship of a cow and also cause the gift of a cow to be made. ||28||
One should cause the gift of land, the gift of clothing, and the gift of gold to be performed;
then, having completed the worship in this manner, one should carry out one's own business on that day.
Likewise at midday, one should indeed offer to the god Mādhava the four kinds of food— eatables, chewables, lickables, and drinkables— which are pure and essential.
In the evening and at night, for the purpose of worshipping Kṛṣṇa, one should have a large and auspicious pavilion constructed,
and therein one should arrange a canopy.
Having performed the worship of Śrī Hari, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to the prescribed rules;
then, having offered the food offering (naivedya) and the request for forgiveness (kṣamā-dāna), one should remain before Hari.
In the pavilion, one should have the verses of Śrī Hari sung in the manner of a *rāsa* dance;
one should keep a vigil at night and delight Kṛṣṇa exceedingly.
Devotees should perform dancing, chanting, instrumental music, and a vigil; then, having bathed in the morning, the Lord Mādhava is to be worshipped.
Various kinds of gifts should indeed be given according to one's capacity, and one should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, and Brahmins with the offered food. 35.
Then one should personally perform the breaking of the fast; when the vow is observed in this manner, the fruit becomes complete and victory shall surely be attained in every respect. ||36||
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to an ancient tale regarding this vow which I shall tell you;
while Mahendra was indeed ruling in the heavenly world, the hosts of deities [were there]. (37)
They all dwell in happiness, nourished by the drinking of nectar, and honored by Apsarases, goddesses, and attendants. ||38||
Honored and happy, the gods delight in the Nandana grove;
they take pleasure with the goddesses, dance, and sing praises. (39)
In the divine forest named Nandana, near the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā,
in a garden rich with the beauty of flowers and served by fragrant breezes.
A dance was performed by the Apsarases for the gratification of Indra;
at that time, the Gandharvas sang there and the Apsarases danced.
And the Gandharvas played their instruments, while women filled out the rhythm;
thus, as the singing and dancing proceeded with great joy, (42)
Mahendra, the spectator, having arrived at the stage by his own will,
danced with joy, he who is the leader of fifty million Indras.
The Gandharvas sing together with him—Puṣpadanta of beautiful voice, Citrasena, as well as his wife Puṣpavatī. (44)
And the son of Puṣpadanta was named Mālyavat;
at that time, Mālyavat was infatuated by the beauty of Puṣpavatī. (45)
By the side-long glances of Puṣpavatī, Mālyavān was brought under her control;
both Puṣpavatī and Mālyavān then performed a dance for the sake of pleasing Indra.
Having come together, their limbs became overwhelmed by desire;
possessed by mental agitation, they fell under the power of the arrows of love.
Indra sang pure songs without fixed gaze or passion,
while he danced perfectly, following the melody of the singing.
He perceived that their destruction would result in the ruin of Tāla and Māna;
for Maghavan reflected upon the union of those two minds.
Seeing the simultaneous discord in the rhythm, the tempo, and the singing, and perceiving the supreme loss of sequence as well as his own disregard, [he spoke].
Enraged, he cursed them there, speaking thus: "Fie upon you two! You are fools, fallen and destroyers of my greatness! (5.1)
Even while constantly enjoying an abundance of sensory objects in heaven, there is no satisfaction; nor do I possess the resolve to maintain the boundaries of excellence.
"Since you both have disregarded my skill and even my encouragement at the time of the dance, why indeed have you danced while being deluded in the midst of the assembly? (53)
Therefore, become a husband and wife as Piśācas; you are not fit for the status of Gandharvas, as you would cause a breach of decorum.
Having reached the world of mortals, experiencing the fruit of their karma and indeed enduring suffering,
they shall remain for many long years.
Thus, due to Mahendra’s curse, those two became piśācas on the most formidable Himavat mountain; tormented by sufferings, they found no peace.
Having forgotten their state as a Gandharva and an Apsaras, they wandered in the forest,
being repeatedly tormented by the intense cold.
As they were grinding their teeth and speaking to one another, the Piśāca spoke to his own dear wife, the Piśācī: 58.
Alas! For such a slight offense, the fruit is so great and most painful—this truly dreadful hell in the form of a *piśāca*. (59)
When will this come to an end? When will peace be attained?
For here, the cold is extreme, and because of it, great suffering arises.
Thus, lost in thought and emaciated by the suffering of hunger,
the two of them took up residence within the trunk of a celestial tree named Pippala.
Due to the falling of snow on the tenth night and on the day of the eleventh,
as well as on the night of the eleventh, those two were [afflicted] by a snowy gale.
Trembling, they went out for the sake of food rather than from their own dwelling;
by the turn of fate, that day was the Jayā Ekādaśī of the month of Māgha.
The night was spent by them in keeping a fast accompanied by a vigil;
there, both of them remained deprived of food, water, drink, and so forth. (64)
Suffering from the harsh Himalayan wind and deprived of all food, they neither committed the killing of living beings nor did they obtain any fruit to eat. (65)
Not even a drink of water was obtained, nor any gratification of the senses;
not even sleep occurred, and the two found no happiness at all.
While those two were thus suffering, the night passed away;
then, when dawn arrived and the sun had risen on the twelfth day, I [approached] them.
Devotion has been established and held in my heart in the form of the Pippala tree;
for I, indeed, become the Ashvattha tree among trees as its embodied manifestation. (68)
I, as the provider of their support, considering the vow of Jayātithi and the two of them,
gave them the fruit of the vow, which was indeed rich in the merit of keeping vigil.
By the power of that fruit, their state as Piśācas came to an end;
they became Gandharvas of divine form, possessing their original appearances.
Filled with their former affection and adorned with their previous ornaments,
Puṣpāvati and Mālyavān ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Having gone to heaven, they joyfully paid homage to the Lord of the Gods;
seeing those two gods, a celestial Gandharva, Indra was amazed and said: ||72||
"Tell me, by what merit was your state as Piśācas destroyed?
And by which sage were you two indeed released from my curse? (73)
Then, by the power of destiny, through the grace of Vāsudeva, and by virtue of his vow for victory, the king of the gods encountered those two.
"Ours—both yours and mine—the state of being a piśāca has been destroyed through the power of devotion to you.
Hearing this, Maghavan was delighted and spoke to them again with respect: || 75 ||
"By virtue of your vows, you two have become the foremost recipients of Hari’s grace;
therefore, by the power of the merit of those vows, you have both become worthy of my worship. (76)
"Drink nectar always from my words with great joy;
and may you two, my dear ones, always sport in heaven according to your pleasure. (77)
Those who perform the vow of Hari and are devoted to the worship of Hari—
whether they be mortals or immortals— they are always worthy of our honor.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, those two—the Gandharva and the Gandharvī—were reborn as Piśācas, dwelling in heaven once more through the power of Jayā’s vow. (79)
For this reason, O Lakṣmī, the Jayā-vrata must be performed;
Jayā is the destroyer of sins, the bestower of merit, and likewise the giver of heaven.
It destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and bestows liberation;
by him who has performed the Jayā-vrata, all gifts have been given. (81)
All sacrifices have been performed by him when the excellent Jayāvrata was observed; and all acts of service to others have been accomplished when the supreme Jayāvrata was observed. (82)
Indeed, by means of the Jayā-vow observed on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one obtains wealth, grain, sons, a wife, a house, cattle, horses, and a virtuous husband.
For one who observes this vow, nothing whatsoever will be difficult to obtain either in this world or the next;
through union with Hari, all things become easily attainable, for there is nothing that remains difficult to find.
Therefore, the vow must be observed in every way on the day of Jayā;
its performer shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha for ten million kalpas and will certainly rejoice there. (85)
From hearing or even from reciting this account of the vow, one shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 86.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Māgha-Śukla-Jaya-Ekādaśī Vow, and How the Gandharvas named Mālyavat and Mālyavan, who had attained the state of Piśācas, were liberated through that vow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O beloved of devotees, Lord of devotees, beloved of Ramā, my husband!
O Gopāla, protector of Lakṣmī, ocean of compassion, you who are my everything! (1)
O Dharmapāla, promoter of righteous conduct, honored by the gods;
tell me, what is the name of that [tithi] in the dark fortnight of Phālguna? || 2 ||
O Lord Hari, tell me all of this: who is the deity to be worshipped on Ekādaśī, what kind of vow is it, and what specifically should be given as an offering?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved, in the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, the Ekādaśī known by the name Vijayā is considered to be the destroyer of all sins.
There, Pradyumna should be worshipped with devotion by those observing the vow;
in the worship, Tulasī should be offered, and a citron fruit for the ritual honor.
As for the food offering (naivedya), meals such as *sohālikā* and the like should be presented;
as for gifts, sandals are primary, along with wealth and other items according to one's faith.
With reverence, a festival should be celebrated and offerings made to the devotees of Viṣṇu by those devotees who are endowed with faith and devoted solely to the Lord of Śrī.
And one should diligently observe the fast that bestows victory;
for just as the bright fortnight is to be observed, so too the dark fortnight should be fasted upon for the sake of attaining the goal of meditation.
From repeatedly drinking water, milk, and other such liquids; from engaging in sexual union;
from anger and the shedding of tears; and likewise from causing distress and the like.
Due to even a slight trace of faults such as theft, the fruit of fasting does not arise;
likewise, charity, self-inquiry, meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, and worship [bear no fruit]. (1.244.10)
These must be performed with effort by one observing the vow who desires the fruit;
his recitation of that [mantra] and his listening to its stories should be done on Ekādaśī, for then victory shall be attained. || 11 ||
O beloved, if anything that obstructs the fast is seen or touched—such as food—it must be abandoned; indeed, on the day of fasting, contact with such things must be avoided by all means.
But one who is unable to observe a fast should perform a vow consisting of fruits;
in this auspicious rite, roots, fruits, milk, and water shall be his means of sustenance.
Likewise, for one who is unable [to fast], there is eating at night, or food consisting of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya),
boiled rice, fruits, sesame seeds, as well as drinking clarified butter, milk, or water.
For the successful completion of the vow, one should abstain from the enjoyment of perfumes and betel;
however, without keeping a vigil and performing the worship of Viṣṇu, the fruit of the vow is halved.
For the observer of the vow, keeping a vigil and performing worship shall yield its fruit in full.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate the account that bestows victory. (16)
In the time following the Kṛta Yuga, the great sage Jamadagni,
who was indeed righteous, dwelt in the forest by the river Kauśikī.
He was always devoted to the sixfold duties such as ritual bathing and the twilight prayers, and was inwardly pure;
he was adorned with virtues such as compassion, courtesy, silence, and forbearance.
He was skilled in sacrifices, rituals, and the like, and was devoted to the service of the gods;
in his hut, the fire-god himself resided in embodied form, consuming the food offered to him.
That famous Jamadagni, dwelling on the bank of the Narmadā while performing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, was propitiating Mādhava.
Reṇukā was his wife, and she too was devoted to dharma and faithful to her husband; that virtuous woman, dedicated to the duty toward her husband, served him daily.
Though they remained content with whatever came by chance and attained peace as time passed, those two, while practicing celibacy, did not obtain offspring.
Once, after bathing, Reṇukā performed the worship of Hari first, and then she performed the worship of her husband; at that time, she fell into reflection.
"The husband is born in the form of a son"—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
"May my husband be handsome, and likewise may I have a son. (24)
My husband is capable, like the three gods, in the creation of new emanations, as well as in their nourishment and even in the withdrawal of creation.
May I have a son who, like him, causes the gods to come daily to his sacrifice and fulfills every desire according to his wish.
"May my son become a lord who possesses in his mind wish-fulfilling trees and the cows of plenty, and may he be a righteous master equal to a god. (27)
His palaces are equal to heaven, his opulences are those of Vaikuṇṭha, and the delights of Goloka indeed reside within his very resolve. 28.

His established status is equal to that of Brahmā, his dispassion is equal to that of Śambhu, and his supernatural powers are equal to those of Śeṣa; moreover, all these abide within his mere resolve. (29)
Liberation rests in his palm; Lakṣmī and the nectar of his benedictory words reside there;
and enjoyments such as the fulfillment of true desires dwell in his presence.
The Vedas, the sciences, the arts, and skillfulness all abide within his form; and all virtues, beginning with celibacy, reside within his heart. (3.1)
May there be a son for that sage Jamadagni who is equal to him;
may the gods grant me blessings for the attainment of such a son. (32)
Thinking thus, she worshipped her own husband and,
with her mind fixed on Viṣṇu, drank the water from his big toe.
At that moment, a voice, moving through the sky and most enchanting, arose there:
"O Goddess, I am pleased with you because of your constant service to your husband."
Viṣṇu exists, always dwelling in the form of a master while accepting service;
O Goddess Reṇukā, I grant this word to you: he shall be born from your womb.
I shall become your son, a lord equal to your husband;
there is no other like a husband for you, for I am a husband in form to this woman.
Therefore, since my husband is equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), I indeed grant all desires to those devoted wives who are properly established in their vows, as well as sons.
Listen, O Mother, for you must perform the vow therein;
it is fruit-yielding, bestowing sons in this world, bringing renown, and a means to liberation. (38)
The vow of the eleventh day, Vijayā, fulfills all intentions;
through it, you shall attain victory in the acquisition of a son, age after age. (39)
Having spoken thus, this voice ceased, and Reṇukā indeed undertook the vow on the eleventh lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
Indeed, he gave various gifts for the gratification of Viṣṇu;
and by the grace of Hari, as well as through his vow, he obtained a son.
This great lord known as Paraśurāma was a portion (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu;
after his birth, Hari assumed his own four-armed form.
The Lord of Śrī-Kamala gave his own divine vision to his mother;
having thus honored Vijayā, that Reṇukā became possessed of a son. ||43||
Listen, O beloved: thereafter this boy Viṣṇu, a young brahmin, became the son of Jamadagni and was devoted to the dharma of sages.
Protecting the duties of the Brahmins, honoring the sages and the gods,
and constantly worshipping the Lord of Śrī, he obtained the sacred thread.
Instructed by his father, he mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches;
through his learning and splendor, he became like another sun.
Even from childhood, he possessed prowess not inferior to his father; like the Lord of Kamalā, his movement was unimpeded throughout the paths of the three worlds. (47)
The prince Vipra was most devoted to Brahman and dedicated to the life of celibacy;
indeed, by the mere sight of him, men on earth attained liberation. 48.
By serving whom the gods attained their godhood and the riches of heaven, and other living beings attained the supreme status of world-protectors. 49.
Thus, he indeed dwells in forest regions within the huts of mendicants;
this is the very sport of Nārāyaṇa, which brings liberation to the distressed.
Now listen, Lakṣmī, once it happened that the Kṣatriyas became arrogant; they no longer took any account at all of their own venerable forest-dwelling twice-born brahmins. 11.
And the king of Māhiṣmatī was named Sahasrārjuna, a descendant of the Lunar dynasty, the son of Kṛtavīrya, and possessed of prowess in his arms. ||52||
Having propitiated the ascetic Dattātreya— an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa—
through his services, he [obtained] a thousand arms for battle.
Likewise, he obtained the perfection of the power of yoga from Śrīdatta while wandering at will for the hunt in the dense forest. (54)
Accompanied by his own great army,
he wandered through the forest regions and arrived at the hermitage of the great sage Jamadagni.
By means of his yogic power, the sage bestowed upon that king, along with his army, ministers, and mounts, abundant honor, hospitality, and respect.
By the grace of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), having manifested there at that time a splendor exceeding even that of heaven, he then worshipped her.
Having beheld the power of the sage, which surpassed his own sovereignty and was never before seen or heard of anywhere, the king and his attendants were filled with extreme wonder.
Having recognized her as the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), who possesses the power to produce all magnificent palaces and other wonders, he indeed seized her by force.
He led her, who was crying out along with her calf, to his own city;
at that time, Paraśurāma had gone outside of his home.
Having arrived and seen his mother weeping in the house,
he then became filled with rage upon hearing of the king’s wickedness.
He said to his mother: "Tell me, what must be done by me, your son?
Tell me how victory may be mine and how its fulfillment may come to pass. (62)
"O Mother, show me such a way; tell me now what I should do.
I shall discipline the Kṣatriyas who have gone astray, for I am invincible. (6.3)
"In that manner, instruct me, O Mother; I am your son and your servant.
The mother said, "O son, may you have complete victory; act accordingly."
O Hari, although I was previously childless, I observed the vow on the day of Vijaya-ekādaśī with the desire for a son.
He became pleased and took birth within my womb in your form;
you are indeed Hari himself—behold the auspicious bow in my hand.
Behold the axe and the banner in the form of lines;
and perform the auspicious vow of the Vijayā Ekādaśī day.
"Victory shall always be yours in battle against Kṣatriyas;
O good son, take up the vow for the training of Kṣatriyas. (68)
"Therefore, go forth to bestow the staff; may victory indeed be yours!
Thus addressed, Paraśurāma performed the rite for the victory of Vijaya.
By the command of his mother, he observed a vow of fasting from water during the dark fortnight of Phālguna;
on the tenth day, he ate only at night and likewise slept upon the ground.
After his morning bath,
he worshipped with heartfelt devotion the Lord Pradyumna, as well as Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Vijayā.
Having prepared a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala there, one should place an auspicious jar endowed with jewels, sprouts, cloth, and so forth, along with water, perfumes, and other offerings.
Having established that [image] there, he should place an auspicious vessel filled with sesame seeds upon it,
and having set it down, install a golden image.
He worshipped Prādyumnī, who stood at his side, with many offerings;
having bathed her with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), he presented her with a sacred thread.

Having adorned [the deity] with ornaments such as garments and jewelry, and having worshipped [him] with fragrant substances like sandalwood, with unbroken grains (akṣata), and with beautiful flowers; ||75||

Having worshipped with fruits and the like, with sprouts and leaves of *tulasī*, and by offering incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as circumambulations, hymns of praise, and other such acts; ||76||
He worshipped with nightly lamps and by making amends for his offenses;
likewise, having worshipped at midday, he offered food and water.
In the evening, he worshipped [him] with the sixteen excellent services;
he kept a vigil with the chanting of the Vedas and the narration of sacred stories. ||78||
When the hour of Brahmā arrived,
he himself bathed once more and, filled with affection, performed the worship of the Lord.
"O Lord, for the sake of victory, he made a prayer through my vow, even though I am a brahmin of limited power and naturally gentle. (1.244.80)
O Kṛṣṇa, may victory be ours in battle against this Kṣatriya host who follows such a cruel and evil path; may we indeed remain unhurt and invincible.
"The time has now arrived for the Kṣatriyas, who stand upon a false path, to be instructed;
O Blessed One, by means of my pretext, you yourself must achieve victory. (82)
While he was thus making his request, the four-armed Viṣṇu appeared and said to him, "May victory be yours in every way."
O best of the twice-born, I am pleased by your vow of Vijayā;
O chief of brahmins, you are my very form, indeed a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
By the fruit of the Vijaya-ekādaśī, may there be victory for you, and may the instruction of the rulers of the earth be for your sake. (85)
If indeed the teachers and the rulers were to fall into a state of confusion, then I have appointed the Brahmins as their governors. (86)
The strength of Kṣatriyas comes from dharma, while the strength of Brahmins is born of the Veda; the punishment of unrighteous Kṣatriyas has been entrusted to the Brahmins.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, fight and subdue the prideless kṣatriyas;
through this vow for victory, you shall achieve triumph here in the world of mortals. 88.
"May you have victory everywhere throughout the three worlds in every direction, leaving me behind!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished from that place.
Parśurāma also, taking up his sharp-edged axe as well as his bow,
arrows, sword, shield, spear, and discus, went forth alone.
He went to where King Kārtavīrya, the lord of Māhiṣmatī, resided—he who was named Sahasrārjuna and was adorned with a thousand arms. ||91||
Having cast the king into his own abode, Rāma shone there and said: "O great villain, slayer of Kāmadhenu! (92)
Go forth for the sake of seizing my life-breaths; experience the fruit of your own karma!
Give me my life, give me battle, and grant me the wish-fulfilling cow.
"Or else, grant me defeat, for the word of Rāma is eternal.
Having heard this, the exceedingly powerful Arjuna was overcome with anger and fought. (94)
However, his thousand arms were indeed severed at their roots in battle by the sharp, divine edge of Rāma’s axe.
Indeed, many akṣauhiṇī divisions of his were torn asunder by the twice-born one;
his sons were destroyed, and Arjuna himself was slain at that time.
Having recovered the wish-fulfilling cow, he himself then went to heaven;
he wandered upon the earth for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.
Twenty-one times he became the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas,
victorious on earth through the power of the Vijaya-ekādaśī vow.
That lotus-eyed Rāma became the most excellent of brahmins;
the cow was obtained, the kṣatriyas were conquered, and Arjuna was slain in battle.
In this world, victory was attained by Rāma through the vow of Vijayā;
indeed, Arjuna became an incarnation of Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana-cakra.
Nevertheless, he who followed the path of false vows was slain by Paraśurāma;
yet, through reading or even hearing this [account], one shall obtain the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. (101)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory of Paraśurāma through Austerity for the Purpose of Destroying Sahasrārjuna," within the section on the Greatness of the Phālguna-Kṛṣṇa Vijayā-ekādaśī Vow, in the first part, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: Kṛṣṇa himself, the Supreme Brahman, having assumed an incarnation for the sake of protecting the world,
even performs his own religious vow.
For the sake of gathering the world, he indeed practices it himself;
and he teaches people this very conduct, which consists of the essence of being.
Speak, O Kṛṣṇa! A virtuous vow must also be performed here by me, just as it was by you, through the power of which liberation shall come into one's grasp.
Even ordinary people, having observed the vow, shall attain the supreme fruit;
this is the Ekādaśī known by the name of Arjuna in the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
"O son of Dharma, speak that [vow] to me, the consort of Nārāyaṇa. Thus addressed, Hari Viṣṇu spoke of the vow to his beloved.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O auspicious goddess, O beloved who bestows all prosperity;
by which vow the great riches of people attain nourishment.
Prosperities and riches indeed always increase for him;
liberation in abundance and great liberation abide according to his will.
In the bright fortnight of Phālguna, let there be the auspicious Ekādaśī known by the name Āmalakī; it bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
In Vaikuṇṭha, Śrī Hari asked Lakṣmī: "What is required? What do you desire, O Lakṣmī? Tell me that, and I shall grant it to you."
There is nothing unattained that remains to be attained through you, O you whose form is Brahman;
for whatever is mine is yours, and is of your very essence.
Therefore, choose [a boon], may it be well with you; I shall fulfill your desire.
Do not feel hesitation, O Lakṣmī; whatever is yours is mine.
Having heard this from Hari, Lakṣmī said: "O Blessed One, I have a most beloved forehead ornament, a *tantikā*; O Lord, give that to me. (12)
Then Hari, having resolved to create an ornament, [produced] a new, auspicious,
golden-hued, and refreshing mark for his forehead that brings coolness to the hands.
He manifested upon his forehead a divine ornament in the form of a *bindu*, which was transparent, radiant like a jewel, equal to the moon, and endowed with excellent qualities.
That drop became a fruit-like jewel, the most excellent of gems, radiant with luster; it was unblemished, spherical, gentle, and resembled a golden gem. || 15 ||
And from that, many other divine jewels were also produced;
a necklace made of strings of them was fashioned as a beautiful ornament.

He is visible like a sun-gem (sūryakānta), equal to a moon-gem (candrakānta) in his virtues; he is like the Kaustubha jewel in his heart-pleasing nature, consisting of the ornament of the sacred thread (tantikā). || 17 ||
To be worn, he is like a crest-jewel; to be touched, he is tender and delicate.
To be honored, he is equal to the sacred Viṣṇu-stone; when worn, he is as cooling as sandalwood.
In Sugandha, he is rich with divine fragrance; in Puṣṭi, he is like breast-milk;
and in Śāśvata, he is the great divine one born from the drop on the forehead of Hari.
The necklace known as the Ornament of Taut Threads, stainless and new, was consecrated by Hari;
it consists of forty-one beads. (1.245.20)
In the middle there are seven beads, and on both sides along the two threads there are twenty-eight beads; at the two ends, it consists of six beads each.
And he was entrusted to Mahālakṣmī by Hari, the Supreme Self;
having obtained one who was radiant like the sun, yet cool and serene.
She rejoiced and exulted greatly at that charming and eternal necklace;
she smelled it, touched it, and gazed upon it with reverence.
He held it repeatedly against his forehead and gazed at it again and again—
it was fresh, resembling gold, and filled with fragrant juices.
Seeing on his forehead that which bestows peace, with a smooth touch and endowed with lines— created by Hari himself for her sake— she rejoiced.
She praised and extolled him; she took him in her hand again and again;
she showed him to her friends; and she became filled with joy. (26)
The Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having observed the purity of the fruit on all sides, bestowed a name upon it according to its qualities.
And Lakṣmī tied an *āmalaka* fruit, fashioned from *tantika-āmalaka* beads, upon his forehead; she shone, surpassing all others. (28)
Just as the sky shines with rows of many moons, so did it shine having attained Mahālakṣmī, who was exceedingly beautiful. 29.
Thus, when great bliss had arisen even here at the beginning of creation by the Creator, and when the elemental creation of moving and non-moving beings had come into being at the start of the Kalpa.
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, Hari himself—the Supreme Self, higher than the highest—came to the earth with great respect, he who is the beloved of Lakṣmī. ||3 1||
And from the forehead of Lakṣmī, Śrī Hari caused the auspicious fruit of the *tantikā* to fall upon the earth for the sake of attaining that essential reality.
From that fruit was born a great *dhātrī* tree itself, bent down by the weight of its own fruit and possessing many branches and twigs. (33)
He is proclaimed as the most excellent of all trees;
endowed with fruits resembling gold, this auspicious tree is dear to Lakṣmī. (34)
Just as the forehead of Nārāyaṇa is dear, so too is this tree dear;
it is of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa and was created by Nārāyaṇa. (35)
For the sake of Nārāyaṇī, this very [liṅga] bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment;
it was first manifested here at Badarikāśrama. (36)
And from that Raivata mountain, that great tree arrived;
all these trees called Āmalaka are givers of liberation. (37)
On the very day that this tree was manifested by Hari, that day was also known by the name Ekādaśī. (38)
There, the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) on which the Āmalakī tree originated was indeed designated by the most excellent divine sages as "Āmalakī. (39)
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
kinnaras, humans, nāgas, ṛṣis, and other sages. ||1.245.40||
Vidyādharas, Kimpuruṣas, yogins, as well as Brahmins, ascetics, renunciants, virtuous women, female yogins, and those established in celibacy. ||41||
Even others who possessed divine vision, though created by the Creator,
all went to see that tree of pure wood after hearing of your great wonder.
Filled with wonder, they proceeded while contemplating the *āmalaka* tree,
praising the *āmalaka* fruits which were worthy of the most exquisite ornaments.
The gods and others arrived at that place where Dhātrī, the beloved of Hari, was located;
upon seeing her, her husbands were filled with great wonder.
Viṣṇu himself said to them: "This Vaiṣṇava tree, the Āmalakī, is indeed preeminent; by its mere remembrance, one obtains the fruit arising from the gift of a cow. (45)
The merit from touching [the *āmalaka* fruit] is twofold, and likewise, from eating it, it is threefold.
Indeed, one should place *āmalaka* fruits on the forehead, the ears, the neck, and the hands. (46)
By those by whom it is worn, their residence in Vaikuṇṭha shall indeed be permanent;
this Āmalaka fruit produced from me is dear and removes all sins. (87)
The *vaiṣṇava* [fruit] leads one to Viṣṇu and purifies sins through its consumption;
therefore, the *āmalakī* should be cultivated by people with every effort. 48.
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke thus, the goddesses then said to Hari:
"O Lord of gods, O All-pervading One, grant us fruits for the sake of our ornaments. (49)
Then, indeed, Śrī Hari, having mentally conceived and manifested countless fruits there, offered them to them as well. (1.245.50)
Then, many ornaments fashioned by them were worn right there upon the forehead,
the neck, and also upon the hands, the ears, and other parts.
They rejoiced exceedingly and accepted him as they desired;
then the gods and others likewise [honored] this Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world.
They said, "O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Lord, hear our request:
this tree is pleasing to us; let the consecration be granted to us. (53)
"By whose residence shall our supreme highest good always be attained?
Hari then said to the gods: 'That which you have requested is worthy. (54)
"Whichever place pleases you for residence, enter that. Having heard these words of Hari, the gods entered according to their own inclinations. (55)
Having entered the Āmalakī tree, they resided there perpetually;
Viṣṇu was stationed at its root, while the Grandfather (Brahmā) was above it.
Lord Rudra resides in the trunk, the sages dwell upon the branches, the other gods are on the twigs, and the Vasus abide in the leaves. ||57||
All the Maruts reside in the flowers, the lords of creatures in the fruits,
the sages in the petals and stalks, and Brahman himself is situated in the bark.
In taste resides the essence of Brahman; in satisfaction resides form;
in fragrance resides union with Brahman; and in touch resides liberation. (59)
The pearl is released from the fruit; the Lord of Śrī resides within the seed, such as the fiber and so forth.
Indeed, this Dhātrī, who gives birth to the world, should be understood as being composed of all the gods.
Bestowing fortune, she is to be served as Ramā; bestowing prosperity, she is exceedingly dear.
Therefore, she is indeed most worthy of worship by all who are devoted to bhakti.
In the month of Phālguna, those men who observe the vow of the Āmalakī tree shall go into the shade of the Āmalakī for my worship. (62)
One should perform the vow and the ritual vigil there with devotion;
on the twelfth day as well, having gone to that very place, one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
O lords of the gods, that fruit is declared to be eternal due to its connection with me;
this applies even when performed beneath an āmalakī tree during the months of Kārttika or Phālguna.
One should perform [the rites] such as eating; the fruit of that is eternal.
With one's limbs smeared with āmalaka fruits and adorned with āmalaka fruits, ||65||
A person who takes food made from *dhātrī* fruit shall attain liberation;
likewise, he who, having taken refuge in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree, worships the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
O beloved, for one who worships Hari-Kṛṣṇa at the foot of a Dhātrī tree, there shall be the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice for every flower [offered].
By feeding virtuous brahmins, he will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha;
by making gifts at the foot of a dhātrī tree, one shall attain heaven.
One who tastes the juice of the *dhātrī* fruit shall fall into a state devoid of merit;
however, the observer of the vow who partakes of the *dhātrī* fruit itself shall indeed attain divine liberation.
If one dies while uttering her name, "Dhātrī,
Dhātrī," then Lakṣmī, like a nurse (dhātrī), arrives accompanied by Nārāyaṇa.
He leads him to the divine, imperishable abode of Hari, Vaikuṇṭha,
which belongs to that very day on which he was born from the earth.
The vow in the form of Ekādaśī should be observed by one desiring liberation;
it bestows wealth and grain, is meritorious, and brings satisfaction to the self. (72)
This supreme vow among vows requires little effort yet yields great fruit;
by performing it, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (73)
If, during the bright fortnight of Phālguna, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should coincide with the Puṣya asterism,
that Ekādaśī is meritorious and destroys even the greatest sins.
This very vow, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, must be performed by the practitioner.
On the tenth day, one should eat only once and likewise sleep on the ground at night.
One who seeks the vows must also protect their state of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Having risen at the Brahma-hour on the eleventh day, within one's own inner self, [one should practice]. (76)
Having remembered Hari and meditated upon Him in that manner, one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford;
then, having approached before Hari, one should formally resolve upon the vow.
"Today, by the grace of the Lord, I shall perform the waterless vow (nirjala-vrata).
O Lord, may it reach completion; let there be no obstacle for me. (78)
Having thus offered this prayer, one should indeed perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and carry out the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) and so forth;
one should then perform the daily worship of Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa.
Then, in the mandala called Sarvatobhadra, which has been fashioned from food,
one should place in the center a vessel made of gold or copper, or one containing the five jewels.
Having arranged garments, sprouts, water, threads, fruits, and so forth, one should place a vessel of sesame seeds and set it there most beautifully. 81.
One should place and worship there an image of Govinda, the lord of Āmalakī, fashioned from gold, together with his wife Candravatī. ||82||
Then, beginning with the invocation and ending with the handful of flowers,
the worshipper observing the vow should perform the worship there with divine articles.
And with sixteen types of offerings, as well as other services—namely, the waving of lights, hymns of praise, food, water, betel-leaf, and various articles. (84)
One should worship the God with flowers such as the *guladāvadikā* and the *kamala*, as well as with rice grains, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood. (85)
In the offering, one should especially present sweetmeats such as *kaṃsāra* and *pūrikā* with great devotion; and for the purpose of worship, one should offer the *akṣoḍa* fruit.
Likewise, one should offer a vessel of sesame seeds, and in the act of giving, gold and other forms of wealth;
having thus performed the morning worship, one should practice devotion. ||87||
On the day of the Dhātrī festival, worship is especially prescribed at midday;
whether by a river, a pond, a well, or in one's home, the practitioner should remain self-restrained. (88)
Having applied earth to the body, one should then perform the ritual bath, [reciting]:
"May all sacred fords come here; I am performing my bath therein. (8-9)
Having bathed in this manner and put on clean garments, and then having applied the *puṇḍraka*,
the *tilaka*, and the *candraka*, one should go to the *āmalakī* tree.
Equipped with all necessary implements and provided with articles for worship,
one should take recourse in the shade of a dhātrī tree, having thoroughly purified the area on all sides.
One should construct a Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala made from seven kinds of grain;
in its center, one should place a pitcher made of gold or copper.
Endowed with the five jewels, perfumed with divine fragrances, provided with an umbrella, sandals, and garments, and anointed with white sandalwood paste. (93)
With garlands of flowers suspended from its neck, perfumed by all kinds of incense, filled with rows of lamps, delightful, and beautiful on every side, it was utterly enchanting. (94)
One should place it in a vessel, and above that, one filled with divine parched grain (lāja);
and in a vessel of sesame seeds, one containing parched grain and a pot provided with a moon-like ornament.
One should likewise install the golden image of Hari Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, together with his axe, as well as the auspicious Dhātrī made of a golden form. (96)
One should offer the invocation, a seat, water for the feet, and the arghya-water;
one should give water for sipping and bathe the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then one should bathe the deity with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) and perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana);
one should clothe the deity in garments, provide the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and offer a gem.
One should offer all ornaments, beginning with the crown, as well as fragrant sandalwood and the like, and attara oil and the like. || 99 ||
With powdered pigment, saffron, *abīra*, agallochum, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
as well as with various kinds of flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, [he worshipped] the God.

By means of the rite of lustration (nīrājana), with water, betel, and excellent fruits, with prostrations like a staff, hymns of praise, obeisances, and requests for forgiveness for one's offenses. || 101 ||
One should worship the Lord of Gods with circumambulations, with sacrificial fees, and likewise with a handful of excellent flowers at the auspicious foot of a Dhātrī tree.

One should meditate upon the form of the Blessed One: oneself as having a gentle luster at the feet, the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa) at the knees, and the nature of radiant energy (tejas) in the thighs.
One should meditate on Dāmodara at the waist, likewise Padmanābha at the belly;
one marked with the Śrīvatsa on the chest, and the wielder of the discus on the left arm.
One should meditate on Gadīna on the right arm, Vaikuṇṭha on the neck, Yajñamukha on the mouth, and Sukhasāgara on the nose.
One should meditate on Vāsudeva in the eyes and likewise on Vāmana in the forehead;
having meditated on the Soul of All in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should contemplate the limbs [of the deity].
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O son of Jamadagni; let there be salutation to you.
Accept this great worship performed by me, accompanied by the offering of *dhātrī* fruits.
"Accept [this] with supreme affection; be the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus worshipped and completed the ritual, one should then indeed partake of food and other such things. (108)
One should give [the remains] to the cows, and likewise cause them to be given even to minute creatures;
furthermore, the prasāda should be offered at the root of the dhātrī tree with a sense of divine devotion.
Water should be offered at the root of the Dhātrī tree as an oblation for the satisfaction of the ancestors;
one should then offer a handful of water to the Sun with devotion, intending it for the ancestors.
One should give a portion of the prasāda to the spirits and to children;
as for the remainder of the prasāda, one should bring it to one's own home and preserve it there.
On the twelfth day, one should consume fruit and water; if these are to be taken by the observer of the vow on that day, they shall not indeed be a violation of the vow.
Having thus performed gifts consisting indeed of jewels and gold— ornaments, garments, various kinds of food, and lands— (113)
Cows and buffaloes, houses, gardens, vehicles, and carriages, as well as most excellent jewels and abundant sweet foods. (1.14)
One would grant him the fruit of the eternal Brahman upon the surface of the Dhātrī tree;
his heaven shall likewise be imperishable and indeed unsurpassed.
Such a vow and such a gift bestow the fruits of heaven and liberation;
having satisfied all with gifts of water, food, and clothing, one attains these results. (116)
Having paid homage to Hari, bowed down, and given something else to the twice-born,
one should go home with supreme devotion at all times, even during the afternoon.
One should pass the time at night in that same manner with devotion and chanting;
having performed the worship according to the rules and having performed the waving of lamps (ārātrika) and other rites.
Having offered the food offering, water, fragrance, and betel leaf,
one should cause the Lord to swing on a swing or a cradle, and likewise perform the night vigil.
One should perform [this] with dances, songs, instrumental music, and the nectar-like stories;
likewise with religious narratives and the singing of verses adorned with the beauty of Kṛṣṇa.
Whether in his home, in a temple, or at the foot of a dhātrī tree,
the observer of the vow should install an image of Paraśurāma by day or by night.
One should perform worship, observe vows, and keep a vigil at the foot of a tree;
they should pass this night with Vaiṣṇava narrations concerning liberation.
Then one should perform circumambulations around the Dhātrī tree while reciting the names of Viṣṇu,
either one hundred and eight times or even twenty-eight times.
Recognizing the Dhātrī tree as Hari, one should perform worship in the morning;
having bathed and performed the lustration rite (nīrājana), one should then worship a Brahmin.
Having worshipped the Guru who is worthy of gifts, one should present everything to him:
a golden vessel belonging to Jamadagni, a pair of garments, and a pair of sandals.
Then he should offer it to his guru, who is the very embodiment of the son of Jamadagni;
having touched an āmalakī fruit and performed a circumambulation, he should speak [the following]. (126)
O Keśava, may you be pleased with me in the form of the son of Jamadagni;
and may you bestow the supreme grace of Viṣṇu upon your devotees.
Having given food and water according to the prescribed rule to those who depend on him,
he should feed the Brahmins, children, virtuous men, virtuous women, and young girls.
Then, surrounded by his family, he himself should eat;
by performing it in this manner, the merit shall be eternal and bestow liberation. || 129 ||
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving,
and whatever merit is found in all sacrifices— that fruit the observer of the vow obtains.
Completely liberated from all sins, he attains supreme liberation;
for one who performs the Āmalakī vow, residence in the world of Viṣṇu is considered certain.
Thus has been told to you all this, the supreme among vows, which bestows sons, victory, splendor, and likewise liberation. (132)
It bestows unimpeded progress and heaven, swiftly grants spiritual accomplishments, yields the fruits of all intentions, and brings about the grace of Lakṣmī. || 133 ||
This auspicious vow, which bestows vehicles, mounts, fine ornaments, utensils, and other such things, is difficult to overcome and liberates one from all sins. (134)
It bestows upon women the nature of Lakṣmī herself and grants the state of being Ramā.
But for the man, it is the bestowal of the four-armed form of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Ekādaśī Vow Named Āmalakī in the Bright Fortnight of Phālguna within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the manifestation of the Āmalakī tree for the purpose of adorning the forehead of Lakṣmī, and the greatness of worshipping the tree-form on earth during the Ekādaśī vow. ||245||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Keśava, my heart becomes exceedingly joyful upon hearing of the vow of Āmalakī as well as the greatness of the Dhātrī fruit. (1)
In the dark fortnight of Caitra, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that is recognized? Which deity is to be worshipped there, and likewise, who is the wife of Hari?
"Tell me what the fruit, the procedure, the gift, and the worship are.
Having heard Lakṣmī's words, Kṛṣṇa, who is indeed Nārāyaṇa, spoke to her.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the Ekādaśī occurring on the first lunar day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, known as Pāpamocanikā, which yields great fruit.
Fulfilling desires, bestowing success, and increasing righteousness—that practitioner who renders [this] waterless shall attain Brahman. || 5 ||
On the tenth day, one should eat only at night, sleep on the ground during the night,
observe celibacy, and as a practitioner of the vow, one should meditate upon Aniruddha in the morning.
One should likewise offer *kundakalikā* flowers during the worship of the Lord accompanied by Suśīlā and Pāpamocanikā.
One should offer a female attendant in the food offering (naivedya), and a jujube fruit (badarī-phala) in the water-offering (arghya);
likewise, other fruits and many sweet foods should be offered here.
One should also give sesame seeds and cows as a gift to Aniruddha;
thus, having risen in the morning and meditated upon Hari in the mind, (one should perform these acts).
Having bathed, one should perform the mental worship of Aniruddha;
one should offer the sixteen mental articles of worship.
Then indeed, the observer of the vow should perform the external worship in due order;
he should invoke the Lord Aniruddha together with Suśīlā.
Having summoned [the deity] into the golden image, one should offer a most excellent seat;
likewise, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
One should offer a bath prepared with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and perform the consecration (abhiṣeka);
then, one should carry out the wiping away of the water from the limbs with garments.
Then he should offer two new, auspicious, and highly valuable washed garments;
he should also offer other very fine cloths for the sake of his satisfaction.
One should give a sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and offer precious gems;
likewise, articles for grooming the hair, a tooth-stick, oil, and a mirror.
One should also offer excellent ornaments to Hari,
as well as collyrium, saffron, vermilion, gulāla, unbroken rice grains, and sandalwood paste.
One should also offer flowers, even a single leaf of *tulasī*,
as well as fruits, incense, lamps, and food offerings to him.
One should offer various kinds of food, milk mixed with sugar,
water, fruit, mouth-fresheners, betel leaf, and fragrant powder.

One should offer superior oil and other substances for the sake of fragrance to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; then one should perform the waving of lights (ārātrika), the hymn of salutation (namaḥ-stotra), and the prayer for forgiveness (kṣamāpana).
One should perform circumambulation and prostrate like a staff, offer a handful of flowers and a sacrificial fee, and entreat the Supreme Lord for the performance of the vow.
"O Supreme Lord, today the Ekādaśī known as Pāpamocanā has been chosen by me in my mind for the sake of a vow. (21)
O Janārdana, may the vow undertaken by her be free from obstacles;
be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Keśava, sovereign of virtuous conduct! (22)
Thus, having completed the worship and the seven kinds of grain,
one should have the Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared and then install it.
A water-pot made of gold or copper, adorned with five sprouts, five kinds of jewels, and provided with water, cloth, and so forth; ||24||
Upon that, one should offer an auspicious vessel filled with sesame seeds,
and therein [place] the images of Suśīlā and the Lord Aniruddha.
Then, having established [the deity], the observer of the vow should worship with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra);
he should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to the rule and carry out the prostrations and other rites.
A couch, a bolster, a secret fastening-strap for the bed, a pillow, side-cushions, as well as an umbrella and auspicious sandals. (27)
A cooking pot together with a water-jar, as well as a small ball,
a fan, a mirror, chowries, a staff, two sandals, and an auspicious leather sandal-sock.
One should indeed offer a *śāṭī*, a *pracchadapaṭī*, a *kañcukī*, a *kucalī*,
a *karpaṭikā* with a moon design, and a *ghargharī*.
The observer of the vow should offer a water-pot, a sacred thread, cold water filled to the brim, and fragrant sandalwood paste to Aniruddha. (1.246.30)
And one should offer sour fruits and sweet laddukas mixed with sugar to Aniruddha within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala.
The observer of the vow should place an unbroken ghee lamp nearby;
having performed the worship in this manner, he may then attend to his own business.
At midday, the observer of the vow, having bathed and worshipped according to the prescribed rules,
should offer various kinds of sweet food and water to Hari.
The observer of the vow should offer to Śrī Hari the fruit, betel leaf, cardamom, cloves for mouth-freshening, and also the areca nut.
And in the evening, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed with plantain pillars, provided with a canopy, complete with water-pots, and featuring archways adorned with green leaves.
In the center, one should construct an altar and likewise fasten a swing;
having installed the Lord who holds the flute there, the observer of the vow should rock Him.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), as well as the offering of incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and worship;
one should provide water for drinking and mouth-fresheners, and proclaim his virtues.
One should keep a vigil at night accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music;
in the morning, one should perform worship and likewise cause gifts to be given.
One should fulfill the auxiliary components of the vow according to one's capacity and according to the facts;
indeed, one should give everything to the preceptor, and in this manner, one should bring the vow to completion.
The observer of the vow should devoutly feed virtuous men and women, as well as Brahmins, the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others, including children, with various kinds of food.
Then, having fed his own people, the devoted observer of the vow should himself perform the breaking of the fast with young girls; he shall indeed attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 41.
O Lakṣmī, listen to this wondrous tale of the past that destroys all sins;
it took place formerly in the middle of a forest in the Caitraratha garden on the Himālaya mountains.
In a divine region covered with green grass, filled with trees heavy with fruits and flowers, frequented by forest goddesses, and served by hosts of apsarases. (43)
In the spring season, in the forest resounded by bees, delightful with the warbling of cuckoos, and a perfect nourisher of the god of love. (44)
The Gandharva maidens sport with musical instruments along with their attendants,
and the gods, headed by Mahendra, the dwellers of heaven, play there as well.
All the rishis and sages perform intense austerities;
likewise, there are virtuous yogins and virtuous yoginīs, as well as true ones. (46)
Those established in vows and observances practice austerities there for the sake of attaining the status of Brahmā;
no other forest region bestows such happiness as that grove of Caitraratha.
There, the inhabitants of the three worlds, in order to dispel their fatigue, always arrive in the evening and depart at their respective times. (48)
There, the Apsaras Mañjughoṣā delights in dwelling within the forest;
she also serves the sages with love day and night. (49)
Like a maidservant or a handmaid, she serves out of a desire for liberation; not with a base mind, but rather with a pure heart. (1.246.50)
She served the sage whether he was a child, a youth, or even an old man;
she attended upon the young wives of the sages as well, like a maidservant. (51)
Thus, she dwelt constantly in the hermitages of the sages in many forms; then, on one auspicious day, that Mañjughoṣā—
He saw the sage named Medhāvin, who was staying in a forest one krośa away, performing austerities while established in celibacy, and endowed with youth and vigor. (53)
He was handsome, well-proportioned, with matted locks as fine as golden threads;
his beard was slightly sprouted with beautiful lines, his lips were red, and his face was round.
His eyes resemble lotus petals, his body is like a land-lotus, he is a treasury of serenity, and his neck is encircled by a halo of radiance. (55)
Hearing that he was handsome even by her own standards and had nails like fine moonlight, she approached his presence with the disposition of a queen in order to serve him. (56)
At first, out of fear of him, she remained near the hermitage; after staying there for some time, she began to strive to win his favor. (57)
She sang sweetly and well, and she swept the hermitage;
then, with devotion, she played upon the beautiful lute.
For the sake of serving him, she went in haste toward the hut;
looking at the sage slowly, the female ascetic touched him as was her custom.
Adorned with flowers, fragrant musk, saffron, and sandalwood,
she displayed various amorous gestures and graceful charms with the intent of service.
In the presence of Medhāvin, she danced beautifully and gracefully;
she offered salutations with her hands and gave her consent with her eyes. (61)
He informed him of his own great devotion and took hold of that sage by the hand;
he also resolved in his mind that he would surely obtain the water-lily.
Having obtained a youth of beautiful form and radiant splendor, she was exceedingly delighted;
yet, though drawn toward that young sage, she remained startled in her inner being.
In embracing the sage, she became permeated with passion (*rājasī*);
for on a path where practice has been established, the minds of such women generally proceed in that very manner. (64)
The god of love indeed made his dwelling within her body;
likewise, desiring victory, he made Medhāvinī his stronghold.
When both were pervaded by desire, their two bodies became greatly transformed;
and their minds, overcome by the impulse of the bodiless god of love, were so again and again.
Then Medhāvin reflected there with his wisdom:
"What is this passion born of association with women that now afflicts me? (67)
"Resorting to patience and fortitude, I shall go to another forest, so that my asceticism may be protected and the impulse of desire shall pass away. (68)
Having reflected thus, that wise lord of brahmins quickly went from his place to another location; meanwhile, Kāma also moved with great speed.
In order to conquer the devotee of Śiva, he indeed assumed a beautiful form outside in the forest; as he advanced, he made himself manifest in every direction.
Having made her brow the tip of the bow, her side-glance the bowstring, and her two eyes, complete with lashes, the arrows in due order; ||7 1 ||
Having taken up the breasts of another woman, he proceeded to enchant her;
Mañjughoṣā became the vanguard of that army of desire here.
By means of desire, the five arrows were discharged at the sage;
the first was characterized by wonder, while the second consisted of wakefulness. (73)
The third is called the carrier of rasa, the fourth consists of delusion, and the fifth pertains to the state of union; he indeed released them.
Led under her influence, Medhāvin united with Mañjughoṣā;
and seeing the sage Medhāvin, she too was tormented by desire. (75)
Then he was joined by the sage whose body had blossomed with youth;
there, having embraced each other firmly, they both shone, united by the god of love.
Adorned with a white sacred thread and appearing like another god of love, the Brahmin, accompanied by Mañjughoṣa, shone like the moon joined with the sky. (77)
Falling under the power of passion, she laughed softly and softly;
with her arms adorned with jingling bracelets, she embraced the sage to her heart. (78)
Making his voice subtle and suppressed like a mute through the affectionate tone of his throat,
he closed his eyes and tasted the face of the Sage with his lips.
Immersed in touch and immersed in bliss, with her anklets and girdle silenced, she embraced the sage with her tactile sensations, her emotions, her eyes, and her body. (1.246.80)
The lute, having fallen to the ground, embraced its own [player] as if by force,
like a creeper clinging to a tree shaken by the force of the wind.
He too took delight with her in manifold ways through various amorous diversions,
having forgotten the principle of Śiva and fallen under the sway of the principle of desire.

When the palace had been accomplished through asceticism— complete with gardens and celestial chariots, as well as vehicles, implements, and various kinds of food to be chewed, eaten, and licked— (83)
When there is the capacity for maintaining [the body], for adornment, for festivals, for social equality, and for the seasons;
and when there are various things suitable for the household and objects of enjoyment along with their means of production. (84)
When it reached its unsurpassed state, he attained satisfaction with her;
yet he went again to thirst, again to satisfaction, and again to thirst. (85)
There is no end to craving; it increases even as one indulges in it again and again.
Thus, by means of that craving which carries the weight of youth, he was indeed youthful. (86)
That lustful man did not even distinguish between night and day;
as he took his pleasure, a long period of time passed while he neglected his customary duties.
Nine hundred years passed for him while he was with her;
yet she took her delight with the sage as if it were but half a night.
Mañjughoṣā prepared to depart for the world of the gods;
clad in armor, she addressed that most excellent of sages with longing. (89)
"O Brahmin, let permission be granted to me to go to the heavenly world.
Having heard this, Medhāvī, being utterly deluded, spoke to him.
"Stay by my side until the dawn twilight arrives.
Having heard this, Mañjughoṣa reflected within his heart.
"Ah! This man does not realize his own agitation caused by desire for years;
overcome by the fainting fit of passion, he thinks it lasts for no more than half a night. (92)
Distressed by the fear of a curse upon her refusal,
she again delighted that sage for many years.
Fifty-five years, nine months, and three days had passed;
then, when that time had elapsed, she spoke again to the sage.
"O Brahmin, let an instruction be given; I must go to my own home.
Medhāvī said: "Blinded by desire and deprived of the light of time (discernment), [you speak thus]. (95)
"The time for retiring has arrived; listen to my words.
O beautiful one, you ought to depart after having enjoyed me for a moment. (96)
Without you, even a single moment will be like an eon for me;
stay with me for a long time, so that even a mere night spent together may endure.
Furthermore, terrified of the curse, she delighted that ṛṣi for forty-five years and more, out of her excessive devotion.
Bowing again, she said to the sage: "O Brahmin, are you satisfied or not? O learned one, please give me your command; I must go to my own home. (99)
Medhāvin said: "In order to protect her, who is so affectionate, by my side at that time, the morning has now arrived; let my words be heard. (1.246.100)
"Stay forever in my palace and delight me according to your desire;
tell me, what satisfaction could I have if you remained here for only a single night? (10.1)
