"Until I perform my twilight devotions, you must indeed remain steady.
Having heard the sage's words, she smiled and spoke to him.
O best of Brahmins, how much of your twilight period has now passed? Consider for a moment: how many years have elapsed for you? (103)
"You know but one twilight and one night; what is your sleep that lasts for an entire aeon?
Hearing these words of hers, his inner eyes were suddenly opened. (104)
Having questioned her regarding the time that had passed, the wise one calculated its measure as nine hundred and ninety-nine in number.
Having clearly realized that nine hundred and nine years had already passed with his beloved,
at the onset of a single night.
Nevertheless, thinking "shame on me who am pervaded by craving," he felt indignation toward that desire,
toward himself, and toward his youth.
Beholding the loss of liberation, the loss of ascetic merit, and the destruction of his own self,
he shed profuse tears from his eyes out of extreme anger.
A woman is the destroyer of ascetic merit, the very form of death, and a demoness;
she is the obstructer of one's own liberation and the consumer of the hard-earned religious merit.
The sage, trembling with agitation, spoke swiftly regarding that cause of his ruin:
"Fie on you, O beloved of wicked conduct, unchaste woman, you who are fond of lust!"
O wanton woman, destroyer of merit, who under the pretext of service causes harm to the sages, you bring about the destruction of their asceticism and lead them onto the path of Yama! 111.
"O wicked woman, you who provide openings for the fulfillment of lustful desires, become a Piśācī!
Thus Medhāvī cursed her; she, bowing low, spoke to him.
Indeed, the fault is not mine alone; you, being young, should reflect well upon this.
When victory in a matter involving two parties is achieved, it is the strong one who is honored. (113)
But when defeat has been reached, one who is weak is slain therein;
let it not be so, O wise one, for the loss shall not be yours alone. (114)
For my part, since you have abandoned me and treated me with contempt,
there shall be for me the loss of self, the loss of the world, and likewise the loss of fame.
I am capable of bestowing a curse exactly as you have said;
nevertheless, a woman should never act in this manner toward her beloved.
For forgiveness has indeed been granted to women by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
though they are faultless, they endure the cruelty of their husbands without distress.
Therefore, show favor; grant a mitigation of the curse.
For the company of the virtuous brings happiness, even when it is formed by walking only seven steps together.
O Brahmin, together with you, I, as a woman in the form of your wife,
have spent many thousands of years constantly serving you.
"For this reason, O Master, abandon your cruelty and be gracious.
Thus, reflecting upon these truthful and pleasing words as well as his own fault, [he spoke].
Seeing her wife thus bowed down in humility, the sage said to her:
"Listen to my words, O blessed lady, which shall bring about both curse and grace. (121)
"What shall I do with you? My great asceticism has been brought to ruin by you.
That which is gone is truly gone; once lost, it never returns again. (122)
I shall perform it again for you as well; may there indeed be auspiciousness for you.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, there occurs the auspicious Ekādaśī.
Known as Pāpamocanikā, it causes the destruction of all curses;
O fair-browed one, when her vow is performed, your state as a piśācī will depart.
Having heard this, Mañjughoṣā then went into another forest;
meanwhile, she became a Piśācī until Caitra returned. (125)
When Caitra had arrived, Mañjughoṣā, remembering her past lives,
then performed the vow according to the prescribed rite on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
With supreme devotion, she indeed worshipped Śrī Hari in her mind;
having kept a vigil at night and performed her morning rites, she [proceeded]. (127)
Released from her state as a Piśācī through the power of Pāpamocanikā,
she indeed assumed a divine form and went to heaven, to her own home.
Abandoned by her, Medhāvin went to the hermitage of his father,
the sage Cyavana, which was exceedingly resplendent with divine ascetic power and splendor.
Seeing him departing with his luster diminished after a long time, his father Cyavana said:
"What is this that you have done, my son? You have brought about the exhaustion of your merit."
"How is it that the fire, produced from the abundance of my asceticism, is not seen?
To this, the wise one replied, "O father, it is because of my asceticism in this forest. (131)
Having obtained the Apsaras, she committed many sins with her;
she enjoyed herself for a long time, and my wonderful ascetic merit was destroyed. (132)
"O father, tell me the expiation by which the destruction of sin may occur.
Then the father said to his son: "I shall tell you the vow; listen to me. (133)
In the dark fortnight of Caitra, there is the Ekādaśī known by the name Pāpamocanī; indeed, when its vow is performed according to the prescribed rules, it liberates one from sin.
"The heap of sins shall go to destruction, and at the end, the observer of the vow shall attain liberation.
Having heard these words of his father, he performed that supreme vow.
His sin went to destruction and his ascetic merit increased;
through the Pāpamocanikā vow, his spiritual luster quickly became pervasive.
O Lakṣmī, those people on earth who perform the Pāpamocanikā rite become truly endowed with austerity just as they were before. || 137 ||
Whatever sin they may have, all of it shall go to dissolution;
even for them, the fruit of a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices is produced.
Enjoyment, liberation, and great liberation—indeed, everything is attained through this single vow;
for such is this lunar day, capable of bestowing these fruits.
A killer of a Brahmin, a stealer of gold, a drinker of liquor, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
by performing this vow, the practitioner of it becomes liberated from those sins.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, or even reciting this, one gains great merit; it bestows the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O Lakṣmī, one must by all means perform this for the removal of curses and sins;
there is nothing superior to this in the world of moving and non-moving beings that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 142.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Caitra-Kṛṣṇa Pāpamocanī Ekādaśī Vow, wherein the Apsaras named Majjughoṣā, who had been enjoying [her boon] for a thousand years by the ascetic Medhāvin, was turned into a Piśācī due to the sage’s curse and attained liberation through the performance of the vow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"In this world, there is no other supreme savior besides the Blessed One;
and in this world, there is no other purifier besides the Sātvatas."
And for living beings, there is no other destroyer of sin than the virtuous;
likewise, in this world, there is nothing other than religious observance that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Apart from Ekādaśī, there is nothing else that destroys curses and sins,
nor anything that bestows heaven, spiritual perfections, wealth and sons, as well as liberation.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear; please tell me:
what is the name of that Ekādaśī which occurs in the bright fortnight of Caitra? (4)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, there is the most meritorious Ekādaśī known by the name Kāmadā; it is a forest fire to the fuel of sins.
She is also called Vimalā, the bestower of all desires;
for Viṣṇu, accompanied by Ramā, is indeed worshipped as her husband.
With the sixteen types of offerings, according to one's wealth and according to the prescribed ritual,
the fruit for the *arghya* offering is *cirbhaṭa* and the like, while *cūta* flowers are used for worship.
As for the food offering, roasted flour, sweetmeat balls,
and cooked rice should especially be presented by one observing a vow for the attainment of the desired fruit.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should either eat a single meal or observe the night-vow;
he should sleep on the ground at night and maintain his state of celibacy.
Having risen at dawn during the time of Ekādaśī, one should remember Hari;
one should meditate upon the form of Śrī Hari and, having bathed, worship the Lord.
One should bathe [the image] with the five nectars and with waters originating from sacred fords (tīrtha);
one should offer garments and ornaments of great value.
One should adorn [the deity] with erotic articles and fragrant substances,
as well as with flowers, necklaces, incense, lamps, food offerings, and excellent fruits.
One should propitiate [the deity] with water for drinking, mouth-fresheners, betel-leaf, cardamom, cloves, lamps offered at dawn, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and other such acts. || 13 ||
One should indeed ask forgiveness from one's inferiors and then perform a hymn of praise:
"O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of attaining the fruit [of my actions], I observe the vow of Ekādaśī. (14)
"By your grace, may that [rite] of mine be fulfilled without obstacle.
Having thus prayed, he should then prepare a *sarvatobhadra* mandala with grains.
Having prepared there an auspicious golden pitcher, or else one of copper,
[he should fill it] with five jewels, nine leaves, water, cloth, and sandalwood.
One should cause [the deity] to be worshipped with unbroken grains, fruits, and flowers;
and there, in each vessel, one should likewise place a vessel of sesame seeds and an image of Hari.
The observer of the vow should install the images of Ramā and Kāmadā according to the prescribed rite;
he should worship them with the mantras for invocation and other rites, and bathe them with water.
One should worship with articles of worship, as well as with garments, ornaments, and weapons; likewise, one should adorn Hari-Viṣṇu and Ramā with clothing and other such items.
One should adorn her with various articles of ornament and decoration;
just as one adorns Viṣṇu, so should one adorn Lakṣmī with many ornaments.
One should groom the hair with oil and fragrant liquids;
there, one should fashion a braided topknot (dhammilla), as well as ornaments and flower clusters (stabaka).
One should fashion a hair-knot with four strands or two strands,
as well as a cord, flowers, a flat ornament, or likewise a golden chain.
One should cause all four types of knots with three strands to be made;
at the front, one should fashion a braid and apply auspicious vermilion.
Likewise, one should apply a tilaka on the forehead with the liquid of kesara-sandalwood,
and place a beautiful mark of saffron in the center of the brow.
Alternatively, one should apply five fine dots of sesame seeds in the center;
and on the sides of the marks on the cheeks, there should be sparse decorations of leaf-patterns.
In the center, one should fashion and adorn the forehead with extremely subtle drops, making it appear like another abode of Lakṣmī.
One should apply collyrium to the eyes with a golden probe,
and one should place a powder rich in white and red fragrances upon the face.
To fully manifest the beauty and charm of her form, one should place a very beautiful red *ṭibakī* mark upon her cheek. (28)
One should likewise apply a tiny, deep red drop of *bindu* upon the chin as well, for the purpose of manifesting the beauty of the two lips as land-lotuses. (29)
One should apply colored ointments of that same kind to the nose, as well as to the nostrils;
one should offer earrings and other ornaments for the ears, and place bracelets upon the wrists.
One should offer necklaces made of gold flowers and excellent gems, as well as fine diamonds such as the Kaustubha, upon the golden Airāvata elephant. || 31 ||
One should wear bracelets set with jewels on both arms,
and golden chains and bangles on the forearms.
One should place gold rings set with gems and other jewels upon the fingers,
and one should color the nails on the palms of the hands with a substance suitable for staining.
One should apply divine sandalwood paste to the chest and also to the breasts;
[one should offer] golden necklaces, flower garlands, and a bodice to fasten the breasts.
One should offer a beautiful girdle made of gold upon her waist, as well as a highly valuable garment with golden threads at its borders. (35)
Likewise, one should wear a triple-strand necklace that is pleasing to the eyes, pleasant to the touch, and made of fine cloth, dyed with colors and variegated with patterns. (36)
One should indeed give a beautiful, soft cloth for the Sudarśana [discus] to hold in the hand, its beautiful folds pervading the interior of the inner space.
A golden vessel in the shape of a lotus, as well as a fine fan, two beautiful chowries, an umbrella, and likewise a pair of sandals; || 38 ||
And ornaments for the feet and ankles, chains with small bells, bracelets,
armlets, and likewise finger-rings and bracelets for the fingers.
Having given [these], one should worship Lakṣmī, Hari, Ekādaśī, and Ramā;
likewise, one should offer ornaments to Ekādaśī just as one does for Ramā.
Just as Ramā is so, Ekādaśī is likewise the beloved wife of Hari;
she is all the necessary implements, all the household articles, and all excellent treasures.
One should also give all kinds of ornaments to her for the attainment of the fruit;
having thus performed the worship with sandalwood and other fragrant substances.
One should offer incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel, and drinks to the God and the Goddess; thereafter, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana). ||43||
Then the observer of the vow should perform circumambulation, ask for forgiveness, offer praise, and prostrate; thereafter, he should offer a handful of flowers—such is the morning ritual.
Having established the form of Hari situated in the center of the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], one should then go to one's own home and perform recitation for the sake of worship. 45.
At midday as well, having performed worship in the same manner, one should offer the food offering (naivedya).
One should give water, betel leaf, and everything else just as before.
In the evening as well, one should likewise perform worship, including the waving of lights (ārātrika) and other rites;
one should observe the entire excellent vow with great festivity, which bestows abundant merit.
At night, one should construct a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars;
one should fashion an archway of sprouts and indeed fasten a swing to a tree.
The observer of the vow should swing Hari Viṣṇu, who is accompanied by Vimalā and Kāmadā;
he should offer food offerings, water for drinking, and other gifts to the God. 49.
At night, the observer of the vow should keep a vigil with great festivities of dance and song; he should propitiate Hari by the ritual method of total self-surrender.
Having bathed in the morning, meditated upon Hari, and worshipped Janārdana, and having given various gifts and performed the lustration ceremony for Mādhava; || 51 ||
Having whirled a wet cloth and offered water from a conch shell,
one should present sweet food along with side dishes and the like, accompanied by tulasī leaves.
Having fed Hari, the Brahmins, the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the children,
and having dismissed them, the observer of the vow should then perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
By performing the rite in this manner, merit becomes eternal;
whatever one desires, whether pertaining to this world or arising from the next world, that shall certainly come to pass.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this delightful story which grants liberation to two Gandharvas.
Long ago, in the beautiful city of Nāgapura, which was auspicious and filled with golden palaces— (55)
For there dwelt Gandharvas known as the Puṇḍarīkas,
who were arrogant with pride, exceedingly cruel, and endowed with great power from intoxication.
Gandharvas, kinnaras, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and likewise kiñjanas; as well as satparya apsarases, goddesses, and maidens dwell there. (57)
In that city, King Puṇḍarīka ruled;
he was known by the name Pauṇḍra, and by him a great festival was well-arranged.
Gandharvas, kinnaras, sūtas, māgadhas, and likewise bandins; kimpuruṣas, singers, and also the reciters known as cāraṇas. ||59||
Brahmins learned in the Vedas, belonging to the rājasa and divine classes,
who were experts in the Gāndharva Veda, arrived there for that festival.
There, in that assembly hall upon the stage, the dance proceeded;
those rich in melody sang, and the instrumentalists played their instruments.
The dancing girls dance, while other people watch; and from Pātāla and the world of the Nāgas, the serpents, able to assume any form at will, also look on.
The Daityas and Dānavas also gathered for that festival;
appearing like gods in form, they too took their places at the celebration.
When the singing and dancing of the other singers had been established, and likewise when the dancing and singing of the female dancers had been concluded; ||64||
The lord of the Gandharvas, a preeminent master of great skill named Lalita, descended upon the stage before King Pauṇḍra.
But Lalitā, the wife of a Gandharva, did not come there to the arena because of her household duties; at that time, Lalita was indeed alone.
Lalita performs singing and music even without his beloved;
indeed, it is because of the absence of his beloved that Lalita [acts thus]. (67)
Deprived of his side and lacking assistance, he nevertheless remembers her in his mind and sings, dances, and plays musical instruments in perfect rhythm.
A beautiful woman dwells eternally in his heart; moreover, she becomes especially well-remembered during moments of intimacy. (69)
The husband dwells eternally within the heart of Lalitā;
both are dyed with passion, a couple bound by the ties of love.
Just as he used to sport at home, that was recalled by Lalita;
with his mind distracted by the memory of his wife on the stage, the dancer [performed]. (7.1)
Remembering Lalitā, his tongue faltered and he stumbled over his foot-binding verses;
his mastery of the meter slipped away, and his voice descended to a lower register.
In the midst of the assembly of the Gandharvas, he became an object of ridicule;
indeed, at that moment, Pauṇḍra’s fame was destroyed by that injury.
Then Pauṇḍraka Puṇḍarīka, afflicted by anger,
cursed Lalita as he was singing on the stage, being himself overcome by passion.
"O evil-minded one, become a Rākṣasa, a flesh-eater who devours men, since you were singing here during the great festival while remembering your wife. (75)
"Because of your lack of attention in the assembly, you have suffered a loss in the art;
thus, both you and I have been made objects of ridicule by the assembly. (76)
"Therefore, having become a Rākṣasa, you shall experience suffering for many years. At these words of Pauṇḍra, he assumed the form of a Rākṣasa. ||77||
With a fierce countenance and deformed eyes, he was terrifying to behold;
his mouth, resembling a cavern, was many yojanas wide. ||78||
The two eyes resemble the sun; the neck is like a mountain;
the nose resembles a range of mountains; and the nostrils are like caves. ||79||
With lips as wide as a *gavyūti* and a height of two *yojanas*,
having become such a Rākṣasa, he was experiencing the fruit of his own actions.
Lalitā went home, and seeing her husband’s deformed appearance, she, distressed by the suffering of her husband, began to reflect.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My husband is tormented by sin.
Having learned the entire account, she remained devoted solely to the service of her husband. (82)
Lalita wandered with her husband in the dense forest;
remembering again and again what had occurred before, she found no peace in her mind.
Though she was capable of assuming any form at will, she wandered through the difficult forest together with her husband, who likewise could assume any form at will.
Though he was graceful in the difficult forest and capable of assuming any form at will, he became pitiless, devoted to evil, deformed, and a man-eater. ||85||
Afflicted by sin, he finds no happiness by night or by day;
seeing her husband so extremely distressed, Lalitā herself became exceedingly sorrowful.
Oppressed by hunger, thirst, and other afflictions, she wandered together with him;
for the husband was in the form of a rākṣasa, while the wife was in the form of a gandharva.
But seeing that extraordinary union of the two, the forest-dwellers were struck with supreme wonder; terrified, they fled from the spot. ||88||
Then the two of them arrived at the hermitage of the sage Śātātapa;
Lalitā went quickly, offered her salutations, and stood before him. (89)
The compassionate sage asked, "Who are you, and for what reason have you arrived?
Lalitā replied, "I am a Gandharvī, the daughter of Vīradhanvan."
"I have a name called Lalitā, and I have come here for the sake of a husband; my husband, who was like Lalita himself, has become a Rākṣasa due to the curse of Pauṇḍraka. (9.1)
Having become thus, I wander in this forest; seeing him, I have no happiness until by some merit my lord is liberated from his state as a rākṣasa. (92)
"O Lord Śātātapa, instruct me in such a meritorious deed.
Having heard this, the auspicious Śātātapa spoke these words that remove the sin of a curse: 93.
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Caitra bestows merit and happiness; O beautiful lady, you should certainly observe its vow according to the prescribed rite. (94)
"The merit that shall arise from this fruit should be bestowed upon your own husband;
once that merit is given, the fault of his curse will vanish in an instant. (95)
Having heard the words of the sage Śātātapa, she became filled with joy;
she remained in that hermitage awaiting the arrival of Ekādaśī.
Her husband dwelt there constantly in that forest;
he had observed the fast of the waterless Ekādaśī, which grants all desires. ||97||
He kept a vigil during the night on the twelfth day, and likewise at dawn, in the presence of Śātātapa and in the vicinity of the image of Hari. (98)
Lalitā spoke these words for the sake of rescuing her husband:
"Indeed, I have observed this vow, the fast of Kāmadā. (99)
By the power of his merit, let this state of being a piśāca perish;
at that very moment, by the words of Lalitā, his piśāca-hood [vanished].
His state as a Rākṣasa departed and he was born again as a Gandharva;
freed from sin, that graceful one became possessed of a divine body.
Adorned with gold and jewels, he took delight with Lalitā;
the two of them, mounted upon a celestial chariot, were auspicious and even more beautiful than their former forms.
Thus, by the merit born of the vow of Kāmadā, both husband and wife, having gone to Nāgapura, shone even more than before; such was their state as Piśācas.
"O Mahālakṣmī, knowing that [the curse] is destroyed, the curse is annulled, and there is a reunion with one's own true nature, this must be performed with great devotion. (104)
It destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and annihilates the state of being a Piśāca;
by reciting or even hearing it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Caitra-Śukla-Kāmada-Ekādaśī Vow, and the Liberation from the State of a Piśāca—born due to the Curse of Pauṇḍra—of the Gandharvas Lalita and Lalitā," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord who bestows liberation, O Master who uplifts the people, O destroyer of the sins of sinners, those cursed, and even those who curse! (1)
This divine vow, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has been revealed by you;
hearing it again and again, I rejoice, and a desire arises in me to hear it further.
Speak, O Lord, ocean of mercy: what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, who is its presiding deity, and what is its ritual procedure? (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: She bestows good fortune, grants the abundance of sons and grandsons,
gives happiness in this world and the next, confers prosperity, and destroys sins.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, there is one named Varūthanī;
by her vow, the practitioner of the vow attains happiness in every respect. (5)
There is the destruction of sins and the attainment of good fortune as well;
even an unfortunate woman who performs this vow shall obtain all good fortune.
For all those who observe vows here, she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
she removes all sins, grants merit, takes away rebirth, and is auspicious.
It destroys latent impressions, bestows eternal bliss and liberation, and grants everlasting stability; indeed, it must be performed by one who observes the vow.
Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, and others who observed vows attained the heavenly path;
therefore, Puruṣottama should be worshipped here together with Śakti and Nandā.
Jātiphala and other such items are for worship; in the food offering, fried cakes (vaṭaka) are auspicious;
likewise, flowers such as campaka and the buds of the kunda flower [are used].
Land-lotuses should be given, as well as land and other gifts; furthermore, the observer of the vow should perform other acts according to his capacity with a state of complete devotion. (11)
On the tenth day, having either eaten a single meal or observed a fast at night, sleeping on the ground and remaining celibate, one should remember Lord Hari in the morning during the vow.
Bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, and likewise kodrava grain;
vegetables, honey, food from others, eating a second time, and sexual intercourse—[these should be avoided]. (13)
A devotee of Viṣṇu who observes the vow should avoid ten things on the tenth day:
gambling, sleep, betel nut, and cleaning the teeth [with a twig]. (14)
On the eleventh day, one should avoid slandering others, backbiting, theft, violence, as well as delighting in them, anger, and false speech. (15)
For one month, he should avoid bell-metal, wine, honey, oil, speaking with those who have fallen from their caste, physical exercise, travel abroad, eating a second meal, and sexual intercourse. (16)
One should avoid tamasic food and lentil-based food on the twelfth day;
on the eleventh day, the observer of the vow, having bathed in the morning, [should worship] Śrī Puruṣottama.
One should worship with new materials and the sixteen excellent offerings;
one should perform the rites beginning with invocation, as well as the five nectars and the anointing.
Bathing in the waters of pure sacred fords, wearing garments and ornaments, giving gifts of fragrant unguents and the like, and applying collyrium and eye-salve. (19)
He offered auspicious forehead marks and crescent-shaped tilakas made of saffron and other substances, clusters of flowers, as well as flower garlands and crests.
There, one should offer [the oblation] to Hari and cause incense, lamps, and so forth to be presented;
having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), bowed down, and completed the circumambulation. ||21||
Having offered praise and asked for forgiveness, one should indeed present a handful of flowers;
having thus worshipped in the morning, one should perform the great worship.
Having prepared an auspicious mandala called Sarvatobhadra with grains, either in a plantain pavilion or in the beautiful temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; (23)
And in the center of the mandala, there should be a beautiful sprout made of the five jewels, accompanied by water, sandalwood, rice, flowers, and fruit. ||24||
One should place a new pitcher made of gold or copper;
therein, one should place a new vessel filled with sesame seeds.
And one should likewise install the form of Puruṣottama together with Nandā and together with Varūthinī upon the tila-maṇḍala.
One should worship her according to the prescribed rite and honor her with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
one should also perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Likewise, bathing with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha), the offering of ornaments and garments, the application of elegant decorations and jewelry, and the offering of fragrant oils; || 28 ||
The offering of sandalwood and other substances, the offering of forehead marks, collyrium, and saffron;
the offering of garlands made of flowers, jewels, and so forth, and the presentation of food offerings (naivedya). ||29||
The offering of water, betel, and the finest desired fruits,
as well as the waving of lights (nīrājana), prostrations, circumambulation, and the request for forgiveness.
And for the sake of fulfilling the vow, one should perform a prayer that destroys obstacles,
as well as the giving of gifts such as beds, elephants, and moon-ornaments, along with a supreme sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
And having completed the act of devotion, one should indeed give [the offering] and then proceed;
at midday as well, one should worship and feed Hari according to this very rule.
Having worshipped Hari in the evening, one should perform the ritual waving of lamps (ārātrika);
one should offer food, water for drinking, and so forth, and likewise observe a vigil.
One should perform dance, song, instrumental music, storytelling, and chanting; having reflected upon the Lord of Lakṣmī in the morning, one should then carry out the worship.
The gift of horses, the gift of elephants, the gift of land, the offering of sesame seeds; the gift of gold, the gift of food, the gift of a daughter, and the offering of cows. || 35 ||
Likewise, one should bestow the gift of knowledge and the gift known as the gift of fearlessness;
in this way, the protective armor (varūthinī) should be prepared, which grants all desired objects. 3.6.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by performing austerities for ten thousand years,
a man obtains that same fruit from the Varūthinī vow.
By constructing a *varūthinī*, one obtains the fruit of all forms of giving.
O Lakṣmī, in the former Kṛta Yuga, a most purifying story took place. (38)
Having heard which, the great majesty of Varūthinī is known:
there was a brahmin seer named Varūtha, the mind-born son of Brahmā. (39)
Less than twenty years of age, engaged in the vow of studying the Vedas and other scriptures, devoted to the service of his guru, and pure, he dwelt in the hermitage of Marīci.
Free from pride and free from ego, with the mirror of his mind made pure, he is constantly devoted to meditation on Brahman and worships the Guru as Brahman. ||41||
The word of the guru is the word of the Veda; the Veda has emerged from the mouth of the guru.
The guru is Viṣṇu, the guru is Brahmā, the guru is the Veda, and the guru is the Creator.
The Guru is Dharma, the Guru is liberation, the Guru is knowledge, and the Guru is sacrifice;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, and the Guru’s command is the Vedic revelation. ||43||
Since the guru must be satisfied by whatever means possible, when the guru is pleased, Brahman is pleased; there is nothing superior to the guru. (44)
The Guru is the reality of Brahman; there is no reality higher than the Guru.
The command of the Guru is the supreme dharma; indeed, the command of the Guru is heaven itself in this world.
Thinking with supreme devotion that there is no other higher dharma than the command of the Guru, the worldly dharma, and the dharma pertaining to the next world, [he remained steadfast]. (46)
He became preeminent in devotion to his guru and performed service for him;
whatever the guru would say, he did exactly that. ||47||
He lived happily, engaged solely in the service of his guru;
through constant attendance upon Marīci, he was perpetually overflowing with bliss.
Established in Brahman, he lived free from attachment to the body;
dwelling in the house of his guru, that twice-born man became one who delights in the Self.
He serves the guru and likewise attends upon the guru’s wife, Kalā, with a sense of non-difference, thinking, "She is indeed the guru himself. (1.248.50)
Kalā was indeed the wife of Marīci; she was the half-body of Marīci.
Both Kalā and Marīca possess the quality of heaviness (gurutva). ||5 1 ||
The household service of the couple also includes sweeping and plastering, as well as fetching water and bringing the materials for worship. ||52||
Massaging the feet, cleaning the bowl after a meal, preparing the canopy for the bed, and likewise withdrawing the bedding. ||53||
Washing clothes, grooming the hair, applying collyrium to the eyes, and staining the palms of the hands with red lac. (54)
Massaging the body with oil, likewise bathing it with water, wiping it with a cloth, and also the application of fragrant scents. ||55||
Every day, he performed his personal adornment with garments, flowers, ornaments, and other such finery.
It indeed brings about the state of qualified Brahman for the couple. ||56||
He does not consider this body to be the self; rather, he considers here that which is other than the body to be the self—the immutable, stainless form of the Self. (57)
That nature of the Self is free from both sin and merit and is beyond all affliction;
the Self is neither bound by sin nor smeared by sin. (58)
Devotion to the Guru is the supreme merit; there is no merit higher than this.
Apart from the Guru, there is no other object of worship or meditation.
Thinking always that he has satisfied his guru,
he never performs the worship of the form of Viṣṇu, nor does he regard it as such.
He does not offer food oblations to Viṣṇu, nor does he offer water;
he does not worship Acyuta Hari with the sixteen types of services and other such rites.
He partakes of food without serenity and drinks water that has not been offered;
he takes bark, roots, flowers, and so forth by himself, without having offered them.
Her intellect, having become turbid through the enjoyment offered to Hari, became pervaded by the quality of passion (rajas) and followed after worldly enjoyments. (63)
Food and other offerings dedicated to Hari are said to be entirely unfit for consumption;
and from the eating of such forbidden food, his notion of identifying the body with the self arose. (64)
And he became embodied, like one who delights in the objects of the senses;
for this proponent of the doctrine that the body is the self, his sense faculties became powerful. (65)
Atheism, youth, and likewise service to the teacher's wife—
through constant practice, these cause one to transcend the intense torment of the fever of passion.
Nevertheless, he too maintains his self-restraint through the power of his mind.
Thus, when a great deal of time had passed, the Seven Sages indeed [arrived].
Then, for the sake of Śaṅkara’s marriage with the daughter of Dakṣa,
they were summoned by Brahmā to the world of truth, into the assembly of Brahmā.
Then they went to Varūtha, and Marīci said to his son:
"Act in such a way that my word is properly protected and carried out. (69)
The word of Kalā must be honored; you must do exactly as she says.
O disciple, my home must be protected by you in every way, just as it is by me.
Having given his command, Marīci departed for the assembly of Brahmā;
and the seven sages, sent by Brahmā, proceeded toward the house of Dakṣa.
But when Śambhu made his decision regarding the granting of the boon for yoga, the Satyas remained steady; they returned to their true state and once again departed. (72)
In this manner, a great deal of time passed while that deliberation continued;
and Kalā too became exceedingly pleased by her service to Varūtha.

Through the assistance of Varūtha, [the attendants] performed service by massaging the body, massaging the feet, and engaging in such acts as sitting and reclining together on the same bed or seat. ||74||
She became attached to the body of the excellent chariot through her state of passion,
having obtained the youth who was very firm by serving him in solitude.
Bowing low, Kalā said: "O Varūtha, take me as your consort here;
O sinless one, grant peace to me who am consumed by the fever of longing. (76)
Varūtha, regarding the words of his preceptor as authoritative and considering Kalā’s speech,
being possessed by a state of passion, enjoyed her in secret.
When their desire was fulfilled and peace had arisen between them, she spoke words of blessing: "May heaven be yours, and it shall be imperishable. (78)
Thus, by the power of desire, these two enjoyers, possessed of longing, took delight in a state of passion, relying upon the words of Marīci. (79)
Having performed that task for the sake of Hara, the seven sages then went to their home;
at that time, Marīci returned to his own auspicious hermitage.
Marīci exists with his retinue and his portion, and likewise Varcas;
both of them abide within their bounds, free from all desire.
Nevertheless, the line of longevity that had previously been full on the foreheads of both the preceptor’s wife and Varutha has now suffered a loss. (82)
It was seen by Marīci to have been severed through direct perception.
There, Marīci said to those two: "How did your life come to its end? (83)
Marīci, filled with wonder, spoke to them exactly as it was:
"Indeed, what was not done has been accomplished by these two; they have truly fulfilled my word. (84)
The word of the Guru is always faultless when spoken for the sake of his devotee;
yet by this [act], my own word has been violated, which is indeed a loss. (85)
The seizing of a Brahmin’s property, violating the teacher’s bed, treachery toward those who trust one, and ingratitude—these indeed are the destroyers of life. (86)
"Whatever has been done by these two, that very merit must be performed by me for them.
While he was thinking thus, the servants of Yama arrived. (87)
They came certainly to lead the two of them back toward the southern city;
Marīci did not speak there, and having taken them to the south, they departed quickly.
And Marīci followed along in that very same body;
then both of them were brought before Dharmarāja by his messengers.
A rod of heated iron and a red-hot metal image were joined together;
Marīci said to the Lord of Dharma, "O All-pervading One, you have acted appropriately."
But since everything was done at my word, there is indeed no fault on their part;
if the preceptor’s speech is wicked, then I alone am the vessel of that fault. (9.1)
It is likewise stated in the *Yamasmṛti*: "The word of a guru does not cause harm;
if the word of Yama is true, then my word does not cause harm. (92)
"How can those two, being attached by my word, be possessed of fault?
Therefore, these two are not fit for punishment; do as you wish. (93)
"As long as you do not release these two, I shall certainly not accept water or anything else;
here is my hospitality for you—do as you wish. (94)
Then Dharma, having heard the words of his aged father Marīci, reflected that his lifespan had been lost through improper conduct.
By what powerful means might these two be reconciled, so that both my word and the word of the Guru may be well-established as authoritative? (96)
What indeed should I do here in this contradictory situation?
If my word is authoritative, then these two are not deserving of punishment. (97)
If these two are deserving of punishment, then our word has no authority;
therefore, what should be done here regarding the act of restoring your life? (98)
Then, by means of that protection, he summoned there the power of his preceptor, saying:
"If I am devoted to my preceptor and carry out my preceptor's command... (99)
Then may Kṛṣṇa, who is identical with the Guru, protect [him] by the Guru’s word;
for as long as he remembers the one in the form of the Guru within that very chariot, [so long shall he be protected].
At that moment, a voice from the sky arose there, saying:
"O Dharmarāja, listen; these two have neither drunk water nor received food."
Marīci, too, exists today deprived of food and water;
for I am the Guru, and they both remember me as their Guru. (102)
"By these [signs], I believe the Ekādaśī vow has been performed on my behalf;
may the line of prosperity for both Kalā and Varūtha be fulfilled today. (103)
By virtue of the extraction of Varūtha, this eleventh day is indeed renowned as Varūthinī,
the one that effects the extraction of Varūtha.
By reconnecting with Kalāyuṣa, she was indeed restored to life;
moreover, she was truly gladdened by the celestial voice that bestows bliss.
"Accompanied by Nandā, Kṛṣṇa shall become her lord;
and those men who worship me together with Nandā," || 106 ||
Indeed, those devoted to the wives of their gurus shall become purifiers;
and women who engage in sexual intercourse with their disciples shall attain purity.
By my power, the men and women of Varūthinī who observe vows shall indeed become sinless; even those whose lifespans have been exhausted shall become long-lived.
Those who seize the property of others and those who are attached to the wives of others shall become dwellers of heaven, purified by the Varūthinī vow.
For them there shall be no fear of King Yama, nor the destruction of their lifespan;
there shall be neither widowhood, nor suffering, nor separation from their kin.
A person who is greatly afraid of the son of the Sun (Saturn) should construct a Varūthinī;
being liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal. || 111 ||
Therefore, those who fear sin should perform this with every effort;
from hearing or reciting it, the fruit of a thousand cows shall be obtained.
Even if one performs this vow for the sake of an army out of ignorance or even by force,
I lead that person, liberated from all sins, to the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Yama, release these two—Varūthaka and Kalā; and instead, accept as your guest Marīci, the best of sages.
Show him honor by giving him your wife as a disciple; thus may you be happy.
Otherwise, this sage will cast a curse upon you on account of the merit of your vow.
"Indeed, that entire region of yours shall become a place for the dead;
let not your spies go to the house of the performer of the Varūthinī vow."
And on the day of the Varūthinī fast, let your messengers not go to one who has fasted and is being honored, for he is performing a religious vow for my sake.
Having spoken thus, that celestial voice uttered by Hari ceased;
and Yamarāja, seeing that their lifespans were complete, released them.
Free from fault, abiding by the words of their preceptor, yet smeared with the faults of their artistic cries,
they returned to their own abode from the abode of Yama along with Marīci.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this festival of the Varūthinī vow been described to you.
Having performed, heard, or recited it, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vaiśākha-Kṛṣṇa-Varūthinī-Ekādaśī Vow, and How Kalā, the Wife of Marīci, was Rescued from the Fault of Association through the Vow despite her Devotion to the Words of the Preceptor’s Wife by Her Disciple Varūtha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, granter of fearlessness to devotees!
O All-pervading Lord, you have duly proclaimed this vow that bestows long life.
O Keśava, ocean of compassion, upon hearing this which destroys great sins, the mind of the brahmin Varūtha becomes serene.
O Mādhava, tell me: what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha; what is its fruit, what is the ritual procedure for it, and who is the presiding deity?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lotus-born one, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
I shall describe that which is the most sacred of all sacred things and the best of all vows.
O Lakṣmī, that Ekādaśī which occurs in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is known by the name Mohinī; it is the destroyer of all sins.
The nets of evil perish and delusion perishes through that vow;
great sufferings perish and happiness arises through that vow.
By her, even through the mere performance of her rites, sin is destroyed;
so too by one seeking the merit of a vow who observes a single meal on the tenth day, or even a night-fast.
One should conduct oneself likewise at night with the vow of celibacy;
having risen in the morning, the practitioner should always remember Kṛṣṇa.
Having bathed, Hari should be well-worshipped by one seeking the vow; he is to be worshipped according to the daily ritual procedure, and one should offer a prayer for the sake of the vow.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Acyuta, today I shall undertake a vow;
by even a fraction of your grace, may it be brought to completion."
Having thus completed the worship that was prescribed as a daily duty,
one should have a Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared with rice and other materials.
In the center of that, one should place a well-fashioned vessel made of gold or new copper,
filled with water, joined with five jewels and five sprouts.
With his neck wrapped in cloth and honored with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice grains,
one should place a coconut fruit at his side, containing water within it.
One should place a beautiful vessel filled with sesame seeds upon the face;
therein one should place substances of gold, silver, and copper, as well as sugar.
Having caused to be fashioned an image of gold of the Lord Madhusūdana, the Master of Ekādaśī, resplendent together with Mādhavī; || 15 ||
One should place that [image] together with Mohinī there in a vessel;
one should install and worship a ladder to heaven made of bell-metal.
Having had a svastika, a brahmasūtra, a crescent moon, and likewise a tilaka fashioned out of gold or silver, one should place them beside the jar.
Various fruits such as betel nuts (pūgīphala) and others,
along with cardamom (elā), cloves (lavaṅga), cinnamon bark (tvaksāra), and nutmeg (jātīphala), should be ground into a powder.
One should cause nine items to be given: sugar, hidden grains, and so forth;
likewise, a couch, a ball with a concealed cord, and a bolster.
A mirror, a fan, an umbrella, a chowrie, an auspicious staff, sandals, a hair-comb, and fragrant substances; || 1.249.20 ||
The performer of the vow should place a new earthen jar filled with water and ripe mango fruits,
and perform the worship according to the prescribed rite.
Among flowers, one should offer the jasmine; the auspicious milk-rice (pāyasa) is the food offering;
the fruit for the water-offering (arghya) is the jackfruit; and the gift of a bed is most excellent.
First, one should invoke that Madhusūdana-Acyuta into a vessel of sesame seeds;
thereafter, one should offer him a most excellent seat.
One should devoutly offer water for washing the feet, as well as auspicious water for worship,
and water for sipping (ācamana) to the deity.
One should provide a moist tooth-stick and fragrant powder;
one should then perform his mouth-rinsing with water from a sacred bathing place.

One should perform purification beginning with cleanliness; one should effect the cleansing of the hands and feet. One should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and thereafter with pure water.
One should perform the wiping with cloths and offer fine garments;
likewise, a clean, subtle, auspicious, white, and new upper garment.
One should offer sandalwood, oil, fragrant substances of the highest quality, camphor, gems, a sacred thread, collyrium, and so forth. (28)
One should quickly offer saffron, abīra, gulāla, auspicious unbroken rice grains (akṣata), flowers in the form of kunda buds, and garlands of flowers. (29)
Then he should offer to Hari all ornaments, the finest articles of adornment,
and beautiful decorations.
The observer of the vow should indeed apply a *tilaka* and a crescent moon mark upon the forehead with sandalwood paste,
and should smear [the paste] all around the body, starting from the heart and so forth.
One should offer incense, a lamp, and food offerings consisting of the finest sweet foods; one should also present sugar-based sweets, the essence of curd, sandalwood, and *pūrikā* cakes.
One should offer sugar-candy, cool water, mango fruit, and a betel-roll made of betel leaves; or whatever else has been prepared.
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering, prostration, hymns of praise, circumambulation, as well as falling like a staff, requesting forgiveness, and the prayer for the fullness of fruits. (34)
One should offer a handful of flowers and a sacrificial fee, and afterwards perform the dismissal; then the observer of the vow, being full of devotion, should attend to his necessary duties. (35)
At midday, one should worship Kṛṣṇa and provide him with abundant food;
then, being endowed with wealth, one should offer fifty-six articles of enjoyment.
One should offer water for drinking and betel leaf for cleansing the mouth;
having paid homage to him, the observer of the vow should perform acts of devotion and the like. (37)
In the evening, he should perform the circumambulation with lamps (ārātrika), offer food oblations (naivedya), and present water offerings;
he should also have a pavilion constructed and adorned with plantain pillars.
The observer of the vow himself should place Hari upon a beautiful and charming swing adorned with arches of fresh sprouts and cause him to sway there.
The observer of the vow should perform worship with the sixteen supreme articles;
at night, he should spend the time filled with devotion together with his devotees.
In this manner, one should perform the vigil preceded by a great festival,
accompanied by dancing, singing, and musical performance endowed with rhythm and measure.
One should cause [others] to remember, chant, and engage in narrations and stories; men and women alike should by all means cause the verses of Kṛṣṇa to be sung. 42.
Engaged in the chanting of Hari's praises, they should likewise keep a vigil;
in the morning, having bathed, one should remember Hari and perform worship once again. (43)
Observing the vow, one should give gifts to the guru with great devotion;
one should feed virtuous Brahmins and honor virtuous women and children. ||44||
One should feed the destitute, the wretched, young girls, those dependent on others, dependents, laborers, women, and members of the household. 45.
One should feed those worthy of worship with sweet food, as well as one's mothers and fathers;
one should feed the elderly and demonstrate a humble disposition.
Then the observer of the vow, remembering Hari, should himself perform the breaking of the fast;
he should also give gifts of beds, elephants, horses, and cows, as well as the offering of land and houses.
One should indeed offer vehicles, draft animals, and wealth to a worthy recipient;
by performing the vow in this manner, the practitioner attains the supreme state. ||48||
And eternal happiness in heaven [was attained] through the grace of Hari as desired;
O Lakṣmī, hear now the purifying story of a Vaiśya from a former birth. 49.
In Saurāṣṭra, not very far from the eastern bank of the Sarasvatī,
indeed in the northern region and to the south of the Bhadrāvatī.
In the city named Bhāṇḍīra, there was indeed a king named Dhṛtisiṃha;
he had a merchant named Dhanapāla, who was a treasury of wealth.
Dhanapāla was always renowned for promoting meritorious deeds; he was the builder of almshouses, wells, monasteries, gardens, tanks, and houses. (52)
He was a devotee of Viṣṇu, a servant of the virtuous, and firm in his vow to assist others;
he possessed great faith in hearing sacred narratives and was always intent upon devotion. ||53||
That wealthy merchant had five sons: Sumanas, Dyutimān, Medhāvī, and Sukṛti. (54)
There were four who were vessels of merit, and the fifth was a perpetrator of great evil,
known as Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, who was utterly devoted to the company of other men's wives.
One who is addicted to vices such as gambling, one who takes pleasure in courtesans, one who neglects the worship of the gods, and one who denies the libations offered to the ancestors; ||56||
He was a reviler of the twice-born, a reviler of the Vedas, devoid of righteousness, evil-minded, a destroyer of his father’s wealth, and a drinker of intoxicating liquor. ||57||

The sinner who eats what is unfit for consumption causes the destruction of all prosperity; he is devoted to acts such as theft, associates with the wicked, and indeed performs no righteous deeds. (58)
He was seen by his father at a crossroads with his hand resting on the shoulder of a courtesan;
thus he was recognized by his kinsmen as being devoted to sinful conduct.
Expelled from his home by his father and banished by his kinsmen,
he possessed only whatever small amount of wealth for his sustenance that had been obtained through his share of the inheritance.
Through constant association with courtesans, he brought everything to ruin:
his ornaments, vessels, garments, and household utensils.
By that very act of consorting with courtesans, his wealth was brought to exhaustion;
consequently, being destitute of riches, he was abandoned by the courtesans.
Distressed by anxiety, deprived of clothing and wealth, and afflicted by hunger, he thought:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? I am destitute of any means of livelihood. (63)
Therefore, I must perform the work of a thief; I live by committing robbery, by force, by plundering, and by seizing, and not otherwise.
In this way, he robs people of their strength on forest paths, and he commits acts of thievery at night in his father’s city. (65)
He constantly drinks liquor, he always eats meat, he perpetually commits theft, and he has fallen into the company of unchaste women. ||66||
At that very moment, he committed the theft of gold during the night;
however, he was seized by the king's messengers at night, yet the gold and wealth [remained] with him then.
Having surrendered his shaven form to the king’s messengers and being released from bondage, he attained liberation; yet, having gone to the forest, he once again committed theft.
Once again, the royal messenger was seized because he had not returned the stolen goods;
having obtained release from bondage, he went once more to the forest in that same manner. (69)
Furthermore, he again began theft and the seizing of wealth;
he oppressed the people and plundered the assemblies.
Then, he went to the city at night to commit theft;
that man of evil conduct was bound with strong ropes by the people.
Punished by the king with shackles and struck with lashes of the whip, he indeed spent his time in prison according to the sentence, and then [was released]. (72)
Having reached the forest with persistence, he rushes about for the sake of food;
fierce as a lion, he slays deer, boars, and monkeys. (73)
Devoted to the consumption of meat, he wanders everywhere in the forest,
holding a bow in his hand and carrying a quiver on his back.
Wandering on foot, he killed wild animals and birds, including ruddy geese, pigeons, doves, and partridges. (75)
He kills cocks, cranes, peacocks, and even mice;
he kills boars, gayals, and even eagles and swans. (76)
Fierce, bold-minded, and indeed merciless, he destroys these and others;
having entered upon the path of evil due to his former sins, he is engaged in sinful deeds. (77)
Overwhelmed by suffering and devoid of even a trace of happiness,
he remained thus day and night among trees, on mountains, in difficult passes, and in forest lands.
Without a seat, he wandered by chance and reached the city named Kuṇḍina, which was rich with the beauty of gardens and situated near forest lands. (79)
Not far from that forest, a great sage named Kauṇḍinya dwells constantly in his own hermitage, bestowing peace upon travelers. (1.249.8)
He honors guests with food, drink, seats, and other necessities; having heard that a sage whose wealth is asceticism had arrived at the gate of his hermitage, he went out to meet him. (8–9)
In the month of Vaiśākha, Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, facing toward his own imminent deliverance, approached the ascetic who had performed his bath in the lake. 8.2.
Having fallen at his feet with a humble disposition and a moistened heart, at that moment drops from the sage’s wet garment fell upon him. 83.
On the head of Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, as well as on his shoulders and hands, [one should recite]:
"We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva. (84)
Even the sound of the King of Sages as he spoke reached his ears;
thus was he purified by the mantra, by the sage, and by the water. (85)
By the mere touch of his feet, he became cleansed of sin;
and at that very moment, the sprout of his desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) broke forth within him.
Standing before Kauṇḍinya with palms joined in reverence, he spoke:
"O Brahmin, O bestower of liberation, having shown compassion toward me... (87)
Tell me of such a meritorious deed or a vow that bestows liberation, by the power of whose merit even a sinner attains release. (88)
Through association with great-souled ones, even those who have committed great sins cross over [to liberation], becoming purified themselves and purifying others as well. 8–9.
And because I committed theft, the drinking of liquor, the eating of meat, and sexual intercourse—
those sinful and wicked practices— I have fallen in every respect.
"O Lord, having purified me who am such as I am, make me a partaker of liberation.
Having heard this, the sage Kauṇḍinya then spoke to him who had come for refuge.
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, there occurs the famous Ekādaśī known as Mohinī; now follow the procedure for its vow.
Sins equal to Mount Meru shall go to destruction through that vow;
for one who observes the vow, those sins accumulated over many lifetimes will certainly perish quickly. 93.
Having heard these virtuous words of Kauṇḍinya, the bold-minded one then duly performed a vow in the vicinity of Kauṇḍinya’s hermitage.
His sins were washed away and he became pure; his latent impressions (vāsanā) dissolved, his life reached its end, and not even a trace of karma remained. || 95 ||
On the twelfth day, subsisting on fruits and leaves, he slept on the bank of the lake while remembering the sage Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and chanting His praises.
Having cast off his elemental body, he became possessed of a divine form;
seated upon Garuḍa, he went to the realm of Viṣṇu. || 97 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this auspicious *Mohinī-sad-vrata* bestows liberation;
there is nothing superior to it in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (98)
Sacrifices, pilgrimages, and gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of this vow, which by the power of Hari removes sins and bestows liberation. 99.
For those who are attached to illusion and delusion, she is the enchantress; for those who destroy delusion, she is the destroyer of delusion.
For those other than those who worship Brahman, she is the enchantress who bestows delusion.
Because delusion does not exist within her, she is therefore called Mohinī; yet that Mohinī by whom the sinner is led to his abode in heaven—[she is truly Mohinī]. (101)
Mohinī, who bestows eternal happiness because of her connection with Kṛṣṇa, grants through this vow a fruit exceeding that of ten million sacrifices. (102)
It should be observed with great effort, as it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation, and serves to remove the many sins of actions committed in previous births. 103.
This should be performed specifically according to the Vaiṣṇava tradition for the sake of quelling delusion, in order to attain the enchantment of the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 104.
One who possesses desire obtains through the performance of this vow everything—sons, grandsons, wealth, wives, prosperity, vehicles, houses, and so forth—that can be attained by it. (105)
One who is destitute of wealth shall obtain wealth, and one lacking wisdom shall attain wisdom;
indeed, whatever the observer of this vow may resolve upon, that he shall surely attain. (106)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vaiśākha Śukla Mohinī Ekādaśī Vrata, and how the liberation of a sinful Vaiśya named Dhṛṣṭabuddhi was attained through performing the vow upon the instruction of Kauṇḍinya," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, in this world, the conduct of living beings is indeed natural regarding food, drink, pleasure, ornaments, and beloved objects. (1)
But humans in this mortal world, having forgotten the human dharma, proceed along the path of beasts, seeking only the gratification of their bodies and senses. (2)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa,
for those [beings], there is no vow other than the Ekādaśī vow that bestows liberation so easily and grants swift release.
O Lord, having heard this, my mind becomes exceedingly serene;
I desire to hear the majesty [of the deity], the ritual procedure, the mode of worship, and the vow.

O Keśava, tell me likewise of that Ekādaśī which occurs on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha: what is its name, who is the deity to be worshipped on it, and what is its fruit? (5)
Nārāyaṇa said: The Ekādaśī known as Aparā, occurring in the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, destroys even great sins and bestows sons and grandsons.
The presiding deity of this is Hari himself, Adhokṣaja, joined with his consort named Trayī; he is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
He is to be worshipped with *ketaka* flowers as well as other auspicious blossoms;
in the water offering (*arghya*), many fruits should be given, and for the meal, milk-rice and other such foods.
Excellent cool water mixed with sugar should be given for drinking;
furthermore, the gift of a cow along with her calf is prescribed here for the preceptor.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should subsist on a single meal taken at night;
he should sleep on the ground at night and maintain his state of celibacy.
Having risen on the eleventh day during the Brahma-muhūrta, one should meditate upon Hari,
who has golden hair, lotus-like eyes, and a nose as beautiful as a sesame flower.
Adorned with earrings and a crown, and equipped with armlets and bracelets;
having red lips, a beautiful chin, and graced by a round face.
Laughing, with teeth radiant like rows of kunda buds,
endowed with emerging youth, and adorned by a circle of splendor.
Adorned with necklaces, gems, ornaments, and the like, he was attended by people;
his limbs were proportionate to his form, and his lotus-like face was serene.
To Kṛṣṇa, who captivates the heart of his devotee, who discharges side-long glances as arrows, who is filled with divine bliss, and who is more beautiful than ten million Cupids. 15.
One should thus meditate upon Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, the Lord;
then, having bathed, one should worship the Master, the Sovereign, according to the prescribed rite.
The observer of the vow should worship the Lord with the sixteen types of rites beginning with invocation, up to the final offering of handfuls of flowers; this constitutes the daily worship.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], he should at the end pray for the pacification of obstacles to the vow:
"O Supreme Lord, today I shall perform the vow of Aparā."
Then the observer of the vow, thinking "May that [observance] be fulfilled for me without obstacle," should have the Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared with unbroken grains and other offerings. (19)
Then, having placed a golden jar filled with water, or one made of copper, provided with the five gems and other such items, and adorned with cloth and sprouts; ||20||
One should worship that [liṅga] and the sacred fords, and then invoke into the water the image of Adhokṣaja fashioned from kunda flowers along with the three Vedas.
Having placed a vessel of sesame seeds upon the head of the jar, one should worship it,
beginning from the invocation and continuing until the final dismissal.
Bathing, ornaments, fragrance, food offerings, water, and betel; the waving of lights, hymns of praise, handfuls of flowers, and the offering of forgiveness and support. (23)
Having performed various acts of giving, one should cause others to give as well;
likewise, at midday, one should perform worship and also the fire-oblation (homa).
The practitioner, having indeed offered one hundred and eight oblations under the name of the Transcendent Lord (Adhokṣaja) according to the three Vedas,
should present sweet food offerings and then offer betel leaves and other items.
In the evening, however, [he should prepare] a beautiful green pavilion made of plantain trees,
adorned with archways rich in fresh sprouts, flowers, and fruits.
One should have a canopy constructed, wondrous with the beauty of various painted designs in the subterranean passage;
there, one should cause Mādhava to be swung upon a swing.
Then the observer of the vow should perceive Adhokṣaja situated upon a throne in the midst of a cool garden, sprinkled with water from a cloud. 28.
Having thus performed the great worship, one should conduct the rites for Hari at night, including the waving of lights (ārātrika) and so forth,
as well as the offering of food consisting of curd and sugar.
One should offer auspicious food consisting of mangoes rich in delicious flavor, along with *pūrikās* and other delicacies;
one should also present a meal to be eaten at night, as well as betel leaves and other offerings.
And for the purpose of a bed, one should prepare a couch provided with a swing—
a well-constructed hammock suspended from a branch of a neem tree in the open air.
One should also prepare a soft cushion made of cotton balls and so forth, as well as a covering;
there, one should swing the Blessed One in the light of a ghee lamp.
Devotees, having gathered together in the presence of Hari, should perform dancing, singing, chanting, remembrance, and likewise worship, as well as keeping a vigil. ||33||
There, one should hear or recite the narrative of Ekādaśī,
and one should cause [others] to hear the divine sports (līlā) and other deeds of Hari through speech and other means.
One should cause the worship of the unbroken [linga] to be performed with sound at night;
likewise, one should offer sweet water, fruits, and other such items to the devotees. ||35||
One should give milk for the pacification of throat ailments, or whatever else may be required; likewise to virtuous men, chaste women, noble ladies, and yogis. (36)
He should perform service, such as massaging the feet, to dispel his fatigue;
likewise, he should remain awake and avoid all censure and reproach. (37)
One who observes the vow of the Ekādaśī vigil should cultivate divine vision, meditate upon Adhokṣaja in the heart, and perform every auspicious deed. (38)
One should eliminate laziness, stiffness of the back, and other such ailments through the practice of *rāsa*;
one should repeatedly engage in leaping, singing, dancing, and laughing. (39)
To destroy sleep and laziness, the devotee should perform running and circumambulation, and engage in play with fellow devotees who are impartial toward all. 40.
One should vividly play out Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes: the rāsa-līlā, the pastime of giving gifts, the pastimes with the gopīs, his sporting with Rādhā, and his wandering in the forest. (41)
One should perform the marriage of Nārāyaṇa with Padmā, as well as his union with Bhārgavī and Ramā, in a festive manner.
At night, one should perform a great festival for Kṛṣṇa as it was performed by the Gopikās, or together with Pārvatī, Prabhā, Māṇikī, and Lakṣmī. (43)
One should perform the marriage festival for Brahmā, the Supreme Self;
likewise, one should sing the birth-verses as well as the festivals celebrating the manifestation of Śakti.
One should recite [the hymn] during the vigil and, having bathed in the morning, worship;
one should also worship Adhokṣaja with the sixteen types of ritual offerings and so forth.
Then one should worship the three Vedas, as well as the eleventh [form], and the Guru;
for Kṛṣṇa’s head is always situated upon the head of the Guru. 46.
Kṛṣṇa’s eyes were in the eyes of the guru; the face of Hari was in the mouth of the guru;
Kṛṣṇa’s ears were in the ears of the guru; and the tongue of Hari was in the mouth of the guru.
The throat of Hari is in the throat of the Guru; the lip of Mādhava is on the lip of the Guru;
Kṛṣṇa’s chest is indeed on the chest of the Guru; and there is a unity of the abdomen between Hari and the Guru. (48)
The hand of Hari is in the hand of the Guru; the waist of Hari is in the waist of the Guru;
the back of Hari is on the back of the Guru; the heart of Hari is one with the heart of the Guru. (49)
In the intellect of the guru is the intellect of Hari; in the speech of the guru is the speech of Hari;
what is protected by the guru is protected by Hari; and the two thighs of the guru are the two thighs of Hari.
The skin of Hari is indeed in the eyes of the Guru; the strength of Hari is in the body of the Guru;
the knees of Hari are in the knees of the Guru; and the oneness of the nails of Hari is with those of the Guru.
The feet of Kṛṣṇa are at the feet of the Guru, and the nails of the Guru are one with those of Hari.
Kṛṣṇa himself resides within the Guru; there is no other Kṛṣṇa higher than the Guru.
"The Guru is Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa is the Guru; salutation to that Śrī Guru.
Having meditated thus, one should properly worship the Guru with the realization that he is Kṛṣṇa. (53)
One should also offer that which is dear to the guru; for when the guru is satisfied, he is truly gratified.
By serving the guru, the merit of serving Kṛṣṇa is certainly attained. (54)
There is no doubt that the offering of the self to the Guru is the offering to Kṛṣṇa;
for I, O Lakṣmī, appear in the form of a Guru to my great disciples. 55.
Abiding with the guru, I shall receive divine service honored by devotion,
by whatever means possible, whether through giving or through worship.
By bowing down, by offering oneself, by service, and by praise;
or even by massaging the feet, or by offering beloved objects. (57)
Even after offering one's home and other possessions, the Guru should always be satisfied;
therefore, one should offer the gift of the Ekādaśī materials to the venerable Guru.
A Guru who is satisfied can indeed deliver the husband, the wife, the son, the daughter, and the entire family; therefore, the Guru is identical with Kṛṣṇa.
Having understood this, one should indeed offer a gift to the preceptor on the twelfth day;
one should cause the Brahmins to break their fast and feed virtuous men and women.
One should feed young girls and give abundant gifts;
thus, the observer of the vow [attains success] on earth, in heaven, or even in the realm of Vairāja.
One who serves the supreme [deity] attains eternal happiness even in the sovereign and indeterminate states;
however, he who serves the lower [deities] attains renown in the world.
One who has committed the murder of a Brahmin, the murder of a cow, the destruction of an embryo,
as well as the murder of a woman or the murder of a friend, and other such evildoers, is liberated from their sin through this vow.
A person who delights in slandering others and likewise takes pleasure in the wives of others becomes free from sin by obtaining the vows of another.
A false witness, a mother who deceives, one who practices fraud and hypocrisy, one who speaks falsely, and a slanderer— these are swiftly liberated from sin.
One who is a fraud regarding the Vedas, a fraud regarding the Śāstras, likewise a fraud regarding the calculation of the stars,
or a physician who is a fraud regarding Āyurveda— such a person is indeed liberated from this [sin] by means of this vow.
Brahmins fallen from Brahmanhood, Kṣatriyas who have lapsed from their duty of protection,
and Vaiśyas who have turned away from giving— these are liberated from this [sin] by means of this vow.
Even Śūdras excluded from the Dharma, disciples who revile their preceptors and others,
and even a son who kills his mother or father, are indeed liberated by this vow.

Whatever fruit is obtained by men at Prayāga when the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, and whatever merit is gained through the vow of Śivarātri at Kāśī—[that is attained here]. (69)

Whatever merit is considered to be bestowed upon the ancestors by the offering of a funeral cake at Gayā, and whatever fruit is obtained at the Godāvarī when Jupiter is situated in Leo; [that fruit is attained here].
The merit from beholding Kedāra is equal to the fruit born of the Badarī-tīrtha,
or from visiting all the holy fords at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse.
By performing a sacrifice accompanied by the giving of elephants, horses, and gold, along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
one obtains that same fruit through the observance of the Aparā vow.
This [wisdom] is the axe for the tree of sin, the forest fire for the jungle of faults, the sun for the darkness of evil, and the lioness for the deer of misfortune. (73)
She is considered the supreme goddess who bestows liberation, worldly enjoyment, and indeed everything desired;
for there remains no higher merit than that which is gained through her vow. (74)
This other [Kṛṣṇā] is meaningful for those who perform vows due to her connection with Kṛṣṇa;
however, through the vows of others here, only fragmented merit is obtained.
By the vow of Aparā here, the fruit of universal sovereignty shall be attained;
for there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be obtained by one who observes this vow. (76)
O Lakṣmī, both the listener and the reciter shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
the observer of the vow, having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
And because others are indeed surpassed by its splendor at the outset, it is called *aparā* (the lower);
yet there is no higher than this supreme one.
Having observed another fast and having worshipped Adhokṣaja together with the Consort of the Three Vedas, one is liberated from even the strongest of bonds, as if from an adamantine paste.
This is declared to be the expiation for sins that lack any other means of atonement;
for a soul that has no other recourse, this alone is the supreme vow and the true refuge.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the narrative concerning Śalabhā in the Kṛta Yuga—a wonderful, auspicious, and liberating account of a female ascetic. 8.1.
Having undertaken the most rigorous initiation of the Bhāgavatas, that virtuous woman worships the god Nārāyaṇa day and night. (82)
In the forest on the mountain named Arbuda, near Puṣkara,
she wanders constantly alone by the power of yoga.
From her childhood, she was an exceedingly great yogini and a disciple of Sanaka;
when a hundred thousand years had passed and she had reached the peak of youthful vigor, ||84||
In the forest, having repeatedly observed the sexual acts of lions and lionesses—the lords of the wild beasts—as well as the various unions of other forest-dwelling animals; ||85||
Her mind became intent upon the pleasure of Kāmadeva;
she [beheld] a red-colored wild monkey situated in her own hermitage. (86)
Having taken him, she delighted him constantly out of passionate desire;
and through the union with the monkey, a fetus was conceived and grew.
Having then heard from the disciple of Vasiṣṭha, named Vedaśruta, that the mixing [of castes] through the yoga of animal sacrifice is a sin that destroys liberation, she—
Having fallen into great remorse, she went to the hermitage of Sanaka;
seeing that the disciple was pregnant, Sanaka spoke to her.
"What indeed is this that has occurred upon your birth? Your studenthood has been violated;
nevertheless, you have described everything to your guru without any deceit. (90)
Tell me how the destruction and purification of this defiling act, as well as this sin of causing a fall from caste, may be brought about so that purity may arise.
Having thus entreated him, she, pregnant and distressed in mind, wept;
for in the event of a miscarriage, there is the extreme sinfulness of causing an abortion and other such heinous crimes.
To her, who was reflecting, "How might my womb be free from defect?", Sanaka said: "Listen. (93)
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, observe the vow of fasting without water;
your sin shall be destroyed and your prārabdha karma shall reach its completion.
"Furthermore, liberation shall be easily attained even before childbirth; therefore, perform the vow.
Having heard this and bowed to the Guru, he went to his own hermitage on Mount Arbuda.
She duly performed the entire auspicious vow of Aparā;
by that, her impurity was removed and her state of degradation was dissolved.
And her life became peaceful through her steady devotion to Adhokṣaja;
then, having joined her self with him through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*), she departed.
Having led the consciousness situated in the womb to the world of Brahmā,
she abandoned her body and, through the practice of the Aparā vow, attained supreme liberation.
O Lakṣmī, this vow alone, which destroys the mixture of sins, must be performed by a woman in every way for the sake of her constant purity. (99)
That [rite] must certainly be performed by an ascetic, one established in Brahman, a yogi, and even a renunciant,
for the pacification of the sin of causing the mixture of castes.

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Vow of the Eleventh Day of the Dark Fortnight of Jyeṣṭha within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning how the pregnant woman Śalabhāyatī was freed from fault and attained liberation through the performance of this vow which destroys sins such as causing the mixture of castes (saṃkarīkaraṇa) and other transgressions, thereby averting her union with a monkey.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the Blessed One himself is the true essence;
by worshipping him, men attain the imperishable state of Nirvāṇa.
Due to its connection with Kṛṣṇa, the dark lunar day bestows fruits equal to those of Kṛṣṇa himself;
by performing its vow according to the rules, an embodied being attains the supreme goal.

What is the name of the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha? Who is its presiding deity, what is the procedure for its vow, what is the nature of the gift, and what is its fruit? (3)
Speak to me, O Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Mercy, O Consort of Ramā,
for You are the one who bestows causeless grace upon Your own devotees.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is indeed known as Nirjalā; on this day, the one named Trivikrama, together with Padmākṣī, is desired to be worshipped.
He is to be worshipped with *yūthikā* flowers; for the water offering (*arghya*), a mango fruit is prescribed.
Curd, rice, and other such items are desired as the food offering (*naivedya*), and the gift of an umbrella and so forth is also recommended.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should subsist on a single meal taken at night;
he should sleep on the ground at night and remain celibate as one observing the vow.
Having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon the Lord of Lakṣmī and contemplate His limbs;
having bathed, the devotee should worship Him with materials endowed with sincere devotion.
