Beginning with the invocation, one should perform the bathing with the five nectars and other substances,
and then provide adornment with garments, ornaments, and fragrant scents.
With betel leaves, saffron, musk, necklaces, sandalwood paste, crest-jewels, and the like; with the waving of lamps, excellent food offerings, drinks, betel nut, and ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having performed the worship of Hari with prostrations, hymns of praise, words of apology, handfuls of flowers, and so forth, one should then prepare a *sarvatobhadra* mandala with grains.
One should have a pitcher made of gold placed in the center, or likewise a pitcher made of copper; similarly, one should place eight pitchers in the eight directions.
Having placed the five jewels, fruits, sprouts, and rice, as well as cloth, a vessel containing sesame seeds, and fragrant substances such as sandalwood. || 1 ||
One should install the form of Trivikrama within the pitchers,
together with Padmākṣī, who is waterless and born of gold.
The devotee should worship according to the prescribed rite and resolve for the sake of the vow:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I perform this worship for the successful accomplishment of the waterless vow. (19)
"May you, who are filled with compassion, become the granter of all desires.
Having thus entreated the leader of the Gaṇas, who is the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, [he spoke]. 16.
One should worship with dūrvā grass, vermilion, agallochum, sandalwood, and unbroken grains; thereafter, one should offer sweetmeats and worship Trivikrama. || 17 ||
Having performed the invocation and other rites, one should bathe Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) derived from a cow,
and with pure water mixed with fragrant scents.
One should offer white garments, the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) and so forth,
as well as crowns, ornaments, necklaces, and armlets.
Scented oils, substances for incense, collyrium, and lac-dye; as well as incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, and betel-leaf.
The rites of the evening lamp-offering, hymns of praise, circumambulation, and processions;
as well as the requests for forgiveness, the offering of handfuls of flowers, and the dismissal [of the deity]. || 21 ||
In this manner, the observer of the vow should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa with every prescribed rite;
thereafter, he should attend to his own duties, and likewise perform them at midday as well.
The essence of sandalwood for the food offering, fried cakes, the excellent juice of mangoes, and cool water fragrant with sugar and cardamom, imbued with devotion. (23)
Afterwards, one should offer the evening ritual to the God and have Śrī Hari placed upon a swing in a flower garden or on the ground of a grove of trees.
In the evening, one should cause Hari to sport upon a soft ground covered with grass that is moist, cool, and sprinkled with water, and which is fanned by a cool breeze.
At night, one should perform the ārātrika ceremony and the hymns of praise and so forth in due order;
one should offer buttermilk with curdled milk as the food offering, along with auspicious ghee.
One should give excellent water of sweet essence for drinking,
as well as substances that cleanse the mouth and an auspicious bed.
The devotee should perform the vigil together with many Sātvatas;
then, having bathed in the morning, bowed to Hari, and worshipped Him thereafter—28.
Having fed other venerable persons, he should indeed perform the breaking of the fast with water;
thereafter, the observer of the vow should take the food offered to Hari.
A king should bestow various kinds of gifts to obtain excellent fruits;
he should give elephants and the like, as well as jewels and cities.
A Brāhmaṇa should give books and the like; a Vaiśya, grains and wealth;
and a Śūdra should give new articles of art and craft. || 31 ||
Everyone should give according to their capacity whatever is to be given before them;
they should perform the gift of cows, the gift of land, and other such gifts.
Whatever belongs to oneself should be offered by the observer of the vow to a worthy recipient;
thinking "I offer this to Brahman," one should give it to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should give it to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa himself, as well as to the venerable Guru;
one should also give it to the protectorless, the poor, and the helpless.
One should give it to a noble woman; indeed, one should likewise offer it to a widow or one who is destitute.
One should also give sugar and other such things to young boys and girls. (35)
The observer of the vow should give alms, accompanied by ghee, to virtuous men and women;
likewise, he should offer sweet foods and other edible items as well. (36)
Having performed this vow in such a manner, the devotee goes to heaven and attains liberation;
this vow is an easy means, essential in nature, and yields great fruit. (37)
Even those who are evil-doers, wicked, most sinful, and devoid of dharma, may achieve that which requires little affliction and is accomplished with few materials through faith. (38)
Those who do not eat when water is scarce, nor drink water and such,
and who practice devotion to Hari, do not go to the presence of Yama.
Listen to the account of this vow which occurred in a former age;
how the world was created by Brahmā at the beginning of the Yuga, just as it was before.
On that first day, during the Satya Yuga, the sage Kratu was there;
Agnīdhra was the mouth of the sacrifice, and Kratu, the son of Vedhas, became the provider of abundant food.
Whatever he obtained and ate was reduced to ashes at that very moment;
even thousands and hundreds of thousands of meals were consumed simultaneously.
He eats all that has been given to him without restriction, and by himself alone;
yet within the span of a single ghaṭikā, he becomes hungry again and all of it is digested. ||43||
Even when overwhelmed by the forest fire of the digestive heat, he desires excessive food; yet when that [desire] is not attained, then— ||44||
He goes indeed to the forest of the Himalayas and the vastest forest of Mount Meru,
and there he devours everything day and night.
For the sake of water, he falls into the ocean of milk;
he drinks the water until he is satisfied, and it is just so.
While the journey was thus proceeding, Kratu, overcome at one point by great hunger, went to Brahmā. 47.
He prayed, "May food that never satiates be obtained by me eternally.
Brahmā said to Kratu, "O son, I grant you satisfaction."
Whosoever among sentient beings, acting as a sacrificer for you, shall offer food at the sacrifice with incomparable devotion; 49.
Let that much hunger arise there for the sake of digestion;
however, in the absence of mental cultivation (bhāvanā), even the destruction of your hunger would occur.
Let your satisfaction there be exactly according to your meditation;
from this moment on, my son, hunger shall no longer afflict you.
Just as he previously oppressed you, O Hotṛ, so shall he not oppress you now;
rather, they will offer even more sacrificial oblations to him who is the very essence of the sacrifice.
"Lest all of you should simultaneously consume what is unwholesome, for that reason your hunger shall indeed arise according to your own individual will. (53)
"Someone will give you as much as you need; let that suffice for you. Then hunger [arises]; "He will not give," then thirst [arises]—thus it is always. (54)
"Be happy, O Kratu, my son; let no greed for the tongue arise in you. Thus addressed with blessings by Brahmā, Kratu departed from there.
With a peaceful heart, he dwelt in the permanent residences of those who maintain the sacred fire (agnihotrins),
while he himself incessantly consumed the offerings in the fires during the sacrificial rites of the priests.
The daily oblation of many kinds is offered morning, midday, and evening;
yet even after eating again and again, his hunger always desires more food.
Thus, by the power of practice, his eating three times [a day] becomes certain;
or even for a longer period than that, it must certainly be performed. || 58 ||
Thus, through the habit of eating, from time to time he desires various kinds of food, whether it be an offering not yet given or one already given. (5.9)
From the greed of the tongue, the desire for food arises again and again;
and by its own will, his hunger increases with great force.
Thus, while Kratu remained there, the great sages Dakṣa, Marīci, and others went to the Badarikā forest to behold Nārāyaṇa and Nara.
And having bathed in the Mandākinī and beheld Hari Nārāyaṇa,
they sat down there in the vicinity of Śrī Hari within the Badarī forest.
He whose limbs were beautiful in form, who was as radiant as a mass of snow or ice,
who was the very embodiment of the vow of Brahman, and who was the Supreme Lord in the form of asceticism.
Having bowed and remembered Hari, Bhṛgu questioned the Supreme Lord:
"O Friend of the distressed, O Ocean of Mercy, O Lord who delivers those who are bound! (6.4)
We bow to you, having sought refuge in you, who reside both within the heart and without;
tell us that which is simple, merit-bestowing, and the giver of worldly enjoyment and ultimate liberation.
By this vow, the faults arising from food— whether they originate from the food of others, from the food of enemies, or from food that is devoid of purity— shall be destroyed in every respect.
Those sins arising from food during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), those born from accepting mixed food, those produced from alms-food, and those originating from stale food; ||67||
O Lord, may those faults—whether committed through ignorance or knowledge, arising from food not offered, or born from the breaking of the row for one's own sake—be destroyed. (68)
"Tell me of such true austerity by which those defects may be destroyed.
Having heard this, Śrī Hari said: "Listen, O best of Brahmins! (69)
The vow considered supreme among vows is the fasting on the eleventh day;
it is austerity par excellence and the cause of the destruction of sins.
This vow is the supreme purifier of all defects rooted in food;
it is simple, easily accessible, subtle, and bestows all fruits. (7.1)
One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
O great sages, one should not eat even during the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) nor during the period of death-impurity (āśauca).
This vow must be observed for as long as one lives by one who desires the highest good;
even by one desiring heaven or liberation, that auspicious vow must be performed. (73)
Countless faults rooted in food do not accrue to the observer of the vow;
for those who do not observe the vow of Ekādaśī, there is indeed no liberation, truly none at all.
Moreover, even those who are of evil conduct, most sinful, and devoid of dharma,
do not go to the presence of Yama if they do not eat on the eleventh day.
"Those who eat food on the eleventh day go to the abode of Yama.
Having heard those words, he trembled within the lotus of his heart. (76)
Kratu said to Nara and Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, I am truly not capable; my hunger is unbearable. (77)
If I do not obtain food in the morning, death will occur at midday;
indeed, I am not able to endure hunger for five periods of time. (78)
In the morning I eat with the gods as my mouth; in the forenoon, with fire as my mouth; and at midday and in the afternoon, with guests and mendicants facing me.
In the evening I eat with all mouths, and at night with all things mobile and immobile;
such indeed is my food, fashioned in every way.
Since even hunger afflicts me during my daily period of practice, I shall therefore bestow gifts and worship Keśava. (8.1)
"I shall perform another meritorious deed; I will not observe the fast," having said this, he ceased speaking; then Nārāyaṇa spoke.
If heaven is desired by you and hell is not wished for,
one must not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
Kratu said to Hari, "O Lord, I speak the truth before you:
I am not capable of eating but once a day; how then could I endure a full fast? (84)
O Lord of Lakṣmī, what is the name of this fire with seven tongues that burns within the belly? In truth, my name is simply "Sacrifice" (Kratu). 85.
That cruel one is the great fire, and excessive eating is its fuel;
when I eat what is too oily, even that [fire] is extinguished.
"If I observe all these fasts, I shall surely die; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, show me mercy so that I may be able to perform them. (87)
"By whatever means heaven is attained, that I shall perform at your command;
and tell me one thing for my sake: that by which liberation may also be achieved. (88)
When he said, "I shall make it easy to practice so that I may attain the highest good," the compassionate Nārāyaṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, heard him.
Having deliberated upon what was appropriate for such persons, he declared this vow:
"When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) occurs while the sun is situated in Taurus or Gemini," || 1.251.90 ||
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, she should be observed with great effort as one who is devoid of water;
having abandoned water for rinsing the mouth and sipping, she should avoid all water whatsoever. ||91||
One may indeed enjoy [the food] here, for it does not become waterless;
if water is swallowed while the [vow] is waterless, the vow becomes deficient in strength. ||92||
By avoiding water from sunrise until sunrise, the observer of the vow obtains the fruit arising from fasting on twelve Ekādaśīs. ||93||
Having observed the waterless vow accompanied by the worship of the deity and a night vigil,
one should perform a ritual bath in water and worship again on the morning of the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
Having given a water-pot filled with water and adorned with gold to a twice-born man,
and having also given gifts of food, he should break his fast with his own people.
The observer of the vow should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, girls, and boys;
indeed, such an observer shall obtain the fruit of eleven years of Ekādaśī vows.
Abandoning all disputations, one should take refuge in me alone;
by fasting on the eleventh lunar day, one is liberated from all sins.
One should not eat on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) of either fortnight;
moreover, on the eleventh day of the bright half of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should remain without water.
By the merit of even a single Ekādaśī occurring within a year, all the Ekādaśīs—both the bright and the dark—are indeed considered as having been observed. (99)
This auspicious [vow], when observed as a fast, bestows wealth and grain, grants sons, health, and other blessings, and provides the attainment of whatever one desires in the mind.
The messengers of Yama—huge-bodied, terrifying, with hideous faces, cruel, and bearing staffs and nooses—indeed do not approach those who observe vows. 101.
Wearing yellow garments, gentle, with discs in their hands and possessing the speed of thought,
these Vaiṣṇavas indeed lead him at the end to the city of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O Kratu, with every effort you must perform that [rite];
O son, carry it out with faith, even though it is waterless and devoid of water.
By that, your internal fire will become intense and you will remain established in discipline;
with enthusiasm and vigilance, the waterless fast should be performed.
If the eating of food or the drinking of water occurs in a dream, then let there be no fault on my part; let there be no violation of my vow in this matter.
O Lord, let there be no violation of my vows for me even through the fault of sleep;
let there be no violation of my vows for me even on account of drowsiness or laziness. (106)
"O Lord of Gods, I shall eat my meal on the following day after the day of Hari"; having thus petitioned Hari-Kṛṣṇa, one should be intent upon fasting.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man, even if it were equal to Mount Meru or the world of light, all of it is reduced to ashes by the power of Ekādaśī.
On the day of breaking the fast on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), a water-cow (jaladhenu) should be given;
a well-constructed vessel filled with water should be offered along with gold.
Indeed, one who observes this vow must not drink water at all;
then, in every watch of the night, he shall obtain the fruit of ten million pieces of gold.
Whatever bathing, charity, recitation, or fire-offering a practitioner performs, even if it be very small,
all that becomes eternal merit through the power of the word of Acyuta.
What need is there for any other rite besides the Nirjala Ekādaśī?
For gold, food, or clothing—whatever is bestowed on this day [yields great fruit]. (1.12)
He who observes a fast without water goes to the abode of Viṣṇu;
whatever merit has been performed by him shall all become inexhaustible.
But those observers of the vow who shall give gifts on the twelfth day, the day of breaking the fast, during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, will attain the supreme state.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, the hater of his guru, and the adulterer—
these are liberated from their sins if they fast on the twelfth day.
O Kratu, listen to the special rule for the day of Nirjala Ekādaśī:
on that day, Hari himself, who reclines upon the waters, is present with men and women endowed with faith.
Likewise, a cow made of water should then be offered for worship;
or else, a real cow with her calf should be given, which bestows liberation.
The virtuous twice-born, the chaste women, and the boys and girls should be gratified with excellent sacrificial fees and various kinds of sweet foods.
When they are satisfied, I, Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of liberation, am satisfied;
those by whom this vow has not been performed are destroyers of their own souls, of this there is no doubt. (119)
Those who eat food on the eleventh day are indeed consumers of sin;
they are evil-minded and ill-behaved, and they are robbed of their merit—of this there is no doubt.
By those who are peaceful, self-controlled, devoted to charity, and worshipping Hari, and by those who keep a vigil at night—by them this fast has been observed. (121)
Indeed, a hundred future lineages and likewise a hundred past ones,
together with himself, have been led by him to the abode of Vāsudeva.
Food, cows, buffaloes, clothing, beds, seats, water,
a staff, a water-pot, an umbrella, a bowl, gold, sesame seeds, and so forth— 123.
He who gives sandals or anything else as an offering for the vessel is honored in the heavenly world by means of a golden vehicle.
Indeed, the vow must be performed according to the rule as one involving complete abstinence from water;
on the twelfth day, Trivikrama, the Lord of the God of Gods, is to be worshipped.
Water-pots containing sugar should be offered in the presence of Viṣṇu;
then, having fed the Brahmins, one should personally partake of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
Thus, he who observes the full Dvādaśī, which destroys all sins,
becomes liberated from every evil and goes to the state free from all affliction.
Having heard this and bowed down, Kratu, filled with joy, went to his own hermitage;
there, on the day of the Nirjala vow, he performed the rite according to the prescribed rules.
He has obtained all the fruit, and so shall another do as well;
he shall obtain the fruit produced by twenty-four Ekādaśīs.
Whoever should hear this with devotion, and whoever should also recite it—both of them shall attain heaven; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.

Whatever fruit is obtained by performing a *śrāddha* and reciting prayers when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu on the day of Sinīvālī, that same fruit shall be attained even from merely hearing this [work]. 13.11.
From both reciting and teaching [this], a fruit equal to that of the vow shall arise;
from the vow, however, eternal heaven and eternal liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Jyeṣṭha-Śukla Nirjala-Ekādaśī Vow, including the Narrative of Kratu who was afflicted by hunger, and the Attainment of Results such as the Pacification of Hunger," in the First Section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O ocean of mercy, O you who always bring about the crossing over of worldly existence for those possessed by laziness,
we have indeed been delivered by you, O Lord, through the description of the Nirjala-vrata.
That practitioners of vows obtain here liberation as well as enjoyment— the fruit of all Ekādaśī observances— is due solely to your compassion.
May your resolve for these living beings somehow be fulfilled, whether it be the supreme ultimate good, or liberation, or even heaven itself. (3)
O Lord, you strive to protect [us] from the ocean of worldly existence like a mother; compassion alone is the cause of this. (4)

O compassionate one, tell me the fruit of the vow, the ritual procedure, the deity to be worshipped, the mode of worship, the greatness, and also the gift for the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
The day in the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha is considered to be known as Yoginī;
on this day, the Lord Hari, named Nṛsiṃha, should be worshipped here together with Kṣemaṅkarī.
Among flowers, bhr̥ṅgarāja is prescribed here, as is the jāmbava fruit for the arghya offering;
in the food offering (naivedya), balls of rice (piṇḍakas) should be given, while for the gift (dāna), a water-buffalo is considered appropriate.
This specific procedure has been declared; this vow, the best of vows, must be performed.
It causes the destruction of all sins and bestows all enjoyments. || 8 ||
The supreme vow of the Yoginīs is the eternal vessel for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra; it is the very essence within the three worlds.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow must indeed subsist on a single meal, eat only at night, sleep on the ground, and likewise observe celibacy and other such disciplines.
On the eleventh day, the observer of the vow, having risen early in the morning, should remember Śrī Hari;
having meditated upon Him and bathed, he should worship Hari with the sixteen articles of offering.
O Blessed One, O Kṛṣṇa, he should pray: "Today I shall perform the supreme vow of the Yoginī; may it be free from obstacles and grant its full fruit. (12)
"O Mādhava, granter of fearlessness to your devotees, [grant us] mercy!
Having thus entreated him, one should then have an auspicious structure constructed on all sides with grains.
Within the center of the mandala, which is beautified by colored powders and other decorations,
one should place a golden jar filled with jewels.
It should be provided with fruits and sprouts, accompanied by water and cloth,
honored with sandalwood, unbroken rice, and excellent saffron, and made from nine metals.
One should worship the conch there, and likewise worship the bell;
one should worship the Śālagrāma and likewise worship Gaṇeśa.
Having worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Narasiṃha with the articles of worship,
one should worship the image fashioned of gold with supreme devotion.

Having placed [the deity] in a vessel of sesame seeds, one should worship with unbroken rice grains and other offerings, with the rites of invocation and so forth, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and with fragrant sandalwood. || 18 ||
With fine garments and ornaments, with the application of fragrant unguents, and with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, fruits, betel, and water. || 19 ||
One should worship with the ārārtika rite, hymns of praise, handfuls of flowers, and so forth;
having requested forgiveness for one's offenses, one may then proceed with one's own business.
At midday as well, one should offer excellent food offerings consisting of mango juice and sandalwood paste,
along with cool, sweet water, *pūrikā* cakes, curd, and sugar.
One should serve fermented gruel, a dish cooked with pieces of pumpkin, and meat broth; as well as mouth-fresheners such as betel nut and prepared betel rolls.
Likewise, at evening he should offer [oblations] and have a new, pleasant pavilion constructed;
having then tied a swing there and installed Hari within it, ||23||
One should cause Janārdana to sway in a garden, have him wander here and there, and let him rest upon a cool, grassy spot.
Thereafter, one should worship with various excellent articles;
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Narasiṃha and offer praise in the lion-like manner (saiṃhikī).
One should keep a vigil at night with songs sung to the feet of Nṛsiṃha;
in the morning, having meditated upon Him with enthusiasm and bathed, one should worship Him. || 26 ||
Having offered all desired and sweet substances according to the prescribed rites,
the devotee should then offer water and perform the auspicious breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
The gift of water, a water-cow, a gold-cow, clarified butter and the like, curds, milk, fresh butter, sugar, and even molasses. ||28||
One should give gifts to a worthy recipient, such as a vehicle or a useful conveyance;
likewise, one should offer a sacrificial fee to the preceptor, as well as a jar and an image of Hari.
One should cause sweet foods and other such items to be given to the virtuous;
one should also cause gifts of houses, fields, cattle, gardens, and slaves to be bestowed.
Having thus performed the vow, the devotee, endowed with faith in the Yoginī, shall enjoy the fruit attainable by yogis: heaven and even liberation (kaivalya). || 31 ||
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this beautiful divine narrative that destroys all sins:
in the city of Alakā, Kubera was indeed a devotee of Śiva.
Whenever he was engaged in the worship of Śambhu, at that time there was always a great yakṣa among his own attendants, known by the name Hemamālī.
He indeed gathered flowers from the nearby gardens;
thus he daily provided the articles for Śaṅkara’s worship.
He always remained there in the presence of Kubera;
however, due to the onset of youth, he was filled with a surging tide of passion. || 35 ||
But together with his large-eyed wife,
he remains especially drawn by the arrow of desire, even during the day.
Even abandoning his duties, he would engage in sensual desire;
thus, being excessively driven by lust, he would occasionally do so even with his wife.
He would indeed go to the trees and other places to fetch flowers and such;
once, however, he went toward the lake named Mānasa with Kubera.
That Hemamālī was indeed sent to Kamalānayanā;
he too, having perceived a beautiful new lake worthy of being seen, [approached her].
He went there with his wife to fetch beautiful lotuses,
as well as water, lush grass, and the shimmering beauty of fine sands.
A delightful region with fragrant flowers and the like, characterized by various passionate states that cause agitation during sexual union. (4.1)
Seeing that he had undergone a transformation, and having cast away the flowers,
he then took delight with his wife in the Mānasa lake.
Though repeatedly restrained by his wife, he remained attached to desire and did not turn back;
yet even when she was satisfied, the wife again set out [for him] and did not desist. (43)
Thus, when they had attained one another’s presence with a state of desire,
especially as they engaged with each other again and again, those two, being deluded, did not realize [the truth].
"Thus, the time for the worship has passed; nevertheless, those two have not yet arrived even though they have brought the flowers, and Kubera is waiting. (45)
Attached to the taste of passion and love, they did not go to the abode of Kubera;
for Kubera performs the worship of Śiva in the celestial realm. (46)
The morning time had passed, and then at the hour of midday,
Kubera, desiring to worship, looked for the arrival of flowers.
He reflected that there must indeed be an obstacle, since the yakṣa did not come;
for a second yakṣa had been sent there to search for him.
Having gone there, he saw Hemamālin enjoying himself;
Hemamālin was sporting in the water together with his beloved.
The servant said to them: "The king Kubera desires flowers;
you must go there quickly, for the worship is to take place at midday."
Having done this, the two went to Kubera, the king of kings;
then, having bowed before him, they repeatedly begged for his forgiveness.
Then the King of Yakṣas replied, provoked by the delay of time, having perceived that he was a lover of women, sporting according to his own desire. (52)
"O wretch, you evil and ill-behaved one! By your attachment to sensual desire, you have indeed committed an insult to the gods by failing to take the flowers. (5.3)
The enjoyment of sensual pleasures is a great obstacle, and it is considered a great fault;
a punishment must be meted out for that, and I must not show compassion. (54)
"O lowest of men, you who suffer from the eighteen types of leprosy and are separated from that beloved wife of yours—driven away from this place, go down to the surface of the earth! (55)
When these words were spoken, the Yakṣa fell from that place,
overwhelmed by great suffering, his body mottled with leprosy.
Then he became afflicted with Galat-kuṣṭha, Śveta-kuṣṭha, and Rakta-kuṣṭha;
he suffered from Carmakuṣṭha, Lalatkuṣṭha, and the foul-smelling Pūyakuṣṭha.
Thus was Hemamālī born upon his body through his own past actions.
He finds no happiness by day, nor does he find sleep at night. ||58||
Whether in the shade or in the heat, in a house, a bower, or a cave;
in a hut, on the ground, or amidst creepers—he finds no happiness anywhere. (59)
He is greatly tormented by burning and is even set ablaze by scraping;
though overwhelmed by his transgression, he remembers his former deeds.
Indeed, due to the power of the flowers and other offerings dedicated to Śiva,
even for one who has fallen or been overcome [by obstacles], his memory does not perish.
Wandering here and there in the vast forest of the Himalayas in a terrifying form, he went to the auspicious hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya, where the gods resided.
O Lakṣmī, that best of sages, a treasure-house of austerity, was devoted to meditation on Brahman;
his lifespan, it is said, lasted for seven days of Brahmā.
He, whose body was afflicted with leprosy, prostrated at his feet from a distance;
Mārkaṇḍeya, having shown compassion toward that trembling, deformed body, [spoke].
For the sake of helping others, he summoned him and said this:
"Why are you overcome by leprosy? Why indeed are you so utterly despicable? (65)
Having heard this, he too— known by the name Hemamālī, an attendant of the King of Kings— then spoke to the sage who destroys sin.
O Sage, having brought a collection of lotuses from the garden every day at the time of Śiva’s worship, I offered them to Kubera.
One day, accompanied by my wife, I was sent by the compassionate Kubera indeed to fetch lotuses for you.
Having beheld the lake named Mānasa, which was exceedingly fragrant and variegated, as well as the new, delightful, auspicious terrestrial region filled with water.
While we were both attached to sensual pleasures, time passed unnoticed;
thus, my morning worship of Śiva was performed without flowers, and for that reason, I am [as I am]. (1.252.70)
"O sage, I have indeed been cursed by the King of Kings in a fit of extreme anger; overcome by leprosy, I have become separated from that beloved wife of mine. (7.1)
"Having wandered about, I have arrived here in your presence; do me a favor.
By nature, the minds of the virtuous are capable of assisting others. (72)
"O Blessed One, act for my sake so that happiness may come to pass.
Having heard those truthful words, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya then spoke.
Listen, I shall tell you the instruction for the vow that bestows auspiciousness:
observe the Ekādaśī vow of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha. (74)
By the merit of the Yoginī vow, your leprosy will surely vanish;
you shall regain your wife and obtain eternal happiness. (75)
Having heard these words of the sage, he fell prostrate on the ground like a staff;
strengthened by his blessings, he became exceedingly joyful.
On the eleventh day, that observer of vows performed the worship of Mārkaṇḍeya and Kṛṣṇa in the vicinity of the hermitage.
Having properly observed the vow according to the sage’s word, he became happy;
all eighteen types of leprosy were completely destroyed from his body. (78)
Having bowed and returned to his own world, the yakṣa became as he was before;
having regained his wife, he lived happily once again in Alakā.
In this way, the removal of curses indeed occurs through the vow of the Yoginīs;
there is the destruction of diseases such as leprosy, and even a lost wife is recovered. (1.252.80)

The world, one's station, home, and prosperity—even if lost—are indeed regained; by the merit of her vow, the practitioner who observes the rite shall shine with that which is attainable through yoga. 81.
O Mahālakṣmī, such is the vow of the Yoginīs that has been described; it is to be observed by a woman who has become a Yoginī, and by a man who is a Yogin. (82)
One should perform this vow, which bestows the fruit of yoga and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for he who feeds eighty-eight thousand virtuous men [attains this]. (83)
A man who observes the vow obtains a fruit equal to that [of the goddess], for she bestows the fruit of the practice of yoga and grants the world of the yogis. (84)
Indeed, this Yoginī-tithi, which bestows liberation through union with Kṛṣṇa, should be observed as a fast;
by reciting or hearing of it, one is liberated from all sins. (85)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Āṣāḍha-Kṛṣṇa-Yoginī-Ekādaśī Vow, and How the Leprosy and Other Diseases of the Yakṣa Hemamālī, Born from Kubera’s Curse, Were Destroyed by Performing the Vow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Salutations to that Blessed One, the Supreme Self and Lord of all powers, who possesses time, māyā, and the individual souls as his powers.
Salutation to You, the bestower of the fruit of the Yoginīs, whose essence is the fruit of the merit of yoga;
salutation to Yoga, which is attainable by yogis, and to the Lord of the Yoginīs. || 2 ||
You alone are the giver of fruits, and you alone are the bestower of liberation;
you alone are the sovereign lord—salutations to that Great Soul.
You are the embodiment of all the gods, and you are the soul of all sacred fords;
you are indeed the essence of all vows—salutation to You, the Soul of All.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?
Who is its presiding deity, what is its ritual procedure, and what is its fruit and the merit of giving gifts? Tell me this. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: I shall relate [the account] known by the name Śayanī, which is highly meritorious, bestows heaven and liberation, and destroys all sins.
Know that very one also by the name Niyamā and Bhāmikā;
by her vow, even a sinful soul becomes purified at that very moment.
By the mere hearing of which the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice is obtained;
there is no other auspicious [work] superior to this, which bestows both heaven and liberation.
The presiding deity of this [tithi] is the god Vāmana, who is Hari;
he is joined by his beloved named Kamalā, and thus Vāmana is indeed to be worshipped.
By whomsoever the lotus-eyed Vāmana was worshipped with lotuses on the day known as Niyamāśayana, by him the three worlds have been honored.
By him who has observed the Ekādaśī, the most excellent day of Hari, three gods are worshipped and all the deities are worshipped.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, Hari lies upon the ocean of milk,
having turned back the flow of all his senses due to excessive yoga.
His worship should be performed with apāmārga plants, offerings of pūrikās and other foods,
coconuts and the like, preceded by the gift of gold and a cow.
The observer of the vow should likewise undertake the observance with devotion;
and listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to this merit-bestowing narrative.
O beloved, in former times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a Dānava named Bali;
he was my devotee, intent upon me, and he worshipped me constantly.
With many sacrifices, the Daitya worshipped me according to the prescribed rites,
with supreme affection and true devotion, through vows, fasts, and offerings.
Thus, by the power of his merit and likewise through his service to me,
he returned from the subterranean realm (rasātala) and became a king upon the earth.
On earth as well, he grew strong through the power of my worship;
by the influence of that merit, he went to heaven in that very body.
He brought the kingdom, including both heaven and the world of mortals, under his own control;
even Indra and the other gods became powerless in his presence.

The Dānavas grew strong and prosperous, becoming kings throughout the three worlds. Then the Supreme Lord Hari, Śambhu, and Brahmā were entreated by Indra and the other gods; they employed the highest stratagem against them.
May Bali perform the sacrifice, and may he be the donor at the ritual.
"Having become a mendicant, let that Kṛṣṇa beg for alms upon the earth.
Having made this agreement, he dispatched Bali for the sake of the sacrifice.
The sages, the ascetics, and the gods—all of us have gone to the vicinity of Mount Revata, where the sacrifice is being performed. ||23||
In that fifth incarnation, indeed in the form of Vāmana, he possessed an exceedingly great form and was the yogi of the entire cosmic egg. ||24||
When the donor, who remained steadfast by relying on the truth, was defeated through a quibble of speech, Śukra restrained him, saying, "I am not Nārāyaṇa. (25)
O Lakṣmī, when the earth was requested by me for only three paces,
he offered it into my hand with merely the water of his formal resolve.
O Lakṣmī, at that time, I indeed filled the entire universe with my form;
having placed my two feet in the Bhūrloka and my knees in the Bhuvarloka. (27)
In the Svarloka he placed his hips, in the Maharloka his belly,
in the Janaloka his heart, and likewise in the Tapoloka his throat.
Having placed my face in Satyaloka, I placed my head in Vairāja;
there the sun, moon, planets, stars, constellations, and comets [are situated]. (29)
Then the gods, along with Indra, the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, praised him with Vedic mantras and various hymns.
Having grasped Bali there with one hand, he filled the earth with one foot,
and with the second, he reached up to heaven along with the shell of the cosmic egg.
But on the third step, O Lakṣmī, my foot was then placed upon the back of Bali;
the Dānava, my worshipper, went to the netherworld (rasātala).
Having been installed in the kingdom of Rasātala, he too then devoted himself to me;
that king of devotees constantly requested me to remain in his own abode.
Then, becoming humble and devoted to my own worship, I assumed both forms and remained in his house with one of them. (34)
In another form, he remains reclining upon Śeṣa;
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, he takes his rest to dispel all fatigue.
From that day forward, I indeed adopted the occasional (naimittika) vow;
therefore, devotees call that Ekādaśī, which bestows great merit, "Śayanī. (36)
"Thus, O Mahālakṣmī, I shall sleep upon the remaining surface in the midst of the Ocean of Milk until the upcoming Kārttikī festival. (37)
That is declared to be the Cāturmāsya vow, which bestows supreme worldly enjoyment and liberation;
even one who performs the Śayana-vrata shall attain enjoyment and liberation. ||38||
Beginning from the day he lies down [to observe the vow] until the end of the four-month period,
a man should remain a virtuous soul, observing the restraints of the vow and the rules of self-control.
There is no vow superior to this, nor any other vow more excellent than it,
wherein the Lord of Gods, the wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, sleeps.
O Lakṣmī, he who thus performs this most excellent vow of Śayanī, which removes all sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, [attains these fruits]. ||41||
Even though he may be insignificant, he becomes dear to me in this world;
one should conduct oneself well on the tenth day by eating only once a day or even by eating only at night.
One should observe celibacy at night, and having risen at dawn during the time known as Brāhma,
one should perform the recollection of the Blessed One.
Having bathed and performed the worship of the deity with the sixteen auspicious articles,
the observer of the vow himself should then complete all the daily rites of worship.
One should have the Sarvatobhadra mandala constructed with nine grains;
in its center, a golden jar joined with five jewels and sprouts [should be placed]. (45)
One should indeed establish that [image] which is rich in water, clothing, and fruit, and worship it;
having placed a vessel of sesame seeds there, one should worship Vāmana. ||46||
One should also worship Kamalā and Śayanī with many offerings;
one should perform the rites beginning with invocation and the excellent sprinkling of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should quickly offer garments, ornaments, decorations, necklaces, sandalwood paste, kajjala, all the elements of erotic passion, and forehead marks (tilaka) and so forth. 48.
Incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel, and fine fruit; the waving of lights, prostrations, hymns of praise, salutations, and the seeking of forgiveness. ||49||
Having offered the *añjali* of dismissal, one should pray in this very manner for the fulfillment of one's own vow: "May my vow be free from obstacles. (1.253.50)
One should perform great worship and other rites according to one's wealth and power;
one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, resembling the royal pavilion.
One should worship the Vaiṣṇavas in the morning and likewise bestow gifts;
standing before the virtuous, one should undertake the vows for the Cāturmāsya period.
Then he should maintain the restraints that bring about happiness and liberation;
indeed, for the sake of asceticism, he should adopt the restraints of the tongue and the sexual organ.
One should undertake the observances and the vow either in the presence of Hari or in the presence of the Guru;
likewise, one should undertake the physical restraints as well as the mental restraints.
Indeed, one should undertake the observances that grant liberation from the constraints of the material world of enjoyments,
as well as vows, gifts, and restrictive rules, specifically in the morning.
The restraint of the senses, the mind, and their fluctuations is austerity;
it should be practiced through constant application, especially during the four-month period.
Sense objects, which cause agitation and create obstacles, must be avoided;
one should certainly not indulge in the nourishment of aesthetic flavor (rasa), for that is considered to be agitating.
Taste is a great defect that captivates the tongue and brings about the full nourishment of all the senses;
it must be especially conquered by those who desire to observe the Cāturmāsya vow. ||58||
Subsisting on fruits, drinking only milk, eating a single food, eating only once a day, subsisting on vegetables while avoiding greens, or the renunciation of ghee—these are forms of austerity. (59)

The abandonment of curd and the abandonment of sesame; the consumption of curd and the eating of sesame; subsisting on bulbs, subsisting on grain-particles, subsisting on potsherds, and eating leaves. (1.253.60)
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should subsist on water alone, renounce sugar and molasses, and eat only tasteless food; in Bhādrapada, one should avoid leafy vegetables and abstain from curd.
In the month of Āśvina, he should eat food devoid of milk; in Kārtika, he should avoid foods made from split pulses; he may eat radish, tubers, and eggplant, but not the *kaliṅgaka* fruit.
It is said that during the auspicious Cāturmāsya, one should observe a vow of austerity;
or rather, the vow known as Dhāraṇā-pāraṇā is declared to yield great fruit.
One should maintain silence, engage in discourse concerning Hari, and, joined with the utterance of His name, one should rotate a rosary of beads a hundred times. (64)
The vow for the eyes is that one must not look excessively at forms;
the vow for the ears is that one must not listen excessively to sounds. (65)
Fragrances belong to the quality of passion (rajas) and should not be excessively grasped; that is the vow for the nose.
The mutual touching of women and men should not be done too much; that is the vow for the skin.
During the four-month period, one must always reside in one place; this is the supreme vow for the feet.
Not breaking leaves, branches, and so forth, is the supreme vow for the hands. (67)
This protection of vigor and the like is indeed the great vow of celibacy (brahmacarya);
it is the consumption of the bodily wind, which is tamasic, and it is the supreme austerity. 68.
The practice of the five fires, hanging from a tree, gazing at the sun, standing on one foot, and raising the arms upward. (69)
Maintaining the head downward, not cutting the nails and so forth, the growing of hair, and the rubbing with ashes, dust, and mud constitute austerity.
One should remain without food for three days, especially while naked;
one should stand in a stream of water, in water itself, and likewise in the heat of the sun.
One should always remain under a canopy, or even dwell beneath a tree; likewise, one should sleep on the ground, lie upon the earth, or rest upon a bed of sand.
A bed of arrows, a bed of iron, likewise sleeping on thorns, sleeplessness, and lack of bedding—these we endure, but never again the drinking of water. (73)
Bathing three times a day, meditating upon the form [of the deity], contemplation, remembrance, and worship—thus, worship is fivefold throughout the day. (74)
The recitation of mantras, meditation upon their meaning, mental austerity, one-pointedness, and concentration—these must be practiced with particular care. (75)
Non-violence [should be practiced] in every way—through mind, speech, and body—and it must be free from [distinctions of] caste, place, time, or occasion. ||76||
One should not even cut a blade of grass, for that vow is indeed non-violence;
freedom from malice toward all beings and refraining from criticism is the great vow.
Not looking at the conduct of others and so forth is the supreme vow;
speaking words that are true, pleasant, beneficial, factual, and conducive to happiness is austerity. (78)
Non-stealing in every way through all the senses and the mind is austerity; the non-arising of desire and discursive thought is the supreme austerity. (79)

That which cannot be grasped should certainly not be guarded, nor indeed is there any need for great austerity; let subsistence on alms alone suffice, for the mere maintenance of the body is the highest penance.
Non-attachment when gains come by chance is great austerity;
providing happiness to others and rendering service to others is austerity. (8.1)
Compassion for the sake of others is the highest austerity;
purity through the waters of knowledge is the supreme austerity. (82)
Absence of deceit in the heart, speech, and action; austerity is unity [of these];
contentment, lack of excessive craving, and freedom from desire—this is the supreme austerity. (8.3)
Contentment with one's own possessions and supreme indifference toward those of others is austerity;
however, taking recourse to the path of liberation is the highest of all austerities. (84)
Freedom from affliction, constant tranquility, and the absence of anger are the great vow;
likewise, freedom from agitation, refraining from reviling, not using harsh words, and avoiding deceitful conduct. (85)
Not seizing what has not been given is mental austerity;
it is constant contentment with what is granted by the Lord, and no longing for that which belongs to another. (86)
Objects of enjoyment such as women and the like must be renounced, as well as beds, elephants, moonstones, and side-chambers; likewise, fragrant oils, massages, ornaments, and beautiful garments.
The renunciation of clothing and ornaments, the renunciation of enjoyments—especially the renunciation of the means of enjoyment—is the supreme austerity for embodied beings. (88)
Carriages, vehicles, smoking [tobacco], drinking, gambling, fine dancing, vices, and the drinking of sweet liquors—these must be abandoned; this is the supreme austerity. (89)
During the Cāturmāsya, the falling [of water] from the feet of the virtuous is nectar;
it is to be drunk as grace (prasāda), and it is to be eaten—such is the vow.
Likewise, honoring the virtuous, the chaste, and the holy women,
as well as massaging their feet and carrying them on one's own body, is a vow that grants liberation.
To bring satisfaction through one's body, mind, speech, wealth, food, clothing, son, and even with one's beloved—this indeed is the great vow. (92)
Constantly beholding, touching, bowing down, serving the feet of, honoring, feeding, and pleasing the virtuous—this is his great vow. (9.3)
One should always dwell in the company of the virtuous and perform service toward them in matters such as ritual bathing and the practice of knowledge; for the righteous are purifiers. (94)
Service to the gods, service to the ancestors, and service to the virtuous are a great vow;
pleasing one's wife is service to the master, and pleasing the husband is the vow of the wife.
For whomsoever this gift, imbued with love, is given according to their need, for them there shall be inexhaustible merit; therefore, there is no vow superior to this.
Satisfying those who depend on him by bestowing gold, food, and knowledge;
and granting villages, fields, jewels, gems, gardens, dwellings, and water. (97)
Constant service with the body shall be the universal vow;
it consists of forgiveness, compassion, freedom from malice, absence of envy, and the avoidance of faults.
Appreciating virtues, performing deeds that bring fame and renown, and supreme austerity;
freedom from pride, bestowing honor upon others, and perceiving the self as equal [to all]. 99.
The absence of heat even when there is its opposite, and the absence of cold even when it is favorable;
the relinquishing of joy, resentment, fear, and agitation—this is the supreme austerity.
Fruits, grains, leaves, petals, flowers, husks, grass, and so forth—whatever is fresh should be offered daily to Śrī Hari; this is the great vow. || 101 ||
Wood, dried cow dung, branches, twigs, stalks, and baskets—these auspicious items for the vow should be offered every day as appropriate. 10.2.
Vegetables, well-prepared sweet foods, salt, ginger, and *dhānaka* (fried grain), as well as parched rice and other such items, should be offered daily; that indeed is the vow.
Solid food, drink, what is chewed, what is eaten, what is sucked, what is tasted, and what is licked; milk, curd, and sweet juice—pippalī should be given [with these]; this is a great vow. 10.4.
Clothing, ornaments, collyrium, sandalwood, and excellent, superior garments; musk, saffron, powder, and lac—these should be given during the vow. || 105 ||
These vows indeed bestow heaven here and grant happiness:
the remembrance of Śrī Hari, devotion, worship, and the offering of oblations.
Worship with the thirty-two modes of service is a vow that grants liberation;
serving others with the thought that they are Kṛṣṇa is a vow that bestows merit.
Performing sacrifices with various rites, providing assistance to the distressed, digging wells, and planting trees—this also constitutes that vow. (108)
The construction of roads, the building of hermitages and dwellings, and the erection of shelters, sacrificial halls, and the like, constitute a vow that bestows heaven. (109)
Training in the arts and crafts, as well as the promotion of agriculture,
the operation of machinery, and providing assistance— such a vow bestows heaven and grants happiness.
The constant offering of flour to fish, ants, and other creatures; the sprinkling of water upon trees; and the giving of water to those who are thirsty—[these constitute his perpetual vow]. (111)
Giving food to the hungry, providing clothing to the naked, and alleviating the various afflictions of those in distress—this is the vow. (11.2)
Giving medicine to the sick, providing a livelihood as a means of subsistence, nourishing, protecting, and guarding them is the supreme vow. (113)
The constant practice of internal yoga, the study of the scriptures, and listening to the stories of Kṛṣṇa constitute the supreme vow that bestows liberation. 114.
Prostrations like a staff and circumambulation are that vow;
the offering of lamps, the giving of water, and the presentation of food offerings and the like constitute the vow. (115)
The vow consists of the daily offering of fruit, the offering of grain, and also the offering of liquids; it includes the offering of sugar, candied sugar, molasses, honey, and so forth. || 11.6 ||
Sweeping, smearing [the floor], cleansing, bathing, and observing vows;
as well as washing the vessels and garments, and the offering of the *nīrājana* lamp. || 117 ||

The drinking from the eyes of the Embodied One (Mūrti), the moving of water-stalls, pavilions, and so forth, and the construction of temples, palaces, and excellent mansions—this is the supreme vow. (118)

Weaving for the sake of the Blessed One includes painting and the like, craftsmanship and the like, as well as stringing together, the composition of books, and the description of meters, verses, and so forth. (119)
Exegesis, narration, fulfilling the desires of devotees, and the vow that bestows happiness, heaven, and liberation—this service is itself the vow. (1.253.120)
I shall describe other vows and indeed penances; listen, O Lakṣmī!
During the Cāturmāsya, sacred stories should be heard and virtuous people should be fed.
The great worship should be performed daily; the three vows grant excellent accomplishment.
The great worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be performed daily as a great vow.
The revolving of a garland of my names one hundred times or more,
along with devotion, worship, oblations, fire-sacrifices, and ritual service, is a vow that bestows liberation.

The vow consists of the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine," the strict observance of celibacy, and the avoidance of milk-rice, sugarcane products, salt, and *phāleya* (a type of grain). 124.
That dharma which is related to Kṛṣṇa is considered by me to be the supreme vow. That vow by which the Blessed Lord, as well as His people,
may be pleased through its performance— that alone is declared to be a true vow, and that alone should be performed.
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, there is the worship of the deity.
Having performed this with a spirit of devotion and offered it before the Blessed One, [he said]:
"O Lord, O Master, this vow has been observed by me for your pleasure. (127)
"May whatever is deficient attain completeness; through this, may you be pleased with me.
Having thus concluded the observances, one should then perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā). || 128 ||
Morning bathing, worship of the gods, daily salutation of elders, and providing food and other necessities after sharing with one's dependents. || 129 ||
He who is free from affliction, well-integrated, and exceedingly affectionate toward his family, and whose home is sweet and pleasant— for him, heaven exists upon this earth.
Whatever vow among the vows may be most desired during the Cāturmāsya period, that must be performed in every way, beginning from the morning of the day of Śayana.
At midday, one should offer food and excellent water to Hari, as well as betel leaf and sweet drinks; and in the evening, one should likewise perform the same.

One should perform the nightly lamp-offering (ārārtrika), hymns of praise, and the ritual of mounting the swing; there, one should cause Hari to be swung and offer milk-filled pastries (dugdhapūrikā) as food.
One should keep a vigil at night with dances, songs, and the nectar of sacred stories;
on the twelfth day, having bathed during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa,
give gifts primarily of gold, and break the fast.
One should feed the virtuous and satisfy them with humility. || 135 ||
Thus, on the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, this auspicious vow accompanied by restraints should be performed;
it bestows the fruits of all sacrifices and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (136)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Āṣāḍha-Śukla-Śayanī-Ekādaśī Vow, the Sleeping Posture Adopted by the Vāmana Incarnation, and the Virtuous Vows of Restraint, Discipline, Self-Control, Subjugation, Austerity, Emaciation, Renunciation, Service, Charity, and Beneficence during the Cāturmāsya," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: Through the yoga of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Hari, everything becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
it bestows heaven, it bestows liberation, and it even grants the form of the four-armed one.
Whatever action is performed— whether for the sake of desire or free from the longing for fruit— if it is done for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa, all of that indeed bestows Goloka.
That alone is the vow, that the delightful rite, that the dharma, and that the worship, by which the Lord Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the master of the virtuous, may be pleased. (3)
That indeed is the Cāturmāsya vow by which Mādhava is pleased;
those are the restraints and observances by which Adhokṣaja is truly satisfied.
Tell me, O Lord: what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa?
Who is its presiding deity, what is its ritual procedure, and what is its merit? Please tell me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, and I shall tell you out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa is known by the name Kāmikā.
Acyuta, joined with Vijaya, should be worshipped there with devotion;
among flowers, Pārijātas are preferred, and for the arghya offering, the Bilva fruit is considered best.
The offering of food with a hundred holes and so forth, as well as the gift of garments for both women and men—
everything should be given by one observing the vow, for it generates love for Acyuta.
Neither at the Gaṅgā, nor at Kāśī, nor at Naimiṣa, nor indeed at Puṣkara,
is that true fruit obtained which is truly gained from the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The fruit that is obtained at the Godāvarī when Jupiter is in Leo and during the Vyatīpāta yoga at Daṇḍaka is said to be even greater than that.
He who observes the Kāmika vow obtains a fruit even greater than that of one who gives away the earth together with its oceans and forests.
He who gives a cow with all its appurtenances, specifically one that is "two-faced" (ubhayatomukhī),
obtains a fruit even greater than that arising from the Kāmikā vow.
Whosoever among the people, observing the vow, worships Śrīdhara Kṛṣṇa in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
by him the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Pannagas are fully honored.
For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, there exists the supreme vow of Kāmikā,
a boat fashioned by Hari that leads them to the further shore.
And the fruit obtainable through the science of the inner self is indeed attained from the Kāmika vow;
having performed this vow along with the night vigil, one never goes to an evil state of existence.
He does not behold the fierce Yama, nor does he encounter a base rebirth;
through the merit of the Kāmika vow, yogins have attained absolute liberation.
The person who worships Hari with leaves produced from the Tulasī plant is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (17)
One bhāra of gold and four times that amount of silver is offered;
the attainment of its fruit comes from worshipping with tulasī leaves.
Kṛṣṇa is not so pleased by offerings of red pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and the like, as He is by a leaf of tulasī.
By whomsoever Mādhava is worshipped with Tulasī blossoms,
his sins of many births indeed go to complete destruction.
She who, when seen, pacifies evil; when touched, purifies the body;
when praised, dispels disease; and when sprinkled with water, wards off death.
Salutations again and again to that Tulasi, who, when planted, brings about proximity to the feet of Kṛṣṇa, and when offered, bestows the fruit of liberation.
Having spoken thus, one should offer *tulasī* to the God, the Supreme Soul;
for him before whom a lamp burns in front of Kṛṣṇa on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), [there is no rebirth]. (23)
His ancestors, residing in heaven, are indeed satisfied with nectar;
therefore, the offering of a lamp should be performed on the peak on the day of Hari.
Even Viṣṇu himself cannot fully comprehend the measure of that merit;
indeed, a lamp of ghee or sesame oil should be offered in the temple. (25)
The donor goes to the heavenly world, radiant with hundreds of millions of lamps;
she removes the sin of killing a Brahmin and bestows the fruit of great merit.
O beloved, the Ekādaśī that bestows the station of heaven, destroys sins such as foeticide, and fulfills all desires must be observed with faith.
The performer of the vow, having indeed become pure and endowed with devotion, attains the world of Viṣṇu and enjoys eternal happiness. || 28 ||
On the tenth day, he should eat only once, sleep on the ground at night,
observe celibacy, and, having risen in the morning, remain steadfast in his vow.
Having bathed and performed the daily worship, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed;
thereafter, one should have the Sarvatobhadra mandala made with grains.
One should reverently worship the golden image of Acyuta accompanied by Vijayā there, according to the prescribed rite, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Then one should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water, and thereafter wipe it clean;
[one should then worship it] adorned with ornaments such as garments and jewelry, and beautified by various decorations.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a sesame tray, one should set the tray atop a water-pot,
provided with the five jewels, auspicious sprouts, fruit, and water.
One should feed [the deity] with various kinds of food and offer betel leaves and other items;
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer hymns of praise, circumambulate, and present the añjali gesture. || 34 ||
"May my vow be free from obstacles"—thus one should pray to Hari;
at midday as well, the observer of the vow should gratify Acyuta with most delicious foods.
In the evening as well, the observer of the vow should likewise perform the great worship and other rites;
he should feed [the deity], worship, swing [the image], and massage its limbs.
One should perform a vigil on the twelfth day, specifically in the morning;
having bathed and performed worship, one should indeed give various kinds of gifts.
One should feed virtuous women and children, and perform the breaking of the fast;
thus is the Sukāmikā vow, which bestows the fruit of all desires. (38)
One seeking wealth obtains wealth; one seeking a son gains a son;
one seeking a wife shall obtain a wife; and a husband who desires his own [wife] shall obtain her.
One who desires houses, fields, cattle, prosperity, grain, or wealth shall obtain those;
likewise, one who desires fame, health, great honor, sovereignty, or the essence of existence shall obtain that. 2.254.40.
One who seeks dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa should acquire them by undertaking a vow;
one who seeks the destruction of enemies, calamities, and obstacles shall attain their destruction.
Thus, this supreme Kāmika vow bestows everything;
it indeed grants heaven, it grants truth, and likewise grants the world of Virāja.
This vow bestows Goloka and grants the supreme imperishable state; it bestows all perfections. Now hear its ancient narrative.
In former times, the Śravaṇas were born into the family of Dharmarāja;
they were appointed by Dharma to bring reports concerning the conduct of living beings. ||44||
Wherever they go to bring back news of living beings,
they neither hear nor see any action more subtle than the subtle.
And they do not know the news; how then could they bring you? Not knowing it themselves, O Yama, how then would they report it to you? (46)
Thus, all of them, overcome with anxiety, gathered together and spoke to Yama in his presence:
"We know everything regarding those who perform subtle deeds exactly as it is."
"O Dharmarāja, please ordain it; we know what the karma of living beings is:
we are twelve in number, yet living beings are countless crores. (48)
How and where could there be pervasion for us without [your] proof?
Therefore, grant us proof, or else show us that ascetic power. (49)
"By which you may indeed possess all powers of perception in your presence.
Having heard this, Yama said to them: "Practice the Kāmika vow."
In the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, that Ekādaśī is considered Kāmikā;
it leads to the perfect fulfillment of all desires and bestows sovereign power. (5.1)
Having heard the procedure for the Kāmikā vow, they then listened to its recitation;
they performed the Kāmikā vow and gave abundant gifts.
On the twelfth day, at the time of breaking the fast, the King of Dharma (Yama), being pleased,
himself arrived having assumed the form of a brahmin guest.
Having clearly uttered, "Give alms," he stood upon the ground of the courtyard;
with great devotion, he accepted the alms offered by the ears. (54)
"Choose a boon, O Kṣatriyas; I am pleased with your vow," said the God of Dharma himself, the progenitor of Acyuta, to them. (55)
The Śravaṇas said to him: "That indeed is the subtle karma of living beings;
grant us that kind of omniscience so that we may truly know it here. (56)
He possesses the power of hearing from afar as well as seeing from afar; likewise, he knows secret deeds and assumes many forms. (57)
Likewise, [he perceives] the pervasiveness among all living beings situated in all places and so forth, as well as the supreme power of omniscience in all its aspects belonging to all of them. (58)
"Grant me also that eternal memory of it exactly as it is.
Having heard this, Dharmarāja then spoke to her.
The vow of the Kāmikā was performed by you, and its fruit is great; for it is from this that I have obtained everything consisting of all perfections and the granting of all desires.
"I grant all perfections so that you may become like the Lord at all times, born from the life-stories of all living beings. (61)
"I grant that all knowledge shall reside in you alone";
having thus bestowed this supreme boon, Dharmarāja vanished.
From that time forward, there were always twelve Śravaṇas,
who assumed countless forms and reported the deeds of living beings.
Always appearing as if they were omniscient before Citragupta,
they report the life-stories of those who have died and gone on before them.
By means of the vow of Kāmikā, they have attained the fruit of all desires;
therefore, Kāmikā, which bestows all perfections, should be performed by people.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story concerning Rati as it occurred in the past,
when Kāmadeva was consumed by Śaṅkara on Mount Himālaya.
Rati, the wife of Kāma, became a widow upon the loss of her husband;
she was greatly tormented and exceedingly emaciated by the agony of widowhood. || 67 ||
Having gone to Śaṅkara, she said: "O Lord, show mercy!
Without my husband, I have encountered this inauspiciousness that brings only suffering. (68)
"O Śambhu, destroy that [suffering] of me, a woman afflicted by pain; grant me well-being.
Having heard her, Śambhu said to her: "Perform the vow of Kāmikā."
"Indeed, misfortune shall certainly depart far from you forever;
even though your husband is bodiless, he will surely meet you at the place of delight."
All your misfortune and ill-fortune shall come to an end;
thereafter, your husband will indeed be the son of Kṛṣṇa, named Pradyumna.
"By means of one who is exceedingly beautiful, you shall obtain a fine body.
Upon hearing this, Rati joyfully undertook the vow of Kāmikā.
And according to the prescribed rites, he gave all kinds of gifts with great devotion;
meanwhile, Śambhu himself, at the time for breaking his fast, appeared as a mendicant.
He arrived for the sake of alms, and she offered him the food;
having eaten it, Śambhu then said, "Ask for a boon, and I shall grant it."
"By virtue of my vow to Kāmikā, I, Śaṅkara, am personally pleased.
Having heard this, Rati then said to her husband Kāma, "Grant it to me. (75)
Having uttered "So be it," Śaṅkara then became invisible;
he had been obtained as her husband by Rati at the proper time and in the appropriate place.
Having entered into every being in all wombs during sexual union, he who was named Pradyumna became incarnate; thus he then became the son of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, by the power of her vow, Rati attained the state of supreme fortune;
she achieved eternal perfection and pervaded all living beings within the universe.
This vow of Kāmikā indeed accomplishes all desires; it sustains the fulfillment of all intentions and bestows all prosperity. ||79||
It is the destroyer of all afflictions, gentle, auspicious, and the bestower of heaven and liberation;
it grants the fruit of all sacrifices and likewise brings about the perfection of yoga.
It bestows lost objects and grants great, eternal sovereignty;
it likewise grants pleasure, fulfills desires, provides a wife, and grants a husband.
It destroys suffering, pacifies affliction, bestows the happiness of sensual enjoyment, dispels obstacles, and fulfills the desires of both men and women. (82)
O Lakṣmī, this supreme rite which brings about non-widowhood must be performed in every way;
it bestows the power of pleasure, the power of passion, and spiritual perfection, and is indeed desirable. (83)
But for those free from desire, it is a vessel of merit that leads to Vaikuṇṭha;
even by merely hearing it, one receives the merit of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices. (84)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kāmika Ekādaśī in the Dark Half of Śrāvaṇa, the Attainment of All Perfections by the Pitṛs known as Śravaṇas, and the Attainment of the Lord named Kāma by Ratī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Nārāyaṇa himself, is the bestower of all desires;
he is indeed the giver of fruits, the giver of happiness, and the one who fulfills the vow.
Merit is attained through faith; he who always abides in faith, Viṣṇu, when accompanied by meditative cultivation and supported by vows, surely bears fruit.
The divine Mādhava, the bestower of liberation, dwells eternally within the means of attainment;
indeed, without those means, he never grants the fruit anywhere.
He alone—Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of Śrī, whose hands hold the banner and the bow—is to be propitiated in every way. (4)
O Lord whose hands bear the marks of the fish and the svastika, O Maṇikīśvara, husband of Pārvatī, speak to me out of compassion! (5)
What is the name of the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa?
What is the ritual procedure for it, what is its fruit, and which deity is indeed to be worshipped in this vow?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The Ekādaśī known as Putradā is considered to be the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa;
here, the Lord Śrīdhara is to be worshipped together with Kāntimatī.
He is to be worshipped with lotuses and fed with cakes;
Kṛṣṇa is to be offered an arghya with sītā-phalas, and a pair of sandals should be presented.
The gift of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā is considered auspicious;
its divine narrative, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be heard. (9)
On the tenth day, he should eat but one meal and likewise observe celibacy;
on the eleventh day at dawn, the observer of the vow should sleep upon the ground at night.
Having bathed daily and performed the great worship within the pavilion,
[he should place] a golden jar upon the Sarvatobhadra mandala that has been established.
Having placed a vessel of sesame seeds accompanied by the five jewels, garments, water, leaves, unbroken rice grains, and fruits, one should then install Śrīdhara.
One should worship with all one's being using the sixteen excellent articles;
one should perform the rites beginning with invocation and the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
With garments, ornaments, cosmetics, collyrium, sandalwood paste, and the like; with flower garlands, unbroken rice grains, aromatic powders, fruits, betel, and food offerings. (14)

Having worshipped Hari with the ārātrika rite, hymns of praise, prostrations like a staff, circumambulations, and the lighting of lamps, one should then pray for the vow to be free from obstacles. || 15 ||
At midday, one should offer food, as well as betel-leaf and water;
in the evening, one should offer milk-preparations, pūrikās, and vegetables.
One should keep a vigil at night with storytelling, chanting, and dancing;
then, on the twelfth day, having bathed at dawn and worshipped Mādhava.
One should give all kinds of gifts according to one's ability and according to one's wealth;
and one should feed virtuous Brahmins, virtuous women, boys, and girls.
Then, having fed one's own kinsmen, one should personally perform the breaking of the fast;
merit will be acquired in this way that grants both desired worldly enjoyment and liberation. 19.
The observer of the vow obtains auspicious wealth, grain, sons, wife, fields, gardens, houses, and so forth, as well as health, honor, fame, and other such blessings. (1.255.20)
Listen, Lakṣmī, to this divine story which occurred in the former Kṛta Yuga:
there was a king named Purūravas, the grandson of the Moon.
Budha’s son, Purūravas, governed his own kingdom;
he dwelt perpetually in Śrīpura on the banks of the Narmadā. (22)
Having heard of his virtues from the mouth of the gods, the celestial nymph Urvaśī, a woman of excellent form,
came of her own accord and presented herself as his wife.
Even after a long time had passed, no offspring was born to her;
for that king, being childless, his kingdom did not bring him happiness.
"For one who has no son, there is no happiness in this world or in the next.
As he was reflecting thus, a great deal of time passed. (25)
And since no son has been obtained by the king, he suffers even in happiness;
for he summoned the wise elders of his own kingdom and informed them of this. (26)
O brahmins, in this life no sin has been committed by me;
nor have I placed wealth acquired through unjust means into the treasury.

Furthermore, the property of Brahmins, the wealth of the gods, and the possessions of widows, orphans, and the destitute—even these were seized by me and never given back; on the contrary, they were always withheld. (28)
The world was protected like a son, the subjects were guarded according to dharma, the earth was conquered through battle, and punishment was inflicted upon the wicked. (29)
No injustice was committed by you toward those sons, kinsmen, and subjects;
the venerable elders were always well-honored and constantly saluted.
Those who stand on the path of justice were not hated; the deities were always honored;
and the Brahmins, the virtuous, the virtuous women, the cows, and the destitute were all revered. (31)
"Sacrifices of material wealth and sacrifices of knowledge have been performed through association with the learned;
nevertheless, no son has been born in my house—let this be reflected upon. (32)
Having heard these words, the twice-born, together with the elders and the family priests,
desiring the welfare of the king, went to the sage Lomaśa.
As each kalpa passed, one single hair of his would fall away;
thus, by the name "Lomaśa" (Hairy One), he attained renown through common usage.
He was performing terrible austerities, fasting, and free from worldly effort;
he was peaceful, a knower of the truth of the sublime Dharma, and an expert in the scriptures and the Vedas.
Seeing that high-souled one— long-lived, knowing the three periods of time, and beautifully adorned with matted hair and beard— the twice-born considered his fortune indeed to be supreme.
Having bowed before the sage Brahmātman, they stood there filled with joy;
seeing them along with their elder brother, the sage Lomaśa spoke to them.
"How and for what purpose have these Brahmins, who serve the elders, arrived? Whatever there may be—whether very great, small, achievable, or even unachievable? (38)
"Whether it be obtainable or even unobtainable, I shall do it for the sake of the Brahmins;
tell me without hesitation, and I will accomplish your welfare. (39)
The word of the Brahmins is the Veda, the command of the Supreme Lord;
by honoring your speech, I shall attain the fruit of my birth.
"There is no doubt that the birth of ascetics is for the sake of benefiting others;
oh, today I shall make my birth fruitful by serving this brahmin. (41)
Thinking thus, he performed hospitality, worship, and so forth;
he gave water, fruit, seats, and other offerings, for even one worthy of worship performs the service for his guest.
Then the brahmins said to him: "O Lord, please hear that which is in our hearts;
for the sake of dispelling our doubt, we are intent upon our own welfare. (43)
We have come into your presence here on account of a certain task; for by the sight of the virtuous, the treasure of sins accumulated in previous lives is destroyed. (44)
It is reduced to ashes instantly; how much more so by serving at your feet!
Indeed, apart from the Lotus-born Brahmā, no one else is found to be superior to you. (45)

You are possessed of great knowledge, you have lived through many eons, and you are a knower of much; endowed with meditative concentration, you know through the power of asceticism the past, the future, and that which is presently arising. (46)
"O Sage, by the power of the identity of Brahman and the Self, you are capable of giving everything;
however, King Purūravas is currently without a son. (47)
We brahmins have always been protected by him like his own children;
seeing him thus deprived of a son, we are pained by his sorrow. (48)
"O Queen, we have come here into the shade of your feet—you who bring about deliverance from suffering; now let what is appropriate be done. (49)
"O one whose wealth is austerity, it is indeed by your good fortune that you have been seen by us;
for by the mere sight of the great, men achieve the fulfillment of their goals."
"How is it that you have no son, or by what means might one be obtained?
Having heard these words of theirs, he entered into meditation for a moment. (51)
Lomaśa then replied to them regarding the king's previous birth:
"In a former life, he was indeed a wealthy Vaiśya named Vardhamāna. (52)
Devoted to the work of trade, he withers people through greed;
driven by the desire for commercial dealings, he travels from village to village. (53)
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
he arrived at a body of water on the outskirts of the village at midday under the scorching sun.
There was a single well, filled with water and beautiful with its descent-staircase;
having gone to that descent, he sat down there for a moment. (55)
