At the very moment he was washing his hands, feet, and face,
a cow accompanied by her calf arrived there, distressed by thirst.
Afflicted by the heat and filled with fear, she quickly descended into the landing-place;
but having stopped her after she had drunk only a mouthful, the dark one [Tāmasa] restrained her.
Having bathed himself, he drank water and performed the washing of his clothes;
staying there for a long time, he did not give the way to anyone seeking to drink. (58)
Though she was thirsty and accompanied by her calf, she waited for a long time on the path;
nevertheless, the wealthy man did not depart from his place for eight ghaṭikās.
The calf, overcome with thirst, said to its mother: "O Mother, my life-breaths are departing from the pain of thirst; when will this [thirst] depart? (1.255.60)
The cow-mother said to her calf: "He will depart in a moment;
meanwhile, maintain your composure, for we two shall drink water in a moment."
The owner did not depart from him, and even Vatsakaṇṭha attained a state of exhaustion;
then the cow said, "This rogue will certainly not leave."
"The life-breaths of my daughter are departing; I shall forcibly drink the water. Having thus resolved regarding her own calf, the cow indeed drank it down. (62)
Vardhamāna, the wealthy man, struck her repeatedly with a staff;
then he was cursed by the cow: "O merchant, you wicked one, you strike me in vain! (64)
O Bhava, may you indeed remain childless throughout all your successive births,
and being deprived of your wife, may you suffer in many ways in the forest.
Having cursed him and forcefully struck him with her two feet and two horns,
the cow drove the wealthy man far away and drank the excellent water in peace.
The calf drank water with composure, but the merchant departed from there;
struck by the cow and overcome by pain, he reached a village and died. (67)
Before his death, he gave all his wealth for the sake of a sacrifice;
the Brahmins performed the sacrifice, and by that merit, Vardhana [was born].
This king born here is named Purūravas;
due to the curse of a cow, he is childless and devoid of the fortune of having sons. (69)
"Indeed, due to this curse, he shall have no son throughout his successive births;
moreover, in the course of time, he shall suffer separation from his wife."
Having heard this, the brahmins said: "The destruction of sin comes from merit, and the warding off of the curse as well occurs through the grace of one such as you. (71)
"There is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for you; let there be a son for the king.
Instruct us in meritorious deeds, and the king will certainly carry them out. (72)
Lomaśa, having reflected upon all of them, declared that the vow which is exceedingly powerful is renowned by the name Putradā, occurring during the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
The Ekādaśī bestows all that is desired; O twice-born ones, observe its vow!
Let the king, the queen, and you all perform the vow with sincere devotion. (74)
On the day of the son's birth, at dawn, Purūravas shall perform the gift of a hundred thousand cows; from that, a son will be born. (75)
"If the vow of giving a hundred thousand cows is performed, a son free from duality will surely be born;
let the king do as he desires according to my word. (76)
Having placed this command upon their heads, the twice-born went to Śrīnagara;
together with the king, they performed the vow according to the rules, including the ritual vigil.
Then a gift of a hundred thousand cows was given to worthy recipients;
by that merit, the queen conceived a beautiful embryo.
But previously, when she had come down from heaven for the sake of her husband, she had made a vow to remain for a long time. (79)
"Upon seeing the king naked, I shall depart from this house.
Then, at that moment during the night, she saw the king without his clothes.
She departed for the forest, and Purūravas followed her;
she, however, being pregnant, remained in the wilderness in the form of a vessel of fire.
Indeed, she gave birth to the excellent son Jātavedas, who is the source of light;
thus, by means of the Ekādaśī vow, Vahni became his son.
In this manner, he indeed performed the gift of a hundred thousand cows at each of the Ekādaśīs and the other six festivals. ||83||
From him, through Urvaśī, six other sons were born:
Āyu, Śrutāyu, Satyāyu, Raya, Vijaya, and Jaya. (84)
Their sons and grandsons were indeed the increasers of the lineage;
through Agni and through progeny, the king attained the world of the Gandharvas.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures and eventually cast off his body in due time,
he departed from heaven to Vaikuṇṭha himself, assuming a four-armed form.
Listen, Lakṣmī: whoever desires infinite golden ornaments and sovereignty must perform this supreme vow, preceded by the gift of cows. (87)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun is situated in Cancer,
one should perform the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Vāsudeva on the twelfth lunar day.
With threads made of linen, gold, silver, copper, silk, lotus fibers, kuśa grass, kāśa grass, fine cotton, hemp, and other such beautiful materials; ||8-9||
Having tripled that thread made of three strands, one should purify it so that it appears like a beautiful gem; for that indeed makes it sacred.
One should indeed offer that purifying object, which bestows the merit of gold, to Hari;
one should wear it on the eleventh day and perform a vigil at night.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, as well as Śūdras, men, and women—
all who are established in devotion to Hari should perform the auspicious Pavitraka rite.
One should offer it to Hari and also dedicate it to the Guru;
by this investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa), I become truly purified.
One should likewise acquire ornaments such as gold, silver, and linen garments;
every year, the people should perform the Pavitrāropaṇa rite for their sons and wives.
Furthermore, it has been stated that by means of this mantra one becomes wealthy;
and through the rite of *pavitrāropaṇa*, one likewise attains both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). ||95||
But for him who does not perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) according to the prescribed rule, his worship performed throughout the year becomes fruitless. (96)
Having heard the greatness of the Putrapradā [Vrati], one is liberated from sin;
having attained heaven with ease, one shall obtain supreme liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Śrāvaṇa-Śukla-Putradā-Ekādaśī Vow, the Acquisition of a Son by the Merchant who had previously offended a cow during his incarnation as Purūravas while being childless due to performing the vow, and the Pavitrāropaṇa ceremony," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
By the remembrance of Nārāyaṇa, the bondage of birth and worldly existence is surely destroyed for people; I indeed bow to that Nārāyaṇa. (1)

I bow to Lord Hari, the husband [of Lakṣmī], the agent, the instrument, the effect, the impeller, the all-pervading master, the giver of happiness, the giver of sons, and the bestower of peace. || 2 ||
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Consort of Ramā!
O Maṇikyeśa, O Prabhāsvāmin, O Lord of Pārvatī, salutations to you! || 3 ||
Indeed, no satiety arises for me from hearing stories from your mouth;
tell me, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that is observed in the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada?
O Lord, who is the deity? What is the fruit of the gift? What flowers and other items are to be offered? What is the procedure for that vow? Please tell me all this in detail. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen with a focused mind, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe in detail the sin-destroying Ekādaśī of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, known by the name Ajā.
Lord Janārdana should be worshipped together with Sundarī;
among flowers, the Pāṭalā is to be offered, and for the arghya, the betel nut (pūgīphala) is considered appropriate.
In the gift, however, a buffalo should be offered; for the food offering, small balls of molasses (guḍalaḍḍukas).
One should act especially according to the time and according to what is available. 8.
On the tenth day, the seeker of the vow should likewise subsist on a single meal;
he should sleep upon the ground and must indeed preserve his Brahmanic conduct.
On the morning of the eleventh day, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa Janārdana and bathed, one should perform the daily worship with the sixteen articles.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, well-adorned with many pillars;
in its center, the observer of the vow should have a Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared.
In the center of that [altar] is a golden pitcher filled with water containing five jewels,
accompanied by cloth, fruit, leaves, a sacred thread, sandalwood, and rice.
One should place [the image] there and keep a bell and a conch nearby;
one should worship according to the rules with mantras and place a vessel of sesame seeds in the jar.
One should place a golden image of Janārdana accompanied by Sundarī, or one made of silver, along with eleven uncooked rice balls (*ajyaikādaśika*), within a vessel.

One should worship and massage the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and liquefied sandalwood following the invocation and other rites, and then bathe the deity with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha).
With rows of garments, ornaments, finery, decorations, necklaces, and the like, as well as with excellent fragrant substances, incense, lamps, and offerings; || 16 ||
With the exquisite fragrances of saffron, agallochum, and musk oils in liquid form, and with collyrium, white and pale powders, crests, and ointments; || 17 ||
With staffs, sandals, umbrellas, chowries, vehicles, and mounts; with the waving of lamps, hymns of praise, prostrations, and the gesture of salutation like a staff, and so forth. || 18 ||
One should worship the God with great devotion using handfuls of flowers, water, betel-leaf, cardamom, and cloves for chewing, as well as through requests for forgiveness and other such acts.
One should give to the God a bed made of gold, provided with excellent soft coverings, and accompanied by a mirror, side-tables, and a fan.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, the observer of the vow should pray for the sake of the observance:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I perform this goat-vow; may it reach completion without obstacles. (21)
One should give various gifts consisting of excellent gems and refined gold;
one should also give auspicious items such as cows and buffaloes that yield milk. (22)
At midday as well, having worshipped Hari Kṛṣṇa, one should offer auspicious items:
a vessel for enchantment, pearls, and powdered sweetmeats.
Apūpas and likewise pūpas, polikās and sweet polikās, pūrikās, puṣpavaṭikās, and even rājikārāddha. (24)
One should offer various kinds of vegetables, delicious vinegars, and curd and milk enriched with the essence of excellent flavors. || 25 ||
The observer of the vow should offer fruits, water, mouth-fresheners, and so forth;
and in the evening, he should properly perform a grand worship.
Having tied Hari to a swing made from a tree or suspended in the air, one should swing Him;
at night, one should indeed offer food consisting mostly of milk, which bestows strength.
One should offer the nightly lamp-offering, hymns of praise, a prayer for forgiveness, and a handful of flowers;
furthermore, one should offer whatever else is appropriate and desired by Hari.
One should keep a vigil at night with dancing, singing, and recitation; through devotion to the praise and names of Hari, by listening to sacred narratives and playful pastimes. || 29 ||
Having bathed at dawn on the twelfth day and having worshipped Janārdana,
one should feed Hari and give various kinds of gifts.
Having fed other virtuous twice-born men who have taken refuge [with him],
as well as children, with sweet food, the observer of the vow should afterwards perform the breaking of the fast during the subsequent observance.
When the vow has been performed in this manner, all the desires of the practitioner shall bear fruit;
whatever he may desire—whether heaven, liberation, or sovereignty—the practitioner shall attain it.
O Lakṣmī, those men who perform such a vow, being liberated from all sins, go to the eternal heaven. || 33 ||
Listen to the auspicious narrative concerning King Hariścandra, together with his wife and son— a story endowed with vows that destroys all suffering.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there lived a king named Hariścandra, the sovereign of the city of Sāketa, who was preeminent and endowed with the quality of truth. (35)
Ruling over the city of Sāketa, which extended five yojanas along the bank of the Sarayū river, the king protected his subjects.
The universal monarch, true to his word and lord of the entire earth,
used to honor his guests and give them whatever they desired.
No seeker ever departs from his house without being honored;
whatever a seeker desires, he always gives that very thing. (38)
The Brahmins [were honored] with offerings of sweet food and alms; the Kṣatriyas with marks of great respect;
the Vaiśyas with the acquisition of assistance; and the Śūdras with the opportunity to join the hermitage.
The gods [are satisfied] by sacrificial offerings and oblations; the sages (ṛṣis) by hospitality;

the ascetics (munis) by devotion to Brahman and the like; those with desires by their wished-for objects; women by the protection of their livelihood and the like; and children by the delight of learning and so forth.
Others are honored by him in every way with whatever they desire to obtain. || 41 ||
All are contented and go to their homes; his subjects live in happiness.
In his kingdom, there is no man who is destitute of wealth or devoid of devotion.
Devoid of service to his father, he felt no compassion for women;
he maintained the resonance of the Vedas, performed sacrificial oblations, and provided a continuous stream of gifts to those in need. || 42 ||
Not a single phenomenon remained without the five names of Hari;
as he lived in this manner, his fame spread throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions.
He became renowned throughout the three worlds as one who never wavered from the truth;
then indeed Brahmā, Hari, Śambhu, Viśvāmitra,
and others arrived for the sake of testing him, wondering how much truth remained in him.
Hariścandra indeed showed great honor to those wearing the forms of brahmins;
he offered them hospitality and service, and announced his desired object. Then Viśvāmitra said, "The entire kingdom is required."
"O Great King, let it be given to me; by this I shall become free from debt.
"So be it," the king replied, and having released the water, he then gave it.
Having accepted the kingdom, the sage separately requested a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

The king had no separate wealth for the sake of a sacrificial fee; to fulfill that requirement, he was deprived of his kingdom and entered into service and menial labor. Having sold his wife and son, he even proceeded to sell himself. (1.256.50)
Having attained the state of a slave to a Pulkasa, that king became a partaker of merit;
by adhering to the truth in the cremation ground as a remover of the garments of the dead,
he indeed became honored by kings, for he never wavered from the truth.
In this manner, many years passed for that king.
He continued to give Viśvāmitra his wages as a sacrificial fee;
nevertheless, the fee required to satisfy the sage was not yet complete.
Whatever clothing or bowl may be obtained, he gives it all for the sake of the offering;
yet, for the sake of fulfilling [the vow], he himself experiences suffering.
Thus is the service fulfilled by one who abides in the duty of a laborer.
Even though he had given away his entire inheritance, he still entered into service for the sake of a livelihood.
Yet the end of his suffering did not come; therefore, he became consumed by anxiety:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can there be an end to this suffering? (55–56)
My wife is a servant in a merchant’s house, my son is a laborer elsewhere, and I am a frequenter of the cremation ground—alas, a servant to the outcastes! (57)
Where is sovereignty, and where is servitude? This wheel is indeed composed of illusion.
Nevertheless, I shall certainly make such an effort so that there may be the destruction of suffering. ||58||
While he was thinking thus, submerged in an ocean of sorrow,
the sage arrived there, having learned that the king was afflicted.
He was a devotee of Viṣṇu, a worthy recipient of blessings for his progeny, and one who lived according to justice;
he was named Gautama, compassionate, and a doer of good for others.
He bestowed blessings upon the king, saying, "May you be happy in every way.
Standing with palms joined in reverence, the king bowed to that brahmin.
He related his own history, which was filled with suffering;
having heard it all, Gautama became exceedingly amazed.
O King, he taught that vow as a means for crossing over suffering;
it is exceedingly purifying during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is named Ajā; it is the destroyer of suffering.
O King, observe its vow, and the destruction of your misery will come to pass.
"Let your wife perform this vow, which brings happiness;
furthermore, let your son perform the 'one-meal-a-day' vow for the sake of attaining happiness. (65)
Having been thus instructed, King Hariścandra performed that supreme vow;
and the sage, having assigned his son to that vow, departed for his wife’s side.
The queen and the prince went to their own hermitage as instructed,
and they performed the goat-vow day and night according to their ability.
When that vow had been performed, the king’s suffering came to an end in an instant;
and the queen’s and her handmaid’s suffering also came to an end in an instant.
There, even during the day, his son died; however, by the power of that very vow, Rohita regained life after the completion of the observance.
That suffering, which was to have been experienced for many years, came to an end;
by the power of this vow, the king emerged from his misery.
Indeed, Hariścandra attained union with his wife, the joy of living through his son,
and union with that very son.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Viśvāmitra, and the others,
appearing in their own forms, arrived visibly to dispel his sorrow.
They declared, "Today the examination of Satya has been completed," and all the gods and goddesses arrived at that festival. (73)
To bestow blessings upon King Hariścandra,
drums resounded in heaven and a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
By the power of Ekādaśī, Hariścandra,
together with his sons and his wife, regained his entire kingdom, free from all thorns.
Having enjoyed [the fruits of his merit] for many years and having performed devotion to Hari,
he then, becoming dispassionate, established his son in the kingdom along with his wife.
Hariścandra, together with his city and his retinue, attained heaven;
having enjoyed that for an infinite time, he went to the abode of Sāketa.
O Lakṣmī, those human beings who shall perform such a vow will be completely liberated from all sins and freed from all miseries. (78)
All shall attain heaven, liberation, and the supreme state;
by reading or even by hearing this, the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice shall be obtained. (79)

Therefore, this story should be heard, and with faith one should perform the vow, as well as the giving of gifts, worship, and adoration that constitute its constituent parts, according to the prescribed rule. (1.256.80)
The performer of the vow becomes a washer-away of the sins of others, a bringer of heaven, and a protector from the fear of Yama and other such realms. ||8 1 ||
Rather, it should be stated that, by virtue of his connection with Nārāyaṇa, he is capable of accomplishing both enjoyment and liberation for his own sake. ||82||
One who observes her vow is never born again; therefore, she is considered unborn.
Liberation is "unborn" (ajā); indeed, through this vow of hers, she is the Unborn.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Bhādrapada-Kṛṣṇa-Ekādaśī Vow, Viśvāmitra’s Test of Hariścandra’s Truthfulness, the Loss of Kingdom, Wife, and Son, and the Cessation of Suffering through the Goat-Vow shown by Gautama," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O remover of suffering, O creator of happiness, O bestower of prosperity, O ocean of compassion!
It is certain that the deliverance of sinners does not occur without you. (1)
Upon whomsoever your compassion may fall—be they even a great sinner or one worse than a sinner—they shall surely be purified; of this there is no doubt. (2)
One may resort to [falsehood] out of desire, anger, fear, greed, or even for the sake of gain.
Whoever shall be released from the snares of saṃsāra, he shall obtain liberation.
Vow, sacrifice, compassion, charity, knowledge, meditation, recitation, and austerity—you alone are these, O Ocean of Mercy; through union with you, they bestow liberation.
Tell me, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada?
Who is its presiding deity, what is its ritual procedure, what is its fruit, and how is it to be worshipped? (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada named Padmā bestows liberation;
here, Ṛṣikeśa is to be worshipped together with Aparājitā.

Kāśa flowers should be used for worship, cooked sesame for the food offering (naivedya), and a pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa) should indeed be given as the respectful offering (arghya); for the gift, an auspicious house of Brahmā is to be given.
One should have a temple, a palace, or a mansion constructed, established with splendor; indeed, one should bestow a beautiful mansion upon the preceptor who worships the deity.
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat only one meal at night;
he should sleep on the ground and must diligently maintain the vow of celibacy.
This eleventh lunar day, occurring on the side [of the month], is considered sacred to Hari;
on this very day, He who lies upon Śeṣa indeed turns over His side.
On the day of Śayanī, on the day of Pārśvavartinī, and on the day of Prabodhinī, men should observe a fast— either without food or even without water— according to their capacity.
"Here, those pitiless ones who eat food cause me pain in my side;
therefore, one must not eat food, but should eat only fruit. (12)
Milk should be drunk by one who has strength; a fast without water must be observed by him, for by this the Lord, the Consort of Kamalā, is pleased.
On the eleventh day, having risen at the time of Brahma, the observer of the vow should remember and meditate upon Hari while reciting His names, and then proceed to bathe.
Having bathed and performed the daily worship of Kṛṣṇa,
the observer of the vow should have an auspicious *sarvatobhadra* mandala constructed with excellent grains.
In the center, one should place a golden jar or one made of copper,
provided with the five gems, unbroken rice, flowers, water, cloth, and fruit.
One should worship [the vessel] equipped with a conch, bell, and so forth, using sandalwood paste and other offerings;
indeed, one should place a bowl filled with sesame seeds upon that jar.
The observer of the vow should install the incomparable image of Aparājitā at Ṛṣikeśa;
he should also install Padmā on the eleventh day and worship her.

Through the rites of invocation and so forth, as well as the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the like, and with waters for clothing, ornaments, and decoration, along with sandalwood paste and other offerings. || 19 ||
With necklaces, armlets, bracelets, crowns, crests, and the like; with sandals, staffs, garments, clusters of flowers, upper cloths, and so forth. || 1.257.20 ||

With incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings; with water, betel-leaf, and fine fruits; with the waving of lights (ārārtika), hymns of praise, prostrations like a staff, and circumambulations. || 21 ||

And having worshipped the Blessed One with a handful of flowers for requesting forgiveness, accompanied by respectful gifts and other offerings, for the sake of accomplishing the vow without obstacles.
Afterwards, having bowed to Śrī Hari, he should offer prayers and attend to other duties;
at midday as well, the observer of the vow should present sweet foods to the Blessed One.
One should offer betel-leaf and water for drinking, and cause sacred stories to be recited;
thereafter, in the afternoon and then in the evening, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to the prescribed rules.
One should perform hymns of praise and recitations, feed [the deity] milk-pudding and other foods, offer betel-leaf and water, and seat [the deity] upon the swing. (275)
The devotee himself, as well as other Sāttvata devotees,
virtuous women, holy men, and even celibate students, should cause it to be swung.
Having joined together, one should keep vigil with festivities preceded by song;
there should be dancing accompanied by the sounding of drums, as well as hymns of praise and the nectar of sacred narratives.
Having bathed in the morning, one should worship Kṛṣṇa in his presence;
one should feed the Blessed Lord and offer the sacred remnants (prasāda) to the devotees of the Sātvata lineage. ||28||
And having caused others to break their fast, the observer of the vow should then himself break his fast;
he should perform the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day and practice charity.
Cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, vehicles, palanquins, and mounts;
houses, gardens, cities, villages, fields, clothing, food, and means of subsistence.
Jewels, diamonds, rubies, gems, gold, wealth, and so forth;
couches, carts, beds, chests, vessels, and door-panels. ||3 1 ||
A grass mat, a linen seat, a lion-throne, a silk cushion, a straw mat, a swing, a grain-sack, a ball, a secret hand-rope, and a cord. (32)
It contained books, household utensils, chains, water-pots,
trees, moving creepers, swaying pillars, and the skins of deer, tigers, and other beasts.
On the twelfth day, one should give whatever is possible for oneself, such as tree bark, a seat, bark garments, silk, wealth, and so forth.
The king should give to the preceptor-guru water-vehicles, land-vehicles, aerial vehicles, and so forth, as well as many kinds of mechanical devices. (35)
Whatever is given by people to a worthy recipient is obtained in the next world:
the gift of knowledge, the gift of land, the gift of a daughter, and the bestowal of wealth. (36)
The gift of food, the gift of water, the gift of clothing, the offering of a house, the gift of a cow, the gift of land, the gift of ritual implements, and the bestowing of vows. ||37||
The gift of merit, as well as the surrender of that which is most dear to each individual, follows the giver to heaven or to another state of birth. (38)

Therefore, one should give according to one's capacity, for it provides assistance in the next world; one should practice the service of the virtuous, which bestows happiness both here and hereafter. (3.9)
By whatever means of devotion the virtuous are pleased in whatever manner, in that very way should the virtuous—who are indeed the very forms of Hari—be served. (1.257.40)
The virtuous are incarnations of Hari’s own form upon this earth;
when served with devotion during a vow, they become pleased if there is sincerity within.
Then, for one who seeks the vow, both enjoyment and liberation are attained, and everything is accomplished:
service to Hari, service to the virtuous, service to saintly women, and the offering of all to Acyuta. ||42||
Knowledge of the self, the yoga of devotion, constant reflection on the qualities of Hari, knowledge of Brahman, and the perfection of yoga—each one individually is a means to liberation. (43)
Vows, austerity, recitation, yoga, sacrifice, and self-surrender—when joined with the path of taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa, these are the certain means for liberation. 44.
Therefore, the observer of the vow should perform this vow which consists of a profound connection with Brahman;
for one who acts with desire there shall be enjoyment, while for one without desire there is the supreme goal. 45.
For one who destroys another's dwelling, one's own dwelling is surely destroyed;
for one who demolishes another's house, one's own house indeed collapses. (46)
For one who commits violence against others, self-violence certainly arises;
and for one who inflicts suffering upon others, personal suffering certainly arises. (47)
For one who bestows happiness upon others, their own happiness certainly arises;
and for one who strikes down the prosperity of others, their own prosperity certainly perishes. (48)
In this world, the destruction of another inevitably leads to one's own destruction;
and for one who steals the property of others, the ruin of one's own wealth is certain. (4.9)

For one who brings about the ruin of another's wife, the ruin of one's own wife will certainly occur; for one who gives fire or poison to others, the presence of fire or poison in one's own home is certain.
For one who deceives others, self-deception is certain;
for one who destroys the domestic life of others, the destruction of one's own domestic life is certain. (51)
For one who destroys the happiness of others, there is the destruction of one's own happiness;
for one whose nature is to help others, there is assistance in helping oneself. (5.2)
The arrival of sensory pleasure occurs for one who bestows sensory pleasure; the acquisition of the means occurs for one who bestows pleasure through those means. (5.3)
For one who creates obstacles, obstacles indeed arise; for one who bestows happiness, happiness surely comes;
and for one who gives everything, all things certainly attend him. 54.
Therefore, all gifts should be given for the sake of future attainment;
for what is given here will certainly not be obtained in vain, neither in this world nor in the next.
The Ekādaśī vow should be performed with great effort for those who have not given and those who are suffering; it will certainly grant whatever is desired. 56.
Suffering caused by the fault of an individual may accrue to that group;
likewise, great merit performed by an individual arises for the community. (57)
In the case of a king, merit or demerit is produced collectively;
likewise, the merit and demerit performed by the king touches the subjects as well. (58)
If the subjects of anyone whatsoever are suffering due to the violation of dharma, the Ekādaśī vow must be performed for the sake of destroying that suffering. (59)
By that, sin is surely destroyed and incomparable happiness indeed arises;
hear how such a thing occurred for King Māndhātṛ in the Kṛta Yuga.
A royal sage named Māndhātṛ, born in the lineage of Vivasvat, became a universal monarch whose dominion extended from the land of sunrise to the land of sunset. || 61 ||
He protected his subjects with righteousness as if they were his own children;
in his kingdom there was neither famine, nor mental distress, nor disease.
His kingdom, endowed with abundance of wealth and grain, was indeed like heaven;
his treasury, too, filled with wealth acquired through righteous means, was like a hidden treasure.
Likewise, the castes and stages of life shine forth and flourish through meritorious deeds.
The earth is the bearer of wealth, the wish-fulfilling cow, and the desire-granting trees.
For him, the virtuous Brahmins were perfected in speech and were stages of yoga;
and his noble women were givers of bliss, tranquil, and auspicious in their grace.
The seasons and the fulfillment of desires were like another heaven for the kingdom;
indeed, the subjects became immersed in happiness, having attained manifold bliss.
Brahmins are established in the duties of Brahman; Kṣatriyas are devoted to protection;
Vaiśyas are intent on the exertion of acquiring wealth; and Śūdras are servants. ||67||
They were followers of their own dharma, and because of that, the kingdom became happy;
as he ruled the kingdom in this manner, the planets always remained auspicious. (68)
The gods were pleased, and auspicious signs appeared in every house.
Then, a certain king of devotees, though born as a *vṛṣala*, desired sovereignty. (69)
Then, due to his abandonment of the dharma of a Śūdra and his adoption of the dharma of a Ṛṣi, he began severe penance in a desolate forest.
Due to the entry of unrighteousness and heterodoxy into this kingdom,
the clouds did not rain for three years, and the subjects were distressed.
Some people were broken and died, afflicted by hunger; [there was no longer] the utterance of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*, nor the study of the Vedas or ritual worship. ||72||
Likewise, the assistance rendered for religious vows, honors, hospitality, gifts, and so forth, as well as all auspicious rites, festivals, and the like, were utterly destroyed. (73)
Due to his misrule, the country became afflicted by fate;
then the subjects, having assembled, spoke thus to the lord of kings: ||74||
Listen, O King: without rain, this destruction of the kingdom occurs.
The Lord Viṣṇu, in the form of Parjanya, is established within the waters. (75)
He alone brings about rain; from rain comes food, and from that, the subjects.
In the absence of rain, O Great King, those subjects go to their destruction. (76)
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, provide for our security and prosperity so that it may be ensured.
Having heard this, the lord of the earth spoke regarding how the welfare of his subjects might be secured. (77)
I shall strive accordingly, since happiness has its root in the king;
for through the misconduct of kings, the subjects suffer oppression. (78)
"Although I have never committed any sin anywhere since birth, nevertheless, I shall strive with the desire for the welfare of my subjects. (79)
Having spoken thus, the king, accompanied by his offspring and a limited retinue,
set out on a journey through the land, intent upon searching for the evildoer.
He heard from the mouths of people that in the dense forest of the Himalayas, a Śūdra was performing austerities; that this very person is practicing unrighteousness (vidharma) within your kingdom.
For Brāhmaṇas and ascetics, righteous austerity is their duty;
for Śūdras, service is their duty, while austerity is indeed contrary to their dharma.
"Due to the fault of the asceticism performed by a Śūdra, a drought arises today.
This very obstruction of a Śūdra’s asceticism shall become a dharma that brings rain. (8.3)
Having heard this, the lord of the earth quickly went to the dense forest;
he visited the foremost sages and their hermitages inhabited by ascetics.
Then the king beheld the sage Aṅgiras, the son of Brahmā,
whose face was pervaded by a halo of splendor like that of the lotus-born one.
The king, humble with palms joined in reverence, paid homage at his feet;
the sage then inquired after the welfare of the kingdom and whether all was free from affliction.
Having sat down on the seat offered to him, Māndhātṛ replied to him: "O Blessed One, as I am protecting the earth according to the ordinances of Dharma... (87)
A drought has arisen and all the subjects are suffering;
three years have already passed—what could be the cause of this? (88)
"I have heard from the mouths of people that a Śūdra performs penance;
nevertheless, tell me the definitive conclusion—what could be the reason for this? (89)
"Bring peace to the subjects by providing for their security and well-being.
Having meditated within himself for a moment, Aṅgiras spoke thus to the king.
In this Kṛta Yuga, Dharma proceeds with its four quarters;
here, the worlds are devoted to Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas are devoted to austerity.
Others are authorized for asceticism, for this path does not exist in the Kṛta Yuga;
yet even a Śūdra may be devoted to asceticism here, provided the proper object [for such practice] exists.
Due to the power of his dharma, the clouds do not rain;
exert effort to slay him, for he is in a forest not far away.
"When this is done, O King, there shall never again be drought.
Having heard this, the highly fortunate king, who was devoted to compassion, spoke.
"I will not kill him while he is performing his penance and engaged in auspicious deeds; rather, I shall gradually obstruct his ascetic practice by means of some pretext. (95)
If there were some other means for bringing rain, then show it to me; for I shall certainly effect the destruction of this affliction.
Aṅgiras said to the king: "If it is so, then it is excellent;
perform the vow named Padma-ekādaśikā, which bestows well-being."
This Padmika vow bestows all accomplishments, destroys all calamities, brings about all peace, and grants security and well-being. (98)
O King, perform the Padmā-vrata together with your subjects and your retinue;
by the power of the Padmā-vrata, a bountiful rain will surely occur. 99.
Having thus accepted the command upon his head and having honored that sage,
he appointed an attendant to prevent the Śūdra from practicing austerities.
Remembering Kṛṣṇa within his own heart, the king returned to his home;
then, during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, he performed the Padmā-vrata.
Accompanied by all his subjects and endowed with the four social orders,
he undertook a vow and performed acts of charity and worship of Hari.
When the vow had been thus performed, O Lakṣmī, the clouds rained down;
the earth, thoroughly saturated with water, became abounding in crops.
The drought was swiftly destroyed by the merit of the Ekādaśī vow;
therefore, the Padmā-vow should be observed for the destruction of one's misfortunes.
Therein are also curd-rice and a jar accompanied by garments and jewels,
as well as a water-filled pitcher, an umbrella, and sandals.
One should give gifts to a Brahmin who knows Brahman and is one's guru with the thought that he is Govinda;
likewise, the twice-born guru should be saluted, fed, and satisfied.
Having thus performed this supreme vow, a person shall obtain their desired goal;
indeed, by hearing or reciting this, the merit of the vow is attained.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Bhādrapada Śukla Padma-ekādaśī Vrata, wherein, during the Satyayuga under the reign of King Māndhātṛ, a drought occurred while a Śūdra was performing penance, and rain was brought about by the vow," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛtayuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Salutations, salutations to you, O Govinda, O Ṛṣikeśa, O Janārdana!
O Witness, O Impeller, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Controller! (1)
O bestower of the visible, giver of sight, you who abide as the seer;
O you whose nature is the seed and the sprout, you who abide in the stalk, leaves, and other parts.
O you who exist as the seed within the stalk, the stem, and the beautiful flower—homage be to you!
O bestower of fruit, abiding in the fruit, you yourself ripen it in its proper season.
O you who pervade the fruit of the seeds of karma, like rain upon seeds, salutations be to you!
Tell me, on which day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina does the Ekādaśī named what occur? (4)
What is the procedure for this, what is its fruit, and what kind of vow is prescribed?
Which deity is worshipped here, and what are the offerings, worship, and so forth? (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, there is indeed a festival known by the name Indirā;
here, Upendra, endowed with auspicious fortune, is to be worshipped with dūrvā grass.
The *āmalakī* fruit is for the water offering (*arghya*), while the fried cake (*śaṣkulī*) is for the food offering (*naivedya*).
The gift of a maiden is the principal rite, and the worship should indeed be performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
The primary libation for the ancestors must be performed, which is auspicious and brings satisfaction;
this vow, accompanied by śrāddha and other rites, provides a means of passage for those who have no refuge.

On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat but one meal, remain celibate, sleep on the ground, and exercise self-restraint; then, on the eleventh day, he should perform the ritual observance at dawn.
Having risen, remembered Śrī Hari, and meditated upon the form of Hari, one should then,
with a pure mind, bathe and perform the daily worship.
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed, one should place a new pitcher made of gold or copper within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
One should place a vessel filled with sesame seeds upon the jar, provided with water, cloth, and the sprouts, fruits, and five jewels.
To the side, one should likewise place cooked rice which provides satisfaction to the ancestors,
as well as water brought from a sacred bathing place in a vessel, and kusha grass.
Then, one should place sugar, fruits, flour-cakes, and other offerings at the sides,
as well as a golden image of Upendra endowed with great beauty.
The observer of the vow should place [the vessel] together with indira in a pot of sesame seeds;
and having worshipped Gaṇeśa, as well as the conch, the bell, and the water-pot.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa and then remembered him in the heart, one should contemplate:
"May his head be upon my head, and may Hari’s eyes be in my eyes and other parts. (16)
May his heart be in [my] heart; may his hands and so forth be in my hands and so forth; may his hips and so forth be in my hips and so forth; and may Hari’s lotus feet be in my two feet.
"May the limbs of Hari be in my limbs; may Keśava be in my soul"—thinking thus, having become divine in every respect, one should worship Hari.
One should perform the invocation and other rites, the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
the bathing with pure water, and the offering of garments.
The grooming of the hair and so forth, worship with various fragrant substances, and worship with gulāla, saffron, barley, sandalwood, and unbroken grains (akṣata). || 1.258.20 ||
One should apply dye, lampblack, and coloring substances such as moistened lac and powder to all the limbs of the deity, and then one should place ornaments and other decorations upon him.
Then, one should extensively adorn the form, made beautiful with erotic grace, with flower garlands and the like, as well as with handsome ornaments such as bracelets and crowns.
Incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel-leaf with lime, the waving of lights (ārārtika), hymns of praise, circumambulation, prostration like a staff, and so forth. ||23||

The practitioner, with a mind endowed with all forms of devotion, should perform the offering of a handful of unhusked rice and flowers as a sacrificial fee, and the rite of seeking forgiveness according to the prescribed rule. (24)
One should give and perform whatever is appropriate, and one should request freedom from obstacles for the vow;
having remembered the ancestors, one should offer a handful of water enriched with grace (prasāda). || 25 ||
One should indeed give gifts in the morning and worship [the deity] at midday as well;
thereafter, one should feed Lord Nārāyaṇa with various kinds of foods.
And after midday, one should perform the Śrāddha for the ancestors;
one should offer water with the appropriate mantras using the specific names [of the ancestors] through the Pitṛ-tīrtha.
One should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas) and other fruits that provide satisfaction to the ancestors;
having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) in the evening, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
One should feed [the devotees] milk-preparations and the like, and offer them water for drinking and so forth;
one should keep a vigil at night and cultivate the company of the virtuous. ||29||
One should engage in discourse, listen to it with devotion, or recite it;
one should also perform dance and song, and hold festivals of great enthusiasm.
Having bathed in the morning, meditated upon Hari, and worshipped Him according to the prescribed rites,
one should offer food-oblations to the Lord and then feed the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having fed the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the twice-born who have taken refuge [with him],
the observer of the vow should then perform the breaking of the fast and give gifts to worthy recipients.
She should honor her teacher, her mother, her elders, her father, and her husband;
she should receive their blessings and thereafter attend to her own duties. (33)
When the vow has been performed in this manner, O Lakṣmī, the desired goal is certainly accomplished;
one should cause food that satisfies the ancestors, as well as water, clothing, and other gifts, to be given.
One should cause other gifts to be made that effect the liberation of one's ancestors, such as cows, houses, gardens, livestock, fields, daughters, learning, and excellent vehicles. (35)

The observer of the vow, with faith and with the intent of pleasing the ancestors, should cause [the image]— adorned with gold and jewels and provided with various new utensils— to be given as a gift.
One should offer it to the Guru, who is Hari; this shall bring about the liberation of one's ancestors.
Since it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, it is most excellent; therefore, one should practice that which grants liberation.
Therefore, for one who has an excessive longing, that very longing must be pacified by him for the sake of its own cessation; otherwise, it will not cease. (38)
Indeed, the reversal of fortune for one born in the lineage may result from the failure to satisfy the ancestors;
therefore, [the offering] may yield either the fruit of desire or even the fruit of non-desire. (39)
A descendant of the lineage should indeed perform [the rite] when the proper time has arrived for the sake of satisfying the ancestors;
during the vow of the dark fortnight of the month of Īṣa, he should perform it so as to bring about the satisfaction that yields special fruit.
Whether it be very small or even vast, one should give [gifts] with the respective auspicious names [of the deceased];
that will certainly bring happiness to those who have gone to the next world. ||41||
If the ancestors were established in liberation, then the fruit would belong to the agent;
thinking that what has been performed must not go to waste, the wise person should act accordingly. (42)
Just as a seed indeed yields a sprout, a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, so too the consecration performed by one endowed with faith in a worthy field never goes in vain. (43)
A seed sown in salt soil perishes, but it is not lost when sown in a worthy field;
when cast into a sacred place, a worthy recipient, or a virtuous person, it certainly sprouts.
What is offered to Hari, whether during a vow or to a worthy recipient, is never fruitless;
therefore, whether it be small or great, one should offer it free from any expectation of reward. (45)
One should give [a gift], for it surely bears fruit by reason of Hari’s grace.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this delightful story which grants satisfaction to the ancestors through the observance of the vow. (46)
The Indira Ekādaśī is the most excellent, bestowing a higher state upon the ancestors who have fallen into lower wombs, and granting the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. 47.
Indeed, by King Indrasena, the Pitṛtāraṇī was propitiated;
he was the lord of the city of Candrāvatī in the great kingdom known as Narmadā.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Indrasena;
he protected his subjects with righteousness as if they were his own biological sons. 49.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, possessed of wealth and grain,
provided with elephants, horses, and vehicles, he remains devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
O Japan, the names of Śrī Hari always grant liberation;
one who contemplates spiritual meditation passes their time through devotion alone. 5.1.
Once, while he was seated at home in a state of tranquility, the sage Nārada descended by way of the sky and appeared before him.
Seeing that Nārada had arrived, he rose with palms joined in reverence;
having offered hospitality to the sage, he seated him upon a beautiful, comfortable seat. (53)
He said, "Welcome to you; I shall do honor to you, O best among the knowers of Brahman.
Today my kingdom, my birth, my deeds, my lineage, and my wealth have become fruitful. (54)
O best of sages, by your grace, my charity, sacrifices, recitations, fire-offerings, and Vedic study have become fruitful; my fortune is most blessed. (55)
Hundreds of sons, grandsons, wives, male servants, and female servants, as well as elephants, horses, and mounts, have become fruitful for me through your arrival. (56)
The sight of a saintly person is meritorious; their touch destroys sin;
serving them bestows heaven; and the offering of one’s self to them grants divine liberation. (57)
Those houses and dwellings in which the dust from the feet of the virtuous does not fall are equal to cremation grounds.
"O divine sage, please show favor to my entire family, who are all my kinsmen, for whom you have come without any desire for gain. (59)
Nārada said: "O royal sage, listen to this which causes wonder:
O lord of the earth, I have come from the world of Brahmā to the world of Yama."
Honored with devotion according to dharma and seated upon an excellent throne,
the righteous ones of truthful character attend upon Dharmarāja.
In their assembly, others who pride themselves on their great merit laughed at your father, who stood behind them, shorn of his luster.
"In the assembly of Śrāddhadeva, your father spoke a message to me for the destruction of my sorrow; listen to it, O lord of the earth. (6.3)
"O Brahmin, tell this message to the king known as Indrasena, the son of Candrāvatī: 'Your father, Candrasena, [sends this]. (64)"
The mass of merit of the King of Dharma remains in his city; for he gave much in charity, yet he did not observe even a single vow. (65)
By that merit, Dharmarāja remained established in his city;
yet by the power of Vṛtra’s vow, he became lusterless and was forced to stay far behind.
He indeed sits in the assembly hall perpetually overwhelmed by extreme sorrow;
therefore, my son, you should perform a vow dedicated to me on the Ekādaśī day.
"O my son, he shall grant me liberation through the gift of the merit of Indirā.
Having been told this, O King, I have come into your presence. (68)
O King, perform the Indirā-vrata for the sake of your father's liberation;
by that merit, your father will certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha. (69)
Having heard his father's message, he questioned Nārada regarding the vow:
"By what procedure is it to be performed, and on which lunar fortnight and on which lunar day? (1.258.70)
Nārada said to the king: "On the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, having risen in the morning and thereafter remembered Kṛṣṇa," (71)
Having bathed and worshipped the Lord, one should perform the midday bath;
having offered food to Hari, one should observe the practice of eating only once a day.
Having bathed in the evening and meditated upon Hari, he should sleep on the ground at night;
and on the morning of the eleventh day, this observer of the vow should indeed abandon sleep.
Having remembered and meditated upon Hari, one should perform purification and other rites while chanting His name;
one should repeatedly rinse the mouth twelve times with water.

One should perform ablutions with the waters of sacred fords and carry out the worship of the deity; having bowed to the form of Hari, one should proceed with the sipping of water (ācamana) and other rites. (75)
The observer of the vow should worship Kṛṣṇa Upendra with the sixteen types of offerings, and he should take the vow of fasting in his presence. (76)
"Having remained today without food and devoid of all enjoyments, O lotus-eyed one, I shall eat tomorrow; O Lord, fulfill my vow. (77)
Having thus established the rule within the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
one should place Kṛṣṇa in the jar and perform the great worship.
Having completed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offer food;
likewise, at midday, having bathed oneself, one should feed Śrī Hari.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the ritual bath, the rite of awakening, and offer water for drinking;
one should fan the Lord, massage him, and bring him joy with offerings of desired gifts.
One should perform the śrāddha rite according to the prescribed rules before a śālagrāma stone;
filled with faith, one should perform the śrāddha for the gratification of the ancestors.
A śrāddha performed with wheat flour is considered middling;
likewise, one performed with barley, rice, sesame, mung beans, wheat, and chickpeas is also middling.
The Śrāddha performed by those observers of vows shall be most excellent;
however, having performed the Śrāddha, the observer of vows must not eat what has been consumed by the ancestors.
For the sake of obtaining the merit of observing the vow, one should indeed smell the offered ancestral food;
having smelled it, the wise man should give it to a cow.
At night, one should perform a great worship as well as a vigil accompanied by festivities;
then, on the morning of the twelfth day, having bathed and worshipped Mādhava, [one should proceed].
Then the observer of the vow, having offered the food offering, fruits, and betel-leaf,
performs the waving of lights (ārātrika) and so forth, as well as the request for forgiveness.
One should give abundant gifts and feed the Brahmins and others;
one should also feed the virtuous men and women, as well as kinsmen, daughters' sons, and sons. (87)
Having fed the poor and the blind, one should eat oneself while maintaining silence;
O King, perform this vow with diligence according to this rule. (88)
"O King, your ancestors shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus to the monarch, O Lakṣmī, Nārada vanished from sight. 89.
In accordance with the prescribed rule, Indrasena performed that vow,
accompanied by his inner apartments and attended by his sons and servants.
When the vow was performed and the gift of cows given, a rain of flowers fell from the sky;
and when the dedication of merit was made, Indrasena’s father indeed [attained his goal]. ||9 1||
Likewise, Candrasena and his other ancestors, established there,
mounted upon Garuḍa and seated in celestial chariots, went indeed to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Indrasena also, having observed that vow protected by Viṣṇu and having enjoyed a kingdom free from all thorns, gave it to his eldest son.
After Mahīsena, he himself went to the third heaven;
having completed his merit there, he indeed went to Vaikuṇṭha. (94)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the greatness of this vow has been recounted by me to you;
by reading or even by hearing it, the merit of the vow shall also be attained. (9.5)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Āśvina-Kṛṣṇa-Indira-Ekādaśī Vow, and the Liberation from the World of Yama of King Indrasena’s Ancestors, Beginning with Candrasena, by the Power of the Merit of that Vow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
You alone are the Lord, the Blessed One himself, composed of all merit;
as an ocean of compassion, you bestow the fruits of actions according to their nature.
Whatever men perform and carry out while forgetting you,
they obtain the fruit of that here and in the hereafter, yet they remain beset by fear.
Whatever they perform or whatever they practice while remembering you,
its fruit— attained through you— is free from the gunas and consists of eternal bliss and liberation.
O Blessed One, beloved one, you bestow such fruit upon that person who has taken refuge in you, because you consist of all actions.
O Omniscient One, O Supreme Lord, having shown compassion, tell me:
what is the name of the Ekādaśī that occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina?
"O Hari, tell me all of this: which deity is to be worshipped there, what is the ritual procedure, what is the fruit thereof, and what gift should be given there?"
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Īṣa is known by the name Pāśāṅkuśā;
it removes all sins, bestows merit, and likewise grants liberation.
Padmanābha, together with Padmavatī, is to be worshipped here with devotion;
for the worship, śamī leaves are used, and the arghya is considered to be the fruit that grants all desires.
Rice cooked with milk (śālipāka) should be offered as a food offering, and rice balls made of grain should be given as a gift;
for the attainment of all desired fruits, everything should be offered to Janārdana.
Having performed most intense austerity for a long time with his senses restrained,
whatever fruit a sage attains, that he obtains by bowing to Padmanābha.
Even after committing many sins, a deluded man who bows to Hari, the lotus-navelled one, while engaged in a vow, indeed does not go to hell.
All the holy fords, sacred sites, and sanctuaries on earth were established by him through the worship of Padmanābha.
For those people who have taken refuge in Janārdana, the god of gods, whose navel is a lotus,
there is never any torment from the world of Yama.
By observing even a single Ekādaśī, even by chance, a human being—
even if established in terrible sin— does not undergo the torments of Yama.
Nothing so purifying exists within the three worlds as this Ekādaśī of Padmanābha, which destroys all sins.
Indeed, sins dwell openly and fearlessly only so long as a living being does not observe the vow on the day of Padmanābha.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī day.
In this world, there is nothing equal to Ekādaśī for washing away sins;
it bestows heaven and liberation, and here it grants wealth, friends, and other blessings. (18)
It bestows physical health and grants wives, sons, daughters, and noble lineage;
he by whom it is performed even under a pretext does not go to the abode of Yama.
Neither the Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, O Lakṣmī, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara,
nor even the sacred field of the Kauravas is superior or as meritorious as the day of Hari.
One should keep a vigil at night and perform the great worship of Hari;
indeed, on the day of Hari, one should observe a fast without even water.
By that indeed is Lakṣmī obtained, as well as my eternal abode;
ten on the mother's side and ten situated on the father's side.
Ten [deities] belonging to the side of the wives lift him firmly from his vow;
they have four arms, divine forms, and their seats are established upon the shoulders of Garuḍas. || 23 ||
Wearing garlands and yellow garments, those whose prowess is equal to that of Viṣṇu,
and women who have become like Lakṣmī herself, go to the abode of Hari.
Whether in childhood, youth, or old age, or even when in a state of dependence, a living being who observes the Ekādaśī fast does not fall into an evil rebirth, even if they are a sinner.
Having fasted while holding a noose and a goad, one indeed goes to the world of Hari after giving gold, sesame seeds, cows, water, food, and likewise clothing. (26)
One who possesses shoes, an umbrella, or other such items does not see the world of Yama;
however, the life of one devoid of merit and vows is considered fruitless. (27)
He whose days come and go devoid of merit does not truly live, even though he breathes like a blacksmith’s bellows.
Performing bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation,
and likewise sacrificial sessions according to one's ability, one should indeed pass the day fruitfully.
In this world, such men who perform meritorious deeds are seen to be long-lived, wealthy, of noble birth, and free from disease. (1.259.30)
Therefore, one should undertake the vow consisting of the noose, goad, and so forth;
on the tenth day, one should eat but once and likewise remain a celibate student (brahmacārī).
He should sleep on the ground at night; having bathed in the morning, he should perform his regular daily worship and seek the fulfillment of his vow through sixteen circumambulations.
One should have a Sarvatobhadra mandala prepared with seven kinds of grain;
in its center, a water-filled jar provided with five jewels.
Having filled it with wealth, one should place it along with cloth and fruit;
upon the jar, one should set a beautiful golden vessel containing sesame seeds.
One should install and likewise worship the auspicious image of Śrī Padmanābha accompanied by Padmāvatī, and provided with the noose and goad.

Having performed the invocation and other rites, he should then install Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances, as well as waters from sacred fords (tīrtha), and clothe Him in garments.
One should offer the fragrance of sandalwood and the like, as well as collyrium and other such items; one should also present necklaces and ornaments made of flowers, gems, gold, and so forth.
One should offer various kinds of food and present sweet water; having given mouth-freshener and fruit, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and bow down repeatedly. || 38 ||

Having offered praise, performed circumambulations, and prostrated like a staff, one should request forgiveness; then, provided with incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should secure the swing in the sky.
One should install Hari there and feed Him well even at midday;
having offered betel, water for drinking, and other refreshments, one should perform the same rites in the evening as well.

Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen types of offerings, one should perform the entire ritual, including the waving of lights (ārātrika) and so forth, according to the proper injunctions, and then offer all food and drink.
Established among the devotees of the Bhāgavata, one should keep a vigil at night, performing dancing, singing, chanting, glorification, and likewise remembrance. ||2||
Having meditated upon Hari at dawn, bathed, and fully worshipped Keśava, one should perform prostrations at his feet, massage his limbs, and attend to his service and so forth. (43)
One should feed the Blessed One and offer him betel-leaf and water;
thereafter, one should feed and honor the virtuous men and women who are dependent upon oneself.
Having bowed to the elders, remembered Lord Hari, and separately performed the five sacrifices, one should then indeed break the fast and give gifts with devotion. ||45||
Having thus completed the vow, one should indeed worship Hari on the twelfth day;
for this practitioner of the vow, the destruction of the bonds of worldly existence becomes certain. (46)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this divine narrative which liberates one from the noose of Yama.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a sage named Vāmadeva.
He had many disciples who were fully accomplished knowers of Brahman;
there were also other sages who were renunciants, as well as householders who were the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman. (48)
When the sun had arrived, they performed their ablutions, twilight prayers, recitations, fire-oblations, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors, remaining devoted to their respective duties.
Among them, one was a sage devoted to the ritual section of the Vedas, known by the name Vedaśiras; he was indeed thoroughly proficient in Vedic rites.
Observing the Cāturmāsya vow, he spent the time subsisting on a diet of tubers;
however, a disease born from the transformation of those tubers arose within his belly. (51)
The digestive fire becomes extremely weak, and the intestines become hot and bloated;
whatever he may eat remains undigested. (52)
Thus, as his body grew emaciated, his incapacity increased;
he became indolent regarding bathing, the recitation of the Gāyatrī, and worship.
Thus, having permanently abandoned bathing and worship due to the cessation of all worldly states, the sage indeed conducts his bodily sustenance like a Śūdra. (54)
And by the abandonment of his duties, he incurred sin according to the Veda;
through that sin, his merit indeed came to an end. (55)
When the end of his life had arrived and the messengers of Yama had come,
Vedaśiras, being thoroughly distressed, then spoke to them.
"How may I avoid seeing the messengers of Yama, and by what action?
The messengers of Yama replied to him, 'Only by abandoning the experience of [the fruits of] one's own actions. (57)
"You may conduct yourself as you please; whatever fruit results from that shall be my dwelling place.
For a Brahmin who has set out upon a wrong path, the abode of Yama is his destination. (58)
"Since this [act] is for the sake of atonement, eat it despite its sinfulness.
Having spoken thus to Vedaśiras, they took him to the abode of Yama.
King Yama, having indeed seen his deed according to its true nature, then said to Citragupta: "His transgression is truly great."
The great sin consisting of the forgetting of the Veda that has been studied.
It is declared to be equal to the murder of a Brahmin; therefore, let him be bound with nooses and led away.
Let him be cast into the Kālasūtra hell for those who slay Brahmins;
having led him to the Asipatravana forest, let them strike him down as well.
Having spoken thus, Yamarāja, the author of ethical treatises, ceased;
then the highly intelligent Vedaśiras addressed Yamarāja.
"In times of distress, the Veda was indeed forgotten by me;
furthermore, out of incapacity, ritual action was abandoned. How then could there be hell for me? (64)
Indeed, the duties of a time of calamity do not fall under the category of unrighteousness;
therefore, there is no sin in me, nor is there anything for me to fill Yama’s realm.
Then the King of Dharma said: "As long as passion still exists, dharma is produced by adversity; in the absence of affliction, we do not consider it such. (66)
The abandonment of many for the sake of a minor misfortune is considered a great unrighteousness;
there is no such disease for you that the Veda has not been recited.
And due to your laziness, you have indeed forgotten the entirety of the sacred revelation;
from that, an offense has arisen, and all ritual action has been utterly abandoned.
A wise Brāhmaṇa who understands should act according to his capacity;
how could it be possible for him to renounce everything all at once? ||69||
Therefore, one who, through the fault of laziness, completely abandons the duties of action and falls away from the path of Brahmanical practice, deserves punishment in every respect.
Then Vedaśiras meditated there in his mind upon his guru, Vāmadeva, who was an incarnation of the Great Brahmā; and he, too, arrived.
Then Vāmadevaka, having been honored by the King of Dharma and saluted even by his disciple, sat down upon the seat that was offered to him.
Vāmadeva heard all that from the mouth of Yama:
that every action which consists of transgression is true [in its consequence], and it does not perish without punishment. (73)
The compassionate Vāmadeva indeed reflected upon that matter so that the punishment might not be endured and the ritual act might not be rendered fruitless. (74)
Having reflected thus, he spoke so that he might cross over;
looking all around there, he then addressed his disciple Yama.
"Listen, both disciples Yama and Vedaśiras:
there is a great vow that destroys the Kālasūtra and Asipatravana hells. (76)
The vow of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is considered powerful;
it is the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and those equal to them. (77)
By performing this with faith, the expiation becomes accomplished;
thus it is through merely hearing the names of the Ekādaśīs at that time. (78)
Furthermore, through his vow and resolve, his life was well-rejoined;
and by the power of his preceptor, he regained his life once more. (79)
Having accepted the hospitality of their guest, the two went to where the corpse was;
the Guru then caused his disciple to enter and spoke the vow.
Having bathed and performed the worship of the Guru, he remained in good health;
then, the eleventh-day vow (ekādaśī-vrata) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha arrived, and it was observed.
In an instant, even the destruction of the sin arising from the forgetting of the Vedas occurred;
at that time, the sins such as the abandonment of ritual duties were reduced to ashes.
Then Vedaśiras obtained long and auspicious life through the power of his guru and indeed by the performance of the Ekādaśī vow.
And by means of this vow of service, his destruction of Yama’s noose occurred;
therefore, this Ekādaśī is considered a goad for nooses.
Just as a goad is used for an elephant, so too should the vow of the noose and the goad (pāśāṅkuśavrata) be performed by people for the auspicious destruction of the nooses of Yama. 85.
It bestows heaven and liberation, brings about all prosperity, grants happiness, confers health, and is the supreme pacifier of the three kinds of suffering. (86)

It is the destroyer of the bonds of latent impressions (vāsanā), the annihilator of sin, and likewise the destroyer of the fetters of the body and its worldly concerns, as well as of calamities. ||87||
It is the destroyer of the fetters of "I" and "mine," the pacifier of hatred and passion, the bestower of good fortune, and the giver of the status of husband and wife. ||88||
It pacifies the forest fire of the afflictions, bestows the eternal abode, grants the yoga of Hari, and likewise bestows Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka. ||89||
O Lakṣmī, the Pāśāṅkuśā vow must be performed with great effort;
for by reciting or even hearing it, one indeed receives the merit of the vow.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Āśvina-Śukla-Pāśāṅkuśa-Ekādaśī Vow," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. It relates how Vedaśiras, a disciple of the sage Vāmadeva, due to indigestion and the resulting laziness, abandoned his religious duties and other virtuous acts; consequently, by the power of his sin, he reached the realm of Yama. There, through the presence of his guru Vāmadeva whom he had remembered and by means of the vow, he was liberated from the noose of Yama.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Salutations to Mahākāla, Mahārudra, Yama, and the servants of Yama—to those whose very selves restrain the entire universe. (1)
Salutations to You, the All-pervasive Lord, from whom the noose, the thunderbolt, the mace, the spear, the staff, the discus, and the trident proceed as Your very self. || 2 ||
Salutations to that one whose essence is virtue, impelled by whom fortitude, compassion, assistance, statesmanship, forbearance, and beneficence prevail.

Salutations to the one who is beyond qualities (nirguṇa), yet by whom everything consisting of the qualities (guṇin) has been created—that which is characterized by "mine-ness," "otherness," self-existence, nourishment, and liberation. 4.
O Blessed One, your compassion for me is always like that between the near and far shores;
tell me, what is the name of the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika?
"Which deity is to be worshipped here? Tell me the procedure for the gift and the merit.
Also, tell me what kind of rite should be performed during the vow."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, this month of Kārtika is indeed the bestower of liberation;
it is the concluding month of the Cāturmāsya, intended for vows, charity, worship, and other rites.
This month is the most excellent for those observing vows;
therein, every auspicious and meritorious deed whatsoever must certainly be performed.
Even there, the eleventh day is the most excellent; in the dark fortnight, it is named Ramā. On that day, Hari, the Supreme Lord, should be worshipped together with Hiraṇyayā.
Among flowers, the *baṭu* and *kunda* are preferred; for the water offering (*arghya*), the plantain is considered best.
For the food offering (*naivedya*), there should be plantains smeared with sugar and ghee, as well as fried cakes (*polikā*).
Whatever one desires for oneself, such as gifts of jars filled with ghee and the like—all that should indeed be given, along with gold, for the increase of prosperity. (11)
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should eat but one meal, sleep upon the ground, remain celibate, and be free from the faults of anger, delusion, and the like. || 12 ||
Having risen early in the morning, one should meditate upon Govinda; having bathed, one should worship Him.
Having performed the daily worship, one should cause the seven kinds of grain to be prepared.
One should prepare a Sarvatobhadra mandala, beautifully adorned with various colored powders; and in its center, one should place a vessel made of gold or copper.
With the five jewels, excellent leaves, and the like, with unbroken grains, water, and fine cloth, combined with sugar, bilva fruit, betel nut, and sandalwood. || 15 ||
The observer of the vow should place a silver vessel containing sesame seeds at the front of that [image],
and there he should install a golden image of Hari, who possesses a beautiful form.
One should serve [the deity] with invocations and so forth, with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and with massages using oil;
then one should offer garments, ornaments, cosmetics, and the like.
One should offer a garland of flowers, as well as bracelets, crowns, and other ornaments;
and incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel leaf, and so forth. (18)
One should offer the *ārārtrika* and other rites, perform hymns of praise and requests for forgiveness,
and then bestow various kinds of gifts upon the venerable Guru.
One should worship at midday as well, feed [the deity], and offer water;
having bathed in the evening and worshipped, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having performed the praise and other rites, one should feed and serve [the deity];
then, adorned by the circle of devotees, one should keep a vigil at night.
One should engage in the delight of singing, dancing, storytelling, conversation, and narration;
on the twelfth day, the observer of the vow, having bathed in the morning and worshipped Keśava, [should proceed].
Whether it be a king, a subject observing a vow, a renunciant, a householder, a woman, or even a man, one should give excellent gifts. (23)
According to one's capacity, one should feed virtuous Brahmins and children;
thereafter, one should indeed break the fast and ensure the successful completion of the vow.
By performing this vow in this manner, a woman will certainly become equal to Lakṣmī;
and a man who performs this vow becomes a god and is truly liberated.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious story of Candrabhāga and Śaśisena.
In ancient times, there was a king renowned as Mucukunda. (26)
That city, known as Indrakūṭana, was situated to the south;
residing there in his capital, he ruled the earth as a sole sovereign.
He formed a very great friendship with Devendra,
as well as with Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and likewise with Agni.
In this manner, he formed a friendship with that very Bibhīṣaṇa;
thus, by means of aerial chariots, he travels everywhere throughout the three worlds.
Devoted to Viṣṇu and true to his word, he rules a kingdom free from thorns;
indeed, all the people in his realm are Vaiṣṇavas.
When the day of Hari arrived, all his subjects, who were devotees of Viṣṇu, did not eat food; they all observed a complete fast.
The drum is beaten for him when the tenth day arrives;
"one must not eat, one must not eat" [is the cry] when the day of Hari has arrived. (32)
On the day of Hari, grass, food, and likewise water must not be consumed by elephants, horses, young calves, or even other animals.
In this manner, he caused all those established in the kingdom to observe the supreme vow;
and the excellent river Candrabhāgā became his daughter.
At that same time, on the bank of the Kāverī,
there was a meritorious king named Candrasena, the sovereign of the city called Kanaka.
Candrabhāgā was indeed given by King Mucukunda to his son named Śaśisena, who was endowed with excellent qualities.
That illustrious Vaiṣṇavī woman was indeed performing her vow;
once, accompanied by her husband, she went to her father’s house.
Her husband became overcome by fever and grew exceedingly weak;
meanwhile, the day of the Ekādaśī vow, which bestows great merit, arrived.
When the vow had commenced, Candrabhāgā thought to herself:
"What will become of my husband, who is indeed utterly incapable regarding this vow? (39)
Sick, emaciated, and utterly weak, he could not endure his hunger;
yet on this very day of the vow, my father was one of stern command. (1.260.4)
Whether capable or incapable, let one observe the vow of the teaching;
if it is transgressed by anyone, that person is undoubtedly subject to punishment. (41)
"Let that which is to be happen; what can be done here by one who is powerless?
Having reflected thus, she remained there as the day of her vow arrived. (42)
The drum is beaten for him when the tenth day arrives:
"One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived. (43)
"One who transgresses my command shall indeed be deserving of punishment.
Having heard the sound of the drum, Śaśisena spoke to his beloved: ||44||
"What must I do, my beloved? I shall die without you. Then Candrabhāgā spoke slowly to her lover, who was distressed with anxiety: ||| 45 ||
"In my father's domain, no one—neither humans nor the beasts, birds, and reptiles that depend upon them—shall eat today. (46)
"Grass, food, water, or flour must not be consumed on the day of Hari.
If you eat them, my dear, you shall then suffer punishment. (47)
"You will incur reproach; therefore, make your mind firm.
Having heard her words, the Moon-crested Lord said, 'I shall observe a fast.'"
"Whatever has been ordained by destiny for me shall happen exactly so.
Having formed this firm resolve, he undertook a vow without water.
Overwhelmed by hunger and thirst, he became greatly distressed;
overcome by fainting at night, he took refuge in the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*).
At the time of sunrise, Śaśisena met his death;
the king had him cremated with wood suitable for royalty.
Candrabhāgā, because she possessed an understanding of the greatness of devotion to Hari,
did not burn herself along with her husband, even though she was a devoted wife.
Having performed the funeral rites for her husband,
Śaśisena, possessing a divine body due to the great merit of the Rāmavrata, remained in the house of Janaka.
He attained in heaven a sovereign empire, independent and like that of Indra,
which was immensely prosperous, invincible, and endowed with innumerable virtues.
With palaces made of golden pillars, adorned with gems and lapis lazuli, consisting of various forms of crystal, and diverse, divine, and radiant; ||55||
Mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot and seated upon a lion-throne, he reached that heaven adorned with innumerable palatial mansions.
Adorned with a crown and earrings, and decorated with necklaces and armlets,
he was being praised by hosts of Gandharvas, gods, and Apsarases.
Surrounded by hand-fans, umbrellas, chowries, and noble lineages,
Śaśisena shines and rejoices greatly in his own heaven.
