Then once, a messenger of Mahendra arrived on earth;
he had been dispatched by Indra to Mucukunda’s house for a specific purpose.
When a great battle between Indra and the Daityas was imminent,
Mucukunda, aided by Indra, then conquered the Daityas.
"He shall indeed be victorious by virtue of a boon granted by Brahmā.
For this reason, the messenger who had arrived was fed and likewise honored.
The king then inquired about the well-being of the gods in heaven;
having been told everything for which the messenger had come, he spoke accordingly.
He said to the king: "I beheld Śaśisena in heaven;
he is an ocean of power, prosperity, and majesty, whose capability is no less than that of Indra."
"O Indra among kings, your son-in-law, a youth endowed with beauty and grace, shines like a god; he has seen me coming to the earth. (64)
He spoke concerning the earth, his father-in-law King Candrasena,
his beloved wife Candrabhāgā, and likewise the city.
"From my presence, you must inquire after his welfare and freedom from illness;
and you must convey my blessings, saying that everything pertaining to heaven is as it is for me."
"And my wife must be told: 'Your husband awaits you.
For thus, O King, there is great happiness for your son-in-law in heaven. (67)
All is well with her, and there exists a marvelous and wondrous thing:
a city, diverse and beautiful, never seen by anyone anywhere.
Divine, it shines like the sky; it is the splendor of those with a good rebirth, illuminated by the light of the heavens;
it is rich in the enjoyment of the delights of nectar, and is served by handmaidens and celestial nymphs.
I am unable to describe this city, which is full of great wonders;
for it has been obtained by your son-in-law through the merit of his vows and is eternal.
Having fasted on that day known as Ramā Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Kārttika,
he died here and attained such a heaven.
Though he had attained the highest heaven, the performer of vows who was devoid of faith desired to go from that celestial realm to a world even higher than it,
by virtue of the Rāmā-vrata performed by his own wife.

Hearing this, Candrabhāgā, the daughter of Mucukunda, who was standing there, was filled with joy and spoke repeatedly: "O messenger, lead me to that place where my beloved husband dwells, for I am overflowing with the impulse to behold my lord. (73-74)
"By the merit of the vow of Ramā, I shall lead him even to the abode of Brahmā;
O messenger, act in such a way that a union between us two may come to pass.
Having heard this and received the command of Mucukunda, the messenger then [ascended] into the sky.
Having transformed Candrabhāgā into one of divine body, he took her and departed. She too, having attained a divine form and youth worthy of heaven,
as well as celestial flight, came into the presence of her husband.
Beholding her husband’s heaven and his great sovereignty again and again, she rejoiced;
Indrasena also rejoiced greatly upon seeing his beloved returned to him.
Having summoned her, he seated her on his own left side;
the messenger, having received excellent hospitality, departed for Indra. 79.
Then, out of joy, Candrabhāgā spoke these pleasing words to her beloved:
"Listen, my dear, to this beneficial speech regarding the merit that resides within me. (1.260.8)
When I was born and became more than eight years old in my father's house, from that time forward I have observed the vow of Ekādaśī. ||81||
By the power of that merit, we two shall go to the imperishable abode,
the eternal station of Śrī Hari, which is enriched with all desired objects.
Having enjoyed heaven for a long time through the power of their merit, they both went to the imperishable abode and became liberated.
This Ekādaśī named Ramā is like a wish-fulfilling gem, or like a cow of plenty, or similar to the celestial Kalpa tree for me. (84)
Regarding the vows of Ekādaśī in both fortnights, just as it is with the dark fortnight, so it is with the bright; one should not make any distinction between them. (89)
Just as a white cow and a black cow both yield milk that is identical for both purposes,
so too the two Ekādaśīs are remembered as yielding equal results.
The Ekādaśī, when observed by men, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
even from merely hearing of it or reciting its account, one obtains a fruit equal to that of the vow itself. (87)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kārttika-Kṛṣṇa-Ramā-Ekādaśī Vow, and the Attainment of Heaven by Indrasena, the Husband of Candrabhāgā—the Daughter of Mucukunda—due to his Death on the Day of the Vow, Followed by the Wife’s Journey to Heaven and Subsequently the Liberation of Both," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: Indeed, Kārttika, possessing great majesty, enters for four months— the rainy season enriched with merit— and performs meritorious deeds.
Indeed, the merit of the Cāturmāsya vow is not truly completed until its dedication;
by performing that dedication in Kārtika, one obtains the fruit of the Cāturmāsya.
He is the destroyer of sins and the bestower of heaven, the world of truth, and the realm of the Vīrajas; indeed, he is the giver of Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the imperishable world (Akṣara-loka).
Whatever merit is performed in Kārtika becomes multiplied a thousandfold;
therefore, for one's own sake, every vow (vrata) should be observed in Kārtika.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, what is the name of the Ekādaśī that is recognized?
Who is the presiding deity, what is the procedure, what is the gift, what is the vow, and what is the fruit? (5)
What indeed is reckoned as the special significance of the final month of the Cāturmāsya, by which those observing vows attain liberation? Tell me this as well.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe that which occurs on the bright fortnight of Kārtika;
it is called by the name Prabodhinī, the most excellent of all Ekādaśīs.
In which the virtuous Lord of Lakṣmī, reclining upon Śeṣa, remains awake;
and by the power of whose vow the darkness born of ignorance is dissolved.

Furthermore, through this, supreme self-awakening arises; therefore, it is called Prabodhinī (the Awakener), the giver of liberation, the giver of happiness, the giver of heaven, and the giver of knowledge.
Having observed the fast there according to the prescribed rites, the Lord Dāmodara should be worshipped;
together with Rādhā and Prabodhinī, He should be honored with many offerings.
Janārdana is to be worshipped with lotuses and the finest flowers;
for the food offering (naivedya), mung-bean cakes (laḍḍukas) are used, and for the water of honor (arghya), lotus fruits.
O beloved Lakṣmī, a bed with its furnishings and other desirable gifts should be given;
this Prabodhinī vow destroys sin and increases merit.
Holy fords, forests, and sacred shrines all roar with pride only so long as the Bodhinī vow of the month of Kārtika does not arrive.
Thousands of horse sacrifices, hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices,
and thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices are not equal to the Prabodhinī [Ekādaśī].
Indeed, Haribodhinī grants even that which is unobtainable, inaccessible, impossible to accomplish, or simply impossible, when she is worshipped by one who has fasted and made a vow.
When observed as a fast here, the Bodhinī bestows knowledge, wealth, royal authority, the favor of the subjects, stainless fame, spiritual perfection, and prosperity. (16)
Indeed, this [fast] burns away all great sins, heinous crimes, and acts that cause social confusion,
whether they be dry or moist.
The vigil performed at night during the Bodhinī vow burns away the mountains of sins and misfortunes accumulated over many lifetimes.
Whether observed knowingly or unknowingly, through illness or other causes, or even if observed out of necessity, this fast bestows both heaven and liberation.
Whatever is performed here according to the rules, with faith and devotion—
even if it is done in a very small measure— its fruit shall become a hundred-thousandfold.
Whatever is performed without knowledge, without following the prescribed rules, or even without mental focus—
yet accompanied by malice and ill-will— is as fruitless as Mount Meru itself.
Indeed, whether it be very small or great, one must certainly not practice censure or malice; rather, it is considered better not to perform even a duty if it involves censure or malice. (22)
Those men who, remembering their ancestors, perform meritorious deeds here, their ancestors go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, fully satisfied. (23)
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed by keeping this vow and by staying awake [in vigil], even those which are difficult to overcome even through sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha. (24)
And whatever may be unattainable even through other excellent means, that is obtained with ease simply by keeping vigil during the Prabodhinī [Ekādaśī]. (25)
Indeed, from the vow and the night vigil, a fruit far greater than that of bathing at sacred fords or offering gold to the earth is obtained. (26)
He alone is born a man of merit who has purified a hundred lineages— by him who, out of devotion, has observed the Prabodhinī festival in the month of Kārttika.
The merit of a vow is declared to be certain, whereas all else is uncertain;
having reflected thus, one should properly perform the vow on the day of Hari.
In the house of one who observes the Prabodhinī vow, all sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell in every way; that house is purified and is itself a king among holy places.
The Haribodhinī indeed bestows sons, grandsons, wealth, and prosperity;
for the sake of sons and other blessings, no other vow need be performed.
For one who performs the Prabodhinī vow, enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of the hand;
knowledge, yoga, austerity, fire-offerings, and self-restraint are all established within this vow.
When observed as a fast, it nourishes righteousness, is dear to Viṣṇu, bestows liberation upon men,
and indeed destroys the sufferings of dwelling in the womb and other such miseries.
Through action, mind, and speech, Kṛṣṇa washes away both dry and moist sins during the vigil observed on the Prabodhinī vow.
Bathing in the Bodhinī for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, as well as fire-offerings, recitation, dedication,
and the libation for the ancestors— all this becomes inexhaustible.
This is declared to be the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), and no other vow is like it;
it destroys the immeasurable flood of great sins accumulated over a hundred lifetimes. (35)
Having gratified Janārdana here by means of the Prabodhinī vow, he,
honored by those residing in heaven, proceeds to the abode of Hari.
By those who earnestly desire the abundance of physical beauty, prosperity, and well-being;
and by those who wish for a wife, sons, a home, fields, wealth, and health. (37)
This Bodhinī [image] should be diligently worshipped by men who desire wealth, vehicles, conveyances, and other riches, as well as cows and prosperity. (38)
By the performance of this vow, the sin committed during a hundred lifetimes—whether incurred through the stages of childhood, youth, or old age—is utterly destroyed. (39)
Whatever fruit is obtained on the land of the Kauravas during an eclipse of the sun or moon,
that is multiplied a thousandfold by keeping a vigil on the Prabodhinī day.
For him whose month of Kārttika passes away in vain,
it should be understood that his human birth is indeed fruitless both in this world and the next.
Even the fruit of meritorious deeds and other actions accumulated over a lifetime goes to waste during a barren Kārtika month; it does not lead to happiness.
One should avoid food provided by others; for that, the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance shall be obtained.
But in the month of Kārttika, for one who narrates the story, the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices shall be obtained.
Kṛṣṇa is not so pleased by sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by recitations and the like,
as he is pleased by discourses on the scriptures during the month of Kārtika.
Furthermore, both those who hear and those who speak of my narrative during the month of Kārttika obtain, for every verse, the merit of gifting a thousand cows. (45)
In the month of Kārttika, one who, with the intent for spiritual welfare and with great devotion before Keśava,
causes the sacred stories to be recited, O Lakṣmī, shall deliver a hundred lineages.
Whoever listens to this story here every day with regularity during the month of Kārttika attains,
through union with Hari, the fruit born of giving a thousand cows.
And whoever, observing the Prabodhinī vow, listens to the life-story of Viṣṇu,
that observer of the vow obtains the fruit of gifting the earth consisting of the seven continents.
Those who, having heard the narrative with the understanding that it is Viṣṇu himself,
worship the narrator of the story according to their capacity with wealth, grain, and garments, are considered to possess an imperishable world.

One should pass the month of Kārtika by means of chanting the names [of the Lord], worship, listening to His deeds, and other such acts; for such a person, there is indeed no returning again to this world.

He who, when the vow has arrived, performs storytelling, singing, instrumental music, dancing, and festivities before the Lord Hari—whether doing so daily or on that specific occasion—is indeed a partaker of liberation. ||51||
Whoever reads or listens to the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā shall obtain, for every single syllable, the fruit arising from the gift of a tawny cow.
One should not practice stinginess with wealth when the day of Hari has arrived, for by the giving of riches, immeasurable merit is produced. (53)
On the tenth day, observing a single meal, the practitioner should sleep on the ground at night;
remaining self-controlled and celibate, he should meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa within his heart.
On the morning of the eleventh day, having reflected that the Lord is awake,
and having meditated upon Him and bathed, one should awaken Hari by sounding a bell.
Having performed the daily worship of Hari, beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal, the observer of the vow should proceed to the excellent pavilion.
One should cause it to be adorned with banana-stalks, leaves, arches, and banners, and one should indeed hang a beautiful, variegated canopy.
In the four corners, one should arrange seven jars each, stacked one above the other;
there, one should also cause decorative bands of color to be made all around.
In the center, however, one should have a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala made with seven kinds of grain,
and a water-pot fashioned from either copper or gold.
One should place a most excellent, new vessel in the center of the mandala;
and there, around the mandala, twenty-four auspicious jars.
One should place therein vessels made of gold or copper, filled with water and fresh,
and adorned with the five jewels, the five leaves, betel nuts, and rice.
Adorned with garments, threads, coconuts, fruits, and sweetmeats, they were honored with flowers, sandalwood, saffron, unbroken grains, and water. ||62||
Fresh vessels of sesame seeds,
rich with sugar, cardamom, and cloves, and accompanied by offerings of fruit, should be placed at their mouths.
Lord Hari himself, in the form of the Śrīmūrti, accompanied by Rādhā-Dāmodara and Prabhāvatī, should be installed in the central vessel. 64.
On one side, a couch should be placed, adorned with bedding and other articles;
likewise, a ball, a bolster, a secret belt, and a cloak.
A fan, a chowrie, an umbrella, sandals, a mirror, as well as a tooth-stick, a water-pot, a vessel, vegetable gardens, and flower gardens. ||66||
Furthermore, other desired fruits and foods should also be placed right there on that couch for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa. (67)
One should worship Śrī Gaṇeśa together with his family and offer the oblation.
And one should worship the bell, the flask, and the conch shell with ritual offerings. ||68||
Afterwards, the observer of the vow should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) and then invoke Hari;
he should then offer a seat, water for the feet (pādya), the guest-offering (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamana).
One should employ a tooth-stick and perform purification for cleanliness;
thereafter, one should perform gargling and consecration with water from a sacred bathing place.
Then one should cause the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) to be performed and offer it;
again, a bath with pure water and likewise a wiping with a cloth.
The offering of fine linen garments upon his limbs, worship with fragrant substances and excellent incense,
and the presentation of the Kaustubha gem, the sacred thread, a tunic, a silken cloth, and so forth.
One should present a divine lower garment, a bodice, and a water-pot; as well as a crown, an upper garment, earrings, a necklace, and so forth.
Bracelets, anklets, bangles, and rings set with gems;
waistbands, jhanjhira ornaments, as well as strings, natthīs, and garlands. ||74||
One should offer other necklaces made of gold and various ornaments,
as well as sandalwood paste, collyrium, powder, saffron, and water with saffron filaments.
One should offer musk, white powder, vermilion, lac,
and other excellent substances that bring good fortune to the Lord of Rādhikā.
One should offer *abīra*, *gulāla*, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers;
with many flowers and fruits, and with camphor, agallochum, and saffron.
And one should perform the worship of Hari at dawn on the day of Bodhinī during the month of Kārtika,
with various kinds of fruits, ritual substances, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
With various kinds of sweet foods, leafy vegetables, as well as sour gruel (āranālaka), with edibles, soft foods, things to be licked and sucked, savory juices, and sweet drinks. ||79||
The observer of the vow should satisfy the Lord with various fruits from the heart;
he should satisfy Janārdana according to the rules with water from a conch shell.
When the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa is worshipped with a single petal of a Ketakī flower, the Lord of Kamalā becomes well-pleased for a thousand years. (81)
One should worship Kṛṣṇa with Agasti flowers according to the prescribed rite;
by the mere sight of the worshipper, the fire of hell is extinguished.
Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, when worshipped with *munipuṣpa* flowers in the month of Kārtika, grants all desired objects—whether celestial or mundane, as well as those that are transcendent. (83)
He who, having set aside all other flowers, worships Keśava with the *munipuṣpa* flower with devotion in the month of Kārtika, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
One who offers Tulasi leaves, flowers, and likewise Śamī leaves to Viṣṇu in the month of Kārtika shall burn away the sins born of a hundred lifetimes.
Whether seen, touched, meditated upon, celebrated by name, praised, planted, watered, or constantly worshipped and bowed to—the *tulasī* [is supreme]. (86)
O beloved, those who perform the ninefold devotion to Tulasī day after day extend their merit for thousands of millions of yugas.
As long as the Tulasī planted by men grows upon the surface of the earth with its branches, twigs, seeds, flowers, and fresh leaves, [so long does it flourish]. 88.
For those born in their lineage, those who will be born, and those who have already passed away— for them all,
there shall be residence in the abode of Hari for a thousand kalpas.
Whatever fruit is found in all flowers and whatever fruit is found in all leaves,
that indeed is obtained by a single leaf of Tulasī during the month of Kārtika.
In the month of Kārttika, Viṣṇu should be worshipped daily with tulasī leaves,
as well as with lotuses, dhātrī leaves, and śamī leaves.
The merit gained by worshipping the gods with hundreds of sacrifices and giving gifts many times over is equaled by the worship of Keśava with Tulasī leaves during the month of Kārttika. 92.

The nightly lamp-offering, prostration, hymns of praise, circumambulations, as well as ritual fees, falling like a staff, and the offering of handfuls of flowers for the sake of asking forgiveness. (93)
After the practitioner has made the prayer for the fulfillment of the vow, he should thereafter perform the worship of the guru with food, clothing, and other offerings. (94)
For the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), many gifts such as cows and others should be given, along with gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 9.5.
At midday, one should worship the God and feed Him according to the prescribed rules;
and in the evening as well, one should perform the great worship and feed Hari.
One should offer water for drinking and other refreshments, then place [the deity] upon a swing;
one should rock it, please [the deity], and perform a massage of the feet. (97)
Observing the vow, one should keep a vigil with singing, instrumental music, and dancing;
with narrations of the Rāsa-sports, and by imitating the divine pastimes and other such acts. (98)
On the twelfth day at dawn, however, having bathed and worshipped Mādhava, one should feed and satisfy [the deity], and increase the merit for Hari with the ārātrika rite. (99)
Having offered praise, one should dismiss them all and feed many with great devotion;
one should feed well the virtuous men and women, the devotees of the Lord, the brahmins, and the children.
One should give various gifts and then perform the breaking of the fast;
having thus performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), one should present the water-pot and other items to the preceptor.
Having thus fulfilled the vow, one shall attain the Imperishable;
one obtains enjoyment after enjoyment and eternal, certain bliss. || 102 ||
Listen, O beloved, to how a certain outcaste, while performing kīrtana in the temple of Hari during the Prabhāvatī vow, was protected from a rākṣasa.
In the forest, in the Raivata field, on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
there was indeed an unobstructed abode of Viṣṇu created by Brahmā.
By the mere sight of whom forest-dwellers attain a happy rebirth—he was indeed some humble person living on the banks of the Bhadrāvatī. 105.
That twice-born man, a *caṇḍāla* by his actions, subsequently became a wood-gatherer;
for his house, wife, and other possessions had been swept away by the flood of a river.
He took delight in dwelling in the forest due to his work of gathering wood;
endowed with auspicious mental impressions, he was constantly devoted to his duties in the evening.
He goes to the abode of Viṣṇu and performs his glorification;
he even brings about a vision [of the Lord] and then returns again to his own home. (108)
In the month of Kārttika, eager to perform the vigil on the Prabodhinī day,
a Rākṣasa seized him on the road as he was traveling at night.
When the outcaste servant Karmacāṇḍāla became a Rākṣasa and was filled with wonder,
he asked the fearless one the reason for his laughter at the time of death.
The outcaste of karma said to him: "I am blessed that death has come;
today is the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), and I have the vow of Prabodhinī. (111)
"I shall go to the temple for chanting and worship;
I shall indeed proceed to the vigil, even if death has arrived. (112)
"Then I shall have a good rebirth; for one who practices devotion does not go to a lower state.
If you are hungry, then quickly eat me here."
"Or else, having performed a vigil or other rites as part of a vow, eat me tomorrow morning.
The Rākṣasa said: "Only that person who is released from the very jaws of death [shall do so]. (11.4)
"Death shall not come to you again, and I have no reliance upon you. The Cāṇḍāla said: "If it is so, then come with me. (115)
"Afterwards, I shall perform my chanting; devour me as you please!
Through chanting there shall be liberation, and through hearing as well, there is deliverance. (116)
The Rākṣasa said: "If it is so, I shall go with you; for previously, I indeed held the office of superintendent over the treasury of the gods. (117)
In the midst of the city of Yaśodātrī, much of the property of the gods was stolen;
by that sin, I was born as a Brāhmaṇa who was a Brahmarākṣasa.
If indeed liberation occurs here through chanting or hearing [the name], then my own liberation shall also occur; I have no attachment to my arm. (119)
Having reflected thus, the two of them engaged in the vow at Viṣṇusthala during the night;
indeed, they performed kīrtana accompanied by dancing and rhythmic clapping, as sung by a Caṇḍāla.
They both also kept a vigil through the night with pure devotion;
in the morning, they became purified, and the celestial vehicle arrived for them.
Having abandoned their bodies right there, they both went to heaven itself;
having enjoyed pleasures for countless years, they were served by hosts of celestial nymphs.
Subsequently, by the grace of Viṣṇu, they both attained liberation and went to Vaikuṇṭha;
thus, he brings about the salvation even of those who have fallen into evil destinies.
The Prabodhinī vow is the most excellent and should be observed by people in every way.
Listen to me as I describe other vows that are also to be performed on this occasion.
When any one of these has occurred, Kārttika is the destroyer of sins;
one should bathe at the Brahma-hour and diligently perform the Kṛcchra penance.
Beginning from the month of Āśvayuja until the end of Kārttika,
one should devotedly perform the auspicious vow known as Māsopavāsa or Cāndrāyaṇa.

During the waning of the lunar days in the dark fortnight, one should eat morsels the size of jujube fruits, omitting one morsel at a time; and during the bright fortnight, one should increase them accordingly.

In the bright fortnight, one should eat morsels the size of myrobalan fruits, increasing them by one each day according to the increase of the lunar days; and in the other [the dark fortnight], one should decrease them.
The first [type] is named *pipīlikā*, the second is named *yava*;
that which is diminished in the middle and then increased is declared to be the auspicious *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Rice-porridge, alms-food, barley-meal, grain-dust, barley-gruel, or even vegetables; milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, or even water. || 1.261.130 ||
These sacrificial offerings (havīṃṣi) are indeed praised as progressively superior during the vow;
one should not eat at all on the new moon day, but on the days of the lunar increase, sixteen [offerings] are prescribed.
But when there is a loss of a lunar day (tithi-kṣaya), exactly fourteen of those mouthfuls (grāsa) are to be taken;
in any case, [the total] of the morsels (piṇḍas) is two hundred and forty. 13.2.
One may consume that [food] for an entire month, and that would constitute the Indu-vrata;
indeed, if one eats eight morsels each day, that is the Cāndrāyaṇa of the ascetic (yati).
Eating four morsels in the morning and four in the evening constitutes the Śiśucāndrāyaṇa.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen with a concentrated mind as I describe other [observances]. 134.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kārttika Śukla Prabodhinī Vrata, the Liberation of the Outcaste-Karma Brāhmaṇa and the Rākṣasa through the Practice of the Kīrtana Vrata on Account of a Brāhmaṇa, and the Nature of the Cāndrāyaṇa," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, what other vows indeed bestow merit during the month of Kārttika? Tell me all of those that ought to be performed by me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
A sky-lamp should be offered by one observing a vow in a temple of the deity;
furthermore, lamps for sacred sites (tīrtha) should be offered by the hundreds and thousands.
Lamps should be offered in rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, and even in the ocean; likewise in wells and large oblong tanks. Such offerings in water are considered to bestow the heavenly realm.
Eating but once a day and the offering of lamps—these are the vows for the month of Kārtika; likewise, the vow is considered to consist of giving split pulses and eating only at night.
One should eat three morsels of food for a month; this is the Ṛṣiśaśi vow.
Furthermore, one should drink cow’s milk from four teats for seven nights.
For seven nights from three breasts, for seven nights from two breasts,
for six nights from one breast, and likewise for three nights he should subsist on air alone.
This is known as Somāyana, considered a great Cāndrāyaṇa;
it is performed by means of eating once a day, or at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for.
With four fasts, thus over sixteen days,
that vow called Kṛcchra is said to be the destroyer of great sins.
One should drink milk, ghee, and warm water mixed together for one day;
then fast for one day—that indeed is the Taptakṛcchra vow.
One should drink hot milk, ghee, and water, each separately, every day;
on the fourth day, one should fast—this is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
For three days each, one should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air; this practice for twelve days indeed constitutes the Atitaptakṛcchra vow.
One should drink this cold water for three days; that is the vow of the Cold Kṛcchra (śītakṛcchra).
Regarding the quantity for drinking, the sequence is three palas, two palas, and one pala.
For one day, one should drink the five products of the cow mixed with darbha-water;
on the second day, by means of fasting, this is considered the Sāntapana vow.
Every day he should consume one [product] derived from a cow; on the sixth day, he should drink water infused with *kuśa* grass.
On the seventh day, he should fast; this is the middle *sāntapana* vow.
By repeating the Sāntapana penance three times, it becomes the Mahāsāntapana, completed in twenty-one days;
one partakes of cow urine, cow dung, and cow curds for three days each, in that order.
Divine milk and cow-ghee constitute the great Sāntapana;
mixed with these for three days, it is the Pañcagavya, the vow known as Yati-sāntapana.
The observer of the vow should drink water boiled daily with the leaves of the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *padma*, and *bilva* trees individually, along with *kuśa* grass.
This Parṇakṛcchra vow is considered to be accomplished in five days;
if one has fasted for three nights, on the fourth day he should drink the decoction of the five [leaves]. (18)
This vow of the leaf-bundle is considered to last four days;
indeed, the month must be passed with fruits, for this is declared to be the *phalakṛcchra*.
The Śrīphala-kṛcchra is performed with *śrīphala* fruits, the Padma-kṛcchraka with lotuses (*padma*),
the Śrī-kṛcchra with *āmalaka* fruits, and the Patra-kṛcchraka with sprouts.
The Puṣpakṛcchra consists of flowers, the Mūlakṛcchra of roots, the Jalakṛcchra of water, and the Dugdhakṛcchra of milk. || 21 ||
That by which a month is passed—consisting of eating once a day, eating only at night, eating food obtained unasked, and fasting—is called the *kṛcchra* penance of that name. (2.2)
That vow is called Pādakṛcchra when it lasts for four days;
[it consists of] three days of eating at midday, three days of eating only at night, and three days of eating whatever is obtained by chance.
Then, one should not eat for three days; that is the Prājāpatya vow.
The Atikṛcchra consists of eating only as much food as fills the palm of the hand for twelve days. || 24 ||
Abstaining from food for three days is considered the Pādakṛcchra vow;
taking whatever is obtained by chance for three days is the second Pādakṛcchra.
Likewise, eating only at night for three days constitutes the third quarter-penance (pādakṛcchra);
eating only at midday for three days constitutes the fourth quarter-penance.
In the middle [period], fifteen morsels are prescribed; for the night-meal (nakta), twelve are traditionally taught.
For a meal taken at will, twenty-four morsels are traditionally taught. (27)
One day should be observed as a fast, the second day as eating only at night;
then for two days one may eat as one pleases, and after that, fasting for two days.
Observing this vow for six days is declared to be the *ardhakṛcchra* penance;
one should drink milk for twenty-one days for the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
One should drink only water for twelve days; this is called the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance.
A Pārāka Kṛcchra is said to consist of twelve days of fasting.
[In another form of it,] one should consume sesame paste daily, as well as barley meal, buttermilk, and fasting.
The Saumya-kṛcchra vow is declared to consist of four days.
Daily, one should consume sesame paste, buttermilk, water, and water infused with Kuśa grass;
followed by a five-day fast—that indeed is another form of the Saumya-kṛcchra.

Sesame paste, boiled rice with its decoction, buttermilk, water, and barley meal—one should practice each of these for three nights; that is considered the Saumya-kṛcchra, which lasts for six days. (33) One should consume sesame paste and the other items individually for three nights each.
That *tulāpuruṣa-kṛcchra* should be understood as lasting fifteen days.
At the end of those fifteen days, one should subsist on air for three days, and then again for three days;
this *tulā-nṛ-kṛcchra* consists of twenty-one days of fasting. || 34–35 ||
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should remain in water and inhale air;
on the full moon day, one should fast—this is considered the Jala-kṛcchra vow.
On the tenth day, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and on the eleventh day, one should fast.
One should perform the worship of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Harikṛcchra vow.
On the seventh day, one should drink water separately from milk, curd, and ghee;
on the eleventh day, one should fast—this is the Paitāmaha Kṛcchra vow. (38)
Starting from the sixth day, the observer of the vow should drink water for three days and fast for three days;
on the twelfth day, he should perform the breaking of the fast—this is the Māhendrakṛcchra vow.

For three days starting from the third day, one should consume rice mixed with sesamum and so forth, and for three days, barley gruel; thereafter, one should fast for three days—this indeed is the Viṣṇu-kṛcchra vow.
The practitioner should consume milk for five days and curd for five days;
he should fast on the eleventh day—this is called the Bhāskara-kṛcchra.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, one should consume, in sequence, beans, barley, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, and water; this is the Saptarṣikṛcchra vow.
The practitioner should gradually drink either milk or boiled water,
separately with the leaves of *palāśa*, *bilva*, *darbha*, lotus, *udumbara*, and *parṇaka*.
This fasting on the sixth day is known as the Agnikṛcchra vow;
from the seventh day onwards, one should consume milk, bilva fruit, ripe lotus-seed, and [lotus-stalk] in successive order.
One should eat lotus fibers on the eleventh day and observe a fast;
this five-day rite is known as the Lakṣmī-kṛcchra vow. (45)
The Brahmakūrca vow is the most excellent, the supreme vow among all vows;
by performing it, human beings are liberated from all sins. (46)
This goal can be accomplished in three days; I shall now describe the procedure for it.
One should fast on the ninth day and consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with water infused with kuśa grass.
On the tenth day he should drink [the five products], and on the eleventh day he should observe a fast;
[he should consume] cow urine, cow dung, milk, water with *darbha* grass, ghee, and curd.
That is declared to be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which is purifying and cleanses the body:
the urine of a copper-colored cow and the dung of a white cow. (49)
The milk of a cow with a golden-colored udder, the curd of a blue one, the clarified butter of a black one, or else the five products from a tawny (kapilā) cow. (1.262.50)
One was golden-hued and tawny; the second was reddish-brown;
the third had red eyes; and the fourth was deep brown.
The fifth is Karburā; the sixth should be Śvetapiṅgalā;
the seventh is indeed Śvetapiṅgākṣī, and the eighth is Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā.
The ninth is the Pāṭalā, and the tenth is the Pucchapiṅgalā;
these ten varieties of the Kapilā cow, which bestows sacrificial offerings, have been described.
In the absence of [the specific materials] of all castes, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are considered auspicious.
There should be eight māṣas of cow urine and sixteen of cow dung.
Twelve māṣakas of *bodhi* [powder] should be taken for milk, ten for curds, eight māṣakas for ghee, and four for *kuśa* water. (55)
Having taken [the water] with the mantra named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, or with the Gāyatrī, or with that specific Ṛk, or with the Gāyatrī, or with the Puṃsūkta; ||56||
Having extracted the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should indeed offer it into the fire with kuśa grass that is green, uncurved, and possesses seven excellent blades.
A fire sacrifice (homa) is prescribed with one hundred and eight invocations of Hari’s names;
the remainder of the oblation, consecrated with the Praṇava, should then be drunk.
That [mixture], supported by the syllable Om and drawn up with the syllable Om, one should drink using either a middle leaf of the Palāśa tree or a lotus petal. (59)
One should drink from a golden vessel, a silver one, or by means of the Brahma-tīrtha;
this is called the Brahmakūrca, which destroys sins and likewise bestows liberation.
Having consumed sesame seeds for twelve days, that is the Agnikṛcchra vow;
one should complete the Yavakṛcchra by subsisting for a month on barley grains abandoned by cows.
One should eat only the barley-meal discarded by cows for an entire month;
this is declared to be the Yāmya-kṛcchra, which destroys the impurities of the body.
One should subsist daily on a handful of sesame paste for one month; this is declared to be the Kuberakṛcchra vow. || 63 ||
One should perform one's bath with cow urine, and one may even consume cow dung;
one should dwell in the midst of cows and likewise sleep upon cow dung.
He should drink only when the cows have not yet drunk; he should not eat while they have not yet eaten.
He should rise when they have risen and sit down when they have sat down. (55)
This vow, known as the *govrata*, should be understood to last for exactly one month;
it consists of dwelling among the virtuous, serving the virtuous, and conducting oneself like the virtuous. (66)
The food and drink of a virtuous person are pleasing, and that indeed is the vow of the righteous;
by means of *āmikṣā* one may subsist for two months, and by milk for a fortnight.
One should subsist on curd for eight days and likewise on ghee for three days;
one should remain without food for three days—this indeed is the Uddālaka vow.
A person desiring prosperity, desiring nourishment, likewise desiring heaven, or desiring to please the gods, should perform the *kṛcchra* penance with devotion. (69)
Thus have these difficult vows been described to you, O Lotus-born One; they destroy sin and grant liberation to all.
Performing all the difficult penances, with speech, mind, and senses restrained,
wearing washed garments and being tranquil, he should bathe and worship Hari.
The observer of the vow should always consume all the substances for the vow, such as milk and the like, only those things offered by Śrī Hari and nothing else. || 7.2 ||
If, while performing difficult penances, he should become bewildered or fall into a swoon,
one should give the nectar-like milk of cows to that seeker of the vow to drink.
Water, juice, fruit, flower, buttermilk, leaf, milk, curd, parched grain, unfermented liquor, medicinal herb, decoction, bulbous root, vegetable, and the word of the guru—[these are all pure]. (74)
The morsel known through the command of the Brahmin, likewise the swallowing of transgressions, the excellent substance fit for mouth-perfuming, fresh butter, and sugar. 75.
Concealed [food] includes preparations of milk and the like, as well as oil from sesame and other seeds;
likewise, the food of sages such as bhivāra, the bhūphalī fruit, and the pulp of trees.
Clove, cardamom, black pepper, cinnamon, fresh ginger, sūpha, gundraka, bitumen, musk, sandalwood, and likewise salt; ||77||
There are indeed forty transgressions of the vow that cause honey-colored smoke;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should feed virtuous men, and its fruit shall be eternal. ||78||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Kṛcchra Vows to be Performed in Kārtika," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"The word *kṛcchra* is said to mean 'suffering,' yet that very suffering, when offered to you, becomes happiness.
This *kṛcchra* vow bestows both happiness and merit; it has been described by you in this context. (1)
The meritorious vow, as well as everything that is to be drunk or eaten, is indeed you alone;
for without you, everything is fruitless, since that is certainly the case.
O Blessed One, tell me regarding the month known as Puruṣottama:
what is the name of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) in the dark fortnight, and what is the fruit of the vow?
What is the ritual procedure? What is the nature of the worship? Which deity is worshipped here? What is the gift, and what are the observances? Tell me everything in great detail.
O Janārdana, tell me: what is the prescribed bath, what is the mantra to be recited, and what food is considered most excellent? Furthermore, what should be avoided during this month? Tell me that.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In the month exceeding [the previous] by one day, she is known by the name Kamalā;
he is called Puruṣottama, and he, her husband, is to be worshipped.
The Lord Hari, accompanied by Lakṣmī, is the embodiment of gold;
Śrī-Lakṣmī and Puruṣottama, residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, are to be meditated upon.
By means of this vow dedicated to Kamalā, one shall become face-to-face with Kamalā here.
On the tenth day, one should eat only once and sleep on the ground at night.
One should indeed be a celibate student (brahmacārī) and abandon anger and the like;
having risen during the Brahma-muhūrta, one should remember Puruṣottama.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, the observer of the vow should undertake the restraint on the first day of the month of Puruṣottama, or in the morning on the first lunar day.
One should indeed undertake the purifying observances (niyamas) to be maintained by embodied beings;
the daily recitation of the Thousand Names or a hundred thousand [names] is the observance for chanting.
Recitation performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; at a river, it is remembered as having a two-fold merit;
at a cow-pen, it is a thousand-fold; and in a fire-sanctuary, it is a hundred-thousand-fold.
In sacred fields of the gods, at holy fords (tīrthas), and likewise in the presence of the virtuous, [the merit is] ten million-fold; but in the presence of Tulasī, it is a hundred million-fold.
In the presence of Viṣṇu, the recitation of mantras certainly becomes infinite;
the turning of the rosary is remembered as the destroyer of the whirlpool of saṃsāra.

During the Cāturmāsya period, those observances (niyamas) should be undertaken every month at Puruṣottama; indeed, they should be observed in both [the dark and light fortnights], as they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
At the commencement of the month, in the presence of the image of Hari, one should accept [the vows];
likewise, the avoidance of meat and the avoidance of oil must be observed.
The avoidance of ghee, the renunciation of oils and the like, the avoidance of pungent substances, the total abandonment of scented oils, and the relinquishing of the enjoyment of flowers; || 17 ||
One should avoid pungent, sour, sweet, alkaline, bitter, and astringent [foods], as well as the avoidance of betel leaf and the avoidance of sweet fruits and the like. (18)
Eating from a leaf of the Palāśa tree, abstaining from oil-massage for the feet, renouncing head-massage, and avoiding curd and milk; || 19 ||
One should avoid the use of collyrium and similar substances, abstain from eating a second meal, observe silence, engage in sacred conversation, and avoid vulgar talk. (1.263.20)
The abandonment of the *sthālīpāka* offering, the avoidance of vegetables alone, the abandonment of food in general, and the avoidance of one or another type of fruit. ||21||
Consuming food upon a stone slab, eating from a plantain leaf, performing ablutions at Puṣkara, and abstaining from bathing at home; ||22||
Touching the lotus feet of the guru, prostrating at the feet of Viṣṇu, eating once a day, eating only at night, or even fasting; 23.
Smearing, sweeping, and washing the house of Hari, as well as performing circumambulation one hundred and eight times, or even more; ||24||

Singing, instrumental music, and dancing; or the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); awakening through the discourse of the scriptures, and awakening through the recitation of the Vyāsa-narratives. ||25||
Worship with *tulasī* leaves, sprinkling water in the temple of Viṣṇu, eating only from leaves, and the avoidance of split pulses and the like. (26)
Accepting only what is offered with pure faith, not eating from copper vessels and the like, not eating from bell-metal vessels, and not eating food that has been cooked for oneself alone. ||27||
Eating only grains cooked in water, eating only cooked grains,
eating from an earthen vessel, drinking water from the hollowed palms,
eating from the hands, and sitting upon the bare ground.
The gift of a tawny cow and food as bright as a lotus petal. ||29||
Alms-food is like nectar; it is an auspicious vow that brings about liberation.
The gift of gold, the gift of silver, the gift of clothing, and the offering of a house [are likewise meritorious].
One who constantly gives food and other gifts according to their ability performs great merit;
such a virtuous person and Viṣṇu—these two are the supreme among men. (31)
Worship should be performed for them daily, as well as service;
whether a Śūdra or a Śūdra woman, one should perform service to the Guru, who is Hari. (22)
The guru is indeed the form of Viṣṇu; the guru is the embodiment of the three deities.
One should perform service with one's body in such a way that the guru may be pleased.
For this [body] is composed of the five elements and is declared to be without intrinsic purpose;
yet by serving the Guru with it, one shall attain infinite fruit.
This Dharma is difficult to find in the world; it bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
This vow must be observed without being asked for, while avoiding malice, violence, and the like. (35)
Generosity, compassion, and self-restraint are indeed the duties even of the great, who bestow upon their teacher the wealth of both their bodies and their worldly possessions. (36)
Indeed, by the power of their charity, they attained the state of being dear to Viṣṇu;
honey was to be abandoned, clarified butter was to be abandoned, and likewise milk and other such things were to be abandoned.
One should avoid pomegranate, citron, and coconut;
one should also avoid the abandonment of rice, the abandonment of barley, and the avoidance of wheat. (38)
A verse, a stanza, a hymn of the Rigveda, a chapter, or likewise a recitation,
as well as a ritual act or a song performed before Hari— this is the vow that grants the abode of Viṣṇu.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse and the renunciation of ritual action constitute the great vow.
One should avoid curd, milk, as well as buttermilk, molasses, and leafy vegetables.
One should perform a bath with *āmalaka* fruits or indeed with sesame seeds;
the *dhātrī* fruit always removes sin, and sesame seeds are indeed purifying. (41)
The vow of silence during the twilight hours must be observed, as must the non-awakening of the sacred fire at night;
likewise, eating in silence is a pure and auspicious vow that brings about purification.
Eating in silence is known to yield fruit equal to a fast;
however, falsehood, anger, and backbiting are characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa).
In the month of Puruṣottama, one’s worldly livelihood must be abandoned in every way;
auspicious meritorious acts should be performed, and sinful deeds must be relinquished. (44)
The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is to be meditated upon, worshipped, propitiated, and remembered;
indeed, even difficult penances should be performed during the month of Puruṣottama. 45.
For one who performs the vow of Kamalā, Kamalā is born in the home;
likewise for Lakṣmī, the consort of Śrī Puruṣottama. (46)
On the morning of the eleventh day, having performed meditation and bathed according to the prescribed rules,
one should perform the daily worship within the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Then, one should worship twelve jars provided with water, gems, and petals, and endowed with unbroken rice, fruits, garments, and other offerings.
In the center, the observer of the vow should place a jar made of gold or copper;
he should then worship it, accompanied by pure water, fruits, jewels, and other offerings. 49.
One should likewise worship the bell, the conch, and the pitcher with ritual offerings;
having placed Puruṣottama upon the vessel atop the pitcher, which contains a bowl of sesame seeds.
The observer of the vow should worship according to the prescribed rite with all materials;
he should perform the invocation and so forth, as well as the anointing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should cause the image to bathe with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and wipe its body;
one should then offer garments, ornaments, decorations, sandalwood paste, and so forth.
One should offer fragrant oil scented with collyrium, agallochum, and musk;
one should also offer ornaments such as necklaces for beauty, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth. ||53||
Having offered various kinds of food for the oblation, fruit, water, powdered incense,
and auspicious betel-leaf, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord.
One should whirl the water from the conch clockwise like a staff,
and having performed praise, salutation, and a request for forgiveness, one should prepare the bed and so forth.
One should perform a foot massage, which will then cause bliss to expand;
one should give abundant gifts and act likewise at midday as well. (56)
One should feed various kinds of food and worship with great devotion;
one should perform the evening ārātrika ceremony, and after offering hymns of praise, likewise provide a communal feast.
One should keep a vigil at night, preceded by dance and song;
then, on the twelfth day, having bathed at dawn and likewise worshipped Hari.
Having fed [the guests] and performed worship of the Guru, one should feed many others;
thereafter, one should break one's own fast and give gifts with devotion.
In this manner, one should indeed perform the vow which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the observances, which yields its full fruit.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, and a mandala made with the seven types of grain;
one should also have svastikas fashioned and cause gifts of beds to be given.
There, the observer of the vow should worship Śrī Hari and Ramā according to the prescribed rite,
as well as the image of the Cow and the one holding the mace (Gadī), and likewise provide food for the virtuous.
And one should give the preceptor whatever is required, such as clothing, food, ornaments,
and so forth, following the great worship of the deity with the sixteen articles.
Indeed, the observer of the vow himself should give various gifts;
furthermore, at the conclusion of the rite, gifts should be given for the fulfillment of the vow.
When the concluding rite (udyāpana) is performed, everything certainly becomes complete;
O Mahālakṣmī, if one performs the vow but does not carry out the concluding rite, [it remains incomplete]. (65)
Having incurred a deficiency in the vow, one will not properly partake of its fruit;
for that which is a mere semblance of the restraint one has undertaken in the vow [is ineffective]. (66)
At the conclusion of the vow, however, the practitioner must personally bestow a gift;
it is traditionally taught that if one has renounced oil, one should give ghee, and if one has renounced ghee, one should give milk.
In silence, sesame seeds and other offerings, together with gold, should be given to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
at the meal, one should provide food accompanied by curd and rice.
One should indeed give sweet food enriched with gold out of great devotion;
however, one who eats from a vessel made of palāśa wood should give sweet items such as ghee and the like.
One who eats only at night should indeed give food endowed with the six flavors;
but for the vow of eating only what is unasked for, one should present a bull along with its equipment.
One who has renounced the *māṣa* coin should give a well-characterized cow along with its calf;
one observing the vow during the bathing with *dhātrī* fruits should give gold weighing at least one *māṣa*.
In the observance of fruits, one should indeed give various kinds of fruits;
in the observance of grains, one should give grains such as rice and wheat.
One should give a bed with cotton and a pillow for sleeping on the ground;
indeed, for the sake of practicing celibacy, one should provide meals for a married couple.

Upon the abandonment of vegetables, one should give vegetables; upon the loss of beauty, substances such as juices; and when there is no oil for daily bathing, one should give ghee and roasted flour (saktu).
In the vow of the nails and hair, one should give a mirror, a fan, and so forth;
upon the renunciation of sandals, one should joyfully give a pair of sandals.
Upon the complete renunciation of milk and other such things, one should indeed give a tawny cow;
during the lamp-vow, one should indeed give a golden lamp-vessel.
But upon the observance of the restraint from sexual intercourse, one should give silver, wealth, and so forth;
likewise, whatever vow was desired and whatever restraint was undertaken [should be fulfilled]. (77)
Having given each of those, one should effect the fulfillment of the observance (niyama) by means of the gift of a cow,
the gift of sugar, the gift of a house, and the offering of wealth.
The gift of land, the gift of a maiden, the gift of the sacred thread, the gift of knowledge, the gift of liberation, and even the offering of one’s own self. ||79||
It surely bestows both heaven and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
What is the use of saying more here? Whatever may be most desired [should be offered]. (1.263.80)
Furthermore, for the sake of attaining this very [state], one should undoubtedly perform the supreme gift of all that belongs to oneself to Hari. (8.1)
Or indeed, one should give everything one possesses to the Guru, the bestower of liberation;
for a skillful person should achieve eternal liberation by means of that which is impermanent. (82)
The arrival of Kamalā indeed occurs in the house of one who performs her vow;
listen, O Lakṣmī, as I relate this narrative of past events. (83)
At Haridvāra, there was a certain Brahmin named Śākaṭāyana;
his cart was small, and his home was merely a place of rest.
Subsisting on alms, with grass and cotton for bedding,
he dwells near the celestial Ganges, using only his hands as a bowl.
Once, O beloved, he had gone to another region to beg for alms; his cart was indeed swept away by a sudden rainstorm.
Seeing his cart stolen, Asva then departed from there; he went alone on foot to the sacred ford known as Prayāgarāja. ||87||
Emaciated by hunger, with a dejected face, he performed his ablutions at the Triveṇī;
afflicted by hunger, he searched there for the hermitages of the sages.
There he beheld the divine and wonderful hermitage of Bhāradvāja,
as well as the assembly of people during the month of Puruṣottama.
In that hermitage, he heard from the mouth of Bhāradvāja a delightful story concerning Sulabhā— a charming tale that destroys all impurity and is centered upon Kamalā.
Having heard the narrative of Ekādaśī, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as proclaimed in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* and which grants wealth. (9.1)
Having heard that story of Kamalā, the Brahmin Śākaṭāyana then remained in the hermitage of the sage and undertook the vow together with them.
He kept a vigil throughout the night, remembering Kṛṣṇa within his heart;
at the Brāhma-muhūrta on the twelfth day, Lakṣmī arrived there.
With divine limbs, divine splendor, and adorned with divine ornaments, she said: "I grant you a boon here; I am pleased with my vow. (94)
The Brahmin Śākaṭāyana, filled with wonder, also asked: "Who are you, whose daughter are you, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks? And how have you become so gracious toward me? (95)
Lakṣmī said: "I have become pleased by the power of this vow;
impelled by the God of gods, I have come here from Vaikuṇṭha. (96)
"Because of your vow regarding Kamalā during the month of Puruṣottama, I have come here to grant you abundant prosperity and fortune. (97)
"My vow was performed by you at Prayāga through the power of the sages;
as the blessings are subject to the influence of that vow, I grant this to you: 'May you become wealthy. (98)
Where Ekādaśī occurs at sunrise, and likewise Dvādaśī at midday and so forth, with Trayodaśī at the end of the night—that is the best of all vows. (99)
In that regard, there is great merit in breaking the fast on the thirteenth day;
this vow has been performed by you, O great sage, and I am well-pleased.
"Take this divine jewel from which gold is obtained," having said this, Kamalā gave the jewel to him and vanished. || 101 ||
The Brahmin Śākaṭāyana also took the jewel and went home;
this great jewel grants him a hundred gold pieces every morning.
The Brahmin Śākaṭāyana also gave gifts day and night;
thus did that excellent sage, the earthly deity Śākaṭāyana.
He obtained prosperity even greater than that of Indra through the Kamalā-vrata:
"Whatever a petitioner desires from my house, all that must be given to him. 104.
Thus was it revealed by Śākaṭāyana upon the surface of the earth;
then once, indeed, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Pulastya, the son of Brahmā.
Having heard this account of Maṇi’s generosity and desiring to beg for himself,
he reflected upon it and went in person to the house of Śākaṭāyana.
Although the sage was free from desire, he gave the alms of that jewel when requested;
Pulastya, having taken the jewel, went to the island of Siṃhala.
There, he fashioned everything—the cities, forests, and so forth—out of gold.
He then offered a jewel to Kubera, the lord of wealth.
Then Rāvaṇa abducted her, and he made it his own golden Laṅkā;
for thus indeed Goddess Kamalā is pleased by the vow.
Whatever vow causes satisfaction, he gives all of that to his devotee;
whether one hears or reads it, the fruit shall be that of Kamalā.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty of the Kamala-Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of the Month of Puruṣottama, the Observances, the Concluding Rite (Udyāpana), the Attainment of Jewels and Lakṣmī through the Vow of Śākaṭāyana, and Subsequently the Acquisition of Gold by Pulastya, Kubera, and Rāvaṇa," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
This which is most worthy of being heard by listeners, the unsurpassed among purifiers, divine, and the destroyer of evil dreams—this must be listened to by me with great effort. (1)
Among all months, the supreme month is known as Puruṣottama,
for in it the Lord himself is truly manifest as Puruṣottama.
All the celestial immortals of heaven, desiring birth upon the surface of the earth,
worship that supreme person, Nārāyaṇa.
The hosts of deities, beginning with Brahmā, constantly worship those who always recite the name of the Lord Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
O Puruṣottama, tell me: what is the name of the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of that month of the God of gods? || 5 ||
O Lord, tell me: what is the procedure, what is the fruit, and who is the deity of giving? And by performing which vow does a human being attain the imperishable heaven? (6)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the bright fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama,
there occurs the Ekādaśī known as Dhāmadā, by which the abode of Brahman is attained.
In this context, the ritual procedure is composed of Brahman, and its fruit is remembered as being composed of Brahman;
the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is considered the master of the abode of Brahman.
This Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is indeed beyond the syllables;
he is accompanied by his own consort, who is likewise imperishable, and is the bestower of the divine abode.
He is to be worshipped with flowers from the *muktālatā* vine and with nectar-like fruits;
indeed, the gift of the knowledge of the *Upaniṣads* bestows liberation.
The gift of initiation, the gift of the Veda, the gift of the Vedas, the offering of one's own self,
and the offering of all one's possessions— among gifts, these are considered the most excellent here.
O beloved, compared to the foremost gift of the Bhagavat’s abode, any other gift is insignificant;
the gift that brings about the attainment of the abode is considered the best of gifts.
On the tenth day, he should eat but one meal, sleep on the ground, and observe celibacy;
having risen in the morning, he should meditate upon the Imperishable Supreme Person.
And having also recollected Dhāmadā, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Having performed the daily worship, one should carry out the great worship.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, featuring a *sarvatobhadra* mandala;
and one should have a flawless jar made, containing gems within and adorned with gold.
Then, one should place upon the maṇḍala a large copper vessel filled with cloth, water, and fruit, and set it atop the pitcher (kumbha). || 16 ||
One should display there a twelve-petaled lotus made with saffron;
there, one should worship Puruṣottama together with the syllables.
Having thus installed [the deity] together with Kamalā according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the great worship (mahāpūjā) with the sixteen types of ritual services (upacāra). || 18 ||
I meditate upon that beautiful and supreme Lord, who is served by the divine Prabhā and others adorned with magnificent celestial ornaments, and who is joined by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and the rest. 19.
I invoke in my mind Kṛṣṇa, the granter of grace to his devotees;
O Kṛṣṇa, O Supreme Person, please sit upon this golden throne.
"Accept the Gaṅgā water for washing the feet along with the imperishable syllable;
indeed, accept this arghya water joined with fragrance, flowers, and other offerings."
"O Janārdana, accept this filtered water from the sacred ford for sipping,
as well as milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar."
Please graciously accept the five nectars for the purpose of bathing;
please accept the waters of the oceans and rivers for the purpose of bathing. (23)
Please accept this woolen cloak, the bodice, and so forth;
indeed, take this cotton cloth, the waist-belt, the bodice, and the rest.
"O Supreme Person, take this silken thread, the sacred thread, as well as the armlet, the bracelet, the ring, the crown, and the anklet. (25)
Let the waist-bands, cords, and necklaces be taken;
let the jewels, gold, flower-garlands, and ornaments be gathered up. (26)
Perform an anointing with musk, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood;
take the kadamba, campaka, lotus, kunda, and jasmine flowers.
O Nārāyaṇa, accept with devotion this incense that bestows fragrance;
O Puruṣottama, accept this beautiful lamp made of ghee.
O Puruṣottama, accept this most brilliant ārātrika, which brings forth an excellence of saffron, bilva, flowers, and collyrium. 29.
Take this food— milk-rice, cakes, and the like, as well as cow-ghee,
fried pastries, curd, milk, clarified butter, and sweets, O Lord of Kamalā!
Drink this cool water from the sacred ford, rich with fragrance, O Mādhava;
and please accept this betel leaf, abundant with pūga nut, cardamom, and khadira wood.
Please accept the plantain, mango, immortality fruit, pomegranate, and wood-apple;
O Kṛṣṇa, take this golden sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the diamonds and other gems.
"Please accept indeed these flowers and unbroken grains held in my joined palms;
salutations to you, O Beloved of Kamalā; salutations to the Supreme Leader of the Imperishable. (3.3)
O Lord, Master of the Imperishable, I prostrate like a staff; please accept me.
There is no other refuge but you; you alone are my refuge. 34.
O Lord of Śrī, complete my vow; O Lord of the Imperishable, protect me!
[Grant] food, clothing, gold, vegetables, a bed, ghee, and so forth. (35)
"I offer this with the thought that it is for Hari; please accept it, O twice-born one.
Having thus worshipped with true devotion, the observer of the vow should spend the remainder of the day.
One should give gifts according to one's capacity and perform the necessary rites;
even at midday, one should offer very sweet food, sacrificial offerings (naivedya), water, and so forth.
In the evening as well, one should perform a great worship with many articles;
one should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) provided with five wicks of clarified butter.
Having offered food offerings, drinking water, betel-leaf, and a foot-massage, and having performed acts of praise, one should keep a vigil at night. (39)
For a man going toward the temple of Hari for the purpose of vigil, or toward the monastery of the virtuous,
there is the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step.
Having bathed in the morning, one should again perform the daily and occasional worship;
then one should feed the Deity and subsequently feed the devotees.
Then the observer of the vow should present gifts of golden images to the preceptor;
furthermore, he should indeed perform many other desired acts of charity.
The observer of the vow should feed virtuous Vaiṣṇavas and virtuous women with delicious food;
thereafter, he should perform the breaking of the fast with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna). 43.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should avoid sleeping during the day, food from others, eating a second meal, sexual intercourse, oil, and any food that is tamasic in nature.
If even a very small portion of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) can be obtained on the day of breaking the fast,
the observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast on that very day and must not let it pass.
The first quarter of the twelfth lunar day is said to be the day of Hari;
one who desires imperishable merit must certainly not eat during that time. (46)
In this manner, the vow of Dhāmapradā should be performed according to the prescribed injunctions;
at the end, the Lord shall indeed lead that devotee to His own abode by means of a celestial chariot.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to an account that occurred long ago during the Dhāmadā vow:
in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Puṇḍarīka. (48)
A devotee of Viṣṇu is a universal emperor who views all things with equanimity; he treats everyone as virtuous and is entirely free from attachment to the body and bodily things.
He spends half the day in worship and the remainder in administering justice;
on the day of his vow, he indeed performs only worship.
He had a queen named Kumudvatī who was devoted to her husband;
regarding her husband's command as the very command of the scriptures, she served her husband with devotion. (51)
Without having asked her husband for anything, she did not form even a thought in her mind;
once, however, she was intent upon the worship of the Dhāma-dāva vow.
The queen, who resided in the inner apartments, was overcome by fever;
yet, for the sake of preserving her health, she went out in the evening without even asking her husband. ||53||
Accompanied by her female servants, she went to the garden in the grove;
there was fruit that was agreeable to her hunger and did not aggravate her fever. (54)
Taking the nine-colored [substances], that devoted wife drank their juice; for since she was a devoted wife, she first caused her husband to drink it before drinking it herself. (55)
Her fidelity was broken and a fever increased greatly within her;
having drunk water out of thirst, she remained right there during the night.
Today, my daily service to my husband in the morning was not performed as usual;
furthermore, I did not behold my husband's face in the morning as I have done before. (57)
She was not permitted to drink even a drop of water from her husband's thumb;
having fallen into a state of utter helplessness while afflicted by illness, her devotion to her husband was brought to ruin.
Then the fever became exceedingly intense and her body withered away;
yet, by the power of her devotion to her husband, the queen remained a partaker of merit.
Facing death and exceedingly tormented by her wasting away,
the life-breaths of Kumudvatī do not depart despite her misfortune.
Puṇḍarīka also heard of the queen’s illness;
when his vow was completed, he returned and rendered service to her.
His lifespan reached its full term, yet his vital breaths did not depart;
then, having offered water, the king presented the fruit of Dhāmadā.
His life-breaths departed swiftly, and a divine celestial chariot arrived,
beautifully adorned by Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and his attendants.
And a second celestial chariot has arrived, adorned by the glorious Puruṣottama together with the Imperishable (Akṣara), bestowing the abode of the Imperishable.
First she was led by Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot accompanied by Ramā;
afterwards, she was brought to Vaikuṇṭha and ascended another celestial chariot.
She was led to the imperishable abode by the Lord of Śrī Puruṣottama;
thus, as the giver of that abode, she went to the abode through the attainment of merit.
And how much more so for one who observes the vow of offering a dwelling?
Therefore, the vow of providing a dwelling should be performed with special care.
The vow of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Puruṣottama bestows the supreme abode,
grants liberation, and likewise bestows prosperity.
By hearing and even by reciting it, one shall obtain a fruit equal to that of the vow;
for those with desires, there shall arise great prosperity, the supreme state, and so forth. (69)
This should be performed according to one's strength by one who desires auspiciousness;
it will bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as imperishable abodes, upon him.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Śukladhāma Ekādaśī Vow of the Month of Puruṣottama, and how Queen Kumudvatī—the wife of King Puṇḍarīka—attained the Abode of the Imperishable through this vow despite being somewhat devoid of service to her husband," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, all the concluding rites (udyāpana) and the worship of all the gods have been described; O Lord, all of that has been understood by me. (1)
If the concluding rite (udyāpana) for all Ekādaśīs were to be performed as a single act, then how extensive would it be? Tell me that as well.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall explain the single characteristic of all [these rites],
namely the concluding ceremony (udyāpana), which indeed bestows the complete fruit in its entirety.
When a beautiful pavilion, adorned with plantain pillars,
has been constructed, one should fashion a *sarvatobhadra* diagram within it and place a water-pot in its center.

It should be provided with the sprouts of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Cūta, and Nyagrodha trees; it should be adorned with jewels, have its neck encircled by cloth, and likewise be filled with water.
One should place a very large vessel filled with saffron before his face,
containing a twelve-petaled lotus endowed with twelve petals.
Having fashioned Vāsudeva, who is attended by Ramā, out of gold and placed him in the center,
one should install twenty-four lords of the Ekādaśīs around him.
One should install them together with their respective consorts in order from the east:
first Śrī and Keśava, then Padmā and Nārāyaṇa on the [next] petal.
Mādhava is with Nityā, Govinda with Candrā,
Viṣṇu with Ramā, and Madhusūdana with Mādhavī.
Trivikrama was united with Padmākṣī, Vāmana with Kamalā,
Śrīdhara with Kāntimatī, and Hṛṣīkeśa with Aparājitā.
Then Padmanābha with Padmavatī, and Rādhā and Dāmodara; on the petals, starting from the east, is Saṃkarṣaṇa together with Sunandā.
Then Vāsudeva was with Hariṇī, Pradyumna with Dhī, Aniruddha with Suśīlā, and Puruṣottama with Nandā.
Adhokṣaja is joined with Trayī; Nṛkesarī is joined with Kṣemaṃkarī; Acyuta is joined with Vijayā; and Janārdana is joined with Sundarī. || 13 ||
Upendra, accompanied by Subhagā; Hari, together with Hiraṇyā;
and Kṛṣṇa, joined by Sulakṣaṇā—these should be installed according to the prescribed rite.

One should perform the bathing of the central deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), preceded by anointing with oil; one should then perform the great consecration (mahābhiṣeka) and offer garments, ornaments, and the like. || 15 ||
One should worship with all kinds of perfumes, jasmine flowers, and tulasī leaves;
one should offer incense, a lamp, sandalwood paste, food offerings, and water. (16)
Modakas, khājās, flour-mixtures, ghee-filled cakes, sohilakas, kaṃsāras, roasted barley flour, sevās, and polikās. || 17 ||
Pūrikās, milk-rice (pāyasa), the essence of milk, as well as rice with curds, cakes, balls, and śaṣkulīs with a hundred holes.
One should offer much sweet food, such as cooked sesame, cooked rice, powdered mung beans, rice with jaggery, plantain fruit, and other varieties. 19.
One should also offer various kinds of vegetables, various kinds of fruits, betel leaf for refreshing the mouth and other such items, as well as water. (1.265.20)
Having performed the great *nīrājana* ceremony, one should then offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*),
as well as hymns of praise, prostrations with the staff-like body (*daṇḍavat*), and a request for forgiveness.
Having performed and completed the worship, one should give gifts with devotion:
cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, horses, elephants, vehicles, and garments.

Then, in a temple or a cow-pen, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and boiled rice mixed with flower-nectar, using the respective names of those [deities].
One should give twenty-four cows, or even one cow accompanied by gold;
likewise, one should worship at midday and feed [the Brahmins] according to the prescribed rite.
In the evening, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), worship [the deity], and likewise feed [the guests];
having kept a vigil at night, one should worship Hari with haste at dawn.
The observer of the vow should give an image fashioned from gold to his own guru;
thereafter, the observer of the vow should also give ornaments, garments, and a bed.
One should feed twenty-four Brahmins, virtuous men, and chaste women;
one should offer water-pots to Viṣṇu and likewise bestow sacrificial fees.
Then he should break his fast after having fed his own people;
when this is done, the fruit of twenty-four Ekādaśīs shall be obtained. (28)
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth during the great festival of the concluding rite;
for Kṛṣṇa himself, the beloved of Lakṣmī, being the bestower of prosperity, is surely pleased.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the gift of a cow, a mountain, and so forth; listen.
Having performed worship, one should then give abundant wealth to the preceptor.
In a vast abundance, the observer of the vow should give ten kinds of cows;
he should also give ten kinds of Merus—listen, O beloved, to the procedure for that.
There, having spread darbha grass upon the ground smeared with cow dung,
ten cows should be stationed with their feet toward the north and their faces toward the east.
The observer of the vow should likewise fashion a cow of jaggery using exactly one hundred *prasthas* of jaggery and twenty-five *sīras* of the same.
Alternatively, having hidden it according to one's faith in the place of the cow,
and having likewise made the calf out of jaggery according to one's faith, then—
And having wrapped both of them in priceless, fine garments,
they were adorned with mother-of-pearl earrings, sugarcane legs, and eyes of pure pearls.
They had copper-colored backs and tails of fine linen, with woolen blankets made of white wool;
they possessed horns of gold, hooves of silver, and were endowed with eyebrows and frowns made of coral.
Having thus fashioned two cow-calf pairs, richly adorned with various ornaments and provided with bronze milking vessels, the observer of the vow should worship them according to the prescribed rite.
A cow of ghee, a cow of milk, an excellent cow of sugar,
a cow of sesame seeds, a cow of honey, and likewise an excellent cow of juice.
Having fashioned a cow of curds, a cow of water, and a cow of gold,
the observer of the vow should worship them after making their respective calves as prescribed before.
One should indeed perform [the rite] according to one's ability, and likewise provide cows and calves;
one should offer them all to the preceptor for the gratification of Puruṣottama.
And likewise, having fashioned ten kinds of delightful mountains provided with trees and ponds, as well as four corner-mountains; || 41 ||
One should worship according to the prescribed rite and offer it to the Guru for the satisfaction of Hari;
having spread kuśa grass upon the ground within the pavilion smeared with cow dung.
In the center, one should fashion Mount Meru made of rice, measuring one thousand *droṇas*;
the best [Mount Meru] should consist of twelve *prasthas* of grain.
One should place pearls and diamonds in the east, rubies in the south, yellow and dark-colored gems in the west, and corals in the north.
One should fashion caves from stalks of sugarcane, rocks and the like from oyster shells,
waterfalls from clarified butter, and clouds from pieces of cloth.

One should fashion the peaks out of gold and silver, the lords of sages and the gods out of gold, and Indra and the other guardians of the quarters out of silver; one should also fashion the trees from the various metals.
Having fashioned a Mandāra, a Pārijāta, a Kalpadru, and a Kadambaka tree,
one should adorn them with flowers and fruits made of gold and silver.
Mandarādri is filled with barley in the east, Gandhamādana with wheat;
Vipulādri is in the west with sesame seeds, and Supārśva in the north with beans. 48.
These mountains should be fashioned, endowed with beauty and furnished with their own appurtenances;
then, having caused the recitation of auspicious prayers, one should invoke the divine mountains.
Having performed the worship, one should present mountains of wealth to the preceptor,
and likewise give twenty-four cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
A mountain of salt, a mountain of jaggery, a mountain of gold, a mountain of sesame seeds,
