a mountain of cotton, a mountain of ghee, a mountain of gems, and a mountain of silver.
One should cause nine mountains of sugar to be fashioned according to one's capacity,
as well as four mountains on each side, likewise.
Having fashioned them as before, one should create manifold beauties;
one should worship all of them according to the ritual rules and present them to the Guru.
One should cause to be performed the gift of a cow, the gift of land, the gift of a maiden, the offering of a house, and the gift of vehicles, mounts, cities, and villages. (54)
One should give one's entire property to the guru, but to the Brahmins according to their merit; to mendicants, the gift of food; and to others, whatever they require.
Having thus performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), one should afterwards dismiss the deities;
all of that should be given to the preceptor or offered to the temple.
Whatever rules regarding prohibited items have been undertaken during the vows,
the gift of those very same items must likewise be performed at the concluding ceremony (udyāpana).
Everything given here indeed meets [the giver] again in the hereafter, but certainly not otherwise;
therefore, according to one's strength, the vow should be brought to completion after its commencement. 58.
In ancient times, the concluding rite was performed by Vaivasvata Manu;
likewise, the concluding rite was performed by Bhṛgu’s daughter, Ramā.
Padmā, the daughter of the Earth, likewise performed the concluding rite of fulfillment;
and having attained Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha, they rejoice there forever.
In former times, Pārvatī performed the entire great concluding rite (udyāpana),
and Prabhā likewise performed that concluding rite in the proper manner.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the vows for all the Ekādaśīs have been described to you according to the ritual rules; what else do you wish to hear? 62.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature and the Great Concluding Ceremony (Udyāpana) of All Ekādaśīs," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Tell me in detail the nature of the vows observed during the rainy season,
by performing which even human beings may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
But knowing that anything other than the means for attaining the Self is inevitably a storehouse of suffering, one should strive for the eternal goal; tell me how this is so. (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall indeed describe all the purifying days consisting of vows, which grant supreme liberation.

Through the power of Hari’s manifestations and through constant association with the virtuous, even time attains a divine nature; one whose soul is devoted to vows shall become a bestower of liberation.
On whichever lunar day a particular vow is observed, what its fruit is, how the worship is performed,
and what its ritual procedure must be— all that I shall declare to you.
In the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, at the beginning of the first day (pratipad), the Creator of the Universe brought forth this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
On that first lunar day (pratipad), a great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) should be performed, which bestows happiness,
pacifies all portents, and grants wealth and good fortune.
This [rite] bestows longevity and nourishment, and grants happiness in both worlds;
having caused a sacrificial pit and a pavilion to be constructed there on an auspicious spot.
The observer of the vow should indeed worship Brahmā, who bears the form of fire,
with water for the feet, respectful offerings, flowers, incense, garments, ornaments, and food.
He should be especially worshipped with burnt offerings, oblations, and gifts, as well as by the gratification of virtuous men and women, using unbroken grains, sandalwood, and excellent juices.
Having fashioned an image of gold, one should worship Brahmā with the sixteen supreme offerings as well as various kinds of food.
One should worship the god Brahmā, who has four faces, four hands, and two feet, who holds the Vedas in his hands and carries a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
After the ārātrika ceremony, the person performing the vow should pray to the deity;
he may then eat fruit and such from the vow, or even a single meal.
One should observe celibacy and give abundant gifts;
one should pray to the Creator for the sake of the continuation of the lineage through sons and grandsons.
One should give an image as a gift to the Guru, who is of the nature of the Imperishable (Aja);
the observer of the vow should also give the gift of a maiden, preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
This vow, which increases one's lineage and bestows all happiness,
should be performed after offering salutations with the syllable *oṃ*, using water from *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken grains of rice.
One should give to a twice-born man clothing, gold, sweet food, cattle, and other wealth according to one's ability. (17)
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to one learned in the Vedas for the sake of completing the vow;
this is declared to be the Brāhma-vrata, which should be performed by those seeking specific desires.
On this very lunar day, in the same manner, the auspicious Sarasvatī-vrata should be performed,
consisting of either fruit-based food or even a single meal.
For Śāradā was born from the mouth of Brahmā in the morning;
she was twelve years and more of age, holding a lute and accompanied by peacocks.
The image should be made very radiant, provided with garments such as blue and golden ones of great value; it should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
Then, having worshipped that Goddess in the morning with the sixteen and other articles,
the practitioner must pray to her for the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman.
Milk-porridge and *pūrikās* should be offered as an oblation (*naivedya*);
on that day, the seeker of the vow should also consume milk-porridge for his meal.
On the second day, it shall be the bestower of wealth for the commencement of learning;
the observer of the vow should give various kinds of gifts to the venerable Guru.
Then, one should offer an image of Svarṇasarasvatī to the venerable Guru;
for that purpose, one should pray: "May knowledge dance upon the tip of my tongue. (25)
The observer of the vow should distribute gifts and give according to his capacity;
he should feed and honor Brahmins, holy men, and scholars. (26)
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
while the churning of the ocean was being performed by the gods and the Daityas, Hari appeared in the form of a tortoise in the morning.
One should worship Vāsudeva in the form of a golden tortoise;
his upper body is human in form, while his lower body bears the shape of a tortoise.
One should place a conch and a mace in the two arms, offer sweetmeats as food, and present sugar, curd, tamarind and other fruits, and sweet water. (29)
One should indeed perform a great festival for the narrative of the Tortoise;
having thus observed the vow, the practitioner shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship in the morning the Karavīra tree, which has come from the celestial garden to the earth.
One should offer a garment of red thread, incense, and unguent;
one should offer perfumes, unbroken rice grains, water, a nāraṅga fruit, and a citron.
Having sprinkled the sprouted grain with *kuraka* water, one should perform a hymn of praise:
"O highly fortunate Karavīra, grant me fruits at all times! (33)
"May the seven auspicious grains dwell within my granaries.
Having thus circumambulated [the deity] and given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the observer of the vow [should perform the rite]. (34)
Having paid obeisance and offered water, one should afterwards return to one's own home;
thus worshipped, the tree indeed bestows wealth and grain. (35)
Salutations! On the first day of the bright fortnight, there is a great vow that bestows fortune and intelligence, and accomplishes virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (36)
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the vow of silence is proclaimed;
one should perform the worship of Śiva according to the prescribed rite upon a water-pot (kumbha).
One should perform the worship of the golden image of Śiva with the sixteen articles;
one should give sixteen sweet, ripe fruits to a Brahmin.
One should offer cooked foods as sixteen gifts to Śiva;
likewise, one should give a cow and other gifts, making sixteen in total.
Having performed this vow for fourteen years to the trident-bearing God of gods, O Lakṣmī, one shall enjoy all pleasures until the end of the body and then go to Śiva.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, there is the vow known as Aśoka;
for the Aśoka, the best of trees, has descended from heaven to the earth. (4.1)
One should perform the worship of the Aśoka tree there with sixteen articles;
by that, one becomes free from sorrow and filled with wealth and grain.
At the conclusion of the vow, in the twelfth year, by devotedly offering an image made of Aśoka wood to the preceptor, one shall become happy in the world of Viṣṇu.
Like the fruit of the Aśoka tree, his subjects bring him freedom from sorrow;
yielding wealth and happiness, they bear fruit upon the earth.
On this very first day, one should observe the Navarātra;
during the Navarātra, one should subsist on a single meal or even on food obtained by begging.
Alternatively, the observer of the vow should always fast, or consume only fruit;
in the forenoon, he should worship Durgā, preceded by the ritual installation of the water-pot (ghaṭa).
One should perform the planting of sprouts using barley, wheat, and rice;
and one should daily carry out worship, recitation, and the chanting of mantras with a rosary. (47)
One should daily recite the auspicious hymn composed by Mārkaṇḍeya;
likewise, one should always perform worship at night and keep a vigil.
One should perform the worship of a maiden with excellent food and other offerings; a person possessing great wealth should fashion an image of Durgā adorned with a thousand [ornaments]. (49)
On the final day, one should release her into the water in the evening;
having performed the vow in this manner, O Lakṣmī, one shall become an abode of all perfections.
Durgā bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon him; of this there is no doubt.
A practitioner of vows must never practice deceit regarding wealth or deceit regarding strength.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should especially perform the vow known as the Annakūṭotsava, which increases the pleasure of Viṣṇu. ||52||
One should offer one hundred and one varieties of sweet foods here, as well as all kinds of vegetables, soups, cooked grains, and leafy greens. (5.3)
There were indeed various kinds of medicinal boluses, tubers and roots, milk products, and sugar-based sweets—various foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked. (54)
One should offer Govardhana to a Brāhmaṇa and likewise worship him;
then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the observer of the vow should partake of the food and receive the sacred remains (prasāda).

The one who performs the festival of the mountain of food shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as the riches of wealth, grain, liquids, garments, ornaments, vehicles, and so forth. 56.
On this very day, in the morning, one should worship the cows, calves,
bulls, and heifers with turmeric, saffron, and other such substances.
Having worshipped them with flower garlands, erotic ornaments, fresh fodder, and other offerings, one should cause them to play in the courtyard of Kṛṣṇa’s temple. 5.8
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the excellent Dhanavrata is prescribed;
for the sake of attaining wealth, one should indeed perform the worship of Viṣṇu at night.
The observer of the vow should have a golden image of Lakṣmī fashioned;
having worshipped that image in the vicinity of the fire-pit, [he should proceed].
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations while reciting the name of Lakṣmī;
one should worship her together with Viṣṇu, covered by a pair of red garments.
And one should give an image to the preceptor and cause other gifts to be given;
by doing so with wealth and grain, one becomes filled with prosperity.
Having become prosperous and cleansed of sin, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The observer of the vow should practice eating once a day, or at night, or subsisting on fruit.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should perform the unsurpassed Bhānu-vrata;
with a spirit of devotion, one should worship the Sun-god with sixteen articles and other offerings.
In ancient times, on this very day, the Sun became twelvefold;
one should therefore offer a golden image of the twelvefold Āditya to the preceptor.
Having become equal to the sun through his vow, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
the man who performs this vow becomes sun-eyed both in this life and the next.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Vahni was born from Maheśvara;
by worshipping Vahni according to the prescribed rites, one shall attain the world of Vahni.
The person observing the vow should perform the offering of the form of fire, as well as the oblation with sesame seeds and other materials,
and carry out all acts of worship and salutation.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, there is the vow known as Dhūlidhūsaraka;
at dawn on that occasion, Śaṅkara [performs the rite] originating from the body of Satī.
His body was smeared with ashes on all sides, and his vow was one of being grey with dust;
therefore, there he beheld Mahādeva, the God of gods, clad in the directions as his garment.
He sprinkled his entire body, which was grey with dust, with water;
and Hara, being pleased by that, granted him union with his own self (sāyujya).
And one should likewise make one's own body naked and smeared with mud;
by this rite, Śambhu, being well-pleased, shall bestow the abode of happiness.
In the month of Phālguna, during the conjunction with the Phalgunī nakṣatra, the man Hari became known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the deity of Dharma, in that very form. ||73||
Having worshipped them on the swing fixed at Dharmāśrama, the gods caused it to be rocked; therefore, a festival should be celebrated here.
In the morning, one should perform the worship of the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa with the sixteen types of offerings, including tulasī, garments, and sandalwood paste.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and jujube fruits (badara) as the food offering;
then, having performed a colorful festival, the observer of the vow should partake of the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
The first day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the supreme Viṣṇujanmavrata;
on that day, one should worship Viṣṇu, the auspicious son of Vairāja.
One should feed Brahmins and virtuous men and give abundant gifts;
by observing the vow of eating but once a day, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||78||
On the pure first day of the bright fortnight, Brahmā, the preceptor of the world, was born;
on that day, his worship should be performed here, and gifts should be given like gold.
The vow of eating but one meal a day should be observed; it shall bestow all perfections, grant the realm of Satyaloka at the end, and provide both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, on the first day of the month, those annual vows have been declared;
among them, celibacy and food consisting of sacrificial offerings yield the fruit.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Vows of the First Day of the Month of Vaiśākha," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. This chapter describes the creation of the world, the birth of Sarasvatī, the birth of the Tortoise, the arrival of Karavīra, the Lakṣmī-vrata, the Mauna-vrata, the Aśoka-vrata, the Navarātra, the Anna-kūṭa-dhana-vrata, the Dvādaśa-bhānu-vrata, the origin of Fire, the Satī-bhasma-dhūlī-vrata, the birth of Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the birth of Viṣṇu, and the vow of the birth of Brahmā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the annual vows of the second lunar day (Dvitīyā);
by them, human beings attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this world.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Brahmā was married;
one should perform the festival for that wedding and likewise observe the vow.
Having constructed a large pavilion, one should worship two golden images of Sāvitrī and Yama amidst festivities, and then feed them with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
One who observes the vow and eats but one meal shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices;
and when there is sufficient wealth, one should give the gift of a maiden and the gift of a cow.
Having obtained the fruit of all desires, one shall go to the state of Brahman at the end;
on this very day, O Lakṣmī, the Moon was born from the ocean.
Therefore, the Candra-vrata, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be performed;
having joyfully worshipped the newly risen crescent moon at the beginning of the night.
One should indeed offer a silver moon and feed a Brahmin as a gift;
the Brahmin, who is the very image of the moon, should be worshipped with white water-lilies.
Likewise, the moon was to be desired by me like a second mother;
[I saw] a hearth joined with a frying pan, two bulls, and a herd of cows. (8)
O Lord of the second house, salutations to you; may my home be endowed with wealth and grain, and may there be health among my people; grant this to me always.
O giver of the medicinal herbs and food that sustain existence, grant me an increase in vital energy;
O nourisher of children, be forever a bestower of happiness upon me here.
On this very day, from Sūrya in the form of a horse, two young boys were born to his wife named Saṃjñā, who was Aśvinī; they became the two Dasras.
The two physicians, the Aśvins, are to be worshipped; for that is indeed the vow. One should observe eating only once a day, and as for the gift, medicinal herbs are prescribed. (12)
One should also present eyes made of gold and silver to a twice-born man;
furthermore, during the Aśvinī asterism, a gift of horses should be given according to one's ability.
The Aśvāśvinī vow should be performed with devotion by both men and women.
Chickpeas should be given to the horses, while the observer of the vow should consume ghee and curd. 14.
Having performed this vow for twelve years, preceded by the gift of eyes and horses,
one shall become the best of kings, exceedingly handsome, and a leader among monarchs.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Rādha, the Unborn One indeed commenced his penance;
one should perform this vow of penance after having fashioned an excellent lotus.
Having placed an ascetic Brahmin there, the observer of the vow should worship him,
or else he should have an auspicious mandala prepared, provided with the seven kinds of grain.
There, having placed the Creator of the Universe upon the water-jar, one should worship him,
as well as the water-pot, the staff, the bark garment, and the seat.
One should give fruits, food, sandals, and a sacred thread; furthermore, one should give the gift of a cow and other gifts to a virtuous Brahmin. (19)
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures, one attains the world of Viṣṇu;
for on the second day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the great Bhāskara, the jewel of the sky, [is present].
Having arisen from the eye of Hara, illuminating the three worlds,
he beheld Hari in the form of the four-faced Brahmā together with Gāyatrī;
and having worshipped the Sun, who is accompanied by his chariot and horses and is of a beautiful ruddy hue, according to the prescribed ritual.
Having observed the vow of eating only once a day, he fed virtuous children.
By performing the gift of a golden sun and likewise the offering of gold,
the observer of the vow shall attain the exceedingly prosperous world of Bhāskara.
The Saṃkarṣaṇa vow is declared to be observed on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha;
on this day, Śeṣanārāyaṇa himself was born in the form of Rāma.
In the first age, the gods indeed placed Rāma together with Bhadrakā upon a chariot and, having circumambulated it, proceeded toward the city and other locations. || 25 ||
Having gone to the edge of the reservoir, they purified that infinite one;
thereafter, a great festival should indeed be performed by all men. || 26 ||
Having placed it at the end of that in a temple of the gods according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony with prostrations and feed many Brahmins.
One should feed virtuous women and children, and perform the gift of ploughs and the like;
likewise, one should carry out the gift of chariots, as well as the gift of fields, villages, and so forth. (28)
The second day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa is the auspicious Viśvakarmavratam;
for on this day Viśvakarman sleeps, and thus it is the Aśokaśayanavrata.
Having fashioned an auspicious four-faced image of Viśvakarman, seated upon a bed together with his wife, and having worshipped him as the Lord of the worlds; ||| 1.267.30 ||
One should pray to the blessed Viśvakarman, the creator of the world:
"O bearer of the Śrīvatsa, O beloved of Śrī, O abode of Śrī, O Lord of Śrī, O Master! (31)
O Lord, may my household life, beginning with this dwelling, not come to ruin;
may there never be for me a separation from dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
In this vow, one should indeed perform the gift of a house, the gift of a wife, the gift of the crescent moon,
the gift of a daughter, and the gift of gold and other such things.
Since the birth of Indra occurred on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one shall surely enjoy the fruit of all sacrifices by worshipping Indra, who is Hari. || 34 ||
And his son, named Jayanta, having fashioned everything— including Śacī’s celestial chariot,
the thunderbolt, the bow, and the arrow— out of gold, [presented them].
Having fashioned an elephant out of gold and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should give everything to the preceptor and observe the vow of eating but once a day.
Having performed this, the observer of the vow shall then attain heaven, the abode of Mahendra,
for a long time, and finally reach liberation in the world of Virāja.
The vow of the second day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is considered to have been established by Durgā;
a gift bestowed on this day shall yield infinite fruit. (38)
In ancient times, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Yama was fed and honored in his own home by his brother Yamunā with many delicious foods.
On the Yamadvitīyā day, a sister should observe this vow in every house;
for this meal at her sister's home increases prosperity.
Having enjoyed his brothers' clothing and ornaments, he should give wealth and other assets to his sister;
by that means, he himself shall become filled with gold, wealth, and grain.
On this lunar day, Yamarāja was fed by Yamunā;
he who eats from the hand of his sister on that day does so out of affection.
That brother shall possess wealth such as gold and gems, as well as grain and other riches;
one should give abundant gifts to one's sister, and even rings to her son.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ancestors, beginning with Aryaman, were born from the body of Brahmā; indeed, that is the vow of the ancestral Śrāddha.
In the morning, one should perform the worship of Sūryanārāyaṇa;
and at the time following midday, one should perform the Śrāddha and the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should perform the worship of the ancestors and offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
The observer of the vow should eat only at night, and as for the gift, it should be coriander seeds.
The observer of the vow should then give food to a Brahmin, as well as clothing and other such items; furthermore, a gift of a cow should be made according to one's capacity. (47)
Remembering all his ancestors and elders, he should indeed offer salutations to the twice-born;
thus he shall attain health and obtain sons and grandsons.
The wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) were born on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa;
the vow of the wish-fulfilling cow should be observed, and the practitioner of the vow should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
One should perform the purification with water from a cow's horn, which grants all desires;
one should bathe with both earth and water from a cow's horn, and one should worship the cow.
One should give gifts of cows and other such things for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
and one should provide grass and other fodder so that cows may obtain their meals.
In the evening, one should perform the sight of the young moon and the offering of arghya;
by doing so, the observer of the vow shall indeed become a possessor of cattle, exceedingly wealthy, and even more prosperous.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Bhāskara was indeed placed upon a whetstone by Viśvakarman and made truly beautiful.
In this context, one should worship Hari in the form of the Sun with red flowers and red perfumes, having fashioned a golden image according to one's means.
Then, one should devotedly offer a full copper vessel filled with wheat and rice to the Sun, and present the water-offering (arghya).
One should give an image as a gift to a virtuous Brahmin according to one's capacity;
when the vow has been performed in this manner, O Lakṣmī, the observer of the vow becomes like the Sun himself in person. (56)
He is born on earth as a Brahmin who is difficult to approach and difficult to overcome;
or else he may be born as a king, a great sovereign emperor. (57)
Having enjoyed various desires here, he goes at the end to the station of the Sun;
or, being praised by all the gods, he goes at the end to the station of Brahmā.
Then, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, Hara himself set out for asceticism at the Nārāyaṇa hermitage on the golden mountain.
Then a golden image of Hara, provided with matted locks, should be fashioned;
Śiva is to be worshipped with flowers that are very white and fragrant.
A canopy should be made with flowers and auspicious floral ornaments, along with various food offerings, incenses, lamps, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and so forth. ||61||
Mahādeva is to be propitiated by one observing the vow for the sake of attaining happiness;
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the observer of the vow becomes free from disease.
Endowed with wealth, grain, and prosperity, he shall certainly live for a hundred years.
In these vows, rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed according to one's means and resources.
The fire itself, appearing in various forms as the body of Hari, should be worshipped by the performer of the *homa* who maintains celibacy and other observances. 64.

Whatever procedure is prescribed for the second lunar days occurring during the bright fortnight, that very same procedure should be performed on those of the dark fortnight by those skilled in the ritual rules.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Vows," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the annual second-day vows (*vārṣika-dvitīyā-vrata*): the origin of Brahmā-Sāvitrī, the conjunction of the Moon, the birth of the Aśvinī Kumāras, the penance of Brahmā, the birth of the Sun, the origins of Saṃkarṣaṇa and Rāma, Viśvakarmā, the Aśoka-śayana, the birth of Indra, the Durgā-vrata, the feeding of Yama and Yamunā, the origin of Aryaman and Pitṛs, the birth of Kāmadhenu, the Sun being licked by Śāṇa, and the penance of Śambhu.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the vows of the third lunar day (Tṛtīyā),
by performing which a man or a woman shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
From the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Gaurī performed a most rigorous penance for the sake of attaining Śaṅkara; indeed, that is considered the Gaurī-vrata.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having fashioned an image of Gaurī together with Śaṅkara—
whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay— || 3 ||
Having worshipped according to the rules with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as auspicious garments and ornaments, and with blades of dūrvā grass, the maiden should remain fasting.
A woman seeking a boon, one desiring sons and daughters, or likewise one desiring a husband,
should perform the lustration ceremony for Mahāgaurī, the daughter of Śaṅkara, who is accompanied by Śaṅkara.
Having bowed down again and again, she should pray for what resides in her mind;
[she may do so] seven, nine, eleven, or even more times, O wives of the twice-born.
Then, having summoned those women who were married or maidens of Gaurī-like form and auspicious marks, he addressed them with great respect.
With her mind delighted by ornaments such as vermilion, collyrium, and garments,
the performer of the vow should honor her and likewise satisfy her with gifts.
One should offer sweet foods, such as rice-balls and fruits;
by thus satisfying them, the practitioner shall obtain the fruit [of her vow]. || 9 ||
One should keep a vigil at night with the desire for the complete fulfillment of the vow;
then, having worshipped her again in the morning, one should joyfully offer her to the preceptor.
Or else, one should dismiss the image and cast it into a sacred ford or a reservoir of water;
having thus performed the auspicious Gaurī-vrata for twelve years.
A maiden, however, obtains a virtuous husband equal to Śambhu;
for the perfection of the vow, she should dedicate and give twelve cows.
What is the use of saying more in this regard? Just as Gaurī is the bestower of good fortune for women, no other such [goddess] exists in the three worlds. (13)
Wealth, sons, a husband, a daughter, knowledge, accomplishment, fame, happiness, and indeed everything desired— Gaurī, when propitiated by this vow, bestows it all.
By means of the vow performed by Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikyā, and Ramā,
the Lord Kṛṣṇa— bearing a banner and a bow in his hands— was obtained as her husband.
Hari has hands marked with the signs of a fish, a trident, a wheel, and a svastika;
therefore, this vow bestows beauty, good fortune, enjoyment, and liberation.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the vow of Akṣaya-tṛtīyā;
that lunar day is the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, and it renders the merit of the Kṛta Yuga inexhaustible.
In this regard, having fashioned the Tretā Yuga in the form of a golden image, one should worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa together with Lakṣmī; or else, one should worship [the deity] thus.
One should satisfy the illustrious Teacher of the World with flowers, incense, ointments, and the like, as well as with the waters of the Gaṅgā, unbroken grains (akṣata), and various kinds of food.
One should feed the Brahmins with barley meal, while the observer of the vow himself should eat only once a day;
for him who has performed the rite in this manner, the fruit is that of fasting.
Even the commencement of an undertaking reaches fulfillment without obstacles;
whether man or woman, one who observes this vow shall attain the state of having accomplished their purpose. ||21||
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, under the asterism Punarvasu, Hari appeared in the house of Jamadagni, bearing his axe.
In this [image], the observer of the vow should have a golden Rāma fashioned holding an axe;
having performed the great worship at midday, he should then take his meal.
From this time forward, one should always wear perfumes, garments, and even white clothes until the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, while meditating upon the Lord.
One should fan the Lord daily with fans made of uśīra root and palm leaves,
and one should offer as food-offerings (naivedya) mango juice and other items mixed with sugar.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, Rambhā descended from heaven to earth;
therefore, the rambhā fruit is to be eaten during this vow, and Rambhā is to be worshipped with unbroken rice grains and water. (26)
One should worship the twice-born together with his wife using perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings;
here, a woman desiring good fortune performs the Rambhā-vrata. (27)
One obtains wealth, sons, intelligence, fortune, riches and the like, a husband, a cow, the earth, a mansion, as well as household utensils. ||28||
One who seeks the vow obtains a delicacy of form comparable to the plantain tree;
in this [vow], there is the gift of *raṃbhā* fruits, as well as sugar and ghee. (29)
Then, on the third day of the month of Āṣāḍha, Ramā commenced her penance for the sake of Keśava; therefore, the Lakṣmī-vrata should be performed by women.
One should worship Keśava, together with Lakṣmī, in the form of golden images, according to the prescribed rite, with the sixteen types of excellent offerings and other requisites.
One should worship with foods, gifts of fragrant scents, garments, and ornaments; and with the offering of lamps, prostrations, and ritual fees (dakṣiṇā). ||3.2||
There, one should honor and feed a Brahmin accompanied by his wife; one should respect him with the words of the Vedas, satisfy him, and likewise gladden him. (33)
Having thus propitiated this goddess in the form of Lakṣmī who has become a Brahmin woman during her vow,
one should bid farewell to both the Brahmin, who is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu, and her to their home.
A woman who observes the vow while remaining at home, desiring good fortune, shall, by the grace of the God of gods, be endowed with wealth and grain. (35)
Accompanied by sons and grandsons, she shall attain the world of Viṣṇu;
and a maiden shall obtain a handsome husband who grants her desired and excellent enjoyments.
The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa is considered the Svarṇagaurī-vrata;
for it was by performing supreme penance that Kālī became Svarṇagaurī. (37)
The observer of the vow should worship Bhavānī with the sixteen types of offerings;
at the conclusion of the worship, he should pray: "Grant me a fair complexion. (38)
O lady of excellent vows, grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me good fortune;
fulfill my various other desires as well—salutations be unto you! (39)
Then one should offer a beautiful wind-instrument to the Goddess who is accompanied by Bhava;
this vow is proclaimed to last for sixteen years.
At the conclusion of that, a fortunate woman should perform a great ceremony of completion (udyāpana) for Satī within a banana grove,
in a mandala known as Sarvabhadra.
One should place [the deity] in the center within a golden vessel endowed with gems and other precious materials;
one should worship the fivefold assembly (pañcāyatana) beginning with Śrī Gaṇeśa all around it.
Upon the water-pot, in a fine vessel filled with unbroken grains of rice,
one should worship a golden image of Śambhu and Bhavānī.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sixteen substances,
using sixteen bamboo vessels filled with cooked food.
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) to Satī, one should present it to virtuous people;
thereafter, one should give excellent betel (vāyana) to kinsmen and others. 45.
One should give the image to the preceptor and likewise offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born;
one should perform many acts of charity for the sake of ensuring the success of the vow.
A woman, whether unmarried or married, shall obtain the full fruit;
having become abundantly prosperous with wealth, grain, and other riches, she goes to the supreme state. ||47||
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the vow known as Haratālika is indeed observed;
for on that day, the joining of Pārvatī’s hand with the hand of Hara took place. (48)

One should perform this vow known as Haratālī, which increases good fortune, with devotion according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the offering of water for the feet and the arghya oblation. 49.
In this regard, having placed the food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, bamboo, or even clay— ||1.268.50||
Having placed roasted sesame, rice, chickpeas, and so forth, as well as fruit, clothing, and ornaments, right here in this very vessel; ||51||
One should indeed give that to the preceptor and then perform the breaking of the fast;
one should feed virtuous Brahmins, virtuous women, maidens, and children.
One should likewise devoutly bestow sixteen vessels made of bamboo, containing auspicious substances, upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
A woman observing the vow should give a more abundant and auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to other Brahmins as well; by that, she shall attain good fortune. ||54||
A woman who has thus observed this vow, having enjoyed delightful pleasures, shall become the companion of Gaurī in the hereafter by the power of that vow. ||55||

Through this vow, which is obtained by the grace of the Goddess and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one attains wealth, grain, daughters, and sons in this world, as well as peace in the next. (56)
When the third lunar day of the month of Bhādrapada occurs here in conjunction with the asterism Hasta,
the chanters of the Sāman hymns should perform the libations for the ancestors, the gods, and the sages.
A new sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be worn according to the ritual prescribed in one's own Vedic branch;
for the sake of prosperity, the vow known as Hastagaurīvrata should be performed.
This [mantra] shall be a protector against the bites of venomous creatures and the like;
for when she assumed ten million forms for the sake of destroying the demon Mahiṣāsura. (59)
Then she became known by the name Durgā Koṭīśvarī, as it was personally proclaimed by the wielder of the Pināka bow; that indeed is the Koṭīśvarī vow.
Indeed, when she assumed the forms of a hundred thousand Caṇḍīs,
the virtuous lady was then called Lakṣeśvarī by the wielder of the Pināka bow himself.
The Lakṣeśvarī vow should be observed for four years;
the worship of Lakṣeśvarī must be performed while fasting.
O Lotus-born One, having purified one hundred thousand unbroken grains of rice or sesame seeds here, one should cast them into milk that has been heated on the fire.
As long as the clay remains firm and solid as a well-formed lump,
one should fashion with that lump a beautiful image of the Goddess.
Having invoked Pārvatī there, adorned with perfumes, flowers, unhusked grains, jewels, hair, and garments, one should worship her with a spirit of devotion. (65)
With perfumes, flowers, water, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prayers;
with various excellent fruits, superior sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and prostrations. || 66 ||
One should cause [the deity] to prosper with nightly offerings while prostrating like a staff, and ask for forgiveness;
one should also request wealth, grain, and so forth, as well as sons, daughters, houses, and the like.
Then one should dismiss Durgā into the midst of the water;
after giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the venerable guru, one should subsequently perform the night vigil.
"Having given gifts to the Brahmins, he should eat on the following day.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the Koṭilakṣeśvarī Vrata.
In the house of the performer of this vow, Lakṣmī, consisting of wealth and grain, always shines and increases eternally through the power of this vow. (1.268.70)
At the end, one goes to the world of Gaurī and indeed attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
the Bṛhadgaurī vow is prescribed for the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
One should perform this for five years to obtain the merit of ten million *kundana* flowers;
one should worship Durgā in the morning with sixteen excellent offerings.
Five auspicious young women (suvāsinyah) should be honored with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste,
as well as with shawls, bodices, earrings, necklaces, and other decorations.
Five types of metal vessels, as well as small bowls and cooking pots,
vermilion, cumin, sweets, auspicious articles, and collyrium.
Fresh cakes made from wheat flour, fruits and the like, various garments, and indeed five types of woven cloths. (75)
One should give to them and feed them; afterwards, being restrained in speech, one should eat.
One should keep a vigil at night, interspersed with the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s praises.
One should wear a fruit on the neck—either a betel nut or whatever else has been offered;
for at night, a fruit worn around the neck bestows the fulfillment of all desires. (77)
Then, in the morning, full of enthusiasm and adorned with ornaments, she should go to the river accompanied by her female companions and musical instruments, and perform her ablutions.
There, one should address Gaurī and speak this prayer:
"O auspicious lady, you have been invoked by me and worshipped according to the prescribed rite. (79)
O Goddess who bestows good fortune upon me, protect everything at all times! O Goddess, may whatever was deficient be forgiven; you may now depart as you please.
Having thus made this petition, having offered salutations with shouts of "Victory! and musical instruments, and having looked upon Gaurī with enthusiasm, one should dismiss her into the water.
Having thus performed the vow with devotion, the practitioner, by the grace of the Goddess, shall enjoy worldly pleasures and, at the end of the body, attain the world of Gaurī. ||82||
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, the Viṣṇu-Gaurī vow is observed;
for it was by Gaurī that Viṣṇu was worshipped for the sake of attaining the fruit of her ascetic penance.
Therefore, this auspicious vow known as Viṣṇugaurī has been proclaimed;
therein, indeed, Gaurī, together with Viṣṇu, should be joyfully worshipped. 84.
With sixteen recitations and various kinds of foods, one should feed Gaurī in the form of a married woman under the name of Lakṣmī. (85)
One should worship with auspicious articles for the pleasure of Viṣṇu and Gaurī;
having bowed to her, one should bid her farewell and give gifts with sincere devotion.
A woman who performs this vow undoubtedly obtains a son;
the Haragaurī-vrata is prescribed for the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Gaurī, having come to the bed of Hara, entered into union with Hara;
through that union with Hara, she became satisfied, endowed with the happiness of her lord. ||88||
In this vow, having prepared a single bed for Hara and Gaurī, one should cause them to sleep there, worship them with devotion, and serve them with a divine disposition. (8-9)
By the power of this vow, having enjoyed delightful pleasures and attained the world of Gaurī, he rejoices together with Hara.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, the Brahma-Gaurī vow is observed;
it was established by Brahmā himself, who arrived there to bestow blessings for the attainment of Śaṅkara.
That vow has been declared; it should be performed according to the proper injunctions.
Having fashioned an image of Gaurī from gold, one should worship Brahmā as well. (92)
One should perform the single meal with the sixteen types of service;
one should give gifts as desired to the guru and feed the twice-born.
By the grace of Brahmagaurī, she rejoices there in union;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, Lakṣmī is Saubhāgyasundarī.
By offering the garland of choice to Viṣṇu, she became beloved;
therefore, one should joyfully perform this vow, which consists of the beauty of good fortune. 95.
There, Lakṣmī is to be worshipped by offering an *arghya* of coconut, along with the sixteen types of services, sweet foods, ornaments, and so forth. (96)
When pleased, she bestows good fortune and even leads one to her own abode;
indeed, every household possession and all objects worthy of being given should be offered to the woman. (97)
The vow of eating but once [a day] should be observed, and a necklace should be offered to Viṣṇu;
that garland of grace should be placed around the husband's neck, for it bestows sons. (98)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, after midnight,
Satī obtained sons who were Rudras through union with Hara.
Therefore, that third vow, consisting of the welfare of the family, has been described;
when worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, Gaurī becomes the fulfiller of one's lineage.
Thus, in all these vows, there is giving, fire-offerings, dismissal, the worship of the gods and goddesses, and the honoring of Brahmins and gurus. (10.1)
One should practice the common observances, such as eating only once a day and so forth;
when performed with devotion, these grant all desires held in the mind.
Among all the gods, Śrī Hari himself exists as their inner self;
he is to be worshipped, for he bestows the fruits of all actions. || 103 ||
Whatever object a man, a woman, or anyone else may desire for the sake of their vow, they obtain all of that through the grace of Śrī Hari. 1.4.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Vārṣika Tṛtīyā Vows, including the Gaurī-tapovrata, Akṣaya-tṛtīyā, the Birth of Paraśurāma on the first day of the Tretā Yuga, the Kadalī-vrata, Lakṣmī-tapovrata, Kālī-gaurī-vrata, Haragaurī-lagnavrata, Sāmaga-śrāvaṇī, Koṭīśvarī, Māhiṣaghnalakṣeśvarī, Bṛhadgaurī, Viṣṇugaurī, Haragaurī-yoga, Brahmāśīrgaurī, Viṣṇuvaramālā, Kulavṛddhi-vrata, and others," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, listen; I shall describe to you the vows of the fourth lunar days (caturthī), by performing which a man or a woman attains supreme worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, who became that Master born from the union of the bodily minerals of Pārvatī in the house of Śaṅkara— || 2 ||
That Kṛṣṇa indeed exists in four forms: having the nature of Vāsudeva, the nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa, and likewise the form of Pradyumna.
And because his essential nature is unceasing, he is the leader of the hosts;
he exists as the embodiment of four forms, and likewise his vows are of various kinds.
On the fourth day of the month of Caitra, having properly worshipped Gaṇeśa in the form of Vāsudeva and having given a gift of gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), || 5 ||
Having performed everything according to the prescribed rules, beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal, one shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.

The vow of eating but once a day (ekabhukta) should be observed; sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) should be offered at the meal, and likewise, durva grass and vermilion (sindūraka) should be offered by the observer of the vow during worship.
Other gifts as well should be given for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa;
however, the observer of the vow himself should perform the auspicious breaking of the fast with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
By performing the vow in this manner in the world, one shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation;
having propitiated Viṣṇu, one shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, saluted by the gods.
On the fourth day of Vaiśākha, the one named Saṃkarṣaṇa is to be worshipped according to the various rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the dismissal.
Having performed [the rite], one should worship the god Gaṇeśa and feed many people;
likewise, one should make gifts such as conch shells and other offerings according to one's capacity.
By that merit, having become a performer of vows and assuming a divine body,
he reaches the world of Saṃkarṣaṇa and rejoices there for many kalpas.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Lord Pradyumna is to be worshipped;
having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas with sixteen types of offerings, [one should proceed].
Having offered fruit, roots, water, and dūrvā grass with true devotion,
the observer of the vow goes by that merit indeed to the heaven of Pradyumna.
On the fourth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, Aniruddha is to be worshipped;
the ritual of worship begins with the invocation and concludes with the dismissal.
One should worship with various flowers and the like, as well as fruits, food offerings, and so forth;
one should give many gifts and perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites. || 16 ||
The observer of the vow should ask for forgiveness when giving; he should give gourds, pumpkin vessels, and even wooden bowls to the virtuous ascetic who maintains his deposits.
Having performed this, the observer of the vow should proceed to the supreme abode of Aniruddha;
thus, having performed the vows of the four forms for twelve years.
One should perform a grand concluding rite (udyāpana) in a beautiful pavilion upon an auspicious mandala;
having placed a golden vessel there, it should be filled with the five gems and other such substances.
Then, having installed the five-faced Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed rite,
the practitioner should perform worship with the sixteen supreme articles.

By the sounds of singing and instrumental music, by Vedic mantras and hymns of praise, likewise by fire-offerings, recitations, and feasts, as well as by the giving of material gifts and so forth. ||21||
One should perform a grand and auspicious festival for the gratification of Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇa;
thus, when the concluding rite (udyāpana) is performed, the full fruit of the vow shall be attained. || 22 ||
Kṛṣṇa himself bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation here and in the hereafter;
whatever the performer of the vow desires, he shall obtain it all, including heaven. (23)
Another vow, the Satī-vrata, is prescribed for the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight;
for in ancient times, Satī was born from Dakṣa of the Brāhma lineage through Asiknī.
The observer of the vow should celebrate the birth festival of Satī; he may eat only one meal, or [partake of] fruit, or observe a fast, and he should perform great worship. (25)
Having thus performed the vow and given gifts to Viṣṇu,
the observer of the vow shall rejoice in the world of Gaṇapati’s mother, equal to Him.
Likewise, on the fourth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, there shall be another auspicious vow,
since that day is indeed the first of the ritual procedure known as Rathantara.
With a mind purified by faith, one should worship for a kalpa the Lord known as Rathantara, who is the form of Time (Kāla) and the form of Kṛṣṇa, or Gaṇeśa. ||28||
One observing the vow should perform the *ekabhukta* (once-a-day) fast; the practitioner shall obtain heaven as the fruit.
On the fourth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa—at dawn, at midday, and at the onset of night—[one should observe this].
One should indeed worship Śrī Gaṇeśa according to all the prescribed rites;
likewise, when the moonrise has occurred, the observer of the vow should worship him again.
One should offer the *arghya* water, food, and so forth, and present vermilion and other offerings;
[he is] pot-bellied, four-armed, three-eyed, and reddish-white in color.
One should visualize [the deity] adorned with various precious jewels and possessing a serene countenance;
one should worship [him] with all the ritual services, beginning with the invocation. ||32||
The observer of the vow should offer sweetmeat balls (modakas) as the food offering to please Gaṇeśa;
having thus performed the vow, he should eat the blessed modakas.
One should sleep on the ground at night and worship again in the morning;
one should give many gifts for the pleasure of Gaṇeśa and Kṛṣṇa.
By the power of this vow, having obtained the desires held in one's mind, one shall attain the supreme station, the state of Gaṇeśa, in the next world. ||35||
Therefore, by one desiring all objects of desire, this must be performed with effort;
indeed, there exists no other supreme vow equal to this.
On this very day, O Lakṣmī, the worship of Dūrvā and Gaṇeśa must be performed; I shall tell you its procedure, which brings about complete merit. (37)
Having appointed a superintendent over the gold and having placed that vessel upon a copper plate within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala; 38.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and then encircle it with red cloth;
thereafter, one should worship it with red flowers and five kinds of leaves.
With the leaves of the Bilva, Apāmārga, Śamī, Dūrvā, and Haripriyā,
one should worship with these leaves, flowers, and excellent fruits.
One should feed [the recipient] with sweetmeats and other such foods, and give an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Likewise, one should offer the water of honor (arghya), a gift, and a bed complete with its furnishings.
Having honored it, one should offer it to the Guru, who is of the nature of Vighneśa.
Having thus performed this auspicious vow of Gaṇapati for five years, [one attains the fruit]. ||42||
Having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, one shall go to the realm of Gaṇapati;
one shall be prosperous in this world and possess great happiness in the next world.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, on a Tuesday at midday, the Lord Varāha was born from the nose of Brahmā. (44)
Having fashioned a golden image of the Boar form, the observer of the vow should worship it;
he should clothe the Lord of Ramā therein with saffron-colored garments. 45.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as the food offering, and especially jars;
likewise, one should cause the hymns on the Boar Incarnation to be sung and perform worship.
Then, one should perform the meal offering with sixteen types of excellent services [to the deities]:
Narāṅga (the human-bodied one) and Sūkarāsya (the boar-faced one), both four-armed and equipped with weapons.
Having taken earth upon the tip of his tooth, he should perform the gift while appearing radiant;
by performing the vow of Viṣṇu in this manner, the observer of the vow shall attain Vaikuṇṭha. (48)
Then, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, Gaṇeśa was born as a son from the bed of Pārvatī, following the excellent vow of the Bahulā cow. 49.
O Lakṣmī, the vow of Gaṇeśa, consisting of four days, should also be performed according to the prescribed rite, preceded by a magnificent festival.
A beautiful pavilion should be constructed with green creepers, trees, branches, plantain trees, and arches, containing a *sarvatobhadra* mandala. ||51||
And Gaṇeśa should also be fashioned from clay or from metal,
or from gold, silver, copper, or even from gemstone.
Furthermore, it should be adorned with vermilion, saffron, and other such substances;
likewise, it should be beautified and worshipped with the sixteen articles.
He should be worshipped every night with sweetmeats and other offerings by one observing the vow;
he should be constantly propitiated and prayed to for the attainment of happiness. (54)
Various kinds of gifts should be given, and one should observe the vow of eating only at night;
at the conclusion, the formal dismissal of Gaṇapati should joyfully be performed.
Having thus performed the vow, the practitioner shall indeed attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, when the full year has passed, by the mother's command and with faith. (56)
On this very day, Gaṇeśa indeed performed a circumambulation of a cow;
therefore, this vow is proclaimed as the Bahulādhenu-vrata.
One should worship it here with effort using garlands, perfumes, barley, and so forth;
thereafter, one should perform circumambulation, and if capable, one should practice giving.
If, however, he is unable [to do so], he should bid her farewell after paying obeisance to her—whether she be five years old, ten years old, or even sixteen years old. (59)
Having performed the vow and its concluding rite, and having given a milch cow, one should complete the vow;
thus he shall obtain his wife and attain the fruit of the lotus-like woman.
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures here, honored by the hosts of deities, he shall attain Goloka together with his wife, sons, and others. ||61||
On this occasion, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, the vow of Siddhivaināyaka must be performed; the practitioner, observing the vow, should worship Śrī Gaṇeśa with devotion. (62)
With all the ritual services beginning with invocation, and with sweetmeats (modaka),
one should meditate with a one-pointed mind upon Gaṇeśa, the Lord of Success.
Through his marriage today to Ṛddhi and Siddhi, the daughters of Viśvakarman,
Gaṇeśa has become the leader of the Siddhis.
Therefore, one should worship that four-armed god with an elephant face, who resembles gold, possesses a single tusk, and holds a noose and a goad. 65.
Having meditated upon the auspicious, pot-bellied Śūrpakarṇa, who is smeared with vermilion and other pigments, the observer of the vow should offer the arghya and worship him once again. (66)
The observer of the vow should offer twenty-one petals with twenty-one names; hear those names as they are. (67)
One should offer a *śamī* leaf to Sumukha, a *bhṛṅga* flower to Gaṇādhīśa,
a *bilva* leaf to Umāputra, and *dūrvā* grass to Gajamukha.
One should offer a jujube fruit to Lambodara, a thorn-apple to Harasūnu,
Tulasī to Śūrpakarṇa, and a Śimbi fruit to Vakratuṇḍa.
One should offer Apāmārga to Guhabhrātṛ, Bārhatam to Ekadantin, Sindūra to Heramba, and Patraja to Caturhotṛ.
One should cause a leaf of the Agasti plant to be offered to the peaceful Lord of All;
one should present fragrant paste, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and a pair of dūrvā leaves. ||71||
One should offer five modakas and present sweet water;
having offered betel-leaf, bowed down, and made a formal prayer, one should then dismiss [the deity]. ||72||
One should offer a golden image, complete with its accessories, to the preceptor or to a Brahmin;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and feed [the recipient] with sweetmeats and other foods.
Having undertaken this vow for five years on earth, a man who worships it obtains his desires pertaining both to this world and the next. ||74||
On this fourth lunar day, one must by no means look at the moon;
for if one does look, one will undoubtedly incur a false accusation. ||75||
Therefore, for the destruction of those defects, one should recite the eternal mantra:
"Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Nṛsiṃha at the onset of night. (76)
The lion was killed by the Śarabha, and the Śarabha became Śaṅkara;
the moon was held by Śaṅkara—may Hara remove false curses. (77)
Having uttered this, no false stigma indeed arises among people;
one should pay homage to Śiva, the moon-crested one, endowed with devotion. (78)
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should worship the Lord Vināyaka Kapardīśa with the Puruṣasūkta and with ritual offerings.
One should give rice grains to the young student (baṭu), who has been honored with perfumes and flowers;
may this Kapardin Gaṇanātha be pleased by these offerings of rice.
"May Gaṇeśa, who bears the form of Kṛṣṇa, grant me both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Having performed the vow in this manner, O embodied being, one shall certainly attain Goloka. ||81||
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Nāga-vrata is proclaimed;
it should be performed by people in every way for the purpose of destroying snakebites and other such harms. 82.

Having performed the morning vow and ritual resolve, and having drunk the pure water from the horns of a cow and bathed, he should then, at midday, [worship] the serpents such as Śaṅkhapāla and others.
The remainder, however, one should worship with ritual services preceded by invocation;
one should perform nourishment with milk and offer milk to the enjoyer.
When the Nāga-vow is thus performed, serpents do not bite at all;
nor do poisons cause affliction, due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā.
In ancient times, Brahmā said to the serpents, "Do not bite those who worship you during the month of Kārttika";
and so they do not bite their worshippers at all.
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, the vow known as Karaka is prescribed;
women alone have the authority for this, and it must be performed by them alone. (87)
Having bathed and adorned his body, he should worship Gaṇanāyaka;
beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), he should perform everything according to the prescribed rite.
In front of that, one should place ten vessels of fully cooked food;
or, one should place ten jars filled with water in front of that.
Having uttered, "May the God be pleased with me," one should thus offer [the gifts];
and one should give ten water-pots to married women.
And then, when the moon has risen, she should offer sweet foods;
having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite, the woman should eat only sweets. (91)
For the fulfillment of the vow, one should give to a twice-born man a jar filled with milk or water, enriched with betel nuts, unbroken grains, and gems. (92)
Having thus observed the vow for sixteen or twelve years,
the woman should then perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and thereby complete the vow.
Or rather, for as long as she lives, a noble woman desiring good fortune should perform this vow; for women, there is nothing equal to this bestower of good fortune. 94.
Indeed, there is nothing else in the world that should be performed with such effort as he who is Maṅgala, the best of planets, and the very son of the Earth. (95)
On this lunar day, that very Bindu of Śaṅkara was produced;
therefore, one who desires welfare should perform the Aṅgāraka vow.
Maṅgala always bestows auspiciousness and prosperity upon him;
one should diligently observe the vow of eating once a day or at night. (97)
Likewise, the worship and recitation of the mantra of Maṅgala should be performed, for they grant one's desires;
so too should the offering of red gems and the gift of red garments and other such items.
At that time, the practitioner should perform the gift of red wheat;
likewise, the gift of red sesame seeds brings about all prosperity.

From the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, for as long as a year, the person observing the vow should pass the time by eating only one meal a day, and for the remainder of the year, by eating only at night.
The third year is spent by means of unasked-for alms, and the fourth by fasts;
thus, for four years, one should perform this vow without sloth. (101)
This is the Vināyaka-vrata; having worshipped the sixteen articles originating from Vināyaka in Kāśī, [one should do so] on all fourth lunar days (caturthī). || 102 ||
One should give all kinds of gifts according to one's ability and according to one's wealth;
at the end of the year or at the conclusion of the vow, one should perform the great rite of completion (udyāpana).
One should have Śrī Gaṇapati fashioned [as] a rat and a golden chariot;
or else, everything may be made of copper, wood, or clay.
Having had it prepared as appropriate— either a lotus with beautiful petals or a *sarvatobhadra* mandala fashioned from grain.
Having placed a suitable and auspicious jar in the center, accompanied by a copper vessel,
one should fill it with rice and install Vināyaka therein.
With invocations and other rites, with ritual ablutions, with vermilion, sandalwood paste, and so forth;
with dūrvā grass, flowers, garments, ornaments, incense, lamps, and fragrant perfumes.

With offerings consisting of sweetmeats (modaka), fruits, and the chewing of betel leaf; with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), handfuls of flowers in the form of hymns of praise, and likewise with vigils (jāgara). || 108 ||
One should worship and please the God with songs, instrumental music, and recitations;
at dawn, one should offer sugar, rice, barley, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and other such items.
One should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite with bilva fruits and white mustard seeds;
[the deities to be invoked are] Gaṇa, Gaṇādhipa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Tripurāntaka.
Lambodara, Ekadanta, Rukmadaṃṣṭra, and Vighnapa;
then Brahmā, Yama, Varuṇa, Soma, Sūrya, and Hutāśana. || 111 ||
With the sixteen names beginning with "Gandhamādin" and "Parameṣṭhin," as well as the name "Vakrasutuṇḍa," there are thus one hundred and eight names.
One should indeed offer oblations into the fire with devotion and perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
then, having worshipped the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas) and twenty-four brahmins.
One should satisfy [the deity] with modakas, milk-rice (pāyasa), vegetables, and pūrikās;
then one should give to the preceptor (ācārya) a milch cow together with her calf.
And he should likewise offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as generously as his means allow;
furthermore, having bowed to the brahmins, he should bestow gifts upon others as well. (115)
Having dismissed [the guests], he should eat with his kinsmen with a joyful mind;
having thus performed this vow and enjoyed these excellent pleasures here. (116)
Through the grace of Vināyaka, one shall attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu.
This is declared to be the excellent vow that bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the fourth day of the month of Pauṣa, having worshipped Vināyaka,
one should feed a single Brahmin and bestow sweetmeats as a sacrificial fee.
When this is done, one indeed becomes a practitioner of vows and a vessel for all prosperity;
on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the vow of Gaurī is highly esteemed.
Gaurī is to be worshipped with devotion by men and women, together with the hosts of Yoginīs, using *kunda* flowers, red flowers, and the like. (1.269.120)
With red threads, lac-dye, incense, lamps, and excellent food, as well as with guḍa-laddukas, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 121 ||
Worthy women who possess good fortune and virtuous Brahmins should especially be honored and given gifts for the sake of increasing one's own good fortune.
Gifts of food, garments, and excellent fruits—this Gaurī-vrata, O Lakṣmī, increases good fortune and health. (123)
This vow of Gaṇeśa, known as the Ḍhuṇḍhi-vrata, should be performed every year again and again; therein Gaṇeśa is worshipped. 1.24.
He has come to Kāśī and remains here for the sake of searching for the devotees of Śambhu;
therefore, this vow must be performed by one who desires his own welfare. (125)
The Kuṇḍavrata, as well as the Śāntivrata and the Lalitāvratam, are indeed this very Tilavrata, which is also celebrated as the Kunda-vrata. (126)
Whatever bathing, charity, recitation, fire-offerings, and libations may have been performed,
they shall become multiplied a thousandfold by pleasing Gaurī and Gaṇeśa.
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should observe the Saṃkaṣṭahāraka vow,
undertaking a fast after observing the rising of the moon.
Having fashioned an auspicious Gaṇeśa with his weapons and vehicle out of clay,
and having placed him upon a pedestal, one should worship him with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
One should offer sweetmeats and sesame powder mixed with sugar;
one should present the *arghya* in a copper vessel blended with red sandalwood.
The observer of the vow should offer kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken grains, śamī leaves, and curd as the arghya offering; thereafter, he should perform the ritual dismissal.
One should feed virtuous Brahmins, holy women, and young boys and girls;
the observer of the vow should then perform the breaking of the fast and give gifts with devotion.
Having thus performed the vow, one who is prosperous shall never encounter distress;
he shall be endowed with wealth, grain, sons, daughters, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth. (133)
Furthermore, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, there is the Ḍhuṇḍhirāja vow.
He should be worshipped collectively with all kinds of articles. || 134 ||
By pleasing Lord Ḍhuṇḍhirāja with offerings of sesame paste and sesame seeds, as well as through gifts, fire oblations, and worship, one shall obtain all prosperity.
By giving a golden elephant-faced [image] along with wealth to a twice-born man, the observer of the vow attains many objects of enjoyment; there is no doubt in this matter. (136)
In whichever month it may be, the fourth lunar day (caturthī) joined with Sunday or with Tuesday yields especially great fruit.
In as many fourth-day festivals as there may be, Vighneśa and Kṛṣṇa alone are indeed to be worshipped;
likewise, the Pañcāyatana should be worshipped with a spirit of devotion.
The concluding rite (udyāpana) must be performed for the vow; likewise, there should be restraint and self-control, and celibacy must be observed, so that the fruit may indeed be eternal. || 139 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vārṣika Caturthī Vows, including the Vows of Gaṇeśa-as-Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; the Satī-janma-vrata, Rathantara-kalpa, Varāha-jayantī, Gaṇeśa-jayantī, Cow-circumambulation, Siddhivināyaka-vrata, Nāga-vrata, Karaka-vrata, Aṅgāraka-vrata, Kāśī-vināyaka-vrata, Ḍhuṇḍhirāja-vrata, and others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the vows of the five [pañcamīs],
by performing which people attain happiness, liberation, and prosperity.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Hari was born as a fish;
a golden fish should be fashioned, and for it a great festival should be celebrated.
This Matsya, the son of Brahmā, who indeed slew Hayagrīva and recovered the Vedas, is to be worshipped by one desiring prosperity.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, he who commanded the fish to protect the seeds in a boat while they were being worshipped— verily, he alone is worthy of worship.
Half of him has the form of a man and half the form of a fish;
he is golden and should be worshipped on the bank of the Kṛtamālā river along with Satyaka.
Holding a conch in his left hand and a mace in his right, he is auspicious and adorned with a crown;
for the food offering, there should be curd-rice as well as vada cakes mixed with curd.
One should give gifts and cause the verse concerning the narrative of the Fish Incarnation to be sung;
one should present offerings to the preceptor and partake of the meal following the *ārārtika* rite.
This is declared to be Śrīpañcamī, wherein Śrī performed penance for the sake of attaining the face of Śrīkṛṣṇa; therefore, the vow and the worship of Śrī should be performed.
With offerings such as perfumes and the like, with food offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and so forth,
with ornaments, fruits, flowers, and excellent articles for the temple.
Lakṣmī does not abandon the worshiper of Lakṣmī, nor the female worshiper;
and on this lunar day, the Earth was lifted upon the waters by the Boar.
A virtuous vow for her should be performed through the worship of the deity's form and other rites;
she should also observe the Candra-vrata here, which destroys all decay.
The waning of the moon was brought to an end through the power of penance and the grace of Śambhu;
and on this fifth lunar day, the incarnation of Hayagrīva took place.
One should perform the Hayagrīva vow and worship the horse-faced deity,
[representing] the human body made of gold, equipped with weapons and accompanied by the earth.
One should worship Vāsudeva Janārdana, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa,
according to the prescribed rite, and likewise feed him with roasted chickpeas.
One should give gifts of medicinal herbs, juices, water, and fruits;
by constantly observing this vow, one shall be free from disease and possessed of wealth and grain.
Then, on the fifth day of Vaiśākha, Śeṣa is to be worshipped here by men;
through that, one obtains the desired fruit granted by the hosts of Nāgas.
The Nāgas do not cause any harm whatsoever in the house of one who observes the vow;
indeed, they become its protectors in the field, the garden, and likewise in the grove. 17.
Then, on the fifth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the wise man should worship the ancestors;
indeed, through these libations to the ancestors, the attainment of the fruits of all desires shall come to pass.
Now, on the fifth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, the Vāyu-vrata is proclaimed;
having gone outside the village, one should remain standing upon a height of earth.
And one should raise a five-colored banner fixed to the tip of a bamboo pole; one should place it thus and worship the base of the pole.
In whichever direction the banner goes when impelled by the wind,
one should perform the worship of the lords of that direction at the base of the staff.
In whichever watch of the night the wind blows during the first and subsequent watches,
one should properly perform worship for each respective lord of that direction.
Remaining thus without food for four watches of the night outside,
he should return in the evening, eat his own meal, and sleep for a moment on the ground.
Whatever dream arises during the night will certainly come to pass;
if indeed anything inauspicious is seen, one should observe a fast.
Having performed the worship of Śiva at night, one should feed eight brahmins;
by that, one enjoys auspicious fruit, and as a gift, one should give cows and other such things.
This vow has been well-proclaimed as an indicator of the auspicious and inauspicious;
it generates good fortune for men and brings happiness both in this world and the next.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, a vow that increases the abundance of food should be performed by people; for it brings about the prosperity of all kinds of food.
On the fourth day, at the end of the day, O Lotus-born One, one should moisten all the grains with water in separate vessels, and then [proceed] in the morning.
When the sun has risen, he should offer those very same waters, as well as well-cooked grains, to the ancestors, the gods, and the deities. (29)
One should offer those very beautiful things to beggars;
then, having gone to the temple of Śambhu at night, one should worship the Liṅga with perfumes and other offerings.
One should recite "Namaḥ Śivāya" and pray for the successful attainment of food—both the autumnal grains and likewise those of the springtime. (31)
"May I be enriched by those [merits] in birth after birth.
Having thus prayed and given food to the Brahmins, he remained restrained in speech. (32)
One should consume only those [fruits], for that is indeed the vow that produces food; it generates all kinds of nourishment and bestows a favorable state of rebirth in the next world. (33)
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the Jīvantikā-vrata is observed;
the observer of the vow should worship Indrāṇī with the leaves, flowers, and other parts of the jīvantī plant.
On both sides of the door, one should draw fierce serpents with cow dung;
having worshipped them and bowed down to the twice-born, [one should proceed].
One should give gifts of gold, silver, and so forth, which bestow infinite fruit;
one should observe the vow of eating but once a day, surrounded by wife, children, and friends. (36)
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should satisfy the nāgas with milk;
his family shall remain entirely free from fear of serpents for seven generations.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should worship the best of sages;
having bathed early in the morning and having fashioned an altar out of clay adorned with flowers.
Having spread kuśa grass there, one should indeed worship the Seven Sages with various perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
One should offer ṛṣyanna for the meal, and especially nivāra rice;
the performer of the vow should cook the food offering with śyāmāka and other grains grown without cultivation.
The observer of the vow, having partaken of the pleasing food, should feed seven preceptors;
he should fashion seven images of matted-hair ascetics, each provided with a sacred thread.
Having placed those [images] made of gold, or [made of silver], in vessels of copper or clay, one should devoutly bathe them with the waters of the five nectars and other liquids. ||42||
Having worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings, one should present the arghya;
then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds, sacrificial oblations, rice, ghee, barley, and so forth.
Having offered oblations with meritorious mantras and names, one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should give seven cows, adorned with garments and ornaments, to the Veda-teacher.
One should indeed give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor for the completion of the vow;
having fed the preceptors and the Brahmins, one should bow down and dismiss them. ||45||

One should personally and respectfully offer palatable food together with one's kinsmen; by thus performing the vow with all its constituent parts, the practitioner shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 46.
O King, by performing this vow, a woman indeed shakes off even the slightest of faults.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, Kṛṣṇa himself is indeed Gopāla. 47.
He was born at Kuṅkumavāpī in the temple of Nimbadevānikā;
Kṛṣṇa should be fashioned with four arms and worshipped according to the prescribed rite. ||48||
A great festival should be celebrated with vows, gifts, and feasts;
he should be worshipped with reverence, together with his wife, Kambharā Lakṣmī. (49)
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina is the Upāṅgalalitā vow;
in ancient times, this vow was performed by Lalitā for the sake of attaining Hari.
O Lotus-born one, having fashioned her image out of gold according to one's ability,
one should worship it with the sixteen types of offerings according to the prescribed rite.
For the completion of the vow, one should give to a Brāhmaṇa cooked food combined with fruit, accompanied by ghee and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), which is pleasing to the sight. 5.2.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, for the sake of attaining Hari through victory,
the Jayā-vrata was performed here with sixteen auspicious articles and other offerings.
Having worshipped, fed, and given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and so forth, the observer of the vow should thereafter dismiss [the deities] and then eat himself. 54.
During the Jayā-vrata, one should perform a bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha) which destroys sins;
one shall obtain the fruit of bathing at the concluding purificatory rite (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
A sonless man obtains a son, and a barren woman becomes pregnant;
a sick person shall attain health, and the observer of the vow shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having worshipped the Nāgas with devotion on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and having obtained freedom from fear from the Nāgas, he rejoices together with his kinsmen.
