On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is to be worshipped;
likewise, the ancestors and the Nāgas are to be worshipped, for they are considered to be bestowers of happiness. ||58||
The Vasantavrata is prescribed for the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha; at that time, worship of Vasanta should be performed and one should observe the practice of eating only once a day.
And with crops of fresh wheat, as well as jujube leaves,
wild dates, black mustard, and various grasses.
Having made the pavilion green, one should worship it with saffron and other substances;
the practitioner of the vow should worship the water-pot filled with colored waters.
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa and cause games to be played with colored powders;
having thus performed the vow, one should cause parched grain and dates to be given to people.
This vow brings about the attainment of enjoyment, liberation, and happiness;
for it was on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna that Lakṣmī was born as Kaṃbharā.
In the morning, that festival should be celebrated at the House of Love, the abode of Om;
for the four-armed Mahālakṣmī is indeed to be worshipped there in golden form. 64.
The vow, along with its constituent parts, should be performed, as it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is to be worshipped.
Then the Blessed One shall pacify the defects suggested by the Holi festival and other such matters;
thus, one who desires happiness should perform these observances according to their capacity.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Annual Pañcamī Vows— namely Matsyajayantī, Śrītapovrata, Vārāha, Pṛthvīvrata, Candrakṣayanāśavrata, Hayagrīvajayantī, Nāgapañcamī, Pitṛvrata, Vāyuvrata, Navavṛddhivrata, Jīvantikānāgavrata, Ṛṣipañcamī, Gopālakṛṣṇajayantī, Lalitāvrata, Jayāvrata, Nāgavrata, Vasantapañcamī, Kambharālakṣmīvrata, and others"— in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe to you the various vows of the Vārṣika-ṣaṣṭhī, which indeed bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In ancient times, the birth of Skanda occurred on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra;
this Kumāra-vrata should be observed with worship and other such rites.
One should worship the six-faced [Kārttikeya] together with his peacock and the commander of the army;
the observer of the vow should offer food and gifts with great devotion.
By means of this vow, a son who is powerful, heroic, endowed with all virtues, and long-lived is certainly obtained by the practitioner of the vow.
For the completion of the vow, one should cause the preceptor to be presented with a golden image of Śaṅkara, Pārvatī, and Skanda, adorned with all kinds of articles.
On the sixth lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha as well, the observer of the vow should worship Kārttikeya;
he obtains the happiness derived from his mother, such as being fondled, protected, and so forth.
On the sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Sun;
by the grace of the Sun, one obtains all desired objects.
Furthermore, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the Skanda-vrata;
thereby one obtains all desired objects and a lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
And on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the one born under the Śara constellation;
by the grace of the Six-faced One, one obtains all desired objects.
On this very day, the devotee should observe the vow of eating only soup and boiled rice;
he should offer it to Hari and then partake of that which is His grace.
Except for rice with soup, nothing else should be eaten during the practice of eating a single meal;
by this vow, Śrī Hari shall then grant rice with soup.
On this very day, I shall indeed become Kalki;
one should perform my birth-vow while I am mounted upon a white horse.
One should worship me with an umbrella, weapons, and adorned with golden necklaces;
I shall provide protection from the suffering caused by heretics and the wicked for one who seeks the merit of the vow.
On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the observer of the vow should worship Lalitā;
a virtuous woman seeking the fruit of the vow, having bathed and wearing white garments, [should perform the rite].
Having taken sand from the confluence of two rivers, one should fashion a lump;
and having fashioned Lalitā with lotuses and oleanders, [one should worship her]. (15)
One should worship with blue lotuses, mālatī flowers, and ketaka flowers.
Then, one should offer one hundred and eight flowers to her.
Standing before her, one should pray to Lalitā, the beloved of Śrī Hari,
at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, or the Nīla mountain.
Likewise, having bathed at Kanakhala, she obtained Hari as her husband;
O increaser of good fortune, grant me also union with Śrī Hari. (18)
Having thus prayed and performed worship, one should place the food offering (naivedya) before [the deity],
consisting of coconuts, cucumbers, pumpkins, pomegranates, and citrons.
One should adorn the front with *cirbhaṭṭa* and *karkaṭikā* fruits,
as well as with fresh sprouts and leaves, rows of lamps, and archways.
The observer of the vow, with sincere devotion, should feed [the deity] with fragrant incenses, various offerings of food, diverse kinds of sweetmeats, as well as *śaṣkulī* cakes and *modaka* sweets.
One should perform the ārārtrika offering and observe a vigil at night with songs,
instrumental music, dances, devotional hymns, and the chanting of the Name.
Accompanied by her friends, that virtuous woman should not close her eyes;
having gone to a river on the seventh lunar day, she should bathe and then worship it.
Having given gifts to the twice-born, having likewise offered oblations into the fire,
and having honored the gods, the ancestors, men, and married women, || 24 ||
The observer of the vow should feed Brāhmaṇas, maidens, virtuous men, and virtuous women;
having prayed, "May Lalitā be well-pleased with me," he should dismiss them. 25.
A man or a woman should thus observe this supreme vow which bestows good fortune;
it cannot be attained by other vows, austerities, gifts, observances, or restraints. (26)
That fruit which is easily obtained in the eternal world hereafter,
the observer of the vow enjoys it while traveling in a celestial chariot together with the goddess Lalitā.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, there is the vow of Candana-ṣaṣṭhī; on that day, Lakṣmī should be worshipped with sandalwood paste, ornaments, and other offerings.
Indeed, when the sixth lunar day is conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism and Mars, it is called Kāpilā;
on that day, one should worship the Sun with sixteen types of excellent offerings.
The performer of the vow shall obtain his desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
This is the Sūrya-ṣaṣṭhī vow, [granted] by the grace of Bhāskara.

Recitation, fire-offerings, as well as giving gifts and the libations to the ancestors, gods, and sages—all auspicious acts performed by one observing a vow are to be known as entirely inexhaustible. (31)
Having worshipped a tawny cow with garlands, saffron, and food,
one should indeed give her, along with all her appurtenances, to the preceptor for the satisfaction of the Sun.
By performing this vow in this manner, a woman shall obtain supreme happiness;
she shall find a husband and a home enriched with flavorful food, fruits, ornaments, and other luxuries. (33)
Furthermore, O beloved, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, Kātyāyanī should indeed be worshipped with fragrant and auspicious substances, and with foods of sweet and excellent flavors.
Pārvatī herself is indeed proclaimed as Kālā, Kātyāyanī, and Prasū;
O beloved, her image made of sand is to be worshipped here, or else that of the wife of a twice-born man.
Having given garments and ornaments, having bowed and asked for forgiveness, he should dismiss her;
thus the maiden seeking the vow shall obtain a most beautiful husband through fate. (26)
A woman desiring a son shall obtain a son through the grace of Kātyāyanī;
this was [ordained] by the high-souled Ṣaṇmukha on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
One should worship Skanda, who is accompanied by Devasenā and honored by all the gods, with offerings, having first obtained a wife named Devasenā. ||38||
Likewise, worship of the fire and the fire-oblation (homa) must also be performed with devotion;
thus the observer of the vow shall enjoy eternal success as desired by the mind. || 35 ||
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the wise Kārttikeya slew the Daitya Tāraka; thereafter, Brahmā and the other gods performed the worship of Skanda.
One who observes the vow should perform the supreme worship with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with fruits and other offerings, and with garments, ornaments, and weapons.
Sweet food is prescribed as the offering, and the gift is traditionally considered to be cattle and land;
if this [lunar day] is joined with Sunday and conjoined with the Śatabhiṣaj asterism, [it is especially auspicious]. ||4||
Then that [day] is called Campā-ṣaṣṭhī; indeed, Hara is to be worshipped there, and every act such as bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, is said to become inexhaustible.
A great worship should be performed for Hara and likewise for Hari; the observer of the vow should, moreover, give various gifts with sincere devotion. (44)
Having obtained happiness through this vow, a man or a woman shall go to the imperishable state.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, the Sun-god Prabhēśvara is to be worshipped.
The protector of the world, having the form of Viṣṇu, was indeed born again from the Creator;
this Nārāyaṇa is the Lord himself, the maker of light for all. ||46||
Those desiring happiness should worship with the sixteen supreme substances and so forth;
thus their visual splendor will increase and they shall become a treasury of wealth and prosperity. (47)
Having had a golden image of Sūrya, adorned with a beautiful crown and accompanied by Brahmā, fashioned, the observer of the vow should give it as a gift to a twice-born man. 48.
The sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha is considered the Varuṇotpatti;
on that day, the Lord of Waters, the Sovereign of Gods who is the very form of Viṣṇu, is indeed to be worshipped.
Worshipped with red perfumes, garments, flowers, incense, food offerings, and lamps by one observing the vow, he shall grant auspicious and excellent flavors according to his desire.
And on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should have an image of the Lord Hara Paśupati made,
either of clay or of gold, and worship it.
Having bathed [the deity] separately with the Śatarudriya and with the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should anoint [him] with white sandalwood and fragrant substances, and offer unbroken rice grains (akṣata) and flowers.
Having worshipped with white dhattūra flowers and bilva fruits along with excellent leaves, one should offer sweet foods as the sacrificial oblation (naivedya).
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), bowed down, and asked for forgiveness, one should then dismiss [the deity].
Having performed this vow, whether man or woman, at the conclusion of their enjoyments, they shall attain the state of Śiva.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Vārṣika-Ṣaṣṭhī Vows, including the Kārtika-Svāmijayantī, Divākara-vrata, the Festival of Skanda’s Birth, the Sūpaudana-āśana-vrata, the Kalki-jayantī, the Lalitā-Hariprāpti-vrata, the Candana-Ṣaṣṭhī, Kapilā-Ṣaṣṭhī, the Kātyāyanī-vrata, the Devasenā-vrata, the Skanda-vrata for the slayer of Tāraka, the Campā-Ṣaṣṭhī, the Viṣṇu-jayantī, the Sūrya-jayantī, the Varuṇa-jayantī, and other vows," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, I shall indeed describe to you the vows of the Saptamīs of the rainy season,
by performing which the observer of the vow attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform a ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha). There, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be smeared with cow dung and covered with white clay.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus there, upon its pericarp one should place the Fire-god,
and on the eastern petal Ravi and Hari.
Then, having placed Anala in the southeast, Śukra in the south, Maṅgala and Yama in the southwest, Nirṛti in the southwest, and Rāhu and Ketu thereafter; || 4 ||
In the west are Śani and Varuṇa; in the northwest, Anila and Candra;
in the north, Budha and Kubera; and in the northeast, Guru and Hara.
Having seated them all, one should worship them with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
as well as with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, betel, fruits, and mouth-fresheners.
The observer of the vow should perform one hundred and eight oblations with clarified butter;
he should offer eight oblations for each individual name-mantra.
Then one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and give an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
in this manner, indeed, one should perform the worship and the vow for the guardians of the directions.
Having observed the vow of eating but once a day, one shall obtain all happiness;
at the end of the body, having pierced the solar orb, one goes to the supreme state.
In ancient times, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Jahnu drank the Gaṅgā and then released her;
this is considered the Gaṅgā-vrata.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, one should worship her with ritual offerings;
indeed, one who desires prosperity should perform the gift of a thousand jars.
This auspicious Gaṅgā-vrata leads seven generations of one's family to heaven;
on this lunar day, the Kamala-vrata is likewise to be understood.
A beautiful lotus should be fashioned from gold weighing only a sesame seed;
having covered it with a pair of garments, one should worship it with perfumes, incense, and other offerings.
In the evening, having bowed to the Sun, one should then offer a lotus to a brahmin;
one should also offer a water-pot, that lotus, and a tawny cow to the brahmin.
One should observe the fast and break it on the following day;
one should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas, as well as virtuous men, women, and faithful wives.
In this manner, the vow should be performed and likewise gifts of cows should be given;
the woman who performs the vow shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, and she shall rejoice in wealth.
On this very lunar day, the auspicious Nimbavrata should be performed;
the worship of the Sun should be carried out, especially with nimba leaves.
One should eat nimba leaves and sleep on the ground; this brings about destruction [of the affliction].
On the following day, having fed the Brahmins, one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
This Śarkarāsaptamī bestows all flavors upon the earth; therefore, those who desire such flavors should observe the vow of sugar. (19)
As the Sun was drinking the nectar from his hand, drops of nectar fell upon the earth, and from them grew rice, mung beans, barley, and sugarcane.
Sugar produced from sugarcane is always beloved by the Sun and is auspicious;
it is pure for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and should be given for the gratification of the deities.
In this matter, the taking of sugar and likewise the eating of sugar must be performed properly by one observing the vow; it increases the lineage of sons.
It pacifies all suffering and bestows the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
furthermore, other gifts should be bestowed and virtuous men should be fed. (23)
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, Indra himself became the Sun;
one should observe a fast and perform the vow, worshipping Indra according to the prescribed rite.
O twice-born one, a gift of gold must be made to Indra;
having fed the virtuous and the children, the observer of the vow should then eat himself. (15)
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the Sun named Vivasvat attained his royal consecration; his worship is prescribed in the vow.
Having worshipped Vivasvant with golden [images] and with flowers and other offerings, one attains union with him and divine, eternal happiness. || 27 ||
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the vow known as Arvya is prescribed;
on this occasion, cotton cloth should especially be given as a gift. (28)
If the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) should coincide with the Hasta asterism, it bestows merit;
on this day, all acts such as giving gifts, recitation, and fire-offerings attain imperishability.
This is indeed the Śītalāsaptamī, a sacrifice to the virtuous Pārvatī;
a garment and food made of flour and other ingredients should be offered to Śītalā.
By that, health shall indeed always prevail within the family of the observer of the vow;
a fast should be observed, and gifts such as fruit and other offerings should be given. (31)
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, there is the vow known as Amuktābharaṇa; indeed, on that day, Śambhu wore the moon upon his forehead as an ornament.
One should perform the worship of Soma and Maheśa with the sixteen [upacāras] and other offerings; having bowed, one should dismiss them for the fulfillment of all desires.
This is considered the "Fruit-Saptamī," consisting of seven fruits:
the coconut, the eggplant, the orange, and the citron. (34)
One should offer these fruits: the kūṣmāṇḍa, the bruhati, and the pūga;
and here, one should also present a beautiful wrist-thread made of seven strands with seven knots.
Having offered it to Śaṅkara, one should then bind it to the left hand;
a woman on the left and a man on the right hand shall preserve it for a year with great care.
At the conclusion of the vow, the observer of the vow, having fed seven children,
should then eat himself along with his wife for the sake of completing the vow.
One should indeed give fruits to the twice-born for the sake of their satisfaction;
thus, having performed the vow according to the rules for seven years. (38)
O Lakṣmī, she who observes that vow attains union with Mahādeva;
her worship should be performed according to the prescribed rules and according to one's wealth. (39)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the Pañcagavya vow is prescribed;
it is proclaimed as Śubhasaptamī, which bestows purity as well as merit.
Having bathed and worshipped the god Hari-Sūrya, the observer of the vow should then worship a tawny cow (kapilā-gau) and pray to her; listen, O beloved. (41)
"I give you to you, O most auspicious lady; may Aryaman himself be pleased.
Protect the entire world through the power of your righteousness and merit. (42)

Having recited this and bowed down, one should offer the liquid to a twice-born man; then, fearing the consequences of the vow, one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform the breaking of the fast on the following day.
Having fed the best of the twice-born, the observer of the vow should partake of the remains;
by the grace of Śiva, he shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now, on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, there is the vow known as Śākāsaptamī.
The observer of the vow should subsist on vegetables and offer seven types of vegetables to a virtuous person.
Then, on the seventh day, one should give food and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a twice-born man;
on the second day, one should perform the breaking of the fast—this is the vow that removes all sins.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Mitra-vrata is proclaimed.
On that day, the Sun, named Mitra, was born to Kaśyapa from Aditi. ||47||
His vow, accompanied by fasting and celebration, should be performed as a supreme duty;
worship should be conducted according to the prescribed rite, and one should feed the virtuous with sweet food.
Having given a gift of gold as a sacrificial fee, the observer of the vow should then dismiss [the deity];
on the following morning, having bowed again to the Sun, he should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
Having thus performed this very vow here, one indeed goes to the world of the Sun;
whoever performs this vow here shall obtain birth in a noble family.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one should observe the vow named Abhaya;
the practitioner of the vow, remaining on the ground, should likewise worship the Sun at the three times of day.
Having observed a fast, he should feed seven other Brahmins;
he should give milk-rice and a prastha measure of sweetmeats (modakas) to the twice-born.
The observer of the vow should offer a greater sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), such as land or gold;
and the Brahmins, being givers of fearlessness, should likewise bestow blessings upon him.
This vow is known as Abhaya, and it is remembered as the bestower of fearlessness upon all.
This vow is also called Mārtaṇḍa; the observer of the vow should worship Mārtaṇḍa.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, there is a vow named Sarvāpti;
on that occasion, one should perform the worship of the Sun while observing a fast.
A vigil should be kept at night; then, in the morning, virtuous people should be fed.
They should be gratified with milk-rice (pāyasa), monetary gifts (dakṣiṇā), fruits, and other offerings. 56.
Having released [the deity] from there, the observer of the vow should eat and go wherever he desires.
This vow, indeed, bestows all attainments and fulfills every wish. 57.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the vow known as Acala is prescribed; one should observe a fast, by which merit becomes as firm and unshakable as a mountain. (58)
Hara, accompanied by Trilocanā, is to be worshipped as Trilocana;
this Jayantī of Trilocanā has been composed as the remover of all sins. (59)
This Rathīyasaptamī indeed bestows the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
one should worship the golden Śrīsūrya seated upon a chariot yoked with elephants.
This is the Bhāskarīsaptamī; on this day, the observer of the vow himself [should offer] seven leaves each of the arka and the badarī.
One should bathe while placing [the image] upon one's head for the pacification of infamy from seven previous births;
this "Vow that Grants Sons" must be performed by one who desires a son.
Sūrya, being greatly pleased by his own portion, shall become his son.
Having fasted on the following day, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the morning. 6.3.
One should feed them curd-rice and milk, and honor the virtuous;
by performing the vow in this manner, one shall indeed obtain a long-lived son.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should observe the Arkapuṭa vow;
one should worship the Sun with Arka leaves and consume Arka leaves.
One should constantly recite the name of the Sun; this is considered the solar vow (arkavrata).
It is auspicious and bestows wealth, sons, daughters, prosperity, a husband, and a wife. 66.
Since this bestows dharma, artha, and kāma, and destroys all sins,
one should perform this vow of sacrifice for the sake of easily attaining all happiness.
The worship of Bhāskara bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
therefore, one should worship the Sun on every seventh lunar day (saptamī).
The Sarvatobhadra mandala, the installation of the ritual jars,
the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the ritual services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
The performer of the vow should always perform everything according to the prescribed rule, ending with the offering of food (naivedya), rice grains, flowers, and the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
One should perform a grand concluding ceremony (udyāpana) and feed virtuous children;
indeed, charity, fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa), and devotion to Śrī Hari are certain [to bring success]. //71//

That which must be performed by one observing the vow so that great satisfaction may arise in Hari, through which both enjoyment and liberation may occur, and the full fruit of the vow may be attained. || 72 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Vows such as the Dikpāla-vrata, Jāhnavī-vrata, Nimba-sūrya-vrata, Indra-sūrya-vrata, Vivasvat-abhiṣeka-vrata, Avyaṅga-śītalā-saptamī, Candrābharaṇa-vrata, Śubhaphala-saptamī, Śāka-vrata, Mitrārka-jayantī, Mārtaṇḍābhaya-vrata, Sārvakāmika-āpti-vrata, Trilocanā-jayantī, Bhāskarī-saptamī, Putraprada-arkapuṭa-vrata, and others," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the vows of the eighth lunar days (Aṣṭamīs),
by performing which, O lotus-born one, the observer of the vow attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the auspicious vow for the birth of Pārvatī [is observed];
a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars and Aśoka archways [should be prepared].
Having constructed a Sarvatobhadra mandala there and having placed a golden image of Pārvatī in its center, one should perform a hundred circumambulations.
One should worship [the deity] with the sixteen excellent articles, beginning with water for the feet and ending with food;
having placed [the image] upon a chariot, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and carry out the ritual of incense.
Devotees should perform a great festival of processions with songs, instrumental music, and other offerings;
in every house, [the deity] should be worshipped with rice, parched grain, water, and fruits.
One should perform the *vardhana* (consecration) with auspicious substances such as saffron, collyrium, and ornaments,
as well as with a coconut fruit or even a water-pot.
Thus, preceded by a great festival, having brought her either to the water or to the temple, one should worship her and then perform the *ārārtika* ceremony.
Having fed the Goddess of Gods according to the prescribed rite, one should dismiss her;
one should give all kinds of gifts, as well as clothing and food to young girls.
By performing this vow in this manner, a woman obtains auspicious good fortune;
and a maiden, having performed this supreme vow, shall attain the status of a queen.
Right here, one should perform the consumption of eight buds of the *aśoka* tree;
for one who thus performs this consumption, sorrow never arises anywhere.
This very same day is known as Mahāṣṭamī; it must be observed with a fast, and the worship of Pārvatī must be performed, concluding with the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should observe a fast;
that is called Durgāṣṭamī, and one should worship Aparājitā.
One should offer an oblation of food mixed with sugar and indeed give gifts at that time;
furthermore, one should feed young maidens on the ninth day before the breaking of the fast.
Abiding in a celestial chariot of light as one observing the vow, by the power of Aparājita’s compassion,
he shall wander through the heavenly worlds and become endowed with both enjoyment and liberation.
Upon the arrival of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should perform the Trilocana-vrata;
such a person shall dwell on Kailāsa for the duration of a kalpa, highly honored.
On the morning of the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the white Durgā;
by the grace of the goddess Śuklā, the observer of the vow attains Kailāsa.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow should worship the Goddess;
he should offer an oblation accompanied by sugar and feed young girls.

Having given gold as a sacrificial fee and having dismissed [the officiants], the observer of the vow himself should depart. By performing this auspicious vow, one shall attain the world of Durgā. || 18 ||
Likewise, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, the observer of the vow should worship Durgā,
feed her with various kinds of food, and perform the ritual dismissal according to the prescribed rules.
Then one should perform the breaking of the fast, for this vow increases one's progeny;
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, this is known as the Daśāphala vow.
One should indeed perform the worship of Śrī Hari while observing a fast;
one should worship with ten leaves of the dark-colored Tulasī plant.
Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, as well as Ananta, Govinda, he whose banner is Garuḍa, Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and the Lord Hari. ||22||
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa day after day with these names,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) one hundred and eight times in the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One should offer oblations with sacrificial porridge (caru), flowers, fruits, and likewise with sugar;
one should perform this for ten days, and thereafter worship the preceptor.
Having placed a golden Tulasī leaf in a golden vessel or another vessel,
as well as a golden image, he should offer them to the Guru.
One should indeed perform the gift of a cow, beautifully adorned with garments and ornaments;
for ten days, one should offer milk-preparations and fried cakes (pūrikās).
He himself should accept the consecrated water (prasāda) and feed brāhmaṇas and virtuous men;
at the conclusion of the vow, he should give ten pūrikās to each of ten virtuous men.
Having thus performed this unsurpassed vow for ten years, one should indeed give [the gift];
after experiencing all the heavens, one shall attain union with Kṛṣṇa.
A man shall become an attendant of Kṛṣṇa, and a woman shall become beloved by Kṛṣṇa;
there is no other vow like this that bestows union with Kṛṣṇa. (29)
In ancient times, the vow of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī was observed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada;
by fasting on that day, the performer’s sins for seven lifetimes are destroyed.
Having fasted and bathed in pure water such as that of a river with sesame seeds,
one should thoroughly cleanse the temple by scrubbing, washing, and plastering it.
One should beautify it with archways variegated by various kinds of colors and with banners;
one should also fasten new canopies and other such ornaments.
One should sweep the lion-throne of the Blessed One and the articles for worship, prepare lamps, and provide a new covering.
Then the observer of the vow should provide offerings for worship, including food, clothing, and so forth, either in the center of the assembly hall or in front of the temple. (34)
One should cause a beautiful pavilion to be constructed, adorned with plantain pillars, joined with cloths, various fine flowers, sprouts, and water-pots. (35)
One should have that area adorned with rows of lamps, fruit, garlands, sandalwood, and the like, and fumigated with incense; then, one should place a water-pot (kalaśa) in its center.
Upon that, one should place a copper vessel, and upon that,
the auspicious golden image of Śrī Hari, covered with a pair of cloths.
The performer of the vow should worship with offerings such as water for the feet;
he should also construct a lying-in chamber for Devakī within the pavilion.
There, one should indeed depict Devakī together with Bālakṛṣṇa, and likewise Yaśodā in Gokula, beautiful and accompanied by her son.
The observer of the vow should have Vasudeva, Nanda, the cowherds, the cowherd women, as well as cows,
bulls, calves, and heifers made of gold.
One should worship those [deities] installed in the pavilion in all directions and intermediate points;
one should cause musical instruments to be played and have auspicious songs sung. ||4.1||
Having performed the bathing, worship, and other rites upon the image, one should perform the ārārtika ceremony;
at midnight, one should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure waters.
One should have them clothed in beautiful garments, ornaments, and strings of jewels, and [anointed] with saffron, kesara, aguru, sandalwood, and flowers. 43.
Then, having offered necklaces, crest-ornaments, flower garlands, and tulasī wreaths, as well as incense and lamps, one should present the great food offering (mahānaivedya).
One should offer as an oblation (naivedya) the five powders— goat meat, ginger, coriander, sugar, and ghee— in a silver vessel.
One should offer rice mixed with ghee, milk porridge, wheat cakes, and other items cooked in clarified butter;
one should present water and give betel leaf for cleansing the mouth. (46)
One should offer a coconut fruit, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and a leaf of Tulasī;
then one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) of Kṛṣṇa, who possesses twenty-four forms.
Having offered the water of honor (arghya) and requested forgiveness, the observer of the vow should then put [the deity] to rest.
At night, he should keep a vigil and listen to the narrative of Him.
Then the observer of the vow should drink the supreme nectar from the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
he should consume a small amount of curd with sugar and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). ||48-49||
Then, having bathed at dawn, one should worship Bālakṛṣṇa;
one should especially offer milk, cooked rice, and sugar.
Thereafter, men and women [should bathe the deity] there with water mixed with curd, milk, and ghee.
They should first engage in play by means of smearing, throwing, and sprinkling. ||5 1||
Having bathed, one should feed the virtuous, as well as virtuous women, boys, and girls; one should feed the Brahmins who are devoted, and also the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and eat the prasāda together with one's kinsmen.

In the morning and evening, at the conclusion of the worship, Hari should be daily rocked by the observer of the vow until the second day of the month of Bhādrapada. Having thus performed the vow together with his wife, children, friends, and servants, the man [attains the fruit]. ||53-54||
Seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, he attains Goloka directly; indeed,
there is no other vow in the three worlds superior to this,
by the performance of which one obtains the fruit of eleven crores [of other rites].
O lotus-born one, gifts worthy of a king should be bestowed here.
O beloved, one should perform the Kṛṣṇa-vow according to one's ability and according to the facts;
the birth of Rādhikā was established on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.
One should represent the Blessed Lord and Rādhā wearing red garments.
At midday, the observer of the vow should worship the form of Rādhikā together with Kṛṣṇa.
One should offer sweetmeat balls, pearls, and even fruits as the food offering (naivedya).
Whatever may be dear to oneself, that very thing the observer of the vow should offer.
One should have the verses concerning the birth of Rādhikā sung by the Gopīs and others;
having observed the vow of eating only one meal a day, one should feed married women.
Having offered the image to the guru, the observer of the vow should indeed eat;
or else, she may observe a fast and offer red garments.
Having performed the vow in this manner, a woman shall dwell in the retinue of Rādhā.
Having always become the wife of Kṛṣṇa, she should constantly acquire the happiness of Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, this Dūrvā-aṣṭamī vow must be performed by the observer of the vow;
on a spot overgrown with dūrvā grass, the observer of the vow should worship the arrow of Śambhu.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, curd, unbroken rice, fruits, and so forth, as well as with *dūrvā* grass; and one should pray: "O *dūrvā*, you who are eternally immortal!
Just as you have spread across the surface of the earth with your branches and sub-branches..."
"Grant me good fortune, abundant progeny, and a lineage free from old age and death.
Having fed the Brahmins and the virtuous, and having bid farewell to Śambhu, the woman who observes the vow shall complete it and become fortunate. (65–66)
Thus, this eighth day, which bestows merit and removes sin, is to be given as a gift by one's lineage;
she who does not worship with *dūrvā* grass shall become a widow for three births.
This Jyeṣṭhāṣṭamī, conjoined with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, consists of a vow;
this is the vow of Mahālakṣmī, which lasts for sixteen days from now. (68)
Until the full moon of the month of Punarvasu and lasting until the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the practitioner must certainly wear a cord tied around the right wrist.
One should constantly worship Lakṣmī, who is endowed with sixteen knots and possessed of sixteen qualities; thereafter, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having constructed a cloth pavilion over a *sarvatobhadra* mandala, one should place a water-pot and a lamp for the object of worship, and having drawn out the cord; || 71 ||
Having placed the four beautiful images of Lakṣmī beneath the pitcher, the observer of the vow should perform their ceremonial bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with water. //7//
Having worshipped with the sixteen and other offerings, one should feed [the devotees];
one should keep a vigil at night and present the water-offering (arghya) to the Moon.
O you who arose from the Ocean of Milk, brother of Mahālakṣmī!
May you be the provider of food and medicine for me; accept this sandalwood offering of mine. (74)
O lotus born from the ocean of milk, beloved of Kṛṣṇa,
dwelling upon the chest of Viṣṇu— be the granter of all my desires.
O sole mistress, mistress of the world, beloved of Gopāla, imperishable one!
O Kambharā, protect me, O Goddess; O Mother of Kṛṣṇa, grant me auspiciousness. (76)
Having thus prayed to Mahālakṣmī and worshipped her with devotion,
and having fed the women, one should offer oblations with bilva, lotus, and kapāvasa fruits.
With *samit* wood, ghee, flowers, and various kinds of fruits, as well as sandalwood, palm leaves, a garland, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), [one should worship] Viṣṇu. (78)
Durvā grass, a pair of safflower threads, as well as a bilva fruit, tulasī, sugar, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍūs), the essence of milk, sesame seeds, and barley; ||7-9||
One should offer water and betel leaf—these sixteen—to Hari;
likewise, one should offer them to Mahālakṣmī, having covered them with a winnowing basket upon a winnowing basket.
Having personally offered it to Lakṣmī and also to Nārāyaṇa,
the observer of the vow should dismiss the worship and thus complete that vow.
One should indeed give four images to four Brahmins;
one should give sixteen sets of articles to sixteen women of good character.
Having gratified them with sweet foods, he should dismiss them along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā);
thereafter, the observer of the vow should indeed perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) in this manner through his observance.
By the grace of Kambharā-Lakṣmī, he shall become a lord of ten million in this world, shall dwell again in the world of Lakṣmī, and indeed enjoy pleasures for a long time.
This is declared as Aśoka-aṣṭamī; one should perform the worship of the Aśoka tree, having observed the vow of eating only once a day and having worshipped Ramā with devotion. (85)
Wherever one may be born, one shall undoubtedly become free from sorrow;
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should observe the fast of the Durgā-vrata.
Or one may perform worship with a single daily meal according to this injunction;
having obtained prosperity from all sides, he rejoices in heaven like a god. (87)
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja, the vow known as Karaka is prescribed;
those desiring sons should worship Umāpati at night by all means. (88)
Having made an offering of gold, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) at moonrise;
the observer of the vow, having performed worship in the morning, should then break his fast.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika, the vow of the Blessed Lord was observed;
on that day, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was born in the house of Gopāla Kaṃbharā.
Then all the gods and sages celebrated a great festival;
having ascended their celestial chariots, they arrived, longing for a sight [of him].
Then they respectfully honored [the deity] with divine flowers and other offerings.
At that time, the pavilion should indeed be prepared early in the morning with the most precious materials.
Then, within the palace, in its pavilion, a golden image of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa should be installed here upon this Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala.
Hari himself should be worshipped in a jar adorned with five jewels, fruits, and sprouts, or indeed in a vessel filled with sesame seeds.
Endowed with glory, as well as joined by his father and mother, that great lord—listen, O Lakṣmī, my worship together with you bestows supreme liberation. (95)
It brings prosperity, bestows all happiness, and grants every desired object;
it should be performed by a woman or even by a man who seeks the fruits of the vow. (96)
Beginning with the invocation, one should perform the bathing with the five nectars, water, and so forth, as well as the donning of garments, ornaments, and other such beautifications. (97)

One should offer incense, lamps, excellent food offerings (naivedya), the waving of lights (ārātrika), sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and so forth; as well as hymns of praise, worship, betel nut, food, and water. (98)
Kṛṣṇa, who consists of all the scriptures, in whom Sarasvatī dwells, in whom all the gods have made their abode, and in whom Śrī, Ramā, and the others have established their home. (99)
One should likewise remember Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, and Māṇikīnātha;
one should give various kinds of gifts and observe a vigil with great festivity.
Having bathed in the morning, having performed worship, and having fed [the guests], one should perform the dismissal;
thus one completes the vow of the Jayantī of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 101 ||
The observer of the vow obtains a wife, a husband, a daughter, a son, a cow, wealth, gold, as well as a field, a house, a vehicle, and health. (102)
Through this vow, one shall indeed attain knowledge, existence, great fame, honor, and all prosperity; one truly obtains heaven and finds liberation.
The birth of Kālabhairava also occurred on that very same Kālāṣṭamī;
therefore, one who seeks the fruit of the vow should perform his worship with appropriate offerings.
This Śaṅkara himself has become Bhairava in the form of Time;
indeed, no fear arises for those observers of vows, such as the Bhairavas and others.
In the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Gopāṣṭamī should be understood as pertaining to cows;
there, one should perform the worship of cows, offer morsels of food to cows, give gifts of cows, and circumambulate cows.
One should perform [this rite]; for Kṛṣṇa became a cowherd and tended the cows, and by the cow-vow (govrata), Lakṣmī, whose essence is rasa, shall always dwell in one's home.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the vow of the pair of Darbha grass blades;
having fashioned a pair of Darbha blades under the names Anaghā and Anagha.
One should place [the vessel] containing both the *suta* and *asuta* on a ground smeared with cow dung and other substances,
and worship it there with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having fed the couple and dismissed them after they have received their sacrificial fee,
the man or woman who has performed this vow shall obtain a son, a daughter, and happiness.
In this very context, one should perform the Kālabhairava-Jayantī vow;
furthermore, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Durgā-vow is prescribed by the Sun.
The rite for the time-vow consists of worship, fire-oblations, gifts, and excellent meals;
it includes fasting and staying awake in the presence of Kālabhairava.
Indeed, having performed an action that causes suffering, it comes to an end through its own power.
Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the Śrāddha known as Aṣṭaka [is performed].
This year, which grants satisfaction to the ancestors and increases the lineage,
must be performed entirely according to the prescribed rite, specifically after midday.
Since the worship of Śiva bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should indeed perform the Bhadrakālī vow on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
One should worship her who slays hosts of enemies and bestows all desires on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha; [then] Hari becomes Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 116.
On the ninth day, the Lord made his descent from the world of Brahmā into Divyakāśī and performed the transmission of the supreme knowledge.
The vow of descent and the vow of knowledge should be performed for two days;
worship should be performed with the sixteen articles, and a gift of gold should be given. 118.
By consuming the essence of milk, the observer of the vow shall obtain knowledge and worldly enjoyment;
one should worship Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Kṛṣṇa.
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, all those radiant women of the city lead the man and the woman to their own abode, the imperishable supreme state.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, the Bhīmādevī-vrata is prescribed;
the worship of Bhīmā should be performed, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (121)
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship Śiva and Śivā;
one should also worship Śītalā with offerings of sweet foods prepared beforehand.
One should recite, without weariness, the mantra of the goddess Visphoṭanāśinī— who is naked, mounted upon a donkey, and equipped with a broom and a water-pot— while standing in water.
For him, however, the goddess Śītalā shall be the bestower of peace from eruptive boils;
for one who observes the vow of Śītalā, the year shall be filled with tranquility.
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, I indeed became Ṛṣabha;
Viṣṇu’s worship should be performed by one observing the vow, for it bestows supreme merit.

Thus ends [the section on] Pārvatī-jayantī, Durgā-ṣṭamī, Daśāha-phala-vrata, Kṛṣṇā-ṣṭamī, Rādhā-ṣṭamī, Tṛrvā-ṣṭamī, Jyeṣṭhā-ṣṭamī, and Kaṃbhara-lakṣmī within the first section, the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

The two hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of Vows such as the Jayantī-Durgā Vow, the Karaka Vow, the Jayantī of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Kālāṣṭamī, Gopāṣṭamī, Darbha Vow, Śrāddha-Ṣṭamī, Bhairava-Ṣṭamī, the Vow of the Incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in Kāśī, the Vidyā Vow, the Worship performed by the Chief Queen, the Bhīmādevī Vow, the Śītalā-Ṣṭamī, the Ṛṣabha-Jayantī, and others."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O child Lakṣmī, listen as I describe to you the vows of the nine Navamīs; by performing these, one attains both heaven and liberation.
The vow for the birth of Rāma is prescribed during the bright fortnight of Caitra;
Śrī Rāmanavamī should be observed with enthusiasm, as it bestows great merit. (1)
Having observed the fast, one should then take only a single meal after the people have finished;
a very large pavilion should be constructed, featuring a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
Having had a jar fashioned and placed [therein], one should cause the image to be set within a vessel;
it should be adorned with a crown and so forth, as well as a bow and arrow, and other ornaments.
The worship consists of sixteen items, including the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā) and others;
for the food offering (naivedya), there is saffron, boiled rice, sugar, curd, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should offer a vigil and perform it; on the following day, one should practice giving.
The observer of the vow should indeed give cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth to the preceptor.
Having gratified the Brahmins and the virtuous, the observer of the vow should break his fast;
by performing the vow of Viṣṇu in this manner, he shall go to the supreme abode.
On this very lunar day, the Hari-jayantī vow should also be observed at Dharmabhavana; it was there that Harikṛṣṇa was born.
On this very day, Bhadrakālī, the most excellent of yoginīs,
was consecrated by Śaṅkara in the sovereignty over all [the others].
This is declared to be the Mātṛvratam; accompanied by Bhairava, the sixty-four Yoginīs, together with Caṇḍikā, are to be worshipped.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the auspicious Goddess Ramā, accompanied by Hari,
who bestows enjoyment and liberation, as well as sons, wealth, and good fortune.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, the vow of eating but once (ekabhukta) should indeed be observed here;
one must perform worship and other rites, as well as the giving of gifts consisting of golden objects.

On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one should indeed worship the goddess Umā, who is most auspicious and established in asceticism; the auspicious vow prescribed for this occasion is eating only at night.
One should feed young maidens according to one's ability and cause various gifts to be given;
one should also give excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and the observer of the vow should eat milk-rice (pāyasa).
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow should worship Lakṣmī;
likewise, the observer of the vow should worship Indrāṇī seated upon Airāvata.
He shall become a possessor of enjoyments in the world of the gods, traveling in a celestial vehicle;
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Bhārgavī Śrī.
One should worship Kumārī, the goddess Lakṣmī who destroys suffering, with excellent offerings of food and flavors,
as well as with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garments, Nepalese shawls, and blankets.
One should also feed young maidens who are the embodiments of the goddess Śrī, the destroyer of suffering;
by performing this vow for Lakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, the practitioner goes to the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa.
This Nakula-navamī should likewise be observed by one who has taken a vow;
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Nandā-vrata is proclaimed.
Nanda should indeed worship Durgā according to the prescribed rites and with the ritual offerings;
having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, the observer of the vow shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.

This ninth day, which destroys suffering, should be observed as "not-suffering" (aduḥkha-navamī); however, this "widow-not-ninth" (avidhavā-navamī) should be observed by those whose husbands are living.
A fast must be observed, and Lakṣmī, the virtuous one, should likewise be worshipped. The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is called Mahānavamī;
it is so designated because Durgā is worshipped there at the conclusion of the Navarātra vow.
Likewise, Mahālakṣmī is to be worshipped, and crores of goddesses are to be worshipped;
all goddesses, whether married or unmarried, are fully honored.

Furthermore, with garments, ornaments, decorations, and other such articles of personal adornment, as well as liquids and the like; and with vehicles, mounts, food, and various objects of pleasure. (24)
In the afternoon, O Dear One, the worship of the Śamī tree should be performed in the eastern direction;
in the evening, one should worship the conch, the mace, the discus, and the lotus.
A sword, a bow, arrows, a spear, a trident, a shield, a buckler, a dagger, an axe, a noose, a staff, a thunderbolt, and a mallet. || 26 ||
An umbrella, a banner, an elephant, a horse, a swan, a lute, a peacock, a bull, a buffalo, a book, a scale, a cow, and [the signs beginning with] the head [of the zodiac]. (27)
Whatever has been protected by her for herself, all that the observer of the vow should worship;
and whatever offering is most dear to her, that the observer of the vow should quickly present to her. (28)
Having completed the worship at night and performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana) in the morning, the observer of the vow should indeed eat cooked food and likewise feed the Brahmins. || 29 ||
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) afterwards, and having offered gifts with devotion,
one should indeed complete the vow and cast the image into the water.
Thus, through their vows, the mothers of the worlds, always bestowing happiness, being satisfied and nourished, sustain the children of the worlds, taking refuge in compassion. (31)
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures as one observing the vow, he shall go to heaven and other realms at the end;
likewise, he shall go to the world of the Mothers, the world of Satīs, and the world of the Goddesses.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika is an inexhaustible [day]; it is a great vow.
One should perform the libation for the gods, sages, and ancestors at the foot of an Aśvattha tree.
Then, having offered the arghya to the Sun, the observer of the vow should feed the twice-born and the children;
he should perform charity, fire-offerings, and recitation, and he should give sacrificial fees.
Whatever is performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) or in a temple shall result in the destruction of all [karmic] reality;
indeed, one should give the gift of a kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, and it shall yield the primary fruit of a sacrifice.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the vow of Navamī is called Nandinī;
having fasted, the observer of the vow should then worship Nandā-Lakṣmī.
One should give a gift of a maiden, and the fruit thereof shall be equal to that born of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should worship Mahālakṣmī.
On the ninth day of the month of Māgha, one should worship Mahānandā;
on the ninth day of Phālguna, one should worship Ānandā Lakṣmī.
Here, bathing, recitation, rosaries, charity, fire-offerings, and fasting—all these attain imperishability through the grace of Kṛṣṇa-Lakṣmī. || 39 ||
Various kinds of gifts should be given to a worthy recipient at an auspicious place and on an auspicious day;
O Kamalā, I shall tell you who that worthy recipient is, for such a recipient delivers people from saṃsāra.
Neither by knowledge alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient; that person in whom both [knowledge and austerity] exist, and who is endowed with devotion, is indeed a true vessel. 4.1.
One who is devoted to sacred study, observant of rules, meditative, endowed with austerity, and has conquered the senses;
one whose nature is forgiveness, who is peaceful in disposition, and truthful—a twice-born man, or even such a person. (42)
One who studies the scriptures, has heard all [the teachings], is free from malice, delights in receiving [gifts],
is firm in his vows, possesses virtuous conduct, and is devoted to worthy recipients (pātra)— such a person is most excellent.
The virtuous, who are devoted to meditation and delight in assisting others, purify even by being seen; how much more so when they have entered into association? (44)
Having given these to them according to their needs, they shall attain the supreme goal;
one should offer them to a learned Vedic scholar who is virtuous and established in Brahman.

Forbearance, compassion, desire for the welfare of others, truthfulness, generosity, virtuous conduct, austerity, and learning—these eight qualities are declared here to be the supreme characteristics of a worthy recipient. (46)
One who is a performer of sacrifices, an expounder of the Vedas, a knower of the Purāṇas, a teacher, and a spiritual preceptor;
one who is compassionate toward women, a servant of cows, and a worthy recipient—[such a person is to be honored]. 47.
One who is naked, devoid of livelihood, afflicted by hunger and thirst, a refugee, and a performer of virtuous deeds is a worthy recipient; what is given to such a person yields eternal fruit.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth, when given to a worthy recipient, are always inexhaustible.
One type of worthy recipient consists of the Vedas; another type of worthy recipient consists of asceticism. (49)
A vessel filled with devotion is one thing, and a vessel filled with Brahman is another;
likewise, a celibate student, an ascetic, a virtuous man, and a virtuous woman are always considered worthy vessels.
Such a capable donor will cause [others] to cross over;
by his own splendor, he delivers both the donor and himself. (51)
A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields a hundredfold merit; to one who calls himself a Brahmin, it is twofold;
to a teacher, it is a thousandfold; and to the virtuous, it is remembered as being infinite.
An oblation offered into the mouths of Brahmins—who are as richly kindled with the fuel of the Vedas—delivers the donor;
likewise, an oblation offered into virtuous women delivers the giver. (53)

Brahmins whose property has been seized and whose entire wealth has been taken away are considered supreme recipients; likewise, guests who have arrived and those of meager livelihoods are also worthy recipients. (54)
To those who delight in the Dharma, delight in knowledge, and delight in devotion; who are compassionate, devoted to austerity, and live on alms—to them, what is given yields great fruit. (55)
If one abandons a recipient present nearby and goes instead to one located in another country for the sake of giving, it burns the family up to the seventh generation.
In whose house there is a fool, yet a man of great learning resides afar, there no transgression or fault occurs; it is as if an oblation were offered into the fire, not into ashes.
Children are vessels for food; women are vessels for ornaments;
the youth is a vessel for pride; and the elderly are vessels for service. (58)
The virtuous are the worthy recipients of worship; mendicants are the worthy recipients of food;
the suffering are the worthy recipients of compassion; and the best of friends are the worthy recipients of truth. (59)

The poor are the worthy recipients of assistance; those who have sought refuge are the worthy recipients of protection; those who give gifts are the worthy recipients of heaven; and those who are well-contented are the worthy recipients of happiness.
That which bestows marriage, the tying of the girdle, consecration, and other rites, when given to the poor, the blind, the wretched, the afflicted, and others, is inexhaustible. (61)
To the slanderer, the malicious, the thief, the rogue, the killer, the destroyer,
the cruel, the deceitful, the envious, and the sinful one devoid of dharma— 62.

Toward a rogue, a deceiver, one who contemplates what is undesirable, one who is envious, a wicked person, one who causes suffering, one who is full of calamities, a murderer, and indeed one who is devoid of devotion; || 63 ||
Everything offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed perishes; of this there is no doubt.
This [gift] weeps while being given; what evil deed have I committed? (64)
A seed sown in saline soil, an oblation poured even into ashes, and that which is given to an unworthy recipient—all this results in total destruction. (65)
Whatever is desired by oneself, whatever belongs to oneself, and whatever is righteous—that indeed should be given to a worthy recipient; such giving alone yields fruit.
There is no end to that which is given with faith and according to the prescribed rite to a worthy recipient;
thus, O Lakṣmī, have I described to you the proper recipient for vows and gifts. (67)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vārṣika Navamī Vows— including the Śrī Rāma Jayantī, Śrī Hari Jayantī, Bhadrakālī Vrata, Ramā Vrata, Umā Vrata, Indrī Vrata, Duḥkhahā Lakṣmī Vrata, Nakula Vrata, Nandā-Durgā Vrata, Aduḥkha Navamī Vrata, the Widow’s Navamī, Navarātra Navamī Vrata, Akṣaya Navamī, Kūṣmāṇḍa Navamī, Nandinī Navamī, Mahālakṣmī-Mahānandā-Nandā Pūjā, and the Worship of Worthy Recipients," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now, O Mahālakṣmī, I shall indeed describe other observances for the tenth lunar day,
by performing which a person attains heaven and peace.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should indeed observe the vow of Dharmarāja;
one should worship him with baths, flowers, fruits, perfumes, garments, and ornaments.
Observing the vow of eating but one meal a day, he should honor fourteen Brahmins;
having fed them and given them sacrificial fees, he shall attain heaven by doing so. || 3 ||
On the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should worship Viṣṇu.
One should perform one hundred circumambulations with the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
By feeding virtuous Brahmins, one certainly attains Vaikuṇṭha;
this applies when Jupiter is in the bright fortnight, the month of Jyeṣṭha, on a Wednesday, and the tenth lunar day (Daśamī). || 5 ||

The *garānanda*, *vyatīpāta*, the Moon in Virgo (*kanyā*), and the Sun in Taurus (*vṛṣabha*): this is the "Tenfold Yoga" (*daśayoga*), which is exceedingly meritorious and indeed destroys the ten types of sin. (6)
The Gaṅgā-daśaharā should be understood as the Gaṅgā who has descended from heaven;
having bathed in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite, one goes to the abode of Hari.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is the anniversary of the Manu (Manvādi-tithi);
on this day, bathing, recitation, giving gifts, or performing fire-offerings bestow the attainment of heaven.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa bestows the fulfillment of all hopes;
one should indeed perform the worship of Śiva, preceded by gifts, fire-offerings, and other rites.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform the excellent vow for the manifestation of the Daśās;
likewise, one should bathe at a sacred ford and offer libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Furthermore, the observer of the vow himself should personally perform the worship of the ten incarnations:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, and Trivikrama; || 11 ||
The observer of the vow, having worshipped golden images of the ten forms— Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Paraśurāma (Jāmadagnya), Buddha, and Kalki— and having offered them,
should provide a single meal for a brahmin and feed the virtuous well.
Having thus performed the vow and partaken of the meal, one shall attain Vaikuṇṭha in heaven.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is considered Vijayā-daśamī;
having placed four balls of cow dung in the courtyard of the house in the morning, [one should proceed].
In the midst of these forms of the discus, one should indeed worship all four: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Having placed moist grain together with silver inside four earthenware vessels that have lids, he should be clothed in white garments. (16)
Having worshipped with unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings, one should then indeed offer salutations;
at midday, one should feed the children, and likewise the observer of the vow should eat sweets.
Then, in the afternoon, having taken earth from the root of a *śamī* tree situated to the east,
and having brought it to his own home, he should worship it according to the prescribed rite.
If he is a Kṣatriya, having fully prepared his own army,
he should go out from the eastern gate of the village without agitation.
There, he [struck] an image of the enemy fashioned from leaves and other materials,
which had been mentally visualized, with an arrow having a golden shaft.
Thinking "he shall pierce [the target]," he would be greatly delighted and then return to his own home;
if he should subsequently engage in battle, he will undoubtedly be victorious. ||21||
One should give here wealth, victory, great sovereignty, sons, cattle, elephants, horses, goats, and sheep; likewise, at the end, one attains the state of heaven.
Today Śrī Rāma has set forth for victory; let there be a festival.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should observe the Sārvabhauma vow;
there, the practitioner of the vow, eating but once a day, should offer cakes and other foods at midnight.
The observer of the vow should offer the bali-oblation in the ten directions, either outside the house or outside the city,
upon a mandala of eight petals on ground smeared with cow dung.
One should perform the offering of the oblation (balidāna), reciting at that time:
"May Indra, the bestower of desired things, shake off whatever sin has previously accrued to me. (25)
May Agni, the granter of desires, shake off whatever sin of mine has entered the fire;
may Yama, the granter of desires, shake off whatever sin of mine has entered the southern quarter.
May the Rākṣasa, the performer of deeds, shake off whatever evil of mine goes toward the south;
may the aquatic creature, the performer of deeds, shake off whatever evil of mine goes toward the west. || 27 ||
May Vāyu, the bestower of desired things, shake off whatever sin of mine has gone to the wind;
may Yakṣa, the bestower of desired things, shake off whatever sin of mine has gone to the moon. || 28 ||
May the Lord, the bestower of desires, shake off whatever sin of mine has gone upward;
may Brahmā, the bestower of desires, shake off whatever sin of mine has gone above. ||29||
"May the Naga, who grants my desires, shake off whatever evil has gathered within me.
Having thus offered the *bali* offering in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the observer of the vow then proceeds.
Outside that [enclosure], one should unweariedly cast the bali offering for the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla).
Having returned home, one should perform a vigil during the remainder of the night.
Having bathed in the morning and duly worshipped the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) and then the twice-born,
he should worship twelve [Brahmins], feed them, and bestow sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having performed the vow in this manner, O Lakṣmī, and having enjoyed auspicious worldly pleasures, and having experienced celestial happiness for a yuga, one shall become a sovereign emperor. 33.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the two Aśvinīkumāras;
one should also worship Dhanvantari, and health shall prevail at all times.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one should worship the Viśvedevas:
Kratu, Dakṣa, the Vasus, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Muni, and Guru.
One should worship the Brahmin Rāma as the forms of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
having seated him upon seats of darbha grass with offerings of incense, lamps, and food.
Having worshipped them with the sixteen articles, one should dismiss them;
the observer of the vow will in every way become an enjoyer of happiness in both worlds. (37)
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should indeed worship the descendants of Aṅgiras:
Ātman, Āyu, Manas, Dakṣa, Mada, Prāṇa, and Gaviṣṭhaka.
One should worship Datta, Satya, and Varhiṣmān with ten excellent substances;
one should offer the forms [of the deities] to the twice-born with the sixteen types of services and others.
The observer of the vow thus attains the higher worlds of the Āṅgirasas while performing the vow;
on the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship the Yamas.
Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, Antaka, Vaivasvata, Kāla, and Sarvabhūtakṣaya; ||4.1||
Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Vṛkodara, Parameṣṭhin, Citra, and Citragupta—these are the fourteen. ||42||
One should worship them, feed them, and satisfy them with water and sesame seeds;
thereafter, one should indeed offer the arghya to the Sun from a copper vessel.
One should feed the Brahmins with water mixed with red sandalwood, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and barley; thereafter, the observer of the vow, restraining his speech, should eat.
Thus, having attained the favor of Dharmarāja by means of his vows,
and having enjoyed supreme pleasures here, he shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu at the end of his body.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Vrata of Dharmarāja, the Vrata of Viṣṇu, the Gaṅgā-daśaharā, the Vratas for Fulfilling All Desires on Lunar Days such as Manv-ādi, the Worship of the Ten Incarnations, the Vijayā-daśamī and Sārvabhauma Vratas, the Ārogya Vrata, and the Vratas of the Viśvedevas, Aṅgiras, and Yama," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, those Ekādaśī vows which were previously described by you are indeed vows that must be completed by performing them for three days.
O Lotus-born one, one should indeed abandon four meals over three days:
one at the beginning and one at the end, and two in the middle.
Bell-metal, meat, lentil soup, chickpeas, and kodrava grain;
likewise, vegetables, honey, food from others, eating a second meal, and sexual intercourse. (3)
On the tenth day, the observer of the vow should always avoid ten things:
gambling, sleep, betel nut, and cleaning the teeth; || 4 ||
On the eleventh day, one should avoid slandering others, malicious speech, theft, as well as delighting in violence, anger, and speaking falsehoods.
Bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, speaking with barbarians,
physical exercise, travel abroad, eating a second time, and sexual intercourse— [these should be avoided].
On the twelfth day, one should avoid these twelve things, including the touch of the untouchable;
or, having observed eating once a day or eating only at night, one should perform the vow.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a sacred thread (pavitra) to Hari;
it may be made of gold, silver, silk, linen, hemp, or cotton.
The most excellent *pavitraka* consists of three hundred and sixty threads;
the ordinary one arises from three strands; and the middling one may be made according to one's desire.
The best [girdle] has one hundred knots, while the smallest has thirty-six;
the best is considered to reach down to the knees, and the smallest is held to touch the navel.
O gods, by performing worship here of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa together with Ramā, one becomes happy and shall attain the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. 11.
On the twelfth day as well, one should offer the beautiful pavitras, which indeed bestow happiness and prosperity, to the Guru and also to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
one should perform the festival of Lord Hari’s playful crossing of the Yamunā in a boat.
As the cowherd women were going along carrying curds for sale, he begged them for a hand’s-breadth of space as a toll;
at that time, one should have them sing his verses.
The observer of the vow should indeed offer curd and cooked rice as an oblation to Kṛṣṇa;
he should present the gift of a waistband and the gift of curd to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, a festival for the worship of Dharma must be performed at midday by one seeking the vow, on account of the birth of Dharma.
Having fashioned a golden image and placed it within a copper vessel situated inside the pavilion, one should worship it upon a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
He has four faces, four arms, and four feet, and is clad in white garments;
he is white in complexion, holding a rosary in his right hand and a book in his left.
He holds well-formed Resolve on his right side,
having placed Ease on his left side, and Devotion in his presence.
The observer of the vow should devoutly worship her who holds the vessel of worship;
having worshipped her with the sixteen types of offerings, he should then feed her.
Having performed a vigil and worship at night, one should dismiss [the deity] at dawn;
one should also give other gifts, for this shall be the strength of one's devotion to Dharma.
Together with Dharma, his thirteen wives, beginning with Śraddhā,
the daughters of Dakṣa, should be properly established, fed, and honored according to the prescribed ritual.
These are the lawful wives of Dharma: Faith, Tranquility, Compassion, Resolve, Intelligence, Contentment, as well as Nourishment, Friendship, Modesty, Action, and Progress. (23)
Those [goddesses] of divine form, known by various names, should be fashioned as golden images; their lineage is also extensive. (24)
One who desires the next world should especially honor [the recipient];
for that purpose, even the most excellent gifts should be bestowed. (25)

The practitioner of vows should perform this penance and observance known as the Ekādaśikā; he shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, and whatever else he desires, he shall obtain all of that. ||26||
Just as the vows for all Ekādaśīs have been previously described,
those vows must in every way be observed here according to the prescribed rules.
The concluding rites (udyāpana) for all of these must be performed according to the prescribed rules;
by doing so, the performer—whether man, woman, or eunuch—shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "Description of Vows such as the Ekādaśī Pālī-niyama, Pavitrāropaṇa, Vrata-dāna, Līlā-vrata, Dharma-jayantī, and others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe to you the vows of the twelve lunar days (dvādaśīs), by performing which people go to the eternal abode of Hari.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe the Madana-vrata;
[one should offer] a jar filled with white rice and adorned with fruits and sugarcane.
Having placed [the image] upon a *sarvatobhadra* mandala, adorned with a pair of garments, gold, and a vessel containing desirable food, and worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings; || 3 ||
One should place the image of Śrī Kāmadeva together with Rati in a vessel and worship it with all kinds of flowers, juices, and fragrances. 4.
One should feed them Rajasic foods and milk-rice (pāyasa);
having worshipped on the morning of the thirteenth day, one should dismiss Anaṅga.
Having thus observed the vow for a year, one should joyfully give as a gift to the venerable Guru ghee, a bed with a calf, gold, desired objects, and pleasure.
One should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, and likewise offer this prayer:
"May Hari, who can assume any form at will, be pleased with me; be the bestower of happiness."
The performer of the Madanadvādaśī vow goes to Goloka;
through the service of Kṛṣṇa, the couple attains eternal happiness.
In this very [context], there is another vow, the Bhartṛdvādaśikā-vrata;
having caused a pavilion to be constructed, one should prepare a Sarvatobhadra mandala.
One should prepare a well-spread, comfortable bed adorned with flowers;
there, one should worship Hari, who is united with Ramā, with the sixteen [upacāras] and other offerings.
Having performed the lustration ceremony for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should place Him to sleep along with Ramā;
the observer of the vow should keep a vigil accompanied by song and instrumental music.
Having worshipped him again in the morning with perfumes and other offerings, one should feed him;
then, one should present to the venerable Guru the golden image of Śrī Hari together with a bed.
Having fed virtuous brahmins, he should dismiss them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
for one who performs the vow in this manner, his marital union shall become eternal. 13.
The observer of this vow, honored in heaven, enjoys pleasures here for seven births;
the worship of the husband must be performed by the wife especially.
The husband is indeed Vāsudeva manifest; he grants all desires.
He bestows every happiness—whether pertaining to the body, the world, or heaven. || 15 ||
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, having worshipped Hari Mādhava, one should offer cooked food along with water; thus one shall attain all desires. (16)
Having duly worshipped Trivikrama on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should offer sweetmeats, water-pots, and other gifts; thus one shall obtain all enjoyments.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Lord Vāmana;
one should observe the vow of eating only vegetables and practice the vow of abstaining from salt.
The righteous-souled one should give gifts— clothing, ornaments, and sacred threads—
and he should offer to the guru a vessel, a seal-ring, a finger-ring, grain, and wealth.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow should worship Śrīdhara;
having completed the vegetable-vow, he should then perform the curd-vow.
One should offer to the venerable Guru a sacred thread made of silk, which is the most excellent;
one should give all kinds of gifts according to one's capacity and thus become happy.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should observe the vow of Vāmanajanman;
one should offer milk-rice to Hari and worship Him with many articles.
One should fashion an auspicious image of Vāmana out of gold, with a beautiful face,
a youthful form, two arms, and holding a parasol, a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary.
In the Sarvatobhadra pavilion, one should worship her at midday;
one should worship Aditi, Kaśyapa, the devoted Bali, and the gods.
The observer of the vow should offer as an oblation sweetmeat balls made of flour mixed with abundant ghee;
furthermore, he should subsist on fruit, eat only one meal a day, or observe the practice of eating only at night.
If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) should coincide with the Śravaṇa asterism at midday, or if the twelfth lunar day should occur at midday on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī); ||26||
When the asterism Śravaṇa coincides with that [lunar day], that conjunction is called Viṣṇuśṛṅkhala;
it is a festival that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants union with Viṣṇu. ||27||
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should worship Padmanābha, feed him sweet foods, and bestow gifts in abundance. (28)
One shall attain the state of Śvetadvīpa and obtain auspicious, desired enjoyments by performing the Govatsadvādaśī vow during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika.

One should indeed perform [the rite] there according to the prescribed rule, and have a golden cow made; one should worship that cow along with her calf with flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings with great reverence.
One should feed him auspicious substances and offer water for the feet;
one should give cakes made of black gram and the like, and provide morsels of food such as grass and so forth.
Having bowed to her and likewise performed a circumambulation, he should make this resolve:
"O Mother, who embodies all the gods, fulfill my desire. (32)
"O Mother, grant me heaven, liberation, and happiness; O Mother, salutations be unto you!
Having worshipped thus, one should give gifts of cows according to one's capacity. (33)
On that day, one should avoid cow’s milk, buttermilk, curd, and ghee;
