one should also avoid food cooked in a pot, food fried in oil, and anything unnatural or deformed.
Or the observer of the vow may worship her in the morning in embodied form, accompanied by a heifer;
indeed, through direct worship and service, the fruit shall be abundant.
O beloved, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, one should worship the Lord Dāmodara with the sixteen supreme articles and feed Hari.
And water-pots filled with water, honored with cloths and sprouts, and adorned with betel nuts, sweets, gems, fruits, gold, and the like. ||37||
The observer of the vow should joyfully give gifts and feed virtuous people for the sake of the Guru;
when this is done, he becomes dear to Viṣṇu and endowed with all enjoyments. (38)
On the twelfth day, the king should perform the supreme vow of *nīrājana*;
for the Lord of the World, having arisen from sleep, should indeed be adorned with excellent articles.
At the arrival of night, having kindled a new fire and worshipped it with mantras,
one should offer oblations of ghee and other items, as well as food fit for sages, accompanied by people holding silver lamps.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the observer of the vow should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Ramā, and Pārvatī. 41.
Brahmāṇī, Caṇḍikā, Gaurī, Māṇikī, and likewise Maṅgalā;
Āditya, Śaṅkara, Yakṣa, Nandā, Gaṇapati, and the planets.
Then one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) for all the Mothers, the Fathers, the mountains, and the Nāgas;
one should perform the lustration of the cows and address them with the words, "Salutation! Victory! (namo jaya).
And bulls, horses, and elephants endowed with auspicious marks;
all royal insignia, such as the umbrella and others, all new. (44)

Having honored the king, the family priest, the ministers, the servants, and the women of the inner apartments as is appropriate, one should cause the conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments to be sounded.
Then the king, adorned with ornaments, should sit upon a new throne; at that time, the assembly hall shall be filled with both courtesans and women of noble family.

Likewise, one should increase [the prosperity] over the head of the lord of men with unbroken grains (akṣata) and flowers, along with gold coins; thereafter, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the king.
Then, let the peace-mantras of the brahmins be heard by the king;
in this manner, this great propitiation (mahāśānti) should be performed every day. 48.
By a king, or even by one who is wealthy, desiring rain and health, that supreme pacification should be performed in whatever kingdom, city, or village [it concerns]. (49)
O Lakṣmī, by this rite called Nīrājanā, those diseases go to their destruction;
this should be performed by people in whatever manner possible, even if it is done in an abbreviated form.
On this very twelfth day, in ancient times during the Kṛta Yuga, Viṣṇu indeed performed the marriage of Tulasī; it is an excellent vow.
One should wear a turban of black Nārāyaṇa silk,
as well as a safflower-colored garment and a red bodice made of golden thread.
One should clothe Tulasī in an auspicious saffron-colored garment and provide her with ornaments,
flowers, and other articles of adornment to make her beautiful.
At the onset of night, one should offer sweet rice mixed with jaggery as a food offering (naivedya) in a beautiful pavilion constructed of plantain trees and other materials.
The observer of the vow should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-Viṣṇu and Tulasī;
at the time of godhūli, he should honor them with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should indeed offer golden garments, a necklace, a nose-ornament, bracelets,
turmeric, saffron, and other such items to Tulasī.
One should offer fruits such as the *amṛta* and stalks of sugarcane;
for the food offering (*naivedya*), one should present yellow-colored *khājaka* cakes.
Having performed the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) between Vṛndā and Kṛṣṇa with a curtain,
and having recited auspicious verses, one should offer Vṛndā to Śrī Viṣṇu.
One should feed virtuous men, virtuous women, Brahmins, boys, girls, and other people according to one's capacity, and should give various kinds of gifts. ||59||
One should indeed have the verses on the wedding of Vṛndā sung by those who relish aesthetic flavor;
in this way, one should perform the festival which protects one's unbroken fortune.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the unsurpassed Sādhya-vrata;
likewise, Manobhava, Prāṇa, Nara, and Vīryavān [are to be worshipped].
One should worship these twelve Sādhyas as gods: Citra, Hayo, Nṛpa, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa, Vibhu, and Prabhu. 62.
One should offer golden [images] fashioned from rice, along with perfumes and other offerings;
one should feed many people delicious food, thinking, "Nārāyaṇa is dear to me."
On this very day, the Āditya-dvādaśī vow should be observed;
[the twelve Ādityas are] Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Śakra, Aṃśu, Varuṇa, and Bhaga.
Having fashioned twelve golden images of those twelve suns—Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu—one should worship them and feed [the Brahmins]. ||65||
One should observe this vow for one year, every month on the bright fortnight.
One should give all kinds of gifts and feed the Brahmins and the virtuous. ||66||
Having thus performed the vow and attained the brilliantly shining world of the Sun,
and having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time, he shall pierce the solar orb.
Beyond Māyā, one should go to the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
then, right here, one should perform the Akhaṇḍa-vrata of Janārdana.
Having fashioned a golden image, the observer of the vow should worship Janārdana;
thereafter, he should feed [the deity] every month for one year.
Eating only at night, one should offer that auspicious golden image of a cow together with its calf to the preceptor, and feed the Brahmins milk-rice and other such foods.
One should pray to Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa: "May my vow be unbroken;
may good fortune, wealth, grain, and health be mine forever. (71)
One should also give other gifts solely for the sake of the next world;
having done so, the observer of the vow goes to the abode of Viṣṇu by means of a golden vehicle.
The Rūpavrata is proclaimed for the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa;
having bathed according to the rules on the tenth day, the observer of the vow should take up cow dung.
O Dear One, for a white cow of uniform color,
one should then dry its hundred and eight balls [of dung] while it is situated in the open air.
Having placed it in a copper vessel or a vessel made of earth, one should indeed preserve it for the sake of the fire-oblation;
on the eleventh day, having fasted and worshipped Viṣṇu with gold, [one should proceed].
One should feed [the devotees] and perform a vigil; then, on the morning of the twelfth day, having placed Hari in a water-pot or a vessel, one should worship him with ritual offerings.
Having worshipped the fire produced by the friction of wood and the pedestal,
one should offer oblations of sesame, ghee, and other substances individually to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the twelve-syllable vidyā, or alternatively with [the deity’s] names; then one should feed [the officiant] milk-rice and fried cakes.
One should offer the clay image of the pot to the preceptor, feed the twice-born, and having bowed, the woman or man should respectfully dismiss them, concluding the vow. (79)
By performing this, one obtains a physical form and the most excellent good fortune.
Now, the vow of Sujanmadvādaśī in the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa is described.
Having bathed in the morning and drunk the water from a cow's horn, and having offered salutations as well as performed circumambulation, one should undertake the annual vow.
Thereafter, one should perform the gift-giving on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight every month;
one should offer a prastha of ghee and four prasthas of rice.
The observer of the vow should offer four *prasthas* of barley, two *raktikas* of gold, half an *āḍhaka* of sesame seeds, and a jar full of milk. (83)
One month of silver, many sweet foods,
an umbrella made of half-a-māṣa of gold, and one prastha of excellent molasses.
The observer of the vow should give each month, according to his capacity, a pala of sandalwood and an auspicious garment measuring ten cubits in length. (85)
For the sake of purification, the observer of the vow should drink cow’s urine, water, or clarified butter;
likewise, he may consume barley-food mixed with curd, or sesame-seeds and clarified butter with sugar.
One should indeed consume milk mixed with darbha-water and vegetables as desired, month after month, for the duration of a year, with sincere devotion.
Having worshipped a golden image of the Sun in a copper vessel,
one should offer it to the preceptor along with a cow, and then prostrate before him.
Having fed the Brahmins, the virtuous, and likewise the unvirtuous, he should dismiss them;
one who observes this vow obtains birth in a wealthy and most excellent family. (8-9)
In that family, which consists of every kind of prosperity, abounds in the vigor of food and drink, serves as a refuge for the power of pleasure, and is attended by excellent women.
Then, having enjoyed countless pleasures here in the eternal heaven,
and having fully experienced the enjoyments of the gods, he goes to the eternal Vaikuṇṭha.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should worship the Śālagrāma;
having placed it in a silver vessel, one should offer gold into its mouth.
One should feed [the guest] with milk-rice mixed with sugar and clarified butter,
and one should present [these gifts], adorned with garments and ornaments, to a knower of the Vedas.
One who observes the vow shall go to Vaikuṇṭha and partake in eternal bliss;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, [one should worship] a golden image of Hari.
Having worshipped [the deity], one should give [the offerings] to the guru and feed the boys and girls;
for by performing this vow, a person goes to the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 95.
Having enjoyed pleasures that are difficult to obtain, one partakes in eternal happiness.
[These include] Trispṛśā, Mīlanī, Pakṣavardhinī, and likewise Vañjulī. (96)
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—these eight Dvādaśīs, when observed with a fast, are destroyers of sin. (97)
If the Ekādaśī has ended before sunrise,
then that Dvādaśī is called Trispṛśā, which yields great fruit.
By the observance of this vow, one enjoys the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices,
provided that on the dawn of Aruṇa, the lunar day of Ekādaśī is pierced by Daśamī.
Then, having completely abandoned that [eleventh day], one should fast on the twelfth;
this Sonmīlitā bestows the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
But when the eleventh lunar day touches the southern solstice at sunrise;
Then that Vañjulikā indeed bestows the fruits of all sacrifices. || 101 ||
When the two full moons (Kuhū and Rākā) fall on the thirteenth lunar day, that is the Pakṣavardhinī;
it indeed bestows all sovereignty and increases one's sons and grandsons.
But when the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) occurs during the bright fortnight conjoined with the Maghā asterism, it is called Jayā; it is considered everywhere to be the bestower of victory. (103)

If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight should be conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa, it is Vijayā; it bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrtha) and grants happiness and enjoyment. 104.
When the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight is conjoined with the Prajāpatya asterism (rohiṇī), it is known as Jayantī, which bestows the fruits of vows and gifts.
But when the twelfth day (dvādaśī) occurs during the bright fortnight conjoined with Jupiter and the Sun,
then that Aparājitā bestows knowledge and liberation, and destroys all sins.
But when the asterism Anurādhā occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, then both vows should be performed; there is no fault here, as they share a single deity.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada when it is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
and on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika under the last asterism (Revatī), one should observe these two vows.
On a day other than these, one should observe the single-meal fast on the twelfth lunar day;
indeed, the vow consists of the twelfth-day day joined with the eleventh.
A separate concluding rite (udyāpana) need not be performed; rather, a gift should be given according to one's wealth.
Thus, O Kamalā, these vows are to be observed on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
Thus, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, [it is described] among the annual Dvādaśī vows.

Chapter Two Hundred and Seventy-Seven: Description of the Madanavrata, Bhartṛdvādaśī, Mādhava, Karaka, Śāka, Alavaṇa, Dadhi, Vrata-pavitrāropaṇa, Vāmanajayantī, Padmanābha-vrata, Govatsadvādaśī, Dāmodara-nīrājana-vrata, Tulasī-vivāha, Sādhyāditya-rūpa-vrata, Sujanma-dvādaśī, Śālagrāma-hari-pūjā, Trispṛśā, Unmīlanī, Pakṣavardhinī, Vañjulī, Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā-dvādaśī, and others.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall fully describe to you the vows of the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī-vrata). By performing them according to the prescribed rite, the observer of the vow becomes the most excellent of those who enjoy worldly pleasures.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship Madana, made of sandalwood, accompanied by Rati, and fan him with a fan.
On a wooden board, one should paint the God of Love with red lead and turmeric pigments—
handsome, accompanied by Rati, and bearing a flowery bow and arrows.
One should have images of Vasantamukha and Vajramukha, as well as Vṛṣadhvaja, fashioned;
one should worship them with perfumes, garlands, ornaments, garments, edible foods, and excellent drinks.
One should worship Madana, Kāma, Manmatha, the beloved of Rati, Anaṅga, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja.
One should also worship the Mind-born God (Kāma), who has flowers as his arrows and resides in uneven places, with *mālatī* flowers; one should indeed cause the gift of a goat to be made.
If that Mahāvāruṇī, which is invincible when joined with Saturday,
can be obtained at the Gaṅgā, it is considered superior to ten million solar eclipses.
When there is a *śubhayoga* and the moon is in the hundredth asterism (*śatarakṣa*) on a Saturday in the month of Kārttika during the bright fortnight,
it is renowned as the *Mahāmaha*, which grants liberation to ten million members of one's lineage.
When the spring season has arrived, one should perform a great festival every year,
or perhaps every month, until the year is completed.
His desire is ever-satisfied, and here he grants him an excellent woman; in the next world, he grants the power of passion and great happiness born of the bodiless god of love.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the Kāmavrata is prescribed;
there, one should worship Kāma with perfumes and other offerings. || 11 ||
One should worship [the deity] every month on the thirteenth lunar day with appropriate offerings;
and at the end of the year, one should give a cow to the preceptor for the successful completion of the vow.
One shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, supreme perfection, and the gratification of desires; as well as heavenly bliss, an excellent woman, and whatever desired objects grant worldly enjoyment.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, there is a vow for the pacification of misfortune;
having bathed in a river, one should indeed worship with incense, lamps, water, and other offerings.
Having gazed upon a white mandāra flower, a sun-like flower, or a red karavīra, the observer of the vow should then pray to the Sun in the sky.
O Mandāraka, Karavīra, and Arka, you who are born from the rays of the Sun;
may you, when worshipped, destroy my misfortune—salutations be unto you!
Thus, the misfortune of the worshipper surely perishes; there is no doubt. Furthermore, Trivikrama should be worshipped here by one who seeks the fulfillment of their vow. (17)
Being contented, one may give away the earth or bestow wealth and enjoyments;
however, one should perform the Sāvitrī-vrata here according to one's desire for prosperity.
The observer of the vow should worship Sāvitrī and Vedhas with many offerings;
he should present clarified butter, milk-rice, and fried cakes.
The fruit of enjoyment and liberation shall always belong to the woman,
and the observer of the vow obtains wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and so forth.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha,
the observer of the vow, having taken a single meal, should duly perform the Jayā-Pārvatī vow.
Indeed, the images of Umā and Maheśvara may be made of gold, silver, or clay;
they may be situated in a temple of the gods, in a lion’s den, in a cow-pen, or in the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having established [the images] according to the ritual rule, one should worship them for three days;
on the third day, those two should be joyfully offered to the Guru.
Every year this vow should be performed; thus for five years, one should provide various kinds of food and various kinds of gifts.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should cause those two to be presented with a pair of cows;
for such practitioners of the vow, there shall be no separation from their spouses for seven births.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one who observes the vow and has fasted should duly perform the auspicious Ratikāmavrata.

Either the maiden or the bridegroom, having placed the [liṅga] made of copper, gold, silver, or clay, and having established it as Rati and Kāma, should worship it properly with perfumes and other offerings. || 27 ||
One should honor a Brahmin couple and give gifts such as clothing and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
then one should feed them and perform the vow for fourteen years.
One should offer two images accompanied by two cows to the venerable Guru;
this vow bestows desired objects and grants the happiness of good fortune.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the Gotrirātra vow is observed;
having fashioned an image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa out of gold or silver.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then placed it upon a seat within an eight-petaled mandala, one should worship it with flowers, perfumes, and ornaments.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offer excellent, sweet food;
thereafter, one should present a vessel containing food and water to the venerable Guru.
One should perform this for three days; at the conclusion of the vow, one should worship a cow.
Five cows were produced when the great ocean was being churned. (33)
Among them, salutations again and again to that cow Nandā.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me. (34)
"May cows be at my side; may I dwell in the midst of cows.
Having bowed down and circumambulated them, one should cause morsels of food to be given to them. (35)
One should offer the image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa to the venerable Guru;
[this is equal to] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the vow of three nights for the sake of one's lineage,
that same fruit is obtained by performing the excellent Śrāddha for children and others on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
One should have [this] performed by all means so that even the slayers may attain a good rebirth;
for this day is declared to be the first lunar day of the Kali Yuga, bestowing merit upon those who observe the vow.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Īṣa, having fashioned a golden Aśoka tree and worshipped it with excellent materials, one should observe the virtuous vow of the three-night Aśoka rite.
A woman devoted to fasting should constantly perform one hundred and eight circumambulations, and while doing so, she should pray to me as the Ashokita.
On the third day, having worshipped Hara upon a tree, one should provide a meal for children and give gifts to worthy recipients, such as collyrium and other items to young maidens.
A woman who observes this vow in this manner shall never encounter widowhood;
accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others, she shall remain beloved by her husband. 42.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should light an oil lamp;
having worshipped it, one should then place it outside at the door of the house. (43)
"May Yama be pleased with me through this offering of a lamp; one should perform this praise.
When this is done, O Mahālakṣmī, the suffering caused by Yama does not arise. (44)
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the worship of Wealth (Dhana).
Wealth is Lakṣmī; wealth is gold; and wealth consists of wife, children, and so forth. (45)
Through the worship of Dhanada, one shall attain stability; of this there is no doubt.
There, the observer of the vow should worship Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and gold. 46.
One should cleanse the entire temple and construct an auspicious pavilion;
one should fashion a most beautiful image of Hari and Lakṣmī out of gold.
One should apply a beautiful black tilaka made with saffron and bind upon the head a cloth-strip decorated with golden borders. (48)
And one should wear other garments and ornaments upon a suitable body:
the goddess Lakṣmī, a green skirt, and a beautiful saffron-colored bodice. 49.
One should wear one's own garments, ornaments, and so forth, and adorn the Goddess Śrī;
one should worship her with the sixteen articles of worship and other suitable offerings, and present them to her.
One should indeed offer auspicious sweet foods such as *śaṣkulī* and *khājaka*, and one should cause many lamps to be waved in lustration (*nīrājana*) everywhere. ||5 1 ||
One should devoutly give gifts of new vessels and garments for four days, performing the worship of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
One should especially have it constructed, for then one shall always be an abode of prosperity;
having given a gift to the preceptor, one should afterwards conclude the vow.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, eating but a single meal at the onset of night,
one should [worship] with thousands or hundreds of lamps, or with a garland of lamps.
One should illuminate the house and the temple, and worship Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen types of services and food offerings endowed with various flavors. ||55||
For the sake of satisfaction, one should worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Prabhā, Hara, Sūrya, and Hari as well. (56)

Having worshipped him at the onset of night and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the observer of the vow, after feeding [the deity], should perform the ritual dismissal; he shall become possessed of gold and other riches.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Ananga according to the prescribed rite;
one should also worship Rati in the morning and feed a Brahmin couple.
When the vow has been performed in this manner, one shall become a vessel for all good fortune;
having worshipped Kamalā and Hari on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa. (59)
One should offer a vessel of clarified butter to a twice-born man for the sake of prosperity and success;
the performer of this vow shall possess wealth, grain, and other riches, and shall be happy.
O beloved, beginning from the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, one should perform ablutions in a river with cold water for three days at the end of the night.
The observer of the vow should worship the Lord while still wearing wet clothes;
sins from previous births and other lifetimes are surely destroyed—of this there is no doubt. (62)
The fruit of the Māgha bath indeed fulfills various desires;
however, the fruit of bathing for even three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha is far greater. || 63 ||
One does not obtain that fruit on earth even by a thousand horse-sacrifices;
bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and worship performed there become infinite.
This very lunar day marks the beginning of the Kalpa and is also the Jayantī of Viśvakarman;
on this day, Hari and Brahmā themselves were born as Viśvakarman.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed and adorn it with artistic designs;
one should worship Viśvakarman, the master craftsman, with all kinds of offerings.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), feed [the preceptor], and give gifts to the wise teacher;
the observer of the vow should also keep a vigil at night accompanied by instrumental music and song.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the morning, having fed [the recipient], and having offered praise, one should bid them farewell.
By performing the vow in this manner, the artisan shall attain the state of Viśvakarman.
Through wealth, grain, sons, daughters, wife, cattle, prosperity, and so forth, one shall be happy and obtain fame for one's own arts both in this world and the next. (69)
In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, on the thirteenth day, is Śivarātri;
it is a great vow consisting of the manifestation of the Great Liṅga through the splendor of Śiva.
Then, with devotion, one should observe a vow that is stainless and free from food;
in the morning, one should indeed worship Śambhu together with Satī, who is beautifully golden.
At midday, one should devoutly offer all kinds of cooked food;
one should cause the Śatarudra, the Koṭirudra, and the Rudrādhyāya to be recited.
One should worship all the incarnations of Rudra and the female incarnations of Pārvatī with the sixteen excellent articles of offering, and one should present bhangā.
One should worship with rudrākṣa, dhattūra, flowers, incense such as guggulu and dhūmra, the waters of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), cool sandalwood paste, and other offerings.

In the evening, one should worship Śaṅkara with all the materials for the ritual services according to the procedure for the Great Consecration (mahābhiṣeka) and by means of the Rudra-hymn (rudrasūkta).
At midnight, one should worship with affection, together with his retinue, using bilva leaves,
jasmine, kunda flowers, dhattūra, and karavīra.
One should bathe Rudra, who possesses eleven forms,
as well as the twelve-fold Self and that which is of the singular form of Brahman, with milk.
Likewise, one should propitiate Śiva and Śivā with incense, lamps, fine musical instruments, and the waving of lights (nīrājana), as well as with dances and hymns of praise.
For the food offering (naivedya), there were hundreds of wheat-based *vaṭaka* cakes, sweetmeats,
vegetables, sour gruel (*āranāla*), cooked grains (*bhāja*), and fruits.
Milk-rice preparations with sugar, products of sugarcane, and liquid offerings; drinks, foods to be sucked, licked, and chewed, as well as roasted snacks. ||1.278.80||
One should indeed offer bulbous roots, tubers, and the like, as well as leaves, flowers, and sprouts, to Śaṅkara and Śivā with supreme devotion. 81.
One should offer to Śaṅkara [an image] adorned with ashes, a trident, rudrākṣa beads, the moon, and the serpent Vāsuki, and one should cause his [Śiva’s] verses to be sung there.
At night, one should hold a festival and keep a vigil together with people;
in the morning, one should perform worship and cause gifts to be given in abundance.
One should feed and likewise honor Brahmins who are renunciants, practitioners of yoga, as well as yoginīs, chaste and virtuous women, ascetics, and holy men. 8.4.
One should feed and honor the gurus, the ancestors, the Gaṇas, the elders, mothers, children, young girls, maidens, married women, and all moving beings. ||85||
One should worship those devoted to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the gods, and Rudra;
one should honor and feed the Brahmins and give gifts in every way.
He should conclude the vow; then he should perform the fire-oblation.
The observer of the vow should then perform the auspicious purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with great celebration.
A wealthy observer of the vow should perform the Rudra-sacrifice, the great sacrifice;
thus, on the fourteenth day of Śiva (Śivacaturdaśī), he should carry out the ritual of feeding.
Having performed the breaking of the fast in this manner, one should partake of food; the fruit shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One shall attain Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the Imperishable Abode.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, one should perform the vow that bestows wealth; on this occasion, one should worship Kubera with sandalwood and other offerings.
Every month, the Lord of Yakṣas himself, the King of Yakṣas, together with his treasure and his retinue, is to be worshipped personally with sixteen articles.
He should be fed with delicious foods, and even a cow with her calf should be honored here;
indeed, the preceptor must be worshipped and provided with food in every way.
And sweet foods and gifts should be bestowed upon the twice-born;
when the vow of eating but once a day is performed in this manner, one shall attain great prosperity.
In this world as well as in heaven, endowed with every prosperity,
he attains a sovereignty of happiness like another Rājarāja.

He shall indeed rejoice together with his family members for eternal years, provided he observes the vow of eating only at night, eating only once a day, or fasting entirely in all circumstances. || 95 ||
According to one's capacity, one should perform [the vow] by subsisting on fruits, water, milk, curd, or jaggery-water. || 96 ||
Thus, in the first section, concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, regarding the vows of the thirteenth lunar day of the rainy season.

The two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Madana-vrata, Daurbhāgya-śamana, Trivikrama-arcana, Sāvitrī, Jayā, Pārvatī, Rati-kāma, Gotrirātra, Bālā-śrāddha, Tithis marking the beginning of the Kali Yuga, the Trirātra, Aśoka-vrata, the offering of lamps to Yama, the worship of Dhanalakṣmī, the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Anaṅga-vrata, the worship of Kamalā-Hari, the tithis marking the beginning of the Kalpas, the Viśvakarma-jayantī, the Mahāśivarātri, the Dhanada-vrata, and others."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the vows of the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī),
by performing which a practitioner in this world obtains his desired goal in the hereafter.
In a former age, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, a great festival was celebrated by Nārāyaṇa for his marriage with Śrī.
One observing the vow should prepare a plantain pavilion here, eating only a single meal;
likewise, a water-pot should be placed within the Sarvatobhadra mandala.
A vessel of sesame seeds should be placed near his mouth close to the fire-pit,
and the worship of Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī should be performed between them.
The offering should be performed with the sixteen types of service;
thereafter, the observer of the vow should indeed cause many musical instruments to be played during the night.
One should likewise manifest the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Lakṣmī,
and have them clothed in garments, ornaments, and fragrant unguents.
Having performed the worldly customs and presented the bridegroom’s garland, and having completed all the worship of the deities and the act of salutation; || 7 ||
Then, having placed an intervening cloth between them, he should cause the joining of their hands;
and having performed the fire-oblation (homa), he should have auspicious songs sung.
Having performed the circumambulation and given her a dowry,
he honored her according to worldly custom and removed the objects from his head.
Having completed the full oblation, one should install [the image] within the house;
after causing Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī to be fed, one should have them sleep in the house.
At dawn, one should indeed untie the knot of the book at the Ganges and bestow many gifts, such as cows, land, and gold.
One should feed the Brahmins, the gods, the sages, the virtuous, and likewise the chaste women;
as well as boys, girls, and others who are wretched, blind, or without support.
And [he sent] servants, mendicants, the helpless, teachers, and the most venerable elders,
who went to the abodes of Brahman, Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the immortal realm.
[He saw] those from the unmanifest realm of Śvetadvīpa, the Vairājas who have gone to the Satyaloka,
those who have come from the world of Brahmā, the liberated ones, and the divine wives of Viṣṇu.
He should likewise feed his mothers and human women, as well as *śaṣkulīs*, delicious *khājakas*, *śatacchidrāṇi*, and *pheṇikās*. (15)
And *ghṛtapūra* cakes, *revālī* sweets, *parpikā* pastries with their essence extracted,
*piṇḍaka* balls, *śarkaraila* sweets, *śārkarā* confections, and likewise chickpea flour treats.
Also inauspicious items such as cotton cloths, delusive vessels, parched grain flour, knotted cords, and bloated medicinal pills. || 17 ||
The essence of milk, milk-rice, curd,
and sandalwood paste, as well as various kinds of vegetables, pearls, and powdered modakas.
Split pulses, decoctions, as well as mustard and red gram soups;
excellent fermented rice-gruel drinks and various preparations of buttermilk.
One should feed them, provide drinks for them, and cause them to perform the cleansing of their mouths;
one should also give them betel leaves and likewise cause gifts to be given.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Lakṣmī, one should bid them farewell;
then, on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), the observer of the vow should partake of auspicious food.
Having thus performed the vow prepared for the marriage of Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī,
through their grace, this conjugal union shall become eternal here.
Moreover, by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the couple who observe the vow shall indeed attain an eternal, supreme, and divine state in Goloka. (23)
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Mahālakṣmī vow is observed;
on this occasion, a procession for Mahālakṣmī should be performed and she should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Furthermore, the worship of Jānakī and Śivarāja should indeed be performed here together, especially by a devoted woman and likewise by a devoted man. (25)
At night, the observer of the vow should perform a vigil here with dancing and singing;
in the morning, they should be fed, honored, and then dismissed with great devotion.
Having performed the worship in this manner, the man or woman observing the vow shall indeed obtain wealth, grain, progeny, and happiness from Mahālakṣmī. || 27 ||
And here also, on the fourteenth day, the worship of Śiva should be performed with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood, as well as perfumes and the like, garments, and jewels.
Having offered canopies, banners, and umbrellas, and having worshipped the Mothers,
the practitioner who observes the vow obtains the great merit of the horse sacrifice and other such rites.
Right here, the practitioner of the vow should perform the worship of the *damanaka* plant with fragrant flowers;
after the worship, he should offer the *damanaka* to Śiva alone.
The great golden liṅga named Hāṭaka came from the netherworld (pātāla) to the earth; indeed, the Lord is there as Hāṭakeśvara. || 31 ||
He alone is to be worshipped here with excellent articles such as the sixteen [upacāras],
including bathing, adornment, food offerings, worship, and the waving of lights (nīrājana).
One should satisfy Hāṭakeśa, for he indeed bestows gold.
Observing the vow and fully endowed with enjoyments, he shall go to the supreme Kailāsa.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, at the arrival of night,
one should worship the Liṅga with offerings such as perfumes and with Bilva leaves.
One should feed them, worship them, offer prayers, and then dismiss them;
thus should the Śiva-vrata be performed by one desiring wealth and progeny.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the Narasiṃha-caturdaśī.
And here, one should perform the evening festival for the incarnation as Nṛsiṃha.
Eating only once or observing a fast, one should worship Narasiṃha, fashioned from gold,
with the sixteen types of offerings and with baths such as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and others.

With incense, lamps, and beautiful flowers, with foods, drinks, and chewables, as well as with the waving of lights (ārātrika) and so forth, and with circumambulations, hymns of praise, and the like. || 38 ||
Having worshipped Nṛhari, the observer of the vow should indeed install him at night;
then he should give various gifts there according to his wealth. (39)
With the tips of his mane like molten gold and eyes like blazing fire,
he was a divine lion, terrifying with claws whose touch exceeded the hardness of a diamond.
With thick shoulders, hips, and neck, a slender waist and a lean belly, he had the face of a lion and a human body, adorned with all ornaments. || 41 ||
His face was wreathed in garlands of flames, with a lolling tongue-tip and prominent fangs,
as he tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with the tips of his claws.
And one should worship Prahlāda and Kayādhū again in the morning;
one should feed them various foods, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and then bid them farewell.
The observer of the vow himself should perform the breaking of the fast for the sake of pleasing Nṛhari;
freed from the fear of clawed and fanged beasts, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
One who seeks the fruits of the vow should perform a pilgrimage here to Oṃkāreśvara;
having bathed the Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and smeared it with saffron, [he should proceed]. ||45||
The observer of the vow should worship the flour-made liṅga with food offerings, fruits, incense, lamps, garments, ornaments, the waving of lights (ārātrika), and other such rites. 46.
By the grace of Mahādeva, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
whatever he may perform shall all become a bestower of knowledge and emancipation upon men. ||47||

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should fetch excellent water for the purpose of the bathing procession; for that [water], one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and other rites. 48.
On the full moon day, the observer of the vow should bathe Śrī Hari with that water at dawn,
worship Him with various offerings, and perform a festival.

On the fourteenth day, performing the penance of five fires during the day, one should offer a cow for the fire-sacrifice at the beginning of the night; one should diligently perform this Rudra-vrata.
Having worshipped Rudra on the fourteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha while observing the vow,
one shall indeed obtain all prosperity through [the excellence of] place, time, the object of worship, materials, and so forth.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) to the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and likewise offer it to Lakṣmī.

Whether a man or a woman, even after worshipping Hari and Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, which are obtained through their grace. ||53||
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform the supreme Ananta-vrata;
then [one should worship] the one named Ananta, as well as Śeṣa and Hari, who is Nārāyaṇa.
Thereafter, the observer of the vow should have [the image] made of gold and worship it according to the prescribed rite;
[he should also provide] a thread made of cotton or silk with fourteen beautiful knots.
Having prepared it and worshipped it with saffron and other offerings, the observer of the vow should bind it upon his own arm—
the woman on the left and the man on the right— and he should then cast the Purāṇa into the water.
Then, having cooked a *prastha* measure of wheat flour mixed with sugar and clarified butter until it is sweet, one should offer it to Ananta.
Having fed the children as well, the observer of the vow should then eat himself;
that vow, accompanied by its sacrificial fee, lasts for fourteen years.
The observer of the vow should indeed perform this rite until its conclusion, and then he should conclude it;
he should prepare a Sarvatobhadra mandala using the seven types of grain.
One should place an image of Ananta in a copper jar or a vessel;
one should worship it according to the prescribed rite, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and offer food.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, the Kheṭas, and the World-Protectors individually;
having performed the fire-oblation with offerings of ghee and sacrificial food, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
On the Śrīmukha day, the observer of the vow should donate a bed, an image, and a cow;
having fed children and virtuous men, he should satisfy them with sacrificial fees.
One should give many gifts and feed virtuous men and women;
thus, the performer of the Ananta-vrata becomes a partaker of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One who desires prosperity should also perform the Kadalī-vrata here;
neither man nor woman [should disregard it], just as one would not overlook the plantain tree standing within the forest.
Having bathed, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, grains, sprouts, and so forth,
as well as with curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, lamps, garments, and an abundance of cooked food.
Having bowed and circumambulated her, he should then offer this prayer to her,
who is worshipped by celestial nymphs, daughters of the gods, and daughters of the nāgas.
"Grant me health of body, beauty, and prosperity; salutations be unto you!
Then, [he should invite] four women—either married women (*suvāsinī*) or virtuous widows (*satī*).
Having fed [the deity] with garments, vermilion, lac, and collyrium,
and having worshipped and concluded the rite, the observer of the vow should return to his own home.
O Lakṣmī, when this vow has been performed in this manner, having obtained supreme good fortune,
one shall sport in heaven by means of a celestial chariot and thereafter worship the highest world.
Served by the *parīs* and having enjoyed great bliss in the realm of Truth (*satya*),
he finally goes to the divine world called the Abode of the Imperishable (*akṣara-dhāman*), the station of Hari.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, for those who have killed a Brahmin and have been slain by poison, weapons, water, fire, serpents, wild beasts, thunderbolts, and the like; ||71||
One should perform the śrāddha rite as appropriate according to the rules for the ekoddiṣṭa ceremony;
one should feed children with sweets, as well as virtuous men, virtuous women, and the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas).

Having offered libations to the cows with mouthfuls of fodder and having given alms to dogs and crows, the observer of the vow, having sipped water (ācamana), should eat together with his own kinsmen. (73)
Having performed such a great śrāddha and having delivered his ancestors,
he shall go to the eternal heaven and, in the end, to the abode of Brahmā within Hari.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, having properly worshipped the golden Dharmarāja with perfumes and other offerings, one should feed him excellent, sweet food.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana), and offer gifts to the venerable Guru.
Thus, Dharmarāja protects the observer of the vow and leads him to heaven.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, having performed an oil massage at the rising of the moon,
one should bathe, worship Dharmarāja, and offer libations to Yama.
At twilight, the observer of the vow should light oil lamps for the satisfaction of Yama and place them at a crossroads outside the house.
One should feed [the deity], perform obeisance, and dismiss Yamādhipa;
having performed the vow in this manner, one shall go to heaven, free from fear of hell. (79)
Then, on that very fourteenth day, one should perform the worship of Hanumān with oil, vermilion, arka flowers, garlands, mung beans, vaṭakas, and other such offerings.
The sons and grandsons of the officiating priests shall attain abundant prosperity;
in the end, they shall reach the eternal and most excellent worlds of Vairāja. ||81||
It is the accomplishment of the Tāmasa beings such as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas, and also the accomplishment of the mantras of the Rājasa deities. ||82||
The propitiation of worldly beings of virtuous nature who cause poison, fire, and paralysis, as well as the invocation of ḍākinīs and yoginīs. ||83||
One who seeks Bhairava should also perform the sādhana of those who dwell in cremation grounds here at night, according to the instructions and the prescribed ritual. ||84||

The observer of the vow should duly perform each respective observance, offering, worship, recitation, dismissal by name, fire-oblation, and ritual action according to the tantra in their proper sequence. 85.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, at Kāśī, Śrī Śaṅkara himself, having bathed according to the prescribed rites, performed the excellent Pāśupata vow. ||86||
Then, one should perform a great worship here at the liṅga with perfumes and other offerings, using *droṇa* flowers, bilva leaves, *arka* flowers, and *ketaka* flowers. (87)
By means of flowers, fruits, sweet ripe offerings, and various kinds of food oblations, the observer of the vow who eats but once a day shall attain Kailāsa through the gratification of Śambhu. 88.
One who desires prosperity should also perform the Brahmakūrca vow in this regard;
he should drink the five products of the cow at night and satisfy the gods with libations in the morning. (8–9)
Having gratified the Brahmins, the observer of the vow may himself eat;
by the Brahmakūrca vow, all sins are certainly destroyed.
Indeed, the urine of a tawny cow, the dung of a black one, the milk of a white one, and the auspicious curd of a red one are to be taken. (91)
Ghee should be taken from Karburā and mixed with those [substances] using water from Kuśa grass;
by drinking that, sins are destroyed from their very roots, even while still fresh.
Even the "stone-vow" (pāṣāṇavrata) is considered fulfilled here by performing it at night;
having worshipped Gaurī with perfumes and other offerings, one should present food cooked in ghee.
If it is ground into a mass shaped like a stone ball,
the observer of the vow shall then attain sovereignty, happiness, good fortune, and his true nature.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped a golden bull and observed the vow of eating but one meal, he should then worship Maheśvara at night.
One should worship with lotus flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
one should feed [the deity] with many kinds of cooked foods, and then one should bid farewell to the god.
One should give gifts to the preceptor and feed virtuous men and women;
having thus performed the Śiva-vow, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And right here, Hari, Brahmā, Śiva, and Datta born of Atri—these three gods having become one—became known by the name Dattātreya. 98.
Having likewise placed Anasūyā, Atri, Dattātreya,
and the Kānakas upon a jar atop an auspicious mandala within the pavilion.
One should properly worship [the deity] in the vessel, feed [the guests], and perform the ritual dismissal;
the observer of the vow should give all kinds of gifts and shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one should observe the Virūpākṣa vow;
having bathed, one should worship Śiva Virūpākṣa with all kinds of offerings.
One should feed and satisfy Śambhu according to the prescribed rite and bid him farewell;
having given gifts to the twice-born, the observer of the vow rejoices in Kailāsa.
The libation to Yama is prescribed for the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha;
having bathed before sunrise, one should offer libations to Yama.
Thereafter, one should feed the excellent food with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water;
one should dismiss the virtuous brahmins, and the observer of the vow should eat.
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna is the Śambhunishāvrata;
however, Śivarātri is observed without water, and its fast should be undertaken with sincere devotion.
Whether it be a Jyotirliṅga or an earthen image, Śiva and Śivā are present in embodied form;
they are worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, bilva leaves and the like, food offerings, and drinks of excellent flavor.
The observer of the vow should worship, feed, perform the lustration ceremony for, dismiss, and bow down [to the deity].
By the power of the vow, the observer of the vow shall attain Kailāsa. || 107 ||
The fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna is considered the Durgā-vrata;
observing a single meal, the practitioner of the vow should worship Durgā and likewise feed others.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), pay obeisance, and dismiss [the deity]; thus one shall become a partaker of Kailāsa.
However, he who desires the fruit [of his practice] must perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for his vows. 109.

In this rite, there shall be exactly fourteen jars— made of copper or clay, unblemished and new— filled with betel nuts, unbroken grains, and sweetmeats, accompanied by sacrificial fees and fine garments.
There were as many bamboo staffs, purifiers, seats, vessels, and sacred threads as there were [of the former]. Indeed, they were all prepared in equal number. || 111 ||
In the pavilion, upon the Sarvatobhadra mandala, water-pots containing fruit should be placed;
the deities should be installed, worshipped, and fed.
The sacrificial fees (visarjanīya) should be given to the preceptor in the form of a gift; likewise, virtuous people, holy women, Brahmins, and young girls should be fed. 113.

With enthusiasm, one should in every way perform the completion ceremony (udyāpana) along with the fire sacrifice (homa), the recitation of mantras (japa), and the ritual union (saṅgama); its fruit is heaven and liberation.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the annual Caturdaśī vows, [are described] the marriage of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, the pilgrimage to Mahālakṣmī, the worship of Śiva, the worship of Damana, the Jayantī of Śrī-Hāṭakeśvara, and the Jayantī of Narasiṃha.

Chapter Two Hundred and Seventy-Nine: An Exposition on Rituals such as the Kāreśvara Pilgrimage, the Bathing Pilgrimage, the Fetching of Water, the Rudra-vow, the Pavitrāropaṇa, the Ananta-caturdaśī, the Kadalī-vow, the Śrāddha for those killed [in battle], the Worship of Dharmarāja, the Naraka-caturdaśī, the Tarpaṇa for Yama, the Oil-Bath, the Worship of Hanumān, the Worship of Bhūtas, Mantra-sādhana, the Pāśupata-vow, the Brahmakūrca-vow, the Dattātreya-jayantī, the Śivarātri, and other such vows.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the vows of the full-moon day (pūrṇimā),
by performing which a man or a woman may obtain an abundance of merit.
Indeed, the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Caitra is a tithi marking the beginning of a Manvantara;
on this day, one should offer a jar containing rice and water for the satisfaction of Soma.
One should perform the śrāddha as prescribed for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors. On the full moon day of the month of Caitra, it is called the Hanumat-tithi.
Worship with oil, vermilion, vaṭakas, and other excellent offerings should be performed here;
indeed, the commencement of the Vaiśākha bath is also recommended at this time.
On the new moon day of Vaiśākha, a Śrāddha ceremony should be performed to satisfy the ancestors;
on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the Kūrmajayantī vow is observed.
There, according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the Lord made of gold, who has two arms, a human head, and the form of a tortoise from the waist downwards.
The observer of the vow should feed [the guests] with the essence of milk and sweetmeats (modaka) prepared from chickpea flour;
he should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana), perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana), and bestow gifts.
For one who has performed such a vow, residence in Vaikuṇṭha becomes certain;
however, the vow of Dharmarāja should be observed here for the satisfaction of Dharma.
The observer of the vow should give cooked rice and a water-pot to his preceptor, as well as a cow;
he should worship Dharmarāja, feed him, and then dismiss him.
One should give an auspicious black antelope skin along with its hooves and horns;
one should also give garments together with sesame seeds, and jars filled with clear water.
A person observing the vow should give fruits and gold as a gift;
such a person rejoices in the world of truth (Satyaloka) for as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
Beforehand, one attains Vaikuṇṭha and enjoys eternal happiness;
Jyeṣṭhāmā is declared to be Bhāvukā, and at that time one should meditate upon Śrī Hari.
One should worship in every way at night, feed [the deity], and then dismiss [it]. On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Vaṭasāvitrika vow should be performed.
Fasting, one should sprinkle the banyan tree with waters comparable to nectar,
and one should also encircle it with a thread while performing one hundred and eight circumambulations.
The observer of the vow should wrap the *pippala* tree and pray to Sāvitrī:
"O Sāvitrī, honored by the world, Mother of the World, whose deity is the husband! (1.5)
"May there be no separation from my husband for me while I remain under the banyan tree; salutations!
Having thus prayed to Sāvitrī and fed the married women, [she performed the rites]. || 16 ||
She who observes the vow herself shall become a partaker of good fortune;
in this regard, the vow known as Bilvatrirātra should be performed with devotion. (17)
Śambhu is to be worshipped with bilva leaves; one seeking the fruits of a vow should consume bilva;
a bath with bilva should be performed, and the bilva tree itself is also to be honored. (18)
One should sleep beneath a bilva tree, and likewise, the offering of bilva fruits is prescribed;
by performing this for three nights, the observer of the vow shall indeed attain Kailāsa.
This is the lunar day (tithi) of Manu and others; Manu is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Likewise, gifts should be given, and virtuous, holy men who bestow great merit should be fed.
On this very day, the festival of the Jyeṣṭhā-abhiṣeka bath should be performed;
there, the Lord of Ramā is to be bathed according to the rite of consecration.
One should bathe Kṛṣṇa with conch shells using pure water mixed with sandalwood, held in radiant vessels, while reciting mantras according to the Vedas.
Then, one should offer yellow garments here to the Lord Śrīpati, as well as a pale-red turban and various ornaments. (23)
One should offer cooked rice, soup, cakes, fried balls, broth, as well as side dishes, food offerings, and sweet drinks.
One should have the verses concerning Hari’s water-sports sung here;
after bidding farewell to Hari, the person observing the vow should then eat.
By that [act], one attains the eternal happiness born of Hari's grace;
on the day of the Aṣāḍhā constellation, a Śrāddha ceremony should be performed for the deliverance of the ancestors.
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, the worship of Guru Vyāsa must be performed with the sixteen types of offerings and other requisites, just as that of Hari is performed.
With sandalwood, unbroken grains, tulasī garlands, fruits, garments, saffron, ornaments, food, most delicious meals, excellent coverings, and water; || 28 ||
The observer of the vow should worship the Guru, Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the Ācārya and the Gurvī with substances such as gold and silver, with fields, and with other types of wealth.
One should drink the water from the big toe of the Guru’s foot for the purification of the sense of taste;
the Guru is declared to be Hari himself, and one should serve him for the sake of one's own liberation.
Knowledge obtained through the grace of the Guru, or service and observance of vows, bestows liberation, happiness, merit, enjoyment, and final release. (31)
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform this supreme Gopadmavrata,
[worshipping] the four-armed [Lord] resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
With a serene face and lotus-like eyes, adorned by Lakṣmī and Garuḍa,
he is golden-hued, beautiful in form, and endowed with golden ornaments.
Having thus bathed Hari—who is served by sages, gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras—with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with water; || 34 ||
Having bathed and observed his vows, he should worship while reciting the Puruṣasūkta;
he should adorn the deity, offer worship, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and feed him.
The observer of the vow should then bow down, seek forgiveness, and dismiss [the deity];
he should then feed the preceptor or the virtuous guru and repeatedly satisfy him.
The observer of the vow should give gifts and enjoy [the fruits] through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā;
he obtains eternal desires pertaining to this world and the next. 3.7.
One desiring prosperity should perform the Kokilā-vrata on this very occasion;
for that vow, one should bathe in water outside [the village] until the full moon of Śrāvaṇa.
The observer of the vow should always worship Kokilā in the form of Gaurī,
who has golden wings, jewel-like eyes, and a lotus-face like coral.
Abounding in the beautiful hue of musk, dwelling in the Nandana forest,
seated upon mango and campaka trees, she resounded with the sound of sweet songs.
One should meditate upon the goddess Pārvatī, who has assumed the form of a cuckoo;
one should worship her daily with perfumes and other offerings, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and feed her. ||41||
At the end of the month, one should then request a golden image made of sesame paste,
when the cuckoo— the beloved of Hara— has appeared in the Caitraratha forest during the dark fortnight.
"O you who have been given to me for the sake of the Brahmin in the form of Hara, be the bestower of happiness!
Then, one should feed thirty or even one twice-born man and a married woman. (43)

Having given a gift of clothing and other offerings, and having bowed to the Goddess, she should dismiss her; by means of the performance of this vow, a woman [attains her goal] through the grace of Kokilā-Gaurī. 44.
One shall obtain worldly enjoyment, heaven, great bliss, Kailāsa, the happiness of a married couple, and good fortune for seven births; and at the end, final liberation.
This lunar day, beginning with the one sacred to Manu, marks the commencement of the Cāturmāsya;
here, the festival of Śambhu’s reclining must be performed according to the prescribed rites.
One should create an ocean filled with water, and upon it, a bed as is appropriate;
there, Hari or Hara should be laid down by one who serves them well. (47)
He is to be fed, honored, and entreated with sincere devotion;
furthermore, the observances of the four-month period must be undertaken by the practitioner during his vow. (48)
Having thus performed worship, as well as the vow and the undertaking of the observances, one obtains divine enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. ||49||
On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the worship of the lamp should be performed according to the prescribed rite with flowers,
sandalwood, rice, sugar, fruits, and water.
A lamp that bestows light upon the eyes shall always grant good fortune;
indeed, the offering of a lamp to the deity grants heaven. 5.1.
And here, a śrāddha ceremony should be performed, which brings divine satisfaction to the ancestors;
and the planting of nine trees should be carried out with great devotion.
Making the earth green, the observer of the vow shall attain the green heaven,
where he is served by vehicles, mounts, female slaves, and other attendants, and remains there eternally.
Then, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow should worship a coconut fruit,
eat it, and also give it as a gift with devotion.
The three—Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva—dwell within the three eyes of the coconut;
they are indeed to be worshipped here within this coconut fruit.
You are Brahmā, you are Kuṣpara, and you are Viṣṇu; Śambhu is the water, and these three are yours.
You are the quality of goodness (sattva), you are Viṣṇu abiding within, and you are the three-eyed one whose central part is the seed-syllable (kuṭhula).
Brahmā is the soul of your matted locks, and Hari is indeed the soul of the three gods;
by worshipping him, one shall obtain eternal worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On this occasion, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, there is the vow of commencing the Vedas (vedopākaraṇa);
therein, the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors must be performed with the Yajus formulas.
The worship of the sages (ṛṣis) should be performed according to the rules of one's own Vedic school;
for that libation (tarpaṇa) is to be performed by the followers of the Rigveda on the fourteenth day.
That libation (tarpaṇa) should indeed be performed by the members of the assembly in the month of Bhādrapada,
on the second or third lunar day of the bright fortnight, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Hasta.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed, and likewise the purification of the body (varṣmaśuddhi) should be carried out according to the prescribed rules;
as well as the libation (tarpaṇa) and worship with water mixed with darbha grass.
Having had a new and auspicious sacred thread (upavīta) made, he should wear it;
and he should feed all virtuous Brahmins, gurus, and chaste women with their favorite foods.
To them he should give a sacrificial fee consisting of gold and silver;
the observer of the vow, together with his kinsmen and others, should eat himself and thus attain happiness.
Likewise, the protective rite must indeed be performed here according to the prescribed rule;
one should use black mustard seeds, red cloths, unbroken grains of rice, and sugar.
Having tied it with a safflower-colored thread and likewise washed it with water,
one should then place it in a bronze vessel and worship Viṣṇu and the other principal deities with perfumes and other offerings.
Being joyful, he should have it tied by means of a Brāhmaṇa upon his own forearm;
he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born, for the cord provides protection.
On this very lunar day, in former times, the great lord Hayagrīva [appeared] for the destruction of Hiraṇyākṣa and for the protection of the Vedas.
Then he understood with devotion what was to be done for him;
the horse’s form was comfortable, yet his auspicious body possessed a human shape. (68)
Having fashioned a golden image and worshipped it with sixteen auspicious articles,
the observer of the vow should feed [the priests], perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and then dismiss the deity.
Thus, for one who has performed the vow, happiness arises here and in the next world;
and on this very day, one should perform the offering of the Rudra-pavitra.
On this day, the observer of the vow should worship Śiva and Śivā with various purificatory offerings and bring the Kokilā-vrata to completion.
On the full moon day of Bhādrapada, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha ceremony, including the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites;
one should fetch kuśa grass from a field, cut with a blade and complete with their roots.
On the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, one should observe the Umāmaheśvara vow;
having bathed and applied rudrākṣa beads, sacred ash, and so forth, one should worship Śambhu.

One should feed [the deity] with bilva leaves rich in fragrance, along with food offerings, incense, and lamps; then one should bow, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and finally put [the deity] to sleep.
One should keep a vigil at night and worship again in the morning;
the observer of the vow should then feed [the deity], offer prayers, and finally perform the ritual dismissal.
The observer of the vow should himself perform the breaking of the fast and shall attain Kailāsa;
having performed this for fifteen years, he should then carry out the concluding rite (udyāpana).
And having worshipped that auspicious golden image of Umā and Maheśa within the central jar among fifteen jars, [he should proceed]. //77//
One should offer the image, complete with a water-pot and accompanied by garments, ornaments, flowers, and the like, as well as sweet foods and auspicious waters, to the preceptor.
Having thus performed this vow here, which is the treasury of all prosperity, the practitioner indeed becomes a vessel for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (79)
Then, on this very day, one should reverently perform the Śakra-vrata;
one should worship Hari with offerings such as perfumes and with food oblations.
Having presented a golden image of Śakra to his preceptor,
the king, if he is wealthy, should feed other Brahmins and indeed bestow sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
This annual rite must be performed by one who desires wealth and grain;
on the first day of the month of Āśvina, the libation for all the ancestors should be offered.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) should be performed, including the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), feeding, and the sprinkling of water;
various kinds of food, as well as those with the essence of milk, should indeed be given.
Brahmins and virtuous men should be fed, as well as truthful women and young girls;
cows should be gratified with grass, and likewise trees with water and other offerings.
Hari-Kṛṣṇa is to be propitiated with water for libation, along with food offerings and fruit;
both Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī are likewise to be propitiated. (85)
Having thus performed the great śrāddha, the fathers, grandfathers, all those beginning with the respective ancestors, and the mothers born of one's lineage [are satisfied]. (86)
They indeed attain eternal satisfaction, and in the end, they follow the path to the state of Brahman;
they shall reach the station of liberation. Therefore, the *śrāddha* is the supreme vow.
In the month of Āśvina, on the full moon day, the festival of the Rāsa-līlā is celebrated;
at night, upon the rising of the full moon, he performed the Rāsa-līlā. (88)
The Blessed One, together with Rādhā and the gopīs, for a long time caused the golden images of Gopī-Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa to shine most brilliantly. (89)
He should wear saffron-colored garments, an upper robe, and a small lower garment;
he should also wear a yellow bodice and a tilaka-mark of saffron on his forehead.
The observer of the vow should wear the yellow garment and the priceless dark [complexion],
as well as a crown variegated with various jewels and likewise earrings.
In his hand, he should hold a golden flute adorned with jewels;
as an offering, sweet cakes (parpikā) should be given, along with rice-balls (piṇḍaka), milk-pudding (pāyasa), and so forth.
One should perfume the garments and the temple of the Lord of Rādhikā with fragrant flower oils and water from land-lotuses. 93.
Having placed [the image] on the moon-chamber seat, one should worship Mādhava at night;
indeed, one should satisfy the Lord of Ramā with songs, instrumental music, and dances. 94.
One should offer him fresh flattened rice mixed with sugar and milk, and cause him to sing the verses concerning the Rāsa-līlā. 95.
From that day forward, one who desires prosperity should perform the autumn vow;
indeed, one should begin the Kārtika bath from this very day. (96)
On the full moon day of this month of Āśvina, the vow known as Kojāgara should be performed while fasting, or one may observe the practice of eating only once a day.
One should worship Lakṣmī in the morning with various ritual offerings, adorn her, and feed her; one should also worship her at midday.
At the sight of the moon in the evening, having placed an image of Lakṣmī made of gold— or even one made of copper or clay— into a vessel or a bowl.
One should illuminate a thousand, a hundred, or a hundred thousand lamps within jars;
one should offer fried cakes and milk-rice porridge to Mahālakṣmī.
One should keep a vigil with dance and song, and having worshipped her in the morning,
the observer of the vow should offer the image to the guru and thus conclude the rite.
"Here at night, Mahālakṣmī, whose lotus-hands grant boons and fearlessness, comes to see who is awake for my sake; therefore, one who possesses good enjoyment [should remain awake]. (102)
To him who is awake and my worshiper, I grant wealth;
by performing this here every year, he shall become prosperous and indeed attain the state of Viṣṇu.
On the first day of the month of Kārttika, the worship of Lakṣmī should be performed especially;
Lakṣmī should be depicted as four-armed, seated upon a lotus-throne.
In the right hand there is a lotus, and likewise in the left a jar of nectar;
below these, in the other two hands, beautiful bilva and conch shells should be depicted.
On both her sides, two elephants should be fashioned, both holding water-pots;
upon her head, a most beautiful lotus should be made.
When a beautiful pavilion has been constructed with plantain pillars and arches,
the observer of the vow should worship her upon a Sarvatobhadra diagram with the Lakṣmīsūkta.
One should offer ornaments and great garments to Śrī;
on her forehead, one should draw a crescent moon, beautified with saffron and unbroken grains of rice.
One should worship with fragrant flowers, garlands, golden ornaments of all kinds, lotuses, jewels, incense, lamps, liquid offerings, and so forth. || 109 ||
One should likewise cause rows of lamps to be arranged all around according to one's ability;
among the food offerings, one should present *śaṣkulī* cakes and *pheṇikā* cakes with a hundred perforations.
He also gave *ghṛtapūra* cakes, *revālī* sweets, *pūrikā* cakes with their essence extracted,
*parpikā* pastries, *piṇḍaka* balls, and vegetables such as chickpeas and the like.
One should offer her edible foods such as rice and vegetables;
having given her a roll of betel-leaf, one should perform the great lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Then the observer of the vow should have verses for the worship of Lakṣmī sung;
he should worship the lamps and illuminate all the sacred sites with lamps.
One should perform the worship of Śāradā on a wooden board (carpaṭa) for the purpose of determining income and expenditure;
or the observer of the vow should have a golden image of Śāradā fashioned.
Betel leaves, areca nuts, cardamom, sugar, cinnamon,
fruits, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, jaggery, parched grain, and so forth.

One should worship Śāradā with incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings, as well as with ink, pens, and other such items; one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with mantras and then bid her farewell.
Thus, for one who observes this vow, Lakṣmī and Śāradā shall always remain steadfast;
indeed, they shall bestow all prosperity and grant the desires of both giving and eating.
Right here, an observant practitioner should perform an oil massage and bath, along with rubbing with oils and the like, by which poverty is certainly destroyed. (1.18)
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Festival of the Divine Lamp (Devadīpotsava) is observed;
one should light lamps at sacred fords, in temples, in houses, and so forth.
One should offer the beloved of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) and the beloved of Prabhā (the Sun) crowns and other ornaments, as well as saṃyāva cakes, fried cakes, boiled rice, kvathikā, soups, and sūraṇa roots.
One should offer vegetables such as eggplant and others to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
by performing the ritual dismissal according to the rules, the observer of the vow shall go to heaven and attain liberation.
On this full moon day of Tripurī, one should worship Tripurāri;
the observer of the vow, being happy, should feed various kinds of food and perform the ritual dismissal.

The conclusion of the Cāturmāsya should be celebrated by the people with festivities; furthermore, the lunar day marking the beginning of the Manvantara should be recognized, and one should worship Manu.
The goddess Bhakti and Jayantī must be protected here in every way;
when the moon of devotion rises, worship should be performed according to the proper ritual injunctions. (124)
One should feed [the deity] and adorn him with auspicious ornaments;
the observer of the vow should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and then dismiss [the deity], becoming an inhabitant of the divine abode.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should perform the vision of Skanda.
A festival must indeed be celebrated there for the sake of victory over all enemies.
In this very place, the festival of Tripura should be celebrated by the offering of lamps.
Even insects, moths, mosquitoes, trees, and creepers are all born as living beings. (127)
Merely by beholding the lamp, they indeed attain the supreme goal:
the Kṛttikās, Kārttikeya, the sword-bearer, Agni, and the Lord of Waters. || 128 ||
They should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, fruits, incense, lamps, food offerings, and drinks; and lamps should be offered outside on the ground away from the house.
Likewise, near the edge of the lamp, a beautiful square pit fourteen finger-breadths deep should be made and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Then, having filled it with cow’s milk and placed a golden fish inside,
one should indeed worship it with perfumes and other offerings, pay obeisance, and present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
By offering it according to that rite, one rejoices in the presence of Hari;
this indeed is proclaimed as the gift of the Ocean of Milk. || 132 ||
By performing the rite of releasing a bull on this lunar day, one shall attain Kailāsa;
moreover, on the first day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the Śrāddha and the libation.
And the ancestors, being satisfied, go to the supreme station of the Bhāgavatas.
On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should give] an āḍhaka measure of salt enriched with gold.
In this gift, one should give to the destitute for the fulfillment of all desires;
on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, one should bathe with waters containing all medicinal herbs.
O Lakṣmī, in former times this world was indeed abandoned by you;
then Viṣṇu, Indra, and Bṛhaspati acted for the purpose of restoring your presence. (136)
Śukra and Soma joined together and, under the asterism Puṣya, made diligent efforts;
they adorned her once again with the playful festivities of auspiciousness.
And for the increase of all good fortune through the majesty of their respective qualities,
the observer of the vow should therefore act accordingly and worship them according to the prescribed rite.
Having rubbed one's own body with a paste of white mustard seeds,
one should bathe with waters containing all medicinal herbs and wear new garments.
Having seen auspicious objects, having bowed, and then having touched them, the observer of the vow should worship Hari, Indra, the Moon, Puṣya, and Jupiter with ritual offerings.
Having performed the fire-oblation, one should feed the planets and the children with excellent milk-porridge;
afterwards, the observer of the vow should dismiss the deities and partake of the breaking-of-fast meal.
This vow indeed destroys misfortune, bestows prosperity, and grants liberation;
in ancient times, it took place here on Mount Raivata on the full moon day.
Then follows the birth of Ambā and Gaurī; one should perform their worship there.
Furthermore, the commencement of the Māgha bath also takes place from this day.
In this very place, the raising of the Holikā staff should also be performed;
or else, jewels, bodices, turbans, sandals, or wealth [should be offered]. (144)
Having given sesame seeds, cotton, and woolen blankets, one rejoices in heaven;
and by worshipping Śaṅkara here, one attains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
The commencement of the milk-vow also takes place on the full moon day of Phālguna;
this lunar day, known as Bodhī, is the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga and brings about auspiciousness. 146.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, the worship of Holikā is prescribed;
having offered oblations into a fire built upon a heap of wood and other materials with mantras that destroy demons (rakṣas).
O Holi, you were created by foolish people who were terrified by the fear of blood;
therefore, I shall worship you—be the bestower of prosperity upon this being.
Having kindled [the fire] with this mantra and having circumambulated it, the observer of the vow should lead forth this Holi, the Rākṣasī who causes fear even to Prahlāda. (149)
Just as people, well-heated by the fire, burn [the effigy] with joy,
so too is this Holikā— the burning of the wicked for the sake of the year.
This burning of Kāma performed by Śaṅkara is considered Holi;
however, the narrative of the burning differs according to the various Kalpas. || 151 ||
Likewise, the festival of the swing (dolotsava) takes place here on the full moon day or on the following day,
when there is a conjunction with the Uttaraphalgunī asterism on Mount Raivata.
In ancient times, having placed Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna upon a swing at the abode of Dharma, the gods caused it to sway; that festival should be celebrated here.
In the morning, one should perform the worship of the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa with the sixteen types of offerings and with the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana).
With garments, sandalwood, flowers, and the like; with ornaments made of tulasī leaves; with milk-rice, fried cakes (pūrikās), and even fruits such as jujube (badara); || 155 ||
One should worship with spring flowers and the like, as well as with colored powders and unguents; one should also feed [the deity], perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and cause delight.
One should cause the Lord to play with mechanical toys and then put him to sleep;
having fed the devotees and the children, the observer of the vow should then eat. 157.
Likewise, there is the ritual of anointing with oil and bathing, the consumption of mango blossoms, dalliance during the spring festival, and even the salutation of dust. (158)
The observer of the vow should perform the rite on the lunar day beginning with Manu and so forth in full detail;
having awakened Nara-Nārāyaṇa in the morning, the observer of the vow should worship them. (159)
One should give many gifts and also complete one's vows;
thus, one attains wives, sons, wealth, grain, heaven, and liberation.
