Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-saṃtāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, [the following are described]: the lunar vows of the full moon and new moon days; the absence of *śrāddha* on the new moon day; the *Anvādi-tithi*; the *Hanumat-jayantī*; the commencement of the *Vaiśākha-snāna*; the *Kūrma-jayantī*; the vow of Dharmarāja; the *Bhāvuka-amāvasyā*; the *Sāvitrī-vrata*; the *Bilva-trirātra-vrata*; the coronation (*abhiṣeka*) of Jyeṣṭhā; the pilgrimage (*yātrā*); the worship of Guru Vyāsa; the *Gopadmaka-kokila-vrata*; the observances of the *Cāturmāsya*; the *Śiva-śayana*; the worship of lamps; and the *Nārikela-pūrṇimā*.

The *Ṛgveda-Śrāvaṇī*, the *Yajurveda-Śrāvaṇī*, the *Sāmaveda-Śrāvaṇī*, the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*), the *Hayagrīva-Jayantī*, the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to Śiva, the taking up of the *kuśa* grass, the *Umā-Maheśvara-vrata* on the full moon of *Proṣṭhapada*, the *Śakra-vrata*, the *Sarva-pitṛ-śrāddha*, the *Āmrā-salīlā*, the *Kārttika-snāna*, the autumn vow (*śarad-vrata*), the *Ko-jāgara-vrata*, the worship of Lakṣmī (*lakṣmī-pūjā*), the festival of lamps (*dīpotsava*), the worship of Śāradā, the oil-bath (*abhyaṅga-snāna*), the festival of divine lamps (*deva-dīpotsava*), the full moon of *Tripurī*, the *Bhakti-jayantī*, the vision of Skanda (*skanda-darśana*), the *Māgha-snāna*, the *Ambā-jayantī*, the raising of the *holi-daṇḍa*, the lunar days beginning with *Dvāpara*, the milk-vow (*payovrata*), the swing festival (*dolotsava*), and the spring festival (*vasantotsava*).
The two hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of Consuming the *Avāma* Flower, Prostration to the Dust [of the Feet], and Other [Rites]."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, O Lotus-born One, I shall describe to you those other meritorious vows which are to be performed during the twelve months; listen.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the Lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī, should be swung with great festivities by the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having rocked the Lord on that [swing] made of fragrant flowers for two ghaṭikās and having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should then bring Him down.
The observer of the vow, having bowed and asked for forgiveness, should feed [the guests] and then dismiss them;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, during the bright fortnight under the Puṣya asterism, he should perform the chariot procession.
One should station the chariot with its horses before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and one should wear garments and ornaments worthy of a king.
The Lord should hold excellent golden weapons, such as swords and other arms;
having fed him with curd, rice, and sweetmeats, one should worship him upon the chariot.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Hari four times again and again,
one should then help him descend from the chariot and have hymns of praise (kīrtanas) sung there.
Then the observer of the vow should take his meal; this is the vow that bestows liberation, lasting for one month beginning from the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
The festival of the swing (dolotsava) is considered to last until the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa;
when the Moon is in the sign of Taurus, one should prepare the well-decorated swing.
Every day at sunset, one should daily meditate upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as the ever-new beloved of Śrī Hari, using ever-new articles and offerings.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered the food oblation (naivedya), the observer of the vow should swing [the deity].
He should cause beautiful verses concerning the swing to be sung and perform a dance.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Nabhas, one should worship Hari and perform the ritual immersion;
indeed, the month of Śrāvaṇa should be spent entirely with vows, observances, and restraints.
It should be spent especially in a manner conducive to sustenance by one desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, the month of Kārtika should be passed through vows, charity, recitation of mantras, and other such practices.
When the sun has entered the sign of Sagittarius (Dhanus) in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the time of the Sagittarius ascendant,
one should perform an oil massage and bathe Hari with warm water.
Having put on fine garments and having placed a small fire before him,
he should perform his daily rites and the decoration of the glorious Lord.
One should offer sweetmeat balls (modakas), fresh butter, ghee, and curd as the food offering; one should present flat cakes, fried snacks, and roasted eggplant.
One should have him drink a decoction and engage him in the study of the Kṛṣṇa-mantras;
thus, for the duration of a month, one should perform a festival for the purpose of instruction.
When the sun's transit occurs in Capricorn during the month of Pauṣa,
the forty ghaṭikās are indeed a particularly meritorious time.
Acts such as giving gifts, ritual bathing, and worship should be performed; furthermore, sesame balls, sweet foods, and other delicacies should especially be given to those who are destitute. (19)
One should give morsels of food and other offerings to the cows, as well as perform a merit-bestowing *śrāddha* ceremony;
likewise, on the fifth day of the month of Māgha, one should celebrate the excellent festival of spring (*vasantotsava*).
From that time forward, until the conclusion of the Holi festival, she constantly performed worship and offered meals, along with the application of saffron, colored powders, and fragrant pastes.
One should wear white garments and put on new ones for Hari;
the observer of the vow should apply colors to the garments of Lakṣmī, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa.
One should repeatedly sprinkle powdered red lead (gulāla) and water with land-lotuses;
one should wear a crest of mango blossoms and feed Lord Hari.
One should wear silken garments of the Kaisara variety, represent Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī, and sing of the springtime sports of the beloved of Holikā during the month of Phālguna. ||24||
Then, from the day of manifestation until the limit of six days,
the observer of the vow should also cultivate the protection of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.

One should have him drink milk and other such things while gently rocking him to the accompaniment of songs; one should serve him with a childlike disposition and repeatedly propitiate the Lord. ||26||
Starting from the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should perform the monthly anointing of the image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with sandalwood paste and other substances mixed with saffron.
On the days of solar and lunar eclipses, one should perform bathing, recitation, and other rites;
on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, however, one should offer safflower-dyed garments.
For Hari, [one should offer] auspicious, soft cloth made from fine, smooth threads;
during the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should satisfy the ancestors with śrāddha offerings.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should likewise invoke Sarasvatī under the asterism Mūla;
one should worship her, feed her, and offer milk-preparations and other foods.
By hearing [this], the wise man indeed becomes one who has fulfilled his vow;
the day of one's own birth should be celebrated by all with festive celebrations. (3.1)
Through acts of charity, feeding the hungry, honoring elders, and visiting the gods,
the twelfth days following the eleventh— those days sacred to Hari— bestow liberation.
Hari is pleased by those who perform acts of worship, festivals, and libations with offerings of food and gifts; He bestows upon them the state of fearlessness.
For whomsoever Hari is truly pleased by whatever means possible, his happiness shall be in this world and the next; for him, the increase of merit itself becomes a vow.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Lord who reclines upon the waters with the sixteen types of offerings; thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, one who is self-restrained should worship Hari with the sixteen types of offerings; he shall enjoy the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should worship the Lord Mādhava with the sixteen types of service and other offerings; thus one shall attain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, a person should worship Govinda with the sixteen excellent articles; thus he shall attain the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa with the sixteen and other ritual services; indeed, such a person shall partake in the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should worship Madhusūdana with the sixteen supreme offerings; thus, the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice shall be obtained.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should indeed worship Trivikrama;
by means of sixteen types of offerings, the fruit of a human sacrifice shall be attained.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the observer of the vow should worship Vāmana with the sixteen types of offerings; he shall partake in the merit of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the observer of the vow should worship Śrīdhara with sixteen immeasurable articles and others; he shall partake in the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should worship Hṛṣīkeśa with the sixteen types of offerings; thus, one obtains the fruit of the Brahmamedha sacrifice.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one should worship Padmanābha with the sixteen types of offerings and other rites; such a person partakes in the merit of a thousand horse sacrifices. 45.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should worship Dāmodara with the sixteen types of ritual services and other offerings; such a person partakes in the merit of two thousand horse-sacrifices.
One should perform recitation, austerity, charity, the feeding of virtuous Brahmins and others, the giving of sacrificial fees, prayers, and keeping vigil while observing the vow. (47)
When a vow is undertaken with devotion, one who has few resources gains a small fruit, while one who has vast resources gains a great fruit; yet the fruit attained is liberation. (48)
Having observed the vow for one year, the practitioner of the vow should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having bathed in the morning and put on clean garments, he should bear a beautiful sectarian mark (puṇḍra) upon his forehead.
One should have a beautiful, spacious, and square pavilion constructed,
provided with bells, chowries, water-pots, mirrors, and small bells.
It was adorned with flower garlands, banners, arches, canopies, and cloths;
it was provided with rows of lamps at its four doors and soft carpets.
In the center of that, one should fashion a *sarvatobhadra* diagram adorned with grains and other offerings;
upon it, one should place twelve jars filled with water.
One should place there golden, silver, or copper [images] covered with white garments and endowed with the five jewels.
Upon a jar placed over a vessel of sesame seeds, one should place the image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
then, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), one should commence the constituent parts of the worship.
One should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and offer ornaments and garments; one should provide fragrant sandalwood and the like, as well as incense and lamps. ||55||
One should offer fragrant substances, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and provide food;
one should give a drink and betel-leaf, put [the image] to sleep, and ask for forgiveness. ||56||
One should keep a vigil at night, perform the morning fire-oblation (homa), and carry out the worship, the feeding, the ritual dismissal (vaisarjana), and the offering to the deity. ||57||
The observer of the vow should himself perform the breaking of the fast and thus complete the observance;
he should then present the image, along with a sacrificial fee, to the preceptor.
Thus, the performer of the concluding rite and the observer of the vow, enjoying worldly pleasures here,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage.
O Lakṣmī, whoever shall hear this narrative of the vow or cause it to be recited,
having obtained the fruit of all vows, shall in the end go to the abode of Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Annual Miscellaneous Vows in the First Section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the observance of the swing-vow (dolāvrata), the chariot procession (rathayātrā), the swing festival (dolotsava), the festivals of Śrāvaṇa, Kārtika, Dhanus, and Makara-saṃkrānti, the spring festival (vasantotsava), the climbing ceremony (pālanārohaṇa), Holi (holikā), the flower-swing (puṣpadolaka), sandalwood, garments, ancestral rites (śrāddha), the Sarasvatī festival, the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśīvrata), the fruit-conclusion rite (udyāpana), and so forth.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow,
which removes all sins, is meritorious, and destroys all suffering.
It bestows the fruits of all desires upon Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise women; it grants the fruit of all religious observances.
It is righteous, the destroyer of evil dreams, and the warder-off of malevolent planets;
by its performance, a heap of tens of millions of sins is pacified. (3)
Having bathed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa during the Brāhma-muhūrta, wearing clean garments, seated on a pure seat, having sipped water for purification, and restrained in speech— || 4 ||
Constantly remembering Nārāyaṇa and having performed the worship of the deity,
one should then make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding place, time, and other factors, [offering it] to the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
One should invoke [the deity], worship, and perform the offering of the seat and other requisites;
having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances, one should present the ornaments.
With perfumes, sandalwood, flowers, and the like; with garlands, incense, and lamps; with erotic delights, foods, drinks, fruits, betel, and songs. || 7 ||
Having gratified him with dances, hymns of praise, worship, and likewise with requests for forgiveness,
[he should do so] before him upon a four-cornered sacrificial mound.
One should duly establish a fire one *aratni* in measure,
having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
One should offer oblations to Varuṇa with sesame seeds, flowers, ghee, fruits,
juices, and other sacrificial foods according to one's capacity.
For the destruction of sin, one should perform expiatory rites such as purification;
having completed the fire-oblation (homa), one should then again recite the Śānti-sūkta.
One should worship Śrī Hari and pray for the fulfillment of the vow;
remaining without food on the full moon day, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the following day.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform [the rite]," one should then offer the water of honor (arghya) to the Moon:
"O Maker of Night, accept this arghya, accompanied by white flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings. (13)
"Obeisance to You, the possessor of white rays; obeisance again and again to the brother of Lakṣmī.
One should keep a vigil at night with narrations, recitations, and dances. (14)
In the morning, one should worship Kṛṣṇa and feed virtuous Brāhmaṇas;
one should give gifts and sacrificial fees, and a chaste woman should feed the children. (15)
The observer of the vow should indeed break his fast together with his servants and others;
having performed this for a year, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika—
One should perform a grand concluding rite (udyāpana) and have an auspicious pavilion constructed;
within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala, upon a jar adorned with gems and petals.
One should worship the Lord Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa in a vessel of sesame seeds;
one should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and bathe the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances. 18.
Worship with perfumes, ornaments, garments, garlands, incense, lamps, and so forth;
offer food offerings such as solid and soft foods, and sweet, cool water.
One should offer betel-leaf, as well as the offering of fruits and other items;
likewise, one should perform the vigil with dance, song, and so forth, as well as the waving of lights (nīrājana) and other rites.
Having performed [the rite], one should cause Kṛṣṇa to sleep; then, at dawn, one should worship him again, give the image to the preceptor as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and feed the twice-born.
One should perform oblations in the fire with sesame seeds and other materials, offer gifts,
feed virtuous men and women, and practice the offering of sesame seeds and so forth.
Having thus properly performed the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, the observer of the vow,
together with his family of sons and grandsons, shall enjoy happiness in this world.
Having enjoyed various pleasures in the end, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
through the sight of Śrī Hari, he attains everything that is difficult even for yogis to obtain.
Listen, Lakṣmī; I shall now describe to you the vow of raising the banner (dhvajāropa-vrata), which bestows sovereignty, grants victory, and is the most excellent means for pleasing Viṣṇu. (241)
Whoever makes a gift of a banner in the temple of the Lord Śrī Hari, or in the temple of His manifestation, shall become worthy of worship by the inhabitants of heaven.
One shall obtain the fruit born of giving a thousand loads of gold;
it is merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā and its fruit is equal to the worship of Śiva. ||27||
The merit arising from the hoisting of a flag shall be equal to the worship of Tulasī.
Oh, how unprecedented! Oh, how unprecedented! Oh, how unprecedented is this vow! (28)
The raising of the banner removes all sins and bestows all merit;
it should be performed on the tenth day of the bright fortnight in either the month of Kārttika or another month. (29)
Having bathed and performed his regular daily worship, the observer of the vow should eat only once a day;
he should sleep on the ground at night, remember Nārāyaṇa, and [worship] again in the morning.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite on the eleventh day and meditated upon Hari,
one should then perform the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu, accompanied by the offering of food and other services.
Then, one should request four Brahmins to recite the benediction (svastivācana);
one should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha and bring forward the flagstaff and the pillar.
Having clothed those two, one should sprinkle them with water while reciting the Gāyatrī;
likewise, one should worship Sūrya, Candra, Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, and Garuḍa.
One should worship the two flagstaffs with white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth,
as well as with the fragrances of saffron and sandalwood, turmeric, sugar, and other such substances.
Then, having smeared a sacrificial ground the size of a cow-hide and having established the fire, one should likewise perform the offering of clarified butter and other rites with Vedic mantras.
One should offer milk-rice and grain with clarified butter one hundred and eight times,
using either the Puruṣasūkta or the names of Viṣṇu.
Having recited the *irāvatī* section, the observer of the vow should offer oblations;
thereafter, he should again offer eight oblations with the mantra "To Vainateya, svāhā. (37)
Then one should again offer oblations with the *soma*, *dhenu*, and *udutya* mantras; one should recite the solar mantras and then utter the hymns for peace (*śāntisūktas*).
Having observed the waterless vow (nirjala-vrata), one should perform a vigil at night;
then, having risen on the morning of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) and bathed, one should worship Hari once again.
Accompanied by auspicious musical instruments, songs, and the like, as well as the recitation of hymns and praises,
one should lead the banner to the abode of Hari and offer salutations once again.
One should properly install a firm flagpole, joined with pillars, either at the entrance of the temple or upon its pinnacle; it should be firmly consecrated with the Nīrājana rite.
One should cast a coconut fruit there as a pure, essential offering;
then one should give it to all, and thereafter adorn Viṣṇu.

One should worship Hari with perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice (akṣata), with incense, lamps, and fragrant substances, and with pleasing food offerings such as various kinds of eatables and delicacies. 43.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, the observer of the vow should ask the Lord for forgiveness:
"O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, wherever [there may be] your banner... (44)
And wherever the movement of the shadow of the peak occurs, there shall always be the destruction of the evils of suffering and poverty. ||45||
May the expansion of sons, grandsons, and so forth; the abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth;
and health, enthusiasm, prosperity, and so forth, increase further and further. (46)
Your banner stands above all; act in such a way that it does so for me as well.
The tail of the banner is consciousness (vijñāna), while the banner itself consists of the nature of pure being, consciousness, and bliss (saccitsukha). 47.
The tip of the bamboo is the abode of Brahmā; the bamboo is the path of the radiant one. The top of the pillar is the abode of Truth; the wooden beam is the ground of the gods. (48)
The uvula is the wheel of the luminaries, and Dharma stands as the pillar established by itself;
the goals of human life are the base of that pillar—salutations to You, the Pillar-Supporter. (49)
I worship daily Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord endowed with Lakṣmī, whom the virtuous indeed declare to be the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (1.282.5)
Having thus praised Viṣṇu, he should honor the preceptor, the true guru, and the twice-born;
he should feed them, give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā).
As long as the cloth of the banner moves upon the lotus by the wind, so many nets of sins of the one who has offered the banner are surely destroyed. (52)
For as many days as the two banners remain during the festival of the deity,
for that many thousands of yugas does one enjoy the state of having the same form as Hari.
Those who, seeing the raised banner, rejoice with delight—their sins, even those as firm as adamantine glue, are destroyed. (54)
A banner, by shaking its cloth, shakes away even the heaps of sins of those who offer it;
the one who causes a banner to be raised goes to the highest heaven by means of a celestial chariot.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there was a king named Sumati born of the Lunar dynasty; he was devoted to the story of Irin, and his queen was Satyamati.
Both husband and wife were constantly devoted to the worship of Hari;
remembering their past lives, they gave water and food and performed religious duties. (57)
On each twelfth day of the month, the king hoisted his banner;
hearing of his fame, the gods sang its praises, and Vibhāṇḍaka went there.
Having offered hospitality to the sage, the king spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Blessed One, I have indeed accomplished my purpose through your arrival."
The arrival of the virtuous brings about all happiness for householders;
wherever there is supreme love for the virtuous, there all prosperity shall abide.
Splendor, fame, wealth, grain, sons, and prosperity increase; indeed, those auspicious things flourish daily wherever there is the grace of the virtuous. (6.1)
He who out of devotion places upon his head the dust from the great one’s feet has bathed in all sacred fords and in the final purificatory ablutions of sacrifices.
My wife, my sons, and my wealth have been entrusted to you;
command me quickly—what dear service may I perform for you? (63)
Having heard this and having touched the head of the king with his hand, Vibhāṇḍaka, being pleased, then said: "O King, that which you have spoken [is true]."
Everything appropriate for your lineage is yours; may you attain many blessings—the fourfold aims consisting of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By serving the great, a living being attains eternal happiness.
May you always be well; now tell me that which I ask.
There are indeed many kinds of worship that grant satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa;
considering the hoisting of the flag to be the foremost among them, why do you perform it? (67)
"Tell me, how is it that even your wife is always devoted to dancing there?
Having heard this, the king spoke of a wondrous event from the past.
In the past, I was a Śūdra named Mālinī, indeed a sinner; I was merciless and a perpetrator of drinking liquor, eating meat, sexual misconduct, theft, and other such acts. (69)
Having committed a murder and abandoned my subjects and kinsmen, I went to the forest and took refuge in a dilapidated temple of Viṣṇu. (1.282.70)
For twenty years he remained constantly subsisting on fruits and roots;
I performed for him the mending of all that was decayed and torn. (7.1)
For my own residence, that ground was smeared and well-prepared by me;
trees were planted there and watered with the waters of the lake. (72)
Having made a secret pact, I took up worn-out rags and raised a banner;
with the insertion of splinters and reeds, the wall of Viṣṇu was well-protected by me.
This woman named Niṣāda was indeed a cuckoo threatened by her captor;
she is the daughter of Dāruka from the Vindhya mountain, who has arrived here by the turn of fate. (74)
"I obtained this unchaste woman and protected her as my wife;
performing service to the gods, we two have entered into the state of husband and wife. (75)
They remained there for eleven years; once, during the night, they became intoxicated by drinking liquor and delighted by eating meat. (76)
Unaware that our garments had been stripped away, we two danced, deluded;
we both remained together until the exhaustion of the fruits of our past actions.
Then the terrifying messengers of Yama arrived to take us away;
at that moment, Viṣṇu, residing in the temple, perceived them as his own servants.
He dispatched his own messengers bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
they said, "O followers of Yama of evil conduct, release the two Arjunas! (79)
"Upon hearing that my two devotees, who were dependent on me and dwelling in the forest, were being worshipped, the messengers of Yama then said: 'These two are indeed great sinners.'"
"Sinners are to be punished by Yama; we shall take these two there.
Hearing this, the Vaiṣṇavas spoke to those who were intent on seizing the sinners. ||8 1 ||
"Released from sin and devoted to the service of Hari, let them be protected by Hari; release them without delay. (82)

She performed a dance, and he likewise carried out the raising of the banner; both were intent on the welfare of Hari’s palace, acting for their own sake while accomplishing the purpose of another. (83)
Even at the time of death, by merely hearing or uttering this name even once, one indeed attains liberation and heaven; how much more so for one who is devoted to its constant service? (84)
One who serves Kṛṣṇa and serves the ascetics attains the state of a Vaiṣṇava even if they are a sinner;
for one who stays in the temple of Hari for even a moment or half a moment [attains that same state]. (85)
Even he goes to the world of Brahmā; how much more so those who perform cleaning, plastering, and the repair of what is worn out or dilapidated for thirty-two years!
How is it that these two, who provided lamps, water, and the shade of trees at the temple, possess such great merit yet are now joined with the experience of torment? (87)
Having spoken thus, they forcibly cast off the nooses of Yama,
took hold of us, and went by means of a supreme celestial chariot to the blissful abode of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed divine and great pleasures there, they came to this earth;
here too, through the favor of service, they obtained a kingdom with its royal banner. (89)
"Even though it was done unintentionally, the kingdom obtained has yielded great fruit;
remembering that, I offer this dance as a tribute to Ketu. (1.282.90)
By worshipping Govinda even with mere desire, we shall attain the supreme goal;
if even when done involuntarily it yields such excellent fruit, how much more so when performed with faith? (91)
Vibhāṇḍaka, having heard that and praised them both, departed for the forest;
know this, O Kamalā, regarding Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa indeed. (92)
Service to all is considered equal to the wish-fulfilling gem;
for Hari, who is devoted to those intent on devotion to him, grants all desires. 93.
Whoever hears or likewise recites this purifying narrative, as well as the speaker who is devoted to the service of Hari— they too attain the supreme goal.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Narration to Vibhāṇḍaka by King Sumati and Queen Satyamati, who had attained their kingdom after being liberated from the messengers of Yama upon the death of the Śūdra Mālī and his wife—a sinner and a woman stained with impurity—through the merit of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, its concluding rite, the raising of the flag over the temple, its plastering, and its protection," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the celebrated Haripañcaka,
a vow that bestows happiness upon both women and men, and is the most excellent of all vows.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, having bathed, one should perform the worship of the deity;
and even after performing the five great sacrifices, one should spend the day eating but a single meal.
Having bathed early on the eleventh day and likewise bathed Hari with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and waters from sacred fords, one should worship Him with fragrant liquids and other offerings.
The ritual action, beginning from the invocation and ending with the dismissal,
is accompanied by incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, betel, and priestly fees.
Having performed the worshipful rite, the observer of the vow should pray before Śrī Hari:
"O Mādhava, from this day forward, I shall remain without food for five nights."
"I shall perform the vow known as Haripañca, and may it be completed for me.
On the tenth day, one should indeed eat only once and sleep on the ground at night. (6)
On the eleventh day, one should perform worship three times a day, offer the three-fold food-offerings,
and keep a vigil at night with songs, dances, and sacred narratives.
On the twelfth, the thirteenth, and the fourteenth days, one should perform the triple rite;
on the full moon day as well, one should perform bathing, worship, and the offering of food.
On the night of the full moon, the observer of the vow should likewise perform a vigil;
furthermore, he should perform worship with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other offerings during the five days.
One should bathe Viṣṇu with milk on the full moon day or on the sixth lunar day;
likewise, one should perform a fire-oblation of sesame seeds, give gifts of sesame, and consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed [the rites], he should feed the Brahmins and worship Hari according to the prescribed rules;
he should also feed virtuous men and women, and then eat himself together with his kinsmen.
In this manner, the auspicious vow should be observed every month for one year;
the concluding rite (udyāpana) should then be performed with magnanimity in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, during this vow of the white fortnight, the practitioner shall remain without food;
then, on the twelfth day, he shall consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having worshipped Hari with flowers and other offerings, he should give [gifts] to a twice-born man.
Milk-rice mixed with sugar, ghee, and fruits.
One should present it accompanied by sweet foods, vegetables, leaves, and so forth, together with fragrant water, excellent jewels, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and garments. || 15 ||
One should give a full water-pot to the virtuous knower of the Self;
one should give all one's possessions to the Guru and feed children, both boys and girls.
One should feed virtuous men and women and then break one's own fast;
this vow, known as the "Five of Hari," has thus been described to you. (17)
Furthermore, for the one who performs that [rite], there shall be no return from the world of Brahmā;
he shall obtain the fruit of giving away thousands of millions of cows.
Whoever should recite this, or hear it, or read it, or cause it to be heard,
for him too there shall be the merit of the vow, and he shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now I shall describe another vow, O Mahālakṣmī, known as Pārāka, which is said to have no equal. (1.283.20)
O beloved, on the first day of the bright fortnight in any one of these months— Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, or Āśvina— 21.
One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and remain in the presence of Viṣṇu;
having bathed and meditated upon Viṣṇu at dawn, one should then complete the daily rites.
Having worshipped Viṣṹṇu, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the month-long fast;
then, one should have the Brāhmaṇas recite the mantras for the pronouncement of auspiciousness (svastivācana).
And the observer of the vow should pray to the God: "O Mādhava, from this day forward for one month, I shall remain without food; please bring about my desired goal. (24)
From that time until the end of the month, he should reside in the temple of Hari;
he should daily bathe the Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and offer a lamp.
He should eat the stalks of the Apāmārga plant and bathe every day;
he should worship the deity constantly and feed children and Brahmins.
In this manner, one should observe fasts for a month for twelve years,
and every year perform the gift of a cow and the satiation of Brahmins and ancestors.
One should give gifts according to one's ability, such as sacrificial fees, ornaments, and food;
by fasting for one month, the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice shall be attained. ||28||
The fruit of two month-long fasts shall be double that;
the fruit of three month-long fasts shall be fourfold. || 29 ||
When performed four times, the merit becomes equal to that born of eight Agniṣṭoma sacrifices;
when performed five times, the merit becomes equal to that born of an Atirātra sacrifice.
If performed six times, it yields the fruit of eight Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices;
if performed seven times, it yields the fruit of eight horse-sacrifices (Vājimedhas). ||31||
If performed eight times, it yields the fruit of eight human sacrifices;
if performed nine times, the merit born of eight cow-sacrifices shall arise.
By performing it ten times, the fruit of eight Brahma-medha sacrifices is obtained;
but by performing eleven Parāka penances, one attains the same form as Hari.
By performing twelve *parāka* penances, one obtains the fourfold liberation;
those who perform the *parāka* vow are indeed liberated, there is no doubt. (34)
Whether a woman or even a man, one who performs this vow shall attain liberation;
or by reading or hearing this narrative of the vow, one shall become a partaker of liberation. (35)
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no teacher equal to one's mother;
there is no god equal to Viṣṇu; and there is no austerity higher than fasting.
There is no mother equal to patience; there is no wealth equal to fame;
there is no gain equal to knowledge; there is no father equal to the Dharma. //37//
There is no brother equal to solitude, nor is there a vow equal to Ekādaśī;
there is no worthy recipient equal to Brahman, and no beloved equal to a wife. 38.
There is no boat equal to the virtuous; there is no vow like that of crossing to the other shore.
O beloved, acts such as giving gifts and performing fire-offerings should be performed when an auspicious day arrives.
The third day of the bright fortnight in Mādhava, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in Bhādra,
the pure ninth day in Kārtika, and the fifteenth lunar day (the full moon) in Māgha.
These have been declared as the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause whatever is given to be inexhaustible:
the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Akṣaya (Phālguna), and the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika. (41)
The third day of the month of Caitra, as well as that of Bhādrapada;
the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha. (42)
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the new moon of Phālguna, and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa. (43)
The fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha are declared to be the beginnings of the Manvantaras; gifts given on these occasions yield inexhaustible merit.
In sacred fords such as Puṣkara, in rivers such as the Gaṅgā, in Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, and on the soil of Kāśī; (45)
In Kāñcī, Avantikā, and Dvārakā, that which is given becomes inexhaustible when offered to a guest who is a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, or to virtuous men, virtuous women, and chaste wives.
A gift given to a god-like man among the gods produces inexhaustible merit;
that which is given to those practicing celibate students (brahmacārins) shall likewise produce inexhaustible merit.
One who observes a vow must by all means perform austerity, charity, and worship; likewise, every act such as eating and so forth should be performed in a manner that bestows inexhaustible merit. 48.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Haripañcaka Vow, the Month-long Fasting Vow, its Concluding Rite (Udyāpana), the Greatness of Gifts on Lunar Days Corresponding to the Yugas and Manvantaras," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the vow of worshipping the planets on their respective days;
by performing which all the planets become pleased and bestow prosperity.
On Sunday, the vow should be observed by eating only at night or taking a single meal;
having bathed in the morning and bowed to the Sun, one should worship him with all kinds of offerings.
Having fashioned a golden sun-god seated upon a chariot drawn by ruddy horses, accompanied by Saṃjñā and Chāyā, and adorned with divine garlands and jewels; || 3 ||
Having performed the invocation and other rites, [one should perform] the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the ceremonial bath,
the donning of garments and ornaments, and the application of fragrant unguents.
The offering of incense, lamps, food, fruits, and betel;
meditation, circumambulation, hymns of praise, prostration, and so forth, ending with the ritual dismissal.
Then one should likewise have [the ritual] performed at midday and also at night;
one should cause the entire worship to be performed, including the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and the offering of food.
One should bathe the God at night, and having bathed in the morning, one should awaken Him;
one should worship Him with lotuses and flowers such as the arka and karavīra.
One should offer water again and again and perform the rite of attendance (upasthāpana),
[visualizing] the Sun holding in his hands a pair of lotuses representing the gift of fearlessness.
One should meditate upon the embodiment of the three Vedas, adorned with earrings, armlets, and bracelets;
and one should duly offer oblations into the fire with red lotuses or sesame seeds.
One should recite for the Sun one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Svāhā," beginning with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyam."
"May we meditate upon the splendor of the divine; may he impel our intellects"—with this Gāyatrī mantra, one should likewise recite it one hundred and eight times.
One should offer oblations with the utterance "svāhā," and one should also address Chāyā;
one should feed, worship, and present the respectful water-offering (arghya) to the form of Bhāskara.
Having restrained his breath, sipped water, and washed his hands,
the worshipper should take up a copper vessel capable of holding one prastha of water.
Saffron, yellow pigment (rocanā), turmeric, sandalwood, red sandalwood, oleander, hibiscus, rice, kusha grass, millet, and grains of rice. || 14 ||
One should cast sesame seeds, bamboo, and barley into auspicious water, holding the pitcher with both hands while kneeling upon the ground. (15)
Having raised the vessel above his head and gazing at the sun in the sky while mentally accepting the invitation, he should offer the arghya with a handful of water.
Having offered a handful of flowers, and having bowed and praised him, one should dismiss him;
or one should daily, or on that very day, offer this arghya to Vivasvat in this manner.
Pleased by that, he shall grant him wealth, fame, and happiness every day;
indeed, he bestows everything desired, including sons and grandsons.
This vow of worshipping the Sun increases longevity and health;
it bestows wealth, grain, cattle, security, fields, friends, and a wife. (19)
Bestowing splendor, vigor, fame, renown, knowledge, power, and enjoyment,
it shall, when performed according to the prescribed rite, bring about the supreme attainment of the solar orb.
One should present an image of the Sun to the preceptor along with a sacrificial fee;
likewise, one should feed the Brahmins with the essence of milk and excellent *supolikā* cakes.
The observer of the vow should eat by himself and thus complete the vow itself;
then, on a Monday, he should perform the Moon-vow according to the prescribed rite.
Having risen early in the morning and bathed, one should bring milk, flowers, and other offerings;
one should worship Soma together with his consort, represented by a golden deer.
The practitioner, beginning with the invocation, should worship the Moon together with his twenty-seven wives using the sixteen auspicious articles.
One should worship with white water-lilies and offer milk and sugar;
one should perform the lustration ceremony at night on the full moon day when the moon is visible.
One should meditate upon the beloved Moon, whose face is naturally radiant like crystal, with dark-blue locks of hair and earrings, holding a white water-lily and a garland of pearls. 26.
One should address Svāhā to Candra, Rohiṇī, and the lunar mansions;
one should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee one hundred and eight times.
One should place a silver vessel and fill it with fragrant milk;
one should offer this *arghya* to the Moon for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims. (28)
One should daily offer arghya and perform worship on that day;
thus satisfied, the Lord of the Night-lotuses shall grant the food of medicinal herbs.
It indeed bestows wealth, grain, daughters, sons, and good fortune;
one should observe the vow of eating only once a day and offer an image to the preceptor.
One should feed milk and *pūrikā* cakes to children and virtuous people;
however, having oneself completed the vow, one should then partake of the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*).
Now, one who desires happiness should observe the vow of Maṅgaladeva;
it should be performed by eating only one meal a day for the accomplishment of all undertakings. (32)
Having bathed in the morning on the day of the Son of the Earth (Mars), one should meditate upon Maṅgala,
situated in Aries, with limbs clad in red garments, and holding a trident, a spear, and a mace in his hands.
One should meditate upon the Lord holding the son of the Earth (Mars), who is marked by perspiration, with his hands.
Furthermore, the commencement of the vow in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa or Vaiśākha should take place on a Tuesday.
At the time of sunrise, one should perform the Bhauma-vrata;
those desiring sons, those desiring wealth, and those desiring prosperity should observe this vow. (35)
Having risen, she should run with her teeth [bared] and restrained speech, wearing red garments and smeared with red unguents and ointments, after having bathed. (36)
One should prepare all the offerings, such as the food oblation (naivedya), in red;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and having proclaimed the place and time, she who seeks the vow [should proceed]. (37)
Having worshipped with the sixteen primary offerings and others, one should present the *arghya*;
then, having offered incense and lamps, one should offer wheat-based food.
In a copper vessel filled with pure water, having cast red sandalwood,
red flowers, unbroken rice, and fruit, one should offer the *arghya*.
O Son of the Earth, I have sought refuge in you for the sake of my daughter; accept this water-offering from me.
Grant me a son, O Son of the Earth; accept this water-offering; salutations be unto you!
Then, one should indeed draw three lines on the ground with charcoal from *khadira* wood;
having done so, one should wipe them away with the left foot and then speak as follows.
For the destruction of suffering and misfortune, and for the sake of obtaining a lineage of sons, I wipe away these three lines with my left foot. (42)
For the destruction of the suffering of debt and for the attainment of my heart’s desired goals,
I erase the three black lines produced from the three births.
Having meditated thus, with auspicious handfuls of flowers in her hands, she should praise him:
"Salutations to you, the remover of debt; may you grant me eternal good fortune. (44)
Salutations to you, who, when having entered a retrograde motion, bestows suffering upon men, yet when worshipped, becomes the giver of happiness and good fortune. 45.
"O Rudra-souled one, whose vehicle is the ram, grant me sons, wealth, and fame.
Having thus praised, bowed down, and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should offer a flower.
Having given according to his ability, he should receive the blessings of the Brahmins;
he should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor and eat what has been offered to him.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] every Tuesday throughout the year; and one should offer oblations with sesame seeds, saying: "Svāhā to Maṅgala, the embodiment of auspiciousness. (48)
Having worshipped the golden image of Bhauma situated in a jar placed within the mandala, one should recite the mantra for the attainment of sons and good fortune. 49.
We know the venerable Maṅgalaka; we meditate upon him who holds a spear in his hand;
may that Bhauma inspire us—thus [one should recite] one hundred and eight times.
Having performed worship once more, one should recite this mantra and feed [the deity] with milk and other offerings;
one should present sugar, very sweet food, and wheat-based dishes.
One should offer water for drinking, betel-leaf, and a handful of flowers;
then, according to the prescribed rite, one should again bid farewell to him in the sky at night.
Having bowed, meditated, and offered water, one should present unbroken grains (akṣata) and flowers;
having prayed for the fulfillment of the vow and its fruit, one should eat, sleep, and remember the planet.

Thus, one who seeks the fulfillment of vows, or even a practitioner of the vow, through the propitiation of Bhauma, obtains children, grain, and so forth, as well as supreme happiness free from obstacles. (54)
Then, on a Wednesday, one should perform the Budha-vrata with a concentrated mind;
having bathed, one should worship a golden image according to the prescribed sequence.
Having performed everything from the invocation up to the final handful of flowers,
one should visualize the son of the Moon (Budha) wearing yellow garments and holding a hand in the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Having meditated upon the left hand resting on the knee, one should offer the *arghya*;
O wise one, son of the Moon, of great intelligence, remove my suffering and grant me happiness. (57)
Then one should offer oblations into the fire with "svāhā" for Budha one hundred and eight times;
having worshipped him and fed him, and having requested his forgiveness, one should join the palms in reverence.
Having honored him with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), he should then dismiss him;
the observer of the vow should feed the Brahmins and view the planet Mercury in the sky at night. 59.
Having offered the *arghya* with lotus flowers, one should complete the vow;
one should feed virtuous men and women and eat oneself with reverence.
In this way, all afflictions caused by the planets for one who observes the vow are averted; there shall be an increase in the abundance of sons, cattle, wealth, and health. || 61 ||
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the vow for the Guru;
having bathed, the observer of the vow should worship an image of the Guru made of gold.
Having worshipped Bṛhaspati, beginning from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the final offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), with sixteen auspicious substances.
Meditate upon him who places his left hand upon a heap of jewels and his right hand scattering all kinds of gems, possessing a golden luster and a beautiful face.
One should meditate upon the Teacher of the Gods, the tranquil one and treasury of all vidyās, who is worshipped with yellow flowers, ornaments, ointments, garments, and other offerings. (65)
One should feed him milk-rice (pāyasa) and likewise bow down and ask for forgiveness;
then, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra "Svāhā to Bṛhaspati."
One should offer oblations with ghee, cooked rice, prepared food, the essence of milk, sugar-candy, and so forth,
during afflictions such as poison or disease, and in quarrels arising among one's own kinsmen.
To bring that [obstacle] to an end, one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks made of *pippala* wood;
furthermore, for three days, one should also offer oblations with night-blooming flowers soaked in clarified butter.
Thinking, "May the calamity be quickly pacified," he should then worship and bow again at night, and perform the visualization of that [deity] in the sky. (69)
Having bowed, the observer of the vow should offer water for the guest-offering (arghya) and pray to the Vidyā;
then he should perform the lustration (nīrājana), offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and dismiss [the deity]. || 1.284.70 ||
One should give a gift to the venerable guru, including an image and a meal;
having thus performed the vow, one should eat afterwards, and thereby become happy. ||7 1||
Then, on a Friday, one should perform the Śukravratam according to the prescribed rite;
having bathed, one should meditate upon the planet Venus as being made of gold and clad in white garments.

The practitioner of the vow should meditate on [the deity] adorned with white ointment, bestowing wealth with his right hand, and displaying the gesture of exposition (vyākhyānamudrā) with his left. 73.
Beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should worship;
thereafter, one should feed [the deity], honor, ask for forgiveness, and bow down. (74)
On a Saturday, one should perform a fire sacrifice with fragrant white flowers;
one should carry out the oblation one hundred and eight times, using ghee and other substances.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offer auspicious water as an arghya to the guru;
at night, one should gaze upon the sky, and having bowed and offered praise, one should dismiss him.
One should give a gift to the venerable guru and thus complete his vow;
the performer of the vow shall obtain jewels, gems, and other riches, and become happy. (77)
One should observe eating once a day, or eating only at night, or fasting during the vow;
or else, according to one's ability, one may drink only milk or subsist on fruit. (78)
Then, on a Saturday, one should observe the vow of Śani;
having bathed in the morning and bowed to Hari, Hanumān, and Pannati.
One should bow to the image of Śani made of iron and worship it;
the observer of the vow should offer seven black māṣa beans during the worship.
Beginning from the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali),
one should perform everything with devotion and offer black flowers and excellent collyrium.
One should offer black garments and ornaments, present black food, and perform a fire-oblation with black sesame seeds and other materials, saying "Svāhā to Śanaiścara! ||82||
One should perform one hundred and eight repetitions, reciting the mantra according to one's strength;
one should meditate upon Him with a sword in hand and a black cloth as an upper garment. (83)

One should bow to him who is seated upon a chariot, has the color of iron, possesses a cruel gaze and face, moves in a crooked manner, and looks ahead; one should offer him water and the respectful *arghya* oblation. (84)
Accompanied by black flowers and black beans, grant peace;
bestow an auspicious glance, O Surya, and increase prosperity and happiness. (85)
"O Tvaṣṭṛ, do not do what is undesirable; O son of Saṃjñā, homage be to you!
O brother of Yama, accept this kṛśara-rice, water, and so forth. (86)

Having thus performed his worship, one should cause gifts for Kṛṣṇa to be bestowed; one should also perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer praise, and dismiss him according to the prescribed rite.
The observer of the vow should generally practice eating once a day or at night;
then, on the morning of the second day, he should worship Śani with his heart.
One should feed children, girls, and Brahmins, and perform the breaking of the fast;
by doing this for one year, one shall overcome the misfortunes caused by Saturn.
One shall attain the perfection of happiness and obtain a bliss equal to that of heaven.
Thus have the vows been proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Complete Rituals of the Vows of the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Lord, O Mādhava, O Keśava!
O Lord of Pārvatī and Prabhā, O Consort of Lakṣmī and Māṇikī! || 1 ||
Only the pure eleventh day is to be accepted in the vow; why indeed is the pierced day not so?
O Lord of the Lotus, O Lord of Nectar, O Hari, tell me the reason for that!
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate this account of Brahmā that has occurred;
indeed, on the Ekādaśī day pierced by the previous tithi, Mohinī remains present at dawn.
The daughter of Vedha (the moon) is a destroyer of merit; therefore, she should not be accepted in a vow.
One should consider that the tenth day, free from the overlap of the ninth, is always to be observed as a fast during a vow.
She bestows heaven and liberation; she grants kingdoms, fields, and sons;
she gives a wife, wealth, food, a loving heart, the body, and health. || 5 ||
Whether at the time of waning or waxing, or when the dawn has arrived, one should fast on the meritorious twelfth day; one should avoid that which is overlapped by the preceding day.
A man who observes a tithi overlapped by the previous day cuts away his merit;
it leads to the destruction of his lineage and the loss of his prosperity. (7)
In former times, that lunar day (tithi) was given to the Dānavas;
indeed, any merit performed on a lunar day joined with the previous one goes instead to the Asuras.
Whatever is given, chanted, offered in sacrifice, bathed, practiced, or offered as worship to Hari on a day of lunar waning goes to destruction, just as darkness does at the rising of the sun.
In Surāṣṭra, there was a sovereign king named Rukmāṅgada,
who was established in the great Vaiṣṇava dharma and devoted to the day of Hari.
That dull-witted man who today, on the day of Viṣṇu, eats while holding a drum to his elephant and beating it on the day of Hari; || 11 ||
Whether it be my father, my brother, my son, my wife, or my friend, whoever [offends] must be punished by me, or executed, or banished from the city. (12)
One who eats on the day of Śrī Hari shall be punished like a thief;
give alms to the Sātvatas and bathe in the waters of sacred fords.
"Having accepted these words of mine, let them remain within my kingdom. Having agreed upon this proclamation, the subjects took refuge in Keśava.
The path to the abode of Śrī Hari was crowded with people going there;
indeed, whoever died within his kingdom went to the palace of Hari.
At that time, men do not go from the earth along the path of Yama;
the hells become empty, being devoid of sinful living beings. (16)
The southern path, scorched by the twelve suns, became impassable;
indeed, all people, mounted upon Garuḍa, went to the abode of Hari.
Then Citragupta also ceased from his work of recording deeds;
indeed, human beings, by virtue of their devotion, shook off even their past karmas.
The Vaiṣṇavas indeed departed for the abode of Viṣṇu, while the Carpaṭas fell into futility;
even the heavens of the gods became empty at that time.
When heaven had become empty and likewise hell was empty,
Nārada approached Dharmarāja and spoke these words.
How is it that the field of Yama is empty and people do not come here?
Even Citragupta has desisted; he no longer writes down their deeds at all.
"Even those who are overcome by deceit and pride, and who delight in evil deeds—why do they not come here? Tell me the reason for this. (22)
Yama, filled with dejection, said: "On earth there is a king named Rukmāṅgada;
he is now a sovereign ruler of the whole world and is devoted to Puruṣottama. (23)
One should awaken with drums and declare: "Nothing should be eaten on the day of Hari;
whatever mortals eat [on that day], they are certainly considered by Me to be deserving of punishment. (24)
Out of fear of him, all creatures observe the day of Hari;
even those who fast merely under a pretext go to the world of Viṣṇu. (25)
By that king, through devotion to Hari, the hells were made empty;
the heavens were also made empty, and the scribes were rendered inactive.
Whatever has been committed or written down [in the form of sin] is wiped away by fasting on the eleventh day;
indeed, prior sins perish by not eating on the day of Hari.
I have become like a wooden deer, my actions rendered fruitless;
today I have abandoned all desire for the office of world-protector, which is devoid of true activity.
I shall indeed go to the world of Brahmā to make known my own suffering;
for a servant who performs no action receives his wages, yet they do not age with him.
"Whether he be a human or even Yama himself, that man goes to a terrible hell.
Having spoken thus, O Mahālakṣmī, [the Lord addressed] Nārada and Citragupta.
Accompanied by Nīravā, Yamarāja himself went to the abode of Brahmā and beheld him seated there,
surrounded by beings both manifest and unmanifest.
He was being worshipped by the various guardians of the world and lords of the quarters,
as well as by the Vedas, the Shastras, the Itihasas and other scriptures, and by the lakes, rivers, and oceans.
[He was filled] with trees, creepers, grasses, and crops; with forests, wild tracts, and hosts of winds; with fields, mountains, and plateaus; and with sages, celestial rishis, and ancestors. ||33||
[The time is reckoned] by means of the digits (kalā) and so forth, the nights, years, yugas, kalpas, and dissolutions;
and by means of pleasure and pain, gain and loss, the serpents as witnesses, the qualities (guṇas), and so forth. ||34||
Indeed, the Unborn is worshipped through both qualities and non-qualities, as well as those illusory attributes not explicitly mentioned;
among them, the son of the Sun entered with his inner heart broken.
Looking down at his lower body, he revealed the loss that had occurred;
he fell before Brahmā, crying out, "Save me! Save me! (36)
I have desisted and am free from duty; what can I do for you in this employment? I am not worthy of wages; take back your royal turban. (37)
Having spoken thus, he cast down the royal decree before Vidhi;
Citragupta also cast down his pen before Vidhi.
The Grandfather consoled the withered Yama,
who was distraught and broken-hearted, and seated him upon his throne.
And he asked slowly: "By whom have you been overcome? By whom were you driven away? By whom was your divine garment wiped away and dishonored? (1.285.40)
"Tell us everything without exception that dwells in your heart—the sorrow because of which all these people are grieving and weeping. (41)
By whom has this son of the Sun been defeated that his face is thus withered?
Or rather, this is a true proverb: "The enemy indeed fears another. (42)
Then, having heard this, Yama said: "Listen, O Grandfather;
he who, being engaged in work, accepts wages without performing the task."
He who lives by unjust means falls into a blind well—the laborer who, driven by greed, does not perform his assigned duty. (44)
He who consumes the wealth of his master shall become a wood-worm;
thereafter, he goes to hell for as long as three hundred kalpas.
But he who, intent solely on his own interest, plunders his master, shall indeed become a rat in village pits for three hundred kalpas. (46)
If an appointed official performs his master's work without being free from desire, and consumes his master's wealth, he will become like a cat in the house. //47//
Thus, I have been appointed by you to govern those who deserve punishment and those who do not—
rewarding the virtuous with merit and the evildoer with sin.
"I shall employ him"—thus thinking, I have now been surpassed in my office by King Rukmāṅgada; I have been rendered inactive. (49)
Out of fear of Rukmāṅgada, the earth, along with its seven continents and oceans,
did not enjoy the day of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins.
Even those who are sinful, devoid of virtuous deeds, and destitute of all religious merit,
indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu by fasting on the day of Hari.
Those who have come from the city of Yama, by virtue of the merit of their lineage, shall leave the city of Yama and place their feet upon my head. (52)
They go indeed to the world of Viṣṇu, my field which has attained emptiness;
by the merit of this vow, a hundred generations of ancestors [are likewise saved]. ||53||
A hundred maternal grandfathers, a hundred people who are the fathers of one's wives, a hundred sisters' sons, and a hundred people who are the wives of one's brothers. (54)
One hundred of the father’s sisters’ sons and one hundred of the mother’s sisters’ people—each reaching one hundred and one—go to the state of liberation of Hari. (55)
This is my supreme sorrow: that after I have had my name inscribed, others go to the highest state through merit earned by another. (56)
"By the greatness of the merit of one person, those of other lineages go to the supreme state after cutting through my snare; because of that, there is pain in my head. (57)
"O King, I have no need for such a command as this;
yet, by fasting on the Ekādaśī day, a single person [purifies] his lineage up to the seventh generation. (58)
Having abandoned my world, he goes to the abode of Śrī Hari;
neither by sacrifices, nor by pilgrimages, nor by vows, nor even by recitations [of mantras] does one attain it. ||59||
One does not attain such a state by means of water, fire,
or falling from a precipice as one attains through the vow of a single day of Hari.
Having become thus despondent, I have now come to make a petition at your lotus-like feet;
please do with this as you desire.
O Grandfather, act in such a way that the realm of Yama, the path of Yama, and even the decree of Yama do not become broken as they were before.
Nowhere has such a thing been seen or heard that is devoid of logic:
those established in their own duties or those engaged in improper acts, whether pure or impure. (63)
"O King, by fasting on the day of Viṣṇu, people go to his abode;
he is our great enemy and must be captured—of this there is no doubt. (64)
For those thousand years, he ruled the circle of the earth;
by his power, the exceedingly wicked people were led to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having mounted him upon a Garuḍa and assumed a four-armed form,
O Grandfather, he leads the immeasurable world day and night.
If he remains for a long time, he will lead everyone to immortality;
for this is the supreme punishment, indeed, which has been unleashed by your two feet.
"By him indeed has our status as world-protectors been rendered futile!
Blessed is that mother who bore him in her womb—he who effects liberation. (68)
Of what use is a son who is born only to cause distress to his mother, by whom there is neither satisfaction, nor contentment, nor service, nor the destruction of enemies? (69)
He has not rescued his multitude of ancestors by means of either knowledge or power,
nor does his fame resound among people, even among those who are wise.
His mother, however, bore her womb in vain, guarding it like a mere mattress;
and he, though born in vain, was a eunuch, being like a disease of his mother's belly.
A son who becomes an adversary to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation is better than that;
for in the case of such a son, suffering reaches its limit.
The life of one who would destroy the Dharma in this world is lived in vain;
yet now, by her, King Rukmāṅgada has been born as a hero.
A devotee of Śrī Hari has indeed been produced for the purification of Malli’s sins;
such supreme worship as this has never been performed by anyone before.
How shall I live, constantly hearing that drum which destroys my path, while I am a partaker in the sin of receiving wages in vain? (75)
Having thus made this announcement, he ceased speaking, deeply distressed;
then, O Lakṣmī, Brahmā, acting to dispel the Sun’s grief, spoke slowly.
What is so wonderful about that for you, or why are you distressed?
O Lord of Yama, how has this anguish arisen in you regarding virtuous qualities? (77)
If by the mere utterance of their names people certainly attain the state of liberation, how could those who have fully observed that vow not lead others to the supreme state? (78)
A single prostration made here to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa yields the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices; yet that [other] fruit is subject to decay. (79)
That [other place] bestows rebirth, whereas a prostration here brings an end to worldly existence; what need has such a person for Kāśī, Gayā, or Kurukṣetra?
He on whose tongue-tip the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside, even if he approaches a menstruating woman or a Cāṇḍālī woman, or eats food mixed with liquor; (8.1)
Even if one commits great theft for an entire month, such a person indeed partakes in liberation;
having shaken off the accumulation of sins, he surely goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
If liberation comes from merely uttering His name, how much more so from fasting for Him, where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is glorified and meditated upon? (83)
Whether out of ignorance, or as a mere pastime, or even with indifference, one who speaks of Hari, hears of Him, remembers Him, or even laughs at Him, attains the supreme goal. (84)
How can there be your instruction regarding his devotees who observe vows, you who were not crushed but were merely bound by the attendants of that very Lord? (85)
Thus, our supreme honor has been preserved, yet you do not perceive it;
for a servant must diligently recognize his royal status. (86)
Those who are recipients of the king's favor must certainly not be appointed even if they have committed offenses; otherwise, the official is punished. (87)
Thus, even sinners who take refuge in the command of a devotee of Kṛṣṇa go to the abode of Śrī Hari; do not issue such a decree regarding them.
O Yama, I shall fill your abode with those who are devoted to others and are full of faults;
I will never provide assistance to those who are devotees of Hari.
There is no subduing of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, if they should commit an insult, I am not your ally.
O son of the Sun, if you provide me assistance even in this matter, let there be the punishment of death for my body and the loss of my status from the rank of Brahmā. (9.1)
What then is your concern in this matter? Therefore, O sir, observe silence!
Let them go to the abode of Hari; do not obstruct them from the realm of Yama.
"O Āditya, let your field be taken away by the power of Hari;
do not fall into grief over this matter, for in due time it shall turn out as desired. (93)

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Yama’s Grief-stricken Report to Brahmā Regarding the Emptiness of Yamapurī Due to the Power of the Ekādaśī Vow," within the narrative of King Mahābhāgavata Rukmāṅgada concerning the non-observance of the Ekādaśī vow defiled by the tenth lunar day (daśamī-viddhā) in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; then Dharmarāja spoke to the Grandfather:
"Aho! What a marvel this is, if the King is the bestower of liberation!"
At that time, all the gods were rendered futile and their instruction was useless;
for there would not have been even the slightest difference between Rukmāṅgada and Hari.
The controller of the city of Yama, the city of the gods, and the city of Brahmā—
Rukmāṅgada was that son of the Earth, for he was indeed Hari himself.
"O Creator, by feeding and honoring even one such person on the day of Hari, I shall have fulfilled my purpose; therefore, accept this from me. (4)
Even if Hari has been remembered, fasted for, or praised by men from the very beginning of time, they are outsiders to me according to my teaching.
Such a conduct of action involving two entities is not recommended;
appoint another who can endure the state of having his own existence shattered. (6)
Having done this, the Lord of Restraint (Yama) abandoned the cloth and remained silent;
then Brahmā, in the assembly, indeed reflected upon who should take the cloth.
Having risen there again and again, they made it public:
"Whoever would take the silk band, I shall grant him the kingdom of Yama. (8)
"However, the command of King Rukmāṅgada must not be transgressed;
therefore, let them accept the seat of Yama on this condition: I shall give you an empty cloth."
Even after hearing it, when no one attains his own teaching,
how could one remain in the service of another's teaching in a state of dependence?
But then Nārada desired to speak to the Grandfather:
"What god would accept a position of sovereignty that is subject to a human being?"
Therefore, O Grandfather, consider here another path by which the way of Yama might indeed be obstructed. || 12 ||
"Act in such a way that even the path to heaven shall not be obstructed.
Having heard these words of Nārada, which were indeed pregnant with profound meaning, [he acted accordingly].
For the sake of Vaivasvata’s task and with the desire to honor him,
the Creator of the Universe reflected upon that which would create an obstacle to liberation.
From himself, he produced a woman who deludes the world;
the goddess, the best of all women, shone forth, fashioned by his mind.
This woman, possessing a divine form and adorned with celestial ornaments, was seen by all with minds struck with wonder as she emerged in the full bloom of youth. (16)
Then all those present in the assembly, born of Brahmā’s creation, were deluded;
for delusion (moha) is the obstructer of liberation, and Mohinī is the destroyer of liberation.
Indeed, as he beheld these, the Unborn One felt a genuine sense of wonder, with a mind full of passion and eyes full of passion. (18)
One might even think of or gaze upon one’s mother, a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a brother’s wife, a teacher’s wife, or a king’s consort. (19)
That person who, upon seeing this woman, falls into agitation— even if she were a dog-eater (śvapacī)— having so intended, goes to a terrible hell.
O sons, the merit earned through his birth becomes fruitless;
by association, ten thousandfold merit goes to destruction. (21)
But through evil, a living being then falls into the womb of an animal;
therefore, one should not think of, look at, or speak of a woman with a sinful mind.
One should not reflect upon women, nor look at them, nor speak to them with a sinful mind;
for if one does so with a mind full of longing, that person falls from his state in that very instant. (23)
Having spoken thus in many ways, Viriñci then beheld Mohinī along with her caravan with his eye of knowledge and reflected for a moment.
Just as this [woman] was fashioned by the mind and causes madness of the mind, so too has she been born for the sake of bondage; Yama will attain satisfaction.
By this [practice], the path of Yama will be properly and well-traversed;
whether toward heaven or hell, one shall never fall into an empty [state]. (26)
Then Mohinī, having bowed to that four-faced one, said:
"O Brahmā, behold this member of the assembly, whose consciousness has become fixed like an inanimate object and who is overcome by a swoon. (27)
Deluded by my form and submerged in the ocean of bondage,
there is no one here today who remains visible upon being beheld by me.
Whether it be slight or great, no agitation has been produced in me by anyone.
O Brahmā, I was created by you for the purpose of causing agitation to someone.
"O Creator, command him quickly; for I shall agitate him in an instant.
Indeed, upon seeing me on earth, even a dull-witted king will instantly become bewildered. (1.286.30)
"Furthermore, how could the conscious soul have been fashioned as a vessel for delusion?
Having said this, she ceased speaking, and Brahmā spoke to her with joy.
"O large-eyed one, it is true that your form is enchanting;
yet all these members of the assembly have become as if insentient upon seeing you. (32)
They exist exactly as they are; may victory always be yours.
O Mohinī, accomplish that for which I have created you.
In the land of Surāṣṭra, there is indeed a king named Rukmāṅgada, whose wife is Sandhyāvalī, who truly resembles you in beauty. (34)
In her was born a son named Dharmāṅgada, who excelled in virtue;
he was wise, never wavering from his word, and always obedient to her command. (35)
"O Mohinī, go to the presence of that very Rukmāṅgada;
on the great mountain named Raivata, that king will come to you. (36)
Enchanted by your song, he will enter into union with you;
there, O Goddess, having rendered him utterly helpless, you must speak to him.
"I shall become your wife, provided that the wager is maintained by you;
when the time comes, I will speak, and you must certainly do what I say. (38)
Having heard this, he will be bewildered and will act accordingly;
at that time, his right hand must be grasped by you with your own hand.
He should be bound by oaths to the observance of the agreement;
thereafter, during the act of sexual union, he should be gratified like one who is utterly innocent.
When deep affection has become firm and the months have passed, O lovely-limbed one, when you are seen to be truly infatuated in love; (4.1)
Laughing, he reminded the king of his own pledged word:
"O King, that oath which was made by you to uphold my speech."
"O Great King, protect that; I believe the time has come.
When you had spoken thus, the king was indeed bewildered by his reverence for the truth. (43)
He will say, "I shall protect you; tell me, what shall I give to you?
When these words have been spoken by you, the king should then be addressed as follows: ||44||
In the state of passion, fasting is considered to cause weakness;
indeed, fasting, which produces hunger, is a great obstacle to the union of sexual delight. 45.
"You must never observe a fast on the day of Hari;
for a fast that causes the loss of my sexual pleasure is an obstacle to me. (46)
He who does not serve a very innocent woman endowed with youth while she is being served,
that wicked and merciless man, who insults holy days, goes to the Raurava hell.
"O King, how indeed could I be able to remain for even three nights without you?
I am not able to remain even for a single day without you. (48)
O King, fasting for you results in great sin, since I burn with the fire of desire without you. (49)
If a young woman is to be protected, the pleasure of love should always be given to her; if one is unable to grant the pleasure of love, then the young woman should not be protected.
The sigh of longing that arises from the hearts of young women is a conflagration that utterly consumes even the merits of those observing vows, burning them away from their very roots.
Therefore, O King, the days of Hari should be observed while one is still in old age;
once my youth has passed, I shall observe the days of Hari.
O lady of beautiful limbs, even when being thus exhorted, if the king does not act upon your words, then you must speak further words.
O King, if you do not renounce the fast on the day of Hari, then cut off your own head with your own hand using the excellent sword of your son. 54.
"O Indra among kings, place Dharmāṅgada yourself upon my lap;
O King, if you do not do this which is dear to me, it will result in injury. (55)
"O Goddess, having heard these words, 'You, whose merit is exhausted, shall surely go to hell before long,' he will not kill his son."
Having obtained the permission of the gods, he will eat on the day of Hari;
likewise, his subjects will also eat on that day of Hari. (57)
Then the path to Yama will be set in motion by people, and it will be as vast as a row of hells. ||58||
When, out of devotion, he shall not eat anything on the day of Hari,
then he will kill that very son who has been consecrated to the kingdom.
Then the king shall undergo the defilement of being conquered by women,
the state of having slain one who was consecrated for sovereignty, and the suffering of the hell named Put.
O King, because he acts as a destroyer of his ancestors and is a slayer of his own self,
he will soon meet his end through these very faults.
Having gone himself upon the path of Yama, he will fill the Raurava hell;
or else, by the power of his vow, he will quickly depart for the abode of Hari.
The teaching will be obstructed, and people will indeed consume [the fruits of] their vows;
the path of Yama will truly be opened wide.
"Go quickly and wait for Rukmāṅgada on Mount Raivata;
once you have accomplished your task, return, for I shall assign a specific lunar day for our meeting at home. (64)
Thus addressed, Mohinī bowed to Aja and the members of the assembly;
watched by the gods on her way, she set out for Mount Raivata.
In the third muhūrta, they reached the mountain peak;
that mountain Raivata, whose nature is like Mount Mandara, shines resplendent in Saurāṣṭra.
For this is indeed a temple of jewels, endowed with many minerals;
it is a playground for the gods and a place of penance for ascetics. (67)
