This place of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is like a pleasure garden,
where the Svarṇarakṣā river flows with a golden luster.
The great Liṅga Bhaveśvara exists there,
and Vāmana indeed dwells in the form of Dāmodara within the mountain caves and forest lands.
Having gone to the bank of Mṛgīkuṇḍa, the young woman drank the auspicious water,
ate the sweet fruit of the sītā plant, and performed an excellent concert.
Accompanied by melodic modulations (*mūrchanā*) and rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), joined with the sound of the *gāndhāra* note, it dispels fatigue, is sweet, and deludes all living beings. ||7 1||
Shrouded by a cluster of ciñcā trees, Śiva, the Lord of Existence, heard [the sound] and then became intensely intent on eating, overcome by desire. ||72||
The temple trembled from where Mohinī was singing;
Svarṇarekhā became motionless, and the forest then grew still.
Dāmodara also arrived, due to the confusion caused by the sound of the rows of forest trees;
and the forest deities, drawn by that sound, came from Mount Raivata.
Absorbed in the enchanting song, she awaits the arrival of the king;
Rukmāṅgada, too, out of world-weariness, desires to go to the forest.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Yamarāja and Pitāmaha under the Pretense of Renouncing His Seat of Authority, the Production of the Woman Mohinī after Being Instructed, the Dispatching of Mohinī to King Rukmāṅgada on Mount Raivata, and the Song of Mohinī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: At that very moment, O Lakṣmī, King Rukmāṅgada,
having enjoyed human pleasures and having fully worshipped Hari Keśava, [attained his goal].
Having rendered the path of Yama empty and having conquered Vaivasvata Yama himself,
he filled the path to Vaikuṇṭha with human beings.
Having summoned Dharmāgada, he spoke to him regarding the granting of the kingdom:
"O son, [accept] this earth, girdled by the seven oceans. (3)
Protect the burden of the kingdom and accept that which is offered by me;
for he who does not hand over the burden when a worthy son has been fully prepared [is at fault].
That father who carries away his afflictions and has fallen away from the fame of the Dharma does not attain elevation in old age, for he fails to nourish the power of his son. || 5 ||
Furthermore, even a son who is capable of performing his duties but does not bear his burden—
having fallen away from his own responsibilities— becomes a miserable old man.
That son by whom his father is not pleased goes indeed to Raurava;
but that son by whom his father is well-pleased is a partaker of heaven.
The kingdom has been governed and the subjects have been led toward devotion to Viṣṇu;
now, having attained fulfillment, I shall go alone to the forest.
Desiring to burn away the mountains, forests, rivers, and various lakes, I shall indeed look upon them after having truly placed this burden upon you.
Having heard this, Dharmāṅgada said: "Janārdana has been described as the father;
great is heaven in the word of a father, and liberation belongs to the one who obeys his father's command."
For there is no other duty for a son than carrying out the father's command;
even one who is most virtuous shall go to a lower state if he does not obey his father’s word.
Therefore, for the sake of your satisfaction, I shall carry out your word;
O father, I shall lift up this heavy burden of your kingdom.
Having heard these words of his son, the king became truly delighted;
he spoke to his wife Sandhyāvalī, who stood there like another Lakṣmī.
Listen, O wife; I am blessed and you are indeed blessed by this son.
Through the ears of a virtuous son, liberation is heard, and it has truly been attained through such a son.
When a son is endowed with discipline, possessed of conduct and valor,
powerful, and fully accomplished, his father’s liberation from household life is certain.
A son who bestows a hundred joys surely delivers the one who provided the seed;
he shall deliver his mother here, and likewise, a son has been obtained by us both.
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to my son and you to its protection,
I shall go to dwell in the forest, recollecting the ancient tradition.
I shall spend the remainder of my life and, at its end, go to the abode of Hari;
be happy with your son through this knowledge that culminates in the realization of the Self.
Do not grieve at the separation; consider this the command of your husband, who is a supreme lord.
Remaining at home out of your nature as a woman, prosperity shall be yours. 19.
Having heard this, Sandhyāvalī said, "O King, you have spoken the truth;
having attained detachment from worldly enjoyments, serve the sages and the virtuous."
I am pleased with your command and with your devotion to your husband;
may you find complete satisfaction, for my liberation shall indeed be aided by you.
Having also taken leave of his subjects and cast the burden upon his own son,
Bhūṣāla took up the responsibility himself and extended his right hand.
Mounting his horse, the king went to the Raivataka forest,
to the hermitage of the brahmin named Patnīvrata, near the Aśvasaras lake.
He entered that exceedingly beautiful grove, adorned with clusters of excellent plantain trees,
filled with Aśoka and Bakula trees, and surrounded by Punnāga and Sarala trees.
It was endowed with mangoes, rāyaṇa trees, rose-apples, and the like, along with kṣīrikās and karmadās; and with wood-apples, long peppers, dates, coconuts, and ketakas.
It was adorned with śrīvṛkṣas, tālas, panasa trees, sandalwood trees, sāla and campaka trees, betel nuts, pomegranates, bamboos, dhātrīs, and nimba trees.
Seeing the ground covered with shrubs, creepers, and grass, yet abounding in crops and grain,
the king beheld the sage, who possessed the brilliance of fire.
He bowed with reverence to the brahmin named Patnīvrata;
honored by the sage with hospitable rites, the king spoke.
Today my sins have been exhausted and the fruit of virtuous deeds has been attained;
I have beheld your lotus feet, and my future is endowed with prosperity.
Then, O King, he who was devoted to his wife spoke, his birth having borne fruit:
"By one as meritorious as you, my hermitage has now been beheld."
Having completely conquered the path of Yama and emptied the hell realms,
he by whom the world was indeed led to the imperishable station of Vaikuṇṭha.
O protector of the earth, he who was a devotee of Viṣṇu and superior even to the twice-born has come within the range of our eyes as we longed to behold him. (32)
But you, O best of devotees, purify the surface of the earth;
dwell happily in this beautiful hermitage and tell me whatever is to be known by me.
"Drink water, O Lord of the Earth; enjoy the fruits appropriate for this hermitage.
All is well with you; dwell happily in this hermitage. (34)
Having received the honors, the king said to the best of sages:
"O Sage, by your grace, everything is well and brings me joy. (35)
And my son has become an obedient emperor, a victorious servant of the earth, renowned as being superior to me in the governance of the seven continents. (36)
In a single day, he traverses the entire vast earth and returns again during the night for the purpose of massaging my feet.
Likewise, this auspicious body of mine is free from all diseases;
my happiness is immeasurable, and my beloved wife is under my control at home. (38)
She who always gazes upon me with a look intensified by passion;
wherever that lady of auspicious marks places her foot—
In various places the earth reveals its treasures for her whose limbs are free from decay and possess fresh youth. (1.287.40)
O Brahmin, even without fire, she indeed prepares food of six flavors;
whatever small amount of food she cooks, millions eat from it. (4.1)
There are horses and elephants, as well as infinite wealth and grain;
and all the people abide by my command in the vow of Hari.
"By what merit indeed do I possess all this auspiciousness?
Having reflected upon it, tell me of the merit performed by me, whether in this world or in another. (43)
Having heard this, the Brahmin, who was devoted to his wife, reflected upon what had been accumulated in a previous birth and said to the king: "In a former life, you were a Śūdra. (44)
Greatly distressed by poverty and accompanied by a wicked wife, you once went on a pilgrimage to sacred fords due to the influence of association with a twice-born man. (45)
Having bathed at the Viśrāntighaṭṭa in Mathurā within the Yamunā lake,
he heard the merit-bestowing narrative at the abode of Vārāha.
This concerns the subject of the Aśūnyaśayana vow, which pleases Hari;
the completion of this vow occurs through four breaking-fast ceremonies. (47)
O King, that vow was performed by you and your wife at home on the second day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O lord of the earth. (48)
This meritorious vow should be accepted; it removes birth, death, and old age, bestows sovereignty, grants wives and sons, and brings about auspicious prosperity. (49)
The practitioner of the vow should likewise eat only once a day for one month;
Viṣṇu, the husband of Lakṣmī, must be worshipped daily at dawn and at night.
With fruits, flowers, incense, and beautiful red ointments;
with gifts of beds, gifts of garments, and likewise by feeding those most devoted to Brahman. (51)
Alternatively, one should observe the fast for seven days within a month;
at the end of those seven days, one should indeed perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) after having eaten wholesome food.
In this manner, one should perform four such breaking-of-fasts within the month;
however, if unable to do so, the observer of the vow should subsist on milk every day.
One should offer a beautiful couch to Viṣṇu along with Lakṣmī;
for without Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu’s bed would be empty. (54)
A bed accompanied by a consort shall be known as the "Aśūnyaśayana" (the non-empty bed);
and the attendants of both the queen and the king should always perform [this rite]. //55//
One should offer all kinds of various services to Śrī Viṣṇu;
then, the observer of the vow will certainly attain it all in another birth. 56.

Since you previously performed all [the rites] for your ancestors along with their concluding ceremonies (udyāpana), you have obtained this great kingdom here; for that is indeed the fruit of the merit of giving (dāna) through prosperity.
You indeed gave the gift of Lakṣmī to Viṣṇu upon his reclining;
as a result of that, you have obtained a queen like a goddess. (58)

Vehicles, mounts, palaces, and so forth were intended by you for the purpose of giving, yet they were not actually bestowed; nevertheless, the fruit born of that intention has been obtained here. (59)
"O King, by the grace of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī, you have obtained a son who indeed carries out his father's word through the power of his mind, speech, and body. (1.287.60)
For him, bathing in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day;
therefore, what was performed and given previously is obtained again in a subsequent birth.
"Thus I have told you this account; what else may I do for you?
Having heard this, the king then spoke regarding his vision of you on Mount Raivata: (62)
"O best of Brahmins, I wish to do so, if you have permission.
"May it be well with you, O King; go," the sage said, blessing him. (63)
Mounting his horse and bowing [to him], the king departed with swift speed to Mount Raivata, where Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Abode, resides, and where Mohinī is present.
She waited for the king and sang sweetly;
the great king, perceiving her beautiful voice, went forward.
He saw a lovely woman standing in Mṛgīkuṇḍa, possessing the luster of molten gold,
appearing less than sixteen years of age, and resembling the goddess Svāhā incarnate.
Upon seeing her, he fell into a state of delusion and was pierced by the arrow of desire;
overcome by the fever of passion, he approached her whose face was like a serpent's.
And having recognized that king, she cast glances from her eyes,
cheeks, arms, breasts, lips, and hips.
Shaking her head like one utterly bewildered, she went before the king;
then she spoke to Rukmāṅgada, who was tormented by desire: "Arise, [you are] under your control."
I am here and I shall indeed do whatever you command in this forest;
or if you have a desire for sexual pleasure, enjoy me, your slave of delight.
Then the king said to the woman: "Even though I have come to the forests for the sake of asceticism, nevertheless, having beheld you, [I am drawn back]. (71)
I am born, O lady with a face like the full moon, filled with desire for you, who possess such a form that deludes all. (72)
"Never before have I seen such a thing even in the work of Brahmā;
show favor, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, for my heart is truly bound to you. (73)
Come to my lap and adorn it as your own, for it is priceless;
I would give even myself, so what need be said of mere wealth and jewels? (74)
"Having given you this most cherished kingdom, I shall indeed dwell here with you.
Thus she spoke, having recognized that the king was utterly deluded and that the moment was opportune.
Having smiled and reflected deeply upon what was spoken by Brahmā, he said:
"O Lord of the Earth, I do not choose a kingdom, wealth, jewels, or anything of the sort. (76)
Whatever I shall say at the proper time, that must be done without hesitation; I shall follow it, there is no doubt—make this agreement with me.
"O Indra among kings, take an oath and say, 'I shall certainly do it';
then I will grant you enjoyment, for that shall not be impossible for you. (78)
Then the king, deluded by her beauty, youth, and charms, said:
"O Goddess, I shall grant you whatever condition by which you may be satisfied. (79)
Uttering an oath, he said, "I shall do your bidding.
Mohinī also said to him, "Give me your right hand."
"By the gift of this ring as a token, there shall be confidence in your word;
then, at the time of the final decision, you shall not speak a falsehood. (8.1)
"A firm wager has been made between us; this path is witnessed by Dharma.
Then the king said to that woman: "What is the use of these firm proofs? (82)
O lady of beautiful thighs, from my very birth I have never spoken an untruth;
indeed, this right hand of mine, which bestows merit through giving, has been extended by me.
O beautiful one, O fair-thighed lady, whatever good deed I have performed since birth—if I do not follow your word, let all of that be for you. (84)
"For in this very place, O lady, I gave you to me as my wife according to the dharma;
I shall speak further of the great king Rukmāṅgada in the middle of the forest. (85)
"You ought to show favor by granting a reply.
Thus commanded by the king, Mohinī spoke these words in response.
"O King, I am Brahmabhavā; having heard of your fame, I have come here for your sake, filled with love for Raivata, who is like a golden mountain. (87)
She worshipped Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, with the gift of song—that very God by whom a great favor was bestowed upon me. (88)
Since you have so soon attained what was desired and beautiful, you are dear to me, O King, and indeed I am dear to you. (89)
"Do not harbor doubt, O Indra among kings; know that the maiden is free from blemish.
Marry me here, O protector of the earth, according to the ritual prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras."
Having heard this, the king married her right there according to the prescribed rites;
he was wedded by Bhava, Viṣṇu, and Dāmodara.
Having subsisted on wild roots and fruits, the couple took refuge in their dharma and enjoyed themselves in various ways, filled with the freshness of youth. (92)
Mohinī delighted him with amorous sentiments day and night,
bringing for him the most excellent objects of enjoyment from Satyaloka as well as from Svarga.
She served that husband and enjoyed pleasures difficult even for the immortals to obtain;
there, a new village of gold was fashioned by divine celestial beings.
With divine male and female slaves and servants, with rows of most delightful palaces, with vehicles, mounts, and gardens, and with wish-fulfilling cows, elephants, and so forth; ||95||
There, at that time, there was no deficiency in food, drink, vessels, garments, ornaments, royal insignia, liquid substances, and so forth. (96)
Twenty years passed for those two who took delight in sensual enjoyments;
the king also became fully satisfied with her.
"Aha! This auspicious form was indeed created by Brahmā for my sake;
her shanks resemble the trunks of elephants and are like gold. (98)
Her rows of teeth are like rows of moons; her ankles are hidden and enchanting;
her eyes are as expansive as lotuses; and her breasts are like golden jars. (99)
Her hips are like those of the king of beasts, her waist is slender and most fragrant;
I am indeed fulfilled by her, yet she will surely ask for what ought to be given.
I shall give even that which is difficult to obtain, and indeed everything that ought not to be given;
if he should ask for my very life, I shall surely give it—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, for King Rukmāṅgada, who was utterly absorbed in amorous pleasure,
four or five years passed by as if they were a mere moment.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Rukmāṅgada’s Renunciation of the Kingdom to His Son and Departure for the Forest, the Hearing of Rukmāṅgada’s Previous Births as Narrated by the Wife and the Vow-observing Ṛṣi dwelling on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake, and the Meeting with Mohinī and the Oath of Time at Raivatācala," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, then his son Dharmāṅgada ruled the kingdom, performing and causing others to perform the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) by the command of his father. || 1 ||
Protecting all his subjects according to the Bhāgavata dharma,
the son always causes the drum to be sounded for the sake of the Viṣṇudinavrata.
The king, too, observed the vow of Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rules throughout the day;
having abandoned all other vows, he enjoyed the company of his youthful wife.
Once, during the month of Āśvina, Mohinī delighted the king with divine pleasures again and again through every means.
Even though the king was extremely simple-minded, he did not neglect his vow to Hari;
the protector of the earth abandoned his play for three days beginning with the tenth day.
One does not abandon the day of Viṣṇu, which cuts asunder birth and death;
indeed, the month of Kārtika has arrived for the awakening of Viṣṇu.
Whatever meritorious deed is performed here by any men whatsoever, it shall indeed become inexhaustible and bestow the world of Viṣṇu. || 7 ||
Having reflected thus, the king spoke these words to Mohinī:
"O Goddess, I have enjoyed pleasure with you for many years."
Fearing to offend you, I have not said anything at all, anywhere;
O fair-browed one, many Kārtikas have passed while my heart was attached to you.
No vow has been undertaken by me for the month of Kārtika, nor even for half a month;
therefore, I desire to observe the Kārtika month accompanied by a vow.
He for whom Kārttika passes without vows has lived in vain; yet those who observe the excellent vows of Kārttika, even if they indulge in liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse, [attain the goal]. 11.
Having become pure, they indeed go to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu;
by the offering of a lamp in Kārttika, the donor shall surely ascend to heaven.
By lighting a lamp for others, even a poor person may go to heaven;
by observing the full moon day at Puṣkara, one is liberated from the sins of a lifetime.
He for whom Kārtika passes while honored by vows, fasts, observances, worship, charity, and other such acts, goes to the supreme goal.
In the month of Kārttika, he who practices the *kṛcchra* penance, or is devoted to the *prājāpatya*, or fasts every other day, or even fasts for three nights; || 15 ||
Having fasted for seven days, ten days, a fortnight, or a month,
subsisting only on fruit, that man goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
By those established in the vow of eating once a day, eating only at night, or eating only what is unasked for, the earth, a wife, a son, sovereignty, wealth, and grain are obtained. (17)
The month of Kārtika is meritorious and bestows devotion through vows, gifts, worship, and other such acts;
within it, the day of Hari is meritorious, as is likewise the five-day period.
Having kept the Prabodhinī vow, which is rich in vigilance, one indeed attains liberation;
during Kārtika, one should avoid oil, honey, soup, and sexual intercourse.
One should diligently avoid flat beans, royal foods, and sensual enjoyments;
for in the month of Kārttika, an undertaken vow cuts away the bonds of men throughout their births.
A person devoid of initiation attains birth in the womb of an animal;
however, one who is initiated on the eleventh day or on the full moon goes to the Imperishable.
Having given water-pots filled with water, one goes to the abode of Hari;
for the conclusion of the vows of the year is the worship performed in Kārtika.
The concluding rite and all other ceremonies shall yield their full fruit;
and the observer of the night-vow (naktavrata) should feed children and virtuous men with food of the six flavors.
To a virtuous twice-born man, one should cause an ox to be given when it is unasked for;
and he who eats the offered food should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee.
During the ritual bath for the Dhātrī tree, one should offer thickened milk-rice (pāyasa) and curd;
likewise, if there is a vow regarding fruits, one should present fruits therein.
Upon the renunciation of oil, one should give ghee; likewise, upon the renunciation of ghee, milk. Upon the restriction of grains, one should give śāli rice or else that very same grain.
If one sleeps on the ground, one should offer a decorated bed provided with a couch;
if one eats from leaves, one should indeed give vessels together with ghee.
In silence, one should cause a bell, gold, or even sesame seeds to be given;
at the morning bath, one should give a horse, and when free from oiliness, one should give ghee and roasted flour.
Upon the shaving of nails and hair, one should give a mirror and clay;
upon the acceptance of footwear, one should give sandals and wooden shoes.
Upon the renunciation of salt and other such items, a cow that yields abundant milk should be given as a gift;
the giver of a lamp should indeed present gold to the image of the deity.
One should give an umbrella and chowries, and offer silken garments;
moreover, the performer of the three-night vow should give a decorated bed.
One who has fasted for seven nights should offer a palanquin and an umbrella;
one who has fasted for fifteen days should give a vehicle and an elephant.
One who performs a month-long fast should offer his entire household property;
for one who observes a single-meal-a-day vow, a goat or sheep; and for one who subsists on fruit, gold.
One should give the fruit of eating vegetables or offer another suitable vessel;
in this manner, one should provide that which follows the vow, according to one's wealth and prosperity.
"In this world, one who performs a vow obtains a kingdom, a wife, wealth, and so forth;
therefore, O Mohinī, I shall perform the observance of a vow during the month of Kārtika. (35)
He whose Kārtika month passes with vows, fasts, and observances, becomes a celestial deity dwelling in a divine chariot and attains the supreme goal. (36)
Therefore, casting aside delusion, give me your command regarding the Kārtika vow;
I shall indeed observe the vow for the worship of Hari.
Having heard these disagreeable words, that Mohinī, who was herself desiring him, said:
"If you desire me as your beloved, you must certainly not perform this vow. (38)
Giving, protection, and warfare—these three are the duties of kings;
the performance of vows and the like for monarchs has not been mentioned anywhere in the authoritative examples. (39)
O Indra among kings, I am unable to remain even for a moment without you, O one who possesses the luster of a lotus-navelled deity; how much less so for a period measured in months!
"If the vow is undertaken by you, my death will surely occur;
therefore, we two shall indeed perform the Kārtika vow in our old age. (4.1)
Having heard those excellent words from Mohinī, the king then said:
"O fair-browed one, I shall not perform the vow; I shall do as you desire. (42)
Having heard this, the slender-limbed Mohinī was delighted; embracing him as he stood in private, she gratified him according to the methods of the science of love.
While he was thus enjoying himself, the awakening dawn arrived;
the sound of a drum reached Rukmāṅgada from his two ears.
"O people, remain for the day of Hari at dawn, eating only one meal; all of you should abstain from pungent and salty food and subsist solely on sacrificial offerings (haviṣya). || 45 ||
Sleeping on the ground as your bed and free from attachment to sensual desires, remember Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods. 46.
Engaged in eating but once, you shall observe the fast; having completed the accumulation of *śrāddha* rites, go to the abode of Śrī Hari. (47)
Tomorrow morning is the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, known as Prabodhinī;
by fasting on this day, one attains the abode of Hari and shakes off the entire web of sins.
O men, perform the worship of Śrī Hari with your own wealth—with garments, flowers, incense, lamps, and excellent sandalwood and saffron. (49)
Having worshipped with food offerings and fruits, go to the abode of Śrī Hari;
whoever does not follow the word of Rukmāṅgada shall not reach the realm of Hari.
"He is to be punished by me and deserves death; this I declare according to the law.
Having heard this righteous proclamation concerning himself from the drum, [he was filled with fear]. (51)
Rukmāṅgada quickly rose from the bed of Mohinī and said:
"In the morning, on the day of Hari, there will be the destruction of sins."
"I shall be self-restrained; may you forgive me, may you forgive me!
This Ekādaśī should be observed; it cuts the bonds of worldly existence and bestows a higher state of rebirth. (53)
O large-eyed lady, you too, along with me,
should propitiate that Adhokṣaja, Hṛṣīkeśa, being devoted to fasting.
By means of this you shall go to Nirvana, which is free from burning and dissolution;
[by means of it] you shall regain your kingdom, or heaven, or else final liberation. ||55||
Mohinī said: "Well spoken by you regarding the vow and worship of Hari!
It cuts through birth, death, and old age; indeed, I shall perform it at your command. (56)
The promise which was previously made by you on this Raivata mountain—accompanied by the granting of tribute and well-marked by your own deed—[remains]. (57)
"The time for her [vow] has arrived; let it be granted by you to me.
Otherwise, all the merit from your birth shall go to ruin. (58)
Having heard and remembered this, Rukmāṅga said: "I shall do what is in your mind;
there is nothing that cannot be given to you by me, even at the cost of my life. (59)
"What more need be said of a kingdom, a city, wealth, or anything else, O beautiful lady?
Mohinī replied, "Having perceived that this was indeed a favorable and auspicious opportunity. (1.288.60)
"O Lord, O Beloved, O Dear One, O King, O Master of my life, O Lover of Rati!
If I am dear to you, this day of Viṣṇu must not be fasted upon; food must be eaten. (61)
"O King, I shall become separated from you without union with you;
therefore, if you desire to enjoy me as your beloved for the rest of your life," (62)
"O King, I must certainly dwell in your house until my death;
therefore, please give up this fast and eat on the day of Hari."
"This very boon was requested by me previously;
if you do not grant it, whether out of delusion or otherwise, you shall become a speaker of falsehood. (64)
One will go to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings for the loss of a wife, the loss of a vow, the loss of one's word, or in matters of strength and weakness. (65)
"Having considered both merit and demerit, seen and unseen, do what you deem most desirable.
The king said: "O fair-browed one, you have been restrained by me during the excellent vow of Kārttika."
"But why, O beloved, do you obstruct us even on the eleventh day?
Reflect upon this: 'We have become happy through the merit of our vow. (67)
Having become the sister of Dharma and the daughter of Vidhi, such conduct is not fitting for you;
being a protector of righteousness, why do you create an obstacle to dharma? (68)
"From birth until now, I have never eaten on the day of Hari;
yet today, being dependent upon you, how could I eat on the day of Hari? (69)
In the final stage of one's life, the service of Svarṇarekhā, her worship, and the constant service of Hari are appropriate. ||1.288.70||
That which I did not do in my childhood or youth while I possessed power—how could I now, in the midst of the forest, perform such a loathsome act? (71)
Do not break your vow, nor do you harbor such persistence;
O fair-browed one, whatever else you desire, I am the giver of royal prosperity.
"Accept this celestial chariot that travels through the sky like a swing;
enjoy the essence of the wish-fulfilling creeper, and do not create an obstacle to your vow. (73)
The man who eats his own flesh on the day of Hari incurs the same sin as one who commits murder in the three worlds; so too does he who engages in sexual intercourse on the day of Hari. (74)
Whatever sin there is in the neglect of one's pasture, whatever sin there is in giving false testimony, and likewise in misappropriating a deposit or betraying trust; ||75||
Whatever sin lies in the killer of a human being, and whatever sin lies in the reviler of one's guru—all that transgression resides within you on this day of Hari. (76)
Knowing this, O large-eyed one, how can I consume such a sin?
And you, being thus possessed of knowledge, why do you destroy your vow? (77)
Mohinī said: Having heard those words regarding the duties of penance toward the king, [she replied:
"Whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or by whatever worship has been performed by you... (78)
One should not let the twelfth day pass by without fruit, fasting, or [eating] wind (i.e., air).
This applies likewise to pregnant women, householders, the emaciated, and the sick. (79)
Of children with delicate limbs who serve on the earth in battle,
and of women rich in devotion to their husbands who are intent upon the enjoyment of sacrifices.
"O King, it is not proper for young women, widows, or husbands to observe the fast;
what is the use of many other words spoken by me? (81)
"If you do not take pleasure in providing me with food on this eleventh day, then even if you were to cut off and offer me your own head, I would have no joy. (82)
O King, if you do not take food on the day of Hari,
then I shall not touch your body, for you would be a speaker of untruth.
By truth the sun shines, and by truth the moon is beautiful;
established in the dharma of truth, the earth sustains the entire world.
By truth the wind blows, and by truth the fire burns;
this entire world is supported by truth, established according to its respective functions. 85.
Like the ocean, it does not waver from truth; like the Vindhya mountain, it does not grow beyond truth.
Trees that are consistent in their conduct of truth blossom when they encounter the proper season.
Truth alone excels even ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
O King, for one who speaks untruth, everything quickly perishes.
O King, may it not be so for you; I grieve that it brings such great loss.
Since profit is seen in feeding many, this is my stubborn insistence. (88)
My father also spoke in this very same way, and I speak it with truth;
if you have no faith in this, do as you wish.
O Lakṣmī, when Mohinī, who accomplishes the rites for the ancestors, had thus spoken and ceased, the king indeed fell into deep reflection.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Mohinī’s Obstruction of Rukmāṅgada’s Desire for the Kārtika-vrata and His Greatness, and Subsequently Mohinī’s Opposition when He Requested Permission for the Prabodhinī-vrata through the Proclamation of His Own Drum," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, on the tenth day of the month of Kārtika, at dawn, Dharmāṅgada,
having caused a drum to be beaten and making a proclamation from atop an elephant, [spoke as follows].
"No one should eat on the eleventh day, the day of Hari.
Having taken his army and subjects with him, he went to the Raivata tirtha.
Joined by Sandhāvalī, he set out to perform a circumambulation of Mount Raivata during the five-day period beginning on the eleventh lunar day and ending on the full moon.
On the Prabodhinī day, the holy fords and deities— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— come to Mount Raivata there to perform circumambulation.
The Ṛṣis, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and likewise the Munis; the Pitṛs, Nidhis, Kāṣṭhās, Grahas, Rudras, and Siddhas. || 5 ||
The Kṛttikās, the lunar constellation-maṇḍala, tens of millions of gods, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Vināyakas; || 6 ||
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vetālas, Gaṇeśas, the Gaṇas and others, Hanūmants, Mahālakṣmīs, and likewise the Yoginīs—[these are the protectors]. (7)
Durgās, Caṇḍīs, and Mānavas; gods, rivers, and lakes;
oceans, mountains, plains, islands, sacred fields, and hamlets.
Cities, forests, days, nights, and even the religious observances of the day—
thus there are others situated in the sky, as well as serpents dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla).
Truthful, virtuous, devoted, and self-surrendered young maidens, as well as men and women intent on offering their bodies to Kṛṣṇa, attain [the supreme goal]. || 1.289.10 ||
There were also forest-dwellers, Kinnarīs, Gandharvīs, and female servants;
as well as Vaiṣṇavas, Śaṅkaras, Sauras, Gāṇapatyas, and those devoted to Śakti.
The Cārvākas, the Bījamārgas, the Nārasiṃhas, the Rāmiṇas, the Dāttātreyas, the Kāpilas, the Ārhats, the Bauddhas, and those who have taken refuge in Śiva. || 12 ||

The great ones, the gurus, the teachers of Dharma, and those who seek the four aims of human life; the Ābhīras, the Ūraṇavāras, the cowherds, and those following the Vāmamārga—[all these are one]. 13.
The Mahābhāgavatas, Merā Nartakas, Naṭajātis, Aghorapathalambas, Gāruḍas, and those who resort to Bhairava; || 14 ||
The Haṃsas and Paramahaṃsas, those with staffs (Sadaṇḍas), the Kuladevins, the Vidyādharas, the Gaṇikās, and the multiform Nāṭikas. || 15 ||
Cowherds, artisans, those accompanied by their wives, and followers of the four castes and stages of life come to Mount Raivata in the month of Kārtika for the purpose of performing circumambulation.
Where, however, countless people come to offer water, food, clothing, their bodies, and so forth, performing acts of self-surrender to the Guru for the sake of merit and liberation. (17)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Hari, and Nārāyaṇa—the manifest forms—come for the sake of the liberation of people, eager for the rite of circumambulation. 18.
The region of Saurāṣṭra is likewise equal to a sacred field of pilgrimage (tīrthakṣetra);
there, on that mountain, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is personally present along with Lakṣmī.
The divine [light], together with the orb of Goloka, shines resplendently upon his head;
indeed, by him a single circumambulation has been performed.
That circumambulation would be equivalent to circumambulating the individual soul, the Lord, and the world of Brahmā;
for one obtains that same fruit which arises from circumambulating the abode of Brahmā.
"Thinking, 'In this place, merit that wards off the cycle of worldly existence is obtained,' Prince Dharmāṅgada [performed] a circumambulation. (22)
Having come on the tenth day to perform [the rite], he arrived before the peak of Yoginīparvata,
on the side of Māhīṣaparvata, on the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā.
Then he spent the night in the great garden in the mango grove;
in the morning, having bathed in the Kuṇḍa, he beheld Dāmodara and Bhaveśvara.
And having likewise seen Nṛsiṃha, he gazed upon Mṛgīkuṇḍa.
There, Dharmāṅgada heard a beautiful verse concerning people.
And here King Rukmāṅgada shines together with Mohinī, who is served by the daughter of Brahmā; he is the father of Dharmāṅgada.
He does not eat on the day of Hari because of the sound of his own drum;
a woman restrains him, saying, "One must eat on the day of Hari."
What was that daughter of Brahmā like, whom the king made his bride on earth, and after whom he had gone forth for the sake of asceticism, having first taken her as his wife? (28)
Indeed, Rukmāṅga served him and did not leave Hari's day;
people went there thinking, "That daughter of a god must be seen. || 29 ||
Dharmāgada also went with his army and his mother to the northern shore of the lake on the river Suvarṇarakṣā.
There, a great celestial palace shines like that of Vairāja,
and a divine village of the lords of heaven shines like a celestial chariot.
Everything was bestowed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śambhu:
his own insignia and all divine implements produced from the substances of Satyaloka.
Likewise, divine male and female servants and everything divine shone forth;
indeed, all that exists which is invisible to those with physical eyes was revealed.
All of that was observed by Dharmāṅgada through his father’s grace;
overcome with great wonder, he prostrated at his father’s feet.
Sandhyāvalī also joyfully prostrated at her husband's feet;
then the daughter of Brahmā honored her elder sister.
Then Mohinī was honored by her sister with the foremost of blessings,
and they both learned of each other's welfare and circumstances.
Immersed in love, they all went forth to perform the circumambulation;
however, Mohinī then did not go to circumambulate by force.
Then, with joy, she prostrated at his feet with the medicine of the Dharma and,
in his presence, inquired about the cause of her broken state of mind.
Having heard all that Rukmāṅgada had reported regarding the nature of his vow, the people were struck with wonder at the one who had obstructed his religious observance. (39)
Then Rukmāṅgada, having conciliated her with auspicious words, said:
"O Mohinī, perform the circumambulation of Mount Raivata."
The vow of Hari’s day, which is the awakening of the Supreme beyond the supreme—the Ekādaśī—on which one must not eat on either of the two fortnights. (41)
For a person who performs what ought not to be done, the slaughter of a thousand cows is ordained;
O Goddess, knowing this, how could I eat on the day of Hari? (42)
Even the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is declared to be equal to something unfit for consumption when the day of the Lord arrives; how much more so, then, the eating of ordinary food? ||43||
O Goddess, for those who have become emaciated, fruits, roots, milk, and the like are prescribed as excellent food during a vow; however, this is never the case for those who possess strength.
For those who possess power, the breaking of a vow leads only to hell;
do not be obstinate, for if I remain true to my word, there would be a violation of my own vow. (45)
"Whatever else pleases you, I shall do that; of this there is no doubt.
Mohinī spoke while Queen Dharmāṅgadā and the others were listening. (86)
"O King, among the sages, seers, gods, ancestors, moving beings, and stationary things, nothing else is pleasing to me except for your food. (47)
I have no need whatsoever even for the gift of my life;
moreover, this fast on the day of Hari is not seen in the Vedas.
How can you, being such as you are, wish to practice a dharma outside the Vedas?
Let all these Brahmins listen, having placed the Vedas before them. (49)
"The king speaks the truth: 'Why shall I not eat on the day of Hari?
For everything, whether stationary or moving, has its life dependent upon food.'"
Even deceased beings in heaven are gratified by food and water;
even ants and other such creatures take food with their mouths with great difficulty. (5.1)
For the sake of the four-month period and to pass the winter season,
these enter their burrows there and gather provisions for their food.
Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings; who would not find food pleasing?
Yet the king eats no food when the day of Hari has arrived. (93)
For ascetics and the virtuous, the renunciation of food is appropriate;
but for kings, what Vedic basis could there possibly be for performing fasts and the like? (54)
The duty of another is not to be practiced; it brings suffering and is fraught with fear.
Yet today this protector of the earth is established in the dharma of an ascetic.
From food arises vital breath; from vital breath arise bodily strength and the like;
through strength, O King, come the dharmas [of a ruler]; one devoid of that is humiliated. (56)
Knowing this, the king whom I am trying to awaken does not understand.
In this matter, all the brahmins are the authority, and not you, O passionate woman. (57)
"Let them speak here according to the truth; I shall do that which is Vedic.
Thus the Brahmins, including Patnīvrata, Vaśiṣṭha, and others, spoke to the king.
This oath of yours that "one must not eat on the eleventh day" was certainly not established through the vision of the Vedas, but was conceived solely by your own intellect.
For those who maintain the sacred fires, it is indeed declared that they should partake of the sacrificial offering at the two twilights;
daily consuming what remains from the *homa* is sanctioned by the Vedas.
Tell me specifically how fasting is prescribed for kings—those protectors of the earth who perform constant sacrifices. (61)
Whether it be Vedic or non-Vedic, whatever oath has been made by you,
let it be fulfilled today by the very word of the twice-born.
"There is no violation of your vow here; eat together with the Brahmins and others.
You should not feel any distress, for the word of a Brahmin is most supreme."
For we are the seers of the Vedas, and Janārdana is the word of Brahman;
he who thinks otherwise than this regarding the Brahmin shall attain the womb of a Rākṣasa.
Having heard these words of the Vedic Brahmins,
Aṅgada, weeping, prostrated himself before those seers of the Vedas and spoke.
"You are the revealers of the Vedas and you certainly speak according to the Vedic tradition;
yet, disregarding the Supreme Veda, there is no instruction for you anywhere."
The sage Nārada, as well as Kātyāyana and Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, and Mahādeva—whosoever else were assembled there [were present]. ||67||
Listen to their words regarding the vow performed on the day of Hari;
O twice-born ones, first listen there to the speech of Nārada.
Those men who are devoted to Viṣṇu and endowed with constant devotion should observe a fast on the Ekādaśī day in every fortnight.
But that man who eats food on the eleventh day is a sinner;
he surely falls into the river that carries excrement, urine, and pus—of this there is no doubt.
O lady of excellent complexion, for men who are weakened, a secondary alternative has been prescribed;
O auspicious one, roots, fruits, milk, and water may serve as their sustenance.
Indeed, O wise ones, no food is prescribed by any for the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), nor on the occasion of my lying down to sleep, my awakening, or my turning upon my side. (72)
O protector of the earth, a man subsisting on roots and fruits might inflict a thorn in his heart;
therefore, one should avoid [the ritual] for three days beginning from the tenth day.
Without the use of perfumes, betel, flowers, and the like; without sexual union with a woman day or night; and without staying awake for the worship of Viṣṇu, a vow yields only half its fruit. (74)
Therefore, having fasted on those two days, a Vaiṣṇava should observe the lunar day (tithi) of Hari;
these are declared to be the obligatory vows for the devotees of Viṣṇu.
All Ekādaśīs are pure, as is the Dvādaśī of Vāmana; the ninth lunar day (Navamī) of the birth of Śrī Rāmāditya bestows divine perfection.
Furthermore, Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī, Nṛsiṃha-caturdaśī,
and Śivarātri are declared to be the principal vows according to their true nature.
"Thus are the words of Nārada and also those of Kātyāyana;
may all of you sages, whose vision is rooted in the Vedas, listen! (78)
Having eaten on the eleventh day, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a full day and night;
otherwise, one should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
That should be known as a fast, entirely devoid of all enjoyments;
let those who perceive the Vedas indeed hear the words of Vasiṣṭha as well.
O King, having observed the fast on the eleventh day, on the twelfth day likewise [one should perform] the recitation of those mantras, meditation, listening to his stories, and so forth. (8.1)
These qualities, such as compassion and others, arise from the practice of fasting;
now let the sages, whose vision is rooted in the Vedas, listen to the words of the Veda.
A man shall obtain the merit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices by means of a single fast on the Prabodhinī day.
On the day of Viṣṇu’s awakening, one should fast according to the prescribed rules;
by fasting on that day with devotion to Hari, nothing whatsoever shall remain difficult to attain.
And may you all, whose vision is rooted in the Vedas, hear the words of Śiva:
"He is neither a devotee of Śiva, nor of Sūrya, nor of Śakti; he is a servant of the Gaṇas. (85)
He who eats on the day of Viṣṇu should indeed be known as superior even to a beast; by that wicked and sinful man, an offense has been committed against [the Lord]. (86)
"Relying on the power of my devotion, he who eats on the day of Hari"—thus you speak, and yet you are also its prohibitors. (87)
"How am I to place full confidence in that which violates my vow?
You all are the ones who show the way for all living beings. (88)
If they were to act perversely, the world would fall into total blindness;
having committed such an improper deed, how could he live for even a hundred autumns? (89)
"Tell me, are those words of yours non-Vedic?
How can I, being such as I am, perform here the eating of food that is unfit to be eaten?"
And how could I ever abandon my vow based on the words of people standing on the wrong path?
It is not fitting for you to speak what is contrary [to dharma] and destructive of one's vows. (91)
Whether they be gods, dānavas, daityas, gandharvas, or rākṣasas; whether they be siddhas or even brahmins—[I do not know] my father or my mother. (9.2)
Whether it be Hari, Hara, Viṣṇu, or even the progenitor of Mohinī,
or even if the sages themselves should say so— I shall not eat on the day of Hari.
For King Rukmāṅgada, who is renowned as a devotee of Hari, will never allow his vow and religious observance to become fruitless. (94)
The sun might turn black, Mount Meru might move from its place, the ocean might dry up, and fire might become cold. || 95 ||
O Brahmins, you may become deluded or even die;
nevertheless, I shall not abandon my vow on the day of Ekādaśī.
A drum was beaten, and my proclamation resounded throughout the worlds:
"He who eats food on the day of Hari shall be punished, executed, or banished. (97)
If, while it is proclaimed thus, I were to eat food on the day of Hari, the drum would become smeared with impurity, and the fault would be joined with falsehood. (98)
My fame would fall into obscurity, and my residence would be in the realm of Yama;
the mother who gave birth to me would have done so in vain, and the ancestors and the gods would be left hopeless. (99)
Yama would rejoice, yet there would be a breach of my vow;
Māyāvinī would have achieved her purpose, and I would become like a dog at the end of its life.
How could I, a king who upholds the Dharma, be a nourisher of unrighteousness?
Neither the Vedas, nor those sages, nor even the seers exist for me.
"Those who adorn the meal-rite on the day of Kṛṣṇa," having said this and bowed down, the king then fell silent. 102.
Having heard this, the brahmins and the gods joyfully praised the king;
however, Mohinī, her eyes bloodshot with anger and burning within, was inflamed with rage.
While they were all listening, she addressed her husband;
she was one who accomplished her own ends, a destroyer of Viṣṇu’s vows, and as sharp-edged as a razor.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between the Sages and the King regarding Mohinī’s Obstinate Attempt to Ruin the Ekādaśī Vow upon the Meeting with Her Father Rukmāṅgada, at the Start of Dharmāṅgada’s Circumambulation of Raivata while Proclaiming the Sound of the Drum," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; then Māyā, becoming enraged for the sake of accomplishing her own desire, made a persistent demand of that king to fulfill his word of promise.
With eyes bloodshot with anger, she addressed her husband:
"If you do not heed my words, you shall become an outcast from dharma."
"O King, you offered me your hand for the granting of a boon;
if you do not grant it, I shall depart, having accomplished my purpose and acquired everything. (3)
"I am not your beloved wife, nor are you my dear husband. Shame on you, a man who speaks with double-tongued deceit and employs the words of dharma as a mere pretext! (4)
"Since you have wavered from the truth today, I shall abandon you who are intent only on your own self-interest.
Having spoken thus, the slender woman, filled with anger, quickly departed with her face cast downward.
At that time, Dharmāṅgada, the son of Rukmāṅgada and himself devoted to his father, stood before his mother and bowed down to her.
Bowing low, he said to her: "O Goddess, beloved of my father, why are you angry?
O Mother, departure is not appropriate for you; I shall tell you what is proper."
Having heard the words of Dharmāṅgada, Mohinī spoke these words:
"O son, your father is a liar, by whom your hand was made otherwise."
By him who performed that virtuous deed, marked by the banner and the goad,
his hand was placed in my hand and these words were offered.
"He does not perform the rites for your birth; what more can I say? I must certainly not dwell among those who deceive by means of falsehoods."
O son, one should never beg for gold, grain, elephants, horses, villages, or clothing; indeed, one should not beg for anything by which one's ruin might be brought about.
"O son, that by which he might satisfy his body and me, his wife, who am in the bloom of youth—that is what I requested; yet, out of delusion, he does not grant it."
That best of kings was entreated by me for my own benefit— for the sake of my happiness and my prosperity— and yet he does not do it for us.
"Having fallen from happiness and having strayed from the truth, I am departing for the abode of bliss.
Having heard that, Dharmāṅgada bowed to Mohinī and then spoke.
O Divine Mother, turn back; I shall fulfill your desire, you in whose truth the worlds—including gods, asuras, and humans—stand established.
By whose power the abode of Vaivasvata was rendered empty by Hari,
and whose fame shines forth, pervading millions of cosmic eggs.
"How could my father become a liar while I am still alive? Out of compassion for me, please turn back; it will be for the best. (17)
Having heard these words of Dharmāṅgada, she, longing for her own desire, turned back from there; then her son Dharmāṅgada spoke to his father.
"Therefore, my mother says of you today that you are a liar.
O King, how could you become a liar while I am present?"
"Give her everything that was promised by you;
I am your servant, O King—let me be sold even for a blade of grass."
"Give her to the goddess if you desire my life; become indifferent [to her].
The loss of fame is a great loss, not the loss of sons or a wife. (2.1)
"Great gain is the acquisition of fame; sons and wives are not true gains.
Having heard the words of Dharmāṅgada, Rukmāṅgada said to him:
"O son, let my fame perish, or let me become a liar, or let me go to the blinding hell; how shall I eat on the day of Hari? || 23 ||
Even if I were to enter a contemptible womb known as that of a worm,
I would still never eat on the day of Hari.
"The drum speaks for the sake of my vow; may it not prove false to me.
Having consumed what is unfit to be eaten, how could one live for a hundred autumns? (25)
"Let what has been spoken be proven false; I shall not eat on the day of Hari, even if I am censured by people or even if I am abandoned by Mohinī. (26)
If death should come to me, I shall not eat on the day of Hari;
how could I feel joy upon seeing those who have gone to the city of Yama? (27)
O son, those rows of hells which have been rendered empty by me shall become filled with people when I have partaken [of the meal] on the day of Hari.
Even though your mother had you eat during the day for Viṣṇu,
that wicked woman now begs for the field of King Yama to be filled.
"I will not give her to Mohinī; this deception has been practiced by the gods.
She is deceitful, and the gods are deceitful; one should employ deceit against the deceitful. (1.290.30)
One might drink poison, enter a fire, throw oneself from the peak of a mountain,
or even cut off one's own head, but I shall not eat on the day of Hari.
Let Mohinī meet her death or go wherever she pleases;
I shall not eat on this day of Hari, the vow that removes birth and death.
How could I consume and destroy that merit which I have earned and that fame which I have accumulated through fasting on the Ekādaśī? || 33 ||
Having heard his father’s words, the exceedingly righteous Dharmāṅgada then said to Sandhyāvalī, "Console Mohinī."
"Just as my father does not deviate from the truth and just as he enjoys his meals, let that be arranged whereby there may be well-being for both of us. (35)
Having heard her son's words, the elder sister, Mohinī, said:
"Follow the king; do not persist in this sinful course. (36)
The king does not taste royal food when the day of Hari has arrived;
choose any other boon that is very difficult to obtain from me, who abide in truth. (37)
"Though I am the youngest, I shall perform the most excellent salutation at your feet;
having been wedded for the sake of my husband, I offer my head [in homage]. (38)
But you have not been married; how else could there be such persistence? You who were deceived after being restrained by mere words and the threat of oaths. (39)
Having caused an image of the Lord to be made, that sinful woman shall go to hell;
and having fallen from hell, she shall be born as a sow for seven and five births.
From that she becomes a Caṇḍālī, and from that she becomes a Kāṣṭhilā;
then she would become a Chuchundarī, and then a female crow or a jackal. ||41||
Having become an iguana, she was indeed not purified even in that state as a cow;
O sister, even for an enemy, the giving of excellent, wholesome counsel is supreme. (42)
Having heard the words of Sandhyāvalī— words by which there would indeed be supreme welfare and constant happiness for the one who brings her joy— the deluded man spoke.
O elder sister, you are worthy of my respect; I shall do as you say, provided that the King does not partake of food on the day of Hari. (44)
O Goddess, perform for yourself another [act] that is even more grievous than death;
for this [present state] causes me pain and brings sorrow to the entire kingdom. (45)
O Goddess, for whom is death desired, and for whom is life undesired?
Indeed, every person possessed by fate performs even that which is undesirable.
Indeed, one whose lines of karma are broken performs that inauspicious deed which is terrible, fallen from the fourfold aims of life, and destructive of fame and fortune. 47.
I, a woman of evil and wicked conduct, am desirous of the vow;
for as the seed is endowed with its own nature, so does the resulting action become. (48)
With whatever state of mind one should emit semen into the womb, with that very same state of mind shall the offspring come into being. ||49||
"Because of my destruction of Rukmāṅgada’s armlet, I was cursed by Brahmā;
thus I became evil-minded and committed this wicked deed against the king."
O Goddess, there is no lunar mansion, no planets, and no auspicious hour for the child; rather, the boy shall become one who is purified by the state of his conception. 5.1.
In that place, there was no powerful sense of courtesy or friendship anywhere;
nor was there shame, nor affection, nor righteousness, nor compassion, and so forth. (52)

Today I shall declare that which takes away the life of the king and his son, as well as of the subjects and their wives—that which is indeed an act that must never be done under any circumstances. (53)
O woman, that which cannot be accomplished even by the mind nor heard even by the ear—
how indeed could that be performed with the body?
If you do so, there will be fame for you, immediate glory for the king, heaven for your son, praise for me, and disgrace for me. (55)
O beloved, having heard the words of Mohinī, Queen Sandhyāvalī summoned her courage and urged that slender woman, saying, "Speak! Speak! (56)
"Do not speak thus, O young bride; for the sake of your husband, everything may be lost—whether it be one's own life or even the life of one's son. (57)
For one who acts for the sake of her husband, there is no pain for me even in the loss of the kingdom;
for it is said that she whose husband is miserable has indeed gone to a downward path. ||58||
O Caṇḍikā, let that [power] belong only to you; let it not belong to my husband, nor even to me, nor let it belong to my son—whatever belongs to you shall remain yours alone. (59)
Once a happy marital union has been established, if the wife becomes an obstacle to liberation and instead becomes a source of suffering, she is no longer a wife, but a demoness.
A wife rescues her husband from sin as he falls into hell;
she is the true wife, while any other is merely a creeping vine of karma that causes worldly existence to flourish.
She who deceives her husband even with her life or her speech shall,
after passing through a hundred births as a worm, be born as a Pukkasa woman.
"For in this world, the husband is a deity who must not be deceived by his wife.
Therefore, speak; for the sake of your husband, I shall give you whatever you desire. (63)
Wealth, the body, a son, or whatever else is very difficult to obtain—what other deity is there in this world for women, except for their one husband? (64)
"Or for his sake, one might sacrifice everything; what could be greater than that?
Having heard this, Mohinī, the casket that enchants with self-interest, replied:
"If you understand it thus, O auspicious lady, that wealth is for the sake of your husband's livelihood, then I shall ask for riches that exceed [the value of] my life. (66)
"Give me the head of your son, which is dearer to you than your own heart, if indeed the king should not partake of food on the day of Hari. (67)
Then, grasping a sword in his own hand, may your husband, the king,
sever the head of Dharmāṅgada and place it upon my lap.
"Or rather, O auspicious lady, do this: that he does not eat food.
Having heard those words of Mohinī, which were harsh in syllable, [he was struck with wonder].
For a moment Sandhyāvalī trembled, thinking [the voice] was that of a Rākṣasī;
then, slowly regaining her composure, she spoke these words of dharma.

One should abandon wealth, one should abandon wife, and one should abandon life; one should abandon home, one should abandon country, one should abandon king, and one should abandon heaven, friend, and teacher. (71)
One should abandon the sacred ford, one should abandon dharma, one should abandon a very dear son;
one should abandon yoga, one should abandon charity, and one should abandon knowledge and meritorious deeds.
One may abandon austerity, one may abandon all supernatural powers, and one may even abandon supreme liberation;
but one must never abandon the day of Hari on either of the two lunar fortnights.
All that is repeatedly attained simply through the vow of Ekādaśī;
therein, for the sake of pleasing her husband, the devoted wife should renounce everything. (74)
"O Caṇḍī, for the sake of your satisfaction and for the purification of my husband’s vow, cause the head of Dharmāṅgada to be given; you are a Rākṣasī, not one born of the gods. (75)
"O fierce one, do not waver from the truth for the sake of a husband or for the sake of a vow," having spoken thus, O lotus-born one, she respectfully grasped her husband's feet.
The queen spoke these words for the sake of Dharmāṅgada’s head;
indeed, Mohinī, whose form is delusion, does not shrink from anything else.
O Lord, taking food during the day of Viṣṇu or even the slaughter of one's own son is better than the abandonment of dharma; indeed, the severing of a son’s head is preferable to that.
O King, having slain your son and cast affection far away, do not commit a transgression of truth; let no unrighteousness touch you. (79)
In this case, a mother’s affection for her son becomes meaningful for the sake of her husband;
this is the nature of the love of dharma that has been adopted, and not the worldly kind.
Having given up one's life, one's beloved, one's son, or even one's entire possession, the vow of truth must be protected for the sake of Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, in this world. 8.1.
Therefore, enough with this lamentation; uphold the truth, O lord of the earth!
By the preservation of truth, O King, one is united with the body of Viṣṇu. (82)
O King, I believe she was instructed and sent by the gods, who are obstacles to your vow, for the purpose of destroying the truth regarding Hari’s observance. (83)
"Because of the killing of your son, the gods will become face-down;
placing your foot upon their heads, you shall go to the supreme state. (84)
O King, the learned ones, together with their lords, have been confounded by your virtuous vows;
they are the obstructors of the path to liberation and the destroyers of your certainty. (85)
The Rītis are indeed the deities who stand as obstacles for those on the path of devotion;
therefore, O King, becoming firm, have your beloved son executed. (86)
"O Viṣṇu, fulfill the words of Mohinī indeed by protecting your own truth; for the sake of maintaining your vow, surrender your son."
Having heard the words of his wife, King Rukmāṅgada then spoke thus to Sandhyāvalī in the presence of Mohinī, "O beloved! (88)
The killing of one's own son is a great slaughter, even greater than the killing of a Brahmin;
having caused the death of a son in this world, what destination will there be hereafter? (89)
"Having killed my son who is childless, what will be my fate?
Why do I kill my son for the sake of another? Why do I kill him on the day of Hari?"
"I shall not eat on the day of Viṣṇu, O beloved, nor will I kill my son;
I shall tear open my own body, O deluder, or let me die. (9.1)
Or rather, I shall once again properly entreat Mohinī;
for if her mind becomes pacified through conciliation, it will lead to our welfare. (92)
Having reflected thus, King Rukmāṅgada spoke these words to Mohinī near Sandhyāvalī for the sake of consoling her. (93)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Dharmāṅgada’s Conciliation of Mohinī, Rukmāṅgada’s Firmness in His Vow, Sandhyāvalī’s Instruction for the Sake of Offspring despite the Conciliation, Mohinī’s Request for Her Son’s Head, and Sandhyāvalī’s Consent to Give Her Own Head," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to what the most eminent devotee of the Lord, King Rukmāṅgada,
spoke to Mohinī after taking refuge in the final Sāman hymn.
O fair-browed one, abandon this wicked obsession regarding your son;
what fruit will there be for you here by killing your own son, Dharmāṅgada?
"O auspicious lady, what gain will there be for you by feeding [me] on the day of Viṣṇu? Ask for something else; choose a boon from me. (3)
Be gracious, O lady of beautiful limbs, and grant me the boon of a son;
for a virtuous son is difficult to obtain, as is the day of Hari.
A wife who obeys one's commands is difficult to find, and service to Hari is likewise difficult to attain;
O son, how could I destroy either your vow or you, who are so dear to me?
Mohinī said: "I have no insistence on that matter regarding the king;
Dharmāṅgada is not my enemy, nor do I slay your son."
"Just as this one is your son, so too is he my son;
how can I kill my own son, who would be my savior from hell?"
"I have already told you before: eat on the day of Hari.
I will not kill my son; rather, there is success in wealth through eating."
O lord of the earth, my purpose will not be accomplished as long as my son remains lost;
the fulfillment of my task shall come through eating on the day of Hari.
Since your wife, sent by the gods in this form, has come into your presence for that purpose, you surely have a beloved son; therefore, let him be enjoyed on the day of Hari.
"Guard the truth with effort; carry out my word. Seeing her thus firm in her resolve, Dharmāṅgada also spoke to her.
"Accept this very [sword]; do not harbor doubt, O deluded one!
Having spoken thus, the son took up the sword and said to his father: (12)
"O Father, you must not delay in causing my downfall;
O King, make the word of my mother true, as was promised."
The self must be protected even at the cost of wealth, wives, daughters, and sons;
let my death for your sake be as one that bestows the world of Brahmā. || 14 ||
Nevertheless, there may be eternal liberation or eternal heaven; therefore, casting aside the suffering for the sake of truth, carry out my execution. (15)

And those who have been slain for the sake of their fathers, for the sake of their mothers, for the sake of cows, for the sake of Brahmins, the virtuous, and the gods, or for the sake of their own dependents, and for the sake of their preceptor— [they attain the highest state].
O King, those who are slain for the sake of dharma go to eternal worlds;
therefore, kill me and protect the truth—do not eat on the day of Hari. (17)
This human sacrifice (naramedha) must be performed for the sake of Hari’s day;
therein there is not the slightest fault, so do not harbor any distress.
At this time, O Lakṣmī, the gods, the hosts of sages, as well as the ascetics, the ancestors, the Manus, and the lords of the quarters [were present]. (19)
Those belonging to heaven, those of the wind, those of the earth, and the inhabitants of the netherworld;
those with visible and invisible bodies, as well as the stationary and the moving.
Crores and arbuds of goddesses also arrived for the purpose of the pilgrimage,
as did Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Standing on the path to Mount Raivata, filled with wonder and desiring to know which was superior— killing or fasting— they gazed upon it.
"Where, then, is the reality of dharma in this life, or even in eating?
At that moment, the lotus-eyed Lord stood in the path of the sky.
Having vanished, he remained there, observing the devotion and fortitude [of the devotees]:
"O King, eat what was spoken by Mohinī; O Father, slay me as was spoken by your son. (24)
Hearing this, Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the examiner of truth, said:
"The king, having bowed to Govinda, took the sword in his hand. (25)
Dharmāṅgada, his speech free from dejection, led his parents and the deities of Raivata and caused them to place their necks upon the path of the sword.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the pilgrims as they wailed;
the entire earth, along with its oceans, cities, and kingdoms, trembled.
Meteors fell by the hundreds, and the sky was filled with lusterless planets; the sacred fords became turbid, and the enchanting river turned pale.
The work of the gods has not been accomplished, and my birth has been rendered fruitless;
the king has indeed eaten no food, and I have been treated as if I were a mere blade of grass. (29)
"The king will surely attain liberation, while I, a sinner, shall go to the realm of Yama"—
with these words, she fell to the surface of the earth in a swoon of grief.
With joy, the king severed his son’s head with a sword,
while Kṛṣṇa remained manifest even as millions of embodied beings looked on.
"O King, held by your own hand, you have said repeatedly, 'I am pleased';
everything has been accomplished for me by your son, by your wife, and by you."
If this has been done for the sake of my vow, no one else shall ever do so again;
the delusive power of Māyā has been conquered, and my foot has been placed upon the head of Yama.
I am pleased; come, along with your sons, wife, friends, and others, to this most excellent celestial chariot.
Accept this pure worship from the three worlds and enter my dwelling within my divine form.
The divine four-armed king, as well as his divine wives, sons, and others, all possessing four arms, became merged into the form of Kṛṣṇa. (35)
Then, celestial voices resounded with proclamations of victory for the Dharma,
and a rain of flowers fell, released by hosts of gods stationed in the sky.
The fierce kettledrums, struck by the world-protectors (Lokapālas), resounded;
the celestial nymphs, filled with joy, sang songs and danced.
Likewise, King Raivata was blessed by those traveling on pilgrimage with the words:
"May you possess eternal abode, endowed as you are with sons, wives, and all else. (38)
And by those of his own [lineage] who were eager for the pilgrimage, their bodies were consecrated with fire in the Nārāyaṇa lake,
and the funeral rites were performed in the morning.
Uttering words of praise, they proceeded to circumambulate [the mountain];
on the twelfth day known as Prabodhinī, they took but a single meal while remaining otherwise without food.
Eating but a single meal on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full-moon days,
they circumambulated Mount Raivata and, on the day of the full moon, proceeded happily.
Mohinī, having fallen into misery, ashamed and disgraced,
and her purpose unaccomplished, became desirous of dying in the forest.
Yama, seeing everything rendered fruitless, said to Brahmā:
"The Mohinī has become useless, like a barren woman at the birth of a child. (43)
The world proceeds toward Vaikuṇṭha; no one at all resorts to me.
Even though the king has died, there is no decrease in the devotion of the people. 44.
Having observed the fast of Viṣṇu for the day, all go to the supreme abode;
but Mohinī, intent on death, does not come into your presence. (45)
"But I am inactive as before; what shall I do? Command me.
Having heard these words of Yama, Brahmā spoke to the son of the Sun.
"Let us go to awaken Mohinī; afterwards, we shall do what is appropriate for your sake. Fate may ordain something else. (47)
Thinking thus, goats and other creatures arrived there in that forest;
however, they saw those dwellers of heaven deprived of their splendor and their purpose lost. ||48||
The gods spoke to Sukālī, who was despondent and humble in nature:
"O knower of dharma, do not grieve; for you have indeed displayed human prowess. (49)
They were sent for the sake of the gods' work, and although that was not accomplished, you should not grieve; for the king indeed attained liberation.
Indeed, no obstacle ever arises for the devotees of Śrī Hari;
when his son was slain, Hari protected his own devotee by fulfilling his vow.
The son, the wife, and the king— these three, being very firm in the observance of their vows,
were led to his own abode by Viṣṇu, who was well-pleased.
Countless embodied beings have been led [to liberation] by those who have attained union with them;
devotion to Hari is certainly the constant protector and the bringer of liberation. 53.
O Goddess, if the fruit of an action already undertaken does not succeed even with all efforts, what fault is there in you now? (54)
Therefore, all the gods have arrived to grant you a boon and to bring about your happiness; make your request for whatever you desire.
Whether success is achieved or not, wages must indeed be paid;
likewise, the group of servants must be supported and protected constantly. (56)
Thus instructed by Surai, the deluded woman, deprived of her husband, exceedingly miserable, and the destroyer of her family's joy, spoke as she was lost in grief. 57.
"Fie on this life of mine, in which my duty has not been accomplished, and the path of Yama, which must be traversed by people without restraint, has not been prepared! (58)
On the day of Hari, nothing was omitted and nothing was eaten on the day of Hari by that king, who was a devoted worshiper;
thus, his beloved son was killed with joy.
Having placed his foot upon my head, King Viṣṇu has attained the eternal state;
my entire wealth has gone to him—what, then, is the fruit of my life?
Those servants who, seeking their wages, do not accomplish the work of their masters,
become consumers of faults on this earth, like horses.
"I am incapable of accomplishing your task, for I am the destroyer of your husband and son;
how then could I accept a boon from you, who dwell in heaven? (62)
"Death is in every way better for an embodied being whose pride has been shattered. Thinking thus, he wept aloud; then the gods spoke words of consolation.
O Goddess, you have exerted great effort in accomplishing our task;
knowing that the fruit depends on destiny, do not grieve, O deluded one. (64)
"Having performed a service for you, we shall indeed be free from debt;
tell us what is desired in your heart that may lead to your happiness, and we shall grant it."
While Mohinī was reflecting in her mind with the desire to go to where Rukmāṅgada resided, in that very moment—
Then the royal priest, who was like fire itself,
arrived there from the Vasu lake at Svarṇarekhā in the cave of Mount Raivata.
Having dwelt there and restrained his vital breath, he emerged from the midst of the water;
and having ascertained everything through yoga, he spoke to the gods who had granted him the boon.
Fie on this woman! Fie on the assembly of gods! Fie on the karma that produces evil!
Why have you come here intending to grant her a boon? Fie on the lords! (69)
"Is this woman, who has killed her husband who was learned in the Vedas, to be considered worthy by the gods?
Indeed, there can be no purification for her in this world even by casting herself into the fire."
Having deluded him with flattering words and becoming devoted to her own interests,
this beloved woman has become a slayer of her son and husband, and a destroyer of her own liberation and heaven.
She has no dwelling even in hell, much less in heaven or in the abode of Hari; nor in any other peaceful world—let her wander, deprived of a home. (72)
For one defiled by the world's censure, there is indeed no standing even here in this world; fie upon her life, which is condemned by its very actions—what more need I say? (73)
Having slain her husband, having slain her son, having slain her co-wife who was like a mother, and having destroyed the entire earth—what destiny indeed will she go to? (74)
Indeed, by her speech as well, she was always a destroyer of the Dharma;
for she had always said to the king, "Let it be eaten on the day of Hari. (75)
If a statement is uttered out of ignorance [regarding the day], one should eat on the day of Hari;
for even that [transgression] is said to have atonement through a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). //76//
"This woman is indeed the one who forcibly enjoys the vow of Hari day after day;
she must not be touched, O Lord of Gods—how then can you be the granters of boons to her? (77)
The denizens of heaven do not protect one who is joined with evil;
the gods are dependent on dharma, and dharma arises from the words of the Vedas. (78)
Service to the husband is proclaimed by the Vedas as the duty of women; pursuing one's own self-interest at the expense of the father is not proclaimed as the duty of a bride. (79)

Whatever the husband says that must be done by the wife should be performed without hesitation; for that indeed is to be known as service by which the satisfaction of the husband is attained. (1.291.80)
The husband’s command was disregarded out of a desire to establish her own authority;
the king was constrained by oaths for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose. (8.1)
She is a destroyer by her words and a bringer of ruin through her actions;
she is this very one who destroys the family, possessing a sinful body and being truly wicked.
How could she, who possesses more than ten thousand murders as her burden, be worthy of being chosen as a bride—even if a god or a demon were to stand on her side? (83)
O best of gods, if anyone should make an effort to protect Mohinī, I would reduce even him to ashes in an instant. (84)
The king attained liberation by casting his sin upon her through truth;
yet, even for one who takes her side, that sin becomes attached to him. (85)
Having spoken thus, his eyes copper-red with rage, he took water in his hand and threw it upon Mohinī’s head; thereupon, fire blazed forth.
While the inhabitants of heaven were looking on, he set the Mohinī ablaze;
meanwhile, great voices in the sky cried, "Restrain your anger! Restrain it! (87)
At that very moment, she became nothing but ashes in an instant;
all the gods, their hopes shattered and their hearts broken, returned home.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of how, after Rukmāṅgada had taught the Sāman hymns, the head of the son was severed with a sword by the will of Krūrā while the gods looked on; and how, despite the attainment of liberation for the king, his son, and his wife, the reproaches directed at Mohinī were rendered futile, and Mohinī was reduced to ashes by the curse of the family priest," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; her body burnt away, she exists as a subtle body of a sinner, being led by the messengers of Yama and opening the path of Yama.
Since she was a companion of Yama, she was forbidden by the Lord of Yama;
consequently, for the sake of opening the path to Yama, she experienced great suffering.
Sent by Yama, she went to heaven, to the abode of the gods;
however, she was rebuked by the messengers of the gods: "O sinful woman, you have no place here! (3)
"O Lakṣmī, because you have neglected the day of Hari (Harivāsara), you shall have no dwelling in the abode of the gods.
Therefore, being distressed, that deluding goddess [Lakṣmī] sought to obtain a place to dwell. (4)
She proceeded toward Pātāla, where she was obstructed by those dwelling in Pātāla—
by gods, sages, Daityas, Dānavas, and likewise by ṛṣis.
By the Pitṛs, Mānavas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas;
and by the Tīrthas, mountains, excavations, oceans, and likewise by the forests.
Mohinī was beheld on Mount Raivata by the Tattvas, the world-protectors (Lokapālas), the Manus, those who dwell in the waters, and by various founders of holy places (Tīrthakṛts).
She was seen by the dull-witted and the conscious alike— as the slayer of sons and the slayer of husbands—
by the stars, the planets, the trees, the creepers, and likewise by the grasses.

Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should either cause him to sleep or dismiss him;
