"This Brahmā, who has offered all as sacrifice, and you, Gāyatrī, shall become husband and wife through this very second vow, by my grace. (102)
"After one hundred years have passed, you two will certainly attain my imperishable abode by virtue of the act of giving this mansion, which is equal to a great city. (103)
"I shall grant you the kingdom of this universe, a prosperous realm higher than the highest," having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa vanished from that place.
Then, even when the dissolution of the previous Brahmā occurred, the couple attained the supreme,
most excellent, and eternal station of Parameṣṭhin for a long time.
Thus King Sarvahuta and his wife Gaurtambharā were born as a divine couple; O Brahmā, you shall create them as your parents, like Gāyatrī.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account of the primordial creation,
as well as the virtuous vow for the second day of the month of Puruṣottama.
"The bestower of the supreme state shall grant the fruit to both the listener and the speaker;
there is no doubt about this," so says the illustrious Puruṣottama. 108.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how, in the primordial creation, King Sarvahuta and Queen Go-Ṛtambharā attained the status of Brahmā and the descent of Gāyatrī through the observance of the second day of the second fortnight, the giving of cities and palaces, worship, and other rites," within the *Puruṣottama-māsa-māhātmya* in the first section, the *Kṛta-yuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the narrative of a former kalpa.
At the beginning of creation, there was a sovereign lord of men who ruled over a portion of the earth.
He was named Brahmasavitṛ; his wife, devoted to her husband and dedicated to the duties of a spouse, was known by the name Bhūriśṛṅgā.
She always served her husband, who was the very essence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
the couple were devotees of the Lord and devoted to the duties of household life.
Performing acts of charity and righteousness, serving their elders and people,
they lived upon the path of Hari, devoted to the service of Viṣṇu.
They honored their guests, were endowed with humility toward their elders,
performed service for cows, and were compassionate toward all living beings.
They were destroyers of the suffering of the wretched, sustainers of the destitute, performers of service for the virtuous, and restrainers of the wicked. (6)
Let it be; for those two were indeed devoted to dharma, intent on protection, and removers of suffering.
King Brahmasavitra, having bathed daily in the waters of the river, [performed his rites]. (7)
He indeed performed the twilight prayers, the recitation of mantras, the fire sacrifice, and the study of sacred texts;
he also gave gifts of food, gifts of clothing, and gifts of wealth.
The wise man goes to the temples to behold the deities and offers well-prepared food, fruits, and other items as an oblation.
At the appropriate time, she indeed performs worship with devotion;
she feeds guests, Brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, ascetics, and sages.
He gives sacrificial fees consisting of gold and silver that bring complete satisfaction,
and he causes food to be distributed from his treasury during food-distributions.
The one who is exceedingly righteous hears the repeated prayers of his groups of male and female servants and brings them happiness by granting exactly what they require.
The queen likewise worships the gods incessantly in her home,
and she travels by means of a vehicle to visit the gods.
He constantly sustains his journey by means of the two feet as his after-drink;
he offers water, leaves, fruits, flowers, sandalwood, and gold as a sacrificial fee.
Having given [the offering] to the god and the preceptor, she returns to that house;
having fed the people, she eats, and the king likewise eats thereafter. (15)
During the Cāturmāsya, the king undertook a vow that unbroken lamps filled with ghee must indeed be offered to Hari in all temples of the gods.
In the seven continents and islands, as well as on the oceanic islands,
wherever there were temples of the gods within his own kingdom and territory, [he restored them].
Of the incarnations of the Supreme Lord, of the lords, of the yogis, of the gods, and likewise of all classes of beings, through their wondrous nature; ||18||
And likewise [he described] the manifestations, the principles, and the various goddesses;
the presiding deities of the sacred fords, both the insentient and the sentient.
And wherever there were dwellings of gods upon the earth, there he established shrines that were marvelous, both stationary and mobile. (20)
He had butter-lamps made with pieces of sugar-candy and of great brilliance,
using purified cow’s ghee in golden vessels with excellent wicks.
Having preserved it, he indeed made it manifest and bestowed it upon all the gods;
and if, in his kingdom, it were given to anyone who was worthy of the gods—‖22‖
If this lamp, though unoffered, recognizes [the thief] then,
the king shall fast and also give a thousand pieces of gold.
Throughout my entire realm, he proclaims everywhere during the four-month period: "This is my vow; throughout my kingdom, lamps shall be offered to the gods on my behalf. (24)
May lamps offered by worshippers to the waters of sacred fords, to the trees at shrines, and throughout all temples become my own lamps. (25)
May there be sky-lamps on all festival days, beginning with Kārttika;
by means of the ghee of cows, may my lights be supreme in every way. (26)
May there be for me the bathing of the gods with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and may there be sweet foods for me when they are offered to the deities. (27)
May all sixteen types of service be mine in every way;
may ninefold devotion to Śrī Hari arise through those fed by me, O Lord. (28)
During the Cāturmāsya, however, vegetables, milk, and juices are for me in the feeding of Brahmins, virtuous women, and the gods. (29)
May there be food for the poor, the helpless, and the wretched;
may there be mouthfuls of grass for cows and fodder for dogs and other village animals for me. (30)
May there be for me the giving of grain fragments and the like to birds such as pigeons, and may there be flour-based food for ants and other small creatures. (3.1)

May there be for me the successful accomplishment of sacrifices and rites through their proper means; and may there be for me the daily performance of the waving of lights and other such services in temples.
May the gift of water and the gift of clothing always be mine through my prosperity;
and may the offering of gold, silver, and other coins always be mine. (33)
Thus did King Brahmasavitr proclaim on earth;
and his wife Bhūriśṛṅgā undertook the vow together with her husband.
Having bathed daily, he worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama in a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars, arches, and other ornaments. (35)
Having constantly caused a new mandala to be made and having filled it with the seven kinds of grain, one should prepare the excellent one named Sarvatobhadra.
And having had a golden image of the illustrious Puruṣottama fashioned, he worshipped it with many kinds of offerings and with great devotion. (37)
At midday she also provided a meal of fifty-six varieties;
and in the evening, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), she danced accompanied by ten thousand female attendants.
Thus, disregarding her own honor, the queen performs this daily to please Puruṣottama;
yet Kṛṣṇa, though pleased by the beautiful singing accompanied by dancing, does not even come within the range of her vision. (39)
Thus engaged and ever devoted to Hari,
that couple heard on the morning of the third lunar day the divine [narrative].
"Listen, O citizens, as well as the forest-dwellers and the denizens of heaven, to this proclamation uttered by the drum, which is most wonderful. (41)
"Let men and women listen; I speak as Śrī Puruṣottama, the Lord of the Abode of Brahman, the manifest presiding deity of the intercalary month. (42)
On the third lunar day of the dark fortnight, men and women shall perform a vow endowed with faith, preceded by my worship. (43)
Whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or by eating fruit, or by eating only what is unasked for, kings or queens shall attain the supreme state. (44)
They shall attain the dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation desired by the world,
as well as sons, grandsons, and lineages, along with the expansion of their family and immediate fame.
"By my vow, they shall indeed attain all sovereign powers;
by observing the vow for even a single day, let them obtain eternal happiness. (46)
Endowed with supreme magnanimity, I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, shall serve as the bestower; I am the one who unites all beings with every form of prosperity. 47.
Today, by the gift of food, I shall bestow the nine eternal treasures;
today, by the gift of gold, I shall bestow the throne of Kubera.
Today, by the gift of juice, I shall bestow the excellent station of Varuṇa;
today, by the gift of jewels, I shall bestow the auspicious sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods.
Today, by the gift of merit, I shall indeed bestow the status of Dharmarāja;
today, by the gift of wealth, I shall bestow the eight Vasus in embodied form.
Today, by the gift of my all, I shall bestow the splendor of the eight supernatural powers;
today, by the offering of a lamp, I shall grant the state of being the eye of the three worlds.
Today, by the gift of milk, I shall bestow the nature of cool nectar;
today, by the gift of food and water, I shall bestow a meaningful sovereignty.
Today, by the gift of a chariot and other such items, I shall bestow upon you a celestial vimāna;
today, by the gift of garments, I shall give you the earth clothed in the waters of the oceans.
Today, by the gift of maidens and the like, I shall give away a thousand women;
today, by the gift of cows, I shall give away the earth filled with its essence.
Today, by the gift of a house, I shall give the cavernous expanse of the universe;
today, by the gift of fruit, I shall give a row of wish-fulfilling trees.
Today, by the gift of ornaments, I shall bestow upon you a well-adorned heaven;
today, through my worship, I shall grant you eternal honor throughout the three worlds. (56)
"Whatever my devotee desires, I shall grant that to him; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, Dundubhi became silent for a moment.
King Brahmasavita and his beloved Bhūriśṛṅgā,
having bowed to that Dundubhi, offered worship to the messenger of Kṛṣṇa.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month, the couple observed a vow of eating only one meal a day, desiring the Sun-god.
O Keśava, by the offering of a lamp during the Cāturmāsya period, I become the Sun;
accompanied by my consort, I manifest as the very essence of the eyes of the three worlds.
Having thus resolved, the king and his wife performed the vow;
having bathed in the morning, they remembered Hari and meditated upon His radiant, desired form.
Having installed the golden Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon the auspicious jar in the pavilion and within the mandala, they worshipped him with devotion. (62)
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and pure water, and having dressed it in garments,
one should then offer ornaments, flowers, necklaces, and so forth, as well as sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped the deity with incense, lamps, and other offerings, as well as unbroken grains and saffron,
one should present fifty-six varieties of food— sweet and savory— as well as water and fruit.
Both of them offered [the flowers] with devotion to Śrī Puruṣottama; they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and made a full circumambulation. ||65||
Having prostrated themselves like a staff, they then offered praise;
they presented an offering of flowers and requested forgiveness. (66)
Likewise at midday and in the evening, they performed worship during the night;
there, with great devotion, they performed dances accompanied by vigils.
The Blessed Lord Hari, the storehouse of all splendor,
became manifest through worship, through the vow, and through the Cāturmāsya vow.
"By the gift of this lamp, I am everywhere pleased with your extreme devotion;
for that which is desired by the three worlds is the most supreme station of the eyes. (69)
"I shall grant you the status of the sun in the sky; together with your wife, you shall become the Sun.
Having spoken thus, Hari vanished from that place.
Having performed the Brahma-savitra dance as well as the Prajagara vigil,
he, together with Bhūriśṛṅga, bestowed gifts in the morning.
Precious gems, cows, buffaloes, elephants, and horses; likewise goats and sheep, as well as vessels of gold and silver and garments. (72)
Male and female servants, couches, houses, and palaces;
fields, gardens, groves, and forests. ||73||
He gave food, wells, tanks, land, cotton,
silk, and likewise woolen garments of priceless value.
He gave various articles of adornment to the Brahmin women, and to the ascetics, he gave mats, alms-bowls, water-pots, and so forth.
To householders he gave articles suitable for domestic life;
to those hungry he gave food, and to those thirsty he gave water. ||76||
To those seeking various forms of happiness, he gave the means for attaining that happiness;
to those seeking wealth, he gave wealth; but to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, he gave everything.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this supreme gift was performed by Brahmā and Savitṛ;
likewise, it was performed by Bhūriśṛṅgī with the approval of her husband.
After having fed the virtuous guests and others, the couple went to eat;
at that moment, Śrī Puruṣottama arrived there in the form of a mendicant.
On his chest shines Lakṣmī in the form of the Svarṇarekhā river, and on his left thigh shines Śrī in the form of the Pāṇḍuraṅga mountain. (80)
O lotus-petal-eyed one, on his right hand shine a banner, a fish, a svastika, and likewise a bow,
which indeed possess a halo of splendor.
Seeing the monk and recognizing him by his marks as Nārāyaṇa, the king and queen fed him and respectfully massaged his feet. (82)
At that time, an internal meditative absorption arose within the two forms there;
however, the great sphere known as Sūrya was beheld by Brahmā-Savitṛ. 83.
There he beheld his own golden body, higher than the highest, by which the entire world, consisting of light, attains illumination. (84)
Having seen the true nature of her own perception, and having beheld the golden wife of the Sun, she attained great satisfaction. ||85||
Hari vanished at that moment, and the two of them arose from their meditative absorption;
filled with wonder and astonishment, they felt their hearts were fulfilled. (86)
They always served Kṛṣṇa and awaited his state as the Sun;
meanwhile, by the gradual process of time, the end of the kalpa occurred.
The king and queen attained dissolution and obtained most divine bodies;
they then departed for Mahastara by means of a sun-crystal chariot.
Having passed that night at the beginning of the kalpa, in the course of creation,
this Lord Brahmā, the progenitor, became the Sun.
And his wife was Bhūriśṛṅgā, born of Viśvakarman;
she was the daughter named Saṃjñā, who had been offered by her father to Aṃśumālin.
Bhūriśṛṅga and Savitṛ became Saṃjñā and Sūrya;
who else could obtain the station of the Sun, those two gods who grant eyes to all? || 91 ||
Thus, having attained the supreme state, as far as heaven shines forth,
by the power of the gift of lamps and by the vow of the third lunar day.
Therefore, lamps should always be offered in temples;
by that, one shall attain freedom from blindness, luminosity, and divinity. (93)
Just as that King Brahmasavita attained the state of the Sun, such indeed shall be the gain for both the listener and the speaker of this narrative. 9.4.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this supreme, divine narrative concerning Sūryanārāyaṇa, which is purifying, merit-bestowing, and beneficial. 95.

Thus ends the three hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the State of Sūryanārāyaṇa, along with the Recovery of His Wife Named Saṃjñā, by King Brahmasavitṛ of the Previous Kalpa and His Consort Bhūriśṛṅga through the Vow on the Third Day of the Second Fortnight and Various Gifts such as Lamps," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-Santāna*, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, listen to this story arising from a former kalpa;
in Saurāṣṭra, on the Raivata mountain, there was one named Samitpīyūṣa.
He became a king, and he had twenty-seven wives:
Ūrjāhuti, Puṣkariṇī, Padmapatrā, and Karīṣiṇī.
Viśvapriyā, Ādityavarṇā, Hariṇī, Hemamālinī, Vasudhīti, Vahniśikhā, Padmākṣī, and Padmamālinī. (3)
Prabhāsā, Jagatī, Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, Iḍā, Piśaṅginī, Suṣumṇā, Purītat, Viśvārcis, and Padmanemikā. || 4 ||
Hiraṇyavarṇā, Candrā, Padmavarṇā, and Vamrikā,
as well as Vidyullekhā— all of them were devoted solely to their husbands.
Devoted to the practice of charity and righteousness, they performed devotion to the Blessed One and honored guests with sincere feeling.
They perform ablutions, meditation, worship of the gods, and the recitation of mantras with devotion;
likewise, they perform the fire sacrifice (homa) dedicated to the gods, the ancestors, and the spirits, as a virtuous rite.
Having fed those who depend upon them, they themselves eat and drink with their own hands,
even though they possess hundreds of thousands of female servants.
They perform service to Viṣṇu and service to their husband according to their own dharma;
for the sake of Viṣṇu, they cook and purify rice and other grains.
Pounding [grain], carrying water, sweeping the house, as well as scrubbing and washing the vessels for the worship of the deity; || 10 ||
Every day, they always gather the first leaves and flowers of the Tulasī with great devotion; they never do so through the agency of another.
Indeed, for the sake of Hari, what indeed could be an unworthy act for devotees?
For when everything has been offered there, what is not accomplished by means of the body itself? 12.
One should acquire eternal merit by means of this impermanent body, so that through the grace of Kṛṣṇa there may be both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (13)
That Supreme Lord alone is to be saluted, worshipped, and propitiated in every way, from whom everything arises—the objects of enjoyment, the food to be consumed, pleasure, and so forth. (14)
Since he is the source of prosperity, abundance, wealth, a wife, a husband, sons, daughters, and so forth, as well as land, heaven, and great sovereignty, the wise man should indeed worship him.
As long as there is health in the body, the circle of the senses remains under control, the digestive fire is youthful and effective, and there is well-being within the physical frame. (1.6)
First, one should accomplish what is beneficial for oneself, whether it be that which is desired or free from desire;
namely, the state of the Supreme Lord, which is eternal, full of perpetual bliss, and everlasting.
If the state of being impaired or absent, there would indeed be no vision and so forth;
therefore, one should always joyfully perform the act of beholding Śrī Hari with one's eyes.
If one were deaf and devoid of discrimination, there would indeed be no hearing of Hari's name; yet, while this path is easy and favorable, the hearing of the Infallible One must be performed.
When one is wounded or impaired, service to Hari by the virtuous indeed does not take place;
Hari himself should be served when one possesses great strength and is well-disposed.
When the feet are strong and move with ease, one may go to the divine temple;
when the mind is undisturbed, vigilant, and filled with vigor.
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of happiness, should be meditated upon; the Lord, who is the inner self, should indeed always be worshipped by means of one's own self. 22.
But when the city is broken, all the obstacles will depart;
there, in that place whose very essence is firm-footedness, the venerable Puruṣottama is to be attained.
Having thus resolved, all those women, who were like nectar to the sacrificial fuel, eternally serve Śrī Hari in the auspicious palace that had been constructed.
King Samitpīyūṣa always performed the three daily ablutions and offered worship to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at the three periods of the day.
As they were living in this manner, a great length of time passed;
in that kalpa, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika—the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī—indeed arrived.
Starting from the full moon of Āśvina, with a seven-day interval before the day of the Dīpotsava festival, they observed the practice of eating only once a day.
On the eighth day, they joyfully observed a fast without water before the auspicious image of Kṛṣṇa known as Puruṣottama.
And having caused a golden image of Kṛṣṇa’s mother,
named Kaṃbhārā, to be made, he likewise had those [other images] fashioned out of gold.
Having had a golden image of Gopāla, the father of Kṛṣṇa, fashioned,
and having constructed a pavilion, they worshipped Śrī Puruṣottama.
They performed a dance accompanied by musical instruments, blended with the melodies of their voices;
at that very moment, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, appeared.
Four-armed, adorned with the Kaustubha gem, wearing yellow garments and other fine raiment,
dark as a fresh rain-cloud and resplendent with white luster.
Having beheld the wondrous Śrī Puruṣottama, they were struck with amazement for a moment; then they became transfixed there before that enchanting, divine form.
Bringing divine ornaments and other items, they presented them to him with great excitement; then they offered him an oblation of *ūrja* and a crown of gold.
She gave him two beautiful earrings made of gold and fashioned a sandalwood mark (puṇḍra) on his forehead with lotus petals.
Karīṣiṇī applied excellent kohl and collyrium to his eyes,
while Viśvapriyā offered garlands of golden flowers to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Ādityavarṇā gave him two bracelets for his wrists, while Hariṇī presented nine new golden rings.
Hemamālinī gave him a beautiful girdle with chains,
and Vasudhīti gave him golden anklets adorned with small bells.
Padmākṣī offered a pair of sandals made of gold, which she had placed upon the crest of the fire, as well as a sacred thread and a meditation band.
Padmamālinī gave him sweet food consisting of vegetables and milk-rice;
Prabhāsā gave him cool water for drinking. (40)
Jagatī offered betel-leaf with its fruit,
while Paṅkti gave fragrant Puṣpasāra and incense.
Bṛhatī gave him a most auspicious lamp filled with ghee;
Iḍā held over his head a golden, radiant umbrella. 42.
The two white chowries, Suṣumṇā and Piṅgalā, are held by Dadhi and Atṛ;
holding the fan of the pericardium (purītat), they perform the fanning with air. ||43||
Then Viśvārci gave a beautiful nakta-ka jewel into Kṛṣṇa’s hand;
then Padmanemi gave a cluster of flowers into Kṛṣṇa’s hand.
Hiraṇyavarṇā presented a discus with a thousand rims;
Candrā gave a lotus fashioned of gold into the hand of Kṛṣṇa. (45)
Padmavarṇā gave him a conch, and Vamrī then gave him a mace;
Vidyullekhā gave a kiss to that Supreme Soul.
She became the supreme object of the Supreme Soul's affection among them all;
moreover, by virtue of that merit, she became even more the recipient of her husband’s love.
"She was indeed Rohiṇī, the wife of the Moon, in a previous birth.
Having spoken thus, they offered gifts and performed the rite of waving lamps before the deity.
But others, seeing the kissing, felt shame in their hearts;
they obtained from the moon no fruit other than excessive pride. ||49||
A maidservant named Sarvajitā performed the massaging of his feet;
because she was devoted to service, she became a vessel of his affection. (50)
Then they all offered handfuls of flowers, unbroken rice grains, and water for the guest-offering (arghya);
thereafter, they performed circumambulations, prostrations, hymns of praise, and other such acts.
Kṛṣṇa, being exceedingly gracious, gave them the milk-pudding of his favor;
having received it, they attained satisfaction and meditated upon him within the lotus of their hearts.
Kṛṣṇa said to those goddesses: "Become consumers of nectar, adorned with necklaces of gold, jewels, and gems; divine beings who have made their homes in heaven. (53)
Having thus bestowed these blessings, Keśava became invisible;
they, having completed the worship, spoke of the event to their husband. (54)
King Samīti-pīyūṣa became exceedingly joyful;
accompanied by his wife, he constantly desired heaven after performing the worship.
The wives also desired the sovereignty of heaven spoken of by Kṛṣṇa;
thus, as time passed, this was heard from Kṛṣṇa at the end of the kalpa.
Making a proclamation with the sound of a drum regarding the command of the Supreme Person:
"Let men and women, and gods and goddesses alike, hear my words! (57)
To whomever, whatever, and in whatever manner I shall give, that shall be exactly so;
for I am known as Puruṣottama, the eternal Supreme Brahman. (58)
I speak indeed out of compassion, without weighing merit;
even when a small deed is performed, I grant an incalculable fruit in every way. (59)
Those people who, performing rites for specific desires, offer me fruit, flowers, leaves, sandalwood, and unbroken grains on the fourth day of the intercalary month; ||60||
I, the Supreme Person, shall fulfill all their desires;
for everything belongs to me, everything is in me, and by me the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
Indeed, there exists nothing whatsoever, whether insentient or sentient, that is separate or independent;
for my reality alone exists in every respect as both the insentient and the sentient.
All places of liberation, as well as the sites of supernatural powers and sovereignty,
the manifestations of the lords, and indeed the stations of the gods— [all these are contained within it].
The prosperities of human beings as well as those dwelling in the netherworld—all this belongs to me alone; whatever they desire, I shall give it.
For one who has performed the vow of Puruṣottama-māsa— whether for a fortnight, daily, or even for a single night—
nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain.
The king should perform vows, give gifts, and offer worship according to his power; the subjects should perform vows, give gifts, and make offerings according to their wealth. 66.
Whether man or woman, one should perform my monthly rite according to dharma;
I shall never forget your vow or my people.
Whether today or at some other time, I shall surely grant abundant fruit according to my satisfaction; of this there is no doubt, for my devotee shall never be without reward.
For the sake of those with desire, the worlds such as heaven have been created by me;
for the sake of those without desire, the world of Brahmā has been preserved by me.
I grant an abundance of happiness in all realms, and infinite [bliss] in the world of Brahmā, to the devoted one who has taken refuge in me and performs vows for my sake.
There is no price for what one has done oneself; rather, the price is my word.
For him by whom my word is upheld, his reward shall also be infinite.
For even when a rain-bestowing sacrifice has been performed, the rain that falls is not like that which occurs during the rainy season—immeasurable and infinite. (72)
The Blessed Lord Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person, rains himself down;
out of compassion, I have indeed become the cloud-form during the month of Puruṣottama.
May they accept what I have offered according to their capacity and as they require;
having made this fruit upon the cloth, let it be scattered and follow them as they depart. (74)
Those who shall offer praise during the month of Puruṣottama will also attain the highest happiness according to their desire. (75)
Even those other embodied beings who grant their approval for the sake of the vow during the month of Puruṣottama shall likewise partake in the happiness of heaven. (76)
Furthermore, to those men who provide assistance to the observer of the vow during the intercalary month, I shall grant whatever happiness they desire. (77)
What indeed could be difficult for one devoted to me to obtain during an intercalary month?
I shall grant him a dwelling, I shall grant wealth, I shall grant wives, sons, and livestock.
I shall grant a husband, I shall grant a daughter, I shall grant a cow, a kingdom, and long life;
I shall also grant health, the delight of the senses, and eternal happiness.
Thus, having heard the Dundubhi drum, King Samitpīyūṣa and his twenty-seven wives— who were indeed established in supreme devotion— [were moved].
And the maidservant, having bowed to Dundubhi and worshipped him with unhusked grains, flowers, fruits,
and other offerings, prepared to perform the supreme Caturthī vow.
Having performed the worship of Hari in the morning, and having likewise performed worship at midday along with their meal,
they performed the final worship in the evening.
Having fed them with milk-rice and fried cakes, they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony;
and with dance, song, and instrumental music, they kept vigil throughout the night.
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with devotion,
they gave gifts of jewels, liquids, and likewise sacrificial fuel.
They gave sacrificial fees consisting of oblations, nectars, and sweet foods, as well as gifts of gold and silver, and indeed various fruits and articles. ||85||
They gave gentle moonstones that were cool and they gave golden gifts;
at that time, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, appeared in the form of a brahmin. ||86||
Then King Samitpīyūṣa, desiring jewels, arrived accompanied by all his beloveds, having become a worthy recipient. 87.
He gave him a garland rich with jewels and bowed down with great devotion.
The brahmin said, "O King, ask for a boon; it shall be so. (88)
Having heard that the moon was made of sacrificial fuel, he chose the excellent kingdom of the moon;
indeed, for the sake of the fuel, he requested a form that would shower nectar.
The wives likewise chose the status of being the wives of the Moon in heaven;
having granted the boon with the words "So be it," the Brahmin vanished from sight. (90)
At the end of the kalpa, having undergone dissolution, that king, at the beginning of creation, acted for the sake of the one named Samitpīyūṣa, fulfilling his purpose by the will of Hari. ||9 1||
And the moon, the possessor of nectar-like rays, became the nourisher of medicinal herbs in the sky; his wives were the daughters of Dakṣa, and from them he begot offspring.
Those twenty-seven were given to him according to the prescribed rite by Dakṣa;
Vidyullekhā became the foremost among them, and for that reason she was his beloved Rohiṇī.
And others as well: Mṛgaśīrṣa, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī. (94)
Hasta, Citrā, as well as Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhikā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Śravaṇa; ||95||
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā;
Uttarabhadrapadā, Revatī, and likewise Aśvinī. ||96||
Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā—these twenty-seven joined together became the goddesses in heaven, the wives of the Moon, who bestow nectar. (97)
A maidservant named Devayutī was born under the asterism Abhijit;
residing with her at midday bestows victory in all undertakings. (98)
And by virtue of the merit of the vow on the fourth [lunar day], they remain so for an entire kalpa;
therefore, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and the fasting on the subsequent fourth day must be performed. (99)
Eating once a day, or eating only at night, or subsisting on fruits—this constitutes my worship; both the listener and the speaker of this shall partake in the merit of the Caturthī vow.

Thus ends the three hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of how King Samitpīyūṣa and his twenty-seven wives, following the hearing of the *dundubhi* drum, attained sovereignty over the moon and the stars in heaven by performing the vow of the fourth day of the second fortnight, and how the maidservant attained the status of the *abhijit* constellation," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Puruṣottama-māsa-māhātmya* of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, listen to this ancient tale concerning the origin of King Vasudhāna and his wife Rādhyāsā.
At the end of a previous creation, there was a king in the south named Vasudhāna,
a great devotee and a servant of Mahādeva.
And his wife, Rādhyāsā, was a servant of Mahādeva, constantly performing the worship of her husband, who is the very essence of Mahādeva. || 3 ||
Devoted to her husband with undivided affection,
she always bathes herself in the morning and then bathes her lord.
One should worship Mahādeva with various liquids such as milk and the like,
as well as with leaves, flowers, fruits, cloth, snakes, sugar, and water.
Having offered the nightly lamp, sandalwood paste, incense, and light, she remained in the service of Vasudhāna like a maidservant. || 6 ||
The king also, having awakened at dawn and abandoned sleep for a moment,
meditated upon the auspicious Śaṅkara-Brahman and performed his ablutions and worship.

Having performed meditation upon Śambhu in his heart and likewise having offered worship, and having distributed food and other provisions among his dependents, the king, accompanied by his wife, partakes of the meal.
Filled with compassion, those two performed the affairs of the subjects as their own royal duties;
they constantly carried out the service of the gods and the distribution of gifts as if they were their own selves.
He gave food to the mendicants, garments to those who required them,
alms-bowls to the worthy recipients of gifts, and wealth as well as fruits.
The word "giving" never ceases at their door,
nor does the act of giving ever come to rest by day or night.
In the two of their houses, the worship of Śambhu occurs day and night for sacrifices, for Brahmins, for virtuous women, and for the righteous as well.
The husband and wife repeatedly gave gifts of cows, gifts of liquids, and gifts of sweets; they were as satisfied as those who had received their desires.
In that kingdom there was no drought, no year without a sacrifice,
no festival without Kṛṣṇa, and no glorification without Śambhu.
The two of them indeed established the righteous laws of Śiva in the kingdom,
and they caused worship to be performed in all the temples of Śiva.
Having summoned all the village headmen residing within their jurisdiction, the two of them commanded them: "Worship must be offered at the temple of Śiva."
Otherwise, this will indeed be the truth, and he shall become punishable by us both;
moreover, through worship and gifts, Śiva, together with Śivā, will be pleased.
Indeed, there are unbroken ghee-lamps in those temples of Śiva;
for every village, as many temples of Śiva as exist in its vicinity [should be maintained]. || 18 ||
In each of those places, an unbroken lamp must be lit by the king's command;
for one who violates the king's command, his head shall be cut off. || 19 ||
The worship of the king must be performed with the sixteen auspicious articles;
otherwise, the king will undoubtedly cut off the head of one who performs it deficiently.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, worship was indeed performed by those two everywhere; out of fear of them, lamps were lit in every temple of Śiva. (21)
Those two, O Great Śambhu, traveled by means of a celestial vehicle throughout the kingdom during the night to behold all the temples of Śiva.
Having performed the ritual viewing of the worship everywhere until dawn, those two return to their residence and perform bathing and worship once more. (23)
Just as those two were sitting down while intending to break their fast,
two mendicants, Śiva and Aśiva, arrived there.
Knowing that the two virtuous ones were hungry, they offered them excellent food;
seeing that it was empty, the two of them struck them with *tulasī* leaves.
If there is the grace of Nārāyaṇa, we two shall eat the sacred food;
as the two Vaiṣṇavas, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, Śiva and Śivā will not eat.
If that which is offered to Śrī Puruṣottama were not pleasing, then the supreme dharma of the Vaiṣṇava and the highest austerity of Vaiṣṇavism would be in vain. (27)
We accept with great devotion whatever is performed or given by Vaiṣṇavas;
indeed, we never, under any circumstances, accept what is given by those who are not Vaiṣṇavas. (28)
"Offerings, food, and lamps are constantly presented to you both;
we merely look upon them, we do not take them, for they have been offered to Brahmā. (29)
This is considered the eternal duty for devotees who have surrendered their very selves:
that which has not been offered to Brahman must never, under any circumstances, be eaten or drunk. (30)
Clothing, a leaf, fruit, a flower, water, food, as well as a seat;
even a mere grain of medicine, or powder, or even something for chewing. (3.1)
Today, whatever is to be tasted, chewed, enjoyed, worn, rubbed, given, or offered— all that has been dedicated to Brahmā— is my own worthy offering.
Therefore, let us accept this and nothing else; for this is our constant duty:
everything—including house, clothing, wealth, and so forth—must be accepted as an offering to Brahman.
Whatever one considers to be one's own—whether insentient or sentient—the king of devotees should offer that indeed to the Blessed One and eat what remains. 34.
Indeed, [he should place] water in the pillars of the house, in beautiful jars,
on grinding stones, on couches, and also on beds and other such items within the home.
Having tied a Tulasī amulet around its neck, that [food] should indeed be consumed;
[this applies to] domestic animals, birds, the trees of the courtyard, and the cart. (36)
Without being a Vaiṣṇava, one must never make use of food, clothing, discus-emblems, or vehicles. (37)
One must never employ for one's livelihood bellows made of iron, storehouses, or merchandise, unless they belong to a Vaiṣṇava. || 38 ||
Furthermore, musical instruments, weapons, missiles,
and objects bearing names [of deities] must be endowed with the marks of the Blessed One by means of the self-consecration.
Sons, daughters, wealth, wives, male servants, female servants, houses, wife, husband, family, and indeed everything—one should offer all to Hari. (40)
That which has not been offered to Hari is unfit to be eaten or enjoyed;
likewise, that which has been offered to Hari alone is fit to be eaten, enjoyed, and drunk. (41)
"Understand this, both of you: that supreme Badarī hermitage was previously reached by me there from Nārāyaṇa along with the sacred mantras."
Then, along with the mantras, the state of being a Vaiṣṇava was bestowed by me upon the goddess Pārvatī and also upon all the Gaṇas in every respect.
My son Gaṇeśa is indeed a Vaiṣṇava who is a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
Skanda has also become a Vaiṣṇava, and even the Rudras are Vaiṣṇavas.
And the goddesses, foremost among them Vaiṣṇavī, are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
Kailāsa has been made by me entirely desirable to the Vaiṣṇavas. ||45||
Through his connection with Badarikāśrama, even Himālaya became a Vaiṣṇava;
his ancestors were Vaiṣṇavas, and their daughter Menā was also a Vaiṣṇavī.
Even the Ocean of Milk is a Vaiṣṇava, for he always upholds Viṣṇu;
his daughters—Śrī, Ramā, and Lakṣmī—as well as the Moon, are also indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
Even Gaṅgā, though belonging to Viṣṇu, was touched by the big toe of Vāmana;
and Vāsuki, the kinsman of Śeṣa, who is a Vaiṣṇava, was held up by me.
The trident was born from the sun; Viṣṇu, the king of the suns, is the twelfth.
The bull came from Gokula; he is the king of Kṛṣṇa’s devotees in Goloka. 49.
He who is Siṃha of the Nṛsiṃha lineage is indeed a great Vaiṣṇava;
and Megha and Vairājakeśa are Vaiṣṇavas nourished by sacrifice.
The peacock and Meghamitra, with its tail-feathers resting upon the crown, possess eternal Vaiṣṇava-nature indeed, both through their connection to Kṛṣṇa and their connection to the clouds. (51)
What more need I say? With the head of Nṛsiṃha upon my neck, I am indeed a Vaiṣṇava; I am a devotee of Viṣṇu in every respect.
Viṣṇu is indeed the all-pervading Brahman; I am that light, Sadāśiva.
Meditating upon Him, I have become manifest in the form of Bāṇa, though possessing a physical body.
The Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, who is higher than the highest, is the soul of all;
from him I and likewise everything are born, and therein they dissolve. (54)
Therefore, O King, receive with reverence this Vaiṣṇava mantra;
I, Śambhu, bestow it upon you, and Pārvatī will give it to the Queen.
Thus instructed, Vasudhāna received the eight-syllabled mantra;
saying, "May Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa protect me," he received it from Śaṅkara.
And Queen Rādhikā received that from the mouth of Pārvatī;
and they both took the tulasī-necklace and the crescent-moon tilaka.
They both took the water used for the worship of Nārāyaṇa and the sacred remains (prasāda) of Acyuta; having partaken of these there, they were indeed born as Vaiṣṇavas.
They offered food and drink mixed with *tulasī* leaves to Viṣṇu,
and they also presented them to Śambhu.
Then they joyfully gave [the gifts] to Pārvatī and accepted them;
they drank water and were filled with happiness.
Śivā and Śiva became exceedingly satisfied and truly joyful;
they bestowed blessings upon the two wealthy ones, who were themselves unimpaired.
"May you both possess a prosperous and eternal kingdom with ten million servants!
Having said this, Śiva and Śivā became invisible.
The king and his queen constantly worship the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with devotion according to the Vaiṣṇava tradition, regarding Him as the very soul of Śiva.
In this way, while Kṛṣṇa was constantly being worshipped by the two of them, the Supreme Person [remained present];
the most divine month arrived and passed day by day.
Then, on the fifth day of the opposing fortnight, they heard the sound of a drum:
"Let the embodied gods and the human beings who possess royal bodies listen! (65)
The Suras, those endowed with divine prosperity, and all things both stationary and moving—
among these, I am the drum of the month of Puruṣottama, which is dear to Hari.
By the command of Hari, I proclaim that for the fruit of a single *kapardikā* coin, one may obtain the entire earth by performing a single day’s *kṛcchra* penance during this month. (67)
[He saw] Alakā, the city of gold, as well as the golden earth,
Goloka, and likewise the golden [city] of the other world-protectors.
Let them go to the royal capital, or likewise to Svarṇapurī, or to a golden body, or even to sovereignty or whatever else they desire from Hari.
It may belong to the Lord of Taste (Varuṇa), or to Sūrya, or to Candra, or to Gaurī;
likewise it may belong to Bṛhaspati, or to Īśāna, or to Agni, or to some other deity.
Whatever may be desired by them, that I shall grant; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether it be the fortnightly or the daily [observance], even when the intercalary month is complete. (71)
Having performed the vow and the worship, may they attain supreme happiness, or even the station of Parameṣṭhin, the Vairāja state, or even Satyaloka. ||72||
May the fierce [Śiva], Śiva himself, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and even the Abode (Dhāman), out of compassion for me today, accept [this offering] merely by virtue of my observance of the Pañcamī vow.
Having spoken thus, Dundubhi then ceased; then both of them, having bowed to Dundubhi and meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, [proceeded].
They indeed honored that musical instrument with golden flowers and unbroken grains of rice;
there they entreated it for the great state of being like gold.
Thinking thus within his heart, Dundubhi then departed elsewhere; the two of them performed the Pañcamī-vrata.
Having bathed in the morning, meditated upon Hari, and bowed with devotion to Śambhu, they worshipped their guru according to the rules and performed their daily rites of worship.
Having fashioned a golden image representing the form of Puruṣottama,
he invoked Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, into it.
Having offered the water for sipping (ācamana), they both bathed him with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and likewise purified him with water.
And these two massaged him with sandalwood paste, fragrant and moist,
and they also dressed him in garments made of gold-threaded cloth.
They also adorned themselves with ornaments such as crowns and decorated one another with collyrium, saffron, and other cosmetics. ||8 1 ||
And they perfumed them with the finest flowers, incense, and other substances;
and they illuminated them with lamps, lustrations, and other rites. ||82||
And they propitiated him with hymns of praise, circumambulations, and other such acts;
they asked for forgiveness for their transgressions by offering precious gifts.
And they both satisfied him with sweet foods, milk-rice, and the like;
they gratified him with the chewing of betel leaves, cardamom, and other spices.
In this manner, they both performed worship at the time of midday; they also provided a meal, and they proceeded in the same way at night as well. (85)
The pavilion was adorned with plantain pillars, leafy archways,
and likewise with very beautiful water-pots and lamps.
The two of them fashioned a beautiful mandala called Sarvatobhadra and filled its center with ever-fresh grains.
Then they both established a golden pitcher;
therein, they placed the five jewels, water, fruit, and likewise a garment. (88)
Having carefully placed a vessel filled with sesame seeds, they two offered worship with devotion;
having installed an image there, they worshipped it with excellent articles.
Bathing water, clothing, sandalwood paste, saffron, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, ornaments, necklaces, incense, lamps, and fruits. || 90 ||

They performed the nightly lamp-offering, offered hymns of praise, circumambulated [the deity], partook of sweet food, and presented water, betel, flowers, and handfuls of offerings while making their requests. (91)
Then they performed a dance accompanied by song and instrumental music;
thereafter, during the night-watch at midnight, that most excellent of men [performed] there in the vigil.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the manifest Lord of Lakṣmī and Śrī Rādhikā;
he is the Master of Pārvatī and Māṇikī, the Lord of Prabhā, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||93||

The Lord who protects those seeking worldly pleasure and those seeking the supreme good, the husband of Śrī Jayā and Lalitā, the sovereign of the imperishable realm, the Lord of the liberated, and the Master of the gopīs. 94.
Then Hari, the Lord of all, the inner self, and the abode of auspiciousness, suddenly manifested, smiling and illuminating the quarters of the sky. 95.
"I have become exceedingly pleased by your observance of the vow on the fifth day," he said.
"I grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire. (96)
"Because of my devotion, two Vaiṣṇavas have been born; therefore, I am exceedingly pleased.
I shall give you my everything—what else could be more difficult to obtain? (97)
Having heard this and prostrated like a staff, they said to Puruṣottama:
"O Lord, you are not unaware of the fact that we two are the masters of the earth."
O Lord, we do not desire even the sovereignty over the fourteen worlds, for that is but a small wealth; indeed, it only brings satisfaction to the destitute. (99)
"O Lord, that state of supreme sovereignty consists of the activities of a potter;
therefore, we do not desire that state. Instead, we desire the position of Indra, which, though oppressed by the Daityas, is [still] desirable."
We do not desire those states, but rather that which is beyond them—that which is supreme even above all the lords, such as Vairāja and the others. || 10.1 ||
That which is beyond Mahāviṣṇu, the station of Hiraṇyādhipati, that which is beyond the city called Śrīpura, and the splendor beyond Vaikuṇṭha—[all these are surpassed by it]. (102)
The station of the Lord of Gold (Kubera) is indeed superior to that of Viṣṇu; it belongs to the Great Kubera, the Person who is Infinite, and consists of a treasury.
That which is the greatest exists within the multitude of lords;
indeed, the infinite multitude of Kuberas of the cosmic eggs is satisfied by but a single grain of it.
From that [divine gold] arises that great kingdom, consisting of an abundance of treasuries;
for indeed, from that [gold], the divine wealth of all lords exists.
Therefore, we truly desire that sovereignty over gold; may you have compassion for us.
For those who are devoted, there is nothing whatsoever that their master does not possess in abundance. (10.6)
If what we have desired is improper, O Supreme Person, may it be forgiven;
O Kṛṣṇa, we desire nothing else than that the Supreme Person be pleased. 107.
Having thus entreated him, the two then fell at the feet of Śrī Hari;
"So be it," Hari said, and he spoke to them once again.
At the end of the lifespan of the current Hiraṇyādhipati,
you two shall indeed become such [beings] again in another creation.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa vanished from that place;
there occurred the destruction of the infinite lords of the Hiraṇyas.
Day after day, [this] was born of Vāsudeva; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, the destruction of one lord of gold occurred therein.
The Lord led Vasudhāna and Rādhyāsa to that station; Hari bestowed upon them the station of Mahākauberaka and the station of Īśa.
Having become the lord of gold, the possessor of wealth shines resplendent;
likewise, the supreme sovereign Rādhyāsā, as Kubera’s consort, shines forth brilliantly.
Of this four-faced Brahmā, born from the lotus, Virāṭ is the father; his father is Mahāviṣṇu, who is beyond that.
That person indeed named Bhūmanārāyaṇa became the lord of the treasury for that king Vasudhāna. || 1.15 ||
This lord of the treasury of the earth acts as a sovereign over all;
he shall remain as the lord of wealth until the dissolution of the world.
Because I am the Supreme Person who perceives directly through immediate intuition, O Lakṣmī, my beloved, I know all; for there is no one else besides me who is omniscient.
"I am of the nature of the Supreme Brahman; I know all, being omniscient and all-knowing"—thus indeed was it said by me to those two at the end of the previous creation.
Indeed, at the conclusion of the fifth vow, an eternal fruit was granted;
for who else but me would be capable of bestowing such a fruit? (1.19)
Indeed, all are swallowed by Time, except for Nārāyaṇa alone;
having created everything, I enter it, I dwell within it, and I withdraw from it.
Nevertheless, I alone possess unimpeded knowledge, and no one else;
therefore, I have related this account of the previous creation to you.
On the fifth [lunar day], for the man who performs the vow as well as for the woman, the fruit for both the listener and the speaker is likewise certainly attained. 122.

Thus ends the three hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Great Office of Kubera, Consisting of Sovereignty over Hiraṇyakośa, in the Present Creation within the Creation of Īśvara— Following the Attainment of Vaiṣṇavahood Granted by Śiva to King Rādhyāsa and Queen Vasudāna, who were devotees of Śiva existing in a previous creation, as a result of performing the vow on the fifth day of the second fortnight during the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this narrative centered upon Śrī Puruṣottama,
which bestows prosperity, grants happiness, and always fulfills all desires.
In a former kalpa, in the region of Maru,
there lived a very righteous and wealthy Brāhmaṇa named Devayava.
His wife was the auspicious Devajuṣṭā, who was devoted to her husband;
their servant was Girikṣita, and likewise their female servant was Adridyuti.
They were always devoted to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
having performed their duties as servants, they engaged in the service of Kṛṣṇa.
Constantly devoted to the duties of Brahmins and dedicated to the sixfold duties and others,
those four indeed became solely intent upon devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
The two Brāhmaṇas were the masters, and the two Brāhmaṇī women were their servants;
for the sake of Hari, they spent every moment with their minds, speech, and bodies.
A temple of Viṣṇu was indeed caused to be built by King Devasakha, the lord of the Maru country, in the city named Bhāsvatī.
It was beautified by seven peaks, charming with three-pointed globes,
delightful with the tops of golden pillars, and enchanting with its three enclosures.
In the center, however, upon a lion-throne situated within the pinnacle, is the four-armed Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Rādhā.
Within the interior of the peaks of Dakṣa, the auspicious triad of Śrī, Prabhā, and Pārvatī shines forth,
each one attended by her own maidservants.
Within the interiors of the left peaks, Māṇikyā, Lalitā,
and Jayā each shine resplendently in three places, attended by their respective maidservants.
Those four, each separately engaged in his service, being seekers of the divine, always perform worship in the middle portion.
Girikṣita became an agent for external tasks such as sandalwood paste;
on the right side was the worship of the splendor and fortune of Pārvatī, which is cherished by the gods.
On the left side, Adridyuti performs worship with rubies and other gems;
the King indeed bestows his wages according to their respective divisions.
A dwelling fit for habitation, a livelihood such as a garden and so forth, annual provisions, and likewise a thousand pieces of gold. || 15 ||
And during the festival, the king gives garments, food, ornaments, and other gifts in abundance; he also provides offerings for the worship of the gods, such as excellent sacrificial foods.
Indeed, for one who lives in this manner, though he is a Brahmin devoted to the gods,
his mind is drawn by greed and he eventually seizes a gambling-die.
In some places, however, he plundered silver coins and gold seals that had been offered to the deity by those intent on pilgrimage, claiming they were indeed "the property of the god. (18)
And by that evil act of theft, the excellent substance of the divine grain became mixed with the wealth of the gods; thus it was defiled and became unstable.
He desired to go elsewhere, for fortunes are considered fickle;
indeed, that which is possessed of divine property goes to destruction along with its very roots.
Even if one's own wealth is acquired through righteous means, if it comes into contact with the property of the gods, it becomes defiled;
indeed, having taken a hundred thousand such items, one perishes as one departs.
Even food mixed with liquor, meat, and the like perishes quickly;
likewise, clothing associated with the garments of gods surely brings ruin to the embodied being. (22)
That which is merely a material object, obtained through theft and not as a gift of grace, yet given by the worshiper, the preceptor, or the guru, takes on the very form of the deity. (23)
Wherever it is cast, it burns even that which is at the very root;
like a fire from wood on a hearth, it consumes the entire forest as it spreads through the wilderness.
The food of cows, the food of beggars, the food of Brahmins, the food of women, the food of the helpless, and the food of the destitute—Agni indeed becomes enraged at these. (25)
The property of a Brahmin, the property of a widow, the property of a deity, the coin of a mendicant,
the property of one who is not wealthy, and a great fire— wherever these fall, there he is consumed.
Whatever fruit or food offered to a deity, even a mere *ḍhabbuka* measure, must not be accepted if one does not possess divinity; for it consumes that entire family. (27)
The gambling coin has been stolen by those of old and even by those of the earliest times;
it is indeed just that the mouse steals yet another such coin.
Even those seeking the gods, in the temple of the Lord in the presence of Hari,
have offered and cast into [the fire] ladles and other such implements, being eager for the festival procession.
He indeed nourishes his own property and deposits it for its increase;
yet, by some cause or other, that [property] comes to destruction. (30)
A terrible war indeed took place between the two kings of Maru and Kosala;
the lord of Maru was defeated by the armies of Kosala. || 31 ||
Then the entire city was devastated by the troops;
indeed, the wealth of the affluent was seized by them by force.
Knowing him to be a Brahmin honored by the king, they seized all of his wealth;
he was then expelled from that place, accompanied only by his wife and servants.
Subsisting on roots and fruits, he went to the auspicious bank of the Hiraṇyā on Mount Raivata, near Somanātha in the forest.
Accompanied by his servants and wife, he passes his days wandering;
having gone to the east along the river Sarasvatī, he reaches a Pippala tree.
Having drunk water, he sat down and rested for a moment;
then he remembered Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world.
They reflected among themselves upon the defeat caused by their enemy;
then a servant of Girikṣit spoke to the brahmin Devayāva.
Even though we are his servants and his worship was properly performed by that wielder of the Śārṅga bow, we were not protected from the enemy’s assault.
Indeed, all his possessions were seized by the armies, including the gold of the palace;
even there, Śrī Viṣṇu did not provide any protection at that time.
"Why should one who does not protect himself protect another?
When this was said, the Brahmin Devayava spoke to his own servant.
"Do not speak thus, O twice-born one; it is not as you say.
Śrī Hari protects all who live, and we have been protected by Him."
Indeed, protection has been afforded to these four so that we may live together here; yet the sin of misappropriating the property of the gods is without end. (42)
That which was done by him was indeed done by me; and that substance was mixed with my own substance.
Because of that, everything has gone away from us, indeed due to my transgression.
If divine property and divine food are digested within someone's treasury, it will certainly result in the destruction of all his wealth. 44.
All one's possessions have gone there, and the appropriate fruit has been earned right here;
indeed, even the world of Yama remains now to be experienced.
Nevertheless, this fruit of our service does not protect us here;
for we have been slain and have not been protected by the Supreme Self.

One must not consume the property of the deity, such as leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth; nor should one ever, under any circumstances, consume clothing, vehicles, houses, or vessels belonging to the deity. (47)
If it has been consumed through injustice, greed, ignorance, or even by force, then that [food] will bring about the destruction of the eater. (48)
O twice-born one, we have not been destroyed at all; this is indeed the mercy of Hari.
Now, an effort must be made so that Yama does not approach us. (49)
For those who have sought refuge, Hari is the protector; Yama shall not move there.
Indeed, the sixfold nature of *prapatti* was demonstrated by Nārāyaṇa. (50)
Trust, choosing [the Lord], entrusting oneself, humility, and firm resolve;
the determination to act favorably and the avoidance of what is unfavorable. (5.1)
In this regard, one should maintain such conviction: "Whatever Hari does for my sake is entirely appropriate for my sake. (52)
One should request the formal acceptance [of the bride] with the words, "You are mine, and I am yours.
Then one should perform the ritual of depositing [the bride] by saying, "I am your entire being; I am placed at your feet."
Even if one is a sovereign ruler of the entire earth, one should act with meekness like a servant;
even in the face of total ruin, one should not give way to despondency, but maintain a steady mind.
"One's own satisfaction is my satisfaction; it is not otherwise"—one should reflect well in this way.
Whatever is delightful to him is indeed delightful to me as well. (5.5)
Thinking always of the devotion to Hari, one should indeed not do anything else;
having had his offenses forgiven, he will surely deliver us. (56)
Whatever sin, such as theft, has been committed out of greed for the sake of one's belly—that the Blessed One will surely consume by means of devotion. (57)
Uttering the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Brahman, while remembering Him, he who departs, casting off his body, goes to the supreme abode. ||5 8 ||
Therefore, having dwelt for a long time right here at this sacred ford (tīrtha) and having propitiated that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, we shall indeed return once more.
Or rather, when his lifespan has expired, we shall attain his desired abode;
Śrī Hari will forgive even thousands of his offenses.
Having reflected thus, the four of them performed the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) at the site of Prācīsarasvatī, chanting the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having bathed in the morning and meditated upon Hari, they worshipped Him daily with whatever was available—
leaves, flowers, fruits, water, roots, and so forth.
They offered prayers and other petitions to Hari for the sake of water;
they did so again and again at dawn, midday, evening, and night.
While they were thus proceeding along the path of the sky,
the drum of the intercalary month was heard, as proclaimed by Śrī Puruṣottama.
On the sixth day, at dawn, during the month of Puruṣottama,
there is indeed a proclamation from the drum that bestows liberation, or else, for those with desires, it bestows enjoyments.
That delightful [sound], having reached the path of his ears, proceeded forth;
yet it was pondered and grasped within the heart by all four who were absorbed in meditation. (66)
Let all human beings listen—whether they be poor or wealthy, innocent or guilty, as well as women and men. (67)
Even if many offenses against me occur during worship,
whether committed by anyone at all, I shall certainly not take them even slightly to heart.
Let them observe the vow this very day on the sixth lunar day of the second fortnight;
in this month of Puruṣottama, I shall indeed forgive their sin.
Today, by means of this vow, I shall indeed wash away sins such as those involving adamantine glue;
I shall subsist on a single meal or eat only at night, without ever soliciting alms.
"Moreover, having taken it on the sixth lunar day, my vow must indeed be performed here;
whether after eating fruit, drinking water, or even inhaling air. (7.1)
On the sixth day, I must perform a vow; I shall grant him whatever he desires.
I will by no means forget that which was previously done wrongly by me.
Today, out of compassion, Puruṣottama will grant that which is desired;
for this month of Puruṣottama prevails throughout the three worlds.
Even in the world of Īśa, this month proceeds by my command;
for this month is the foremost of all, derived from Puruṣottama, the foremost of persons.
"Therefore, grant me the supreme fruit of the *mūrdhan* stage; choose whatever you desire.
Having spoken thus, Dundubhi departed from that place to another location.
Those four brahmins, however, afflicted by the suffering of poverty,
undertook a vow on the sixth lunar day after hearing the sound of the drum.
Poverty shall go to destruction, and happiness born of prosperity shall arise;
there shall be even greater wealth than before, and vast riches shall expand.
If vehicles, carriages, palaces, male servants, and radiant female servants were all present—even more than a kingdom—then there would be happiness. (78)
Having thus desired this, they all undertook the vow of fasting;
for those who previously indulged in sensual pleasures later yearn for the abundance of enjoyments. (79)
Beings follow their own nature, but restraint is difficult to maintain;
as long as desire is not pacified, the knower continues to act. (80)
Even for devotees, there is engagement with desired objects of enjoyment;
however, for one who is free from passion and views all things with equanimity, there is no such engagement at all. //81//
If, after reflecting and abandoning it as if it were poison, passion does not subside, then when a favorable opportunity arises, one desires to take it up again. (82)
Therefore, those who are well-disciplined in yoga establish the weakness of the senses;
with the power of their sins washed away by austerity, they conquer the illusory world. 83.
Victory comes through fasting, or victory through great hardship;
yet for those who indulge in food, victory comes through laxity. 84.
But by these Brahmins, though joined with wives, victory was not achieved;
rather, they indeed desired a kingdom of illusion that was superior even to the former one.
Whether it be the station of the Supreme Lord (Brahmā), or the station of the sun, the moon, and so forth, there is nothing else equal to the station of Indra, like that of the King of the Gods. (86)
Brahmā, however, is always subject to old age in relation to his own progeny;
the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies wander in the sky under the control of another. (87)
For those who dwell abroad, there is no happiness and indeed no rest anywhere;
being constantly distressed without rest, the station of Indra is therefore superior.
Indeed, the sovereignty of all the gods, as well as wives, dwellings, wealth, and so forth—the eternal Lakṣmī and prosperity of Indra exist in heaven. (89)
Therefore, one should accept the auspicious state of Indra, which bestows the highest enjoyment;
thereafter, having acquired Vaikuṇṭha through devotion, it becomes a divine means of accomplishment.
Having thus resolved, they all performed the auspicious vow on the sixth lunar day;
having bathed in the morning, they then had an image of Hari fashioned out of clay.
Then, having placed a crystal stone at their side, they invoked Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person. ||92||

Having bathed [the deity] with the nectar of the five milks and so forth, as well as with water, and having honored [him] with garments, ornaments, flowing substances, unbroken grains, flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings; ||93||

Having worshipped with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, fruits, leaves, water, and so forth, and having offered the *arghya* consisting of bilva fruits, one should perform the salutation and praise. (94)
Having offered prayers, hymns of praise, and handfuls of flowers to Viṣṇu,
they began to swing upon swings made of creepers, ropes, and other materials.
At midday, as well as in the evening and at night, they performed worship along with a vigil;
through their dancing, singing, and other rites, Keśava appeared there.
"Choose boons, for you are my devotees; through my vow, your suffering has come to an end.
I have arrived to grant whatever you desire, and I am well-pleased."
Having seen and heard of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari, the four-armed one,
they bowed at his feet and then offered a handful of flowers and water.
They chose the abode of the gods, the prosperous station of Mahendra;
having granted the boon, saying "So be it," Hari vanished from sight.
In the intercalary month, on the eastern bank of the Sarasvatī at Supippala, four [ascetics] abandoned their bodies on dry land and ascended to heaven. || 100 ||
Upon the destruction of Prāntendra’s lifespan and following the dissolution of the ten worlds,
those four went to the auspicious Maharloka and remained there for a long time.
Furthermore, at the beginning of another kalpa, four [beings] arrived in heaven;
indeed, through the merit of his vows, Mahendra became one devoted to the gods (devayava).
Devajuṣṭā became Mahendrāṇī, the beloved of Hari;
Indraputra was born as Jayanta by name, the son of Indra. || 103 ||
Adridyuti became the victorious wife; she was born from the mind (Mānasī), the daughter of Viśvakarman, and is considered the daughter-in-law of Indra.
Pulomajā became Indrāṇī; she was his mind-born daughter and became the wife of Indra, accompanied by hundreds of millions of male and female servants.
By means of that Ṣaṣṭhī-vow, those brahmins attained the auspicious station of Indra;
through the grace of the illustrious Hari, they attained the blissful station of the Lord of Gods.
Whoever should recite this discourse or listen to it with a concentrated mind,
for him there shall indeed be the fruit of the sixth [vow], and he shall likewise obtain his desired object.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Titles Mahendra-jayantī and Mahendrāṇī-jāyantī by the Couple Devajuṣṭā and Ārdradhuti—Inhabitants of the Maru Country, Descendants of Devaya and Giri—the Brahmins, Following the Loss of All Their Possessions Due to Stealing Temple Property, Through the Vow on the Sixth Day of the Second Fortnight of the Intercalary Month," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder that arose from the vow of the seventh lunar day (Saptamī), which was performed by Sandhyā, the daughter of Brahmā; that I shall now relate.
At the commencement of creation, Brahmā himself, the creator, [beheld] his mind-born sons:
Atri, Marīci, Pulaha, Pulastya, Aṅgiras, and Kratu.
She brought forth the great lords Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Dakṣa, and Bhṛgu—
handsome and endowed with youth as soon as they were born.
When those divine beings, who were skilled in their tasks and agitated the mind, departed from there, then a woman of beautiful form was born from the mind of Aja.
By name she was Sandhyā Divakṣāntā, the evening twilight known as Japantikā;
she was exceedingly beautiful, with lovely eyebrows, and she enchanted the minds of the sages.
At that time, creation was indeed mental and not born from the womb of desire and the like;
thereafter, Dakṣa and others, who followed their own desires, were meditated upon by the Creator.
There, Kāma, the mind-born son of Brahmā, appeared;
he had the splendor of molten gold, was restless, and possessed a face resembling the moon.
His hands, eyes, face, feet, and arms are slightly reddened;
his eyes are like the petals of a full-blown lotus, and he is adorned with a flowery bow.
Then Sandhyā and the others, beholding that charming man who was captivating their two eyes with the casting of side-long glances, were filled with desire.
They experienced supreme longing as well as the restlessness characteristic of the *rajas* quality;
they attained the state of sensory delight and fell under the sway of desire.
At that time, Kāma indeed took up the flower-arrows known as Harṣaṇa (the exhilarating), Rocana (the pleasing), Mohana (the bewildering), Śoṣaṇa (the withering), and Drāvaṇa (the liquefying).
Then Brahmā said to Kāma: "Deluding both men and women with your five flower-arrows, provide assistance for the work of creation."
Whether it be I, or Vāsudeva, or Sthāṇu, the Supreme Person—we shall all come under your control here; what need is there to mention other mere sustainers of life?
Always entering the hearts of living beings in a concealed form,
become yourself the cause of their happiness and carry out the eternal creation.
Having given his command, Brahmā sat down upon his own seat;
Dakṣa and the others sat down as well, and Sandhyā also took her place.
Then, for the sake of testing all those who had been praised by Kāma,
he diligently assumed the ālīḍha stance and drew his bow with great force.
For the sake of desire, he indeed equipped his arrows with various kinds of flowers;
Dakṣa and all the others were deluded and underwent transformation from the very beginning.
Beholding the twilight, they all underwent many transformations;
at that very moment, forty-nine states arose from their bodies.
Even as they gazed upon Sandhyā, she cast glances full of emotion;
then, seeing Sandhyā filled with such feeling, they were overcome by extreme agitation.
Seeing those youths, Sandhyā underwent a profound transformation; and Madana, perceiving the attainment of his desired fruit, placed full confidence in his own mission.
"That which has been assigned to me as the task of Brahmā—that indeed can be accomplished by me; this is certainly determined by you, and it shall surely bear fruit. (21)
Then, seeing them thus transformed, his son Dharmadeva himself spoke with discernment to his father, his brothers, and Sandhyā.
Madana was born for the sake of dharma, never for the sake of adharma;
indeed, it was through Madana that the family fell into mutual discord.
This is not fitting for the subjects, for it will not bring them security;
if entry into desire were permitted as soon as one has reached youth. (24)
Then the traditional designation of "mother," "sister," "brother's wife," as well as "daughter," "father," "brother," "husband," and "son" will perish. (25)
O Creator, act in such a way that desire does not arise for one as soon as he is born, so that youth may become a forest for dharma. (26)
"You have indeed practiced both righteousness and desire, yet you have committed a slaughter that was unbecoming and untimely; therefore, you shall be reduced to ashes."
And Dharma said to Dakṣa and the others: "Go to Badarikāśrama;
having bathed in the Gaṅgā, bowed to Hari, and performed austerities, you shall become purified. (28)
"Therefore, let them always perform creation according to dharma.
Dharma then said to his father, "O Grandfather, achieve glory! (29)
At the beginning of creation, Brahmā performed a Vedic sacrifice;
from that were born the rain-clouds, which always bestow satisfaction and provide food.
Then Dharma said to Sandhyā, who was possessed by the defect of transformation:
"Become the daughter of a dog-cooker; thereafter you shall become pure."
Then Sandhyā said to Dharma: "I shall strive by means of asceticism so that this desire may not trouble him for long, even from the moment he is born. (32)
After these events had transpired, they all departed from there according to their respective instructions;
at that time, Sandhyā too, overcome with indignation, became absorbed in meditation.
She reflected: "This would be appropriate and would bring future happiness;
for as soon as I was born, I became a beautiful young woman, infatuated by desire. (34)
Dakṣa and the others were likewise born thus, deluded by passion for me;
the minds of all were churned by Madana, the domestic fire.
May I receive the fruit of this sin in the form of this disease;
I myself shall perform the expiation for this sin. (36)
I desire to quickly accomplish the means for that purification;
I shall offer my own self into the fire of austerity in accordance with the path of Dharma. (37)
However, I shall establish a single boundary here in every respect, so that embodied beings do not become possessed of desire immediately upon birth. (38)
For this purpose, having performed most rigorous penance,
I shall establish the boundaries of conduct and renounce this wicked life.
With this very body, I have indeed manifested lustful desire toward my family and kinsmen; that is not a means for accomplishing wholesome merit.
Having thus reflected with the mind through the meditative absorption of yoga at the twilight hour,
she became mental [in nature], even while possessing that very body composed of shadow.

Having become minute for the sake of destroying her sin, she was born as a daughter in the house of a dog-cooker; having been born, she immediately possessed the memory of her past lives and attained youth.
Her father was Rākhāla and her mother was Mātaṅginī;
having attained the state of outcaste laborers (karmacāṇḍāla), they then lived on the Himālaya mountain. 43.
In such a land where there is no drought whatsoever, where there are no fruitless trees, and where there is no desert region, while dwelling upon the earth... (44)
Constantly remembering the curse of her former life as a result of her past karma,
she spent her time performing purificatory acts such as ascetic penance.
He served his parents, who possessed the power to wash away his sins,
waiting for that time by which his purification might be achieved.
While they were thus wandering upon the earth, rescuing those who had fallen [into worldly existence],
the Seven Sages then departed through the sky toward Badarī.
Having seen her there on that spot in the forest with their yogic vision,
they descended into the house of a dog-cooker under the pretext of seeking alms.
Even if he is a Cāṇḍāla by his actions, he is indeed the son of Brahmā;
he should be solicited for alms for the sake of fruit and other provisions, provided that no harm is caused thereby. (49)
"There is no fault even in uncooked food; there is no impurity (sūtaka) regarding mere grains.
Having reflected thus, they begged for alms from the trees belonging to the outcastes (śvapaca).
Recognizing those twice-born ones as such and identifying them as his daughters in every respect,
the dog-cooker joyfully gave them alms, preceded by a formal speech.
The outcaste, having bowed at their feet and drunk the nectar-like water from their feet, entreated the Seven Sages, the effectors of the world’s salvation. (52)
"May the stainless sages accept alms rich in fruits, rice, and maidens;
may they deliver us, their daughters; I give these maidens as alms to you. (53)
With the consent of the sages, Vasiṣṭha, a portion of the Creator, accepted the alms and the girl; and having taken her, they departed for Badarikā.
Having bathed that maiden in the Gaṅgā at Badarīvana,
they [performed] her entry into the mouth within the body of Kāmadhenu.
Having fashioned her by their power, they then expelled her through the urinary passage;
she thus entered into another birth.
Indeed, having been consecrated by the sacred thread (upavīta), that girl became purified; she attained the status of the twice-born and became fit for ascetic practice. 57.
Nevertheless, desiring to establish a boundary for the sake of her asceticism while she was still in the bloom of youth, she smiled and spoke to the seer: (58)
O Great Seer, the worldly order is maintained for the sake of establishing it among living beings; yet, as soon as one enters youth, that order is no longer observed. (59)
I desire to perform penance on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river, if there is the command of the divine Brahmā; I wish to practice asceticism.
Having understood the profound and extensive inner intention of his own [disciple],
Vasiṣṭha, the treasury of austerities, said "Om" to her there.
There he beheld the great lake known as Lohita,
and from that wall [he saw] the Candrabhāgā river and the southern ocean.
And he beheld that great river as it was flowing from the mountain with its attendants; for she, the Candrabhāgā, had indeed burst forth from the western side of the mountain.
Purifying the people and the lands, she flows slowly toward the ocean on that mountain, Candrabhāga, at the great red slope of the Sattavatī.
Descending from the path of the sky, Vasiṣṭha said to her:
