By his own will, for the sake of protecting the Dharma and for the promotion of devotion, he himself manifested in the very form of Pativratā. (109)
In Goloka, that quality called *patnīvrata* which issued from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa became manifest, accompanied by the Goddess of Fortune known as *pātivratya*.
Thus, for the sake of establishing the Dharma, Śrī Puruṣottama himself became the son of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as Puruṣottama during the intercalary month (adhimāsa).
The celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell;
there, the apsarases danced and the singers performed songs. || 11.2 ||
In every abode dwell the lords, the gods, the great sages,
their incarnations, and their goddesses— the Śaktis beginning with Abjā, Arbudā, and Antyakā.
Accompanied by shouts of victory, they worshipped the Supreme Lord everywhere throughout the cosmic eggs, including all incarnations of the Lord of living beings.
There was a great festival consisting of an infinite feast for the Brahmins;
it became a source of gratification and satisfaction for all living beings of the creation.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, when the moon is in the asterism Punarvasu and five ghaṭikās have passed after sunset, at that moment— || 1 16 ||
At the beginning of the night, the primordial, beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, was born in the home of Gopāla Kaṃbharā.
And here, as everywhere else, there was a light like that of many suns in another world;
perceiving that [the Lord] had been born, the Vedas and the sciences offered hymns of praise. (1.18)
He is the supreme beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the sovereign treasure-house of all sciences, and the lord of Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Śrī, and the other goddesses. 1.19.
The Compassionate One displayed countless wonders;
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, he received initiation and the sacred thread.
On the morning of the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, he descended at Kāśī;
on the ninth day, the Lord established the transmission of the Brahma-vidyās.
Having heard from the mouth of his own father that all knowledge, consisting of the Vedas and their branches, was established within himself, he indeed taught it to Lakṣmī.
Listen, Lakṣmī, what shall I say? He who is Hari, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Brahman beyond the Imperishable, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (123)
He alone exists as the Lord of Rādhā in the realm of Goloka;
he is the husband of Rukmiṇī, the cowherd, and the lord of Kaṃbhārā.
He is the sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha, the Lord of Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa;
he is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all, the Supreme Person.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am Nārāyaṇa, and you are that Lakṣmī, my beloved;
the multiplicity of my forms is perceived by me through the differentiation of their locations.
I am the speaker of the sciences of the Nigamas and Agamas, the Supreme Person;
you are my listener, my servant, my beloved, and my disciple. 127.
O Lakṣmī, here I, Nārāyaṇa,
bestow upon you that knowledge and realization which is established within the Self and is ever directly perceived by me.
It consists of ten million verses and comprises the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, originating from the successive stages of creation and dissolution, beginning with the first, the second, and so forth.
Fifty lakhs must be given by you to Vairāja,
in which the preeminence of the Īśvaras is described for the sake of the creation of Īśa.
O Creator, you must indeed grant twenty-five lakhs [of verses] wherein there are countless accounts such as those concerning the spheres (gola) and the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 13.1 ||
And having offered twelve and a half lakhs [of coins] to the ancestors, O beloved,
you have reached that place where all their branches are honored as the ultimate truth.
"O beloved, you must grant five hundred thousand [gold pieces] to the preceptor in heaven;
for that knowledge of Bṛhaspati concerning the gods indeed follows the ways of the deities. (133)
Furthermore, you must give five hundred thousand [coins] to Śukra, who dwells in the netherworlds (pātāla) and other regions, and who follows the path of Tāmasa and the like. || 134 ||

One hundred and twenty-five thousand [verses] should be given as a purifying gift for the Brāhma and Ārṣa [Vedas], which brings about the attainment of Brahman for those supreme sages who are inclined toward renunciation. 135.
Indeed, among men, it should be given to the Brahmins along with a quarter-kṣetra;
for by studying it, men shall accomplish the four aims of life.
When time has passed away, I shall appear again and again in the form of sages such as Vyāsācārya for the sake of illuminating various forms of knowledge.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I reminded you of our former history as it was;
formerly, the fluctuations of water and land used to undergo dissolution into one another. (138)
Millions of Vairājas have perished; what need is there to mention those beginning with Brahmā?
I am the form of Puruṣottama, the creator of the great dissolution.
The creator of the universe, possessed of eternal consciousness, the inner controller of all,
and the stable treasury of inconceivable power, I do not forget even the slightest thing.
Where there are mountains, there water shall appear after a period of time;
where there is water, O Earth, let there be dry land, and where there is a dwelling, let there likewise be a forest.
In battle he was as if in a forest, and likewise in a forest he was in a city or a cave;
in caves he was a great bridge, and upon every layer of grass he was the open sky.
Where, when, or what has occurred—I know this, and I shall also know what is yet to come; everything indeed exists within me, for nothing whatsoever is separate from me.
At the commencement of creation, this nectar of our life-story was indeed [revealed] under the pretext of the vow for the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month.

O Lakṣmī, I have reminded you of that which is purifying for embodied beings who hear it, which bestows heaven upon those who recite it, which grants liberation, and which yields the supreme merit of vows. 145.
In this festival, there is no doubt that the performer of the vow attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and a wife who desires a husband shall obtain one.
One seeking wealth shall obtain riches; one seeking land shall obtain land;
one seeking dharma shall become meritorious; and one with desires shall attain their fulfillment.
One attains fame and renown, achieves preeminence among the virtuous, and all inauspiciousness comes to an end through reciting this in every way. (148)
A Brāhmaṇa shall become possessed of wisdom, a Kṣatriya shall obtain victory,
and likewise a Vaiśya shall be endowed with the abundance of wealth, grain, and prosperity.
A Śūdra shall become prosperous in all respects and indeed happy by hearing this;
he shall attain the highest welfare and fortune, and obtain splendor and heroism. || 150 ||
Strength, beauty, virtues, prosperity, cattle, wealth, fields, and gardens;
wives, sons, male and female servants, houses, kingdoms, horses, and so forth—[all these he gives]. (151)
One shall attain health, independence, and freedom from bondage;
likewise, one shall attain fearlessness, freedom from calamity, and liberation.
Thus, O beloved, the fruit arising from the eighth-day vow has been told to you;
by performing the vow and worshipping, one shall attain Puruṣottama. (153)
My incarnations are indeed innumerable, for I am Śrī Puruṣottama;
I am the Great King who takes descent, the eternal Supreme Brahman.
"Whether it be Brahmā, Virāṭ, or even the realms of Vaikuṇṭha—in all places I shall remain as the Supreme Person, the Exalted Month. (155)
As long as the moon and the sun shall remain, and likewise the earth,
so long shall [this] endure eternally at the holy site of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, adorned with the banner, the Śārṅga bow, and other emblems,
served by Lakṣmī and others, shall remain there as Puruṣottama.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the *Puruṣottama-māsa-māhātmya* of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*: when Puruṣottama became the presiding deity of the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), a great festival and *rāsa*-dance were performed in Goloka; subsequently, the moonlight from the crest-jewel of Kṛṣṇa’s crown separated from the crown and descended to earth in the form of Nimbadeva and Iṣṭādevī in the Ānarta country; Kṛṣṇa descended into their home in the form of Gopālakṛṣṇa; and Rukmiṇī-Lakṣmī descended into the house of Premamaṇi in the form of Kaṃbhārā.

The three hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of Śrī Puruṣottama into the Homes of Kambharā and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa Following Their Marriage, Upon Hearing the Sound of the Drum, and by the Performance of the Aṣṭamī Vow, as Well as the Composition of the Koṭiśloka Saṃhitā."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the sin-destroying story of this vow from a previous kalpa, which took place on the ninth lunar day within the final month of the intercalary period.
In a kalpa even more ancient than the previous one, there was a lord of the gods named Dyumerujit;
when his dissolution occurred at the end of the day, he was indeed born again through the remainder of his merit.
Having spent the night in Satyaloka, at the dawn of the beginning of the Kalpa,
he became the sovereign emperor Śatamakha during the first Tretā Yuga of creation.
Endowed with the virtue of generosity and compassion, he was intent on protecting the world;
he bestowed honor upon gods, demons, and mortals alike, having conquered his senses.
Traveling by means of a celestial chariot, he wandered through the three worlds,
honoring cows, holy places, Brahmins, ascetics, chaste women, and virtuous people.
Upon the palm of his hand, there indeed shone divine marks in the form of a vajra, a parasol, and a sword, which were indicators of his divinity.
His wife was the great queen Dyuvārṇā, devoted to her husband;
she was constantly intent on serving her husband as well as on serving the gods.
She is devoted to the duty of hospitality, the destroyer of the poverty of the wretched and the helpless,
the bringer of prosperity to maidens, and the eternal protector of the female sex.
Gandharva women, Naga maidens, goddesses, and Dānava women, as well as Kinnara and human women, indeed came and dwelt there for the sake of training.
Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Saṃjñā, Svāhā, Arundhatī,
Mahendrāṇī, Satī, Lakṣmī, Rohiṇī, Pārvatī, and Svadhā.
Prabhā, Māṇikī, Śrī, Jayā, Bhakti, and likewise Diśā—
these and other rivers, beginning with Kṛttikā, then became her companions.
Campā, Dayā, Ramā, Hemnī, Muktā, Godā, Jayantikā, Śānti, Śāntā, Premapātrā, Dīpotsavī, and Nandinī. || 12 ||
Ojasvatī, Suratnā, Damayantī, Caturmatī, Devikā, Kāntikā, Revā, Savitrī, and Mūlayoginī. (13)
Kastūrikā, Maṅgalā, Haṃsā, Ruci, Mañjulā, Nirmalā, Amṛtā, Rālijaṭinī, and Pānaputtalī. (14)
Vanitā, Miṣṭikā, Puṣpā, Manu, and Kṛṣṇā are the maidservants;
Kāntā, Sarasvatī, Padmā, and Śāradā are the sub-maidservants. || 15 ||
In that kingdom called Prāgjyotiṣa, there were wish-fulfilling trees, jewels that grant desires, cows of plenty that bestow what is wished for, and celestial creepers.
Thus King Śatamakha and Queen Dyurvarṇikā,
as a husband and wife, conducted themselves according to the duties of sovereignty upon the surface of the earth.
By the turn of fate, that kingdom became like a fortress on the Snowy Mountain;
they established their capital at Sāketa along the Sarayū river.
Having appointed Pradhāna as their protector and having resolved to undertake the journey,
the two of them then set out with devotion for the pilgrimage to Badarī.
Accompanied by their auspicious servants and maidservants, whose movements were limited and disciplined,
the two proceeded while observing all the regulations of the sacred ford.
Morning bathing, celibacy, the vow of truthfulness, subsisting on fruits, sleeping on the ground, and the renunciation of ornaments, fine seats, and the like. ||21||
Non-violence, freedom from slander, the practice of recitation with a rosary, being devoid of passion and hatred, generosity, and the worship of the gods and other deities. ||22||

Worshiping elders at sacred fords, rendering assistance to the spiritual preceptor at sacred fords, beholding cows, drinking the nectar from the feet of Hari, and listening to the sacred narrative. ||23||
The renunciation of sense objects, behaving like a virtuous person, meditating on Nārāyaṇa at night, and auspicious pilgrimage to sacred sites during the day. (24)
In the evening, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā), hymns of praise, chanting, and remembrance;
and one should practice forbearance toward all beings, whether moving or stationary, without causing them agitation. ||25||
Protecting [the world], those two became ascetics and went to Badarī;
there, having sipped water from the celestial river, they bathed and drank the water. ||26||
They clearly beheld the sages who embody the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the sacred fords themselves;
and having seen Nara and Nārāyaṇa, they performed worship with ritual offerings.
Then the king and queen fed virtuous brahmins and guests in order to please Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (28)
Right there, in the presence of the image, he performed dance and song, and offered a pair of golden umbrellas and two crowns. (29)
A pair of armlets, four chowries, a pair of staffs, necklaces, and likewise twenty finger-rings. ||30||
A pair of two bracelets, a pair of chains for the waist, a pair of two sandals, and likewise a pair of two lion-thrones. ||3 1 ||
There was also abundant sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), excellent vessels of gold, garments of bark and deerskin, and fruits native to the region. ||32||
Everything was offered up, addressed as "thine own";
his feet were touched, and the water [of his bath] was drunk, even as it was called the nectar of his feet.
Golden garlands were placed at the feet of the king and the lord of men,
and the two supreme lords were honored with sandalwood paste and other excellent offerings.
Then blessings were received: "O King, may you be possessed of a son;
may the queen become a mother of a son. Having heard this praise, they departed. (35)
Just then, on the ninth lunar day, at the very dawn,
a drum resounded there clearly, fulfilling the desires of the mind and speech.
Today, let them perform their vows and receive their desired fruit;
for this month of Puruṣottama is the bestower of fruits and is itself the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||37||
May they receive from Puruṣottama the auspicious desires residing in their hearts;
and I shall grant abode, splendor, and prosperity to the seeker of this vow.

For one who performs the Navamī vow, that which is unapproachable becomes approachable by the intellect, that which is unobtainable becomes indeed obtainable, and even that which is inconceivable becomes conceivable. (39)
"Success in all intentions shall be yours, as well as the attainment of the Supreme Person," he said,
naming him Dundubhi, after beholding that man, the lord of men.
Having honored the two excellent sages,
the king and queen, husband and wife, departed for the northern region after reflecting upon what they had heard.
Then Nara and Nārāyaṇa quickly became absorbed [in meditation];
within their two hearts, they beheld two most beautiful forms of divine appearance. (42)
Captivating the mind, speaking with gentle words, adorned with beautiful matted locks, well-nourished, youthful, divine, ascetics, and attended by Śrī. (43)
Both of them were residents of Vaikuṇṭha whose feet were worshipped by sages;
they were worthy of a royal palace and deserving of being cherished, protected, and honored.
With eyes like the petals of a lotus and faces like the beautiful moon, they are abodes of virtue; dark as a rain cloud, they are heart-pleasing and charmingly beautiful. (45)
Having seen that such two sons had been conceived for them by him,
the Queen and the King then emerged from their meditation and looked upon one another.
Nara-Nārāyaṇa said, "Let your resolve bear fruit.
Having heard this, they both became exceedingly satisfied; and having performed the rites prescribed for sacred fords (tīrtha), they departed.
Having turned back from that place, they went to the riverbank;
there, having sipped water and bathed, they then worshipped the golden image.
Having bathed Hari with the waters of the Gaṅgā and wiped him dry with garments,
they offered the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then performed an ablution with water.
Having thoroughly wiped [the image], offered fine garments and ornaments, prepared the beauty of its adornment, and presented incense and lamps; ||50||
Then, having perfumed the offering of lights with sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, saffron, collyrium, and liquid resin,
they performed the ārātrika ceremony.
They fed the Lord, magnified Him with hymns of praise, and offered Him handfuls of flowers along with fruits and other offerings. ||52||
Having offered them betel for chewing, they begged for their forgiveness;
thus, after sunrise, when five ghaṭīs had passed, [they spoke] again.
And having made an agreement at that time, they performed bathing, worship, hymns of praise, and so forth, as well as the offering of food, drinks, betel, sacrificial fees, and other gifts. (54)
Having offered food for the sages, the gods, and the earthly deities (brahmins), as well as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he should likewise present a handful of flowers as an arghya offering and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having offered praise, they performed the ritual dismissal;
thus, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama. (56)
Having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa and completed the ritual for the sacred ford, he [went] to the newly renovated capital city before the time of midday. (57)
Having arrived by celestial chariot at Sāketa along the Sarayū river,
he entered a great palace in the garden, beautifully adorned with trees and creepers.
The two of them had a pavilion constructed, adorned with gold and other precious materials,
as well as with water-pots, necklaces, ornaments, garments, decorations, banners, and so forth.
It was beautified with colored creepers, sprinkled with fragrant waters and the like,
provided with a sacrificial fire-pit, and resplendent with an altar.
It was adorned with mats made of *kaṭa* grass, couches, seats, and woolen carpets;
it was enriched with archways made of *kammānika* wood and supported by pillars of plantain trees.
With mirrors, moon-ornaments, the sounds of drums beaten at night, water-waves from mechanical devices, and streams of cool breezes; ||62||
It was beautified and adorned with various descents of gods and others;
its appearance was distinguished by nets [of light] through the reversal of water and land. 63.
It was adorned like a celestial chariot with instruments for hearing from afar, mirrors for seeing from afar, and devices for the accomplishment of grasping distant objects.
There, in the center of the pavilion, two mango trees were fashioned, and four *aśoka* trees were constructed at the side corners. (65)
And those two fastened a divine swing to the branches,
and there they bound the embodied gods and the goddesses to the chains.
And they prepared the chamber and soft coverings;
there, indeed, was a golden image in the form of Puruṣottama.
The queen and the king likewise placed [the image] upon it and caused it to sway there,
near the deity, within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
They fashioned a beautiful golden pitcher in the center, well-mixed with the seven types of grain and gold, jewels, diamonds, and other precious things. (69)
They placed upon it a vessel filled with sesame seeds, accompanied by the five jewels, water, flowers, fruits, ritual substances, and garments. (70)
Then they both wore a seal-ring bearing the *śrīphala* fruit, and [they established] a second golden image known as Śrī Puruṣottama. (71)
They placed it in a vessel and honored it with sixteen types of offerings; they performed the ritual waving of lamps (ārārtika) with great devotion.
At that very place, they then caused dances and songs to be performed;
likewise, they caused a fire-oblation to be offered into the midst of the sacrificial pit.
They fed the brahmins, the gods, virtuous women, the righteous,
as well as the wretched, the helpless, groups of weaklings, the poor, beggars, and others.
They caused sacrificial fees to be given and offered handfuls of flowers and unbroken rice grains;
as long as they were doing so, [they remained] there in that beautiful pavilion.
The god was seen with his younger brother, possessing a divine form, youthful, as beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud, dark-complexioned, and wearing matted locks. (76)
At the time of midday, the divine Puruṣottama appeared in embodied form, his face radiant with a smile and enriched by a halo of divine splendor. ||77||
Filled with the oil of divine vision, nourished, and accompanied by his well-nourished younger brother;
wearing yellow garments and bearing a bow, a shield, a sword, a conch, and matted hair. ||78||
Adorned with a golden crown and endowed with golden earrings,
his other hand was raised in blessing, and his mind was rich with compassion for service.
The Lord, who desires stability and exerts himself for the sake of providing delight and peace,
was born in the pavilion within the grove, as radiant as the midday sun.
Summoned there repeatedly by his younger brother with the words "O Rāmāditya," [he went] to that place where yogins delight in the Supreme Lord, who is radiant as the sun.
For this Rāmāditya was born as Śatakratu, and here Keśava appeared;
this is indeed proclaimed as the first incarnation of Rāma. ||82||
Upon seeing the Lord Keśava, a youth, as soon as he was born, both the queen and the king were struck with wonder and amazement. (83)
The blessed Lord Rāma, out of affection for his parents, said to them:
"I am pleased; ask for a boon as you desire, and I shall grant it."
Therefore, service in the form of an embodied image has been accepted by me;
having manifested myself, I, the Supreme Person, am present before you to grant a boon. (85)
That Hari who was seen at Badarī together with Nara as an ascetic, and those two of divine form and great beauty whom he beheld within his heart—[they are present here]. (86)
Thus, O Supreme Person, I have arrived here with my brother;
Narāditya, my brother, though an ascetic, is also with me. (87)
"Driven by compassion, he has come here to grant his own vision;
choose a boon, do not delay, for I am indeed departing. (88)
Having heard this, King Śatamakha and Queen Dyurvaṇikā became greatly agitated, their minds filled with intense anxiety.
"Saluting you, we remain; remain, do not go, do not depart!
O Lords, grant us your vision here in this abode forever. (90)
"O two monkeys, you shall obtain what is beautiful and desirable;
take this delightful food, drink, betel, and worship. (91)
"O children, always enjoy yourselves here in this garden, granting whatever you desire! Why is there such haste, my dear sons? Do not go away from me! (92)
Having spoken thus, the queen, filled with natural affection,
drew her two sons close to her, touched them, and her eyes became filled with tears.
Her breasts began to flow with milk, yet she could not bring herself to abandon him;
the king, his limbs filled with love, as did the others, was utterly enchanted by Hari. (94)
The two Blessed Ones said, "So be it," in the beautiful pavilion;
then, for a moment, both boys became intent on drinking from the breast.
Having been made to drink that milk which was as bright as the sky, she attained fulfillment;
being a virtuous woman, she became possessed of sons named Rāmāditya and Narāditya.
Then, at that great festival of bliss, she became truly happy;
for at midday, the King indeed performed the manifestation of Rāma. (97)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the sages Sanaka and others, Nārada and the other seers, and the devotees dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha—[all these were present]. ||98||

The inhabitants of Satyaloka and other realms, the gods of heaven, and human beings; those dwelling in Pātāla and elsewhere, as well as other insentient and sentient creatures—[all these abide within it]. (99)
Sacred fords, rivers, mountains, wildernesses, and forests; as well as world-ages, wish-fulfilling trees, thought-gems, and the cows of plenty. || 100 ||
At that festival, the Mantras, the Vedas, the Vittayas,
all the other Tattvas, and all the mind-born sons of Brahmā arrived.
The ancestors, the kings of the gods, and millions upon millions of earthly monarchs arrived on the ninth day to increase [the merit] with every kind of blessing.
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month, while the sun was situated in the middle [of the sky],
O Rāma, they beheld that man, Rāmāditya Jayantī, in the same manner as you.
Having received hospitality such as food and other honors, they felt their purpose was fulfilled;
and having attained Rāma’s favor, they performed songs and beautiful dances.
The performer of a hundred sacrifices gave away hundreds of millions and billions of cows;
so too did the carpenters, the world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the gods, and the rest. || 105 ||
They all went to their own places, and the people departed for their respective worlds;
meanwhile, the midday worship was performed by the queen and the king there in the pavilion.
In that same manner, the evening worship was completed at night;
then there was a vigil during the night, and in the morning, the ritual bathing and other rites were performed.

The worship of the image, the feeding of worthy recipients, the offering of sacrificial fees, and so forth—all this was performed according to the proper rite; thus, the vow was then brought to completion.
And he, together with his wife and their virtuous son, performed the breaking of the fast;
an inconceivable joy indeed arose for him on that ninth lunar day.
"By means of this vow of the month of Puruṣottama, which bestows sons—thus, O Lakṣmī, has this most excellent of vows been described to you. (110)
Whoever reads or listens to this account of the former deeds of Prāgrāma, which is the most excellent merit of the vow known as Rāmādityajayantī, [attains the highest goal]. (111)
One who causes [this] to be heard with supreme devotion shall partake in the merit of the vow;
he shall obtain his own desire, he shall obtain a kingdom, and he shall obtain sons, wealth, and so forth.
One shall also obtain the fruit of visiting sacred fords (tīrtha) established at Sāketa and on the Sarayū river,
and one shall obtain a powerful son who resembles Puruṣottama.
By the grace of the Supreme Soul, one may obtain whatever is desired—enjoyment, liberation, happiness, heaven, or even the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. 1.14

Thus ends the three hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled “The Description of How the Two Divine Sons Named Śrī Rāmāditya and Narāditya, the First Incarnations of Puruṣottama, Were Born in the City of Sāketa through the Performance of the Ninth-Day Vow of the Second Fortnight Following the Vision of Nara and Nārāyaṇa by King Śatamakhara and Queen Dyurvarṇā during Their Pilgrimage to Badarikāśrama,” within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, specifically the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of her who is Vikuṇṭhā, the daughter of Rādhikā in Goloka; a maiden born of mere resolve, her life is filled with vows.
During the intercalary month, the Lord, the Supreme Person Kṛṣṇa, together with Rādhā, performed the rāsa dance at that festival.
There arrived cowherds and cowherd-maidens, girls by the hundreds of millions and billions,
as well as housewives with their daughters, all endowed with the perfection of beauty and charm.
Seeing the gopīs, Rādhā herself desired her own daughter among those who were not her children;
the divine daughters of the gopīs then called out to their respective mothers. (4)
O Mother, these maternal goddesses indeed bring me such joy;
for she who is deprived of her daughter, even if united with her husband, is not truly fulfilled or happy.
A daughter is the very embodiment of a mother; indeed, she is a servant to her mother's needs.
In every way, through constant companionship, the daughter serves her mother.

Having bowed her head in humility and recognized Śrī Puruṣottama, the ant fell at the feet of that very one who bears the discus and the lotus. (75)
"O Goddess, I, Puruṣottama, am pleased by your vow;
choose a boon, and I shall grant it here, whatever dwells in your mind. (76)
Then the female ant, having bowed at his feet, held water to her mouth,
placed dust upon her head, and set his lotus-foot upon her breast.
Placing his hands above his throat, fixing his mind within the expanse of his heart,
and directing his eyes toward his own eyes, he took hold of Puruṣottama.
"Take your wife as your handmaid," she said;
but Mādhava, Hari, perceiving her supreme devotion, replied, "So be it. (79)
And he said to that female ant: "Remember what you previously requested in my presence—that you might have ten husbands one after another. (80)
"I alone am to be your husband, the manifest Śrī Puruṣottama;
become one of divine form and come together with me. (8.1)
In the supreme, imperishable abode, my eternal consort shall be;
you shall become her mind-born daughter, Satī, ever devoted to service. (82)
The maiden Vaṭasāvitrikā always resides here;
she is the daughter of Rudra, the Yakṣiṇī of the banyan tree, and the guardian of wealth. ||83||
Even within the mines of the earth, you remain in the form of Rudrī;
remember how, upon seeing Pracetas, your mind became filled with affection. (84)
Therefore, those ten pure Pracetasas shall become your husbands;
however, they are considered unsuitable for you in this present body. (85)
Therefore, O beloved, you shall likewise become the daughter of whichever trees are present here for the purpose of this worship and by whom you are requested.
"By my command, your name shall certainly be Vārkṣī;
O Goddess, become the daughter of a tree, assuming ten forms. (87)
Listen, I shall tell you this: assume those various forms—trees, pillars, crops, vegetables, and grasses. (88)
Receiving the status of father for these ten—the *nalas*, creepers, stalks, leaves, and tubers—become tenfold. (89)
Indeed, among those having only branches and fruit, and those having only flowers and no branches;
indeed, among those having only branches and flowers, and those having only fruit and no branches. || 90 ||
Indeed, among those with branches, fruits, and flowers, and among those without branches, fruits, and flowers;
indeed, among those with branches, fruits, and flowers, and among those without branches, fruits, and flowers. ||9 1 ||
"O you who possess only branches and leaves, and you who are merely without branches or leaves, having become a daughter, grant us juices; let there truly be ten daughters."
Having spoken thus with great devotion, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa assumed the form of an ant suitable for his splendor, took her, and departed joyfully. (93)
One form remained in the guise of a daughter for the sake of Satī,
while the other forms became youthful tree-maidens.
Then those trees of various species, having come into being, brought [the fruits] and,
according to dharma, gave them to the ten Pracetas.
In every respect, they bestow aesthetic delight and indeed grant the fruits [of their practice], through the instruction of Nārada during the liberation of the Pracetasas. (96)
"Even for those born of trees, there will indeed be liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, having performed the Ekādaśī vow, Vamrī, the daughter of a virtuous woman," 97.
For by means of her spiritual body, she attained the eternal, supreme abode;
indeed, she reached the state of being the wife of Puruṣottama, which bestows desired happiness. 98.
Likewise, the divine female bees (vamrī-devīs) were born from the drops of Hari’s compassion, as well as those born from trees;
these divine bees, however, were the first-born on the altar of Rudra, O excellent one. 99.
On the earth, at the sacrifice of Makha where the gods were victorious, there were sacrificial fuel-sticks;
by reciting this [text] from the month of Śrāvaṇa, one obtains the fruit arising from the vow of Ekādaśī.
He who obtains or causes this to be recited becomes possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain;
through pleasing Puruṣottama, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how Satī and Rudra’s mind-born daughter, the Yoginī Vamrī, by performing the Ekādaśī vow of the intercalary month attained a Brāhmī body fit for her desired abode of the Imperishable Brahman, and subsequently assumed various other forms such as being the wife of the ten Pracetas and becoming a tree-daughter," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, concerning the majesty of the month of Puruṣottama.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the goddess Joṣṭrī, born from the feet of Vairāja, who appeared as a servant at the commencement of creation.
The Vairāja Puruṣa, having produced his son Brahmā from the region of his navel,
then entrusted to him a female servant named Joṣṭrī.
But the Unborn One caused you— who were born from the feet of Vairāja and who served the Creator—
to dwell eternally in Satyaloka as if you were a servant.
Meditated upon by Brahmā with his mind, that attendant gave birth again and again to attendants of various births, as if born from a dream.
Having given birth to his daughter named Ṛṣisvanā, he offered her to the Ṛṣis; and having given birth to a daughter named Pipāsā, he offered her to the Pitṛs.
Having given birth to a daughter named Aśanā among the gods, he established [her] there;
having given birth to Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and others, he established his latent impressions (vāsanā) therein.
Among the mountains, Karā gave birth to a daughter and established her;
among humans, Vyavasāyā gave birth to a daughter and established her.
Having forcibly begotten a daughter among the Dānavas, he bestowed her [in marriage];
and having begotten a daughter named Vilāsā among the Daityas, he bestowed her [in marriage].
Having given birth to Viśvāsā as a daughter among beasts and birds, he entrusted her;
having given birth to Meghā as a daughter among trees and creepers, he entrusted her.
Having given birth to mud, she produced worms, moths, and other small creatures;
having given birth to the water-lily, she placed her daughter among those dwelling in the waters.
Having thus given birth to twelve daughters according to their respective lineages,
she respectfully presented them, one by one, as attendants to the subjects.
Thus, the female camel, ever devoted to service as the attendant of the Creator,
remained constantly engaged in the duty of service within Satyaloka.
Just as there are six duties for a Brahmin that indeed grant liberation,
so too is service considered to bring about liberation for the fourth caste.
Just as protection is considered to bring about the highest good for Kṣatriyas,
so too does service bestow the highest good upon the class of servants.
Just as charity indeed brings welfare to a Vaiśya in both worlds, so too may a group of female attendants obtain blessings through their service. 15.
Just as for a maidservant, constant obedience leads to liberation, so too does service by a group of attendants lead to liberation. 16.
Just as moral conduct within the vow of celibacy provides protection, so too must the service of the female attendant always provide protection. || 17 ||
Just as the honoring of the duties of a householder becomes a protection, so indeed does the service of the class of servants become a protection. || 18 ||
Just as penance is considered to bring happiness to those dwelling in the forest, so too does the happiness of service always accrue to the one who performs it. 19.
Just as the renunciation of those who possess the spirit of renunciation is considered to bestow supreme bliss,
so too service performed with devotion truly grants joy to the servant.
Just as sacrifice, austerity, meditation, recitation, charity, oblations,
and so forth grant happiness in both worlds, so too does service grant happiness everywhere.
Through service, heaven is attained, as well as sovereignty, prosperity, wealth and the like, fame, renown, merit, and the eternal, certain liberation. 22.
Service to Kṛṣṇa, service to one’s mother, service to one’s father, service to oneself, service to the gods, service to people, service to the elderly, and service to the distressed. ||23||
Service to one's husband is service to a virtuous woman; service to one's wife is worship of the Lord;
service to cows, the earth, the righteous, and the protectorless, as well as service to those who have sought refuge, is honoring the subjects. ||24||
Service to one's master, service to guests, and the act of pleasing others—these bring happiness in this world and the next, as well as merit and peace. (25)
Through the increase of the Supreme Person, however, that which is performed becomes a means to liberation;
such as service to the body, service regarding wealth, and the massaging of the feet and so forth. (26)
Service to virtue, service to material objects, service through food, the service of water, service to the home, service to the sick, and likewise service to the world, and so forth. ||27||
Everything performed with the vision of Brahman becomes a giver of happiness and liberation; therefore, the dharma of service should be understood as being inaccessible to all embodied beings. 28.
Everything else may be present, but there can be no service without faith;
indeed, even if joined with all else, service cannot exist without meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
Service may arise from the desire for liberation, or it may arise from the desire for happiness;
service may also arise from the desire for one's own self-interest, or from the longing for rewards.
But that which is performed without desire indeed bestows ten millionfold merit;
for the Supreme Person is the bestower of fruit for an action done without desire. 3.1.
Having reflected thus, that camel-mistress caused her daughters to perform service for all people, insofar as it would satisfy her inner self.
When satisfied by service, the elderly Brahmins bestow blessings; indeed, they offer their benedictions to the one who serves them.
The body goes to destruction, but service rendered to the Supreme attains companionship in the world; therefore, one should practice service. ||34||
Service rendered to others never goes to waste anywhere;
even service rendered in the past never becomes fruitless at a later time. (35)
That which is not given does not remain; only that which is given remains.
Non-service does not endure; service that has been performed endures. (36)
With body, mind, and speech, a living being should always serve their father and their infallible guru; the fruit of that shall be eternal. (37)
Thus the Joṣṭrī always serves the Supreme Lord in truth;
and with her daughters, she performs auspicious service to the subjects every day. (38)
Once, however, there was an assembly in the Sudharmā hall, consisting of sages, seers, gods, ancestors, humans, and trees. (39)
Likewise, the Piśācas and others, as well as the Kandas, the Vallyas, the Daityas, and the Dānavas—all embodied beings residing in the fourteen worlds—arrived there. (40)
Both invisible and visible, they arrived together with their wives;
all twelve of them came along with those various leaders of the assembly. 41.
Maidservants, female slaves, camel-riders, daughters of Aśanas, and others—those assemblies were served by them for the sake of those who are worthy. (42)
Having performed each of those services, all the beings were satisfied;
being pleased, they gave them rewards as well as blessings. (43)
May all become truly fortunate, filled with eternal bliss, and honored for their wealth, grain, fame, renown, respect, and virtues. ||44||
Endowed with supernatural powers and sovereignty, they possess beautiful forms;
they perpetually increase the lineage of the Joṣṭrī clan and always bear great splendor. 45.
O Goddesses who illuminate the world, although you are my attendants, may you always remain as the powers of Brahmā, possessing eternal and stable youth. (46)
Thus, having received their blessings when the assembly had concluded,
all the sisters went for a moment to the house of their mother’s eldest sister.
There, in Satyaloka, the great drum of Śrī Hari was heard, uttering the sound taught by Puruṣottama. 48.
"In this intercalary month, let embodied beings perform my worship on the twelfth day; let them observe my vow, which is my sole refuge. (49)
"I, the Supreme Person, shall grant you whatever your heart desires;
you must not be distressed, for though the vow is brief, its merit is great. (50)
"May those whose fortune is indeed radiant accept that fruit;
I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, am in every way the giver out of compassion. (5.1)
I shall grant you perfections, I shall grant you my abode, and I shall indeed grant you eternal happiness;
I shall grant everything, and I shall grant myself, except for that which is not desired.
Observe the vow by eating once a day, by eating only at night, by subsisting on fruits, by drinking only water, by consuming curd, or by eating only wild-growing grain. //5.3//
Whether one's vow was performed by means of leaves, roots, and tubers, or by subsisting on air alone— even if the vow was performed through even a small fraction of my grace— (54)
Whether with buttermilk or milk, with sesame seeds or a handful of mung beans—
by whatever means the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata) has been undertaken.
I shall fulfill all his desires in every way;
my worship must be performed in the morning, at midday, and at the onset of night.
A vigil should be observed, and meals should be offered;
furthermore, gifts should be bestowed according to one's ability and according to what has been acquired. (57)

One should offer me a handful of flowers, likewise a handful of unbroken grains (akṣata), one should offer a handful of water, and one should offer a handful of meditative visualization (bhāvanā). ||58||
The observer of the vow should offer a handful of oil, he should offer a handful of himself,
and he should offer everywhere the most excellent handful of total surrender.
I am to be reached through contemplation, reached through affection, and reached through love;
I am to be reached through the reality of things, reached through self-interest, or whatever else I may be. 60.
Long life will pass away, and youth will pass away;
all prosperity will go to destruction, yet my compassion is considered eternal.
Yogic practices will fall into decay, nourishment will turn to decrepitude, and the body will be reduced to ashes; yet my compassion is considered eternal.
Whatever has arisen—be it merit, sovereignty, wealth, or the like—is subject to destruction;
yet my compassion for awakening is eternal, for its destruction is never found. (63)
May the wretched receive compassion; may they cast far away their poverty.
By my command and through this very vow, may they indeed become eternally prosperous.
Having thus heard the sound of the drum, those twelve daughters of Mātṛvardhana undertook a vow of subsisting on milk for twelve days of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Moreover, the two beloved ones (Joṣṭrī) performed a vow imbued with devotion;
having bathed in the morning and remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa thirteen times, they observed the rite. (66)
Having fashioned an image of gold, they worshipped Puruṣottama;
[they constructed] a pavilion with pillars of plantain trees and archways of Aśoka, mango, and other trees.
Adorned with strings of flower garlands, beautified by golden garments and the like, and decorated with festive lamps, fine jars, archways, and other ornaments. ||68||
In the center of that, having caused a beautiful and excellent maṇḍala to be made,
[he should place] a lovely golden pitcher with sprouts of the five jewels.
Having placed a garment, fruit, sandalwood, and unbroken grains in the center,
and having set a golden vessel containing sesame seeds and sugar upon its head— 70.
Having installed there the Lord of Gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama,
they worshipped him with devotion using the sixteen articles of worship.
Having performed the invocation and other rites, and having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and waters,
one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) and offer garments and ornaments.
Having adorned Śrī Kṛṣṇa with saffron, collyrium, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, and sandalwood, and having offered incense and a lamp; ||73||

The food offering consists of excellent milk-rice (pāyasa), sweet foods such as fried cakes (pūrikā) and the like, fruit such as mangoes and other varieties, and the drink is nectar-like sweet water. (74)
Having offered everything that was desired by the Lord—betel, fruit, and whatever else—they performed the ritual waving of lights (ārātrika). ||75||
In the morning, they offered prostrations like a staff, hymns of praise, circumambulations, beautiful joined palms,
a request for forgiveness for their offenses, and final water for the feet.
They continued their service in that same manner at midday and even at night;
during the night, they kept watch with dancing, singing, and other such activities.
And those twelve maidens were endowed with amorous gestures and expressions,
just as Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Nārāyaṇa, and Śrī Puruṣottama are.
Through the sentiment of the erotic (śṛṅgāra-rasa), the Supreme Person becomes gracious;
being drawn [toward him], that compassionate one grants his vision. (79)
Thus, with great joy, they performed dancing and singing;
then, at the time of Brahma, in the morning, Hari appeared, smiling.
He was young, robust, and handsome, the abode of the minds of young women; he possessed a beauty exceeding ten million desires, and his limbs were endowed with great vigor. ||8 1||
"Pervaded by pleasure in every hair, illuminated by the bodiless god (Kāma) in every limb, I am pleased, I am pleased! he said repeatedly while being served. (82)
The female attendant chooses her desired boons in every way:
the status of Indrāṇī, or the status of Śivā, or even the status of Brahmāṇī. (83)

Whether it be the state of being Kṛṣṇa, the state of being Vaiṣṇava, the state of being Brāhmī, or even that which is beyond them—whatever desire you may have, I shall grant that very thing today; of this there is no doubt.
The worlds beyond the highest were conquered by her through twelve incarnations—women who served with faith, meditative cultivation, and hearts moistened with affection. (85)
"Even you maidservants have today become mistresses indeed through your service;
choose now the one dwelling in your minds, O heart-entrancing ones! Do not delay. (86)
I am the servant of servants, the teacher of teachers;
I am the friend of friends, and the right-hand man of the left-handed ones. ||87||
Among the affectionate, I am the most affectionate; among those who provide refuge, I am the protector;
and for those who have renounced all their possessions for my sake, I am the giver of all their possessions. (88)
I do not attain such satisfaction through wealth, servants, or service as I attain through the service performed by my own self. (89)
Where service is not divided into "I am the servant" and "He is the master," where the devotee indeed serves me himself with his own very being—[therein lies true devotion]. (90)
Therefore, let my beloveds speak: "What shall I give? What shall I say?
What shall I bestow upon my beloveds—my very all, together with my heart? (91)
"All of us, our beloveds, have offered ourselves to the Supreme Self—to the supreme lover, the beloved husband, Śrī Puruṣottama. (92)
Likewise, the duty of female slaves is the total surrender to the Teacher;
and likewise, the duty of beloveds is the total surrender to the dear husband. (93)
Likewise, it is the duty of a master to always accept those who have been offered;
indeed, the duty of beloved women is to act for the pleasure of their beloved. 94.
The beloved is the entire possession of the beloved; for the sake of the beloved, everything is dear.
And for the beloved as well, the beloved alone—the very treasure of compassion—is everything.
Thus, O Keśava, act as you wish in this great matter;
my mind and my entire being are offered unto you—do whatever you deem right.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord, then said:
"I know everything; likewise, I accept all within my heart. (97)
Holding their hands even from the outside, I make them heart-pleasing;
through the touch of my hand, may they come to possess divine forms for me. (98)
May my beloved wives always abide in the abode known as the Imperishable;
may my power, consisting of light, be the one who delights in my own essential nature. 99.
The Goddess, who bestows all bliss, consists of consciousness and is my very own nature;
she, who is consciousness in the form of existence, knowledge, and bliss, has been made by me as my own self.
And let there be twelve other wives for me eternally;
by their respective names, let those wives dwell in my house there.
All those wives, who were in every respect identical to me, did not indeed seek any pleasure or anything else whatsoever without me. (102)
Thus has the thirst known as "the caravan-leader" been described; now hear about "the desire for wealth" according to its meaning:
she who always desires to drink my own semen and no other. (103)
That wife of mine, Pipāsā, who has taken my own form, has been protected by me;
likewise, my wife Aśanā, who always eats me. (104)
"She enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahmā"—
thus she was called Sārthāśanā, and that wife of mine was protected by me.
And she who eternally causes me, her supreme husband, to dwell within her own self— that wife, whose latent impression is filled with love, has been well protected by me.
She whose name must be spoken here, and whose meditation has been cultivated by me—
she, my beloved, comes to my hand, for she is indeed dear to my hand.
"Ka" is happiness, my supreme bliss; "Śam" is Lakṣmī, the divine prosperity.
She who, through service, attains and receives these from me is Karāyikā. (108)
"Resolute effort is dear to me because it possesses the meaningful certainty that 'she has performed every action, both in deed and in spirit, solely for my sake.'"
She who is capable of enduring all my actions is dear to me;
she who intensely endures my pleasure is Prasahyakā. (110)
For my sake, my divine wife named Vilāsā, who acts in accordance with my every whim, shall sport in every way for my enjoyment.
Her breath indeed cannot remain without me;
and I am hers, for she is my wife for the sake of happiness.
Thus, having attained confidence, my beloved became full of trust;
for her, there is no life and no breath at every moment without me. 11.3
She mists her husband with rain, showers love upon her lord, and indeed bestows affection upon me; she is considered by me to be a cloud dear to my heart. 1.14
She who, out of devotion, restrains all her actions within me—
she for whose sake the subduing of actions is dear, like mud— is my beloved.
She who daily contemplates her own self as my field for my sake,
sustains me within her own soul just as water is contained within a jar.
She is my wife Kumbhikā; you are proclaimed to be my wives.
May those twelve divine ones dwell within my abode of twelve syllables.
Now, indeed, in other forms consisting of twelve powers,
they exist in yet other guises, offered to Mahākāla.
Then it pervaded the universe, both that which eats and that which does not eat;
indeed, the flow of thirst runs at the forefront of this world-process.
This world, composed of a mixture of the insentient and the sentient, dwells by means of latent impressions (vāsanā);
herein, through the power of karma, there occurs the exchange between embodied beings.
The year is maintained and nourished by the passage of time through its various efforts; it endures both seasonal afflictions and the pairs of opposites by means of its persistent power.
Through *vilāsa* (sportive charm), he causes living beings to cast off their weariness;
through *viśvāsa* (trust), embodied beings engage in action out of desire for the fruit. 122.
Indeed, through the rain of affection that is like a cloud, they delight the subjects for many years;
but when the subjects have become like mud, they remain within me in that very mud.
In these jars, globes, and cosmic eggs, she is in every way considered the one who establishes and protects them in their respective places.
Thus, may the powers of Time— which is my own power—
become effectors of action day by day in the world, and may they be dedicated to Time.
Then, just as the daughters of Joṣṭrikā were dwelling there, may they likewise dwell within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), O Creator, having fashioned it so. (126)
By my desire, let them dwell with Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through their own third forms as the mother of the camel.
Thus, having been properly enjoined by me through these three forms,
let them perform service here toward Mahākāla as well as toward me.
"I am your master and husband, the Supreme Person;
sport with me freely in the supreme imperishable realm."
Likewise, there are others who are my powers, accompanied by Mahākāla;
and likewise, others in my creation who always carry out their respective tasks.
Thus, in three ways, I have bestowed this service upon you;
indeed, the eternal fruit of the vow of the twelfth day has been granted.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person,
took those divine women with him and likewise established others there.
Having given [the boon] to Mahākāla, Hari went to another imperishable abode.
Speak, O Lakṣmī, of Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, the supreme among persons. 133.
"What does she give, and out of compassion, what infinite fruit does she yield from even a small gift?"—thus has this entire narrative of the goddess Joṣṭrī been told to you. (134)
The two divine sisters, the bestowers of wealth, having reached the god Indra, the bestower of vitality, the great Vedic speech increased toward the Supreme Person. || 1.35 ||
Whoever causes this to be heard, or listens to it, or recites it, shall also certainly obtain such a fruit as that of the vow. || 136 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Puruṣottama-Nārāyaṇa, who was pleased by the service of the twelve daughters beginning with Joṣṭrī—the daughter of Vairāja—and by the vow of the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), as well as His assuming the threefold form," in the section on the Greatness of the Month of Puruṣottama within the first book, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; having seen the excellent Rādhikā who possessed a son, Śrī also spoke to the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 1 ||
O Hari, just as Rādhā, who possesses a daughter, shines most brightly, so too does she attain honor in every respect among all those who possess daughters. || 2 ||
O Supreme Person, by whatever means possible, when shall I become a mother of a daughter?
Having shown mercy to me, please grant me a daughter who is a source of auspiciousness.
Thus entreated by her, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then granted Śrī a boon,
saying, "So be it," and sported with her in beautiful play.
By the mere glance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there was a daughter who graced the couch of Śrī;
she was divine, equal to Kṛṣṇa in form and equal to Śrī in beauty.
She appeared suddenly, youthful as soon as she was born;
like a wish-fulfilling cow, she was endowed with all perfections and was given the name Sudughā (the Good Milker).
Summoned by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and by Śrī as well, she is indeed called "the good milker";
that daughter of Kṛṣṇa is the "good milker" who yields all desires.
Equal to Śrī, possessing the very form of Śrī, and as exceedingly radiant as Śrī herself; with all her limbs fully developed, she was endowed with a golden luster.
From the very moment of her birth, she was naturally inclined toward the work of milking cows;
she appeared devoted to that task and was likewise beloved by the cattle.
When she was born there, a great festival took place,
performed by sages and gods for the abiding of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s own Śrī.
During that great festival, there was the dancing of the goddesses, the singing of the Apsarases, and the exquisite dancing, singing, and instrumental music of the Gandharvas.
The sages received blessings that the girl would be well-protected by the gods, and the voices of the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses were indeed filled with words of auspicious increase. 12.
Likewise, handfuls of flowers fell upon Sudughā;
and seeing the girl’s mass of splendor like milk, the young maidens [beheld her].
The female companions rejoiced greatly and took delight with her again and again;
they entertained her, she delighted them, and they all sported together with her.
Then, desiring to know her purpose, she milked again and again; for she reflected from the depths of her heart, "What must I do here? (15)
Having learned that her father and Kṛṣṇa had instructed her thus regarding the power of yoga, O daughter, she milked the cow Urjāhuti; with its milk, Indra was nourished.
Thus commanded, the excellent milch-cow was then greatly delighted; having bowed to her parents, she reflected upon the prosperity and nourishment of Indra.
In whatever spheres and cosmic eggs there may be,
such is the station of Mahendra and the divine sovereignty that exists in heaven.
Having meditated with his heart upon all those kingdoms and their constituent parts,
he contemplated a means for their eternal prosperity.
I am the illustrious Śrīputrī, the one who yields milk well; I exist in the form of milk, and having bestowed the milk of nectar upon the gods in heaven, I dwell there.
At the beginning of the great [creation], having become the immortal self of well-performed deeds, I dwell there;
and I offer water, funeral cakes, milk-rice, and other such oblations to the ancestors.
Having extracted the nectar of essence from cattle, humans, and trees,
and having given it, I bring nourishment even to the earth with this divine, delicious nectar.
Having made the moisture in water into nectar, I provide nourishment;
for fire, I give the sweetness of digestion, the nectar of maturation.
I offer the nectar of sense-objects to the Self dwelling within the body;
Indra is this Self, whose powers are the senses resting upon their objects. (24)
By means of these, indeed, they become eaters of nectar within their very selves;
for the butter residing in the principles is the clarified butter, the nectar that effects all things.
Thus, I exist as one of many forms, consisting of action;
for the sake of Indra’s attainment of happiness, I abide as the milch-cow Śakti.
And having become the two offerings of strengthening oblations (*ūrjāhuti*) in the sacrifice, I bring about nourishment;
I act in such a way that Indra's protection may be complete in every respect.
"Having become [this] again and again, I shall enter everywhere this very day";
having reflected thus, that maiden, who was like a cow yielding much milk and possessed of many forms, [acted]. (28)
She became visible and invisible, entering at her will;
she then entered Indra’s beautiful heaven and increased there in prosperity.
All the nectars were milked out and increased with extreme velocity; in all the worlds, the earth became filled with glory, and prosperity was enchanting.
The gods and goddesses shone with ever-increasing splendor even than before;
all their abundant riches, though being expended and enjoyed, remained intact. ||3 1||
They did not diminish even slightly, nor were they exhausted due to their noble lineage;
and a prosperity, unseen and unheard of before, became manifest as bliss. (3.2)
Thus, when that auspicious time had passed and the first Kṛta Yuga had gone by,
there was a venerable sage named Medhāvī, a great performer of sacrifices.

For the sake of rain, for the sake of sons and so forth, for the sake of happiness and so forth, for the sake of heaven, and for the attainment of merit, he performs sacrifices according to the rules and causes them to be performed as well. (34)
For the sake of obtaining a pair of sons and daughters, he indeed performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice;
then Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, manifested himself in many ways.
With his own two hands, he took the excellent sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered by him and said:
"I am pleased; choose a boon as you desire. (36)
The earth, sovereignty, delicious tastes, milk, heaven, a son, or a daughter—whatever you desire, I give it to you; do not delay.
Having heard this, the wise Brahmin said to his son: "Give [the wealth] to me;
this sacrifice called Putreṣṭi has been performed by me for the sake of a son. (38)
The Blessed One said: "Indeed, for seven births you shall have no son;
a son is born through the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, but regarding his longevity there is doubt. (3.9)
"O Brahmin, choose this daughter if it pleases you—she who gives happiness at birth but brings misery immediately after death. (40)
O sinless one, the line on your wife’s forehead shines as a sign of a daughter;
she will be even more renowned than a son and will be devoted to your service.
"O brāhmaṇa, act in such a way that there shall indeed be no grief; O lord of the earth, take the consent of your wife. Having accepted her words, the brahmin took her counsel.
Then the Blessed One granted him the favor of a meal;
having accepted it, the brahmin said to Hari, "My daughter is like Śrī herself."
O Lord, may she who is peaceful, who bestows happiness upon all beings, and who grants the drinking of nectar like a wish-fulfilling cow, be auspicious. 44.

"So be it," Hari replied, and he sent forth the cow who yields all desires for the sake of Medhāvin’s daughter; yet, by his command, even that cow who yields all desires [remained] for the sake of the daughter.
Then she appeared upon the bed of Medhāvin’s wife;
she was a divine, mental creation, shining like another Śrī.
Exceedingly beautiful from the moment of birth, endowed with full maturity, charming with beauty and grace, she cast glances from the corners of her eyes. (47)
Endowed with qualities such as cleverness, she was the sole object of praise for her parents; beautiful with every excellent virtue, she was exceedingly dear to them. 48.
Lalitā was always cherished like a son and was never reproached;
she was skilled in ethics and literature and was proficient in the knowledge of the self. 49.
The maidservant always served her parents, and they were pleased by her service;
as time passed, O Lakṣmī, their mother met her death. (50)
She was cherished with joy by her father as a daughter among those who were like sons;
and as time passed, she likewise became like a yoginī.
Seeing the happiness of those standing by their wives, and longing for the happiness of sons and grandsons,
that wise maiden Medhāvatī formed a desire for the life of a householder.
And she reflects upon me alone: "How might there be happiness and the rise of good fortune?
How might my husband possess the fortune of virtues and my sons be givers of joy? (53)
For that purpose, which sage or which lord of gods shall I worship?
I am a young woman in the midst of my friends, a maiden experiencing great sorrow. (54)
"I am not acquainted with my husband's happiness as my circle of friends is.
Even though her father recognized that the young girl was thus distressed by anxiety, [he did not speak].
The wise one wandered over the earth, searching for a bridegroom equal to him;
failing to find such a match, his resolve shattered, he fell into a state of intense fever.
Even as he was coming toward his own abode, he fixed his mind upon Hari;
he remembered Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men. (57)
He fell upon the courtyard of the house, and the messengers of Kṛṣṇa arrived;
seizing that sage by the hand, they went to the lotus-like heart of Kṛṣṇa.
Perceiving that his life-breath had departed, the daughter cried out, "Alas! Alas!
and, placing her father's body upon her lap, she lamented in extreme distress.
"Alas, alas, father! Having abandoned your own daughter who is bereft of her mother, and likewise having left her without a protector, where indeed have you gone? (60)
There is no brother, nor kin, nor mother, nor protector;
how shall I remain, O father? I shall die, without a doubt. (6.1)
Having heard these and other such lamentations, the ascetics arrived there;
they beheld the deceased sage and, filled with grief, cremated him.
Having consoled that maiden, they all went to their own abodes;
the maiden, maintaining her fortitude, performed the funeral rites for Śakti.
O Lakṣmī, when some time had passed, by the power of destiny, the sage Durvāsas, a devotee of Śiva,
arrived at that house, impelled by his future strength.
Seeing him approaching, the maiden bowed at the feet of the sage and respectfully worshipped him with offerings of water, flowers, and other honors.
Salutations to you, O son of Atri! From where have you come, O Sage?
By serving your sacred ford, the dawn of my good fortune has occurred.
Today my birth has become fruitful, and today my vow has borne fruit;
today my merit has reached its fulfillment, since I have beheld one such as you.
Having heard her, Durvāsas said: "Excellent! May it be well with you, my daughter.
I am coming from Kailāsa; I am going to the Badarī forest."
"If you have a purpose to inform the Lord Nārāyaṇa so that he may be seen, let it be reported.
Medhāvatī said to the sage, "There is nothing at all to be reported to the Master. (69)
From now on, auspiciousness shall prevail through the grace of beholding you;
neither mother, nor father, nor kinsman—no one at all—is my protector. (70)
"No one desires me for the sake of taking my hand in marriage, O Brahmin; I am as if wishing for death—what shall I do? Please act for my benefit. (7.1)
Having heard this, the sage reflected well upon the means and spoke to his daughter:
"O fortunate one, three months from now shall be the month of Puruṣottama. (72)
One who bathes there at Janatīrtha is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
indeed, no other month exists that is equal to this, the best of months. (73)
All months, as well as fortnights, lunar festivals, and seasons,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the month of Puruṣottama.
All spiritual practices together with thousands of baths in the Gaṅgā and Godāvarī are not worth even a sixteenth part of the intercalary month.
The month is the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, known by the name Puruṣottama; when that youthful month is properly observed, every desired object is accomplished.
Therefore, O daughter, you too should always serve that Supreme Person for a month with devotion, just as I do, serving the Supreme Person constantly.
If you desire that which is to be attained, then perform a vow according to your pleasure;
O daughter, I shall go to the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, Medhāvatī then departed quickly from there,
intent on awaiting the intercalary month, which bestows auspiciousness and its fruits at that very time.
Holding him in her heart and directed toward him, she practiced difficult austerities:
during the day she stood in the midst of five fires, and at night she remained in cold water. (80)
Taking no food and carrying out her meditations, she remained as if established in samādhi;
the Blessed Lord, the husband of Pārvatī, was pleased with her austerity.
He revealed his own form, visible to the eyes, to the young girl;
she prostrated before Hara and worshipped him with flowers and other offerings from her mind.
With a spirit of devotion, he offered praise: "Salutations to you, who are easily pleased;
salutations to you, Śaṅkara, the support of the son who is himself without support. ||8 3 ||
Homage to the three-eyed one, who is Sūrya, Agni, and Soma; homage to Death!
Homage to you here, who fulfills the desires of Pārvatī and the female ascetics. 84.
"O Śaṅkara, effect the deliverance of this maiden who is without a protector.
Having praised him thus and bowed again, the daughter of the sage fell silent. (85)
Having heard this, Sadāśiva, with a serene countenance, said to her:
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you! I am pleased; I shall grant it to you. (86)
The girl said: "O ocean of compassion, if you are pleased with me, grant me a husband!
Grant me a husband! Grant me a husband! Husband, husband! (87)
Having heard this, Mahādeva then spoke to the daughter of the ṛṣi:
"Since you have requested a husband from the Lord five times," (88)
Therefore, O daughter, there shall be five righteous kṣatriya kings for you— performers of sacrifices, true to their word, and filled with your essence.
Now, let those five Indras born in a former kalpa who dwell in Satyaloka become the husbands of your daughter.
"Indeed, with this very body now rendered divine, come today to his presence with me as your helper, O Satyabhāmā. (91)
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, having endowed her with a most divine body,
led Medhāvatī through the celestial path to Satyaloka.
He heard a divine drum sounding: "Perform the supreme vow on the thirteenth day of the intercalary month; it shall grant whatever fruits one desires. (93)
"By means of a single vow, may my attainment be equal to his attainment.
Having heard this, Medhāvatī said, "How can the attainment of Kṛṣṇa be achieved? (94)
Having heard this drum, a desire for knowledge has arisen within me;
act in such a way that Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa may meet with me.
Śambhu said: "O auspicious daughter, may all prosperity be yours in every way;
I am pleased by your words, which are solely intent upon attaining Kṛṣṇa."
Whether it be sovereignty, heaven, the supreme station of Brahmā, or even the state of Īśvara—all of this becomes tasteless without Kṛṣṇa, the best of men. (97)
Through devotion, that supreme person Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is attained;
perform the vow of the thirteenth lunar day as it was spoken by Dundubhi. 98.
Having observed a fast and subsisted on fruit, one should worship the Supreme Self with sixteen articles, and likewise feed and cherish Him.
"One should keep a vigil at night and, being well-pleased, give everything as a gift.
Having said this, he sent her to Satyaloka and [performed] the five-fold Indra-rite.
Having given her away in the form of his wife, Hara spoke again to his daughter regarding the vow of the thirteenth day of the month of Puruṣottama.
Hari will indeed find you when he has assumed a human form;
there, by the power of your asceticism, you shall be born without the aid of a womb.
There, these five husbands will arise, born from portions of the gods;
they are produced from portions of Dharma, Marut, Mahendra, and the two Aśvinī-kumāras.
Then Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa will indeed meet her as her protector;
having attained the happiness born of a husband, she shall thereafter go to the supreme abode.
But those who are devotees of Puruṣottama, endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, have attained, will attain, and are attaining success in both this world and the next. (105)
"We are all leaders who serve Puruṣottama.
Having spoken thus, Hara Nīlakaṇṭha quickly vanished.
Having consulted her husbands, Medhāvatī, following the instruction of Śaṅkara,
observed the vow of the thirteenth lunar day, including fasting and a night vigil.
Having bathed Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, with the five nectars and water,
[one should offer] garments, ornaments, food offerings, fruits, betel, and so forth.

Having performed the offering of incense, lamps, beautiful flowers, and other items, as well as the *akṣata* with joined palms (*añjali*) and the request for forgiveness, and having conducted the *ārātrika* ceremony and other rites, he made his petition to the Supreme Lord.
"O Father, grant me your vision; be my helper in this world.
Just then, the Lord of Śrī arrived there, mounted upon Garuḍa.
"I am indeed pleased with you, my daughter, because of this vow on the thirteenth day; O daughter, I shall always protect you and remain with you as long as I live in the forest. (111)
Again that daughter spoke: "O Guru, O Father, may my liberation come about at the end of my life in such a way that I desire no other wish. (11.2)
"So be it," Hari said, and he spoke further in detail:
"Listen, my daughter, at the end of the Dvāpara age, I myself shall be the Lord Kṛṣṇa."
"I shall indeed descend upon the earth for the purpose of removing the burden of the world,
from the midst of the sacrificial altar of the king named Yajñasena."
You shall be born as the maiden Kanakaprabhā;
you shall become known as Yājñasenī, Vairājī, and Kṛṣṇā.
And at that very same time, five Indras shall be your husbands;
they will be portions of the gods, lords of immeasurable prowess.
But when, O daughter, having made you my instrument, I have destroyed the asuras, daityas, and dānavas, and shall depart for my own abode— then [you shall follow].
Having restrained you, I shall lead you at the proper time and for the sake of the necessary task;
then you will regain your abode in Goloka, where your birth took place.
Then, O daughter of noble birth, I shall lead you with your body to the supreme abode of the Vedic syllable (Om),
my own auspicious refuge at my feet.
"Thus, my daughter, this narrative of what was to happen has been told to you.
Dwell in truth and happiness, my daughter; I am now departing for my own abode."
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Puruṣottama then vanished;
that daughter of Kṛṣṇa, Yājñasenī, shall become a cow that yields milk at will.
By means of this vow on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the intercalary month, she shall attain the supreme abode, according to the word of Puruṣottama. || 122 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this story of Śrīputrī.
They are blessed, they possess true birth, and they are worthy of worship as well as purifiers.
By those who have worshipped Puruṣottama with various observances,
one shall obtain the fruit of this vow through hearing it or even through reciting it.
One obtains the assistance of Kṛṣṇa, who is esteemed by the Supreme Person;
indeed, whether it be a man, a woman, or even another, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, within the *Puruṣottama-māsa-māhātmya*: the transformation of Sudughā, the daughter of Śrī, into the essence of nectar (*rasāmṛta*) by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of Indra’s prosperity in Goloka; her birth as one not born from a womb in the house of the wise sacrificial priest; the death of her parents; the arrival of Durvāsas; the instruction on the vow of the *Puruṣottama-māsa*; her penance upon Śaṅkara; and her prayer for a husband five times over in Satyaloka.

The three hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Status of Five Indras, the Vision of Puruṣottama through the Trayodaśī Vow, and the Granting of the Boon that Yājñasenī, having become the mistress of five husbands on earth, shall attain liberation."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, how by the vow of the fourteenth day, the excellent king Citradharma obtained a virtuous son renowned as Dṛḍhadhanvan. || 1 ||
He obtained a kingdom, sons, grandsons, and a devoted wife;
and in the end, he attained the world of the Lord, which is difficult even for yogis to reach.
Endowed with all excellent qualities, a master of the Vedas, and a protector of his subjects, he became the son whom his father had beheld [in vision]. (3)
Having reflected upon those various dharmas, he consecrated him in his own kingdom;
then, he propitiated the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
For that purpose, the forest land is indeed entirely suitable;
[there,] Dhruva, Ambarīṣa, Śaryāti, Yayāti, and Śaśabindu [attained their goals]. (5)
Bhagīratha, Śibi, Rantideva, Rukmāṅgada, and others—
Divodāsa, Abhayakhaṭvāṅga, and other such most excellent royal sages (rājarṣis)— [all attained their goals].
These and other kings of great being have gone to the forest in various kalpas and other kalpas, having renounced manifold enjoyments.
Having attained the eternal by means of the transient through the propitiation of Puruṣottama,
I too must therefore perform the service of Hari in the forest.
Having severed the bond called latent tendencies toward wife, children, home, and so forth,
and having resolved thus in his mind, Citradharman went to the forest.
Having reached the hermitage of Pulaha, he performed austerities while remembering Hari;
having become pure and possessing a divine body, he went to the abode of Hari.
Then Dṛḍhadhanvā performed the funeral rites for his father;
having established the capital at the city of Puṣkarāvarta, he [ruled there]. (11)
Together with his wife Guṇasundarī, the princess of Vidarbha,
and his four sons, the king ruled over the entire earth.
Once, while Dṛḍhadhanvan was sleeping at night, he had this thought: "He possesses eloquent speech, a splendid chariot, and jeweled earrings of wonderful design. (13)
I have indeed never performed charity, austerity, recitation, or fire-offerings;
nevertheless, by what fortune has this sovereign kingdom come to me? 14.
Rising at the hour of Brahmā, that king, intent on hunting,
mounted his horse and went to the shore of a lake in the forest.
At that banyan tree, there was a parrot with a human voice;
it recited a single beautiful verse again and again.
Even though you possess great wealth, sovereignty, and such things as the body that grant pleasure, why do you not contemplate the Lord of Lakṣmī? How will you reach the further shore?
Having heard the words of the parrot, the king rejoiced as they brought him liberation;
having gone out on a hunt, the king reflected upon the parrot’s speech.
He returned home, and at that moment Vālmīki arrived there;
having honored Vālmīki, the king asked him about what the parrot had spoken.
"What did he say? How did he speak? Who was this Śuka, O Sage?
Having heard this and meditated upon it for a moment, Vālmīki spoke to the king: kimuvāca kathaṃ prāha ko’sāvāsīcchuko mune | śrutvā kṣaṇaṃ ca taddhyātvā vālmīkirāha bhūpatim || 20 ||
Listen, O King, to the account of your deeds in a previous birth:
in the Dravidian country, on the banks of the Tāmraparṇī river, you were a twice-born brahmin.
And Sudevā, the wife of Gautama born of Gautama, being childless, spoke to her husband in great distress because she lacked offspring. (22)
A lineage that is pure in descent leads to happiness both in this world and the next;
yet, without obtaining such an excellent son, life here is indeed fruitless.
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining a virtuous son, we two must constantly propitiate the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣottama, through ascetic penance.
Heeding the words of his lawful wife, on the auspicious bank of the Tāmraparṇī river,
he subsisted on dry leaves and water, taking food only every fifth day.
For four thousand years they performed supreme austerity;
by that, the worlds trembled, and Mādhava appeared.
