Seated upon Garuḍa, Hari said: "O Sudeva, may it be well with you;
O Gautamī, may prosperity be yours as well. Do not perform excessive penance. (27)
Having heard this, the two bowed to Kṛṣṇa and said, "Victory to you, O Mādhava!
Sudeva said, "O Blessed One, O Lord Hari, grant me a son. (28)
Hari said: "All the letters upon your forehead have been seen by me;
therein, for seven births, there is no happiness from a son for you."
Gautamī said: "If the Lord of Ramā is useless at the forefront of fortune, and if fate alone is to be relied upon, then what is the purpose of Hari? (30)
Having heard this, Garuḍa spoke to Hari Janārdana:
"O You who cannot endure the suffering of Your devotees, make my purpose meaningful for the sake of Hari."
The greatness of worshipping you is never, never indeed fruitless;
do not render your power to act or to refrain from acting useless. (3.2)
Seeing Garuḍa’s persistence, Hari said, "So be it";
however, the suffering caused by that will certainly befall the couple.
Having spoken thus and mounted upon Garuḍa, Hari departed for Goloka.
After some time had passed, an auspicious son was born to the wife of Sudeva.
As time passed, he grew up, was invested with the sacred thread, and then instructed in his studies.
At one point, the divine sage Devala, the destroyer of sins, arrived there.
Seeing his hand marked with the signs of the parasol, lotus, barley-corn, and chowrie, and with the lines of longevity clearly visible, he then spoke while shaking his head.
"O illustrious lady, this son of yours, Sudeva, will meet his death in the water during his twelfth year; therefore, let there be no grief for you."
Upon hearing this, the two of them lamented, and then Devala emerged from there.
When that time of misfortune arrived, his son went indeed to the pond.
Having fallen into the bottomless water, he sank and died;
and learning of their son's death from his friends, the father and mother [were overcome]. (39)
Having taken up the corpse there, they were both deeply moved and wept profusely; they lamented excessively and renounced water and food. (40)
That month became dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; it was Puruṣottama itself.
Even though those two were unaware, their service to Puruṣottama took place. ||41||
Being thus exceedingly purified, Hari himself appeared;
the twice-born man, together with his wife, prostrated himself like a staff before Śrī Hari.
Hari said, "O Sudeva, you are fortunate at this moment;
I have made this son of yours one whose lifespan shall be twelve thousand years. (43)
O twice-born one, because of the majesty of Puruṣottama, I have been pleased and have restored this son to life; may he indeed grant you happiness for a very long time.
Having always enjoyed incomparable domestic life together with your son,
you shall then go to the world of Brahmā and experience great happiness there.
Having enjoyed [this] for a thousand divine years, you shall go to the surface of the earth;
thereafter, you will become a Cakravartin king named Dṛḍhadhanvan.
"You shall enjoy the sovereignty of the earth for ten thousand years.
Gautamī, whose name is Guṇasundarī, shall be your wife. There, four sons and one daughter are destined to be born to you."
When you cease from me, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||48||
"O Brahmin, this son of yours, having become a parrot in the forest at that time, will awaken others through words of devotion that contemplate Kṛṣṇa. (49)
Vālmīki will relate to you the entire story exactly as it happened;
then, having attained detachment and having performed supreme devotion to Hari, [you shall proceed].
"You shall go with your wife to liberation, the supreme abode of Hari.
While Mahāviṣṇu was speaking thus, the son of the twice-born rose up.
Upon seeing that son, the couple were filled with great joy;
Śukadeva also bowed down to Śrī Hari and to his parents.
Garuḍa and the Brāhmaṇa, together with their wives, bowed down to Hari.
Kṛṣṇa said: "By the effortless observance of the intercalary month (adhimāsa)..."
Indeed, the happiness of sons, wives, husbands, wives, fields, and kingdoms certainly comes to pass;
of this there is no doubt—how much more so the life of one's own son? (54)
He who observes even a single fast at Puruṣottama, having burned away infinite misfortunes, shall obtain treasures of merit. 55.
Having ascended the celestial vehicle, the embodied soul goes to Vaikuṇṭha;
on one side are all merits, but on the other side is Puruṣottama alone.
The Creator weighed [the worlds], and Puruṣottama indeed became the Guru;
he himself presides over the creation of Īśa, the creation of Jīva, and even the creation of Brahmā.
The great month of Puruṣottama prevails everywhere.
"By protecting him indeed, victory shall be yours here.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, went to his own abode;
and Sudeva, together with his wife, worshipped him for that month.
Then, having enjoyed all sensory objects day and night for thousands of years,
that best of the twice-born went to the world of Brahmā together with his wife.
Having experienced the happiness found there, he returned to earth accompanied by his wife.
He himself is you, the renowned lord of the earth, Dṛḍhadhanvan.
This queen of yours is Gautamī, beautiful in her virtues;
and Śukadeva is your son, who was brought back to life by Hari. 62.
Having lived for twelve thousand years, he went to Vaikuṇṭha;
indeed, having become Śuka himself, he awakened you to the remembrance of Hari.
"Your son became a true benefactor, a savior from the hell named Punnāma.
Thus, O King, has this past event been related to you exactly as it occurred. (64)
Then Śatadhanvā questioned the sage regarding the procedure for worship;
Vālmīki, however, explained that entire ritual to the king in full detail.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate the Supreme Brahman;
thereafter, carrying a water vessel, one should go toward the southwest direction for the purpose of purification.
Having placed the sacred thread over the ear, one should discharge urine with cleanliness;
having washed the pair of organs with water, earth, and so forth.
Having performed purification by removing the stains of odor and having taken many mouthfuls of water,
and likewise having cleansed his teeth, he should bathe in the waters of sacred fords and the like.
For one who has performed the ritual bath, longevity, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, and wealth, as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and retentive memory, increase day by day. (69)
Having put on clean garments, facing eastward with his topknot tied,
he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with his hand holding a pavitra grass ring.
One should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) together with a dot using sandalwood paste or clay;
one should also draw the conch, discus, and other symbols, and wear a garland of tulasī.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
In a pure place, one should prepare a mandala with cow dung, rice, and other materials.
Having had it constructed, one should place a water-filled jar in its center;
Viṣṇu is always situated at the mouth of the jar, and Rudra at its neck. (73)
Brahmā stands at its base; the Mothers stand in its center;
and within its belly reside the seven oceans together with the earth and its continents.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas stand there, together with their auxiliary limbs;
likewise the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Sauryā, Kāverī, and Sarasvatī.
May the rivers that bring about the destruction of sins remain here in this water;
I offer sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and flowers—Oṃ Namaḥ! (76)
"I offer the food offering, fruit, and betel; Oṃ, obeisance.
Having thus worshipped, one should then worship the conch with unbroken rice grains and other offerings. (77)
One should worship the beautiful bell with unbroken grains, saffron, and other offerings;
one should place a vessel filled with sesame seeds and sugar upon the jar.
One should worship that Hari, the deity of the month of Puruṣottama, who is clad in yellow garments, auspicious, golden, and accompanied by Rādhā.
Having performed the extraction of the anus, one should maintain the vital breath;
indeed, having touched those two skull-halves with the right hand. (80)
And having placed his thumb upon her heart, he should firmly fix the vital breaths there, [reciting]: "May her vital breaths be established; may her vital breaths flow. (8.1)
" Svāhā to this one endowed with divinity, indeed to Nārāyaṇa!
Then one should meditate upon the God and invoke the Lord who resides within the heart. (8.2)
I invoke Puruṣottama together with the glorious Rādhā;
I offer a seat to this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
I offer water for the washing of your feet;
and I present this arghya, accompanied by fruit, to the Supreme Self.
O Lord of Rādhikā, I offer you the waters of sacred fords for sipping;
I offer you milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar. (85)
O Keśava, I shall likewise perform for you the fivefold bath and the water-bath; I offer you this yellow, washed upper garment.
O Lord, I give you the Kaustubha gem, the sacred thread, and ornaments;
I offer you sandalwood paste, the essence of fragrant oils, and other such things. ||87||
I offer saffron, unbroken grains, and flowers; please accept them.
O Lord, I also offer you incense endowed with divine fragrance. 88.
O Lord Hari, I offer to you a lamp blazing with ghee;
O Keśava, I present this milk-rice as an oblation.
O Mādhava, I offer you water for sipping, drinking water, fruit, betel leaf, and likewise a fragrant powder for rubbing the hands. (90)
O Keśava, I offer gold as a sacrificial fee, along with necklaces and unbroken grains;
I perform the lustration rite for the Lord of Gods and circumambulate him.
I offer this handful of flowers and I prostrate;
O Puruṣottama, forgive whatever deficiency there may be in your worship. (92)
One should perform an uninterrupted fire sacrifice (homa) and maintain a lamp of ghee for the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama and for the attainment of the fruit of all goals. 93.
Thus one should worship him constantly and give gifts according to one's ability;
one should feed those worthy of food and bow at the feet of the elders.
The observer of the vow should partake of sacrificial food (haviṣya) which propitiates the gods:
wheat, rice, mung beans, barley, sesame seeds, and sugar. (95)
Millet, dates, wild rice, grapes, tubers, cucumbers, roots, vegetables, leafy greens, edible flowers, and radishes. (96)
Plantains, bananas, curd, milk, as well as fresh ginger, long pepper, mango fruit, buttermilk, jackfruit, and myrobalan. ||97||
Long pepper, cumin, emblic myrobalan, tamarind, as well as betel nut and all products of sugarcane— these constitute the sattvic food for one observing a vow.

One should avoid food that is rajasic, such as that prepared with mustard seeds; tamasic, such as meat and the like; and vātalā, such as split pulses and so forth, as well as the food of others and similar items. 99.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, eat from a leaf-plate, observe the vow of eating only once a day, and avoid even the slightest censure of others. || 100 ||
Puruṣottama should be worshipped with fasting, milk, curd, water, ghee, leaves, or even fruits. || 101 ||
One should take food in such a way that there is no violation of the vow;
by worshipping with a hundred thousand *tulasī* leaves, the merit is infinite.
Even one who observes the vow of the month of Puruṣottama becomes the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*).
He shall indeed become four-armed and will dwell eternally in Vaikuṇṭha.
An unbroken lamp should be offered during the month at Śrī Puruṣottama.
In ancient times, there was a king named Citrabāhu in the city of Saubhāgya. 104.
His wife was Candrakalā, and both were indeed very righteous;
then the sage Agastya came to his house.
Having honored him with humility, Citrabāhu said:
"Today, indeed, the sovereignty of my home, my birth, and all else have become truly fruitful."
Since you, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, have come to my home today,
I give everything today to you, the high-souled Vaiṣṇava.
Even a slight offering made to you for Viṣṇu or a devotee of Viṣṇu shall yield fruit equal to Mount Meru; however, a day not offered [to them] is fruitless.
The Vaiṣṇavas are worthy of service through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
blessed are all his subjects in whose house there is a person devoted to Viṣṇu.
One should indeed dwell in a Vaiṣṇava land and in a kingdom where the sovereign is a Vaiṣṇava;
likewise, a kingdom that is not Vaiṣṇava should be understood as inauspicious and one-eyed.
O Sage, the kingdom of the king who has taken refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa prospers;
likewise, my fortune and my vast kingdom are free from all obstacles.
"Tell me, by what merit did my wife become devoted to her husband?
Having heard this, Agastya spoke to him: 'Long ago, in the city of Camatkārapura...'"
You were born of the Śūdra caste as Maṇigrīva, an extreme nihilist and an ocean of evil qualities such as liquor, meat, sexual indulgence, and theft. (11.3)
"This wife of yours is indeed devoted and always possesses a virtuous disposition;
yet you, having been banished by the king, have gone to the forest accompanied by your beloved. (11.4)
But you, who live by hunting, saw in the forest the sage Ugradeva,
a twice-born man who was then thirsty and on the verge of death.
Having risen and lifted up water, and having offered a fruit, he gladdened him;
the sage, being well-pleased, said: "O Maṇigrīva, may you be happy. (116)
"You have granted me my life; tell me, what shall I give you?
Maṇigrīva then replied, "May my poverty perish! (1.17)
"May there be incomparable riches; may my desires be fulfilled"—when he expressed this wish, the sage said, "So shall it be for you."
Indeed, during the coming intercalary month at the holy Puruṣottama,
a lamp should be offered in the temple for the satisfaction of the illustrious Puruṣottama.
Your intense poverty shall not perish even with its very roots, [if you worship] with sesame oil, clarified butter, or even with ingudi oil. (120)
"Having bathed daily for one month and offered a lamp to the God after bowing down,
you shall indeed obtain a great kingdom upon the earth."

Sacrifices and other rites, as well as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, the recitation of the Vedas, the Śrāddha at Gayā, and likewise the pilgrimage sites of Kurukṣetra and the planets—these [are the means]. || 1.22 ||
All sacred fords, all acts of charity, and whatever religious duties there may be,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of Puruṣottamadīpa.
The vow of the intercalary month is supreme; it is a lamp that illuminates from within, bestowing wealth, grain, cattle, sons, grandsons, wives, and fame. 1.24.
This vow destroys barrenness in a woman and ensures she does not become a widow;
it is a vow that bestows a kingdom, grants all desires, and provides both a husband and a wife.
"The vow of offering a lamp bestows knowledge, success, wealth, and liberation;
thus, you previously offered a lamp to Śrī Hari in the forest. (126)
By that merit, O Indra among kings, you have obtained a virtuous kingdom, prosperity, and a devoted wife; by performing it again, you shall obtain them once more.
Having spoken thus, Agastya, the king of sages, departed for Prayāga;
and by that king as well, [the pilgrimage] was undertaken according to the prescribed rites at Śrī Puruṣottama.
"Having offered a gift of lamps, he then attained liberation.
Having said this, Vālmīki took the offerings and departed.
Then, when the month had arrived— the excellent month of Śrīpuruṣottama—
at dawn on the fourteenth day, Kṛṣṇadundubhi was [confronted] by Dṛḍhadhanvan.
"Having heard this, let them perform today itself the vow of the lamp and the vigil;
by that merit, through my boon, may they attain heaven and liberation. (131)
Having heard this and remembering his entire vow, Dṛḍhadhanvan then,
together with his family, remained without food and performed a vigil by lamp-light.
He celebrated a great festival and gave gifts of cattle and land;
then, during the night, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, arrived here.
He, along with his family, was led by Garuḍa to the world of Brahmā;
O Mahālakṣmī, what more need be said regarding the greatness of the month of Māgha? 1.34.
Where Śrī Puruṣottama is the creator, the sustainer, and the deliverer;
where Śrī Puruṣottama is the nourisher, the gratified one, the giver, and the enjoyer. (1.35)
O Lakṣmī, whoever hears this, reads it, or causes it to be read,
shall indeed attain the fruit of an intercalary month and proceed to the world of Brahmā.
Having attained heaven according to his desire, as well as the station of Parameṣṭhin and the rank of Maheśa and others, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
By those by whom this month has been fully honored, everything has been honored;
by them everything shall be attained, for they have attained Śrī Puruṣottama.
The intercalary month (adhimāsa) is rendered fruitless by him by whom it is disregarded;
indeed, all his merits become fruitless, and every merit performed becomes fruitless—of this there is no doubt. || 139 ||
O Lakṣmī, whatever beings there may be who possess happiness— whether gods, humans, or dānavas— it is the fruit of the month of Puruṣottama, and nothing else.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, within the *Puruṣottamamāsamāhātmya* of the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*, [Dṛḍhadhanvan] heard the verse spoken by Śuka in the forest of Dṛḍhadhanvan; having questioned Vālmīki regarding its meaning, he learned his own past existence as the twice-born Sudeva, his state of having sons, and how upon the death of his son, he restored the boy to life by performing the *Puruṣottamamāsa* rites. He realized that this very son was Śuka, the speaker of the verse, while he himself had now been born as Dṛḍhadhanvan. Such was the account he came to know.

He learned the ritual for the worship of Puruṣottama-māsa; he also learned what was told by Agastya regarding how, through the offering of a lamp during an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), the Śūdra Maṇigrīva attained the state of King Citrabāhu and the acquisition of a kingdom in another birth. Furthermore, having performed the Caturdaśī vow, Dṛḍhadhanvan, together with his family, attained liberation. This concludes the three hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of [these] Matters."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; at the end of the intercalary month, on that day in the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣara-dhāman), the concluding rite (udyāpana) was performed by all in the temple of Puruṣottama.
Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa, and all others residing in Goloka arrived;
the emanations (vyūhas), such as Vāsudeva and the rest, arrived together with their own progeny. || 2 ||
We, Nārāyaṇa and the others, residing in the world of Mahāvaikuṇṭha,
have gone together with you and the subjects to the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Then all those beginning with Nyāyeśvara went there with joy—the women who were the foremost in the city of Śrī on the ground of the Avyākṛta, Amṛta, and Dhāman realms. || 4 ||
Mahāviṣṇu and the others, born from the creation of Hiraṇyagarbha, along with the Pravairājas and the Āvaraṇas, went to the Imperishable Lord.
Likewise, those residing in Vaikuṇṭha, situated above the watery covering of Viṣṇu, departed;
and those born of Mahāmāyā, residing in the abode of Sadāśiva, departed.
Thus those lords and incarnations, having gone to the supreme Imperishable One,
performed there the concluding rite for the Puruṣottama month-long festival.
The sages and ascetics in the world of Brahmā,
as well as the hosts of Mothers, the Pitṛs, and the Vaiṣṇava deities, all departed.
The celestial beings who performed the concluding rites departed, as did the men and others;
all the holy fords, the deities, and the goddesses likewise went to their respective quarters.
The principles (tattvas) also went there, as did the rivers and the oceans;
likewise the mountains, the chasms, the islands, and the continents went there as well.
The planets, the stars, the circle of constellations, trees, and creepers;
indeed, the divine ones, the excellent devotees, as well as the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas. (11)
Then the herbs, serpents, nāgas, and stainless birds— those dwelling in water, on land, and in the air— all departed.

Then those dwelling in the netherworld, those in the chasms, and those who were divine or non-divine— vow-observers, co-residents, and devotees— all went forth for the sake of the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Out of reverence, they went into the presence of Satya, the world of Brahmā;
and they also went for the purpose of performing the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the month of Puruṣottama.
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Sūtas and others, as well as gods and humans;
Bhaṭṭas, Cāraṇas, and servants, and even the fierce attendants of Śaṅkara. || 15 ||
These and others went to the festival for the sake of the fruit of completing their vows;
listen, Lakṣmī, how they did so in various places according to their power and according to their wealth. (16)
The concluding rite (udyāpana) was performed by all, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
indeed, it was performed by them preceded by the giving of wealth, granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Listen as I relate to you the concluding rite (udyāpana) performed by them,
which was spoken by Hari himself regarding the month of Puruṣottama.
On the fourteenth day of either fortnight, on the new moon day, on the full moon day,
on the eleventh, the ninth, or on the eighth lunar day— the day of the vow— || 19 ||
On whichever lunar day there is auspiciousness, or even on that very lunar day,
one should indeed perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) for the sake of completing the vow.
In every place, the drum proclaims throughout the month of Puruṣottama:
"Go indeed and perform the auspicious concluding rite (udyāpana)."
"The fruit of the month of Puruṣottama will become complete.
Having heard even this much, others performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) at home, [beating] the drum (ḍiṇḍima). || 22 ||
Having slept on the ground at night and strictly observed celibacy,
they all rose early in the morning and then performed meditation upon Hari.

Having performed all bodily rites such as purification and so forth externally, and having then performed the bath and other rituals according to one's physical capacity, whether divine or non-divine; ||24||

Having performed their recitation of mantras (japa), fire-offerings (homa), twilight rituals (sandhyā), self-study of scripture (svādhyāya), libations (tarpaṇa), and so forth—according to local custom, according to their physical capacity, and as was appropriate for them—they [proceeded]. (25)
Having performed the daily worship and the honoring of elders, and having completed the rites of worship, offering, and so forth,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and prepare the ground with great elaboration.
And they constructed there a pavilion provided with many pillars, adorned with jewels, diamonds, necklaces, and other ornaments, as well as archways made of mango, *aśoka*, and other trees.
With plantain trunks, leaves, and the like; with the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavallī);
with water-pots, colored creepers, and garments adorned with gold. || 28 ||
Having bound it with lamps and adorned it with fragrant scents,
one should perfume its interior with the five grains and the seven [herbs].
Or, having caused a Sarvatobhadra mandala to be made with grains,
one should invite devotees of Viṣṇu together with their wives according to one's capacity.
He should place four water-pots in the four directions within the mandala,
provided with fine cloths, bilva fruits, betel nuts, and betel leaves.
There, having filled them with unbroken grains mixed with sugar and other substances,
[one should worship] Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Having performed the sequential placement starting from the northeast, one should place [the deity] in the center within an auspicious jar that contains its fruit,
is covered with a cloth, and is provided with betel nut, a golden seal, and unbroken grains of rice.
They enshrined Śrī Puruṣottama, possessing a divine form made of gold and endowed with the five jewels,
together with Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, within a golden vessel.
In this manner, the installation of Śrī Hari was performed by all those observers of vows;
and the preceptor, the guru, was ushered in there for the purpose of worship. (35)
The purification of the body was indeed performed by him for the patron;
then the deity was invoked and a seat was offered. || 36 ||
Water produced from an excellent sacred bathing place was indeed offered for the purpose of washing his feet;
lamps were lit in the four directions, and fragrant incense was burned there.
The *arghya* consisting of fruits and other offerings was presented by the couple,
and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) originating from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) was offered to the God.
Curd, milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and likewise nectar—
these were indeed offered as water for the consecration bath to Keśava.
The two deities were wiped with a cloth and adorned with garments and ornaments;
they were made fragrant with the essence of sandalwood, excellent oils, perfumes, and other scents. ||40||
He was beautifully adorned with saffron, collyrium, powdered sandalwood, and other unguents;
he was further embellished with necklaces of jewels, diamonds, and pearls, as well as a sacred thread.
Adorned with a crown, earrings, bracelets, armlets, and chains, he was protected by an umbrella, a staff, a turban, chowries, and leaf-shields. ||42||

He was provided with a couch, a bolster, and a pillow, and was beautifully adorned with offerings such as flowers, *tulasī*, and lotuses, as well as with *puṇḍra* marks shaped like the crescent moon. ||43||
Then, in that pavilion, a fire sacrifice was performed using sesame seeds,
ghee, and excellent fruits, with the mantras consisting of the names [of the deities] in the dative case.
Then, the libation was performed one hundred and eight times with the words:
"May the gods and the ancestors, as well as Puruṣottama, be satisfied. (45)
Then the Lord was honored with the *nīrājana* rite by means of many wicks and fires;
he was saluted, praised, and circumambulated by the Vaiṣṇavas. (46)
Śrī Puruṣottama was honored like a staff-bearer, meditated upon, and Hari was asked for forgiveness; a handful of flowers was offered to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then the god was served a meal, satiated with sweet foods like nectar, offered water, and provided with sweet fruits and betel-leaf for chewing. ||48||
The Supreme Person was massaged with fragrant unguents on his hands;
the Lord was refreshed with comforts and massaged at his feet. (49)
Thus worshipped by all, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, appeared before them; becoming invisible, he bestowed infinite fruit upon them.
Then a gift of gold and silver was bestowed upon the preceptor,
and the gift of a cow, adorned with golden horns and ornaments, was also made.
There, a vessel of ghee, cloth, and sesame seeds was given to a brahmin;
furthermore, an image was bestowed and a compendium of scriptures was offered. ||52||
At that time, thirty bronze caskets were indeed given;
each was filled with thirty cakes in their center.
O Lotus-born One, this gift of the cosmic egg has indeed been fashioned for Puruṣottama; for as many apertures as there are in each of its limbs, [so many gifts should be given]. 54.
For that many thousands of years one shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha; thereafter, one shall dwell in Goloka, and then in the supreme, imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāman). //55//
Alternatively, cakes that are uncooked due to a deficiency in their preparation may be given to a twice-born man;
then the virtuous Brahmins and the children are to be fed.
With milk-rice, sweet dishes, and side-dishes such as amṛta and others—by means of the fourfold foods: those to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked. (57)
Then [one should offer] liquids such as milk and water mixed with sugar, cardamom, and so forth;
thereafter, water for rinsing the mouth, betel leaf, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Indeed, garments and most excellent ornaments were offered;
they were presented to the goddesses, to the deities, and even to the preceptors.
Indeed, those principles (tattvas) belonging to each respective world which are worthy of being given as gifts—
food has been offered by me to all beings, to those who have taken refuge, and to guests.
Then, together with his kinsmen and those observing vows, he respectfully partook of suitable food such as fruits and the like, provided it did not cause a violation of the vow. ||61||
Likewise, it was performed at midday and similarly during the night;
the Lord was worshipped and fed by people engaged in a vigil.
Singing, dancing, and worship were performed by the people;
having bathed in the morning, [the deity] was honored, asked for forgiveness, and then bid farewell.
That Supreme Lord, in the form of an image, was presented to the preceptor;
having thus performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), they all went to their own abodes.
And an infinite fruit has been attained through service to the Supreme Person;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, one should observe this vow according to one's ability. (65)
There shall be the destruction of suffering, poverty, and misfortune, and one shall obtain what is desired;
thereafter, the person observing the vow should perform the relinquishment of the restrictive observances (niyamas).
One who observes the vow should eat only at midday or eat only at night, and should feed the Brāhmaṇas; if food is obtained during the "unasked" (ayācita) vow, one should perform the gift of gold.
One who observes the month-long fast (māsopavāsa) should give a milch cow along with a thousand [gold pieces] as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
one who observes the Dhātrī-vrata should likewise give curds, milk, and sugar.
O Lakṣmī, when there is a restriction regarding fruits, one should provide an offering of fruit;
when oil is restricted, ghee should be given, and when ghee is restricted, milk should be offered. (69)
In the observance of grains, one should give those very same grains;
in the practice of sleeping on the ground, one should give beds, couches, pillows, and covers.
In the observance of fruits, leaves, and so forth, one should give those to a twice-born man;
in the observance of silence, O Lotus-born One, one should give bells, conchs, and musical instruments to the God.
One who wears nails and hair should give a mirror and a comb;
and one should give sandals when sandals and such items are not being used.
Upon renouncing salt, one should give flavorful juices; upon giving lamps, however, one should give lamps.
And fasting on alternate days, one should cause eight jars to be given.
Whatever desired prosperities belong to kings in this world,
all of those should indeed be given as gifts according to one's ability and according to one's wealth.
One who observes the vow while eating only once a day attains the supreme goal;
likewise, by fasting and eating only once, one shall obtain all desires.
The gods eat in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday, and the hosts of ancestors in the afternoon; a man should be one who eats at night.
One who eats only at night obtains daily the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
one who observes the vow of the twelfth day goes to the abode of Hari by means of Garuḍa.
Whichever specific rule one may have, one should apply oneself to the giving of that very thing;
by that, the vow becomes complete and shall bestow the world of Brahmā.
O Lakṣmī, the state of liberation is always to be achieved through this impermanent body; indeed, there is nothing equal to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) in the three worlds.
Even by asceticism performed for a thousand births, that fruit which is attained in this world through service to Puruṣottama is not reached. (80)
By bathing here for three nights, even a monkey attained the Imperishable;
for there was once in the land of Kerala a twice-born man who was exceedingly greedy for wealth. (8–1)
Because of that, he became known among living beings by the name "The Miser" (Kadarya);
he neither enjoyed good food nor fine clothing, nor did he ever offer the *svāhā* or *svadhā* oblations.
Wealth was guarded on the earth, yet no work of dharma was performed; there were neither vows nor festivals, nor eclipses, nor the ritual of the water-jar (kumbha). ||83||
Having begged for alms repeatedly like a miserable wanderer seeking wealth, he went to the garden of a florist, weeping constantly in distress. (84)
The gardener, having shown compassion, kept him by his side;
having appointed him as the protector of the garden, the florist departed for the village. (85)
Afterwards, he ate ripe fruits and bartered for others;
in this manner, ten thousand years passed for that perpetrator of thievery. (86)
He died there in the forest, failing to obtain the firewood for cremation;
being led by the messengers of Yama while being beaten, he was taken to the abode of Yama. (87)
As he was departing, he said: "Indeed, the fruit of evil deeds has been obtained by me today;
having attained human birth, not even a single virtuous act was performed. (88)
Wealth accumulated through theft and other such means lies useless upon the ground; it is neither retained nor consumed, and thus no merit has been earned from it. (8-9)
His family was not supported, and his wife was subjected to hardship;
lamenting thus, the miser then departed for the city of Yama.
Citragupta spoke of dharma, [and] two very terrible sins:
the theft of fruit, as well as the supreme and great betrayal of trust. 9.1.
Having heard this, Yama said to his messengers: "Designate him indeed as a preta;
however, let this one be a monkey for a moment, undergoing the torments of hell."
Thus, having been sent by messengers to the state of a preta in a waterless forest,
he then became a monkey on the formidable Kālañjara mountain.
There, a sacrificial pit known as Mṛgasutīrtha was formerly constructed by Indra;
it was there that [the monkey] was born due to a small amount of merit from his previous life. (94)
Listen to the merit performed in a former life, the praise of Puruṣottama:
there was a Vaiśya named Citrakuṇḍala who was devoted to the excellent vow of Puruṣottama.
In the past, that miser had gone for alms to the one who was a giver of gifts;
out of greed for wealth, the beggar praised that Vaiśya. (96)
The vow of the month of Puruṣottama that has been performed by you according to the prescribed rite—
such a thing has never been performed by anyone else here on this earth.
You have achieved your purpose, since you have served the glorious Puruṣottama;
this month of Śrīpuruṣottama is the bestower of prosperity and the giver of liberation. ||98||
He entreated him for a month, saying, "Give me some wealth";
by that merit, he attained the state of a monkey at this sacred site.
From birth, there was pain in his mouth arising from blood and wounds;
his teeth fell out, he was overcome by hunger, and he became excessively afflicted by fever.
Puruṣottama fell near Kuṇḍanika;
from the tenth day onwards, he remained in the waters of the Kuṇḍa for five days.
Having bathed in the waters of the sacred ford, he was born assuming a divine body;
he became four-armed and was served by divine goddesses and attendants. || 10 2 ||
Just as [the merit] arises from bathing at a sacred ford, so it arises from bathing for five days with due honor;
and since it arises even from bathing done unknowingly, how much more so from that performed according to the prescribed rite? (103)
They are always fortunate and meritorious, and their existence is fruitful— those for whom the month of Pumuttama has passed with ritual bathing, charity, and recitation.
These [merits] were indeed multiplied ten millionfold for that Supreme Person;
the monkey, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, went to Goloka.
Thus, although he was both miserly and a thief, and had even attained the state of a monkey,
he reached Goloka itself through union with Puruṣottama.
Even by merely hearing the narrative of the month of Puruṣottama, one obtains in its entirety the fruit of fasting throughout the month, performing worship, and other such rites. 107.
Having heard the Dharma, one understands it; having heard it, evil is destroyed.
Having heard it, delusion ceases; having heard it, one attains the nectar of knowledge.
One who observes the vow should read or hear the Veda known as the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* during the month of Śrī-Puruṣottama; for it indeed bestows liberation. (109)
If a woman has not observed the month-long vow at Śrī Puruṣottama,
yet her husband honors it, she shall obtain that excellent fruit.
If a virtuous woman is always devoted to the duty of fidelity to her husband,
the month becomes like her husband, the Supreme Person Śrī Puruṣottama.
Whether he be ugly, ill-behaved, or even of wicked nature and a drunkard;
whether he be diseased, wrathful, or corpulent; or even mute, blind, or deaf—(11.2)
Whether he be fierce, dejected, or miserly; poor, or even contemptible; timid, or a gambler; or even a sensualist or a libertine— (113)
For a virtuous and faithful wife, Lord Hari is her husband, who must be worshipped constantly like a god;
for a widow and for a maiden as well, the husband alone is always Lord Hari.
He is to be served, worshipped, meditated upon, and dwelt upon—likewise through speech, action, body, and mental cultivation. || 11.5 ||
A husband’s business must not be treated with negligence, nor should the lord be made to feel anxious;
whether she be a child, a young woman, or an old woman, a wife should remain devoted to her husband. 116.

Whether by desire, greed, or even by force; by a state of wretchedness, or by seeking refuge; by beauty, by residence, or by wealth and the like; or by thirst, or by the nourishment of the sense-faculties and elements— || 1.17 ||

She who does not worship anyone else, even with fine garments, excellent vehicles, mounts, ornaments, millions of diamonds and gems, beautiful dances and songs, or many seats—she indeed possesses the characteristics of a virtuous woman. 118.
A virtuous and beloved woman indeed does not adorn herself for the sake of being seen by another; she thinks only of a man who is worthy of her. 119.
She who, upon seeing one who is handsome, youthful, charming, and beloved by women,
does not undergo any change of state, is indeed to be known as a great virtuous woman.
She eats when her husband has eaten; she is sorrowful when he is sorrowful;
she rejoices when he rejoices; she sleeps when he sleeps; and she remains awake when he is awake. (121)
Devoted to her elders, she is compliant in her husband’s affairs and does not spend excessively;
when her husband returns home, she rises to greet him with a seat and water. (122)

With a serene countenance at the proper time, she should provide food and other necessities; once he has eaten, she should not speak anything unpleasant to him, but rather bestow peace upon him. (123)
She should always be intent on service and always act for the pleasure of her beloved;
as the guardian of the household, she should not spend excessively on material things. 124.
One should wear ornaments such as excessive jewelry for the pleasure of one's husband;
however, in the Tretā age and those following it, women shall indeed undergo the ritual impurity of menstruation.
During those four days, she should not touch any household chores;
having bathed and beheld the Sun and the Lord Kṛṣṇa, she should thereafter be devoted to her religious duties.
A woman desiring a son should approach her husband on even nights, being fond of sexual union;
but one desiring a daughter should serve her husband on odd nights.
Indeed, until sixteen nights have passed, the power of conception remains;
beyond that, the door of the lotus becomes closed.
One should never be loathsome, nor should one speak harsh words;
one should not catch the wind from a winnowing basket, nor should one sit upon the bare ground.
One should not sit upon a door, a wooden beam, a hearth, or a grinding stone;
nor should one consume food that is excessively hot or when it has not yet been digested. 130.
By this means she shall have offspring; otherwise, there would be a miscarriage. A co-wife is the seat of jealousy; therefore, a virtuous woman should avoid jealousy. || 131 ||
She should not create domestic distress, but should protect the household in every way;
she should not look upon her husband with anger, nor should she revile or treat him with contempt. (13.2)
She should always grant pleasure to her husband, who is her protector;
she may go outside at her husband's command for the purpose of beholding the gods.
When her husband has gone to another country, the virtuous wife should conduct herself in every way as one devoid of cosmetics and dyes, always obeying the commands of her mother-in-law and others.
She should not remain with soiled garments or limbs; she should maintain purity.
She should devoutly consume the food and water that are the remnants of her husband's offerings and his grace.
One should bathe while not devoid of clothing; one should never be naked.
One should not bathe on a mortar, nor on a pestle, nor on a water-jar or similar vessel, nor on a stone.
A virtuous woman should never sit upon a machine or on a road;
she should drink the water used for washing her husband's feet, which bestows the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
A wife should never perform vows, fasts, or religious observances in defiance of her husband;
she should always eat only after having honored her husband’s feet. 138.
Saramā is one who rejects her husband; Ulūkī is one who fills only her own belly;
Sūkarī is one who stays by the side of another; and Vāgurī is one who eats in secret. || 13.9 ||
A woman who causes humiliation becomes mute; one who is jealous of co-wives becomes unfortunate;
and a woman who brings suffering to her husband shall be ugly and diseased. (14.0)
The husband is Brahmā, Hara, and Viṣṇu; he is the preceptor, the sacred ford, the vow, and the recitation of mantras.
He is purity, heaven, auspiciousness, and the act of charity; therefore, one should serve the husband well. 141.
A body devoid of life is impure; a virtuous wife devoid of her husband is impure.
Yet, a devoted wife who is dear to herself leads her husband to heaven.
Upon seeing a virtuous woman from afar, the messengers of Yama flee;
indeed, for as many hairs as there are on her body, they flee for tens of millions of crores of yojanas.
A devoted wife, taking delight with her husband, enjoys the happiness of heaven;
however, a widow, remembering her husband, must perform the libation (tarpaṇa) every day.
She should accumulate merit through offerings of *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and water, as well as ground grains, fruits, morsels of food for cows, and other such acts of giving.
She should present a *brahmāṇḍa* (the cosmic egg) fashioned from bell-metal in the form of a casket.
It was filled with thirty middle-sized cakes and well-wrapped with thread.
A virtuous woman should offer that which has been honored with unbroken grains, flowers, and saffron; likewise, a man who is devoted to his wife becomes one who is dedicated to his wife.
One should always honor one's own life-force, body, field, auspicious place of peace, and wife, and should look upon them with sweetness. || 148 ||
One should give her sweet things, speak to her, and act with a spirit of love; one should not treat the wife with contempt, nor beat her, nor insult her. (149)
One should always gratify one's beloved with garments, ornaments such as jewelry, liquid sandalwood paste, flowers, oil, thread, collyrium, and other such things. 150.
One should not cause distress, nor should one eat by force, nor should one restrain her;
one should not cause the wife suffering through hunger, thirst, or labor. 151.

A husband should not disregard his beloved wife, even if she is of humble status or a servant; rather, he should nurture her—who bestows progeny and gives delight—as one would a climbing vine that clings to and supports him. 152.
Then the husband should neither say "I do not wish" nor even utter "no";
rather, having uttered "Om," he should bestow whatever wealth and other things are desired.
One should cause great delight in her as she performs her duties of serving food, household tasks, sexual pleasure, bodily care, service to her husband, and whatever else there may be.
He should not look upon another woman, nor should he engage in sexual union with another;
he should never be fond of any other woman, having abandoned his wife, who is indeed Lakṣmī herself. (155)
He shall not provide nourishment to another woman, nor indeed shall he take pleasure with another;
[this applies] even among vehicles, mounts, regions, festivals, and social gatherings. (156)
If one truly desires heaven, one should never be anything other than devoted to the Dharma; for in this world, a husband and wife who are thus intent upon righteousness partake in liberation.
Indradyumna, Śatadyumna, Yauvanāśva, and Bhagīratha—these and other Vaiṣṇava kings and Brahmins existed in various Kalpas and Kalpāntaras. || 158 ||
Having propitiated Puruṣottama, they went into the presence of the Blessed One;
by whomsoever the drum of the month of Puruṣottama was heard. || 159 ||
And in every place, a festival was indeed celebrated;
furthermore, the worship of the drum was performed by Nārāyaṇa.
Whenever an intercalary month (adhikamāsa) should also occur,
at those times a proclamation of the royal command must be made with the sounding of kettledrums and tabors.
He is eternally protected in the imperishable abode by Śrī Puruṣottama,
by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama who wields the Śārṅga bow.
Accompanied by Rādhā, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Prabhā,
Māṇikyā, Jayā, and Ramā, this Lord,
the Supreme Sovereign, is to be worshipped every day during the intercalary month.
For the sake of food, one should serve and meditate upon the Supreme Person. || 164 ||
This chapter, complete with its verses, which should be heard as the greatness of the month, shall yield the fruit of all holy places such as the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
It possesses the merit of circumambulating the earth and the merit of rescuing the universe.
By hearing this, liberation shall likewise be attained within a month.
Those belonging to the castes and stages of life who have attained excellence in every respect—even people engaged in the conduct of beasts—attain liberation upon hearing this. 167.
Having had the majesty of Puruṣottama written down along with its commentary, one should give it as a gift; the fruit of this is that for three generations, one shall go to Goloka.

In a house where a book concerning his majesty is kept as its foundation, all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) dwell in every way, the deities likewise reside there, and Puruṣottama himself is present. || 169 ||

The listener, the speaker, the one who causes others to hear, the one who describes, the one who praises, the protector, the observer of vows, and the giver—all these are supreme among men (puruṣottama). || 170 ||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beginningless Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the teacher of the Saṃhitās and Upaniṣads, is especially worthy of worship. (171)
Having heard this, Lakṣmī was exceedingly satisfied and worshipped Puruṣottama;
she worshipped her own husband, Lord Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. || 172 ||
"By drinking the nectar of your mouth, I have attained my life's purpose," she said;
and she worshipped and bowed down to Vyāsa, who was her husband in form.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the speaker, and you are Lakṣmī, the Narāyaṇī; I accept the worship performed by you. What else do you wish to hear? || 174 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Conclusion of the Puruṣottama-māsa Vow Performed by All the Lords of Creation in the Abode of Akṣara within the Greatness of the Puruṣottama Month, along with Gifts for the Fulfillment of Observances, the Fruit of Offering Lamps, the Liberation of the Miser, the Release of Monkeys, the Duties of Chaste Wives, the Duties of Husbands, the Gift of the Cosmic Egg in the Form of a Brass Casket, the Worship of the Drum, and the Fruit of Hearing [this]," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Lord, O Supreme Self, O One higher than the highest! O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Inner Controller, O Supreme Lord! (1)
O Supreme Person, O Lord of the Self, O Lord of my life, O Beloved, O Giver of honor!
As you have said, I have thirteen lawful wives.
What are they? From what, when, and where did they arise, and by what cause?
What is their purpose, and by whom were they spoken? Tell me this, if indeed it is to be told. (3)
I have been delivered, purified, and brought to fame by the compassionate one,
who caused me to hear the story concerning the Goddess, the Yoginī Puruṣottamā.
O Lord, for the sake of remembering the wives of dharma, please tell me in detail the divine narrative concerning those women of dharma, which bestows both heaven and liberation.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious story of the wives of Dharma which bestows liberation;
it indeed originated at the beginning of creation—listen to me as I relate it.
The Supreme Person abides in the imperishable, supreme abode;
within that, divine powers exist by the hundreds of thousands.
Then, [the Self], being one, formed the thought, "May I become many";
at that time, eternal, divine qualities, consisting of power and possessing form, came into being.
Faith, friendliness, compassion, tranquility, contentment, nourishment, exaltation, action, intellect, wisdom, forbearance, and modesty—these are the twelve. (9)
There, that which is called "form" (mūrti) is always spoken of by the name of "devotion" (bhakti).
Indeed, these female powers were born from the very nature of Hari. (10)
Even in Hari, eternal shadows exist for the liberation of the world;
assuming a second form, they dwell among the classes of living beings.
When they had become endowed with beautiful forms through the power of Brahmā’s form, then Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men, desired them.
O Keśava, since we have been offered as oblations by your resolve, we exist in embodied form consisting of your own form; therefore, we go nowhere else.
"O Lord, please command whatever task is appropriate for one such as us.
Thus entreated, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, [replied].
Having reflected, he said to them all: "Become indeed of the nature of shadows;
let those forms of yours that appear here be composed of shadow."
"May all these move within embodied beings during creation"—
having received this hope from Śrī Hari, she became composed of the qualities (guṇas) at the time of creation.
Those pervasive powers came into being by the will of Lord Hari;
however, they were entirely absent among the asuras, the daityas, and the dānavas.
There was no happiness for those who were dominated by darkness (tamas) in their homes;
therefore, they all gathered together and went to the auspicious Badarī forest.
Desiring the Supreme Lord, they performed most fierce austerities,
having reached the banks of the Gaṅgā and remained there subsisting on no water.
For a period of a thousand years, with their minds fixed on Puruṣottama,
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself then appeared.
He said to them, "Why and how is such a severe penance being performed?
By the power of your practice of austerity, I have been nourished. (21)
My qualities and my powers are entirely devoted to my growth;
you are, in every way, the providers of my nourishment and the givers of my happiness. 22.
Since I have indeed come here for the purpose of assisting you, please declare your desire; what do you seek through these ascetic penances?
Having thus informed him, Hari remained silent there for a moment;
then all those Śaktis said, "O Lord, regarding the Dānava and Daityaka... (24)
O Lord, there is no happiness at all for us among the Asuras;
indeed, we are miserable there because of our dwelling in unrighteousness. (25)
"Therefore, O Blessed One, draw us out and make us forever happy.
Then Hari, having reflected for a mere moment, spoke to them.
Perform the great vow on the final day of the month of Puruṣottama; here, on the bank of the celestial river, your desire shall be fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, the god vanished; and when the time for the intercalary month arrived once again, at its very end, those ascetics—
Every day, they all performed the worship of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with various articles and diverse dispositions, using flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
In the evening, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama appeared there, saying, "O goddesses, choose a boon; I have come to grant you whatever you desire."
Then, filled with fear, they chose the protection of dharma, saying:
"O Kṛṣṇa, we are devoted to dharma; may we be protected in every way. (31)
"O Śrī Puruṣottama, you must always provide protection.
Having heard this, Hari then replied, "So be it."
He said to all those auspicious Śaktis: "Go to the house of Dakṣa;
thereupon your father shall have you as daughters."
Dakṣa will indeed give thirteen daughters to Dharma as wives;
you shall become renowned by those very names, each according to her respective order.
Then, from my own form, I myself as Hari shall manifest in the forest of Badarī as Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, in the personification of the dharma of celibacy (brahmacarya).
"I shall always provide protection for you who have acted unrighteously.
Having said this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vanished.
Then, abandoning their asceticism, they entered the river Asi;
by the mere thought of Dakṣa, they then became those maidens.
Born as soon as they were conceived, they were youthful, beautiful, and worthy of being chosen as brides;
remembering their past lives, they were of excellent form and dedicated their bodies to the pursuit of dharma.
Seeing those women longing for the Dharma, he who was resolved upon the goal of the Dharma—being skillful—waits for the auspicious time for the practice of Dharma. (39)
Meanwhile, Dharma, having observed the house of Dakṣa on the path to Badarī-āśrama by way of the sacred ford, paused for a moment to rest.
Having learned that the house of Dakṣa was adorned with hospitality toward guests,
and having recognized his brother as the son of Brahmā, he went there, remembering him especially.
Seeing this, Dakṣa was exceedingly pleased and prepared a grand reception;
having honored them all, he gave thirteen of them to Dharma.
Having performed the marriage rites for his daughters, Dharma then became fulfilled; taking them with him, he went to Badarikāśrama.
Having drunk from the Gaṅgā and bathed in its waters,
Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, went to Dharmāraṇya and entered into dharma.
Accompanied by his wives, Dharma traveled for a year,
visiting all the sacred fords (tīrthas) before proceeding to the Badarī forest.
There, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born in person from his own form through austerity, due to their excellent vow toward Puruṣottama. (46)
The two sons of Dharma, the two sons of Mūrti, were most great as soon as they were born;
those two divine youths were always devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Two ascetics, bringers of welfare to the world, appeared.
Then, from Śraddhā and Dharma, Kāma was born as their son.
Desire (kāma), which possesses the power of merit and virtue, was said to be Saṃkalpa;
from Saṃkalpa was born a son named Vyavasāya.
Maitrī gave birth to Snehā, and Upakārā was born from Dayā;
Śānti gave birth to her son Kṣema, while Tuṣṭi’s son was Santoṣa. (50)
From Puṣṭi comes Lābha as a son; from Unnati comes Abhyudaya as a son;
from Kriyā come Naya, Daṇḍa, and also Samaya as sons. (5.1)
The awakening of the intellect and heedfulness are both sons of Intelligence; the two sons of Wisdom are Auspicious Learning and its opposite; and the son of Forbearance is Renunciation. (52)
O Badrī, the lineage of Dharma consists of four: Hriyā’s son was Niyama; from his form [Mūrti] came Nara and Nārāyaṇa; and Kṛṣṇa and Hari. Thus, O Badrī, is the family tree of Dharma.
He lived happily, devoted to the service and attendance of Lakṣmī,
in the world of the Creator, in the Satya realm, at the site of the assembly of Brahmā.
At the conclusion of the month of Puruṣottama, there is the worship of Puruṣottama with a great festival and with many tens of millions of offerings.
It was performed by celestial sages, hermits, humans, and those of other species,
with great devotion and intense emotion, preceded by the offering of their very selves.
Because of that, Dharma, his wives, and his sons—Puruṣottama being among them—became gracious and attained supreme satisfaction. (57)
At midnight, at the end of the day, or after the meal,
they desire to grant an audience to their devotees and those observing the vow.
Invisible, they gathered in the sky, distinguished by their singing;
then, indeed, he manifested in the midst of the devotees of Puruṣottama.
Suddenly that mass of splendor pervaded the sky instantly;
that light became condensed, resembling millions upon millions of moons.
Then stability manifested and attained firmness, illuminating all directions;
the scales, the musical modes, the melodic modulations, and the sounds became enchanting. (61)
Then, while the gods and others were looking on, a single woman was seen there—captivating, of divine form, and pleasing to the mind. (62)
Clad in divine saffron garments and adorned with celestial ornaments, she possessed a beauty that perfectly matched her form; serene and radiant as molten gold. (63)
Abounding in the splendor of every ornament, adorned with all types of jewelry,
she bore flowers upon her mass of hair and was playful with her beautiful smiles and eyebrows.
Clad in spotless garments and adorned with a girdle and anklets,
she captivated the minds even of women by her exquisite beauty.
Playing the lute, her voice was harmonized by her female companions;
indeed, by her singing alone, she could humble even the pride of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
And twelve other women performed the song of Nārāyaṇa with proper rhythm and measure, truly captivating even the minds of others.
Their sons were also most divine, serene, and skilled singers; together with their musical instruments, they stood in His presence, while in their midst was Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The intercalary month, as well as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and other divine women,
were all seen there in that assembly hall within the house of the Creator.
The lotus-eyed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the sovereign of syllables, the beginningless Śrī Puruṣottama, appeared while uttering blessings.
The four-armed god of Dharma appeared, radiant white,
speaking with Vedic verses and showing his favor to his devotees.
And Brahmā and the others, seeing that great wonder at that time,
were bewildered for a mere moment, but then they rejoiced in them with exceeding joy.
Having recognized Kṛṣṇa as the glorious Puruṣottama, they bowed down;
and Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and the others likewise bowed to Dharma, his personified form, and his sons.
Then Śraddhā and the others, having bowed down, praised him with supreme devotion:
"O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you; salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī. (74)
O Dharmadeva, homage be to you; repeated salutations to those who are righteous. Let there be homage to faith and the other virtues, and let there be homage to the embodiment of devotion.
Salutations to Rādhā, Ramā, and the other Śaktis, and to the Supreme Person,
the deliverer of the worlds, and especially of us.
"You have indeed granted your vision, O Supreme Lords;
we have been made successful by you, O Gods, right here. (77)
"Having shown compassion, if you have a command, let it be known and instructed.
Having heard this, Puruṣottama then spoke to the gods, headed by Brahmā: 78.
During this month of Puruṣottama, devotion has been shown by you, the leaders of the world, and by the subjects alike toward me, this Puruṣottama. (79)
Dharma has been performed to the utmost extent, and faith and the other virtues have likewise been nourished; I, along with my family, have been sustained so that you might grant us your vision. (80)
I have come here out of compassion; may the greatest welfare be yours.
Otherwise, my vision would not be perceptible even to yogis. (8.1)
"Choose a boon; I am pleased; you shall have your heart's desire.
Hearing these words of compassion, they prostrated themselves and performed worship. (82)
May they dwell forever within our hearts; likewise, may they protect us as we abide by your instructions. O Guru, always protect me in my duties. (83)
O Mādhava, lead the desireless devotees to Your own divine abode;
fulfill the desires of those who possess them; shower upon us the rain of Your compassion, shower it down! 84.
Having praised him thus, they ceased; and Keśava, the Supreme Person, having granted a boon to Brahmā and the others along with their families, said, "So be it. (85)
Hari suddenly vanished, producing wonder;
in this way, the desires of his own devotees were fulfilled by that Blessed One. (86)
O Lakṣmī, all things are fulfilled and protected moment by moment for those who are devotees of Puruṣottama; indeed, there is nothing that cannot be attained by them. 87.
Whoever shall read or hear this [account] which pleases Puruṣottama, Hari will indeed fulfill all the desires of his heart.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Dharmadeva, His Wives, and His Sons, and the Granting of a Vision and Boons by Śrī Hari—Who was Pleased by the Vow of the Puruṣottama Month Performed by Brahmā and Others—to the Family of Dharmadeva," within the section on the Greatness of the Puruṣottama Month in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O Lakṣmī, I am pleased; this is my grace.
When the month of Puruṣottama arrives, grace alone is the cause."
If he wishes to make me exceedingly pleased during other months,
I become exceedingly pleased even with a single leaf of tulasī.
A person should worship with a leaf joined with a flower-cluster (mañjarī),
or with both a leaf and a flower-cluster, or with several leaves joined with flower-clusters.
One may worship with a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand [flowers];
yet, O beloved, seeing you, Tulasī, again and again, I am as pleased as if seeing you yourself.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama, O Keśava! O Lord, why do you consider Tulasī to be as pleasing to you as I am?
Tell me everything exactly as it happened, provided there is nothing to be hidden; and even if something must be concealed, tell it to me if you consider me a fit recipient.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this ancient narrative in its full detail,
concerning how Vṛndā, who brings me satisfaction, was accepted by me.
Do not entertain doubt in this matter, and do not feel envy upon hearing it;
you must always maintain your friendship with Vṛndā.
For a devoted wife, there is dharma, and she never takes account of suffering; but one who is solely intent on her husband always regards the happiness derived from rival wives as her own.
Having heard again and again of the happiness of her husband arising from union with other women,
the devoted wife finds satisfaction by regarding the bliss of her own self as supreme.
"Indeed, thousands upon thousands of wives shall be mine;
and Vṛndā too has been made my wife by me, and she is devoted to me. (11)
Listen, I shall tell you this narrative exactly as it happened in every respect:
having made the accomplishment of my purpose a pretext, Vṛndā was made my wife by me.
Vṛndā was indeed my wife in Goloka, equal to Rādhikā;
she saw me, her own husband, sporting together with Rādhikā. (13)
Afflicted by jealousy, she experienced a burning heat in her heart that was hostile to pleasure;
unable to speak to me, she did not express what was in her mind.
Then, after a short while, although she was summoned by me to sport, she did not come;
because of that fault, she is wicked and does not deserve to serve me.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the narrative of Jālandhara and Vṛndā in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*: Having observed the amorous union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, Vṛndā—the consort of Kṛṣṇa residing in Goloka—departed from Goloka due to the fault of jealousy toward her co-wife. Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; once Jālandhara himself, the lord of Vṛndā, arrived together with the asuras for the purpose of worshipping Śukra.

Having heard this and remembering Śiva, Śukrācārya said to him:

Following the path shown by Viṣṇu, those heroes, devoted to the practice of deceit for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose, then made peace with the Asuras.

"I shall grant you the fruit quickly; be ready, O Lord of Asuras.
