Viṣṇu said: "Indeed, for the sake of protecting the lords of the gods, I must go there by all means; I shall not kill your younger brother."
"O beloved, because he is a portion of Rudra and by the word of Brahmā—and not by my own word—your brother must not be killed; do not despair, my dear."
Having spoken thus and consoled her, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa went to where Jalandhara was, having taken the gods and others along with him. (108)

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Viṣṇu of Vaikuṇṭha and Other Matters," following the defeat of the gods in the battle between the Suras and Asuras waged by Jalandhara for the sake of destroying Viṣṇu and the other deities; after seeing Rāhu headless among the hosts of Asuras who worship Śukrācārya on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, and having understood the cause thereof—the drinking of nectar from the churning of the ocean—and his partiality [for the gods]. Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā, First Part: The Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga, within the narrative of Jalandhara and Vṛndā. Chapter 325.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, tell me what my brother did after seeing Viṣṇu, and what was done by Viṣṇu; speak to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how the father, daughter, and likewise the son—all are indeed fickle and restless; what, then, does not happen therein?
Seeing Viṣṇu, he became exceedingly enraged, filled with pride in his own strength;
and beholding the army of the gods prepared for battle, he blazed with extreme fury.
Jalandhara commanded the Daityas for the sake of battle:
"O all you excellent Daityas, [go] for the purpose of war with the immortals! (4)
"Let the great weapons go forth and wage a battle difficult to overcome, such that the gods shall not return again, until their great end is brought about. (5)
Then there were Mauryas numbering one hundred thousand, Dhaumras numbering one hundred,
Asuras numbering ten million, and Kālakeyas numbering ten million.
Hundreds of thousands of Kaṅkas, as well as those protected by Śumbha and Niśumbha,
and crores of the great Daityas known as Tālajaṅghas, marched forth from there.
Rākṣasas and Dānavas, too, numbering in the millions and hundreds of billions of foot-soldiers,
having formed an alliance, arrived there with the firm resolve to destroy the gods.
Then the battle-flags appeared in the sky like eyes,
and the kettledrums and war-trumpets indeed sounded terrifyingly.
By the command of Jalandhara, the Daityas fought with the gods using missiles,
arrows, bhūśuṇḍīs, and śataghnīs from afar.
Then Trita, having arrived running with clubs, spears,
and javelins, as well as sharp-edged spears, axes, swords, maces, and other weapons, [attacked].
With trees and mountains, as well as with thunderbolts and spears, with iron arrows and crescent-shaped shafts, and with javelins, they struck one another.
Those hosts of Daityas struck them, and the deities also struck with their discuses;
those great heroes fought, uttering roars like lions.
Some were struck down by arrows, others were killed or wounded by lances;
some were slain by axes and spears within the forest of battle. (14)
Seeing the great slaughter of the Daityas, Jalandhara blew his battle-trumpet and, shouting himself with force, [advanced]. 15.
Having made the Dānavas powerful, he descended to the forefront of the battle;
consequently, the Daityas of great heroism then became filled with enthusiasm.
And having become blind in the battle, let those most cruel deities encounter one another;
let them kill, let them cut, and let them rend each other asunder. || 17 ||
May they crush them, trample them, and grind them like sesame seeds;
may they not flee from the battle, but perform the fire-oblation for their own selves.
The sacrifice of battle for heroes indeed does not come again, nor can it be obtained;
let the gods drink the blood, and let those dear to them enjoy it thereafter. (19)
Thus there was a great outcry at that time within the realm of the Daityas;
for the blows dealt by the Daityas were powerful and destructive to the gods.
At that time, no blow whatsoever was dealt by the gods;
rather, wherever [a wound] was seen, there the deities themselves were seen to have been struck down. ||21||
At that moment, a great terror arose within the heart of Viṣṇu for an instant;
even Vāsava fled, and the remaining gods likewise fled.
Seeing them intent on flight, Viṣṇu indeed entered among them.
Having rendered the gods entirely powerless, Hari [confronted] those who remained after the slaughter.
Mounted upon Garuḍa, he challenged him again and again for battle, saying:
"I shall restore all the gods to life, but I shall destroy the Dānavas."
"Do not flee from the battle; I shall fight, standing at the forefront.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu then [issued a command] from his Sudarśana [discus].
At that very moment, he fashioned hundreds of thousands of Sudarśanas and dispatched them to destroy the Dānava army.
Having created hundreds of thousands of fires, Hari dispatched the Asura army to slay them, and he also hurled the Sudarśana [discus].
Just as the fire-wheels completely reduced the Asuras to ashes,
the gods, having observed this, struck down those who were fleeing.
Challenging one another, exceedingly bold, desirous of victory, and most terrible,
they were thus revived by Viṣṇu after he had sprinkled them with water.
They too then struck the Dānavas with swift weapons and missiles;
Viṣṇu beheld everywhere that the Dānavas had fallen into a state of terror.
Then, they were seen as if in a forest—severed, destroyed, and cut to pieces;
the survivors fled from heaven, abandoning the field of battle.
Thus, a great defeat befell the asuras there;
the ocean-dweller, who inspired fear in the hosts of gods, could not endure it.
Pointing toward Śukra, who was the life-giver of the asuras, he advanced to do battle;
and Śukra quickly restored to life the Daityas who had been consumed by the [enemy's] magic power.
Jalandhara let out a great roar that pierced the ears;
by that terrifying sound, the entire world was then filled.
At the roar of Viṣṇu as well, the entire world trembled;
both of them, having taken up their bows, produced a clanging sound.
For the husband of the sister and the son of Śālaka fought each other, moving through the opposing ranks; with their arrows, they then made the sky appear as if it had no space at all.
Viṣṇu cut off the asura’s banner, umbrella, bow, and arrows with his shafts,
and struck him firmly in the heart with an arrow.
Then, leaping up with mace in hand toward Hari, the lord of the Daityas ran with force and struck Garuḍa on the head in his rage.
Having exerted great force, he indeed struck Viṣṇu in the heart with a spear;
Viṣṇu, with his sharp sword, cut down both the mace and the spear.
Then the Daitya, having again taken up another bow equipped with arrows,
struck Viṣṇu in the heart and also cut his sword.
And Viṣṇu, having cut that approaching arrow in half with his sword,
quickly took up his Śārṅga bow and discharged a fierce arrow.
The powerful Daitya, his lower lip bitten in rage after being displaced from Sītā,
severed the Vaiṣṇava bow Śārṅga with another arrow.
Furthermore, he struck Viṣṇu in the chest with exceedingly sharp arrows;
his bow being severed, Hari indeed hurled the Kaumodakī mace.
Irresistible like a flash of lightning, he possessed strength equal to that of the ocean;
even when struck with the mace, he did not waver in the least.
The Daitya hurled a trident that rained down fire at Hari;
Hari, with his sword Nandaka, cut that trident to pieces.
The Daitya [hurled] the thunderbolt-born spear named Lambā, which was one yojana in length,
possessed eight edges and a thousand bells, and was capable of destroying mountains and other such things.
Having seized it, he then hurled it for the destruction of Hari;
a great and terrifying cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods.
And the Daitya’s final thunderbolt took the form of a spear, [thinking]:
"If I destroy it, he will certainly not engage in battle. (48)
Therefore, having seized him with the beak of Garuḍa and brought him under my control,
I shall grant him victory so that there may be battle once again.
Having reflected thus, Hari held her with the beak of a bird; as she approached, she was protected by him within a single feather of his own wing.
Having witnessed this great marvel, the asura arrived from the sky;
descending into the lake, he struck Viṣṇu forcefully with his fist.
Just as [the serpent] had struck Garuḍa’s neck with his foot-lash,
Viṣṇu then seized the Daitya firmly by the head.
But Garuḍa, seizing that Daitya by the feet with his beak, lifted him up and hurled him; he fell indeed a great distance away, a hundred yojanas.
Having risen again, the ocean-born one approached by way of the sky;
at that moment, Viṣṇu, exceedingly enraged, struck him once more in the heart.
And he struck Viṣṇu repeatedly in the chest with his fist;
there, upon Garuḍa, those two of great strength continued to fight.
With arms, fists, and knees,
the powerful Daitya fought on, disregarding death as he faced his end.
"I must either die or be victorious; for I have a stake in both outcomes.
Where indeed is death from the hand of Viṣṇu, and where is the state of being a conqueror of Viṣṇu? (57)
"There is a great gain for both of us; let whatever is destined to happen surely come to pass.
Having reflected thus, he considered his own death as ordained by Śambhu. (58)
Laughing, the Blessed One said: "Blessed are you, O you who are intoxicated by battle, who fall like a moth before me, the imperishable one, for your own destruction."
O son of Śaṅkara, you who have come to the forefront of battle having surrendered your very life and vital breaths, thus upholding the duty of a warrior.
"You are certainly not afraid of my weapons, by which many heroes have been slain;
for no hero equal to you has ever been seen, one who engages in combat by seizing the enemy by the throat."
"Choose a boon, O Lord of Daityas; I am pleased with your prowess.
Even that which is not to be given must be granted to you, for you are such a one upon the field of battle."
O Lakṣmī, having understood the intention of the bridegroom, the intelligent Jalandhara replied to Hari, bringing the Lord under his own control.
"If you are pleased, O Blessed One, and if you grant me a boon,
then dwell in my house together with my sister, myself, and your retinue."
Having heard that, the Blessed One said to him, "So be it"; then the Lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī and his retinue, [departed].
Having gone to the house of Jalandhara and being honored by Jalandhara,
he dwelt there at [the demon's] word, bound and awaiting further combat.
Jalandhara established the city of Jālandhara upon the earth,
and he held sovereignty over a vast portion of the world extending as far as the ocean.
All the Dānavas were appointed as officials in heaven and other realms, while the Daityas themselves were made to hold authority in the netherworld (Pātāla) and other regions. 68.
He dwelt indeed upon an island in the midst of the western ocean on earth;
whatever jewel was accumulated among the gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, [he possessed it].
Having brought all those under his own control, he enjoyed the earth free from thorns—
the lords of the gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, as well as the serpents, rakshasas, and kings of men.
Having made the Nāgas his subjects in his own island, Hari ruled over the three worlds;
he restored to life all those gods who had died in battle.
Śukra restored to life whichever Daityas were slain;
the gods, however, returned to Mount Meru and other forests as they had been before.
Not even a small fruit was obtained; it was like the threshing of husks.
The news spread throughout all the worlds that Viṣṇu had been defeated.
He who is self-controlled becomes subject only to devotion and not by anything else;
he was brought under control by Lakṣmī, by Śālaka, and by affection.
Having abandoned his divine duties, he has taken refuge in the house of his brother-in-law;
thus the gods have become destitute, miserable, and without a protector.
The goddesses, too, having fallen into misery and being greatly oppressed by the Asuras, [asked]:
"What should be done? Where should we go? Viṣṇu has resorted to the Vṛndā creeper. (76)
Then he thought, "May the destruction of the Daityas indeed occur swiftly," [receiving this] from the Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who resides within his inner self.
The gods and goddesses who were citizens of Jālandhara-dvīpa became such that no one could recognize them as demons. ||78||
Having deliberated thus, those excellent ones went into the presence of Śaṅkara;
they praised Śaṅkara for the removal of their own suffering.
Then Mahādeva, having summoned Nārada who was intent on performing his duties,
dispatched him to that city with the desire to accomplish the work of the gods.
Then Nārada also went quickly to the city of Jālandhara;
having first met with the gods and learned of their sorrow, he returned once more.
Having accepted the worship performed by the gods and the hospitable reception of guests,
and having heard about the departure of the sun, moon, dharma, and fire, and so forth.
Having heard of Viṣṇu’s defeat and the misconduct of Jalandhara, he comforted the gods and informed them for the sake of accomplishing their purpose.
Having declared, "I shall indeed perform the work of the gods according to my intellect," the sage himself bowed to the gods and went to the assembly hall of Jalandhara.
Having bowed to the sage who had arrived, Jalandhara offered him a seat;
and after worshipping him according to the prescribed rites, the Daitya spoke to Nārada with a smile.
"May it be well with you, O best of sages! From where have you come here? For what purpose have you arrived? Tell me, and I shall do it. (86)
Having heard that, Nārada, with a serene soul, spoke to the Asura:
"Blessed are you, O powerful king; you now abide as a lord of kings. (87)
"I have heard in heaven that you are the enjoyer of the luster of all jewels, and subsequently I have heard of the most excellent of enjoyments belonging to Śaṅkara. (88)
In a great forest of wish-fulfilling trees extending for ten thousand yojanas,
crowded with hundreds of wish-granting cows and brilliantly illuminated by wish-fulfilling gems.
It was divine, made entirely of gold, and possessed of wonderful beauty on every side;
it was attended by vehicles, mounts, male servants, and female servants.
There, upon the peak of Kailāsa, I indeed beheld Śaṅkara—fair-complexioned, beautiful in every limb, three-eyed, and crowned with the moon. 9.1.
It was well-served by young women less than sixteen years of age,
who were as if formed from the mass of the moon or emerged from the gold of the sun.
Śiva rejoices there on that mountain with many beautiful women;
thereafter, without reflection, I heard of the happiness of Jālandhara.
"Of what nature might such prosperity be, or perhaps it is not like this?"—having reflected thus with wonder, I have come to your house. (94)
Desiring to behold him, I have come here into your presence;
for your island is beautiful and adorned with gardens and groves. (95)
"It is beautiful, for it is adorned by a surrounding moat," said [the architect].
To him who had spoken thus, the Daitya showed [the site] in every respect. (96)
Having seen prosperity residing within the house, outside the house, and established in the depths,
the king of sages, having reflected upon it, declared that it was produced by the acquisition of divine power.
Impelled by Viṣṇu, he spoke so that delusion might enter the Daitya:
"O Jalandhara, there is no end to your prosperity! (98)
In the palace of the Lord of the Three Worlds, there is indeed nothing surprising:
the dwellings are variegated, as are the vehicles and mounts. (99)
Requisites, jeweled offerings, treasuries of gems, pearls,
diamonds, gold, and hundreds of lands.
Elephants, horses, and other such creatures do not exist elsewhere as they do here; for instance, there is Airāvata among the capable elephants, and Uccaiḥśravas is the horse of the Sun.
The wish-fulfilling Kalpa-mandāra trees, the treasures of Kubera, Brahmā’s swan-vehicle, and Viṣṇu’s Garuḍa as well; 102.
The buffalo of Yama, as well as Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus, the jewel of King Śeṣa, and likewise the nectar of the Moon; || 103 ||
The umbrellas of the Manvantaras, as well as their golden staffs,
the chowries of the lords of the directions, and the bracelets of the goddesses.
Thus all these jewels shine within your home;
indeed, you possess the preeminence over both women and female servants.
But not even a single jewel among wives shines like that which is before Śaṅkara; indeed, you are deficient by that much.
The palaces of the king shine with that most excellent jewel of a wife, who resembles the sun and the moon, rather than with [other] riches.
The king’s palace does not shine with even a hundred thousand Kirāta women as you do, O lady of celestial fame; indeed, no wife of yours equals you.
Or rather, what is the use of beautiful slave-girls if one’s fame has not been spread by marriage?
Without a white-complexioned wife, everything is like the palace of a jackal king.
Indeed, without a wedded wife, the king could never possess splendor;
the queen would be the mother of the kingdom, divine, and the increaser of the lineage.
The prince is not considered by the king to be among the thousands of slave-girls;
nor are those born of slave-girls, even by the hundreds, deemed worthy of consecration.
Therefore, you ought certainly to bring back that maiden, a jewel among women;
I shall go to those worlds where jewels are gathered.
Having heard this, the exceedingly arrogant Jalandhara said to the celestial sage:
"O celestial sage, just as I possess the preeminence among all jewels," || 113 ||
If such a most excellent and supreme thing exists among the fourteen worlds, and it has been known by you, then show it to me according to your will.
By you have been seen everywhere women, queens, and maidens—even the daughters of the Vedhas, the Śaṅkaras, and the Viṣṇus. (115)
There were also daughters of the sages, of the ancestors, and of the gods;
and of humans, of the nāgas, and of the daityas, dānavas, and rākṣasas. (116)
O Sage, all those maidens have been seen by you everywhere,
possessing supreme beauty, form, youth, and excellent qualities.
Show me that jewel where it dwells;
I shall take it to my assembly of queens from the fourteen worlds.

"O learned one, show me such a man, before whom all queens will surely fall like moths; I shall lead him away and marry him."
"I shall carry such a jewel among maidens as that.

How slender was her waist, and how much like the seat of desire (the vulva) was it?

Otherwise, that task could not be accomplished; for what is there that cannot be achieved by heroes?

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of the Kṛta Yuga lineage, in the narrative concerning Jalandhara and Vṛndā, [described are] the battle between the armies of the Asuras and Suras; the resuscitation of the dead Asuras and Suras; the battle between Jalandhara and Viṣṇu; the granting of a boon consisting of residence in Jalandhara’s home by the gratified Viṣṇu; the renewed suffering of the gods; their report to Śaṅkara; Nārada’s journey to Jalandhara’s house; and [the account] of Jalandhara regarding the bringing of his beautiful wife, Pārvatī.
The three hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Delusion" (Mohanam), etc. || 326 ||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Great King Nārāyaṇa,
after Nārada had departed, what was indeed done by the enemy Jalandhara?
Speak in detail, O Lord, O Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
what did the great Daitya Jalandhara do for the sake of Pārvatī?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how the Daitya thereafter made a thorough effort according to the instructions spoken by Nārada; I shall relate it to you exactly as it happened.
Thinking only of that slender woman, afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, his fortune now subject to Time, he was bewildered and his intellect utterly lost.
He summoned his wise messenger, the son of Siṃhikā;
when the great Rāhu had arrived, he, the accomplisher of tasks, spoke to him.
For the sake of accomplishing my purpose, go to Mount Kailāsa;
there dwells the yogi Śaṅkara, who does not touch even the most excellent of women.
Nārada told me that he possesses a jewel of a maiden in his hand,
and that this very jewel must indeed be obtained by me.
Indeed, that name "Pārvatī" must certainly be attained by me;
having gone there, you should speak with a fearless heart.
O forest-dwelling great yogi, what use have you for the jewel of a wife?
Give her to me, who am named Jalandhara; take back that jewel-handed one.
Whatever jewels exist throughout the three worlds, all of them have been brought by me, the king, from there to my palace by force.
Airāvata, Uccaiḥśravas, the Kalpavṛkṣa, and the Pārijātaka tree;
a celestial chariot yoked with swans, the thunderbolt, the spear, and the fly-whisk.
The pearls, the diamonds, and that renowned parasol—
all of that is indeed for my enjoyment, for I have brought it to my own home.
The treasures, the great garland, the noose, the staff, and likewise the nectar—
all that exists in my house, O Hara, with the exception of the jewel of a maiden.
"O yogis, these nine maidens must not be touched; indeed, let them be given to me.
Having received this command, Rāhu went to where Śaṅkara was.
Because he had been appointed as a messenger by Nandin, he was ushered into the midst of the assembly hall [to see] Śaṅkara, whose every limb was divine and who was adorned with celestial ornaments.
He prostrated before Hara there and likewise approached his presence;
he said to Śaṅkara, "I am indeed the messenger of Jalandhara."
"Sent by the Lord of the Three Worlds, I have come here into your presence;
listen to that which he said concerning you, a yogin. (17)
"O Digambara, this jewel of a maiden, lovely as gold and like a mass of moonlight, would be of no use to you, a yogi; therefore, give her to me. (18)
"I am the enjoyer of the jewel of light; that jewel of a woman shall not be yours.
For one who subsists on alms, whence could there be a jewel? But the jewel of a wife belongs to a sovereign. (1.9)
"Whatever jewels exist in the three worlds have been gathered by me in their entirety;
this auspicious maiden is also desired by me—let her be given to me."
"Give me the jewel of your wife; subjects bring happiness to a king.
O Hara, because you are contained within the three worlds, you are my subject. (21)
Behold, O Lakṣmī, how this one of ruined intellect spoke to his father and mother, saying, "Give me Pārvatī"; what indeed is the nature of Hari’s illusion? 22.
In this world, those of ruined intellect who contemplate only their mothers—all these are to be known as Jalandharas, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu. || 23 ||
Even though he has female slaves, he still desires another's wife;
that Jalandhara, too, should be understood as being consigned to the mouth of destruction.
Listen now to what happened next, which Rāhu spoke of at that very moment:
a most terrible host arose, with a roar like a violent thunderbolt.
Great, with eyes blazing from the wrath of Īśa between his eyebrows, having a lion’s face and a flickering tongue, and with hair standing erect, he was terrifying. || 26 ||
Tālajaṅgha, afflicted by hunger, rushed toward Rāhu;
seeing him approaching to devour him, Rāhu fled. || 27 ||
Nevertheless, he forcibly seized Rāhu to devour him;
having reviled Śaṅkara, Rāhu said, "Protect me, who have sought refuge! (28)
Save me, save me, O Lord! Protect me, protect me, O ocean of compassion!
This servant of yours is devouring me, your messenger who has come for refuge. (29)
O Śaṅkara, protect me so that he does not devour me;

Having heard those words, "O Brāhmaṇa," Śaṅkara then said to his own attendant:
"O messenger, do not devour this Brāhmaṇa named Rāhu."
Having heard these words of the messenger, he released Subhojana;

"Hunger afflicts me, O Śambhu; give me something to eat, Maheśvara.

"O great hero, I grant you the status of being worshipped alongside me under the name Kīrtimukha; dwell at the door of my house."
From that time forward, he remained at the gateway of Śambhu’s abode;

Then Rāhu went to where Jalandhara was stationed and reported his own death as well as how he had survived.
But Jalandhara, enraged upon hearing of Śaṅkara’s conduct,
regarded the insult to his messenger as a great personal humiliation.
He said to the foremost of the Daityas: "Be ready indeed in an instant!
Let all the Daityas, such as Kālanemi and the others, set forth. (41)
And there were tens of millions born of the lineage of heroes, headed by Śumbha and Niśumbha;
those of the Kaṃbu lineage, the Daurhṛdas, the Kālakeyas, and the Kālakas.
The Mauryas, the Dhaumras, and other Dānavas and Asuras—
all having assembled and prepared themselves— Jalandhara took them with him.
He quickly went forth, surrounded by tens of millions of Daityas;
Rāhu, with his head severed, was placed at the front as an inauspicious omen.
Śukra was one-eyed, yet he went at the very front for the sake of inauspiciousness;
moreover, Śumbha’s sword fell from his hand, which was likewise for the sake of inauspiciousness. ||45||
There was the crushing of Niśumbha and others, as well as the stumbling in their flight;
furthermore, the crown fell from the head of Jalandhara.
All of that became an ill omen for his departure, causing distress; moreover, there were even inauspicious signs indicative of a great sleep [of death]. ||47||
Then the terrified gods, seeking protection, went toward Śaṅkara;
they offered hymns of praise for the destruction of the wicked and for the attainment of happiness by the deities. 48.
O Mahādeva, absorbed in meditation, established in samādhi, salutations be unto you!
Jalandhara, your son, has been surrendered for destruction. (49)
Having caused the slaughter of the gods, as well as the assault upon Pārvatī,
and having committed an insult against you, he was then prepared for destruction.
Or rather, O Lord of Compassion, was the demon previously intended for destruction? Or has it been so determined by you, the Lord of Lakṣmī? (5.1)
It is better to destroy poison before consuming it;
it is better to punish the wicked before they cause joy to the evil-doer. (52)
Viṣṇu dwells in his house, served by Vṛndā;
Śaṅkara dwells in his own house, absorbed in meditation upon Brahman.
O Lord, O Śaṅkara, consider what will happen to Pārvatī here, and also behold the miserable plight of the gods. 54.
Brahmā does not cease from his activity in the construction of the cosmic egg,
and the guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds have fallen under the sway of Jalandhara.
No protector exists for us, and Fortune herself is our companion; therefore, become our protector, for we have been dislodged from our place and our minds are distraught. (56)
"O son, he whom you slew for the sake of protection—that son of the Ocean—now approaches, arrogant in his strength, to engage you in battle. (57)
"You ought to slay him without delay, for he pursues contrary goals;
being distressed yourself, protect all the gods and us who have come to you for refuge. (58)
Having heard these words of the god, Śaṅkara remembered Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu arrived swiftly so that the asura might not perceive him. (59)
Śambhu said to Hari: "O Viṣṇu, how was Jalandhara slain by you?
And why do you still dwell in his house even today?"
Viṣṇu said: "O Mahādeva, Śrī is your brother and [this being] is your son; for this reason, he has not been killed. Do not slay him, O Śaṅkara. (61)
I engaged him in battle with the intent of seizing his life in every way;
however, restrained by Lakṣmī, I did not kill him at all.
O Śambhu, he was indeed not killed by me out of respect for you;
rather, by your grace, I have been established in my own abode and am no longer a bird.
His wife was the highly fortunate Vṛndā, a resident of Kṛṣṇa’s Goloka, who was rich in virtue, chaste, and ever devoted to her husband.
"By her power, that Daitya will not die; indeed, it was with the desire to know the cause of this that I took up residence in her house. (65)
O Śambhu, that is known in every way to be the powerful cause;
therefore, O Mahādeva, engage in battle, for I shall provide assistance. 66.
In that Vṛndāvana, some form of deception will have to be practiced;
however, I shall act only according to justice, never unjustly.
"And that Daitya desires to seize your wife out of passion;
there is a vulnerability in this situation where something must be done by me. (68)
The destruction of one who pursues wealth obtained through the corruption of his mother is certain;
this is not a son, but an enemy created by you upon seeing Indra. (69)
He alone is the one who goes astray from justice and must be destroyed; no deliberation is required in this matter.
In the meantime, the Daitya arrived accompanied by Mahāsena.
Having arrived at the vicinity of Kailāsa, he roared, obstructing the mountain;
hearing the tumultuous clamor of the army, Śaṅkara then became enraged.
He commanded Nandi and the other leaders of the Gaṇas for the sake of battle— those experts in warfare headed by the general Nandīśvara, who has the face of an elephant.
All the Gaṇas descended from Kailāsa, filled with wrath;
indeed, those Gaṇas were by the millions, as were the foremost of the Daityas.
Making the sounds of battle in the valleys of Kailāsa,
those heroic Pramathas and Dānavas roared most terribly.
They shone with showers of spears, javelins, and arrows, with clubs, nooses, and sharp-edged spears,
as well as with tridents, missiles, thunderbolts, mallets, and various weapons.
Resounding with the booming sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs that gladden heroes,
and with the noise of elephants, horses, and chariots, the earth shook as it was made to vibrate.
In that place, terrifying sounds arose from both armies,
accompanied by roaring and the fierce mutual slaughter.
Then, O Lakṣmī, a most terrible slaughter commenced;
elephants were slain, horses were slain, and heroes were killed by the thousands. (78)
The hosts of Daityas were struck down by the Pramathas, and likewise the Gaṇas were struck down by the Daityas;
having fallen into the great sleep, the earth, covered by them, shone resplendently.
At that time, the earth became impassable, thick with the mire of fat, blood, and flesh;
yet Śukra brought the Daityas back to life by the power of the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* mantra.
"The Gaṇas who have died do not rise again; this is a great and terrifying calamity.
And the Gaṇas reported this destruction to Śaṅkara.
Having learned all the deeds of Śukra, Hara became enraged;
from his mouth, with eyes copper-red with anger, there emerged a terrifying Kṛtyā.
With shanks like palm trees, a mouth like a cave, fingers like palm trees, and breasts like mountains,
she reached the battlefield and moved among the asuras.
While devouring those Daityas, she went to where Bhārgava was; seizing Śukrācārya by the throat, she indeed cast him into the middle of her womb. 84.
Having placed it within her own body, she vanished into the sky and departed;
the Daityas, seeing this destruction of Śukra, became dejected with their faces withered.
Intent on preserving their lives, they fled from the battlefield;
then the great army, struck down by the hosts, was utterly shattered.
Śumbha, Niśumbha by name, and Kālanemi— these three,
engaging in battle, struck down the divine army of the Pramathas.
Discharging showers of arrows, they shook the army of the Gaṇas;
and the Gaṇas, in turn, obstructed the Daityas with rains of shafts.
The hosts of Dānavas became as radiant as the kiṃśuka flowers of spring;
then that army of Dānavas took to the sky.
He obstructed that army of the Gaṇas with an exceedingly terrible rain from the sky;
then the host of the Pramathas, being shattered, fled into the mountain caves.
Having seen this reversal, Nandin, Bhānumukha, Ṣaṇmukha, and other exceedingly powerful gaṇas took hold of the sky. ||9.1||
Supporting themselves upon the sky, the armies, having brought forth great boulders,
rushed forward in indignation to destroy the foremost of the Daityas.
Leaping up again and again, the powerful goddesses struck down the foremost of the Daityas protected by Jalandhara,
shattering their heads with weapons of stone.
Others, however, fell upon the earth, while still others fled. ||93||
Thus that army of the Asuras, having been shattered and abandoned the sky, took refuge in the forest of Kailāsa and remained hidden for a moment. 94.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Jālandhara Sending Rāhu as a Messenger to Śaṅkara and His Being Repelled by Kīrtimukha; the Arrival of Jālandhara’s Army; Śukrācārya Being Cast into the Vagina by Kṛtyā; and the Occurrence of the Fierce Battle," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Tell me, what happened there after Śukrācārya had been placed within the womb of Kṛtyā, and what was the nature of that battle?"
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Until the destruction of Jālandhara was accomplished, Śukra was crushed within his own womb by Kṛtyā; at that time, he was unable to emerge.
By the power of yoga and mantra, this man, though on the verge of death, somehow sustained his life through self-restraint; he remained there in a state of deep sleep, as if unconscious.
When Jālandhara had been destroyed by the magical rite (kṛtyā), he was urinated upon outside;
having fainted for a long time, he eventually regained consciousness.
Now, O Lakṣmī, hear of the incidental battle between them;
from that, a great duel arose between those two great warriors.
The great asura Kālanemi rushed toward the one named Nandin;
Śumbha rushed toward Lambodara, and Niśumbha toward the six-faced one (Ṣaḍānana).
Niśumbha pierced Śikhin in the heart with five arrows;
then Kārttikeya [pierced him] in turn with five exceedingly sharp arrows.
He pierced his horses, his charioteer, and even his banner;
with a single sharp arrow, he struck Niśumbha.
Niśumbha also roared at the roaring six-faced one (Kārttikeya),
and he struck him with many arrows, piercing his armor.
Then Kārttikeya, enraged, seized a spear with his hand;
the powerful one forcefully and swiftly hurled that life-destroying weapon.
Niśumbha, who was conversant with the rules of combat, struck her down with his own power;
meanwhile, Skanda then hurled at him a second weapon that brings an end to life.
She hurled it with great speed; as it struck his heart, it caused him to fall.
Then Nandīśvara [struck] the great asura Kālānemi there.
He pierced him with five sharp arrows, then with seven, and likewise with four; he struck the horses with two, the standard with one, and the charioteer with another.
Then Kālanemi cut Nandin’s bow with arrows,
and likewise pierced Nandīśvara on the head with feathered shafts.
Nandīśa also struck Kālaka in the heart with his trident.
Kālaka, his entire essence destroyed and the interior of his heart pierced by the trident, [fell].
Having uprooted a peak from the mountain, he struck Nandin;
Nandin, seizing a spear, struck Kāla in the chest.
Kāla fell into a swoon, stretching out his hands and feet;
then the auspicious Hastyānana pierced him in the heart with a feathered shaft.
He pierced the horses with eight arrows and struck the charioteer with one;
then Śubha, with great speed, indeed struck Mūṣaka with a single arrow.
Having made the sound "cūcū," he pierced him in the head, and Ālu fled;
Gaṇeśa, the leader of the hosts, abandoned him and proceeded on foot.
Then, with a spear, he pierced Śubha and struck him down upon the earth;
thereafter, Kālanemi and Niśumbhaka, having cast off their swoon, [arose].
Both of them, fierce and formidable, came together to slay Gaṇeśa;
they seized him, threw him down, and pierced him with arrows.
Seeing him thus afflicted, Vīrabhadra rushed forward;
he seized him by both sides and crushed him repeatedly.
Those two great asuras, nearly dead, were cast upon the earth;
they became kūṣmāṇḍas, bhairavas, pretas, bhūtas, and piśācas.
The Vināyakas, Vetālas, Vīras, and Rākṣasa hosts, as well as the Yoginīs, Kṛtyakās, and Ḍākinīs, all marched forth with their armies.
Then, indeed, the sounds of "kila-kila," lion-like roars accompanied by gurgling sounds,
and the loud blasts of hand-drums caused the earth to tremble at that time.
They devour the Dānavas and slay them with tridents;
they cut off their throats and crush the great Asuras. ||26||
Then they struck down the Daityas and Dānavas with mountain-like peaks,
as well as with elephants, horses, and chariots converted into weapons.
And by the Dānavas and Daityas, both those who were armed and those who were not,
she was seized by the feet one after another, and they in turn struck her with them.
Thus, a great slaughter was indeed wrought by the armies of Bhūta and the others;
those who were the warriors, such as the Daityas and the rest, became weapons themselves.
By those very weapons having attained their power, the foremost warriors of one's own army were destroyed—
wherein there were spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, and vināyakas.
What impossible feat was not conceivable there for the warriors?
That army of Jalandhara was cut to pieces, shattered, and destroyed.
When not a single asura or dānava remained there— whether crushed, destroyed, pulverized, or shattered into pieces— [he saw that none were left].
Then the great hero Jalandhara, overcome with extreme distress and filled with intense grief at the destruction of Śukra, shed tears again and again.
With the destruction of Ujjīvaka, everything of mine has indeed perished today;
I too must die here, having displayed my prowess in battle. (34)
Having thus resolved, he suddenly seized the Kṛtyā by her feet;
at that moment, she discharged her own semen into his urine for the purpose of tearing him apart.
When he had placed [the chariot] there and rested for a moment,
Śukra then regained consciousness by means of his knowledge.
Then, reviving the Daityas with the Saṃjīvinī herb, he roared;
meanwhile, Vīrabhadra [attacked] that Śukrācārya and Jalandhara.
Having brought the entire chariot together, he entered the cave;
having delivered Śukrācārya to the Kṛtyās, he took Jalandhara away.
Vīrabhadra brought him before Hara and roared;
meanwhile, Jalandhara assumed many forms.
Departing from that place in his original form out of fear of death,
he was accompanied by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and leaders of the gaṇas.
The Daityas who had been cut, pierced, and slain were then restored to life by Śukra;
however, seeing his army thus utterly devastated, Jalandhara then [acted].
Again, with his chariot adorned with many banners, he advanced against the hosts;
like a cloud, he released a rain of arrows upon the army of Śiva.
Then the sky became covered by the cloud-like arrows of Jalandhara;
Gaṇeśa, the leader of the hosts, was pierced by five shafts.
Vīrabhadra was pierced by twenty [arrows] and Kārtikeya by seven;
then Kārtikeya also, having been struck by that Daitya, quickly [acted].
He pierced that hero with his spear and felled him to the ground;
then Jalandhara, blazing with rage, rose up in an instant.
He struck Kārttikeya with a mace and crushed him;
then Vīrabhadra, with a spear, crushed the son of the Ocean.
Jalandhara, rising up and armed with an iron club, leaped forward;
rushing swiftly, he struck Vīrabhadra.
Vīrabhadra fell to the earth and Jalandhara roared;
a great tumult arose among the beings in the presence of Rudra. 48.
Hearing this, the fierce Mahārudra arrived at the battlefield laughing aloud;
indeed, upon seeing the terrifying Rudra, all the Daityas fled. ||49||
Then the Daitya Jalandhara, having resolved upon his own death,
rushed toward Caṇḍīśa while discharging arrows by the thousands.
But those preeminent Daityas who had been restored to life by Śukra,
as well as others who remained after the slaughter, rushed toward Śaṅkara.
Śumbha, Niśumbha, Ghasmara, Kālanemi, Balāhaka,
Pracaṇḍa, Khaḍga, and Romāṇa, their lips quivering with rage, [advanced].
They pierced Rudra and the hosts of Rudras with arrows;
the sky became completely shrouded on all sides by the darkness of those shafts.
Hara, having torn apart that net with his arrows, covered the sky;
then Śaṅkara severed Khaḍgaroman’s head from his body with his shafts.
Having slain Balāhaka, he also killed Ghasmara;
he then cut down Mahāvīra and Pracaṇḍa with his triple-pointed spear.
Thus indeed many were slain there and did not rise again;
then Śaṅkara himself dispatched the great spear Jaladhara.
Assuming another form, he vanished into the sky for a moment;
that spear, rendered fruitless against the earth, struck down other Daityas.
Then the remaining great daityas fled from the battle out of fear;
but Jalandhara, seeing them, spoke again, uttering words of reproach: "Shame! (58)
What is gained by you who have fled after drinking your mothers' milk?
And what indeed is gained by being slain from behind, such that heaven or liberation is not attained? (59)
For brave warriors, death in battle bestows heaven and even liberation;
let there be death by weapons that grant immortality while facing the enemy.
May death not come to one who turns away from battle, for such a person goes to a hellish state;
rather, having pierced the solar orb, let the warrior go to the supreme goal.
That great yogi who is slain face-to-face in battle is a wandering mendicant;
indeed, the wise should not entertain fear of death, which is truly unavoidable.
Indeed, death is fixed and certain for the body from the very moment of its birth;
therefore, O Asuras, casting aside the fear of that death, fight in battle! (6.3)
Even after saying this, those Daityas, being terrified of Śaṅkara at that time, did not go to the battle of Aṇa; Jalandhara became exceedingly enraged.
He said to Śaṅkara, "Show me here that strength which you possess.
Having spoken thus, Bāṇa struck his father Hara with seven arrows.
Before they could reach him, Mahādeva cut them down with sharpened arrows;
then the Bearer of the Ocean rushed forward and hurled a mace at Śaṅkara.
Śiva, by means of his power, indeed split her—who was traveling through the path of the sky—into two;
then the Daitya then endeavored to strike Hara with his fist.
He was struck down at a distance of one yojana by Śaṅkara with his trident;
then Jalandhara, perceiving Rudra to be supported by great strength, [acted].
He created an illusion of Gandharvas and Apsarases that bewildered Rudra;
and appearing forth, the Gandharvas sang in a manner enchanting to the ear. (69)
The Apsarases danced with songs sung in sweet tones,
while others played cymbals, flutes, and drums.
There, Śambhu as well as his attendants were indeed deluded;
forgetting the battle, those devotees of Śambhu and Śaṅkara remained absorbed in that [state]. ||7 1||
Seeing Śumbha and the others lying unconscious, the Daitya left them on the battlefield and,
overcome by desire, went quickly to where Gaurī was in her abode.
He has ten arms, five faces, and three eyes; he wears matted hair and is adorned with rudrākṣa beads, the serpent Vāsuki, a trident, a hide garment, and other ornaments. || 73 ||
Having become Rudra through his asuric power of illusion, he went inside the house;
seeing Rudra approaching, Pārvatī, the beloved of Bhava, [stood there]. (74)
Knowing him to be desirous of sexual union, she went to her bed in the house, being a virtuous woman as brilliantly radiant as the sun, the moon, fire, gold, and lightning. (76)
As soon as he saw her, that dull-witted one discharged his semen;
seeing such a thing, Pārvatī reflected within herself: ||76||
"He has certainly not touched me, nor has he come onto my bed;
he did not even see me naked—how then could he have discharged his seed? (7.7)
Therefore, this cannot be Mahādeva; rather, he must be some other Dānava.
Or perhaps he is a son of Śaṅkara, born from a mere drop of breast milk? (78)
Having reflected thus, she vanished out of fear;
not seeing her, his vigor destroyed, he went to fight with Śambhu. (79)
Pārvatī also repeatedly remembered Mahāviṣṇu in her mind;
Kṛṣṇa arrived there, and Pārvatī spoke to Keśava.
"O Viṣṇu, Jalandhara has arrived here at my house having become Rudra;
he is overcome by passion and seeks to deceive me—is this not known to you? (81)
Viṣṇu said, "It is known to me; command me here as to what I should do.
Pārvatī said, "O Lord of Lakṣmī, [bestow] such [a boon] upon one who is such. (82)
Perform the very task that has been shown by him in that same manner;
destroy the virtuous conduct of Vṛndā's chastity according to my command. (83)
Otherwise, that great Daitya will die, not by his own power;
for devotion to one's husband is a supreme dharma, providing protection as well as liberation. (84)
She was likewise in Goloka; you incur no fault in that enjoyment.
All living beings are your wives—what concern is there for you here, O Lord? (85)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, having heard this himself and informed Hara, the Lord Viṣṇu departed to employ a stratagem for the purpose of destroying Jalandhara. (86)
In that city on the island of Jālandhara, Vṛndā resides;
longing for a vision of her husband, she awaits him as the victor in battle. (87)

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first book concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, within the narrative of Jalandhara and Vṛndā: the death of the generals in battle; the restoration of life by Śukrācārya; the casting of Śukrācārya’s vital essence into the womb of a *kṛtyā*; the subsequent destruction of the Daityas; the duel between Jalandhara and Vīrabhadra; the battle between Jalandhara and Śaṅkara; Jalandhara’s production of the *gāndharvī* illusion and his approach in the form of Rudra to deceive Pārvatī; and Viṣṇu’s approach to deceive Vṛndā.
The three hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Jagāma," etc. ||328||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa! What was done by Viṣṇu after that? How did Jālandhara die for the sake of deceiving Vṛndā? || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, during Vṛndā’s vow of devotion to her husband, the army of Jālandhara appeared;
Viṣṇu acted in order to break Vṛndā’s chastity.
Viṣṇu went there at night and, taking refuge in the garden,
showed her a dream indicating widowhood.
Indeed, Jālandhara’s head, its eyes torn out by a vulture and its ears and tip of the nose severed, was carried away by a man after it had been decapitated by Śaṅkara.
He was departing, mounted upon a buffalo, smeared with oil,
naked, adorned with ornaments of black flowers, and attended by hosts of flesh-eating spirits.
With disheveled hair, languid, and dark-complexioned, wearing crimson garments,
Kālī devoured the head that had fallen from the neck toward the south.
Vṛndā beheld a dream in which her own city, along with herself, was suddenly submerged in the ocean, endowed with the quality of the destruction of the Daityas.
Then, having awakened, Vṛndā reported her dream to the Brahmins;
and having heard it, the Brahmins declared that the dream itself was indeed most formidable.
That indeed yields inconceivable fruit and brings about great misfortune;
therefore, give gifts to the twice-born, for they destroy inconceivable fear.
Cows, garments, jewels, elephants, and ornaments—
these gifts were indeed bestowed by her, which grant the pacification of all misfortunes.
Moreover, at that time, throbbings occurred in his right limbs,
and he beheld the risen sun as being spotted and likewise devoid of luster.
Realizing that even this was undesirable, she remained submerged in an ocean of grief;
she found no peace anywhere, even upon the floors of the palace towers.
Drawn away by Viṣṇu through his illusory power (māyā), she went to the garden in distress;
accompanied there by her two friends, she found no happiness anywhere.
Wandering from forest to forest, she beheld two terrifying Rākṣasas with lion-like faces, her own emissaries dispatched by Viṣṇu.
Seeing her two servants created by means of illusion, she became exceedingly distraught;
intent on flight, she ran toward the protector. || 15 ||
Then, in that forest, she saw the sage Viṣṇukṛta;
thinking him to be her protector, she approached him and sought refuge with him.
Grasping his throat with both arms, he said to him, "Protect me! Protect me!
Then, by the power of the sage and by the sound of the syllable *huṃ*, both of them [were struck down].
The two Rākṣasas were put to flight, and Satī was protected from their fear;
then Vṛndā, her mind composed, bowed and spoke these words: || 18 ||
O holy man, dispeller of distress, protector from the fear of the wicked;
O Brahmin, if you know him, tell me: is Jalandhara my husband? (19)
He has indeed gone toward Rudra for battle; what is his current condition, his state, his well-being, or his victory? Tell me this or anything else regarding him.
The sage said: "I am the son of Bharadvāja; I shall explain this to you:
the state of great sleep is your condition of remaining without further awakening."
Hearing these most terrible words— that her husband’s well-being had departed for heaven and his victory had indeed gone elsewhere— she wept, utterly overwhelmed.
Then the two monkey lords arrived and stood before Vṛndā,
holding his head and his headless trunk in their two hands.
Seeing this, Vṛndā wept once more with a piteous voice;
beholding Jalandhara dead, she wailed like a female osprey.
Alas! My destiny is shattered; all my wealth is lost.
I have fallen into widowhood, and indeed, my auspicious fortune has vanished. (25)
"I requested that I should not have to fight with Śambhu on my way;
nevertheless, O Lord, because of your heroic nature, you did not heed my request. (26)
"O Vīraka, I too must die today by means of your body.
Having said this, when Vṛndā desired to burn that corpse, [the gods intervened].
Then that bull among sages, having bestowed courage through his own compassion, said to her: "I shall restore him to life by means of the very fire he himself produced. (28)
Having spoken thus, that sage Viṣṇu, having restored her husband to life, made that illusory corpse— Jalandhara, who was his own self— truly alive.
Having had it constructed, caused to be made, and displayed, he then held a great festival in that forest for the sake of Jīvaka.
Vṛndā too, having regained her husband—her very life—at that very moment, cast off her grief; embracing him, she then kissed his face.
Viṣṇu, the wielder of the net of illusion, took delight there on his bed again and again according to his will, while describing the field of battle.
"O beloved, my head was severed by the fierce Rudra with his discus;
it has been swiftly brought here into your presence by your messenger. (33)
"O Goddess, by this mantra spoken by me, take back your life through your chastity; accept this betel and delight in the skill of lovemaking. (34)
Having spoken thus, Mahāviṣṇu took delight with her again and again;
from the sweat of Vṛndā’s body, there appeared upon the earth that which is exceedingly purifying.
Vṛndā is said to be Tulasī, and Vṛndāvana is that sacred place;
Jālandhara’s seat is the kingdom consisting of Jālandhara. (36)
Thus it became well-known there from of old, O Ocean-born one:
that Viṣṇu took delight here with Vṛndā in exceedingly amorous play. (37)
Then, through the violation of the dharma of Satī and her devotion to her husband,
the splendor and strength of her lord Jalandhara came to exhaustion.
O beloved, in whatever manner Jalandhara approaches and delights there, he indeed becomes diminished moment by moment.
The battle lasted for exactly five days and was even more terrifying than that;
meanwhile, Viṣṇu enjoyed Vṛndā again and again in the garden palace.
Keśava Hari dispatched Garuḍa in a disguised form day and night to ascertain whether Jalandhara was dead or not.
But on the fifth day, when she had engaged in amorous play upon the bed and Vṛndā had fallen asleep, Garuḍa arrived at that moment.
Since Viṣṇu, having gone inside the house, became four-armed, Garuḍa reported the entire incident to Viṣṇu. ||43||
The Daitya has not died until this very day; he is about to die, do not delay.
Whether today, tomorrow, or the day after, he will die—of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken these and other words, just as Garuḍa was about to go outside the house, Vṛndā saw him and quickly rose up in apprehension. (45)
He saw within the house Viṣṇu with four arms; [he thought], "Who is this? Who is this other man who has entered the interior of my house? (46)
Having thus reviled her husband, while she was searching for him in the house,
Viṣṇu then arrived, having assumed the form of Jālandhara.
"Speak, Vṛndā! Who is here? Where is he? Having spoken thus, Keśava remained as if unaware; yet, no one was found there at that time.
On another day, Vṛndā became filled with suspicion once again;
she feigned sleep at the conclusion of their lovemaking in order to ascertain what was happening.
Just then Garuḍa arrived there, and Mādhava,
having become four-armed, reached the interior of the house at that very moment.
At that moment, she indeed perceived this one with certainty as Viṣṇu;
filled with wrath, she rebuked him and spoke these words to Viṣṇu.
Shame on you, who violate another’s wife and assume a deceptive form;
for though the son of Dharma, you yourself, having become a monkey, have committed unrighteousness.
"Enjoy the fruit; I grant you this: let a curse befall you, and become exactly like those two Rākṣasas whom you showed me here through your magic. (53)
For those two Rākṣasas will indeed carry off your wife;
and you too, afflicted by the grief for your wife, shall be in the forest with the monkeys as your companions.
"Because of this delusion, he who is your servant here shall become a serpent.
Having been cursed thus by her, Viṣṇu vanished in an instant.
Vṛndā said to her friend: "Behold that deceitful act committed by Viṣṇu!
My devotion to my husband has vanished, and my beloved has fallen into doubt. (56)
Having spoken thus, he performed his ablutions with the water of the Pārśva lake;
then, having assumed the lotus posture on the bank and having made his mind free from sensory objects, he sat. (57)
Then Vṛndā herself, having piled up a heap of dry wood and reflecting upon Viṣṇu’s deceit, entered the sacrificial fire.
Then Vṛndā blazed forth and in an instant became ashes;
and those ashes there turned into a dark forest of tulasī plants.
From the perspiration of Vṛndā, the green forest of Tulasī was born;
through the ritual of marriage with Tulasī, she again obtained Hari as her husband.
Meditating upon Viṣṇu, she indeed merged into him, becoming one with Viṣṇu;
yet by the will of Viṣṇu, Tulasī attained Viṣṇu once again.
Although that goddess was in the form of a tree, she was always accepted by Viṣṇu;
she who was his own in Goloka became here the daughter of the golden Apsaras.
A daughter was born in the house of Kālanemi; she was indeed beloved by Viṣṇu.
Due to the fault of being Rādhā’s co-wife, she became the beloved of Jalandhara.
Having embraced Viṣṇu once again, she was indeed born as Viṣṇu’s beloved;
at that time, Vṛndā’s splendor merged there into the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu.
That Vṛndā Tulasī was indeed born on earth in the form of a tree;
for at the end, her conduct and her destination were exactly as they had been.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you the deceptive stratagem of Vṛndā’s dharma,
which was then employed by Viṣṇu for the destruction of Jalandhara.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of Jalandhara and Vṛndā during the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga: the inauspicious dream shown to Vṛndā by Viṣṇu; the ill omens at sunrise and other times; the protection of Vṛndā, who was terrified by two artificial Rākṣasas in a garden, by Viṣṇu in the guise of a holy man; the restoration to life of the artificial Jalandhara who had died while in the form of an artificial sage; the enjoyment of pleasure with Vṛndā by Viṣṇu, having become the artificial Jalandhara; and [the account] from the sweat of Vṛndā...

Then, having learned that Vṛndā had entered the funeral pyre and thus attained the form of *tulasī* from her ashes, as well as Viṣṇu’s grief and the curse [pronounced] because his wife was abducted by two demons and so forth—this is the three hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description [of these Events]. || 329 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; then the messenger went quickly to Jalandhara and spoke of Vṛndā’s burning with grief; upon hearing this, the son of the Ocean wept.
Whatever action is performed by whom, that very same [result] is experienced by him;
thus, Gaurī has been deceived by me, and the bride has been deceived by Hari.
A person should by no means allow the husband of his sister to remain in the house;
he gradually takes possession of everything, including wealth, wife, and so forth.
A wise man should never place his trust in a son-in-law who remains living in the house;
indeed, a prudent man, having given his daughter to him, should send him away.
"Relying on my power of illusion, my wife has surely been deceived by Viṣṇu;
shall I go now to conquer Hari, or rather the formidable Hara? (5)
If I go to conquer Hari, Hara will strike me on my back;
for one who abandons a present opportunity to follow others surely perishes.
Both my very powerful enemies have been conquered, yet victory has become uncertain;
half of myself is defeated, as is the wife who has been reduced to ashes. (7)
Therefore, having conquered Paśupati, I shall indeed proceed against Viṣṇu afterwards;
having conquered Śambhu, I shall become the Lord of all lords in the world.
"Or else, having died by the arrows of Śiva, I shall go to his state.
Having reflected thus, he went right there to fight with the wielder of the Pināka bow.
In the battle, Jālandhara beheld a field terrifying with heaps of headless trunks,
impassable due to a flood of corpses, beautiful flesh, marrow, fat, and bones.
In the battle, he beheld the Lord of Pārvatī mounted upon his bull,
as well as many sharp and exceedingly thick arrows that resembled iron pillars.
The invincible one released [them] in battle like a rain-cloud at the onset of the monsoon;
then, he was struck with fury by Rudra with fierce showers of arrows.
Then, by Rudra’s arrows, his armor was cast down to the earth;
his body, pierced by the shafts, assumed the color of the *kiṃśuka* flower.
Much blood flowed from Jalandhara’s body;
the gods became powerful, while the Dānavas trembled with fear.
Hara quickly pierced the son of the Ocean in the heart with a sharp arrow;
his body mangled by the shaft, the son of the Ocean fell down unconscious.
Meanwhile, Jalandhara’s army was struck down by Rudra with iron arrows;
Jalandhara, however, remembered Śukra in his mind and called him to mind.
But he, being dependent on others, was unable to come to that place where the battle was raging, as he remained in a mountain cave occupied by a magical spell (kṛtyā). || 17 ||
Jalandhara, slowly regaining consciousness from his faint,
arose and quickly fashioned an auspicious illusory Gaurī of similar appearance.
Śiva beheld Pārvatī, bound upon the chariot and crying out in distress,
while being struck by the Daityas Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Seeing Gaurī in such a state, Śiva’s mind became exceedingly distressed;
with his limbs slackened and his soul despondent, he then cast his face downwards.
Then Jalandhara, with speed, pierced Rudra with three arrows— embedded up to their feathers—
in the head, the chest, and the belly.
Thereupon, Śaṅkara, assuming a fierce form, became exceedingly enraged; at that time, Rudra became as terrible as the fire of universal dissolution.
Then Śuṃbha, having taken that illusory Pārvatī from his chariot into the sky, released her upon the tip of his trident; she fell down upon the trident.
Weeping before Śaṅkara, she died, pierced by his trident;
seeing Māyā-Gaurī dead, Hara was overwhelmed by grief and delusion.
Gaurī cursed those led by Śumbha, saying, "She shall slay you all";
and having become Caṇḍī, she indeed slew them all on the field of battle. || 25 ||
Then Brahmā, having arrived there, spoke to the illustrious Śaṅkara:
"O Hara, this is an illusion created by Jālandhara; she is Pārvatī."
But Satī, protected by me and by Viṣṇu as well,
remains within the interior of a lotus bud, having attained a state of subtlety.
"Fight and destroy the multitude of enemies, but consider Pārvatī to be Māyā"— thinking thus upon the words of Brahmā, the Great Lord Maheśvara, who possesses supreme wisdom, [acted accordingly].
Having recognized that demonic illusion, he released a massive boulder;
he shattered the deceptive form and reduced it to dust in that very instant.
Then, beholding Śarva abandoned by his illusion, the son of the Ocean quickly manifested another illusion of exceedingly great power.
Jālandhara, possessing ten thousand arms and having stones and trees as his weapons,
became enraged in battle and repeatedly obstructed Śambhu with missiles and handheld weapons.
Then, disregarding Hara, he spoke these forceful words:
"Behold, O Śaṅkara, what kind of power I possess; do you not know it at all? (32)
"Who in the three worlds is so powerful that he cannot be pierced by my arrows?
Viṣṇu, however, is protected in his own home by his childhood nature. (33)
And by his ascetic penance, Brahmā himself— the bestower of boons— was gratified,
as were Indra, Agni, Yama, Kubera, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Īśvara, and the others.
I have brought all [beings] under my control; I have seized their mounts;
all the mountains have been subdued by me, and the rivers have been obstructed with ease.
The inhabitants of heaven were indeed conquered; Vaḍavāmukha was firmly bound;
Airāvata and the others were cast down, as was Indra along with his chariot.
Even Garuḍa was bound by me and the goddesses were brought to my home;
O Rudra, you do not know me, the conqueror of the three worlds.
Having heard this, Mahādeva laughed again and again;
Jalandhara quickly struck the laughing Śiva with his arrows.
Then the Dānava was struck in the chest with a trident by Rudra;
from the mouth of that Dānava, a supreme fever issued forth.
Jambha, who had the face of a lion and the body of a man, rushed toward the Lord;
the Lord uttered the syllable "Huṃ," and there Śarabha appeared.
Then the lion, struck by Śarabha,
seized the Dānava bull by the tail with force and whirled him around upon the ground.
Then the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain released an exceedingly fierce trident;
seizing it with his hand, the Daitya rushed toward Hara.
Then the Daitya Ayutabhuja bound Śiva in battle;
Śiva, with his own sword, cut off the forest of his hands.
Even with his hand severed, he continued to fight; then Maheśvara was pleased and spoke for the purpose of granting a boon, and the Daitya then chose a boon from Hara.
"Quickly grant me success; give me your own state!
"So be it," said Hara, and he took [the vessel] filled with fire. (45)
The Lord Hara hurled the Sudarśana discus, whose prowess was equal to ten million suns,
for the destruction of Jalandhara.
He swiftly seized that head with its large, wide eyes;
his body then fell in two parts like a mountain of collyrium.
From his throat emerged hundreds of thousands of Daityas, equal to Jālandhara in battle; they were all slain by him with that discus.
That headless trunk of Jālandhara danced, crimson with blood;
the entire earth was saturated with the fat of the son of the Ocean. 49.
The world became filled with his fierce blood;
where that blood had dried, it indeed became the city of Śoṇitapura.
Then Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Kaumārī, and whichever others there may be, [gathered] the heaps of flesh.
Having led those yoginīs in all directions and caused them to be destroyed,
the splendor that had issued from his body then dissolved into Hari.
The hosts of Yoginīs eat the flesh of Jālandhara and drink his blood;
therefore, even now, he does not rise, though slain in battle.
Seeing Jalandhara slain, the gods attained great joy; and the lords of the gods, siddhas, and great sages uttered cries of "Well done! (sādhuvāda). ||54||
Showering a rain of flowers, they sang the auspicious praises of Śiva;
and the gods, honored by the Apsarases, danced all around.
All the directions became serene and free from obstruction, as did the gods and others;
the sun, the moon, Varuṇa, and the rest were liberated from his bondage. (56)
Furthermore, they were appointed by Viṣṇu, Hara, and Brahmā;
and the lords of the gods bestowed jewels upon them.
Released by the magical rites (kṛtyās), Śukra went back again to his own place;
and after the destruction of the Daityas, the sovereignty of the gods was established once more in every region.
The gods, having attained lordship over the worlds, enjoyed their sacrificial portions;
the goddesses and the other deities likewise remained happily in their respective abodes. (59)
Then Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, having brought forth the Droṇa mountain and the oceans from outside, obtained the life-restoring herb (jīvanī).
Wherever the Pramathas, the hosts of Śambhu, were defeated on the battlefield,
there he employed [the weapons] consisting of bones, flesh, corpses, and so forth.
All those hosts of Rudras who were slain in battle were restored to life once more;
without exception, they all went happily to Kailāsa.
Just as Parvata was previously situated in that place for the sake of the world, he was established there by the vehicle of Viṣṇu; in due time, what is appropriate comes to pass.
O Lakṣmī, know this without doubt: everyone experiences their own karma;
as long as the body exists, actions and the resulting pleasure, pain, and so forth continue.
Having heard this history, one is not overcome by sufferings;
even the afflictions that have arisen repeatedly become distant from him. (65)
Whatever kind of union one has, such is one's bondage; yet by practicing yoga in Vṛndāvana, even for Viṣṇu there is a firm bondage [to that place].
Everything occurred according to worldly custom; listen further, Lakṣmī, how Viṣṇu was again enchanted by Vṛndā for the sake of attaining Vṛndā. (67)
Though exhorted by the gods and others, he did not abandon the sacred ground of Vṛndāvana;
and because she meditated upon him, Vṛndā indeed became a Satī. ||68||
He desires Viṣṇu right there once again in Vṛndāvana,
existing outside and further outside the very body of Viṣṇu in a subtle form.
She becomes manifest in solitude and dissolves again into Viṣṇu;
she is the threefold power of Viṣṇu, namely Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā.
Those who always exist within Hari as both visible and invisible forms—
by them Hari was seen there, and he was utterly enchanted by Vṛndā.
Vṛndā, moreover, upon the destruction of her husband, desired another husband;
yet, having been accepted by Viṣṇu, she now desires to obtain Viṣṇu himself. (72)
In a secluded place, she indeed became manifest in bodily form and served Viṣṇu;
she said to Viṣṇu, "Since I have been accepted by you in every way," (73).
Therefore, O Lord, take my hand according to the marriage rite;
first you shall dwell in the abode of Goloka, and afterwards you shall be the beloved of Jalandhara. (74)
"Furthermore, you have made me your own; therefore, carry me as your own.
Viṣṇu said, "Become the daughter of Kedāra; I shall carry her. (75)
That was indeed beheld and seen by Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and she who is named Ramā;
then, at that time, gifts were indeed bestowed there by those Śaktis.
And seeds were cast by them upon that spot for the sake of the deities;
from those seeds sown there, three auspicious trees came into being.
Dhātrī, Mālatī, and Tulasī—these three are [the manifestations];
that Dhātrī is remembered as a portion (aṃśa) of Gaurī, and Mālatī is remembered as a portion of Lakṣmī. ||78||
Rama became Vṛndā, while Tulasī became a tree;
and those women there also assumed divine forms.
Seeing the trees possessing the forms of beautiful women, Viṣṇu was filled with great joy;
and seeing Viṣṇu, both Tulasī and Vṛndā were likewise exceedingly delighted.
In this way, she gazed at him with passion; Tulasī gazed at that Viṣṇu with passion, and Dhātrī likewise gazed at him with passion. ||8 1 ||
At that time, you, Lakṣmī, offered the seed out of envy alone;
therefore, the woman born from it became possessed of envy toward Viṣṇu.
Therefore, she acquired the exceedingly contemptuous name "Barbarī";
yet, out of affection for her, the Dhātrī and Tulasī plants always grant pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Having taken both of them away, Viṣṇu reached Vaikuṇṭha;
there, having married them, Viṣṇu remained accompanied by Vṛndā.
Having become the daughter of Kedāra, Vṛndā indeed attained Viṣṇu;
there in that forest, a captivating garland was woven by Vṛndā. ||85||
O woman of excellent complexion, goddesses and gods arrived at the auspicious site of Vṛndāvana, bringing flowers of the mandāra and pārijāta trees. 86.
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed and having prepared a sacrificial pit,
he kindled the fire there and performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rules.
Having performed the purification of the body and the decoration of the Tulasī plant with garments, ornaments, and finery, as well as auspicious fragrant bathing, [he should proceed]. (88)
Having caused the Tulasī plant to be fashioned, he devoutly fed Viṣṇu, as well as the millions of deities beginning with Brahmā, after having adorned them. ||89||
Accompanied by vehicles and carriages, followed by goddesses,
and joined by groups of singers, they resounded with the music of musical instruments.
All of them, mounted upon their divine vehicles, went to the home of Gaurī;
there, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Ramā, and the others worshipped Viṣṇu with great reverence.
Having performed the customary worldly rites, they brought the young maiden Vṛndā, who was now a youth, into the interior of the pavilion and settled her there.
Having caused the fire-oblation to be performed and having caused them to circumambulate,
Bṛhaspati paid homage to that fire and to those two.
Having placed hand upon hand and having caused the bridegroom’s garland to be laid down,
he then performed the taking of the bride's hand with the permission of Gaurī and the others.
There, cries of "Victory! from the gods and goddesses, auspicious songs, showers of flowers, and words of increase arose for the sake of both.
Then, having been given wedding gifts and food,
all of them— the gods and the others— departed from Vṛndāvana for their respective countries.
Having heard this sinless narrative—which leads to heaven, removes evil, is meritorious, destroys grief and delusion, and is dear to the hearts of the virtuous—[one attains these benefits]. 97.
A Brāhmaṇa attains knowledge, a Kṣatriya becomes a possessor of a kingdom,
a Vaiśya becomes endowed with prosperity, and a Śūdra becomes happy upon hearing this.
One should satisfy the reciter with gold, sesame seeds, garments, and the like, as well as by the gift of cows and land; for when he is satisfied, the fruit [of the rite] shall be attained.
When the teacher and the reciter have been honored, may the deities be propitiated;
then, having bestowed gifts of food, one should worship the Brahmins and others.
"One becomes eternally victorious and endowed with the prosperity of sons and grandsons"—thus, O Lakṣmī, was the cause of Tulasī’s birth described by you under this pretext. (101)
Having heard that which has been proclaimed, one obtains the highest merit;
even the Tulasī planted in one's own home is a destroyer of sin.
By the mere sight [of it], sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should worship Tulasī abundantly during the months of Vaiśākha, Kārtika, and Māgha.
One should worship Viṣṇu with Tulasī and likewise offer a thousand blossoms;
by offering these to Viṣṇu in the morning, the fruit of ten million sacrifices shall be attained.
Where Vṛndā and the green Tulasī of dark luster were born in Vṛndāvana, there Viṣṇu became exceedingly enchanted. || 105 ||
Keśava took up his residence there, yet he did not abandon his delusion;
at that time, three powers of his own self were manifested.
They illuminate the quarters of space with their own most wonderful splendors;
then, by means of those [energies], seeds were deposited right there from their own portions.
Then, in Vṛndāvana, the Dhātrī, Mālatī, and Tulasī became trees; seeing them there, Keśava [was moved]. || 108 ||
He was infatuated with her, and both Tulasī and Dhātrī fell in love with him; because of that passion, Dhātrī and Tulasī were always objects of his affection.
Then Viṣṇu took her away and returned to Vaikuṇṭha;
there, Lakṣmī, acting out of jealousy, separated Barbarī from him.
Whoever should constantly recite this, cause it to be recited, or likewise listen to it, for him there shall be a good state, residence in heaven, and liberation. || 111 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Jālandhara’s Deception of Gaurī through Illusion, the Illusory Battle, the Destruction of Jālandhara by means of Śiva’s Discus, Vṛndā’s Request for a Boon from Viṣṇu, Vṛndā’s Becoming the Daughter of King Kedāra, the Marriage of Tulasī by Viṣṇu, and how the Portions of Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Ramā in Vṛndāvana Manifested as the Dhātrī, Mālatī, and Vṛnda Trees, and Lakṣmī’s Becoming Barbarī," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! The majesty of Tulasī is equal to that of Viṣṇu;
by hearing it, even liberation may be attained, for she bestows the presence of Viṣṇu. (1)
But she who is eternally devoted to one will certainly not belong to another;
thus Vṛndā, though formerly a tree-dweller, became the wife of Viṣṇu and has now attained Viṣṇu once again.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: "Indeed, when Vṛndā had been reduced to ashes in that place,
for how long did she remain invisible, meditating upon Viṣṇu?"
The female species is truly pure, and all of them are devoted to their husbands;
for at the beginning, all castes were created by the Creator as being of one kind.
All of them are portions of Prakṛti, pure, wise, and embodiments of prosperity;
how then has dharma, which consists of devotion to one's husband, truly come to destruction?
For Viṣṇu is indeed the husband of women, and he is the eternal Dharma;
men are always portions of Viṣṇu—how then has Dharma come to destruction? (6)
Indeed, at the beginning of creation, when there was only the service of primordial nature (prakṛti) by the souls (puṃs), dharma alone was supreme; how then did it come to decline?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this divine narrative which destroys many doubts;
formerly, women were always pure, as was their inner heart.
A man must always be served by a woman solely for the sake of the increase of creation;
for this was indeed the most ancient and eternal dharma in the beginning.
When any woman became pregnant by serving someone, then the service of a mere man was the eternal dharma for women. (1.331.10)
At that time, there was indeed no desire or craving born of passion;
for that Dharma had gone to ruin due to the curse of Kedārakanyā.
Then, out of anger, the Creator made women filled with passion;
from that time onward, a different dharma was established for women.

O Lotus-born One, in that age, passion was indeed unrighteousness when a man, full of lust, sought union with women for the sake of satisfying his desires; this occurred due to the distinction between the ages.
If there is no passion in the woman, there is likewise no passion in the man;
if their union is solely for the sake of conception, then dharma consists merely in the bestowing of the seed.
If yoga is practiced with a desire for enjoyments, it is proclaimed to be unrighteousness;
according to the differences between the ages, passion and craving have arisen among people. (15)
Because of that, the engagement with sensual desires became of the nature of unrighteousness;
consequently, the dharma of devoted wives became a mere semblance of dharma.
The former dharma was destroyed and a new, different dharma arose;
all of this occurred in the past due to the agency of Vṛndā.
I shall tell you in brief; understand from me how it truly was.
In ancient times, there was a son of Brahmā named Manu Svāyambhuva.
His wife was Śatarūpā, who was devoted to her husband;
they had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda. (19)
Uttānapāda’s son was Dhruva, who was indeed a Vaiṣṇava;
his son was Nanda Sāvarṇi, and Kedāra was his son.
This lord of the seven islands, Kedāra, became a devotee of Viṣṇu;
for his protection, the Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu was always present in his house.
He constantly gives as a gift a hundred thousand cows with golden horns, various kinds of garments, and likewise a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
He constantly gave gifts of jewels, diamonds, and pearls;
he fed hundreds of thousands of brahmins every day.
He gives water-vessels and food-bowls made of gold,
as well as sacrificial threads, rings, and seats fashioned from gold.
That king bestows gifts upon the poor, the helpless, and the twice-born;
there are one hundred thousand brahmins, two hundred thousand cooks, and two hundred thousand servers.
Indeed, at every festival, there are for him enjoyments possessing a hundred million splendors:
delightful streams of ghee, streams of honey, and streams of curd.
For him, streams of molasses and streams of milk flow day and night;
likewise, there is constant worship of the virtuous and the worship of virtuous women.
He constantly performs acts of service, such as honoring the elders;
he performs the daily worship of cows, deities, and Brahmins. || 28 ||
O Lotus-born One, subsisting on fruits and roots, the king is solely intent on offering everything to me; having made all things an offering to me, he always accepts them.
He constantly chants my name alone and remembers me, the one endowed with Śrī;
indeed, he always worships me as this very Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Once, on the morning of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), for the purpose of breaking the fast (pāraṇā) in the king’s palace,
ten lakhs [of gold coins] were presented solely for the feeding of the Brahmins.
Having quickly caused a sacrificial offering to be performed by the king,
they were indeed fed with sweet foods and other delicacies, including seasoned dishes and milk-rice.
With various kinds of *pūrikās*, as well as milk, curd, and other such foods,
the excellent twice-born attained satisfaction, their minds filled with the [gift of] sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Auspicious blessings were bestowed upon you: "May Lakṣmī indeed dwell in your home.
Then, during the midday oblation, the sacrifice was performed in many ways with clarified butter.
Then, through the grace of Viṣṇu, Vṛndā remained in Vṛndāvana, having performed worship with sesame seeds, fruits, milk-rice, flowers, and leaves.
Devoted to her husband and faithful to Viṣṇu, she remained performing austerities for the sake of obtaining him as her husband;
indeed, due to the destruction of the clouds, she existed in another form.
By the command of Nārāyaṇa, Kamalā arrived at the sacrifice of Kedāra; she was born from the sacrificial pit as a partial incarnation (kalā).
