Clad in garments purified by fire, adorned with jewel ornaments,
the lotus-eyed maiden was full of divine splendor and full of desire.
As soon as she was born, that young woman, who was to carry out the command of her lord, said to the king: "O Great King, I am your daughter. (39)
Having honored his daughter and entrusted her to his wife, the king remained there;
and that mother, the queen, spoke to her father Kedāra.
From that time forth, by the power of this king’s fortune,
five hundred thousand lords of kings were constantly present in the assembly at Kedāra.
He offered to Kedāra a priceless ruby, a pearl necklace, a sovereign gem, the jewel of an elephant, and the jewel of a horse as tribute.
Thus his kingdom became filled with prosperity and comprised of the seven continents;
however, the maiden, rich in her longing for Viṣṇu, set her mind solely upon asceticism.
Having paid obeisance to her mother and father, she went once more to Vṛndāvana,
specifically to the vicinity of the Yamunā where she had previously been reduced to ashes.
Through her ascetic penance, she chose me as her boon, the most excellent of boons;
Brahmā granted her that boon, saying, "You shall obtain Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa."
Then one day, while the beautiful woman was sleeping on the bank of the Yamunā,
Dharma went there to test that female ascetic, Vṛndā.
In private, she beheld a supreme young man,
sixteen years of age, possessing the luster of gold, who was like the god of love himself.
Richly scented, adorned with ornaments, and captivating to women; a lover possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, with a face like the full moon. (48)
With eyes resembling lotus petals, smiling and filled with divine emotion,
he stands at his side singing and playing a beautiful lute.
Yayāti also, displaying his inner disposition here and there,
sat down there upon seeing Sundarī, honoring her greatly.
Then Vṛndā also rose up and offered him hospitality;
she honored him with fruits, roots, flowers, leaves, water, and other offerings.
Having accepted the offering, he joyfully and affectionately said to her:
"Whose daughter are you, and why do you perform such severe penance?
What is the reason for this, O maiden, and what is your name? Tell me."
"O auspicious one, why do you desire to dwell here alone in this desolate place? (53)
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever dwells in your heart.
Thus did Vṛndā, the daughter of King Kedāra, speak to that brahmin.
"O Vṛndā, I am performing penance here; I meditate upon Hari as my husband.
If you are capable of granting it, bestow upon me this supreme boon. (55)
"If you are unable, O Brahmin, I shall worship Him from another direction.
Dharma said to Vṛndā: "He is the Supreme Self, the Lord. (56)
Who, other than the virtuous Lakṣmī, Śrī, Rādhā, Ramā, Pārvatī, Śāradā, and likewise Prabhā, would have the patience to become his wife? (57)
He is four-armed in Vaikuṇṭha with Sarasvatī, Māṇikī, Śāradā, and Virajā; however, in Goloka, he has two arms.
In the supreme abode known as Akṣara, he indeed exists with two arms;
his consorts are innumerable, and they are exclusively liberated beings.
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others— those beginningless women— worship Him who is as beautiful as His beloved, filled with the power of ten million Cupids and other perfections.
That which constitutes a single blink of an eye for Brahmā is indeed equal to seventy-one cycles of the Satya Yuga for Indra; such is the duration of his fall.
A day of Brahmā consists of a period of time delimited by fourteen Indras;
his night is of equal duration, and he likewise possesses a lifespan of one hundred such years.
Sanaka and the others serve [Him] until the end of their lives, and for tens of millions upon tens of millions of kalpas; there is nothing so great that cannot be accomplished by Him.
And Śeṣa, who possesses a thousand mouths, serves him and also chants his name with devotion day and night for hundreds of millions upon millions of kalpas.
Nevertheless, even Brahmā, whose nature is Brahman, does not attain Him who is difficult to propitiate and higher than the highest; may I worship Him birth after birth.
Even by him the Blessed One cannot be overcome; how then could he be attained by you? Even Rudra, the destroyer of the worlds, does not meet his end.
If even he did not attain it at that time, how indeed will you attain it, O young girl—
you who are the supreme sovereign, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), whose very form is Brahman?
She is Nārāyaṇī, Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the eternal Vaiṣṇavī;
even the supreme goddess Sarasvatī is unable to praise her.
"How do you wish for a husband who has transcended material nature, O auspicious one? O highly fortunate lady, accept me as your husband, the sovereign lord of kings. (69)
"Enjoy all pleasures in my house, O lady of excellent complexion;
for beyond the seven oceans lies my city of gold."
Come right there—blessings be upon you—and take delight with me, O Rāma. Come, set your mind on enjoying me, for I am a young woman. (71)
Thus addressed, that princess spoke to him from her righteous seat with indignation:
"O Lord of the Earth, maintain your composure; penance and truth are your vow. (72)
"However, this practice of not associating with one's wife for your sake is unrighteous; because of it, misfortune will arise, leading to the destruction of everything along with its very roots. (73)
In this matter, my ascetic merit would be destroyed, and likewise yours would be ruined;
having perceived this secret calamity, you desire to violate me.
But here, the world-protectors, Dharma, Yama, Hari, Śaśin, Sūrya, Earth, Water, Fire, Buddhi, and others likewise are the witnesses. (75)
They dwell within all living beings; where is it hidden, where is it secret?
Forgive me, go, may you be blessed; for a Brahmin is considered inviolable.
"I am capable of reducing you to ashes; go, O Brahmin, as you please.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the inner self of all, protects me, O twice-born one. (77)
"Viṣṇu is always the protector of the helpless, the young, and the aged.
Even though he was addressed thus by Kāma, Viṣṇu proceeded to enjoy her company.
In anger she cursed Dharma: "O wretched Brahmin, go to ruin!
O man of evil conduct, O destroyer of dharma, go to ruin! (7.9)
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara arrived there;
seeing Dharma thus cursed, those lords of the thirty gods wept.
O Vṛndā, forgive this Dharma, who is motionless, soiled, burnt, and struck by the fire of Satī’s wrath; he is the remover of birth, death, and old age.
"Give life to Dharma; protect Dharma, O devoted wife!
Thus Viṣṇu spoke then, and Brahmā likewise spoke to her.
O Vṛndikā, the world has become filled with darkness due to the absence of Dharma;
both the moon and the sun tremble, as do Śeṣa and the earth.
May there be well-being for you and may prosperity attend you; O auspicious one, restore this bull to life!
You practice dharma through asceticism, so why do you now destroy dharma? (84)
Dharma, assuming the form of a twice-born, has come to test you;
urged by Brahmā, he has been slain even though he was faultless. (85)
Dharma is acquired by men through austerity, and the fruit [of action] comes through dharma.
How could there be a fruit from austerity if dharma has gone to destruction? (8.6)
The ritual action of those who perform rites is fruitless without righteousness, O righteous one;
when righteousness has perished, even your unprecedented asceticism will perish.
"O beautiful one, you have come here to perform the acquisition of your own duty;
yet you destroy that duty through ignorance—live according to dharma immediately! (88)
Having heard this, the ascetic Vṛndā then said to the gods:
"O gods, I do not know the Dharma in the form of a Brāhmaṇa. (89)
Out of anger, I have destroyed one who desired to overpower me;
I shall surely restore the eternal Dharma, though it be dead, to life once again.
But he who has died shall not become that very same person here again;
due to differences in place, time, and other factors, this dharma will be different. || 91 ||
If my austerity and truthfulness are real here, and if my worship of Viṣṇu is true,
then by that merit may this Brahmin be restored to life immediately.
If my vow of truth is true, and my austerity is true,
then by that merit may this Brahmin here be restored to life immediately.
Then the personified form of his lawful wife spoke to the Lord of Kamalā:
"If I am devoted to righteousness, may Dharma be restored to life. (94)
Having bowed at the feet of Nārāyaṇa, Mūrti and Vṛndā performed a salutation for the sake of Dharmajīva; then Nārāyaṇa spoke.
This Dharma exists in embodied form and as a multitude; may it live for the sake of the Kṛta age.
It shall have four feet in the Tretā, three feet in the Dvāpara, and two feet [in the Kali].
"In the Kali age, however, let there be only one-footed [Dharma], possessing the curse that leads to threefold decay.
Having said this, Hari summoned Dharma by means of his voice.
May Vṛndā, who is the very life of Dharma personified, be pleased;
Dhruva was honored there, and Vṛndā was praised. (98)
Commanded to grant a boon, she requested Viṣṇu himself:
"I have performed penance for the sake of Viṣṇu; may Viṣṇu himself become my husband. (99)
"Having married me, may Viṣṇu himself lead you to Vaikuṇṭha.
"So be it," Hari replied, as Vṛndā became filled with joy.
There, the maiden Vṛndā was married by Viṣṇu.
Having reached Viṣṇu, that princess went to Vaikuṇṭha;
yet Vṛndā did not wish to leave beautiful Vṛndāvana.
Then Viṣṇu said to Vṛndā: "Stay here, embodied as Tulasī;
having come, I shall marry you with great honor. (103)
I cannot bring myself to abandon this delightful Vṛndāvana;
having found another pretext, I shall remain here with you.
"O Tulasī, you shall attain fame in the world as Viṣṇu’s bride;
I shall act accordingly, O Vṛndā, so dwell here in the form of Tulasī."
Then, after some time, you shall indeed become the shadow of Rādhā;
at that time, I shall marry you once again as the daughter of Rāpaṇa.
"I am the son of Vasudeva, Kṛṣṇa himself, the husband of Rādhā; O beloved, I shall become your husband here as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
Viṣṇu, the infallible Acyuta, having taken that Tulasī and Vṛndā with him, went to Vaikuṇṭha;
the other gods likewise went to their own abodes.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Vṛndā Becoming the Daughter of Dhruva’s Grandson Kedāra, Her Austerities in Vṛndavana, the Test by Dharma, the Curse upon Dharma for His Attempted Assault and Death, the Arrival of the Three Devas, the Resurrection of Dharma, the Decline of Dharma, His Internal Transformation into the Form of Śīla, Vṛndā’s Abiding in the Form of Tulasī, and Her Departure to Vaikuṇṭha in the Form of Vṛndā," in the narrative of Jālandhara and Vṛndā within the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall narrate the story of the most excellent yoginī Vṛndā;
Tulasī, the wife of the Lord, became a small tree in Vṛndāvana.
Just as she was born, so in the course of time she was wedded by Viṣṇu;
I shall relate her story exactly as it happened—learn it from me.
Understand from me what occurred in my own abode, Goloka;
by the mere hearing of which one is liberated from all sins.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Gaṅgā— these three wives of Hari also remain constantly in the presence of Hari, equal to one another in their love.
Once Gaṅgā, filled with desire and casting sidelong glances, beheld Acyuta;
she looked at him again and again, causing Sarasvatī to tremble with agitation.
Kṛṣṇa laughed many times in vain upon seeing Gaṅgā;
Hari took his pleasure with Gaṅgā, but not with Sarasvatī.
She delighted her, who was pervaded by desire and full of longing;
yet Lakṣmī, being patient, did not perceive any internal distress at all.
Sarasvatī was fickle and could not endure her inner anguish;
Lakṣmī awakened her and consoled the sorrowful woman.
Nevertheless, her speech, though filled with anger, did not become calm;
trembling with the force of her wrath, she spoke to Gaṅgā and indeed to her husband.
A virtuous husband maintains an attitude of equanimity toward all his wives;
however, an unvirtuous husband, being selfish and base, treats them with partiality.
Your affection for Gaṅgā is known, and your love for Lakṣmī is constant;
however, it appears indeed deficient toward me, your lover and co-resident.
"The life of her who is deprived of her husband's love is fruitless.
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa went silently out from the house.
When Nārāyaṇa had departed, the goddess of sound said to the Gaṅgā:
"O shameless one, O lustful woman, you are obstructing Hari in his home!"
"I shall strike her who is full of pride in her beauty and youth; receive the fruit of your actions!
O you who are dear to your lover, what will your husband do for you? (14)
Having thus rebuked her as she rose to seize Gaṅgā’s hair,
Padmā then went between them and restrained her with words.
Enraged, she cursed Padmā, saying, "You shall become a tree.
Enraged, she cursed Gaṅgā, saying, "You shall become a river. (16)
Having heard the curse and understood it to be the work of Viṣṇu, those two goddesses did not utter that speech; rather, Gaṅgā spoke to Padmā.
Since this playful speech is by its very nature fickle, it does not distinguish between what should and should not be said; how indeed can I not swear an oath against it? (18)
And you, O Speech, become like a river; be barren without a season.
Let her always remain without menses, forever devoid of desire.
Thus did Sarasvatī receive that curse at that time, O beloved;
in the meantime, the Blessed One arrived there.
Having pacified the quarrel, he spoke to those grieving women: "O beloved ones, do not grieve; this sorrow has arisen solely by my own will."
"O Lakṣmī, go with a portion of yourself to the auspicious house of Dharmadhvaja;
having become a maiden born not from a womb, you shall indeed enter later under a pretext. (22)
"O Tulasī, after you have come together [with him], you shall subsequently become the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa and, through the rite of marriage, become my wife."
"You shall become a river named Padmāvatī by means of a portion [of yourself].
Then, O Gaṅgā, take the form of a river and become the destroyer of the sins of embodied beings. (24)
For the sake of the liberation of the Sāgaras, become the beloved of the Ocean;
O Sarasvatī, be the one who desires Brahman in the abode of Brahman.
Become the river Sarasvatī in form, free from menstruation;
become the bestower of liberation, eternally devoted to celibacy. || 26 ||
"O my beloveds, I shall carry out for you your respective acquisition and preservation; grief and delusion are not to be entertained. (27)
Three wives, three houses, and three dependents who are kinsmen are certainly adverse to well-being; for these do not bestow auspiciousness. (28)

And for those householders in whose home the man is under the control of the woman—just as in the case of a wife and husband—their birth is indeed fruitless, and they encounter misfortune at every step. (29)
He whose wife is corrupt in speech, corrupt in her womb, or fond of quarreling must dwell in the forest; he should never indeed live with such a woman.
Dwelling in a place infested by tigers is better than living in the house of a wicked woman;
the flames of disease and poison are preferable to the fire from the mouth of a corrupt woman. (31)
In this world, the life of a man conquered by a woman becomes fruitless; moreover, the coexistence of many rival wives in one household is not conducive to welfare. (32)
A man with a single wife is happy somewhere, but one who has many wives is not;
indeed, the husband of many wives is impure, miserable, and as good as dead while yet alive.
Go, O Gaṅgā, to the abode of Śiva; go, O Sarasvatī, to the abode of Brahmā.
Let Kamalā, the all-enduring one, remain here for my sake.
For him whose wife is easy to manage, virtuous, and devoted to her husband,
there is the happiness of heaven in this world, as well as dharma and liberation in the next.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa indeed ceased;
then they wept, trembling with tearful eyes and pained by the sorrow of separation.
O Lord, grant us that expiation which is appropriate for these three;
show us favor so that there may be an end to the curse. (37)
Having become rivers, when shall we go and behold your feet?
How long will your stay there be, and when shall we attain you once again? (38)
"O Lakṣmī, I am the virtuous one named Tulasī, the daughter of Dharmadhvaja;
having thus assumed the form of a tree, when shall I attain your abode? (39)
Due to the curse of the Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā was cursed; due to the curse of Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī was cursed.
When will they both be released from their curses, and when will they find you?
"Therefore, O Lord, forgive me; do not send me to another place.
Having spoken thus, Kamalā took hold of her beloved’s feet and wept. (4.1)
The Compassionate One, placing that radiance upon his chest, said to her:
"Let all three of you go to the earth in other forms, according to my word."
"It is my wish that those of divine form should always remain here, for it is on their account that the necessary tasks must indeed be performed. (43)
Having brought those to completion, I myself shall indeed remain here in the form of the river Padmāvatī and in the form of the Tulasī plant. (44)
Let Sarasvatī, in the form of a river, go to another world;
for when four thousand years of the Kali age have passed, she shall become the best of rivers. ||45||
"Age after age, you shall come to my house again and again;
for misfortune is the cause of prosperity, and suffering is the cause of happiness. (46)
The greatness of prosperity does not arise without adversity;
therefore, adversity must first be experienced, for it is indeed the price of prosperity. (47)
"These rivers have been created by me for the sake of destroying the sins of sinners;
through bathing in them, the sins of you virtuous devotees of mine shall be destroyed. 48.
The state of being purified by countless holy sites arises from the touch and sight of my devotees;
my devotees purify the entire earth with their footsteps. 49.
Wherever my devotees reside, they wash their lotus feet;
that place shall indeed become a great sacred ford (tīrtha), a means of liberation for sinners.
A killer of women, a killer of cows, an ungrateful person, a killer of a Brahmin, and one who violates the teacher’s bed;
One who has violated his vows or is an atheist becomes purified by serving my devotees. ||5 1 ||
A betrayer of trust, a destroyer of dharma, one who falsely casts aspersions, a killer of friends, and one who misappropriates deposits—all these are purified by the sight of my devotee. 5.2.
One who is uninitiated, unconsecrated, impure, a reviler of others, and one who eats what has not been offered—such a person becomes purified by serving my devotees. (53)
One's mother, father, wife, brother, son, daughter, teacher, family, sister, dependents, kinsmen, and so forth— (54)
He who does not support his mother-in-law, his father-in-law, the elderly, and his wife shall become a sinner; yet he is purified by the touch and sight of my devotee.
Those who have stolen the wealth of gods, brahmins, and others, those who sell their daughters, and those who cause the mixing of liquids—these are purified by serving my devotees. (56)
By association with them, may rivers always be purified;
by the dust of their feet, may the earth be purified through the water used for washing their feet.
All sacred fords are purified by the bathing and immersion of the virtuous;
the gods desire their sight and touch in every way. (58)
The meeting with Vaiṣṇavas is the supreme gain among all gains;
neither water-tirthas nor earthly gods are equal to it. (59)
Neither the fire-sacrifices and other rites, nor the meditations on the vital breaths, purify one over a long period of time; oh, how wonderful! Those devoted to Viṣṇu purify in an instant.
He into whose ear the excellent Viṣṇu-mantra enters from the mouth of the guru becomes a knower of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Śāstras, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and most excellent. ||61||
He at whose birth the denizens of hell attained liberation is a great devotee of Viṣṇu, the most excellent among all the excellent. (62)
By the mere inclusion of births among animals and other such states,
living beings become liberated through that yoga by which one becomes a most excellent devotee of Viṣṇu.
Endowed with devotion to me, intent upon my worship, possessed of my qualities,
worthy of praise for my virtues, absorbed in me, and consisting of me.
Merely by hearing of my virtues, he was filled with joy, his hair stood on end, his voice became choked with emotion, his eyes were filled with tears, and he even forgot his own self. (65)
They do not desire happiness, liberation, or the fourfold states such as *sālokya*;
rather, they long for the service of my feet day and night.
Such devoted, virtuous, and saintly women, who act for my sake, shall purify the rivers; do not grieve, my beloveds. (67)
Let all [the goddesses] go, or let them remain in the form of water, trees, and so forth;
at that time, the divine Sarasvatī herself remained at the feet of Hari.
By her second form, she became Brāhmī Sarasvatī;
she is celebrated here as the presiding deity of speech and the beloved of Brahmā.
Then, impelled by Brahman in the form of water,
she became the river Sarasvatī, a most purifying embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites.
Then Gaṅgā, possessing a divine form and consisting of water, emerged from the hollow of Viṣṇu’s foot;
stationed within Brahmā’s water-pot, she was touched by the tip of his dwarf-sized thumb.
Brought down by Bhagīratha and clinging to the matted locks of Śarva, the river that purifies the world arrived in her portion. 72.
But Padmā herself, in her divine form as a young woman, remained at the feet of Hari;
and through a portion of herself, she became the auspicious river Padmāvatī.
By her second form, Lakṣmī was born in the house of Dharmadhvaja as a daughter named Tulasī, in the form of a maiden. ||74||
But Lakṣmī herself, possessing a divine form, dwells there eternally.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you your former birth and your deeds.
She who is Vṛndā is Ramā-Lakṣmī; she who is Lakṣmī is Ramā and she is she. She who is Ramā is Vṛndā-Lakṣmī; she who is Lakṣmī is Vṛndikā. ||76||
In Vṛndāvana, Rāmā herself took the form of a tree;
she, that very same one, having been cursed by Gaṇeśa, became the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī became rivers, and how Lakṣmī took the form of Tulasī, due to a mutual curse among the wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Goloka for the sake of sexual pleasure," within the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, tell me how and when did that Tulasī become the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa? Why was she cursed by Gaṇeśa, and when did that happen?
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī! Having received the command of Hari, the lotus-born Brahmā caused Lakṣmī to become Padmāvatī, a river in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Once she became beautiful, radiant with the brilliance of youth;
the maiden, possessing excellent limbs, was like heaven itself and overwhelmed by desire.
Wandering at sacred fords through her ascetic penance, she who was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa beheld Gaṇeśa on the bank of the Gaṅgā, endowed with youth.
Exceedingly beautiful, captivating the heart, and fragrant with sandalwood; illuminated by excellent ornaments and possessing a splendor of countenance that is exceedingly heart-stealing. || 5 ||
Tulasī said: "O Brahmin, you who are free from desire, upon whom do you meditate—upon that beautiful woman with well-formed and nourished limbs? (6)
"How is it that you have a hanging belly and the face of an elephant?
How is it that you have such a face with but a single tusk? Why do you perform meditation on Hari? (7)
"Abandon your meditation, O greatly nourished one; evening has arrived.
One should not remain alone at evening, at the onset of night. (8)
Having spoken thus, she placed her joined palms upon his belly;
consumed by the arrows of desire, she laughed again and again.
He touched his cheeks and temples, his chest and the region of his abdomen,
and even the area below that, with the gesture of his hand.
At that moment, his meditation was broken; then she, who was fond of pleasure, struck his linga and her own hip in vain with the tip of her forefinger.
When his meditation was destroyed, Gaṇeśa’s anger became uncontrollable;
opening his eyes, he beheld the beautiful woman Kāmanāvatī.
She was in the full bloom of youth, overflowing with the impulse of passion; she was distressed, devoted to playfulness, and scorched by the forest fire of desire.
But Lambodara, seeing her, reflected for a moment with compassion:
"For the goodness of the virtuous consists in removing the suffering of those who are distressed. || 14 ||
"How can I reject her, who is tormented by the forest fire of desire?
In rejecting her, there would be great suffering, and I would obtain an undesirable result. (15)
Even in accepting [him], there would be a great fault, namely that she would become pregnant;
therefore, having reflected upon this, one should treat him with supreme discipline.
I console her, who is tormented by the impulse of desire, with words of peace:
"Come, O maiden, O female ascetic, you who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa!"
"Stay, sit in this comfortable place, and dwell here in happiness indeed. What do you require? Tell me whether it be food, water, or something else. (18)
"I am the god Lambodara, and I am the deformed Vrindala.
O Goddess, perform your bath in the water; remember Viṣṇu and remain steadfast. (19)
"Maintain your composure—blessings be upon you—and you shall experience my touch.
Come, let us bathe in this lake and then enjoy ourselves."
"Your distress shall be pacified; therefore, perform your ablutions and other rites. Who are you, my child? Whose daughter are you? You possess the form of Lakṣmī; what is your auspicious name? (2.1)
Worthy of worship and adoration, O Mother of the World, you appear before me; tell me, who are you and how have you come?
O Consort of Kṛṣṇa, this is a disruption of my meditation and a destruction of the ascetic penances of the sages.
May Kṛṣṇa bring about our welfare and destroy the obstacles of us two;
let not the mind be fickle, for fickleness causes the breaking of one's vows.
For those who practice meditation and observe vows, passion and desire cause the destruction of their vows;
therefore, the agitation of the senses must especially be endured.
"Resolve must be slain, especially by an ascetic.
You are an ascetic woman, O fair-browed one, and I am a practitioner of vows, possessed of meditative concentration. (25)
"We two are capable of conquering the mind and restraining desire itself;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, wife of Kṛṣṇa, do not perform such a deed toward Kṛṣṇa. (26)
"Be steadfast, O young girl; I am Gaṇeśa, conquer the hosts!
Hearing these words of Gaṇeśa, she, tormented by passion, spoke to him.
"I am the daughter of the son of Dharma, and as an ascetic woman, I have performed penance for the sake of a husband;
the fruit of my penance is the attainment of a lord—be you my lord and husband. (28)
Having heard Tulasī’s words, remembering Hari, he said to her:
"O Mother, I have no desire for taking a wife, as it would indeed cause me suffering. (29)
Taking a wife is a great net, a bond, and a house of strife; the pursuit of sensual desires is an obstacle to attaining Hari and does not grant liberation.
Austerity without food is considered a bolt on the door of liberation;
it acts as a noose around the neck and provides residence in the prison of the womb.
She is the destroyer of the knowledge of reality, the instiller of doubt, the giver of birth,
the supreme mother of all rash acts, and the casket of all illusions.
One should not take refuge in faults, for that destroys the flow of desire. Turn back, O Great Illusion; seek out another lover.
"Only through union with a lover can a woman's desire be fulfilled.
Upon hearing this, the maiden Tulasī became deeply distressed and overcome by longing.
He said to Gaṇeśa: "Since you do not accept me even though I am devoted to you, my wife shall become one who does not worship you because of my curse. (35)
Then Gaṇeśa said to her: "You shall be seized by an asura;
afterwards, you shall become a tree by my curse as well."
Having heard the curse, Tulasī wept; the Gaṇa said to her, "Do not weep, O worshipful one; you shall become the essence of flowers."
"O Patrasārā, you shall always be affectionate toward Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa;
and by you, Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation, shall always be worshipped. (38)
"I shall not eat from your leaf, nor your flower-cluster, nor even your wood.
O fair-browed one, become one to be enjoyed by Kṛṣṇa; welfare shall be yours. (3.9)
Having spoken thus, that Gaṇeśa went to the Badarikā forest;
Tulasī also departed for Puṣkara, her inner self tormented with grief.
Having performed penance there, she subsequently became the beloved of Śaṅkhacūḍa;
thereafter, that lord of the asuras was slain by the trident of Śaṅkara.
That beloved of Nārāyaṇa attained the state of a tree by means of a portion of her essence;
and as a maiden, she was married to Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rites.
Once again she attained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the dweller of Goloka. Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the story of Tulasī’s return. 43.
O Daughter of the Lotus, that Tulasī, who has beautiful limbs and was indeed accepted by Hari as the bride of Hari, washes away all sins.
Leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, branches, bark, and what is known as the trunk—
all these originating from the Tulasī plant, as well as earth and other such things, are purifying.
For that deceased person whose funeral pyre is even partially composed of tulasī wood,
there is never again a return to this world, as he has attained liberation.
Even if a person has accumulated great sins or even more heinous crimes,
if they are cremated with Tulasī wood, they are liberated from the onset of death.
Even one who merely touches *tulasī* is liberated from all sins;
likewise for him whose name of Hari is uttered at death and for whom *tulasī* fuel-sticks are used during cremation.
And when a gift is made to the Blessed One at a śrāddha ceremony, there is no returning for him;
even if there were but a single piece of wood remaining in the heap of wood used for cremation.
His sins are destroyed and he becomes destined for liberation;
waters that are well-mixed with the water of the Gaṅgā attain the state of merit.
Words mixed with the name of Hari attain sanctity;
pieces of wood mixed with tulasī wood attain sanctity. (51)
As long as the funeral pyre mixed with Tulasī wood remains ablaze,
his sins, even those accumulated over ten million kalpas, are consumed.
Seeing a corpse upon which Tulasī wood has been placed, the attendants of Yama flee,
abandoning the man, and the associates of Viṣṇu lead him away.
One who is united with the wood of the *tulasī* plant goes, liberated, to the abode of Hari;
in the excellent heaven, the gods and apsarases honor and celebrate him. (54)
Viṣṇu becomes exceedingly pleased with one who offers a handful of flowers, who dwells upon the corpse of Tulasī, and who enjoys the company of Tulasī.
Wherever a fire produced from Tulasī wood is maintained,
that ground destroys all sins and is of the nature of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Wherever there may be a fire-sacrifice on a festival day using the wood of the *vṛndā* tree,
for him there shall be the fruit born of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for every single piece of that wood.
By offering incense of tulasī in the temple of Kṛṣṇa,
one obtains merit equal to a hundred sacrifices and the fruit born of giving a hundred cows.
Whoever offers to Keśava as an oblation food that has been cooked over a fire of Tulasī wood shall obtain a fruit equal to Mount Meru. ||59||
Even if one offers a lamp to Viṣṇu using only a Tulasī twig as the wick,
the merit of that act shall be equal to that of offering thousands of lamps made with clarified butter.
To the giver of sandalwood paste produced from Tulasī wood,
the Lord Viṣṇu grants the station of Viṣṇu and bestows His own equality.
One should worship Hari with sandalwood paste produced by rubbing it upon *tulasī*;
the grace of Hari, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is to be understood as resulting from that. 62.
Anointed with *tulasī* and sandalwood paste, he performs the worship of Hari; indeed, honored by Tulasī in the abode of Hari, he rejoices there. (53)
Even when offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the ancestors, whoever offers only a tulasī leaf,
his merit here bestows the happiness of enjoyment.
Satisfaction of the ancestors for a hundred years is also obtained by offering oblations on a Tulasī leaf;
indeed, bathing with Tulasī mud is considered equivalent to bathing at a sacred pilgrimage site.
Whoever performs the worship of Viṣṇu with the fresh leaves and blossoms of the mañjarī plant,
by him has been performed a worship with all flowers that bestows liberation.
The Tulasī plant should be specially protected, nurtured, and sustained within the home;
by seeing it and touching it, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is dissolved.
In whatever village, house, courtyard, or garden there may be Tulasī,
there Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, dwells everywhere.
In whatever house Tulasī is present, there is no illness;
nor is there fear, sorrow, poverty, or separation for the members of the family. (69)
If one specifically plants a Tulasī plant in a sacred field of the gods,
one obtains the merit arising from the nourishment of all trees planted.
The gift of *tulasī* in the temple is superior even to the gift of *lakṣmī*; by planting *tulasī* here, one attains happiness and, in the end, the abode of Hari.
Indeed, Tulasī drives away portents that cause fear, bring about the loss of fortune, and are ill-omened, even when they appear suddenly. (72)
Wherever the wind, mixed with the fragrance and other qualities of the *tulasī* leaf, blows through the ten directions, it purifies all embodied beings.
Where there is the union with the root of Vṛndā, there are Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu;
where there is the union with the leaves of Vṛndā, there is the circle of the gods and others. (74)
Where there is the application of that *mañjī*, there the sages and seers (*ṛṣi-munayaḥ*) are remembered;
where there is the water of *tulasī*, there the hosts of ancestors (*pitṛ-gaṇaḥ*) are remembered. (75)
Where there is indeed a tulasi stem, there is Vaikuṇṭha itself;
where there is indeed a tulasi jewel, there is Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Wherever there is the shade of a Tulasī plant, the satisfaction of the ancestors is eternal;
wherever there is a heap of Tulasī, whatever is given there becomes eternal.
At its root Brahmā always resides, Viṣṇu dwells upon its branches, and Śambhu is present in its blossoms and so forth; thus Tulasī embodies the three gods. (78)
People should always plant Tulasī in the temple of Śiva;
for as many seeds as are produced from it each year, [so many rewards are gained]. (79)
For each seed, they attain an unbroken celestial realm measuring a yuga,
on the eleventh day, the full moon, the new moon, and on the day of their vow.
During the auspicious time of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), one should offer Tulasī at the temple;
with great devotion, one should plant it and cause it to grow by watering it. ||81||
One who worships with offerings such as lamps shall become wealthy even if poor;
wherever there may be a Śālagrāma stone or a Tulasī plant, [there one should worship]. (8.2)
There, bathing, recitation, and giving are more than a hundred times superior to those at Vārāṇasī;
they are more than a hundred times superior to those at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, and Naimiṣa.
The person who meets their death having made use of Tulasī—O Mahālakṣmī, Tulasī leads that person to the abode of Hari. (84)

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Tulasī, the Journey of Padmāvatī—who had assumed the form of a young woman through the force of her youth—to Gaṇeśa, Her Petition to Him for Him as a Husband out of Desire, the Curse Pronounced by Gaṇeśa that She Become a Tree and a Wife to a Daitya, and the Greatness of Tulasī," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, where was Tulasī, your beloved, born?
In whose lineage was she born, and which demon was her husband? (1)
By what austerity did she regain Nārāyaṇa as her husband?
O Hari, tell me in detail this story of mine which has been forgotten by me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, listen as I relate to you the story beginning from Manu;
though it was forgotten, I shall tell it to you now that it has been reminded by your questions.
Manu Dakṣasāvarṇi was indeed born as a portion (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu;
his son was Dharmasāvarṇi, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and then his son [was likewise].
He is called Viṣṇusāvarṇi; his son was indeed Vaiṣṇava; Devasāvarṇi was the son of this one, and Rājasāvarṇi was his offspring.
His son was Vṛṣadhvaja, who was devoted to Śiva;
for Śiva’s affection for Vṛṣadhvaja was even greater than that for his own son.
When the king, like one intoxicated, no longer regarded Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, nor Sarasvatī; nor did he regard sacrifice, the Sun-god, or the deities, [then he was overcome by passion].
Then Ravi cursed him, saying, "O King, may you be deprived of your fortune! Thereupon, the king quickly went to Śiva for refuge in order to be protected.
Śambhu, taking up his trident, came to strike the Sun;
terrified, the Sun fled and went to Brahmā for refuge. || 9 ||
Placing Sūrya at their head, Brahmā quickly proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha;
they bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and made a full report of everything.
Then Nārāyaṇa, out of compassion, granted them freedom from fear;
meanwhile, Śiva, trident in hand, followed behind them in a rage.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, he sat down upon the offered seat;
Nārāyaṇa said to Śiva, "Tell me the reason for your arrival."
Then Mahādeva spoke to Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"The Sun has cursed my devotee Vṛṣadhvaja, who is very dear to me."
Out of grief born of affection for my devotee, I went to slay the sun;
he, placing Brahmā at his head, has now come to you, the protector, for refuge. (14)
Those who have come to you for refuge, whether by meditation or even by word alone, are free from calamity and devoid of fear; by them, indeed, old age and death are conquered.
"But, O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, tell me what will become of me, your devotee, who have indeed been deprived of my splendor by the curse of Sūrya? (16)
Nārāyaṇa said to Hara: "The bull-bannered one has arrived here;
his son, Haṃsadhvaja, is now the king and has reached old age. (17)
O Hara, their two sons, Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja, who are devotees of Viṣṇu,
have today fallen from prosperity along with the wives of those two.
"Lakṣmī shall become my wife in two ways, and she will have two daughters;
they both shall be endowed with prosperity, devoted to me, and become the best of kings."
Half a ghaṭikā in Vaikuṇṭha indeed becomes twenty-one yugas on earth; O Śambhu, there is nothing strange in this.
Having been addressed thus, they all departed to their respective places;
Vṛṣadhvaja, having returned to his own kingdom, met his end.
In the course of time, Haṃsadhvaja also met his end;
thereafter, the two kings Dharmadhvaja and Kuśadhvaja performed fierce austerities.
Having propitiated Nārāyaṇa, they obtained their desired boon:
"Lakṣmī shall certainly become your daughter in two forms. (23)
"By its power, you two shall become endowed with the excellence of sovereignty.
Then the two of them performed the worship of Lakṣmī. (24)
The vow was fulfilled and Lakṣmī became gracious; she granted them both a boon:
"May you two be lords of the earth, endowed with wealth, sons, and prosperity."
"By the grace of Nārāyaṇa, may you both be honored by kings.
Flooded with this blessing, they replied, "So be it."
"O Lotus-born one, make the statement 'endowed with Śrī' come true. Having thought thus, Lakṣmī then assumed a twofold form.
In the house of Kuśadhvaja, a daughter was born in due time who brought him prosperity;
the beloved wife of Kuśadhvaja gave birth to that daughter, who was born from a portion of Kamalā.
As soon as she was born, the maiden Vedavatī made a sound;
by that, she attained fame at that very moment by the name Vedavatī.
Having paid homage to her parents, she went to a virtuous forest for asceticism;
while practicing penance at Puṣkara, that virtuous woman heard a voice from the sky.
"But in another birth, Hari himself shall become your husband.
Having heard this, she became angry once more and performed penance again.
Having taken refuge on Mount Gandhamādana, she remained there for a long time and practiced austerities;
then, she beheld before her a brahmin named Rāvaṇa.
Having paid homage to her guest, she offered him water for his feet, fruit, water, and other refreshments; yet that wicked man indeed experienced a transformation of mind.
Having drawn her toward him with his hand, he prepared to engage in sexual union;
however, Vedavatī paralyzed him with a glance of wrath.
And she cursed him, saying, "You shall perish along with your kinsmen on my account.
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman dissolved her body and vanished from sight. (35)
She was Vedavatī, the daughter of the Earth and the joy of Janaka;
she became the goddess Sītā, for whose sake Rāvaṇa was slain.
This very Lakṣmī was you yourself in all ways throughout other kalpas;
you become Sītā, and I become Rāma.
Indeed, this has been ordained by me for the destruction of the Rākṣasas;
for there is no other cause for the destruction of these beings of darkness except you. (38)
The great ascetic Lakṣmī obtained Hari, Rāma, as her husband;
remembering her former births, she endured only suffering.
By the command of his father Śataratha, Rāma went to the forest together with Sītā and his younger brother Lakṣmaṇa.
There Rāma beheld the Fire-god in the form of a brahmin.
The venerable Fire-god said: "For he is indeed the one who shall bring about the end of Rāvaṇa."
Through the occasion of Sītā’s abduction, the time has arrived;
I am Agni, sent by the gods, assuming the form of a brahmin.
"Having entrusted Sītā to me, indeed take this shadow-Sītā;
I shall give you the real Sītā at the proper time for the testing of my offspring. (43)
Having heard those words, Rāma immediately acted accordingly;
Lakṣmaṇa did not even realize it—what then to say of others? ||44||
In the meantime, Rāma saw a golden deer;
out of Sītā’s insistence, he indeed went after it to destroy it.
Lakṣmaṇa also followed behind, while Rāvaṇa carried away Sītā;
that attendant named Vijaya, having died in battle, went once again [to his divine state]. (46)
Moreover, even though Savarṇa was victorious in the midst of battle, having died, he went to the state of a preta for the sake of Tṛtīyajanman. (47)
By Rāma’s arrow, many Rākṣasas were slain in Laṅkā;
Vibhīṣaṇa became his devotee, and Hari gave him the kingdom. ||48||
Then, for the sake of purification, Rāma underwent an ordeal by fire;
there, the Fire-god presented him with the real Jānakī.
The Blessed One said to Chāyā, "Go to Puṣkara, my dear;
having performed penance there, you shall become the goddess Lakṣmī of heaven."
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years, she became Lakṣmī in heaven;
that very same Lakṣmī will be born as Draupadī in the sacrificial pit.
In the Kṛta age she was Vedavatī, the daughter of Kuśadhvaja;
in the Tretā age she was Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and the wife of Rāma. (52)
Her shadow-form will be Queen Draupadī at the end of the Dvāpara age,
while in the Kali age she will be Queen Māṇikī, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa ascends [to his supreme state] in age after age;
this has been declared to you as the first form. Now hear the second.
The wife of Dharmadhvaja was renowned as Mādhavī;
she became pregnant upon the peak of Mount Gandhamādana. (55)
On the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, she gave birth to a daughter, Padminī,
who was resplendent with rubies upon her pair of lotus-feet.
The sovereign lady of kings, Lakṣmī, beautiful in every limb, endowed with the marks of royal fortune, the presiding deity of royal prosperity. ||57||

She has a moon-like face, eyes like lotus petals, and beautiful lips red as the bimba fruit; her palms and soles are crimson, her navel is deep, and she possesses the three folds [of skin] on her waist.
She who possesses the luster of the color of a white campaka flower and is known by the name Tulasī— she is the daughter Tulasī, in whose presence the comparison of all other women fails.
As soon as she was born, that exceedingly beautiful young woman, with a gentle smile upon her face, became certain: "Nārāyaṇa shall be my husband."
She went to the forest of Badarī in order to attain Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
there, she performed for a long time supreme penance that bestows Kṛṣṇa.
In the summer she performed the penance of the five fires, and in the cold season that maiden remained in the water;
during the rains, enduring the downpour of rain, she practiced asceticism.
First she ate fruits, then she ate leaves, then she drank water;
then she subsisted on air, then she remained without food, standing on one foot. (63)
Seeing that ancient and severe austerity, Brahmā arrived at that Badarikāśrama to grant a boon.
She bowed down to Brahmā, and Brahmā spoke to her:
"Choose a boon, O Tulasī, whatever is desired in your heart. (65)
Listen, my dear, to how I attained devotion to Kṛṣṇa, or even liberation and freedom from old age and death; formerly, I was established in the supreme abode, Goloka.
At that time, I myself became Kṛṣṇa’s wife, his servant, and his dear friend; I was Ramā, Vṛndā, and Lakṣmī. (67)
Then, out of anger, Rādhikā cursed me, her servant, as I stood in the midst of amorous play, my mind fixed on Govinda while Vṛndā was in the form of a beautiful woman. (68)
In that very same manner, he cursed Vāṇī, Padmā, and me as well:
"Go to a human womb; I remember this from my former birth."
Then, in the past, Gaṇeśa cursed both Padmāvatī and me, saying:
"Go to the state of a tree," and likewise, "Become the wife of a Daitya."
After the curse, Kṛṣṇa spoke joyfully with a smile in Goloka:
"O Lakṣmī, Sudāmā is indeed my own attendant; he is a portion of myself."
He too, due to the curse pronounced by Rādhā, will become Śaṅkhacūḍa;
you shall be his wife, according to what was foretold by Gaṇeśa.
"Therefore, after you have performed austerities, you will obtain me without a doubt—I, Nārāyaṇa, my ancient beloved husband. (73)
Now I wish to obtain a boon; grant it to me in this way, so that I may remember my past lives and know all that has been told to you. (74)
"Therefore, O Brahman, pronounce a curse such that it may be appropriate.
Brahmā then said: "O beautiful Lakṣmī, you know everything. (75)
You yourself are one who remembers her past births and are the daughter of Dharmadhvaja;
that asura Śaṅkhacūḍa has been born on this earth as Sudāmā.
Now, O auspicious and beautiful lady, become his wife;
afterwards, you shall obtain Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa himself, as your husband.
O Tulasī, you shall become a tree in Vṛndāvana;
you shall be the foremost among all flowers and shall become a purifier.
Just as the worship of all would be fruitless without you, so too will Kṛṣṇa hold you dearer even than his own life. (79)
"In Vṛndāvana, you shall indeed become Vṛndā and Vṛndāvanī in the form of trees; people shall worship Keśava with your leaves."
Thus you shall dwell constantly with him among the people;
you, O fortunate one, shall become equal to Rādhā for Govinda.
"You shall become equal to Rādhikā's very life-breath and the life-breath of Kṛṣṇa.
Hearing this, Tulasī said, "May it be so; act quickly to make it happen. (82)
Then Brahmā spoke this supreme mantra for the purpose of recitation to Lakṣmī:
"Oṃ, I surrender my very self to Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa; obeisances. (8.3)
Having thus bestowed [the boon] enriched with sixteen syllables, he vanished from sight;
she, for her part, recited that mantra at the holy Badarikāśrama.
In a very short time, through the mantra, perfection in austerity was attained;
with a tranquil mind, she beheld the divine Kṛṣṇa standing before her. (85)
Kṛṣṇa said to Tulasī: "The perfection of your penance has been attained;
from this day forward, O beloved, having become the wife of my attendant, you shall obtain me. (86)
Having spoken thus, he vanished from sight; she too abandoned that penance, and having eaten and drunk, being fully satisfied, she slept upon a beautiful couch.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sun’s Curse upon Vṛṣadhvaja of the Lunar Lineage, the Birth of Lakṣmī named Sītā in the House of Kuśadhvaja of that Lineage, and the Birth of Lakṣmī named Tulasī in the House of Dharmadhvaja, as well as Tulasī’s Austerities and Their Accomplishment at Badarī," in the section concerning the Marriage of Tulasī within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, what then happened to Tulasī in the forest named Badarī?
O Master, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the remover of distress, tell me all of that.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen; I shall relate what happened afterwards—understand it from me.
I shall cause you to remember everything exactly as it occurred, for you have forgotten it all.
While sleeping on her auspicious bed, she indeed beheld a vision for a moment;
in that dream, she saw Tulasī and Sudāmā arrived together.
He who was seen by her in a dream, known as Śaṅkhacūḍa,
was seized by her, his hand grasped, and he was kissed upon the hand.
Having suddenly vanished from sight due to the power of delusion,
she then quickly woke up, becoming agitated for a moment.
For a moment she was consumed by fire; for a moment she fell into heedlessness;
for a moment she regained her senses; for a moment she was overcome with despondency.
For a moment she rises from her bed, and in an instant she goes near him;
for a moment she wanders about in agitation, and in a moment she enters the house.
Out of agitation, she fell asleep for just a moment;
yet once more, in her sleep, she beheld that well-attired man.
He was handsome, youthful, and smiling,
a lord of connoisseurs who spoke of the stories of the Sun and kissed [her] again and again.
Then the virtuous woman spoke again to him as he lay well-reclined upon her bed, embracing her with affection, and was about to depart once more.
"Where are you going, O you who are as dear to me as my own life? Stay!"—thus she spoke to him. Then, regaining her senses, she lamented, longing for him.
Thus she attained her destined state there in that penance grove.
At that very time, however, the yogi Śaṅkhacūḍa was at Puṣkara.
Having attained from the sage Jaigīṣavya the perfection born of penance and mantra,
and having received the boon of Brahmā by the command of the Creator, || 13 ||
Where that Tulasī was staying, he went to that Badarī;
and [he saw] the youth approaching, whose splendor was equal to that of Kāmadeva.
Beholding Śaṅkhacūḍa, who possessed the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, was adorned with all ornaments, was handsome, and had very firm limbs, she— || 15 ||
Having closely observed Sudāmā, who was adorned with earrings, a tilaka mark, and a necklace, he mistook him for Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Modest and bashful at their first union, she looked upon him with her face cast down, covering her face with her garment. || 17 ||
With her gaze fixed upon his lotus-like face, she became covered in horripilation;
Śaṅkhacūḍa also saw her there, well-seated and veiled by her garment.
Thinking, "This is Tulasī," he beheld the large-eyed woman,
whose palms and soles were reddish and who was surrounded by her own radiance.
She has full limbs, a golden complexion, and is in the bloom of fresh youth;
she wears a line of vermilion and her braided hair is adorned with jasmine flowers.
Having observed her—whose forearms were adorned with bracelets, who was graceful, possessed beautiful teeth, and was virtuous—he reflected and spoke to her with words full of deep emotion:
21. Having thus observed her, he made a decision and spoke to her with words pregnant with feeling.
"Who are you, O lovely one? Whose daughter are you, you who enchant the sages?
Abandoning your silence, please converse with me as I have approached you. (22)
Having heard this, she, with a face of humble smile, spoke to him with desire;
and the daughter of Dharmadhvaja said, "I am indeed established in ascetic practice."
Go wherever you wish to go; who are you to ask such an improper question? One born of noble family does not inquire of a woman who is alone and in private.
Upon merely seeing women, one should never apply [the gaze] with the heart;
for there, a calamity may arise even if it were unintended. (25)
In the heart it is like the edge of a razor, yet on the tongue it consists of sweet syllables;
at first it is pleasant, but afterwards its grasp is like that of Death.
Resembling the indravallī fruit, she is pleasant on the outside but unwholesome within;
she is intent on her own interests, dependent on her master, and always seeking refuge elsewhere in the end.
Outwardly appearing detached through guile, yet inwardly longing for enjoyments and the like;
saying "no" to external things while inwardly desiring ever-new pleasures. (28)

There was no counting the foot-soldiers of the Daityas and Dānavas,

There were indeed autumnal winds, aerial vehicles, water-vehicles, and subterranean vehicles,
as well as akṣauhiṇīs of three hundred thousand soldiers there.
Having thus led thirty of the foremost and most excellent warriors away, the great asura emerged from the camp,
remembering Śrī Hari in his mind.

Skanda, possessed of great strength, became the commander-in-chief of Śaṅkara’s army.

Marīci, the son of Brahmā, spoke; his son was Kaśyapa, to whom Dakṣa gave thirteen daughters in accordance with dharma.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, as well as Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, and Irā. (68)
Kadru and Muni were among them; indeed, their offspring were born as various species.
From Aditi, the twelve Ādityas were born as her first-born sons.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga;
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is recorded as the tenth.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu—these were the sons of Kaśyapa;
and from Diti came two sons, Hiraṇyakaśipu along with his elder brother.
Hiraṇyākṣa was another, and both of them had a daughter, Saṃhikā;
that goddess was the mother of Rāhu and the wife of Vipracitti.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of great strength:
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Saṃhrāda, and Hlāda. (73)
And Hiraṇyākṣa had six sons, all of whom were indeed possessed of great strength:
Utkara, Śakuni, and another named Kālanābha; ||74||
Mahānābha, Vikrānta, and Bhūtasantāpana—
these were the hundred sons of Danu, the Dānavas headed by Vipraciti.
Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkukarṇa, as well as Śaṅkunirāmaya, Śaṅkunāsa, Mahāviśva, Gaveṣṭhi, and Dundubhi; ||76||
Then Ajāmukha, Bhagahṛt, Śila, Vāmanasas, as well as Marīcirakṣaka, Mahāgārgya, and Aṅgirāvṛta. ||77||
Vikṣobhya, Suketu, Suvīrya, and likewise Suhṛda; Indrajit, Viśvajit, and also Suravimardana. ||78||
Ekacakra, Suvāha, the mighty Tāraka, Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Pravīṇa, and Mahāśiras; ||79||
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the great asura Muṇḍaka;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candra, Indra, and Tāpana. ||1.336.80||
Sūkṣma, Nicandra, Ūrṇanābha, Mahāgiri, Asiloman, Sukeśa, Sada, and likewise Balaka. ||8 1 ||
Vyomamūrdhā, Kumbhanābha, Mahodara, Mahāhanu, Pramodāha, Kupatha, and the powerful Hayagrīva. ||82||
And the Asura Virūpākṣa, Supatha, and the great Asura Aja; also Hiraṇmaya, Śatamāyu, and Śambara. ||8.3||
Śarabha and Śalabha were also prominent sons of Danu;
these and other Dānavas indeed arrived for the battle. ||84||
From Kālā were born sons such as Kṣaṇa and others, who were themselves of the nature of Time;
and from Ariṣṭā were born thousands of sons known as the Ariṣṭeyas and the Vighnas.
From Surasā were born the serpent-dragons, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and others;
from Kaśyapa, Surabhi gave birth to the eleven Rudras as her sons.
Aṅgāraka, as well as Sarpa, Nirṛti, Sadasaspati, Ekapāda, Ahirbudhnya, Ūrdhvaketu, and likewise Jvara. (87)
Bhuvana, Īśvara, Mṛtyu, and the renowned Kapāla;
and the two sons of Vinatā were Aruṇa and Garuḍa.
And there were thirty-six sisters who were known as younger;
among them were Śukī, Krauñcī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Pakṣiṇī, the daughters of Tāmrā.
Śyenī, Bhāsī, and others likewise became progeny as birds;
furthermore, twelve daughters are recorded as having been born to Krodhavaśā.
Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Haribhadrā, Irāvatī, Bhūtā, Kapiśā, Daṃṣṭrā, Niśā, Tiryā, and another likewise. (91)
Śvetā, Svarā, and the renowned Surasā—then Irā indeed gave birth to these three daughters of beautiful eyes. (92)
Latā, Vallī, and Virudh—these were her numerous offspring;
Kadrū gave birth to a thousand nāgas, who are known as the Kādraveyas.
Then, from the sage Mauneya, those Gandharvas and Apsarases arose;
the expansion of their lineage became more than ten million in number.
Aditi is known to be of a virtuous nature, Diti is remembered as being of a powerful nature;
Surabhi is of the nature of austerity, while Danu is remembered as being of the nature of illusion. || 95 ||
Muni was indeed Gandhaśīlā, while Ariṣṭikā was Gatiśīlā;
Kālāsyā was Kṣudhāśīlā, and Kadrū was of a cruel nature.
Irā is of a benevolent nature, while Ariṣṭā is characterized by anger;
Vinatā is of a swift-moving nature, and Tāmrā indeed possesses a noose.
By their nature, their conduct, their intellect, their forbearance, and their strength and form, the noble-born offspring of Kaśyapa were like mothers to all creatures. 98.
Gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas; piśācas, beasts, and also wild animals, birds, and plants. ||99||
O Śaṅkhacūḍa, recognize those who have gathered on your side;
they are these Daityas and Dānavas belonging to the faction of the Asuras.
O Asura, those who are the adversaries of the gods shall be your guests at my sword; and those who are equal to the gods and belong to the side of the gods shall also be yours, O Asura.
"O Dānava, you must remain ready here; all of them are to be protected by me.
Now, the son of Vipracit, the son of Danu, named Dambha—" || 102 ||
"My friend is a devotee of Viṣṇu, and you are his great son.
For the sake of obtaining a son, your father recited the mantra of Kṛṣṇa at Puṣkara. (103)
Your father performed severe penance for a thousand years;
by the power of that, you were born as his son Sudāmā Śaṅkhacūḍa.
What is the use of this quarrel with you today, if you know me to be Hara?
If you know Sudāmā the Dānava to be your own devotee. || 105 ||

Vaiṣṇavas do not accept even the granting of residence in the same world (sālokya), equal power (sārṣṭi), identical form (sārūpya), proximity (sāmīpya), or oneness (aikya) with Hari, without [the continued] service [of the Lord]. (106)
O Dānava, what use have you for a kingdom or for strife, you who are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa? Give the kingdom back to the gods and show me your affection.
"Remain happily in your own kingdom; let the gods abide in their own places. Enough with this enmity toward your brother, for we are all indeed sons of Kaśyapa. (108)
There are no sins whatsoever equal to the betrayal of one's kin;
in due time, destruction will surely come even to Brahmā—what then need be said of you?
"O Lord of Devotees, equanimity toward all states of being exists at all times for no one; abandon it through knowledge, O King of Dānavas, not through opposition."
The sun, the moon, and all others wax and wane;
by time the earth becomes rich with crops, and by time it is bereft of prosperity. (111)
In due time you were greatly prosperous; that time for you has now turned away.
I am Kāla, the conqueror of death, and I withdraw embodied beings.
I constantly perform the chanting of the true qualities and names of Kṛṣṇa; you, however, having renounced everything, should likewise perform the chanting of Kṛṣṇa. 113.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, ceased;
nevertheless, the mind of Śaṅkhacūḍa did not change even in the slightest.

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Dispatching the Flower-Bearing Messenger Puṣpavant to Śaṅkhacūḍa," within the narrative of Tulasī’s marriage in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, it is described how Śaṅkara, armed with his trident, sent the messenger Puṣpavant to Śaṅkhacūḍa; how Śiva reminded him of his knowledge of Śaṅkhacūḍa and Tulasī, of Śaṅkhacūḍa’s departure for battle at dawn, of his birth as a Dānava in the lineage of Kaśyapa’s thirteen wives, and that he was named Śaṅkhacūḍa and Sudāman; and the instructions given by Śambhu. || 336 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkhacūḍa spoke these ethical words to Śaṅkara:
"War is rooted in pride, it causes destruction, and it is indeed of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). || 1 ||
O Lord, everything that has been spoken by you is true and not false;
O Śaṅkara, if there is great sin in betraying one's kinsmen, [then why have you done this]? (2)
How was Bali, along with his brother Hiraṇyākṣa, seized of all his possessions and sent to the netherworld? And how indeed was he destroyed by the gods?
How was the nectar consumed by the deities during the churning of the ocean?
Why do you slay the Dānavas, and not the gods nor your own Gaṇas?
Why was her father then killed on account of Satī?
And why is Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana effective only against the Asuras? || 4-5 ||
"O Hara, when a great conflict arises between two related parties—the descendants of Kaśyapa and their offspring—how can we endure such rivalry? We feel profound shame."
A man who upholds his paternal lineage goes to heaven,
whereas one who is intent upon the lineage of others falls into a low state.
Let that which is destined by time indeed come to pass here in my abode.
Whether it be defeat or victory, that which is determined by Time is indeed respected by me.
Now you are Mahākāla to me, O Lord of Pārvatī;
whatever may come about through Time, I am content with that—engage in battle!
"Upon death, I shall go to Goloka; in victory, I shall enjoy the fruit ordained by Brahmā.
There is no loss for me in battle, nor is there even the slightest gain for you. (1.337.10)
Having reflected thus, O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, desist;
for when the great associate with the small, there is only loss, not gain.
I pay homage to you, O Śambhu, and I shall rise up for battle.
Having resolved thus, he mounted his own chariot and departed for his army.
Therein were those who belonged to the faction of the Asuras—the Daityas, Dānavas, and others—who, as adversaries of the gods, followed the Asuras in battle. || 12-13 ||
Those who were equal to the gods and belonged to the faction of the gods became followers of Hara;

they all arrived in the armies of Śaṅkhacūḍa and the wielder of the Pināka bow. At that time, the two armies, consisting of combatants numbering ten million, a hundred billion, and a trillion, resembled the ocean.
O Lakṣmī, you were truly beautiful when the battle-drums suddenly sounded upon your victory. In heaven, kettledrums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Here, Skanda became the commander-in-chief, and Rāhu became the king.
A battle took place in the sky between the two [armies] with *śataghnīs*, arrows, and spears;
with axes, clubs, *bhūśuṇḍīs*, javelins, and discuses;
and also with arrows, *śilīmukhas*, hissing darts, and iron balls. (17)
And with thousands of slaying weapons and grass-bundles, there was a wonderful and fierce battle. || 18 ||
Between the two armies, there was a crushing, tearing, cutting, and splitting in two, resembling the great dissolution of the universe.
There was indeed cutting, pulverizing, the mangling of living beings, and crushing,
as well as a rain of arrows, crescent-headed shafts, spears, javelins, and triple-edged missiles.
The slaughter of both armies was all-pervasive, causing terror among the elephants, horses, and mules alike. (21)
There was destruction of chariot-warriors and infantry; indeed, there was no counting them.
Chariots were shattered and vehicles were crushed by the thousands.
Horses were cut down by the hundreds of thousands, and lords of warriors by the millions;
they perished, were mangled, and lay lifeless, forever prostrate upon the earth.
Day and night, a most terrible battle, constantly characterized by dissolution, raged there; even hunger and thirst were not taken into account.
Then, the arrows of the archers, the weapons of those bearing arms,
and the armor of those clad in mail were entirely brought to destruction.
When the dissolution of the hosts of Dānavas occurred as if it were a natural cosmic dissolution (prākṛtika-pralaya), they became terrified and fled from the field of battle. ||26||
Kārtika indeed caused a great slaughter with a rain of arrows,
and Rāhu also performed a supreme cutting down with a rain of arrows.
And they constantly brought down upon the mountains, serpents, rocks, and trees a rain that was difficult to endure and terrifying. (28)
Shrouded by a shower of arrows from Rāhu,
the son of Śiva cut off Skanda’s bow and shattered his chariot and horses.
He rendered the peacock shattered by means of a divine weapon;
then Rāhu hurled a spear, radiant as the sun, which pierced the chest [of Garuḍa].
Having crushed him with his mace, Skanda took up a divine bow and rained down weapons in every way for the destruction of Rāhu.
The son of Śaṅkara, with divine weapons, furiously cut down all the serpents, mountains, trees, and rocks as well. (32)
Guha indeed warded off the fiery weapon with the Varuna weapon;
he effortlessly severed both the chariot and the bow of the son of Siṃhika.
Having killed both his charioteer and his horses, he hurled a spear at [the god's] chest;
struck there, the Dānava then fell into a swoon.
Śaṅkhacūḍa, the best among illusionists, arrived swiftly mounting his chariot and,
by means of his illusory power, unleashed nets of arrows.
Then, having covered you with a web of arrows in the battle, he seized the spear named Śatasūryā, which was endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu. ||36||
He hurled it at Kārttikeya; it struck him and he then fell down unconscious.
Kālī took him in her lap and carried him into the presence of Śiva.
Śiva quickly urged on his own army and the gods for another terrifying battle with the lords of the Dānavas and their hosts.
There, Mahendra fought with Vṛṣaparvan,
while Bhāskara fought with Vipracitti like the fire of universal destruction.
Candra was with Dambha, Kāla with Kāleśvara,
Kṛśānu with Gokarṇa, and the king of the Yakṣas with Kālakeya.
Maya and Viśvakarman [were present], as was Mṛtyu with Bhayaṃkara;
Yama was there with Saṃhāra, and Varuṇa likewise with Kalaviṅka.
The Wind was born from Cañcala, the wise Budha from Ghṛtapṛṣṭha,
Śani from Raktākṣa, and the Vasus from the hosts of Varcas.
Jayanta with Ratnasāra, the two Aśvins with Dīptimat, Nalakūbara with Dhūmra, and Dharma with Dhanurdhara. (43)
Ishana fought with Shobhakara, Mangala with Mandukaksha,
and Manmatha also fought with Pithara, using missiles and weapons.
With Ulkāmukha, Dhūmra, Khaḍga, and Dhvaja;
with Kāñcīmukha, Piṇḍa, Ghanas, and Nandin.
The Ādityas fought fiercely with Viśva and Palāśa,
while the eleven Mahārudras fought with those called Bhaya.
Then Mahāmārī fought with Progradandyā and the others, while Nandīśvara and all the rest [fought] together with Daṇḍi and the other dānavas.
Thus those commanders of the armies fought their forces on all sides;
likewise, Śaṅkhacūḍa rested for a moment, as did Kārtikeya.
The Dānavas, Asuras, and Daityas fought on all sides;
the gods trembled with fear and fled in the ten directions. ||49||
Skanda became enraged and granted fearlessness to the gods;
then, out of great wrath, he fought together with the hosts of Dānavas.
In that battle, he slew a hundred akṣauhiṇīs;
then the enraged Kālī drank blood and danced upon the field of combat.
Taking up ten lakhs of lordly elephants and a hundred lakhs of horses,
he effortlessly cast them into his mouth one after another.
By the nets of arrows from Skanda, the Dānavas and others fled;
Kālī, having reached the battlefield, let out loud, boisterous laughs.
Ugradaṃṣṭrā, Ugradaṇḍā, Koṭarā, and the hosts of Yoginīs,
as well as the Ḍākinīs, devoured the Asuras and drank the honey-wine.
Seeing Kālī, Śaṅkhacūḍa then rushed toward her for battle;
thereupon, Kālī hurled an āgneya weapon, equal to the fire of universal dissolution.
Śaṅkhacūḍa indeed effortlessly neutralized that [weapon] with the Vāruṇa missile;
however, the Dānava countered Kālī’s Vāruṇa missile with a Gāndharva one. ||56||
Then Kālī cut and cast away the Māheśvara weapon;
at that time, the Dānava effortlessly struck it down with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
Then the Dānava hurled the Nārāyaṇa weapon at Kālī;
she prostrated herself on the ground like a staff, and by her devotion, that weapon was pacified.
She discharged the Brahmāstra, and he swallowed it with the Brahmāstra;
she discharged the Pāśupata, and he destroyed it with the Pāśupata. (59)
The Goddess hurled that spear, and he destroyed it with his own spear;
then Mahākālī, becoming enraged, [discharged] the Mahākāla weapon.
As he was about to cast it down with a mantra, a voice from the sky spoke:
"Death does not exist for this Dānava; on his neck is the armor of Hari. (6.1)
As long as the chastity of Tulasī truly remains,
so long shall neither old age nor death affect him, except through the destruction of that chastity.
Having heard this, Kālī retreated, and he let out a roar of victory;
at that moment, Viṣṇu arrived at the banyan tree, assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa.
"O Śambhu, take up the power (śakti) offered by me and go to the field of battle for the destruction of the Daityas; I am Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world. (64)
"I am going as a mendicant to entreat the Dānava for armor, O Lord of Beings; afterwards, I shall go to Tulasī."
O Lord, for the sake of bestowing seed through the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, the death of the Dānava will indeed come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu, assuming the form of an old brāhmaṇa, approached the lord of the dānavas and said, "Give me alms. (67)
"Take it; what is your desire? the Dānava then asked.
The Brāhmaṇa replied, "Give me the armor; become a Dānava. (68)
Having heard that, the best of the Dānavas gave him the supreme armor;
having taken the armor, Kṛṣṇa went toward Tulasī.
In the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa, he went to Tulasī’s house;
he sounded his kettle-drum and raised a great cry of victory.
Having heard that, she, filled with supreme bliss, rose up in agitation and beheld her husband through the window of the royal highway from where Tulasī was standing.
She gave wealth to the Brahmins, the reciters, and the monks;
she had them pronounce auspicious blessings and also gave wealth to the bards.
Descending from his chariot, Kṛṣṇa went to the abode of Tulasī;
having approached her beloved, Tulasī washed his feet.
With great joy, she embraced him who was seated upon a golden throne and bringing victory; she massaged his limbs for the sake of his well-being. (74)
And he gave him betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other spices, saying:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; I behold your victory. (75)
"How did victory come to Viśva in battle against the Destroyer?
Tell me that, O Lord of Life," so spoke the virtuous Tulasī.
Viṣṇu said: During that great destruction of the gods and the Dānavas, Brahmā arrived there and brought about a reconciliation.
May the gods be fearless in their offices;
O Śaṅkhacūḍa, remain happy with your wife in your kingdom. ||78||
Thus, a reconciliation was indeed brought about by Brahmā between us two;
I have returned to my own abode, while Śiva has gone to the world of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa made Tulasī his bed;
there, the Lord of Ramā took delight in amorous pleasure upon the bed of Tulasī.
She too, due to the excess of her pleasure and because it was distinct from [ordinary] acts such as pulling [the hair],
and because her state of being was unshaken, inferred that he was someone else.
"Tell me, who are you, O Great King? You have assumed this form here through illusion. My virtue has been cast aside; I have been enjoyed by you through your power of illusion. (82)

"Speak quickly to me; having heard this, I shall curse you out of fear of my curse. Hearing this, she playfully assumed her own form as Nārāyaṇa—dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like autumn lotuses.
Having likewise seen Nārāyaṇa, who possessed the loveliness of ten million Cupids, adorned with jewel ornaments,
his face brightened by a slight smile, and graced with yellow garments,
as well as the passionate woman who was fainting with desire; ||84-85||
And again, having fallen into a state of delusion, she embraced Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
then Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed deposited his seed within Tulasī.
Then Śambhu indeed struck Śaṅkhacūḍa with his trident;
the soul of the deceased, four-armed Sudāmā, went to his own abode. ||87||
Having fallen into a swoon once more, and having regained consciousness again, she said to Kṛṣṇa: "O Lord, you have a heart of stone! (88)
"Devoid of compassion and lacking even a shred of shame, you have killed my master by deceit under the guise of dharma, while he lived his life through the strength of his virtue. (89)
Therefore, you shall now become a stone-like deity upon the earth;
consequently, you will be devoid of knowledge for one lifetime.
Having spoken thus, Tulasī fell at the feet of Hari and wept;
she lamented, and the Blessed Lord then spoke to her.
And because my devotee Śaṅkhacūḍa and Sudāmā were to be led to Vaikuṇṭha, I indeed employed a stratagem against you. (92)
For his destruction, I indeed gave a trident to Śaṅkara, blazing with the splendor of a hundred midday suns in the summer season. (93)
Its tip is presided over by Nārāyaṇa, its middle by Brahmā, its root by Śiva, and its supporting base by Kāla. ||94||
It was difficult to ward off, likewise useless [to others], and a destroyer of all weapons;
it was unbearable for Śaṅkara, Keśava, or anyone else, and capable of destroying the cosmic egg.
It was a thousand *dhanus* in length and a hundred *hasta*s in width.
Śambhu cast that living form of Brahmā upon the Dānava.
O Daitya, because my seed was deposited in you, Śaṅkhacūḍa, along with his chariot, was then reduced to ashes. ||96-97||
And once again he became the divine one with two arms, holding a flute, surrounded by millions of cowherds adorned with various excellent jewels. 98.
Having mounted the vehicle that had come from Goloka, he went to that city;
then the trident quickly returned to the hand of the Wielder of the Trident.
With that trident, Śaṅkara quickly cast the skeletal framework of the Dānava out of affection into the salt-water ocean.
That which is born from a conch is the most excellent and pure for the worship of the gods;
likewise, water from a conch is highly praised and brings delight to the deities. || 10.1 ||
Where there is a conch, there is Lakṣmī; here too is Tulasī and a sacred ford.
Conch-water is the water of a sacred ford; where there is a conch, there is Hari.
Abandon your grief, O lotus-eyed one; become one who remembers her past lives, my dear.
O virtuous lady, you performed penance for my sake in the Badarī forest.
For your sake, Śaṅkhacūḍa performed penance at Puṣkara;
having made you his beloved, that lustful man enjoyed her as a result of that merit.
He has gone for refuge to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the Rāsa-maṇḍala; that devotee resides in Goloka. You, O beautiful one, must go there. 105.
Having abandoned this body here and having assumed a divine form,
you shall become like Ramā and sport with me in the Rāsa dance along with Ramā.
"By your curse, I shall indeed become a stone known as Śālagrāma;
unable to endure separation from you, I curse you: 'Become a river! (107)
May this body, in the form of the river renowned as the Gaṇḍakī, be purifying and bestow liberation upon men through the merit-giving act of bathing. 108.
May the multitude of your body hairs indeed become sacred trees;
may the trees born from the hairs of Tulasī truly become Tulasī plants.
In the river, I, Śālagrāma, carry water and *tulasī*;
and among all flowers and leaves in the three worlds for the worship of the gods— 1.337.11.0.
May Tulasī, who is the very embodiment of Pradhāna, always be dear to me;
your separation from me, caused by Rādhā’s curse, has come to an end. (111)
"Out of compassion for me, O Padmā, remain here in this abode; O Tulasī, I shall marry you, a virtuous maiden, according to the marriage rites in Vṛndāvana."
"I shall seize you and take you along as my companion; I shall go.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu proceeded to where Śambhu stood in the fray.
Hara and Hari paid homage to one another and praised each other;
all the gods were raised up, and Śiva’s army was restored to life. 11.4
Then, by Viṣṇu and even by Śaṅkara, the dead were restored to life; and by Śukra, the army of the Dānavas was brought back to life by means of the Sañjīvinī [mantra].
They celebrated a festival there, and after the presentation of the gifts was made,
they all went to where the future Śālagrāma stone of Hari would be.
Where the form of the Gaṇḍakī and also that of Tulasī were to exist, the gods and others, having attained those forms, worshipped them. || 11.7 ||
They went to the beautiful Vṛndāvana, where the auspicious Tulasī grows;
having performed their ablutions in the Yamunā, they celebrated a great festival there.
And by the will of Hari, she was born there in the form of a Tulasī tree;
likewise, she then became a divine maiden of excellent form.

Thus, in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the narrative of the marriage of Tulasī, [is described] the speech of the Dānava to Śaṅkara; the battle between Skanda and his army; the battle waged with the weapon of Kālī; the begging for the armor of the Dānava by Viṣṇu in the form of a Brahmin; the infusion of Tulasī’s vital energy by Viṣṇu in the form of Śaṅkhacūḍa; the death of Śaṅkhacūḍa; and the two curses—by Viṣṇu that Tulasī would become the stone Śālagrāma, and that the Tuṅgaṇḍakī river and the Tulasī tree would come into being—[all occurring] during the battle.
The three hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Revival of the Dead and the Arrival at Vṛndāvana," etc.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Upon beholding the Tulasī plant adorned with clusters of excellent leaves,
the gods and others were then overwhelmed by great wonder.
Likewise, Lakṣmī and the other goddesses paid homage to Tulasī.
Then Mahāviṣṇu Nārāyaṇa spoke of her greatness to them:
"Listen, O Lakṣmī, at that time the maiden Tulasī possessed a divine form."
Though she stood by my side, she was listening to her own greatness;
for she is indeed Tulasī, in whom the comparison of all things perishes—
