in heaven, on earth, in the netherworld, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in the imperishable abode.
May Tulasī trees always remain in my presence—
in Goloka, on the banks of the Virajā, in the Rāsa dance, on the earth in Vṛndāvana,
at Bhāṇḍīra, in the Campaka forest, in Aśoka, and in the sandalwood grove. || 5 ||
May there be forests of mādhavī, ketakī, kunda, mallikā, and mālatī;
and where I am, may there be tulasī trees along with tulasī.
Furthermore, on the ground at the root of the tulasī, there shall be the residence of sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
Where a Tulasī leaf falls, there is the presence of the gods and others;
one who has bathed in Tulasī water and eats Tulasī leaves [is purified]. || 8 ||
He who takes refuge in Tulasī has bathed in all holy fords, is initiated into all sacrifices, and partakes in the merit of all pilgrimages and acts of charity.
O gods, I do not experience such satisfaction from the gift of jars filled with nectar as I do from the offering of a *tulasī* leaf.
He who drinks the water of the tulasī at the time of death,
being liberated from all sins, goes to Vaikuṇṭha as a king among devotees.
He who daily drinks water touched by *tulasī* with devotion should be known as one liberated while living; he obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
One who performs my worship with *tulasī* possesses the merit of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices;
and he who, placing a *tulasī* leaf in his mouth, should give up his life, [attains the highest state].
He who meets his death while wearing a garland of *tulasī* around his neck enjoys [bliss] in heaven for ten million *yugas* and then proceeds to the world of Viṣṇu.
A person who obtains even a single drop of Tulasī water during their meal gains at every step the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice by bearing the name of Tulasī. (15)
Whether at the time of death or upon falling into sin, he who obtains a leaf of Tulasī ascends a chariot of jewels and goes to Vaikuṇṭha, my abode.
O gods, a pure *tulasī* leaf remains fit for three nights even if it has been kept overnight;
it is suitable for use in ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), religious observances (*vrata*), giving gifts, consecrations, and the worship of deities.
Having washed that which has fallen on the ground or fallen into water, one should offer it;
thus dedicated to Viṣṇu, it becomes divine and pure.
On festival days, at the two junctions of day and night, and during the night, that leaf must not be cut;
for Tulasī is my most beloved abode, the dwelling place of the presiding deity of trees.
The river goddess Gaṇḍakī, the beloved of the ocean, is dear to me on earth; and Ramā, Padmā, and Svarūpā are also dear to me in Vaikuṇṭha.
By virtue of Tulasī’s curse, she will dwell on the bank at the root of the Gaṇḍakī river, constantly delighting in the Rāsa dance together with me.
Today I become a mountain-form consisting of the Śālagrāma stone;
and those worms shall be Vajrakīṭas with adamantine fangs within them.
"The insects shall fashion my discus; they are my attendants (pārṣadas). I am established as a stone-form, enriched by a golden-lined discus. (23)
Having a single door, four wheels, adorned with a forest garland, and endowed with golden lines—that indeed is known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. ||24||
If it has a single opening, four rims, and is devoid of a forest-garland (vanamālā), yet is marked with golden lines, it is indeed called Lakṣmī-Janārdana. 25.
One should know that the name "Raghunātha" consists of two gates, four wheels, and is endowed with a "cow's footprint," yet it is devoid of a forest garland. (26)
One should know that the small [cakra] named Prabhā-Kṛṣṇa, which possesses two wheels and a golden line as its garland, bestows happiness upon householders.
The thick, two-wheeled [discus] devoid of the golden line is known as Pārvatī-kṛṣṇa; it is remembered as bestowing happiness upon renunciants.
The one known as Dadhivāmana is very small and has two wheels;
it may be marked with lines or a pair of garlands, and it bestows happiness upon householders. (29)
The two-wheeled [vehicle] is joined with a garland, possesses Śrīdhara, and always bestows prosperity;
it is large, circular in shape, and devoid of a forest-garland (vanamālā).

The [yoga] named Dāmodara, characterized by two wheels, should be known as bestowing grain and wealth; likewise, it should be understood as producing fields, gardens, and groves, and granting excellent garments. (3.1)
The middle one should be understood as being circular in shape, possessing two wheels, pierced by arrows, named Raṇarāmā, and equipped with a quiver of arrows. || 32 ||
The middle [form] has seven wheels and is provided with a parasol and quivers;
it should be understood as the Lord of the Kings of Kings, bestowing royal prosperity upon men. (33)
The gross [element] has fourteen wheels (cakras) and is like a hooded serpent with its mouth turned upwards;
it is to be known as named Ananta, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life. || 34 ||
That which is reddish in the middle, possessing two wheels, and known as Māṇikī-kṛṣṇa, indeed bestows wives, children, a home, jewels, and vehicles. || 35 ||
That which is wheel-shaped, possesses two wheels, is endowed with splendor, and has a cow-path [around it], is known as Madhusūdana; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sudarśana is indeed the single-wheeled [discus], while Guptacakra is the wielder of the mace;
Hayagrīva is proclaimed as the two-wheeled one, resembling the face of a horse.
The five-faced one, whose essence is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, is proclaimed;
it has an exceedingly wide mouth, two wheels, and is named Nṛsiṃha. || 38 ||
That which bestows dispassion and renunciation, and if it possesses an assembly hall, it grants happiness;
that which is known as Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha is likewise considered to be a destroyer of obstacles.
That which has two wheels at the entrance, is beautiful and symmetrical,
is indeed known as Vāsudeva, and it fulfills all desires.
The subtle wheel (*sūkṣmacakra*), however, is hollow with many apertures and belongs to Pradyumna;
it bestows happiness upon householders and indeed increases good fortune and other such qualities. ||4 1 ||
Two wheels with a single axle and a broad, thick rear [part] should be known as the *saṃkarṣaṇa* [chariot]; it always brings happiness to householders. (4.2)
Aniruddha is yellowish in luster, circular, and exceedingly beautiful;
it bestows happiness upon householders and increases their prosperity. ||43||
Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, there Lakṣmī and Hari likewise reside;
all sacred fords dwell therein, and its worship destroys all sin. 44.
If it is shaped like an umbrella, there is universal sovereignty; if circular, all prosperity;
if shaped like a cart, there is suffering; and if shaped like a trident, death shall occur. ||45||
If the mouth is distorted, there will be poverty; if it is tawny, there is indeed loss.
If the circle of the ascendant is cracked, disease occurs, but if it is split asunder, death is certain.
That man who bathes with the waters of the Śālagrāma stone has performed ablutions at all sacred fords and is well-initiated into all sacrifices. ||47||
Vows, charity, the consecration of temples, ancestral rites, and the worship of deities—when performed in the vicinity of a Śālagrāma, they yield ten million times their merit. (48)
Circumambulating a Śālagrāma stone is considered equivalent to circumambulating the entire earth;
the merit of the Vedas and the merit of ascetic penance are obtained through the worship of the Śālagrāma. (49)
One who drinks the water from a Śālagrāma stone shall always be liberated while living;
indeed, all sacred fords (tīrthas) desire the touch of its feet.
The earth is purified by his feet; it is the liberation of the lineage of that *lakṣa* family.
At death, by the falling of its water, one shall go to the world of Viṣṇu. ||51||
He who causes a separation between the Śālagrāma stone and the Tulasī plant attains Nirvāṇa and is absorbed into the feet of Viṣṇu. ||52||
For him who indeed causes the removal of a *tulasī* leaf from a conch shell, there will certainly be the dissolution of his marriage and the separation from his wife. (53)
For him who places the Śālagrāma, Tulasī, and the conch together in one place, there shall be separation from his wife and sickness for seven births.
He provides for and protects [the devotee], and there shall be no separation from wealth or wife;
one who desires a wife should always offer *tulasī* to the *śālagrāma*. (55)
Therefore, let the gods always worship me with Tulasī.
O highly fortunate Tulasī, become for me here in the form of a tree. (56)
"Having said, 'And I shall marry you here in your true form as a celestial maiden,' Śrī Hari then ceased speaking, and she likewise [ceased]."
Having abandoned his former body, he assumed a divine form;
like Śrī and like Lakṣmī, he dwelt within the heart of the Lord.
In the form of the Śālagrāma stone, Viṣṇu resides within the dense water; situated on the earth, he is tawny-hued and established through fervent heat.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Padmā, Tulasī, Ramā,
Rādhā, Śrī, Prabhā, Vṛndā— all these are the consorts of the Lord.
Jayā, Pārvatī, Māṇikyā, Pāñcālī, Lalitā, as well as Joṣṭrā and others, are indeed the Śaktis of that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 61.
Then, when the maiden Tulasī assumed a divine form and clung to Kṛṣṇa’s chest, Sarasvatī and the others could no longer endure it.
Sarasvatī could not endure it and glanced at her with a sidelong look;
out of fear of that, Tulasī vanished from that place once again.
Then Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having awakened Sarasvatī,
meditated upon her, worshipped her, and composed a hymn of praise for her.
Chanting the twelve-syllable mantra— "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ Vṛndāyai Tulasai Svāhā"— Viṣṇu performed that worship.
The person who worships according to the prescribed rite with a lamp of ghee, incense, vermilion, and sandalwood shall obtain all accomplishments.
With food offerings, flowers, garments, ornaments,
collyrium, red lac, and various presents, the Supreme Lord performed worship.
Pleased even by his hymn of praise, she emerged from that tree and,
having fallen at his feet, this very maiden sought refuge in Hari.
Viṣṇu granted her a boon, saying, "Become worthy of worship by the entire world;
I shall bear you upon my head and upon my chest."
All the gods and others shall themselves bear you upon their heads;
then, O Goddess, Tulasī will be worshipped even by the gods.
The invocation was performed for her and a seat was offered;
then water for the feet, the respectful offering, and water for sipping were presented. ||7 1 ||
Then oil was also offered by the gods for the purpose of massage,
as well as curds, milk, clarified butter, honey, and sugar.
He was bathed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with water from sacred fords (tīrtha); garments, a water-pot, a bodice, and other such items were offered to him. (73)
Musk, sandalwood, agallochum, collyrium, and the like;
saffron, hair-oils, vermilion, and so forth have been offered. (74)
Lac-dye ornaments, decorations for the body such as jewelry, as well as the sacrificial thread, purificatory grass rings, meditation bands, and so forth—[he gave these]. (75)
[He saw him] wearing the Kaustubha gem, with the auspicious thread and its cord,
along with his night-garment, fan, mirror, hand-cord, and the liquid of the bindu-mark.
It was offered by the gods with saffron, unbroken rice, perfumes, incense, lamps, and other articles,
as well as sweet foods, milk-rice, sweetmeats, fruits, betel-leaf, and water.
In the pavilion, adorned with banana pillars and clothed in archways,
upon a *sarvatobhadra* pedestal and atop a water-pot containing the five jewels.
Then, by them, the arati rite with Tulasī was performed fruitfully;
a cloth, conch-water, incense, and a lamp were waved before her.
Then, bowing down, offering the water of honor (arghya), presenting handfuls of flowers, circumambulating, and pleasing [the Lord] with hymns— all these were performed with Tulasī.
A twelve-year-old girl was meditated upon by them as being like gold;
then Hari praised her—listen, O Lakṣmī, as I speak. (8-1)
I always worship my beloved wife Padmā, as well as Tulasī, Ramā, Vṛndā, Gaṇḍakī, Vanaspati, and Kanyā. ||82||
In Goloka, my beloved is eternal; I worship that beloved wife with whom I delight in Goloka—I worship that wife, Ramā. ||83||
The river Padmāvatī was born; I worship her as my wife Padmā.
I worship that Tulasī whose equal does not exist in all the worlds. (84)
In Vṛndāvana, I worship that Vṛndā, the mistress of Vṛndāvana;
I worship that Gaṇḍakī river, which is joined with the Śālagrāma. ||85||
I worship her who possesses breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant; I worship that tree-like one, whose essence is flowers, the sovereign of the forest.
"I worship that dark-complexioned maiden of beautiful limbs," having thus offered this hymn of praise, the Lord of Ramā remained there. (87)
Then Viṣṇu beheld the maiden Tulasī bowing at his feet, and he granted her a boon, saying, "Become worthy of worship by the entire universe."
"By the boon of Viṣṇu, that goddess became truly satisfied, thinking: 'She is to be borne upon the heads of all, and she is to be saluted and honored by me. (89)
Smiling, Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī,
Virajā, Rādhikā, Padmā, and Śrī— the consorts of Kṛṣṇa— honored him.
On the full moon day of Kārtika, however, is the auspicious birth of Tulasī;
on that occasion, worship should be performed, as it was ordained by Hari himself. (91)
The man who offers a Tulasī leaf to Viṣṇu during the month of Kārtika obtains the fruit of giving ten thousand cows. ||92||
Through the recollection of this hymn, one shall obtain sons, beloved ones, wealth, clothing, houses, food, vehicles, and carriages; as well as health, fearlessness, merit, and so forth. (93)
There is no comparison for her among flowers, nor likewise among goddesses;
Tulasī, who has purified all things, is the purifier of the universe. (94)
Thus honored by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the maiden Tulasī, the tree-like goddess of Hari, became joyful. 95.
The maiden said to Śrī Hari: "O Lord, O Master, if you have daily made me your own through your word, or through your heart, or through your very self," (96)
"My hand must be taken according to the rites of marriage," [Viṣṇu said];
"So be it," Hari replied, and the gods and goddesses sang likewise. (97)

Thus ends the three hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Nature, Greatness, Worship, Hymns, and so forth of Tulasī and Śālagrāma," within the account of the marriage of Tulasī, in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, I desire to hear in full about the marriage of Tulasī—
the side of the bride, the side of the groom, and even the wedding festival itself.
Who were the parents of the maiden and likewise the parents of the bridegroom? Where and how was she married, and who was her priest? || 2 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you; I relate to you this account which destroys sin and grants liberation, through both its recollection and its hearing.
Vṛndāvana is exceedingly beautiful, adorned by the banks of the Yamunā;
it is the most splendid site for the marriage ceremony of Tulasī and Viṣṇu.
Beginning from Govardhana and extending as far as Western Kosala,
and likewise beginning from Kurukṣetra and extending as far as the Khaṇḍakāraṇya forest.
Then that great field was prepared as the site for the wedding;
Viṣṇu remembered the divine plowmen for the sake of purifying the ground.
They arrived there in an instant, and by them the terrestrial site was consecrated;
then Viṣṇu remembered Viśvakarman, and he arrived.
He constructed a preeminent pavilion in Vṛndāvana measuring eight yojanas,
and he also built other pavilions extending for a hundred yojanas.
Now, since King Vṛṣadhvaja was a devotee of Śiva, Dharmadhvaja was born in his lineage; Tulasī was his daughter.
Therefore, may Pārvatī and Hara become the parents of Tulasī.
Thus were the two commanded by Viṣṇu regarding that marriage ceremony.
For the purpose of performing the rite of giving away the daughter in marriage, both parents were honored by all as they were accompanied by Satī and Hara; Tulasī, too, became filled with joy.
Then, Viṣṇu’s parents, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa— who reside in Goloka and are highly esteemed— desired to know the nature of his boon.
Reminded by Viṣṇu, they both arrived there together with their retinues;
indeed, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, was present there as the preeminent Viṣṇu.
Summoned by Viṣṇu, Bṛhaspati, the priest of the gods and the preceptor, arrived as the family priest for the maiden’s household.
And Viṣṇu remembered Dhaumya, who was a family priest residing in an excellent household; as the priest of Kṛṣṇa, he arrived together with Garga.
Auspicious rites were performed and the customary social traditions were observed;
furthermore, a marriage proposal letter, smeared with saffron and written, was dispatched.
There, on the bank of the Yamunā in a grove of Tulasī trees, a new wedding pavilion four yojanas in extent was constructed by Tvaṣṭṛ.
Likewise, the sacrificial pit, the altar, the installation of the water-pot and so forth, the worship of Gaṇeśa, and the installation and worship of the Mātṛkās and other deities. || 18 ||
The worship of the planets, the planting of the pillar known as the *māṇikā*,
the customary local practices, and the application of a paste of turmeric juice upon the girl.
Sadaśiva caused all of that to be performed according to the prescribed rites,
and they summoned their respective kinsmen from every direction.
The camp for the bridegroom's party was established in the Khāṇḍava forest,
while the camp for the bride's party was established in the Tulasī grove.
In the great principal pavilion in Vṛndāvana,
those on the side of the bridegroom's party stayed for the wedding ceremony, while those on the side of the bride remained in Khāṇḍava.
And there, at the command of Rādhākṛṣṇa, the god who is devoted to his wife arrived; that brāhmaṇa was one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas, sciences, and other branches of knowledge.
By him, letters written with saffron were likewise sent out,
concerning the creation of living beings, the creation of Īśa, and also the creation of Brahmā.
Those who were skilled in such matters were dispatched by the experts to indicate the auspicious moment;
the pavilion was prepared on the twelfth day, and the public auspicious rites were performed on the thirteenth.

On the fourteenth day, the consecration of the ground is performed; on the full moon day, the marriage ceremony; and on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the erection of the pavilion and other rites are carried out.
Likewise, on the thirteenth day, the highly auspicious local customs were performed;
and on the fourteenth day, all the great lords arrived from every direction.
In the abode of Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable realm, the Lord Puruṣottama, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is served by both the liberated and the unliberated, arrived.
From Goloka, the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, as well as the wives of Kṛṣṇa and the attendants of Kṛṣṇa,
also arrived and refreshed that forest of Kṛṣṇa.
And from Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa arrived together with his consort;
his male attendants and female attendants arrived from all sides.
Then Vāsudeva and the other Vyūhas, together with their wives and their attendants,
all arrived at the marriage ceremony of Tulasī and Viṣṇu.
From that neutral abode, the realm of the Bhūman-Puruṣa arrived,
and the Vairāja Mahāviṣṇu came along with his own mandala.
Likewise, all the Saṃkarṣaṇas, as well as the principles (tattvas) and primordial nature (prakṛti),
and the primary elements (pradhānas), approached Tulasī who was clinging to Viṣṇu.
The incarnations and their consorts—Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Jayā, Ramā, Lalitā, and others—along with the Goddesses of the Īśvaras, arrived there. (34)
Śrī Rāma, Sītā, and all the others arrived there;
the sages, seers, gods, and ancestors also assembled.
The wife of Brahmā, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, and others, as well as the creators of the universe—
the seven Ṛṣis who were the mind-born sons of Brahmā— also arrived.
The guardians of the quarters, the Manus, the lineage of Dharma, the groups headed by Artha and Māna, the Śrāvaṇas, the years, the followers of Yama, the Pretas, and the Vahnis arrived.
Indra, Candra, Sūrya, Maṅgala, and Budha as well—
the planets, the stars, and the constellations— came to the festival of Tulasī.
The Siddhas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, as well as the Nidhis, the Kṛttikās, the other Mothers, the Suras, the Kāṣṭhās, and indeed the Kalās; || 39 ||
The thirty-three kinds of lunar days and the gods arrived,
as well as the yakṣas, the classes of bhūtas, and the hosts of Śaṅkara.
Herein are the maṇḍalas of the Yoginīs, the goddesses beginning with Caṇḍī, the Bhairavas, the Piśācas, the Vīrabhadras, Jvara, and the others. 41.

The other creation was of the nature of *tamas*; those belonging to the side of Śiva arrived, including Brahmins such as Patnīvratas and others, as well as women such as devoted wives (*pativratās*) and others. 42.
Likewise, those belonging to the castes and stages of life arrived, as did those dwelling in the water and those moving through the sky;
the household deities, the rivers, the mountains, and the forests also came. ||43||
The oceans, villages, islands, and trees arrived there, as did the creepers, shrubs, grasses, beasts, and birds. 44.
Living beings, as well as crops, elephants, and serpents, arrived;
those dwelling in jujube trees, those dwelling in white [shrubs], and those dwelling in milk [trees] all came together. || 45 ||
All women of creation and the men there who were destined for it arrived at the great festival of Tulasī, summoned by Śiva and Viṣṇu. ||46||
Possessing umbrellas and chowries, they are the glories of kings and supreme sovereigns;
mounted upon excellent celestial chariots, they ride on swans, Garuḍas, and elephants.
Resembling Campaka flowers, they are without blinking, adorned with golden crowns, neck-ornaments, and earrings.
Accompanied by male and female servants, they arrived at the great festival of Tulasī. || 48 ||
There were vast quantities of foods to be chewed, foods to be swallowed, foods to be licked, and substances to be sucked;
of drinks, the essence of milk, and nectars;
as well as sweetmeats, side dishes, vegetables, and soups.
There, mountains were fashioned of rice, sugar, roots, and fruit; and lakes were prepared of fresh butter and ghee,
while excellent rivers of cool, refreshing drinks were gathered there.
There were streams of ghee, streams of curd, streams of juice, and rivers of wine;
there were also rivers of honey-wine and lakes of Varuṇī liquor.
Salt, bitter, pungent, sweet, and sour—just as they are, however they may be, and according to one's desire, they are all gathered together like the ocean. (53)
There were couches for reclining, flowers, millions of male and female servants,
dancing and dancers, as well as bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists.
There were crowds of hired singers, bards, scholars, astrologers, and innumerable mendicants;
as well as virtuous women, truthful wives, and the wives of Sāṃkhya practitioners, yogis, renunciants, and forest-hermits. ||55||
Apsarases, courtesans, and celestial chariots were present at the festival of Tulasī;
so too were sacred fords, gods, Gandharvas, actors, and the melodic sounds of songs.
The Vedas and all branches of knowledge arrived at the festival of Tulasī;
likewise did drinks of cold and warm water, as well as foods that were cold and warm. (57)
O Great One, there are infinite things to be enjoyed by the senses of cold and heat; likewise,
there are sacrificial fuels of every kind, sesame seeds and other grains,
as well as the various implements for the fire-oblation, all numbering in the millions.
And twice-born men performing the Cāturhotra sacrifice arrived there by the tens of millions. ||59||
Having taken up residence in their respective quarters on all sides, the dignitaries,
having been offered a welcome and food and other provisions, rejoiced and shone with splendor.
On the full moon day, having performed their ablutions, worship, and other rites, the gods and others,
by the command of Śiva, carried out oblations and sacrificial activities.
Those who have Agni as their mouth indeed become exceedingly satisfied at that time;
and the tumultuous sounds of musical instruments become exceedingly great at that time. (62)
At that time, the songs and melodies of women become exceedingly prevalent,
and the performances of dramas and entertainments become exceedingly common.
At that time, the chanting of the Vedas by the Brahmins becomes exceedingly great;
at that time, the dances of the Apsarases become exceedingly great. (64)
At that time, the songs of courtesans will become exceedingly prevalent;
at that time, displays of sorcery will become exceedingly prevalent.
Then, objects created by illusion are seen most clearly;
then, excellent songs and poems come forth most vividly. (66)
At that time, the currents of marriage with those previously mentioned arise in great abundance;
at that time, the teachers' discourses on reality prevail in great abundance. (67)
At that time, the efforts of the artists' skills are seen most clearly;
indeed, at that time, all tastes, all fragrances, and all forms [are manifested]. 68.
At that time, all sounds and all touches are experienced to the utmost degree; what could be lacking where the Blessed One causes even a tuft of cotton to resound? (69)
In the morning, an excellent army arrived there from Khāṇḍava;
the two heroes were Viṣṇu, who had four arms and was less than sixteen years of age.
He is resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and forest garland;
he is endowed with the Kaustubha gem, earrings, a crest-jewel, and bracelets.
At that time, his face was encircled by a fresh garland of lotuses;
mounted upon a divine white horse, he shone brightly with a sword in hand.
Adorned with the splendor of excellent garments shimmering with golden stars,
he was decorated with ornaments of gems, diamonds, pearls, jewels, gold, and the like.
The Lord wears yellow garments and is endowed with lotus-like feet wearing sandals;
he is as tawny as yellow pigment and shines with the color of a lion's mane.
Adorned with armlets, garlands, a crest-jewel, and necklaces; graced by a forehead mark consisting of saffron, unbroken grains of rice, and a crescent moon. ||75||
Adorned with glory, prosperity, modesty, splendor, beauty, accomplishment, and fortune,
he traveled by means of a river ten yojanas in length.
[The city] was served by male and female slaves holding parasols, whisks, and staffs, and was frequented by supreme lords who were kings of kings and sovereigns of kings. (77)
For the purpose of establishing worldly conduct, Sadāśiva remained present;
and having accepted food and drink from the emperors, including Koṭīśvara,
they stood with water-pots upon their heads, filled with water and adorned with bilva leaves.
Fortunate daughters of the gods also approached the bridegroom. 79.
Flowers, saffron, bilva fruits, and unbroken grains held in a golden vessel, as well as garlands, parched rice, and svastika figures, were indeed offered by Satyā to her chosen husband.
He was then honored with sandalwood paste, flowers, parched grain, and unbroken rice by his female attendants;
saluted by the followers of Śiva and blessed with benedictions by the brahmins.
He was celebrated in every way by the women and gazed upon by those of great honor.
Delighted by the sounds of musical instruments, they were led to the pavilion of rest.
Honored, worshipped, refreshed, and treated with hospitality, those dignitaries from both sides attained enduring happiness. (82–83)
Tulasī wore all the garments, ornaments, and other items sent by her husband, as well as the jewels and other articles belonging to her father-in-law. || 84 ||
At the rising of the moon, having brought him to a house illuminated by the light of ten million moons, suns, and lightning, Hara performed the honors for the bridegroom.
Then, having performed the customary worldly rites, offered water for drinking,
and honored [the guests] with various articles, Hara [prepared] the wedding pavilion.
Then, as musical instruments were sounded, they led that excellent king away;
at that time, there arose the sounds of the Vedas, the sounds of songs, and the sounds of trumpets.
Then the goddesses rained down a shower of flowers mixed with unbroken rice and other offerings.
Having shattered the skull with his foot, Śrī Viṣṇu approached the sacrificial altar.
Then that excellent one sat upon a magnificent throne there,
seated on a cushion near the sacrificial pit.
Joined there with the thread of the forearm and the fruit of the desire-yielding tree (kalpavṛkṣa),
it was consecrated for the sake of well-being by the preceptors who had mastered the Vedas.
Then, adorned with a *tilaka* by Śaṅkara and honored by him, he had a *tilaka* applied by Pārvatī with her two hands and was made auspicious.
Then, having brought that Tulasī from the left side, he was made a bridegroom.
Those two were marked with an auspicious tilaka dot by the two family priests.

Then, having been sprinkled and consecrated with flowers, unbroken rice, water, and other substances, and having sipped water for purification, the two were urged toward the fire-oblation and performed the sacrifice.
And the bridegroom’s garland was placed by the maiden around the neck of Viṣṇu.
The priest joined the couple with the bridegroom’s garland,
and after that, having had them perform the worship of the limbs, the deities, and so forth,
he caused them to place morsels of food into each other's mouths.
Having caused [the disciple] to drink water and having recited the Vedic mantras,
he should place his left hand upon Viṣṇu’s right hand.
As he caused them to hear the mantras beginning with "May you two practice the dharma together," at that moment,
a drop of sweat appeared on both of them and their hair stood on end.
Then musical instruments were sounded, the sounds of the Vedas arose, and cries of "Victory! were raised by Viṣṇu upon his taking of Tulasī.
Having circumambulated the fire, the two of them sat down again;
and having performed the remaining oblations, they engaged in the game of rings.
Hara gave to the Brahmins cows, land, gold, rubies, garments, various jewels, and plots of ground, numbering in the millions, tens of millions, and hundreds of millions.
Kṛṣṇa gave to the brāhmaṇas jewels, diamonds, queens, vehicles, mounts, excellent elephants, houses, fields, wealth, and all manner of prosperity.
Then they gave gifts for the groom and the bride;
subsequently, the pestle, winnowing basket, and other items were lowered from the head of the groom.
Having led both the bride and the groom to the house, they were served food;
then, having provided them with a private bed, [the rites continued] after their morning bath and other duties.

Having caused food and other offerings to be prepared, and having bestowed the nuptial gifts according to the prescribed rules, as well as countless treasures such as gems, diamonds, gold, and so forth; || 104 ||

Tens of millions of horses, elephants, cattle, living beings, vehicles, and mounts; male and female slaves by the hundreds of millions, and household utensils and the like—[all these were given]. (10.5)

Having bestowed all those things— given by his own father and by others according to what was appropriate and according to their wealth— and having offered betel-leaf in accordance with worldly custom, he made them over to the bridegroom.
Then, having offered him water for drinking and requested his forgiveness,
he seated his daughter, who was endowed with excellent qualities, upon a vehicle.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings and received the prostrations of the maiden,
Śambhu sent the two of them to the pavilion of rest.
The followers of Varuṇa, borne by the people, went to their place of rest;
the followers of Śiva, having turned back, set out for the hermitage of Śiva.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, having fed everyone with great devotion and having honored the common folk,
Hara sent forth his excellent followers.
Then Hara sent away the lords of his own abode, and having caused the dismantling of the pavilion and other structures by the Gaṇas and others, he departed.
From that place, the Lord went to Kailāsa by means of his celestial chariot;
and Tulasī remains there on the ground at the site where he was joined [to him] in the form of a tree. || 11 2 ||
Having gone to the Khāṇḍava forest in the form of a bride,
she also performed there the dismantling of the pavilion and other such tasks.
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa and the others, and having taken his new bride with him,
Viṣṇu departed for his own Vaikuṇṭha along with Garuḍa and his attendants.
Viṣṇu took delight with his newly wedded wife in various desires;
in this way, she, his own wife, was liberated from the curse by him.
And Tulasī too, having obtained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her husband, was led to her own abode, which is filled with supreme bliss.
Her desires fulfilled, she remained in the world as Tulasī.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, those people who shall worship me incessantly—‖ 1.17‖
My devotees, who have taken refuge in me, shall lead men and women— just like the Tulasī plant— with the blossoms and leaves of Tulasī to my own feet.
On earth, I myself exist here in two forms: as the Tulasī tree and likewise as the Śālagrāma stone. (1.19)
By means of water, stones, leaves, flowers, grains, or clay—by whatever means possible—I grant liberation from living beings; that is my pretext.
Having heard this account of the marriage of Tulasī,
one should then worship the preceptor and the reciter according to the prescribed rite— the latter being honored by all.
With wealth, garments, ornaments, vehicles, and conveyances;
with food, silver, gems, and the like, as well as gold, diamonds, and various [precious objects];
with leaves, flowers, fruits, water, milk, curd, clarified butter, and so forth.
With sugar, grains, wheat, dates, and so forth, measured in khārīka units. || 123 ||
With *śrīphala* fruits, sandalwood oil, umbrellas, chowries, and couches; with cows, land, houses, mansions, and the like; and with gardens, vehicles, and horses. || 124 ||
With couches, beds, and royal thrones; with bedsheets, mirrors, and vessels; with sesame, rice, and excellent food; and with fresh butter and fine cakes. || 125 ||
One should honor the guru with many articles of domestic utility and should give abundant gifts according to one's capacity and wealth. (126)
One should feed many Brahmins and virtuous men, and one should cause virtuous women to be fed; likewise, one should feed boys, girls, the destitute, the blind, and the wretched. (127)
One should gratify the ancestors with offerings of water and perform the śrāddha rite;
one should perform worship of the gods and conduct the great pūjā.
One should perform the worship of Śiva and Śivā, as well as the worship of Tulasī and Viṣṇu; one should worship Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa and offer oblations to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having bestowed grace upon all the listeners,
and having caused the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) to be performed, he praised the couple.
Having asked for forgiveness for any offense and having given an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should dismiss [the deity] with prostrations and remember Tulasī and Mādhava. || 131 ||
Thus, one should worship Tulasī and Mādhava with these sixteen supreme and most excellent objects; the worshipper shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 132.
By worshipping Kṛṣṇa with Tulasī and by listening to this [narrative], one obtains wealth, a wife, offspring, sons, fields, a kingdom, a home, and so forth. (133)
A barren woman indeed obtains a son; one who is destitute becomes wealthy;
a sick person shall be freed from disease; and a debtor shall attain freedom from debt.
One bound in shackles shall be liberated; the sinner shall attain sinlessness;
and a maiden shall obtain a husband equal to Kṛṣṇa, which always bestows good fortune.
One shall obtain everything as desired and attain the state of being a vessel for all prosperity;
the suffering of those who suffer shall be destroyed—provided one causes this to be heard or listens to it oneself. (1.36)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, within the narrative of the marriage of Tulasī in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, [is described] the construction of the pavilion for rest and other facilities on the bank of the Yamunā in Vṛndāvana on the twelfth lunar day; the camp of Viṣṇu’s ancestors in the Khāṇḍava forest; the camp of Tulasī’s ancestors in the Tulasī forest; the arrangement of the sacrificial pits, pavilions, and so forth; the arrival of the bridegroom’s entourage and the arrival of the procession of people carrying the groom's party; the marriage rites of Tulasī on the full moon of Kārtika; the joining of hands; and the departure and other concluding events.
The three hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Fruits of Performing the Marriage of Tulasī, Hearing [Her Story], and Other Deeds."
Śrī Lakṣmī said: O Viṣṇu, how indeed was the name Śālagrāma always given to this?
What kind of place is it? O Hari, Lord of Śrī, please narrate this story to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this narrative which clarifies the purpose of the Śālagrāma;
by hearing it, such devotion shall arise, and likewise liberation shall be attained.
Listen as I relate to you everything that occurred there, exactly as it happened, concerning that great river which was born with the name Gaṇḍakī.
Having recognized that the ground known as Śālagrāma was to the east of the Tulasī plant, Acyuta was then bound by oath: "Let it become the Śālagrāma stone."
And from the temples of Hari as he was performing penance, a wondrous water emerged, and it fell indeed upon that region in the form of streams. || 5 ||
Having known that field to have already arisen in the past as the Gaṇḍakī field, it was then cursed by Viṣṇu in ancient times, saying, "Become the Gaṇḍakī! (6)
In the Siddhakṣetra of Śālagrāma, Keśava became a stone;
in the spring of the Gaṇḍakī, that [stone] became the river Gaṇḍakī.
Listen to this field, adorned and fashioned, in detail:
there was a supreme Brahman-sage known by the name Sālaṅkāyana. (8)
In the former Kṛta Yuga, this great devotee, accompanied by his desire for a son, wandered through the ten directions to propitiate me.
For the sake of a son, he performed austerities with a concentrated mind on the peak of Mount Meru,
as well as at Piṇḍāraka, Lohārgala, and on Mount Raivata.
Since peace does not come to me at all without his direct presence,
he has arrived there in the vicinity of the Himalayas for the sake of performing austerities.
The sage named Sālāṅka constantly performed austerities for many years;
by him, a small leaf-hut was constructed there for the sake of his wife.
Other forest deities as well, dwelling together with their wives,
made a village of *sāla* trees among the *śāla* trees in that forest.
The founder of the lineage was Sālaṅkāyana, who resided at a *sāla* tree;
because he lived among the *śāla* trees in a village, the site became known as Śālagrāma.
Having learned of that previous history of Tulasī,
I, who am of the nature of stone, was told, "Become a resident of Śālagrāma," and so I became thus.
Having arrived there, I indeed abide in the form of a mountain by my own will;
for I was then pleased with the fierce austerity of Sālaka.
Having granted his own vision and being joined with the blessing of a son, he said: "O Lord, let there be a son for me who is indeed equal to you. (17)
I replied, "So be it," and from that time forth, my sons were born;
I took up my residence on the mountain of Śālagrāma.
O beloved, I have always remained there like a stone, as if dull-witted;
meanwhile, the sage Sālaṅka met his death right here. (19)
And my mother, known as Śalākā, was virtuous and remained with him;
having indeed brought about their liberation, I, Viṣṇu, am present in that very place.
Having become invisible, I dwell eternally within this heap of stones;
yet, being cursed, I indeed reside here with even greater intensity.
In that sacred field, the Lord Hara, endowed with the form of a fish,
resides upon that Śālagrāma mountain in the form of a stone.
I remain in that very place eternally in the form of a mountain; all the rocks therein are my own form, without a doubt. (23)
All of them are indeed worthy of worship, how much more so those marked with the discus;
on this mountain, the stones in the form of lingas should be understood as being the very form of Śambhu. (24)
Śambhu is the stones with Śiva as their navel, while I am the stones with the discus as their navel;
this was due to the power of the asceticism of the sage named Sālaṅkāyana.
O my beloved, having consulted with Śambhu, we two remained there;
the Śālagrāma mountain is Viṣṇu, and that Śiva-peak is auspicious. (26)
Between those two mountains, there is indeed a stone named Viṣṇuśivā;
formerly, Revā performed penance there which brought great satisfaction to Śiva.
With the desire, "May I have a son like you," he indeed granted a boon to Revā in the form of a Liṅga.
"O beloved of Śiva, I shall dwell within your womb as your son.
Having spoken thus, that Śiva departed from the Śālagrāma mountain.
Indeed, the soul of the Liṅga, having assumed the form of stone, went into the waters of the Narmadā;
thus, at the base of the Narmadā, there were stones that were the peaks of the Śiva-liṅga.
"All of them are indeed of the nature of Śiva, and likewise, I myself am Hari here";
thus, O Lakṣmī, has this been told to you for the purpose of understanding the significance of the Śālagrāma.
Moreover, listen to this account: much austerity was performed by me, and from the sweat-water upon my cheeks, a stream of water came into being.
That lotus-eyed maiden also became conscious of her own form;
and there she performed severe penance out of a desire for a son.
Having subsisted on withered leaves and thereafter even consuming only air,
she performed penance for a hundred divine years, always intent upon meditation of Viṣṇu.
Being present there in person as Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, I,
pleased and affectionate toward those who bow before me, spoke sweetly to her.
"O Gaṇḍakī, O sinless one, I am pleased with you and amazed by your asceticism;
because of your uninterrupted devotion, choose a boon, O female ascetic! (36)
"O lady of excellent complexion, tell me quickly what should be given; I am pleased.
Even Gaṇḍakī, having first seen the one who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus," [spoke thus].
Having prostrated herself like a staff, she then began to offer praise:
"O Lord, having manifested from your rod as the nature of water... (38)
"As long as I remain here, you have become invisible;
O Keśava, how shall I dwell alone in this forest? (39)
Indeed, he who is difficult even for yogis to behold was seen by me once again;
having entered his own yoga-māyā, you have assumed this form.
Standing in the midst of this deluded world, knowing nothing at all, I have been created and sustained by you, unable to distinguish between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. (41)
O noble one, you have indeed seen me today as I have been elevated to greatness by you;
since I have made this request out of ignorance, it behoves you to grant it to me.
"O Soul of All, you are compassionate, especially toward the wretched.
Having spoken thus, he joined his palms in reverence and requested the boon he desired. (43)
"O Viṣṇu, having entered my womb, become my son.
Then Viṣṇu said to her, "Listen, O Goddess, to my words. (44)
In the form of the Śālagrāma stone, I shall always abide within your womb as your son, for the sake of bestowing grace upon my devotees. (45)
"Come with me to Vaikuṇṭha, O blameless girl; stay here for now, for my wife Tulasī, who is in the form of a river, will arrive here."
"She shall be known by the name Gaṇḍakī, and she will be my great future consort.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One led the girl away by means of a bird.
Having protected both Vaikuṇṭha and her right there, he returned once more to where that stream of water, the Gaṇḍakī, flows, and into its waters he [entered]. ||48||
He dwells in the form of stone for the sake of granting boons;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, I am Viṣṇu, eternally embodied in the form of stone. Because of my presence, that river has consequently become most excellent.
By seeing, touching, bathing, drinking, and immersing oneself [in her],
she removes great sin born of speech, mind, and body.
He who bathes in the Gaṇḍakī and offers libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors— ‖ 5 1 ‖
Having delivered his ancestors, he shall go to the world of Brahmā;
and if he should give up his life there, he too shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Then Lakṣmī said to Viṣṇu: "How indeed did the Blessed One [attain this] in the past?"
Indeed, Gaṇḍavārigaṇḍakī performed most rigorous penance.
Then Nārāyaṇa said to Lakṣmī: "Listen always, O beloved, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, for their prosperity, and for the protection of dharma."
"I perform various kinds of austerity for the sake of auspiciousness and for my own satisfaction.
This sacred ford existed in a previous creation as being of such a nature;
there I began my penance for the sake of many blessings."
I know all that, but no one else knows it, O you who have acted in the past.
O Lakṣmī, when even Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the sons of Dharma, were not present on the Himālaya for the protection of the worlds, [then... (57)
Supreme austerity was performed by me near the Himalayas;
at that time, the great sacred field of Śālagrāma became my dwelling place.
While I was performing penance there, indeed, after a long period of time had passed—
A fierce radiance appeared, by which the worlds, both moving and unmoving, were illuminated. ||59||
Greatly agitated and amazed by that heat, they looked in every direction;
and from that heat, a flood of sweat arose upon his cheeks.
From that was born a divine river that removes the sins of the worlds.
Desiring to know his power, they were not able to do so in any way whatsoever.
Then all the gods, filled with eagerness, went toward Brahmā;
and Brahmā, though ignorant of the cause, went together with the gods to the illustrious Śaṅkara.
He asked: "O Lord, tell us what this is, why it has occurred, and how it came to be—this being of wondrous splendor."
Having meditated for a moment, Śiva replied to Viṣṇu, who was established in penance.
"Let us go where he dwells," they said, and they went to that place.
Śambhu, smiling, said to him: "O Lord, how is it that you practice asceticism?
For one whose every desire is fulfilled, what is the purpose of your penance?"
Thus addressed, Mahāviṣṇu, having paid homage to the lords of the gods, [proceeded].
He said, "For the sake of the welfare of the world, I have prepared to perform austerities;
having obtained the sight of you, I have indeed become one who has achieved his purpose today."
May this field be a divine land and the most excellent of sacred sites;
likewise, may the gods always show their grace through words of blessing. (67)
Having heard that, Brahmā, Śambhu, and the other deities then said: "O Viṣṇu, because of your vision, this is indeed a sacred field (kṣetra) that grants liberation."
Moreover, because of the vision of the gods, this place shall become a field of liberation (muktikṣetra), where the Gaṇḍakī, the best of rivers, was born from the sweat on [the god's] cheek. (69)
There is no doubt that [this shall come to pass] for her in whose womb you shall be;
while you, the Lord of the World, abide therein, it shall be by virtue of your presence.
O Lord of the worlds, we— the gods, the sages, the Vedas, the sacred fords, and the sacrifices— shall dwell here forever at the Gaṇḍakī.
He who bathes in its waters throughout the entire month of Kārttika will be liberated from all sins and shall partake in liberation; of this there is no doubt.
It is the supreme holy site among all holy sites and the most auspicious among all auspicious things;
by remembering it, seeing it, or touching it, one obtains a fruit greater than that of the Gaṅgā.
This is that most meritorious Gaṇḍakī, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is joined by another river named Devikā.
Formerly, Pulastya and Pulaha performed supreme austerity there,
having each established a separate hermitage for the purpose of carrying out creation.
Thereafter, the capacity for the performance of creation was obtained by those two;
from that, the daughter of Brahmā arose, who indeed merged with the Gaṇḍakī.
There, at the confluence of the three rivers, Hari liberated the elephant and the crocodile;
with his Sudarśana discus, he swiftly tore open the mouth of the crocodile.
Furthermore, that wheel was thrown again and again, striking against the rocks;
and from that striking of the wheel, the rocks were marked by the wheel.
Then, in that same manner, those [images] were always nourished by the gods through Vajrakīṭas;
indeed, this was for the sake of protecting the devotees in the sacred field of Śālagrāma. (79)
I commanded Sudarśana, which always revolves there;
by that discus, all those stones were indeed marked.
Extending from Muktikṣetra as far as Hariharakṣetra,
that sacred field consisting of Śālagrāma stones spans twelve yojanas.
O beautiful one, wherever I have established my presence for the sake of protecting my own devotees, there also exist *sāla* trees, which are portions of myself. (82)
"This tree which was seen by Gaṇḍakī is undoubtedly I myself;
this place, amidst the high rocks of the mountain peak, is pleasing to me. (83)
The place known as Śālagrāmasthala grants liberation from the cycle of existence to devotees;
indeed, in the region of Cakrasvāmī, there are stone discs (cakras) scattered here and there.
By virtue of my yoga, that entire region is seen as sacred;
the Gaṇḍakī, Tulasī, Vṛndā, and Padmā have taken refuge in my body. (85)
By the power of Me, O beloved of Mine, one who relies upon the Śālagrāma, the Gaṇḍakī river, and Tulasī will certainly attain My world. (86)
I have related to you exactly what occurred, as well as my own abiding in asceticism for the purpose of establishing sacred fords and for the sake of the welfare of the world. (87)
In the form of stone, you exist for the sake of the benefit of embodied beings; in the form of iron filings and so forth, you exist for the sake of the benefit of living creatures. ||88||
For the sake of providing water, drink, shelter, and so forth for all beings, I assumed my various forms at the moment of creation. (89)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this is my compassion for one who is intent on the liberation of living beings;
this chapter, O highly fortunate lady, brings about all auspiciousness.
Those who follow my path and recite this indeed obtain splendor, glory, fortune, all desires, and abundant prosperity. (91)
O wise woman, for as many syllables as there are in this chapter,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in my world.
One who desires the supreme goal should never forget this at the time of death—not even a single verse or a single quarter-verse. (93)
This secret, the source of all blessings, has been told to you, O blessed lady;
it is my sacred field, O highly fortunate one. What else do you wish to hear? (94)

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of the Kṛta Yuga lineage, in the narrative of the Śālagrāma field, there is the ancient history explaining the meaning of the names Gaṇḍakī and Śālagrāma; the penance performed by the sage Sālaṃkāyana and his son Viṣṇu, who remained right there in the form of stone; the penance of Revā for the sake of a son; the presence of Śambhu in the river Revā in the form of a Liṅga that is his son; and how the stream from the cheek (*gaṇḍa*) of Viṣṇu, while he was performing penance at the Śāla tree, became known as Gaṇḍakī. That [is the account].

Chapter Three Hundred and Forty: The Description of the Nature of Tulasī, the Marks of the Discus [imprinted] by the striking of the discus thrown at the crocodile for the sake of liberating Gajendra, and the stone-insect [incident], and so forth. || 340 ||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
Having heard of the Śālagrāma stone, the Śambhu stone, the Gaṇḍakī river, the Śāladruma tree, the Munisālaṅka, and the virtuous Tūlasī— || 1 ||
My mind finds no satisfaction in its longing to hear [of them];
O Keśava, tell me of the sacred fords situated within the Śālagrāma field.
By hearing which, even the sinful shall be uplifted;
and by performing which, one shall possess wealth, wives, and other such blessings even in this world.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Oh, what fortune! Oh, what merit! Is it not the hearing of the stories of Śālagrāma?
Oh, what destiny! Oh, what liberation!—the worship of the Śālagrāma stone! (4)
Oh, what heaven! Oh, what sovereignty! Is this dwelling at the sacred site of Śālagrāma?
Oh, what prosperity! Oh, what contentment! This is the service of the waters of the Gaṇḍakī.
O Lotus-born One, when the rise of great merit occurs for living beings, the opportunity to reach the site of Śālagrāma arises; it does not happen otherwise.
"Having gone to Śālagrāmasthala, I shall perform ablutions and libations in the waters of the Gaṇḍakī"— one who makes such a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) attains results pertaining to this world.
Indeed, satisfaction arises for the ancestors when one performs [this rite]; what more need be said?
It serves to destroy the sins of the sinful and to lead those endowed with merit to heaven.

At the beginning of creation, I fashioned the Śālagrāma sacred site for the fulfillment of the desires of those with worldly aspirations, and for the sake of liberation for those endowed with devotion.
The Śālagrāma stone is my form; it is my image fashioned by me.
For one who performs worship with the sixteen articles, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And I grant whatever else is desired, such as wealth, wives, houses, and so forth;
these have been created by me solely out of compassion for the sake of uplifting living beings. (11)
Listen, Lakṣmī, to all those holy places that exist there on land;
I shall describe to you in their entirety how and why they came into being.
At the Sālaṅkāyana-tīrtha, indeed, is the mountain named Śālagrāma;
there the Lord Hara was installed by Soma as Someśvara.
Someśvaragiri and the Gaṇḍakī have also been described to you;
[the latter flows] from the southern side of Someśa after Bāṇa had pierced the mountain.
After Rāvaṇa performed penance, the Bāṇagaṅgā, which bestows great merit through its streams of water, was manifested at this supremely purifying sacred site (tīrtha). 15.
To the east of Someśa, there is the penance grove of Rāvaṇa;
there stands the mountain famous as Nartanācala because of Rāvaṇa’s dancing.
Pleased by his dance, Śambhu then granted him a boon:
the auspicious Bāṇeśvara, which bestows heaven at the holy site of Bāṇagaṅgā. (17)
Staying there for three nights, one shall obtain the fruit of austerity;
by bathing, one gains the fruit of a bath in the Gaṅgā, and by beholding [the deity], one obtains the fruit of worship.
Now, there is indeed the Triveṇī Tīrtha, the most excellent among all holy places,
where the river named Devikā meets the Gaṇḍakī.
For the sake of regulating the penance of the gods as they were performing austerity,
that river indeed manifested, bestowing liberation upon the gods.
Then, from the hermitage of Pulastya and Pulaha, the river Devikā merged with the Gaṇḍakī; that confluence of three streams is known as the Gaṇḍakī-triveṇī.
That great holy place (tīrtha) is most efficacious for desires and supremely grants satisfaction to the ancestors;
it is renowned as Triveṇī—listen now to its narrative here.
In ancient times, Viṣṇu performed austerities on the Himalayas out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; at that time, an exceedingly long period passed.
Then, from the body of Hari, a fire as intense as that [of the sun] appeared;
by its heat, a profusion of sweat was produced upon his cheeks.
From that was born the divine river Gaṇḍakī, the best of streams;
at that time, the river known as Devikā entered into union with it.
Born there through the ascetic power (tapas) of the gods, she is considered Devikā;
another river was born from the ascetic powers of Pulastya and Pulaha. 26.
Then, through their ascetic penance, the knowledge of creation was indeed obtained by those two;
she is the third, the illustrious river named Brahmaputrī.
The Gaṇḍakī joins there and is celebrated as Triveṇī;
by bathing there, a human being obtains the fruit of ascetic practice. ||28||
Now I shall tell you something else regarding that site of Triveṇikā:
at that place, Hari brought about the liberation of the lordly elephant and the liberation of the crocodile.
Formerly, the two sons of Vedanidhi, named Jaya and Vijaya,
having propitiated Hari, were born as attendants in the abode of the Lord.
Due to the curse of Rādhikā, those very two returned once again to the earth in another kalpa as the two sons of Tṛṇabindu.
Born as performers of sacrifice, masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
they worshipped Hari with devotion, their senses and minds fixed solely upon Him.
At the time of worship, Hari always attains their presence;
once, they were both invited by Marutta for the sacrificial rites.
Satisfied by the king who had completed his sacrifice with sacrificial fees and other gifts,
the two began to divide the wealth and other possessions between themselves.
They disputed; the elder said, "The division should be equal," but Vijaya said to him, "For whatever has been acquired by someone belongs to him. (35)
"I am indeed skilled; therefore, I have obtained this especially.
You are not capable in that way, so I will not give it to you as an equal share. (36)
Jaya said: "Why do you speak thus, thinking yourself incapable?
Since you do not give back what you have seized, therefore you shall attain the state of a crocodile. (37)
Vijaya also said, "Surely you have become blind with wealth;
become an elephant, blinded by rut! Thus, by their respective curses, the two became separate.

Indeed, Jaya and Gaja were born as an elephant-catcher and an elephant; both were rememberers of their former births (jātismara). Jaya was in the forest of the Triveṇī region, while Vijaya was within the water.
In that forest, there was a crocodile that had come to bathe; remembering its former enmity, the crocodile dwelling in the midst of the water seized the elephant. (1.341.40)
A battle between those two took place for many years with various maneuvers;
then Hari, moved by devotion, was entreated by Varuṇa.
By the gift of the elephant Kamala, he reached Triveṇī;
with his Sudarśana discus, he tore apart the mouth of the crocodile.

Liberation was granted even to the elephant, and release was achieved even for the crocodile, through the act of striking against rocks and other such obstacles by means of the Sudarśana [wheel]. (43)
The wheel-marks have appeared; thus has your greatness been proclaimed.
In this way, this sacred ford is the supreme savior for embodied beings. (44)
O beloved, the great god Jaleśvara shines there;
when my discus was hurled upon the earth, it became water. (45)
That place indeed became the Jaleśvara Tīrtha, consisting of a wheel;
a person who dwells there for five days shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In former times, there was a Gaṇa named Nandīśvara, the grandson of Śālaka;
he dwelt in Vṛndāvana, constantly tending the cattle.
Once, having taken the cows, he went to Harikṣetra;
Nandin was himself told by Hara, "Go to Harikṣetra," and so he went there. ||48||
He made his dwelling for many nights on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī,
in that field where cattle graze upon the lush pastures day and night.
From that very day, that famous sacred field came to be known as Hariharātmaka;
and because the gods wandered there, it is also remembered as Devāṭa.
Once the Blessed Lord Śambhu was seated upon an excellent throne;
there, from the three matted locks of Śambhu, there issued forth three streams.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the holy river Sarasvatī—this is the Tīrtha of the Three Streams where Śambhu is eternally present. (52)
Bestowing knowledge upon his devotees by which they are liberated from saṃsāra, he is himself liberated after bathing, propitiating the ancestors, and worshipping the gods. (53)
In the eastern direction of that very place, there is indeed Haṃsatīrtha;
once, hungry crows flew up from there. (54)
Having taken food, one crow was indeed departing when another crow saw him;
they fought there, and then both fell into the pit.
Having become two swans, they departed and went indeed to Lake Mānasa;
because of that wondrous event, it was made known as Haṃsatīrtha. ||56||
From Muktikṣetra, the sacred site of Haṃsatīrtha extends for twelve yojanas; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who visit holy places, and it has been resorted to by me. (57)
Then, because that sage Sālaṅkāyana performed penance there, that cluster of *sāla* trees became renowned as Śālagrāma. (58)
There, fifteen secret sacred sites (tīrthas) exist; there is a field named Bilvaprabha, possessing four groves. 99.
There, by bathing in the river and residing day and night, a person obtains the fruit of four horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas). || 1.341.60 ||
Furthermore, there is the Cakrasvāmin Tīrtha, consisting of a stone disc;
it is three yojanas in extent, and a person should dwell there for three nights.
One who dies at a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) certainly attains the merit of a three-night sacrifice;
moreover, when the abandonment of life occurs there, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Now, at that sacred field called Viṣṇupada, where three streams fall from the Himālaya,
one obtains the fruit of the holy ford simply by bathing there.
One who gives up their life there shall partake in the merit of three Atirātra sacrifices;
in that place is a most purifying holy site named Kālīhrada.
Indeed, from the foot of the Badarī tree, a stream flows into the lake;
by bathing there, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice and is liberated.
Now, at midnight on the twelfth lunar day, at the holy ford (tīrtha) called Śaṅkhaprabha, conch sounds are heard; those who hear them become partakers of liberation.
Then, having bathed in the holy pool known as Gadākuṇḍa at the southern stream, a human being obtains the fruit of the knowledge of Vedānta and other such attainments. ||67||
Then there is the auspicious Agnisuprabha Tīrtha, whose water flows toward the northeast;
its water is warm during the winter and becomes cool during the summer.
It falls in the form of a stream; having bathed there, one partakes in the five fires and the moon. Then, that sacred ford (tīrtha) consists of all weapons and is composed of seven currents.
Having bathed, one shall become a great king; he should dwell there for seven days.
Now, there is the Devaprabha Tīrtha, endowed with four streams.
Having bathed there, one obtains the awakening of the four Vedas.
Next is the Vidyādhara Tīrtha, which is endowed with five streams.
Having bathed there, one undoubtedly goes to the world of the Vidyādharas;
that sacred bathing place on the river is covered with rocks, groves, and creepers. (72)
One should perform a bath there; one shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Having bathed at the Gāndharva-tīrtha, which has a single stream, one shall become happy. (73)
He rejoices among the world-protectors and goes to my own realm;
then there is the sacred ford Devahrada, where the fish dwell along with the Cakras.
And golden lotuses are seen at the rising of the sun;
those who bathe there, purified from the impurities of speech and body, go to heaven. ||75||
A human being obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices at every place where the divine rivers meet, O beloved;
for there the gods and goddesses abide in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha).
The Gandharvas and Apsaras, along with the daughters of the Nāgas and the serpents themselves;
the celestial ṛṣis, all the sages, and even the lords of the gods; the Siddhas, the virtuous ones, and the Kinnaras—indeed, they all descended from heaven. ||77–78||
In the Himalayas and in Nepal, on this very land of Paśupati,
various rivers flow across the earth from those respective locations;
having joined with the Śvetagaṅgā, these many rivers follow the forests.
Those originating from Śiva have reached the confluence of the Gaṇḍakī and the Kṛṣṇā.
That Triśūlagangā has become the assembly of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
likewise, Siddhāśrama is a purifying holy site that increases merit. ||8 1||
Furthermore, by bathing at the hermitage of Śambhu and at the confluence of two meritorious rivers,
one will certainly obtain the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
By bathing there on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
furthermore, by bathing in the month of Māgha, one obtains the fruit born of bathing at Prayāga.
In the month of Kārttika, by bathing at Satulārava, one attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
By bathing there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Sacrifice, charity, austerity, burnt offerings, ancestral rites, and worship performed at the Śālagrāma, the great sacred field, and at the confluence of the two divine rivers yield indeed infinite merit. ||85||
"O Lakṣmī, I always dwell here facing the east, bestowing liberation;
Śiva is on my right side, and Brahmā is always situated on my left.
That place is indeed composed of both Hari and Hara, and composed of both Viṣṇu and Brahmā. (86)
Upon death, they surely attain liberation, and indeed reach the eternal and certain heaven. ||87||
First is Muktikṣetra, then Rurukhaṇḍa;
next is the confluence of the two divine rivers, and after that, Triveṇī. ||88||
This very field of Gaṇḍakī is indeed where it meets with the Gaṅgā;
there, the Gaṇḍakī has joined with the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā. (89)
That sacred field is known as Hari-hara; its greatness is difficult even for the gods to attain.
By reading or even by hearing [of it], the fruit of bathing at a holy pilgrimage site shall be obtained.
Thus, in the first section, concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter Three Hundred and Forty-one: The Display of the Tīrthas, beginning with Śāligrāma-kṣetra, Sālaṅkāyana, Someśvara, Gaṇḍakī, Bāṇa, Gaṅgā-triveṇī, Devikā, Brahma-putrī, Gaja-grāha-tīrtha, Jaleśvara, Traidhārika-tīrtha, Haṃsa-tīrtha, Śāligrāma-tīrtha, Cakra-svāmi-tīrtha, Viṣṇupada, Śaṅkha-prabha, Gadā-kuṇḍa, Agni-prabha, Sarvāyudha-deva-prabha, Vidyādhara-ekadhāra, Devahrada, Triśūla-gaṅgā, Hari-hara-kṣetra, and others.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
How did Ruru-kṣetra come to be, and what is the nature of Ruru-tīrtha?
O ocean of mercy, tell me that; I desire to hear it in its entirety.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In ancient times, there was a brāhmaṇa named Devadatta, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu,
who formerly performed divine penance in a hermitage abounding with deer.
Ten thousand years had passed while the sage remained engaged in austerity;
then Indra thought of creating an obstacle for him as he practiced penance.
He sent forth Kāma along with Vasanta, the Gandharvas together with their companions, Pramlocā, and even the Malaya breeze.
Taking Indra’s command, they went toward his hermitage,
which was situated in a delightful grove nearby, resonant with the warbling of cuckoos.
It was cooled by breezes pervaded with the fragrance of *rasālaka* flowers,
resounded with the humming of bees, and echoed with the songs of Gandharvas.
Having entered that place, exceedingly beautiful with water and land, which was made radiant by the splendor of the lotus-eyed one, Pramlocā sang a most sweet song.
When the sage ceased his meditation, the Gandharvas began their singing,
and Kama, finding his opportunity, then drew his bow.
Perceiving that the sage was agitated, he aimed his arrows;
meanwhile, the sage wandered through the hermitage, listening to beautiful songs.
From afar he beheld the slender-limbed woman engaged in playing with a ball;
he approached her, and she likewise came near him.
Deluded, the sage asked her, "Who are you, and how have you come to the forest?
She replied, "I have come for the sake of serving the sage; take me [as your wife]. (11)
Then, as she was smiling, he took his pleasure with her according to his desire;
thus, sporting at will, many series of days passed.
Having immediately attained world-weariness, he spoke again and again:
"Alas! Behold the power of Māyā, by which I have been utterly deluded! (13)

Even though he knew it would result in the loss of his ascetic power, the man, being rendered utterly deluded, was overcome by the force of the gods and melted away at the mere sight of the woman. || 14 ||
"Therefore, the fault does not lie with the woman, but with the man whose senses are unsubdued.
Having reflected thus, the sage then dismissed her.
Having abandoned that place filled with obstacles and gone toward the hermitage of Bhṛgu,
he performed his ablutions in the Gaṇḍakī river in a secluded spot in the eastern direction.
He performed severe penance upon Bhṛgutuṅga for the sake of Śiva;
Śiva himself, having arrived in person, spoke to that best of sages.
By perceiving Viṣṇu and Śiva as non-different, you shall attain perfection;
this Liṅga at the site of Śiva was fashioned by him as "Samaṅga. (18)
That Samāṅgeśvara Tīrtha was indeed born on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī;
having realized this, Devadatta likewise attained supreme union (sāyujya).
O beloved, Pramlocā also abandoned the sage’s mature embryo, which was in the form of a girl, in the hermitage and departed for heaven.
That maiden, having been raised by the excellent ruru deer,
did not find anyone in her heart even though she was sought after by young men.
Meditating upon Hari-Kṛṣṇa, that young woman remained steadfast in her ascetic penance;
during the first month, she was devoted to subsisting on fruits alone.

Having reached the first day after an interval of one [day], on the second [day] after an interval of three days, on the third [day] on the fifth day, and on the fourth [day] after an interval of seven days. ||23||
In the fifth [period], it lasts for nine nights; in the sixth, for fifteen days;
in the seventh, for a month; and in the eighth, one subsists on withered leaves.
Having abandoned even those, that young woman subsisted on air alone;
when a hundred years had passed in this manner, [the Lord] appeared before her.
When I, Viṣṇu, said, "Ask for a boon that is difficult to obtain," she bowed to me upon seeing me and replied with palms joined in reverence.
"In this very form, you ought to remain in my place;
and let this sacred field (kṣetra) become known by my name in every way. (27)
"O Maddeha, let this place of pilgrimage here be known as Rurutīrtha, which is purifying;
may every person who has performed their ablutions in my tīrtha be cleansed of all sins. (28)
"Grant me boons, O Lord of the World, so that I may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having granted her these boons, he vanished on the spot and remained there.
In time, she too became like a sacred ford;
for by her restraining her senses, the Ṛṣika attained direct perception.
It is renowned as Ṛṣīkeśa, and its location is likewise such;
Ruru-kṣetra is the field of Ṛṣīkeśa, and that is called a holy ford (tīrtha). || 31 ||
Now I shall describe the sacred field known as Goniṣkramaṇa; listen to that, O beloved. In a former kalpa, there was a Prajāpati named Aurva.
Having arrived here at this place of creation, he performed severe penance;
yet he desired no fruit thereof, and thus a great length of time passed.
He too, having come from the peak of the Himālaya mountain, arrived at Gaṅgādvāra;
for at that time, Śaṅkara himself was there for the sake of obtaining lotus flowers and other offerings.
Knowing that the sage had departed, he reduced the hermitage to ashes;
then, Aurva saw that the hermitage was burnt upon his arrival.
With eyes copper-red with anger, as if burning the burner himself, he said:
"May he by whom this hermitage was set on fire likewise be tormented in every way. (36)
O Goddess of the gods, at that very moment, even Śambhu, the burner of Kama,
being tormented by a great burning sensation, spoke to the Goddess.
But seeing the ascetic power of Aurva, the gods, filled with fear, declared:
"The entire world is being consumed here, yet he does not desire even the slightest [reduction]. (38)
"What indeed is the remedy there so that it might be possible for everyone?
When I had spoken thus, his hermitage was consecrated by me with wrath. (39)
He was consumed in an instant, and we emerged from him;
tormented by this sorrow and overwhelmed by grief.
Aurva cursed us out of anger; we are tormented by it, O auspicious one.
Afflicted by that burning heat, I am unable to move.
Therefore, let us go to Nārāyaṇa for the sake of pacifying the curse.
Then, having recognized Nārāyaṇa and informed him,
they went together to Aurva and said to him, "Ward off the torment of the curse.
Aurva replied, "O Mādhava, bring the assembly of Surabhis here."
"Let them bathe Śaṅkara and the others with milk, and the curse will be pacified. In the meantime, O Lakṣmī, I brought down seventy-seven auspicious, milk-yielding cows of the Surabhi lineage.

Their bodies bathed by that [water], they attained supreme peace. Śaṅkara and the others declared this sacred field and supreme, most meritorious pilgrimage site, named Goniṣkramaṇa, to be the excellent Aurvakṣetra. || 45-46 ||
One should perform a bath there; by that, the Gāloka world is attained.
Endowed with the conch, discus, and mace, one is glorified in my own realm.
Here, at the root of the Mūlavaṭa tree, the five rivers fall down.
Having performed the bath with five streams, it bestows the fruit of the five sacrifices. || 48 ||
This sacred field, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is proclaimed to have five streams.
Now, this field of five quarters is where the five great stones (mahāśilās) exist;
because they are situated very firmly, taking recourse to the direction to my east.
There, in the center of the pool, is a stone marked with two *brahma-padas*.
Above it, the circumference of the stalk is my own *viṣṇu-pada*.
Those who bathe there go to the pure worlds beloved by the devotees of the Lord.
This is the field of the Brahma-abode; here, in the west, the stream falls.
Having bathed there, one rejoices in the world of Brahmā together with Brahmā.
Now, in the direction of the wind (the northwest), there is the certain sacred site named Koṭivaṭa.
One should perform the ritual bath there, even if it is situated within a distance of five krośas.
Having enjoyed the fruit of ten million sacrifices, one attains my world.
Now, to the northeast is the beautiful Viṣṇusaras,
a supreme holy place (sutīrtha) five krośas in extent, and the mountain is likewise as long.
O beautiful one, as many steps as he takes while circumambulating it, [so many merits shall he obtain].
For as many as a thousand years, he wanders about;
then, that meritorious soul is honored in the world of Brahmā at every step.
In that sacred field, a great marvel occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
On the twelfth day, however, the sounds of cows are heard from the path of the sky.
This is the holy site of Gosthalaka, which destroys both physical suffering and sin;
and for both the speaker and the listener of this chapter, O sinless one, it brings the same benefit. || 57-58 ||
For every syllable [of this hymn], one shall indeed dwell in my abode for a thousand years,
and likewise, there shall be the upliftment of twenty-one generations.
O highly fortunate lady, the sacred field of cows (Gavākṣetra) is a circle of five yojanas.
I indeed always abide here on the eastern side of the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, O beautiful one, having reached the Dvāpara Yuga, I abide there in that supreme sacred field named Stutasvāmin.
Śāṇḍilya, Jājali, Bhṛgu, Kapila, Sāyaṇa,
and others shall establish me, who have descended to the earth as the embodiment of Dharma.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—
they too shall indeed abide there for the welfare of the world.
By my grace, those humans shall attain the perfection that is supreme to me;
whereas those who act with envy toward my dharma and my form [shall not].
For those whose minds are afflicted by envy, this next world does not exist;
envy leads to total ruin, and envy is the destroyer of Dharma.
Engaged in many ritual acts, devoted to giving and study,
or endowed with austerity and knowledge, they are constantly intent upon virtuous deeds.
Furthermore, those consumed by stinginess do not see me anywhere at all;
therefore, no one should ever practice stinginess, for it destroys peace.
Many have met their end through the fault known as stinginess;
listen, Lakṣmī, on Mount Bhūta there was an iron image of mine. (68)
She indeed remains in the form of a boar; she is seen as indivisible, yet some perceive her as made of bell-metal, while others even perceive her as made of iron.
Others see her as a stone, and still others as a diamond-pig;
some behold that form situated upon Mount Maṇipūra.
Released from all sins, they indeed go to the supreme goal;
this very Vārāha-kṣetra assumes the form of the earth's upliftment.
Now I shall describe another sacred ford called Pañcārūma;
one who bathes there shall dwell in heaven, served by celestial nymphs.
Now, the Bhagukuṇḍa holy site is on my right side;
one who has bathed there becomes liberated and rejoices in the region of Dhruva.
Then there was the Maṇikuṇḍa holy site, an unfathomable ocean and abode of the gods,
where jewels were seen and the restless Malaya mountain stood.
Having bathed there, one becomes a king possessing jewels and is liberated;
it is my [tirtha] named Dhūtapāpa, situated three krośas away.
The sacred field at Kuṇḍa has water with the luster of gold, radiant with the brilliance of emeralds;
one who bathes there, having shaken off their sins, attains the sovereignty of Indra.
And a miracle occurs on my mountain Maṇipūra:
the stream of water does not fall as long as sin has not been shaken off. (77)
The tree there is said to be the Aśvattha; one who is stainless goes there.
And in the west is the Āmalaka tree, which brings forth all fruits.
It washes away even the sins of the most wicked through mere touch;
praised by the gods, it resides daily in the great field of Maṇipūra.
"Stutasvāmī" is the name assigned to me by the gods themselves;
through its recitation or even its hearing, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men.
Now, there is the field of Lohārgala, situated on the Himalayas;
it is excellent, fifteen yojanas in length and five yojanas in circumference.
There, in the northern direction, I dwell within a golden image;
at that time, the Dānavas were indeed causing suffering to the gods there. (82)
And the Daityas were constantly afflicting the humans there;
so, having employed my Vaiṣṇava illusion, I indeed created an inner man. ||83||
