By that alone, one shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
thereafter, one should bathe in the Saṃkarṣaṇa Tīrtha and perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
The destruction of sins such as the killing of a cow or the killing of a Brahmin shall occur;
thereafter, one should perform [the rites] at Śakratīrtha near the heap of food (annakūṭa).
It was there that the destruction of Mahendra’s sacrifice was indeed brought about by Kṛṣṇa; then Indra, out of wrath and with the desire to destroy the world, sent down a torrential rain.
And Kṛṣṇa held up the mountain for the protection of the cows and others;
there, the gods, goddesses, cows, and great sages were fed.
The cowherds, cowherdesses, moths and other insects, as well as beasts and birds—[all these were there];
and thus that mountain became renowned by the name Annakūṭa.
In that place, by the gift of food, the offering of water, and likewise by libations,
a pilgrim shall obtain the fruit of a hundred sacrifices.
Then, one should indeed bathe in the Kadamba-kuṇḍa, which bestows the world of Brahmā.
Thereafter, one should go to Devagiri, bathe, and behold it with devotion. One should gaze upon Mahādeva and offer libations to the ancestors in the kuṇḍa.
Having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and enjoyed liberation in heaven, he shall go to Hari.
From the northern bank of the Gaṅgā as far as the land of Kṛṣṇa, the God of gods who bears the discus, a battle took place with the demon Ariṣṭa. || 1.348.20–21 ||
Having slain the demon Vṛṣāsura, Hari bathed there again and again;
then, having come together with Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa was bathed by her. That auspicious place, which removes all sins, became famous by the name Rādhākuṇḍa.
By bathing there, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha and Rājasūya sacrifices. ||23||
The sin of killing a Brahmin, even one as great as Gonara, is destroyed by bathing there;
having bowed to the tīrtha named Mokṣarāja, one should proceed to Indradhvaja.
Having bathed at the Indradhvajocchraya tīrtha and performed obeisance, one should return;
then one should go to the pool named Pañcatīrtha and complete the pilgrimage.
Having offered the fruit of the pilgrimage to Śrī Hari, one should keep a vigil at night.
Then, on the morning of the twelfth day, it should be performed at Govardhana.
Having bathed, offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and bowed down, one should depart while worshipping Hari;
he who performs the pilgrimage in this manner delivers even his ancestors.
Having completely shaken off all evils, one attains the Supreme Brahman;
even during the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the circumambulation of a heap of food.
Whoever hears this, reads it, or likewise causes it to be read, shall obtain the fruit of a pilgrimage, the merit of a ritual bath, and the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Listen, Lakṣmī: there was indeed a Vaiśya named Suśīla in the southern region.
He was a resident of the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, possessed of many sons, and endowed with great prosperity.
He is merely a glutton, intent on the maintenance of his family;
he performs neither ritual bathing, nor charity, nor recitation, nor fire-offerings, nor worship of the gods. (31)
He never once had the company of the virtuous; he neither listened to sacred discourses nor performed any religious duties. (3.2)
He had no devotion toward the gods or the brahmins;
for one immersed in sin, his intellect does not turn toward the giving of dharma. (33)
Having reviled and utterly insulted the giver of his wisdom, he met his death in the course of time while behaving in such a manner. (34)
Having attained the state of a preta upon a dry, waterless place, he remains there in misery, wandering through a desert region overcome by hunger. ||35||
In a thicket in the desert lived a fierce and terrifying preta,
with long fangs, a protruding jaw, a cat-like face, and a massive belly.
Then, along that very path, a certain merchant engaged in buying and selling came out; dancing, he spoke to him at that time. (37)
"I have obtained my prey; where do you wish to go now?
I shall devour your flesh and drink your blood. (38)
Having heard the words of the preta, the merchant summoned his courage and said to him: "I am going out of a desire for wealth in order to support my family. (39)
"My aged father is at home, as is my mother and my devoted wife;
O Rākṣasa, when I am devoured, my family will perish."
"Furthermore, being joined with sin, you shall not be released from the state of a preta.
Having heard this, that preta asked him, "From where have you come? (41)
The merchant said: "I have come from Mathurā to your forest;
here is Govardhana, the best of mountains, and the great river Yamunā. (42)
Between those two, I have lived in Mathurā for many generations;
being poor, I go to foreign lands for the sake of acquiring wealth. (43)
The preta said: "Listen, O wretched one; if you have any business, do it for me.
On this condition I shall release you: go toward Mathurā. (44)
Having performed your bath according to the rules at the confluence of the four oceans, offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) with great care in my name. (45)
"And grant me the fruit of this bath: liberation shall be mine.
O merchant, you possess wealth in your house; there is no poverty for you. (46)
"A load of gold, gathered and kept in a pit, remains in your house. Return home well-contented, O merchant, and grant me my release. (47)
The merchant asked, "How do you know that the well is a means of deliverance?
The Rākṣasa replied, "In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, there is the great sage Agastya. (48)
He recited the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā;
at evening time, I went to the temple of Viṣṇu to hear the story. (49)
Then I heard that there is a well that grants liberation to the departed spirits (pretas),
where indeed the four oceans are said to be gathered together.
Thus was the story heard there by many people, and they gave much alms to the reciter; out of deceit, I too gave a copper coin. (51)
Then, when my time had come, my death occurred by the decree of King Yama and through the power of my past karma. (52)
Having attained the state of a preta, being devoid of both giving and burnt offerings, he did not then visit sacred fords, nor were his ancestors ever satiated with libations. (53)
I did not perform any religious duty, and thus I would have attained the state of a preta;
however, by the power of the *ḍhabbuka* and by hearing this story, [I have been saved]. (54)
"Knowledge still exists; go and effect my liberation.
The merchant named Vibhu said, "Tell me, how do you live? (55)
The Rakṣasa said: "I planted this Pippala tree in the courtyard of my own house and nurtured it with water for the sake of its shade. (56)
In that year, fruits indeed appear twice;
by their merit, living beings live, as do I. (57)
"My satisfaction is constant, just like that produced by water and food";
having heard this and comforted the preta, the merchant went to Mathurā. (58)
Having indeed removed the funeral materials from the ground, he performed the rites for the deceased;
he offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into a well containing the waters of the four oceans.
Having arrived there, that preta ate the alms-food and departed for heaven;
likewise, the merchant, having obtained wealth, rejoiced in his own home.
Whether at a sacred ford, in a house, in a forest, in a temple, or at a crossroads—
wherever they may die, those who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) attain liberation.
For one who has committed sins elsewhere, liberation at a sacred ford is indeed certain;
even for one who has committed sins in Mathurā, there is destruction [of those sins] at Kūpārṇava.
Sin committed in Mathurā perishes right there;
this city is immensely meritorious, wherein no sin exists. (63)
An ungrateful person, a drinker of liquor, a thief, and likewise one who has broken his vows—
upon reaching Mathurā and the Yamunā, such a person is liberated from all sins.
If someone were to stand on one foot for a thousand yugas anywhere,
the merit of a resident of Mathurā would be even greater than that.
All the inhabitants of Mathurā are indeed divine gods in human form;
even they, who are devoted to bathing at sacred fords, are truly gods in human bodies.
Whatever fruit is obtained elsewhere by worshipping a thousand Brahmins, that same fruit shall be obtained here by worshipping a single person from Mathurā. 67.
Indeed, a person from Mathurā is like the Ṛgveda itself, whereas another may possess all four Vedas;
yet, nowhere can one equal to a person from Mathurā be found even through the four Vedas.
All holy fords, sacred shrines, and indeed all auspicious things exist wherever that twice-born man of Mathurā resides.
All the liberations for embodied beings that have occurred and will occur in the future exist there, where indeed the Mathurā Tīrtha and the waters of the Yamunā are found.
The attendants residing in Mathurā are indeed four-armed;
by reading or hearing this, one shall attain the state of having four arms.
Listen further, I shall proclaim another greatness arising from Asikuṇḍa.
In ancient times, there was a king named Vimati who resided in Puṇyanagara.
While Vimati was in his house, Nārada arrived there at some point;
Vimati then offered him water for his feet as well as the respectful arghya offering.
Having accepted it, Nārada, the upholder of dharma, then said:
"O lord of kings, you are capable of discharging your debt to your father. (74)
My friend was always my father’s giver of honor;
his name was Sumati, and it was immediately after his death that [this occurred]. (75)
"You have performed great acts of giving and accumulated abundant merit;
yet, since you have not undertaken a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), you cannot thereby discharge your debt to your father. (76)
"Having discharged his debt to his father, this son shall become a partaker of dharma.
Having spoken thus, Nārada indeed departed for the Badarī forest.
The king also then desired to go on a pilgrimage for the sake of his father; the thought arose in him: "Let us go to the city of Mathurā. (78)
Having thus resolved, that king came to the city of Mathurā, thinking, "I shall indeed dwell in Mathurā for the four months of the rainy season. (79)
"All sacred fords dwell here during the Cāturmāsya," having reflected thus, that king indeed made his residence there for a long time.
Accompanied by a thousand men and attended by male and female servants,
his attendants perform the removal of waste at all sacred bathing places.
Male and female slaves of the Śūdra caste engage in sexual intercourse even on days of religious observance; likewise, they bathe without restraint in the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites.
They forcibly seize the household utensils and other belongings of brahmins and others;
they revile virtuous men and brahmins, and indeed they utter threats and abuse. (83)
People perform acts such as voiding urine upon the ground of the gods without restraint;
they eat those sinful fish, yet the king inflicts no punishment upon them. (84)
That sin fell upon the very head of King Duṣṭatāra as well.
When the month had passed, the holy fords spoke to one another out of distress: (85)
"The king must be expelled from this place for the sake of our own well-being; we ourselves are not able to engage in battle with one who is so obstinate. (86)
"Let us go to Kalpagrāma and report our distress to the Supreme Lord Varāha; he will surely do what is appropriate. (87)
Having arrived at Kalpagrāma, they earnestly prayed with devotion:
"Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O Lord of the Earth! Victory to you, O Lord of Kings! (88)
"O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you for the sake of destroying the hardships of the heretics.
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord Varāha spoke respectfully to the holy places: 89.
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever dwells in your minds.
The holy places said, "O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, it behoves You to grant us fearlessness."
A most terrible terror was produced by that wicked-minded and great sinner;
restrain that most sinful meat-eater who is frequented by the wicked. 9.1.
Then Śrī Varāha said, "I shall slay the great enemy;
thus, by the command of the sacred ford, I have come to the city of Mathurā. (92)
The boar engaged in a fierce battle with King Svāsī;
then the boar slew the king with his sword.
Having placed the tip of his sword’s edge upon the ground,
he sat down on the surface of the earth to obtain a moment's rest.
That ground is purifying where the pool was created by the celestial sages;
it is called Asikuṇḍa, a most sanctifying holy site (tīrtha). ||95||
Indeed, bathing in the Kuṇḍa on the twelfth or fourteenth lunar day bestows liberation;
at that time, I abide here at Varāhatīrtha, granting the gift of emancipation. (96)
At that sacred ford (tīrtha), my fourfold forms are to be installed:
one known as Varāha, and the second as Nārāyaṇī. (97)
The third day belongs to Vāmana, and the fourth to Rāghava;
for these [days], there should be viewing, worship, installation, and likewise the giving of gifts. (98)
One must by all means perform [this] there; consequently, one becomes a partaker of liberation.
He who, having bathed in this pool named Kuṇva, beholds these four [deities], [attains that same state]. 99.
By him the earth, bounded by the four oceans, has been traversed;
he shall certainly partake of the fruit of the sacred fords of Mathurā.
Even one who has risen from sleep on the twelfth day, having bathed in the Asikuṇḍa, beholds those forms; such a person is fit for absorption into Brahman.
By the grace of Nārāyaṇa, there is no returning again;
indeed, by reading or hearing this, one shall attain liberation after having experienced worldly enjoyment.

Thus ends the three hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Circumambulation of Govardhana Hill, Annakūṭa, and Other Holy Sites; the Liberation of the Vaiśya Suśīla who was in the Form of a Preta; and the Destruction of Vimati by Vārāha, along with the Greatness of Vārāha-kṣetra," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of Viśrāntighaṭṭa on the Yamunā.
In Ujjayinī there lived a brāhmaṇa who had fallen from right conduct and was an atheist.
Abandoning virtuous conduct, he does not even perform ritual bathing;
he does not worship the gods, nor does he pay homage to the holy sages.
Agitated by desire, sleeping at twilight, a reviler of his ancestors,
a destroyer of ancestral rites (śrāddha), associated with sinners, and evil-minded— (3).
Constantly supporting his own family's belly by means of theft and other such acts at night,
once he was engaged in thievery at night together with other sinners.
While being watched by the king’s soldiers, fleeing with great speed along a wrong path,
he then fell into a deep blind well as he was running away.
Having died and fallen, he then attained the state of a Rākṣasa;
he lived constantly in a Jīrṇa tree situated on the path by his side.
He devours and drinks the blood of living beings, including beasts and winged creatures. Once, a great caravan arrived by that very path.
Protected by a Brahmin standing in their midst who recited mantras that destroy demons,
the caravan, being utterly exhausted, fell asleep beneath a tree near a well.
Having arrived there, the Rākṣasa said to the Brāhmaṇa: "O twice-born one, I shall give you whatever wealth resides in your mind."
"O Brahmin, this food, obtained after a long time and held in high esteem, give it to me to eat; go elsewhere and have mercy. (1.349.10)
"By which means I may devour this caravan until my hunger is satisfied.
The Brahmin said, "I am ungrateful; I shall not do so under any circumstances."
What friendship can I have with a wicked one? What gain is there from being with a Rākṣasa?
Friendship and gain from a Rākṣasa result only in the loss of life and the destruction of counsel.
My profit lies with the caravan, and not with you in any way; having set out on this journey as part of a single caravan, I will not abandon my fellow traveler.
Therefore, O Rākṣasa, depart, leaving my caravan;
you are truly unable to look upon it because of the power of my mantra.
The Rākṣasa said: "If my prey is killed, you will incur guilt;
O best of Brahmins, have mercy and let food be given to me. (15)
To the Rākṣasa who was thus seeking his purpose, the twice-born one asked:
"By what fault of action have you come to this state of being a Rākṣasa? (16)

The Rākṣasa explained that he had attained the state of a Rākṣasa due to the faults of his thievery and immoral conduct, and that the Brāhmaṇa likewise had reached this state through his own sinful deeds.
Then Kṣmādeva, who had joined the caravan, hearing this, was moved by compassion and said to the Rākṣasa: "Tell me, and I shall wipe away [the debt] for you, O twice-born one."
Whatever sins there may be, and how liberation might be attained—
even as one who has rendered you service, what dear thing may I do for you?
Having heard this, the Rākṣasa said to the Brahmin: "You have performed many pilgrimages;
indeed, you have bathed at Viśrāntitīrtha in Mathurā."
"And grant that fruit of the bath by which I may attain liberation.
Having heard this, the brahmin questioned the rākṣasa regarding his previous history.
"How do you know, O Rākṣasa, that this sacred ford is named Viśrānti?
And how did it receive such a name? Tell me everything, if you know."
The Rākṣasa said: "O best of Brahmins, formerly my residence was always in the city of Ujjayinī; indeed, I lived there in the temple of Viṣṇu. (23)
The brāhmaṇa, however, daily recounts the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā with great devotion for the sake of the people. (24)
O twice-born one, I then heard the majesty of Viśrāntitīrtha;
by the mere hearing of it, devotion took root in my heart. (25)
That name, when heard there, brings about the understanding of the meaning through rest;
Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (26)
On that bank of the Yamunā where he always took his rest, that place, being near the water, became known as Viśrānti. ||27||
Having bathed there, one enjoys heaven for ten million aeons (*koṭiyuga*), and thereafter,
having enjoyed the worlds known as Vairāja, one goes to the supreme state.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, grant me the fruit of a single bath, by which I may be liberated from this demonic state and attain the way to heaven. (29)
"May liberation also come to me; have mercy upon me!
Having heard the words of the Rākṣasa, the merchant-brahmin then spoke: [1.349.3]0.
"O Rākṣasa, the fruit of a single bath has indeed been granted to you. Having spoken thus, as he was about to give the water to the Rākṣasa—
Becoming pure, he attained a divine body and went to heaven;
there, having enjoyed supreme pleasures, O lotus-born one, he obtained liberation.
Then that brahmin indeed departed with his caravan toward his own country.
Listen, Lakṣmī, in ancient times Śambhu [performed penance] for the sake of pleasing Hari. (33)
He performed severe penance; consequently, I, being pleased at that time, approached Śaṅkara and granted him my very sight.
Being told, "Choose a boon," Hara chose a boon from him:
"If you are pleased, O Blessed One, [grant it] within the circle of the sacred field of Mathurā. (35)
"O Kṛṣṇa, let a place for me always be granted wherever it may be.
Then I said to him, "You shall become the guardian of that sacred field (kṣetrapāla). (36)
O Mahādeva, when you are seen, may the fruit of my field be realized;
O Śambhu, grant protection on all sides to my field forever. (37)
Upon entering my field, worldly existence indeed ceases;
for Mathurā, the city of Vaikuṇṭha, is dear to me. (38)
My domain in Mathurā extends for twenty yojanas;
by virtue of my yoga, the fruit of horse-sacrifices shall accrue at every step. (39)
Indeed, sixty thousand crores and six hundred crores of holy places that bestow heaven and liberation reside here.
Having heard this and obtained the boon, Śambhu remained right there;
he is the supreme Vaiṣṇava, the king of devotees, existing in the form of my Kṣetrapāla.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this supreme majesty which bestows liberation;
those who read it and those who hear it go to the highest state.
Even two hundred and twenty families are delivered when a person, upon reaching the point of death, remembers Mathurā, the sacred ford. (43)
He shall attain the supreme perfection that destroys this cycle of existence;
for among all sacred sites, the one at Mathurā is the most excellent and great. (44)
The sacred site where Kṛṣṇa played is indeed pure at every step;
the region of Mathurā, the circle of land between the southern and northern oceans, is eternally so. ||45||
Having departed from his home in silence, he should indeed continue until the time of the ritual bath;
after the worship is completed, he should speak and give milk-yielding cows as gifts.
One should give gold and wealth, feed virtuous Brahmins,
reside in Mathurā during the Cāturmāsya period, and perform the prescribed rites.
There is no return for him; he is glorified in my world. O Lakṣmī, those who die in Mathurā indeed go to my world. 48.
Furthermore, for those who die elsewhere but are cremated within the Mathurā maṇḍala, there is residence in heaven as well as in my abode, Goloka. 49.
Whatever form belongs to the people of Mathurā, that very four-armed form is mine;
O son of Vārddhi, when the people of Mathurā are satisfied, I am always satisfied.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of how the high-souled Garuḍa came to Mathurā, desiring a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
In the presence of Kṛṣṇa, Garuḍa offered praise and bowed down:
"Victory to you, O Lord of Lakṣmī, Kṛṣṇa! Victory to you, O Lord of Māṇikī! (52)
Victory to the Lord of Light! Victory to the Lord of Rādhā! Victory to the Lord of Śrī Pārvatī!
Victory, O Viṣṇu! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Ramā! (53)
Victory, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Gopīs! Victory, O Garuḍādhipati!
Victory, O Brahmā, Lord of all! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa; let there be salutation unto You! 54.
Thus praised by the high-souled Garuḍa,
O Kṛṣṇa, the Lord stood before Garuḍa, assuming a beautiful form.
The king of birds said, "Tell me quickly what you intend to do and why you have come; having heard it, I shall grant it. Then Garuḍa spoke.
Having come to Mathurā with a longing to behold you, I did not see your form, and delusion took possession of me. ||57||
In Mathurā, you remain with the people while concealing your true form;
this was not known by me, and therefore delusion has taken possession of me. (58)
"Now that I have seen your divine form, peace has come to me.
Having heard the words of Garuḍa, Mādhava laughed and said: (59)
O best of the twice-born, I exist in my true form among the people of Mathurā; those who do not behold the people of Mathurā as my very forms are indeed sinful.
"I dwell in that very place, yet I wander elsewhere at times.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa then vanished on the spot.
Garuḍa also went to Vaikuṇṭha at the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
the residents of Mathurā, indeed, having remained in Mathurā, attained divinity.
They purify everyone, just like the attendants of Kṛṣṇa;
even a worm, a moth, or one situated in the womb of an animal [is purified].
By the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they indeed became four-armed.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen to another marvel concerning Mathurā. 64.
In a former age, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Patnīvrata, a resident of Mount Raivata in Saurāṣṭra, who lived together with his family.
Having set out for the Yamunā, he reached the region of Mathurā;
there, while resting by the Yamunā, he bathed and performed a circumambulation.
Likewise, one should perform circumambulation of Mathurā, Govardhana, other forests, Vṛndāvana, and even the Tulasī grove.
Having fed many Brahmins and taken waters from sacred fords, Marudeva returned to his own country. ||68||
There, in that forest consisting mostly of śamī trees, upon a dry plateau made of horn-stone,
he beheld a caravan of more than a hundred ḍākinīs and śākinīs.
Dancing and speaking haughtily, "Eat!
Devour!", he was deformed, naked, black in color, and terrifying.
Upon seeing the multitude of magical spells (kṛtyās), he who was devoted to his vow as a husband immediately remembered Kṛṣṇa; and lo, the blazing [discus] appeared at once.
Having the forms of pretas, they burned that wheel from the outside;
they wept, they wailed, and they entreated him most intensely.
"Save us, O Brahmin! We shall not be devoured;
protect us here, for we were the one hundred and more wives of the king of the Maruts. (73)
Consuming liquor and meat, committing evil deeds, and devoid of Dharma,
the king met his death during a great pestilence and a major epidemic.
Our kingdom was seized by Tripura, and we were rendered destitute by him; when the earthquake struck and our palace collapsed, we all perished there, tormented. (75)
"O Brahmin, we have entered the wombs of *ḍākinīs*, *śākinīs*, and *bhūtas*;
O Keśava, grant us liberation through the water of a sacred ford! (76)
Having heard this, that Brahmin Kṛṣṇāṃśa, who was devoted to his wife's vow,
took water in his hand from the Yamunā and then sprinkled them with it.
Having cast off their forms as hungry ghosts, they then became divine four-armed beings in the form of Lakṣmī; having bowed down, they praised [him] with devotion.
"O Kṛṣṇa, you yourself are indeed he; you have been lifted up from the ocean of suffering.
O Kṛṣṇa, lead me to your own abode. When this was said, a celestial chariot arrived.
That brāhmaṇa, who was the very form of Kṛṣṇa, led her indeed to Goloka;
then, together with his family, he went back to his own country, Raivata.
Thus has the divine majesty of Viśrāntitīrtha and the waters of the Yamunā, which effects the liberation of the deceased, been proclaimed to you. 81.
And I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, joined with the waters of the Yamunā; wherever I was then, there was heaven, Goloka, and even liberation itself.
O Lakṣmī, for those who hear this, as well as those who recite it or cause others to hear it, there shall be heaven, and even liberation in Goloka. ||83||

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the *Māhātmya* of Mathurā-kṣetra: the liberation of a Brahmin residing in the city of Ujjayinī who, having fallen from right conduct, had become a Rākṣasa, through the fruit of bathing at Viśrānti; the protection of the sacred field performed by Śambhu; the divine vision of Garuḍa through his hymn of praise upon meeting Kṛṣṇa in His form as a resident of Mathurā; and [the account] of how Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, in the form of the Brahmin Patnīvratavipra, [acted] by sprinkling the waters of Viśrānti.
The three hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation from More Than a Hundred Ḍākinīs and Śākinīs," etc. || 349 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, listen as I recount the majesty of Gokarṇeśvara on the bank of the Yamunā in Mathurā, which bestows sons, heaven, and liberation.
There was a Brahmin named Subhadra, the son of Pāribhadra, who followed the livelihood of a Vaiśya and sustained himself through buying and selling. || 2 ||
Dwelling in the region of Saurāṣṭra on the bank of the river Śatrujit,
he practices agriculture here and also tends to cattle and other livestock.
His wife, known by the name Jīvantī, was renowned for being rich in virtuous qualities;
she was a chaste woman who acted for the pleasure of her husband, yet she had not given birth, as she was advanced in age.
She constantly felt grief upon seeing women with children;
she had gone to her father's house for a festival at the Kuṅkumavāpī pond.
Her father was a brahmin named Kratu, a great yogi;
seeing her so full of grief, he immediately asked her the cause of her sorrow.
She too spoke to her father, saying that childlessness was the cause;
and the sage, having meditated for a moment, spoke to his daughter Jīvantikā.
"Come, daughter, and report this before Kṛṣṇa;
having decided upon it, they are destroying the temple of Kṛṣṇa, who observes the vow of his wife."
Having gone and bowed to that god, they reported the matter:
"O Sage Kṛṣṇa, this unfortunate woman has no happiness in offspring. (9)
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke to her who was longing for a son:
"By the grace of Kambharā Mahālakṣmī, you shall have a noble son."
"It will surely come to pass for you; therefore, set out on a journey to Gokarṇavakeśvara on the bank of the Yamunā in Mathurā, which bestows excellent sons. (11)
O lady of virtuous vows, that delightful sacred site yields the fruit of obtaining a son;
go there quickly with your husband and propitiate it.
Propitiate him with offerings of baths, lamps, and various hymns of praise;
remain steadfast in this, O Bhava, for you shall live together with your sons.
When she had been told this, she bowed to her husband and went home;
then she reported everything that had been said by Hari.
Having heard those words, he was well-pleased and said to his beloved:
"O wife, this is my own opinion as well, regarding what has been spoken by Hari."
On the tenth day of the month of Caitra, having traveled through the sky by means of a splendid vehicle to Mathurā,
he bathed in the Yamunā at evening and bowed to Śaṅkara.
These two fell asleep on the ground right there at Gokarṇeśvara;
and having risen in the morning, they performed their ablutions and worship with devotion.
Then the blessed Lord, the lord of Uma, being pleased, said to them both:
"You two shall have a son endowed with virtues, beauty, and wealth."
Thus addressed by the Lord, the two of them performed their ablutions in the Sarasvatī,
bowed to Yamunā at the confluence, and stood for a moment before giving [the gift] to the twice-born.
Having performed the pilgrimage in the Mathurā region on the Ekādaśī day, they gave wealth, food, clothing, and other gifts along with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
By means of a beautiful aerial vehicle, the two of them returned to their own home;
while his wife was still living, the brahmin performed the rite of conception.
In the tenth month, she gave birth to a son who possessed the splendor of the moon;
at that time, she gave away a thousand cows along with gold and fine garments.
On the great festival of the birth of his son, he performed the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*), and the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) many times for all the castes.
"Let this one, given by Gokarṇeśvara, indeed be named Gokarṇa. Having been consecrated with the sixteen purificatory rites, he became a youth.
He married those four women as his wives;
yet they were all childless, for not even one among them had a son.
Therefore, that very man, accompanied by his wife, indeed undertook religious works:
the digging of ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as the construction of temples for the deities.

There, on the bank of the Śatrujit river, he established water-stations, rows of alms-houses, sacrificial feasts, and service for the gods and the distressed; and there is the auspicious Gokarṇeśvara Śaṅkara.
To the east of Gokṣurapattana, he established a shrine on the Yamunā and had a temple for Hari built with five sanctuaries.
There was a vast grove there, containing various kinds of flowers as well as various kinds of fruits, along with varieties of vegetables, leaves, and tubers. || 29 ||
He caused a wall to be built, encircled by a moat,
along with water-lifting machines at the wells by which he might irrigate the gardens.
All those excellent women gather flowers,
perform his bathing and worship, sweep the ground, and attend to the lighting of lamps.
His wives always perform [worship] in the temple of the deity, while the gardener himself daily waters the branches. (32)
The trees have come forth, abounding in beautiful blossoms and rich with fruit;
from this festival, fruits and other offerings are constantly given and enjoyed by all.
By him, Śaṅkara is always worshipped with devotion;
he performs labor and agriculture, and even causes them to be performed.
Once, having resolved in his mind to adopt the life of a merchant and having firmly fixed this intention in his heart,
he assembled a caravan and set out for the western region.
There, having purchased excellent wares from the city of Vāmanasthala, and having bought precious gems and jewel-like horses on Mount Raivata; 36.
On the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā, he established an excellent dwelling;
having deposited his goods there, he ascended the mountain.
It was an abode inhabited by many gods, frequented by siddhas and gandharvas, endowed with divine flowers and fruits, and adorned with many caves. ||38||
Then, in the middle of the earth, in a valley within a deep gorge, he hears a welcome greeting; having gone there, he sees the parrot in its cage.
He said, "O sir, come here; I shall offer you hospitality.
Here are these delicious fruits and cool, desirable waters."
"O illustrious caravan-leaders and brahmins, please accept this; may it be auspicious for you.
One who turns away from honoring a guest who has arrived here would be acting improperly. (41)
Therefore, the ancestors of that householder certainly dwell in hell;
yet, when he is honored, they are honored and rejoice in heaven for imperishable time. ||42||
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, that person gives away their own merit and takes upon themselves the other's demerit. (43)
Therefore, with every effort, he should indeed be honored by the householder—
whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time— for he is just like Kṛṣṇa himself.
Having heard such auspicious words, Gokarṇaka said:
"Who are you, O knower of the highest dharma? Are you a ṛṣi, or a god, or perhaps a guhyaka? (45)
"Or is it a Siddha, or an inhabitant of Raivata, or a Mānava? Tell me, sir, who is here, you whose gracious form possesses such superhuman speech? (46)
Thus addressed, Śuka related everything concerning his own past deeds:
"I was a disciple of Vāmadeva, named Śukodara. (47)
Having heard the teacher’s words endowed with wisdom, even in his presence I asked questions that required reasoning and analysis again and again. (48)
Although I was repeatedly forbidden by him, I did not follow his word;
then, out of extreme anger, he cursed me, saying, "Become a parrot! (49)
Having attained the state of a parrot at that very moment, I dwell here on Mount Raivata;
remembering my past lives, I perform the worship of Hari.
But here, I was captured by a house-dwelling sage named Brahmasūri;
he kept me confined in a cage, and thus I live happily at home.
Vāmadeva, entreated by me out of compassion, spoke to me who was exceedingly dejected:
"After you have died in Mathurā, you shall go to the world of Brahmā. (52)
"Therefore, I shall always say, 'Mathurā, Mathurā!
Having heard Śuka’s words, Gokarṇa spoke to the bird: (53)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place equal to Raivata Hill;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants the abode of Mokṣa-Goloka. (54)
"O bird, having abandoned this place, why did you go to the Mathurā region for the sake of liberation? If you know, tell me about it here. (55)
Having heard that, Śuka said to him: "Since my [karmic] line is such, liberation from death occurs in that very place; there is no certainty of my death here."
Therefore, O Brahmin, you must perform this very service for me:
take me to Mathurā, O merchant, if you are indeed going anywhere. (57)
While the two of them were thus conversing, Brahmasūri, carrying sacrificial fuel, arrived there from the forest; and upon seeing those guests, he too [approached].
Having performed hospitality with fruits and other offerings, he became serene and said:
"Who are you? From where have you come? Having established this conversation, tell me, what may I do for you? (59)
Thus addressed, Gokarṇa bowed to the sage and requested:
"Please grant me this parrot in its cage for the sake of a son."
"I shall go to Mathurā solely for the sake of his liberation;
indeed, by the gracious sage, Śuka was entrusted to him. (61)
Having bowed to the sage, Gokarṇa departed for the city of Gokṣura,
accompanied by all his treasures and joined by his entire caravan.
Śuka [went] to the garden of a Brahmin on the bank of the river Śatruñjitā.
Seeing her endowed with fruits, flowers, and other such things, he set his mind on staying there. ||63||
Once, while he was being protected by Gokarṇa in the enclosure and subsisting on food consisting of fruits, flowers, and the like, he said to his four wives, "O mothers! (64)
"Why are your sons not seen, and why are your daughters also not here? Those who were watering [the plants] said this to that wise parrot: 65.
"O bird, we four are barren; tell us how there might be sons for us.
The parrot said, "I shall tell you, provided that I remain here. (66)
When the year had passed in this manner,
Gokarṇa, accompanied by Śuka, went toward Kaccha once again with a desire for business, filled with joy.
The wives and female attendants also went to Kaccha along with their master;
having crossed the ocean by boat, they proceeded to Nārāyaṇasaras.
There, thousands of divine goddesses were seen in the midst of the lake, radiant with forms corresponding to their beauty, and exceedingly fragrant due to dwelling in the water.
But, withered by grief, they questioned the parrot: "From where have you come? Tell us, what business do you have here? (1.350.70)
The parrot said: "My master has arrived here for the sake of jewels;
if there is any business of yours that needs to be done, please inform me of it. (71)
Having heard that, they then spoke to Śuka, who was supremely wise: "The suffering of one who destroys disease must be fully related. (72)
There lies Kuṅkumavāpī, which bestows liberation upon men, where Aśvapaṭṭasara shines, served by the gods. (73)
The heroic lord of Gūrjara, the king named Dharmavīra, accompanied by a fourfold army, [was at] Raivata in the month of Kārtika. (74)
He set out for the purpose of a pilgrimage, including circumambulations, and traveling very slowly,
he performed a pilgrimage at the lake of Kuṅkumavāpī along the way.
He bathed, performed the rites of the śrāddha, and provided a feast for the Brahmins;
he honored Kaṃbhārā and Gopāla with gold and jewels. (76)
There was a vision of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, as well as a fire sacrifice,
in the great garden of the temple, which was exceedingly beautiful with its seven stories.
The garden groves were bright, enclosed by low walls, provided with wells and water-wheels, and beautifully scented with various kinds of flowers. ||78||
There, the trees were laden with fruit and enchanting throughout all seasons;
in their vicinity, that royal sage established his excellent dwelling.
"The entire grove with its fruit-bearing trees has been destroyed by the servants;
we are all those very trees and creepers, the deities of the gods."
Having spoken thus, they wept with great distress, uttering cries of their own suffering;
the sounds of all those women wailing were like the calls of female ospreys.
Those [women] were heard to be givers of pain, yet Śuka indeed comforted them;
he spoke to them there once more, saying, "By all means, take these jewels."
"My master will go; he will bring us back to life."
As soon as these words were spoken, they all regained their senses. ||83||
Desiring to speak with Śuka’s master and likewise to know him,
they all questioned the merchant with a sense of oneness.
"You are the giver of life to us; who are you, and from where have you come here?
Gokarṇa said to those goddesses, "O fair-eyed ladies... (85)
"How is it that those with such beautiful faces and such lovely limbs are overwhelmed by grief?
Then, the eldest sister, adorned with various flowers, spoke to him.
Abiding in the garden, nourished by food and water, pleasing and protected by our master, we are always devoted to the growth of flowers. (87)
We have been oppressed by the royal officials through such acts as cutting down and uprooting [trees].
They were deeply distressed, greatly agitated, and overwhelmed by that grief. ||88||
Deprived of fruits and flowers, with only roots and trunks remaining—having become such as these, we remain here, our consciousness lost. (89)
The divine Aśvapaṭṭasara lake is a witness there;
furthermore, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the brāhmaṇa, is also our witness.
It was a meritorious pond, filled with water and beautified by blooming lotuses;
it was frequented by swans and served as a watering place for the trees.
That lake was not destroyed by the destruction of its trees; it remains there in a state of deformity. Go there and restore our lives. (92)
Sacrificial rites (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*) are the primary means for the twice-born to achieve dharma.
Through *iṣṭa* one attains heaven, and through *pūrta* one reaches liberation. (93)
He who rescues ruined step-wells, wells, tanks, and temples of the deities enjoys the fruit of *pūrta* (meritorious works). 94.
Those worlds that are proclaimed to be attained through the gift of land and the gift of cows are all fully obtained by the planting of trees. (95)
Whoever [plants] the Pippala, the Vaṭa, the Nimba, the Tulasī, and the Udumbara, as well as the Āmalaka, the Bilva, and the Khadira—[these nine trees]. (96)
O twice-born one, he who increases ten species of flowers, two each of pomegranates and five of mangoes, or even a single tamarind tree here [attains great merit]. 97.
One who plants trees bearing flowers and fruit never goes to hell;
for trees, once grown, support their nourisher just as sons do.
Through their fuel, shade, and shelter for travelers weary on the road, and through providing nesting places for birds, trees and creepers bring happiness. (99)
Through medicinal herbs such as leaves, roots, and bark, may there be comfort for embodied beings;
through wood, houses are produced, as well as the dwellings of small creatures.
In this way, those embodied beings always serve others for their benefit;
indeed, by means of their fruits, leaves, petals, branches, trunks, and roots, they bestow life.
They bestow heaven and even liberation when employed in the worship of the gods;
therefore, accept these precious jewels of Gokarṇa from our land, which are so dear to us.
And likewise, having ascended a celestial chariot in the sky, take us along with you and go to where our pleasure garden is situated.
"By the gift of our life, may your beloved wives become mothers; having brought Śuka back, they shall possess excellent offspring. Go indeed! (104)
We, the cowherds and cowherd girls, though residing in Goloka, perform service to Kṛṣṇa here on earth, consisting of trees, creepers, and grass.
We, the maidservants and attendants, though residing in Vaikuṇṭha, shall also perform service to Nārāyaṇa while staying on earth at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Other attendants and female attendants were liberated and went to the abode of Sāketa;
in Sāketā we became trees and creepers, devoted to the worship of Śrī Rāma.
We are male and female messengers, residing on Kailāsa as well as upon the earth.
"Residing in sacred fields such as Kāśī, they take the form of creepers and trees.
Thus has our inner heart been described to you, O brāhmaṇas;
here, the maṇḍala of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is remembered as being composed of the servants and handmaidens of Kṛṣṇa. || 108–109 ||
Thus addressed, Gokarṇa took up jewels by the millions,
as well as all the goddesses and his wives, and departed, O Śuka.
He cultivated a flourishing garden with edible seeds, water, and other necessities;
indeed, through his service, the trees, the creepers, and the goddesses all became well-nourished.
In that service, much wealth such as jewels and other riches was employed;
the temple was maintained, and the trees were also well-nourished. || 112 ||
By that merit, his wives became pregnant;
and those goddesses of divine form praised him again and again. || 113 ||
Having granted the boon as desired and said, "May it be well," he vanished.
Gokarṇa remained there, performing all auspicious rites according to the prescribed rule.
And he served Śuka, his parents, and his four virtuous wives equally, according to the extent of his wealth and capacity. || 115 ||
He himself performed there a great sacrifice known as Vaiṣṇava,
and he constantly gave gifts of various kinds of food and edibles to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having renovated the dilapidated temple of Kṛṣṇa at Kuṅkumavāpī so that it became a new and excellent one, he likewise made that pond appear as if it were newly created once again.
Furthermore, having bound the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake with a dam,
he established [a shrine] on its bank under his own name, known as Gokarṇeśvara.
Having performed the rites for Mahādeva with the aid of Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas,
he went to his own residence, the city known as Gokṣura.
Whoever should hear this or likewise recite it with devotion,
and should undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords, shall become possessed of sons and wealth.

Thus, in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorification of Mathurā-kṣetra, [is described] the obtaining of a son by a Brāhmaṇa named Subhadra from Saurāṣṭra through the vision of Gokarṇeśvara and other rites in Mathurā; his name was Gokarṇa. By him, after conquering his enemies, Gokarṇeśvara was installed on the bank of the Śatrujit river. For the sake of wealth, Gokarṇa went to Vāmana-parvata and obtained a parrot on Raivatācala. Having returned home again, he went to Kaccha for the sake of wealth.

Chapter Three Hundred and Fifty: An Account of the Vision of the Forest Deities at Lake Nārāyaṇa, the Restoration of the Saffron Pond in the Garden Destroyed by the King of Gūrjara, and the Description of the Greatness of the Trees and Creepers Standing at the Holy Site as Being None Other than the Attendants of the Lord’s Abode.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; in that city of Gokṣura, Śuka spoke again and again to a brāhmaṇa for the purpose of undertaking a pilgrimage to the Yamunā.
Śuka indeed reminded Yāmī of his own death;
"Lead me to the land of Mathurā; set out on the journey with your beloved sons."
O Gokarṇa, make your birth fruitful in every way;
behold the Lord Gokarṇeśvara, who is your giver.
Having heard the words of Śuka, the brahmin Gokarṇa, together with his family,
traveled by means of an aerial vehicle to the region of Mathurā.
Having bathed at the holy ford of Viśrāntitīrtha and performed the vision of Gokarṇeśvara with devotion, he set out toward the district of Mathurā.
In Mathurā, he quickly performed a Viṣṇu-sacrifice accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees;
when the sacrifice was completed, Śuka, the son of Śukī, met his death.
Having reached an excellent celestial chariot and become a god, he went to heaven;
embracing Śuka to his heart, that merchant indeed wept aloud.
Where Śuka died, there the high-souled Gokarṇa established a beautiful and great shrine of Śiva named after Śuka.
Having installed Śukeśvara, he performed a divine sacrificial session (sattra),
providing two hundred brahmins with a meal of excellent sweet foods.
Every day at midday, they reach that famous Śuka-sattra;
there, surrounding the sacrificial session, is an excellent grove that yields fruits and flowers.
He also had a garden constructed by the people residing in Mathurā,
wherein those goddesses of divine form indeed took the nature of creepers.
Having arrived, they stayed there and were observed by Gokarṇa;
he then set up a water-wheel for them to drink from.
And Gokarṇa, having performed his bath and worship at the confluence of the Sarasvatī, remained there together with his wife, sons, and servants.
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he returned toward his home;
meanwhile, the Brahmin set his mind upon performing a pilgrimage to the Puṣkara tīrtha.
Having reached the Puṣkara forest,
he brought down the celestial chariot upon a level spot near the Puṣkara lake, amidst the clusters of trees.
While Gokarṇa sat there for a moment with his wife, son, and servants,
he beheld five most terrifying ghosts.
Seeing those beings of deformed appearance, he cast aside his fear from afar; summoning his courage, he asked, "Who are you, you of such fierce forms? (17)
The pretas said: "Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst and exceedingly miserable, we do not know even the cardinal or intermediate directions, day or night. (18)
"This one who has fallen into such suffering due to his own evil deeds is named Paryuṣita; indeed, this other one is Sūcīmukha. (1.9)
"May there be a third quickly; there is a fourth, Rodhaka, and a fifth, Lekhaka; such are we by name according to our functions. (1.351.20)
"I always eat delicious food myself, yet I give stale food to the twice-born;
by that fault, I have become known as Paryuṣita myself. (2.1)
"Many mendicants desiring food were indicated by him;
by this deed, he was born with a needle-mouth. (22)
Indeed, in the midst of giving, he quickly proceeded toward cessation;
by this deed and by this name, he became the supreme Śīghraga. (23)
Having deceived many people and then closing the door all alone, he eats out of fear of other beggars; for that reason, the other is called a "blocker" (rodhaka).
Even when requested by those worthy of receiving gifts at the proper time, he did not write upon the earth; because of that action, the scribe never gives anything away.
Behold, O Brahmin, our fate here due to this evil deed:
the scribe goes upward with pride, while the obstructer indeed goes head-first downward. (26)
Though lame, he moves swiftly; though lacking a mouth, he is like a needle;
he has large testicles and long lips, is foul-smelling, and has a protruding belly. (27)
Thus we are in great suffering, eating the food of the wicked and the fallen.
O Brahmin, that which you have heard and for which you now reproach me is certainly not worthy of being heard.
Phlegm, urine, and excrement left in the houses of children or women, or in a field—impure things thus discarded, the hungry ghosts (pretas) indeed consume them. (29)
Those offerings devoid of dedication to the gods, filled with impurities of feces and urine, and cooked in a state of impurity—these indeed the pretas consume. (1.351.30)
Indeed, those [foods] that have been thrown into a tube, those placed in broken vessels,
and those defiled by a woman in her menses and the like— these the pretas consume.
The hungry ghosts (pretas) always consume those foods that are devoid of offerings to guests, which provoke quarrels, and are likewise censured. (3.2)
The food of those who perform evil deeds, the food of those in a state of birth-impurity, and the food of those who are putrid do not affect him;
nevertheless, hunger never abandons the preta at any time.
Water touched by impurity does not reach us even in small measure;
nor would there be drinking of water anywhere except where it is guarded by the servants of Varuṇa. (34)
O twice-born one, if a man dies after eating food that has been discarded,
he is born as a preta with that very food still remaining in his belly.
Those who eat from the skull-bowls of human heads and others, having died, go to the state of a preta, eating together with animals. ||36||
One who consumes liquor and meat, who is utterly deluded by wicked latent impressions,
and who steals the property of gods, brahmins, or gurus, is born as a preta.
That sinner who abandons his mother, father, brothers, sisters, wife, or son—provided they are not at fault—will certainly become a preta. (38)
One who associates with those who perform evil deeds is born as a preta due to that sin;
this applies even to a killer of a Brahmin, an ungrateful person, a killer of a child, or a killer of a cow. (39)
One who seizes the bride-price or the wealth of a woman, one who hates his guru, and an atheist—that sinner is born as a preta, deprived of food and other necessities. (1.351.40)
Therefore, one should perform meritorious deeds and never harbor hatred;
indeed, one who acts for the benefit of others is never reborn as a preta.
By always practicing loving-kindness toward those who are happy, compassionate goodness toward those who suffer,
and sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit, one is not reborn as a preta.
He who never becomes attached to those devoid of merit, but instead maintains equanimity toward them, is never born as a preta. ||43||
He who performs vows for the gods, such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and others,
being free from passion and possessing a clear intellect, is not reborn as a preta.
He who provides food and water with faith, performs acts of dharma,
and honors virtuous people, gods, and ascetics, does not become a preta.
One who performs service for others, is intent on nourishing others, and is compassionate toward all living beings is never born as a preta anywhere. (46)
O Brahmin, he who performs the worship of the ancestors, the gods, guests, and those worthy of honor, and who brings supreme satisfaction to the Supreme Self, is never born as a preta anywhere.
One who is free from desire, anger, great greed, delusion, and thirst, and whose nature is characterized by forgiveness, generosity, and compassion, shall never be reborn as a preta. ||48||

He is always a performer of the Jayantī vow and a reciter of sacred stories; he honors cows, the earth, brahmins, virtuous women, the righteous, and holy pilgrimage sites, and he possesses excellent dharma. (49)
One who performs bathing, twilight prayers, recitation, and fire-offerings does not become a ghost;
likewise, he who serves his mother, serves his father, and serves his guru [does not become a ghost]. (1.351.50)

He who serves cows, serves his husband, and brings happiness to his wife, and who performs service for the poor, the helpless, and others, is never born as a *preta*. He who indeed employs pure food and purifying substances for his own sake [is likewise saved].
One who gathers all blessings is never born as a preta anywhere. ||52||
If you know the destiny of the high-born pretas, tell it; and if you are worthy of delivering us, grant us deliverance. (53)
Having heard these words of the preta, Gokarṇa then said to them:
"Those fools who are averse to dharma and devoid of compassion and generosity... (54)
Even those born as pretas find their destination at the confluence of the Mathurā;
having bathed in the Yamunā during the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī conjunction in the month of Bhādrapada, they attain it. (55)
Then he should perform the worship of Vāmana and likewise have the fire-oblation (havana) performed;
he should cause the gift of an umbrella, sandals, gold, food, and clothing to be given.
By that [offering], one should satisfy the ancestors; thus the deceased go to the supreme state.
Having bathed at the Mathurā-tīrtha, one should meditate on the people [there] and remember Hari. 57.
If one hears the greatness of Pretatīrtha, one shall attain the supreme goal;
ascending an excellent celestial chariot, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the month of Bhādrapada, the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight conjoined with the Śravaṇā asterism—
whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or performed as a ritual bath on that day shall become a hundred-thousandfold meritorious.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Yamunā and the Sarasvatī, having worshipped Vāmana,
and having offered a water-pot according to the prescribed rite, the state of being a ghost no longer exists.
By giving a hundred tawny cows equipped with golden ornaments and utensils on the twelfth lunar day, one shall indeed obtain that same fruit by bathing at the confluence of two rivers.
One's state as a rākṣasa is destroyed by the vow of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī;
one indeed dwells in heaven for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Then, descending from heaven to earth, he becomes a Brahmin learned in the Vedas;
a great yogi who remembers his past lives and is devoted to the path of liberation.
Through a state of being joined with meditation, by service to the Supreme Self, and by the blessing of his parents, he is liberated and goes to the state beyond rebirth. //64//
Having had a dwarf image fashioned with gold as it was obtained,
one should worship it according to the prescribed rite, together with sandals and an umbrella.
One should likewise invoke him and bathe him with the five nectars (pañcakāmṛta);
one should also consecrate him with water and provide him with garments and so forth.
One should offer ornaments, fragrant substances, excellent oils, and so forth,
as well as sandalwood, saffron, collyrium, and a sacred thread.
And likewise, one should offer incense, a lamp, and excellent food offerings (naivedya),
as well as fruit, betel leaf, water, a bilva fruit, or even the water of honor (arghya).
One should offer gifts, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the deity, present an umbrella and chowries,
as well as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), prostrations, the gift of a cow, and the offering of a water-pot.
One should offer praise before him and then dismiss the deity;
by performing it according to this rite, the liberation of the deceased will certainly occur.
But for one who performs [this rite] according to this procedure at the excellent confluence of the Yamunā with the Sarasvatī, his merit is increased by a hundredfold. (71)
One should observe the vow on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādra, in conjunction with the Śravaṇa asterism;
by that, liberation will certainly be attained, granting residence in Goloka and other realms. (72)
The pretas, having come for refuge, said to that brahmin Gokarṇa:
"O wise one, the pretas do not even have the power to perform that vow. (73)
Therefore, by bestowing merit, bring about our liberation;
having made Gokarṇa the sky, he gave the merit of his bath and prayers. (74)
He gave them the dust of his feet and likewise the water from his feet;
by that, they were all liberated and indeed released from the state of being ghosts (pretas).
Then a sound of celestial drums arose in the sky, created by the gods;
and hosts of pretas arrived from all sides to witness the scene.
Then the divine messenger spoke these words while the pretas were listening:
"From conversing with this brahmin and from partaking in the merit of his bath..."
"By obtaining the dust of his feet and by obtaining water from him, you have been entirely liberated from the state of a preta, even by merely hearing of this sacred ford."
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice visiting sacred fords (tīrthas);
one should engage in conversation with the virtuous and properly serve the righteous. (79)
Faith in sacred fords, faith in vows, and faith in sacred narratives must be cultivated in the mind by all means, for that indeed bestows liberation upon the departed spirits.
Water used for washing the feet of a person who has bathed at sacred fords (tīrtha) should also be drunk for the sake of liberation, just as it grants these [sages] their release. 8.1.
Through the power of the sacred ford, the preta-s attained an imperishable heaven at the confluence of the Sarasvatī;
indeed, they obtained this fruit by hearing [the name] Śravaṇa.
The celestial chariots of the pretas with divine bodies and those of the gods arrived;
having ascended them, they went to the highest heaven.
Lakṣmī went to the highest world without the perfection of spiritual means;
Gokarṇa, having visited the holy site of Puṣkara, came to Gokṣura. ||84||
He who recites with supreme devotion, listens while intent on devotion, causes others to hear it, or remembers this Tīrtha, goes to the highest goal. ||85||

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Gokarṇa’s Journey to Mathurā through the Words of Śuka; the Liberation of Śuka; the Installation of Śukeśvara; the Lamentation of the Five Pretas to Gokarṇa upon his Return on the Way; the Dialogue at Puṣkara Concerning the Causes of Being a Preta or Not Being a Preta; the Worship of Vāmana on the Twelfth Day of the Bright Fortnight of Bhādrapada; and the Liberation of the Pretas through the Merit of Bathing and Giving," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, specifically regarding the majesty of the sacred field of Mathurā. || 351 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā-tīrtha located in the waters of the Yamunā, where the Lord Vyāsa himself, the Blessed One who understands the nature of creation, resides. (1)
In the first Kṛta Yuga, having bathed, he would constantly teach the Vedas;
he remained there on the land of Yamunā for as long as that age lasted. || 2 ||
Hari shall bathe daily at that spot in the waters of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā;
indeed, that Kṛṣṇagaṅgā is considered to lie between Soma and Vaikuṇṭha. ||3||
In that divine hermitage, sages of celestial form,
invisible to the eye, arrive for the purpose of observing the Cāturmāsya vow.
Compassion arises for those who are indeed merciful toward others; those sages come within the range of vision of such people, and not otherwise.
At the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā-tīrtha during the Cāturmāsya, it was beheld by a Brahmin,
a worthy recipient of compassion, named Vasu, who was the sole thread of the Pāñcālya lineage.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell a story that effects the deliverance of sinners.
There was once a certain Brāhmaṇa from Pañcāla known by the name Vasu.
Greatly afflicted by famine, he went with his wife to the excellent city on the banks of the Bhadrā and took up residence there, subsisting on alms.
While he was residing there, two children were born to him—a son and a daughter.
The daughter was given in marriage to a Brahmin for the sake of increasing his wealth and grain.
Then the Brahmin, the husband of the maiden, being afflicted by disease in his youth, died,
destitute of kinsmen and likewise deprived of his family.
Having collected the bones of the maiden, he indeed came to Mathurā;
this is the account of the casting down of the bones as told in the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. 1.1.
In that region of Mathurā, on the site of the Half-Moon (Ardhacandra), a maṇḍala has been established;
any embodied being who performs it there shall indeed attain liberation, even without desire.
Then, by the hand of a Brahmin, the bones of the maiden were cast into the current of the Yamunā according to the prescribed rite; at that moment, liberation was attained for her husband.
That lovely young widow had dark, curly hair;
she was beautiful with delicate limbs, yet she was without support and deeply distressed.
Her thighs were very fleshy, resembling the trunk of a plantain tree;
her feet had well-knit toes, and her auspicious nails were bright and copper-colored. (15)
Her navel was deep and spiraled to the right, adorned with the three folds;
she had a slender waist and symmetrical hips, and her breasts were full and elevated. || 16 ||
She has a neck like a conch shell, a well-covered mouth, beautiful teeth, and lovely lips and jaws;
she has beautiful ears, beautiful eyes, beautiful eyebrows, perfect proportions, and speaks with grace.
With beautiful hips and a slender waist, with a moon-like face and lotus eyes,
Tilottamā was perfect in every single form.
Named Tilottamā, golden-hued, young, and beautiful—
such was she, devoted to bathing at various sacred fords (tīrtha).
Whomever that woman of beautiful limbs looked upon, and whoever looked back at her,
each one became for a moment as if transfixed in a painting, deprived of his senses.
In that manner, he chose his own residence in Mathurā.
At that very moment, the king who was the sovereign of the Kānyakubja region—
In Mathurā, at Devamārteśvara, he established a perpetual feast of food;
there indeed were truthful Brahmins and virtuous Brahmin women as well.
A hundred virtuous mendicants, poor and helpless, eat there;
yet this excellent woman, Tilottamā, who is of noble character, eats there as well. (23)
At the time of his meal, music is performed beautifully, with instrumental music and songs just like those in the palace of Śakra. (24)
But she was enticed by the dancers, singers, female messengers, and courtesans belonging to that king.
Devoted to singing, dancing, and other such arts,
that virtuous woman, though surrounded by unchaste women, attained their way of life within just a few days.
Having come into the presence of the king, she became possessed by the enjoyment of his pleasures;
as a young woman, she desired him ever anew due to the burning of her passion. (27)
Thus she became one who followed the path of transgression regarding sensual pleasures.
Now, her brother was a Pāñcāla, born of a Brāhmaṇa father. (28)
Having become destitute at home and having reflected upon his livelihood,
he arrived in Mathurā when the time had come, finding himself without any support.
At that time, he became a servant to a certain eminent merchant;
at the end of the year, through his business acumen, he too obtained profits from trade. (1.352.30)
Indeed, through the conjunction of fortune, Vidhura became wealthy;
he would always go to the Yamunā for the purpose of bathing, where that river flows.
He constantly beheld her of beautiful limbs, and upon seeing her, he fell under the sway of delusion;
having bathed there in that best of holy places, he was adorned with garments and ornaments.
Having beheld the gods and others, and having worshipped Garteśvara,
he took the path of Tilottamā and proceeded slowly thereafter.
Where that palace was, there he beheld the foster-sister;
and by her, the youth was invited into the house as one who was charming.
And with a delighted mind, he went into the interior of the dwelling of that young woman, preceded by great respect for her nurse.
Deluded, he gave her garments of fine texture, golden bracelets, necklaces made of jewels, and wealth. (36)
And he gave her the essence of agallochum along with camphor and sandalwood;
she dwelt day after day in that excellent house of his.
When half a watch of the day has passed, he then goes to his own camp,
having always bathed in the nearby holy ford born from the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā.
Thus, constantly attached to that, he performs his own livelihood;
and as he goes, he is always observed by the sages who are well-disposed toward him. (39)
Then one day, as he was going forth to bathe, that brahmin was seen by the divine Sumantu, who remained at his own hermitage, covered with worms and insects.
Worms are seen falling in great numbers from the pores of his skin;
indeed, they continue to fall for as long as he performs the bath.
When the bath was performed, they were no longer seen, and he was born with a beautiful form;
thus was this miracle witnessed by Sumantu for many days.
Sumantu called out to him and asked his name and occupation;
then the Pāñcāla said to him, "I am born in the land of Pañcāla. (43)
"Having resorted to trade, I, a brahmin, now dwell here alone;
having spent the night in this camp protected by Tilottamā and the asuras. (44)
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped the Lord of Trigarta every day,
I carry out my business during the day and reside in the camp at night.
Then Sumantu said: "Listen, O Brahmin, to the truth as it is;
I constantly behold a wonder issuing forth from this body of yours. (46)
"When you have not bathed, it is filled with worms; when you have bathed, it possesses stainless luster.
There must be some great sin of yours arising from what is concealed. (47)
By bathing in this [place] through the power of the sacred ford (tīrtha), one goes far away;
indeed, through contact with the Lord of Trigarta, the body is seen to be purified.
"Having investigated, tell us indeed what hidden sin you have [committed].
Having heard this from the sage Sumantu, who knows the three periods of time, [he spoke]. (49)
"I shall take pleasure with women in my own camp," he announced;
having gone there, he then questioned her in private from the very beginning.
Who are you? Whose daughter are you? And from what country have you come here?
For I shall surely give up my dear life if you do not speak the truth.
Perceiving his persistence, she spoke her own words with difficulty:
"In the land of Pañcāla, in the excellent city of Varapattana, there is a Brāhmaṇa named Pañcāla. (52)
There lived one named Vasunāmaka; I am his daughter, Tilottamā.
I was married, but my husband perished, and you have taken his bones to Mathurā.
Requested by the King of Kānyakubja, she came through the power of passion; having entered into the practice of sexual union, she lived according to the ways of desire.
My brother, however, is a Panchala living in his father’s house;
for there, on the bank of the Bhadrā river, my own home once stood.
"I dwell here as one who is protectorless, resorting to the conduct of an unchaste woman.
Tell me your own story, if you consider me a worthy recipient. (56)
Having heard this, that Pāñcālya then became tearful-eyed;
Tilottamā questioned him regarding his family, whose consciousness had been restored.
Then he related his own story, including his lineage and name; indeed, he became extremely despondent on account of having approached one who was forbidden.
The twice-born man, filled with despondency, set his mind upon performing a penance;
he considered [approaching] his mother, his teacher’s wife, his sister, his daughter, and his daughter-in-law. (59)
Having gone there, she should enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed.
For the princess of Pañcāla, having realized that her brother was of the nature of her husband, [she entered the flames].
He bestowed all his jewels, garments, wealth, and so forth upon the twice-born;
having given the lord of Kāliñjara and Trigarta ornaments, wealth, and the like, [he departed].
Having constructed a funeral pyre according to the prescribed rites at the Kṛṣṇagaṅgodbhava Tīrtha,
she kindled the fire for her own purification.
The King of Pañcāla also, having given his own wealth as a gift with nothing remaining,
duly set aside a portion for the sake of the funeral rites.
Having bathed, and having likewise bowed to the gods, the brahmins, and the sage Sumantu,
he approached him and spoke of the sin incurred by coming to one who should not be approached.
"Indeed, for the sake of purifying that sin, I shall abandon my body.
Having said this, he prepared a funeral pyre and set it ablaze, drenched with ghee.
Just as he was about to enter it, an incorporeal voice spoke;
at that very moment, his sister too was intent upon entering.
"Do not commit such a rash act, for you two are indeed free from sin;
wherever Kṛṣṇa moves, there sport arises according to one's pleasure. (67)
That place is truly divine, where the footprints marked with wheels are found;
it is the very form of Brahman, the abode of light, wherein the destruction of sin occurs.
For a sin committed elsewhere is destroyed upon reaching a sacred ford (tīrtha);
however, a sin committed at a sacred ford becomes as indelible as adamantine cement.
But the destruction of both [sins] occurs at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
at the junction of the Gomatī and the ocean, and at the five sacred sites (pañcatīrthaka) of the Yamunā.
Whatever fruit is considered to arise from bathing at all the sacred fords on earth is not equal even to that obtained by bathing at the five sacred fords of the Yamunā. ||71||
For on the eleventh day one should rest; likewise, on the twelfth at Saukara;
on the thirteenth at Naimiṣa; and on the fourteenth at Prayāga. ||72||
By bathing at Puṣkara on the full moon day, by observing vows on the Kārttikī day,
and by bathing at every sacred ford (tīrtha), a person is liberated from all sins.
In Mathurā, at Sarvatīrtha, Viśrānti, Pañcatīrthaka, Asikuṇḍa, Sarasvatīyoga, and likewise at Garteshvara; ||74||
Indeed, by bathing even once in the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, ten times the merit arising from [ordinary] bathing is produced; of this there is no doubt. (75)
Whether committed knowingly or unknowingly,
even a misdeed as formidable as a thunderbolt perishes upon touching the waters of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā.
For Mathurā is indeed the form of Kṛṣṇa; likewise, its river consists of Kṛṣṇa.
Men and women there are the very form of Kṛṣṇa; no sin exists therein.
In one part of whose ear there is indeed only a mere trace of space, and into the corners of whose eyes light is likewise dissolved; ||78||
In whose breath the wind is dissolved, in whose sweat the water is absorbed,
and in whose belly the subtle earth remains forever established.
In whose womb all the oceans are always dissolved,
and from whose body-hair the cosmic eggs constantly come into being.
Since Kṛṣṇa, by whose will the incarnations such as the Boar and others come into being, is present here, not even a trace of sin exists. (81)
Where the Lord Varāha, the protector of the earth, resides, the destruction of great sins occurs there through the sight of him. 82.
O best of Brahmins, at that very moment [the result is attained]; there is no need for deliberation here.
By bathing in the waters of the dark Gaṅgā on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, [one attains this]. ||83||
A human being is indeed purified from sins by giving lamps at Sūkara for three nights;
even Mahāvajrā is liberated from great sins at Tilottama. (84)
Having bathed on the twelfth day at Kāliñjara and having fully worshipped the deity, one becomes divine and four-armed, and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. ||85||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Devavāṇī and Tilottamā were enlightened by Pāñcāla; they both then went to the hermitage of Divyasuman.
Falling at his feet, they said to him: "O Brahmin, you are our father and our teacher;
tell us with your divine vision what we should do here."
The sage said: "The voice from the sky was true and never false;
I have personally witnessed the sin upon your bodies. (88)
Since there is no sin incurred either before or after bathing, always perform your ablutions at the five holy sites (pañcatīrtha) in Trigarteshvara. 89.
"Stay constantly in my hermitage and perform your recitations;
remain free from sin for as long as you live."
And by my blessing, both your brother and sister shall become free from sin; you two shall go to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the great sages such as Suyajvan and others dwell in that hermitage with divine bodies; therefore, it is remembered as the most excellent of sacred fords (tīrtha). 92.
Having attained divine bodies, both that brother and sister were born there in the hermitage as sages, granting liberation even by their mere sight. (93)
Then, having ascended the celestial chariot, those two went together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa to the eternal abode of Goloka, belonging to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 94.
Such is the power of the sacred ford at Mathurā in the waters of the Yamunā,
as well as that of the site of the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā and of Kāliñjara.
O Mahālakṣmī, what need is there to speak of even a pig-tirtha?
That sin which is not of a sinful nature is that which has been offered to Kṛṣṇa. (96)
Even a non-virtuous act may take on the form of virtue if it is offered to Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, one should perform some kind of meritorious great gift, whatever it may be. 97.
That which is faultless or even faulty must be given by me to Kṛṣṇa;
for desire, anger, great greed, pride, and the relish of taste have deluded me.
All these divine [narratives] dedicated to Kṛṣṇa indeed lead to steadfastness;
O Mahālakṣmī, he who hears them with faith certainly recites them. (99)
It removes all the evil committed during seven lifetimes;
indeed, reciting this once in the morning during the Cāturmāsya period [achieves this].
People shall obtain the fruit of giving a hundred cows;
indeed, there is not even a trace of sin for him, and immortality is firmly established for him.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Sinlessness," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes the majesty of the Mathurā Tīrtha, wherein the sin arising from the illicit union of a Brāhmaṇa from Pāñcāla residing in Varapattana in Saurāṣṭra with his sister named Tilottamā—who were unaware of each other’s presence in Mathurā—is shown to be non-existent through the power of the five holy sites (pañcatīrtha) and the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā Tīrtha, as revealed by a celestial voice and the sage Sumantu.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the conduct of women, which is always fickle;
having seen a handsome son, or a father, or another person.
For a moment, that passionate woman may come under the sway of her own volition;
for the mind is likewise fickle, as is the experience of passion born of the *rajas* quality. (2)
He will indeed make him dependent on others, just as he did with Sāmba;
listen, for Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s son shall be named Sāmba. (3)
There, through delusion regarding the Mothers, he shall become a vessel for a curse;
at that time, the disease of leprosy shall afflict the body of Sāmba.
Having arrived at Mathurā, he will likewise perform the worship of Āditya,
establish [the deity], and bathe in the waters of the Yamunā.
By that, his leprosy will be destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Such is the Māthura Tīrtha, which destroys diseases.
Listen in detail, O Lakṣmī; I shall relate that which will happen as he dwells in Dvārakā together with his wife, sons, and daughters.
The sage Nārada arrived there at Kṛṣṇa’s abode;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa joyfully offered him a welcome as was appropriate.
Then, in private, Nārada made this representation to Hari:
"O Kṛṣṇa, desiring to say something, listen; I have heard it in heaven. (9)
The son of Kṛṣṇa named Sāmba was a youth of extraordinary beauty, desirable to women; indeed, there was no other so handsome as him.
Even the wives of Kṛṣṇa longed for him upon seeing him,
as did those who belong to the divine species, numbering sixteen thousand.
"Upon seeing Samba, the minds of all women indeed become agitated.
How is it that this is sung by the deities even in the worlds of heaven and elsewhere? (12)
"O Great Lord, heaven indeed is residence in glory, while hell is its opposite;
I have come here for the sake of your pleasure to speak.
As long as one's merit is heard of, so long is that person said to exist."
For one who hears that which is not meritorious, hell is indeed proclaimed as the destination.
Therefore, whether it be true or false, I shall indeed characterize that;
so, summon Sāmba as well as the host of goddesses to the assembly.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa likewise summoned all the goddesses;
having seated Sāmba and summoned him as well, he placed him by his own side.
Upon seeing the exceedingly beautiful form of Sāmba there, all the excellent women were agitated, even as Kṛṣṇa himself looked on.
Having paid homage to Nārada, they departed for their respective abodes;
Kṛṣṇa remained there with Sāmba, his face cast down in shame.
There is no moment of privacy, nor is there secrecy; there is no deliberation regarding what ought not to be done.
Upon seeing a handsome man, women always lose their self-control. (19)
This is the very nature of women; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as a chariot cannot move with only a single wheel, [so it is with a man without his wife]. (1.353.20)
Without a man, women—who are by nature fickle—let flow their human fluids;
they consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose merely by the casting of a man's glance. (21)
Upon seeing Pradyumna, they all experienced intense shame;
but upon seeing Samba, they were all tormented by the god of love. ||22||
