This manifestation of the excitant is Śambhu, who deludes even your wife;
for that report which has arisen in Satyaloka concerning you is difficult to overcome. (23)
"I have heard this repeatedly from the world and from the brahmin-sages;
O Keśava, you ought to wipe away that infamy by abandoning Sāmba."
Having spoken thus, Nārada then observed a vow of silence;
thereupon Hari cursed Sāmba, saying, "O son, become deformed!
Immediately, Sāmba became afflicted with leprosy and was indeed disfigured.
Then, seeing Samba thus filled with grief, Narada said:
"O Samba, Samba, son of Krishna, listen, O son of Jambavati!
O sinless one, you must always pay homage to the rising sun. (26-27)
"O dear son, the Sun, being pleased, will destroy your leprosy.
Having gone to Mathurā, you shall obtain the fruit of the Six Suns (Ṣaṭsūrya).
O sinless one, worship the Sun in the morning at the Ṣaṭsūrya Tīrtha."
Likewise at midday and in the evening; obtain the fruit immediately. || 29 ||
Having bathed at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇa and Gaṅgā and having diligently worshipped the Sun,
one is liberated from all sins and freed from leprosy and other ailments.
Thus addressed, O Mahālakṣmī, Sāmba departed by the command of Kṛṣṇa;
he beheld Mathurā, the remover of faults and the bestower of liberation. Restrained in his ritual bathing and libations, he worshipped the six suns.

Sāmba constantly worshipped the sun as it rose toward the Brahma-world, as it moved upward, as it reached the meridian, as it inclined, and as it had set. Satisfied, the Sun appeared before Sāmba in a very short time.
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; your leprosy and other ailments have departed.
Having said this, Sāmba touched every limb of Sāmba, and at that very moment—
Free from leprosy, he shone with a luster equal to the sun;
he appeared like a second sun existing together with Sāmba.
In the Brahma [direction], Sāmba established the sun known as Virāj;
in the south, he established the sun called Udaya. (36)
At the end of the Ūrdhvāyaṇa, he installed Kālapriyaravi on the Cakra;
at the western Cakra of Vaikuṇṭha, he installed Mādhyandinīyaka Ravi.
Descending [to earth], he established Sāmbārka in Mathurā;
and as the sun was setting, he established Kṛṣṇagaṅga on the south of the Arka mountain.
Established in Sāmbapura, Sāmba performed the rites of worship and other ceremonies there;
however, that Sāmbapura became known as Kuleśvara in Mathurā.
Those people who shall perform the chariot procession of Sāmbasūrya toward the divine city of Sāmbapura on the seventh day of the month of Māgha—
Having bathed in the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā and beheld the six solar discs, people shall go to that peaceful state which pierces the solar orb. || 41 ||
"Released from evil diseases and other afflictions, they shall go to the supreme state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you that which destroys mental sins and the like. (42)
The sin of approaching those who should not be approached, as well as the sin of approaching [prohibited women], quickly sets ablaze the sixfold solar pilgrimage site. 43.
But whatever mental wickedness one shakes off through desire, Hari himself quickly removes even all those offenses in Mathurā. (44)
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa, who is honored by the multitude of gopīs, did not take account [of Sāmba];
Sāmba became cleansed of sin and vanished right there.
Always remaining upon the sun-chariot, he would inquire about the future;
having made everything new, the son of Kṛṣṇa understood it all. ||46||
Having established Sāmbapura in Mathurā, he departed for his own home;
by reciting or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of worshipping the six Ādityas.
At the end of life, he attains the world of the Sun and the abode of Kṛṣṇa;
listen, O Lakṣmī, my dear, even to the offenses committed by devotees. 48.
A man who is entirely unknown and pure may, due to the disparity of place and time, become guilty even though he is without fault. (49)
Indeed, transgressions occur through action, mind, and speech;
namely, the failure to bathe, violence, and sexual intercourse.
The discharge of feces and urine, as well as the birth of a child and so forth, and touching a corpse and the like, are indeed offenses during the worship of the deity. (51)
Likewise, stretching out one's feet in the presence of the temple or the image, turning one's back [to the deity], urinating, and eating as one pleases; || 52 ||

Eating impure and unclean food, worshipping with prohibited flowers, and failing to remove the floral remains (nirmālya) when the worship has concluded and darkness has fallen—[these are the faults]. (53)
Entering a temple while wearing shoes, eating liquor or meat, and waking a deity in the dark. ||54||
Likewise, failing to offer salutation, vulgar speech, caviling, smoking, spitting, and so forth, are transgressions of ritual action. (55)

Furthermore, there is non-meditation, non-remembrance, and non-retention of the glorious Hari, as well as the formation of thoughts regarding others and the contemplation of sense objects and the like. (56)
Attachment, aversion, as well as craving, latent impressions, and censuring others;
fallacious reasoning, doubt regarding causes, delusion, and likewise error. (57)
Laziness, lack of inquiry, pride, conceit, desire, anger, greed, intoxication, and envy as well; ||58||
For envy, malicious intent, harmful deliberation, and the like are mental offenses;
likewise are [offenses against] mother, father, friends, companions, teachers, the twice-born, deities, and so forth. (59)
Satīs, virtuous women, beloved wives, children, young and old cows, and so forth; grass, insects, sentient beings, and all others—within them all dwells Nārāyaṇa. (1.353.60)
Those who have taken refuge with one's dependents must never be offended;
this includes idle chatter, false news, and even pointless speech. (61)
Lack of devotion, giving way to faults, the employment of wicked words, quarreling, reviling, clamor, and scolding; ||62||
Excessive noise, shouting, and even the uttering of insults;
the proclamation of vulgar speech, as well as the slapping of thighs and so forth—[these are the faults]. (63)
O you who have committed offenses, this first speech of Anargalaprahāya has been made for you;
having reflected upon it, you must not act [further], for it will yield results undesirable to you. 64.
One should never commit offenses against deities, sacred fords, gurus, brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, or devoted wives—all of whom are saviors. (65)
A man who has committed an offense does not perceive Viṣṇu at all;
he should never perform worship characterized by demonic or tamasic qualities.
O Dear One, worship that involves the offering of meat and liquor is called demonic;
that worship which is joined with acts such as violence is considered to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasī).
Adultery, the seizing of another's property, the harming of others, and actions that cause the destruction of others—such deeds are proclaimed as Rākṣasa rites. (68)

The purification of those who have committed offenses through their actions occurs by means of bathing and other rites, as well as by bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). ||69||
By means of fasting, by sacrifice, by the long-duration rite, by the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and likewise by the Brahmakūrca vow; ||1.353.70||

Purification for those who have committed offenses with the mind is sought through service to the gods and service to the virtuous; purification for those who have committed mental transgressions occurs through meditation and other such means. (71)

Through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, through the restraint of the senses, through knowledge, through the abandonment of defects, and through austerity by virtue of its meritorious nature. ||72||

Through hearing and reflecting upon this discourse, and by reaching a definitive conclusion through inquiry into the Self, one attains the discrimination between consciousness and the unconscious. ||73||
Purification of the mind is desired through the realization of the nature of the self and primordial matter;
however, purification for those who have committed offenses by speech shall be achieved through recitation and other such means. (74)
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Hare, Mādhava, Keśava;
O Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Ramā, Lord of Śrī, Lord of Pārvatī! ||75||
O Lord of the Gopīs, O Lord of Māṇikī, O Lord of Prabhā; O Lord of the virtuous, O Lord of the Imperishable, O Lord of the Liberated, O Supreme Person! 76.
"O Lord of Goloka and other realms, O Supreme Brahman, O Śrī Puruṣottama"—by chanting these names in this manner, as well as by chanting the syllable Om and so forth, [one attains the goal]. (77)
Through the requesting of forgiveness, as well as through discourse and recitation, by performing the glorification of Kṛṣṇa, and by wearing a garland of Kṛṣṇa; ||78||
Purity of speech is desired through being established in the vow of truth;
however, a person who recites the hymn of Viṣṇu is liberated from transgressions. (79)
One is indeed purified by bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) even after a year;
likewise in Kāśī, Mathurā, Dvārakā, and Puṣkara,
as well as in Badarī, the city of Jagannātha, and the city of Sāketa.
At Haridvāra, at the Gaṇḍakī, at the Godāvarī, and at Janārdana;
at the Kāverī, at Setubandha, at Padmāvatī, and at Raivata; in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā, at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, and at Mānasa.
At Nārāyaṇa, Indradyumna, Kāverī, Padmanābha,
Kāñcī, and on the Narmadā, during the avabhṛtha bath and the festival of the crown—
by bathing, drinking [the water], as well as by meditating, chanting, and wearing [the sacred ash or marks]— [one attains the goal].
Through hearing, reflecting, and also through seeing [the Lord], there is the destruction of sin.
Having wandered to all the sacred fords (tīrthas), one arrives at the district of Mathurā;
for ultimate rest occurs only at Viśrāntighaṭṭaka. ||84-85||
In Mathurā, the fruit is produced multiplied by a parārdha;
for those seeking a goal, Mathurā is the supreme goal.
That which is the goal of one disciplined in yoga and likewise of one possessing the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, [is attained there].
For one who gives up their life in Mathurā, that is the goal; of this there is no doubt.
(87) There is no sacred site equal to Mathurā, no deity like Kṛṣṇa, no liberation possessing the splendor of the abode of Brahman, and no being higher than Puruṣottama. (88)
"When this is made the support, there shall be the dissolution of all sins;
when it is held within oneself, one's own ultimate liberation approaches.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you the supreme knowledge among all knowledges.
"By hearing or even by reading this, a person shall partake in that fruit.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Mathurā-tīrtha in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning how Sāmba contracted leprosy due to the mental agitation of Kṛṣṇa’s wives upon seeing his form as Sāmba at Dvārakā and the subsequent curse given by Kṛṣṇa; how his leprosy was cured through the worship of Āditya in Mathurā, the installation of the six Ādityas, and the removal of physical, verbal, and mental offenses.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the Dhruva-tīrtha in Mathurā, which bestows excellent liberation;
through libations and the gift of food, it brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
In Mathurā there was a king named Candrasena, who performed righteous deeds.
His wife was Candraprabhā, a mother of heroes who gave birth to heroic sons. Among her hundred maidservants, there was one maidservant named Prabhāvatī.
O beautiful lady, Prabhāvatī’s ancestors, numbering one hundred,
have all fallen into hell due to their own faults;
yet Prabhāvatī neither performs nor causes to be performed the libations for them.

Whether it be a *śrāddha* ceremony or some other gift for the sake of satisfying the ancestors, they certainly perform it; yet they do not even offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) for her or for her family members.
Once, a host of her ancestors, having fallen [into hell], arrived as a subtle multitude of living beings at Dhruvatīrtha on the bank of the Yamunā.
The ancestors, black in color and resembling gnats as they moved about,
were seen by the seer who was known for his knowledge of the three periods of time.
He who knows the three periods of time always offers handfuls of water to the ancestors on this river;
thus he satisfies them, and the satisfied ancestors go to the realm of light.
That sage always observes the vow of subsisting on milk, eating only at the sixth meal-time;
he subsists by drinking the rays of the sun and moves according to the movement of the sun.
Upon seeing the assembly of his ancestors who had arrived, he was instantly bewildered;
out of compassion as he gazed upon them, he did not perform his vow or recitation.
And the day drew to a close with only a fourth part remaining.
Some ancestors descend there from the sky to the earth.
Other ancestors by the hundreds of thousands likewise gathered there at Dhruvatīrtha from the east, the north, the south, and the west.
Seeing those who were coming and going, he was struck with wonder;
there he beheld one group, joyful, with well-nourished limbs and full of contentment,
which, having received the *svadhā* offerings from its sons and drunk the water, ascended to heaven.
Another ascetic was seen, who was emaciated in body.
Rough-skinned and devoted to bathing, he drank water and went to the earth; then another group was seen, adorned with garments and ornaments,
their limbs joyful and well-nourished, and having drunk water, they went to heaven.
Then another group was seen, with naked bodies. || 16 ||
Well-nourished and endowed with happiness, he drank the water and went to the sky;
then, at the end, many were seen seated upon excellent celestial chariots (vimānas).
Taking various vehicles filled with abundant food, they travel through the path of the sky to Mahārā and other such places.
Then others, being looked upon by you, uttered auspicious blessings;
they were satisfied, seated upon the backs of swans, garuḍas, and the like, or mounted on elephants and horses.
Others besides them were seen to be deformed, enraged, and excessively tormented by hunger; with bellies clinging to their backs, they were devoid of pride and intent on uttering curses.
Then others were likewise seen, honored with garlands of flowers;
having eaten at the śrāddha, they were full of great enthusiasm and as radiant as gods. (21)
Some, holding alms-food in their hands, and some, having eaten fruits; others, endowed with the sixteen articles and so forth, proceed toward the people and other such things. || 22 ||
Some were seen engaged in beds, provided with objects of enjoyment and pleasures; yet they were content, with serene minds, intent upon the practice of austerity.
Some, wearing crowns and fanned by royal parasols and yak-tail whisks,
were seen departing for Satyaloka in celestial chariots, honored by millions.
On the Yamunā, the ancestors were seen wandering about, dressed in new garments and adorned with ornaments and other finery; others likewise appeared in such a manner.
Indeed, at the Dhruva-tīrtha on the Kālindī, after midday and until evening,
the ancestors are likewise beheld by the ṛṣis who know the three divisions of time.
When the assembly of ancestors had departed, these sons, householders with their wives,
who were the performers of the śrāddha rites, went each to his own home in the evening.
Then Dhruvatīrtha became deserted and devoid of people;
even the king of sages, though knowing the three periods of time, arose from there in astonishment.
He saw one man with emaciated limbs, wasted by hunger, his gait unsteady,
trembling as he waited, his small belly pressed against his back.
Trembling with pain in his thighs, skin, and bones, yawning again and again,
with sunken eyes and a withered face, he was emaciated and made only a faint, low sound.
Then that compassionate sage asked him: "Who are you, who are so distressed, deformed in appearance, and swarmed by so many mosquitoes?"
"You do not go, nor is there a place for you; you are without support—what do you say?
Today, indeed, many millions of ancestors have been seen by me here. (32)
"The time for my daily observance has now entirely passed while looking after them;
today, indeed, there is no performance of my regular ritual duties. (33)
But now that you have been seen by me, my ritual action is surely destroyed;
tell me the truth: shall I perform my daily rites afterwards? (34)
"I shall indeed do as much as I am able, provided it is beneficial for you.
Having heard this, Jantu spoke to the sage, telling him everything exactly as it was. (35)
This very day, Bṛhannimitta performed a Śrāddha ceremony at Dhruvatīrtha that brings satisfaction to the ancestors; he offered water with sesame seeds and other oblations. (36)
Food, clothing, fruit, flowers, water, as well as bedding and so forth, sandals, a house, an umbrella, ornaments, milk, and likewise other things. (37)
Whatever is given today by sons, daughters, grandsons, wives,
and kinsmen becomes a hundred-thousandfold, providing complete satisfaction as an offering to the ancestors.
O Brahmin, at Dhruvatīrtha, everything given becomes eternal—be it a vehicle, a mount, a cow, a garden, or even a field. (39)
Taking what has been given—gold, wealth, and other things—the ancestors depart together; satisfied by the sesame seeds, fully satisfied, and gratified today, they go forth.
Today all the ancestors, having sons, go to heaven satisfied—their bodies nourished by their descendants who have offered śrāddha and performed the water-libations. (41)
Those whose lineage remains thus undecaying and endowed with offspring,
go to the supreme goal through sons honored by the ancestral offerings (svadhā).
Today, the ancestors of King Candrasena have been honored;
likewise, others who have gone to heaven were seen by you through your divine vision. (43)
For Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and those of Śūdra occupation—indeed for all who perform the Śrāddha rites, whether born of inverse (pratiloma) or natural (anuloma) unions. ||44||
"You have seen the ancestors whose lineage is imperishable;
as for me, I am standing here waiting indeed for the śrāddha. (45)
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope, hungry despite his desire for satisfaction,
he indeed went to hell in the past due to the fault of mixing castes.
"Neither by the atheists nor by those of my lineage has a śrāddha been offered to me today;
indeed, though I have come here every year, I have received no śrāddha. (47)
O Brahmin, having taken up the occupation of a slave to another's father, I live;
today, at this performance of the Śrāddha, even after a hundred years, [I have not attained my goal]. (48)
I have not obtained even a family member; indeed, I have found no satisfaction today.
I have become unable to move, and being tormented by the three fevers, I am deeply distressed. (49)
All went forth endowed with strength; for what recourse is there for one who is weak?
Indeed, some will come who shall satisfy all their ancestors.
"For then, having obtained something [of merit], I shall go to a nearby forest;
these are the tiny mosquitoes that exist within my body. (51)
"Because the lineage has come to an end, these people have taken refuge in my body;
for I am indeed their ancestor, and these people are born of my own line. (52)
"At times of hunger, they devour me, distressed by the breaking of the thread;
in this lineage of mine, there exists a single daughter made of thread. (53)
In Mathurā, there was a maidservant named Prabhāvatī who served as an attendant to the queen of King Candrasena and was devoted to her service.
Her son was a servant named Virūpanidhi;
he was the thread of our lineage, and we [performed] the śrāddha rites for him. (55)
With hearts bound by our intentions and desiring to satisfy the ancestors with offerings of faith, we have remained thus far; beyond this, we shall go to the forest.
Whether in a bottomless hell or in old age with broken spirits, if that thread [of kin] should offer water, śrāddha, and handfuls of sesame seeds; (57)
Then, having become nourished, we shall go to the lowest heaven.
Listen: even that which is offered by one of the lowest birth is indeed received as an oblation. (58)
May we be satisfied by what is given by her and become blessed with good sons;
for, due to the ripening of past karma, whatever downward path [we might have entered], [may she deliver us]. (59)

The ancestors who have ascended to higher realms— those with sons and those dependent on daughters— attain the merit of the funeral feast (śrāddha), the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), the water libation, and the gift bestowed through the act of adopting a daughter as a son.
There would be no other refuge for our ancestors; by having a daughter, our fathers truly possess a son.
May there be someone in our lineage who shall offer us handfuls of water.
Especially in rivers with abundant water that are cool,
one should offer a handful of water mixed with sesame seeds and fruits in the midst of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, with darbha grass in hand, one should offer even water mixed with silver; by that, we are always satisfied.
Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, the son, reciting the names of the ancestors belonging to the three lineages (*gotra*), should say: "May he whose name is so-and-so be satisfied; *svadhā*! (64)
One should offer one añjali to the gods, two añjalis to the sages,
and three añjalis to the ancestors, reciting, "May they be satisfied."
One should first give to the father, then one should give to the mother;
one should give to the maternal grandfather and also to the paternal grandfather.
One should offer three handfuls of water to the ancestors who have passed beyond;
likewise, one should offer to the paternal grandmother and also to the great-grandmother.
By this offering of a ball of rice, I cause you to perish so that you do not see the sun;
this water given by me—may it bring you inexhaustible satisfaction. (68)
Even water given with faith leads to infinity;
yet some ancestors, while receiving it, become agitated in appearance. (69)
Listen, O Brahmin, to the reason why a Śrāddha may become fruitless:
that which is given at an improper place or time, devoid of ritual procedure, and lacking a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (1.354.70)
A filthy substance in an unworthy vessel does not lead to satisfaction at all; likewise, food that is untrustworthy, unfit for the company, or looked upon with a wicked gaze [is of no avail]. (71)
That which is devoid of sesame seeds, mantras, and kuśa grass becomes demonic;
likewise, impure houses and the sacrificial offerings of an impure śrāddha are indeed impure.
Gifts given while possessed by anger, funeral rites (śrāddha) performed without following the rules or for unworthy recipients, and those lacking ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), indeed fall to the rākṣasas.
Indeed, the Rākṣasa partakes of the fruit of a sacrifice devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
likewise, he partakes of the fruit of those who utter false oaths in the presence of gods, Brahmins, or gurus. (74)
O Lakṣmī, those dwelling in the netherworld enjoy all that has been performed:
Śrāddha rites offered by those ignorant of the Vedas, and oblations or gifts given without mantras. (75)
The disciple who lacks devotion to the guru [is to be avoided], while the proclamation of meritorious deeds and the prior revelation of dharma shall be performed by one who is about to act.
All this has been prepared for the satisfaction of those dwelling in the netherworld;
indeed, that vow which was performed with false and vain ostentation is in vain.
Indeed, that gift, ancestral rite, austerity, and burnt offering would belong to the Rākṣasas;
it does not reach the ancestors, for the hosts of Pitṛs are then naked. (78)
Indeed, they are robbed by Rākṣasas and others who consume the fruits of their gifts;
thus, as they were summoned, so they go forth without fruit and without food.
Having resorted to silence, they all remain hungry and thirsty;
they come and go, yet they do not partake in merit.
All this has been told to you regarding the cause of his father's disfigurement;
he is one who gives what is new, highly valuable, excellent, and essential. (81)

If one gives at a śrāddha that which is worn out, insignificant, inferior, or worthless, then his ancestors indeed go to heaven seated upon vehicles that are equally decrepit, meager, lowly, and unsubstantial.
Their ancestors indeed wander and travel on foot as paupers;
they are impoverished for those who are impoverished, and they partake in the prosperity of those who are prosperous. (83)
Having spoken thus, that aged assembly of ancestors then ceased;
knowing the three periods of time and moist with compassion, they spoke to him for his benefit.
“Until you have reached full satisfaction, I shall not eat; remain steady and wait for my return, for I am going to bring that daughter back. (85)
Having said, "Then I shall perform the Śrāddha," he departed from the king.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, the king bowed at his feet. (86)
I am blessed, I am favored; my home has been sanctified.
Today my birth has become fruitful; please accept water for the feet, the guest-offering, and the cow.
Having received such honor from the king as he was thus conversing, he said:
"O King, listen and do that by which I have been satisfied. (88)
"Bring the queen together with Prabhāvatī.
Having been brought by the king and having bowed to the sage as he sat upon his seat, she was addressed by the muni: [89]
I shall tell you of the wonder that I beheld at Dhruvatīrtha:
all my ancestors, numbering in the tens of millions, went to heaven, honored by their sons.
There was a single old man, his body withered, emaciated by hunger, and his flesh dried up;
hopeless, he desired to go to hell at the Dhruva-tīrtha. (91)
Out of great compassion, I asked him, "Who are you? What do you desire?
He replied to me, "In my lineage there was a maidservant named Prabhāvatī. (92)
"O Brahmin, my son is indeed named Virūpakānidhi;
if he were to perform the śrāddha for me, I would attain satisfaction. (93)
Indeed, Prabhāvatī must perform the libation for the sake of the ancestors through her son;
whatever gift, water, fruit, or the like is given for the sake of the ancestors [is effective]. (94)

"O Svadhā, this milk-rice śrāddha shall be a giver of satisfaction and a giver of liberation. Having said this, for the sake of providing proof, the sage struck her, who was overwhelmed with intoxication. (95)
"Did you offer water for the satisfaction of your ancestors, or not?
She replied, "I did not; moreover, I do not even know those ancestors. (96)
"I do not know ritual action, nor do I ever perform it.
The sage said, "Let us come together; you shall witness a marvel today. (97)
Having resolved thus, all the citizens, the Brahmins, the king, and many other people then went to Dhruvatīrtha.
The Sage showed them an old, senseless man, emaciated, surrounded by tiny gnats, and excessively tormented by hunger. (99)
The sage said to him: "O living being, your daughter born of your lineage has arrived here with her son for the sake of prosperity; tell me what you desire."
Then Agati said: "Having bathed here according to the prescribed rite, let him perform the libation (tarpaṇa) by my name, and thereafter let him perform the Śrāddha ceremony."
Let him offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) together with sesame seeds and cloth of a similar color;
likewise, let him indeed give other gifts here according to his ability.
"By which, indeed, you all behold me here endowed with happiness; therefore, perform the *śrāddha* and the gift according to your ability through this thread. (103)
Having heard this, the king’s wife had the śrāddha ceremony, accompanied by very liberal sacrificial fees,
performed entirely by her maidservant and her son.
Silk cloth, fruit, incense, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
*tilottara*, milk-rice, sweet food, and cakes with rice-balls. 105.
Satisfied by all that water and water with sesame seeds which had been offered, he,
being virtuous and full of splendor, shone like a god with radiant luster.
But even the mosquitoes born there were similar to them—satisfied, handsome, like gods, and exceedingly well-nourished; they shone with great splendor.
The sky there was indeed covered with celestial chariots descended from heaven;
all those ancestors, their minds full of contentment, were like gods.
May the thread of our lineage increase through those born of a noble family, who shall forever deliver us by means of various ancestral rites (śrāddha). 109.
"May all of you—hear my words, which bring satisfaction to our father:
the sacred fords, the rivers, the wells, the mountains, and the lakes. (1.354.11)
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Gaṅgā, and other sacred sites and shrines—
there has never been, nor will there ever be, anything else that grants liberation to the ancestors.

Then, having bathed on the full moon day of Bhādrapada (Proṣṭhapadī), they reached the sacred ford with haste, beginning from the first lunar day and continuing until the end of the bright fortnight of that month.
The ancestors, who receive the funeral offerings and rice-balls, have certainly taken their place in the month of Āśvina,
having vacated the city of the departed spirits for heaven and the netherworld.
Striving for our own sons, as well as for the continuance of our family lineages and younger brothers,
we remain here together with the ancestors born of our respective clans.

Whoever shall offer a śrāddha and perform libations at Dhruvatīrtha during the month when the sun has entered Virgo, for the sake of their ancestors during the sixteen-day period, [shall obtain great merit].
We are forever fully satisfied; we shall go to the supreme goal.
You have indeed seen the means by which the ancestors are delivered. || 1.16 ||
"By the grace of the Knower of the Three Times, this sin, which was otherwise difficult to cross, has been crossed over.
Having thus proclaimed this to the king, the people, and the sage, they all [departed].
Having addressed the queen, the maidservant, and their son, saying,
"May it be well with you," they mounted excellent vehicles and went to heaven, surrounded by the gods.
Then the king, the queen, the son, the maidservant, the subjects, the women,
and the men departed toward their own homes, filled with great wonder.
And they always performed the ancestral libations (śrāddha-tarpaṇa) at the appropriate time;
by the power of Dhruva-tīrtha, their ancestors were thereby delivered.
O Lakṣmī, this majesty arising from Mathurā has been told to you;
by the remembrance of which the sins of previous births are destroyed. (121)
Whoever recites or even hears this shall possess the merit of the Dhruva-tīrtha;
he shall possess the merit of bathing in the waters of the Yamunā at Mathurā.
Standing anywhere near water, one should indeed offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa),
having remembered the eternal holy site of the Yamunā and having invoked the ancestors.
Therein, satisfaction of the ancestors arises as if from the waters of the Yamunā; likewise, the increase of one's lineage, health, and prosperity are well produced for him. (124)

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrāddha Rite and its Greatness, Bestowing Liberation upon the Ancestors, by Means of a Daughter in the Form of a Slave Girl Belonging to King Candrasena—Recognized through Her Lineage—After the Satisfaction of Ten Million Ancestors at Dhruvatīrtha, Following the Arrival of the One Named Trikālajña," within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, specifically the majesty of Mathurā-tīrtha.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe, I have heard this glorious majesty of Mathurā-kṣetra, which is fruitful and bestows both heaven and liberation. (1)
O Hari, you have out of compassion heard from me about the śrāddha and the fruit of the śrāddha;
now tell me in detail by whom the śrāddha was first originated.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall tell you the definitive account of the origin of the Śrāddha.
At the beginning of creation, Brahmā was born from the lotus of my navel.
And he brought forth as his sons the gods and others,
including the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts.
For the sake of delivering all beings everywhere on earth—Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, those of the Vaiśya caste, as well as Śūdras and even animals. || 5 ||
He created birds, stationary beings, and animals such as insects as required;
likewise, through Diti he created the Daityas, and through Danu the Dānavas.
In this way, there were also Vedic scholars and sages whose wealth was their asceticism;
their sons and likewise their grandsons were born, by whom the world was filled.
From the eye of Vedhas was born the mental son Nṛpa;
from him also was born a glorious son named Mānasa.
A mere youth by birth, yet remembering his former lives and likewise remembering the Vedas,
he performed supreme austerity, having fixed his mind on Hari.
He practiced the penance of the five fires, subsisted on air alone, stood on one leg with arms raised upward,
fed on withered leaves and water, and during the cold season lay within the water.
Performing the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances for more than ten thousand years,
he reached the time of death and attained the state of the five elements.
Nimi, having fallen into extreme grief on account of that, reflected;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, he created a mental realm.
Out of faith, she pondered, "What indeed shall I do for the sake of a son?
At that moment, a son with a divine body [appeared] from the path of a celestial chariot in the sky.
Having arrived at Nimi, he said: "Give gifts for my sake;
give water, give fruit, sweet food, and garments."
"Give me ornaments, vehicles, vessels, and milk-rice;
give me whatever foods I may eat, as well as roots and juices. (15)
"Give me those vegetable dishes which are most dear to me"—having spoken thus, he stayed there on the bank of the Devadhūnī in the cold season. (16)
Having addressed the seven seers, Nimi, becoming pure and composed,
caused all those best of seers to proceed in a clockwise direction.
Seven times they sat down together simultaneously in various places; they gave you various kinds of grains, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
O beautiful one, Nimi, having honored the brahmins seven times and having then carefully arranged the *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing southward, remained composed.
He offered to the illustrious one— pronouncing his name and lineage—
water, fruit, leaves, food, milk-rice, garments, and so forth.
He gave it to his divine son, and he accepted it in every way;
he brought everything before his very eyes, and he ate and drank it all visibly.
Likewise, having entered among the Seven Sages again, he ate repeatedly; and having approached Vastuka, he exclaimed, "I am satisfied! I am thoroughly satiated! (22)
Having ascended a celestial chariot, he went to heaven, gratified by the funeral rites;
when the sun had set, the king performed the evening twilight devotions.
At night he began to reflect on what he had done for the sake of his son;
having performed the offering of funeral cakes and other rites, he felt deep remorse.
What was never done by the sages of old have I now performed:
the rite of scattering offerings, which is impure, has been undertaken for the sake of a son. (25)
"Ah! By the power of affection, I have performed what surpasses death;
I have not merely performed the work upon a corpse, but a deed that is beyond reproach. (26)
And what will all those who stand in the place of fathers say to me—the gods, asuras, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas? (27)
As he was reflecting in this manner, the morning dawned;
he performed his twilight devotions, offered oblations into the fires, and again engaged in reflection.
"Alas! My life is in vain where my son is not seen;
indeed, the hell named Pūtika is described as the very sorrow within my heart. (29)
When there is a son, there is indeed no sorrow; heaven is attained in every way.
Through a son one obtains heaven, and through a grandson, the ancestors do so as well.
"Moreover, the great-grandfathers rejoice through the grandson of a son;
deprived of a glorious son, I have no desire to live. (3.1)
In the meantime, O Lakṣmī, Nārada arrived;
seeing him radiant with splendor, the king indeed worshipped him. (32)
Having been honored, Nārada sat upon the seat and said to him:
"O Nimi, listen, O highly wise one; do not grieve, O destroyer of grief. (33)
The body is impermanent and transitory; why, O wise one, do you grieve for it?
Those of noble intellect do not mourn for what is dead, lost, gone, or passing away. (34)
Once gone, he never returns; people laugh at one who grieves. I see no immortality in the world of mortals, whether among the moving or the unmoving. (35)
All people, from the world of truth down to the netherworld, are subject to time;
for every living being that is born, death is indeed certain. (36)
"You and I, O Creator, must certainly go;
you have had a high-souled son named Śrīmat, a treasure-house of fortune. (37)
Having performed great and complete austerity, he went to the supreme goal;
thus, for one who has attained liberation, you ought not to grieve at all. 38.
Thus addressed, Nimi, bowing his head at the feet of the sage, spoke to Nārada with shame, sighing and terrified like one in distress. (39)
"I have been consoled by you, O Brahmin; however, I shall say something—listen to it.
Once gone, he is indeed gone; once gone, he does not return again. (1.355.40)
But that which was performed by me after fashioning the corpse—this has never been heard of before, nor has it ever been done by the gods or my ancestors. (41)
Under the very influence of grief, he performed for the sake of the corpse the rite of satiating seven brahmins with food, drink, and even fruits. (42)

Afterwards, having spread darbha grass upon the ground, he should offer the food that has been set aside; and likewise, the fetching of water should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya). 43.
"Indeed, all this has been newly created, and because of that I am truly afraid.
Having heard that, Nārada said: "O King, you should not be afraid."
"I see no unrighteousness in this; go for refuge to your father.
Thus addressed, Nimi reflected and went for refuge to his father. (45)
At that moment, the illustrious son Tapodhana arrived and said, "O Nimi, this ancestral sacrifice has been prepared by you. (46)
Indeed, the dharma consisting of the sacrifice to the ancestors was ordained by Brahmā;
and that, which is essentially ritual action, has been revealed by you through my mouth. (47)
The dharma of the śrāddha, the sacrifice to the ancestors, has been established by you;
it is the ancient dharma of creation, handed down from each preceding age. 48.
That very rite, whose essence is the *śrāddha*, was established of old by the Self-Existent One;
the duty of the *śrāddha* for the deceased must be performed by people in every way. (49)
For one who is born, there is inevitably a final resting place somewhere after death;
for the sake of attaining that state, one must here offer dedication with faith.
For one who has not attained liberation, there may be satisfaction; however, in liberation, satisfaction is eternal.
Liberation is certainly attained through specific ritual acts and through expiation.
For even those of long life pass away, how much more so those of short life?
In another age, people will become short-lived. (52)
They will become especially characterized by tamas and rajas;
however, for them, the śrāddha ceremony will provide a means of attaining a good rebirth even from an evil state. ||53||
One should know that hell, the animal realm, and the state of a rakshasa are characterized by tamas;
for cruelty, fear, despondency, violence, and shamelessness are indeed darkness (tamas).
Ignorance and the state of a Piśāca are born of the nature of those characterized by Tamas;
one should know him to be Tamasic who, even when being instructed, does not understand. ||55||

One who is intoxicated with pride, lacks faith, and is intent on harming others; such a person is dominated by the quality of passion (rajas), is powerful in speech, and always holds his own people dear. 56.
The hero, who is manifest everywhere and whose desires for sense objects have been fulfilled—for the sake of their satisfaction in the next world, the Śrāddha is requested for these [ancestors]. (57)

One who is characterized by sattva will partake in liberation; he is patient, self-controlled, pure of heart, full of faith, endowed with austerity, and possessed of the practice of sacred study and other virtues. ||58||
If, even regarding these, there is the desire for sons, the desire for worlds, as well as the desire for wealth, the desire for a wife, or the desire for sensual pleasures; ||59||
By that continuous flow, he may go to the state of a preta in another life;
for his satisfaction, the rites of śrāddha, giving, and fire-offerings [should be performed].
This conception was first formed by the Creator and then expanded by you;
reflecting thus, you ought not to give way to grief.
Abandon your grief, O one of great wisdom; grief is the destroyer of all.
Grief burns the limbs, and by grief the intellect perishes.
Modesty, fortitude, righteousness, prosperity, fame, memory, and policy—
all virtues and all religious duties abandon a man who is overwhelmed by grief.
Thus, having abandoned grief, O King, become free from sorrow;
for it is the fool who, through the power of affection, enters the bondage of saṃsāra.
Therefore, having restrained attachment, one should apply the intellect to righteousness;
for righteousness is for the sake of the welfare of the world, consisting of faith, charity, and worship.
The śrāddha rite, consisting of hospitable reception and the offering of oblations, is generally considered to be fivefold;
it provides satisfaction to the deceased, while giving (dāna) brings happiness to the living. (66)

The worship of an image is auspicious; honoring living beings brings happiness; and offering oblations to those who have gone to heaven is auspicious; furthermore, the giver shall partake in the fruit [of these deeds]. (67)
If a wish should arise at the time of death, it must especially be fulfilled;
for the contentment of one who is dying bestows a favorable rebirth in the next world. (68)
When the life-force has reached the throat, one should quickly expel it from the house;
having placed the person upon a bed covered with a mat of kuśa grass, one should recite [the scriptures] to them with an attitude of affection.
One should place gold in his mouth, offer water, and perform vows and other rites;
one should bestow merit and give a cow, which brings benefit in the world beyond.
By the gift of cows that yield milk, one is swiftly liberated from sin;
one should whisper the name of Hari, the means to liberation, into its ear.
One should offer the madhuparka—honey, clarified butter, and curd—to his lips;
when the vital breath has thus departed, one does not enter the cycle of worldly existence again.
Then, having purified the body with fragrant substances such as ghee and the like,
one should cause the ritual bath at the sacred ford (tīrtha) to be performed while placing the head toward the south.
Having constructed a funeral pyre according to the prescribed rite with the wood of the finest trees,
and having placed [the body] with its head toward the south, he took the fire into his hand.

Then, having said, "Now [touch] his limbs," and having performed a circumambulation, one should cause the ashes to be applied to the location of the head after the state of being reduced to ash has occurred. (75)
Having washed his limbs and his garments, he should turn back;
then, intending it for the deceased, he should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) upon the ground.
On the third day for one whose life has ended, one should perform a bath in river water;
one should offer a rice-ball with cūṛṇa and give three handfuls of water.
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth [days], one should offer a single morsel of food and a handful of water;
likewise in the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth.
In the tenth [day], the purification of the clothes and the purification of the body must be performed in every way by the kinsmen of the lineage, using sesame seeds, myrobalan, and oil.
Having completed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna), one should have the shaving performed;
then, on the eleventh day, having bathed together with one's kinsmen, [one should proceed].
Having bathed, one should engage a deceased person with Brahmins or cause it to be done;
indeed, one should feed a single Brahmin with excellent materials for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Having bathed again, one should assign that deceased person among the pretas;
for the three castes, the Ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed with cooked food.
One should set aside the uncooked ingredients for the fourth caste;
on the thirteenth day, one should feed virtuous Brahmins with cooked foods.
Becoming like the wind through your mind, take refuge with virtuous brahmins; service rendered to brahmin-saints will bring happiness to the deceased. (84)
The body for the enjoyment of the preta was indeed fashioned from the two brahmins;
then, when the night had turned to dawn and the sun had risen, [he departed]. (85)
The barbering of the Brahmin must be performed according to the prescribed rule; likewise, bathing and anointing should be carried out, as these bring satisfaction to the deceased. (86)
One should prepare a sacrificial mound on the ground and perform the rites for the deceased;
however, one should choose a place that neither cocks, dogs, nor pigs can see. (87)
A dog drives [the evil] away with its barking, a boar with its snorting, a cock with the wind of its wings, and a *cāṇḍāla* by his mere sight. (88)
Whatever śrāddha they perform there brings bondage to the ancestors;
one should offer the portion for the deceased (pretabhāga) upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and that should be done in the forenoon.
And one should perform the formal dedication of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-saṃkalpa), pronouncing the name and the lineage (gotra);
thereafter, those born of the family, belonging to the various lineages, eat together as a single meal.
In this way, those who have gone to the world of the hungry ghosts (pretas) are satisfied by what has been given.
One should give an umbrella to ward off fire, ashes, rain from rocks, and other such calamities. (91)
One should also give sandals that ward off the thorns and other obstacles of the path;
one should offer incense, a lamp, garments, and ornaments.
One should indeed offer fruits that are well-ripened for the enjoyment of the pretas;
having thus completed everything, one should feed a twice-born with cooked food.
First, the Brahmin there should set aside the portion for the deceased;
then, having performed the purification of his hands, the Brahmin should indeed eat the sweet food. (94)
The portion for the deceased should be given to a Brahmin again and again by kinsmen, relatives, and friends; it must not be withheld by anyone. (95)
When an obstruction is placed there, the ancestors certainly do not accept [the offerings];
thus the Dharma is subverted, and the deceased spirit is not satisfied therein. || 96 ||
When the Brahmin is satisfied, cool and auspicious water should be given;
however, the remnants [of the food] should indeed be offered to the fish in the river and other such places. (97)
One should also give a bed and a seat, as well as collyrium and a bracelet;
then, having arrived at the place of the funeral offering (nivāpa), one should offer water with sesame seeds.
Having lifted up the tail of a cow, one should place it in the hand of a Brāhmaṇa, having prepared water with black sesame seeds using a vessel made of udumbara wood. 99.
Then, having sprinkled [the area] with water purified by mantras, one should dismiss the deceased from the Brahmin; one should give gifts to the twice-born.
One should assign a portion for the deceased among beings such as ants;
through those devoted to the poor and the helpless, the deceased becomes satisfied. (101)
Thus, this purificatory rite (saṃskāra), which consists of faith and cleanses one of all states of being a preta, must indeed be performed; yet it has been performed by you, O Nimi.
This ritual procedure for the offering of faith (śrāddha) is proclaimed as a single sacrifice;
from this point forward, the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) shall exist in the worlds.
"O Nimi, as the performer of the sacrifice, you shall go to the world of Brahmā;
likewise, the share for the deceased must be offered by all on the third day."
In the seventh, ninth, and likewise the eleventh month,
one should then perform the annual rite for the liberation of the deceased.
When a full year has passed and the funeral rites have been performed,
some beings attain liberation, while others wander in the sky.
Grandfather, daughter-in-law, wife, kinsmen, relatives, and friends—
thus these many exist here, but they are like a dream to you.
Having wept for a moment, they all indeed turn their faces away;
bound by the snare of affection, they are released in the next instant.
To whom do mother and father belong? To whom do wife and children belong?
Day after day they revolve, bound by the snares of delusion. (109)
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, are experienced throughout the cycles of existence; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?
The procedure for the consecration of the deceased has been proclaimed by Svayambhū;
indeed, this sacrament for the dead must be performed with a spirit of affection. (111)
Once the funeral rites have been completed, the status of being a father arises;
indeed, the libation to the ancestors must be performed month after month on the new moon day.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather, are satisfied by the oblation offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa and by the feeding of the virtuous. (113)
Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best of sages, departed for heaven.
In this manner, the Śrāddha was performed by King Nimi in a former age.
From that time forward, the Brahmins perform the Śrāddha and the offering of the Piṇḍa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the origin and details of the Śrāddha and the Piṇḍa.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of Śrāddha and the Sequence of its Ritual," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, specifically regarding the majesty of Mathurā-kṣetra: wherein King Nimi performed a śrāddha for the sake of his deceased son named Śrīman; and subsequently, when Nimi was grieving upon realizing that the rite he had performed was unestablished, Nārada instructed him that śrāddha is an ancient duty and explained the procedure for performing the śrāddha ceremony.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Keśava, by your grace I have heard about the Śrāddha, which is food for the departed;
indeed, do the Brahmins accept the gift of food as the portion for the departed? (1)
By what rite is a Brahmin released after having eaten food that is undesirable, censurable, or even that which has been entered by a *preta*? (2)
"How can that censurable person save the donor, O Supreme Person?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: You have asked well, O Lakṣmī; I shall destroy your doubt.
As for that brahmin who is an ascetic and a great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavata), [he is as follows]. || 4 ||
He was a great yogi and a possessor of great wisdom, adorned with supernatural powers and lordly sovereignty;
he was one whose wealth was his great asceticism and who was proficient in the Vedas and the Shastras. || 5 ||
He who possesses meditation, mental retention, and concentration as well; who knows the three periods of time and is adorned with the excellent virtues of restraint, observance, and the rest.
Constantly devoted to the six duties and intent upon the worship of Hari,
a deceased person is born as a god in heaven by the touch of the dust of his feet.
One of virtuous conduct, ever pure, should be a purifier like fire;
he indeed, having taken even the food of a preta as a gift, [is purified]. (8)
Having performed the rites for the deceased, he is not tainted by that fault,
for he knows the distinction between the individual soul and primordial nature and is devoted to the supreme unity of Brahman and the Self.
Capable of washing away evil, he is not defiled by its fault;
the darkness produced by night never obscures the sun in any way.
Just as darkness turns into light in the presence of the sun's rays,
so too does the state of a preta become that of a deity through such a yoga.
Through the yoga of Brahman, the state of a preta is transformed into divinity;
even sin becomes most meritorious, and for one who is capable, there is no fault.
But he who is neither rich in self-strength, nor devoted to Brahman, nor perfected in the vow of Brahman, nor engaged in the yoga of the six duties and so forth; || 13 ||
He who knows neither the Self nor the means of discernment—that Brahmin is indeed defiled by sins;
by eating for the dead, he becomes a dead spirit himself, born impure through his eating.
For the sake of purifying his own body, he should observe one fast;
having performed the morning twilight ritual and having offered libations to the sacred fire. (15)
The twice-born man, reciting the pacification mantras, should perform a sesame oblation;
having gone to a river flowing eastward and bathed, he should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having drunk the honey-mixture (madhuparka), he should sweep the house and sprinkle it with water;
having gratified the gods beginning with Agni, he should perform the bali-offering to the spirits.
One should give food to the Brahmins and perform the gift of a cow;
the Brahmin who acts in this way certainly becomes pure. (18)
When this has been done, he goes to the supreme goal upon death;
otherwise, when the law of time arrives, he enters the belly of a *pretānna* demon.
He would become a hungry ghost (preta) or dwell in hell;
he would attain the state of a rākṣasa, and only then be released from that sin.
The mind should perform atonement, which brings happiness to both the giver and the receiver,
and bestows cattle, elephants, horses, wealth, jewels, fields, female slaves, and ornaments.
He who accepts [the gift] with the mantra and performs the penance shall become pure and shall also deliver the donor; of this there is no doubt. ||22||
On an auspicious day for the gods, on one's birth star, at the time of a śrāddha, on the major lunar nodes (parvan),
and in all funeral rites, [one should invite] a Brahmin who is devoted to the six duties.

One who has completed the ritual bath after studying the Vedas and their branches, who is most righteous and ascetic, endowed with virtues such as good character, contentment, and truthfulness, and possessed of forgiveness. (24)

Having obtained a worthy recipient who is devoted to non-violence and other such virtues, and who has the Blessed One as his supreme refuge, one should indeed perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha), give gifts, and offer worship.
That pure one shall deliver all beings and deliver himself as well;
for indeed, a stone can never deliver another stone anywhere without a savior.
For one who is impure and burdened by sin cannot save others anywhere; indeed, only one who is pure can save others. Therefore, one should employ [one's gifts] upon a worthy recipient.
Listen, Lakṣmī: formerly there was a great king named Medhātithi;
in Avantī, Candraśarman was his domestic priest.
The king, having given a gift of a hundred cows, ate day after day;
then the day for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) of the king’s father arrived during the month of Vaiśākha. ||29||
Having bowed to the invited Brāhmaṇas and performed the Śrāddha according to the prescribed rules,
and having offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in the Śrāddha, he gave abundant food that had been prepared for the rite.
Likewise, he gave gifts of garments and ornaments to the brahmins;
among them was a certain brahmin who was weak and exceedingly wicked. ||3 1 ||
Born of an illicit union and mixed with the seed of a Śūdra and others, he consumed the food of the śrāddha ceremony there; by that fault, [the sin] fell upon the king.
The ancestors, fallen from heaven and cast down into the thorny forest,
are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, and they indeed cry out again and again.
By the turn of fate, Medhātithi went to the forest for the sake of wandering;
as they were wandering, he asked them, "Who are you, so deeply distressed? (34)
Then his ancestors said to him, "Indeed, there exists in our lineage a king named Medhātithi; we are his ancestors, dwelling here in the forest. (35)
"O King, we have fallen, dropped from heaven due to the fault of the *śrāddha* offering;
for that most wicked pseudo-Brahmin requested the food of the *śrāddha*. (36)
To those twice-born ones who have fallen from their duties and are merely Brahmins by name alone, arising from sexual misconduct—
desiring to go to hell because of that very defect in their conduct,
they shall experience great suffering there and then return again to heaven.
But by giving cows to Brahmins, through that merit, he goes again to heaven. || 38 ||
"We shall go there, but there is no food there that will provide satisfaction.
Hearing this, the king said, "I am indeed that Medhātithi. (39)
"For the sake of your deliverance, tell me what further task must be done.
The ancestors said to him: "In such a way that we may indeed be satisfied, the śrāddha must be performed again, and the best of the twice-born must be fed."
Having heard those words of theirs, Medhātithi went home.
He invited virtuous brahmins who had exerted themselves in the study of the Vedas—
men who were meritorious, devoted to dharma, patient, of excellent character, and great ascetics.
Then the king performed a śrāddha ceremony for those virtuous and highly devoted bhāgavatas who were endowed with the yamas and niyamas, after having offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in every way.
Having honored the Brahmins with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) and fed them, the king bowed to them and dismissed them; thereafter, he himself partook of the meal. ||44||
Then, having gone to the forest himself, he saw his own ancestors,
joyful, nourished, endowed with strength, and prepared to ascend to heaven.
Upon seeing this, the king rejoiced greatly, and the ancestors said to the monarch:
"May it be well with you; O King, we shall now depart for the heavenly realm."
It must never be given to an unworthy recipient or to one who is a great sinner;
for whatever is given there, whether as an offering to the gods or to the ancestors, is entirely fruitless.
If, in a rite for the gods or the ancestors, a worthy Brahmin recipient cannot be found, that prepared food should be given to cows according to the prescribed rule. 48.
In the absence of cows, one should diligently cast the food into a river;
it must not be given to an unworthy recipient, nor to an atheist, nor to one who betrays his guru. It must not be given to a golaka, a kuṇḍa, or a person of mixed caste (saṃkara).
Having spoken thus, all the ancestors departed for heaven in celestial chariots.
Medhātithi returned home, having understood the strength and weakness of the recipient.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, even a single excellent Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to righteousness [is superior].
They undoubtedly deliver one from misfortunes and the objects of the senses;
therefore, at a śrāddha, virtuous brāhmaṇas who are devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) should be fed.
Or else, month after month, or during the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa), those whose wealth consists of their penance should be fed as worthy recipients.
The stars are indeed to be enjoyed by the gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas;
likewise, those people who are devoted to the awakening of Brahman,
who are virtuous, truthful, and dedicated to celibacy, are to be enjoyed.
Thus it has been told to you, O Lakṣmī: a worthy recipient delivers his ancestors, whereas an unworthy recipient causes them to fall; therefore, one should perform an expiation.
Having heard that, Śrī Lakṣmī said to Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"Embodied beings go to other wombs according to their own karmas. (56)
How is it that beasts, birds, humans, and others come and eat? O Kṛṣṇa, who are these ancestors who have arrived to partake of the śrāddha? (57)
Some who have died have fallen under the power of Yama’s noose in hell;
others, indeed, have come under the control of householders among the ranks of the gods.
Due to the power of karma, some embodied beings in this world are subject to control within the eighty-four thousand classes of birth; they have fallen there and remain forever bound. (59)
"O Lord, they are capable of performing the *śrāddha*, yet they are unable to come; how then do they partake of the *śrāddha*? Pray, dispel this contradictory doubt of mine. (1.356.60)
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) must be performed so that the lineage is protected;
it must be performed in every age and even in the intervals between ages so that it is preserved. ||6 1 ||
Having heard these words of Mahālakṣmī, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke to Lakṣmī, clearing away her doubt.
Listen, Lakṣmī: those who partake in the ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña) at all times are the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather. (63)
These three indeed are the lords who partake of the offerings of the faithful;
the father, however, has Brahmā as his deity and was fashioned from the body of Veda.
The grandfather is the god Viṣṇu, fashioned from the body of Viṣṇu;
the great-grandfather is Rudreśa, fashioned from the body of Rudra. ||65||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have been appointed here for the Śrāddha;
first, one should offer the Śrāddha with the Piṇḍas to the portion of Brahmā.
One should offer the second śrāddha, together with the piṇḍas, to the portion of Viṣṇu;
one should offer the third śrāddha, together with the piṇḍas, to the portion of Rudra.
For to the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa himself assumes the form of the three gods. 68.
Wherever they die and attain birth,
Kṛṣṇa, abiding as the all-pervading Inner Controller, brings them satisfaction even there.
In this way, that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the inner controller, dwells within the virtuous brāhmaṇas;
at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, the Lord assumes the form of whoever is the intended recipient.
Having received the śrāddha offering and the funeral cake (piṇḍa),
Hari Kṛṣṇārāyaṇa causes it to reach that place where the deceased has gone.
Know this, O Mahālakṣmī: in this śrāddha, I myself appear in the form of the ancestors and others, bestowing the intended objects upon those who have entered other wombs. (72)
Now hear something else, O Lakṣmī; I shall explain it to you in detail:
some indeed perform the Brahma-sacrifice in the form [of the deity] or in the mouth of the virtuous. (73)
Some indeed perform the sacrifice to the gods in the sacrificial pit or the fire;
some indeed perform the sacrifice to the spirits in an animal or in the mouth of a cow.
O twice-born one, some perform sacrifices to men in the form of a human being;
others indeed sacrifice to the ancestors in water, fire, or on the earth, O twice-born one.
All of them abide in me; I tell you this as the truth.
Furthermore, in every kind of sacrifice, fire is the primary [deity], being the very essence of the mouth. (76)
The spirits, ancestors, sages, and deities eat through the mouth of Agni;
and I, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, indeed eat through the mouth of Agni.
I am the fire situated in the sacrificial pit, and likewise I am the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni);
I am also the āhavanīya fire, the purifier and the purifying one.
I am indeed the Vaiśvadeva fire, and likewise I am the Gārhapatya;
I am also the Bārhaspatya, and I alone am the Āvasathya as well.
Facing them, I, whose self consists of the three gods, eat in all sacrifices;
in the sacrifice to the ancestors, I, whose self consists of those three, eat with Brahmā as my mouth.
At a śrāddha, one should feed a twice-born who is learned in the Vedas, whose character is righteous, who is a great devotee of the Lord, whose senses are subdued, and who is truly contented.
Having first given [the offering] to the Fire, who is the embodiment of the divine tīrtha,
one should afterwards give it into the mouth of a Brahmin for one's father and grandfather.
One should indeed give repeatedly, even for the great-grandfather, having remembered him;
one should feed a Brahmin in secret and there invoke the ancestors.
Three balls of rice should be offered together with condiments;
with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered month after month.
I, as the Supreme Self residing within the body, carry [the offerings] for the deities;
likewise, the ancestors are pleased by what is given, of this there is no doubt. (85)
Three gods and three indeed are the ancestors, emerged from Hari;
they shall become the ancestral deities and the enjoyers in age after age. (86)
The ancestors bestow long life, fame, strength, splendor, wealth, sons, cattle, and women, as well as health, upon that person who offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍas). ||87||
When the Brahmin has been fed and is satisfied, those who are animals, hell-beings, humans,
or others situated anywhere else, are also satisfied by the offerings of the Śrāddha.
Satisfied, they go by the pure path of sattva to the supreme heaven.
O beautiful one, listen as I shall explain another matter according to its true nature. 89.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, sinful, fallen, and deceased people,
bound by hundreds of snares of affection, are cooked in the impure hell.
Their sons and grandsons, as well as those born in their lineage, may at some time shed drops of water upon reaching this lake. (91)
By that very [act], those who are destined for hell find satisfaction;
likewise, the libation, the śrāddha rite, the funeral cakes, and the water with sesame seeds [bring them relief]. (92)
A twice-born man, through a spirit of devotion, should deliver his ancestors by making an offering;
furthermore, a blue bull should be given, for it destroys the agony of hell.
If one were to draw up even water from the tail of Nīlaṣaṇḍa, the ancestors would be satiated by that for sixty thousand years. (94)
If a lump of mud has been lifted by its very horn, then by that act the ancestors are truly uplifted and led to the world of Soma. ||95||
For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years, they rejoice in the worlds of Soma, entirely free from hunger and thirst.
Thus, this duty of the householder, consisting of the śrāddha rite, was established by sons, grandsons, and others for the sake of the deliverance of those possessed by craving. ||97||
Ants and other creatures, moving beings and birds, as well as stationary things, all depend for their livelihood upon householders; of this there is no doubt. (98)
Those who perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) every month while in the householder stage of life,
on the proper lunar day, during a festival, and under an auspicious constellation, deliver their own ancestors.
Those ancestors indeed emerged, residing within the bodies of Brahmā and Viṣṇu:
the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
In this manner, they subsequently became the Kāśyapa deities;
thereafter, they were indeed appointed to preside over the śrāddha rites. || 101 ||
At that time, during the ancestral sacrifice, they gave [the food] solely into the mouth of a Brahmin;
consequently, the ancestors suffered from indigestion and were afflicted by it.
Accompanied by Soma, they went and bowed to the Grandfather (Brahmā), saying:
"We are indeed afflicted by indigestion; please provide us with an elephant."
Brahmā then spoke of that which exists as the excellent son of Śāṇḍilya, by whom indigestion is destroyed and the ancestors attain happiness.
Dhūmraketu is Vibhāvasu, the radiant one who brings about decay;
at a śrāddha ceremony, an offering should first be given to him among human beings.
One should eat together with that very person after the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍas) have been offered;
for as long as [the impurity lasts], the fire-god, the carrier of oblations, is remembered as a consumer of all things.
Engaged by Brahmā in all rites through the five sacrifices,
O Fire, you should first partake of that which has been offered as a funeral pinda for the ancestors.
The deities and these ancestors shall eat through you;
the second śrāddha must be eaten together with the fire and the ancestors.
The third offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), however, should be consumed by Soma, the ancestors, and the fire-god together; thus, there will be no indigestion.
Thus addressed, they always eat together at the sacrifice to the ancestors;
[the three are] Vahni, Pitṛ, Pitāmaha, and Prapitāmaha.
The ancestors, the gods, and the fire-eaters indeed consume [the offerings] as "Soma.
At that time, those Brahmins who are unworthy of the row (apāṅkteya) should never be fed. || 111 ||
I shall now declare those who are excluded from the company of diners (apāṅkteya), who have fallen to a state of deficiency due to their actions:
eunuchs, painters, cattle-herders, and revilers. || 112 ||
Likewise, those who steal gold, the one-eyed, those afflicted with leprosy, atheists, as well as dancers, singers, and those who live by acting; 113.
Also those who sell the Vedas, those who perform sacrifices for all kinds of patrons,
servants, laborers, royal attendants, and likewise those who deal in leather.
Those devoid of sacred refinement, the fallen, those who subsist on the labor of Śūdras, astrologers, village priests, scribes, and likewise hypocrites; || 115 ||
Those who perform all manner of forbidden acts, who have fallen from their path, and who consume liquor, meat, and engage in sexual intercourse—
those others who are thus defiled are indeed Rākṣasas in the form of twice-born Brahmins.
Seeing the ancestors partaking of them, the ancestors would experience great suffering.
Then one should quickly perform an expiation and perform the śrāddha rite again;
one should offer clarified butter into the fire and gaze upon the sun.
Having performed the re-sowing of seeds, one [should offer for] the father and the grandfather.
One should offer perfume, incense, a lamp, water for honor, and water with sesame seeds; one should also feed a Brahmin, for by that the ancestors are satisfied.
As for that Brahmin who never eats food from the dead, he is always pure.

To him, gifts should be given; however, one should not employ rice grains in the Vaiśvadeva offerings, nor wheat, ghee, and so forth, nor sugar, nor vegetables, nor milk, nor curd, nor clothing in the Śrāddha rites. || 1.356.120–121 ||
For those who eat the food of the hungry ghosts (pretas), an expiation is prescribed:
on the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, one should offer excellent milk-rice mixed with ghee.
Then, for the sake of purifying the body, one should smear [the image] with honey;
likewise, for one's own purification, one should give away a tawny cow (kapilā) along with its calf.
Furthermore, one should bathe at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and likewise recite the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times.
Or rather, one who desires the purification of both the body and the self should perform the *śrāddha*.
Having bathed and smeared the ground, he should address the most excellent Brāhmaṇa:
"O Mahālakṣmī, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one should not use a tooth-stick. || 1.24-25 ||
If Soma, the deities, or the ancestors should be harmed,
that Brahmin must, at dawn, have his beard and nails clipped;
he must also perform a bath, anoint himself with oil, and partake of cooked food.
When the time of midday has arrived, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) to the Brahmin.
One should lead him into the interior of the house, provide a seat, and offer excellent water for the guest-offering (arghya).
Having worshipped him with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps, one should present water and sesame seeds.
Having given the auspicious vessel for the purpose of eating, one should place it before the Brahmins;
one should draw a mandala with ashes to ward off the defects of the row.
Having offered oblations into the fire, one should serve sweet food to the Brāhmaṇa.
One should say to the twice-born, "Eat as you please.
Having satisfied the Brāhmaṇa, one should then offer the *vikira* (scattered food).
Having offered an upper garment as a seat, one should then pose the question regarding the alms-food.
Facing the south, having spread darbha grass upon the ground,
one should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the triad beginning with the father.
One should perform the worship of the rice-balls according to the prescribed rite for the increase of the lineage;
the self-possessed person should place them in the hand of a Brāhmaṇa so that they become inexhaustible.

Having satisfied them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and having had the benediction (svastivācana) recited, one should dismiss them. However, the three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should remain right there upon the ground. ||134||

The ancestors remain in the house for that long while being nourished. Having sipped water and become pure, one should then offer the waters of peace (śāntyudaka) after bowing to the Vaiṣṇavī earth, the inexhaustible domain of Kaśyapa. || 135 ||
One should eat the first ball; the middle one, however, should be given to the wife. || 136 ||
One should offer the third portion into the water and dismiss the ancestral deities;
one should bow down according to this rite, for thus the ancestral deities are satisfied. || 13.7 ||
They bestow long life, as well as sons, grandsons, and wealth.
Listen, Lakṣmī: one should offer the *madhuparka* at the time of the departure of the vital breaths.
Indeed, the *madhuparka* is a person who has emerged from my right limb. || 138 ||
By me he has been engaged in all undertakings for the sake of liberation from existence (bhava-mokṣa).
Where there is the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), there is liberation;
where the honey-mixture offering is absent, there liberation is not found. || 1.356.140 ||
One should likewise prepare honey, curd, and ghee in equal parts as this "trika";
one should give it to a Brahmin for the sake of merit and for the liberation of the deceased.
At the conclusion of rites such as the Śrāddha, one should cause the recitation of peace-mantras (śāntipāṭha) to be performed.
Salutations to You, the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Lakṣmī;
salutations to the pervasive Lord of Māṇikī, the Lord of Pārvatī, and to Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Prabhā. 1.42–1.43.
Look toward the quarters, look downward, and protect yourself constantly from diseases.
Be gracious toward your own kingdom, the king, and all his forces;
likewise, be gracious toward pregnant women, the elderly, the rice crops, and the cattle.
Bring peace to the Brahmins and the virtuous; bring about auspiciousness. || 141 ||
"Provide food and bring about good rain; grant us abundance and fearlessness.
O Lord, may the kingdom flourish, and may there be peace forever for the gods, for human beings, for your devotees, and for the young maidens. (146)
May there be constant peace for all beings, including domestic animals. || 147 ||
Having thus recited the Śānti, one should offer the Madhuparka:
clarified butter, honey, and curd, placed together in an equal measure within a vessel made of Udumbara wood.
In the absence of honey here, one should mix it with jaggery;
O Mahālakṣmī, in the absence of ghee, one should mix it with parched rice.
And in the absence of curd as well, one should mix it with milk.
One should prepare curd, honey, and ghee, or indeed all three in equal measure.
"O Lord of Gods, O Kṛṣṇa, I offer clarified butter, ghee, and honey.
However, if none of these are available, one should simply place water in the mouth.
He who indeed releases the vital breaths and offers the honey-mixture (madhuparka) into the mouth—this is pure, stainless, and the fulfiller of all desires. 152.
He who hears this supreme narrative concerning the madhuparka and other rites attains the highest divine liberation by virtue of my grace. (153)
Whether at the king's gate, in a cremation ground, or likewise in times of fear and calamity, for those who recite this peace-mantra, their own desired goal will quickly be realized. (154)
One without a son obtains a son, and one without a wife obtains a beloved; a woman without a husband obtains a lover, and one who is bound becomes free from bondage. 155.
"By the mere remembrance of this, one shall also partake in the fruits of śrāddha and other rites.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you the supreme inner meaning of śrāddha and so forth. (156)

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga, concerning the majesty of the Mathurā-tīrtha: the purification of one who eats at a *śrāddha* through penance; the downfall of the ancestors when King Medhātithi of the city of Avantī feeds unworthy Brahmins at a *śrāddha*, and their return to heaven when he performs the *śrāddha* for worthy recipients; the fact that his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather were born from the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa respectively; and that the Soma, Pitṛs, and Hutāśana [are present] in a virtuous Brahmin.
The three hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Shared Meal, the Gift of a Blue Bull, the Offering of Madhuparka, the Recitation of Peace Hymns," and so forth. ||356||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, Yamarāja, the elder brother, was fed and worshipped by the daughter of the Sun.
And Yama, being pleased, spoke to Yamī regarding the granting of a boon:
"Whether in the water at your sacred ford, or on its banks upon the ground, for all embodied beings—" || 2 ||
O sister, whether they be sinful or meritorious, even those who have entered the four modes of birth,
if they abide having attained yoga, they are not to be punished by me.
Then Yamunā said to her elder brother: "If you have compassion for me, release me completely from dwelling in the city of Yama today."
Likewise, I [know] the great fruit of bathing, the great fruit of drinking water,
and also the merit of giving Tulasi leaves from a multitude.
"I shall indeed give them to the denizens of hell; release them from their bonds!
Having accepted his sister-in-law's words and saying, "So be it," [he acted accordingly].
Yama, having bestowed the merit earned by Yamī, sent all the inhabitants of hell to heaven,
leaving the realm of Yama empty.
