Then, as time passed once more, she was brought forth by the wicked on the far shore beyond the Lokāloka mountain, in dense darkness.
Indeed, that court of justice was established by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa for the purpose of bestowing the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions upon living beings.
To the sinful and to the meritorious alike, the Lord of Yama,
the King of Dharma himself— whether cruel or gentle— bestows the fruit according to their deserts.
All living beings who have died— whether sinful, meritorious, or performers of ritual actions—
go to that place, and from there they proceed either to the other world or elsewhere.
Those with much evil and those with little evil, according to their karma in the abode of Yama,
having experienced the fruit of their actions in the hells, indeed go toward further existence.
Indeed, the hellish regions are innumerable;
they are mental realms fashioned by Dharmarāja within those very places.
He bestows that punishment upon him according to his karma.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: "O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the place where the fruits of the ripening of karma occur. (14)
Of what kind is it, what is its measure, what is its form, and by whom is it seen?
What kind of fruit from the ripening of karma is experienced by human beings? || 15 ||
Explain all of this for the benefit of people: how may a person never go to the abode of the King of the Dead? (16)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this most beautiful ancient tale,
which is purifying of all sins and brings about auspiciousness when undertaken.
Born during the churning of the ocean, you were given as a lawful wife by the gods and others to the sage Uddālaka, though you are Alakṣmī.
Born of her was a son born of her mind (mānasa), a knower of the true essence of the Vedāṅgas,
renowned as Naciketas, who always abided by his father’s command.
In the forest, he possessed a wealth of cattle numbering ten thousand;
therefore, every morning at dawn, the great sage Naciketa [would go forth].
Having performed his ritual duties in the morning, he indeed gave a hundredfold gift;
among those gifts, he gave cows to a brahmin.
Having experienced their enjoyments, they have reached the state of old age; their teeth are broken as they approach the end of life.
They are like cows that have already eaten the grass, whose milk has dried up, and whose signs of pregnancy have vanished.
When his father was about to give away such cows as these, the son Naciketas, moved by compassion, spoke to him. (23)
O father, cows that are fit for gifting are always those capable of yielding milk;
such ones as these, who are worn out and deprived of the power of conception, are not at all suitable. (24)
Having heard this, the father said: "The old cows have already been given away;
there are no young ones remaining in our house at present that could be bestowed as a gift. (25)
Having heard this, the son indeed desisted;
then, on another day, a certain brahmin mendicant arrived for the sake of a cow. (26)
That Naciketas also begged for the gift of a cow;
and he indeed gave that aged bull, which was the only one remaining from his wealth of cattle, to the twice-born man.
Then the son Nāciketa said repeatedly to his father:
"Father, those cows which have never yielded milk must not be given. (28)
Those cows, however, were merely a burden, with nothing remaining but death;
their father, becoming somewhat distracted in mind, spoke to that son.
"What then shall I give? I give you here on this ground of cows.
Having heard this, the son spoke again, "Give me! (1.357.30).
Then the father, out of anger, spoke these terrifying words to his son:
"O son, why do you repeatedly obstruct me so swiftly? (3.1)
"You say 'Give me,' yet you have been given to death by me.
As soon as her father had spoken these words, Death arrived there.
"O son, let it be so," he said; "Om. In an instant, he vanished.
"Let not the word of my father be false; I shall go to the abode of Yama."
Having heard his son’s words, the father, with a distressed mind, said:
"O child, you are alone; indeed, no other kinsman exists. (34)
"O son, you have been entreated by me not to go there;
indeed, what I spoke out of anger was not my considered view of the true nature of dharma. (35)
The word of one's father must indeed be honored, provided that unrighteousness does not touch it;
yet, this would not be so if King Vaivasvata were to release you back.
Behold, I am perishing as the destroyer of the bridge of my lineage!
They know that "pud" is the name for hell, and indeed, hell is suffering. (37)
The protection of one who has sons shall exist through his sons in every way, both in this world and the next; [for it is said:
"The oblation has been offered, the gift has been given, austerity has been practiced, and the ancestors have also been nourished. (38)
For one who has no son, all that—whether it be vast asceticism performed or gifts given according to dharma—becomes certainly in vain. (39)
Having performed oblations in the fire and recited the series of mantras, one who is childless shall not attain heaven; this I have heard from the three gods.
The father is counted by the son, and the grandfather by the grandson;
but the great-grandfather rejoices through the great-grandson of his son. ||41||
"My child, I shall not abandon you, who increases my lineage;
even when entreated with great effort, you ought not to go there. (42)
Having heard that, the humble Nāciketa said to his father:
"O father, you should not despair; you shall see me returned here."
Having seen King Yama and having made your words come true, I shall return here again; therefore, I have no fear of him.
Truth is the staircase to heaven; may you indeed abide in truth.
Through truth everything is obtained; all that is beneficial is established therein. 45.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices. (46)
The great Vindhya mountain, though growing, does not increase when it stands firm in truth;
likewise, Bali, the son of Virocana, remains bound while observing his own vow of truth.
Truth and righteousness, when protected, protect their own protector;
therefore, practice truth today and protect yourself by yourself. 48.
Having spoken thus, Nāciketa, with a serene mind, went to Death;
he reached the abode of Yama, where at that time Yama was not present in the house. (49)
When the great festival of the sacrifice performed by the Guardians of the World had commenced,
a Brahmin guest named Nāciketa stood in the courtyard of the house.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, and without even a welcome,
one day passed and then a second, all spent without that welcome.
On the third day, there was the falling of the crown upon the earth;
then it was known that some great sin had been committed somewhere. ||52||
The cause has been understood; it was sought out by messengers who recognized that the guest's lack of welcome indeed destroys merit. (53)
Yama said to the messengers there: "I arrived here yesterday;
indeed, no excellent messenger whatsoever informed me that I was a guest. (54)
Let them offer a welcome to that truthful Brahmin whose wife remains at home deprived of water, food, and a seat for a guest. (55)
The merit of that householder is entirely reduced to ashes;
one should receive food from him only after washing his feet and placing them upon one's head. (56)
Water should be offered by a householder; by that, his merit increases.
Whether it be little or much, it should be given according to one's ability with great faith. ||57||
If a guest turns away from a house with his hopes frustrated, he departs taking away the merit of the householder and leaving behind his own sin. (58)
A learned brahmin, a virtuous man, a chaste woman, and a celibate ascetic—these indeed are the guests of Dharma; what is given to them yields infinite merit. (59)

These are the hungry ghosts, the aged ancestors, those who have their own dependents or are without support, the wretched, children, the dull-witted, the blind, and these guests who arrive by chance. (1.357.6) 0.
One should perform the washing of the guest's feet, the massaging of his limbs, bathing him, feeding him, providing water for drinking, and offering auspicious gifts. 61.
Having thus instructed his servants, Yama himself returned to the gate to meet Naciketas and asked him about that happiness.
"O Brahmin, you have arrived at my life's fulfillment; it is my greatest good fortune.
O virtuous one, please accept this sweet food, a meal, and a drink of water. (63)
Enter here into my house; accept water for the feet and the guest-offering;
accept from me various seats, garments, and ornaments.
"How and for what purpose have you come? Speak, O Brahmin; I shall grant it to you.
Naciketas said to Yama: "Indeed, [I have come] out of compassion for you. (65)
May whatever clothing, ornaments, and the like I have obtained become for me the very knowledge of the Self;
may Yama, the Yogin, and Hari manifest the inner Self before my eyes.
"Then I requested that vision of the Self: 'If you have great compassion, grant it to me.
Yama said: 'Take this gold and this collection of jewels.'"
Furthermore, he gave him a wish-fulfilling tree, the moon-creeper, a wish-granting gem,
a beautiful golden mansion, and hundreds of male and female servants.
O sir, take these vehicles—elephants, horses, and other mounts—as well as beautiful gardens, pleasure groves, and a treasure-store of gold. 69.
"But I shall never give the knowledge of the Self to one who is not directly perceived [as a worthy recipient]. May it be so; O Lord, by Your grace alone has everything been obtained by me.
Having spoken thus, Nāciketa requested him for the sake of self-knowledge.
Yama said, "Accept from me the sovereignty over the earth, a universal empire."
Whether it be heaven or the netherworld (pātāla), the kingdom of Brahmā, all sovereign powers, and the supernatural accomplishments (siddhis) beginning with atomization (aṇimā); ||72||
O friend, take hold of such powers as entering the bodies of others;
do not, however, crave self-knowledge, which is difficult to attain even for yogins. (73)
"May it be so; by your grace alone, O Lord, everything has been obtained by me.
Having said this, Naciketas then requested from him the knowledge of the Self. (74)
Yama said: "Choose something else that dwells in your mind;
however, the realization of the Self is not easy for those who are poor in yoga. (75)
Nevertheless, Naciketas thus requested knowledge of the Self;
Yama said, "Listen: the Self is perceived through divine vision. (76)
"I grant you divine vision; behold the Self abiding in your heart.
Having spoken thus, Dharmarāja gave him water of great merit.
By means of the collyrium for the eyes, Nāciketa indeed beheld the conscious one—resplendent, being-consciousness-bliss, subtle, embodied, and a mine of all qualities. (78)
Having seen that which is the locus of all accomplishments, shining, and abiding within as the inner self, Nāciketa, possessed of divine vision, rejoiced exceedingly. (79)
Then Yama, seeing his firm resolve regarding the knowledge of the Self, was pleased and said to the Brahmin: "Choose another boon as you desire."
Then Naciketas said: "Let my corpse become undecaying, where my life may be eternal and divine, free from destruction. (81)
Thinking, "May there be no offense against my father," I beheld that which bestows peace;
thus, by the name Naciketas, I become the fire. (82)
"May my fame endure forever everywhere, reaching even unto the abode of Brahmā; I pray for these boons previously mentioned, which have been granted by you. (83)
"So be it," Yama said; he offered everything to his guest:
his own palace and the auspicious dwellings of his administrative officers.
Then he showed him the prisons of the wicked,
the places of punishment for those in hell, and the celestial realms of the meritorious.
Yama himself showed everything to his venerable guest;
having seen all that wealth, prosperity, and excellent sovereignty, he took it with him. (86)
Nāciketa went to his own home where his father was;
indeed, the corpse, becoming endowed with consciousness, rose up most divinely.
Then, with a joyful mind upon seeing his son, Lakṣmī, that treasure-house of asceticism, embraced him with both arms and, smelling his head, said to him: [88]
I hope you have not been killed, my child, nor indeed bound in the abode of Yama;
I hope your path was auspicious as you went forth, my son. (89)
"O son, I hope no diseases have arisen in the abode of Yama;
what did you do upon going there, and what did you see when you returned home? (1.357.90)
"Have you seen Yama? Is he harsh or very gentle?
Is he pleased or filled with wrath? How is it that you have been sent away so quickly? (91)
I hope he was not detained by the gatekeepers there or ushered inside;
I hope that the fruit of his merits and sins did not become an obstacle for him. (92)
"Has the path been reached by you without hindrance, or was it well-honored?
Having spoken thus to his son Naciketas, [the father addressed] Naciketas.
With a joyful mind, he embraced the ascetics who had arrived and said,
"Behold the power of my son, which bestows victory."
Having seen the abode of Yama, he returned once more to his body through the power of service to his ancestors and also through service to his teacher. 95.
"By the truth of what was seen by the gods, my son has been restored to life.
Oh, how supreme is my fortune! My son has returned, having crossed over death. (96)
The deities, the sages, and the holy lords are indeed pleased with me, because my dear child Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has joyfully come to me. (97)
While he was speaking thus, the forest-dwellers heard it from ear to ear and, having heard it, abandoned their vows, recitations, and worship. (98)
Abandoning their asceticism and fire-offerings, they all assembled to behold [him];
some stood with arms raised aloft, while others remained balanced on one foot.
Some had their eyes fixed upon the sun, while others had their heads bent toward the ground;
some were naked, and others likewise used their teeth as mortars.
There were those who subsisted on heaps of stones, those who observed silence, those who fed on withered leaves and grass, and others who drank smoke, drank vapors, or drank water. (101)
Having surrounded him, they all questioned Nāciketa:
"O, O you who are devoted to truthful vows and conduct, you who delight in service to your teacher!"
"O Nāciketa, speak the truth: what have you seen and what have you heard?
Whatever conduct of Yama there may be, whether secret or manifest—" || 103 ||
You must recount everything, including whatever was done for your sake—
the suffering, the rebukes, the insults— and even that which was to be kept secret, as well as that which was made public.
Speak all that consists of instruction for the world, concerning what will happen here, and how that which is performed in this life is of benefit in the next.
Living beings who look only toward the further shore do not see the end of what they have done;
has Citragupta been seen by you, or does he perhaps do nothing at all? (106)
What is the form of the King of Dharma, and what is his form as Time?
Likewise, what is the form of Death, and what is the nature of diseases? (107)
And what kind of ripening of the fruits of karma is experienced? How do those who have conquered themselves and whose conduct is meritorious proceed in such a state? (108)
How do the sinners go, and how indeed do the indifferent ones go?
[They go] exactly as it was seen, exactly as it was born, and also exactly as it was experienced. 100.
"Tell me everything in detail and according to the truth, O Nāciketa: what was eaten by you, how it was eaten, and likewise whatever else remains in your memory."
Having spoken thus, they, being exceedingly eager to hear that which was indeed supermundane, became fixed in heart; then Naciketas spoke to them.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of How the City of Yama was Emptied by the Prowess of Yamunā, How it was Again Filled with Ritualists (Karmis), Nāciketas’ Journey to the Abode of Yama due to his Father’s Curse, His Return to His Own Body after Receiving Yama’s Blessings, Attaining Self-Realization, and Beholding the Fullness of Yama’s Realm, Including the Rishis’ Questions Regarding What Was Seen and Heard There," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of Mathurā-kṣetra. ||357||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; Nāciketa recounted his own experience to them.
O brāhmaṇas, listen as I relate this account of Yama’s wondrous deeds.
As I was traveling on the path of Yama, I indeed beheld embodied beings who were meritorious, moving happily along with their meritorious celestial chariots and other vehicles.
Deprived of the means of purification and severely beaten by the messengers of Yama,
the wicked travel along the rugged path to the abode of Yama in great suffering.
I shall describe those evildoers whom I have seen on the road: liars, cruel men, and those who kill living beings, women, and children. (4)
Wicked slayers of Brahmins, causers of suffering, betrayers of trust,
rogues, ungrateful, greedy, and violators of others' wives.
Those who kill virgins, those who destroy the path of Dharma, those who commit evil acts by force, and those who indulge in liquor, meat, and the like; || 6 ||

Those who are deceitful, those who revile others, those who kill their mothers, fathers, or gurus, those who abandon their mother and father, and those who cause great suffering to chaste and virtuous women; || 7 ||
Those who harbor hatred toward their guru, those who hate the gods, deceivers, and the wicked; likewise, those who seize houses and fields, and those who destroy bridges and embankments. || 8 ||
Those devoid of faith, atheists, merciless, and lacking in purity; those bereft of wife and sons, and those who cause the breaking of vows and the like. || 9 ||
The twice-born have lost their status as twice-born; they are fallen from right conduct and unrighteous.
They eat all things, perform all tasks, and engage in sexual union with everyone.
Also those who are assassins, as well as those who associate with evildoers; women who cause suffering to their husbands or wives, and those who inflict suffering upon their husbands. (11)
Those who cause suffering to women, those who indeed steal away wealth, those who practice deceit and pride, and those who inflict false blame and stigma; || 12 ||
Those who administer counterfeit medicines, those who deceive with false news, those who strike with fire or weapons, and those who crush sesame seeds and other crops in oil-presses; || 13 ||
Those who destroy temples, food-distributions, and other charitable works; those who destroy trees;
those who forge edicts; and those who are informers or backbiters. || 14 ||
Those who defile sacred fords, those who are excessively cruel in quarrels and desires,
as well as men, women, and laborers— I have seen them on the path.
They went to the abode of Yama, presided over by Citragupta and others;
I, however, quickly reached the courtyard of King Yama’s palace.
Those soldiers of mine read my very words of truth upon the plowshare,
bow down, and show me the path.
I beheld for three days the delightful abode of King Yama, surrounded by a great wall, and his throne at the city gate.
After I had finished my task, Yama himself arrived to welcome me;
having honored me, he led me into the interior of his vast palace.
Then, having granted me boons, that great city of the King of Dharma was shown to me by his soldiers at his command; I beheld it on all sides.
It is one thousand yojanas in width and twice that in length;
it is twice as much in circumference and is surrounded by moats.
It was covered with divine and auspicious palaces made of Jāmbūnada gold,
consisting of mansions with hundreds of stories and towers adorned with spires.
It was surrounded by palatial mansions provided with watchtowers, by temples adorned with finials, and by a great golden rampart.
There, the servants of the city of Yama, as well as the chief officials,
the messengers of Yama, the Kālas, and the soldiers and others, indeed reside.
There, rivers with desirable waters, lakes, oblong ponds, wells, tanks, and lotus-pools shine forth, surrounded by creeping vines and trees. (25)
Female slaves, female messengers, wives, servants, daughters, and sons—these families of the subjects of King Yama dwell there. (26)
Elephants, horses, royal swans, camels, cows, bulls, and other animals of various species also exist as providers of assistance. (27)
Flocks of birds such as parrots, cranes, and peacocks indeed dwell there;
the virtuous city of King Yama is filled with all kinds of living beings. ||28||
The river Puṣpodakā was beautifully adorned with trees, creepers, and groves; its banks were graced by flourishing gardens and the like, and it possessed golden stairs and sands. 29.
In that place, where lotus-ponds served as water-channels for every palace,
there were lakes of sweet, cool water for those of divine form.
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, messengers, and most beautiful Kinnarīs as well—broad-hipped, their limbs shimmering with ornaments, they were bestowers of delight. ||3 1||
At the time of bathing, women who can assume any form at will indeed sport there; men delight them there according to their desire and according to their pleasure. 32.
Agitating that river, they sing together with their beloveds;
its broad flights of stairs are fashioned from divine pearls, gems, and other precious materials.
The river named Vaivasvatī flows through the middle of the city;
its waters are divine, it is ever full, and it is adorned with swans as white as kunda flowers.
It was adorned with lotus creepers, clusters of flowers, and the Vālakhilyas; its waters were fragrant, nectar-like, pure, and resonant with the sounds of birds.

Women, appearing in their natural forms and overcome with intoxication, plunge into the ponds filled with groves of fruit and flowering trees and with bulbs, roots, and other edibles, and sport therein. (36)
Likewise, groups of maidens sing together with vocal and instrumental music and rhythmic beats in the riverbanks, gardens, and groves. (37)
At the descents and the ghats, charming men and women sport and sing with the melodies of stringed instruments and clay drums. (38)
The wind, fragrant with the scent of aguru and sandalwood, blows pleasantly through the palaces—cool, gentle, and creating a delightful aroma. (39)
Celestial palaces and vehicles that travel through the air move about upon the water and in the sky, accompanied by their beloved women.
The royal roads and dwellings were overflowing with joy, endowed with every kind of prosperity, and adorned with marketplaces and other such sites. ||41||
There are divine assembly halls and places of divine sight, as well as houses for divine dramas, dances, and songs. ||42||
Thus was seen the vast city of Yama, filled with happiness;
it is said to be like a second Vaikuṇṭha for those possessed of merit.
Then that beautiful gateway, resplendent with a golden ground,
was ten yojanas in width and twice that in length.
He painted the sky as if it were adorned on both sides by ramparts beautified by hundreds of palaces, and filled with various mechanical devices and lattices.
It was like heaven, rich in splendor, the entrance for those who perceive dharma;
it was easily accessible to the celestial sages who perform meritorious and virtuous deeds.
Right there, a gate was fashioned, possessing the luster of a mass of autumnal clouds;
therein, an entrance was created for those humans who have performed meritorious deeds. (47)
Then, there was an iron southern gate of terrifying appearance, smoke-colored and possessed of many defects. 48.
Fierce, scorching, and causing torment, it is the place where sinners enter—those who are cruel, murderers, eaters of raw flesh, and evil-minded. (49)
Indeed, for all those evils that inflict suffering upon living beings,
there was a western gate constructed there with many weapons and other materials.
Smeared with a net of fire from the *audumbara* tree and causing intense burning,
it was personally constructed by Yama for the purpose of admitting evildoers.
In that city, there was a divine assembly hall made of all kinds of jewels;
it had been constructed by Yama for the sake of those men who were devoted to their duty and asceticism.
That assembly hall is truly adorned by those who speak the truth, those who have conquered anger, and those free from greed and passion;
that assembly hall belongs to the righteous, and that assembly hall belongs to the doers of evil.
That assembly is the dispenser of justice for all the world regarding both auspicious and inauspicious deeds; it is the embodiment of the dharma for everyone. (54)
Where the reciters of the Dharma, remaining impartial and free from partiality, contemplate only the fruits [of their actions] for the benefit of the entire world; 55.
They reported according to the rules, according to the written records, and at the proper time:
Manu, Vyāsa, Atri, Āpastamba, Śukra, and Bṛhaspati. (56)
Nāciketa, Gautama, Śaṅkha, and Likhita;
Pulastya, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vahni, Vāyu, and likewise the Yugas. ||57||
Pulaha, who is devoted to his wife, as well as others who recite the Dharma,
all together with Yama, deliberate upon a remedy.
All of them were preoccupied with their duties, adorned with earrings and armlets,
and difficult to look upon due to the splendor of the crowns and other ornaments bestowed by Brahmā.
Then, on both sides of him were divine sages who discoursed on Brahman,
who were masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs, and who held truth and righteousness as their foremost principles.
And there, having seen the sages and the ancestors indeed singing ancient tales in the abode of Dharmarāja, I [listened]. (6.1)
Beside them, I beheld one who was black in color,
with large jaws, tall in stature, with hair standing erect, possessing great tusks, and terrifying to behold.
Enraged, he held a most formidable staff in his left hand,
constantly displaying the terrifying and hideous aspect of his own face.
Commanded by the King of Dharma for the sake of instruction, Kāla assumes many forms; he hears the final judgments and likewise unites embodied beings [with their results].
Likewise, there are others resembling Kāla, attendants intent on calculation; here, tens of millions of executors of the command are indeed the proclaimers of the fruits [of karma]. (65)
Properly honored by Yama with divine perfumes and ointments,
she is the destroyer of all worlds, truly terrible and consisting of torment.
For the Asuras, the sages whose wealth is penance, the Asuras and the gods alike, and even the highly powerful yogis, all fear her.
From her body arose diseases created by Time—most terrible and causing great affliction—which were intensely intent upon inflicting punishment. (68)
Just as they were seen by me, so was that most dreadful Mahākrodha seen;
he is by nature ill-behaved and exempt from old age and death. (69)
A great being, terrible in appearance, a man named Death,
was seen composed of divine splendor and endowed with all the nooses.
I also saw singers and jesters who awaken all living beings; they were knowers of the proper time, adorned with splendor and wearing fine garments. (71)
Many kinds of fevers, diseases, and likewise agonies have been seen;
they indeed take the form of women and men, and they are devourers of living beings. //72//
Women who bestow the forest fire of anger, who are observed in various forms, who possess intense wrath, who are destroyers, and who assume diverse appearances—[these are the obstacles]. ||73||
There, a cruel sound of "halahalā" was heard incessantly near Dharmarāja, intended for the purpose of withering living beings. ||74||
The Kūṣmāṇḍas, Yātudhānas, and flesh-eating Rākṣasas—those with one foot, two feet, three feet, and many feet. ||75||
Some had one arm, some two arms, some three arms, and others many arms; some had ears like spikes, some ears like winnowing baskets, and others ears like reeds.
Some had faces like lizards, while others had faces like sea-monsters.
Others had the faces of tigers and cats, with terrifyingly distorted eyes. ||77||
Carrying axes, spades, and wheels, with spears in their hands;
holding pikes, javelins, tridents, bows, and mallets in their grasp.
Others, however, were bearing swords and holding various kinds of food in their hands;
then other men were seen, adorned with every kind of beauty.
Adorned with armlets, chains, variegated crowns, and bracelets;
wearing garlands, enriched by the splendor of their garments, and gladdened by the fragrance of sweet perfumes.
Others, however, travel in vehicles drawn by horses, elephants, swans, and the like; while others are seated upon śarabhas, bulls, cranes, wheels, and peacocks. ||81||
Thus, some gentle beings were seen by me, while others were seen to be terrifying; some there were radiant, and others were entirely soiled.
Some wore fresh, bright garments, while others wore tattered rags; some were of a sattvic nature and well-disposed, while others were cruel-minded.
Others, such as Mṛṣṭavacanamādhurī and the hundred Śatamārakas, as well as Kali, Kṛṣṇā, Mahākṛtyā, and Kālī, were also beheld. ||84||
Some have the Dharma in their hands, some have fame in their hands, and others have glory in their hands;
these remain in the presence of Kṛtānta, devoted to his word.
Others are devourers of animals, devourers of men, and likewise devourers of women.
They were indeed eaten by many kinds of corpse-eaters, child-eaters, and bird-eaters. ||86||
They feed on raw flesh and devour birds; they hold lotuses in their hands and follow Yama;
they possess great fangs and are terrifying, yet they cannot be overcome by fire or water. 87.
I have seen these whose bodies are fire, whose bodies are water, and those with bodies of clay; others who are struck by weapons, and likewise others who are untouched by the wind.

For these soldiers of King Yama, when visualized as possessing supernatural powers, are seen to be equipped with weapons and wings, capable of traveling everywhere through the sky and other realms. (89)
Subjected to the power of the suppression of their vital breaths, they were gazed upon by the servants of Yama;
they were seen as objects to be seized by all, touched by all, and beheld by all.
And however many beings there are here in the cosmic egg and throughout the worlds, as well as the inherent natures of embodied creatures and their various qualities of consciousness; ||91||
Whatever qualities the insentient possess, whether they be manifest or unmanifest, and whatever manner of beings there are, both stationary and moving—[all arise] by her. ||92||

Indeed, for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon all those types of beings, those soldiers are endowed with all powers, possessed of all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis), and are the restrainers. ||93||
Moreover, they are unassailable and likewise beyond the reach of others;
O Pārtha, what more can I describe? No [such beings] exist for them.
Assuming desired forms, endowed with the power to accomplish desired ends, providing desired reasoning, they possess irresistible strength when meting out punishment. ||95||
Some indeed possess subtle bodies, while some take the form of mountains;
some assume a size equal to the cosmic egg when their functions are joined.
Some take the form of flowing rivers, some have the nature of flames;
some are as hot as the sun, and some are as cold as the Himalayas.
For indeed, they become exactly as the principle of punishment is;
I have seen them in many forms, and I have been struck with wonder. (98)

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Appearance, Form, and Capabilities of Kṛtānta, Kāla, Mṛtyu, Kiṅkaras, and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the sinners seen on the path of the southern wheel, and the city, palace, walls, and gate-towers of King Yama.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; Nāciketa beheld the torments of Yama. He spoke to all the brahmins; I shall tell you what he saw.
Nāciketa said to the twice-born: "The king who is the lord of the city of the departed was seen by me in the midst of the assembly, highly skilled in the management of many affairs. (2)
Yama likewise gave me a single bull for the sake of hospitality;
he offered me a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, and performed my worship according to the prescribed rite.
He seated me upon a golden throne adorned with flowers;
though previously he had a fierce countenance, at that moment his face became gentle.
His two eyes also became red like lotuses;
seeing him thus there, full of devotion, I felt confident.
Then, with a truly peaceful heart, he offered this praise to him:
"You are indeed the supreme and great bestower of the fruits of karma for the ancestors."
O Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the Śrāddha, O Dharmarāja, salutations be to you!
O Kālakāla, knower of karma, Lord of the Pretas, salutations be to you! (7)
O wielder of the staff, O one with the noose in hand, O embodiment of Dharma, salutations be to you!
To you who are the color of the sun and the color of black, and who consume the offerings to gods and ancestors, salutations!
Obeisance to you, O embodiment of justice, who possess both beautiful forms and even cruel forms;
neither ascetics nor sages are able to move you from your path.
Having heard this auspicious hymn of praise, King Yama said to me: "I am well-pleased; may it be well with you. Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
Then I said to him: "O Lord, show me that region;
I desire to see the torments of both the wicked and the virtuous. (11)
"I wish to see Citragupta, your chief; show him to me.
Having summoned me, Yamarāja sent me as a messenger. (12)
Seeing me with affection, Citragupta rose up toward Citragupta and, with palms joined in reverence, offered him a most cordial welcome.
He said to him, "Let the servants show him the abode of the dead, and let protection and guarding be provided for him by you. (14)
Urged by my message, the messengers hurriedly led me to Phalālaya;
listen to this terrifying sight that I beheld near the gate. (15)
The messengers of Yama bind and burn embodied beings;
they tear them apart with blows and strike them again and again. (16)
And those sinners strike them with blows from bamboo staves;
they are broken, pierced, their limbs mangled, and their backs and necks shattered. (17)
They weep piteously and terribly, yet they find no protector;
some are cooked in hell and burned in fierce fires.
They are cooked in boiling oil and likewise dissolved in caustic lye;
some are crushed in machines, from which blood flows out.
There flows the river Vaitaraṇī, which is difficult for those with evil deeds to cross;
they are impaled upon great spikes and likewise bound by their feet.
They are cast into the Vaitaraṇī river, where fanged beasts bite them;
tossed up and down by whirlpools of water, they are tormented by the waves.
Thousands are seen withering away in the wind;
other embodied beings are sinking, vomiting, and fainting.
Many are seen there who find no protector;
then others are made to ascend the Kūṭaśālmalī tree by many messengers.
They are struck with blows from swords and spears and by iron thorns;
and the kūṣmāṇḍas and yātudhānas go about crushing some of them to pieces.
The flesh-eating rākṣasas devour some and kill others;
some, having sucked the blood of others, likewise discharge them onto the ground.
Then, though they have been sucked and even consumed by the living being,
they are born again just as before, and they suck those [beings] once more.
Even as the followers of Yama say, "O sinners, protect us!
Release us!", they strike them again and again for the sake of the ripening of their sins.
Some are crushed by showers of stones, while others by showers of dust;
fleeing, they enter caves and burn.
Slain by messengers, they are roasted in a great fire while being beaten with bamboo canes;
they say to us, "Give us water! Be gracious to us! (29)
And heated water is given to them, which they drink within their hearts;
then they are burned by internal torments and cry out most terrifyingly.
Then the land of the meritorious was seen by me, where living beings, though indeed happy, were observed to be overflowing with joy. (31)
Before whom there are heaps of desired foods and edibles,
as well as the flavors of curd and milk, rice-and-pulse porridge, and milk-rice.
There were also heaps of fruits, jars and pools of drinks, and many kinds of foods—eatables, chewables, and lickables—all kept in readiness. (33)
Substances such as oil and betel for chewing shine forth;
and the divine things acquired through austerity remain for those of virtuous soul. (34)
Garlands, incense, perfumes, garments, ornaments, and furnishings—charming, lovely, and radiant—delight them as well. (35)
Adorned with every ornament, young women, having been gazed upon, served food to their beloveds while they sat upon golden seats. (36)
Others, carrying water-pots and jars, with bowls in their hands,
and others with flowers and water for the feet in their hands, fed them by the thousands.
Adorned with anklets and chains, and resonating with the beautiful sound of networks of tiny bells, they stand nearby, enchanting and ready for enjoyment.
And at the proper time, women serve those who are deeply rested—young men who are mines of beauty and virtue—and speak with sweet and melodious voices. (39)
Then the instructors and the messengers were also seen—cruel and harsh-spoken, striking and laughing. (1.359.40)
O you ungrateful ones, greedy, and always devoid of compassion; you people who delight in slandering others and who inflict suffering upon the bodies and souls of others! ||41||
When worldly wealth was available, things that are easily obtained—water, wood, and delicious food—were not given away; thus, happiness has come to me. (42)
Therefore, you have indeed become subject to execution here by the servants of Yama;
having brought about the exhaustion of your karma, may you be liberated and go to the earth. ||43||
Those born into impoverished families must not commit sin again;
they should practice merit correctly, for it is through merit that one enjoys heaven. (44)
Therefore, becoming devoted to truth, compassionate, and very righteous, may they go to the supreme station or into a great family on earth. (45)
Through devotion and the worship of Kṛṣṇa, the supreme goal will be attained;
or else, you shall obtain the opulent heaven of beautiful women.
Thus I clearly heard that excellent instruction there;
nevertheless, my servants led me further to another location. (47)
Wherein there is piercing, striking, crushing, and likewise cutting, grinding, splitting, and burning like refuse and the like. (48)
Indeed, I have seen that which causes terror to living beings who are sinful;
yet, because my heart is moistened with compassion, I do not venture to describe it. (49)
Nevertheless, because of my persistent insistence, I shall speak further:
there, the entire surface of the earth is covered with iron thorns. (1.359.50)
It was uneven, smeared with poison, pervaded by fire, and filled with darkness;
moreover, there were those here whose feet were severed, and whose hands and necks were cut off.
Those of evil conduct, though possessing beautiful forms, are cast down by the servants of Yama; and women in the form of *kṛtyā* spirits await those who indulge in sexual misconduct.
They cast those who have arrived onto a stone surface heated by fire;
many wicked ones suffer there and find no protector. (53)
Then I saw others being devoured from the soles of their feet to the tops of their heads by fierce dogs, crying out again and again.
Then I saw others as well—those with large fangs and emaciated bellies—who, hungry and thirsty, were being tormented by those needle-mouthed beings. (55)
Neither food nor drinkable things meet [with her], not even water;
for this Kṛtyakā is a woman made of the essence of iron, heated by fire. 56.
There she embraces the man, and as he runs away, she runs after him;
she says, "I am indeed your sister, for I am the wife of your son. (57)
"You are my maternal aunt, my paternal aunt, and my maternal uncle's wife;
I am indeed your teacher's wife and your daughter, yet previously I was forcibly violated by you. (58)
"O sinner, this manhood is the fruit of your evil deeds; you shall not be released from your misdeed.
I shall burn you and I shall kill you! Why do you run so far away? (59)
They cause the sinners to hear [the truth], awaken them, and rush upon them;
having tormented the evil-souled one, they utterly crush that most cruel being.
"Why do you cry, O evildoer? Make love with me while you embrace me!
Wherever you may run, I shall not let go of you, you adulterer! (6.1)
Having seen this curiosity, young women repeatedly strike such men with blows from iron rods and other weapons. (62)
Then others were seen suffering, beaten with sticks and mallets, and [attacked] by tigers, lions, jackals, and the like, as well as by rākṣasas, donkeys, and dogs. (63)
They were being devoured by beasts of prey, crows, vultures, and lizards;
furthermore, others were seen by me torn apart and split asunder. (64)
In the Asita forest and the Jvālāvana forest, they have been set ablaze by messengers;
cut, burned, struck, and tormented, they cry out.
Then birds with iron beaks, as well as dogs and other carnivorous,
predatory beasts such as tigers, angrily devoured them.
In Ṛkṣadvīpa, I saw some who were torn apart by the bears of Yama, others whose limbs were crushed by mallets, and still others impaled upon spikes. (67)
Others were seen by me cast by me into ponds, lakes, and rivers, as well as into pools of blood, wells, and lotus-pools. (68)
Sinners were seen smelling the stench of putrid flesh, worms, insects, and filth in the lakes, while they themselves sank into them. (69)
Thus pulverized by rains of bones, stones, and blood, they ran and leaped about, crying out, "Alas! We are destroyed! (1.359.70).
There I heard those crying out piteously—men who were imprisoned, pierced, bound to massive pillars, and some even suspended by hanging. (71)
Others were crushed by rocks and hacked to pieces by weapons;
I indeed saw them in great suffering and heard their terrible wailing. (72)
Then, by means of messengers, the eight terrible hells were shown to him:
Tapta, Mahātapta, and both Mahāraurava and Raurava.
Saptatāla, Kālasūtra, Tāmisra, and Andhatāmisraka;
in the first [hell] there is the first degree of suffering, while in the second it is double.
In the third [house], the suffering is threefold; in the fourth, it is fourfold;
in the fifth, fivefold; and in the sixth, the suffering is sixfold. (75)
In the seventh [hell], the suffering is sevenfold; in the eighth, it is eightfold. For those who are suffering there, the pain is more painful than pain itself.
In this world there is only suffering, not happiness; suffering increases through sufferings.
There is no means whatsoever by which even a small amount of happiness might arise. (77)
In sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, evildoers are tormented by physical and mental sufferings that lead to the end of misery.
The ground was covered with glowing, heated iron thorns;
the sky was filled with flocks of birds whose tongues were like flames.
Hunger, thirst, heat, and even excessive heat;
cold, and even extreme cold; and wind mingled with flames—[these are the sufferings]. (1.359.80)
Desiring to drink water, he is led by messengers to a warm lake;
he gazes at it, runs toward it to drink, drinks, and then burns from within. (81)
Rākṣasas, fish, and other creatures, having seized and torn away his cooked meats, eat them and laugh.
Then they are indeed thrown by them into a great lake of alkaline water;
the Kṣārahūtas devour them, and they are born again with flesh.
In the terrifying Kumbhīpāka hell, which is heated by a pit of dried cow-dung,
they tear out the well-cooked flesh from the bodies of embodied beings, piece by piece.
"Those who relish flavors devour [the flesh] after grinding it with their teeth," I saw such sinful beings crying out nearby. (85)
Then, those who were seen in Śṛṅgāṭakasthalī with its intensely heated sands are burned on that ground, cut, and pierced by thorns.
The sinners are split apart, cast down, and tormented by the messengers of Yama; they are dragged along, slaughtered, and indeed torn limb from limb. (87)
Dark, brindled dogs devour them, as do snakes and scorpions;
furthermore, another hell was seen by me, called Kūṭaśālmali.
There, sinners are dragged about until nothing but their bones remain;
there, living beings are crushed and ground to powder by fierce messengers.
With their limbs severed in every part of their bodies, they experience intense suffering;
then another river was seen by me, consisting of mud and sand.
And there is a river with a torrent of blazing fire, filled with fiery serpents and crocodiles, and completely pervaded by fiery fish; yet mortals are carried across it.
Likewise, the river Vaitaraṇī was seen, filled with salty mud, with skin, flesh, and bones for its mire, and marrow, saliva, and blood for its waters. (92)
There are creatures with diamond-like fangs and claws, and those with diamond-like tongues;
there are also highly venomous crocodiles and fish that can pierce bone. (93)
In that place, they devour, swallow, and vomit up their sins;
yet those sinners become fleshly once again, just as before. (94)
Then, on the ground in front, he saw an empty house with a deep cavity; there, rats with adamantine teeth and venom were devouring them. (95)
Their limbs were devoured by rats until only their bones remained;
yet, when touched again by the wind, they became fleshy once more.
Then, ahead of them, they saw a forest of rough trees inhabited by fierce birds, where even those perched upon the trees were devoured by flesh-eating fowl. (97)
Fleshless, skinless, and bone-like, likewise devoid of the network of veins,
and without eyes or ears, the sinner is made thus by those with sharp beaks.
Then, in front of me, I saw a great, deep-red banyan tree,
with vajra-wood that was indeed unburnable, joined by thousands of swings.
That which is below is indeed the Yama-cullī, ten yojanas in width and three yojanas deep; it is perpetually ablaze.
Thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of hungry ghosts (pretas) are constantly cast into this place by the Rākṣasas, the servants of Yama.
Having bound the sinner upside down within the intermediate space by means of a cord attached to the branch of a banyan tree, they roast him and devour him.
Some throw them into cauldrons, and some even eat them roasted;
likewise, the servants of Yama and the pretas taste them with great delight.
From the belly of Cullī flows the swift river named Śakunikā;
carrying fat and marrow, it flows there where they cast the sinners.
Then, having seen those seven extremely fierce places of torment,
each one difficult to cross and terrible, the sinner experiences them in due order.
There are ten great *śūla* hells and thirteen *kumbhīpāka* hells;
there, they are indeed roasted, impaled upon spikes heated by fire.
In a dry, smoke-filled well, he hangs with his head downward;
likewise, he is set ablaze and cooked in a cauldron of boiling oil.
Cast into a pit of dried cow-dung, they are cooked by the fire of their own fat;
thus have I seen living beings being roasted and severely scorched.
Moreover, the river Yama was seen, flowing with molten lead;
having plunged into it, living beings who are evildoers are indeed cooked there.
Then a long pond was seen, with cool waters and a cool forest, where one could drink the cool water and obtain rest for a moment. (1.359.1) 10.
There, Yami, the sister of Yama, indeed provides food and drink;
there also is a stone named Śūlabhra, extending for a hundred yojanas.
For I have seen Mount Parvata; there the cloud rains, living beings sink there, and then they indeed emerge from it.
Then the Śṛṅgāraka forest was seen, filled with gadflies and mosquitoes;
and whoever saw or touched a sinner there was indeed born in the form of a worm. || 113 ||
Then another stage was seen, wherein he beheld his kinsmen—
his mother, father, sons, wives, and likewise beloved people.
Being beaten before them, he then cries out in terror,
struck by clubs, mallets, staffs, knees, and likewise by bamboo poles.
With fists, clubs, whips, chains, and so forth—then another state is seen that bestows the condition of a stationary preta. (116)
Having gone there, the deceased being proceeds to whatever stationary state it may be;
however, for sixty thousand years, it experiences the condition of a beast.
Thereafter, he is born from sweat, and from that, he is born as a bird; then, having entered the womb of a cow, he becomes a human being once again. || 1.18 ||
Just as the wheel of saṃsāra is indeed marked with its various features,
so too, after undergoing those torments, one is born among the Brahmins and other castes.
Thus far indeed was it seen by me, as shown by the messengers of Yama;
exhausted, the messengers went with me to Citragupta.

Thus ends the three hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Nāciketa’s Praise of King Yama in the Southern Wheel, the Command of King Yama to Behold the Various Hells, the Observation of the Torments of Painful Infernos, the Description of Those Torments, and the Return of the Messengers Accompanied by Nāciketa to Citragupta," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate what was seen by Nāciketa in the house of Citragupta; Nāciketa spoke thus to them.
"Let all the Brahmins listen in the courtyard of Citragupta;
whatever was seen by me there, I shall relate all of that to you. (2)
Commanded by Citragupta, the Rākṣasas named Mandehas and other messengers were informed to carry out the torments of those who have performed [evil] deeds.
Assuming various forms, these fierce beings, armed and flesh-eaters—O heroes Mandehakas and likewise messengers endowed with valor! (4)
Let them bind the living beings, seize the sinners for the sake of torment;
let them kill, devour, and crush them according to their deeds.
Thus commanded, those Rākṣasas and messengers, capable of changing their forms at will,
quickly prepared themselves— terrible elephants and those in the form of lions.
They take the forms of tigers, jackals, buffaloes, serpents, and scorpions;
they assume the shapes of vultures, hawks, hooded snakes, bears, donkeys, and the like.
Those messengers of terrible prowess, with spears and javelins in their hands, carry clubs and iron-tipped missiles; they are equipped with sharp-edged spears, swords, and scimitars.
"Break! Cut! Seize! so cry those with blood-red eyes;
impelled by Citragupta, the Mandehas devour and strike.
There are thousands of diseases, tens of thousands of messengers,
and thousands of fevers, Kālamuṇḍas, and Keṃkarākṣas.
They began to perform the crushing of the sinners, those who had committed evil deeds,
by the command of Citragupta as instructed by Dharmarāja.
Some, deserving punishment according to their deserts, were bound by the Rākṣasas with various bonds;
some were scorched by fire and others were gnawed by the fangs [of beasts].
Dogs, beasts of prey, and wild animals devour those evil-minded ones who are of wicked conduct, devoted to sin, merciless, and sinful in heart. (13)
Citragupta stands there and proclaims the legal judgments regarding the fevers, as well as the messengers and the Rākṣasas; indeed, I have heard this directly with my own ears.
Having impaled the killer of a father and the killer of a cow upon a śālmali tree, let the messengers tear them apart with very sharp thorns; do not delay! (15)
Let these birds cook this lowest of men in a cooking pot;
as for other animals and creatures, let them roast him in a cauldron of boiling oil. (16)
Having cast them onto a heated copper floor and into a blazing fire,
let them roast this scorcher of living beings according to his own deeds.
Let them cast the one who steals his bed or seat, as well as the one who sets fire [to his dwelling],
into the Vaitaraṇī river, and thereafter cast them into fire.
May they indeed cause him to fall, destroying the sacred fords, the holy fields, and the field of Dharma;
may they pierce his vital organs with stakes heated by fire.
Let fire-stakes be driven into the ears of this slanderer and false witness, and into the tongue of this reviler.
"Indeed, let this fraudulent priest—a rogue, a cheat, and a hypocrite—be bound to a stake in prison, and let him be given nothing at all. (21)
May the tongue of the speaker of wicked falsehood be cut off; may the violator, through the force of lust and delusion, be severed by the edge of a sword.
Having cut away the mark of evil, let caustic alkali and fire be applied;
by means of this sixfold treatment, many people have been cured of their inheritance-disease. (23)
Let them, for the sake of their own interests, destroy him with arrows—
him who is a thief of gold, ungrateful, and the destroyer of his father.
"Having crushed this Brahmin who abducted the maiden with mallets, let them roast him in alkaline fire! Let the Kṛtyās devour him swiftly! (25)
May tigers with sharp fangs devour the treacherous Brahmin;
may they cook him, who pierces the vital organs, in various ways in their ovens. (26)
May they release from the Karkaṭa hells those who neglect the worship of gods and fire, those who slay heroes, those who revile the gods, and those who destroy the property of the gods.
"Let them cast this wretched twice-born man into a heated lake—he who performs sacrifices for all comers, who refuses to give gifts, and who sells the Dharma! (28)
Let them strike with most terrible punishments the one who steals their water or food—using bamboo staves, whips, iron rods, and clubs. (29)
Water and food must never be given to him;
having gained his trust, let them cook the killer in a great fire.
Let them also cause him who has stolen the property of the gods to undergo punishment,
as well as those who kill the king, those who kill their teacher, and those who kill children.
Let them afflict with the disease of royal consumption; let them cast [the sinner] into the mountain cave.
Let them indeed cause the slayer of a woman to be executed at the Kūṭaśālmalī tree.
"Let the followers of Yama devour that meat-eater for a hundred years;
thereafter, let that lowest of men be cooked in terrible hells. (33)
Then, having attained human birth, let him die repeatedly while still in the womb;
having died ten times in the womb, let him be born as one who partakes in suffering.
"Let this betrayer of his friend's trust be constantly tormented there by the afflictions of hunger and disease, and let him be crushed by a machine. (35)
Then let him burn in a terrible fire for two hundred years;
thereafter, having entered the womb of a dog, let him be afflicted by disease forever. (36)
Then, may this man, whose body is afflicted by disease, be born [as such];
may he who steals juices and he who steals salt and other things be born as a worm.
"May he be born as a dung-worm for five hundred years;
thereafter, may he become a bird, and after that, a wolf in a waterless place. (38)
Let them heat this giver of fire in the flames again and again;
thereafter he shall be a deer for a hundred years, and then a worm for a hundred years.
Then, joined with extreme suffering, let this man be born as one who feels revulsion;
and let those who steal the property of others fall into the Raurava hell.
Having been thoroughly cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells, let them be cast into a family of donkeys;
thereafter, into a family of pigs due to their impurity, and then into a family of thieves among men.
There, those overwhelmed by suffering indeed experience the results of their deeds; having bound this person who harms others with his head downward to a tree, they make him eat it.
"Let them cook him with fire and cast him into births as hunters;
then, when a hundred years have passed, let the followers of Yama release him. (43)
Having crushed the slanderer with the edge of a vajra and cast him into a boat,
they should then throw him into the womb of a pig, and thereafter into the births of mongooses.
Cast this liar, this stealer of fields, and this false witness into the Andhatāmisra hell, and thereafter into the wombs of animals and trees.
Having obtained birth according to their karma, may they be born again and again among humans as deaf, blind, mute, one-eyed, and afflicted by disease. 46.
"Having bound this usurper of land and fields, cook him;
thereafter, let that wicked man be born as a hungry cat. (47)
May these wicked fowlers be struck down by dogs and fierce vultures,
and thereafter may they be cast into the family of cocks.
May they cast this evildoer into the wombs of gadflies and mosquitoes;
may the buffaloes surely slaughter this sinful swineherd. (49)
Then, having passed successively through the wombs of a pig, a buffalo, a cock, a hare, and a jackal, let him become food there.
"Then let this evil-souled one become a hunter dwelling in the forest;
furthermore, let them repeatedly roast the giver of leftover food with glowing coals. (51)
May those women who have violated their conduct, who are of evil character, and who commit offenses against their husbands, embrace seven iron men on all sides. (52)
"May she become a distressed female dog, and then a miserable sow;
afterwards, having obtained birth as a maidservant, may she become one who has many enjoyments. (53)
"By this man many servants have been deceived and made miserable;
therefore, cast him into the Raurava hell, which is difficult to approach. (54)
Afterwards, may he be born into a cruel species such as a serpent and the like;
then in a pig, a jackal, a crane, a ram, and a horse. (55)
Having been born again and again among donkeys and the like, in the species of dogs and in the species of bulls,
he shall indeed then be born in the class of slaves, for this [existence] is most miserable.
"O Brahmins, all of this has been heard and seen by me directly;
furthermore, Citragupta assigned other sins as well to them. (57)
For those who are devoid of religious vows and the like, and who follow the side of evil,
their residence shall be for a thousand years in the grasp of Yama’s servants.
May the messengers of Yama indeed inflict such [torments] upon those who take pleasure in violence, as well as upon informers, those who corrupt affairs, and those who betray their gurus. (59)
Let the soldiers perform the ripening in fire for those who set the forest fires,
and then cause them to be impelled into a womb within a human being.
Due to their own sins, they will have short lifespans and be afflicted by disease;
they will die even in the womb, or else infants will perish.
Some who have not yet reached youth will die as destroyers,
by means of a wooden noose, a weapon-noose, or in wind, fire, or water.
By falling, they will likewise meet their destruction, or by poison;
as well as the suffering of killing mother and father, and the taking of life.
Those who inflict harm, as well as killers, smiths, artisans, ditch-diggers, and those who injure living beings, shall suffer misery from their own kinsmen. (64)
Those who destroy the urine and testicles, those who administer poison, those who set cities on fire, those who construct cages, and those who strike with spears and other weapons; ||65||
Those who are slanderous, quarrelsome, and those who bring about false accusations;
those who cause the destruction of livestock, those who terrify living beings, and those who are murderers. (66)
May they behold themselves again and again in the terrible hells undergoing torments;
and upon the exhaustion of their karma, may they be born with deficient limbs.
There, the poor suffer the cutting off of their ears,
as well as the cutting off of their noses and the cutting off of their hands and feet, on account of their past actions.
May they always experience mental and physical suffering;
may they have throbbing pain in their heads and ailments in their bellies.
They were dull-witted, blind, deaf, mute, lame, and crawling on their hands; some had a withered arm, others were one-eyed, those with deformed nails, and those afflicted by disease. (1.360.70)

Hunchbacks, the lame, the deformed, those with swollen feet, pot-bellied men, those suffering from trickling leprosy, those with vitiligo, those with testicular hernias, and those devoid of testicles. (71)

Those afflicted by urinary disorders and diabetes, those suffering from pain in the female reproductive organs and the eyes, those with pain in the breath, heart, and private parts, and those suffering from diseases such as splenic enlargement and abdominal tumors; ||72||
May they exist in human form as enjoyers of the fruits of their own karma;
may the followers of Yama cause those cruel liars to undergo their retribution.
The messengers [carry away] those who are harsh, abusive, malicious, and likewise bitter;
those who cause the depletion of affection, who are cruel, who strike at the vital points, and who corrupt speech. (74)
Let those lowest of men—who give abuse, who are cruel, shameless, deceitful, merciless, envious, jealous, and violent—be bound. (75)
Then, let them indeed be cast among the animals, insects, birds, and beasts;
thereafter, let them exist in human form as destroyers of the world.
Despised, ignorant, ruined in mind, and devoid of reputation;
unworthy of honor and undeserving, they were held in contempt even by their own kin. ||77||
Causing hatred in the world, loathsome, and rejected by friends and kinsmen, they are consumers of false accusations and [victims] of weapons such as the vajra and poisons. (78)
"May these false accusations and defamations come to naught.
Then, much else was heard there that had been spoken by Citragupta.
He who commits robbery, assault, and the taking of property by deceit, and those who perform acts of theft and forcible seizures; ||| 1.360.80 ||
Those who eat the flesh of dogs, those who subsist on the shadow of the king, and those who oppress all subjects—those are the most wicked sinners among men. ||81||
Those who mimic the fraudulent purchase of gold, gems, pearls, and the like; those who are ungrateful at the proper time; and those who are devoted solely to their own self-interest. (82)
[They are] those that destroy spirits, ghosts, and malevolent spells; likewise, those that cause the separation of the bodily constituents;
those that steal the purpose of ritual deposits; and likewise, those that cause the delusion of mantras and so forth. ||83||
May those who provide water at drinking stations cause the kings who inflict suffering upon the wretched, the poor, the miserable, and those dependent on others to suffer for a long time. (84)
Let them be cast into a great pit of darkness filled with scorpions;
when their karma is exhausted, let them be joined there with common folk.
Where there is fear of thieves, fear of water and hunger, fear of the king, great fear of calamities, fear of severe afflictions, and likewise fear of disease; ||86||
Where the people possess the intellect of rogues and the city is inhabited by the deceitful, there calamities never abandon it for even a moment. (87)
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, hear again another thing that I have heard:
"May these evildoers be born where there is suffering. (88)
Afflicted by manifold sufferings even while dwelling in the womb, they are born with only one hand or two hands, or with limbs severed and deformed bellies. (89)

Those who suffer from the pain of diseased veins, those with deficient limbs, those afflicted by wind-related diseases, those who are constantly wailing, those bereft of wives, and those who are sexually promiscuous; ||1.360.90||
Childless and wretched, their children crying out with terrifying sounds, they eat the remnants of others' meals and are utterly overwhelmed by intense agonies. (91)
Inferior in form, in qualities, in strength, and likewise in conduct—even to your servants, let them be as mere blades of grass. (92)
Where the king’s punishment is constant—whether execution or severe hardship—there all undertakings meet with ruin due to the distress caused by rain and cold. (93)
They shall share in ill repute and, even when it is auspicious, they shall share in what is inauspicious;
indeed, even during a good rain, the rain shall avoid their fields. (94)
Wherever a thunderbolt might fall, even that field would be destroyed;
yet for those who possess the *bhālaka*, there is neither happiness nor death, but only suffering. (95)
Let those evil ones, such as thieves and others who cause suffering to the world, remain there;
but now, let there be torment for those who have forcibly attached themselves to wives and other [possessions]. (96)
Listen, O soldiers, to where those sinners must indeed be cast:
those who are lustful and who have forcibly violated the bodies of animals and humans. (97)
Or those who dwell as lustful women, corrupting the practice of Dharma; or those who, having used force or intimidation, behave improperly toward women of noble family. (98)
May those who cause the intermixture of castes be repeatedly cast into fire;
may they be made to cook there for many thousands of years. 99.

May they be cast into human existence where they are born from mixed wombs— such as courtesans, those who have transgressed their vows, impostors, and those conceived through multiple acts of intercourse.
They are captives to women, destroyers of women, dressed as women, sporting with women;
they are slaves to women, objects of women’s enjoyment, possessed of feminine natures, and performing the acts of women. || 101 ||
Let people cast those who are loathsome to behold here and there;
let even women, possessing that same nature, likewise fall into suffering.
"Thus I have heard everything that Naciketas said to them;
thus, O Lakṣmī, has the instruction of Citragupta been told to you."

Thus ends the three hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Torment of Hellish Beings by the Rākṣasas, such as Mandeha and others, through Various Tortures at the Command of Citragupta for the Purpose of Inflicting Punishment upon Sinners in the Yāmya-cakra," within the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the instruction of Citragupta,
and furthermore, that which was spoken by Nāciketa to them.
"Let the messengers seize him quickly so that time does not pass by. What compassion is shown in this matter? Seize him and kill him without delay! || 2 ||
One should not feel shame; do not stand with faces turned away.
Why do you not go with speed? Do not be procrastinators.
Go quickly to that very place and bring them back with all haste;
you must not show any incapacity, nor should your service be considered as a matter of mere calculation.
Neither marriage, nor the state of an ascetic, nor lifelong celibacy,
nor even dalliance with a new wife constitutes true devotion to a husband or the virtue of a faithful wife.
Whether it be the state of being virtuous or childhood, the state of giving gifts or the stability of passion;
whether it be the affairs of state, the assembly hall, travel through the sky, or worship—(all these are attained).
Do not let anything delay you so that time may not pass;
bring him here quickly indeed, according to the command of his duty.
"Quickly become a serpent, and you too become a tiger; become a reptile, a crocodile in the water, or even a tiny worm. (8)
Become the form of disease, and also become dysentery;
furthermore, become vomiting, ear-disease, and cholera.
May fever become the disease of the wind of worldly existence, and may you become dropsy;
may you become epilepsy, insanity, constipation, and delusion.
"Run, run with speed; all of you go without delay!
According to what is right, according to their karma, and according to the time, [lead] these embodied beings."
Let them overpower him, let them emaciate him, let them bring him under their control without delay;
let them kill him at the end of his lifespan, so that death does not arrive prematurely. 1-2.
Whether he is awake, asleep, unconscious, or in deep sleep,
act according to what must be said so that the proper time does not pass.
Just as Rudra commands, just as the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa,
just as Brahmā and Dharmarāja, so too does the Lord Citragupta.
Thus commands Citragupta, and so they proceed;
the messengers of Yama bring the embodied beings into his presence.
Having observed their deeds, Yama and Citragupta indeed mete out punishment there; I shall relate that which I have heard. (16)
"Let this meritorious donor go to the heaven of the lords of the earth;
let him indeed become a tree and be born as a sanctuary for animals. (17)
"Let this Nāga indeed attain the supreme goal;
let him who has insulted his own ancestors go to a terrible hell. (18)
"Indeed, let them exhaust this man—who causes the abandonment of his wife—in the Raurava hell;
let these others be released, freed from their sins. (1.9)
May those most righteous ones, having dwelt for many kalpas in heaven,
go to birth as humans upon this earth which abounds in every prosperity.
Having met their end for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or for the sake of the kingdom,
let them dispatch [this message] to Śakra in Amarāvatī without delay.
May his residence there for one kalpa bring him happiness;
for he is devoted to giving much and is compassionate toward all living beings.
Let them worship him with perfumes and garlands and present him with offerings;
let him be fanned with yak-tail whisks, and let a vehicle be provided for him. (23)
May he travel by means of a celestial vehicle to the city of Indra;
honored by the sounding of conchs and trumpets, may he obtain happiness. (24)
"May this man go to the world of the virtuous, the auspicious abode of the renowned;
through his virtues, such as his service and other merits, may he indeed possess the lifespan of Indra in the third heaven."
May this giver of jewels and gold indeed go to the world of the Aśvins;
may this performer of the gift of abundant food indeed proceed to the world of Śiva.
The giver of sweet food and milk, the milker of cows for the purpose of charity,
and the donor of gold and clothing— these three [reside] in heaven for thirty million years.
Let it be that this best of sages remains here on earth even after passing away;
let him, as one who has gratified his ancestors, indeed go to Satyaloka.
Bestowing all desires and devoted to the welfare of all beings, this giver of the earth shall indeed go to the third heaven for a very long time. (29)
Thus may those who have performed meritorious deeds go to the heavens that grant their desired enjoyments;
and may those who have committed evil deeds indeed go downward to the hells, which are a mass of afflictions.
Thus have I heard, O Brahmins, and the arising of its fruit has also been heard;
I shall relate all of that, so listen with concentrated minds.
This man is one who honors guests, shows compassion toward all living beings, provides food equally to all, and eats only what remains as his portion. (32)
May he go to the realm of Vairāja, endowed with all fortune and happiness;
the Gandharvas shall sing of him there, and likewise the Apsarases shall dance at his arrival.
"Let a divine seat be given; let a vehicle that travels through the sky be given;
whatever desires one may wish for, let them be granted at my command. (34)

Let them indeed bestow upon him those desiring heaven, those desiring the ancestors, those desiring truth, and those singing the Virāj hymns, along with male servants, female servants, and household furnishings.
By him were given gifts such as jewels, gold, and cows;
buffaloes, elephants, and horses; fields, and gardens and groves. (36)
"Since there have been many gifts of maidens and gifts of food here, let that illustrious one be observed as he enjoys them in heaven along with his followers. (37)
Until celestial chariots arrived from heaven in their entirety; then, with his followers and retinue, he departed in those most excellent vehicles.
May he go to the abode of the gods, well-honored by the deities; may that meritorious one rejoice right there for as long as heaven endures. (39)
Then let them honor this performer of sacrifice, the giver of many daughters, with all their desires; may he indeed attain the station of Viṣṇu.
"Let this meritorious man, who is compassionate toward all beings, enjoy himself there for a thousand times ten thousand years; let his worship be performed. (41)
May he remain in heaven like a god for ten thousand divine years;
furthermore, let him possess the parasol, the alms-bowl, and likewise the robe bestowed by him.
Offer him sandals, foods, and worship;
let this man become a Vidyādhara, a marvel with hands like lotuses. (43)
May these four great lotuses remain forever in heaven, [as a reward] for this milk, curd, and ghee given by him to the helpless and the wretched. (44)
"Lead him to the flavorful heaven; offer him worship, and present him with vessels filled with cow's milk. (45)
Having given [this] to his own kinsmen and having drunk [it] with his own people and relatives, let him go to the heaven of Anasūyā and rejoice there for ten million years. ||46||
Constantly served by many beautiful women, may this immortal one always dwell in the Golokas, provided with all objects of enjoyment. (47)
This person is a giver of the essence of sugarcane, and indeed this one is a giver of the essence of milk;
likewise, he is a giver of the essence of food, as well as a giver of garments and ornaments.
The giver of a house and land, and the provider of all household utensils,
shall be led to the Goloka worlds, accompanied by the bull-vehicle.
There dwell goddesses who embody all the deities as their attendants;
auspicious, they hold the nectar of immortality and serve [him] day and night.
Curd, milk, ghee, nourishment, the purifier, the sacred ford, and nectar—through curd the gods and others are satisfied, while through milk Maheśvara is satisfied. ||51||
Pāvaka is always pleased by ghee, and Pitāmaha by milk-rice;
by giving these even once, they are gratified for thirteen years.
By drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
The product of the cow is supremely pure, for cows are indeed deities worthy of sacrifice.
The Marut gods reside in the tamed parts; Sarasvatī is in the tongue;
the Gandharvas are in the middle of the hooves; and the Pannagas are in the tips of the hooves. (54)
The objects to be accomplished reside in all his joints; the moon and sun are in his eyes;
the constellations are in his hump; and Dharma is established in his tail.
All sacred fords reside in his downward breath; Lakṣmī dwells in his excrement;
the goddess Jāhnavī is in his urine; and the oceans are in his breasts.
The sages reside in the pores of his skin, while the Vidyādharas dwell in his body hairs;
Vaikuṇṭha itself is in his skin, and the two paths [of inhalation and exhalation] are at his sides.
Forgiveness, fortitude, peace, nourishment, growth, memory, intelligence, wisdom, modesty, physical splendor, fame, learning, tranquility, and progeny—[these are the attendants]. ||58||
The wives of Dharma, such as Kriyā, Utkarṣiṇī, and others, are established among cows;
where there are cows, there are the gods, Lakṣmī, and Dharma as protectors. (59)
The giver of a cow obtains everything: palaces, mansions, young women, male and female servants, beds, seats, and drinks. (1.361.60)
Objects of enjoyment, stores of drinks, houses, edibles, and meals; horses, elephants, vehicles, mounts, and gardens.
O followers, by the command of Citragupta, deliver this giver of cows, as well as this giver of mangoes and the donor of a garden! 62.
"By giving away the beautiful Tāmravaṇa forest and the excellent, divine maiden Parī," thus was it heard in many ways there, and it was seen as well.
As he went from house to house and from place to place,
he experienced what was more painful than pain and likewise what was more pleasant than pleasure.
The destruction of karma and the great success of karma have both been observed by me;
therefore, O Blessed One, I am here in this assembly of the King of Dharma.
Just then, Nārada, radiant with splendor, arrived there;
Yamarāja, having honored him, seated him upon a throne.
They said, "We are all purified, and this land has been purified by your arrival.
O Blessed One, tell us what must be done, or by whom it must be done. (67)
Having heard this, Nārada said: "Sever my great doubt:
by what means do they attain immortality—through charity or through religious observance? (68)
By means of what—whether through vows, austerity, recitation, or worship—do people attain incomparable prosperity, fame, and an eternal station? (69)
By what means do people go to the most wicked hell, which is censured by the world?
Tell me everything in accordance with reality; it will be for your supreme benefit.
King Yama said to him in the hearing of those present there:
"By means of dharma, people go to heaven, which is earned through merit. (71)
But through unrighteousness, O Nārada, one goes to hells and various kinds of bonds; however, one who has performed the fire-sacrifice never at any time goes to the Naraka hell.
One who bestows land becomes possessed of sons, heroic, and proficient in the Vedas and Shastras;
one becomes endowed with knowledge, a follower of the path of truth, and devoted to his wife, while a devoted wife likewise attains these qualities. (73)
Embodied beings who are free from deceit and hypocrisy, devoted to their masters, non-violent, ungratefulness-free, and firmly established in celibacy and other virtues; ||74||
They are generous, devoted to the twice-born, and devoted to their ancestors; they are virtuous, servants of the righteous, free from adultery, and compassionate. (75)
Those who know the Self of all beings never go to hells—those places filled with torment, full of suffering, inhabited by the most wicked, and shrouded in darkness. (76)
Those people here who possess knowledge, those who have attained supreme learning, and those who, though indifferent, have been slain for the sake of their master—[all these] do not depart. (77)
Those who are devoted to the welfare of all, who are intent on service, and who are indeed givers—specifically those who perform the gifts of sesame seeds, cows, land, gold, and maidens; ||78||
Those who give food and water, as well as those who organize sacrificial sessions (satra), those who perform sacrifices, the virtuous, and those who observe the Cāturmāsya vows; ||79||
Those who observe vows such as the Kārtika-vrata, who abide by the commands of their guru, who possess virtues such as silence, and who constantly engage in the study of sacred texts; ||1.361.8||
