They were self-controlled, gentle, and established in their own true nature; likewise, through the conquest of the senses, they had withdrawn from all desires, were free from longing, and had mastered their faculties.
They do not go to the hells and they attain immortality;
indeed, through devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they truly attain immortality.

Through the granting of knowledge and fearlessness, through the rule of lifelong commitment, through the vow of Brahman, and through the austerity of the self-nature of knowledge, [one attains] Hari by the recitation of "Oṃ. (83)
Indeed, through the worship of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, one attains eternal immortality;
for service to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa bestows the fortune of Lakṣmī. (84)
Service to the virtuous and service to cows indeed bestow fame and a high station; however, through an action censured by the world, one goes to a censured state.
Through austerity heaven is attained; through austerity fame is attained;
indeed, longevity and enjoyments come about through austerity alone. (86)
Through austerity, everything is attained: knowledge, discernment, health, beauty, good fortune, wealth, a wife, sons, and servants. (87)
Thus, through silence one attains perfection of speech; from contentment comes supreme happiness;
through giving come enjoyments; and through celibacy, long life. (88)

Through non-violence comes freedom from agitation; through initiation, birth in a noble family; for one who subsists on fruits and roots, there is sovereignty; and for one who subsists on leaves, there is heaven. (89)
Those who subsist on milk go to heaven; those who give wealth attain prosperity;
through service to the guru and the giving of ancestral offerings (śrāddha), one attains a virtuous lineage.
By giving milk and other products, cows and the like become the bed of grass for those who sleep upon it;
by performing the three daily ablutions oneself, one becomes a Brahmin; and by offering water, one shares in the eight worlds.
The performer of sacrifice goes to heaven and rejoices in good fortune;
through the gift of food, one obtains food, intelligence, memory, and the celestial realm.
Through the gift of an umbrella one obtains sovereignty; through the gift of a house, houses and the like;
and through the gift of a chariot or vehicle, one becomes possessed of vehicles and mounts. (93)
The giver of clothing shall obtain beautiful ornaments, wealth, and sons;
the giver of water indeed attains eternal satisfaction in heaven. (94)
Through the gift of food, drink, and so forth, one is well-satisfied with the enjoyments of desire;
the giver of trees bearing flowers, fragrance, and fruit possesses a home like a jewel among women. (95)
He who gives beds, ointments, perfumes, collyrium, incense, garlands, a couch, a garden, and fruit-bearing trees; ||96||
He attains a home abounding in women and filled with elephants and horses;
and the giver of incense and lamps attains equality with the Vasu gods.
By the gift of an elephant, a cow, and a bull, eternal heaven is attained;
by the gift of clarified butter, one is born indeed radiant and delicate.
By the gift of oil, one indeed becomes smooth and charming;
by giving honey, sweet things, sugar, and so forth, one becomes a master of a satisfied household. (99)
By the gift of a lamp one becomes radiant; by milk-rice, the body becomes firm;
and from kṛsarā rice, one attains an oily and gentle disposition as well as beauty of form.
Through fruits one obtains a son, and through flowers, good fortune;
likewise, through chariots one obtains a divine celestial vehicle (vimāna), or other means of transport and conveyances.
Furthermore, by the granting of fearlessness, by the gift of life,
and by the granting of all desired objects, one shall attain all desires.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you the fruit as it was spoken by Yama;
he told it all to Nārada, and Nāciketas told it to the Brahmins.
Having heard this and having bowed repeatedly to Yamarāja, Nārada took his honors and departed through the air for Satyaloka.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Activity of Messengers to Bring Sinners to the Wheel of Yama by the Order of Citragupta in the First Kṛtayuga Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Arising of Fruits for Those Who Have Given Gifts; the Arising of Fruits as Told to Nārada by Dharmarāja; and Their Arrival," and so forth. ||361||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, and I shall tell you what happened there after that—how Nāciketa truthfully related to the twice-born what he had seen. || 1 ||
Let the Brahmins there listen: by the wise Dharmarāja, those traveling toward heaven in celestial chariots as radiant as the sun were seen. || 2 ||
Those ascetics were possessed of supernatural powers; they were accompanied by their wives and kinsmen, full of affection, and their faces shone with a mass of merit.
Then, in an instant, Dharmarāja became exceedingly distressed;
his face turned pale with rage, and he was deprived of his luster and splendor. || 4 ||
Seeing him in such a state, I asked him directly: "Though you are so radiant, how have you come to this change of complexion? (5)
"O King, why do you burn with grief? For I desire to know this.
Then Yamarāja spoke concerning the cause of his pallor and sorrow.
They were wanderers devoted to the practice of gleaning, engaged in the study of the Vedas,
hospitable in their reception of guests, practitioners of yoga, and masters who had conquered their senses.
But those virtuous men who are devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), as well as faithful wives—they all go above me, O twice-born one, disregarding me. (8)
They do not wait upon me, nor are they under my control;
accompanied by their wives and followers, they pass over my very head.
With their limbs smeared with divine perfumes and adorned with garlands and ornaments,
they shall speak in such a manner that I become withered.
We do not take Yama, the lord of death, into account; we go to that supreme state.
O Death, for whose sake do you stand? Who is death, and who is Yama?
On our account, this Yama and even Yameśvara have become useless;
you always strike down those who are full of faults, the most wicked, and devoid of dharma.
"Even though you are capable of obstructing us, we shall go to the supreme state"—thus speaking, the celestial beings in their aerial chariots depart; this I have heard.
"O best of the twice-born, though I am capable, I cannot perform acts of restraint or favor for yogis; hearing this, I am distressed. (14)
"O twice-born one, perceiving my own lack of power regarding them,
I am deeply distressed," thus did Dharmarāja speak to me there at that moment.
A certain virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, arrived before him in a celestial chariot;
she was of great splendor, accompanied by her followers, her husband, and her attendants.
Full of joy, she spoke words that were pleasant and beneficial to the King of Dharma:
"O King of Dharma, most worthy of worship, O Lord, do not fall into despondency. (17)
Brahmins, ascetics, the peaceful, the virtuous, and female ascetics are worthy of being seen and worthy of being saluted; by their own power, they have reached the further shore.
O Dharma, the majesty, power, and even the nature of these austerities grant the attainment of liberation, bestow the world of Īśa, and are higher than the highest.
Virtuous Brahmins are inconceivable to all beings;
Brahmins who are virtuous are always to be honored as all the gods.
Existence should not be attached to there, and stinginess must indeed be abandoned;
likewise, passion, anger, and delusion should never be committed by the virtuous. (21)
Having spoken thus and paid her respects, she departed for the highest heaven.
Then I indeed questioned Dharmarāja as to who she was.
Then the King of Dharma related the entire story to me:
"O Brahmin, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a highly illustrious man named Nimi. (23)
There was a king endowed with righteousness, splendor, valor, and the vow of truth;
his son was named Mithi, by whom Mithilā was built.
Because he was the progenitor (janaka) of Mithilā, his secondary name was Janaka;
his wife, named Rūpavatī, was most dear to him and acted for his pleasure. (25)
Devoted with great affection and carrying out the words of her husband, old age, disease, and death do not prevail in their kingdom. (26)
The god rained continuously, yet no person anywhere was afflicted by disease.
Then the queen, upholder of dharma, spoke these words with humility to the king: ||27||
O King, you have performed sacrifices and fed the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas) therein;
you have given various kinds of gifts, for no small amount of wealth has been distinguished [in your giving]. (28)
Whatever wealth there was of your servants, of the twice-born, and likewise of your attendants— whatever existed on earth and whatever was in your house.
All of that has indeed been entirely employed for the purpose of giving;
you do not understand this, O King—how then could one ask for food?
There was nothing in the house, nor anywhere else, not even a single cowrie shell;
yet leaves, flowers, fruits, and roots had indeed been given to the sages.
The fields, the gardens, and the entire kingdom were all made over to the Brāhmaṇas; there was not even a cow or anything else, nor ever any garments [given]. (32)
Moreover, there is no income for food whatsoever during the rainy season;
tell me, O Lord, how one should subsist for the sake of pacifying hunger? (33)
Having heard these affectionate words, Janaka spoke to the beautiful woman:
"Listen, I shall speak what is beneficial; if you consider it credible, then hear it. (34)
"O beloved, while we have been subsisting on sacrificial offerings, these hundred years have passed;
indeed, we have been preparing the field with a spade and wood. (35)
Then, the acquisition of food, drink, clothing, and so forth will become your dharma;
having obtained what is to be chewed, what is to be eaten, and other things, you shall attain happiness. (36)
Thus addressed, the queen, greatly delighted, spoke to the king:
"In your residence, there are thousands of male servants and female slaves."
There were tens of millions of horses, elephants, and cows;
and also tens of millions of camels, buffaloes, and donkeys.
And there are tens of millions of bulls and servants in your house;
O King, employ them all in your desired agricultural work.
The king said: "O Queen, those very things were indeed given by me as gifts:
oxen, donkeys, horses, elephants, camels, and men."
All are appointed to the acts of giving; indeed, I have no ownership over them—whether they be made of iron, tin, copper, silver, or gold.
"O knower of dharma, I do not see any wealth at all here— not even gold or iron— that has been employed for charity or sacrifice within this house."
"O Queen, with what shall I make a spade for the work of cultivation?
Having been addressed thus, Rūpavatī, exceedingly delighted, spoke to the king.
"Let us go, O King; may it be well with you. Diligent effort bestows prosperity.
Having been addressed thus, the son of Nimi went to the sacred field accompanied by his wife.
This auspicious field of mine is always composed of forest trees;
it is unconditioned and likewise unplowed, for what is given that is useless? (45)
"Stay here; I shall cut down those small thickets and thorns.
And you, my dear, clear away these very few blades of grass and such."
Thus addressed, the great queen, devoted solely to her husband,
took refuge in the shade of a tree and began to cut grass and shrubs.
Then, by virtue of her merit, that woman who protected her husband’s word beheld beside her a great thicket of gold that bestowed gold.
That gracious queen spoke these sweet words:
"A golden tree is seen here nearby, an excellent shrub. (49)
Just then, she saw another tree, adorned with fruits and the like; immediately thereafter, a third tree was seen there, provided with articles for food.
But no water was seen there on the forest ground despite its proximity;
delighted, she said to the king, "Food has been obtained, but indeed no water. (51)
"How has this come to pass?"—seeing this, the king also said to her:
